ACTION STATEMENT OF DR. MICHAEL P. BALZANO, JR., DIRECTOR ACCOMPANIED BY: 

NICHOLAS W. CRAW, ASSOCIATE DIRECTOR OF ACTION FOR INTERNATIONAL OPERATIONS EMERSON MARKHAM, CHIEF, BUDGET DIVISION, ACTION APPROPRIATION REQUEST 

Senator INOUYE. The subcommittee will please come to order. 

This morning we will begin our fiscal 1975 hearing on appropriations for foreign assistance and related programs. 

Incidentally, we are again the first subcommittee to begin our hearings. If it were within my control, I would here and now pledge the subcommittee to report a timely bill before the beginning of the fiscal year. Inasmuch as new authorization is required for several major items, especially security assistance, such an accomplishment is contingent on timely authorizing action by the Legislative Committee and the cooperation of our sister committee in the House of Representatives.

I can only cite a timely bill as our goal and pledge our best efforts to achieve it.

It is significant to note that this year's request for items funded in this bill totals $5,197,326,000, an apparent decrease of $633,383,000. 

A more careful examination, however, will reveal that $2,350,000,000 of last year's total was for emergency military assistance to Israel and Cambodia. Excluding these, we find an increase of $1,716,617,00 in the entire bill and more than $1.8 billion in bilateral assistance carried in title II.

II. 

HIGHLIGHTS OF BUDGET CHANGES 

I. 

More than half of the increase, $2.6 million, will support the modest growth of 100 trainees and 310 additional volunteer manyears.

Over $2 million of the increase is for mandatory cost increases: $966 thousand for rental and related services formerly budgeted by the GSA, just over $350 thousand for the full year effect of the government-wide October 1973 Federal pay increase; higher costs of telephone and postal service, and some necessary accounting improvements,

Finally, the remainder of the increase is a result of restoring multilateral grants to the statutory level and of devoting 1% of the total request to strengthen the planning, program development and evaluation capability of the Peace Corps.

B. Program Highlights THE NEED 

Host Country demand for Volunteers, with their increased maturity and experience, is at the highest rate since 1968, exceeding 6,500 requests per year.

• 85% of these requests address the acute problems of the developing world in education, health, and agriculture.

The Peace Corps now operates in 68 developing countries, the highest number in its history; 

39 of these countries receive no other U.S. bilateral assistance.

The value host countries place on Peace Corps Volunteers is apparent from their support of the Volunteers. Host Country Contributions increased 22% last year, from $3 million to $3.6 million. In FY 1975 they will be $3.8 million, almost double those in FY-72.

When compared on a proportionate per capita income basis, Host Country contributions are more than the 

U.S. contribution to Peace Corps operations.

II. PUBLIC SUPPORT FOR PEACE CORPS 

Applications to serve in Peace Corps have increased from a 1970 low of 19,022 to a high of 33,637 in 

FY 73, the highest since 1967. 

The Volunteer of the 70's also better represents the broad spectrum of the American people. The average 

Volunteer is 28 years old, and the number of Volunteers with graduate and professional degrees has risen to 11% while the number of Volunteers with special skills but no college degree is now 14%. 

An October 1973 Overseas Development Council Survey indicated that 88% of the people polled considered the Peace Corps effective, out-ranking all other foreign assistance organizations covered by the survey.

III. PROGRAM EMPHASES 

The three major legislative goals of the Peace Corps Act remain as central principles in programming: 

1. Help developing countries meet their need for trained manpower, 2. Help promote e a better understanding of the

American people on the part of the people served, and 

3. Help promote a better understanding of other peoples on the part of the American people. • With special emphasis in Food Production/Distribution, Water Resources Development, and Health Care in FY 75,

IV. 

the distribution of Volunteers by program sector will be approximately:

Agriculture and Rural Development Business and Public Management Education Health Urban Development and Public Works

MANAGEMENT PRIORITIES 

Maintaining or reducing unit costs. 

Volunteer manyear costs for FY-75 have been held constant, below the costs of 

FY 1971. 

238 38 48% 98 138 4% 

Direct training costs have been reduced by 40% since 1970.

We have absorbed, through management efficiencies, pay raises of 41.1% since 1967 and recent inflation and devaluation in excess of $3 million have not changed Volunteer manyear costs.

Reduction of Early Terminations 

In FY 73 the termination rate for Volunteers was only 98 which compares favorably with industry, government, and academic rates. However, better quality control of training, job assignment, and support of Volunteers will be a high priority of country plans to further reduce Trainee and 

Volunteer attrition.

Improved Resource Control and Allocation 

In order to better control and allocate the scarce resources of budget dollars, Volunteer skills and staff positions, a new Country Management Planning system will combine budgeting and programming into one coherent process in a greater level of detail than currently available. It will become the primary management tool for supporting good programs and spotting weaker projects for improvement or termination.

In addition, a significant effort will be placed on evaluation by: 1. 2. 3. 

Creation of a central evaluation unit 

Installation of new internal evaluation systems 

Development of impact assessment procedures 4. Assessing individual program sectors and countries.

Mr. BALZANO. 

I have with me today the Associate Director for International Operations, Mr. Nicholas Craw; also Mr. Emerson Markham, our Budget Director.

REVIEW AND REPORT ON FISCAL YEAR 1974 BUDGET REQUEST 

Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, the last time we came before your committee we discussed at length our proposed operational plans for fiscal year 1974. These included plans to alter practices in the areas or recruiting, training, and evaluation to qualitatively improve the Peace Corps program in the field. 

Also included in last year's plans was the commitment to upgrade our management practices, where necessary, to strengthen program administration.

Today we would like to report on the progress we have made in implementing those plans and making good on those commitments, and share with you our plans and budget proposals for fiscal year 1975. 

In order to conduct the Peace Corps program in fiscal year 1975, we are requesting $82,256,000, an increase of $5,016,000 above the fiscal year 1974 level. Approximately $1 million of the increase is for building rental costs formerly paid by the General Services Administration. 

We must also absorb the full-year effect of the October 1973 Government-wide Federal pay raise.

More than half of the increase, or $2,625,000, will cover the modest rise in trainee and volunteer levels planned for the year. This includes support for an additional 100 trainees, an additional 131 interns and an additional 310 volunteer man-years above the fiscal year 1974 level. 

We are also requesting a $583,000 increase for planning, program development, and evaluation.

These proposed increases in the program budget reflect our continuing strong concern for three major areas-recruitment, training, and program evaluation. Changes in focus in these 3 years have also evolved an increasing participation of host countries in the Peace Corps. 

The development of a strong binational partnership with each country we serve remains a high priority of the Peace Corps. 

During fiscal year 1974, our recruiting, selection, and placement efforts have improved. We have sharpened our recruiting methods, making a concerted effort to recruit individuals with the skills requested by the host countries. This has been done, in part, through utilization of intern programs with American colleges and universities.

In addition, recruiting costs will have been reduced from $6.9 million to $6 million since Peace Corps' merger into ACTION in 1971. 

The shift in preservice training for volunteers has continued toward training in the country where the volunteers will later serve. In-country training has resulted in the phasing-out of the Virgin Islands 

Training Center this past summer. The Puerto Rico Learning Center will be phased-out on June 30 of this year, at which time practically all volunteers will be trained in country.

The benefits of in-country training are impressive. It enables host countries to share fully in all phases of the training and to accept increasing financial responsibility as well. Such training is more realistic as it helps the volunteers adjust to the environment in which they will be working for the next 2 years. Since 1970, in-country training has cut by more than one-third the cost of training of each volunteer. 

To increase the value of the in-country training program, we are continuing to use a preinvitational staging (or PRIST) system. Recently, however, we studied its effectiveness and found mixed results. 

PRIST proves cost effective in particular situations and in particular countries we serve. As a result of the study, we are going to cut back on the number of people we PRIST, but we will continue to use the PRIST mechanisms in the instances in which we have found it is costeffective.

We have intensified evaluation activities in fiscal year 1974 and look forward to greater improvements in fiscal year 1975. 

At the request of Congress, we completed in fiscal year 1974 a twovolume survey of Peace Corps accomplishments since its inception, and also prepared an annual operations report for fiscal year 1973, which is more of an assessment of the Peace Corps than a mere recitation of program activities. 

We have developed an entirely new country management plan which is now being utilized by each country staff in developing future programs and budgets. Country staff and regional staff in Washington have been trained in its implementation. 

A major study of living allowances paid to volunteers is in progress and will be completed later this spring. 

The National Academy of Sciences has been commissioned to undertake an independent assessment of the future role of the Peace Corps, with primary emphasis being given to an investigation of program areas where the Peace Corps can have its greatest impact. 

A comprehensive evaluation of program activities in Micronesia has been completed, and another major administrative and program assessment of the Peace Corps activities in Zaire is in progress. 

Task forces have been created to recommend ways of measuring the Peace Corps' impact overseas, of increasing host country contributions, and of capitalizing more on non-Peace Corps resources. One impact assessment model is now being tested in two countries overseas. 

Mr. Chairman, at this point I would try to briefly discuss what we have done to resolve problems in our management practices, and, in particular, our accounting procedures.

As you know, an imbalance of $315,000 has built up since the beginning of Peace Corps between the amounts of readjustment allowances owing to volunteers and amounts held in a Treasury Department trust fund account for that purpose. We are confident now we have solved the problem. 

In April 1973, we contracted with Arthur Young & Co., certified public accountants, to determine the exact amount of the discrepancy, to provide reconciliation schedules, and to establish a system to reconcile the accounts and prevent a recurrence of the imbalance in the future.

This system is now in place and our latest figures show that for the last half of fiscal year 1973 and the first quarter of this fiscal year,

no variance at all occurred on the imbalance figure arrived at by 

Arthur Young. 

Our authorizing legislation this year proposes that we be authorized to use $315,000 to correct the imbalance. Further, our authorizing legislation this year requests authority to waive claims against those volunteers who may have been overpaid. We believe these proposed measures and the accounting procedures now operating will prevent this from happening again.

Another budget matter which I know is of concern to you is the reduction of staff and staff salaries in Peace Corps. 

It is our intention to continue to reduce the cost of operations both by reducing unnecessary staff and by filling positions at lower grade levels. A net reduction of 90 headquarters staff positions funded under 

Peace Corps has been made since the merger alone. In all cases, however, such reductions will be made in light of their impact on programing. Our goal is to produce a better program for less money. 

Mr. Chairman, I would now like to shift my remarks away from accomplishments of fiscal year 1974 to discuss briefly some of our proposed plans for fiscal year 1975. 

One major priority will be to improve our resource management. 

Keeping the Peace Corps concept of service healthy and effective in its lost countries must be based on sound management of the volunteer, staff, and budgetary resources available to the program. 

To achieve this objective, steps have already been undertaken through the development of specific systems and procedures to make concrete improvements in the Agency's goal-setting operations, measurement of its impact and achievements, and the placement of volunteers, staff, and budgets in our host countries where they can be most effectively utilized. Our new country management plan system currently being implemented is only a good first step in this direction. 

Another priority area for fiscal year 1975 will be the increasing of support for several critical program areas where the Peace Corps has proven successful in the past. These volunteer activities are in the fields of food production and distribution, water resources development, and public health.

A final high priority area for the coming fiscal year will be an expanded evaluation effort on several fronts to enhance our ability to achieve our goals in the other priority areas in addition to solving specific policy, program, and administrative issues as they arise. 

Before concluding, Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a few words about ACTION, Peace Corps, and our volunteers.

The goal of the Peace Corps has not changed. It remains the firm desire to promote peace and friendship by confronting the world's developmental problems. Nor has the essence of the program changed. 

It is the spirit of volunteerism, the desire to serve others without material reward. Our volunteers live and work at the grassroots level. 

They sacrifice comfort and affluence in order to break through communication barriers and cut down social distance, enabling them and the people they work with to attack the problems facing these growing nations. This person-to-person service is what makes the Peace 

Corps unique in the field of foreign assistance programs. 

But it is this kind of service and the spirit which sustains it that gives Peace Corps its common bond with the domestic volunteer pro-

grams of ACTION. As a part of ACTION, Peace Corps shares the cause of voluntarism with our expanding domestic volunteer programs, and offers the opportunity for the exchange of ideas and experiences strengthening both programs.

Common recruitment and placement facilities gives the Agency greater flexibility in the utilization of the best volunteer skills available. If we cannot place a volunteer in the Peace Corps, for example, we can attempt to find a place for him in a domestic program. 

From the beginning of 1973 to date, we have been able to place 773 international applicants in a domestic program and 617 domestic applicants in the Peace Corps.

We also propose to develop career possibilities for returning Peace Corps volunteers by giving those who have proven themselves worthy the opportunity to reenlist in volunteer leader capacities. This enables the volunteer to gain a solid management background which will help him when he returns to the United States, and benefits our Nation by the continued use of valuable Peace Corps' experience in work at home.

The unity of purpose and flexibility of service found in ACTION as one agency offers those Americans who want to serve others a greater opportunity to act on that desire. This can only serve to improve every program we have in ACTION. 

Thank you, Mr. Chariman.

My colleagues and I are now prepared to answer any questions the committee may have.

ADDITIONAL SUBCOMMITTEE QUESTIONS 

Senator INOUYE. Before proceeding, without objection we will now insert in the record our questions and your responses. [The questions and answers follow:] 

VOLUNTEER READJUSTMENT ALLOWANCE 

Question. Have you finally identified the shortage in the Peace Corps Volunteer Readjustment Allowance? How much is it? How did it occur? Who is responsible? How do you propose to acquire the funds necessary to make these payments to returned volunteers?

Answers. (1) Identified Shortage? A. Yes. 

(2) How much is it? A. $314,363.81. (3) How did it occur? A. Probably through a combination of: 

Improper coding of financial transactions resulting in the crediting of transactions to an account other than the Volunteer readjustment account. "Float" on any given date or transactions which have been reflected on individual pay cards but not yet reflected on General Ledger or Treasury account. 

Payments to former Volunteers who did serve and were entitled to readjustment allowances, but for whom accruals were not credited in the appropriate 

Treasury account.

Collections or claims on overpayments to former Volunteers which were returned to general Treasury funds rather than to the Treasury fund for allowances. This would typically result in the funds being "lost" to the Peace Corps but available for other governmental uses. 

Record-keeping errors associated with early terminated Volunteers delayed entries on the payroll records and Volunteers assigned to projects through transfers from other countries or local placements. (4) Who is responsible? A. Since the imbalance was disclosed in a GAO audit conducted in 1966 and 1967 and probably existed from the earliest Peace Corps days, the determination of responsibility is extremely difficult. There is attached an identification of individuals responsible for administration of the accounting function during the period under discussion.

(5) How to get funds? A. Provision for obtaining the funds is included in the FY-75 budget.

REVIEW PROGRAM 

Question. In last year's hearing the Committee pointed out several apparent inequities and excesses in these scales. In its report it also called for a review of salaries and operating costs. What has been done? 

Can you illustrate with specific examples?

Answer. We have begun a program to significantly reduce the average grade level of the Peace Corps by filling high level positions with lower-level persons as they become vacant. Since September 1973, roughly one quarter of the fiscal year, we have saved over $100,000 (est). The annual rate of saving will be a bit lower than that because part of the total saving results from unfilled positions that will have to be filled. 

We have instituted a Country Management Plan for our programming and budgeting activities that we think will have great impact upon our ability to determine and control costs. We have instituted wide-ranging studies for our personnel and administrative policies and practices with a view to cost-reduction and control.

TRAINEE COSTS AND PERSONNEL AVAILABILITY 

Question. In his statement last year (page 111) Mr. Howe indicated that training costs per trainee would be reduced to $2,210 by shifting to "in-country" training. Did you meet this target?

Answer. As a result of the continued shift to in-country training during fiscal year 1974, the average training costs per trainee are projected to be $2,148. 

Question. Mr. Howe projected 7,265 Volunteers and trainees on board at the end of fiscal year 1974. What is your present projection?

Answer. The number of Volunteers and trainees projected to be on board at the end of fiscal year 1974 is approximately 8,000. 

GAO REPORT ON TRAVEL EXPENSES 

Question. On September 20, 1973 the General Accounting Office reported that the Peace Corps had at least $75,000 worth of unused travel tickets ranging in age from a few weeks to two years.

It is also advised that 4,500 tickets on which nearly $800,000 had been refunded had not been forwarded to GAO for audit.

Can there be any justification for these slipshod practices? 

Answer. The problems relating to unused travel tickets raised in the September 20, 1973 report from GAO refers to a situation they found in March of 

1973. ACTION requested a further review of the problem by GAO in July of 1973.

As noted on pages 4 and 5 of the September GAO Report, recognition is as given by GAO that corrective measures had been taken by ACTION and that ACTION was properly handling travel tickets.

COUNTRIES SERVED BY PEACE CORPS PERSONNEL 

Question. At the time of your budget presentation last year you were operating in 58 countries with an expectation that it would rise to 62 or 63. What changes have occurred?

Answer. At the time of the budget presentation last year, Peace Corps volunteers were, in 64 countries served by 58 country-administrative units. The information outlined below is based on countries in which volunteers are serving. At the present time, Peace Corps volunteers are serving in 68 countries with the addition of two new countries, Cook Islands and Gilbert and Ellice Islands, planned for

FY 1975. 

In FY 1973, the Peace Corps entered one new country (Central African Republic) re-entered Nigeria (first time since 1970) and left one country (Uganda) for the welfare of Peace Corps volunteers. 

In FY 1974, the Peace Corps has entered 4 new countries (Bahrain, Oman, Yemen and the Seychelles) and re-enetred Gabon which we left in 1967. Also requests have been received to enter Cook Islands. Peace Corps program in 

Uruguay has been phased out at this time.

The countries now being serviced by Peace Corps Volunteers are:

Answer. Approximately 66% of all Volunteers serving in the Peace Corps today are "skilled." Of all Peace Corps Volunteers, 87% are college graduates. The breakout is as follows: Graduate Degrees, 11%; Bachelor Degrees, 76%; Other 

Degrees (RN, AA, etc.), 3%; Some College, 8%; and High School Only 2%. 

Requests for new Volunteers for FY '74 are still emphasizing skills. Of a projected total of 7,000 requests for FY '74, a total of 71% of those requests are for skilled Volunteers.

HOST COUNTRY CONTRIBUTIONS 

Question. In fiscal year 1974 you projected $3,389,000 in host country contributions. What does this represent and how much local support do you expect for next year.

Answer. The FY 1974 estimated level of host country contributions is $3,- 

653,000. This represents an increase of $658,000 above FY 1973. In FY 1975, host country contributions are expected to increase to $3,835,000. We feel this increasing level of support reflects a continuing growth of interest by the host country governments in the Peace Corps programs. 

VOLUNTEER COMPENSATION 

Question. Just what compensation does a volunteer receive? 

What is the purpose and amount of his readjustment allowance?

Many volunteers feel that it is inadequate. Why has no request been made to increase it?

Answer. The volunteer compensation package has two major parts. First, the volunteer receives a living allowance based upon the cost of living in the country where he is posted. The second part is a readjustment allowance amounting to seventy-five ($75) dollars per month for each month of service. 

This amount is held for the volunteer until the completion of service. Its purpose is to provide a "nest egg" for the volunteer until such time as he can find employment in this country or as is that case often, returns to school. We have considered this in the past. However, the increased costs were not possible at a time when the Executive Branch was required to reduce spending overall. 

That pressure to cut spending continues, and we do not feel the proposed level of spending for FY 75 will allow us to increase the allowance. Our recruitment figures suggest the readjustment allowance is not a significant deterrent; although it clearly works a hardship on some returning volunteers. 

Using fiscal year 1974 as an example, each volunteer receives:

A living allowance which averages (per year) - 

And a leave allowance which averages (per year)

At the time a volunteer is sworn in, he receives a settling-in allowance, a one-time payment which averages--. 

Volunteers with minor children also receive a dependent support allowance, which averages (per child). $1, 821 216 171 1,858

Upon completion of service a volunteer receives a readjustment allowance. (The basic readjustment allowance of $75 per month of service averages, including 5.2 percent employer share of benefits. (per year). 

Volunteer leaders and volunteer heads of household, however, receive a readjustment allowance of $125 per month which, on the average, including 5.2 percent employer share of benefits, provides an additional (per year) –

Total 

947 631 

5, 644

The purpose of the readjustment allowance is to provide the returning volunteer with a source of income until he finds a job or returns to school. 

No request has been made to increase the readjustment allowance because we believe the current allowance is adequate for its purpose and because we place a higher priority on using funds to increase programs rather than increasing average volunteer costs.

Dear Senator Inouye: 

A space utilization study of that portion of the ACTION headquarters staff located at 806 Connecticut Avenue has been completed.

The results of these findings indicate that the office personnel of ACTION are housed in approximately 33,000 square feet of office space in excess of the General Services Administration guidelines for space occupancy. Based on a cost of $5.99 per square foot at this leased location, this represents an annual expenditure of $197,670.00 for under-utilized space.

The General Services Administration has forwarded a copy of this report to ACTION along with a request that they prepare a plan for releasing space to us for reassignment to other agencies. 

Members of my staff will be available to work with ACTION administrative personnel to devise a workable plan towards this end. Sincerely,

HOUSING OF EMPLOYEES 

Senator INOUYE. Would you care to comment on this observation, sir?

Mr. BALZANO. Mr. Chairman, it is our basic desire to put the employees in one building as fast as possible. This, of course, we will not be able to accomplish in this fiscal year. We do hope, however, as soon as we get some GSA space available in one of our buildings, to consolidate.

Senator INOUYE. Before proceeding, I would like to clarify a few things so that there is no misunderstanding. 

In our questioning, we have no desire in any way to detract from the great contributions made by ACTION personnel. As you know, there is great pressure upon the executive and legislative branches to keep down the cost of Government to the best workable level possible. 

In this spirit, we are, as you might feel, nitpicking. 

So. I hope you understand we are doing this with every agency. 

TABLE ON DISTRIBUTION OF PERMANENT PEACE CORPS EMPLOYEES 

Without objection, there will be inserted in Appendix II a table reflecting the distribution of Peace Corps employees in permanent positions. This table indicates an annual salary level of over $20,000 per year for foreign service reserve personnel which remains very high and especially for an agency dedicated to providing volunteer services.

I have noticed some specific adjustments which have been made since Mr. Craw undertook to revise these. 

The subcommittee will continue to monitor the situation closely and perhaps ask for another table prior to our markup of your appropriation. 

Do you wish to comment on this salary level, sir? 

Mr. CRAW. Yes, sir, I would.

EMPLOYEE SALARY LEVEL 

We share the committee's feelings on this subject. 

When I took office in September. I initiated a number of steps designed to examine the facts and to lay out a prospective course of action to address these issues with the equity of the employees kept in mind.

One of these was a personnel management survey. 

Another was a complete position classification for all Peace Corps. positions, both here in Washington and overseas.

It was our view at the time, and it remains our view today, that Peace Corps employment should not constitute a financial windfall. 

Since the time I took office, as I think you may have noted with the insertion in the record, there has been a rather substantial reduction in the number of positions at the GS-14 and above equivalent level in the foreign service reserve system. The number of positions in that category which we reported a year ago has been decreased from 93 to 

74. This constitutes a reduction of 20 percent.

Since the time I took office, I have made 12 country director appointments. The average country director appointment which has been

made since I took office has been made at $4,500 a year less compensation and we have hired a number of other people below the country level and almost uniformly have obtained savings. 

I would like to point out, Mr. Chairman, that on the face of the statement of an average salary of over $20,000 for foreign service reserve employees it is accurate. I should also like to point out there are three other personnel classifications in the Peace Corps. 

To look solely at that statement would be somewhat comparable to looking at General Motors president who earns $600,000 or $700,000 without respect to the other employees which he has under his jurisdiction.

We have a total of 705 employees in the Peace Corps. The average of all those salaries is $10,736. 

I should like to put that into context.

The average salary in the U.S. Government as a whole is $13,834. So, our average salary throughout the Peace Corps is 21 percent below the average for the Government as a whole. 

Senator INOUYE. Excuse me. 

That includes overseas volunteers, does it not? 

Mr. CRAW. No, sir, it does not include volunteers. Staff only. 

Senator INOUYE. Just staff? 

Mr. CRAW. Just staff. 

Senator INOUYE. Foreign nationals, also? 

Mr. CRAW. That is correct, sir. 

Senator INOUYE. How do you pay your foreign nationals? 

Mr. CRAW. Foreign service local appointment, sir. 

Senator INOUYE. They are pretty low, aren't they? 

What is the average for foreign nationals?

Mr. CRAW. The average salary for foreign nationals is slightly more than $5,000, I believe.

Senator INOUYE. So, you put that into the average to bring down everything else. I just want to put that into context, also. 

Mr. CRAW. That is correct, sir.

I also would like to point out a statistic which we learned, somewhat to our dismay that the continuing effect of federally mandated pay raises, Government-wide pay raises, is such that any improvement or decreases which we are able to effect are frequently either negated or superseded by pay raises.

LENGTH OF SERVICE 

Let me give you the classic example.

There is a 5-year rule in Peace Corps which governs the length of service that any Peace Corps employee can serve. If I had hired an employee 5 years ago and his pay rate was roughly equivalent to GS- 15, $22,376, and had never given that man a promotion, he would now be at the pay rate of $36,000, as a result of periodic step increases and 

Government-wide pay raises.

I think you can appreciate the magnitude of the problem as well as the efforts that we are making in attempting to deal with it. 

Senator INOUYE. In 5 years? 

Mr. CRAW. That is correct, sir.

Senator INOUYE. I wish something like that could happen to Members of Congress. We have not had a pay raise in 10 years now, not-

withstanding all those who criticize us for being overpaid. I would hope to think that some of us do just as much as the country director in India.

Mr. CRAW. It so happens our country director in India is currently compensated at the rate of $14,000. 

Senator INOUYE. Last year he was $45,000. 

Mr. CRAW. We have a new man, sir. 

Mr. BALZANO. Part of the new improvement.

VENEZUELA 

The country that the subcommittee will openly touch upon is Venezuela. Although Venezuela has gold and foreign exchange reserves in excess of $1 billion and has been enjoying balance-of-payments surpluses, we know that its contribution toward the cost of the Peace Corps program has been much lower than could be expected for a country in its financial condition. 

Although Venezuela has a much higher annual per capita income than nearly all of the countries in which Peace Corps operates, its contribution toward the cost of Peace Corps activity was only equal to the average made by all other countries even though the other countries are poorer.

The Peace Corps, itself, recognized that because of the status of its economy it was questionable whether to characterize Venezuela as an underdeveloped country.

Venezuelan cash and income contributions for Peace Corps activity for fiscal year 1973 totaled about $59,000, while the Peace Corps spent more than $1 million for Venezuela programs:

One of the unfortunate results of this situation is that Peace Corps programs are either being delayed or not implemented at all because of the failure of Venezuelan agencies to make their promised contributions.

For example, the food study program for which Peace Corps recruited three highly qualified agroscientists did not get off the ground because the Government of Venezuela did not contribute the $22,000 in local funds for the program as needed. As a result, the three Peace 

Corps volunteers were assigned to other activities. 

Another example is that for the physical education teaching training program the Government of Venezuela Ministry of Education

failed to provide all the sports equipment needed. As a result, the volunteers were using their personal funds to buy needed equipment. 

And the question I have for Venezuela, and these will be similar for other countries: Why can't Venezuela pay all of the local costs of the 

Peace Corps program in the country?

Mr. BALZANO. Mr. Chairman, shortly after I became Director of the 

Agency and Mr. Craw became the Associate Director for International

We have, however, been able to determine that there is an inverse relationship between a country's ability to pay and that country actually making payments in kind. We feel at this point that this is basically a management problem. That is, we have not, in the past, evaluated the performance of our country directors or regional directors on their ability to obtain host country contributions for their programs. Mr. CRAW. I would like to point out, Mr. Chairman, that one of our priorities, as alluded to in our statement, is the design and implementation of a management system whereby we can better allocate our resources, and clearly host country contributions are one of our resources as are our volunteers, our budget dollars, as well as our staff. 

There appears to be an inverse relationship between the GNP or per capita figures and rates of host country contributions. 

An example of that would be the fact that the African countries who are among the poorest in the world, and using GNP and income statistics, proportionately provide a greater level of contribution to the Peace Corps program in Africa.

There are some difficulties, however, in using the PCI or GNP as a standard against which to measure host country contributions. The two primary difficulties are:

First, as you well know, the GNP in many of the lesser developed countries is a highly inaccurate system. It can be seriously affected by foreign assistance transfers, other types of transactions which we would not normally count in our conception of the GNP here in the 

United States.

Second, there is a danger in establishing a direct connection between the country's GNP and its apparent wealth and our request that they contribute to the program. The Peace Corps is a voluntary program. 

We believe that host country contributions should be of a voluntary 34-192 - 74-3

nature. I do not think that we should be placed in the context of attempting to extract, if you will, those kinds of contributions from host countries.

I do think that there is a discrete relationship between the existence of host country contributions and their rate and the kind of value that that host country places on the Peace Corps resources and Peace 

Corps program.

LACK OF COMMUNICATIONS

February 1971)

Saw In Guinea in late 1970 a politically tense situation existed and public executions of people who opposed the government were taking place. A Peace Corps 

Volunteer witnessed the hanging and mutilation of a personal acquaintance and was prompted to send the following commercial telegram to the Ambassador on January 30, 1971. "Lost a friend last week. a hanged dead man beaten. Please stop this madness."

He also sent a similar telegram to a Volunteer at the Peace Corps office. The telegram was intercepted by the Internal Security Police. There was fear on the part of Peace Corps and the Embassy that the 

Volunteer would be arrested for intelligence activities. 

He was removed from Guinea. 2. 

India (August 1971) 

3. 4. 

A Peace Corps Volunteer wrote a letter to the "Times of India Illustrated Weekly" in which he discussed the Indian political system. The Country Director terminated the Volunteer for violation of Peace Corps' apolitical policy on November 1, 1971.

Ethiopia (November 1971) 

A Peace Corps Volunteer was serving in Gambella, a politically sensitive area near the Sudanese border and an alleged center for insurgent activity. His supervisor, the District Governor, wrote a letter to the Vice Minister of National Community Development asking for the Volunteer's removal due to political involvement in local affairs. The Country Director felt that the charges were due to the Volunteers close relationship to the Sudanese Consul and not due to any political activity. However, no transfer possibility existed and therefore the Volunteer was terminated effective January 1, 1972. 

Senegal (February 

March 1972)

Two Volunteers sponsored a film show at their social. center in Louga and invited a Senegalese film producer to show some of his films. After the showing there was a discussion during which the producer made antigovernment remarks. On February 15 the Minister of 

Information held a press conference over national radio in which it accused the Volunteers and Peace Corps of sponsoring anti-government activities. On 

March 2, 1972 the Minister of Interior, with the concurrence of the Prime Minister, issued orders of deportation against the two Volunteers. Peace Corps and Embassy officials worked to clear the Volunteers and President Leopold Senghor intervened to suspend the deportation orders while an investigation of the charges was carried out. The Volunteers were found to have followed all the proper procedures in organiz-

5. ing the film show and no fault could be found. However, their transfer from Louga was demanded by the government. 

As no alternative assignment was available for the remaining three months of their tours the Volunteers terminated service effective May 10, 1972.

Liberia (May 1972) 

A Peace Corps Volunteer filed a written complaint to the Assistant Supervisor of Schools of Loffa County charging that the teachers of Gorlu School were lacking in seriousness and dedication. An investigation of the charges was held during which the Volunteer told the audience that the whole Republic of Liberia was plagued with inefficiency and irregularity and called the Assistant Supervisor a fool. His statements were reported to the 

Minister of Education as "derogatory remarks" against the Republic of Liberia. Another investigation followed during which the Volunteer repeated his remarks and the investigating official recommended the Volunteer be prosecuted by the government. The Acting Country Director decided to terminate the Volunteer immediately to offset any prosecution which might damage Peace Corps relations with the government. 

July 20, 1972. 

Termination was effective 6. 

Sierra Leone (April 1971)

A Peace Corps Volunteer befriended a Guinean who had just been released from a prison for illegal entry into Sierra Leone. He obtained a travel permit for his new friend "under the table." He also went to the Guinean 

Embassy on behalf of his friend. He later realized that both Guinean officials and Sierra Leone APC party stalwarts were very interested in the case and found he was being followed everywhere. He decided to terminate for fear he had become over-involved. 

Afghanistan (September 1973) 

On September 13, 1973 Peace Corps staff discovered that a newsletter had been distributed in the Peace Corps 

Kabul office and was available for anyone to pick up.

The document was found to be insulting to Peace Corps staff, and to the Afghan people, government and country. 

All copies were collected immediately. There is no evidence that any copies were distributed. Two Volunteers readily admitted writing the newsletter and after discussions with several staff members including Host Country Nationals the Volunteers realized the seriousness of their actions and regretted having printed the newsletter. The Volunteers were terminated from Peace Corps/Afghanistan.

SAHEL SPECIAL DROUGHT REPORT 

The extent to which the Peace Corps has involved itself in the problems of the drought in West Africa has been severely underestimated and in some instances completely overlooked. David B. Ottaway's article which appeared in the Weshington Post on February 11, 1974, clearly attests to this fact. Whether this is done out of (in an attempt to focus attention on large donor agencies such as AID and FAO) it is disturbing that Peace Corps is not recognized for its decided contribution in drought-related projects over the years.

An historical look at Peace Corps' role in programs help to clarify this concern. ignorance or by design

HISTORICAL OVERVIEW 

Since the early 1960's Peace Corps has been one of the principal agencies providing development assistance to the Sahelian and East African nations which are now suffering from the drought. Initial efforts took the form of community development projects which involved Volunteers in a wide range of activities, from child care to wells construction. As the needs of the host countries were defined more specifically and the skill levels of Peace Corps Volunteers increased, a variety of drought-related projects were launched. The most prevalent were projects in irrigation, well construction and repair, reforestation, health and nutrition. 

The severity and magnitude of the current situation in the Sahel and Ethiopia have made it impossible for both Peace Corps and the Sahel countries involved to attempt to develop and implement any massive relief efforts. Material support is a key element in most projects that deal with drought conditions. Peace Corps is a manpower agency and we have traditionally relied upon the host governments and foreign donor agencies for material support.

The absence of material support limits Peace Corps' effective involvement and recognizing this fact we have sought actively and successfully to expand our current activities. We have initiated new activities making use of funds provided by international donors to specific projects. Many of these international donors have had and continue to have excellent working relationships with Peace Corps.

PEACE CORPS INVOLVEMENT IN EMERGENCY DROUGHT-RELIEF EFFORTS 

In recent months, drought-relief measures have centered around massive grain distribution operations in West and East Africa. Peace Corps Volunteers assisted wherever possible, primarily as interpreters for the grain lift teams.

A nutritional survey team from the U.S. sought and obtained manpower assistance from Peace Corps whose familiarity with the country and people of the Sahel were an asset in obtaining the full cooperation of government officials and the local people in the study. 

Recently, three Volunteers in Ethiopia were transferred from their community development projects to a drought-specific project concerned with increasing water supplies to northern Ethiopia. Here, the expertise of the PCVS and their unique knowledge of the area, language and culture at all levels of society have made it possible for them to function effectively as liaisons between the ministry and UNICEF, the supporting agency, while at the same time developing programs at the village level. 

The concept of cooperative relief efforts which bring together a variety of agencies and resources has proved successful over the years. Based on this experience, PC 

Washington and PC field-based drought coordinators have pursued vigorously and persistently joint programming possibilities, funding for drought projects and other forms of joint involvement. Pledges of over $4 million to support drought programs (medium and long-range) have been received by countries from USAID, OXFAM, UNICEF and other donor agencies. Peace Corps by countries will provide the manpower for these programs. 

DROUGHT PROJECTS IN THE PLANNING STAGE 

As a result of working very closely with AID over the past few months, Peace Corps is preparing to send an additional forty-three Peace Corps Volunteers to 

Senegal, Mauritania, Niger, Upper Volta and Mali specifically to work on drought projects. Approximately thirty-three of these PCVS will be working on projects totally or partially funded by AID. Some examples are listed below. 

MALI: In Mali, AID has made available $50,000 for the construction of pit silos. Peace Corps will 6 w

1 provide six PCVs to work as livestock extension agents to insure that villagers will have the capability of storing feed in pit silos at minimal cost. Approximately 200 farmers will be selected to participate in the project. 

SENEGAL: In Senegal, AID will provide $140,000 for range rehabilitation and protection. Four PCVs have been requested to work with the Ministry of Rural Development in the development of plan nurseries and irrigation systems.

UPPER VOLTA: In Upper Volta, Peace Corps will be working with Catholic Relief Services and the 

Rockefeller Foundation in the construction of earthen dams.

A $150,000 grant has been made for this purpose. 

AID will be providing $340,000 for equipment, materials and operating costs.

MAURITANIA: Mauritania, the driest of the Sahel countries, will receive $600,000 from AID for vegetable production. 

The primary objective of this project is to encourage Nomadic involvement in agricultural production during the dry season.

A second Mauritania project being funded by AID will assist the Government of Mauritania in equipping to repair and construct earthen dams. AID will donate $535,000 for support of eight Peace Corps construction specialists and mechanics.

CHAD: Peace Corps has worked in well drilling in 

Chad for the past five years with noticeable success.

AID will provide the Chadian Government with $200,000 for the purchase of vehicles, equipment materials and operating costs. Peace Corps will provide six additional 

Volunteers that will construct 180 wells in the 

Lake Chad/Kanem regions over a period of two years.

OTHER DONOR AGENCIES 

In addition to UNICEF working closely with AID in drought-relief projects, Peace Corps is working with several other agencies. The Director of UNICEF in

Mauritania is a Peace Corps Volunteer, assigned to that position, and there are plans to appoint another 

Peace Corps Volunteer as the Director of UNICEF in

Senegal. It is hoped that UNICEF will continue to draw on Peace Corps Mauritania's ability to staff and implement health and nutrition projects dealing with the drought.

CHURCH WORLD SERVICE AND CATHOLIC RELIEF SERVICES Church World Services and Catholic Relief are collaborating with Peace Corps in both Niger and Upper Volta. A school garden project currently underway in Niger is supervised by PCVs.

SUMMARY 

Peace Corps Volunteers represent the largest contingent of qualified manpower available to host government ministries which concern themselves with the eradication of drought conditions in the Sahel and the drought stricken areas of West Africa. For years, the Peace Corps has figured importantly in literally all aspects of drought relief and will continue to do so for as long as the need is present. Peace Corps has served as a catalyst in bringing together, through cooperative programming strategies, the resources of a number of international assistance agencies. Because

Peace Corps Volunteers occupy a unique position in the developmental assistance endeavor in Africa, U.S.

Ambassadors at Peace Corps posts view them as a valuable lever in promoting cooperation and coordination while making a significant contribution to the countries' developmental efforts, especially during this period of crisis.

IMPACT 

Although it is difficult to measure the long-range impact of PCV efforts, it is clear that there are significant accomplishments as a result of several years of assistance in this area. One example is the 

Senegal Animation Rurale project which has programmed approximately 175 PCVS between 1964 and 1973. One of many activities in this program is a wells project which has resulted in the construction and repair of over 800 wells in villages throughout Senegal. An estimated 88,000 people are served by these wells. 

In Upper Volta, over 700 new wells were built by PCVS since 1967. Similar achievements were realized as a result of crop extension and reforestation projects in Niger where we currently have 20 PCV foresters working with the Government of Niger. 

Peace Corps' role in the crisis in the Sahel and in 

East Africa has and will continue to be a vital one.

Both Volunteers and staff have shown the traditional intimate involvement and dedication in their attempts to assist in any way possible in dealing with the problems of the poor countries in Africa.

DISCRIMINATION PRACTICES AGAINST BLACK PEACE CORPS VOLUNTEERS 

Senator BROOKE. Mr. Craw, I have received letters expressing dissatisfaction with the assignment of black Peace Corps volunteers to countries where they are encountering either real or imagined racial discrimination.

Is this a factor in Peace Corps assignments and, if it is, what have you done about it, and what is the basis for the assignment of volunteers?

Mr. CRAW. We never assign a volunteer on the basis of his race, creed, color or her sex, as the case may be.

We also refuse to have a program in a country where discrimination is practiced on any one of the EEO criteria. 

It is a known fact that discrimination does exist in the world at large. I have spoken with volunteers in Liberia and in Zaire, black volunteers, who have expressed to me the opinion that if you thought discrimination was bad in the United States that you had better come over and find out what it is like over there. 

I have also had other instances reported to me of orientals who have contended, although not a critical vein of the Peace Corps, that discrimination, in fact, exists at various levels of society in which they were functioning.

I think that those volunteers recognize the difficulty of their situation and have attempted to adjust to it as best as possible. 

I do not know of an instance where minority volunteers from whatever segment of our society have terminated because they felt that such discrimination was a complete bar to their effective service. 

Senator BROOKE. You say you do not know of any? 

Mr. CRAW. I do not know of any.

DISCRIMINATION 

Senator BROOKE. Have you received many complaints about assignment because of racial discrimination?

Mr. CRAW. In writing, I have not. I have spoken to volunteers personally out in the field. I have had a number of them express to me a feeling that discrimination existed in a black society between blacks from various levels of that society as well as foreign nationals, not necessarily Americans, but it was an expression of opinion as opposed to a perjorative statement.

We have had the same type of situation, if you will, in Latin America, where we have Mexican Americans or Spanish Americans from the United States serving in Latin countries. 

Senator BROOKE. Dr. Balzano, what measures do you utilize in determining whether or not your program is successful? 

Mr. BALZANO. I am sorry, sir?

Senator BROOKE. What measures do you utilize in determining whether or not your programs are successful? How do you determine the success of a program? 

Mr. BALZANO. Mr. Craw?

Mr. CRAW. Our present standard, we feel, is not adequate. I will give you the two levels of definition at which that occurs. 

The most simple generalized answer I can give you is that so long as a significant number of Americans continue to apply for the program, and so long as we continue to receive a larger and larger number of requests, we can judge the program to be effective. 

That is an overly generalized definition and one with which we are not satisfied.

MEASURING IMPACT 

One of the agendas we are working on is a determination of an appropriate form of measuring impact. It is an issue with which the 

Peace Corps has been wrestling for a long time and has never come to a satisfactory closure on.

What we are looking for is a definition of impact which goes beyond the anecdotal or generalized statements which have been used to quantify the kind of impact which the Peace Corps has had in the past. 

These have largely been confined to reiterations of accomplishments or to the kinds of relationships which have been set up between host country nationals and Americans and the kind of understanding that has accrued from that. Those still are at the crux of the Peace Corps mission.

What we are looking for now is to build on that foundation and move somewhat beyond that and design an impact assessment formula which enables us to not only determine how successful we are but also to provide us a management tool to enable us to allocate, or reallocate, if necessary, our resources; again, those resources in the areas of volunteers, staff and budget.

We do not presently have a discrete formula which enables us to make judgments between countries, between projects within countries, or even between regions, so that we can allocate or reallocate our resources for the optimum impact which we would like to achieve. 

It is an extremely difficult problem, Senator, because of the two goals, the second and third goals, in the Peace Corps Act, which are essentially nonquantifiable.

It is also a dangerous problem to wrestle with for the simple reason you can appear to give the impression of stressing only the first goal, which is technical assistance and provision of trained manpower. 

It is very important for us as we examine this issue that we not appear to stress any one goal over the others.

The basic mission of the Peace Corps is to maintain a balance between all three of those goals. It is a problem. The definition of impact alone is a problem. We believe we have made some headway on it. We have not completed it.

Senator BROOKE. How many minorities do you employ on your staff and how many minorities are there among your volunteers? 

Mr. CRAW. On the staff, sir, 27 percent of the American staff members are minorities. 

DEFINITION OF MINORITIES Senator BROOKE. How do you define minorities? Do you include women as a minority?

Mr. CRAW. No, sir; we are talking about a racial minority. 

I should point out, sir, that we have the unique situation in the Peace Corps, particularly with respect to the host country nationals or foreign service locals whom the chairman referred to earlier. As you know, a very large proportion of our employment force is comprised of host country nationals. Consequently, the remaining number of Americans is small as a percentage of the total. 

Therefore, the 27 percent figure which I gave you earlier is a good deal larger than it would appear. 

If you wanted to use a similar, broader definition and include host country nationals as minorities, which, in many respects, they are, 68 percent of our total staff are minorities. 

So, in effect, the Americans are the minorities. 

Senator BROOKE. These foreign nationals are very lowly paid, aren't they? I am talking of the American staff.

Mr. CRAW. Of the total American staff, 27 percent are minorities; that is correct. 

Senator BROOKE. Volunteers? Do you have many minorities in the volunteer program?

Mr. CRAW. Frankly, not as many as we would like. 

Senator BROOKE. Do you still have a recruitment program for this purpose?

Mr. CRAW. Yes; we do. It has achieved varying degrees of success and varying degrees of cost-effectiveness.

While I was still Associate Director for the Office of Recruitment, we examined our minority recruitment programs globally and in some detail, each individual one. We found there were a number of them which we could no longer justify from a cost-effectiveness standpoint. 

We reprogramed some of those activities. We are still not satisfied. We are not getting as many people as we would like. 

One of the reasons for that, we have determined in more than one study, is that a majority of minority applicants or who could potentially be applicants, in the Peace Corps have undergone some financial sacrifice to achieve their education. They frequently have debt obligations and they have a family or relatives to support. 

Consideration of the Peace Corps volunteer service is usually not an important part of their financial and career plans. It therefore becomes extremely difficult for us to compete for their attention and for their service. That does not excuse any lessening of effort on our behalf. It does explain to a certain extent why minorities in this country are somewhat less inclined to be motivated to the volunteer service in light of their career and other aspirations.

CLASSIFICATIONS AND RANK OF MINORITY VOLUNTEERS 

Senator BROOKE. Could you supply for the record their classifications and rank?

Mr. CRAW. I can provide it to you for the record. 

 MINORITY VOLUNTEERS 

There are approximately 310 minority Volunteers currently serving overseas. (There are no classes or grades of Peace Corps Volunteers except in the distinction between Volunteers and Volunteer Leaders and no minority data is collected by the Peace Corps on Volunteer Leaders.)

Mr. CRAW. Excluding volunteers.

PERCENT OF VOLUNTEERS WITH COLLEGE DEGREES 

Senator INOUYE. I have three further questions here. 

In last year's summary sheet, you advised the subcommittee that in fiscal 1973 only 45 percent of your volunteers had college degrees, whereas in fiscal year 1966, 81 percent had college degrees. 

I have been told that these figures are incorrect. 

Mr. CRAW. That is correct, Mr. Chairman.

I am not exactly sure how it happened but we checked the record. 

The committee was given an incorrect figure in the hearings last year. 

We attempted to correct that in the fiscal 1973 Operations Report to the Congress on page 11.

The correct figure would have been 86 percent. Where they got the 

45 percent figure, I do not know. 

Senator INOUYE. Something went wrong with the computer.

Mr. CRAW. I think something went wrong with the typewriter, not the computer. 

Senator INOUYE. In the Sunday, January 20, 1974, issue of the

Washington Post, the organization got some publicity involving your country director in Thailand. 

What is the situation today?

UNFAVORABLE PUBLICITY 

Mr. CRAW. As a general statement, Mr. Chairman, I would like to point out that that publicity was not particularly favorable with respect to our country director. I believe our country director's rights in that respect should be respected.

Some of the allegations contained in that story, as well as other stories which appeared in the New York and the Los Angeles papers I will try to deal with. 

One allegation was made that three Thai senior staff assistants had quit for lower-paying jobs elsewhere in Thailand. 

One of those three Thai staff members was attempting to hold down two jobs at once, one of which was a Peace Corps job, and the time he was allotting to his Peace Corps responsibility was insufficient. His work performance was substandard. He was informed of this fact and he quit.

The second of these three individuals was seriously suspected of misappropriating Peace Corps funds and equipment over an extended period of time. He was confronted with the suspicion and he chose to resign. Those suspicions have since been confirmed. 

The third staff member left for a position voluntarily which he chose on his own.

Another allegation which was made in the story was that the Peace Corps Director had entertained a group of people at Peace Corps expense to the tune of $700. We have taken a few steps in this respect. 

One was to inquire of the country director whether this allegation was correct. He said it was not; he had paid for that party out of his own funds. However, we also exhumed the records from records center in Maryland and looked over every single voucher for the period involved, as well as a few months before and a few months after. We found no evidence whatsoever to indicate that party was paid for out of Peace Corps funds.

I might point out that there is a legal representation allowance provided for the Peace Corps but which we rarely make use of. 

It was also pointed out in the story that the country director had installed certain management practices and had begun to look for greater cost-benefit for the program in Thailand. I do not view that as criticism. I would view that as a very positive trend. 

TERMINATION OF TRAINEES AND VOLUNTEERS 

Senator INOUYE. Last year, as you are well aware, we undertook to review a surprising and disturbing statistic. A large number of trainees and volunteers were terminated prior to expiration of their contract. 

The committee staff and I have been lost in a maze of conversions and formulae submitted with your presentation. 

In the fiscal year 1972, you reported that 36 percent of Peace Corps trainees and volunteers terminated their services prior to expiration of their contracts.

Will you provide us with the number of volunteers terminated early at their own election in fiscal year 1973 ?

Mr. CRAW. Sir, I would like to try to address first the issue of that 

36-percent figure.

I share your confusion with the maze of statistics involved because I have determined there have been at least several formulas supplied in the Peace Corps history to determine attrition rates. 

The figures, as I understand it, that were provided last year were the total number of early terminees, including those who had become volunteers in previous fiscal years, divided by the total number of new volunteers in the current year regardless of the expected date of their close of service or any other factor. To me, in management terms that is a useless statistic. It tells me how many people attrited earlier but only as a proportion of the total number of volunteers attriting in that year, even though the vast majority may have been terminating at or beyond their scheduled term of service.

MAN-MONTH FORMULA 

The formula we are currently using, I believe, is a good deal more denfensible, both from a management standpoint and programmatic standpoint. The formula we have constructed which we call the available man-months formula, is applicable at any time in the fiscal year over a period of years in any quarter, in any month, in any week. 

The purpose of it is to establish at the time a volunteer is enrolled the number of man-months of service we expect from that volunteer, traditionally 24 months. At any one point in time, we can determine what percentage of our manpower resources is being lost through early termination.

That is the kind of management information we need to know to run the program appropriately, and I think that is the kind of information to which the committee has a right to determine if we are making good use of our management resources. 

That available man-months formula excludes volunteers who complete their service and then extend past their 24 months. 

For example, if you had a Peace Corps that was comprised of only one volunteer and he served his full 24 months, which was what his

commitment was to us, and the host country, we would have a zero attrition rate, a zero loss of man-months. If he served only 1 year, we would have a 50-percent loss.

My problem with the existing formulas that have been used in the past and including the ones that were reported last year is that it is both useless as a management tool to us and I think reports statistics both unfairly as well as inaccurately. 

DROPOUT PERCENTAGE 

Senator INOUYE. It may be useless to you from the management standpoint but the question was just what percentage of those who volunteered and who were trained and who signed contracts and decided, on their own initiative, to quit before the expiration date, it was 

36 percent. What is the percentage this time?

Mr. CRAW. I can give you the figures for both fiscal 1973 and the first half of fiscal 1974.

The number of man-months lost 

Senator INOUYE. No. 

What percentage of those who quit, whether it was the 1st or 23d month?

Mr. CRAW. That I can't give you for the current year. We did not compute it for that. 

Senator INOUYE.. You don't know how many of them quit? 

Mr. CRAW. Yes; I do. 

Senator INOUYE. How many quit early? You must have that number.

Mr. CRAW. I would have to go back and refigure it for you, sir, because the way in which we derive the figure was the number of manmonths which we lost against the total available man-months we would have expected. That way it is 9 percent.

In fiscal 1973, we should have had a total of 79,265 man-months. We, in fact, lost 7,130 man-months against that total expected figure, or a rate of 9 percent.

In the first half of fiscal 1974, we should have had a total potential man-month figure of 22,281. The amount of actual man-months lost prior to the completion of term of service was 1,445, a 6.5 rate for the first half of fiscal 1974.

Senator INOUYE. As I said, I can understand from the standpoint of management those figures on man-hours and man-months, but I have another question to follow.

I just want to know: Of the number of volunteers who signed a contract, how many quit before the expiration date? 

If you have that figure, do you further have their reasons for quitting?

I would think from your management standpoint it would be well to know why they are quitting, whether it is in the 1st or the 23d month. 

Mr. CRAW. Absolutely, on both counts. I agree with you. 

Senator INOUYE. It does not give us any hint as to what your problem is by knowing the man-months lost. If you knew that 36 percent or 40 percent for some reason or another decided to quit, it should raise a red flag for all of us. 

Mr. CRAW. Absolutely.

Senator INOUYE. This man-month business, it shows it is not too bad; it is what General Electric has or General Motors has; we are running a good shop.

When you come out with 36 percent who quit, I would say you should check and find out why.

Mr. CRAW. For the validity and the value to us of the 36-percent figure, let me postulate an example.

Let us imagine that 36 percent of the volunteers did, in fact, quit early but quit 1 week prior to their 2-year term of service. That tells you one thing. Let us imagine they quit 1 month into their service.

That tells you something completely different. That figure has limited utility, depending on what term it is applied to. 

PROGRAM REFLECTIONS 

That is what we are trying to get at by finding out the actual number of man-months we have lost, which does, in fact, reflect on the kind of program that they are operating, the kind of supervision they are getting, the kind of program development that was done, the viability of their job, et cetera.

We are very much concerned that attrition statistics do reflect a very wide number of factors.

One category is unmanageable and is beyond our control. That would be a difficulty in the family at home, compelling financial obligations that would require a volunteer to return, an illness, an injury, a disability, or a number of other factors which we can't control. 

There is a significant amount, we feel, of attrition which occurs within the manageable area which we feel we should be held accountable for and which we can hold our country directors and our country staff accountable for. These relate specifically to job development, the type of support and supervision that a volunteer is given, the kind of satisfaction that he derives from performing his job. It is that area that we have had to attack.

EARLY TERMINATING VOLUNTEERS 

Senator INOUYE. So, if you could furnish us just the raw number and percentage and give us an idea as to why these men and women quit, because if someone quits on the twenty-third month his reason may have some bearing as to why he remained longer than the fellow who quit on the first month, the same reason but one had greater patience; that is all. 

Mr. CRAW. Fortitude.

ACTION WASHINGTON, D.C. 20525 

February 22, 1974 

Dear Senator Hatfield: 

Thank you for your February 14, 1974, letter to Mr. Balzano, in which you requested information relating to the Peace Corps Volunteer readjustment allowance. We will respond to your questions in the order that you presented them in your letter. 

1. What is the present readjustment allowance for 

Peace Corps Volunteers, Volunteer Leaders, and 

PCV's with one or more minor children? 'Section 5 (c) of the Peace Corps Act provides that Peace Corps Volunteers are entitled to receive a readjustment allowance at a rate not to exceed $75.00 for each month of satisfactory service. This section also provides that in the cases of 

Volunteers who have one or more minor children at the time of their entering a period of pre-enrollment training ("Volunteer families"), one parent shall be entitled to receive a readjustment allowance at a rate not to exceed $125.00 for each month of satisfactory service. The other 

Volunteer parent receives the normal readjustment allowance of $75.00 a month for each month of satisfactory service. 

Section 6 of the Peace Corps Act provides that Volunteer Leaders are entitled to receive a readjustment allowance at a rate not to exceed $125.00 for each month of satisfactory service. 

2. How long has the allowance been at this level?

The readjustment allowance for Peace Corps Volunteers and Peace Corps Volunteer Leaders has been the same since the Peace Corps Act was enacted in September 1961. A separate allowance for Volunteer families was established by amendment to the Peace Corps Act in 1970. 

3. How many PCV's are presently in service or in training? 

At the end of December 1973 there were 6,554 Volunteers in service, and 708 trainees. 4.

Of these, how many PCV's have one or more minor children?

The number of Volunteer families was approximately 157. (For purposes of section 5 (c) of the Peace Corps Act, a Volunteer family is defined as Volunteers who have one or more minor children at the time they enter Peace Corps training. Volunteers who marry during their service and have a child are not eligible for the higher readjustment allowance provided by section 5(c) for "volunteer families".) 

5. How many Volunteer Leaders are presently in service?

Section 6 of the Peace Corps Act provides that the ratio of total number of Volunteer Leaders in service at any one time shall not exceed 1 to 25. At the end of December, 1973 there were approximately 103 Volunteer Leaders in service. 6. 

What is the FY74 cost of readjustment allowances for Peace Corps Volunteers? 

The estimated FY74 cost of readjustment allowances for Peace

Corps Volunteers is $7,238,000. This total is divided accordingly: Trainee man-years $861,000; Peace Corps Volunteer man-years $5,607,000; Peace Corps Volunteer Leaders and heads of household $390,000; U.S. Government contribution to social security - $380,000. 

(Note: For budget purposes, the costs of readjustment allowance are calculated on a man-year basis. Because the total number of Volunteers in service at any one time fluctuates, the man-year figure, which represents a division of total volunteer and trainee man-months by 12, provides the most accurate index of the average number of Volunteers and trainees in service during a given fiscal year.) 1. 

How many Peace Corps Volunteers do you expect to have in service or in training in FY75? 

In FY75 the Peace Corps expects to reach a level of 6,800 

Volunteer man-years and 957 trainee man-years. 8.

Of these, how many are expected to have one or more minor children?

The Peace Corps anticipates having slightly fewer families (i.e., Volunteers with one or more minor children at the time they enter Peace Corps training) than the 157 who were in service at the end of December, 1973. We anticipate that we will have approximately 150 Volunteer families in service or training during FY75.

9. How many Volunteer Leaders do you expect to have in service in FY75?

We anticipate that we will have approximately 122 Volunteer 

Leaders in FY75. 

10. What would be the estimated cost of implementing the proposals of Senator Mondale's S. 2814 

for FY75?

The estimated cost of Senator Mondale's bill would be an additional $7,539,000 to the present readjustment allowance estimate for FY75. The total readjustment allowance cost under S. 2814 would thus be $15,078,000. This total includes the United States Government contribution to social security. 11. 

What is the expected FY75 cost of readjustment allowances for PCV's, PCVL's, and Volunteers with one or more minor children?

The estimated readjustment allowance cost for FY75 is $7,539,000. This total includes the United States Government contribution to social security. 12.

What would be the estimated cost of increasing the readjustment allowance for PCV's to $125 a month, and to $200 a month for PCVL's and 

PCV's with one or more minor children?

The estimated cost of increasing the readjustment allowance from $75 to $125 a month for PCV's, and from $125 to $200 a month for Peace Corps Volunteer Leaders and heads of household would be an addition of approximately $5 million to the presently estimated FY75 cost. The total readjustment allowance cost under this proposal would thus be $12,539,000. 

This total includes the United States Government contribution to social security.

I trust that the above information is sufficient for your purposes. Please do not hesitate to let me know if I can provide you with any further information. 

With best wishes. 

Sincerely yours, Jelly Kammeur 

Carlton Kammerer

Assistant Director of ACTION
