INTER-AMERICAN FOUNDATION STATEMENT OF WILLIAM M. DYAL, JR., PRESIDENT ACCOMPANIED BY LEON M. PARKER, EXECUTIVE OFFICER BUDGET REQUEST 

Senator INOUYE. The subcommittee will now take up the Inter- 

American Foundation.

The subcommittee is glad to have with us this morning Mr. William 

M. Dyal, Jr., President of the Inter-American Foundation, who will present a statement regarding the fiscal year 1975 request for the Foundation which is the limitation of $10 million, the same as for fiscal 1974. 

Please proceed, sir. 

Mr. DYAL. Mr. Chairman, and Senator Brooke, with me today is 

Leon M. Parker, the Executive Officer of the Foundation.

Since you have before you my complete statement for the benefit of time I will just highlight briefly this statement. 

On March 16 of this year the Inter-American Foundation began its 4th year of operations, facing, as most organizations at this time, a range of both issues and opportunities. 

Our basic approach continues to be a unique emphasis on man as the focal point of development and on responsiveness to the people of Latin America and the Caribbean as our method of operations. 

Our brief 3-year history confirms, frankly, that we must even more carefully, yet still risk oriented, commit our limited resources to those indigenous efforts of Latin America and the Caribbean designed to enable the people so often bypassed by other assistance programs to become no longer objects but subjects of their own destiny. 

This subcommittee, I think, summed it up unusually well in your own report on the 1974 foreign assistance appropriation bill. 

You stated: "Development with maximum grassroots involvement and participation by those being assisted must be at the core of our future assistance."

FOUNDATION PROJECTS 

To date the Foundation has participated in the funding of 87 projects and 25 evaluations in 24 countries. We don't speak of them as the 

Foundation's projects. Neither did we design them nor are we carrying them out. They are the projects of the people of the region in those countries.

As we become better known, both the number and the quality of proposals we are receiving continue to increase. It would be difficult to talk about examples or typical projects we are funding. 

In the statement I speak of those which illustrate the kind of project proposals before us. One of them, for example, in Bolivia is for a federation of 14 production and marketing cooperatives in southern Bolivia for a total amount of $434,000, to help raise their (81)

output in hog production, provide additional employment and raise incomes, and I might say to provide one other viable organization in the mountains of Bolivia for the people to have the force and voice to express themselves.

It is interesting that this entire grant reflows to a development trust fund providing further uses of the money for projects in surrounding communities.

A second project is $62,000 for a major land redistribution project in Dominica, one of the smaller islands in the Caribbean which seeks to replace a traditional estate structure controlled by wealthy landowners with a cooperative structure allowing landownership and control by the workers of the land. 

A third illustration of $70,000 in Guadalajara, Mexico, to aid local self-help efforts to build minimal housing for some 12,000 people whose incomes fall under the $1,000 range. 

Mr. Chairman, thanks largely to the efforts of this subcommittee last year, together with an agreement signed in December with the Inter-American Development Bank granting the Foundation access to a portion of the reflows to the social progress trust fund, we are operating for the first time during the second half of this fiscal year at our full budget request.

PROGRAM SUPPORT COSTS 

Last year both in the hearings before you and in the subcommittee's report you expressed concern over the Foundation's then excessive program support costs which were running at approximately 30 percent of total obligations.

Although the low continuing resolution figure was the primary cause, I shared your concern and told you that the percentage would be cut at least in half this year. 

For this fiscal year, our projections call for obligations of $13.3 million in program funds, and program support costs of $1.7 million or a maximum ratio of 11 percent for program support. 

Our budget request for fiscal 1975 is based on a projected total of $20 million. We are requesting a $10 million limitation on obligations of our original appropriated funds, the same as we received from the 

Congress for this year.

The additional $10 million will come from reflows to the Social Progress Trust Fund. Program support costs are budgeted at $2 million or 10 percent of total obligations for the coming fiscal year. 

In reviewing program support costs, I think it important to describe the type of staff we have. It is a small staff of 58 people. We have purposely not created a far-flung bureaucracy with regional offices all over the hemisphere. 

Neither have we created a massive support services staff. 

The bulk of our program support costs goes to pay the salaries and travel expenses of the program staff. This staff is made up of professionals who must travel throughout Latin America and the Caribbean, have the sensitivity and language skills to establish relationships with a wide variety of groups and individuals, and carefully analyze and respond to every project proposal that the Foundation receives. 

In comparison with many other funders, our preaward assessment of a project must be very thorough. We do not have the luxury of cor-

recting errors midcourse, since we neither direct the project nor do we provide technical assistance staff in residence. 

Therefore, we must make the maximum feasible effort to do sound preliminary analysis. The record thus far attests to the economy of this approach, with only one of 87 projects having been terminated without achieving the proposed objectives. 

It is also important to note that we do not designate our staff's time as part of the project costs. Program grants go totally to the grantee. This is routine even though our staff have additional and complex tasks relating to the projects through evaluation and dissemination.

Yet another staff role is as brokers, in leveraging other resources to projects we have identified. This would be true whether the project resources would come from private foundations or from international lending agencies or others.

POPULAR PARTICIPATION 

I wish to underscore the fundamental importance the Foundation places on popular participation by those being assisted. 

The Spanish have a very interesting verb, "habilitar" which I believe has real importance for what we are about. It is best defined as "To give one the necessary capital in order to be able to negotiate for himself."

We are not talking only about economic resources and this kind of capital but also the kind of motivation resources, leadership capacity. 

I believe the concept is crucial in problem solving social ills. 

It is increasingly evident that solutions can succeed only if designed both by the people and for the people, thus expressing their own desires, aspirations, values and commitment.

PREPARED STATEMENT 

Senator INOUYE. Thank you very much, sir. Your prepared statement will be placed in the record at this point. 

[The statement follows:] STATEMENT OF WILLIAM M. DYAL, JR. 

Mr. Chairman and members of the Subcommittee, I would like to read a brief opening statement and then we can proceed with the questions I know you have. 

At the beginning of the fourth year of operations, the Inter-American Foundation faces both issues and opportunities. But our basic approach will continue to be a unique emphasis on man as the focal point of development and on responsiveness to the people of Latin America and the Caribbean as the method of operations.

The Foundation's brief three-year history confirms for me that we must even more carefully, yet still risk-oriented, commit our limited resources to those indigenous efforts designed to enable the people so often bypassed by traditional aid programs to become no longer objects but subjects of their own destiny. 

This Subcommittee summed it up well in your report on the 1974 Foreign 

Assistance Appropriation Bill. You stated: "Development with maximum grass roots involvement and participation by those being assisted must be at the core of our future assistance." 

You have before you a report entitled "First Steps" which is one attempt to describe the Foundation's record of the past three years. During this period the staff has been establishing relationships based on mutual respect and trust with countless groups and individuals throughout Latin America and the Caribbean. 34-192 - 74 - 5

FOUNDATION PROJECTS 

To date the Foundation has participated in the funding of 87 projects and 25 evaluations in 24 countries. We don't speak of them as the Foundation's projects. 

Neither did we design them nor are we carrying them out. They are the projects of the people of the region. 

As we become better known, both the number and the quality of the proposals we are receiving continue to increase, thus requiring greater selectivity and deeper analysis by staff. Illustrative of the projects currently pending are: 

1. $434,000 for a federation of 14 production and marketing cooperatives in southern Bolivia to raise their output in hog production, provide additional employment and raise incomes. The entire grant will reflow to a development trust fund to provide further uses of the money for projects in surrounding communities. 

2. $62,000 for a major land redistribution project in Dominica which seeks to replace a traditional estate structure controlled by wealthy landholders with a cooperative structure allowing land ownership and control by the workers of the land. 

3. $70,000 in Guadalajara, Mexico to aid local self-help efforts to build minimal housing for some 12,000 people whose incomes are under $1,000 per year. 

Mr. Chairman, thanks largely to the efforts of this Subcommittee last year, together with an agreement signed in December with the Inter-American Development Bank granting the Foundation access to a portion of the reflows to the Social Progress Trust Fund, we are operating for the first time during the second half of this fiscal year at our full budget request. 

PROGRAM SUPPORT COSTS 

Last year both in the hearings before you and in the Subcommittee's report you expressed concern over the Foundation's then excessive program support costs which were running at approximately 30% of total obligations. Although the low continuing resolution figure was the primary cause, I shared your concern and told you that the percentage would be cut at least in half this year. 

For this fiscal year, our projections call for obligations of $13.3 million in program funds, and program support costs of $1.7 million or a maximum ratio of 

11% for the program support. Our budget request for fiscal 1975 is based on a projected total of $20 million. We are requesting a $10 million limitation on obligations of our original appropriated funds, the same as we received from the Congress for this year. The additional $10 million will come from reflows to the 

Social Progress Trust Fund. Program support costs are budgeted at $2 million or 10% of total obligations for the coming fiscal year. 

In reviewing program support costs, I think it important to describe the type of staff we have. It is a small staff of 58 people. We have purposely not created a far-flung bureaucracy with regional offices all over the hemisphere. Neither have we created a massive support services staff. The bulk of our program support costs goes to pay the salaries and travel expenses of the program staff. 

This staff is made up of professionals who must travel throughout Latin America and the Caribbean, have the sensitivity and language skills to establish relationships with a wide variety of groups and individuals, and carefully analyze and respond to every project proposal that the Foundation receives. In comparison with many other funders, our pre-award assessment of a project must be very thorough. We do not have the luxury of correcting errors mid-course, since we neither direct the project nor do we provide technical assistance staff in residence. Therefore, we must make the maximum feasible effort to do sound preliminary analysis. The record thus far attests to the economy of this approach, with only one of 87 projects having been terminated without achieving the proposed objectives.

It is also important to note that we do not designate our staff's time as part of the project costs. Program grants go totally to the grantee. This is routine even though our staff have additional and complex tasks relating to the projects through evaluation and dissemination. 

Yet another staff role is as brokers, in leveraging other resources to projects we have identified. For example, during the past year the Clark Foundation, a private foundation located in New York City, approved almost a half million dollars in grants to projects which the Foundation staff identified for them. 

Also during this past year, in El Salvador, the World Bank made a soft loan of some $7 million to a group that we had funded at a first stage and later brought to the Bank's attention.

More recently the Inter-American Development Bank sent representatives to Bolivia to study a pilot project we funded last summer. They are seriously considering replicating the model in four other areas of Bolivia with a loan of more than one million dollars. 

One final note on the subject of program support costs should be emphasized. 

As I stated earlier, our budget for fiscal year 1974 calls for $13.3 million in program funds and the 1975 budget for $18 million. Frankly, these projections are our best estimate of the money we can place in good projects based on expected requests and staff capacity. Based on our experience to date, we should come out somewhere near those figures. 

I refuse, however, to succumb to a traditional end of the fiscal year obligations race and to make program grants just to cut the program support percentage to a certain figure. The Foundation shall continue to try to choose its projects wisely, placing quality above quantity.

POPULAR PARTICIPATION 

In conclusion, I wish to underscore the fundamental importance the Foundation places on popular participation by those being assisted. The Spanish use a verb "habilitar"—which I believe has great importance for those concerned with foreign assistance. The idea is best defined by the Spanish Royal Academy as "to give one the necessary capital in order to be able to negotiate for himself.” 

I believe the concept is crucial in problem-solving social ills. It is increasingly evident that solutions can succeed only if designed both by the people and for the people, thus expressing their own desires, aspirations, values, and commitment. 

An article reflecting on the Foundation in the winter issue of the Harvard Political Review captured this unique responsiveness to local initiatives. I will let an "outsider" speak to this by quoting him ; "IAF's funding exposes the increasingly active role that private development groups can play in the hemisphere's social development. The tendency has too often been to think of central planning, government financing and externally controlled projects as the means to upgrade living standards in Latin America. IAF demonstrates the contributions that small, private groups can make. Second, it is bringing to the fore active and dedicated private citizens who are fighting for small social development programs, usually this resource has been ignored in the past. Third, IAF allows the program benefiting an area to be initiated by the people affected by them. 

Funds probably are more wisely administered and less likely to end up in the pockets of top political leaders. Fourth, times have changed and bilateral aid is becoming increasingly unpopular in the U.S. and Latin 

America. IAF is establishing the continued importance of various types of bilateral aid which are still feasible and vital to the future of Latin America. 

Fifth, just as the programs are indigenous, so too are the evaluations, conducted during the lifetime of the project rather than simply "post-mortem." 

The results from the evaluations can be related to host government assistance programs, and this is already being done. "Though foreign aid proposals are a dime a dozen these days, the notion of linking the individual to the social institutions which control his environment is central to IAF's operation and should be encouraged throughout the foreign assistance programs. Possibly it is time to apply the New Federalist argument to Latin America. For the growing population to manage the coming decades initiatives from the lowest rank and file must be encouraged and honored."

Which leads us back to the false dichotomies that so dramatize the cruel choice. 

Development is a complex and still not fully grasped phenomenon. 

We know, however, that it requires capital, technology, production and markets as well as planning and controls. The question is not one of control per se, but the source and legitimacy of control. Discipline, austerity, and restraints on self-gratification for the common good are controls that can be effective in the long run only if they are self-imposed and voluntary.

Do specific examples provide evidence that this is so, or is it but wishful thinking? It may be both. 

Switzerland is evidence,

PREPARED STATEMENT 

The subcommittee has received your prepared statement. Without objection it will be inserted in the record in toto at this time. If you prefer to summarize it, you may do so. 

[The statement follows:]

Mr. Chairman, members of the Committee, it is indeed a pleasure for me to discuss with you the FY 1975 budget proposals of the Export-Import Bank and some significant events of the past year which affect the Bank. 

As you know, Henry Kearns, the Bank's President and Chairman for the past four and one-half years, resigned and returned to private industry in October 1973. Since then I, the First Vice President and 

Vice Chairman, have been serving as President and Chairman, as provided for in our enabling legislation, and it is in that capacity that I appear before you today.

FISCAL YEAR 1973 

In FY 1973 the Bank had gross authorizations of $8.5 billion which supported more than $10. 5 billion of United States exports. 

Regular loan authorizations were $2.4 billion, up 5. 1% over FY 1972.

Because of the general tightening of liquidity experienced by commercial banks in FY 1973, commitments under our commercial bank discount program rose 66%, from $989 million in FY 1972 to $1.6 billion in FY 1973. Guarantee and insurance authorizations totaled $4.5 billion, up from $3.9 billion the prior year. +

Gross revenue to the Bank from its operations totaled $376 million. Out of these funds, the Bank paid interest expenses of $215 million, administrative expense of $8.5 million, and net claims of $12.5 million, leaving a profit for the year of $139.7 million. We paid a $50 million dividend to the U. S. Treasury from these profits and added the remaining $89.7 million to our retained earnings, which now amount to $1.503 billion.

FISCAL YEAR 1974 

The first seven months of FY 1974 have been ones of continued high levels of activity. Equipment and services loans have totaled $1,736.3 million, nearly double the same period of last year. Guar-

78 1 antees and insurance authorizations were $2.1 billion and discount loan commitments totaled $513 million, both down somewhat from the previous year. The contract value of export sales supported by all these activities was $6.2 billion.

FY 1975 BUDGET REQUEST 

For FY 1975 the Bank is requesting authorization levels of $3.4 billion for equipment and services loans, $75 million for commodity loans and a $50 million contingency for emergency loans. Two billion dollars are requested for discount loan commitments and $8 billion for guarantees and insurance. Administrative expenses are estimated to be $10.2 million which, of course, will be paid from the Bank's revenues. We believe that these levels are the minimum amounts necessary for us to provide the support needed for United States exports in FY 1975. In keeping with the provisions of our enabling legislation and the policies of the Administration, larger increases are requested for our guarantee and insurance of private sector credits than for the lending of our own funds. 

These are the highlights of our 1975 budget requests. We have submitted detailed justification data on these requests to your Committee and we will be pleased to answer any questions that you may have with respect to that data.

PENDING LEGISLATIVE PROPOSALS 

There is, as you know, legislation pending in the Congress to amend the Export-Import Bank Act of 1945. S. 1890, introduced in the 

Senate last year, would extend the life of the Bank for four years--from 

June 30, 1974, to June 30, 1978. It would also increase the Bank's loan, guarantee and insurance authority from the present $20 billion to $30 billion outstanding at any one time, and increase the Bank's authority to issue guarantees and insurance on a fractional charge basis from $10 billion to $20 billion. 4

As you can see from the budget schedules, it is anticipated that at the end of FY 1974, only $2.2 billion of the $20 billion authority and $674 million of the $10 billion guarantee authority will be uncommitted. Thus, these increases are necessary to permit the Bank to continue its operations as called for by our export trade in FY 1975 and beyond. 7

CHANGES IN EXIMBANK'S LENDING RATE 

Under the Bank's Participation Financing Program, the Bank assists U. S. exports through direct credits for the purchase of U. S. goods and services by foreign buyers. The foreign purchasers must pay at least 10% of the contract value of the export in cash. We will then lend up to 50% of the financed portion, with a commercial bank or other private financial institution lending the other 50%. The blend of rates--that is, the rate charged by us on our 50% and that charged by the commercial bank on the other 50%--is intended to produce an effective rate which makes the financing package for the U. S. export competitive in the international marketplace.

Recently, after extensive analysis by the Bank and the National Advisory Council on International Monetary and Financial Policies, we raised the rate charged on our 50% of the financing from 6% to 7% per annum.

This change reflects the considered judgment of the Board of Directors of the Bank that an increase in the rate would not be detrimental to the Bank's efforts to assist U. S. exports. Obviously, the 7% rate, blended with the commercial bank rate, results in a total effective cost of funds to the foreign obligor which is slightly higher than was the case when the Bank's rate was 6%. However, under current international economic and financial conditions, we believe that the higher effective rate is still competitive and that this new rate is generally in line with the rates charged by Eximbank's 34-192 O-74-6

counterparts in other industrialized countries. In addition, the increase reflects existing over-all cost of funds to the Bank which, in FY 1974, for the first time, rose above 6%.

EAST-WEST TRADE 

Over the past several months there has been a considerable amount of discussion concerning the Bank's loans to the Soviet Union. As you know, the Bank's enabling legislation precludes it from engaging in transactions with communist countries unless the President of the United States determines that it is in the national interest for the Bank so to do. As of this time, Presidential Determinations to such effect have been made for Yugoslavia, Romania, Poland and the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics. As of February 15, 1974, the Bank had outstanding and undisbursed credits and guarantees in Yugoslavia of approximately $433 million, in Romania, of approximately $85 million, and in Poland, of approximately $94 million. As of the same date, there were outstanding and undisbursed credits for the Soviet Union of approximately $245 million in support of U. S. exports having a value of $545 million. 

It will be noted that in the case of Poland and the Soviet Union there are no financial guarantees. This is because in both instances, the countries have obtained the standard 50% commercial bank financing of each transaction without the necessity of the Export-Import Bank's issuing its guarantee to the commercial bank lenders. The terms and conditions of the loans to these communist countries are the same as those granted by the Bank to other borrowers. In other words, contrary to some statements that have been made in the press and other places, the Soviet Union was not given preferential treatment on the loans made by the Bank to that country. 

SUPPORT FOR SMALL BUSINESS 

Permit me now to discuss for a moment the ways in which Eximbank assists the export effort of small- and medium-sized

businesses, a matter which I believe is of some interest to this Committee.

Eximbank has in its active files the names of over 5,700 U. S. suppliers who have used one or more of its programs in support of one or more of their export sales. 

While it is impractical to research and classify this many suppliers into small, medium, large, or whatever, it is obvious by their numbers that the vast majority of them cannot be large companies; even if all of the companies in the Fortune 1,000 were included--which is most definitely not the case--that would still leave over 4,700 companies whose annual sales are less than $67 million.

Further, our files often include only a small portion of the total suppliers involved, particularly in large credits where one or perhaps a few major contractors handle the over-all contract even though thousands of subcontractors are participating. For example, as we have often noted in testimony before Congress and elsewhere, commercial aircraft manufacturers such as Boeing and McDonnell tell us there are as many as 16, 500 subcontractors involved in the sale of a wide-bodied jet aircraft, and nuclear power station contractors such as Westinghouse and General Electric tell us there are 5,000 sub-suppliers involved in the sale of such a power plant. 

By their very nature, the medium-term guarantee, insurance, relending, and CFF programs are especially attractive to, and used by, smaller businesses. Seventy-six percent of the export sales supported by the Bank in FY 1973 were under these programs; for FY 1974 through 

January the figure is 77 percent. Seventy-nine percent of the authorizations under these programs were in support of export sales of less than $250 thousand.

We are all quite aware of what significant changes have taken place in the past year or so on the international financial scene. The energy crisis and, more specifically, the spectacular rise in the price of petroleum, is probably the most significant single factor affecting world trade today. After a large trade deficit in 1972, the 

United States moved into a trade surplus position in 1973. We at the 

Export-Import Bank like to believe that the Bank made a significant contribution to the United States achieving this surplus. The estimated value of exports included in the trade figures for 1973 which were supported by the Bank amounted to about $4.5 billion and so far as the cash balance of payments is concerned, the Bank contributed $4.1 billion during 1973. Whether the United States can achieve another surplus year in 1974 may well depend upon how serious the impact of the energy crisis may prove to be, both here in the United States and abroad. The Bank will, of course, continue to support the overseas marketing efforts of U. S. business through the Bank's various programs of loans, guarantees and insurance, and in so doing, will help to mitigate the adverse impact on our trade account of the increased outlay for petroleum imports and of the other unfavorable factors which may result from the energy crisis.

Mr. SAUER. Yes, I will do no more than that. We have figures here for fiscal year 1973 and the first months of fiscal year 1974. As you just stated, we are asking for these limitations for the fiscal year 1975. 

We have submitted detailed justification data on this request to your committee. We will be pleased to answer any questions that you may have with respect to the figures. 

Senator INOUYE. Mr. Sauer, before proceeding will you introduce those gentlemen who are with you today?

Mr. SAUER. I can do that and I should have done it. 

I have on my left a member of our board of directors, Mr. Alex 

McCullough; Mr. John Corette, general counsel; Mr. Patrick Dugan, our senior vice president and treasurer-controller; Mr. James Hess, deputy treasurer; and Mr. Warren Glick, our acting executive vice president.

CONTINGENCY FOR EMERGENCY LOANS 

Senator INOUYE. I have a few questions here. I just noted new words which appear on page 2 of the fiscal year 1975 budget request, on the last line, "$50 million contingency for emergency loans." This is the first time I have seen these words appear in a justification. 

What are emergency loans, sir?

Mr. SAUER. In the past, Senator, we have been called upon to extend loans in situations in which a country finds itself in dire stress with respect to its balance of payments. It may need dollars to continue its imports of U.S.goods. 

We have extended credits for such purposes. We have not done that in the last several years, but we do include an amount for such contingencies in our backup here. We don't ask for a specific limitation figure in the legislation, but in arriving at our overall figure, with the Office of Management and Budget's consent, we include an item for emergency loans.

Whether we will be called upon to do anything like that, we don't know. That is the explanation.

NEWSPAPER ARTICLE ON EXIMBANK LOANS 

Senator INOUYE. I am certain you are aware, sir, of an article which appeared in the December 26, 1973 issue of the Washington Post.

[The article follows:]

Wednesday, Dec. 26, 1973 THE WASHINGTON POST 

Eximbank

Loan Setup 

Debated 

By Josh Fitzhugh 

Associated Press

NEW YORK-While Americans have found it costly and sometimes impossible to borrow money recently, their tax money has helped provide relatively cheap and easy loans for U.S. exporters and foreign companies seeking 

American goods. 

The loans-some $2.4 billion worth in fiscal 1973-are made below domestic rates to boost exports, to improve a country's balance of payments or for international political reasons.

They are made by the governmentbacked U.S. Export-Import Bank, the 

American contender in a worldwide credit war in which countries offer prospective overseas buyers loans at low, subsidized rates.

Eximbank loans, which also draw on commercial bank funds, have financed exports of nuclear power plants, jet aircraft and military equipment. Last year, the bank loaned $157 million for an Algerian gas facility, $86 million for a Russian truck factory and $21.6 million for an oil refinery in Iran, its biggest customer.

Today, no major domestic company, without a government subsidy, can borrow money at less than the current prime lending rate of 10 per cent. But a foreign firm wishing to buy American goods, or a U.S. exporter wishing to finance a foreign order, can get a 6 per cent, long-term loan from the Eximbank. "Call it a subsidy to help U.S. exporters," said John Petty, a partner in the international investment banking firm of Lehman Brothers and a former assistant secretary of the Treasury. 

Observers note that Eximbank loans can sometimes have undesirable domestic side effects, however. In April, the bank lent $75 million to the Bank of Tokyo to finance raw cotton purchases from the United States. The loan, for purchases from the 1973-74 crop, comes at a time when short supplies of cotton in the domestic market have already contributed to higher prices for cotton clothes. 

Warren Glick, Eximbank's senior vice president for financing, said: "At the time we made the loan, it was not clear the cotton market was that tight. 

We would take a much closer look if we considered the loan today." 

Since 1969, the Eximbank-established in 1934 to expand trade between the United States and Russia-has enlarged its direct grant loans from $1.1 billion to $2.4 billion for fiscal 1973.

The loans are approved by the bank's board of directors, which is appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate, and then matched by private commitments from U.S. commercial banks. Eximbank guarantees the private loans.

The Eximbank has granted 6 per cent loans since the mid-'60s, despite wide fluctuations in domestic money market rates. Petty and Glick said the 

6 per cent rate is necessary for "planning and consistency" and to remain competitive in world markets, where Germany, France and Japan finance exporters at 6 to 7½ per cent. 

Earlier this year, the bank and the Nixon administration resisted attempts to raise the rate. "If we charged the prime rate, we would make the American exporter grossly uncompetitive," Glick said. 

Committee said there was a "dubious need for the bank" and low rates were "simply a hidden subsidy to U.S. exporters."

A study by the General Accounting 

Office, an investigatory arm of Congress, criticized the bank for not making "a concerted effort to maximize private financing." "Although Eximbank sees its role as a lender of last resort because its interest rate has been lower and its repayment terms longer than comparable commercial financing, borrowers tend to seek Eximbank financing as a first resort," the GAO said. "Prestige, patented materials and a preference for U.S. products by borrowers suggest that purchases would have been made from the United 

States without Eximbank financing,' the GAO-concluded, summarizing a study of loans to Japan. 

How can Eximbank lend at 6, per cent when commercial banks charge 10 per cent? 

The principal reason is a $1 billion grant from the Treasury in 1945 and $1.3 billion in retained earnings, said 

Lehman's Petty. For the use of this capital, the bank pays the Treasury a yearly dividend of $50 million, or roughly 2.2 per cent. Other funds to cover 1973's total authorization of $8.5 billion come from loan repayment, sales of Eximbank bonds and 180-day 

Treasury borrowing. 

Despite the Treasury capital, the bank's reliance on private borrowing 1 may cause "a problem in funding the institution if the prime rate stays high much longer," Glick acknowledged. 

The Treasury dividend may by dropped, he said. 

Dr. Peter Beter, a former counsel for Eximbank and author of a new book, "The Conspiracy Against the 

Dollar," said the low interest rate and "bad loans made at the insistence of 

President Nixon and Henry Kissinger" have caused bank directors to dip into reserves. "They have absolutely plundered the bank," Beter said, noting that both Eximbank chairman Henry Kearns and executive vice president Don Bostwick resigned for personal reasons last summer. 

U.S. exporters, in concert with 

American banks and investment houses, arrange most Eximbank loans for foreign buyers. The usual practice is for Eximbank to establish a credit at a commercial bank, which in turns pays the exporter and is reimbursed by Eximbank. Eventually, the borrower repays Eximbank in dollars. 

Devaluations of the dollar have made loans easier to repay, Glick concedes, thereby further reducing the real interest. Officials agree another result of the subsidized loans is increased inflation. "Export financing is inflationary." said Petty. "But one must remember that the purpose is to stimulate U.S. exports."

DENIAL OF ACCUSATIONS 

Senator INOUYE. In this article Dr. Peter Beter, former Counsel of 

Export-Import Bank, charged that a combination of low interest rates and bad loans, made at the insistence of our President and the Secretary of State, has forced the Bank to dip into reserves. He is further quoted as having said, "They have absolutely plundered the Bank." 

Would you care to respond to these charges, sir?

Mr. SAUER. Yes. The members of our Board of Directors categorically deny such innuendoes and the direct charges of Peter Beter. I personally happen to know him. He was a member of the Bank's legal staff for some years. He has, shall we say, a superficial knowledge of what the Bank does and is doing these days. What provoked him to make these statements and write a book that included some of these statements, I don't know. But there is nothing of substance to the charge.

Our record speaks for itself. We have taken no actions that we have not publicized. We believe that each and every one of our actions at the Bank over the past 4 years, which is the period in question, is subject to scrutiny.

Eximbank loans also draw on commercial bank funds.

Eximbank loans are extended to overseas purchasers (non-U.S.) of U. S. exports, not to exporters. 

These loans are repaid in dollars with interest.

However, monies actually disbursed by Eximbank never leave the U. S. They are disbursed through a U. S. bank directly to the U. S. exporter. 

Eximbank receives no annual appropriations or other tax monies from the Congress. The Bank operates with its own resources, makes a profit ($140 million last year), and pays a $50 million dividend to the U. S. Treasury. Dividends paid into the Treasury over the Bank's life total $856 million. In addition, Eximbank funds its operations primarily through the sale of debentures in the private market. No.

Loans are made to support U. S. export sales. 

In fact, the Bank's operations since inception have contributed $27.2 billion to the credit side of the U. S. balance of payments. 

No. Eximbank is a member of the Berne Union, an international association with memberhsip from 24 nations, which oversees international credit transactions to assure that terms offered are those customary to international trade, thereby working to prevent such "credit wars. "1 Eximbank will lend up to 45% of the cost of exports. 

The balance consists of a 10% cash payment and 45% financing from private sources. Eximbank's lending *rate is 6% per annum and the rate on the private source financing is that rate negotiated directly between the buyer and the seller.. When Eximbank's financing is combined with private financing it yields an effective interest rate which is competitive with the government-supported rates offered by the other industrialized countries. 

Eximbank's funds in support of its direct financing are raised from its $1 billion capital stock, its $1.5 billion of reserves, borrowings in the private market, repayments of prior loans with interest, receipts from guarantee and insurance fees and premiums.

Eximbank lends its own funds. Commercial banks make their own lending decisions, voluntarily participating with Eximbank in financing certain large transactions.

INFORMATION FROM SOVIETS 

Senator INOUYE. In sales to the Soviet Union, the Government is the importer? 

Mr. SAUER. That is correct.

Senator INOUYE. Has the Government provided all of the information normally required for private importers or have these requirements been waived in connection with early sales? 

Mr. SAUER. No, they have not been waived. We are proceeding in extending credits to the Soviet Union on information that they have furnished us with respect to their domestic economy and certain statistics with respect to their foreign trade. Our Board of Directors has found, in the cases that we have approved, that we have reasonable assurance of repayment as required by our act and that the individual transactions are sound.

Now we have said, and we continue to say, that if we go forward in the Soviet Union over and above figures that we are now talking about of, shall we say, $250 million, $300 million, $350 million, without naming a particular figure, we will have to get more information from the Soviet Union as we go along on their economy, their balance of payments and their reserves. 

As of the moment we are satisfied that we have all that is necessary to substantiate and support the credits that we have made to the 

Soviet Union.

Senator INOUYE. It is your response then that as far as the sales made up to this moment to the Soviet Union, none of your requirements relating to importers have been waived? 

Mr. SAUER. I think that is a fair statement.

CRITERIA FOR FUTURE SOVIET LOANS 

Senator INOUYE. What will be your policy with reference to future sales?

Mr. SAUER. We envisage that if we were to go forward, if we are to extend larger credits to the Soviet Union, which have been described as "substantially larger," we may need more information on their reserves and other aspects of their financial situation in order to make a finding that we have reasonable assurance of repayment. But as of this moment we take cognizance of the fact that a country the size of the Soviet Union supported by the statistics they have given us, is well able to pay credits in the amount of $250 million. 

EXIMBANK EXPOSURE IN SOVIET UNION 

Senator INOUYE. Is the $250 million or $248-plus million the total exposure of the Bank in relationship to the Soviet Union? 

Mr. SAUER. That is the total exposure, yes.

Senator INOUYE. Doesn't the Bank normally guarantee the commercial part of the finance? 

Mr. SAUER. Yes, we do.

Senator INOUYE. Isn't it actually making the total exposure $500 million instead of $250 million? Ter

Mr. SAUER. It would have been if we had been called upon to guarantee the other 50 percent, but we were not called upon to do so. The 

Soviets were able to obtain credits in the commercial banking system of the United States for the other 50 percent, that is, the other $250 million, without our guarantee. We have no exposure, no liability whatsoever, with respect to that $250 millon. 

Senator INOUYE. So the total exposure as of this moment is $248plus million? 

Mr. SAUER. That is correct.

RELATION OF EXIMBANK BORROWINGS TO DEBT CEILING 

Senator INOUYE. Recently when the Treasury's debt ceiling authority had lapsed, the Export-Import Bank announced its intention to market $1.8 billion of 91-day notes. Eximbank canceled this plan when the Senate acted on the authority. What was the purpose of the Eximbank in issuing this notice? 

[Article from Wall Street Journal, dated December 4, 1973, fol lows:]

DEBT BILL CLEARED WITHOUT A RIDER ON ELECTION FUNDS SENATE RAISES DEBT LIMIT TO $475.7 BILLION UNTIL JULY, AVERTING MONETARY MOVES 

WASHINGTON.-Senate advocates of financing presidential elections with public funds gave up their fight and allowed a bill raising the national debt limit to be sent to the White House.

The debt-bill delay forced the Treasury into considerable monetary maneuvering yesterday, though the late-afternoon passage of the bill cancelled the need for some fancy financial footwork planned to avoid issuing more debt. The weekly 

Treasury auction of $4.3 million of short-term bills, usually held each Monday, was postponed until today.

Proponents of the campaign-financing plan, which was attached to the Housepassed debt-limit bill, abandoned the effort after they were unable to break a filibuster against the legislation. Senators expressed alarm that the government this week would head into serious financial trouble without passage of the measure raising the debt limit to $475.7 billion through June. Without the legislation, the debt ceiling had reverted Friday to $400 billion, a level well below the actual debt. 

With its debt authority lapsed, the Treasury early yesterday postponed its regular Monday auction of Treasury bills, and the Export-Import Bank, in an unusual action, announced it planned to auction $1.8 billion of 91-day notes today. 

But the backdoor borrowing by the Ex-Im Bank, which isn't covered by the debt ceiling, was cancelled when the Senate acted. The Treasury announced the cancellation of the Ex-Im Bank note auction and said it will hold its own bill auction today.

After the Senate action, the Treasury also said it's instructing savings bonds issuers to resume their sales, which were ordered suspended over the weekend. 

The Treasury said it will resume its normal debt operations in light of the Senate passage of the bill.

One emergency action that wasn't affected by the Senate turnabout is the Treasury's calling in of some $2 billion in funds it has on deposit in commercial banks. Early yesterday, the Treasury ordered all these tax and loan accounts to be paid over to its accounts in the district Federal Reserve banks. 

Though this will reduce the amount of funds available for lending, a Treasury official said the impact wouldn't be great. He said a large part of the balances would have been called in routine Treasury operations yesterday even without a debt-bill delay. 

Yesterday's Senate vote represents a victory for the Nixon administration. which quietly fought the campaign-financing proposal. A majority of the Senate favored the provision, but Sen. James Allen (D., Ala.), with help from the White 

House, staged a successful filibuster against it. After votes to end the filibuster

over the weekend and again yesterday failed to get the required two-thirds majority, Sen. Allen proposed that the Senate go along with the House and simply increase the debt limit without any campaign-financing provision. 

This was narrowly defeated, 43 to 42. But after this close vote, Senate Republican Leader Hugh Scott of Pennsylvania, a chief sponsor of the campaignfinancing measure, warned that the impasse was jeopardizing the country's financial position. "We aren't hurting each other as much as we're hurting the country," Sen. Scott said, and switched to back a simple increase in the debt ceiling. Democratic Leader Mike Mansfield of Montana concurred, and after the changes by the two party leaders, the motion carried 48 to 36. 

But Sen. Howard Cannon (D., Nev.), chairman of the Senate Rules Committee, promised that his panel would consider the campaign-financing provision early next year. And a number of proponents vowed they would continue their efforts, perhaps trying to tie the provision to other bills. 

LIMITATIONS ON DEBT CEILING 

Mr. SAUER. Senator, at that point we were asked by the U.S. Treasury to go into the private market to borrow funds and use them to repay the Bank's outstanding borrowings from the Treasury if it became necessary for the Treasury to raise funds because of the limitations of the debt ceiling. We responded, yes, we were prepared to do this if it were necessary so to do. 

We are going into the market pretty regularly. We are raising most of our borrowed funds in the private market. Now it is true that we did not have this particular operation in mind until the Treasury spoke to us about the possibility, but it was not illegal, nothing unusual except perhaps the term that we were talking about. Subsequently we went into the private market for $400 million without any request from the Treasury.

I mention that because it demonstrates that we are going into the market to raise our funds. 

Senator INOUYE. Then, Mr. Sauer, you are advising this subcommittee that under our present law it is possible to circumvent the debt ceiling?

Mr. SAUER. I believe agencies are doing that all the time. I don't know about the word "circumvent," let me put it this way. As I understood the law, the debt ceiling does not apply to obligations that are not the direct obligations of the U.S. Treasury. It does not apply to Export-Import Bank obligations, although we are a part of the U.S. 

Government. It does not apply to the multiple other agencies that issue paper in the market-the home loan banks, the various agricultural banks, and so forth.

It only applies to the direct Treasury obligations. So, when the debt limit is tight, the other agency obligations are not counted. 

Senator INOUYE. Is it a common practice for all of these agencies that you refer to to issue notes as you attempted to in this case? 

Mr. SAUER. It is a regular practice for all of these agencies to be raising their money in the marketplace, including the Export-Import Bank, regularly apart from the question of the debt limit. But when they do, I repeat, their obligations are not included within the debt limit.

Senator INOUYE. In this case it was related to the debt ceiling? 

Mr. SAUER. This is true, sir.

POTENTIAL LOSSES 

Senator INOUYE. What is now the amount of the Bank's potential losses? Does the Bank believe that its reserves will be large enough to cover these losses? 

Mr. SAUER. What was the first part of the question, Senator? 

Senator INOUYE. What is the amount of potential losses that the

Bank envisions at this point? I am certain you are about ready to declare that certain loans should be charged off?

Mr. SAUER. Well, we are not ready to do that at the moment, that is, loans of any consequence, although as I have indicated, we have some defaults. We believe that our loans will be repaid for the most part. We believe as we go along the reserves that we are building up will be adequate to take care of whatever losses we do incur. 

That reserve at the moment is $1.5 billion. We are not ready to concede that some of these delinquencies and defaults should be charged off.

Senator INOUYE. Your reserves of $1.5 billion will remain constant, but I note you have been expanding your loan program. So, won't it be logical to conclude that your potential losses will thereby increase?

Mr. SAUER. Well, if you get more of a portfolio, the potential losses increase, yes, sir.

Senator INOUYE. And your contention is that at the present time your reserve of $1.5 billion is sufficient to cover these loans? 

Mr. SAUER. That is not a static figure. We add to it each year, Senator. We add the excess of our income over our expenses, after paying a dividend to the Treasury on our capital stock, into the reserve. For instance, in 1973 I believe we added the sum of $89 million to our reserves.

Senator INOUYE. But the rate of increase in the reserve is not equal to the rate of increase in your expansion program? 

Mr. SAUER. That is correct, Senator. If there were a worldwide catastrophe, if I may say it in that way, in which a number of countries were unable to meet their foreign debts and if a rescheduling wouldn't cure the situation, we might be confronted with serious defaults. 

Otherwise, we continue to believe that we are in pretty good shape. 

INCREASE IN INTEREST RATE 

Senator INOUYE. Your Bank recently increased its lending rate from 

6 to 7 percent. What was the reason for increasing the lending rate from 6 to 7?

Mr. SAUER. Senator, our Board of Directors acting, I might say, on the recommendation of the National Advisory Council, which is a body set up by the Congress composed of the Secretary of the Treasury, the Secretary of State, the Secretary of Commerce, the Chairman of the Federal Reserve Board and the President of the Export- Import Bank came to the conclusion that our rate of 6 percent was low.

For the first time in the history of the Bank we were paying more than 6 percent on the average for our money and, second, we found that from a competitive standpoint with respect to the other industrialized countries our rate of 6 percent was too low and that 7 percent was a more realistic rate.

Senator INOUYE. Aren't you paying more than 7 percent at the present time?

Mr. SAUER. Well, we are paying more than 7 percent for an individual issue, but not overall, Senator.

Senator INOUYE. What is the overall? 

Mr. SAUER. Mr. Dugan says 6.7 percent. Now we are watching this matter of the rate to see that it is competitive. My colleague on the 

Board of Directors, Mr. Alex McCullough, who sits on my left, has just attended a meeting in Bonn, Germany, at which the other industrialized countries were present and the matter of interest rates and terms of credits being extended by the industrialized countries was very much an issue and a subject of discussion. 

If I may, I would like to have Mr. McCullough say a few words on this point.

Senator INOUYE. Fine. 

COMPARISON OF INTEREST RATES OFFERED BY OTHER COUNTRIES 

Mr. MCCULLOUGH. Mr. Chairman, we are very much aware of the directive that Congress has given the Eximbank, that we shall be competitive with the other exporting countries of the world. In this ad hoc meeting in Bonn with the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Japan, and Italy we arrived with our interest rate just having been changed to discuss the rates that prevailed in their countries on long-term export credit-long term being defined generally as more than 5 years, in some cases 4 years, in some cases 7 in certain of these countries, but substantially the same.

Since that meeting there have been two increases in the rates provided by these countries that were in the meeting, one by France and one by Japan. Germany already had a higher interest rate than our 

7-percent rate. The United Kingdom has a flexible rate varying from 

6to 8.5-percent basic rate, and in discussions this week here in Washington with the head of the ECGD agency we were advised that with our rate at 7, their rate would not be below 7 in any instance. 

So, the effective rate that exporters are paying in these countries would run something like this, including insurance, fees, and other charges that might get involved in an effective rate. 

Keep in mind, of course, that the Eximbank provides only 50 percent of the financing on any transaction which we support with a direct loan. So our rate of 7 is mixed, or blended, with the commercial bank that is lending the other portion of the financing, so that the average comes out somewhere between 7.53 and 8 percent as best we can calculate at the present time. 

The United Kingdom is 7.5 to 10.5 percent; France, 6.5 to 6.75 at the present time; Germany, 9 to 10; and Japan, 6.75 to 8.5. So, the effective cost to the borrower on direct lending in the major industrialized nations is approximately in balance. 

EXPORT EXPANSION FACILITY 

Senator INOUYE. Thank you very much, sir.

The Export Expansion Facility is designed to provide the Eximbank greater latitude in financing high-risk exports. By nature this

program is designed to assist the transactions of small exporters since adequacy of capital is generally a point of concern. 

I have three questions here. The first, to what extent has this program benefited small exporters?

Mr. SAUER. Well, I don't know that that program was intended to benefit small exporters particularly. We have other programs which do. I don't want to get argumentative here, but I would question whether the Export Expansion Facility program was designed for smaller exporters. It was designed more specifically for breaking into markets where the United States had not been in previously and, second, for more risky markets, but it might be used by either small or large exporters.

My answer truthfully must be that I don't think that program has directly or indirectly specifically aided smaller exporters, but we have other programs that we think do.

Senator INOUYE. Would you like to expand on that and tell us how small exporters have benefited?

SUPPLIERS 

Mr. SAUER. Yes; we are going to do that and we believe that we can do it.

We have in our files the names of over 5,700 U.S. suppliers who have used one or more of our programs. Now while it is impractical to research and classify these many suppliers into small, medium, large or whatever, it is obvious by their very numbers that the vast majority of them cannot be large. Even if all the companies in the Fortune 1,000 were included, which is most definitely not the case, that would still leave 4,700 companies whose sales were less than $67 million. 

Then we point out further that when we finance jet aircraft, for instance, there are as many as 16,500 subcontractors involved in the sale of a wide-bodied jet. When we finance a nuclear power station for such big companies as Westinghouse or General Electric, there are 5,000 subsuppliers involved.

More particularly, our medium-term guarantee and insurance programs and our cooperative financing programs are meant to serve smaller businesses. Seventy-six percent of the export sales that we supported in fiscal 1973 were under these programs. We think that we do have programs that are suited to and are being used by small exporters.

EXAMPLE OF ASSISTANCE TO A SMALL EXPORTER 

May I just run though an unsolicited letter that was sent to U.S. 

Senator Edward J. Gurney and Hon. Claude Pepper, Member of Congress? This is on the letterhead of a firm called M&M World Marketing, Inc., Miami, Fla. 

Dear Senator Gurney: We have been very alarmed at the news appearing in the enclosed copy of page 22 of the American Metal Market Review. This is one of these articles that says that the Export-Import Bank is in trouble on the Hill because of its loans to the Soviet Union. 

To the growing number of exporting companies in Florida, the Export- Import Bank of the United States, together with its affiliate. . 

The affiliate being the Foreign Credit Insurance Association in New York.

Represent the difference between being able successfully to compete in foreign markets and having to abandon these markets to French, English, German, Japanese and other foreign exporters, all of whom have the assistance of a similar government financing organization in their respective countries. 

Ours is a small exporting organization and of the more than $3 million of export sales this year I would estimate that 90 percent have been made possible by the assistance of the Export-Import Bank. 

We were sent a copy of this letter. We didn't recall the people. We looked them up, and did find that we had been assisting them. 

We will furnish specific cases as you requested.
