[The letter follows:]

November 30, 1973

The Honorable 

Edward W. Brooke 

United States Senate 

Washington, D.C. 

Dear Senator Brooke: 20510 I am replying to your recent letter with which you attached correspondence from Dr. Elihu Bergman concerning Export-Import 

Bank financing of U.S. export sales, particularly to the Soviet Union.

We are very pleased to be able to comment on Dr. Bergman' discussion because we believe that his understanding of Eximbank's operation with respect to Soviet as well as other credits is not accurate.

As you know, the Export-Import Bank is a wholly-owned United States Government corporation which operates under authority granted to it by the Congress in the Bank's basic enabling legislation, the Export-Import Bank Act of 1945, as amended. That Act, which has been amended and extended periodically by the Congress since 1945, sets forth the purpose of the Bank, which is to aid in financing and to facilitate exports and imports between the United States and any foreign country. The Act instructs the Bank in furtherance of this function to "supplement and encourage and not compete with private capital" and further, in an amendment added by the Congress in 1971, to provide export credit support for U.S. exporters at rates and on terms and conditions which is competitive with the official Governmentsupported export credit financing available from the principal countries whose exporters compete with U.S. exporters. 

The Act provides further, in section 2(b)(2), that the Bank shall not assist in the financing of U.S. exports to or for use in, or sale or lease to, any Commmist country unless the President of the United States determines that such support is in the U.S. national interest and so reports that determination to the Congress within 30 days. On October 18, 1972, President Nixon made a determination that it is in the national interest for Eximbank to support U.S. sales to the Soviet Union and so reported that determination to the Speaker of the House and the President of the Senate by letter of the same date. The Fresident also informed the Congress that Eximbank would report such financing assistance to the Congress monthly, which the 

Bank has done.

Eximbank has several programs through which it assists in the financing of U.S. export sales. Under the Bank's direct loan program, operated through a procedure called Participation Financing, the Bank requires a cash payment by the foreign borrower of at least 10 percent of the contract price of the U.S. goods or services, and then will provide up to 45 percent of the contract price from its own funds, at an interest rate of 6 percent per annum, and requires the remainder of the financing to be obtained from private commercial sources, either in the U.S. or abroad, at whatever intarest rate the borrower is able to obtain from the private lending institutions. The Bank generally offers to guarantee repayment of the private source financing if requested. This

participation financing procedure insures maximum private participation in the transaction, while at the same tire providing an effective interest rate and repayment term for the U.S. sale which will be competitive with the officially-supported export financing offered from other foreign countries.

This standard lending practice applies to Eximbank support of sales to the Soviet Union for the same reasons, and under the same conditions, as U.S. sales supported by the Bank worldwide. Commercial banks and other private sources of export financing are unable or unwilling to extend credit in the amounts and for the length of repayment term required for most major transactions. Commercial banks generally will not extend credit for longer than five to seven years. Thus Eximbank participation provides the additional funding and an effective interest rate and repayment tern on the whole transaction (by permitting the private portion of the financing to be repaid from the early installments when necessary) required to obtain the sale for the U.S. supplier. 

To date, Eximbank has authorized six credits totaling $119,943,000 in support of U.S. sales to the U.S.S.R. with a contract value of $266,548,000. The Eximbank amount represents 45 percent of the contract price on these sales transactions and is based on the standard lending criteria described above. No guarantees on the private portion of the financing on the Soviet transactions have been requested. 

The rate of interest on Eximbank's portion of the financing on these transactions is 6 percent per annus on outstanding balances, the same as on all Eximbank loans worldwide. On these credits, as on all others, Eximbank charges a commitment fee of one-half of one percent per annum on undisbursed balances, commencing 30 days from date of authorization of the credit.

All Eximbank loans are repayable in dollars, with interest, in the United States. However, while the Eximbank loan is extended to the foreign buyer, the Bank's funds never actually leave the United States because disbursements under the credits are made through commercial banks directly to the U.S. suppliers. 

Repayment terms on transactions in which Eximbank participates are those customary in international trade and are based on the product or the project to be financed. Generally, for products to be used immediately upon delivery, the first repayment of principal is required to be made six months after shipment of the goods, which permits sufficient time for the products to be used to generate income to repay the debt, and semiannually thereafter. However, interest is required to be paid from date of disbursement of the Eximbank funds. 

On project loans, it is the policy of the Bank to set the repayment terms based on the ability of the project to generate income which can be applied to repayment of the debt, thus insuring that the project is economically viable. During the construction period of the project, interest only is required to be paid semiannually, with the first principal repayment on the total financing required six months after completion of the project. As explained previously, under the participation financing program, when necessary Eximbank is repaid from the later maturities on the total credit, thus enabling private source financing to participate to the maximum degree possible and moderating the interest rate to a competitive level for the whole transaction. I believe that Dr. Bergman's misunderstanding of a ten-year "grace period" on Eximbank credits may have resulted from the fact that the Bank in its general literature lists only the start of the repayment period on its portion of the financing, whereas repayments on the whole transaction actually start to the private institutions participating with the Bank in accordance with the previously described

procedure. The repayment terms on the six Soviet transactions in which the 

Bank is participating range from seven to twelve years, with Eximbank to be repaid from the later maturities. These

In addition to the six Soviet credits already authorized, at the present time the Bank has an additional potential exposure for Soviet transactions amounting to approximately $217.1 million in loans. transactions involve pending loan applications and outstanding Preliminary Commitments (which, as you know, are not firm commitments until an actual loan application is received and authorized by the Bank). Although we have seen many press reports mentioning Soviet-American business ventures in a magnitude as great as the $3 billion cited by Dr. Bargman, Eximbank has not been requested, even in a most preliminary way, to support transactions in this order of magnitude, and, in fact, would be unable to entertain such requests under its current fiscal year budget authority levels, which must be approved by the Congrass.

Eximbank does not use appropriated, or tax-receipt, funds to finance its activities. When the present Export-Import Bank was incorporated in 1945, the U.S. Treasury purchased $1 billion of capital stock in the Bank which it still holds. Eximbank uses these funds, receipts from repayments of principal and interest on outstanding loans, fees collected under its various programs, funds in its retained reserve, and borrowings from the private market, primarily, and from the Treasury to finance its activities. The Bank borrows from the Treasury, as necessary, at current Treasury rates for comparable maturities to fund its daily disbursement requirements, but refinances most of these borrowings on an annual basis through periodic borrowings in the private market so that the Bank's annual net borrowings from the Treasury at the end of a fiscal year are minimal.

With respect to the impact which Eximbank borrowing has on the U.S. private credit market, in calendar 1973 Eximbank has had net borrowings of $600 million in the private market, the last of which cost 7.37 percent, against total net demand for credit estimated at $185.2 billion for the year.

This amounts to less than one-half of one percent of the estimated total credit demand. The Bank estimates its need for net borrowings in the private market for the next few years to be about $1 billion annually, thus maintaining approximately the same percentage of net impact on that market.

Until the middle of this year, Eximbank's average interest expense on its outstanding debt was less than its 6 percent lending rate. Because of rising interest rates in the economy, after midyear Eximbank's average interest expense rate moved slightly higher than 6 percent. It should be noted, however, that this does not mean that Eximbank is losing money on an overall basis. In terms of the Bank's total capital and debt structure, its total effective interest expense rate is only 5 percent at this time. 

This effective rate takes into account the inclusion of the capital stock and the retained earnings reserve, both of which are utilized continuously in the Bank's lending activities.

Eximbank, in fact, has made a net profit on its operations of over $100 million annually for many years ($139.7 million in fiscal year 1973). 

From this profit its pays an annual dividend of $50 million to the Treasury 'on its stock and places the remainder in its retained reserves. From inception of the original Bank in 1934 through the last fiscal year, the Bank has paid a total of $856 million in dividends to the Treasury. Its retained reserves, against which it charges any losses, now total $1.5 billion. Losses under the Bank's loan program have amounted to only two one-hundredths of one percent of loan disbursements since inception of the Bank.

Eximbank has maintained a 6 percent interest rate on its portion of financing since 1966, during periods of both high-cost and low-cost money. It has done so in order to provide an assured source of available and acceptable financing on U.S. export sales into the future, which va believe is necessary to encourage the marketing efforts necessary by U.S. suppliers. Because the variations in the market rates of money are reflected in each transaction through the private source funds, Eximbank participation moderates the fluctuations and reduces the rate when the private cost is high, thereby providing an effective rate to the buyer that is comparable to that offered by the government-supported export financing of other industrial countries. The average effective interest rate on export transactions supported by Eximbank over the last several months has ranged from 7.25 percent to 7.5 percent, depending on the length of the repayment term. Further, it should be remembered that the financing being offered on export sales, through a combination of Eximbank funds and private source funds, is competing in markets abroad, not on sales in the U.S. domestic market.

Contrary to Dr. Bergman's initial statement, Eximbank financing is not considered to be a component of the U.S. Government's foreign economic assistance program, which is operated primarily through the foreign aid program. Eximbank financing is provided whenever it can be demonstrated that the Bank's participation in an export sales transaction is necessary to obtain the sale for the United States supplier and that the transaction offers "reasonable assurance of repayment, 11 as required by the Bank's legislation. Moreover, it should be noted that U.S. export sales benefit substantially the entire U.S. economy through increased U.S. jobs and personal income, increased corporate profits which permit industrial expansion and lower unit costs to all buyers, both domestic and foreign, and increased tax revenues to all levels of government. Eximbank's fiscal year 1973 authorizations will support $10.5 billion in U.S. export sales, although the Bank's direct loan authorizations in the period amounted to only $2.4 billion. 

I trust that the foregoing will be helpful to you in replying to Dr. Bergman. If you have any further questions concerning Eximbank, please do not hesitate to contact us. Sincerely, (Signed) Walter C. Sauer 

Walter C. Sauer

PUBLIC CONCERN OVER CREDITS TO SOVIETS 

Senator BROOKE. Mr. Sauer, the Congress has received many expressions of concern over the risk involved in doing business with the 

Soviet Union. 

What is your evaluation of these risks?

Mr. SAUER. I think one has to look at it, Senator, from the standpoint of, one, political risk and, two, commercial risk. As I indicated earlier this morning, our Board of Directors has found, and we are so convinced, that from a commercial standpoint the Soviet Union can pay the credits that we have authorized. We take cognizance of the fact that the Soviet Union is a country with resources that can stand a debt certainly of $250 million and well beyond that. 

Now, as to their willingness to pay, the political aspects of it, we know of no evidence that would indicate that they are not incurring the credits from our Bank in good faith and with every intention of making payment. On the contrary, the evidence is that the Soviet 

Union has paid its commercial debts to the West which the Soviet Union, itself, incurred, although it has not recognized some of the czarist debts.

Now, we don't live in an ivory tower or work in a vacuum. We know there is a real political problem here. We think that under our act we are entitled to guidance on this political question and we have sought and obtained it.

In the first place, the Congress said that we should not make these loans unless the President of the United States found it to be in the national interest to do so, and the President has made that finding. 

Furthermore, the Congress in 1945 created a statutory body called the National Advisory Council on International Monetary and Financial Policies. That body still exists. The Secretary of the Treasury is 

Chairman, and the other members are the Secretary of State, the Secretary of Commerce, the Chairman of the Federal Reserve and the 

President of the Export-Import Bank. 

That body has passed judgment on our loans to the Soviet Union, if not each and every loan, the several big ones that we have made, and generally speaking they are continuing to do it. That body has continued to find that it is in the national interest, both from the foreign policy standpoint and from the domestic standpoint, that those loans should be made, provided that the bank, itself, finds that they are sound commercially.

So, my answer must be, Senator, that we feel that we are meeting the statutory requirement both in the political and the commercial basis, that is, that our loans to the Soviets offer reasonable assurance of payment.

CRITERIA FOR SUBMITTING CASES TO THE NAC 

Senator BROOKE. Do you have a formula or standard by which you submit the loan applications to the Advisory Council? 

Mr. SAUER. Yes; we do.

Senator BROOKE. What is that figure? 

Mr. SAUER. Where the Eximbank liability is $30 million or over we submit the case to the National Advisory Council prior to final

authorization. As a result, the Kama River loans were sent under that criteria. We also sent over others in order to get the continued view of the National Advisory Council.

Senator BROOKE. If you have any political question you would submit that? 

Mr. SAUER. Yes, sir.

Senator BROOKE. That is generally the rule by which you work? 

Mr. SAUER. That is correct, sir.

REPAYMENT GUARANTEE ON SOVIET CREDITS 

Senator BROOKE. Would you supply for the record a detailed compilation of the Soviet repayment record on loans which have been granted in the past? I am sure the committee will appreciate the details of the repayment record.

Soviet Borrowing in the United States and Other Western Countries 

In the twenty-year period (1954-1974) of rapid growth of East-West trade, the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe have borrowed billions of dollars on short, medium, and long-term credit from Western banks and suppliers to finance imports of capital goods, various industrial commodities, consumer goods and foodstuffs. All of the matured hard currency debt incurred by the Comecon countries has been repaid promptly. 

The Comecon countries value trade with the West largely because of their need for Western equipment and technology and other materials in short supply in Eastern Europe. 

Western Creditors 

Eastern Europe's principal creditors in the industrial West are the large West European commercial banks, and Western governments. 

Western commercial banks absorb much of the westward flow of Soviet and East European notes and bills, which are either retained in bank portfolios or rediscounted through various outlets, including Western 

Central banks.

At present, at least one-half of Eastern Europe's and nearly all the USSR's medium-term and long-term debt is covered by export insurance offered by agencies of Western governments. 

Since the late 1950s, there has been a steady increase in the use of Western credit facilities to help breach the gap between the East's desire to import and its ability to pay for Western goods. At present, Soviet and East European outstanding medium and long-term indebtedness to the West is on the order of $9 billion to $10 billion. The extension of such credits has been largely from Western Europe. 

The Soviet Experience 

The Soviet Union has made use of significant amounts of Western government-guaranteed credit only in the last ten years. Before 1965, the USSR financed its trade deficits in the West primarily by selling gold. From the mid-1960s until 1972, the USSR used Western credits instead of gold to finance imports. In that period the USSR borrowed at least $2 billion, mainly in Western Europe, on favorable terms and generally at prime interest rates.

The basis for the Soviet Union's prime credit rating has been its large gold reserves, the very size of its economy, and, most important, the USSR's unblemished record of prompt repayment established over the years, the maintenance of which is thought to be an important element in Soviet economic foreign policy. 

An added dimension to Soviet financial credibility is the successful development of its fifty year-old banking network in the West, which has grown from a single bank in London into a $3 billion eight-institution system based throughout Western Europe. These banks have been instrumental in facilitating the growth of East-West trade, and in providing over the years invaluable contacts with the West for a number of East European countries with little prior experience in Western financial dealings.

Recent Developments 

In 1972-1973, the USSR made use of unprecedented amounts of medium and long-term credit together with gold sales to finance record trade deficits in the two-year period amounting to a combined $3 billion. 

Large imports of grain and other agricultural products, machinery, equipment and industrial materials accounted for much of the deficits. 

Soviet medium and long-term debt rose to about $3.6 billion at year-end 

1973. In spite of this, the burden of the USSR's indebtedness will be lightened considerably as a result of recent swift changes in the world economy which have worked to the benefit of the USSR in the form of hard currency windfalls arising from sharp increases in the price of gold and crude oil. Soviet crude oil exports to the West (35 million tons) in 1973 were worth about $840 million. Oil exports of 42 million tons in 1974--a reasonable estimate--would generate about $3 billion in earnings. Gold sales of 250 tons in 1974 could bring in an additional $800 million - $900 million. 

Soviet Borrowing in the United States

Other than the current Soviet debt at Eximbank, Soviet borrowing from the U.S. Government since World War II 

is limited to medium-term credits from the Commodity Credit 

Corporation (CCC) to finance recent grain purchases here.

On July 8, 1972, the USSR received a three-year $750 million line of credit at a floating interest rate based on commercial rates prevailing when credits are drawn. This line is secured by letters of credit issued by Vneshtorgbank (the Soviet Foreign Trade Bank) which are confirmed by Chase 

Manhattan Bank in New York.

So far the Soviets have drawn $549.3 million under the line and have repaid $86.6 million of the outstanding principal plus interest. The interest rate on initial drawings was 6.1 percent, but it has subsequently increased to 9.5 percent following trends in commercial rates. Repayments of principal and interest have been made promptly and in conformity with agreed terms and conditions.

In addition to the CCC line, the Soviet Foreign Trade Bank and several foreign trade organizations have, for a number of years, borrowed from U.S. commercial banks and suppliers on varying terms to finance imports from the United States. 

At present, U.S. commercial banks and suppliers have roughly $300 million to $400 million outstanding in short and medium-term credits to the Soviet Union. The USSR is considered a prime risk by the U.S. financial community, having acquired a reputation for prompt repayment of debts.

SOVIET UNION RECOGNITION OF PROJECT COMMITMENTS OF EXIMBANK 

What guarantee does the United States have that the Soviet Union will honor its commitment on projects that the Export-Import Bank is involved in even if there should be a new crisis in our relations with 

Moscow ?

Mr. SAUER. We have nothing specific by way of security. We have nothing more than an IOU, an obligation of the Soviet Union. 

Now, it is complete in that we have the Bank for Foreign Trade as obligor on the paper, and we have the government itself guaranteeing that obligation of the Foreign Trade Bank.

So, we believe that our General Counsel has protected us legally. 

The Soviets have no way to disavow the debt legally, so it comes down to the question of willingness to pay. 

YAKUTSK LNG PROJECT 

Senator BROOKE. Concern has been expressed as to the propriety of the Export-Import Bank's involvement in the Yakutsk natural gas project in Russia.

Will you supply for the record a detailed description of the Export- Import Bank's involvement in this project and your estimation of the risk and potential benefits relating to this project?

Mr. SAUER. We will provide the story for the record. May I say this, Senator, we have not made that credit.

Description and Status of Proposed Financing Relating to Yakutsk Natural Gas Project in the USSR 

In October of 1973, the Soviet Union submitted to Eximbank an application for what is called a preliminary commitment for financing relating to exploration of a natural gas field in eastern Siberia; that is, it is a request by the Soviet Bank for Foreign 

Trade (Vneshtorgbank) that Eximbank formally indicate whether it would be prepared to extend a loan of $49.5 million for the purchase of U. S. equipment and services with a contract value of $110 million that would be used for exploratory work in the gas field in Siberia, and if so, the terms and conditions of the loan.

Eximbank's Board of Directors has not reached a decision on this pending application, and, in fact, is still in the process of discussions with the U.S. companies involved in the project and with the Export-Import Bank of Japan because the Japanese also are considering participating in the project. 

The project is one which involves the liquefaction of natural gas present in the Vlyuy Basin of Siberia near the city of Yakutsk.. The gas would be liquefied in the Soviet Union and sold to United States and Japanese companies. The American companies are the El Paso Natural Gas Company and the Occidental Petroleum Corporation. The principal Japanese company is the 

Tokyo Gas Company, Ltd. The American companies and the 

Japanese company intend to enter into agreements with the Soviet Union under which the Soviet Union would supply to each of the two an amount of liquefied natural gas equivalent to one billion cubic feet of gas each day over a period of 25 years.

The gas destined for the United States would be brought to the West Coast and distributed by the El Paso Natural Gas pipelines serving California and the Southwest United States.

It is estimated that at least 37 trillion cubic feet of natural gas reserves will be necessary to enable the Soviet Union to meet the proposed supply of liquefied gas to the American and Japanese companies. The Soviets have been conducting exploration in the 

Yakutsk field and state that something like 8 trillion cubic feet of natural gas have been confirmed. Before going further with their part of the project, however, the American and Japanese companies are requiring that more exploratory work be done in order to prove up the necessary amount of gas they are to purchase. 

This has been agreed to by the Soviets. The proposed exploratory work calls for extensive geological investigations and the drilling of approximately 200 exploratory wells. The actual work will be conducted by the Minister of Geology of the Soviet Union. The program will be initiated during the last six months or so of this year and will require up to three years for completion.

In order to conduct the type of geological work called for, the Soviets will have to purchase in the United States and Japan drilling rigs and bits, seismograph equipment and other equipment of various types. The extimated cost of this equipment, together with the relatively limited amount of services that would be furnished by the Americans and the Japanese, is tentatively estimated to be between $200 and $300 million. Included in the proposed services would be a feasibility study to be made by Bechtel Corporation of the gas liquefaction project. 

It is proposed that the Export-Import Banks of the United States and of Japan, respectively, finance the purchases of this equipment and these services through loans to the Soviet Union. 

Each of the Banks would finance approximately one-half of the purchases, but Eximbank at least, would not finance anything but United States equipment and services. It is understood that the terms of the loans by the two Banks would be essentially alike. Neither Bank, however, has as yet acted upon the Soviet request for the loans and so Eximbank is unable to state what the precise terms of the loans would be if approved. However, in the discussions the Bank has had with the Soviets, as well as with our Japanese counterparts, Eximbank has talked about a medium term (5 years or so) loan, with the understanding that if the second stage of the gas liquefaction project should come into being the Bank were to assist in financing it, the loan for the exploratory work would be incorporated in the second loan with the result that the repayment of the exploratory loan would be spread over the longer period which would be called for by the development loan.

There would be a 10 percent cash payment by the Soviet Union on the contractual price of the U.S. equipment and services being financed by Eximbank, with 45 percent of the contract price to be financed by a direct loan of the Export-Import Bank and 45 percent financed by a United States commercial bank. The Export- 

Import Bank direct loan would carry the 7 percent interest rate currently being charged by the Bank on all of its direct loans. 

While it is believed that the Chase Manhattan Bank has not made a commitment to finance the other 45 percent, it has indicated its interest in doing so, and it has further indicated that if it agrees to make a loan, it would do so without requiring the guarantee of the Export-Import Bank. 

Eximbank believes it safe to say that the Soviets would not be able to borrow the funds needed for the exploratory program without the participation of the Export-Import Bank of the United States. Certainly, the Export-Import Bank of Japan has strongly indicated that they would expect the United States Government, through the Export-Import Bank, to participate along with the Japanese Government, through its Export-Import Bank, in this first stage of the gas project. Likewise, the Chase Bank has indicated that it would not be prepared to lend the entire amount needed to finance the U.S. equipment and services involved.

This initial loan would be made on the obligation of the Soviet Union to repay regardless of the outcome of the exploratory work. If Eximbank were later to make a loan for the production of the liquefied natural gas, the Bank at that time would give consideration to enacting assurances from the Soviet Union with respect to the disposition of the liquefied gas. 

The Bank does not intend to make a commitment at this time with respect to financing the development stage of the project. 

However, if Eximbank does make a loan for the exploratory phase of the project, the Bank would thereby be manifesting an intent at least to consider a loan for the principal stage of the project if the exploratory work should prove up the feasibility of the project. 

The Bank has no estimates as to what the foreign exchange costs of the ultimate project would be, but its experience with other LNG projects would indicate that these costs for the facilities in the Soviet Union for gathering and liquefying the natural gas, together with the costs of the tanker fleet for carrying it, would run to several billion dollars. 

Before making a commitment to finance even the first stage of the project, Eximbank would submit the matter to the National Advisory Council on International Monetary and Financial Policies to obtain the opinion of the Council as to whether a loan by the Bank for the purpose would be in furtherance of the domestic and foreign policy objectives of the United States.

QUESTION OF LNG TANKERS FOR PROJECT 

Senator BROOKE. U.S. involvement in that project is to be for the purpose of our having access to Russian natural gas, some arrangement would be necessary for the transportation of natural gas to the U.S. Shipping interests in the United States would be extremely interested in this aspect of the project. 

Have you any preliminary indication as to whether the needed carriers will be built in the United States or would they be procured from overseas suppliers?

Mr. SAUER. We have not reached that second stage by any means. 

But to try to answer your question, if the Export-Import Bank were called upon to finance the tankers that brought the liquefied natural gas to the United States, or to Japan for its share, they would be built in the United States because that is the only way we would finance them. Now, if we were not called upon, I can't speculate where they would be built. 

Senator BROOKE. You can see that there is a problem.

Mr. SAUER. Yes; I do. There is also a question, as I see it, of who is going to own and control the shipment, whether it will be the U.S.flag vessels or some other country's flag vessels. 

ACCESS OF UNITED STATES TO SOVIET GAS 

Senator BROOKE. Have you made any preliminary arrangements that justify optimism that we will indeed have adequate access to Russian natural gas if the Export-Import Bank does grant credit to the 

Yakutsk project?

Mr. SAUER. All we can say is that two responsible companies in the United States tell us that they have understandings, agreements if you will, with the Soviet Union that if the gasfields are developed and if liquefied natural gas facilities are constructed, they will be given their share of that liquefied natural gas for delivery to the United States and that it will be brought here and distributed throughout the United States.

POLICY GUIDELINES TO BANK ON SOVIET LOANS 

Senator BROOKE. I know that the Export-Import Bank does not set policy. However, it must operate under some policy guidance in specific cases such as the granting of credits to the Soviet Union. 

Can you provide for the committee some indication of the policy guidelines given your organization in regard to the Soviet Union? 

Mr. SAUER. Yes; we can. We will put in a statement with respect to our relations with the National Advisory Council and how they have answered our questions on the Soviet loan. 

Senator BROOKE. Will you supply that for the record? 

Mr. SAUER. We will, Senator. 

 NAC REVIEW OF SOVIET CREDITS 

The National Advisory Council was established by the Bretton Woods Agreement Act of 1945, as amended, to coordinate the policies and operations of all agencies of the Government which make or participate in making foreign loans 1

or which engage in foreign financial, exchange or monetary transactions. The 

Council is composed of the Secretary of the Treasury as Chairman, the Secretary of State, the Secretary of Commerce, the Chairman of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, and the President of the Export-Import Bank. 

The NAC provides the Bank with overall guidance with respect to policy considerations of the Administration. In addition, the NAC reviews, prior to final authorization, all loan applications in which Eximbank's exposure would be over $30 million and post-audits many smaller transactions, for the purpose of expressing their opinion on the policy aspects of these specific credits. 

In the case of credits in support of U.S. exports to the Soviet Union, the NAC has reviewed all such credits, regardless of their amount. In all Soviet cases approved by the Bank, the NAC has expressed its opinion that approval of the credit would be in the U.S. national interest and is in accordance with the domestic and foreign policy objectives of the United States. 

AVAILABILITY OF FINANCING FOR SOVIET PURCHASES 

Senator BROOKE. If the Export-Import Bank did not provide the credits to the Soviet Union, would the Soviet Union have alternative sources of financing and if Moscow turned to the alternative sources what would be the implications for the United States as you see them?

Mr. SAUER. In respect to the credits we have authorized to date, we believe that the equipment involved could be bought in other countries of the world. If we didn't extend the credit we are convinced that the other countries, the industrialized countries of the world, would be extending credits for these particular purposes. 

We don't think there is anything so technologically esoteric about these particular items that forces the Soviets to come to the United States for them with the result that we are, I repeat, meeting the mandate of the Congress. We are living up to the letter and the spirit of our act in financing these items of equipment that are going to the Soviet Union under our credits. We are thereby doing all that we are called upon to do to assist the U.S. exports. 

CREDIT FOR CHEMICAL COMPLEX TO PRODUCE FERTILIZER Senator BROOKE. One final question. The Export-Import Bank may enter into a credit agreement with the Soviet Union for export of machinery for a fertilizer complex.

In view of the short supply of fertilizer in the United States what advantage would this have for the United States?

Mr. SAUER. Again, let me say that we have not authorized this particular credit, Senator, but we are studying it. Also, let me say that we would only be financing the equipment and services that were going into the construction of the fertilizer or the chemical complex in the Soviet Union. We are not financing the export of fertilizer. 

However, the entire transaction does have a dual aspect. We are financing the machinery and equipment that would go into building a plant. But complementary thereto is a proposal by the Occidental 

Petroleum Co. that it will sell and ship to the Soviet Union superphosphoric acid which will be produced in the State of Florida from the phosphate deposits there which are owned by Occidental Petroleum. These phosphates, after having been converted to superphosphoric acid, will be shipped to the Soviet Union. 

How this works chemically, I don't know, but it is treated by the natural gas there, the thing that the Soviet Union has, and it is thereby turned into ammonia, urea, and other fertilizers. 34-192 O-74-9

This fertilizer will be exported by the Soviet Union through the Occidental Petroleum Co. We are told in writing that Occidental 

Petroleum has the market for the sale of this fertilizer, and we are told further that the Occidental Petroleum intends to sell it in the United States.

So we would achieve a dual purpose if we make this particular loan. 

QUESTION OF EXPORTING ITEMS IN SHORT SUPPLY 

Senator BROOKE. You know, Mr. Sauer, that there is an understandable growing concern about the sale of vital commodities to foreign countries when we have shortages here at home. I am sure the Bank is cognizant of this.

Mr. SAUER. We are quite sensitive to that, Senator. But as I understand it, phosphate rock is not in short supply. What is in short supply is natural gas. 

Senator BROOKE. But you are sensitive to this problem?

Mr. SAUER. We definitely are. We are not financing short supply commodities at this time.

OCCIDENTAL PETROLEUM CORPORATION 10989 WILSHIRE BOULEVARD SUITE 1500 

LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA 90024

March 1, 1974 

Dear Senator:

I am writing to you about the fertilizer transaction between Occidental Petroleum and the Soviet Union because there have been scveral misunderstandings which have arisen, and I think if very important that the precise facts of the matter be made available to you.

Unfortunately, I cannot be in Washington to present this to you personally. Hence, I have asked Bill McSweeny to undertake its delivery and also to answer any questions you may have. 

As you know, this agreement required the exchange of letters of approval between the governments of the United States and the U. S. S. R. After thorough consideration of the many advantages of this agreement by all concerned departments of the United States government, letters were exchanged on June 1, 1973, between the two governments, at which time the Secretary of Commerce stated on behalf of the United States government that there was "no impediment to the agreement concluded." Subsequently, on June 4, 1973, the U.S. Export-Import Bank issued a preliminary commitment letter for $180 million. A matching $180 million credit was arranged by the Bank of America and subscribed to by a consortium of private banks. An additional $40 million cash contribution was committed by the Bank of Foreign Trade of the U. S. S. R., making a total of $400 million in credit necessary to pay for the equipment and services purchased in the 

United States.

On the basis of the above, work has proceeded on the part of Occidental, its U.S. subcontractors, and the U.S.S. R. To dute, several million dollars have been expended by Occidental and its subcontractors for designs and design approvals. Technical specifications and appendices have been signed and agreed between the U.S.S.R. and 

Occidental, and we anticipate that the supplemental agreements will be signed in Moscow next month.

I would like to clarify the many advantages which will accrue to the United States as a result of the fertilizer agreement. As you know, the agreement requires approximately $500 million of ammonia plants, storage, terminal and distribution systems to be built. Of this, $400

million of equipment will be designed, produced and manufactured in the United States by approximately 100 United States firms. The advantages to United States business, labor and balance of payments are self-evident. The additional $100 million necessary in excess of the $400 million expended in the United States will be provided by the U.S.S.R. from credits outside the United States. 

Additionally, the agreement provides for a long-term trade whereby the production of ammonia and urea from these plants is purchased by Occidental, partially to service the United States equipment loan and partially to pay for superphosphoric acid we will be shipping to the U.S.S.R. in dual purpose ships, which will back haul ammonia from the U.S.S.R.

We shall give the United States market and farmers the right of first refusal for the ammonia and urea obtained from the U.S.S.R. 

Since these products are made from natural gas, of which there is a severe shortage in the United States, the advantages of making them available to the United States are obvious. 

The superphosphoric acid we will be shipping to the U.S.S.R. will not come from existing plant facilities. All such shipments will be made from new plant facilities and mines, which are presently in the design and/or construction phase. The superphosphoric acid will be made from existing phosphate rock, of which this country has a surplus. 

Therefore, there will be no adverse effect on the domestic supply and market.

As you can see from the above, the trade has all of the advantages favorable to the United States economy in that it will increase jobs, supply our farmers with needed nitrogen fertilizers, substantially improve the balance of payments, and conserve our natural energy resources.

It has been some time since I have had the pleasure of talking with you personally, and I hope that in the very near future that will be possible. 

A good deal of my time is spent in Los Angeles. Should you have occasion to be here, I would be delighted to have the chance to visit with you at lunch or dinner and renew our friendship.

Until then, I close, as always, with warmest regards, Sincerely, Award Hammar 

Armand Hammer

ARTICLE FROM MIAMI HERALD 

Senator CHILES. Mr. Chairman, I would just like to include in the record this particular article. 

Senator INOUYE. Without objection, it is so ordered. 

[The article follows:] UNITED STATES-POLAND TRADE PACTS INCREASING WARSAW SEEKING INTEGRATED CIRCUITS (By Dusko Doder) 

WARSAW-In the midst of reported Soviet-American tensions over the Middle East crisis, a team of U.S. Defense Department experts arrived secretly here to inspect Polish computer industries and determine whether this Soviet bloc country should be given access to some of the most advanced U.S. computer technology. 

The visit was unprecedented since it presumably involved inspection of military related industrial facilities. Both Polish and American officials here refused all comment.

It was learned, however, that the Poles wanted to obtain U.S. integrated circuits, a technology extensively used in modern weapons systems as well as in third generation computers and that they have concluded an $18-million deal with Fairchild Corp.

Fairchild is seeking export license from the Commerce Department since integrated circuits are still on the government's list of strategic goods and which cannot be exported to Communist countries. 

It has been the view of U.S. officials that advanced technology obtained by any 

Warsaw Pact country would in turn be made available to the Russians. 

The visit Oct. 19-23 of three Pentagon officials is believed to have been arrangea at the insistence of the U.S. Defense Department, which apparently sought that its experts assess on the spot possible military implications of the Fairchild deal. 

The deal is one of a series of commercial transactions concluded in recent months that have brought a dramatic increase in Polish-American trade. It is expected that bilateral trade for 1972 will exceed one-half billion dollars. 

Major deals signed in recent months include a $94-million contract awarded to Epstein Co. of Chicago for the construction of three meat processing plants; a $43-million contract with Swindell Dressler Co. of Pittsburgh to build an iron foundry near Lodz.

The upsurge in Polish-American trade followed President Nixon's decision last November to make export-import bank credits available to Poland. Thus far the Poles have received nearly $200 million in exim bank credits or credit commitments.

Henry Kiesel, deputy chairman of the State Planning Commission, said that Poland intends to continue its expansionary trade policy over the next two years despite a growing trade deficit.

He said that he would welcome cooperative agreements with American firms, particularly those in the electronics and computer fields. The Polish government is currently preparing regulations to permit joint U.S.-Polish ventures in Poland, he said, but he stressed that he favored industrial agreements over joint ventures. 

Poland's current five-year plan, redrafted after the workers riots that brought Edward Gierek to power three years ago, is designed to impove domestic conditions and upgrade the nation's competitive position in world markets.

QUESTIONS FROM SENATOR BROOKE 

The following questions from Senator Brooke will be inserted in the record at this point: [The questions and answers follow:] 

Question. What is the present status of the Export-Import Bank involvement with Chile?

Answer. Presently, the Bank is not assisting U.S. exports to Chile. In fact, no direct loans were authorized after May 7, 1970 and no supplier credit cover was approved after June 10, 1971.

As you know, Chile suspended service on its foreign debt as of November 1, 1971, later that month declared a unilateral moratorium, and then sought a rescheduling from its major creditors. Twelve creditor countries comprising the "Paris Club" reached a multilateral agreement with Chile on April 19, 1972 for the rescheduling of the bulk of its debt maturing from November 1, 1971 to

December 31, 1972. The rescheduling was implemented by bilateral agreements between each country and Chile. The United States and Chile concluded such an agreement in February 1974.

Question. Can you provide the committee with an account or listing of the level of delinquency of the Chilean government? 

Answer. As of December 31, 1973, Chile had delinquencies of 30 days or more on loan installments to the Bank totaling $107 million. The delinquent interest amounted to $43 million, or a total of $150 million of principal and interest. A rescheduling agreement has been reached for the installments falling due between November 1, 1971 and December 31, 1972. These amount to about $83 million of the delinquent principal and interest. 

Question. What indications has the present Chilean government given as to its intent to repay outstanding loans? What arrangements have been made for it to do so?

Answer. The Chilean Government has made an initial payment of $12 million toward the payment of the amounts due pursuant to the rescheduling of the November 1, 1971 to December 31, 1972, maturities. We have no reason to believe that they will not continue to make payments under the rescheduling. We are currently holding preliminary discussions with representatives of the Government of Chile concerning rescheduling 1973 and 1974 maturities. 

Question. Because many of your undertakings are large projects such as aircraft or nuclear facilities, many people assume that the small businessman does not receive his fair share of your attention. Is this an accurate assumption? I am especially interested in obtaining information as to the involvement of small businesses in these large projects through subcontracts. It would be useful for the record if you would provide an illustrative breakdown of how small business, through subcontracts and other means, participate in large projects. Will you do that?

Answer. Although the large transactions capture the headlines, smaller transactions make up by far the largest percentage of Eximbank's authorizations. In 

FY 1973, about 76% of the Bank's authorizations were for the guarantee and insurance programs. By their nature, these programs support small and mediumsized transactions.

In addition, as you note, there are many smaller businesses involved in large projects. For example, there are as many as 16,500 subcontractors involved in the sale of a wide-bodied jet aircraft. General Electric and Westinghouse tell us that there are about 5,000 subcontractors involved in a nuclear power project. 

Thus, many small businesses benefit from Exim support exports of equipment and services for large projects and products. 

Question. What sources does the Export-Import Bank draw on for its funds? 

Answer. The Eximbank has several sources of funds. The Bank utilizes receipts from principal and interest payments on its outstanding loans, fees, sales of loan maturities, borrowings in the private market, and borrowings from the U.S. Treasury. Most of the Bank's funds are derived from borrowing in the private market and receipts of principal and interest on our outstanding loans. For example, in FY 1973, the Bank had $1.1 billion of loan repayments, sales of loans of $144 million, net income from operations of $139 million, net borrowings in the private market of $401 million and net borrowings from Treasury of $144 million. 

In addition, the Bank utilizes its $1.0 billion of capital stock and $1.5 billion of reserves in its operations.

Question. How does Export-Import Bank borrowing impact on the private market?

Answer. The Bank's borrowings have very little net impact on the private market. In FY 1971, the Bank had a net impact of $732 million, in FY 1972 a minus $806 million and in FY 1973, $401 million. Thus, over the last three years, the net draw of the Bank on the private money market has been only $372 million. 

Question. At what rate does the Export-Import Bank borrow from the Treasury? 

Answer. The Bank pays the current market rate on its Treasury borrowings.

This rate is changed weekly and is equal to the rate which the Treasury must pay on its 6 month bills. The rate paid by the Bank on its Treasury borrowings has ranged this year from 7.13% to 9.5%.

Question. How does the rate at which the Export-Import Bank borrow affect the rate charged by the Bank?

Answer. The rate charged by the Bank on its loans is designed to make a financing package competitive in order to assist U.S. exporters to capture overseas

sales. This rate, which was 6% until recently when it was raised to 7%, changes at very infrequent intervals. Prior to the recent change to 7%, the Bank's rate had remained at 6% since August, 1966.

The rate paid by the Bank on its borrowings, however, is determined by the market and fluctuates constantly. Thus, there is no direct relationship between the rate paid by the Bank on its borrowings and the rate charged by the Bank on its loans.

However, one of the factors considered in increasing the Bank's lending rate was that recently for the first time, the Bank's overall cost of funds rose above its 6% lending rate.

Question. Can you describe for the Subcommittee the exact process the Export- 

Import Bank goes through when calculating the risks involved in any given proposal?

Answer. The factors which must be considered to support such a determination are numerous and varied depending upon the size and character of the transaction being financed. They relate to the borrowing country, the nature of the undertaking for which financing is sought, and the creditworthiness of the individual borrower involved.

With respect to each proposed transaction it is important that the undertaking be one which is not opposed by the host country, and that it offer prospects of cash generation adequate to service and repay the proposed debt within an acceptable repayment period. Uncertainties on this latter point are sometimes resolved by means of a repayment guarantee from an acceptable third party or by another security arrangement appropriate to the undertaking. 

Factors involving the proposed borrower are closely related to those affecting the contemplated transaction and the Bank necessarily looks to the loan applicant to provide the financial and other data required for their consideration. The quantity and character of these data will vary in the size and complexity of the particular undertaking but in all cases they include a clear description of the project for which financing is sought and statements disclosing the proposed borrower's current and prospective financing position. 

In large and complex cases, more extensive factual material may be required, including data on the borrower's corporate history, a description of the markets it serves or intends to serve, an outline of its past operations, and the financial results thereof as embodied in its financial statements for a representative past period. It would also include a description of the overall plan for financing the proposed project and specifically, requirements for financing items which Eximbank may not finance, together with the proposed sources, terms and conditions of all such financing. To afford the Bank a means of appraising the borrower's outlook and prospects for the future, it is required in large complex cases that the applicant furnish financial projections in the form of earnings and cash flow forecasts covering a representative future period supported by market data describing its sales outlets, pricing policies, and the competitive situation with which it must deal. 

In addition, continuous evaluations are made of each country's overall foreign trade position and the potential future availability of the dollars necessary to repay the Eximbank loan.

Question. Would you describe the flow pattern of Export-Import Bank funds once a positive loan decision has been made? I ask this question because of the concern that is expressed by some that the Export-Import Bank is contributing to our Balance of Payments problems. Is this the case?

Answer. All of the Bank's disbursements remain in the United States. They are made through a United States bank to the U.S. exporter to pay him for the goods and services which he exports to the foreign purchaser. The foreign purchaser then repays to the Export-Import Bank in dollars with interest the funds which were loaned.

The repayment to the Bank by the foreign purchaser causes funds to flow into the U.S. and assists the Nation's balance of payments. 

Question. Do you have any information as to whether or not Export-Import 

Bank activities contribute to a net exporting of jobs? 

Answer. The Board of Directors is required, by law, in authorizing loans and guarantees to take into account any adverse effect on the U.S. economy. We do not believe that the Bank's activities contribute to an exporting of jobs. On the contrary, Exim supported exports sales have created thousands of jobs in the United States.

Question. Do you have figures as to how many jobs are created domestically through Export-Import Bank activities?

Answer. We have no exact figures on this, but we estimate that approximately 

620 thousand jobs have been or will be created or sustained by the export sales supported by FY 1973 authorizations.

Question. Many Americans are finding it difficult to understand why the 

Export-Import Bank should grant credits to Egypt at a time when it has been one of the countries contributing to our energy problems. Can you provide the 

Committee with a detailed rationale for your authorization of $100 million in loans for the SUMED project?

The history of the SUMED loan goes back a long time. The project has been under consideration for many years, particularly since the closing of the Suez Canal after the 1967 Arab-Israeli War. The project encountered various delays, and for the past year it was thought that a European consortion would build the pipeline.

However, because of sharply escalating costs and other considerations, the Egyptians encouraged a group of United States firms to submit a proposal. At that time, the Bank was approached about supporting the U.S. exports involved in such a project. After a detailed analysis, and thorough consideration by the 

National Advisory Council and the Bank's Board of Directors, a Preliminary Commitment was approved in August 1973, well before the recent Mid-East hostilities.

This Preliminary Commitment was issued to assist U.S. exporters to obtain the business. They faced very stiff competition from European suppliers who were bidding to build the pipeline. The Board of Directors felt that Eximbank support was essential for the U.S. exporter to win the business and also believed that the revenue produced by the pipeline provided reasonable assurance of payment.

The final application was approved in January 1974. It should be noted that, as in all Exim credits, the Bank's loan, or any private loan guaranteed by Exim, will be used only to purchase United States goods and services. 

From an overall standpoint, it is the judgment of the Administration that U.S. participation in the proposed pipeline project will be helpful in settlement of the Middle East problems, including alleviating the worldwide oil shortage and thereby indirectly benefiting the United States in addition to the direct benefit which will result from the U.S. export sales. 

Questions. Many of us have been struck by the coincidence that the SUMED loan was authorized at approximately the same time Secretary of State Kissinger was in the Middle East negotiating the disengagement of forces between Egypt and Israel. Would you provide us with the details as to the linkage between this loan and Secretary Kissinger's endeavors?

Answer. As I just described, the SUMED pipeline credit has a long history. 

In fact, a preliminary commitment had been issued prior to the recent Mid-East War. The timing, then, of the final approval depended upon Eximbank's obtaining the necessary information and performing the analysis required before we could make a credit judgment, not upon Secretary Kissinger's Middle East negotiations. Obviously, it might have been helpful that the Secretary knew of the 

Exim credit, but the timing of the Bank's approval was primarily dependent on the time necessary for the credit evaluation.

Question. Some of us are concerned that Egypt's repayment record on loans such as this may indicate that somewhere downstream some difficulties may be encountered. Would you provide the Committee with the details of your evaluation of the risks involved? It would be helpful if you would also provide for the record a summary of Egypt's past track record regarding repayment of loans. 

Answer. The repayment of the loan is not dependent upon the ability of Egypt to pay but upon the profitability of the pipeline itself. There is no doubt that a market exists in Europe for the oil, and the supply of oil for the pipeline is likewise assured by the 13 companies involved, 5 of which are U.S. Thus, the Board of Directors concluded that reasonable assurance of repayment exists. 

SUMMARY OF EXIMBANK REPAYMENT EXPERIENCE WITH CREDITS TO SUPPORT EXPORTS TO EGYPT 

Eximbank has made several loans over the years in support of U.S. exports to Egypt. The first loan was authorized in 1947 and was fully repaid by 1957. Two loans were authorized in 1955, one of which was not used, the other was repaid by 1959. In 1958 a fourth loan was authorized. Repayments under this credit were completed in 1965.

In 1960, an $18 million credit (Credit 1265) was authorized to support U.S. exports to Egypt and in 1963 a $12.5 million credit (Credit 2110) was authorized, Credit 1265 became delinquent in 1967, after paying the first nine installments of the 16 semi-annual installment loan. Credit 2110 became delinquent in September, 1966 on the second installment of a 16 semi-annual installment loan. 

These two loans were rescheduled in 1971. Egypt made payments under this rescheduling, however, the payments were from 16 to 63 days late. The October 

1, 1973 installment, which was delinquent at December 31, 1973, was paid on

March 1, 1974. 

Question. The Bechtel Corporation is involved with this project as well as with the Algerian liquified natural gas project. Charges have been made that because 

Stephen D. Bechtel, Sr. served on your advisory committee during and just prior to the granting of loans in these two cases, there is a likely conflict of interest. Is this the case?

Answer. The Advisory Committee is a group which is legally constituted under the Export-Import Bank Act and is broadly representation of production, commerce, finance, agriculture, and labor. This committee meets three or four times a year to consult with the Bank on the effectiveness of its programs in meeting the needs of the U.S. exporting community. It does not review, nor is it consulted on, individual credit or guarantee applications. It has absolutely nothing to do with the day-to-day operations of the Bank. 

Question. Recently, the charge was made that a basic conflict of interest was evident in the Export-Import Bank decision to grant over $157 million in loans related to the liquified natural gas project in Algeria because Stephen D. Bechtel, Sr. served on your advisory committee at the same time that the 

Bechtel Corporation was chosen to serve as the "coordinator" of U.S. business involvement in this project. Would you like to comment on this charge? 

Answer. Again, we deny there was any conflict of interest. I would like to point out that the Bechtel Corporation is the largest international engineering firm in the world. The fact that Mr. Bechtel, Sr. served on the Bank's advisory committee had absolutely nothing to do with Eximbank's decision to support the U.S. exports involved in this project. I would point out that for many years 

Eximbank has been financing exports for projects in which the Bechtel Corporation has been one of the U.S. companies participating, as the Bank has for many other American engineering firms operating abroad. 

Question. A similar situation to the Algerian one exists vis-a-vis the SUMED project in that Bechtel Corporation is the primary American business involved in the project. While Mr. Bechtel was no longer serving on your advisory committee when the SUMED loans were authorized, the loans were authorized shortly after he left the committee. Was there any conflict of interest involved here? 

Answer. My answer is again categorically no.

Question. During the history of the Export-Import Bank have there been many instances similar to the Bechtel one. If so, can you explain why this is the case? 

Answer. Senator Brooke, over the years the members of our Advisory Committee have been distinguished men and women, most of whom are directly or indirectly involved in exporting or export financing. It is only natural that in order to advise the Bank on its programs of export assistance, the members of the committee must be familiar with the problems encountered by the U.S. exporting community.

In the course of their export sales endeavors, the firms or banks with which these advisory committee members are associated quite naturally might seek Eximbank assistance to consumate certain sales, as do a great many other U.S. exporters. Eximbank programs are available to all U.S. exporters and we do not discriminate for or against firms of banks who might have an officer serving as a member of Exim's Advisory Committee. Such a factor is never taken into consideration in the application evaluation process. 

For example, the President of the Bankers' Association for Foreign Trade has been included as a member of the Bank's Advisory Committee for many years. 

This position rotates among bankers involved in export financing. 

I repeat, therefore, there is no relationship, and never has been, between the fact that a person is a member of the Bank's Advisory Committee and any export assistance the Bank might authorize for the sales of the member's firm.
