OVERSEAS PRIVATE INVESTMENT CORPORATION STATEMENT OF MARSHALL T. MAYS, PRESIDENT ACCOMPANIED BY: 

RUTHERFORD POATS, VICE PRESIDENT FOR DEVELOPMENT PAUL MULLER, TREASURER BUDGET REQUEST 

Senator INOUYE. We will now consider the Overseas Private Investment Corporation.

Our next witness is Mr. Marshall T. Mays, President of the Overseas Private Investment Corporation, who will justify the fiscal year 1975 request which is $25 million as an additional appropriation to 

OPIC's reserves. 

PREPARED STATEMENT 

Mr. Mays, we have your prepared statemeent which will be inserted in the hearing record at this point. You may proceed as you wish, sir. 

[The statement follows:]

Mr. Chairman and Members of the Committee: 

I appreciate this opportunity to report to you on the activities and financial condition of the Overseas Private Investment Corporation (OPIC). In the year since OPIC last appeared before this 

Subcommittee, the Corporation's financial position has been strengthened by a continued growth of earnings and a decline in claims payment and new claims. 

Use of OPIC's insurance services by U. S. investors has increased markedly in the last four months from the low level of Fiscal 1973, despite increased rejections by OPIC of private investment proposals that we found potentially harmful to the U. S. economy. 

OPIC has taken major steps in the past 12 months to increase private reinsurance and to open the way to direct participation by private insurers in the OPIC insurance program. The report to 

Congress which we submitted on February 28, in compliance with Section 240A(b) of our statute, describes our efforts to analyze and our plans to test the possibilities of transferring OPIC programs to the private sector.

Appropriation Request for Reserves: 

OPIC requests an appropriation of $25 million in FY 1975 to complete the restoration to the insurance reserves of the $50 million in insurance premiums which were transferred by law to the AID Housing Guaranty reserve at the time of OPIC's establishment separate peso AID. This request represents the balance of the $50 million restoration approved by the House of Representatives last

year but which was reduced by the Senate-House Conference to $25 million.

This appropriation is needed to assure users of the insurance service and prospective private insurance partners that premium payments will be accumulated in ready reserves for prompt payment of claims rather than diverted from the premium pool to other Federal programs. This appropriation is not needed to meet presently foreseen losses which might seriously reduce OPIC's present insurance reserve of $186 million.

During the recent floor debate in the Senate on the extension of OPIC's authorization, it was argued that OPIC's continuing request for reserve appropriations proved that the program is a public subsidy to U.S. corporations or, as some argued, OPIC is "insolvent." 

These are understandable misconceptions. The facts demonstrate, however, that they are wrong.

OPIC's financial position has strengthened during a period of unusual challenge--the wholesale expropriations in Chile. Under a recently concluded debt rescheduling agreement with OPIC, the Chilean Government has agreed to make payments, on a stretchedout basis, for past due installments of certain debt owed to U. S. investors and with respect to which compensation had been paid by 

OPIC. 

The insurance program has produced, over a period of 15 years of substantial operations in developing countries, a record of user fee payments greatly exceeding claims payments and administrative costs. U.S. investors insured by OPIC and its predecessors havesv 34-192 O-74-10

paid insurance premiums totaling $189 million. 

Cash claims payments have totaled approximately $33 million, and guaranties of host government commitments in connection with expropriation claims now total about $90 million.. Administrative costs are now running at about $4 million per year for the entire OPIC operation; this is less than the interest earned annually on the investment of premium income.

In view of widespread misconceptions of OPIC's appropriations record, it may be in order to review the record of reserve appropriations at this time. Reserve appropriations totaling $106 million have been received by OPIC and its predecessor, AID, in the five fiscal years 1970-74.. The FY 1970, 1971 and 1972 reserve appropriations totaling $69 million helped fund the separate Loan Guaranty (finance) Reserve required by the 1969 legislation and restored to the insurance program funds taken from it for this new Reserve. 

The FY 1973 and 1974 appropriations totaling $37.5 million partially restored to the Insurance Reserve premiums totaling $50 million transferred by law from the investment program's reserve to the AID Housing Guaranty reserve, plus interest OPIC has foregone on these funds.

Claims: 

Calendar Year 1973 was one of notable progress in claims settlements. In January, 1973, there were 18 outstanding claims totaling about $114 million. At the end of the year there were only seven outstanding claims for about $27 million. Early in 1974, one investor company withdrew its claim for $9 million. In addition,

OPIC has reason to expect that negotiations between,the Government of Chile and an OPIC-insured copper company will soon result in settlement of the major pending claims case amounting to $14 million. 

This would leave only five claims outstanding, totaling about $4 million. 

During Calendar Year 1973, OPIC settled 16 claims by paying insured investors approximately $5.4 million. An additional $9.5 million was paid by OPIC pursuant to one of the guaranties of host government commitments referred to earlier. OPIC recovered approximately $1.5 million during the year, mainly through sale of local currencies acquired in the course of settling inconvertibility claims, resulting in net claim payments of $13.5 million. 

In addition to these recoveries, OPIC received reimbursement of nearly $1.7 million from the Government of Chile pursuant to the debt rescheduling agreement. Chile is obligated to pay the rest of the defaulted debt covered by this agreement, amounting to $6.6 million plus interest, over the course of the next seven years. 

Also during Calendar Year 1973, OPIC denied three claims and three other claims were withdrawn. OPIC's denials of the $92.5 million claim of International Telephone and Telegraph and of Anaconda's $154 million claim have been submitted to arbitration. 

OPIC has been advised by independent legal counsel that it has no obligation to pay compensation in either of these cases. 

Risk Management: 

OPIC has expanded and refined risk management and risk sharing measures aimed at reducing the probability of severe claim losses. Among these steps were:

An increase in the amount and length of the term of expropriation reinsurance obtained by Lloyd's of London. 

A new three-year Lloyd's commitment effective January 1, 1974, provides for Lloyd's liability to pay approximately 45% of any expropriation claim accepted by OPIC on a first-loss basis up to annual limits of about $18, 255, 000 per country and $54, 765,000 worldwide. This represents an increase in both the absolute amount of reinsurance and Lloyd's share of losses in countries of major OPIC exposure. 

The opening of negotiations with Lloyd's for reinsurance of inconvertibility risks.

The adoption of a refined system of controlling the growth of OPIC's insurance concentration in countries of strong investor attraction, so as to limit the possibility of large losses in a single country. 

Countries' exposures were weighted according to risk factors common to the several types of coverage. In line with this new country concentration guideline, OPIC has identified a growing insurance volume in Brazil and is restricting the volume of additional insurance written in Brazil by generally declining to cover new investment in the industrialized areas of the country (Sao Paulo and Rio de Janeiro). This should help spread OPIC's portfolio in the country and assure that any coverage issued in Brazil will be for investments in the poorer regions of the country where the need for development is the greatest. 

Adoption of a systematic program of project and country monitoring designed to obtain early warning of potential political

risks and assure constructive approaches to resolving potential conflicts between the insured or guaranteed U. S. investors and their host governments or other local institutions. 

Small Business and Developmental Impact: 

OPIC has increased its efforts to assist small U.S. businesses through a formal program to better inform smali business of the availability of various OPIC services to assist them in developing overseas sales and investment opportunities. As part of this effort, OPIC has begun holding a series of informational seminars in various business centers around the country. 

OPIC also has undertaken several new initiatives as part of a program to find and promote investment opportunities in some of the least developed nations. These initiatives include: 

An intensive effort to identify and promote investment opportunities in five African nations, Kenya, Ivory Coast, Cameroon, Zaire, and Gabon, particularly through closer cooperation with their local development banks and agencies. 

A similar approach in Latin America, focusing on 

Central America. 

Consultations with Brazilian officials and private agencies on how U.S. private investment can best assist the development of the Northeast region of that country. 

1973 Operational Results: 

OPIC's net income during the first half of FY 1974 rose to almost $17.6 million, an increase of 8. 4% from the $16.2 million recorded during the first half of FY 1973. Total gross income

rose to $19.4 million, while gross income from insurance fees totaled $12.7 million.

OPIC management has continued to maintain firm control over administrative expenses. Fiscal Year 1975 administrative costs are expected to total $4, 673, 000, an increase of $689,000 over the actual results of FY 1973, two years previously. While 

OPIC has maintained its full-time staff at approximately 130 persons over the last three years, pay raises authorized for all Federal employees and normal employee within-grade increases will result in increased personnel costs accounting for the majority of the increase in administrative costs. Other major increases come from increased investment survey costs and travel expenses. 

The volume of new insurance issued lagged during the early and middle months of 1973, largely due to the absence of any new contracts covering large mining, smelting, or refining projects. 

However, in November the insurance volume began to increase noticeably, a trend which is continuing. During CY 1973, OPIC insured $197 million of new investment compared with $224 million in CY 1972. However, OPIC new insurance volume in CY 1974 is already far ahead of the level of 1973, and we expect to insure approximately $300-350 million of new investment in this calendar year, and issue about $15 million of new loan guaranties. 

Conclusions: 

We believe that the investment insurance program has been and continues to be in the best interests of the United States and the participating less-developed countries. Numerous studies by various

and noted groups, as well as Department of Commerce trade and investment data, have clearly shown that foreign investments by U.S. companies and individuals have, in the aggregate, been vitally important to maintaining the volume of America's exports and in making positive contributions to our balance of payments. The 

United States sells 29% of its total exports to the developing nations of the world. OPIC's selectivity in carefully screening applications for insurance and finance assures that the investments OPIC encourages will not harm the domestic employment and balance of payments interests of the United States.

The need of the developing nations for the technological and capital contributions of foreign investment in stimulating their economies is growing. Their already great problems have been intensified by the recent sharp increases in the costs of oil and other necessary imports, including manufactured goods. Government-to-government aid alone cannot meet our responsibilities for international development cooperation. OPIC's work in encouraging private foreign investments which are of benefit to both the developing nations and the United States is as important to our national interests today as it has ever been.

FINANCIAL CONDITION 

Mr. MAYS.  I might just mention in the introduction that OPIC's financial condition has continued to improve since our last appearance before this subcommittee. 

Our earnings have continued to increase. In December of 1973 our board of directors allocated an additional $25 million from earnings to our insurance reserve. We have today about $12.5 million of unallocated earnings.

We have in the last month received in payment from Chile $1.7 million which is a repayment of some funds which we had disbursed on claims in Chile so our financial prospects to date we think are indeed very good.

Our request for an appropriation of $25 is not to pay anticipated claims. We are requesting it as an addition to our insurance reserve because when OPIC was created $50 million of premium income paid in the program in AID was left behind in AID to fund a reserve for the Latin American Housing Guaranty program. 

These premiums were paid for our political risk insurance. We think and our policyholders think they should be part of OPIC's insurance reserve.

Last year we received an appropriation of $25 million, so we are asking for the balance of $25 million this year to restore those premiums to our insurance reserve. 

Senator INOUYE. Before proceeding, would you please introduce your colleagues? 

Mr. MAYS. Yes. On my left is Paul Muller, Treasurer of OPIC and on my right in Rutherford Poats, our Vice President for Development, who will respond also to questions of the committee. 

PAYMENT OF CLAIMS 

Senator INOUYE. Speaking of reserves, in last year's hearings on page 348 I asked if it were not true that there was never any commitment to appropriate $50 million to OPIC reserves at some future date. 

Mr. Mills replied that this statement was correct and he went on to state, "I am trying to maintain the financial solvency of the program." 

Do you know what was meant by this statement?

Mr. MAYS. I don't think that Mr. Mills or I have considered that there was any obligation or commitment on the part of the Congress to restore it if OPIC was to be operated as an insurance business. 

Our insurance reserve has since OPIC was created increased from $85 million to $186 million to date. 

Senator INOUYE. Is it my understanding that OPIC invests its earned reserves in interest-bearing U.S. Government securities but is required to place appropriated reserves in a noninterest-bearing Treasury account No. 0083.

During the past 4 fiscal years $68,750,000 in funds appropriated to OPIC's reserves (including $25 million in fiscal year 1974, and $1212 million in fiscal year 1973) have been appropriated and placed in account No. 0083.

Is it true that during this time every dime OPIC has made in claims which is $30,393,877, has been drawn from the appropriated funds while OPIC's earned reserves have been left untouched? 

Mr. MAYS. Senator, I am not familiar with the account numbers or those exact balances but in responding to the question on the use of appropriated funds to pay claims it is true that OPIC has paid insurance claims from appropriated funds in the insurance reserve as distinguished from premium income which has gone into the insurance reserve.

This has been done because it seemed to be a good business practice to have our premium income earn as much as possible. This year we anticipate $9 million of interest income on our invested reserve. You have probably noted from reports of insurance companies generally that most of their profits are derived from the investment of their funds as opposed to underwriting profit. Most insurance companies will be very close to a break-even point or may even show a loss on underwriting.

They make their profit on the investment of their reserves. So, it is quite important if OPIC is to succeed in operating without cost to the U.S. taxpayers and to operate on a basis on which private insurance companies will participate in OPIC and share its risks, that we invest our premium income in this way, particularly with regard to use of these appropriated funds to pay claims. 

If we look at these appropriated funds, for example the $25 million appropriated last year, as being a substitute for premium income which was earned by the program in AID I think it is certainly justifiable and is sound business to pay the claims in this way. 

Senator INOUYE. I can understand from the standpoint of your organization it would appear to be sound and it would look good on the balance sheet but why should the American taxpayer be called upon to cover OPIC's losses while your earnings are free to draw interest? Why can't you pay it out of your earnings as other organizations do? 

Mr. MAYS. We could.

Senator INOUYE. There is no one appropriating any money to insurance companies.

Mr. MAYS. We could do that and it would reflect a reduction in our earnings because we would have less funds, of course, to invest. However, until we have reached the point of paying from appropriated funds more than $50 million which represents the premium income we lost it seems perfectly justifiable to my mind to pay it from the appropriated funds. After we reach that $50 million point I think we should look again to see which source of funds we should use for the payment of the claims.

Senator INOUYE. Yet, you also concur that this is not a commitment on the part of Congress to appropriate $50 million? 

Mr. MAYS. I know of nothing in the legislative history that would indicate a commitment on the part of the Congress to restore those funds. I do know that when OPIC was created in 1969 it looked like it had been such a profitable operation to that point that it was probably felt that the program could afford to have $50 million of its premium

income taken to fund this other program. I think, however, if that practice were followed in the future it would be not only of concern to our customers who paid in this premium income and who justifiably feel they are being taxed in this way to support a separate Government program, but it would also be of concern to the private insurance companies that we are now trying to get to share in OPIC's risks, that if OPIC were to be in a position of reinsuring these private companies there should be adequate reserves for OPIC to pay on its reinsurance obligation.

Senator INOUYE. If I recall, the amounts appropriated for your reserves, based on discussions which ensued between your organization and the Appropriations Committee, would suggest that the Chilean loans were about to collapse and appropriations from Congress were necessary to cover this. 

I gather now that Chile is making payments and that your reserves picture is a very good one. Are you still going to insist upon using appropriated funds to cover losses and not use the premium funds for this purpose?

Mr. MAYS. My own judgment, Senator, would be that we should continue to do so until we have used $50 million of appropriated funds which would be the equivalent of this premium income in the absence of further indication from the Congress as to what their intention was. 

There was a change in the law when OPIC was created in regard to the use of these funds to pay claims. There is no legal question, I believe, with regard to the way these funds have been used to pay claims. 

JAMAICA, CHILE, AND THE DOMINICAN REPUBLIC 

Senator INOUYE. In its fiscal year 1974 report the subcommittee expressed some concern regarding OPIC's exposure of $480 million to Jamaica, $249 million to Chile, and $253 million to the Dominican 

Republic. What is your present exposure in these countries? 

Mr. MAYS. As of January 1 of this year, Senator, our exposure in

Jamaica on expropriation risk being the largest of the three, was $479 million. Our exposure in the Dominican Republic was $202 million and in Chile it is $168 million. 

These, of course, are concentrations in our portfolio which we inherited from AID and today OPIC would not write insurance in that concentration under a policy adopted by its Board of Directors at either its first or second meeting in 1971, which was to avoid exposures of more than 10 percent of its worldwide portfolio in any one country. 

Senator INOUYE. What is your outlook so far as these loans are concerned?

Mr. MAYS. In these three countries we do not perceive any undue risk at the present time. 

Senator INOUYE. Would that be the same for Chile at this time? 

Mr. MAYS. Yes, it would, Senator.

SOUTH VIETNAM 

Senator INOUYE. An article appeared in this morning's Washington 

Post which cites the refusal of the U.S. Government to extend its foreign investment insurance as a major obstacle to South Vietnam's economic recovery. What is OPIC's position on this?

Mr. MAYS. There has been no real change since last year when Mr. 

Mills explained to the subcommittee that we were under injunction from the House Foreign Affairs Committee against the issuance of political risk insurance in South Vietnam. However, since that time a subcommittee of the House Foreign Affairs, chaired by Congressman 

Culver, has recommended that the injunction be removed.

There has not yet been action by the full Foreign Affairs Committe. However, on the Senate side this year the Subcommittee on Multinational Corporations, chaired by Senator Church, put into its subcommittee report a somewhat similar injunction against OPIC's doing business there. It was later modified to state in substance that OPIC should not take any risk in Indochina unless private insurance companies participated in those risks.

As a practical effect, that may prevent us from doing any business in Indochina. It was stated in terms of direct underwriting by private insurance companies. However, on the floor of the Senate last week the bill reported by the Senate Foreign Relations Committee was amended by an amendment offered by Senator Javits that permits OPIC to obtain participation by private insurance companies by more than one route. That is through reinsurance or participation in direct underwriting.

Now, if that action by the full Senate is construed to apply to this section of the report, I would say that the risk which Lloyds of London shares with OPIC in South Vietnam, qualifies as private participation in expropriation risks in South Vietnam. But that is a question of interpretation of the report and this Senate action which I have not yet carefully considered to determine exactly what we could do. 

However, the most significant thing is that we see no possibility that private insurance companies will write insurance in South Vietnam against war, revolution or insurrection, which may be the most critical coverage there in order to encourage U.S. investment to go into 

South Vietnam. We are aware that the Japanese Government has opened its investment insurance program in South Vietnam and 

Japanese investment is going in there.

We have expressions of interest from numbers of U.S. companies who would be willing to make some investment there if our insurance were available. But we are at present still under the injunction of these committees not to operate in Indochina. We would be interested in an expression of opinion of this committee in its report with regard to the conduct of OPIC's business there. 

OIL PRICE INCREASE 

Senator INOUYE. It has been reported that the recent price increases in the Middle East oil will mean an additional financial burden on these developing countries to the tune of about $30 billion that these price increases will also affect the trade picture of the Western in-

dustrialized countries of Japan and where they made a profit last year they estimate a deficit of approximately $40 billion. 

Has this price increase of Middle East oil affected the risk factor in your operations?

Mr. MAYS. It would probably have some effect on the commercial risks involved with many of these countries. The effect of the increased cost of oil can indeed be devastating to these countries. 

However, we have not perceived that it would make any significant difference in the political risk which we insure. It may well mean that it will be all the more important to encourage additional investment in these countries since it would be impossible probably to make up the necessary funds from official AID flows. 

I suppose that we might have some more claims on our unconvertibility coverage because some of these countries will have problems on convertibility. 

Senator INOUYE. Are you anticipating this?

Mr. MAYS. We have examined a particular country and the amount of our convertibility exposure in these countries. I might comment our convertibility insurance program has not lost money because although we pay many claims we are able to use the foreign currencies to pay the operating expenses of our U.S. embassies which therefore does not result in a loss to our program.

PROMOTION OF INVESTMENT OPPORTUNITIES Senator INOUYE. Senator Hatfield. 

Senator HATFIELD. On page 7 I notice that you have indicated that you are making some intensive effort to identify and promote investment opportunities in five African nations and you list them. You also suggest a similar approach should be used in Latin America, focusing on Central America.

Will you first of all identify some of the types of projects, also the philosophical framework, into which you see these projects fitting in relation to these countries and the United States through this means of investment?

Mr. MAYS. Starting with the applicant countries, Senator, these five countries which we have identified for a special OPIC effort are in conjunction with five U.S. companies who are sharing the cost of this program with OPIC.

They wish to survey this market to see what types of investment may be most suitable for it. Of course, like other markets in the developing world, these countries represent substantial portions of the populations of the markets of the future.

These companies are naturally interested in trying to participate in these markets. One of the areas in which we are directing our attention presently in Africa, is cattle raising. 

There have been problems with disease in terms of producing cattle and beef in Africa but these seem to have been overcome to a degree. 

That is where we expect some of the first investment to occur. 

There have been already some substantial cattle investments in Kenya, one of which was described in our recent annual report. 

Senator HATFIELD. Is that cattle raising for export business or for domestic consumption?

Mr. MAYS. Domestic consumption and some exports to the Common Market.

OTHER PROJECTS IN DEVELOPING COUNTRIES 

Senator HATFIELD. What are some other types of projects that you envisage here in these countries that are representative of, say, the developing countries of the world in which you are interested? 

Mr. MAYS. I am afraid I did not understand the question. 

Senator HATFIELD. What other types of projects besides the cattle raising projects are you now involved in? What types of projects would you envisage as possible future involvement in the areas identified generally as the developing countries of the world? 

Mr. MAYS. In addition to the cattle project, West Africa looks like it has considerable potential from the standpoint of the production of timber which has not yet been developed, at least by U.S. companies. 

Most of the U.S. investment has tended to go to Central America and to the Far East, Indonesia, the Philippines. This is an area which has had considerable attention.

Senator HATFIELD. Now, would you put all these projects in a basic philosophical context which you are pursuing in looking specifically at some of these developing parts of the world that you would like to place investment in? What is the basic philosophical motivation that you have?

PURPOSE OF OPIC PROGRAM 

Mr. MAYS. The purpose of the OPIC program is to develop these countries, to improve their economic development and consequently their social development. OPIC is quite selective, more selective than 

AID was in the type of projects we support. 

We want to make certain of the economic contribution that they make. What the effect will be on the balance of payments of each of these countries, what effect it will have on their employment. 

But similarly we are also examining projects from the standpoint of the effect on the U.S. economy, the U.S. balance of payments and 

U.S. employment, and we have made a practice since the first year 

OPIC was created of refusing to support any projects that would have a detrimental effect on U.S. employment. 

In fact, it was at OPIC's initiative that we suggested that the law be changed to require such consideration on OPIČ projects. 

Senator HATFIELD. Do you perceive the purpose to be partially at least to have the indigenous economy of these countries improved and least to have the indigenous economy of these countries improved and broadened, diversified, and strengthened? Do you evaluate such efforts both in terms of economics of those countries and the social implications of such development?

Mr. MAYS. That is indeed our primary purpose and it will always be, I think.

Senator HATFIELD. You see the capital that flows into these countries in a sense as another representation of the American image or profile that will be portrayed and presented to these people; is that correct? Mr. MAYS. I do. 

Senator HATFIELD. As with the people in striped trousers in the official lists of legations and embassies, this is another type of American image?

Mr. MAYS. An American present in these countries of the type of which I think we can generally be quite proud, that these investors are generally very good corporate citizens and they do a lot to strengthen the ties between these countries and the United States. 

HABITATION LE CLERC OF HAITI 

Senator HATFIELD. Did you have an opportunity to invest in the 

Habitation Le Clerc in the country of Haiti?

Mr. MAYS. We do have a loan to that project. 

Senator HATFIELD. $400,000; is that correct? 

Mr. MAYS. Yes.

Senator HATFIELD. The New York Times article of Sunday, Janu ary 6, 1974, which lists the funding as being from the Agency for 

International Development then is in error. It was really OPIC? 

Mr. MAYS. It was really OPIC's loan.

Senator HATFIELD. You made this loan of $400,000 for the Habitation 

Le Clerc from your reserves as part of your investment that you were talking about a while ago, bringing the profits into your reserve program?

Mr. MAYS. It is part of our direct investment fund, Senator. It is made on commercial terms. I believe in this case it is a 12-percent loan for 10 years. 

Senator HATFIELD. Did you make the judgment and evaluation and therefore the decision on this particular project? 

Mr. MAYS. I was at that time the General Counsel of OPIC. As such 

I was a member of the investment committee that considered this particular project. 

I might say what the reasoning of the committee in justifying this project recognized from the start that this was appealing to a particularly luxury market in tourism. 

At that time there was practically no private investment interest in Haiti. Haiti had just come out from a period of oppression and there had been no investment interest in the country. 

We have observed that investment in tourism can indeed be developmental and beneficial to the country concerned. 

The argument was presented that where the luxury trade goes in tourism it is quickly followed by mass tourism and that this would occur in Haiti. And examining developments since this loan was originally approved we have found that to be the case. 

There are now in OPIC applications for five hotels of medium priced class aimed at mass tourist business. 

So, we think this will indeed contribute to the development of Haiti. 

Our loan was of fairly modest proportions, as you notice. 

Ours is $415,000. There is a similar private loan of that amount and $1.2 million of equity by the investors in the project. 

It has, unfortunately, gotten some rather lurid publicity which the operators of this hotel are using apparently to attract business. I don't approve of their advertising techniques. If it is successful I guess it will mean that the occupancy of the hotel will improve and our loan will be safer but the advertising seems to be of questionable taste. 

COMPREHENSIVE STUDY OF OTHER HAITIAN DEVELOPMENT POTENTIALS 

Senator HATFIELD. Had you made a study of the potential economic factors in Haiti and come to the conclusion that tourism was the only, or at least the most immediate, project in which you could become involved? Do you have a comprehensive study of what other potential development could occur in Haiti outside of tourism? 

Mr. MAYS. Yes, we have, Senator. Haiti, of course, is one of the least developed countries in the world. It has the least per capita income, in many ways it is the most backward. 

Senator HATFIELD. Do you have any projects pending for investment other than the tourist industry in Haiti?

Mr. MAYS. I don't know the breakdown on this but we have applications pending for $51 million of new investment in Haiti. 

So, apparently this new interest in Haiti is beginning to stimulate investment interest.

Senator HATFIELD. Outside of the tourist industry?

Mr. MAYS. Let me review the list for just a moment, Senator, and 

I will tell you. There are 28 applications pending for investment in

Haiti now; $61 million investment and noting the dates on the applications I think they have all come in since we undertook this project.

It includes that particular project and the other five hotel projects that I mentioned but none of the others seem to be tourist type investments. 

Senator HATFIELD. Would you define that a little bit further for me as to what percentage, or rough estimate, of the $61 million total request represents projects of the tourist type and projects of nontourist type?

Mr. MAYS. I believe about 20 percent of them in number are tourist. 

I don't know if that applies to the dollar amount as well.

Mr. MAYS. I can give it to you for the record. I cannot guess the types. I am having to guess from the name.

TOURIST AND NONTOURIST RELATED PROJECTS 

Senator HATFIELD. Mr. Chairman, if I might make this request to have in the record an extrapolation of these projects and to have them distinguished as to tourist and nontourist.

Why I ask for this is that simply you are quite right that there has been some rather interesting publicity surrounding the luxury resort called Habitation Le Clerc.

There is one thing that I would like to observe and get your response on-I do not disagree that the tourist industry is a legitimate part of an economic potential of a State, but I have a feeling that if the people are to be only servants and locked into a servile cast to provide the comforts for the tourists coming from other countries, then we are not building a good foundation for human relations or political relations. 

I would further observe, and I would like to get your response, that where accommodations are now renting at this particular project at $150 a day per couple, that is equivalent to the total annual income of a native couple in Haiti.

When 2,000 of them stood outside the gates and watched this opening night soiree, and considering the American profile projected by the 34-192 O 74 - 11

guest list, I cannot believe in my mind that we are doing more than providing some short term economic gains at a very serious long term risk of unhappy American relationships.

It is quoted in the New York Times, and I would like to submit this for the record, "The president of this company, described this as the most extraordinary, lascivious and decadent place in the world. 

When I say decadent I don't necessarily mean sex. For me decadent is just a beautiful way of living where everything is beautifully lazy and all you have to do is raise your hand and you get service."

Interestingly, when they provided the service they are talking about including not only the swimming pool, a private pool for every two villas, but also three servants for every guest; it is obvious that those three servants are coming out of the general population of Haiti. 

A Haitian government official said, "If we are to postpone indulgence and luxuriousness until every last person on Earth is fed and clothed, then it would be a very boring world indeed." 

I think that kind of attitude and philosophy and being identified with that kind of project is not to our long term interest. 

Now, that is my own personal observation. Would you care to respond? 

[The article follows:] [From the New York Times, Jan. 6, 1974] A NEW RETREAT FOR THE RICH-SURROUNDED BY TUMBLEDOWN SHACKS (By Judy Klemesrud) 

PORT-AU-PRINCE, Haiti-Jean-Claude ("Baby Doc") Duvalier didn't show up as promised, but his sister, Nicole, did. So did the cream of Haitian society and a gaggle of Beautiful People-1,500 in all-for the opening-night party of a new retreat for the rich, billed by his owners as "the most extraordinary, lascivious, and decadent place in the world."

It is Habitation Leclerc, a $1.8-million hilly hideaway nestled amidst almond trees, magnolias, breadfruit and palms on a 15-acre estate that was once supposedly owned by Pauline Bonaparte Leclerc, the fun-loving sister of Napoleon. "When I say decadent, I don't necessarily mean sex," said Olivier Coquein, president of the resort, who also founded such fashionable watering holes as New York's Le Club, Ondine, Cheetah and Hippopotamus. "For me, decadent is just a beautiful way of life, where everything is beautifully lazy, and all you have to do is raise your hand and you get service."

SURROUNDED BY STONE WALL 

Decadent could also mean that the $150-a-day-per-couple paradise is surrounded by some of the worst squalor in the Western Hemisphere, and that tumbledown shacks of Haitians—whose per capita income is around $80`a year—can readily be seen by guests who might happen to be sipping a rum punch around the swimming pool while their investments earn them $80 a minute. But management is quick to point out that the natives are friendly, and anyway, the resort is surrounded by a stone wall, which has chunks of broken glass embedded on top. "My friends are always saying, 'How do you dare live in that country. You'll get killed, you'll get mugged, you'll get robbed,'" Lawrence Peabody of the Boston

Peabodys, co-owner and interior designer of the resort, said shortly before the party begun. "I tel Ithem, 'I can't stand the poverty in the United States,' I say, 'Look, here the people are smiling, if nothing else, they can always pick fruits and vegetables if they get hungry.' 

Mrs. Mary ("Sisi") Cahan of New York, resplendent in a bib of imitation diamonds by Kenneth Jay Lane, nodded in agreement. "It's tropical poverty as opposed to cold poverty, which is much worse," she said. 

Other guests at the Thursday soiree were Mrs. H. Loy Anderson and her son and daughter-in-law, Mr. and Mrs. H. Loy Amierson, Jr., of the Palm Beach banking

family, Michael Butler, the theatrical producer and polo player; Mrs. Fernanda

Wanamaker Leas, the socialite; Edward Gilbert, the former Wall Street wonder who was later convicted of embezzlement; Alan Hamilton, whose husband, George, the actor, arrived the following day; Alexis Smith, the actress; Jean

DeNoyer, the clothing designer and restaurateur; Pia Lindstrom, the newscaster, her husband Joseph Daly, who is in real estate, and their 1-year-old son, Justin; Barbara Valters, the television personality; Alexis Lichine, the wine expert; Joe Eula, the fashion artist; Thomas Corcoran, charge d'affaires at the 

United States Embassy, numerous other officials from foreign governments, and members' of Haiti's "200 families," who run the country's businesses, professions and government. "I'll go anywhere," said Miss Smith, one of several celebrity guests whose airfare (from her California home), as well as her hotel bill, were taken care of by the resort's management. “If there's an arrow pointing in some direction, I'll always follow it."

Almost 2,000 Haitians stood outside the gates of the resort as the guests arrived for the party. One 15-year-old Haitian girl was run over by a car and had to be rushed to a hospital.

INTO THE POOL 

Once inside the vast resort complex, the guests sipped drinks beside the large circular pool, visited Hippopotamus, a discotheque modeled after the one in New York, and strolled on the grounds of the resort. Later, they dined buffet style on such Haitian dishes as chicken and rice, beans and rice, and roast pig. 

There was, as might be expected, at least one couple who jumped into the pool together. They were Patti Adelson, 23, of Boston, who said she was vacationing here with her sister, and Alex Flambert, a 28-year-old Haitian she had met. "It [the pool] just looked so beautiful," she explained as she padded by the poolside, soaking wet.

The highlight of the evening for most of the Haitians seemed to be the arrival of President Duvalier's sister, Nicole Duvalier Foucard, who wore a long white lace dress and was accompanied by two beefy bodyguards. "Elegant," she said, in French, as Mr. Peabody guided her around the resort. "Finally Haiti has something no other country has." 

When asked about news reports that her 32-year-old sister, Marie-Denise, wielded the real power in the Haitian Government, Nicole smiled slightly and replied, in French: "I'm not in politics; I don't know."

People at the party, both Americans and Haitians commented on how much Haiti had changed since 1971, when the title of President for Life passed from the late tyrannical Francois ("Pappa Doc") Duvalier, to his then 19-year-old son, Jean-Claude. No longer, they insisted is Haiti the terror-ridden country depicted in Graham Greene's novel, "The Comedians," with its dread secret police known as the Tontons Macoutes (Creole for bogeymen).

Today Haiti courts tourism, and last year 206,000 tourists visited here, according to one of the partygoers. Theo Duval, the suave executive assistant to the director general of the National Office of Tourism. This was more than double the 

1972 figure, he said.

When asked about Habitation Leclerc, the paradise-amidst-the-poverty, Mr. Duval replied: "If we are to postpone indulgences into luxuriousness until the very last person on earth is fed, and clothed, then it would be a very boring world, indeed."

The indulgences at Habitation include 44 individual villas (there is a private pool for every (two villas), designed by Albert Mangones, a Haitian architect, to "look terrible ancient." Each residence is rented on a daily flat rate ($150-a-day per couple in season; $85 off-season) that includes meals, liquor, three Haitian servants at one's beck and call, and a jeep with chauffer. Tipping is prohibited. 

According to Mr. Coquelin, the resort was financed by two $400,000 loans, one from a New York bank, the other from the Agency for International Development, and $1 million from 14 backers, including Giovanni Agnelli, George Plimpton, the Duke of Bedford, Prince Egon Von Furstenberg, Mick Jagger, Jean- 

Paul Belmondo, Roger Vadim and Baron Edmund de Rothschild.

But you don't have to be a somebody to stay at Habitation Leclerc, Mr. Coquelin said. All you need is to be "groovy" and have enough money. He did say, though, that he would discourage people who come to Haiti for 24-hour divorces. "I don't want them," he said, with a wave of his hand. "They come here for 

24 hours, and they have something else on their minds. I want people here who

are in love, fall in love, or stay in love. These other people, they are depressed."

Habitation Leclern has certain liabilities that perhaps should be pointed out : 

At present, the tennis courts are badly studded with pebbles; the nearest beaches are an hour away on rutted and potholed roads; and the city's one gambling casino is dingy and mediocre.

The resort's owners, however, see no real reason for guests to ever leave Habitation Leclerc. "When [Lee Radziwill] and Peter Beard were here last week, they almost never left," Mr. Peabody said. "They just relaxed and ate."

But even though the resort has its faults, there seemed to be general agreement that the opening-night party was an unqualified success. At least Haiti's expert on such matters thinks so. "This was the most beautiful party in Haiti in years," said Lavinia Williams, who is in charge of entertainment for the Haitian Government. "The last big party we had was when Nixon came here while he was still Vice President. 

More than 5,000 people came for that one."

TOURIST BUSINESS 

Mr. MAYS. I would agree, Senator, that if this were the only investment we could support in Haiti, we never should have supported it in the first place. But if you look at it from the standpoint of breaking through a barrier where there had been no investment before and that it would lead to further investment in moderate priced tourist business and the $60 million of investment which is in large part in nontourist business, then I would think that our participation in this project did serve a useful purpose, rather than looking at this project by itself. 

Senator HATFIELD. I appreciate your comment. I would only close my questions by just recalling that I don't know that we can really separate the means from the objectives. 

It was Mahatma Ghandi who observed that the means are the ends of making. Therefore, I think sometimes, when we look at these as merely a means to a better and greater goal, and maybe less than the most preferred system or project, it can taint the future objectives so much that we can't really achieve them. 

I am really very unhappy about this type of identification of American capital in Haiti. I am only hopeful that somehow we can move expeditiously with these other nontourist projects which will help free these people rather than lock them into a servile role to white Americans who are shown there living lasciviously, in that kind of life.

Mr. Chairman, this committee ought to include such matters in its forthcoming personal investigation.

Senator INOUYE. To further explain why our distinguished colleague is interested in Haiti, it should be noted that the Appropriations Committee has instructed the subcommittee to conduct intensive investigations in Haiti to determine our future course. We have received many letters and other communications relating to the status of its 

Government, its economy, and such.

Most seem to be very unfavorable. In light of that, the committee will be taking the extraordinary step of investigating a foreign country. 

Usually we investigate the area or region. In this case, two members of this committee will be personally visiting Haití with their staff and come back after making their personal observations. 

This is part of the assignment. I hope you will keep that in mind. 

We will be calling on you for further assistance involving the Republic of Haiti.

Mr. MAYS. We will be delighted to assist the committee in any way we can.

Senator INOUYE. Senator Chiles. 

Senator CHILES. Mr. Mays, before I ask some questions, and since you are new as the president of OPIC, I want to give you the thinking

I have done with respect to OPIC over the last year or so since becoming a member of this subcommittee.

I think this is especially important in light of last week's votes on 

OPIC. 

SKEPTICISMS ON SOME OPIC OPERATIONS 

Last year as I began to delve into the operations of OPIC, I became skeptical about a number of things of continuing concern. These ininclude: 

1. The degree to which OPIC aggravated rather than alleviateu 

Government-to-Government conflict in cases of foreign investment disputes in other countries. 

2. The degree to which OPIC depended on congressional appropations and extended subsidized insurance premiums to private companies. 

3. The degree to which OPIC benefits the large enterprises of our country rather than the small businesses which are trying with limited resources to invest abroad; 

I am not totally satisfied on any of these issues. I found that OPIC insurance did sometimes alleviate Government-to-Government tension created by a disputed investment in another country and that this has been useful in some cases like Bolivia to our overall foreign policy.

Obviously, this is a two-edged sword since sometimes the fact that OPIC is involved makes these disputes more difficult as in Chile. 

But at least there are two edges, and there is some advantage for us at times governmentally in having this instrument available. 

I think you should know that I am not in favor of additional appropriations for OPIC for OPIC's reserves until these become necessary. At that time, I feel you should come to the Congress and request these appropriations, and we will make a decision at that time rather than handing over the money to you now before you actually need it.

In my view, even though your requests are based on what you construe to be past moneys owed to you, they are in fact highly arbitrary in terms of your actual needs, and therefore their appropriation must, I feel, await the time when there is a clearer case to be made. 

This is shown in the very fact that last year you were seeking, I think, some $72.5 million in appropriations for your reserves, and the 

Congress, I think, appropriated $25 million. So you have made up $25 million for your reserves, but now you are asking for $25 million. 

I think the Congress is not going to write any more blank checks ahead of time without full knowledge of the facts. I really think that this is a different reserve.

OPIC is different from a private insurance company; it is the full faith and credit of the Government that stands there, and I think it stands in a different situation than a private agency.

I am not satisfied yet that OPIC is making enough of an effort to meet the needs of the smaller businesses of this country, who really need a larger umbrella to bear the risks of investment in developing countries. I would like to see more efforts along these lines. 

For me, OPIC is fundamentally an instrument of our commercial policy abroad. I harbor no illusions about the great benefit OPIC is bestowing upon developing countries. 

It is a shield for our businesses against expropriation primarily in some of the world's less developed countries. The fundamental reason 

I think OPIC should continue to exist is to promote competition. 

Other industrialized countries have such a mechanism to help their business communities compete in the world economy, and my view is that we should have such a facility available to our business community.

So, I would not want to abolish OPIC. But I do want to see it promote competition by helping the little guy and not just the giants, and to operate as much as possible on a businesslike basis free of the public purse strings.

I found myself very much in agreement with the Church bill seeking to assure that OPIC begin to transform its activities into the mold of a reinsurer by beginning to transfer its portfolio over to private insurance agencies.

If this can be done, it will go a long way to take care of my concerns by reducing the dependence of OPIC on the public till, by reducing the Government exposure to political friction and public indebtedness, and by placing the operations on a more free market, competitive basis. 

I think you would make a very serious mistake to read from last week's votes in the Senate the conclusion that your mandate is one to go ahead with "business as usual."

I think there is solid sentiment in the Senate to turn the OPIC insurance program as much as possible as quickly as possible over to the private sector.

The key question is not whether but how-how to legislate that. The decision in the end was not to throw what you felt was a straitjacket on you which you said you couldn't live with of mandatory transfer of the portfolio under tight time constraints.

That decision was made by a one-vote margin which shows I think the degree to which the Senate does want to see some action on this even at the risk of putting you in a straitjacket. The ultimate decision was to curtail the 5-year authorization contained in the Church bill to 2 years. 

This was by a decisive vote of 53 to 37.

My own reading of this which I would strongly urge you to adopt as your own is that rather than having gotten off the hook, you are now on very clear notice to meet the 25-percent private insurer requirement on future OPIC insurance policies by the end of the 2-year authorization or run the definite risk of losing your authorization altogether. 

Because now you have gotten the free hand you asked for to carry out the will of the Senate and to meet the objectives of spreading the risks of OPIC insurance to the private sector which OPIC has said it agrees with.

If the Javits amendment 970 had not been agreed to, then, if you had not been able to meet the deadlines the Church bill contained, you could have said that the straitjacket imposed by the Congress kept you from it.

Now all the responsibility is on you to carry out what I think is a very clear mandate. 

I considered my votes on OPIC last week very carefully. I am pleased with the outcome. But I wouldn't want you to misread what the Senate decided.

And I do want you to know that I for one will be watching with great interest to see how the mandate of the Senate is carried out. 

Mr. MAYS. I appreciate those comments, Senator Chiles. 

I would like to assure you that we haven't misread that mandate.

If I can comment on your points in sort of reverse order, OPIC was taking these initiatives to involve private insurance and we were delighted to have the approval of both House and Senate and committees in our efforts to do so.

We did think that this specific provision in the Senate bill would have made it impossible to achieve greater private participation and we were therefore pleased that the Senate amended the bill in that respect.

You are indeed correct that it is our responsibility to get the maximum participation for private insurance companies and I think we will, just as we were able to get a larger participation each year from Lloyds of London. After 2 years of experience they are now willing to go into a 3-year contract with us, which was very significant because up until now they had only been willing to do 1 year at a time. 

We have been talking about a long-term insurance policy which is indeed necessary for an investor to make a long-term commitment. 

OPIC has been quite active in trying to get greater participation of smaller investors overseas to show them the potential of export markets and how they could increase those exports with some investment on their part.

These companies, of course, because of less staff and less financial resources, aren't as well equipped to make investment abroad as the large companies are which have been doing investment for many years abroad.

So, our assistance to them is important. I think in dollar terms they will continue to be a relatively small part but we will continue to do all we can and we welcome the amendment offered by Senator Kennedy on the floor of the Senate for OPIC to give preferential treatment to small businessmen in their efforts to invest abroad. 

I recall last year you asked some rather penetrating questions about claims settlements, I think with regard to the claims in Bolivia and in Chile.

I am not sure that I understood that you were concerned as to whether or not OPIC's insurance had in any case caused a confrontation between governments. I think that in all cases where we have insured investors against expropriation we have made a positive contribution toward helping that investor negotiate for compensation, avoid claims against OPIC, and helped to make those settlements possible.

If you have in mind anything in particular I will be glad to respond to that. 

Senator CHILES. I have several questions.

Could you give me a clear breakdown of how much of your coverage is for small and medium-size companies? If you cannot do it now, furnish it for the record. I would like to see some statistics on the percentage of your liabilities which are for the small insurer as opposed to the large and also the number. 

Mr. MAYS. This is the entire portfolio as of May 1973 of companies in the Fortune 500 and of course that is a fairly arbitrary cutoff. itself.

Fifty-eight percent of our coverage was to large companies and 

42 percent to companies smaller than the Fortune 500. In dollar terms, 71 percent was for the larger companies and 29 percent for the smaller companies.

In the last 6 months, in the period July to September of 1973, OPIC assisted 15 projects and 5 of the 15 fell into the small category; in the period October through December 1973, OPIC assisted 24 projects in 16 countries and 4 of these fell into the small category. 

Senator CHILES. Now that you have this flexibility is it your feeling that you are going to be able 2 years from now to meet the 25-percent target?

Mr. MAYS. I think we can, Senator. Our difficulty with meeting that under the bill as reported by the Foreign Relations Committee is the provision which was referred to as "sudden death" penalty. 

Our issuing authority would be terminated if we failed to achieve by January 1975 a 25 percent participation in expropriation and in convertibility coverage.

We were in the process of trying to negotiate with private insurance companies a division of the premium income paid by our customers and a division of the risk.

Obviously, you want some relationship between the division of the premium and the division of the risk. It is understandable also that the private insurance companies coming into a program like this for the first time on an experimental basis would like to get as much premium and as little risk as possible.

If we were in a situation where we would go out of business at the end of the year unless we accepted their terms, any agreement we reached with them would, I think, have to be suspect in that we were under duress to reach an agreement. Now that we are not under duress 

I think we can reach a fair division and we can continue to get some competitive elements involved so that we can assure that we are not paying too much for their participation.

QUESTIONS SUBMITTED BY SENATOR BROOKE 

Question. Do you anticipate making further requests for appropriations after this year?

Answer. We do not anticipate any future requests to augment reserves. The only appropriation requests which I envisage in the future would be made to replenish the reserves if they were drawn down significantly as a result of large claim payments.

Question. What was OPIC's claim situation in 1971 when you took over the program from A.I.D.?

Answer. When we were set up in 1971, we had some $400 million in claims pending primarily on Chile contracts which we inherited from A.I.D. 

Question. What is your claim situation today?

Answer. I am pleased to say that this situation has been dramatically reversed. 

At the end of 1973 we only had 7 outstanding claims for about $27 million. Early in 1974 one investor withdrew its claim for $9 million. In addition, we have reasons to believe that negotiations between the Government of Chile and an OPIC-insured copper company will soon result in settlement of a major pending claim case of $14 million. This would leave only 5 claims outstanding totalling about $4 million.

Question. How were you able to reduce the claims from over $400 million down to just a few million dollars today? 

Answer. As of December 31, 1973, OPIC in its first three years settled 32 claims amounting to over $120 million to the satisfaction of the insured, either through cash payments or through the issuance of OPIC guaranties backing host government commitments. This represents nearly three times the number of claim settlements by OPIC's predecessor agencies during the prior 23 years of the investment insurance program. OPIC has denied 2 claims totaling $246 million because the companies did not maintain effective coverage, or failed to comply with several requirements of the OPIC contract. Several claims have been withdrawn, and as I indicated earlier, only a few remain today. 

Senator, I think the key to OPIC's success, first and foremost, has been an ability to attract highly professional personnel. In negotiations with investors and local governments, we have shown a willingness to experiment and try out innovative settlements. It has required a fine mixture of flexibility on the one hand, and toughness in negotiations on the other. Our claims experience has shown that the basic contract of insurance between OPIC and the investor is sound.

Question. In what specific cases are you susceptible to large claims? What are you doing to counteract the possibility that claims may occur in such areas as Jamaica?

Answer. Our largest current exposure, taking A.I.D. and OPIC portfolios together, are in Jamaica ($479 million), Dominican Republic ($203 million), Chile ($168 million), and Korea ($165 million). In all countries where there are significant investments, we have instituted a project monitoring system. OPIC officers visit these large projects and we have senior management reviews of such projects periodically in Washington in consultation with the companies involved. At present we have only a few investment situations which we consider to be in the possible claim stage. These projects have a total dollar value of less than $29 million.

You mentioned Jamaica. Its Governments have repeatedly reaffirmed respect for property rights, noted the value of foreign direct investment. and actively sought additional foreign investment. We have no reason at this time to believe there will be claims in that country. As I suggested earlier, such investments would fall under the purview of OPIC's project monitoring system. 

Question. During recent Senate consideration of your authorizing legislation, the allegation was made that the OPIC program creates a potential for government-to-government confrontations. Have any such confrontations arisen as OPIC has worked out claim adjustments, particularly in Chile? 

Answer. I am glad you asked that question, Senator. The argument seems to be based on logic-that is, the financial stake of the U.S. through insurance would produce a greater involvement. In fact however, the weight of evidence from our claim experience supports just the opposite conclusion. 

OPIC has paid or settled nearly 20 claims in Chile without any governmentto-government confrontation. Any confrontations that arose involved major Anaconda and Kennecott equity holdings not insured by OPIC. Indeed, witnesses

before the Senate Subcommittee on Multinational Corporations and the Hous Subcommittee on Foreign Economic Policy testified that one of OPIC's principai benefits is that it provides a practical mechanism for resolving investment disputes without directly involving the U.S. Government. 

Our experience has shown that insurance has helped to depoliticize disputes and focus attention on financial matters. Our insurance contract with the investor requires investors to pursue negotiations on their own with the local government, gives OPIC access to company records, and puts us in a position of being able to have an important influence on settlements. 

Question. Please review for the Committee OPIC's earnings since you were formerly organized in 1971, versus the claims you have actually paid out. 

Answer. Since 1971, we have earned about $86 million after administrative expenses, and we have paid claims totaling about $28 million. Over the life of the program, the financial record is even more impressive. Total earnings including interest and premiums have been $207 million. Net claims paid (not including settlements guaranteed by OPIC in the amount of $90 million) and estimated administrative expenses have been about $46 million, resulting in net receipts to the U.S. Government of over $161 million. 

Question. Some members of the Congress are concerned about the payment of claims out of appropriated funds. Section 235 (d) of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, as amended, states that all insurance claims payable by OPIC are to be "paid first out of the Insurance Reserve, as long as such reserve remains available, and thereafter out of funds made available pursuant to section 235 (f).” 

Have you complied fully with this provision? If not, can you provide a legal basis for not doing so? 

Answer. Yes, Senator, we have fully complied with the express language of the statute. The Insurance Reserve referred to in section 235(d) is made up of both income of the Corporation and appropriations. The funds appropriated in 1974 have been allocated by OPIC's Board to the Insurance Reserve pursuant to the next to last sentence of 235 (c). Hence, these funds are available for the payment of adjudicated claims along with other funds in the Reserve. 

There is no requirement in OPIC's statute that OPIC pay claims out of corporate income in the Insurance Reserve before using appropriated funds in the Reserve. This used to be the rule under the A.I.D. program, but Congress changed this in 1969 when OPIC's enabling legislation was passed. Unlike A.I.D., OPIC is permitted to invest its revenues in U.S. obligations and it makes good business sense for OPIC which is enjoined by Congress to be businesslike in its operations, to preserve its premium income for investment purposes where possible. 

As you know, Senator, appropriations made in FY 1973 and FY 1974 and the appropriation requested in FY 1975 are to restore to OPIC's reserve premiums which were transferred to other Federal programs. Consequently, on both legal annd logical grounds these appropriations should be regarded as properly usable in paying claims.

Question. Although the legislation recently passed by the Senate involves your authorization rather than appropriations, please briefly review your efforts to achieve private insurance participation in your program. 

Answer. We started to investigate ways in which we could secure private participation in the program as soon as OPIC was created in 1971. Initially, we were unsuccessful in our discussions with U.S. insurance companies, so we turned to Lloyd's of London with whom we negotiated a quota-share reinsurance contract for calendar year 1972 amounting to about $8 million per country. Subsequently, we increased this quota-share reinsurance protection to $14 million per country for calendar year 1973. The experience with Lloyd's was quite favorable and based on this experience Lloyd's agreed to significantly expand its reinsurance coverage for 1974. We now have a three-year Lloyd's commitment to pay 

45% of OPIC losses, up to $18.25 million per country and $54.75 million globally.

Meanwhile we have been negotiating with several U.S. companies who have expressed some interest in establishing a joint public/private direct underwriting consortium for expropriation and inconvertibility risks. We are pursuing these negotiations.

Question. What are the prospects for negotiating with additional private insurers in the near future?

Answer. If Congress provides us with the necessary enabling legislation I am quite hopeful we will be able to carry this experiment forward. Long-term political risks never have been underwritten in the U.S. insurance market, and

consequently, we will need flexible legislative authority so that we can encourage broad participation by U.S. insurance companies. 

Question. There now exist important public policy objectives in the OPIC programs. Projects must assist in the economic development of poor countries. In addition, they must be helpful to the U.S. balance-of-payments and not harm domestic labor interests. How do you propose to retain these public policy objectives as private insurers participate in your program? 

Answer. An experimental approach is required for us to test U.S. Governmentprivate working relationships. I am pleased to say that the Senate recognized this when it adopted the amendment offered by Senator Javits. The proposal we have discussed up to now with the private insurers envisages that OPIC would manage the program under a management contract with the private association. 

OPIC would maintain policy controls over the underwriting through direct participation in the consortium and through reinsurance of the consortium itself. 

Question. Can you describe for the Committee the process by which you evaluate whether or not a project is a success or a failure? What quantitative or qualitative criteria do you use to make this determination?

Answer. We evaluate our programs and investments which we assist, in several ways: (1) We have a project monitoring committee which reviews the large projects in our portfolio each year and OPIC case officers make on-site visits to these projects periodically. With your permission, I would like to place in the record at this point, a copy of the questionnaire which OPIC officers complete on projects which they visit. (Information retained in committee files.) (2) From time-to-time we sponsor research on a sampling of projects in our portfolio. For example, in 1972 we had Harbridge House study the economic effects of a sample of 20 private investments on the four developing countries in which they were located and on the U.S. balance of payments. The study looked at the efficiency of the projects with respect to labor-intensity, national value added, cost effectiveness; the extent to which the ventures contribute to local capital development, including local ownership, reinvestment of profits, integration in the local economy, etc. At this point I request that an Executive Summary of this study be placed in the record. (Information retained in committee files.) (3) We also evaluate the overall effects of the OPIC insurance program. For example, recently we asked the Harvard Business School to review the U.S. economic effects of U.S. private investment in the less developed countries. In sum, this report found that U.S. manufacturing operations in less developed countries had a net positive effect in 1970 on the U.S. balance of payments of approximately $820 million and a net positive effect on U.S. employment of about 120,000 jobs. (4) We seek to assure, when we first approve a project, that it will have a strong development impact and that it will not harm the U.S. economy. With your permission, we would place in the record a copy of our development effects guidelines. (Information retained in committee files.) 

Our insurance portfolio is composed of some 1,500 projects in 73 countries. 

It would be uneconomic for us to re-evaluate each and every investment in our portfolio. Thus, from time to time, we sample the private investments in the portfolio as was done with the Harbridge House study a year and one half ago. 

As is true of insurers generally, we do not normally make assessments of the commercial success or failure of projects which we insure because we are liable only for the political risks of the project. 

Our finance portfolio is much smaller-31 projects in 11 countries. There we are concerned with commercial, managerial and financial factors, both at the time of our decision to invest and throughout the period of our loan. We receive regular financial reports from each of the OPIC-financed projects and visit them occassionally.

Question. I have already mentioned the new important public policy objectives for OPIC that are contained in the recent Senate legislation. Have you done any thinking as to how you will determine whether or not you are fulfilling these objectives? If so, can you describe in detail how you will do so?

Answer. Well Senator, with respect to the private participation guidelines contained in the Javits amendment which was adopted, I believe it will be a rea-

sonably clear-cut percentage test. We either will or will not achieve the goals. 

As to the mandates to provide preferential consideration for small business and for the least developed countries, we have not had an opportunity yet to develop any new criteria, in addition to our existing policies, which we would use to measure our success in achieving the legislative mandates. When this is finally adopted, we will, of course develop guidelines in an effort to fulfill these objectives.

PREPARED STATEMENT 

Senator INOUYE. You may proceed, sir. Thank you.

[The statement follows:] 

Mr. Chairman, I am John M. Thomas, Assistant Secretary of State for Administration. I appreciate this opportunity to appear before your Committee to present our 1975 request for funds for Administrative and Other Expenses, State Department.

The funds requested in this appropriation item cover the cost of four activities administered by the Department of State. They finance the salaries and operating expenses of the United States Mission to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (USNATO) in Brussels, Belgium; the United States Mission to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (USOECD) in Paris, France; the staff responsible for administering the Mutual Defense Assistance Control Act; and the staff responsible for administering the Military Assistance and Arms 

Sales Supervision activity.

The United States Mission to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and the United States Mission to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development are responsible for the direction, coordination and administration of the United States policy and activities related to the international organizations. 

The staff responsible for administering the Mutual Defense Assistance Control Act is concerned with prevention of the shipment of strategic items to nations threatening the security of the United States. They recommend to the Secretary of State, who is administrator of the Mutual Defense Assistance Control Act, commodities to be included on the Battle Act list, report on shipments, coordinate the activities of other United States agencies concerned with security trade controls, and conduct bilateral and multilateral negotiations. 

The primary function of the Military Assistance Arms Sales Supervision staff is to ensure continuing foreign policy control and coordination over the level and character of worldwide United States military assistance and sales program. 

Mr. Chairman, for these activities we are requesting an appropriation of $5,370,000 for Fiscal Year 1975. This represents a reduction of $530,000 below the $5,900,000 transmitted in the President's January budget. This reduction is a result of actions we are taking this year and plan for next to curtail expenses to the amount approved for these activities for 1974. To achieve these reductions we are deferring controllable 1974 expenses and reducing the previously authorized staff.

The 1975 request for $5.3 million represents an increase of $570,000 above the 

1974 appropriation and an increase of $440,600 over the estimated availability for 1974. This increase is requested to maintain the 1974 level of operations during 

1975. It will provide for statutory salary and benefit increases, overseas operating expense increases resulting from inflation and full staffing of the reduced number of authorized positions.

Mr. Chairman, that completes my prepared statement. I will be pleased to answer any questions you and your Committee may have regarding our request for 1975 funds. With your permission, Mr. Chairman, because of the diverse activities financed by this appropriation, I should like to ask that my colleagues here with me who are the Department's principal officers concerned with each of these activities assist me in providing any information the Committee may desire. 

TRANSFER OF ACTIVITIES TO  

Senator INOUYE. In our fiscal 1974 report the Senate Appropriations Committee stated:

The committee believes that these activities have no place in the foreign assistance appropriation bill and urges that they be transferred to the budget of the Department of State in fiscal year 1975. 

It appears from our session this morning that this committee has very little influence with the Department. Can you tell us why these miscellaneous agencies have not been transferred to the regular State 

Department budget? 

Mr. THOMAS. If I may, Mr. Chairman, I would like to say that we are in complete agreement with your position and would have no objection whatsoever to having this transferred to the Department of State appropriation. However, we need the concurrence, sir, of six congressional committees. We have discussed this with these committees, we will continue to do so and we would hope that we can effect this transfer to the Department of State. 

Senator INOUYE. Would you just enlighten us as to why certain committees in the Congress would prefer to have this in the aid bill? 

Mr. MURRAY. Mr. Chairman, I am not certain that I can speak for each one of those committees. However, if I may go back into the past, back in 1962 or 1963 the State Department did propose this transfer from the foreign assistance bill into the State Department's regular Appropriation Act. It was proposed by a transfer in the appropriations. The Foreign Assistance Committee naturally did not hear it because it was not presented to them. The House and Senate appropriations subcommittees on the regular State bill failed to pick it up and the entire appropriation was lost. There was action taken in the 

Senate to save the situation that would have been created by that loss. 

We now would like to have the State Department's subcommittees in the House and Senate agree to let us move this over as a single item or merge it within the appropriation structure. We would also have to present it to each of the authorizing committees since all of our appropriations are now under prior authorization. The committee staffs in my discussions with them have indicated to me that they didn't wish us to try this; that is, transfer to the regular State committees, this year. 

I can only conclude that since there were changes taking place in those subcommittees, that there would be confusion if the effort to effect the transfer occurred in 1975.

Senator INOUYE. Do you find any resistance on the part of Congress to bring about this change? 34-192 O 74 - 12

Mr. MURRAY. I have not found that resistance in the Senate except the suggestion made by one of the staff members who is no longer with the committee that this should not be done this year. I would like to say, sir, that we agree completely with what Mr. Thomas said. We will make every effort in 1976.

LAOS, CAMBODIA, AND VIETNAM

ECONOMIC ASSISTANCE VERSUS MILITARY

the Department and the executive branch the need for military assistance in this particular year is just as great as it was in past years.
