MUTUAL DEFENSE ASSISTANCE CONTROL ACT 

Senator CHILES. I see in the prepared statement it says:

The staff responsible for administering the Mutual Defense Assistance Control Act is concerned with prevention of the shipment of strategic items to nations threatening the security of the United States. They recommend to the Secretary of State, who is administrator of the Mutual Defense Assistance Control Act, commodities to be included on the Battle Act list. 

What about technical know-how? We have been questioning some witnesses about Poland seeking the latest in computer technology and third generation computers that we are manufacturing-not only seeking it but also seeking loans through the Export-Import Bank and others to finance this equipment. Would this fall within the items of strategic nature? 

Mr. THOMAS. Senator, if I may, I will ask Mr. Wright from that office to answer your question.

STRATEGIC TRADE CONTROL PROGRAM 

Mr. WRIGHT. The so-called Battle Act list is, as you know, a list of arms, ammunition, implements of war and equipment necessary to make these goods. It is matched by an international list that also includes strategic items. The international list as well as the Battle Act list covers as well the technology for the production of items that are covered on the strategic list. So the purpose and effect of the strategic trade control program is to control not only the hardware and end items but the important technology for their production. 

Mr. CHILES. Well, specifically then into computers they can be used certainly and are used in guidance systems and missile tracking systems in offensive and defensive weaponry today as well as having commercial uses. Are they included on the Battles Act list?

Mr. WRIGHT. Yes, they are, as well as quite a range of components and peripheral equipment that is associated with advanced computers. 

Senator CHILES. Can you tell me whether this agency was asked to make a recommendation or made any recommendation with regard to the request by the Poles seeking computer equipment? 

Mr. WRIGHT. Yes, we have been. That case is under active consideration still and there has not been a decision made on it. Like so many problems that arise in this area it has a civilian side and a potential military side and it is very difficult to draw the line on what would be a permissible and a safe industrial facility without running some

risk of its being used for military purposes. This is the point at issue certainly in the case that you refer to and there are different views on this matter but it is still under active consideration. 

Senator CHILES. Who has the different views?

Mr. WRIGHT. The case involves American companies so that the resolution and decision that would be made on it would be made by the Department of Commerce since it is a U.S. export licensing decision. 

Senator CHILES. The Department of Commerce is going to make the final decision on something as to whether it is or is not in the best interest of the strategic defense of the United States? 

Mr. WRIGHT. Yes, the Department of Commerce would make that decision under the Export Administration Act which of course sets standards for decisions on exports that might have an impact on the national security. Of course whatever is done by the Department of 

Commerce in making a decision on an American case of that kind has to take full account of the international obligations that we have in the Coordinating Committee organization and the international list to which I referred and to the judgment of the strategic character of the equipment and technology in the Battle Act list so that we certainly hope and expect that whatever decision is made by the Department of Commerce will be fully consistent with the Battle Act list. 

Senator CHILES. I can't understand that answer.

Would that answer mean then that if the Battle Act listed this kind of third generation computer equipment then the Department of Commerce would not be able to make that kind of a decision if it was listed as being a strategic item?

Mr. WRIGHT. The presumption would be that they would not but the fact is that the international strategic control system does provide for the possibility of exceptional shipments of goods and technology when it can be demonstrated that they are for civilian purposes and when adequate safeguards can be attached to the particular transaction. So it is not quite a black and white situation in that the inclusion of an item on strategic control list does not necessarily mean that a decision could not be made to permit the transaction involving those items. There is a qualitative factor and a judgmental factor that does apply in the area but the presumption certainly is that if the goods or technology are on the list the transaction would not take place. 

Senator CHILES. But the waiver and the exceptions with the safeguards, if they felt that could be done, that still can be done by Commerce if Commerce has the ultimate authority?

Mr. WRIGHT. Well, it could be done by Commerce if Commerce decided after consulting with us and with Defense and with the other agencies that they normally advise with on these matters and if everyone agreed that it was a desirable transaction, then it would be necessary for the U.S. Government to go to our colleagues in the coordinating committee organization, present the case and our justification for it and find out whether they agree with that. We could not go forward with the U.S. transaction until we had received the concurrence and the support of the other 14 members of this international organization if the technology involved strategic items. 

Senator CHILES. Thank you. 

Senator INOUYE. Mr. Secretary and gentlemen, I thank you very much for your assistance. 

Mr. THOMAS. Thank you very much.

Senator INOUYE. Our next witness is Mr. Howard H. Palmatier, Director of the Cuban refugee program.

The fiscal year 1975 request for this program is $60 million which is $69 million less than the amount appropriated for fiscal year 1974. 

PREPARED STATEMENT 

Mr. Palmatier, we are very pleased to have you with us. Your statement will be inserted in the record at this point in total. 

[The statement follows:]

Mr. Chairman and Members of the Committee, I am pleased to have this opportunity to appear before you again to present the appropriation request for the Cuban Refugee Program. 

An appropriation of $60 million is requested for fiscal year 1975 $69 million less than the $129 million appropriated for the current fiscal year. There are three principal reasons for the decrease: 

First is the renewal of our proposal to phase down the reimbursements to States for financial and medical assistance for needy Cuban refugees. 11 Second is the first full-year effect of the program of Supplemental Security Income (SSI) for the Aged, Blind, and Disabled which began January 

1, 1974. The SSI program includes needy aged, blind, and disabled Cuban refugees, and therefore the Cuban Refugee Program is no longer responsible for financial assistance to these refugees. 

Third is the continued effect of the termination of the Cuban refugee airlift on April 6, 1973. Without the substantial, continuing influx of new refugees to Miami via the airlift, reductions have occurred in the need for welfare and medical assistance. 

As you will recall, last year we proposed a phasedown in the Refugee Program which was scheduled to begin last July 1. This proposal was in response to a Congressional recommendation that "the Executive Branch exert every effort in bringing about the termination of this program as soon as reasonably possible"l/ a recommendation with which the Department concurred. 11

However, Congress took action in the Continuing Resolution for fiscal year 1974 to continue the Cuban Refugee Program at the 1973 funding level, and the Department responded to the Congressional intent by suspending 

1 Conference Report, Foreign Assistance Appropriations; Report No. 

92-849, February 23, 1972, p. 7.

the phaseout pending further action by the Congress. took final action on the 1974 appropriation nonphaseout level of $129 million 

After Congress funding the program at the the Department again responded to the Congressional intent by suspending the phaseout until the end of the present fiscal year.

The Department continues to believe that it is appropriate to begin phasing down the Cuban Refugee Program, in light of the termination of the Cuban refugee airlift nearly a year ago and the fact that the vast majority of Cuban refugees are self-supporting and paying Federal, State, and local taxes on the same basis as other residents of the communities in which they live.

We believe that the emergency situation which gave rise to the Cuban Refugee Program and to the special Federal assistance to States and localities has passed, and that the proposed phasedown presents an orderly means of reducing and terminating the program. 

The phasedown plan which we expect to begin next July 1 is similar to the plan developed last year, with these differences: (1) It will be starting a year later than originally proposed. This means that State welfare agencies and the Dade County, Florida, Public Schools will have received one additional year of Federal Refugee Program assistance on a nonphaseout basis. (2) We have adjusted slightly upward the proposed assistance to the Dade County Public Schools for 1975 as compared with the phaseout plan which was submitted to the school system a year ago. 

Phasedown in Welfare Reimbursements to States The major points of the welfare phasedown plan are as follows: 

1. Beginning July 1, 1974, this program will no longer reimburse

States for refugee assistance cases in which the head of the family has been in the United States for 5 years or more. Their needs will be met from the regular Federal/State and State/local

welfare programs. An exception to one aspect of this policy will enable the State of Florida to continue to be reimbursed 100 percent from the Cuban Refugee Program for financial and medical assistance required by those needy refugees, without regard to their length of residence in this country, who are not eligible for assistance under either the SSI program or the federally aided program of Aid to Families with Dependent Children (AFDC). These are the so-called "General Assistance" type cases which in Florida only the Department plans to exempt from the 5-year policy during fiscal year 1975. This exemption is designed to offset the impact which would otherwise fall on locally financed assistance programs in Florida, where approximately half of the Nation's Cuban refugees are located. The possible continuation of this exemption during fiscal year 1976 and 1977 will be reviewed annually by the Department. 

2. Although responsibility for financial assistance to needy aged, blind, and disabled refugees was transferred to the SSI program when it began January 1, 1974, the Refugee Program has continued to reimburse States for medical assistance to refugee recipients of SSI. Under the phaseout plan, such reimbursements would be made only on behalf of those refugees who had been in the U.S. less than 5 years. 3.

All reimbursements from the Cuban Refugee Program would terminate by June 30, 1977.

This plan for reducing the costs of the Cuban Refugee Program is based on the minimum amount of time that it takes a person to become a citizen of the United States. It retains the Federal role of reimbursing the States for assistance to those refugees who have been here less than 

5 years, and would require States and localities to include under the regular programs those who have been here more than 5 years. In the AFDC

and Medicaid programs, there would still be substantial Federal funding although not from the Refugee Program 11 for those refugee recipients over the 5-year mark since these are Federal-State programs. Those needy refugees over 5 years in the U.S. who do not fall into the categories of 

SSI, AFDC, or Medicaid would have to be assisted under the so-called "General Assistance" programs which are financed entirely from State and/or local funds. An important exception, of course, is made for General 

Assistance in Florida, which would continue to be funded by the Cuban Refugee Program, at least during 1975, regardless of a refugee's length of residence. This exception is planned in recognition of the fact that so many of the refugees live in Florida, and especially in Dade County. 

The projected final termination date of the program on June 30, 1977, means that the special Federal assistance will have been continued for more than 4 years after the final flight of the refugee airlift on April 6, 1973.

We believe this to be a fair and reasonable plan for reducing and terminating the Cuban Refugee Program. While it does require additional expenditures by States and localities, these are no more than are required in the regular domestic assistance programs for citizens and other aliens. 

In light of the self-supporting status of the vast majority of the Cuban refugees, and the fact that they are paying taxes on the same basis as everyone else, we find it difficult to justify the continuation, on a nonphaseout basis, of special Federal refugee assistance to States and localities.

Phasedown in Aid to Dade County Public Schools 

In our appropriation request for fiscal year 1974, we proposed $10.4 million for assistance to the Dade County Public Schools to help offset the cost of educating Cuban refugee children and to help provide support for special staff and materials.

This amount represented a reduction of

20 percent from the base of $13 million budgeted for fiscal year 1973. 

Under the plan proposed last year, a reduction of 20 percent per year until the final termination date of June 30, 1977 was anticipated.

The Congressional action on the 1974 appropriation added $2 million for assistance to the Dade County Public Schools, raising the amount from $10.4 to $12.4 million.

In developing the 1975 appropriation request, the Department considered that a reduction from $12.4 million in 1974 to $7.8 million anticipated for 1975 in the original phaseout plan

Therefore we have included $8.5 million in the present budget request for assistance to the Dade County Public schools, an increase of $700,000 over the previously planned phaseout amount for 1975. 

As in the case of welfare reimbursements to the States, we believe that this reduction in aid to the Dade County Public Schools is fully Justified by the fact that most Cuban refugees in Dade County are fully self-supporting and tax-paying members of the community. 

Cost of Phasedown to States and/or Localities 

If the phasedown were not scheduled to go into effect July 1, we estimate that a total of approximately $104 million would be required for the CRP in fiscal year 1975 rather than the $60 million actually being requested. The additional $44 million would include $40 million for welfare reimbursements to the States and nearly $4 million which would be required if aid to the Dade County Public Schools were to be maintained at the 1974 level.

Of the $40 million reduction in welfare reimbursements due to the phasedown, it is estimated that approximately $25 million would be met from State and/or local funds, and the balance of $15 million from Federal financial participation under the regular programs of Aid to

Mr. Chairman, I would like to address myself briefly to each of the major activities of the program. 

In recognition of the changes which have occurred in the refugee situation 

the end of the airlift, the resulting decrease in resettlement activities, and the inclusion of most refugees in Medicaid-type health services as the result of a Federal court action in Florida last year we have organized our presentation under three major activities this year rather than the six activities identified in previous years. 

These three activities are: (1) Welfare Assistance and Services (which includes health); (2) Education; and (3) Other Services (which includes program services and administration and the services of the voluntary resettlement agencies). 

The activity in previous years entitled Movement of Refugees from Cuba, which covered funds transferred to the Department of State for the airlift, has of course been eliminated, and we have proposed deletion from the Appropriation Act of the language which related to this activity. 

The reductions which are indicated in all activities of the program in 1975 are the result of the three principal factors cited previously the phasedown proposal, the full-year effect of the SSI program, and the fact that the refugee airlift terminated.

Costs budgeted for these types of training were reduced by more than 10 percent between 1973 and 1974, and a further reduction of 20 percent is estimated between 1974 and 1975, due primarily to a more stabilized Cuban refugee population because of fewer new arrivals.

Activity 3: Other Services 

This activity covers Federal direction and day-to-day operation of the program, including a variety of services for newly arriving refugees und for those already in the U.S. Provision is made for reception services for new refugees, as necessary, and for placing continued emphasis on training and employment and arrangements for other services to help overcome barriers to self-support as effectively as possible. Also included under this activity are the services provided by the voluntary resettlement agencies.

Beginning with the interruptions in the airlift and following its termination, substantial reductions have been made in this activity, including substantial decreases in the staff of the Cuban Refugee Program and in the activities of the resettlement agencies.

1974 to $1.7 million in 1975 a decrease of 37 percent. 

Mr. Chairman, I cannot close without noting again this year the excellent record which the Cuban refugees as a group have established for themselves in the United States. Almost all reached this country in a state of complete destitution, deprived of all possessions and resources by the Cuban government, and many after suffering several years of forced labor and harassment by the authorities in Cuba. The fact that the vast majority are self-supporting, tax-paying residents of this country is a tribute to their considerable skills, determination, and initiative.

STATUS OF PHASEDOWN PLANS 

Mr. Chairman, as you will recall, last year we proposed a phasedown which was scheduled to begin last July 1. We sincerely believed that this proposal was in response to a conference committee recommendation that "the executive branch exert every effort in bringing about the termination of this program as soon as reasonably possible' mendation with which the Department concurred. -a recom- Subsequent to that, however, in the continuing resolution for 1974 and in the final appropriation, Congress took action to postpone the phaseout. An additional sum was appropriated, and the Department again responded to the congressional intent by postponing the phaseout throughout fiscal year 1974. We continue to believe, however, that it is appropriate to begin phasing down the program in light of the termination of the airlift nearly a year ago and the fact that the vast majority of Cuban refugees are self-supporting and paying Federal, State, and local taxes on the same basis as other residents of the communities in which they live. That is, we believe that the emergency situation which led to the creation of the Cuban refugee program and to the special Federal assistance to States and localities has passed, and that the proposed phasedown presents an orderly means of reducing the program and terminating it on June 30, 1977. 

As you will note from the prepared statement, the phasedown plan which we expect to begin next July 1 is similar to the plan developed last year; that is, the Cuban refugee program would discontinue reimbursements to the States for those refugee assistance cases in which the head of the family has been in the United States for 5 years or more. This would mean that these cases would be included under the regular welfare programs which are partially-or, in the case of general assistance, entirely-dependent on State and local funding.

We would once again recommend an exception for general assistance-type cases in Florida, which would continue to be fully funded by the Cuban refugee program at least during 1975 in order to avoid an undue impact on locally financed assistance programs, particularly in Dade County where approximately half of all Cuban refugees are located. We would also begin a phasedown in fiscal 1975 in assistance to the Dade County public schools. And we would recommend the complete termination of the refugee program by June 30, 1977.

IMPACT OF CUBAN REFUGEE INFLUX 

I have done a little studying and I gather that the rationale for this program is a rather simple one; that as a result of national policy the sudden influx of refugees has caused the economic dislocation and disruption of certain communities primarily in Florida. 

Mr. PALMATIER. That is very true, Senator.

Senator INOUYE. And it was felt that these communities should be compensated; otherwise, they would have to carry this unusually high burden.

IMPACT OF ASIAN IMMIGRANTS IN HAWAII 

Senator INOUYE. I am just wondering if this rationale could be applied to another rather similar situation. As you know, a few years ago the Congress of the United States and the administration amended the immigration and naturalization laws taking away the quota system and thereby making it possible for increased immigration activity from Asia. We have noted in recent years that, as a result of this liberalization of the laws, Hawaii has had to play host to most of the 

Asian immigrants.

The immigration has been disproportionately very high in Hawaii and as a result we have had to bear a disproportionately high financial burden, such as medical costs, because even with all of the sophisticated examinations that we conduct overseas before a person is permitted in we find that after a few months these immigrants do come up with Hansen's disease, for example. Then the State of Hawaii becomes obligated to carry the burden of care and treatment. If you would visit our Hansen's Disease Hospital you will notice that a large segment of the patients are recent immigrants.

We also find that our welfare requirements have been further increased because of economic problems. In the event of an economic crisis as we have today, unemployment becomes commonplace. The first to become unemployed are the recent arrivals. So we, in Hawaii, must bear the burden of providing unemployment compensation and welfare payments. 

Do you think that the Cuban refugee assistance rationale could be applied to the Hawaii immigration situation to justify a special request for compensation by the State of Hawaii? Please bear in mind that it was a national policy that brought about this increased Hawaii immigration.

Mr. PALMATIER. I cannot respond specifically to the situation in 

Hawii, Senator, and I don't know if the persons coming there came on the basis of the regular Immigration Act and therefore there was supposed to be an affidavit of support involved which would assure, to a certain extent, that they not become a public charge, or whether they came as refugees.

With respect to the total question, I would give a personal opinion. 

Based on the sum of 20-odd years that I have been involved in refugee work since the end of World War II, I personally have always had the feeling that if a government-be it ours, be it Germany, be it Austria, or any other country-makes the decision to provide political asylum, if that is the case, for a group of individuals, then it should be equally prepared to provide them with the necessities of life once they are accepted.

In general response to your question about impact, and that is what you are discussing, I certainly feel that if in any situation the impact on a local community or a State as a result of an immigration policy places an overburden on the State or locality, that that State or locality should be assisted, as was the case in the Cuban refugee situation. 

Senator INOUYE. Thank you very much, sir.

CUBAN REFUGEES ENTERING THE UNITED STATES FROM SPAIN 

Will you please advise the committee of the circumstances under which Cuban refugees who sought asylum in Spain were recently brought to the United States? My first question, how many were there? 

Mr. PALMATIER. I am not trying to be evasive, Mr. Chairman, but as you know in HEW we are responsible for refugees only after they are admitted to the United States legally by the Immigration Service and by the Department of State, and therefore I am not familiar as an expert with the Cubans and the situation of the Cubans in this thing. 

I would talk to it generally, however, because I do have some knowledge.

There has been, since the takeover by Castro in Cuba, a steady movement of Cubans from Cuba to Spain via commercial aircraft. Likewise, there has been a consistent movement of Cubans from Spain and several other points-such as Mexico-to the United States. This has been going on since 1959. The movement was relatively free prior to 1968 when the provisions of the new Immigration Act went into effect which placed for the first time a numerical limitation on the number of persons in the Western Hemisphere who could enter the United States. This resulted in a buildup of the Cuban refugee population in Spain. I think that at the present time the estimates are that it is somewhere in the neighborhood of 25,000 persons. 

RECENT POLICY ON ADMITTING REFUGEES FROM SPAIN RELATES PRIMARILY TO TIMING 

It is further my understanding that all of these persons would have eventually come in. I believe a high percentage of them are relatives, many first degree, Cubans who have become American citizens. I understand further that the situation of the Cubans in Spain was desperate in the sense that it is quite difficult to obtain work there and that a large amount of money, dollars, was flowing from the United States, from relatives here, to Spain to assist in the support of the Cubans who were still there.

I believe the rationale in expanding the program to bring them in in a 1-year period-rather than the 2or the 22-year period that would normally be required to bring them in-was on the basis of these factors, and one of them certainly was the dollar outflow, that the Departments of State and Justice made the decision to bring them in within a 12-month period. We in the Cuban refugee program do not normally become involved with these people after they have come. The majority of them are joining relatives here. They have to meet the requirements that any normal immigrant does in passing the physical and having an affidavit of support provided either by a family or church group involved with their movement to the United States. 

Only in those instances when through no one's fault the affidavit. breaks down--perhaps a catastrophic illness or something of that type hits the relative who had provided the affidavit-would we become involved. There has been very, very little impact on our program as a result of the movement of Cubans from Spain to the United Statesbut with respect to specific statistics and so on, Mr. Chairman, I don't have them because we are not directly involved.

Senator INOUYE. Then you are not able to respond to a question such as who made the decision?

Mr. PALMATTER. It would have to be the Secretary of State and the 

Attorney General. It is required by the law. 

Senator INOUYE. I believe you were in Spain recently, were you not? 

Mr. PALMATIER. Yes, about a year ago. 

Senator INOUYE. Did you investigate the Cuban problem then?

Mr. PALMATIER. I assisted the Department of State in this-in terms of the types of persons who were there, age groups, their capacity to obtain employment in Spain, or their lack of capacity, as well as their employment potential in the U.S., also in terms of the other point I mentioned on the outflow of dollars. 

Senator INOUYE. Was the Spanish Government seriously taking up their responsibility as we are for their refugees? 

Mr. PALMATIER. I think the Spanish Government was expending some moneys in their behalf but not to the same extent that we provide assistance to those to whom we grant asylum. No, definitely not. 

FINAL PHASEOUT OF CUBAN REFUGEE PROGRAM 

Senator INOUYE. Final question. Are you satisfied that this program can be phased down by June 30, 1977?

Mr. PALMATIER. I am satisfied that it can be phased out if conditions remain relatively normal with respect to current influx. If something should happen and we would have another large influx of Cuban refugees to the United States of the magnitude experienced under the airlift, I think we would all have to reconsider the phaseout or if something should happen and large numbers of Cubans might become unemployed, because, as you mentioned, it is true in some instances that when there is unemployment, the most recently employed are the first who lose their positions. However, as we see the situation-and we can see it only in terms that now exist-we believe that the program can be phased out.

When we talk about phasing out the Cuban refugee program, Mr. 

Chairman, I would not want to be misleading. This does not mean that you are not going to continue to spend money on the Cuban refugees, it does. It merely means that the Cuban refugee program is going to be spending less money. It does not necessarily mean that less money is going to be required to provide for those who through no fault of their own cannot be self-supporting.

DEPORTATION OF REFUGEES 

Senator INOUYE. When an immigrant misbehaves in the United 

States and gets involved in some illegal activity, he becomes subject to deportation and he can be summarily sent back to the land of his origin. In the case of refugees this does not apply, does it? 

Mr. PALMATIER. No, it does not. Not to my knowledge. 

Senator INOUYE. A refugee is forever guaranteed residence here? 

Mr. PALMATTER. Well, No. 1, he goes through the normal judicial process. Even though I feel that the Cubans as a group have certainly proven they are outstanding citizens Senator INOUYE. I have no question about that.

Mr. PALMATIER [continuing]. If they break the law, they go to jail. To my knowledge no Cuban has been deported. I cannot speak with respect to all refugees; I don't know. 

Senator INOUYE. Thank you.

Mr. PALMATIER. I assume it would depend in part whether we did or did not have diplomatic relations with the country from which the person came and the seriousness of the crime. 

Senator INOUYE. Thank you very much, sir. 

Senator Chiles.

DIFFERENCE BETWEEN AIRLIFTED REFUGEES AND THOSE FROM SPAIN 

Senator CHILES. Mr. Palmatier, we had a national policy that affected the Cuban refugees as they came into Florida based on from the time that Castro said that if anybody didn't want to stay in Cuba they were free to leave, and based on those statements President Johnson said we would take in anyone who wished to leave. 

Mr. PALMATIER. That is correct.

Senator CHILES. At that time, as I understand, they signed on a list if they wanted to leave and we began to honor, through the airlift and through our program of trying to help those people when they came to this country, those people that signed up on that list. 

Now, the 25,000 that are in Spain really are in a different category from that, are they not? 

Mr. PALMATIER. Yes, some of them are.

Senator CHILES. They are not people that went down and in effectmaybe some of them did, but they just chose to leave another way. 

They didn't sign their name on the list as wanting to come to the United States and then lose their possessions, as many of them did, and were sent to the canefields and just waited until they got a chance to come out on the State Department list. These are people that exodused via Spain and are likely to go another route entirely. 

Mr. PALMATIER. By and large that is true. As you mentioned, Senator, there are those who went off through Spain who were of course on the original list and were in the canefields and so forth. 

Senator CHILES. The reason I am laying this predicate is that I think we have a different obligation. We have always felt we had a particular obligation to those people who gave up in some instances perhaps life but certainly gave up property and their status and citizenship and everything else when they signed their name on that list based on a commitment that the President of the United States made that, "We will grant you asylum, we will grant you refuge in this country."

I think this 25,000 that are residing in Spain, we don't have that commitment to. We have not made that same commitment to them that we made to the others and that is why personally I am a little perplexed that a decision is made by an acting Secretary of State and an acting Attorney General to grant this immediate program. 

NUMBER OF REFUGEES FROM SPAIN WHO MAY SETTLE IN FLORIDA 

I am perplexed again as to what the outcome of Florida is going to be in that regard. I note that in some of the statements that they have made they estimate that only one-fourth of these 25,000 people will come to Florida.

CONDITION OF REFUGEES IN SPAIN 

At the time that you went to Spain what did you notice about the conditions in which these refugees were living? Were they in desperate condition?

Mr. PALMATIER. Well, the principal problem in Spain that I saw was the high unemployment rate among the Cubans there, and second that it was requiring a tremendous outflow of dollars from relatives here to support them during the period of time that they were required to remain in Spain. 

I would like to go back, Senator, and say that in 2 or 21½ years the problem of the 25,000 would have been resolved anyhow, since most would have qualified to come. They were on the waiting list. I think that these decisions were made greatly on the basis of the dollar outflow and knowing that they would come anyhow. But the existing time frame presented a problem because of the waiting period. So the policy was changed in order to resolve the problem more rapidly.

MOVEMENT WITHIN THE UNITED STATES OF REFUGEES 

Senator CHILES. What way do we have of actually determining whether these people do move again? Let's say when they come over they will go somewhere other than Miami. What way will we have to know whether later they are moving to Miami-6 months, a year, a year and a half?

Mr. PALMATIER. In terms of pure statistics of course you can pick it while they are still aliens because each alien is required to register with the Immigration Service in January of each year. In terms of whether a person becomes a public burden after reaching Florida with respect to welfare or medicaid or things of that type, we do see that because as I mentioned before, if someone returns who is obviously not capable of supporting himself and he meets eligibility requirements in the State of Florida for welfare, he is picked up and we reimburse 100 percent. So we are aware of the ones that return and go on welfare, but if they come back and go into self-supporting situations, we don't necessarily know of their return. 

Senator CHILES. That is all the questions I have. 

Senator INOUYE. Thank you very much, Mr. Palmatier. We appreciate your appearance.

WORLD REFUGEE PROBLEM 

Ambassador KELLOGG. Mr. Chairman, you have before you our fiscal year 1975 appropriation request for Migration and Refugee Assistance. My statement will be confined to aspects of the world refugee situation as we see it today.

The committee is aware that the programs under discussion represent only a part of what the United States is doing in refugee affairs. 

They are, however, basic programs authorized by the Migration and Refugee Assistance Act of 1962. Along with assistance to move and resettle Soviet Jews and other refugees from the U.S.S.R. funded, as you know, under other appropriations, they are the programs actually administered by my office. Whether bilateral or multinational in function, they enable the United States to meet its fair share of the demands of what the world has come to endure as continuing predictable refugee needs. And-very important in my opinion-they help insure that mechanisms are available in place, ready to rise to meet sudden, usually unanticipated major refugee disasters, threats to the safety and the rights of masses of human beings and also to our foreign policy interests.

ASSISTANCE PROVIDED 

Whether continuing programs covered by this appropriation or of emergency nature, our assistance is rendered almost invariably in co-

operation with our great American voluntary agencies, usually in support, with other countries, of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) or the Intergovernmental Committee for

European Migration (ICEM). Sometimes, in especially difficult situations, they involve the participation of the International Committee of the Red Cross. These are the necessary mechanisms to which I refer, and the following is a rundown of some of their operations during the past year:

ALIEN REFUGEES IN CHILE 

Prompt application of human rights treaties resulted in protection of alien refugees in Chile, and has acted to speed their resettlement in other countries. ICRC, UNHCR and ICEM all have played significant roles.

CUBAN REFUGEES 

Movement through ICEM of U.S. bound Cuban refugees stranded in Spain was expedited in cooperation with UNHCR, Catholic Relief 

Services, Church World Service and the International Rescue Com mittee, under 1-year immigration parole procedure authorized by the 

Attorney General.

SUDANESE REFUGEES 

Repatriation of Sudanese refugees from a civil war was brought close to a successful conclusion by UNHCR, helped by Catholic Relief 

Services, Church World Service and Lutheran World Relief. 

BANGLADESH AND PAKISTAN REFUGEES 

The transfer of refugees between Bangladesh and Pakistan was negotiated and is on the way to completion in one of the great airlifts of history, with ICEM, UNHCR and ICRC all involved. 

ASIAN REFUGEES FROM UGANDA 

New homes were found in a dozen countries for all but a handful of Asians expelled from Uganda; organizations concerned were 

ICEM, UNHCR, ICRC, the American Fund for Czechoslovak Refugees, U.S. Catholic Conference, Church World Service, Lutheran

World Relief, the Tolstoy Foundation, United HIAS Service, Inter national Rescue Committee and many other governments and voluntary agencies abroad.

OTHER REFUGEE SITUATIONS 

The programs I have enumerated here have helped or are helping more than a million dispossessed people to the opportunity to achieve dignity and self-sufficiency. But other refugee situations still plague international relations, complicate foreign policy interests, arouse concern and sympathy among citizens of our country and other freedom-loving nations.

WORLDWIDE REFUGEES 

There are, depending on how you count them, up to 8 million refugees in the world today. Among them are freedom-seeking people

still coming out of Communist countries, including those of Eastern Europe. As long as oppression continues in those countries, individuals are going to manage to escape. I am confident that in concert with other free nations we are going to continue to help these refugees establish new lives. International commitments aside, I believe American public opinion will permit no other course. 

But the number of European refugees is not high on the scale; the large concentrations are Africans, Asians, and Latin Americans. Not only Communism is creating refugees but all forms of totalitarianism, along with revolution, war and racial, tribal and religious persecution. The UNHCR spends more than half of his resources to meet 

African problems. ICEM, established originally to meet European problems, has come to operate globally, for the benefit of refugees in 

Africa, Asia and Latin America as well as Europe.

For the future, we are watching with special concern situations in a half dozen nations which conceivably can result in explosive exodus of new masses of refugees. Perhaps the most certain things we know about refugees are that some existing movements are going to continue and also that major new problems inevitably are going to arise with frequency, in expected or unexpected places and from anticipated or unanticipated causes.

U.S. REFUGEE ASSISTANCE 

The rationale of U.S. refugee assistance has not changed. Our programs reflect response of successive administrations and each successive Congress to American traditions of humanitarianism and dedication to freedom, and to the realities of our national interests. To help meet the challenges, our requested appropriation:

Provides a fair share of support for mechanisms and organizations able to respond to real human needs in refugee affairs. 

Furthers foreign policy objectives.

Helps maintain U.S. leadership in the protection of human dignity and human rights. 

This concludes my statement, Mr. Chairman. 

Senator INOUYE. Thank you very much, Mr. Ambassador.

EASTERN EUROPEAN REFUGEES 

With the exception of the Russian Jewish refugees for which there is a special program, how many Eastern European refugees have fled the Iron Curtain in fiscal year 1973 ?

Ambassador KELLOGG. Approximately 6,900, Mr. Chairman. The total number was 41,929, and the refugees ex-U.S.S.R. totaled about 35,000. 

Senator INOUYE. And fiscal 1974 and 1975 ?

Ambassador KELLOGG. There, of course, we would have to estimate. 

We don't see any diminution of these numbers, Mr. Chairman. 

OTHER COUNTRIES' CONTRIBUTIONS FOR REFUGEES 

Senator INOUYE. As you may recall, in the fiscal year 1972 report, this committee expressed a view that "European countries of original asylum, principally Austria, West Germany, Italy, Turkey, Lebanon,

and Greece, are fully capable of meeting the need for care and maintenance of those seeking temporary refuge within their borders." 

Are these countries less able today to provide food and shelter than they were 3 years ago?

Ambassador KELLOGG. Mr. Chairman, other countries are making a tremendous contribution to the whole expense of caring for refugees. 

For example, I have before me a table of refugee assistance by other countries for the latest 12-month period. This shows that 14 countries, not including the U.S. Government, contributed in a 12-month period over $3 billion. Therefore, my answer is that these countries are perhaps not less able to provide care and maintenance as you ask, but that they are doing a tremendous amount of work at a tremendous cost to handle the refugee situation. 

Senator INOUYE. What countries are these 14, sir?

Ambassador KELLOGG. Australia, Austria, Belgium, Canada, Denmark, France, Greece, Germany, Israel, Italy, Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, and Spain.

Senator INOUYE. These 14 countries have spent $3 billion? 

Ambassador KELLOGG. Yes, sir. 

Senator INOUYE. How much have we spent, sir?

U.S. CONTRIBUTIONS FOR REFUGEES 

Ambassador KELLOGG. In the 12-month period of calendar year 1973 the U.S. Government spent a total of $330 million for refugee assistance. You might be interested, sir, to know that of the larger categories of this total amount, the largest single sum is $145 million for Čuban refugees in the United States. The second largest amount is for Southeast Asian refugees. The third is UNRWA, followed by our own program, Mr. Chairman. 

Senator INOUYE. By your own program, what do you mean?

Ambassador KELLOGG. The program that is before your committee this morning.

Senator INOUYE. Does the $330 million include the Russian Jewish refugees?

Ambassador KELLOGG. Yes it does; for a total of $50 million in 1973. 

DISPARITY BETWEEN U.S. ASSISTANCE TO REFUGEES 

Senator INOUYE. In justifying your $1,340,000 administrative budget you state that your office has primary responsibility to "formulate comprehensive policy and enunciate goals of U.S. Government refugee and migration efforts."

The information available to this subcommittee indicates that there is a great disparity between U.S. assistance to European refugees, rough estimates of up to $1,000 per refugee per year in the case of Russian refugees, and Asian refugees, rough estimates at less than $50 per person per year in Cambodia and Vietnam. 

This year your own office will oversee the spending of some $45 million, of which about $500,000 is identified with the staggering load of refugees in the Far East. As our Government's chief spokesman charged with "formulating comprehensive policy and enunciating goals of U.S. refugee efforts," can you tell the subcommittee or explain this difference in the tangible evidence of American concern? 34-192 O 74 14

Ambassador KELLOGG. Mr. Chairman, that is a very broad question. 

I will try to deal with the various questions within the broad area of your thrust and then, if I may, summarize.

To begin with, it would be a mistake to relate our administrative costs to the programs that are before this committee this morning. As 

I believe you also noted in your question, the $9.4 million that we are requesting this morning is only a portion of what my office is responsible for.

The $500,000 for the Far East is for a small program of assistance to Chinese refugees in Hong Kong and Macao. Bearing for a moment on the question of the difference in the amount of dollars by which refugees are assisted, it is true that there is a disparity between, for example, refugees from Eastern Europe and those of Africa or the Asian countries. This is because most refugee problems vary and are very different one from another. For example in the Sudan, some 500,000 refugees were moved within the Sudan itself from the bush, and several more hundreds of thousands from outside of the Sudan. There were mass migrations, mass movements that didn't require airplane transportation, that didn't require complicated resettlement, that were not done on an individual basis. Therefore, the cost per capita is a great deal less than in the case of Europe where a refugee family is going to find a new home outside the country of first asylum and, therefore, he has to be fed and housed, given care and maintenance, until transportation can be arranged. The country that is going to take him has to agree, and it is a vastly more complicated and expensive procedure. 

There is also, of course, the difference in the standard of living between European refugees and those in Africa and Asia. 

Have I answered your question, sir?

Senator INOUYE. Taking aside the cost of transportation are other costs comparable?

Ambassador KELLOGG. No, sir, because the refugee in Europe for sake of argument must have papers processed, and he must decide in which country he is going to resettle. All of this is expensive in terms of time. He has to be counseled to this effort, whereas, to take the instance of 10 million refugees in India who fled out of what is now Bangladesh, obviously when they returned they returned on foot without any advice or counsel from technical people. 

ICEM ACTIVITIES 

Senator INOUYE. In the committee's 1972 hearings you advised at that time that most refugees resettled by the ICEM were in Australia, the United States, and Canada in that order. 

Are Canada and Australia currently members of the ICEM?

Ambassador KELLOGG. No, Mr. Chairman. Australia unfortunately has decided to withdraw. This decision was made in 1973. Part of the effect of the withdrawal was felt by ICEM in that year and the final total withdrawal of Australia was effective January 1, 1974.

Senator INOUYE. In fact, isn't it true that Canada, France, Sweden, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom have all dropped out? 

Ambassador KELLOGG. Yes, sir, I believe that is correct.

Senator INOUYE. What is the rationale for the United States con tinuing to shoulder this increasing burden with reference to ICEM costs when these major European countries have dropped out?

Ambassador KELLOGG. Well, perhaps I should start my reply to your question by saying that countries that have dropped out have done so for varying national interests. For example, Australia, which has been historically a large supporter of ICEM has also been a large country of immigration. This changed in recent years. Australia had brought in vast numbers of people, but had not completed the assimilation of these people, when she ran into unemployment. And when a change in government occurs, very frequently other changes are made simply to demonstrate that a new hand is in charge. 

The United Kingdom dropped out some years ago because it no longer was bringing people in to that small island. 

On the other side of the coin, Mr. Chairman, there are many reasons why the U.S. Government should continue to support ICEM. ICEM is a vital mechanism to move refugees; without it there would be a stagnation in the ongoing movement of people which would have a deleterious effect on countries of first asylum. For example, Austria, if not assured of the ongoing movement of refugees, would quickly have to close her borders for those who managed to escape from Eastern Europe. Obviously, those refugees must be moved out of Austria, or that small country would become clogged and have to close its borders. 

Senator INOUYE. Have we made any attempt to convince our friends abroad that they should pick up their just share? 

Ambassador KELLOGG. Indeed we have, sir. This is an effort which the U.S. Government has participated in as well as a constant effort by the Director of ICEM, Mr. John Thomas. It is an effort on the part of my office and the U.S. Government which is unremitting. 

We are trying to bring pressure on the other countries to take a greater share, and there is a working group that is meeting on this very subject this week in Geneva to further this program. 

U.S. SHARE OF ICEM BUDGET 

Senator INOUYE. Is it true that at the present time we are sharing about 40 percent of the operating and administrative budgets of ICEM?

Ambassador KELLOGG. That is correct, Mr. Chairman, and I should fail in my duty if I didn't say that we are very conscious of this large share of the total ICEM budget. However, I think I should make the point that the total number of dollars which the U.S. Government has given to ICEM each year, for example since 1966 with one exception when it dropped below $3 million, has been very constant in the $3 million range, so that in terms of actual dollars the U.S. Government contribution to ICEM has not increased. What has happened is that with the withdrawal of Australia there is a larger proportion of the total budget that must be picked up by the U.S. Government in order to keep this organization going.

NOTES (1) Refugees from North Korea in South Korea: 

The five million North Korean refugees who fled to South Korea between 1945 and 1953 are now integrated within the economy of South Korea. Escape from North Korea today is virtually precluded by stringent North Korean controls. 

(2) East German Refugees in West Germany: 

Between 1945 and 1961, 3.7 million German refugees fled from the East Zone into West Germany, across the zonal border or via West Berlin. Between the erection of the 

Berlin Wall and January 1, 1972, this flow totaled approximately 139,000, including 30,000 who came over the Berlin Wall or who fled across the border. These refugees have been integrated into the West Germany economy or are being assimilated without international assistance.

CUBAN REFUGEES FROM SPAIN 

Senator INOUYE. In 1974 ICEM plans to move about 17,000 Cubans to the United States from Spain. The committee first learned of your office's allocation of $411,000 to this program in your letter of February 11, 1974. In that letter you stated that the movement of Cuban refugees from Spain to the United States was important for both "humanitarian and political reasons." Would you tell us these political reasons? 

Ambassador KELLOGG. Yes, sir, I will be glad to.

The fact is that this large number of Cubans, the total number having risen at one point to about 25,000 in Madrid and in that area has been a cause of concern between the United States and the Spanish government. These Cubans had no other choice but to take the air transportation to Madrid to get out of Cuba. Probably a great many of them had no idea that they were not going to continue right away to come to the United States, which had promised them a haven. And yet for technical reasons they were hung up in Madrid. The result of this has been that the Spanish government has had to provide care and maintenance at a rather substantial cost, and the sooner this irritant is removed from Spanish-United States Government relationships the better it will be.

Senator INOUYE. You have just indicated that we have made a commitment to those who were in Spain that we would eventually provide a haven for them? 

Ambassador KELLOGG. No, sir. I am sorry. I didn't make myself clear.

Senator INOUYE. I was under the impression that those who had decided to go to Spain did so voluntarily, they elected to do so. Isn't that correct, sir? 

Ambassador KELLOGG. Yes, sir, it is correct. And the reason 

Senator INOUYE. Then why should it be the cause of friction between the United States and Spain? We did not force this upon Spain, did we?

Ambassador KELLOGG. No. These people to get out of Cuba had no choice but to take the airlift that was provided for them. There was not sufficient space in the regular airlift to the United States and, therefore, they took the airlift to Madrid, which was their sole means of leaving an oppressive regime.

Senator INOUYE. I was under the impression that there was sufficient airlift to go to the United States if they so elected, but they elected to go to Spain. In fact, we provided haven for half a million of them. 

Ambassador KELLOGG. Well, that brings me to the other part of your question which is that it has been a policy of the United States Government to accept any Cuban that has been able to get from Cuba to the shores of the United States, and this was only a cruel quirk of fate that these Cubans ended up in Madrid where they didn't have any intention of remaining-that is, the great majority of theminstead of having come directly to the United States. 

AUTHORIZATION FOR CUBAN REFUGEES FROM SPAIN 

Senator INOUYE. For the record, when was this program authorized, and by whom, sir? 

Ambassador KELLOGG. May I ask which particular program?

Senator INOUYE. The Cubans in Spain.

Ambassador KELLOGG. In 1961 ICEM began moving Cubans from 

Spain and other third countries to the United States. 

Senator INOUYE. The specific move of 17,000 Cubans?

Ambassador KELLOGG. Right. That was a decision taken by the State 

Department the Secretary of State and the Attorney General on 

October 26, 1973.

SOUTH AFRICAN REFUGEE PROGRAM 

Senator INOUYE. AID reports to the committee that it granted $300,000 to the South African refugee program in fiscal year 1972, and that this amount has carried the program up through the present time. This equals just over $100,000 per year. 

How will you utilize $600,000 in this program during the last 3 months of this fiscal year and next?

Ambassador KELLOGG. To begin with, Mr. Chairman, we are asking for a total of $300,000. This was designed to begin the support of students on January 1, 1974. 

Senator INOUYE. Have you spent any of the $300,000? 

Ambassador KELLOGG. No, sir, we have not. 

Senator INOUYE. So you have 3 months left in this fiscal year?

Ambassador KELLOGG. Yes, sir, but it is a calendar year program and, therefore, the $300,000 that was appropriated in fiscal year 1974 is for a 12-month program beginning January 1, 1974, with 9 months to go because actually the AID has financed the students until March 31. 

We would hope to commence this program on April 1. 

Senator INOUYE. How do you propose to spend this? AID has been using about $100,000 a year, and your program calls for $300,000. Can you tell us how you except to spend $600,000 in 21 months?

Ambassador KELLOGG. Mr. Chairman, we are asking $300,000 for fiscal year 1975. This will support up to 100 students with scholarships in Zambia and 45 students in post-secondary education elsewhere in Africa during calendar year 1975. The total of these students at just over $2,000 each comes to the amount that we are requesting; namely, $300,000, which is the same as AID's program. 

Now the major reason that AID has been able to finance the program this long is that the program has not been running at its full capacity of 145 students. This is changing. Almost all of the 45 postsecondary scholarships are now filled and there are at the moment 84 students in the school in Zambia with applications being processed for the remaining 16 slots. In other words, Mr. Chairman, we budgeted for a full capacity program. 

RATIONALE FOR SOUTH AFRICAN PROGRAM 

Senator INOUYE. What is the rationale for this program?

Ambassador KELLOGG. There are- 

Senator INOUYE. Put it another way. What are the foreign policy interests involved in this program? 

Ambassador KELLOGG. Might I suggest, sir, that Mr. Coote who is representing the Bureau of African Affairs should speak to this point. 

Senator INOUYE. Please do so. 

Mr. COOTE. Shall I proceed to answer your question, Mr. Chairman?

Senator INOUYE. Please do. I just wanted to know what the foreign policy interests are on the part of the United States in being involved in the South African students program.

Mr. COOTE. We have always strongly supported in the United 

Nations and other bodies the goal of self-determination for the African people still under the minority regimes in Southern Africa. 

This program is one of the few positive demonstrations that we give to the refugees and to the other African countries of our support and sympathy for this goal of self-determination. 

I think in recent months many of the African countries have felt that we tend to express ourselves and make statements in support of this goal but that our actions sometimes don't follow through on these particular statements. This program has been a successful program for the past 10 years in demonstrating to Zambia and the other African countries that we in fact do support our statements. 

There are, I think, secondary advantages, too. The program permits us to maintain continuing contacts and dialogue with the liberation movements themselves. Secondly, a number of these students who are qualified students especially selected for the course may eventually become the important officials in successor regimes and we will have a built-in relationship with these individuals. 

Senator INOUYE. The areas involved include Rhodesia, Angola, 

Mozambique, the Union of South Africa, and Southwest Africa. 

Mr. COOTE. Yes, sir.

Senator INOUYE. By training these students for eventual selfdetermination are you training them to change the government there? 

Mr. COOTE. No, sir, we are not. In fact these individuals don't otherwise have the opportunity to develop skills of their own and to obtain an education. This particular course is aimed at providing certain basic skills and education for peaceful purposes to these individuals who participate. 

Senator INOUYE. Are you convinced that we are not involved in the internal affairs of these countries?

Mr. CoOTE. Yes, sir. This particular program has been in effect for over 10 years. It is well known to the countries of Southern Africa and in fact accepted by them because they are fully aware of our position in favor of self-determination through nonviolent means. 

Senator INOUYE. Thank you very much, sir.

Ambassador KELLOGG. Sir, might I add two small footnotes to what 

Mr. Coote has said? 

Senator INOUYE. Please do, sir.

Ambassador KELLOGG. I think it could be pointed out that the United 

States, in contrast to some of the Communist countries that are training guerrilla groups in the areas, is taking peaceful means to educate students. There is a very wide disparity between that course of procedure and our own.

Secondly, in the long period of the civil war in Sudan, refugees were also educated by voluntary agencies during that 17-year period, and the proof of the value of this is in Southern Sudan today where these refugees have returned to their own country and many of them are in key positions that are helping to keep the fragile peace viable in that country. 

Senator INOUYE. Thank you, sir.

This program transports nonrefugee migrants from developed Western European countries such as Germany, Italy, and Spain to Latin American countries. I believe in 1973 

Brazil received 673, Venezuela 258, Argentina 172.

TRANSPORTING COSTS OF MIGRANTS 

Why was it necessary for the United States to pay 55 percent of the cost to transport these migrants to these countries? 

Ambassador KELLOGG. Here again, sir, the judgment was made that this was a very important way of helping Latin American countries fill a need for skilled and technical people. There is a choice. Another method of doing it is to send an expert for 2 years on a loan basis. It has been estimated that the cost of that sort of a program is in the area of $50,000 per expert. 

Senator INOUYE. These are nonrefugees?

Ambassador KELLOGG. That is correct, they are nonrefugees. 

Senator INOUYE. And the recipient or nonbeneficiaries are not in the less developed category are they? I gather that Brazil and Argentina have foreign exchange reserves.

Ambassador KELLOGG. No, sir, they are not in the lesser developed category, but they have a great need for this sort of development assistance, and it is also in the interest of the United States to continue to show its friendship and concern over the needs of its Latin American neighbors.

Senator INOUYE. The United States is now suffering from unemployment. If some of our unemployed decided to go to Latin America- 

Brazil, Venezuela, Argentina-to use their talents there, would this Government provide transportation under the ICEM program? These are nonrefugee Americans.

Ambassador KELLOGG. The answer to that is that certainly in theory at any rate ICEM would be available to transport Americans who wished to go to Latin America. There is no prohibition for that movement. I am not aware, however, that there is any appreciable group of 

Americans who wish to take advantage of such a possible movement. 

Senator INOUYE. Have we made this known before this morning? 

Ambassador KELLOGG. I don't believe so, no, sir.

MOVEMENT OF AMERICANS UNDER ICEM PROGRAM 

Senator INOUYE. If an American group came to you seeking transportation assistance to go to Brazil, would you provide this?

Ambassador KELLOGG. It would have to be on a fully reimbursable basis, Mr. Chairman, before ICEM will move anybody. 

Senator INOUYE. Fully reimbursable. Does the beneficiary country reimburse the cost? 

Ambassador KELLOGG. Yes, sir. 

Senator INOUYE. Have they? 

Ambassador KELLOGG. I believe they have, yes, sir.

Senator INOUYE. If they are reimbursing, why then do we have to put up the cost year after year? I would assume that moneys are coming in. I gather from the bookkeeping that they have not reimbursed anything. It is just in theory and in principle. 

Ambassador KELLOGG. May I ask Mr. Carlin to answer this?

Senator INOUYE. Yes. I realize this question is a miniscule one, but it is my responsibility as Chairman of this Committee to be able to respond to every question that the Senators may have. 

Ambassador KELLOGG. Certainly, sir. I understand that. 34-192 O 74-15

REIMBURSEMENT FOR COSTS INCURRED 

Mr. CARLIN. Mr. Chairman, any program which ICEM would undertake outside of Europe-ICEM is constituted to move migrants and refugees from Europe; if a program involves non-Europeans-and sometimes ICEM at the request of a particular government does become involved in a program outside of Europe-that would have to be on a fully reimbursable basis, not necessarily to be reimbursed by the receiving country of the migrants but by interested governments or other parties. 

Senator INOUYE. Have they reimbursed this money? 

Mr. CARLIN. Have they, sir? 

Senator INOUYE. Have these costs been reimbursed in the past?

Mr. CARLIN. In the case of the normal selected emigrant program from Europe to Latin American countries there is international financing for that. As you indicated earlier, I think the United States has been bearing the lion's share of that national burden, but the Latin American receiving countries in recent years have been increasing their financial participation, and we from our side are endeavoring constantly to try to get that on a more equitable basis, sir. 

Senator INOUYE. We are bearing about 55 percent of the costs, aren't we? 

Mr. CARLIN. You are correct, sir.

Senator INOUYE. And so it is not being reimbursed. 

Mr. CARLIN. Only in the sense that it is joint financing from various governments. Some contributions from the receiving countries- 

Senator INOUYE. I didn't want the record to indicate that whatever we put in we will be reimbursed. That is not the case. 

Mr. CARLIN. No. The case of the reimbursement is if there is a program outside of Europe, because that would be outside the normal ICEM constituted program and would have to be on a fully reimbursable basis with financing coming from interested governments and other interested parties.

Senator INOUYE. Last year, I believe Latin American countries all together put up about $160,000. 

Mr. CARLIN. I think your figure is close to the mark, yes, sir.

CAPABILITIES OF LATIN AMERICAN COUNTRIES FINANCING 

Senator INOUYE. Is it your view that countries such as Brazil, Venezuela, and Argentina with their booming economies now will not be able to pay the transportation costs of these nonrefugee European migrants?

Mr. CARLIN. Sir, I think the record would indicate in the past 3 to 

4 years we have made fairly significant progress in getting those particular Latin American countries to pay increased per capitas toward the skilled migrants they receive. The record suggests that it is still not adequate and we are constantly urging them to take more of their fair share.

Senator INOUYE. Later in the hearing we will be receiving a report from the GAO which indicates something that many of us have been suggesting for a long while, that reassessment should be made of the beneficiary countries because oftentimes when the United States de-

cides to share its treasury and good will with other countries this program continues indefinitely, even if the recipient country becomes all powerful, and we make very little attempt to change this because we feel that might cause some diplomatic friction. 

In fact, up until recently, as part of the military program we were sharing destroyers with Japan, and Japan is far from being an underdeveloped country. We are now providing assistance to countries such as Brazil and Argentina which, on a per capita basis, are doing pretty well, not as well as the United States. 

REASSESSMENT OF LATIN AMERICAN PROGRAM 

I am just wondering if there is a point where we should stop and say, "Sir, I think you are now back on your feet. We would suggest you begin walking by yourself." Or do we want to continue in providing them assistance even if they are economically viable and powerful? 

Ambassador KELLOGG. I would like to make a response to that. 

Senator INOUYE. Because the countries we are talking about in 

Europe, none of them are less developed. 

Ambassador KELLOGG. Recently, Mr. Chairman, we sent out cables to each of our Latin American Embassies requesting them to make an assessment of this program. In each case we got a very enthusiastic response for the need for this particular program as evidence of the interest and friendship and concern of the U.S. Government for the various South American countries involved and Central American countries.

Also I should point out that in recent history the Latin American countries have taken a greater role in ICEM's affairs than in the past. 

As a matter of fact, Venezuela recently returned as a full member of ICEM, and there are now a total of 16 Latin American countries that are members of the ICEM organization. 

Therefore, there is reason to think that with this increased influence of the Latin American countries in ICEM's affairs and because of the growing prosperity in many of these countries, there will indeed be greater support by them as contrasted to the United States, for this particular program.

In light of that, we intend to look at this program very carefully, with an idea of reducing our participation in it. 

Senator INOUYE. I am certain all of our embassies in Latin America and elsewhere view with great enthusiasm all these programs, not just this program but all the AID programs because if we decided to cut out these programs they would have to experience the discomfort of facing the Chief of State and I don't suppose they would like to experience this discomfort, but somewhere along the line someone has to experience this discomfort.

The question is, can the taxpayers of the United States be called upon forever to bear the load of these programs when the recipient countries are obviously in an economic position to pull their own oar? 

I would hope that your office will keep this in mind very seriously and come forth in the next presentation with a few changes because in the few years I have been in this position instead of cutting down our share in each case we have gone up, and yet at the same time your testimony indicates that all of these countries are interested.

In the case of Latin America you just said that 16 countries are interested. They put up $160,000 when we put up 55 percent, or something like $1.2 million. I am just wondering if we should be satisfied with just a token interest on their part, especially if they can bear the load.

I am not picking on any country, but I think this should be a message from the Congress to all countries that we want to share our bounty with the rest of the world if there is a need for this. 

I am certain you realize that we were able to pass this program by a very narrow margin last year, and I hate to go through that experience with this again.

Ambassador KELLOGG. Sir, I shall be attending the ICEM Council meeting in May, and I will make sure that the ideas that you have just expressed are transmitted to that body.

CONSOLIDATION OF REFUGEE ACTIVITIES 

Senator INOUYE. In our fiscal 1972 report the committee expressed the belief that there was an urgent need to consolidate refugee activities into a single office. As our Government's principal officer for providing leadership guidance and coordination for these programs, what have you done to bring this about?

Ambassador KELLOGG. Well, with your permission I would like to step back in history momentarily. You will recall, sir, that in April 

1971, the President embodied in the AID reorganization requested legislation for a central bureau for refugee and humanitarian affairs. 

For reasons not having to do with that particular request that legislation did not pass.

Since that time at least two bills have been introduced in Congress to create a bureau of humanitarian affairs. Neither of these has survived.

Within the Department of State, I can tell you that at the present time a management study is being made in connection with the very question that you ask.

SOVIET REFUGEE OBLIGATIONS 

Senator INOUYE. Mr. Ambassador, in last year's hearings you advised the subcommittee that the $50 million made available in fiscal year 1973 for Soviet refugees would cover assistance for both fiscal year 1973 and fiscal year 1974. I will refer you to page 110 of the committee's 1974 report. 

I quote my question and your answer:

Do I understand that this appropriation we are talking about, $50 million, will cover assistance to both the 30,000 who expect to immigrate to Israel in calendar year 1973, and an additional 30,000 expected in calendar year 1974? 

Mr. KELLOGG. That is correct, yes, sir.

[From the Christian Science Monitor, Dec. 12, 1973]

U.S.-SAIGON REFUGEE PROGRAM CRITICIZED 

(By Daniel Southerland, Staff correspondent of the Christian Science Monitor)

SAIGON.-There are signs of disillusionment among American AID officials here over the way the U.S. and Saigon governments are handling the Vietnam refugee problem.

Among the criticisms voiced are these: 

Refugees are being "resettled" on land which is too poor to lead to economic self-sufficiency. In cases where forests are available, they are often denied to the refugees because (it is alleged) government officials can reap sizable profits by letting private contractors sell the timber. 

The Saigon government, with U.S. support, is moving refugees to insecure areas in an effort to consolidate and expand its territorial control. 

These were two of the main objections voiced by one of two former assistant relief and rehabilitation officers of the U.S. Agency for the International Development (AID), Edward L. Block, who recently resigned because of their misgivings over the handling of the refugee program. The other is Leon J. Van Wagoner. 

Both have considerable background and experience in Southeast Asia. 

Mr. Block indicates there are others who share their criticisms and have either quit or decided against another tour of duty here. 

For the past five or six months, Mr. Block's job has been to work with the 

Saigon officials responsible for land development and for drawing up resettlement guidelines. His work has taken him on number of trips to the provinces. 

Mr. Block described Dr. Phan Quang Dan, the Minister of State for Land 

Development and Hamlet Building, as a hard-working official. But he said that 

Dr. Dan had taken so much responsibility into his own hands that he could not possibly provide careful coordination and planning. 

Dr. Dan had made an effort to cut down on the thousands of nonexistent refugees, called "ghost refugees," who had swollen the aid rolls. But much too little was done too late, said Mr. Block.

He said he was convinced that very high-level Vietnamese officials were profiting from the aid supposedly going to "ghost refugees."

LARGELY FUNDED BY U.S. 

The refugee relief and rehabilitation program is a big one, involving close to a million refugees. It is almost entirely U.S. funded. 

But according to Mr. Block, U.S. officials refused to use the leverage which they possessed to bring significant changes in Saigon's handling of the refugee problem. Higher-level U.S. officials routinely suppressed critical reports coming from Americans working in the field, he said. 

Mr. Block explained that he had not made known his views to U.S. aid investigators who questioned him about his resignation because he feared that they might distort what he had to say in their reports. 

He believes that the channelling of American aid to refugees through private voluntary or international agencies would be more effective than continuing to pump it through AID and the Saigon government. 

LABELED "AN INSULT" 

In a recent letter to a staff member of the U.S. Senate subcommittee investigating refugee problems, Mr. Block described the U.S. aid-funded relief and rehabilitation program here as a "massive bonanza for the government of Vietnam, a disaster for the refugees, and an insult" to the American people. "Many of the new refugees sites (even the highly praised Suo Nghe project) are in danger of eventually collapsing or are already collapsing due to insufficient land and lack of required support from the government of Vietnam," wrote 

Mr. Block. "We have come to discover in South Vietnam that if an area has good soil, plentiful water, and is safe, there is inevitably somebody farming or claiming it," 

Mr. Block said in his letter. "If an area has poor soil, few water resources, and the government of Vietnam would like to make it a buffer zone, then the land is available for refugee resettlement," he said. "Return-to-village and resettlement site-development projects are usually bogged down in 'administrative delays' while the 'administrators' decide on their own cut. . . . To make matters worse, controls over the expenditure of AIDprovided funds are practically nonexistent, and this has led to inexcusable fiscal irresponsibility. 

"AID-provided refugee relief funds are being spent for such unauthorized items as government of Vietnam social events, additional allowances to military dependents, the installation of telephones, land rentals, and even roofing for churches."

Senator INOUYE. Our next witness is Mr. J. K. Fasick, Director of the International Division of the General Accounting Office.
