[The statement follows:] 

Mr. Chairman and members of the subcommittee, we are pleased to appear before your subcommittee to discuss that work of ours related to the Foreign Assistance Appropriations Bill for fiscal year 1975. Our statement will highlight some of our recent work concerning foreign assistance, some of our current efforts which will provide reports of interest to the subcommittee in the near future, and several issues which we are of the opinion need continuing attention by the 

Executive Branch and the Congress.

We are pleased to note that several significant actions were taken by the Congress in the foreign assistance area last year during the consideration of the authorization and appropriation bills. Particularly noteworthy were the provisions included in these bills which require disclosure of debt service rescheduling, require the administration to seek independent review groups for the World Bank, the Asian Development Bank, and the United Nations organizations; tighten the control over the use of excess foreign currency by the executive agencies in administering their programs; and functionally realigns development assistance programs. The subcommittee obviously was a prime mover or supported these improvements in the foreign assistance area. 

Subsequent to our appearance before this subcommittee last April, we have continued to work very closely with your staff in order to be responsive to the specific requests of the subcommittee and subcommittee members and to maintain (237)

a communications channel which on a day-to-day basis keeps us aware of the subcommittee's overall and long-range interests. Our objective is to tailor our self-initiated work to respond to your needs to the extent possible. 

We issued 74 reports on international programs during fiscal year 1973. From 

July 1, 1973, through February 1974 we have issued 39 reports-13 to the Congress, 18 to committees or Members of the Congress (2 of which were to your subcommittee) and 8 to agency officials. The two to your subcommittee were:

Excess costs to the United States because of monopolistic transportation practices in Thailand.

Utilization and maintenance of equipment provided to Thailand's armed forces by the United States.

This year will again devote about 250 man-years of professional staff efforts to international programs. Of that total, roughly 25 percent will be applied in response to specific congressional requests. 

HIGHLIGHTS OF GAO DIRECTION OF EFFORT IN THE INTERNATIONAL AREA 

Our reports over the past year relative to international operations have dealt with broad country programs, selected development and security assistance aspects of overall country programs, balance of payment issues, management and profits on wheat exports, international aspects of the energy crisis, financial aspects of EX-IM Bank and OPIC operations, and various subjects involving foreign trade. We have prepared an attachment to this statement which excerpts those reports which have been submitted to the Congress since we last met with the subcommittee in April 1973, and which are concerned with areas of interest to this subcommittee. With your permission, I would like to submit this listing for the record.

We currently have a number of studies underway which we believe will provide reports of interest to the Congress and the subcommittee in the near future. I would like to briefly describe some of these efforts in terms of our study ob jectives and the current status of our studies. 

AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT STAFFING 

This subcommittee requested the GAO to review aid personnel staffing. In addition to three specific areas mentioned in the request-establish a base against which future action can be measured, compare AID's salary and related personnel benefits to those of other Government agencies and private nonprofit organizations, and evaluate the utilization of AID personnel in offices performing services not directly related to program support-we are also reviewing AID's personnel policies and its staffing trends since 1968 for the purpose of identifying other areas where problems exist. 

With regard to the utilization of AID personnel, we have recently learned that AID is currently making its first in-depth study of its personnel requirements. 

We plan, as part of our review, to analyze pertinent portions of this study as soon as it becomes available (tentatively scheduled for early April) and intend to present our views to the subcommittee on the proposed actions and the additional actions that we believe should be taken.

IMPLEMENTATION OF PUBLIC SAFETY PROGRAM PHASEOUT 

In the fall of 1973, we started a survey of Agency for International Development public safety program's. Our objective was to gain an insight into the nature of the programs and identify problem areas for in-depth review. Shortly after we began our survey, we received a series of requests from various Members of the Congress for specific information related to public safety programs, such as cost, type of support provided, and the purpose for which funds were expended in certain countries.

Subsequently, the foreign assistance act was amended to provide that, "No part of any appropriation made available to carry out this act shall be used to conduct any police training or related program in a foreign country." Accordingly, the scope of our work in the public safety area was tailored to give recognition to this amendment.

AID is currently taking steps to terminate its funding of public safety programs in all foreign countries. We are monitoring this phaseout, and we are also looking into Department of Defense military assistance programs with a view toward reporting to the Congress on the nature and scope of continuing support, if any, to police organizations, law enforcement, and public safety programs.

INTERNATIONAL NARCOTICS CONTROL 

We are in the process of reviewing the U.S. Government's international narcotics control efforts. In fiscal year 1973 $20.5 million was allocated to overseas narcotics control programs and in fiscal year 1974 $42.5 million has been made available.

We are looking into U.S. assistance activities involving training and advising enforcement personnel and providing economic alternatives to farmers producing opium. Narcotics assistance in the areas of health, education, and treatment is being examined. U.S. efforts to promote and participate in multilateral narcotics control activities are being analyzed. We are also considering the issue of foreign government cooperation and the adequacy of opium for legal medicinal needs. 

In connection with this assignment, fieldwork is being performed in 10 European and Mid-East countries and in 8 South Asia and Far East countries. 

We expect to be able to report on the results of this work by the fall of 1974. 

EVALUATION OF THE NEED FOR MAAG'S IN TODAY'S CLIMATE 

The question as to whether the United States should continue to maintain military assistance advisory groups (MAAG's) throughout the world has been of considerable concern to the Congress. This was particularly evident during hearings on the 1973 Foreign Assistance Act and in the Senate recommending that MAAG's be eliminated by 1976.

In view of this concern, GAO has undertaken a review of the MAAG's to evaluate their functions, duties and purposes so as to be in a position to report to the Congress on the role played by the MAAG's in U.S. foreign policy. Primary emphasis will be placed on determining whether all of the MAAG's, which in fiscal year 1973 were staffed with about 2,300 military and 1,100 civilian personnel in 46 countries, are still required to assist our allies improve their defense capabilities or whether such functions could better be handled through other elements of the U.S. country team. 

EVALUATION OF U.S. PARTICIPATION IN MULTILATERAL ORGANIZATIONS 

The principal channels for providing multilateral assistance are the international financial institutions, the organizations of the United Nations System, and the organization of American States. The executive branch believes that the multilateral approach to international development assistance offers unique advantages, such as the ability to share the aid burden with other industrialized nations. They also consider that the international organizations have done a creditable job and merit continued U.S. support. Accordingly, it is the policy of the executive branch to promote and support the continued expansion of the role of the multilateral organizations. 

GAO is placing more emphasis on evaluating the U.S. participation in the 

World Bank, the Asian Development Bank, the Inter-American Development 

Bank, the United Nations and its specialized agencies, and other international programs.

The objective of GAO work in these areas is to suggest ways in which the U.S. agencies involved can seek improvements through membership and participation in these organizations. 

We have made a number of reviews of U.S. participation in these organizations and have concluded in general that: 

The Executive Branch has not obtained the information or developed the necessary procedures to adequately analyze proposed programs and and activities of the international organizations. Therefore, it has a very limited factual basis for making informed judgments, except in very broad terms, as to what the organizations plan to do with U.S. contributions. 

The data submitted by the organizations and the procedures for appraising it provide little or no opportunity for member governments to exercise an effective voice in the direction of the programs. 

From our observations, we believe that improved capability for monitoring and evaluating the results of U.S. development assistance channeled through international organizations is needed. Thus we will continue to emphasize the need to improve management of U.S. participation in these organizations and currently have in process a number of reviews addressed to this need. 34-192 O-74 - 16

UTILIZATION OF EXCESS FOREIGN CURRENCIES On November 19, 1973, the Chairman, Senate Foreign Relations Committee, asked GAO to make a study of U.S.-owned foreign currencies with the aim of finding possible ways to put them to more effective use. GAO was asked to develop information on : 

1. The nature and extent of current and projected holdings including debts, 2. The nature and extent of partially controlled currencies, 3. Current and prospective uses of currencies by agencies and estimates of dollar savings, and 4. Applicable laws regarding usage and debt settlement. 

GAO has also been requested by others to do work in the field of foreign currencies. On December 14, 1973, the Chairman, Subcommittee on the Near East and South Asia, House Committee on Foreign Affairs, requested work by GAO. 

On December 21, 1973, work was requested by Congressman John D. Conlan. 

The information asked for in these two requests is similar to the information requested by the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. 

We plan to issue our first report on these foreign currency assignments this spring.

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE ISSUES NEEDING CONTINUING ATTENTION 

Our studies and reviews of foreign assistance programs have resulted in the identification of a number of issues which need continuing attention on the part of the administration and the Congress in order to effect management improvements. These involve questions such as: 

When should concessional assistance be stopped?

Is the coordination of family planning, health and nutritional programs adequate? 

What improvements are needed in Ex-Im Bank's operations?

Has AID moved expeditiously in using the fixed cost reimbursement approach to development assistance projects? 

Are inconsistencies in overseas allowances sufficient to warrant corrective actions?

I would like to discuss each of these issued briefly. 

1. When should concessional assistance be stopped?

We believe there is a need for criteria to enable judgments to be made on when countries no longer require United States assistance. 

In our report on U.S. concessional assistance to Brazil (July 30, 1973, B-133283), we stated that Brazil's need for $50 million and $17 million in concessional aid for fiscal years 1973 and 1974, respectively, was questionable. 

Brazil's gross national product had grown at an average annual rate of about 9.9 percent since 1968; it had accumulated $3 billion in foreign exchange in 

1971 and 1972, and at the beginning of 1973 total reserves were about $4.2 billion; and it is able to obtain substantial economic aid from other sources. 

The State Department and AID said that current U.S. assistance levels were consistent with U.S. foreign policy objectives, but U.S. officials have not addressed the question of when does an AID recipient like Brazil reach the point in its development when it no longer needs further U.S. concessional aid. 

The need for developing a plan for the phaseout of U.S. economic aid is also addressed in our draft report on U.S. economic aid to Turkey. In Turkey we noted that recent economic trends have created a favorable climate for the phaseout of U.S. economic aid. Certain types of U.S. assistance are no longer needed non-U.S. aid levels have gone up substantially; and most importantly, Turkey's economic performance has improved greatly since 1970. The State 

Department and AID have not developed a plan with specific target dates for the phaseout of U.S. concessional economic aid to Turkey. 

In our report on U.S. assistance for the economic development of the Republic of Korea (July 12, 1973, B-164264), we pointed out that while Korea's economic growth indicators have been most impressive since 1965, economic success has not been all that it appears on the surface. Economic development has been achieved at the expense of a steadily growing external debt and trade deficit. U.S. assistance stimulated economic growth, but at the same time it contributed to Korea's economic problems. The report suggested that the Congress inquire into what plans the Department of State and AID have for terminating the development loan program in Korea.

In a recent survey of U.S. programs and activities in Panama, we noted that the activities of the major U.S. bilateral programs are closely tied to the successful negotiation of the new canal treaty and that the canal issue tends to override other considerations which could affect the direction, magnitude, or scope of specific U.S. programs in Panama. The economic assistance program administered by the agency for international development is an example of this type programming. On the basis of Panama's continued economic growth and development, there are serious doubts as to whether U.S. economic assistance programs in Panama should continue at their present level. U.S. officials agree that the agency's program levels in Panama have been justified on other than purely economic grounds. Although the canal isssue is an added element in the case of U.S. economic assistance to Panama, the question of criteria concerning termination of assistance still pertains.

Deciding when to end an AID program in a developing country is just as important as deciding when to start one. Prolonging the program can create self-help disincentives, while a premature ending risks loss of development momentum. We suggest that the subcommittee may wish to consider requiring that AID include a discussion of this aspect of economic assistance management as an element for consideration in its foreign assistance budget presentations. 

2. Is the coordination of family planning, health, and nutritional programs adequate?

The world food situation has increasingly been a matter of concern particularly since the massive sales of grain to Russia in 1972. This period has been marked by a rapidly upward spiraling of prices-some grains increasing by as much as 300 percent on the world market-depletion of world grain stocks, and export restraints by various countries. In the United States during 1973, the consumer price index for food increased from 128.6 to 151.3 compared to an increase from 127.7 to 133.5 for all items.

Such increases were not confined to the United States. The food and agricultural organization (FAO) reports that in some developing regions, 20 percent increases were experienced over a year's time. 

This situation came about even though the 1972 world grain output was the second largest on record; only slightly smaller than 1971. 

Solutions to the food situation are complicated by population increases. Over the past 15 years, food production in developing countries increased about 60 percent but per capita production increased less than one-half of one percent. 

Thus production increases are offset by population increases. The less developed countries now account for 83 percent of the world's population increases as compared to 68 percent only a score of years ago. A further problem is that almost half of the population in some of the less developed countries have not yet reached their reproductive years.

In addition to food shortages and large scale population growth, disease and malnutrition are common conditions in the developing countries. 

It seems obvious, therefore, that increased food production, decreased population growth, and improved health go hand-in-hand, and solutions to these problems must be approached on an integrated basis. We intend to focus on each of these areas in our future work. 

We have already initiated work in the food and nutrition area. In recognition of the increased concern throughout the world that we face a global food crisis, we are reviewing the extent and adequacy of bilateral and multilateral efforts to resolve both long and short range food problems. In subsequent review efforts, we plan to review population planning and health programs. 

Because of the interrelation among AID's programs in the fields of food supply, nutritional levels, population planning and health, these programs should be closely coordinated. therefore, in examining AID's appropriations request, the subcommittee may want to explore the level and effectiveness of coordination in these areas. 

3. What improvements are needed in Ex-Im bank's operations? 

Our reviews of Ex-Im bank's operations have resulted in conclusions that improvements in its management information system would aid the bank in making judgments on such matters as whether its financial assistance was essential to an export sale. Also we strongly believe that it is inappropriate for the 

Ex-Im bank receipts and disbursements to be excluded from the U.S. budget and that there is need to clarify Congressional intent as to whether the bank is required to maintain funded reserves of not less than 25 percent of its contractual liabilities of outstanding guarantees and insurances.

With respect to the "additionality" criteria, we issued a management report on Ex-Im bank's capital loan program in fiscal year 1973 in which we concluded that improvement in Ex-Im bank's management information system would aid the bank in making judgments crucial to financial operations. We pointed out that an improved system would assist the bank's management in: 

Determining whether its financial assistance was essential to an export sale,

Selecting products most in need of its financial assistance, Documenting the basis of its actions, and Evaluating the effects of its financing on exports. 

Let me say that we know of no system that can be devised to absolutely insure that regular commercial financing is not displaced or that the availability of Ex-Im bank's financing is the crucial factor influencing the sale. We believe it is possible, however, to develop a system for acquiring information which will increase the probability of bank assistance resulting in increased exports. 

Fundamental issues are, how much evidence is needed to judge whether the financing is necessary to complete a sale or whether prospective borrowers are trying to take advantage of the attractive rate and terms available, and how much risk to take on losing a sale. We do not try to minimize the difficulties in making these judgments.

In responding to our report, Ex-Im bank strongly advised us that its decisions were a matter of judgment made by its board of directors as a result of access to a variety of facts surrounding the circumstances of sale. We were unable, however, to find any large amount of material explaining the reasoning process on which the judgments were based. 

It is highly important that the integrity of the unified budget be maintained. 

If the Congress is to exercise effective control over Federal expenditures through the budget, it should resist efforts to remove Federal activities such as the export-import bank from the budget. 

The fundamental purpose of a unified budget is to bring together, in one place, competing needs so that priorities may be more readily established and resources allocated with due regard to all potential demands of the Federal Treasury. 

During fiscal year 1973, excluding the bank's receipts and disbursements from the budget understated the budgetary deficit from what it otherwise would have been by about $498 million. This amount represented a sharp increase over the approximately $145 million involved in the previous year. 

A bill has been reported in the Senate to include the Ex-Im Bank and other organizations currently excluded from the budget. Further, the Senate Subcommittee on International Finance is considering a bill to expand Ex-Im Bank's loan program which includes a provision to clarify the intent of the fractional reserve requirement. 

Another matter which may be of interest to the subcommittee is a recent decision rendered by the Comptroller General concerning the type of presidential determinations required with respect to Ex-Im Bank's loans to Communist countries.

On October 18, 1972, the President determined it to be in the national interest for the Export-Import Bank of the United States to guarantee, insure, extend credits in connection with the purchase or lease of any product by the USSR in accordance with section 2(b) (2) of the Export-Import Bank Act of 1945, as amended. Subsequent to this presidential determination, Ex-Im Bank has extended credits to the Soviet Union in numerous transactions, and the bank has reported such transactions to the Congress. However, no separate determination of national interest for each individual transaction has been issued by the President.

GAO on March 8, 1974, in response to an inquiry from Senator R. S. Schweiker held that the language of section 2(B) (2) of the present act, together with its legislative history, clearly requires a separate presidential determination for each loan. The GAO ruling is also applicable to other Communist countries holding export-import credits including Poland, Romania, and Yugoslavia. 

The Export-Import Bank has suspended action on further loans to Communist countries pending resolution of its response to the GAO ruling. 

1 Section 606 of S. 1541 which provides for the inclusion of Export-Import Bank activities in the Budget effective July 1, 1975.

4. Has AID moved expeditiously in using the fixed cost reimbursement approach to development assistance projects? 

The subcommittee in its report on the fiscal year 1974 appropriations bill expressed a strong belief that AID should make greater use of the fixed cost reimbursement method for dispensing economic assistance. It was noted that this method has been used with success in the Philippines but despite the subcommittee's recommendations AID had little inclination to use the method elsewhere. 

However, during the hearings, we noted that AID planned to use the fixed cost reimbursement method for rural programs in Bangladesh beginning in fiscal year 1974.

Since last year we have found that AID has taken only limited actions to expand the use of the fixed cost reimbursement method. We currently have several members of our staff in Bangladesh and, among other objectives, they plan to observe the progress that has been made to date. The subcommittee may wish to pursue this matter further with AID officials during the course of these hearings. 

5. Are inconsistencies in overseas allowances sufficient to warrant corrective actions!

During last year's consideration of the appropriation for AID by this subcommittee, concern was expressed regarding the payment of benefits and allowances to U.S. employees overseas. We have just completed a review of this matter.

We found that there are at least 50 different benefits, allowances, and privileges available to U.S. employees serving overseas depending upon their post and circumstance. The U.S. Government has about 737,000 employees-mostly military-from 38 agencies and departments assigned to positions in foreign countries and nonforeign areas overseas. Benefits and allowances, exclusive of salaries, amount to about $1.5 billion annually ($1.3 billion for uniformed personnel, $150 million for civilians in foreign countries, and $100 million for civilians in nonforeign areas). 

In our review, we found: 

1. Innumerable differences in the type and amount of allowances available and paid to U.S. civilian employees overseas in different agencies and within the same departments. These differences resulted from the fact that there are four different benefit and allowance systems, for U.S. Government civilians, which involve different legislative authority, agency regulations, and discretionary decisions by agency officials at varying levels. 

2. Significant differences between civilian employees in foreign areas and nonforeign areas overseas. 

3. Differences between uniformed personnel and civilian employees. 

4. Indications that the lack of uniformity in allowances and benefits result in significant morale problems. 

For the most part, allowances for civilian employees in foreign countries are authorized as (1) an overseas premium to recruit and retain employees or (2) as reimbursement to employees for extra costs which they would not incur in the United States. Some allowances like the housing allowance are designed to serve both purposes.

In many cases, additional compensation and benefits related to overseas service can be more than an individual's salary. Our question is whether the post differential allowance, which costs $36 million a year, and the premium portion of the housing allowance are serving the purpose for which they were authorized. Moreover, the overseas premium seems high in relation to other systems checked-Canada, the United Nations, and U.S. private industry. 

The basic aim underlying all nonpremium overseas benefits and allowances should be that they neither result in financial gain nor loss for an employee but reimburse the employee for extra costs of maintaining a standard of life equivalent to that which could be maintained in the United States. Notwithstanding, GAO found that the system of nonpremium allowances, as presently managed, permits civilian employees in many instances to realize substantial financial gain. 

In a draft report we have just released to executive agencies for their review, we are making a number of tentative proposals aimed at correcting these inequities.

ACCESS TO RECORDS 

One last matter we would like to discuss today concerns the current status of our access to records problems in the foreign assistance area. In our testimony last year, we presented to the subcommittee a description and examples of some of our access to records problems. 

Since last year's hearings, there has been some improvement in gaining access to records with respect to foreign assistance and related programs. We want to emphasize, however, that the access to records problem has not been resolved. 

The principal concern to us are continuing delays on the part of the agencies in responding to our requests for documents essential to our reviews. These instances which continue to arise are part of a long pattern of difficulty we have experienced in obtaining prompt access to information which we need in connection with our reviews of the security assistance programs. 

This completes my prepared statement, Mr. Chairman, and we will be pleased to respond to any question which you may have.

EXCERPTS FROM DIGESTS OF CERTAIN GAO REPORTS ON INTERNATIONAL MATTERS APRIL 1973 THROUGH FEBRUARY 1974 U.S. AGREEMENTS WITH AND ASSISTANCE TO FREE WORLD FORCES IN SOUTHEAST ASIA, DEPARTMENT OF DEFENSE,  

B-159451 of April 24, 1973

In recent years the Congress has been concerned over the number and scope of agreements concluded by the executive branch committing the United States to provide substantial assistance to foreign countries. To illustrate some of the agreements or arrangements and to report on the costs and financial administration of the assistance provided, GAO reviewed U.S. commitments, agreements, and assistance to allied governments that provided forces to Vietnam, namely Australia 

Nationalist China

Republic of Korea 

New Zealand

The Philippines 

Spain Thailand

GAO found that assistance provided under the agreements was often funded from multiple sources and not always fully identified or reported to the Congress. Documents committing the United States were signed by military commanders in some cases and by ambassadors or other officials of the American Embassy in others. The agreements and arrangements were not well defined. We concluded that the executive branch needed to exercise more coordinated control and management over the execution of such agreements.

We also found no evidence that the Congress was notified or advised by the executive branch prior to its entering into specific agreements or commitments obligating the United States to incur substantial expenditures. 

GAO recommended that the Secretaries of State and Defense should require that agreements and commitments providing assistance to foreign countries are clearly understood and adequately defined prior to providing the assistance. 

GAO also recommended that the Secretary of State: --Establish procedures to require that all agreements be subject to his approval. This would include those subordinate to or designed to implement basic government-to-government agreements requiring expenditures of substantial amounts of money. --Require a central repository to be established within the State Department for all such international agreements and arrangements.

--Provide annually to the appropriate committees of the Congress a list and description of all such agreements, together with estimates of future years' costs that each agreement involves. 

IMPROVEMENTS NEEDED IN SYSTEM FOR MANAGING U.S. PARTICIPATION IN THE ASIAN DEVELOPMENT BANK 

B-173240 of May 8, 1973

This review assesses how U.S. officials managed U.S. participation in the Asian Development Bank (ADB). The report is one of a series of three dealing with U.S. participation in the international financial institutions.

We noted that the Treasury does not yet have a fully functioning system for managing U.S. participation in the Bank, although some improvements were made. Consequently, we observed that Treasury is not in a position to assure the Congress that funds contributed are being used efficiently and effectively for intended objectives. 

This report made a number of specific recommendations to improve management of U.S. participation in the Bank. We suggested that the 

Secretary of the Treasury should arrange for: --More timely, substantive information on proposed Bank loans, before receipt of the formal loan proposal documents. This would allow U.S. missions to make more meaningful and timely comments and thereby improve the NAC review and approval process. --Guidelines for U.S. officials to follow in appraising and evaluating loan proposals. --Instructions requiring U.S. missions to furnish available information on Bank activities to Washington, D.C., including prospective loan requests from would-be borrowers and progress in implementing Bank projects. 

INTERIM REPORT ON THE AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT'S HOUSING INVESTMENT GUARANTY PROGRAM 

B-171526 of May 22, 1973

The Housing Investment Guaranty Program (HG) authorized under the Foreign Assistance Act and managed by the Agency for International Development (AID) is designed to guarantee private U.S. capital for long-term financing to housing projects and programs in developing countries. The Chairman, Senate Committee on Foreign Relations asked 

GAO to review this program and initial efforts focused on the program in Central America.

In attempting to fulfill its legislative objective, the HG program: --Financed functional, attractive, and generally selfliquidating housing.

--Contributed to an unmeasurable degree, to the development of housing institutions and the mobilization of savings. --Had no appreciable impact on improving housing conditions for lower income families because only the upper 25 percent of the economic stratum could afford housing under the program. --Had no appreciable impact on improving housing conditions when measured against relative need. 

On the basis of the results of the review in Central America, GAO is undertaking a worldwide review of this program. 

GAO recommended that the Administrator, AID, have the agency review the HG program's role in meeting the statutory objectives of constructing homes for lower income families and improving housing conditions in Central America. This review should determine whether alternatives, such as building homes at lower prices, exist which could make the HG program effective in constructing housing for lower income families. 

ASSISTANCE TO FAMILY PLANNING PROGRAMS IN SOUTHEAST ASIA, AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT 

8-173240 of May 23, 1973

In 1967 the Congress enacted an amendment to foreign aid legis lation entitled "Title X--Programs Relating to Population Growth." 

Thereafter amounts earmarked for population and family planning programs increased sharply--from $35 million in fiscal year 1968 (up from $5 million the previous year) to $125 million for both 1972 and 1973. AID provided $35 million directly to family planning programs in Indonesia, Laos, Thailand, and the Philippines between 1968 and 1972. GAO reviewed AID's problems in implementing programs in these 

Countries, particularly in view of the relatively short period AID had to develop and implement programs to use the large amounts of money provided.

For each of the four countries, title X funds were used to a greater or lesser degree for purposes related indirectly to controlling population growth rates. Various maternal and child health and nutrition programs in the Philippines, Thailand, and Laos previously funded by regular AID appropriations were considered family planning projects when title X funds became available. In addition, AID obligated large amounts during the last month of the fiscal year for undefined program requirements so that funds would not be lost to the program. 

Recommendations or Suggestions

AID used title X funds for health and nutrition programs not related directly to reducing population growth rates, because it believed that such use in some cases was the best means to promote family planning. 

GAO therefore suggested that the Congress consider whether title X may need to be revised to provide for a coordinated program of family planning, health, and nutrition.

AID said it would concur in this recommendation, provided that additional funds for health and nutrition are included in the title X appropriation. In implementing a coordinated family planning, health, and nutrition program, AID would be glad to give increased emphasis to health and nutrition but would in no way wish to reduce the emphasis given to family planning.

PROGRESS AND PROBLEMS OF U.S. ASSISTANCE FOR LAND REFORM IN VIETNAM, AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT,  

B-159451 of June 22, 1973

As of March 31, 1973, the United States had contributed about $38 million to the land reform program in Vietnam. The primary aim of the program was to broaden the political base of the Government of Vietnam (GVN) by breaking up large landholdings and giving rural families title to the land they farm. 

The program consisted of two subprograms: the Land-to-the 

Tiller (LTTT) program and the Montagnard program. Under the LTTT program 1,007,217 hectares had been distributed to about 650,000 tenant farmers as of March 1973. This exceeded the initial goal of 1 million hectares. The Montagnard land reform program, however, has made slow progress. It has been carried out poorly, has not received adequate 

GVN support, and has received a disproportionately low share of U.S. support. In many cases where land has been transferred, problems exist which prevent the Montagnards from receiving full program benefits. 

These problems include allocations for less than the amount of land area indicated in program guidelines and land encroachments. 

If the United States continues its past level of support to the GVN budget, the cost of the program to the United States might reach over $300 million. Compensation payments to former landlords under the LTTT program alone are expected to cost about $537 million. This will place a serious additional burden on the GVN budget. 

Agency officials agreed problems still exist in the land reform program but contended that since November 1972 progress has been made in overcoming some problems hindering the attainment of the program's initial objectives.

NET FOREIGN EXCHANGE COSTS OF U.S. 

MILITARY FORCES IN EUROPE B-156489 OF July 6, 1973 

This report estimates the net foreign exchange cost to maintain U.S. forces in Europe for calendar years 1970, 1971, and 1972 and evaluates a DOD computation of these costs for fiscal years 1972 and 

1973. The report also estimates the impact of the two devaluations of the dollar on the cost of U.S. participation in NATO. 

Despite the base period difference (fiscal vs. calendar years) between the DOD computation and the GAO estimate, GAO believes the significant difference is that DOD includes additional items to offset U.S. expenditures in NATO and as a result DOD computed a much smaller net cost. Thus DOD's computation of the deficit for fiscal

years 1972 and 1973 amounted to $400 million compared to GAO's estimate of about $1.0 billion each in calendar years 1970 and 1971 and $1.7 billion in 1972. 

As a result of the 1971 and 1973 devaluation of the dollar, DOD costs for programs in NATO countries have increased. GAO estimates the total impact of the devaluation on U.S. participation in NATO from fiscal year 1972 to fiscal year 1974 to be roughly $600 million. 

RUSSIAN WHEAT SALES AND WEAKNESSES IN AGRICULTURE'S MANAGEMENT OF WHEAT EXPORT SUBSIDY PROGRAM, DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE 

B-176943 OF July 9, 1973

The President announced the signing of an agreement with Russia on July 8, 1972, making credit totaling $750 million available over a 3-year period for purchasing U.S. grains. By then Russia was already purchasing U.S. wheat. Within a few weeks, cash and credit wheat sales to Russia, heavily subsidized by the U.S. Government approximated $700 million, the largest private grain sales in U.S. history. The large sales of U.S. wheat to Russia and other exports in the summer of 

1972 caused a dramatic rise in the price of U.S. wheat. 

Agriculture paid over $300 million in subsidies on the Russian and other export sales. GAO believes many of these sales would have been made even with reduced subsidies and that Agriculture should have responded more rapidly to the available information and reduced or eliminated the subsidies sooner. 

GAO made several recommendations to the Secretary of Agriculture to overcome general management weaknesses observed in the wheat export program concerning the payment of subsidies; and for the dissemination of foreign agricultural information.

GAO suggested that Congress should consider requiring that agencies develop definitive ground rules so that expected benefits from exports can be appropriately weighed against their impact on various segments of the domestic economy. 

U.S. ASSISTANCE FOR THE ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT OF THE REPUBLIC OF KOREA 

B-164264 OF July 12, 1973

Korea's economic growth indicators, such as gross national product and manufacturing output, have been most impressive since 1965, but this economic success may not be as great as it appears. Indicated accomplishments have been achieved at the expense of a steadily mounting external debt and an increasing trade deficit. Expansion of industry has been emphasized with much less attention being given to social and welfare needs. The rural-urban income gap and food grain production-consumption gap also have widened.

During 1971 and 1972, most of the AID development loan funds were used to import rice. Therefore, in essence, the development loan program has been an extension of the Public Law 480 program. With the 

United Nations and international lending institutions increasing their assistance to Korea, the Public Law 480 program generating increased

amounts which can be used in the lagging economic sectors, and the Korean Government's continuing emphasis on the industrial sector, GAO questioned the need for continuing the AID development loan program. 

The review also disclosed a number of problems involving the administration of the AID and Public Law 480 programs, e.g. --AID loans, intended for developing small and medium size firms were used to assist large well-established firms. --The Korean Government improperly used $1.8 million in funds and commodities provided by the United States. 

Korea had not refunded this amount at the time of the review. --AID recorded as obligations large amounts of funds for family planning activities without defining the requirements, and commodities obtained for the program were either used for activities other than family planning or were not used. --The U.S. had incurred financial losses totaling $404,000 due to late Korean Government deposits of local currencies generated from the sales of Public Law 480 commodities. 

The Administrator of AID should (1) urge the Korean Government to reassess its roles as investor and as competitor with the private sector, (2) exercise closer controls over the use of funds as provided for in existing agreements, (3) implement follow-up procedures to assure the timely receipt of required reports on textile production and exports, (4) continue to press Korea for final settlement on refund claims, and (5) strengthen procedures for determining commodity requirements before obligating funds.

The State Department and AID expressed the belief that the timing for a phasedown of U.S. economic aid should remain flexible because of the irregular performance of the Korean economy and events which have clouded its economic outlook.

MANAGEMENT OF INVESTMENT INSURANCE, LOAN GUARANTEES, AND CLAIM PAYMENTS BY THE OVERSEAS PRIVATE INVESTMENT CORPORATION 

B-173240 OF July 16, 1973

Because OPIC supports projects in underdeveloped countries and insures political risks, it is vulnerable to catastrophic losses. 

Catastrophic losses would compel OPIC to ask the Congress for funds to satisfy claims. --OPIC has made considerable progress in sharing its risk with private insurers although it still retains the primary risk for catastrophic losses. --Recent contractual changes should reduce OPIC's risk significantly, but OPIC has not yet had sufficient experience to determine how acceptable the changes will be to investors.

--A monitoring system appears to provide OPIC a reasonable basis for decisions to suspend or terminate insurance programs in countries that become high political risks, but OPIC's existing interests in those countries would remain vulnerable to whatever political actions occur. 

OPIC has made good progress in obtaining information related to the developmental effects of projects, and recognizes the need to expand its monitoring of project results. OPIC has given increased attention to the problem of insuring runaway industries and has recently established procedures which, if properly implemented, should provide reasonable assurance that U.S. interests are protected. 

GAO was unable to make any overall conclusions on the general adequacy of procedures, guidelines, and criteria used by OPIC in evaluating claims presented by companies.

SOCIAL DEVELOPMENT ACTIVITIES IN LATIN AMERICA PROMOTED BY THE INTER-AMERICAN FOUNDATION, FISCAL YEAR 1972, B-135075 OF July 23, 1973 

The Congress created IAF to rectify social development shortcomings in prior U.S. assistance efforts in Latin America by providing assistance privately through private channels rather than through governmental channels, meaning that the principal participants in the development effort would be United States and Latin American private groups. During its first year: -- IAF provided assistance to Latin American private groups, but none to United States private groups. -- IAF relaxed the terms of the assistance, i.e., it gave grants to projects or types of projects previously promoted with loans, and it softened the prior practice of requiring the Latin America recipients to obtain local matching funds.

GAO believes that the exclusion of U.S. private groups and the relaxation of assistance terms are potentially detrimental to the U.S. social development program in Latin America. 

GAO recommended that IAF broaden its approach, but IAF rejected the recommendation because it apparently perceives its intended role to be more limited than that perceived by GAO. 

The Congress may wish to consider whether IAF's intended role is adequately defined and understood. 

U.S. FOREIGN AID TO EDUCATION: 

DOES BRAZIL NEED IT? 

B-133283 OF July 30, 1973

The United States has given education development in Latin America priority attention since the mid-1960's. Brazil, which accounted for a substantial part of this assistance, received about $187 million direct and indirect aid for fiscal years 1965-1972. GAO observed shortcomings in the implementation of the U.S. education assistance including the

program not being designed to improve inequities in the Brazilian education system; U.S. efforts not being directed to solving the basic course of the shortage in qualified primary school teachers; and planned increases in secondary school enrollment being adversely affected by school site locations. GAO made suggestions for improvements.

GAO's review of U.S. assistance for education development necessarily required that it be examined in the context of Brazil's overall development. 

The United States provided about $50 million in concessional aid to Brazil in fiscal year 1973 and planned to provide about $17 million in fiscal year 1974. Brazil's need for such assistance, however, is questionable. --Its gross national product has grown at an average annual rate of about 9.9 percent since 1968 and totaled about $50 billion in 1972. --It accumulated $3 billion in foreign exchange in 1971 and 1972. Total reserves at the start of 1973 were about $4.2 billion. --It is able to obtain substantial economic assistance from other sources. --Brazil, in turn, pledged some of its resources in 1972 to the Special Fund of the African Development Bank. The resources of this fund, like the more concessional loan funds of the Inter-American Development Bank and the Asian 

Development Bank, will be used to finance high-priority development projects. --Authorized but undisbursed Agency for International 

Development (AID) loans amounted to over a quarter of a billion dollars as of May 1, 1973. 

The question of when a foreign aid recipient, like Brazil, reaches the point in its development when it no longer needs further U.S. concessional assistance has not been addressed by State and AID. GAO believes that the 

Congress should require the Department of State and AID to identify precisely and objectively that point at which a country, such as Brazil, no longer requires U.S. concessional assistance. 

SUMMARY OF UNITED STATES ASSISTANCE TO JORDAN, AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT,  B-179001 OF August 8, 1973 

Jordan plays a key role in United States Middle East policy. It has received $887.2 million in U.S. economic and military assistance for fiscal years 1952-72. about half of which has been in untied cash grants for budget support. Other assistance includes project assistance grants, Public Law 480 loans and grants, capital development loans and Export-Import Bank loans. The U.S. programs appear to have been successful in helping to maintain a moderate government in Jordan. 

The June 1967 war with Israel drastically changed Jordan's growth. 

It lost (1) the West Bank of the Jordan River, (2) one-third of its 2= ? 2. 2 2

agricultural production, (3) one-fifth of its light industrial production, and (4) its major tourist attractions. 

The refugees and displaced persons in Jordan have placed a heavy burden on its economy. While the United National Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA) has assumed the major share for the necessary financial support, Jordan has accepted responsibility for the needy displaced persons. 

Overall, the refugees and displaced persons have had a major negative impact on Jordan's economy.

U.S. GRANT SUPPORT OF INTERNATIONAL PLANNED PARENTHOOD FEDERATION NEEDS BETTER OVERSIGHT, AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT 

B-173240 OF September 14, 1973

The Agency for International Development (AID) is providing about $10 million annually as grant budgeting support for private family planning activities carried out by the International Planned Parenthood 

Federation (IPPF).

IPPF's income has grown substantially, from about $900,000 in 1965 to over $19 million in 1971. Rapid growth has contributed to a number of organizational and operational problems.

AID's limited grant review and monitoring and its strong reliance on the management control system of IPPF's central office in London provides minimal control upon the use of funds. 

At IPPF's central office, GAO noted several problems bearing on IPPF's ability to implement effective programs and to reasonably assure donors of program effectiveness. Management review and control over family planning activities by family planning associations is uneven and weak. 

IPPF is making improvements in personnel practices, programing, auditing and reporting.

GAO perceives the grant arrangement as a realistic attempt to insure effective use of U.S. population assistance funds and to enlarge the scope of the program. 

IPPF is qualified to sponsor the inception and improvement of indigenous family planning programs and is of value to AID in carrying out its congressional mandate on population assistance. 

GAO also concluded that AID and IPPF needed to provide greater assurances that the purposes of the grant are being achieved. Therefore, GAO recommended that AID provide for a program of increased assistance and advice to the grantee for working out a specific phased plan for more effective and timely implementation of management controls. 

GAO recommended that AID improve the review and evaluation of IPPF operations by making a more complete review of IPPF's management system to provide greater assurance that grant objectives are being met. GAO believes that the Agency's evaluation capability should also be improved by obtaining appraisals of national associations' programs, where feasible, from a larger number of Embassies and Missions.

U.S. ASSISTANCE TO THE KHMER REPUBLIC (CAMBODIA), , AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT, DEPARTMENT OF DEFENSE B-169832 OF October 10, 1973 

not

The United States provided $516 million in military assistance and $216 million in economic assistance to Cambodia during fiscal years 1970-73, not including the cost of combat air operations. Problems existed concerning compliance with the congressional restrictions: all costs of U.S. activities in Cambodia were reported to the Congress, even though reports of U.S. expenditures were prepared and Military 

Equipment Delivery Team members were not assigned as advisors to Cambodian combat units, but they were acting beyond their primary function of auditing deliveries.

Management deficiencies inpaired the effectiveness and efficiency of U.S. assistance. Procedures for receipt, transfer, and maintenance of military equipment after turnover to Cambodia were inadequate during 1971 and 1972, and management of the ammunition program was deficient. By 1973, considerable improvements had been made, or were planned, but equipment accountability still needed attention. Other problems with the military program included (1) the failure to cancel a $1.4 million requisition for construction equipment after it was known that AID was satisfying the requirement, (2) the improper purchase of U.S. military equipment by 

Cambodian military personnel from South Vietnamese military personnel, (3) the improper payment of as many as 100,000 "phantom troops", and (4) logistics support and distribution problems related to trucks purchased from Australia.

AID's $180 million request for economic assistance in fiscal years 1971 and 1972 greatly exceeded the level the Cambodian economy absorbed effectively due to the slow arrival of the commodities financed. 

Cambodian tax policies delayed the movement into the economy of some commodities financed by AID and it approved procurement of some commodities of questionable necessity to a war economy; then, as a result of congressional inquiry, canceled them. 

Because the Congress has been concerned about the extent of U.S. 

Involvement in Cambodia, GAO recommended that the Secretaries of State and Defense fully inform the Congress of the type and organizational level of advisory assistance provided to the Cambodian military as well as all costs against the dollar limit including those outside the Foreign Assistance Act and Public Law 480. 

Also a number of specific recommendations were made to the 

Administrator of AID and the Secretary of Defense. 

EXPORTERS PROFITS ON SALES OF U.S. 

WHEAT TO RUSSIAN DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE 

B-176943 OF February 12, 1974

The estimated financial results of the sales to Russia of 316 million bushels of hard winter wheat as reported to GAO by five grain companies ranged from a profit of 2 cents to a loss of 1.9 cents per bushel. Hard

winter wheat sales constituted about 91 percent of the sales made to Russia by the five companies. 

In view of several limitations, GAO believed that the financial results of the Russian sales could not be precisely determined. Subject to these 

1imitations, GAO believed that the companies' estimated financial results of the hard winter wheat sales to Russia were a reasonably accurate and fair presentation. The grain exporters had opportunities to make unusual profits on their non-Russian sales through September 1972 since these sales were made at higher prices while still obtaining subsidies. 

Available records concerning the background of the Russian wheat sales tended to support the view that exporters either did not have inside information on Russian buying intentions or did not take advantage of any such Information.

GAO discussed the results of its review with the five exporters. 

There were no major disagreements with the exporters concerning the financial results of the Russian sales. Most agreed also that opportunities for unusual profits existed because of the changed business environment. 

UNITED STATES PROGRAMS IN GHANA 

B-179421 OF February 12, 1974

GAO reviewed U.S. aid to the Republic of Ghana to --Observe the relation of U.S. assistance programs to other donors and --Evaluate the relation of assistance from all donors to Ghana's significant external debt problems. 

For a 5-year period through fiscal year 1971, the United States, the largest single source of economic assistance, gave about $155 million, or an average of $31 million a year, in bilateral economic assistance to Ghana. U.S. assistance for fiscal years 1972 and 1973 was at a lower level due to U.S. concern with resolving Ghana's debt problems.

The U.S. assistance program in Ghana operates within a multilateral group led by the World Bank. This approach has improved the coordination of aid to Ghana. Efforts are being made to further relate 

U.S. assistance with projects of other donors. GAO believes that these efforts can be productive and should be encouraged. 

Ghana's external public debts totaled almost $1 billion early in 1972. Interest and principal payments on these debts, together with 

Ghana's trade deficit problems, resulted in a shortage of foreign exchange, which has hampered Ghana's economic development and threatens future progress.

Debt relief has been given primarily by rescheduling interest and amortization payments on pre-1966 suppliers credits--about three-fourths from Western European sources. 34-192 O 74-17

The United States, the World Bank, West Germany, and Canada have been the major providers of net assistance (i.e., the excess of assistance provided over debt repayment) to Ghana from 1967-71. Because of the seriousness of Ghana's debt problem, the Congress may wish to review with the Department of State and AID the role that foreign donors, including the United States, play in providing a net-aid flow to support 

Ghana's economic development.

AID assistance to a textile manufacturer in Ghana has raised questions about the priorities given to further Ghanaian development and U.S. trade interests. GAO found a need for developing more definitive criteria to help resolve such conflicting U.S. interests. Criteria for determining eligibility for a loan should specify such matters as the permissible percentage of the production that could be exported to the United States; how much displacement of U.S. trade should be permitted; and the benefits, if any, that could flow to third-country interests.

SUMMARY OF STATEMENT 

Senator INOUYE. Now, if you wish to summarize, or to go through the whole statement, I will leave it up to you, sir.

Mr. FASICK. I would like to summarize the statement. Senator INOUYE. Please do. 

Mr. FASICK. First of all, I would like to introduce our staff that is here today. 

On my left Mr. Hylander, Deputy Director; Mr. Milgate, Associate 

Director; and Mr. Zappacosta, Assistant Director. 

On my right is Mr. Duff, Associate Director; and Mr. Conahan, Associate Director.

We also have several people in the back in case we should need them. 

We are pleased to appear before the subcommittee, Mr. Chairman, to discuss our work. Our statement basically concerns three areas: The recent work we have done that would be of concern to this subcommittee, our current efforts which we are now involved in, and several issues that we think are pertinent and should be considered by the administration and by the Congress in connection with the foreign aid program.

We are pleased to note that last year the Congress had taken several significant actions in the foreign assistance area. Particularly noteworthy were the provisions included in these bills which require the disclosure of debt service rescheduling, require the administration to seek independent review groups in selected international organizations, tighten the control over the use of excess foreign currency by the executive agencies in administering their programs, and functionally realine development assistance programs. 

Subsequent to our appearance before this committee last April, we have continued to work very closely with your staff in order to be responsive to the specific requests of yours or the subcommittee members and to maintain a communication channel which on a day-to-day basis we believe keeps us aware of your overall and long-range interests. Our objective is to tailor our self-initiated work to respond to your needs to the extent possible.

In this connection, we spent about 250 professional man-years' worth of effort in international programs. Many, if not most, of those programs are of concern to this subcommittee.

Of that total, roughly 25 percent are applied in response to specific congressional requests. 

Our reports over the past year relative to international operations have dealt with broad country programs, selected development and security assistance aspects of overall country programs, balance-ofpayment issues, management and profits on wheat exports, international aspects of the energy crisis, financial aspects of the Eximbank and OPIC operations, and various subjects involving foreign trade. 

We prepared an attachment to our statement which with your permission we would like to submit for the record. These concern a number of reports which we believe will be of specific interest to this subcommittee.

We currently have a number of studies underway which we believe will provide reports of interest to the Congress and the subcommittee in the near future. I would like to briefly discuss several of these 

AID STAFFING 

The first concerns AID staffing. This subcommittee requested this particular study of GAO, and in this request you specifically asked us to establish a base against which future action can be measured, compare AID's salary and related personnel benefits to those of other Government agencies and private nonprofit organizations, and evaluaate the utilization of AID personnel in offices performing services not directly related to program support. 

I think it is pretty obvious even at this early stage in our review that AID does have problems in connection with overstaffing and overranking of their personnel. I think their real problem is a determination as to what action would be appropriate in order to alleviate these situations.

PUBLIC SAFETY PROGRAM PHASEOUT 

The second study we have underway involves the implementation of the public safety program phaseout. In the fall of 1973, we started the survey of Agency for International Development public safety programs. Our objective was to gain an insight into the nature of the programs and identify problem areas for in-depth review. Shortly after we began our survey, we received a series of requests of various Members of the Congress for specific information related to public safety programs, such as cost, type of support provided, and the purpose for which funds were expended in certain countries. 

Subsequently, the Foreign Assistance Act was amended to provide that: "No part of any appropriation made available to carry out this act shall be used to conduct any police training or related program in a foreign country." Accordingly, the scope of our work in the public safety area was tailored to give recognition to this amendment. 

We have found to date that AID is taking steps to terminate its funding of public safety programs in all foreign countries. We are monitoring this phaseout, and we are also looking into the Department of Defense military assistance programs with a view toward reporting to the Congress on the nature and scope, if any, of continuing support to the police organizations, law enforcement, and public safety programs.

INTERNATIONAL NARCOTICS CONTROL STUDY 

The third study I would like to mention with possible interest to you is the international narcotics control study. We are looking into 

U.S. assistance activities involving training and advising enforcement personnel, and providing economic alternatives to farmers producing opium. Narcotics assistance in the areas of health, education, and treatment is being examined. U.S. efforts to promote and participate in multilateral narcotics control activities are being analyzed. 

We are also considering the issue of foreign government cooperation and the adequacy of opium availability for legal medicinal needs.

In connection with this assignment, the fieldwork is being performed in 10 European and Mideast countries, and in 8 South Asia and Far East countries. We expect to be able to report on the results of this work by the fall of this year.

EVALUATION FOR MAAG'S 

Please proceed, Mr. Fasick.

Mr. FASICK. The next area is an evaluation of the need for MAAG's in today's climate. The question as to whether the United States should continue to maintain Military Assistance Advisory Groups, MAAG's, throughout the world has been of considerable concern to the Congress. 

This was particularly evident during hearings on the 1973 Foreign Assistance Act and in the Senate recommending that MAAG's be eliminated by 1976.

In view of this concern we have undertaken a review of the MAAG's to evaluate their functions, duties and purposes so as to be in a position to report to the Congress on the current role played by the MAAG's in U.S. foreign policy.

Primary emphasis will be placed in determining whether all of the MAAG's, which in fiscal year 1973 were staffed with about 2,300 military and 1,100 civilian personnel in 46 countries, are still required to assist our allies improve their defense capabilities or whether such functions could be better handled through other elements of the U.S. country team.

Senator INOUYE. On the MAAG, are you finding that DOD is cooperating with you? 

Mr. FASICK. Yes, sir. So far. 

Senator INOUYE. Thank you, sir.

Mr. FASICK. We have several efforts underway directed toward evaluation of U.S. participation in multilateral organizations. We are placing more emphasis, for example, on evaluating the U.S. participation in the World Bank, the Asian Development Bank, the Inter- American Development Bank, the United Nations and its specialized agencies and other international programs. 

The objective of GAO work in these areas is to suggest ways in which the U.S. agencies involved can seek improvements through their membership and participation in these organizations. We have made a number of reviews of U.S. participation in these organizations in the past, and we have concluded in general that improved capability for monitoring and evaluating the results of U.S. development assistance channeled through international organizations is needed. Thus, we will continue to emphasize the need to improve management of U.S. participation in these organizations and currently have in process a number of reviews addressed to this need. 

U.S.-OWNED FOREIGN CURRENCIES 

The utilization of excess foreign currencies. On November 19, 1973, the chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee asked us to make a study of U.S. owned foreign currencies with the aim of finding possible ways to put them to more effective use. We were asked to develop information on the nature and extent of current and projected holdings includings debts; the nature and extent of partially controlled currencies; current and prospective uses of currencies by agencies and estimates of dollar savings; and applicable laws regarding the usage and debt-settlement.

We have also been requested by others to do work in the field of foreign currencies. On December 14, 1973, the chairman of the Subcommittee on the Near East and South Asia, House Committee on 

Foreign Affairs, requested work by GAO. On December 21, 1973, work was requested by Congressman John D. Conlan. The information asked for in these two requests is similar to the information requested by the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. 

We plan to issue our first report on these foreign currency assignments this spring.

Now I would like to address myself to some foreign assistance issues that in our opinion need continuing attention. Our studies and reviews spanning back over the past several years of foreign assistance programs have resulted in the identification of a number of issues which need continuing attention on the part of the administration and the Congress in order to effect management improvements. These involve questions such as: 

When should concessional assistance be stopped?

Is the coordination of family planning, health, and nutritional programs adequate? 

What improvements are needed in Eximbank's operations?

Has AID moved expeditiously in using the fixed cost reimbursement approach to development assistance projects? 

Are inconsistencies in overseas allowances sufficient to warrant corrective actions?

With your permission I would like to discuss each of these briefly. 

We believe there is a need for criteria to enable judgments to be made on when countries no longer require U.S. assistance. This question was raised by us in reports that we have issued as a result of four country program reviews in Brazil, in Panama, in Turkey, and Korea. 

Senator INOUYE. May I add my amen to that, sir. 

Mr. FASICK. Very good.

Now deciding when to end an AID program in a developing nation is just as important in our opinion as deciding when to start one. Prolonging the program can create self-help disincentives, while a premature ending risks loss of development momentum. We suggest that the subcommittee may wish to consider that AID include a discussion of this aspect of economic assistance management as an element for consideration in its foreign assistance budget presentation.

I think, Mr. Chairman, the remarks you were making to Ambassador Kellogg were very, very pertinent. It usually is far easier to start a program than it is to stop it. We have found this to be the case, as I indicated, in a number of countries that we have reviewed recently. 

Is the coordination of family planning, health, and nutritional programs adequate? The world food situation has increasingly been a matter of concern, particularly since the massive sales of grain to 

Russia in 1972. I don't think the sales to Russia themselves triggered the problem, but they highlighted it to the American public. 

Solutions to the food situation are complicated by population increases. Over the past 15 years, food production in developing countries increased about 60 percent, but per capita production increased less than one-half of 1 percent. Thus production increases are offset by population increases. The less-developed countries now account for 83 percent of the world's population increases as compared to only

68 percent a score of years ago. A further problem is that almost half of the population in some of the less-developed countries have not yet reached their reproductive years.

In addition to food shortages and large-scale population growth, diseases and malnutrition are common conditions in the developing countries. It seems obvious, therefore, that increased food production, decreased population growth, and improved health go hand in hand and solutions to these problems must be approached on an integrated basis. We intend to focus on each of these areas in our future work. 

For example, in connection with AID's appropriation request, this subcommittee may want to explore the level and effectiveness on the part of AID in these areas. 

Senator INOUYE. Are you suggesting that there is a lack of coordination? 

Mr. FASICK. From what we can discern so far, sir, yes.

EXPORT-IMPORT BANK IMPROVEMENTS 

Our reviews of Eximbank's operations have resulted in conclusions that improvements in its management information system would aid the Bank in making judgments on such matters as whether its financial assistance was essential to an export sale.

With respect to what we call the additionality criteria, we issued a management report on Eximbank's capital loan program in fiscal year 1973 in which we concluded that improvement in Eximbank's management information system would aid the Bank in making judgments crucial to financial operations. We pointed out that an improved system would assist the Bank's management in determining whether its financial assistance was essential to an export sale, selecting products most in need of its financial assistance, and documenting the basis of its actions and evaluating the effects of its financing on exports. 

Let me say that we know of no system that can be devised to absolutely insure that regular commercial financing is not displaced or that the availability of Eximbank's financing is the crucial factor influencing the sale. We believe it is possible, however, to develop a system for acquiring information which will increase the probability of Bank assistance resulting in increased exports. Fundamental issues are, how much evidence is needed to judge whether the financing is necessary to complete a sale or whether prospective borrowers are trying to take advantage of the attractive rate and terms available, and how much risk to take on losing a sale. We do not try to minimize the difficulties in making these judgments.

In responding to our report, Eximbank strongly advised us that its decisions were a matter of judgment made by its board of directors as a result of access to a variety of facts surrounding the circumstances of sale. We were unable, however, to find any large amount of material explaining the reasoning process on which the judgments are based. 

It is highly important that the integrity of the unified budget be maintained. If the Congress is to exercise effective control over Fedcral expenditures through the budget, it should resist efforts to remove Federal activities such as the Export-Import Bank from the budget.

UNIFIED BUDGET 

The fundamental purpose of a unified budget is to bring together, in one place, competing needs so that priorities may be more readily established and resources allocated with due regard to all potential demands on the Federal treasury.

During fiscal year 1973, excluding the bank's receipts and disbursements from the budget understated the budgetary deficit from what it otherwise would have been by about $498 million. This amount represented a sharp increase over the approximately $145 million involved in the previous year.

A bill¹ had been reported in the Senate to include the Eximbank and other organizations currently excluded from the budget. 

The Senate on Friday did pass this bill which does include the provision for bringing the Eximbank back into the budget of the United States.

That was a matter that I was going to discuss in more detail today, but the action of the Senate on Friday overcame that. 

Another matter which might be of interest to the subcommittee is a recent decision rendered by the Comptroller General concerning the type of Presidential determinations.

On October 18, 1972, the President determined it to be in the national interest for the Export-Import Bank of the United States to guarantee, insure, extend credits in connection with the purchase or lease of any product by the U.S.S.R. in accordance with section 2(B) (2) of the Export-Import Bank Act of 1945, as amended. Subsequent to this Presidential determination, Eximbank has extended credits to the Soviet Union in numerous transactions, and the Bank has reported such transactions to the Congress. However, no separate determination of national interest for each individual transaction has been issued by the President.

We on March 8, 1974, in response to an inquiry from Senator R. S. 

Schweiker, held that the language of section 2(B)2 of the present act, together with its legislative history, clearly requires a separate Presidential determination for each loan. Our ruling is also applicable to other Communist countries holding export-import credits including 

Poland, Romania, and Yugoslavia.

SUSPENSION OF LOANS 

The Export-Import Bank had suspended action on further loans to Communist countries pending resolution of its response to the GAO ruling.

We understand that the Attorney General now has concurred in Ex-Im's opinion that our decision had no merit and Ex-Im has resumed actions on loans to Russia.

Senator INOUYE. This decision made this past weekend by the Attorney General and the State Department, are you still concerned that the Ex-Im Bank is operating outside the scope of the law? 

1 Section 606 of S. 1541 which provides for the inclusion of Export-Import Bank activities in the Budget effective July 1, 1975, required with respect to Eximbank's loans to Communist countries.

Mr. FASICK. We are, sir, and we adhere to our opinion. As I understand it, that concurrence in Ex-Im Bank's opinion was made by the 

Attorney General, Mr. Saxbe. 

Senator INOUYE. And it is your view notwithstanding the Attorney

General's decision that every separate transaction requires a Presidential determination? 

Mr. FASICK. Yes, sir.

Senator INOUYE. And on the record you have just one blanket determination? 

Mr. FASICK. That is right, sir. One country determination. They have one for each of the four Communist countries involved on the loan program. 

We expect to testify on this matter before the Subcommittee on International Finance of the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs on April 2, at which time we will respond in detail to the opinion of the Attorney General and the General Counsel of the Ex-Im Bank.
