含​晶 ​ttoma Pr

Dear Ms. Chairman: 

COMPTROLLER GENERAL OF THE UNITED STATES 

WASHINGTON, D.C. 20548 

March 21, 1974

d

Recently, this Office was called upon by Senator Richard Schweiker to render an opinion as to whether Export-Import Bank credits involving Communist countries required a separate determination of national interest by the President for each transaction. After careful review of the wording of the law and its legislative history, we determined that such credits would require separate Presidential determinations. Our reasons are set forth in the enclosed letter to Senator Schweiker. 

The General Counsel of the Export-Import Bank has rendered a contrary opinion and we understand the Bank has requested the Attorney General's concurrence in the General Counsel's opinion. This opinion concludes that the practice of making general "by country" determinations is consistent with the law and its legislative history, and that neither the Congress nor our Office has heretofore objected to this practice. 

We adhere to our view that the statutory language and relevant legislative history clearly require separate determinations for each transaction. 

We were fully aware of the past practice at the time we rendered our opinion. 

However, the fact that objections have not been raised in the past does not render a practice immune from challenge. I might add that our reviews of the financial statements of the Export-Import Bank are concerned primarily with whether such statements fairly present the Bank's financial position and the results of its operations. The manner in which the Presidential determinations were made were not questioned by us during our annual reviews of the Bank. In retrospect we believe that this should have been done.

In our opinion, there is a most important principle involved. Congress, in many instances in the past, has provided the executive branch authority to expend funds on the basis of a Presidential certification. This has come about usually under circumstances similar to those involved in the present case, namely, to assure full consideration of all the policy implications involved at the highest levels in the executive branch, particularly in matters involving foreign relations. In our opinion, this principle was involved in the legislation authorizing credits to 

Communist countries.

Inasmuch as the Export-Import Bank has been classified as a Government corporation and its expenditures made in accordance with the Government Corporation Control Act, this Office does not have authority to disallow payments as we do in the case of many other activities. 

We expect to testify on this matter before the Subcommittee on 

International Finance of the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing and

Urban Affairs on April 2 at which time we will respond in detail to the opinion of the General Counsel of the Export-Import Bank. I will send you a copy of our statement at that time. INS 

Sincerely yours,

Tunes & Staate

COMPTROLLER GENERAL OF THE UNITED STATES 

WASHINGTON, D.C. 20348

March 8, 1974 

The Honorable Richard 8. Schweiker United States Senate 

Dear Senator Schweiker: 

Your letter of January 31, 1974, raises several questions concerning the participation of the Export-Import Bank (Eximbank) in transactions involving the Soviet Union. These questions arise primarily in view of section 2(b)(2) of the Export-Import Bank Act of 1945, as amended, which prohibits the Bank from guaranteeing, insuring or extending credits in connection with the purchase or lease of any product by a Communist country except in the case of any transaction which the President determines would be in the national interest and so reports to the Congress. 

You state it to be your understanding that on October 18, 1972,

President Nixon determined it to be in the national interest for Eximbank to extend credits to the Soviet Union. Subsequent to this Presidential determination, Eximbank has extended credits to the Soviet Union in numerous transactions, and the Bank has reported such transactions to the Congress. liowever, no separate determination of national interest for each individual transaction has been issued by the President. 

You also indicate that Eximbank is presently considering an application by the Soviet Union for a $49.5 million direct loan to be invested in an energy development project in the Yakutsk area of Eastern Siberia, and that the Soviet Union is expected to seek additional Eximbank credits to finance a $7.6 billion North Star energy development project in Western 

Biberia. 

In consideration of the foregoing matters, you request our response to the following specific questions: 4 (1) In view of the restrictions contained in the Export- Import Bank Act of 1945, as amended, has the Bank acted in compliance with applicable law in extending credit to the Soviet Union in the absence of individual Presidential determinations, submitted to Congress, to the effact that each such transaction is in the national interest? (2) Regardless of the legality of prior loans, in view of the present American energy crisis, can the Xximbank legally extend credit to the Soviet Union for the pending Yakutsk energy development project in the absence of a specific Presidential determination, submitted to Congress, that such transaction is in the national interest? (3) What is the total amount of Eximbank funds presently outstanding in loans, guarantees or insurance to the

Soviet Union, and what is the total amount of Federal funds presently committed to energy research and development in the United States?

As you indicate, the President made a determination concerning extension of Eximbank credits to the Soviet Union on October 18, 1972. 

The full text of this determination, as published at 37 F.R. 22573 (October 20, 1972), is as follows: "The White House, Washington, October 18, 1972. "I hereby determine that it is in the national interest for the Export-Import Bank of the United States to guarantee, insure, extend credit and participate in the extension of credit in connection with the purchase or lease of any product or service by, for use in, or for sale or lease to the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, in accordance with Section 2(b) (2) of the Export-Import Bank Act of 1945, as amended. [signed] Richard Nixon"

This determination was reported to the Congress on the date it was made. 

See Congressional Record for October 18, 1972, H10409 (Executive Communication No. 2432). Obviously this document evidences a determination that it is in the national interest to extend credits to the Soviet Union as a general matter, and without reference to any particular transaction or transactions.

Your first question, as to the validity of such a general determination, requires consideration of the legislative history of section 2(b) (2) of the Export-Import Bank Act and prior appropriation act provisions. 

Section 2(b) (2) of the Export-Import Bank Act of 1945, as amended, 12 U.S.C. 635(b)(2), provides, quoting from the United States Code: "The Bank in the exercise of its functions shall not guarantee, insure, or extend credit, or participate in my extension of credit-- "(A) in comection with the purchase or lease of any product by a Communist country (as defined in section 2370(f) of Title 22), or agency or national thereof, or "(B) in connection with the purchase or lease of any product by any other foreign country, or agency, or national thereof, if the product to be purchased or leased by such other country, agency, or national is, to the knowledge of the Bank, principally for use in, or sale or lease to, Commmist country (as so defined), "except that the prohibitions contained in this paragraph shall not apply in the case of any transaction which the President determines would be in the national interest if he reports that determination to the Senate and House of 

Representatives within thirty days after making the same."

The above-quoted provision was added by section l(c) of the act approved 

March 13, 1968, Pub. L. 90-267, 82 Stat. 47, 48. The 1963 act was in this regard based upon a somewhat similar limitation which had been carried in appropriation acts for prior years. 

The appropriation act limitation first appeared in the Foreign Aid and Related Agencies Appropriation Act, 1964, approved January 6, 1964, Pub. L. 88-258, 77 Stat. 857, 863, as follows: "None of the funds made available because of tha provisions of this Title shall be used by the Export-Import Bank to either guarantee the payment of any obligation hereafter incurred by any Communist country (as defined in section 620(f) of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, as amended) or any agency of national thereof, or in any other way to participate in the extension of credit to any such country, agency, or national, in connection with the purchase of any product by such country, agency, or national, except when the President determines that such guarantees would be in the national interest and reports each such determination to the House of Representatives and the 

Senate within 30 days after such determination."

The same language was included in the appropriation acts for 1965 (78 Stat. 

1022), 1966 (79 Stat. 1008), 1967 (80 Stat. 1024-25), and 1968 (81 Stat. 943).

The appropriation act limitation, as originally enacted in 1964, represented a compromise between proponents of a flat prohibition against Eximbank participation in my transactions involving Communist countries, led by Senator rundt and Representative Findley, and those members who insisted upon according discretion to the President. However, the legislative history indicates that this language was intended to require a specific Presidential determination for each transaction to be exempted from de prohibition. Thus Senator Hundt commented as follows in a statemant appearing at 109 Cong. Rec. 25619: "★ ★ ★ The compromise language which we finally developed in the conference report and which has been adopted by the Bouse is a significat and important policy recommendation by Congress md a firm expressional intent. It contains the same specific prohibition against extension and guarantees of cradit to the Commumist nations contained in S. 2310 but it provides an escape clause to be used by the President of the United States only and I repeat only when he himself finds in the case of each proposed credit transaction that he believes it to be in the national interest ★ ☆ *, "I am confident there are many in Congress and throughout the country—and I inclixle myself among them--who will want to scrutinize each such transaction most intently and carefully if it should actually eventuate and be authorized. "Thus, I am well satisfied with the policy daclaration sad the specific prohibition in this matter contained in the conference report and by the work accomplished by the Hous�–

Senate conference committee in writing into this foreign aid appropriations bill a prohibition which can be voided only by specific Presidential ection to be publicly reported in each case within 30 days to both Houses of Congress. "

The same intent seems to be manifested during House consideration of the conference report. Hr. Passman observed: $ The "✯ ✯ ✯ The so-called Mundt amendment which was agreed to by the conferees requires two things specifically: 

President must determine that financing such assistance by the Export-Import Bank is necessary, and the President must report each such determination ***. * If, for example, there are 20'such determinations, the President will report 20 different times * 

109 Cong. Rec. 25416-17.

In response to m observation that the President had already in offect determined that sales of wheat and other agricultural products to the Soviet Union were in the national interest, Mr. Rhodes stated: "Of course, the gentleman realizes that a new determination has to be made with each transaction under the terms of this amendment?" - Id. at 25418. 

As noted previously, the present statutory provision was enacted in 1968 by Public Law 90-267. The report on the 1968 legislation by the 

Senate Committee on Banking and Currency noted the similar provision contained in prior appropriation acts, but pointed out: "the committea provision goes beyond the existing provision in two respects. First, as indicated, it would require a determination of national interest by the President in the case of indirect as well as direct transactions with Communist countries. Second, the provision becomes a part of the Bank's statutory charter and does not need to be adopted each year by the Congress as in the case with the appropriation act. S. Rept. No. 493, 90th Cong., 1st sess., 4. (Underscoring supplied.) 

The conference report commented with reference to the provision enacted: "The Bank is also prohibited from participating in credit transactions in connection with the purchase or lease of any product by a Communist country * * * except after a 

Presidential determination communicated to Congress within 30 days after it is made, that the transaction would be in the national interest. H. Rept. No. 1103, 90th Cong. 

2d sess., 4. (Underscoring supplied.)

Finally, in explaining the conference version of the 1968 legislation, Senator Muskie reiterated that section 2(b) (2) was patterned after the similar limitation which had been carried in appropriation acts. 

114 Cong. Rec. 3336.

Thus the language of section 2(b)(2) of the present act, togather with its legislative history, clearly requires a separate determination for each transaction. Your first two questions are therefore answered in the negative.

With reference to your third question, the materials enclosed herewith indicate the present status and extent of Eximbank participation in transactions involving the Soviet Union. Finally, a report to the 

President dated December 1, 1973, from the Chairman of the Atomic Energy

EXIMBANK'S CHAIRMAN ANNOUNCES ACTION BY THE BOARD OF DIRECTORS ON CREDITS TO POLAND, ROMANIA,U.S. S. R. AND YUGOSLAVIA William J. Casey, Chairman and President of the Export-Import Bank of the United States announced today that the Bank's Board of Directors has resumed its normal processing of credits to Poland, Romania, U. S. S. R., and Yugoslavia. Eximbank had suspended action on credits to these countries on March 11 in order to study and receive advice on an opinion of the Comptroller General of the United States to the effect that each individual transaction involving these countries had to be the subject of a finding by the President that such transaction was in the national interest. Since 1964, Eximbank has been making loans and issuing guarantees and insurance to these countries pursuant to determinations made at various times by Presidents Johnson and Nixon that it would be in the national interest for Eximbank to facilitate exports to these particular countries. 

In resuming action on transactions involving these four countries, the Bank acted on the opinion of its General Counsel, and a concurring opinion which the Attorney General submitted to the President on March 21, 1974. 

Mr. Casey also announced that he had signed two Agreements that had been delayed for Eximbank credits to Yugoslavia in support of sales of jet aircraft to JAT, the Yugoslavian Airline.

In addition, authorizations for two credits to Romania, four credits to Poland, four credits to the U.S. S. R. and one credit to Yugoslavia have been approved by the Bank's Board of Directors. 

Eximbank's credits total $73, 692, 165, in support of sales of U. S. goods and services totaling $163, 760, 366.

New York, will also extend financing of $19,691, 550 to finance another 45 percont of the U. S. costs. The obligor, Bank Handlowy w Warszawie, S. A. (Handobank) will make cash payment of the balance of the U.S. costs of 10 percent or $4,375,900.

[From the Washington Post, Mar. 23, 1974] Ex-IM BANK RESUMES CREDITS FOR SOVIETS (By Dan Morgan, Washington Post staff writer) 

The Nixon administration, buttressed by a legal ruling from the Attorney General after 12 days of uncertainty, resumed its program of credits to the Soviet Union yesterday with a $44.4 million package of loans. 

The administration's announcement that it was going ahead with the credits to the Soviet Union and three other Communist nations ended a brief showdown between the White House and Congress over the program, which is a key element in the policy of expanded economic cooperation with the Communist world. 

The credits had been halted March 11 over a legal technicality. 

After Attorney General William B. Saxbe upheld the loans' legality, the U.S. 

Export-Import Bank yesterday aproved a total of $74.9 million in credits for 11 projects in the Soviet Union, Poland, Romania and Yugoslavia. 

Included in the $44.4 million in loans earmarked for American projects in the 

Soviet Union was financing for constructing and equipping the $80 million international trade center in Moscow. The center is symbolic because it is to be headquarters for American and possibly other Western businessmen seeking to expand trade with the Soviet Union.

White House officials had indicated concern about the unexpected suspension of the loans last week. One purpose of Secretary of State Henry A. Kissinger's trip to Moscow, which is to start this weekend, is to convey the message that the Nixon administration is ready and able to continue its policy of economic cooperation. 

Soviet officials had begun to express concern about the future of this cooperation.

The Senate is considering a trade bill whose provisions-opposed by the administration-would have the effect of cutting off the credits and denying Moscow's exports to this country preferential tariff treatment. 

A number of senators, led by Henry M. Jackson (D-Wash.). have attacked the government credits and guarantees as a form of unjustified "foreign aid" to the 

United States' main adversary.

Yesterday's action was also a sign to Congress that the administration will fight for detente. 

Sen. Richard S. Schweiker (R-Pa.) said yesterday that he was "greatly disappointed" with the Attorney General's upholding of the legality of the credits. 

Last week Schweiker released a finding from the General Accounting Office the investigative arm of Congress-that the credits to the Communist countries had been extended under an illegal procedure. 

Export-Import Bank President William J. Casey told Schweiker at a private meeting yesterday that Saxbe had concurred in the resumption of the loans. 

The GAO had contended that the President should have made a finding that each individual transaction involving a Communist country was in the national interest and reported this to Congress. 

Schweiker said last week that he favors East-West trade but fears that huge sums of American capital will be invested in Siberian natural gas developments, instead of in energy exploration at home. 

USE OF FIXED-COST REIMBURSEMENT METHOD 

Yesterday he introduced a measure to block Soviet-American energy deals and to prevent the bank from approving a pending loan application for $49.5 million for natural gas exploration by an American consortium in the Soviet province of Yakutsk.

The four loans approved yesterday for Soviet projects will finance the construction of the trade center, as well as the shipment and installation of machinery for a motor factory, a canal and a valve-making plant. 

At the time the bank ordered suspension of business with Communist countries "pending clarification" last week, it had extended $255 million in direct loans for Soviet projects. The credits have promoted an upsurge in American exports and, the administration argues, helped this country's balance of payments. 

Yesterday's decision also cleared the way for approval of financing for a number of projects involving petrochemicals, computer systems, textiles, aircraft sales and machine plants in Poland, Romania and Yugoslavia. 

Two deals involving the sale of four Boeing aircraft to Yugoslavia-blocked after the GAO ruling-were ratified by the bank yesterday.

USE OF FIXED-COST REIMBURSEMENT METHOD 

Mr. FASICK. The subcommittee in its report on the fiscal year 1974 appropriations bill expressed a strong belief that AID should make greater use of the fixed-cost reimbursement method for dispensing economic assistance. It was noted that this method had been used with success in the Philippines but despite the subcommittee's recommendations AID had little inclination to use the method elsewhere. 

During the hearings we noted that AID planned to use the fixed-cost reimbursement method for rural programs in Bangladesh beginning in fiscal year 1974.

Since last year we have found that AID has taken only limited actions to expand the use of the fixed-cost reimbursement method. We currently have several members of our staff in Bangladesh and, among other objectives, they plan to observe the progress that has been made to date. The subcommittee may wish to pursue this matter further with 

AID officials during the course of these hearings. 

Senator INOUYE. Has AID advised you why they are reluctant to pursue this method?

Mr. FASICK. They have not, sir. They have provided us with some indication that they plan to expand it but again, in fact, it hasn't been expanded beyond this trial effort in Bangladesh.

Senator INOUYE. I realize that this program may be a bit insulting to the recipient country because they would have to produce before payment is made, and therefore underlying this principle is an element of incomplete trust, shall I say. But if we are to account to our constituents, and we should be accountable, something like this method of fixed-cost reimbursement must be carried out, and I have tried to impress the AID of this. Would you, if it is feasible, look into all of the programs wherein you feel that the fixed-cost reimbursement principle could be applied? 

Mr. FASICK. Very well. We can do this. 

Senator INOUYE. I realize you cannot apply this principle to all activities, but if you could share with us your views on where this could be effectively applied, I can assure you that as chairman of this subcommittee I will insist that it be applied. Otherwise I am certain we can take steps to bring this about. 

Mr. FASICK. Very good, sir. We will be pleased to include this in our studies. 

Senator INOUYE. Thank you.

PAYMENT TO OVERSEAS EMPLOYEES 

Mr. FASICK. During last year's consideration of the appropriation for AID by this subcommittee, concern was expressed regarding the payment of benefits and allowances to U.S. employees overseas. We have completed a rather complex and difficult review of this matter and have a draft report prepared which is with the agencies involved for comments on the positions we have taken.

Senator INOUYE. When do you think this subcommittee can receive a copy of this report?

Mr. FASICK. We are hopeful that we will receive the comments. within 30 days from the agencies and can incorporate them where

pertinent into the report. I would suggest that within 90 days we would have a copy of the report for the subcommittee. 

Senator INOUYE. We are very much interested in this, and we would hope that we can get a copy before we begin marking up this measure. 

Mr. FASICK. We think that we will be able to make a copy available by markup.

In this review we found that there are at least 50 different benefits, allowances, and privileges available to U.S. employees serving overseas depending upon their post and circumstance. The U.S. Government has about 737,000 employees-mostly military-from 38 agencies and departments assigned to positions in foreign countries and nonforeign areas overseas. Benefits and allowances, exclusive of salaries, amount to about $1.5 billion annually: $1.3 billion for uniformed personnel, $150 million for civilians in foreign countries, and $100 million for civilians in non foreign areas. 

In our review, we found:

One, innumerable differences in the type and amount of allowances available and paid to U.S. civilian employees overseas in different agencies and within the same departments. These differences resulted from the fact that there are four different benefit-and-allowance systems for U.S. Government civilians, which involve different legislative authority, agency regulations, and discretionary decisions by agency officials at varying levels.

Two, significant differences between civilian employees in foreign areas and non foreign areas overseas. 

Three, differences between uniformed personnel and civilian employees.

Four, indications that the lack of uniformity in allowances and benefits result in significant morale problems. 

For the most part, allowances for civilian employees in foreign countries are authorized as (1) an overseas premium to recruit and retain employees or (2) as reimbursement to employees for extra costs which they would not incur in the United States. Some allowances like the housing allowance are designed to serve both purposes. 

In many cases, additional compensation and benefits related to overseas service can be more than an individual's salary. Our question is whether the post differential allowance, which costs $36 million a year, and the premium portion of the housing allowance are serving the purpose for which they were authorized. Moreover, the overseas premium seems high in relation to other systems checked-Canada, the United Nations, and U.S. private industry. 

MAINTAINING STANDARD OF LIFE 

The basic aim underlying all nonpremium overseas benefits and allowances should be that they neither result in financial gain nor loss for an employee but reimburse the employee for extra costs of maintaining a standard of life equivalent to that which would be maintained in the United Statee. Notwithstanding, GAO found that the system of nonpremium allowances, as presently managed, permits civilian employees in many instances to realize substantial financial gain.

R S Again as I have mentioned, in a draft report we have just released to executive agencies for their review, we are making a number of tentative proposals aimed at correcting these inequities.

AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT 

WASHINGTON, D. C. 20523 

Dear Mr. Chairman:

This letter concerns A.I.D.'s operating expenses which were the subject of debate in the Congress during the recent adoption of the Conference Report on the Foreign Assistance Appropriations Act for fiscal year 1974. I share your interest and concern with the operational management of A.I.D. I intend to institute a management system that will respond to your interests and concerns, which are also mine. 

I have two basic goals for the management of A.I.D. First, that we operate efficiently and economically, in terms of manpower and money, and second, that we effectively meet our program objectives. 

In regard to the second goal, I believe we must sharpen our program objectives to insure that we carry out the mandate of the new A.I.D. legislation. I believe we must do more to measure the effectiveness of our programs against these objectives.

In regard to the first goal, we are now taking a number of steps to achieve better efficiency. As you know, we have taken the essential step of defining total Agency operating expenses, consolidating all the components that heretofore had been handled separately. A number of actions are underway or planned to reduce these expenses. Annex A describes the major components of A.I.D. operating expenses and some of the actions we are taking to achieve greater efficiency. In addition, to help identify and control these expenses, we have established an internal A.I.D. Operating Expenses account. Details of how this account will function in FY 1974 and FY 1975 are set forth in Annex B. 

The establishment of the Operating Expenses account constitutes a major step in the direction of obtaining better management control over the Agency's total operating costs. In particular, the new approach will focus attention on the action components of the Agency's operating costs. 

While there are certain minor areas which need refinement, our work in defining the operating expense concept has proceeded to the point at which establishment of such an account is possible. 

Establishment of this new account will give the Appropriations Committees additional information with respect to A.I.D.'s operating costs which should be useful in the appropriations process. The A.I.D. Congressional Presentation will include an explanation of total operating expenses and will track the amount which each appropriation account contributes to the Operating Expenses account. A final statement of the Operating Expenses account will be presented as part of the Operational Year Budget. Changes from the original estimate will be fully and completely explained. 

We believe this approach will give the Appropriations Committees substantially the same amount of information regarding A.I.D.'s operating expenses as would be obtained were the Administrative Expenses account replaced with an operating expenses authorization and appropriation. We prefer this approach, at least in fiscal year 1975, for the following reasons:

We have already obtained an authorization of $45 million 

for Administrative Expenses for fiscal year 1975.

An authorization for operating expenses for fiscal year 1975 would require readjustments in most of the A.I.D. program accounts for which authorizations have already been obtained.

For fiscal year 1976 and beyond, we would welcome the opportunity to discuss with you the possibilities for further refinements in the operating expenses concept and the funding methods to be used. Prior to holding such a discussion, I have secured the services of a top-notch private accounting firm to assess our work to date and to make recommendations for further improvements. further.

When this effort is completed, I will be in touch with you · Meanwhile, we are faced with rising operating costs in FY 1974 notwithstanding the fact that we have been able to make savings in our operations. 

As a result, our operating costs have increased a net of $18 million over the estimate contained in last year's Congressional Presentation. In addition, as we have worked to improve the definition of operating expenses, we have included in the concept certain personnel who were previously charged to specific assistance projects; the cost of these personnel is $8 million. (Part of these increases have been borne by the recipient countries themselves in the form of increased contributions to local currency trust funds that support A.I.D. operations, which are included in the operating expenses total.) Annex A

OPERATING EXPENSES Definition of the Concept end Improvements to Date 

A.I.D. operating expenses cover the salaries and supporting costs for personnel engaged in the basic operating functions of policy, planning, programming, coordination, management, and support in Washington and Overseas. This type of personnel comprises about 85 percent of A.I.D. direct-hire employment. The 15 percent of A.I.D. personnel who are directly responsible for program and project implementation, as technical advisors attached to specific projects, are excluded. Operations personnel and costs are grouped by functional categories representing the major operational and management responsibilities of the Agency. These functions (and their approximate share of total operating expenses) are: 

16 

Executive Direction (5%) includes the top policy formulation and direction of the Agency. 

Program Planning and Budgeting (9%) includes identifying development needs, setting priorities for resource use, and resource allocation. 

Technical Analysis, Management and Evaluation (16%) includes technical planning and review of programs and projects, project management, and program evaluation.

Central Backstopping of Overseas Operations (3%) involves program and administrative contact between overseas missions and the Washington Country Desks in. each of the Regional Bureaus. 

External Relations and Information (1%) includes legislative liaison and public affairs activities. 

Administration of Special Programs (2%) includes management of the American Schools and Hospitals Abroad program, Disaster 

Relief, Food for Peace, and Private and Voluntary Cooperation programs.

Legal Services (1%) involves provision of legal advice and services to all clements of A.I.D. in Washington and overseas.

Audit and Inspection Services (4) includes the Agency compre hensive internal audit program and the investigation of alleged irregularities and deficiencies relating to compliance and integrity of operations. 

Program Support Services (9%) includes functions directly supporting individual A.I.D. programs and projects; commodity management, contract services, engineering services, and participant training services. 

Financial Management Services (8%) includes the functions of accounting, statistics, internal financial control, advice and assistance on financial practices and procedures, and financial reporting.

Management Support Services (42%) encompasses the full range of administrative management services (personnel, data processing) and the cost of general logistics support (communications, vehicles, buildings, supplies) provided for all functions. 

During the past year and a half we have worked to build and refine the Operating Expenses concept and to apply it to our budgetary requests and our internal financial operations. At the present time, we believe that the concepts are reasonably clear, but that further work remains to be done to apply the concepts to our individual programs and operations. 

This is a continuous process of refinement that will result in changes · from time to time.

For several years we have also been working on many fronts to make our operations more efficient and to reduce operating expenses. Following is a description of some of the major efforts that are underway, plus an assessment of results to date and future work to be done. 

1. Kanpower reduction. In line with overall Government efforts to reduce the Federal work force, particularly overseas, we have cut A.İ.D. directhire employment 45 percent since 1968. The primary vehicle has been a general employment freeze. With overseas staffs (other than Indochina) already reduced to a minimum, our attention is shifting more particularly to Washington. Recent enactment of foreign service retirement legislation should assist us in this effort. The

A.I.D. will continue its policy against general Reductions in Force, "bumping" process involved in general RIF's is extremely disruptive and time consuring. It would result in the release of younger people with less tenure 'thereby increasing the already heavy concentration of A.I.D. employment in the more senior grades. Even the possibility of a general "RIF" substantially diminishes the attractiveness of the Agency to young personnel of high caliber. 

While we remain opposed to general RIFs, we may need to employ specific reductions in force involving selected job categories. 

2. Study of future manpower requirements. Closely related to our efforts to reduce manpower, we now have underway a study to project the types and numbers of direct-hire employees that we will need to carry out the new directions for the A.I.D. program over the next three to five years. The study is divided into two parts: technical/program management personnel and administrative/support personnel. The technical/program management personnel portion is already completed and the administrative/support portion will be completed very shortly. When the entire study is finished, we will use the results for future personnel planning. The study of technical/ program management personnel has indicated that a major problem we will face in the next three to five years is a shortage of certain skills and a surplus of others, assuming present personnel policies remained unchanged. Policies to cope with these problems are being developed. 

3. Experimentation with organizational change. Under the A.I.D. reform plan of January 1972, two new bureaus were established in Washington: a 

Population and Humanitarian Assistance Bureau to consolidate responsibility for population and family planning, disaster relief and rehabilitation, and relationships with voluntary non-profit organizations; and a Bureau for 

Program and Management Services bringing together various common services to achieve greater uniformity, flexibility, and speed of response with less manpower. Less well known but no less significent, we are experimenting with several new regional servicing arrangements in Africa which provide project development, accounting, housing guarantee program support, and population program support to several missions from regional locations. 

We will continue to assess the effectiveness of these efforts to determine if replication elsewhere is feasible and desirable.

4. Personal support policy. We are now installing worldwide a uniform policy for the types and levels of support services to be provided for overseas employees. The key element of this policy is to place much greater reliance on the individual employee to arrange for his own support and to use the facilities of other existing Government organizations instead of setting up parallel A.I.D. capability. We hope to have this policy operative by the end of FY 1974, with resulting savings in A.I.D. support staff which we believe is excessive in view of the greatly reduced size of today's typical A.I.D. field Mission. 

5. Improved systems. As part of the A.I.D. reform plan, we are now studying the feasibility of installing a Planning, Budgeting, Accounting and Reporting system that will strengthen our ability to manage the more highly focused A.I.D. program envisaged in the new legislation enacted this year. Key elements of this system will be simplified procedures, greater focus on program outputs, comparison of plans with actual results, and exception reporting. Other system improvements include the installation of more efficient but cheaper automatic data processing equipment and standardized costing procedures for participant training that will save many man years in the areas of accounting and financial reporting. 

6. Personnel training. In line with the above-mentioned study of future 

A.I.D. manpower requirements, we are taking steps to identify the specific skills that our employees will need which they now lack, and are revamping our approach to training so that in the future the training of our employees will be focused more clearly on acquisition of the skills needed to manage the A.I.D. program in line with the new directions. I 7. Grade Creep. A.I.D. is concerned that adequate internal management controls be developed and established on the pay grade levels of its staffs in Washington and overseas. Our Office of Personnel is now identifying ways of achieving such a control with particular attention to vacancies which may result from enactment of the recent Foreign Service Retirement legislation. 

These are only the major elements of our ongoing effort. to operate more efficiently. There are, of course, countless smaller efforts that taken together add a significant dimension to the effectiveness of our work. 

In addition, we have just begun a special series of reviews of our operations that we expect to complete shortly. From these reviews we hope to develop: 

An agency Consolidated Operations Report, primarily for 

AID/Washington managers.

Data and information for the FY 1975 Congressional Presentation and hearings.

Recommendations on the validity and usefulness of our present Mission Operations Budget system, together with refinements in our operating cost concepts.

Action recommendations for top management regarding improvement's in agency operations.

AN A.I.D. OPERATING EXPENSES ACCOUNT Annex B 

We believe it would be desirable to simplify our financial procedures end strengthen accountability through establishment of an internal A.I.D. account for Operating Expenses. Following is a description of the steps necessary for establishment of such an account, and a description of how the account would be maintained. These actions are now underway. 

Step 1 

Define Operating Expenses 

The first requirement is to classify A.I.D. obligations into two categories; substantive program obligations and operating expenses obligations. This step is nearly complete already. For the past year we have been working to define A.I.D. operating expenses, and we have already promulgated guidelines for such classification. Our initial testing of the guidelines in preparation of our FY 1974 and FY 1975 budget requests leads us to the conclusion that they are clear and susceptible of practical application. The only work that remains is the classification of obligations for a few A.I.D. activities that do not neatly fall into the "substantive" or the "operating expenses" category. Handling these few obligations involves a continuous process of refinement based on further research into the activities in question. The number of such cases is small and the amounts marginal, and we believe we can proceed with subsequent steps concurrently without waiting for a final determination in each case. 

Step 2 

Determine the Operating Expenses Charges to Each A.I.D. Appropriation 

It is impossible to calculate specifically the amount of operating expenses that should be charged to each A.I.D. appropriation. Indeed, it can be demonstrated that certain of our operating expenses (for example, the salary of the A.I.D. Administrator) benefit more than one and perhaps all A.I.D. substantive activities. Given this situation, we believe it is best to develop a simple formula that charges all A.I.D. appropriations for operating expenses on an equitable basis. So long as A.I.D. receives an appropriation for "Administrative Expenses", we can assume that that entire appropriation is available for operating expenses, and the first step, then, is to subtract that amount from total appropriated fund requirements for operating expenses. 

Beyond that, we believe the remaining requirements for appropriated funds should be generally divided among the other applicable A.I.D. accounts on the basis of the ratio that each bears to the total and charge each in proportion to its share of the total (if all such accounts totaled 100 and Account A totaled 10, Account A would be charged with one-tenth of the remaining Operating 

Expense requirement, and so on.)

This general approach could properly be modified in the event that the facts demonstrate a purely pro-rata allocation is unjustified. In any event, the planned charges to each appropriation using the finally established formula would be clearly identified in the annual A.I.D. Congressional 

Presentation, and would be further reviewed and approved by the Administrator as part of the Operational Year Budget that is formulated following enactment of A.I.D. appropriations by Congress.

Step 3 - Establish an Internal A.I.D. Account for Operating Expenses 

Once the Operational Year Budget is formulated and approved, the amounts from each appropriation account to be used for operating expenses (plus the entire Administrative Expenses appropriation) would be merged to form an internal A.I.D. account for operating expenses. 

All allotments,

obligations, accruals, and disbursements for operating expenses would be charged initially against this internal account, and periodically all such fiscal activity would be finally charged proportionally to the A.I.D. appropriations that make up the internal account's resources. These fiscal charges to each A.I.D. appropriation would be made in periodic lump sums only, and no attempt would be made to charge any specific obligation or other fiscal transaction to a particular source appropriation. Instead, detailed accounting records would be maintained by Missions or similar organizational units on the basis of the ten management categories (and further sub-categories) that have been established within the Operating Expenses concept. These management categories are the meaningful breaks for control of operating expenses, and our accounting records would thus support management in making operating expenses decisions. Meaningless and complicated categorizations of individual operating expenses transactions back to the appropriation accounts from which the funds originally came would be eliminated. Our attention, as well as the attention of the Congress, could thus be focused on what we believe are the meaningful points of control in a clear, simple way. 

If any funds originally earmarked for operating expenses turned out not to be needed for that purpose, they would merely remain in the source appropriations and could either be used for substantive program activities or left unobligated at the end of the fiscal year.

JAMES R. CALLOWAY CHEF COUNSEL AND STAFF DIRECTOR LETTER FROM SENATOR DANIEL K. INOUYE

COMMITTEE ON APPROPRIATIONS

March 20, 1974 

Honorable Daniel Parker Administrator 

Agency for International Development 

Department of State 

Washington, D. C. 20523 

Dear Mr. Parker:

I have your letter of March 20 with further reference to the Agency for International Development's operating costs. .

After several years of growing Committee concern regarding the high cost of carrying on AID's operations, Mr. Campbell, the Agency's Assistant 

Administrator for Program and Management Services, appeared before the Subcommittee on Foreign Operations and addressed the matter as follows:

Modern management and business has long been concerned with evaluating the components that go into the cost of the major management functions. To provide a more meaningful and comprehensive analysis of such costs, AID has this year consolidated all costs related to like functions from all sources of funding. 

This new system permits improved analysis of the effectiveness of each major management task and provides a better understanding of the relationship between the various aspects of the agency's management responsibilities. This is permitted us for the first time, to include in our congressional presentation to you, Mr. Chairman, a summary of the discussion of the total AID operating expenses. 

Under this new cost system, we define operating expenses as the salaries and the supporting costs for personnel involved in the policy, planning, coordination, managerial, and program support functions of our Washington office and our overseas operations.

In essence, they include all the costs of management, managing and implementing the AID programs.

We have excluded from operating expenses those technicians who work directly with the developing countries as advisers under specific country projects, since these costs are more properly charged to the projects themselves.

These operating expenses are funded from three primary sources: first, from the AID administrative expense account and the major program appropriations, such as development grants, supporting assistance, population, et cetera; and, second, a limited amount of non-appropriated funds to the agencies, such as the housing guaran-

tee program and the excess property funds; and, third, from the foreign country trust funds contributed by host governments. 

AID operating expense requirements are decreasing from $204 million in fiscal year 1972 to $191 million in fiscal year 1974. This decrease is particularly significant in view of the increased salary rates imposed on us and the general price increases, both in the 

United States and overseas. (Above excerpt from page 1000 of Senate Appropriations Committee's fiscal year 1974 hearings)

In both the authorizing and appropriations bills the Senate substantially reduced that small portion of AID operating expenses which was exposed to view under the heading of "Administrative Expenses." 

The conference report on the appropriation bill further restricted shifts of funds or activities between other accounts and the Administrative 

Expenses account.

In response to the personal appeal contained in your letter of December 20, 1974, I sought to reduce the impact of this provision if the Committee was convinced "the Agency is moving as fast as possible to correct the situation and reduce its excessive overhead." 

Recalling this series of events, you can perhaps understand my great surprise and keen disappointment to learn from your letter that $8 million of operating expenses which were not earlier identified as such and $17.6 million in increased costs net will now increase fiscal year 1974 operating expenses $25.6 million above the $191 million which the Committee sought to reduce.

I appreciate your assurance that you intend to institute a management system that will respond to the Committee's interests and concerns. Singerely, Fund Wun

DANIEL K. INOUYE 

Chairman, Subcommittee on Foreign Operations

AID LOANS TO TUNISIA 

Several weeks ago this committee received information indicating that AID loans to Tunisia were being used to buy household refrigerators and that spare parts for automobile air-conditioners were being financed under the Vietnamese commodity import program. It was particularly distressing to hear that these parts were intended for the repair of units in the vehicles of high-ranking Government of Vietnam officials and members of the Saigon diplomatic corps. 

These reports were forwarded to GAO. Did you check into this matter, sir?

Mr. DUFF. We are looking into it. We did check with the AID people, and we do have this statement from them as to how the items were used. We will continue to look into it in our work. 

Senator INOUYE. When do you think we can expect to have something for the record. 

Mr. DUFF. I think we can have one within a few days, sir. 

 GAO ANALYSIS OF THE TUNISIA REFRIGERATOR AND VIETNAM AUTOMOBILE AIR CONDITIONER PARTS TRANSACTIONS 

A review of documents and discussions with AID/Washington officials showed the following with respect to AID financing of household refrigerators for Tunisia and automobile air conditioner parts for South Vietnam. 

HOUSEHOLD REFRIGERATORS FOR TUNISIA 

In December 1972 the Government of Tunisia (GOT) requested that household refrigerators, normally ineligible for AID financing, be made eligible. The GOT said that, because of changes in living standards and patterns, refrigerators were now considered a necessary household item, not a luxury, and they were needed to improve health conditions.

On February 7, 1973, AID/Washington replied to the AID Mission in Tunis that it was receptive to the idea, but that AID financing should be available only if (1) the refrigerator size did not exceed 350 liters (approximately 12.4 cubic feet) and (2) the unit cost and number imported were limited. AID/Washington said that these conditions were necessary to preclude the importation of deluxe models. After additional discussions between AID/Washington and the Tunis 

Mission, AID, on March 30, 1973, authorized the financing of refrigerators for household use as follows:

Refrigerators from Code 941 Countries (Selected Free-World) other than the U.S. would be limited to 360 liters and $98 per unit cost before customs duty.

Refrigerators from U.S. sources would be approved up to 425 liters (about 

15 cubic feet) and $250 per unit cost before customs duty.

In accordance with AID/Washington approval to finance refrigerators, the GOT and the AID Mission in Tunis agreed to set aside for this purpose $1 million from AID Loan 664-H-050. (AID Loan 664-H-050, dated January 1, 1973, au thorized $11 million for the agriculture sector.) The initial purpose of the loan was to finance imports for the private sector to generate local currencies to support the GOT agricultural development budget.

In October 1973, the Tunis Mission advised AID/Washington that the GOT 

proposed to purchase refrigerators on the basis of international competitive bids with awards going to the low bidders. The invitation for bid would not indicate 

AID financing. If attractive offers were received from code 941 countries, the 

GOT would propose AID financing for that portion. As of March 5, 1974, the 

GOT had not initiated any such procurement. 

AID/Washington had received information that if the procurement did take place, the GOT would probably purchase on a negotiated basis rather than on a formal competitive bid basis. Accordingly, on March 8, 1974, AID/Washington told the Tunis Mission that in view of the lagging interest and indications that

procurement would not be competitive it should suggest to the GOT that AID funds not be used to purchase household refrigerators. On March 15, 1974, the 

AID Mission in Tunis conveyed this message to the GOT. It was agreed that 

AID funds would not be used to finance household refrigerators at the present time, and, should the situation change, prior AID/Washington approval would be required and AID regulations must be observed. 

AUTOMOBILE AIR-CONDITIONER PARTS FOR SOUTH VIETNAM 

Automobile air conditioners, per se, are not eligible for AID financing in accordance with AID's commodity eligibility listing. However, AID informed us that spare parts for automobile air-conditioners are considered eligible commodities on the basis that such parts are sometimes needed by automobile repair garages the same as other automotive replacement parts. 

We noted that automobile air-conditioner spare parts were not specifically identified as eligible commodities in AID's commodity eligibility listing (Condensed Schedule B) or the special eligibility listing for South Vietnam. Rather, automobile air-conditioner parts were consolidated within the broad categories for air conditioning and refrigeration parts and equipment. Unlike the specific type or nomenclature of the spare parts are identified by the U.S. supplier on the Application for Commodity Eligibility Approval (AID form 11), AID man agement personnel in Washington cannot ascertain whether the requested parts are intended for institutional (hospital) air-conditioners or automobile air-conditioners. For example, the automobile air-conditioner spare parts financed by 

AID, discussed below, were included in the eligibility listing in the broad categories of: "Parts for air-conditioner and refrigerator equipment (including parts for compressor and condenser units)." "Condensers, except for household refrigerators." "Compressors (except ammonia) 3 HP and under, refrigerator and air-conditioner type."

QUESTION FROM SENATOR BROOKE 

Senator INOUYE. The following question from Senator Brooke will be inserted in the record at this point: [The question and answer follow:]

Question. Would you supply the committee a statement as to the method or process by which you take into consideration policy-oriented problems in formulating your suggestions as to improving management practices in the foreign assistance area? This would be very helpful to the members of the committee as we attempt a reconciliation between the monetary amounts requested, the management techniques desirable, and the necessarily complex and, at times, vague policy implications of the foreign assistance program. 

Answer. In our reviews of foreign assistance we are concerned primarily with how executive agencies manage their responsibilities in accordance with the intent of the Congress, as expressed in legislation or committee reports, and in accordance with pronouncements on foreign policy by the President, the National

Security Council, or department heads. We try to disclose in our reports whether expressed policy is being carried out in program management. Our reports may also point out problems and issues in day-to-day administration of foreign assistance programs which may be of interest to the Congress or top officials in the Executive Branch in their deliberations as to whether expressed policies should be continued or changed.

For example our reports on U.S. participation in multilateral organizations do not take a stand on the advisability of furnishing assistance through bilateral or multilateral channels. This is essentially a policy issue. It is the policy of the 

Executive Branch to support an expansion in the role of multilateral organizations and members of the Congress have at times given their views on this issue. 

However, GAO reports on how multilateral assistance is being administered may be useful to the Congress in determining the extent to which U.S. assistance should be authorized on a multilateral basis.

34-192 O-74-20 (808)

Having assumed my new duties on April 1, my appearance here today is among my first official acts as Senior Adviser to the Secretary of State for International Narcotics Matters. As I take up the challenge of managing the highly important International Narcotics 

Control Program, I welcome the opportunity to appear before this Committee in support of the request for funds for the coming year's operations.

We are seeking an appropriation of $42.5 million for fiscal year 1975, an amount which has previously been authorized under the Foreign Assistance Act. This is the same level appropriated for fiscal year 1974.

In a landmark message to the Congress on June 17, 1971, President Nixon called for an all-out attack on both the supply and demand sides of the problem of drug abuse. On the home front, he asked for significant increases in expenditures and manpower in the area of enforcement, prevention, and treatment. And they were forthcoming. On the foreign front, the President called for an acceleration of international cooperation and elevated drug control to a top priority foreign policy objective. With the establishment in August 1971 of the Cabinet Committee on International Narcotics Control 

(CCINC) and the designation of the Secretary of State as Chairman, the President gave the Department of State

primary responsibility for developing an intensified network of international cooperation and controls. And this has been done.

Over the past two and a half years, while our collective anti-drug abuse efforts moved ahead at home, the United States has at the same time succeeded in convincing other nations that drug abuse is not a United States problem, but a world problem, one that will gain in scope and intensity in the absence of prompt and effective international cooperation. For this reason, an increasing number of countries have worked with us both on a bilateral basis and through various regional and international programs designed to eliminate illicit supplies and to suppress illicit trafficking. 

Through the collaboration of Washington agencies within the Cabinet Committee and the activity of our diplomatic missions abroad, the United States has encouraged and developed, and presently participates in, narcotic control action programs with some 60 countries considered to have a current or potential involvement with illicit hard drugs. With emphasis on more effective law enforcement and an increased exchange of narcotics intelligence information, our efforts in these programs have been devoted largely to augmenting the capability of foreign governments to immobilize the traffickers and to prevent illegal

supplies of narcotics 

base, heroin, and cocaine international markets. principally opium, morphine 

from entering illicit

The United States as well as many other nations have benefitted directly from these cooperative efforts.

There has been in the process an expansion in activities abroad by U.S. drug enforcement personnel. 

Whereas 10 years ago there were only 14 narcotics agents stationed overseas, the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) today has 174 Special Agents in 58 embassies and consulates in 39 countries. 

Pursuant to programs approved and monitored by the Cabinet Committee, of which I am Executive Director in my interagency capacity, the DEA personnel overseas work with foreign narcotics enforcement officials under the policy direction of our ambassadors.

There has, moreover, been a sharp step-up in our training of foreign narcotics enforcement officials. 

Our training program, which is planned and coordinated by the CCINC Training Subcommittee, includes inputs from 

DEA, the U.S. Customs Service, and AID. Since 1969,

DEA and its predecessor agency have held courses and seminars here and overseas for more than 4,300 police officers from 40 countries. Within the past year, the 

Customs Service has trained in the United States and abroad more than 1,300 foreign customs officers and

executives representing 29 countries. 

Since mid-1970, the International Police Academy has provided narcotics instruction for 152 ranking supervisory and management personnel from 30 countries. This significant program has paid off in improved enforcement techniques abroad as reflected by the growth in arrests and seizures. 

The allocation of funds for training in FY 1974 is $6.8 million; we are asking for $6.5 million for this program for FY 1975.

Our narcotics control funds have also been used to provide vehicles, communications equipment, laboratory equipment and other basic police equipment for use by recipient countries in their narcotics control efforts.

We are also assisting foreign governments with income substitution projects and other long-range programs which provide economic alternatives to the production of drugs of abuse. Such programs have ranged from traditional agricultural research on alternative crops to trades and crafts development and farm demonstration programs. 

Finally, some assistance has been provided in the health and education fields. 

For the past two years, the principal funded international narcotics programs have been in Turkey, Mexico, Thailand and Laos. Other sizable amounts have gone for

programs in Pakistan, Colombia, Ecuador, the Philippines,

Peru and Brazil. The country allocations for FY 1973 and FY 1974 as well as our requests for next year are shown in the table attached to our Congressional Presentation.

In addition to our bilateral action programs, we have also strongly supported the United Nations in its expanded efforts to suppress the illicit drug traffic as well as the supply of and demand for drugs for illicit purposes. In February of this year I had the honor to lead the United States Delegation to the 

Third Special Session of the United Nations Commission on Narcotic Drugs (CND). There I became better acquainted with the wide variety of activities which the UN and associated agencies are carrying out. I was impressed by the broad consensus within the international community on the threat posed by drug abuse and on the need for international cooperation to deal effectively with the problem. In addition to discussing the latest information available on illicit traffic and on the medical and sociological aspects of drug abuse, the Commission considered the report of the 

International Narcotics Control Board 

the regulatory organ under the narcotics treaties. It also considered the world supply and demand situation for opiates for medical use and the activities of the UN Fund for Drug

Abuse Control. It is my initial firm impression that the policy objectives of the United States and the United Nations are consistent and complementary in this important area of international cooperation. 

In order to help maintain the momentum of the United Nations program, the Department is requesting an additional $5 million as our contribution to the UN 

Fund for Drug Abuse Control for fiscal 1975. 

It is my judgment that the Fund, in its short three-year period of existence, has conceived some very sound projects, a number of which are in the process of implementation. 

In Thailand and in Lebanon (in cooperation with the FAO) the Fund is assisting in comprehensive programs designed to develop alternate economic opportunities for those who grow opium in the case of Thailand and cannabis in the case of Lebanon. In Thailand, the UN Fund in cooperation with the World Health Organization is also rendering assistance in the improvement of treatment and rehabilitation facilities for addicts. 

Another significant role for the United Nations relates to the world opium supply situation. U.S. 

Government policy is to cooperate with the international community in seeking to assure an adequate level of supply of opiates for medical purposes, while keeping opium production under effective control until such time as acceptable synthetic substitutes for codeine become

available.

At the recent CND meeting, the U.S. called for further research on the poppy straw process, research in which we would participate.

We proposed that such research be coordinated internationally by the laboratory of the UN Division of Narcotic Drugs and also that international research on the straw process be conducted through programs administered by the UN Laboratory. We asked that the results of the research be shared inter- We believe that improved processing of poppy straw could give higher opiate yields and could also result in more effective controls. At the meeting, the nationally.

United States in announcing its contribution of an additional $2 million to the Fund stated that $800,000 of that amount was being contributed for such international research. 

We believe there is room for improvement in the operations of the UN Fund, which was launched at the initiative of the United Stated States in 1971. We are disappointed at the slow progress being made in preparing programs in several critical countries which have requested UN assistance but these, of course, require agreement on the part of the governments concerned. We recognize and have repeatedly stated in UN meetings that the Fund cannot survive as a viable instrument if it depends too much upon one nation for its support for an extended period of time. We have

urged the Acting Executive Director, therefore, to intensify his efforts at fund raising and have used our influence with other UN members to persuade them to 

As of make periodic and increased contributions. 

March 1, the total funds pledged to the UN Fund stood at $13.5 million, to which a total of 38 countries had pledged or contributed. The United States has contributed $10 million or 74 percent of the total. The single highest contributor next to the United States is our neighbor to the north, Canada, which shares our problem and which through 1976 has pledged a total of Other major contributors until now include $1 million. the Federal Republic of Germany, $500,000; Japan, $400,000; France, $300,000; and the United Kingdom, $240,000. We will continue to exert our influence to the end that all members of the UN family bear their fair share of this common burden. 

The United States was also one of the principal formulators and supporters of the Convention on Psychotropic Substances, which would provide international controls over such drugs as LSD and other hallucinogens, the amphetamines, barbiturates, and tranquilizers.

The President sent the Convention to the Senate on June 29, 1971, requesting early advice and consent to ratification. The Convention is still before the Senate Foreign Relations Committee which

has deferred action until the approval of enabling domestic legislation.

Hearings on an Administration approved bill were held on February 25 of this year, and we look forward to early approval of this legislation by the Congress as a forerunner to ratification of the Convention. 

I am glad to report that the Amending Protocol to the Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs already has 28 of the 40 necessary ratifications to bring it into effect. As the Committee will recall, the United 

States took the initiative in pressing for these strengthening amendments and the United States was the first to ratify the Protocol on November 1, 1972.

The results of the cooperative efforts throughout the world over the past two years have been encouraging. 

Worldwide seizures of illicit drugs have increased, important traffickers have been arrested, and illicit traffic routes have been disrupted. In the United States a shortage of heroin has developed, particularly on the 

East Coast. The quality and quantity of a heroin fix are down and the price is up. The price of one milligram of heroin on the East Coast was less than 50 cents in late 1971. By mid-1973, it had risen to $1.52. During the same period, the street level purity of heroin sold to addicts was cut in half, from 7.7 percent to 3.7

percent. The rates of overdose deaths, drug-related hepatitis and drug-related property crimes have declined throughout most of the United States for the first time in six years.

The heroin addict population, which peaked at an estimated more than one-half million persons in 1971, is on the decline. 

As heartening as these indicators are, they should not serve as a signal for the United States in any way to relax our efforts. The elimination of illicit supplies of opium, morphine base, and heroin remains the number one priority in our international narcotics control program. The progress we have made in conjunction with other governments has put the heat on traffickers throughout the world. However, we also know that illicit narcotics exist in storage and are under cultivation, ready to respond to high profits should worldwide suppression efforts subside. So, rather than let up, we must seek to strengthen international controls and international action to reduce drug abuse. Toward this end, I urge the Committee to support our program request of $42.5 million for fiscal year 1975.

BACKGROUND IN NARCOTICS CONTROL 

Mr. VANCE. This is indeed one of my first acts as senior adviser to the Secretary and Executive Director of the President's Committee for International Narcotics Control. 

I was sworn in only on April 1, however, I led the U.S. delegation to the third special session of the United Nations Commission on Narcotic Drugs in Geneva in February which gave me an opportunity to meet my foreign counterparts and begin to participate in the activities of the international organizations which are directing their efforts to the control of narcotics traffic.

I also last week attended the meeting of the Economic and Social Council of New York City which considered and ratified the resolutions adopted in Geneva by the Commission on Narcotic Drugs. 

REQUEST FOR FISCAL YEAR 1975 

As you stated, sir, we are seeking an appropriation of $42.5 million for fiscal 1975. These funds were authorized under the Foreign Assistance Act.

Our request is at the same level as last year. 

I should like to make only a few brief remarks before endeavoring to reply to the subcommittee's questions. 

NEW CONCEPTS FOR NARCOTICS PROGRAMS 

This program is only a little under 3 years old. It has been a difficult program to launch for a variety of reasons. Like all foreign policy activities, particularly operational, we have to rely on the cooperation of foreign governments.

It is also a new program involving new concepts and new approaches. Also in one of the aspects of our program, that of crop replacement, we are operating in what is generally regarded in economic development work as the most difficult sector in which to be effective, that is the agricultural sector.

To make it worse for us, we are not down in the great fertile plains where governments have effective operations, where there are roads and markets.

We are endeavoring to operate up in the hill country where, for the most part, governments do not have effective controls, where there are no roads and no ready markets.

We are quite pleased that we have now been able to program the whole of the $42.5 million which we had appropriated in the current fiscal year, notwithstanding the fact that we had to ask for just under $10 million in unprogramed moneys. We are requesting a similar amount of unprogramed moneys for fiscal year 1975. 

The reason for this request last year and this year comes from the difficulties of program administration that I have just described and the fact that the basic reason for the creation of this program was to be flexible and innovative in this very important field. 

We have to be able, we think, to reply and respond to opportunities that develop in the changing circumstances during a given fiscal year.

SUPPORT OF UN FUND FOR DRUG ABUSE CONTROL 

We operate also in support of United Nations activities and have contributed very substantially, as you have no doubt noted, to the U.N. 

Fund for Drug Abuse Control. 

That Fund now has approximately $13.5 million either granted or pledged of which the United States has contributed $10 million or about 75 percent.

We hope very much, and I am pressing very hard, to reduce the U.S. percentage of contributions by urging the Fund to undertake more active fund raising activities and by urging bilaterally and internationally that other governments increase their contributions.

REVIEW OF CURRENT PROGRAM 

I am looking in the early weeks of my assignment at every aspect of this program to see how we can make it an even more dynamic and effective one in the coming year.

However, we believe that the administration's overall efforts to reduce the effects of the scourge of drugs on our population has begun to show measurable success and we think a good part of it is due to the activities of this program and its predecessor programs abroad. 

For example, there is a measurable shortage of heroin in the United States today, indicated by the fact that the price has risen. It has tripled in the last year.

At the same time the purity of heroin available in the street is reduced approximately 50 percent. 

SUCCESS OF PROGRAM TO DATE 

The last thing I would like to point out in connection with the degree of success of this program is that we estimate there were about 50,000 heroin addicts in the United States in 1960. This ballooned to something like 600,000 or 700,000 in the 1970-71 period and we think that this figure is down now to the neighborhood of 200,000 untreated heroin addicts in the United States.

The remainder of this 600,000 or 700,000 breaks down as follows: 

There are about 160,000 in treatment clinics, there are about 100,000 in prison. We estimate about 200,000 have abandoned it due at least in part to the price and more difficult availability. That leaves about 

200,000 untreated addicts today.

I should be very happy to try to respond to any of your questions.

[From the Washington Post, Feb. 19, 1973]

TURKS EYE RE-DRAWING OF POPPY BAN 

(By Dan Morgan, Washington Post staff writer)

Turkey's new left-of-center government has reopened its discussion with the United States of a 1971 agreement that banned cultivation of opium, poppies in exchange for cash compensation by Washington.

A ban went into effect last year, and according to Turkish officials it has resulted in hardships for the more than 73,000 farmers who once raised the poppy crop. The Nixon administration pressed hard for the prohibition of poppy growing in Turkey as part of its effort to cut off a primary source of the heroin used illegally in this country. 

State Department spokesman George Vest said that difficulties confronting the former legitimate growers of the poppy were the topic of a long, wide-ranging discussion Feb. 13 between U.S. Ambassador William Macomber and Turkish Foreign 

Minister Turhan Gunes in Ankara.

U.S. officials said that the poppy growing problem was among several points in the Turkish-American relationship that Gunes wished to discuss again. However, they denied other reports that Gunes had either rescinded the ban on poppy growing or demanded more money as compensation. 

In 1971, the United States agreed to pay Turkey $35.7 million to aid the farmers and to make up for losses in Turkey's legitimate exports of medicinal morphine refined from opium. Of that amount, $20 million has already been transferred to Turkey.

Officials said Gunes had reaffirmed Turkey's desire to meet its commitments to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and to continue close cooperation with the United States.

[On Saturday, the state minister and secretary general of the Republican Peoples Party, Orhan Eyuboglu, said the opium-poppy ban would be lifted soon by a government decree, the Associated Press reported. [But in an interview published Sunday in the newspaper Cumhuriyet, Gunes said Turkey would not alter the ban without consulting the United States.] 

The new government is the most left-leaning ever to come to power in Turkey. 

Turkish officials believe it will move cautiously toward a more independent foreign policy in the months ahead. 

The program of the two governing coalition groups, the Republican Peoples Party headed by Prime Minister Bulent Ecevit and the National Salvation Party of Deputy Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, was revealed in a protocol issued 

Jan. 25.

It called for the nationalization of one industry, the borax trust; a continued tough policy to limit foreign investment, and a solution of the opium poppy "problem." It also contained a strong statement on Turkish control of the Turkish- 

American military bases in the country. 

During a resurgence of Turkish nationalism in 1969, all the bases were placed under joint command, under a defense cooperation agreement. However, prolonged negotiations aimed at spelling out exact American rights at each base are still dragging on.

Although Turkey received $69 million in American military assistance in 1973, as well as credits enabling it to purchase 40 F-4 jet fighter-bombers, Turkish governments have been consistently sensitive to suggestion that they are satellites of Washington.

Prime Minister Ecevit's party won an upset plurality in last October's parliamentary elections.
