[From the New York Times, Feb. 15, 1974] TURKEY TELLS UNITED STATES SHE WILL RESUME OPIUM CULTIVATION 

ANKARA, TURKEY, Feb. 14 (UPI).—Turkey has notified the United States that it will resume cultivation of the opium poppy, banned 13 months ago at Washington's request, the Foreign Ministry said today. 

A spokesman, Semih Akbil, said that Foreign Minister Turan Gunes had given notice of his intention in a meeting with Ambassador William B. Macomber Jr. 

He denied a report in an Istanbul newspaper, Huriyet, that Mr. Gunes had asked for more compensation from the United States as a price for retaining the ban. 

Foreign Ministry sources said that opium cultivation was just one of many outstanding issues between Turkey and the United States. They said the two countries were negotiating amendments to 55 existing agreements. [From the Washington Post, Apr. 14, 1974]

LIFTING THE TURKISH OPIUM BAN 

(By Jack Anderson) 1 The streets of America have become safer since opium growing was outlawed in the distant hills of Turkey. But by early summer, barring a political miracle, the Turkish government will tell the impoverished opium farmers in the remote Afyon region that they can once again plant their traditional money crop: the opium poppy which gives Afyon its name. 

This expected Turkish action would have an inevitable impact on the U.S. crime rate. For out of the new opium harvest would come an illegal flood of heroin into this country. As more heroin became available, hundreds of thousands of young people would try it and become addicted. Most of them would be forced to turn to crime to support their habit. 

The effect on U.S. cities, narcotics officials tell us, would be measured in robbery, violence and death. They use words like "disastrous” and “catastrophic" to describe the consequences. 

Yet the pressure to lift the opium ban is coming, in part, from a few U.S. pharmaceutical firms looking for cheap morphine. They are in strange company, ranging from opium growers and international smugglers to Mafia mobsters and corrupt Turkish legislators-all eager to revive the heroin traffic.

Before 1972, when opium growing was banned in Turkey in exchange for $35.7 million compensation from the American taxpayers, huge opium shipments were diverted to France for refining into heroin and then were smuggled into the United States.

We have obtained a secret House report, which estimates at one point "up to 80 percent of heroin in the United States came from Turkish opium." The 

1972 ban dramatically reduced the flow into this country until only the hardcore addicts could obtain heroin. Suddenly, it became almost unavailable to the young drug "chippers," who like to live dangerously.

The House report, authored by Narcotics Subcommittee Chairman Lester 

Wolff (D-N.Y.), describes what happened after the Turkish connection was cut off. "Heroin addiction," it states, "(was) reduced from between 500,000 and 700,000 to about 200,000 active addicts.. "The price of one milligram of heroin in New York City was 44 cents in 1972; by mid-1973, (it) had risen to $1.52. The street level purity of heroin sold to addicts decreased... from 7.7 per cent to 3.7 per cent."

With the decline in addiction came a corresponding reduction in crime and misery. "Overdose deaths, drug-related hepatitis and drug-related property crimes," declares the report, "have declined throughout most areas of the 

United States for the first time in six years."

The end of opium planting in Turkey caused repercussions, indeed, throughout the subterranean world of drugs. In Europe, the Corsican criminals who had made huge profits from heroin smuggling were compelled to invest their money in more or less legitimate businesses. The federal narcotics investigators warn, however, that the Mafia is keeping its investments semi-liquid in anticipation of a reopening of the opium traffic. 

In Southeast Asia, opium traders in the mountainous Golder Triangle of Burma, Thailand and Laos began to feel out the United States on an exchange deal similar to that made with Turkey. One group offered to sell 400 tons of opium to the United States to get it off the market. 

In India, the Soviets began buying up legal opium feverishly for medical purposes. Suddenly India, which leads the world in legitimate opium sales, also found about 25 per cent of its crop being diverted to criminal elements. 

But in Turkey itself, an outcry against the ban began to swell. The farmers who were supposed to get the American aid complained it arrived. late when it came at all. They suspected, with some justice, that the U.S. payments were going into the bottomless pockets of corrupt officials.

Chairman Wolff, accompanied by Rep. Charles Rangel (D-N.Y.) traveled into the Turkish hinterland to get, as the report puts it, "some insight into the poppy ban in Turkish eyes." Feeling among the opium traders ran so high that the two congressmen had to be guarded by armed Turkish and American security men. 

The congressmen met a 70-year-old farmer who "had grown poppies on those hills every year until 1972," they relate. "He had, at the government's suggestion, grown sunflowers as a substitute . . . But he did not like the taste of sunflower seed oil. He also planted barley now... but it earned less money than the poppy. 

Wolff asked him whether he wanted to grow poppies again. "Yes," said the old farmer simply.

Most of those interviewed along the rocky roads of Afyon felt the same way. 

Some said grudgingly they would abide by the government decree. But others were openly rebellious, admitting they had illegally sold opium gum. "Two opium pressers spoke with indignation about how their small businesses disappeared with the end of the poppy seed supply," recounts the report. "A local doctor said that the ban was imposed with haste and without adequate consideration."

But perhaps Wolff's most disturbing discovery was the role of some U.S. pharmaceutical firms in the backstage campaign to lift the opium ban. He found the firms were quietly but actively lobbying with the Turkish government, Geneva narcotics conference and even the U.S. Congress. In short, these pharmaceutical firms are more interested in reducing the price they have to pay for opium than in preventing drug addiction and street crime. 

The secret report concludes gloomily: "An apparently insoluble problem faces the United States and Turkey concerning the opium ban. Each has taken a course which, when fulfilled, will probably result in a frontal collision with the other. 

The report urges that the channels be kept open with Turkey and that the crop diversification program be pursued. "Raising the level of understanding in 

Turkey about the international drug problem is a vital basis for any future cooperation," states the study.

[Translation on Narcotics and Dangerous Drugs, No. 145] GENERAL SURVEY OF OPIUM SITUATION [Article by Ege University Agriculture Faculty member Dr. Sukru Hazim 

Emiroglu: "Possibilities for Resumption of Poppy Cultivation"; Istanbul, Milliyet, Turkish, 15, 16 March 1974]. [Mar. 15, 1974, p. 5] 

The Turkish farmer, in having bound his fate for centuries to the opium poppy, has lived a life in which the good days are good and the bad days are bad. Both have shared the life filled with its color, its smell, its pungency, in short, every aspect of it. In hard times, they have fought together to survive on the Anatolian steppes. But today they have been separated, and they, themselves, do not even 34-192 O-74-21

know why. However, many things devolve on them in which they have no say. 

Finally the subject has been turned to again and has returned to the point in the vicious circle where it is useless except for killing time. 

I have worked for a long time on this beleaguered plant of the God-fearing Turkish peasant. Owing to my closeness to it, I would like to add some views to the discussions of resumption of its cultivation in our country. However, in order to be precise, it would be well to take the matter briefly from its beginning. 

Although researchers have differing views, our researchers and the publications of the American narcotics bureau show Asia Minor as the native soil of the opium poppy. As scientific support of this view, investigations show that almost every type of opium poppy is encountered in Anatolia and that Anatolia has the characteristic of being the best ecological field in the world for this plant. 

WORLD OPIUM PRODUCTION 

Opium production has declined significantly in recent years as a result of restrictions placed by the world narcotics bureau. Although the production in 

China, which has been a leader, is not known for recent years, this country behind the iron curtain is one to say that it could venture significant increases, no matter what restrictions there might be. In fact, Russia is the most beautiful example of this. In comparison to Russia's production in the pre-war years, it has tripled production recently, and it would be naive to say the least to think that China, being in the same position as a country behind the iron curtain, would adhere to measures to restrict production. Furthermore, China has great reason to make acceptable increases. Even if we should presume that China's production remained at prewar levels, we would still see that China has a very large share of the world's production, around 80 percent. 

Another important opium producer, India, has had no change in pre-war and postwar levels. This country produces 4 times more than we ever have. On the other hand, Iran, Yugoslavia, Pakistan, Afghanistan, and certain other secondary countries produce so little as not to bear discussion here. 

SITUATION IN TURKEY 

Turkey's place in world opium poppy production requires examination from 2 distinct aspects. For us, the essential goal of oplum poppy cultivation would be first the seed products, then opium production. The importance of fundamental seed production in our country will be covered later. Let us first review the facts of our opium production, which was the reason for the opium poppy cultivation ban.

Turkey's opium production is nowhere near the 24 percent of world production, as has been so much written and publicized. We see it as 3 percent. The reason for the writers' making this mistake is probably a calculation according to the countries outside the iron curtain. If we were to look at our country's production using this mistaken method of evaluation as a country outside the iron curtain, we would see that it should be, not 24 percent, but 17 percent. However, should the opium producing countries be divided up according to whether they are inside or outside the iron curtain? Of course, opium, which is involved in international smuggling through clandestine organizations, has nothing to do with free trade and culture. This brings us to the fact that the guilty party that is being sought among the countries of the world is not Turkey, and if there is such a guilty party (and I think they should look to their own countries), Turkey's share in it is mall (3 percent) as to be almost nothing. This is very important to the attempts we will make toward resumption of opium poppy cultivation. 

Furthermore, the recent spread of the synthetic narcotic LSD has more or less eclipsed the classic importance of opium in this regard. The basic goal of opium production is to provide the pharmaceutical industry its raw material. The only buyer and seller in our country is the Soil Products Office. The very small amount of smuggling that might escape the eyes of our laws occupies a tiny place in the opium trade carried out through normal means, and the world attention which is concentrating on us should be directed to China, Russia, and India. In fact, it is obvious that they have a 96 percent share of total production. How much of a reduction has the 2-year ban on opium poppy cultivation in Turkey (the interval will be 3 years, even if there is a 1974/75 crop) shown in the world use of narcotics and smuggling? We have no doubt but that the answer to this question will be one more proof to world public opinion of our country's innocence.

Seed production is the basis of opium poppy cultivation in Turkey. Our country joined the international opium production restriction in 1934 and, by a decision of the Council of Ministers, divided our cultivation regions into the "soft" districts and provinces of Malatya, Corum, Mecitozu, Amasya, Tokat, and Zile and the "druggist" districts and provinces of Afyonkarahisar, Kutahya, Usak, Eskisehir, Balikesir, Isparta, Burdur, Manisa, Bilecik, and Konya. These were categorized as (a) regions where both seeds and opium would be produced and (b) regions where only seeds would be produced. In the decisions, action was taken so as not to suffer loss in seed production in either case. 

Seed production was a primary source of our peasants' livelihood, which came from pressing the seeds, which are 44-54 percent oil. The oil is prized for its flavor and aroma in cooking various dishes in which it is used alone or in combination with olive oil. It is used also in many areas of local industry where it is valued for its semi-dry nature. The cake left after pressing the seeds for oil contains 28 percent protein and up to 10 percent oil, making it an excellent animal fodder. It is even used to feed the cows that produce the cream-laden milk made famous by Afyonkarahisar, Eskisehir, and Kutahya. Also, the poor people of Anatolia use the seeds as food in the form of various sweets. There is no alkaloid in the seed, but the seed may spoil the opium in the deep cuts. (1) 

Seed production of the opium poppy grown in our country to serve all these needs is shown on the accompanying chart by year. 

Poppy seed production in Turkey has varied between a low of 8,675 tons for the 4 years 1944-47 to a high of 21,225 tons for 1956-59. The drop in recent years was dictated by changes in the laws. Our average annual production over the 32 years covered in the chart was 15,500 tons. If one figures the oil production from this amount of seeds as 50 percent, it is clear that this more than meets the oil needs of the local people. 

Also, making a rough economic evaluation of our poppy seed production, though based on no statistics, the oil would amount to at least 100 million Turkish liras per year and the cake 20 million liras. Furthermore, 1 dekar of land produces 250-500 kilograms of stalk and stem which can be used for fuel and, in this country where wood is scarce and dried dung is burned for fuel, this is equivalent to the annual amount of fuel wood obtained from 1 dekar of pine forest. Also the farmer knows that just as an opium poppy crop does not exhaust the soil, the stubble continues to feed it. 

RESUMPTION OF POPPY CULTIVATION IN TURKEY 

Opium poppy cultivation and opium production in our country were banned on 26 June 1971 by Council of Ministers decree number 7/2654. At the moment,

though there has been no official permission to resume planting, we are on the brink of a positive decision. However, even if permission were granted to plant immediately, it would take time to get things underway again after the 2-3 year interval. It would be necessary to take care of such things as renewing the very small available seed stocks, much of which is no longer good, reopening the abandoned oil presses, reestablishing market situations, and so forth. 

Many views are being put forward for the resumption of cultivation. The most interesting among them is that planting should be carried out on the state farms. This may be the right way to ensure that opium poppies be cultivated only for the needs of the pharmaceutical industry. But it must not be forgotten that the opium poppy is also the food and bread of the poor peasant, as explained above. In fact, it was our peasants who suffered most from the ban. 

Looking at it from other angles, how many state farms have the ecology to support opium poppies? Opium poppy culitivation is something that has taken form over the years under ecological conditions with its own technique. 

There is certain to be some hesitation in resuming cultivation because of the effects it would have elsewhere. For this reason, those in the responsible positions have been trying to find solutions outside the formerly applied system. However, various arguments may be offered to all of them : 

1. The old system should be maintained.-Just as there is bound to be conflict in the application of any new system, there may also be defects in the old system. Our view is that except for the problem of implementation, the major problem is economic. There should not be such a large gap between the price the state pays for opium and the smugglers' price. In practice, the difference is 3-4 times higher for smugglers' prices. If this difference were eliminated, the entire crop would be gathered into official hands. The money paid out for opium production would thus be 3-4 times more, but opium would not be smuggled. This method would be a correction of the old system. Many measures to prevent opportunism could be considered. such as establishing an effective control system in every province and district, careful enforcement of the laws, and daily purchases of the opium at harvest time. 

2. Opium production should be tightly restricted.-This method has already been attempted with a law that went into effect in 1934 and was retained in spirit with a new law in 1959 that required licensing for planting opium poppies and producing opium. This may be the way to handle the matter-making more new laws and tightly restricting opium production-if the goal is to be only eliminating the shortage of raw materials in our pharmaceutical industry. The hardships caused to the farmers by the production of opium would have to be eliminated or lightened, and foreign exchange would not be spent on opium for use in our pharmaceutical industry. New types would have to be developed from among our rich poppy population to find varieties to produce high quality opium and numerous seeds. 

3. The gum should not be drawn before harvesting the pods.-A report prepared by the United Nations narcotics laboratory in 1972 showed that there was a shortage of codeine alkaloid, a vital material for the pharmaceutical industry, as a result of reduced world opium production. It was then proposed that the "papaver brecteatum," a close relative of the opium poppy which is known as the source of thebaine and is native to Turkey's high plateaus, should be planted and improved in our country. The incising method cannot be used on this plant because its pods are very small. The oil content of the seed is high and thebaine is obtained by grinding the entire pod after the seeds are harvested. 

It would be possible for our regular opium poppies to be treated this way also. 

To harvest the seeds, the pods would be snapped off the stems and, after removing the seeds, the pods would then be processed for alkaloid in state-run plants In this way, the various objections presented above would be avoided. The peasant and the national economy would both be saved from a great deal of hardship, and the humane solution-both intelligent and moral-would be found to the problem of the countries of the world looking with suspicion on our decision to resume opium poppy cultivation. Thus the opium poppy could be rid of distrust and could resume its position, not of destroying mankind, but on the job in medicine of relieving the agony of those millions writhing in pain.

LICENSED, CONTROLLED CULTIVATION OF OPIUM POPPIES TO RESUME 

Ankara-Minister of Agriculture Korkut Ozal reported that the licensed and controlled cultivation of poppies is planned for a 200,000-donem area in Turkey during the fall of this year. As much as 200 tons of raw materials for pharmaceuticals will be obtained. Opium capsules will be sold for up to 15 lira per kilogram to the drug industry to be established by the state. 

Ozal, who, at yesterday's Ministers' Economic Council meeting, presented his ministry's proposals on resumption of opium-poppy production in Turkey and on investments to be made in the opium region, told this newspaper: "In complete accordance with the principles of the only agreement we have signed, the supervised and licensed cultivation of poppies, within a specified area is planned. The goal is to reach the level of cultivation of 1967, to fill the need for raw opium in the world, and to obtain approximately 200 tons of the raw material. 

The written decision will be made public by 1 July at the latest and will clearly define the areas and conditions for cultivation. "It is our opinion that very effective supervision will be ensured through the licensed cultivation of poppies. This method was applied in four of our provinces in which poppies were last sown in Turkey in 1971-1972, and very positive results were achieved. Licensed cultivation is nothing new in our nation. For example, much experience has been gained in Turkey with the licensing of tobacco production. "In addition to widespread and strict supervision conducted during the period when the poppies can be incised, state organizations which will purchase the capsules from the producers will stipulate that opium poppies are to be delivered before they are incised. This will be the third control mechanism that will be put into effect."

TO PAY FULL VALUE FOR CROP 

"At present, the official price on the world market is between 500 and 600 lira per kilogram for opium gum. However, since it is proposed that the uncut poppy rather than opium gum be purchased from the producer, estimates have been made by taking into account world prices. It has been established that it will be possible to pay up to 15 lira per kilogram for opium capsules which will be used in the pharmaceutical industry. "According to studies conducted by specialists in our ministry, if opium gum obtained from poppies is sold abroad, a farmer would receive 2,000 lira per decare of land. However, if an establishment is founded in Turkey to use this opium gum as a raw material in the pharmaceutical industry, it will be possible for a producer who turns over his uncut opium capsules to the state to increase his total income to 3,300 lira per donem." 

1 Tarim Istatistikleri Ozeti (Various years).

PHARMACEUTICAL RAW MATERIAL ESTABLISHMENT 

"It is proposed to set up in Turkey a factory which will manufacture every type of chemical product requiring opium alkaloids that is needed by the pharmaceutical industry. Preliminary studies show that this can be done with an investment of 250 million lira. Until this factory goes into operation, Turkey will export raw opium. "It has been demonstrated that, since our farmers are ensured incomes of between 2,000 and 3,300 lira per decare through the cultivation of poppies, this is a very productive crop. In fact, studies show that if other supposedly valuable crops are substituted for opium poppies, our economic loss per decade at today's prices is 15.000 lira. The loss for 200,000 donems is 3 billilon lira. This is only an estimate of economic loss at present prices and does not cover harm from the social standpoint that confronts the producer."

COMPENSATION TO BE PAID 

"Because of the ban on poppy cultivation, indemnification will again be paid for the 1973-1974 period to farmers who had grown opium poppies in the past. 

In addition, a decision to compensate owners of oil-pressing mills who earned their living by producing poppy-seed oil and who suffered great harm due to the ban has been sent to the Prime Minister. "Since the prohibition on poppy cultivation went into effect, 20 million dollars from a United States' assistance fund has been appropriated. Of this, 111 million lira for indemnification and 71 million lira for investment projects for a total of 182 million lira or 13 million dollars has actually been spent. "Work will continue on investment projects that have been started in the opium-producing region that have no connection with the ban on cultivation. 

Furthermore, several investment projects with the goal of diversification begun after the ban was imposed will coincide with an investment policy that will take into account our development plan and that will ensure the maximum economic development in the region."

TURKEY CAN FIGHT SMUGGLING AS WELL AS AMERICA CAN 

Minister of Agriculture Ozal pointed out that Turkish administrations have always demonstrated understanding of the opium-smuggling problem and that poppies were cultivated in 42 provinces in 1960; 22 provinces during the Inonu administration in 1965; 9 provinces in 1970; 7 provinces in 1971; and 4 provinces in 1972. He said: "There is a clear and decisive opinion on this topic in Turkey. The government fully comprehends its responsibility. It well knows, within the framework of sovereign rights, its obligations to prevent smuggling. We, keeping an eye on defense, first of all, of our villagers' and Turkey's interests in this area and on humane considerations, are undertaking a constructive, sensitive, and meaningful task. We definitely believe that Turkey's ability and success to prevent smuggling of dangerous drugs within its own borders is not inferior to that of other countries that deal with the problem."

TURKEY PLANS TO LIFT OPIUM BAN; U.S. RELATIONS STRAINED 

(By Sam Cohen, special to the Christian Science Monitor) ISTANBUL, TURKEY.-The Turkish poppy, expected to reappear soon in the fields of western Anatolia, already has started to show its poisonous effects on the relations between the U.S. and Turkey. 

The new government's intention to lift the opium ban, enforced in 1972 following American pressure, has become a heated political issue between the two allies. 

Tension is running high in Turkey and there are signs of a new wave of anti- Americanism.

Observers are concerned the clock could be turned back in U.S.-Turkish relations to attitudes of the late 1960's, when anti-American feelings soared over the 

Cyprus issue.

PLANS UNDER STUDY 

Premier Bulent Ecevit's coalition government is expected to announce soon a total end to the poppy-growing ban. Recently the administration has decided to allow the planting of poppies only in state-owned experimental farms in order to preserve the seeds, which are regarded as of the highest quality in the world. 

This is seen as the first significant step towards reintroduction of the poppy cultivation in private farms as well. 

In fact the government is now discussing plans drawn up by the Ministry of Agriculture and already approved by the cabinet's economic agency for the lifting of the ban. Under the program, the cultivation of poppy will be allowed on fields limited to about 50,000 acres, under license. The controlled cultivation is expected to yield 300 tons of crude opium per year. A state agency will buy the poppy directly from the farmers for 15 lira (about $1) a kilogram (2.2 pounds).

Government sources say the cultivation of poppy will be resumed next fall. 

Meantime talks between Washington and Ankara on the question are continuing. Washington is pressing for continuation of the ban and seems prepared to help the 100,000 Turkish farmers who are said to have been suffering economically from the prohibition. The U.S. is paying Turkey a $35 million grant for compensation to the farmers and for the introduction of substitute crops.

DETERMINATION SEEN 

However, Ankara does not seem to want to use the issue for bargaining or pry more money from the U.S. Foreign Minister Turan Gunes said recently "Money is not important. We cannot allow the farmers to depend on charity of a foreign country, no matter how friendly that country may be." 

American diplomats here think that the Ecevit government is determined to go ahead with its plan to lift the ban. Their concern is that any harsh move to prevent it may cause more damage than good. 

In fact, some unofficial angry reaction for the U.S. already has provoked resentment and tension here. Two U.S. congressmen, Reps. Lester Wolff and 

Charles B. Rangel, who came to Turkey on a fact-finding mission, were coolly received. When they were quoted as saying that Congress may revise the foreign aid program to Turkey if the ban is lifted, Turkish parliamentarians, politicians, and newspapers reacted strongly. 

The congressmen and other American diplomats who visited the opiumgrowing areas were told by farmers that they wanted to go back to the cultivation of opium, more than anything else. One diplomat observed that poppy growing had been "a way of life" for these people for centuries, indeed the Turkish farmer-who does not use the opium as a drug himself-draws several benefits from the by-products as cookng oil, fuel and fodder. 

FARMERS LONG CRITICAL 

The farmers have been most unhappy with the ban. Their main complaint was that nothing or very little was done in way of introducing substitute crops or new jobs.

The Americans blame previous Turkish governments and agencies for this, claiming that they were unable to produce or implement regional development projects, which Washington was prepared to finance. "The Turks are going the easy way, by lifting the ban and keeping the farmers poor, instead of trying to introduce new crops and improve their living conditions," a high-ranking U.S. diplomat said.

The government, and almost all the parties, argue that the ban was imposed by an Army-appointed government and therefore did not reflect the wishes of the people. With a democratic regime now, it appears inevitable that such an unpopular measure should be revoked. The Turks say that any attempt by the 

U.S. to influence Turkey to maintain the ban is an "interference in its internal affairs and sovereignty."

COMPLETION CITED 

Another argument is that the Turkish farmers cannot be forced "to pay the bill for other people" who use drugs. Said a Turkish editor, "it's like asking the car factories in Detroit not to manufacture automobiles, because they cause accidents here."

The Turks also say, on the ground of recent international studies indicating that the world output of raw opium was inadequate for medicinal use, that Turkey should not be stopped from producing the world's best-quality poppy. Reports that the U.S. was ordering large quantities of opium from India for medicinal use provoked an angry reaction here. Foreign Minister Gunes said, "This means our legitimate income will flow from now on to other countries." 

The American-trained Premier Ecevit seems to be aware of the "humanitarian problems," as he puts it, that opium causes, particularly in the U.S. He wants for this reason to keep the opium production in Turkey "limited and controlled." He is interested in a close cooperation with U.S. authorities on this to prevent illicit growing and smuggling.

In the light of the past experience American experts doubt that this would be possible. Before the ban, experts estimated that 80 percent of the heroin smuggled into the U.S. originated from Turkish poppies.

However the Americans' immediate and main concern now is the serious political implications which the issue is causing. Emotional reactions on both sides may lead to a deterioration of U.S.-Turkish relations, at a time when the Western alliance is already facing a crisis. 

STATUS OF AGREEMENT WITH TURKEY 

Senator INOUYE. Mr. Ambassador, your statement and the Department's justification paint a rosey picture of your international control

program. However, most other information received by this committee indicates this program was in great trouble. 

The cornerstone of the program appears to be the agreement with Turkey to refrain from opium production. 

Mr. Ambassador, exactly what are Turkey's obligations growing out of the 1971 agreement whereby the United States committed itself to a vast new aid package of about $35 million? 

Mr. VANCE. The obligation of the Turkish Government in our opinion is to continue the ban. It was envisaged at the time of the agreement the ban was not a temporary one but a permanent one. 

Senator INOUYE. This is oftentimes referred to as an agreement and sometimes as an understanding of cooperation. 

What is this, an agreement or just an understanding?

Mr. VANCE. Mr. Chairman, our reply to that question is that it was an agreement. We had been discussing the problems created for the international effort to control illegal heroin with the Turkish Government for a number of years.

The Turkish Government's ban was in response to these discussions and, more appropriately I might say, was their effort to meet their commitments under the 1961 Single Convention, of which they are a signatory, as are we and most other countries of the world, which obligates signatory countries to make their best efforts to prevent narcotics from getting into the illegal market.

The Turkish Government under Prime Minister Demirel, starting back in 1967, began to reduce the number of provinces in which poppies were legally grown. By 1971 the Government had reduced the number of provinces from 21 to 7.

Then a new government came into power in Turkey under Prime Minister Erim and it decided to reduce the provinces in which poppies might be legally grown from seven to four and then to zero. 

In the growing season 1970-71, which meant the harvest of 1971, there were only seven provinces permitted legally to grow poppies. This covered a production by what is estimated at something like 

80,000 peasants because their plots of opium are very tiny. 

In the 1971-72 year the number of provisions were reduced to four and the Turkish Government decree provided there would be no further legal poppy growing following that season.

In that 2-year period, they worked out an internal arrangement whereby they compensated the farmers who turned-in those seven provinces and the next year four-those farmers who turned their opium over to the Government and a record was taken of how much opium each produced during those years and in subsequent years each has been paid what the Turkish Government regarded as a reasonable amount for their loss of this income. 

The agreement grew out of the discussions between the two governments and the Turkish Government informing us officially that they were moving to reduce from seven to four and then to zero the number of provinces in which poppies would be grown. 

Our commitment to provide them with a little over $35 million in grant assistance was conditioned on that undertaking, on that decree by the Turkish Government to ban the production of poppies. 

So we feel that there very clearly was an understanding, it was very clear on both sides.

Senator INOUYE. From all the articles we have seen, especially those 

I have just put in the record, the Turkish Government intends to break this agreement and proceed with the growing of poppies, is that correct? 

Mr. VANCE. That is not our understanding, Mr. Chairman. 

May I give just a little background? 

Senator INOUYE. Yes.

NEW GOVERNMENT IN TURKEY 

Mr. VANCE. The Turks held elections last October and during that election campaign, I might add, the government was in the hands of the Justice Party. The opposition parties were the Republican Party and the National Socialist Party. In the election campaign both of those opposition parties included in what we would call their campaign platform statements that the decision of the predecessor government to ban poppies had been badly based, badly reasoned, and badly implemented and they promised the electorate if they came to power they would review the whole situation with regard to this ban. 

The Turks had some difficulty forming a government because no one of the parties had a majority and the two opposition parties finally formed a government in the latter part of January of this year, a coalition government.

RESTUDY AND RECONSIDERATION OF AGREEMENT BY NEW TURKISH GOVERNMENT 

Shortly thereafter the Government-the Prime Minister and the Foreign Minister-informed our Ambassador, referring to these electoral promises, that the Government was restudying and reconsidering the decision of the earlier government and that the Government's decision would take into account the interests of Turkey, including the interests of the farmers who had been prejudiced, the interests in the Turkish economy and also Turkey's obligations under the 1961 Single Convention not to contribute to the presence of illicit drugs on the world markets.

They have told us they have not yet made a decision, that their studies are not yet complete and they informed us further that they would consult with us before they make this decision. That is the present status.

COST OF TURKISH PROGRAM 

Senator INOUYE. What has this entire Turkish opium program cost the United States?

Mr. VANCE. The program consisted of two different aspects, actually two major aspects and one quite minor one. Ambassador Handley was Ambassador at the time and he informed the Turkish Government in the light of their decree banning the growing of poppies, that, subject to appropriations by the Congress, we would make two sorts of grant payments to them. One was a series of three separate annual payments of $5 million each, which was an estimate of the foreign exchange loss to the Turkish Government of their legal or licit opium sales in export. 

The second aspect was two successive grant payments of $10 million each which was envisaged as being available to the Turkish Government for economic assistance programs in the poppy-growing provinces designed to improve the economic standing of the inhabitants of those provinces to counter losses caused by the ban. 

Those were in successive fiscal years and the present fiscal year is the last during which these payments were envisaged. We have not obligated or turned over to the Turkish Government the moneys in the current fiscal year which are $5 million of the first level of payment and $10 million of the second type, so we have retained this year's funds until we are sure Turkey has decided to maintain the ban. 

Of the moneys obligated in the previous fiscal years, there are some $4,700,000 of the first $10 million payment that are as yet undispersed so that makes a total that is not yet in the hands of the Turkish Government for expenditure of some $19-plus million. 

TURKISH EXPENDITURES OF U.S. CONTRIBUTIONS 

Senator INOUYE. I gather from an audit submitted by the Turkish 

Government only $1 million has been actually expended by the implementing agencies of that government?

Mr. VANCE. Well, our information from our Embassy, which they obtained from the Turkish Government, indicates that the Turkish Government has expended $5,308,206 of the first $10 million transfer which was envisaged for economic developments. 

We have a breakdown of how those moneys were expended which I can put in the record if you so desire.

CLASSIFICATION OF AGREEMENT 

Senator INOUYE. At the request of this committee, your office furnished a copy of former Ambassador Handley's memorandum of his understanding of the United States-Turkish Agreement dated July 16, 1971. A copy was supplied to the Government of Turkey. 

Why does the Department of State persist in maintaining a secret classification on this document?

I have looked over the document and can't see why it would cause any harm if we made it public. I think the people of the United 

States should know what sort of arrangement we have with Turkey. 

Mr. VANCE. Mr. Chairman, the substance of the agreement and the payments to the Turkish Government pursuant to it have just been described by me for the record. 

The reason why this letter was secret and is still secret is the following: the Turkish Government at the time described its action to its people as being a unilateral decision of the sovereign government to fulfill its international obligations under the single convention. 

One of the fears then, I believe, of the Turkish Government was that if it appeared to the Turkish public that their action was pursuant to an agreement with the United States, political problems might be created for the Government. 

I believe this anticipation has proved accurate because the pressures in Turkey now for the lifting of the ban are essentially political. The assertion is that the Turkish Government knuckled under the pressure from the United States, the great power, that it was an unfair agreement, and the decisionmaking it was improperly made by the Government.

If we lend credence to the statements of the opponents of the ban, it would defeat our purpose. Our purpose is to see Turkey decide to continue the ban. That, I think, in addition to the fact that we promised another government that we would not publish it prevents our doing so.

I think the former is a substantive, reasonable, and rational position. 

PLIGHT OF AMERICAN CITIZENS ABROAD 

Senator INOUYE. I noted with some dismay articles which have appeared and TV documentaries which I have seen relating to the plight of American citizens, the latest being a group of military personnel, airmen stationed in Turkey who were caught with, a hashish stick in their possession and the first case involving two or three women transporting several pounds of hashish. The articles all indicate they were given extremely stiff sentences, something like 20 years to life and in the case of the military personnel there was evidence indicating some sort of physical torture and long-term imprisonment.

I gather that our Embassy there almost refused to lift a finger in representing the interests of those citizens. 

On one hand, I note the Turkish Government clearly is willing to knowingly permit its citizens to enter into the legal drug traffic and suddenly, on the other hand, going on a great crusade giving 20-year sentences to someone who just picked up a cigarette and smoked it.

Have we entered into discussions involving our citizens who have been apprehended by them?

Mr. VANCE. We have indeed, sir, and I think those press articles suggesting that we have not lifted a finger are erroneous.

The responsibilities, as you know, Mr. Chairman, of the U.S. Consular officers and Embassy officers abroad very clearly include making our best efforts to protect the rights and interests of American citizens abroad whenever they get into any kind of difficulty. 

We are, of course, when it comes to American citizens who have been arrested for a crime committed abroad, or charged with a crime, we have to recognize the criminal legislation and the criminal justice procedures and structures of foreign governments. 

Therefore, our efforts on behalf of citizens who fall into such troubles have to be restricted to making sure that they are receiving the same treatment that is accorded by that government to their own nationals and urging the foreign governments to treat them humanely. 

We see to it to the best of our ability that they are given legal advice and we see to it that they are put in contact with their families so they can raise funds for their defense and, if in prison, to improve, if permissible, their living conditions. 

We have taken those actions with regard to these people to whom you are referring in Turkey as well as in other countries. The problem has been accentuated in Turkey because the drug problem in Turkey itself is essentially one of Cannabis and Hashish. 

CRIMES SUBJECT TO LOCAL LAWS 

Turkey does not have drug abuse of heroin, therefore their laws are very strict on hashish. The two girls and one young man to whom you are referring who are in prison, I think, for sentences of 20 years or life, were apprehended by the Turkish authorities, as I recall, driving three Volkswagen mini-buses with several hundred pounds of cannabis secreted in them.

We have repeatedly approached the Turkish Government saying the sentences, it seems to us, greatly exceed the crime. But the sentences are in conformance with Turkish legislation and Turkish judicial practice.

So far we have not gotten very far in persuading the Turkish Government to grant leniency in these cases. We feel strongly these are verv excessive sentences.

We are helpless so far to find some way of improving their situation. 

SITUATION OF MILITARY PERSONNEL 

Senator INOUYE. In the case of the military men, according to the articles, the only American representatives present when these men were being questioned were several U.S. military police and throughout the questioning the military police didn't do a thing even while our men were being tortured and assaulted. 

In fact, it appears that one of the military men suggested to the defendant that they should confess, otherwise they would be tortured continuously.

This is the sort of representation our men received in Turkey. 

I am wondering if this is considered reasonable. No representative from the Consul's office there, the only highest ranking officer was a sergeant in the military police. 

Mr. VANCE. I am not familiar with this case. I will be happy to look into it further and submit a statement for the record. 

Senator INOUYE. I would appreciate that, sir. 

The airmen in question were picked up by the Turkish police while on a weekend outing. Ten of them were charged with use or possession of hashish, while the eleventh was charged with trafficking in that drug. At the first judicial hearing two men pleaded guilty, and the others not guilty. As the judicial proceeding unfolded, the two who initially pleaded guilty stated that they were not guilty.

Under the NATO Status of Forces Agreement, the host government has primary jurisdiction in cases involving alleged infractions of local law by foreign military personnel unless the host government decides to waive jurisdiction. Turkey has usually chosen to exercise jurisdiction in such cases as those being discussed here.

As in all court proceedings abroad involving American citizens, the U.S. 

Government is very much interested in seeing that these airmen receive fair trials. The Government feels a special responsibility, of course, to ensure that servicemen who have been sent abroad on government orders are provided the necessary legal and other assistance to ensure that their rights are protected. 

From the time the airmen were picked up in mid-February to the present, a wide range of US civilian and military officials in Turkey and in Washington have paid close attention to their cases. As soon as American authorities in 

Turkey learned of the airmen's incarceration, they undertook to arrange appropriate legal and translation assistance. We understand that a team of US Air 

Force lawyers has been aiding the men throughout and that the Air Force has arranged for local lawyers to assist in their defense as well. Moreover, the Air 

Force has organized regular visits to the jails in which three of the men are being held to deliver rations and other necessities. US consular officers in the area have also visited the men and have been present at each of their court hearings. Present in court for the most recent hearing were the following US officials: an officer from the US Consulate at Adana, a trial observer from the 

Judge Advocate General's Office, four US Air Force colonels, and two US Air 

Force translators. The men were also assisted by two Turkish lawyers.

JUSTIFICATION OF CERTAIN ITEMS REQUESTED FOR FISCAL YEAR 1975 

Senator INOUYE. As I go through your justification, I am wondering about justification and cost effectiveness of the following items: 

I hope you will bear with me; $15,000 for TDY psychiatrists for

Indonesia, $10,000 for two launches and two motor boats for Colombia, $12,000 for temporary duty of DEA agents in Jamaica. 

I realize these are small items but what are two temporary duty psychiatrists doing in Indonesia? Does this help in your international narcotics control program? 

Mr. VANCE. I can speak generally to the occasional expenditures that we envisage in the treatment field. We, of course, are not going to get into major expenditures for treatment of foreign populations; however, in our efforts to bring home to and elicit the full cooperation of foreign governments, in our efforts to restrain and hopefully eliminate eventually illicit trade in narcotics, we have to use various means. 

Many of them started out 2 or 3 years ago with the impression that the great noise and great activity in which we were engaged in launching this program indicated the problem was ours, not theirs. 

Therefore, a good part of our initial efforts this is still ongoing with regard to some countries-is to point out to them that the problem is also theirs. It is a worldwide program and theirs as much as ours and that of other countries.

In the course of these efforts they are either discovering or have talked to us about existing treatment requirements in their own countries and they want to find out or learn what we have learned in our efforts and therefore we do send occasionally our experts on relatively brief visits to foreign countries.

We also find we don't know all the answers and therefore these experts when they go abroad to convey what we have learned are able to learn what other people have learned.

PUBLIC SAFETY PROGRAM

POSSIBLE SITUATIONS IN COUNTRIES NOT COOPERATING IN MATTERS OF DRUG CONTROL

Mr. VANCE. Mr. Chairman, I am not qualified to comment on other aspects of requests for foreign aid appropriations and authorizations. But to reply generally to your statement, we are well aware of congressional intent that assistance not be given countries that are not taking, to quote section 481:

If the President determines that the government of a country has failed to take adequate steps to prevent trade in narcotic drugs, he shall suspend economic and military assistance under this and any other Act. 

Thus far, no such determination has been made and we think there is no appropriate basis for making this determination.

EXCERPTS FROM GAO REPORT 

Senator INOUYE. Without objection, there will be inserted in the record at this point an excerpt from a recent GAO report which offered several quotes from a recent private study on the economic studies of heroin. The subject of this report contended because of the relatively small amount of heroin needed to supply the U.S. market and high profits involved in providing an illegal supply, it is unlikely that risks can be raised high enough to force dealers out of business. 

A year-long study by a private group offers several observations on the economics of heroin:

Past reliance on law enforcement measures has not stopped an epidemic growth of the heroin addict population.

U.S. national policy, by resorting almost exclusively to criminal sanctions to eliminate addiction, has bred a thriving illegal market that can be sustained only by criminal activity.

The amount of opium needed to supply the demand for heroin in the United States is only a minute portion of total world production. 

It is probably impossible to curb all opium production, licit and illicit, everywhere in the world.

The profits earned in domestic distribution are so great that it is unlikely that the risks can be raised high enough to force dealers out of business. 

The illegality of heroin is the sole reason for its high cost in this country: in England the pharmacy cost of heroin is $0.04 per grain compared with a 

U.S. street price of from $30 to $90 per grain.

BRITISH PROGRAM 

In England the pharmacy cost of heroin is 4 cents per grain while the U.S. street price is $30 to $90 per grain. Is the rate of addiction and illegal use so much greater in Britain than in the United States?

Mr. VANCE. I am not familiar with the situation in Britain. I can endeavor to find out something for the record. 

Senator INOUYE. I believe there is a Mr. William Durkin here. He is in the Drug Enforcement Administration. 

Mr. DURKIN. Yes, sir. 1 

Senator INOUYE. Could you give this committee your views on the

British practice where narcotics are being dispensed under government supervision at very low cost? 

Mr. DURKIN. Only to the extent, Senator, I don't think the so-called

British system would work in the United States. 

History has demonstrated it won't work in the United States. At one time the United States did have drug clinics, drug-free clinics which were established in the late twenties or early thirties. They proliferated the problem rather than solved the problem.

The current use of methadone is also now having an impact on the drug problem, a positive impact but at the same time it is opening the door for additional enforcement problems.

I think comparing England's system and the situation in the United 

States is comparing apples and oranges. 

Senator INOUYE. Is the British system working in Britain? 

Mr. DURKIN. That is very difficult to answer. 

The British are divided on that question, sir. 

Senator INOUYE. What would be the street price of heroin in England? The street price I noted is between $30 to $90 per grain depending on location. 

Mr. DURKIN. The pharmaceutical price for heroin in Great Britain would be considerably lower than the illicit street price in the United States.

I might add that reports we are getting from Great Britain now indicate that Great Britain is considering moving toward a methadone program of some nature because their experience with providing heroin to the addicts is not being as beneficial as they had anticipated. 

Senator INOUYE. Thank you very much, sir.

Vehicles thus represent a significant portion of our programs with about a dozen countries where law enforcement activities are being strengthened to break up illicit trafficking operations. Effective enforcement is, of course, emphasized in our international program as a means to meet the top objective of curtailing the flow of illicit substances into our country. Increasing the enforcement

capabilities of foreign governments is the most effective use of our funds.

Concurrent with our efforts in the enforcement field, we are also providing important assistance in crop replacement programs and other agricultural projects to eliminate drugs at the source. These are, of course, more long-range in nature, and it is difficult at this juncture to provide any definitive information on the chances of their success. 

In Turkey, where we hope the ban on opium poppy cultivation will be maintained, the U.S. Department of Agriculture has recently completed a survey which contains some promising indicators. There are prospects for the development in 

Turkey of winter lentils; winter oil seeds, particularly 

Syrian Scabis and safflower; such winter cereals as wheat barley, oats, and rye; and such legumes as millets, sorghum, and broad beans. As far as we know, there has been no research for the development of the castor bean in Turkey. 

The problem of reducing and replacing the opium production in the Golden Triangle area, roughly 600-700 tons a year, defies a short term solution. None of the three governments involved Thailand, Burma, and Laos 

effectively controls the rugged, isolated area where opium is grown and where a mixed collection of wellarmed dissident groups, communists and ordinary bandits operate. Little can be done until the area is fully controlled by the central governments and until income substitutes are found for the substantial numbers of hilltribes who depend entirely on opium as their cash crop. 

To date no crop substitute has been found for this region

as easy to store and transport and with such a ready market and lucrative return as opium. 

It will be necessary to develop not a one-for-one replacement for opium but an agricultural community and market based on a number of income substitutes. This effort has begun in northern Thailand through crop research being undertaken under the guidance of the U.S. 

Department of Agriculture, the agricultural extension project of the United Nations Fund for Drug Abuse Control 

(UNFDAC), and complementary projects in marketing and improved village transport being developed by the U.S. 

Agency for International Development. Projects are being developed for deciduous fruits, legume seeds, coffee, essential oils, tree nuts, and strawberries.

In Burma, the government has been studying crop substitutes and plans a phased reduction in opium growing in areas it controls. Also, an UNFDAC crop substitution project is now in the process of negotiation. Most of the new crops being developed in Thailand would be equally suitable for Burma.

Although opium production declined in Laos as a result of the fighting in the growing areas, a return to peacetime may prompt the hilltribes to return to this cash crop; hence it is important to continue efforts similiar to those in Thailand in research and agricultural training in other crops. We are working with the Government of Laos in resettling some of the opium producing hilltribes and providing them assistance in a variety of activities including

alternate crops, the raising of silkworms, handicrafts production and livestock breeding.

In Pakistan, illicit production of opium is estimated at 150-300 tons annually. We are engaged in a serious dialogue with the Pakistan Government authorities to bring about an effective narcotics control program. Projects under discussion include possible U.S. assistance in conducting aerial surveys of opium growing areas, technical aid in formulating crop substitution and development programs, and direct assistance to growing areas tied to an effective ban. The U.S. Department of Agriculture has developed crop substitution proposals for cultivating deciduous fruits, sugar beet seeds, and mushrooms. programs have as yet been activated. No

In Afghanistan, annual illicit production of opium is estimated as high as 200-300 tons, the bulk of which is smuggled into Iran. The Afghans face numerous problems making the control over production and trafficking of narcotics difficult. Its terrain limits access to many areas; subsistence farming is still the dominant employment pattern, with opium being a valuable source of income for the marginal farmer; Afghan tribesmen have engaged in smuggling for centuries; and the capability of Afghan law enforcement agencies to interdict the production and flow of narcotic drugs in the traditionally independent tribal areas is extremely limited. 

Working with representatives of UNFDAC, the United States is planning to contribute to the anti-narcotics control program of Pakistan principally in the area of law enforcement. ་ང་

PEOPLE'S REPUBLIC OF CHINA'S ATTITUDE TOWARD DRUG PROBLEM 

Excuse me, I have one final question. 

Mr. Ambassador, we have also had conflicting information as to just how much the People's Republic of China is involved in the so-called drug traffic and conflicting data, statements, allegations, and so forth. These more or less tend to create the image that there is some involvement; other persons think there isn't.

Can you give us information as to what the People's Republic of China's attitude and policy is toward the drug problem and whether or not Peking has shown any willingness to cooperate in controlling the drug traffic in the world at large? 

Mr. VANCE. The International Narcotics Control Board, which is the policing organization of the international structure which reviews the compliance of all the countries of the world with the international conventions, has stated that they have found no evidence and we have found no evidence of drugs illicitly entering the world market from the People's Republic of China. 

So the stories, some of which I have also seen, asserting the contrary, we do not believe are accurate.

I mentioned earlier that I was in New York City attending the Economic and Social Council during its debate last Thursday and Friday on the activities of the international community in the field of narcotics.

The People's Republic of China was present at that meeting and I heard their statement to the council which was along the following lines, that opium had been imposed on China historically from abroad and, when the present Government took control, there was a serious drug addiction problem in China which they assert has now been completely eliminated.

We believe that there is legal production of opium in China for their legal pharmaceutical and research requirements.

As I have said, there is no evidence contrary to the Chinese official's assertion, that there is illegal traffic in opium from China. 

Senator HATFIELD. Would you insert for the record what date this position, this view and policy, or attitude, was established by our State Department? 

Mr. VANCE. Yes, sir, I will do that.

Senator HATFIELD. Contrast it to any previously held view in terms of date, please. 

Mr. VANCE. Yes, sir, I will do that. 

A mass of articles has been disseminated in the United States since early 1950's to attempt to convince the American public that the People's Republic of China (PRC) produced thousands of tons of opium annually and was actively engaged in the illicit export of opium and its derivatives to the U.S. and other 

Western countries. The campaign has been promoted here and abroad by a number of groups who have consistently opposed normalization of relations between the U.S. and PRC. Although we are unable to locate any record of official pronouncements by the State Department on these stories before the early 1970's, I think the stories were fairly widely accepted as authentic by the public and by some U.S. Government agencies as well. It should be pointed out that this was a time when we knew much less about the world illicit narcotics trafficking market and no concerted effort was being undertaken to improve our knowldge of it.

Then in the early 1970's when the heroin epidemic reached an all time high in the U.S. and drug abuse was found to be extensive among U.S. troops in Viet- 

Nam, U.S. narcotics agents began extensive investigative work in Far East trafficking centers in cooperation with local police. In the process, we have learned a great deal about the structure of the opium trade in the Far East: 1) Not one investigation into heroin traffic in the Far East in the past few years has led to PRC involvement; in each case, the traffickers were people engaged in criminal activity for the usual profit motive. 2) Where the origin of the heroin could be traced, it was to refineries in Southeast Asia owned by non-communist consortiums. 3) The origin of the raw opium used in the production of heroin could be traced to the poppy growing area of Southeast Asia known as the Golden Triangle which encompasses portions of Burma, Thailand and Laos; production of raw opium in this area is more than enough to account for all the opium and heroin traded in the Far East.

Senator HATFIELD. No further questions, Mr. Chairman.

[From the Chicago Tribune, Feb. 24, 1974]

DRUG FOE ON WAY OUT; DID HIS JOB TOO WELL (By Bob Wiedrich) 

WASHINGTON, Feb. 23.-Former Ambassador William J. Handley, the man hailed two years ago as a master diplomat for negotiating an unprecedented pact with Turkey to ban opium poppy cultivation, has become a victim of his own good work.

Several weeks ago, while in Southeast Asia, Handley was informed he will be relieved soon as President Nixon's global watchdog of the narcotics traffic. His replacement will be Sheldon Vance, ambassador to Zaire in the Congo. In effect, the career diplomat has become a casualty of the very agreement he so skillfully negotiated with the Turks in exchange for a $35.7 million American subsidy to help Turkish farmers find alternate crops to the opium poppy. 

Handley's downfall is partly due to the intense domestic crisis generated by the pact as Turkish farmers have pressured the new government of Premier Bulent Ecevit to resume cultivation of the sole cash crop of many peasant farmers for centuries. The 70,000 poppy growers complain the subsidy is inadequate, and 

Turkey has notified the United States it will resume growing poppies this spring. 

In recent months, as it became more apparent Turkey would do just that, there was growing concern at the White House. Turkish opium accounted for 80 per cent of the heroin pumped into the United States before the pact. And shutting off that source had allowed American agents to concentrate their efforts on other illicit drug sources in Southeast Asia and Latin and South America. 

But when Handley was asked to reopen discussions with Turkey in the hope of reaching some compromise, Handley reportedly became adamant in his refusal to do so. As one White House official declared, Handley was unable to view the matter objectively. He would not even entertain the thought. 

At the heart of the matter is the growing worldwide shortage of opium for medicinal purposes, humanitarian pain killers of far greater effectiveness than the synthetics developed by man. The United Nations calculates there have been shortages in seven of the last 11 years and the 1973 shortage was an estimated 300 tons. Thus, the Nixon administration stands squarely in the middle of a perplexing problem.

On the one hand, White House officials are encountering increasing pressure from the pharmaceutical industry to legalize opium poppy cultivation on American soil to ease the shortage and end dependence on medicinal opiates from India, the sole legal exporter of such drugs. On the other, administration officials find it unthinkable to even entertain such a step when the United States is importuning every opium growing nation to curb production in the hopes of smashing the international narcotics racket, which has destroyed so many 

American lives.

As a result, White House spokesmen indicate they may have to bend a little in meeting Turkish demands to resume opium production even though they are distraught at Turkey's efforts to dissolve the poppy growing ban agreement. 

It is this acceptance of the realities of Turkey's internal affairs that apparently was summarily rejected by former Ambassador Handley, with whom the end of Turkish opium poppy cultivation had become a labor of love. 

The White House reportedly has flatly refused the demands of the American pharmaceutical makers.

However, the Department of Agriculture has been ordered to explore other methods of extracting the needed opiates from the poppy plant before it reaches the degree of maturity in which it produces opium gum from which is made morphine base and eventually heroin. Such alternative production methods could be used in discussions with the Turks to temper and control resumed opium production if that is the final outcome. 

Right now, the Agriculture Department reportedly has three acres of opium poppies under cultivation and has requested approval to increase that figure to 150 acres. But experts point out the methods under study involve mechanical extraction from green opium poppy straw, another issue almost certain to clash head-on with the political, economic, social, and cultural realities of many opium producing countries. 

This is already reported to be the case at the U.N. Commission on Narcotic 

Drugs conference now under way in Geneva, Switzerland, where such U.S. proposals have encountered a buzz saw of opposition from such opium producing lands as India, Turkey, Thailand, and Laos. 

In each of these nations, the opium poppy is a labor-intensive crop. And mechanical extraction means—as envisioned by the United States-would sorely affect the labor force. 

Rep. Morgan Murphy Jr., the Chicago Democrat whose worldwide investigations highlighted the heroin traffic problem and prompted the opium poppy growing ban in Turkey, believes a reasonable synthetic substitute must be developed by American drugmakers. "I don't care how limited we would go into domestic poppy cultivation; the move would be viewed as worldwide evidence of a lack of sincerity on the part of the United States," he said. "We can never ask other nations not to do what we might be proposing to do."

In any event, Handley will soon be relieved as senior adviser to Secretary of State Henry Kissinger on internationl narcotics matters and executive director of a White House cabinet's Committee on Global Narcotics Control, a victim of his dedication to an ideal and the swiftly changing patterns of diplomatic political realities.
