LATIN AMERICAN DEVELOPMENT 

Senator INOUYE. Our first witness is Mr. T. Graydon Upton, president of the Pan American Development Foundation. 

Welcome to the subcommittee, sir.

Mr. UPTON. Mr. Chairman, my name is Graydon Upton, and I 

make this statement as president of the Pan American Development

Foundation, an organization whose chairman is Mr. Galo Plazo, Secretary General of the OAS and among whose trustees are several distinguished Members of the Congress.

My remarks are based on experience gained in Latin American development problems in former years as an Assistant Secretary of the Treasury, as U.S. Director of the IBRD and U.S. negotiator for the establishment of the International Development Association (IDA), as a Director of the old Development Loan Fund, and for some 12 years, as executive vice president of the Inter-American Development Bank.

The Pan American Development Foundation (PADF) is a non profit, U.S. foundation, closely associated with the OAS. Its chief activity is the promotion of national development foundations in Latin America, whose function is to make very small development loans to marginal communities and individuals who have no other access to credit, and to orient such communities and individuals in preparing requests for credits and in properly executing their small development projects.

In appearing before you, I wish to thank the Congress for its persistent role in trying to persuade administrations, both Democratic and Republican, to make greater use of private sector organizations in the delivery of funds in Latin America.

It was the Congress which a number of years ago developed the various aspects of title IX of the Foreign Assistance Acts, specifically directing AID and its predecessors to recognize and respond to the need for participation by private organizations in grassroots development, and participation by the beneficiaries in formulating their own programs.

It was the Congress which at a later date worked for the organization of the Inter-American Foundation (formerly the Inter-American Social Development Institute), which now funds a number of such private sector grassroots activities, where the sponsoring organization is located physically in Latin America. 

And it was the Congress which passed the Moss amendment to the Aid Act of 1969, which provided a trial mechanism for partial guarantees of small loans to marginal individuals and groups by local banns in Latin America, or by other lenders.

Indeed, throughout the annual deliberations of the Congress on foreign aid, during many years, we find two strong undercurrents of thought: A greater use of nongovernmental organizations, and more effective procedures to assure that aid funds reach the little man, and not simply develop infrastructure and add to the well-being of the middle and upper classes.

Both of these themes are central to my observations, and are cer-

tainly familiar to the Congress which passed such recommendations long before the practitioners of aid recognized their importance. 

The development "gap" in Latin America. The development "gap" in Latin America is not just one of inadequate funding or failure of income per capita to reach a designated figure. It is rather a gap in development thinking, and to the extent that such thinking is now changing, it is a gap in the ability to develop mechanisms which will get development aid down to the poorest groups. 

During the past 15 years, development aid in Latin America has been subject to frequently changing emphasis. At an early period there was great weight on infrastructure, then during the early days of the Alliance for Progress this shifted to social projects, low-cost housing, potable water, and agricultural land reform and development. 

Still later the shift was to financing local development banks, and more recently to the restructuring of capital markets, to agricultural development, and to population control. All of these are important, because development is an integrated process, but all of them have had great difficulty in contributing in any significant degree to the improvement of the life of the masses, many of whom are outside the monetary economy. 

"TRICKLE DOWN THEORY" 

In short, the "trickle down theory" of raising the living standards of the poorest 40 percent has been a failure.

The clearest description of this failure, and of the need for new approaches, has been given by Mr. Robert S. McNamara, president of the IBRD. The points which he has repeated in the last 2 years are to be found in these extracts of his address to the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development in April of 1972, and I quote.

A recent study of income distribution patterns in more than 40 developing countries estimated that at the beginning of the First Development Decade the average share in the national income of the richest 20 percent of the people was 

56 percent-but the share of the poorest 60 percent was only 26 percent ** *

Preliminary indications are that this severely distorted income distribution is not only continuing but in many countries may be growing worse. The poor are sharing only to a very limited extent in the benefits of growth. 

What can be done about it? What must be done is to reduce the crushing disparities of opportunity.

The Role of the Pan American Development Foundation and its Associated National Development Foundations in Latin America in "Reducing the Crushing Disparities of Opportunity." The Foundation which developed the first principles on which all other national foundations now operate was the "Penny Foundation" established in Guatemala, in 1964. It was initiated and carried forward for many years by Sam Greene, who many of you know, and who was one of the intellectual authors of the Moss amendment to which I have previously referred.

This foundation collected contributions from the Guatemalan private sector, principally businessmen, and made small development loans to Guatemalan Indian communities which were completely outside the aid and development scope of the country, and largely outside the monetary economy.

The loans were made on normal commercial terms, generally 10 percent, with interest capitalized. The maturity of the loan and the total capitalized amount, was based on the total of the pennies per

week, hence the term "Penny Foundation" which each family could afford to pay, with the village fathers collecting the payments. 

The participants largely carried out the physical aspects of construction, and the village itself selected the project, in which the substitution factor was often a consideration. That is, the substitution of potable water for contaminated water more than paid its way in savings on medicine expenditure, and the substitution of a small diesel generating plant more than paid its way in the savings for lamps, kerosene, and candles.

Other typical projects were a truck to bring produce to market and eliminate costly middle men, a fishing boat with an outboard motor, a ceramic oven, and looms to make available to the tourist market the Indians' inherent artisan skills, a schoolhouse, purchase of land, fertilizer, a small tractor, et cetera, et cetera. 

In the event that there was a deliberate failure of payment, the truck or fishing boat was repossessed, or the diesel generator removed. 

There were, needless to say, very few payment failures. 

Borrowers recognized that this was the only loan capital available to them other than usurious loans at several hundred percent per annum, or more. That Foundation is still very active.

The second Foundation was established in the Dominican Republic in 1966. Shortly after the revolution and the U.S. intervention, Sam 

Greene was sent to the Dominican Republic by the PADF, where he made contact with the forward-looking young businessmen in the Santiago and Santo Domingo areas, who then organized the Dominican Development Foundation, to make small development loans to rural communities.

Partly due to the initiative and leadership of its founders, and partly due to the important funding by AID, which was anxious to contribute to political stability in that then turbulent country, the DDF has enjoyed rapid growth, until at the present time it is one of the most important entities in agricultural development in the Dominican Republic.

It currently has a staff of some 40 people, including specially trained "promotores" who work on developing the actual projects. It currently has hundreds of small loans outstanding and since its inception has loaned in total about $4 million. 

Its staff is professional and its loan administration is fully computerized. This foundation has the support of much of the Dominican business community through whose contributions it has assured its own administrative self sufficiency.

An important innovation which this Foundation was the first to develop was that of working with the local banks, not only in terms of their contributions, but in persuading them to make small development loans directly to communities, once the latter had proved their credit worthiness by promptly repaying prior Foundation loans.

Now many of the Foundation's original clients are borrowing directly from local banks, which have revised their concepts of the creditworthiness of these marginal groups. 

Time will not permit me to tell you of the stories of other foundations, and of how they have adapted the original concepts to their own local needs by moving into low-cost housing, in guaranteeing bank loans, in training loan agents ("promotores"), and through other innovations.

Suffice it to say that there are now some 12 such independent but associated foundations in Latin America and the Caribbean which have extended small development loans in an amount of $10 million and there are others in formation, but which have not made headway because of lack of funding.

Well organized, operating foundations exist in Mexico, Guatemala, Nicaragua, Honduras, El Salvador, Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, and in the Caribbean in the Dominican Republic and Trinidad and Tobago. Foundations are being helped to organize in Bolivia, Jamaica, Costa Rica, and in Chile.

In addition, the national development foundations have now formed their own association for dissemination of information, for technical assistance, and for aid in funding, et cetera. It is called El Consejo de 

Fundaciones Nacionales Solidarios. Its present seat is in the Dominican Republic, and its President is Mr. Alejandra Grullon, one of the founders of the Dominican Development Foundation, and the president of a large Dominican Development Foundation, and the president of a large Dominican bank. 

PRINCIPLES OF THE NATIONAL DEVELOPMENT FOUNDATIONS 

At this point permit me to summarize the basic principles under which these foundations operate. 

1. They are essentially private sector organizations, although in some cases Latin American governments have been so impressed by their work that they have guaranteed loans to them, or made contributions. 

2. They work exclusively on a loan or loan guarantee basis, at commercial terms of interest, and make no grants. This is important not only because the funds revolve for new loans and are not dissipated, but it also permits the borrower to enter into a transaction with the full sense of dignity which comes from participating in a business transaction, and not being an object of charity. 

3. They establish contact between their borrowers and local banks once they have established their credit standing in order that subsequent loans may be made by the latter, thus integrating the borrowers into the normal credit life of the community. On occasion they guarantee such loans wholly or in part. 

4. They loan only to groups and/or individuals who have no access whatsoever to credit other than through local money lenders. In a sense, the foundation movement is a specialized credit movement, at the very bottom of the credit scale, as at a higher level of the economic scale are savings and loan organizations, credit cooperatives, and workers banks. 

5. They are funded from abroad on a matching basis: $1 of local contributions is matched with $1 of loans or grants, although occasionally exceptions are made. It is sad to note, that in a time when so much aid is available to governments on a very long payout basis, the PADF is unable to direct or obtain modest amounts of matching funds to assist the foundations in formation. 

6. The foundations are completely independent and decide what field they will work in, in the accord with the above principles. Most of them work with rural community loans, but some work in low-cost

housing-where the Salvadorean Foundation has had such a notable success that it may be the executor of a World Bank loan-and some work in loans to very small businessmen and artisans, or to market women, as in Guayaquil and Managua. 

7. They have very close relationships with the borrowers, give technical assistance, loan orientation, and most if not all physical loan projects involve a substantial degree of participation and self-help. 

The borrowers play a major role in developing their own projects. 

Funding of the PADF and the National Development Foundations. 

The PADF operates with a staff of some seven individuals and has a budget of about $200 million a year. It receives about 30 percent of its funding from the OAS and the balance from corporate and individual contributions, with some U.S. foundation support, and some earnings on the interest differential between funds received as grants or loans from AID some years ago, and loans made to NDF's.

Currently the PADF is having difficulty with its funding due to a reduction in private contributions. There is also, unfortunately, a tendency for a number of funding sources to wish to work exclusively with innovating, experimental programs, and not to give funding for an operation already successful on a small scale, thus denying it the opportunity to expand. 

The National Development Foundations are funded locally with contributions from the business sector and efforts are then made to obtain matching funds from abroad. Some AID funds have been channeled to them through the PADF, the last of these in 1972, and AID missions do some modest grant funding locally. 

Recently, the Inter-American Foundation has been an important source of funding, having given to the various NDF's some $3.5 million since its own formation. In addition, NDF's receive funds from other sources, such as European and Canadian foundations, and religious groups.

Without exception, all the National Development Foundations are underfinanced. Although the movement has proved its viability and its freedom from dominance by any individual or groups of individuals, the sums currently available to it represent a very small base for expansion. When we think of the development potential which the movement has among poor people, and compare its total financing with the amount allocated for a single loan for a highway or a steel mill or a hydroelectric plant-the type of loan to which the lending institutions are still very partial-it is clear that the long-expressed ideas of the Congress for stimulating grassroots development are still at the bottom of the priority list for U.S. developmental assistance. 

What conclusions can we draw with respect to the significance in the development process of the National Development Foundation movement? I believe that there are three very simple but essential points:

First, the most crushing disparity of opportunity in a capitalistic world is the lack of access to credit on reasonable terms for the marginal groups in the developing countries. The marginals are human beings of dignity, of capacity, of ambition, and frequently of considerable ability in terms of their own circumstances. But without access to credit they must remain objects of uncertain and very limited government assistance through services which all too frequently do not reach down, and out to them.

5 The second conclusion is that in the National Development Foundation movement, there do exist proven, viable, and effective ways to reduce this crushing disparity of opportunity-the lack of credit for the very poor man at the community level. 

The third lesson is a sad and somewhat bitter one. That is, despite all the efforts of the Congress to persuade various governmental organizations throughout the years, to encourage private sector operations such as this, which truly transforms U.S. foreign aid into economic opportunity for poor people, we find a lack of interest on the part of many development organizations, or else a bureaucratic maze of regulations which we cannot overcome.

Despite several favorable studies and reviews in depth of the National Development Foundation movement, one by AID itself, it has proven impossible during the past 3 years to obtain from U.S. public sources more than a very modest amount of funding. 

If the Congress were to find ways of allocating through one or more of the appropriations which find their way to Latin America as little as $5 million a year for the NDF's through the Pan American Development Foundation, for the purposes outlined in these remarks, it would give a tremendous stimulus to this movement. 

By thus setting up attainable incentives for matching local, private sector contributions, it would enable the movement to break through to greater international recognition, financial participation, and developmental effectiveness.

Indeed, a senior economist of the World Bank once said that the simplest and most effective way of narrowing the income gap in the less developed countries would be to base the selection of development projects not on the size of the benefits, but on the part of the total return that accrues to the beneficiaries below a certain income level. 

If that criterion were to be adopted, within months the national development foundations would be transformed into major development factors.

PAN AMERICAN DEVELOPMENT FOUNDATION 

Mr. KENNEDY. Mr. President, during the annual meeting of the Pan American Development Foundation, I think it appropriate to call to the attention of riy colleagues the work of this unique organization.

As a member of the board of trustees, along with Senator JAVITS, T have watched with some admiration the nccomplishments of this independent and nonprofit agency which is sponsored by the Organization of American States and whose chairman is Galo Plaza. For over. n decade, PADF lins attempted to provide a mechanism to provide low-interest ioans to finance community self-help projects in various countries in Latin America.

Beyond the value of the particular project which is determined by the community rather than by any remote governmental agency, the lonas guaranteed by the local national development foundations force traditional credit Institutions to reach out to the poorest communities which are on the periphery of the economic and socia! structure of most: developing nations.

The national development foundations formed in each nation have become not only a source of technical assistance to these communities but serve as a vital condult to enable local communities to take a small step toward ultimately becoming integrated into the ongoing econote, social, and political life of the country.

In a recent article in Vislon magazine by Winthrop Carty, the work of the 

Nicaraguan Development Foundation following the devastating earthquake a year ago is shown in sharp contrast to the concerns of traditional sources of credit. The banks' concerns were with corporations and those with established credit ratiors. The foundation's concern was with the "tle man at the boltoin of the entrepreneurial heap."

'PAN AMERICAN DEVELOPMENT FOUNDATION 

(The following is the English version of a story on the Managuan recovery program. 

The story, written by Winthrop P. Curly, appeared in Vision Magazine.) 

What are the consequences to a nation's economy the capital's commercial center virtually disappears? Manga sadly found out last December 25. A series of giant fren ors tumbled the downtown men and the en suring fires and looting ravaged the region, Perhaps 8,000 people died in the holochtest. 

Today, roughly 500 city blocks have been scaled off by barbed wire Gutted bulldings have been dyunnilted and much of the pubble has been pushed tato Luko Manalo ko Only a few high-rise ulice buldrops fee main--two unsafe for occupancy to bro..k the picture of utter desolation. 

The layout of the city, stular to many world capitals, dictated the economie results of the duster. Large conunercial enterprises, small business, and goverumental agencies were januned into the bustling center. Woven nto the downtown area and the immediately surrounding area was the housing of the white-collar workers enployed in the com. mercial institutions, government othees, and shops. The outer ring of Manngus was come posed of factories and the housing of blugcoter workers.

Roughly 65% of the commercial area ww. wiped out. The surviving clerks, accountants, secretaries, small shop-keepers and other center city workers were left jobless. Their housing, located in the epicenter and made mostly of adobe, fell, and Managua's predominantly lower middle class residents Bed to outlying areas. But in sharp contrast of fortune, only 10% of the city's outer ring of factories and Industrial worker's housing was seriously damaged.

Of all the major categories of financial Interests, the biggest question mark is attached to the fate of urban landowners. The value of highpriced property in downtown Managua tuinbled in the wake of the earthquake. Landowners possess title to formerly prized land which now brings no rent and lles forsaken behind barbedwire. The hope of revived real estate values turns mainly on exactly how tLe government rebuilds the city. 

At the very least, realtors expect some return by selling their property to the governinent for an integrated reconstruction effort. On the other end of the scesaw, property-owners en the outer circles of the city held strategically located land and stand to make windfall profits.

Manufacturers suffered the least. No mora then 10% of Managuan iactories, strung along the outskirts, hod production seriously interrupted. The Managuan Pepel Cola plaat is cited as an admirable example of the manufacturing sectors's resullency. The management quickly removed the rubble of the collapsed roof, found the machinery basically intact, and placed a jerrybullt canvass cover over the plant. Pull production was reached within a month. Meanwhile, permanent steel roofing was constructed before. the rainy reason set in: "From ashes to production in 28 days," exciairas a sign outside the factory. Industrial capacity is now reaching 100%. and some manufacturers have expanded into new lines during the renovation period.

The larger commercial and retall enter prises survived the disaster with unexpected case. The large firms bad branches in nearby 

Masaya, Grenada, and Leon, Nicaragua's other population centers. The branches became the headquarters while the companies scrambled for a new roof in Managua. A human wave followed the same pattern. Pcsbly half of Managua's population of 400,000 Aed the city and often found lodging with relatives in the secondary cities. The uprost. ed brought manpower and clients to the Arms' temporary headquarters. 

The Managuan headquarters of the Nic aragusa Branch of the Bark of America, the world's largest private bank, was the kind of business well able to jump back into operation. The original downtown headquarters was built of re-inforced concrete but fire weakened the structure beyond repair. 

Armando Ortega, the Nicaraguan-born manager took a route familiar to many business leaders. The government assigned a day when police would escort the transfer of assets from the wrecked headquarters to a new location. The Banco Nicaraguense lent the Bank of America a window at Its Masaya branch. At first some depositors raced to withdraw their savings but the bank paid cheerfully and confidence was quickly rectored. Subsequently, Ortega rented a house in Masaya to enlarge the operation. Finally, a colorlal-style house. only one-third constructed in Managua, was purchased and converted into the permanent headquarters. "A high percentage of the destroyed enterprises have a credit relationship with the banking community," notes Ortega, "and we, like other banks, are serving our clients." 

The banks are experiencing high liquidity. 

Clients with cash on hand and policy-holders of earthquake insurance have reserves they don't wish to invest until they have a clear picture of the government's plans to reconstruct Managua.

The large Insurance companies survived 

Jasncial pay-outs and business dislocation.

Leonel Argüello, the executive director of the Companta Nucional do Eeguros, the largest Nicaraguan usurance company, points cut the substantial companies have a hedge against being swamped by a disaster like the 

Mannguan earthquake. The companies Lelong to an international system of catastrophic insurance that provides back-up foreign reserves in case of an overwhelming national calunity.

Argüello's first task was to save the company records. After the six-story main once vas dangerously cracked by the quake, employees, numbering 70. formed a human chain to pass out the irreplaceable records and load them on trucks. Private houses were rented in residencial suburbs, and the company began the job of processing the fallout of claims. The superintendent of banks has announced that $56 million in claims were honored in the Arst half of 1973, and Industry sources estimate as much as $75 million may be paid out by year's end. 

Argüello notes that foreign companies fended to have more earthquake insurance 'ban local firms. "After the 1931 earthquake." be observes, "people thought lightening doesn't strike twice; furthermore, a local claims movement puts the Nicaraguan insurance in a public-relations bind. The earthquake triggered fires and looting. Policyholders with are and theft Lasurance are pressing claims. But the international consortium as well as local companies, under the terms of their contracts, only pay for coverage of the prime cause of the disaster, the earthquake.

The survival of shop-keepers, restaurateurs, commercial district suppliors and the like turns on access to credit. Some shops in the center represented the owner's place of business, warehouse and residence. In a few tumultuous hours, a man could lose his established location, inventory, home, helpers, and. If a property-owner, the value of his land. A scant 10% of an estimated 900 small 

Managuan enterprises were located on the spared outskirts of town, and only 12% of all small businesses had any form of insurance. 

The established entrepreneurs were able, despite financial loss and dislocation, to resume business. An industrial fairground was redesigned to accommodate 200 shops pre- Tious'y situated in the center. The rents are relatively low and the government is providing some recovery financing, but many relocated entrepreneurs suffer doubts. "Bus!ness is slow here." wearily said a druggist, "but we are waiting for the city to begin bus service to this shopping area. We have another small pharmacy on the other side of cown-Just in case."

With the final design of the reconstructed capital not yet settled, many entrepreneurs are hedging their beta. Italian-born Annunziato Esposito, who ran the popular El Coloseo restaurant in the oid center, has converted a house on the main road to Masaya, but he too has purchased a spot in a different section of town in case the city grows away from his present site. Come what may, Esposito is confident: "I'll make it-I work hard, know my business, and have faithful customers." 

Familiar Managuan commercial names are popping up in suburban houses. Casa Commercial Gertsch Molina is typical of the estabisted enterprise which has survived the earthquake. arid can look to the future with reasonable confidence. Federico Gertsch, a

Swiss-born engineer, ran a machinery import business next door to his wife's successful Jewelry shop. Relojeria Omega. Married three months before the 1931 earth-' quake, they maintained earthquake insurance for 25 years, but let the policy lapse two 

Jears ago. The elderly couple owned six houses, three of which were in the devastated center. With funds saved over the years, they are back in business in one of the three undamaged houses.

The lasting economic victims of the Ma- Arguan earthquake are the small entrepreneurs without access to credit, and whitecollar workers who lost their homes. Housing to the old commercial center, it should be remembered, represented proximity to 

Jabs. In common with most Latin American hations, the Nicaraguan economy isn't geared to extend credit to small entrepreneurs, or constructing appropriate housing for whitecollar workers. Both government and private banking lack & sma-loan delivery system for the little mau at the bottom of the entrepreneurial heop Usurers provide the firancis for the marginal members of the cash economy.

With varying success, private foundatious 

Latin America have tackled the problem of making proper credit available to "mar ginated" persons. The Nicaragusu Develop ment Foundation (FUNDE) is one of the beat run private-sector, non-proft foundations in the Americas. "We cannot pretend to solve the nation's problems," explains William

Beez Sacasa, FUNDE's executive secretary, 

"but we can experiment and seek new approaches to old problems." 

FUNDE has been virtually alone, for instance, in helping the vivanderas (market women), the lowest-level entrepreneurs but, by definition, classic symbols of the freemarket economy. Before the earthquake. 

Managua's three main markets-Boer, Santo 

Domingo, and Oriental-represented 2,500 selling locations in such basic wares as bread, candy, simple jewelry, shoes, furniture, and clothes.

The economics of the ancient markets are complex. A woman operating a retail stand, needs between 815 and $150 daily to do business. Dally working capital for a woman with a basket runs from $5 to 87. Most women with medium or large stands receive loans from usurers for repayment over a one or two-month period. The daily interest rate averages 25% of the loan.

Some of the more enterprising woinen had built up a relatively substantial business. 

Cigar-maker Lila Garcia, for example, rented a house fronting one of the markets for $115 monthly, and employed four women to roll tobacco. Her most popular pack was 50 small cigars for 50 cents, and, on an averago day. she would sell as many as 5,000. Her cigars were sold in the front of the house, while they were fashioned and the tobacco stored in the back rooms.

Lua started her business in Managua at a conspicuous corner of a main market, and rolled her cigars in public as a way of advertising her product. She considered herself "established" after six months of maintaining her corner station and building up a regular clientele. 

During the earthquake, her cigar business literally went up in smoke. The house, serv. ing as her retail outlet, storage facility and home, and her modest inventory of tobacco, were completely lost. She raced to the countryside. But 15 days later she was back in

Managua rolling tobacco. FUNDE loaned her money sufficient to regain her position in the market place. "Littlo by little I shall build back my former production," the rugged vivandera claims. Aware that a lack of a trademark and transportation limit her operation to her door front, she adds, "I hope some day to own a well marked truck to deliver well packaged cigars" to put the business on a higher commercial level. "She unquestionably will receive the money she needs from 

FUNDE," says Bacz Sacasa, "once she raises her daily production." 

Even an enterprising woman like Lila

Garcia is intimidated by the formal lending system. At first FUNDE attempted to draw the vivanderas into forming cooperatives and collectively applying for bank loans. The women, however, rejected the prospect of entering the marble halls of a bank for a loan, end clung to their tradition of borrowing from usurers who keep their accounts in a booklet. As a Arst step toward overcoming the vivanderas' cultural resistance to formal banking procedures, FUNDE designed a booklet similar to that of the usurers. The group then accepted the foundation's loan and their weekly repayments are recorded in the familiar booklets which the women are given to hold. The vivanderas also have been encouraged to form cooperatives-to buy in buk, build adequate storage facilities, etc.and their repayment record is excellent. The fact they traditionally Anance their businesses with money borrowed at usurious rates indicates the inherent strength of their operations.

In the first half of 1973, FUNDE had completed 186 projects, including 48 small businesses, eight inall businessineu's coopera tives, 27 other cooperatives, and extended technica: assistance to 44 sma!! enterprises.

But the work among the market women best illustrates FUNDE's ability to reach the thousands of little people who are generally bypassed by disaster relief.

Housing for white-collar workers is another aren hardly touched by the government. With great fanfare, Ger. Anastasio Somoza and 

Ambassador Turner Shelton earlier this year opened a US.-ananced housing project called "Las Americas". The project, originally designed for 11,000 shelters, is a manifest fallure. The housing project is only partially occupied and blacks basic facilities. Popularly called "the concentration camp", Las Americas was erected in the worker's district, where damage was relatively Ught. Inconveniently located and crudely serviced, the drab units are of no use to needy white-collar workers.

FUNDE constructed a cheaper, portable house. The pre-fabricated units were designed with the help of the Pan American Development Foundation, the OAS-associated stimulous for the Latin American national development foundations. The pre-fabs can be placed on land people already own, in a relative's backyard, or near existing public faculties. White-collar workers, who were 

Boattered badly, and the mobile houses more practical than the government's poorly serv iced, fixed units. 

The Managuan experience spotlights many of the problems surrounding disaster relief. 

Poreign governments and agencies can send medicine, food, clothing and other items of immediate help, but aid for long-range economic recovery is another matter. Foreign disaster relief often raises unfulfilled hopes among the recipients and disillusionment among donors. Among the many extraneous supplies reportedly sent stricken Managua and were Spanish wine frozen German chickens. In the chaos following a major earthquake or flood, there is no sound way of accounting for relief items. The Somoza dynasty naturally engenders doubts about the disposition of foreign assistance. Many observers quietly bellere President Luis 

Echeverria was prudent in politely turning down offers of International ald after 

Mexico's recent earthquake. Mexico has the resources to help its own people, and can avoid the misunderstandings which all too often attend foreign relief programs. 

Most Latin American nations, unfortunately, simply lack the grassroots agencies to assist the little man beyond charity. Tho

Peruvian government is still attempting to reconstruct Huarez, tho picturesque town demolished three years ago in an earthquake. "Over the fundations that romain we will not reconstruct misery," the recovery program's slogan proclaims. But the process of making Huarez into a model town and redistributing local wealth has been painfully slow. "People's values change after an earthquake," notes Baez Sacasa. "Property doesn't seem so important-people discover that possessions can crumble in 30 seconds, and one is lucky just to be alive. But Managuans soon found that it was important to get back to work-it gave them a chance to for get the past and regain a sense of purpose about the future."

BUREAUCRATIC REGULATIONS 

Senator INOUYE. Thank you very much, Mr. Upton.

If I may refer to your last page, you speak of the bureaucratic maze of regulations which we cannot overcome. 

Can you provide us a bit more of the specifics describing what you mean by bureaucratic regulations? We would like to give you some assistance.

Mr. UPTON. I think you get into this in various fields. The international lending agencies find themselves in the position of generally just making loans where there are adequate guarantees, and frequently these are guarantees which have to be given by the various governments. We worked for some time in trying to get a loan from the Inter- 

American Development Bank which had previously given some technical assistance. We found that we could not overcome this question of the guarantees.

We have found with AID that although they did support us at one time and although instructions have gone out to the field in support of these programs, that at least under the last administration, we have not yet had too much contact with the current one, it has been cult to get anything to come out of it. very diffi I would say that the major support of the foundations, and this has been very constructive, has been the Inter-American Foundation. 

About 60 percent of the grants which it has given since its organization have been directed to these foundations. 

The amounts are quite small, but they are effective. The reason they are directed to these foundations is because that institution has found that these were one of the best developed groups in the sense of having a good organization, good administration, good executives, and therefore can carry out a program. 

Another problem we have run into is the fact that this is an effective ongoing program, and a number of institutions, this is particularly true with the private foundations but it has been also true of AID, have said that they want to work with more innovative programs, experimental programs.

I cannot agree with this because it seems to me the objective of an experimental program is to create something that will work on an expanded scale, and this can work and it has been shown, but one of our foundations was declined when the request came in from one of the Embassies for a fund for it on the basis that the program has been in existence for several years and was no longer innovative or experimental. 

Senator INOUYE. You speak of $5 million a year assistance from AID would provide you with tremendous stimulus. What would you use this $5 million for?

Mr. UPTON. We would use it, I would say, in two different forms. 

The first thing we would do with it is to get four or five foundations which we have been working to develop to give them matching funds or even more than matching funds, to get started. 

Our experience, Senator, is that when a foundation is just getting off the ground, it has tremendous difficulties. We have been unable to get funds for new foundations.

Both AID and the Inter-American Foundation have taken the philosophical attitude that they prefer to work with the foundations with a good track record, where the organization has been established, is in being and moving forward. 

So the first thing we would do would be to allocate certain amounts of this to get these new foundations moving. The next thing we would do is make either grants or low-cost loans to assist foundations in order to get them to expand their activities. 

Senator INOUYE. What is your experience on default or nonpayment of loans?

Mr. UPTON. It is extraordinarily good. The overall record is around 

95 percent. The reason for this, I think, is that these people have absolutely no other access to credit. 

They know that if they default, they are all through. One of our foundations, the one in the Dominican Republic, gives their borrowers a certificate after the first and second and third loan has been repaid, showing that their credit standing is good. With that they take them to the banks; they say, this man or this group has repaid one loan or two loans, we think you can now safely make this loan, yourself. 

There are problems sometimes, particularly if you get a bad crop year, since most of these are rural, and some of these loans have to be carried over, but on the whole it is an outstanding record of repayment.

Senator INOUYE. Can you be a bit more specific on the statement attributed to a senior economist of the World Bank, to wit, that the simplest and most effective way of narrowing the income bank in the less developed countries would be to base the selection of development projects not on the size of the benefits but on the part of the total return that accrues to the beneficiaries below a certain income level? 

Mr. UPTON. Mr. McNamara has been very much concerned with the failure of programs to get down to the lowest classes. 

During the last several years, he has made this one of his major objectives to try to develop World Bank programs, particularly in the agricultural field which will overcome this problem. 

This statement was in a story in Business Week several months ago discussing the present occupation of Mr. McNamara with the inability to get down, and they interviewed one of the economists, I believe it was Mr. Adler, and he made this comment, which was a rather unusual one, because actually most projects go on what is called the cost-benefit ratio where you compare the financial money put in with returns in economic terms, whereas this concept was to transfer it to the human benefit which is not measurable under normal economic processes. 

Senator INOUYE. Once again, I thank you very much, Mr. Upton. I appreciate your appearance and your assistance this morning. 

Mr. UPTON.  It is a pleasure to be here.

Pan American Development Foundation 

1725 K Street, Northwest Suite 1409 Washington, D. C. 20006 .

June 10, 1974 

Dear Senator Inouye: 

This letter is in answer to your request for additional information on the following two points in my testimony of May 24, before the Senate Sub Committee on Appropriations, on the Pan American 

Development Foundation. 

1) "We find a lack of interest on the part of many development organizations or else a bureaucratic maze of regulations which we cannot overcome.' 11 

The PADF and/or the National Development Foundations have had moderate financial support over some years in the form of loans, grants, technical assistance, or contracts from OPIC, the OAS, AID, IDB, and the IAF (Inter-American Foundation), and we are currently having talks with the World Bank, for all of which we are most appreciative. Funding continues to be made in moderate and helpful amounts from time to time to the National Development Foundations directly, particularly by the Inter-American Foundation. The PADF itself has received no public funding in recent years except some significant budget support from the OAS, and is hard pressed to continue its operations.

The basic problem here is to convince the various agencies, international and national, that this movement has great promise, and should be given a real priority in funding considerations. That such conviction does not exist is shown by the fact that funding of the PADF, and through it of the National Development Foundations, has been declined on various occasions because it is located in Washington and not Latin America, because it does not have adequate credit standing and cannot obtain adequate guarantees, that it is not policy to do so, etc. Funding directly of National Development Foundations has also been at times declined because' they have sufficient funds, because no funds are available for new Foundations but only for Foundations with an established reputation and good record, because an established foundation is not engaged in new and innovative programs, because they can only be funded on the basis of government guaran-

1 tees (which they can generally not obtain as they are small private sector operations) that technical assistance requests do not conform to existing policies, etc? In one case funding of two Foundations was promised two years ago but still has not become effective because of technical reasons. The reasons for declining funding are not of importance they simply add up to the fact that except for the Inter-American Foundation, whose availabilities are limited, other institutions and agencies pretty much have the Foundation movement near the bottom of the list in recent years. 

The second statement concerning which you requested elaboration was as follows: "A senior economist of the World Bank once said that the simplest and most effective way of narrowing the income gap in the less developed countries would be to base the selection of the development projects not on the size of the benefits, but on the part of the total return that accrues to the beneficiaries below a certain income level." 

This statement as reported in Business Week magazine of May 6, was made by Mr. John Adler, who is also author of a paper entitled "Development and Income

Distribution" which shows convincingly that those countries (none of which are in Latin America) which have adapted effective policies to make credit (and other inputs) available to small farmers have not only increased agricultural production, but have succesfully redistributed income. This paper gives strong economic backing to the policies of the Congress as expressed in the AID act of 1973, and also to the National Development Foundation Movement. Mr. Adler has been kind enough to give further elaboration on his statement, which is attached.

Your interest, Senator Inouye, in this important foundation rural credit movement is appreciated, and I hope it will lead in due course to still further strengthening it. Respectfully, Miptin 

T. Graydon Upton President

May 31, 1974 

Mr. T. Graydon Upton 1776 K Street, N. W. Suite 600 

Washington, D. C. 20006

Dear Graydie: 

Thank you for your letter of May 29. What I meant by my suggestion (in the attached article on Development and Income Distribution) to select "development projects not on the basis of the size of the total net social return (or total net benefits), but on that part of total returns that accrues to beneficiaries below a certain income level" is illustrated-I think rather clearly-in the remainder of the same paragraph (p.341) and in the paragraph that follows the quotation.

If I were to generalize I would say that what is required is to determine that part of the increase in the net national product which accrues to the income groups below a predetermined dividing line. There is nothing unusual about aiming at a measurement of the net increase in GNP in cost/benefit analysis-that is what the modification introduced through shadow pricing is all about. What is novel is that I suggest that one should forget about those benefits which accrue to people over and above a certain income level. In many instances that will mean not counting profits of industrial entrepreneurs when it comes to the evaluation and selection of projects. Perhaps I should add that I certainly would not object if profits and benefits in other forms accrue to entrepreneurs. I only do not want to count them in the evaluation and selection of projects. I shall be delighted to expand on my explanation to you or to anybody else who is interested in my approach. 

With kindest personal regards and best wishes, Sincerely yours,

Jol 

John. Adler frector

GEORGETOWN UNIVERSITY INTERNATIONAL POPULATION PROGRAM STATEMENT OF FATHER T. BYRON COLLINS, SPECIAL ASSISTANT FOR FEDERAL RELATIONS, GEORGETOWN UNIVERSITY INTERNATIONAL POPULATION PROGRAM 

Senator INOUYE. Our next witness is Father T. Byron Collins, special assistant for Federal relations, Georgetown University. 

Father Collins, welcome. 

Father COLLINS. Thank you.

It is a pleasure to appear before you again. 

I am Father T. Byron Collins of the Society of Jesus. I am at 

Georgetown University.

Dr. Conrad Taeuber was unable to be with us this morning. He is at the United Nations. In his place, Father Harold Bradley, director of international programs at Georgetown is with me.

This is a brief report on the program concerning universities in the field of international populations. 

As you will remember, this committee has indicated interest in and support of an international population program through a consortium of universities to be embarked on with certain foreign countries. 

Foremost among these countries is Latin America. The program would work through a consortium of universities in the various countries. I refer you to the attached report of December 13, 1973.

Our efforts to get universities in Brazil to work on this program were successful. The Brazilian universities had obtained a letter of approval dated March 14, 1973, from the Brazilian Minister of Education.

Our review of these documents and the proposal of the consortium of universities with AID representatives met with difficulties. I attach copies of correspondence with AID representatives over a period of some 9 months to illustrate this. At the present time, it does not seem feasible to pursue the hope of working with AID. 

However, we are pleased to inform this committee that the United Nations, through its United Nations Fund for Population Activities, immediately saw the value of our approach and immediately approved a small planning grant to start the Brazilian program as the first phase of an international university program wherein a group of universities in a Latin American country would establish a center in their country and would work with population centers in other countries. 

For this reason we support the full funding, as a line item, of the President's request for a United Nations population program as an indication of the continued interest of this committee in the university 

Latin American program.

Last year, we are informed, the United Nations did not receive the full amount programed to the United Nations Fund for Population 

Activities as presented to Congress.

The universities in other countries are much more willing to work with the United Nations agencies than with AID. This is particularly true of the universities in Latin America, who are able to persuade their own governments to accept the United Nations approach. On the other hand, the AID approach and program constantly presented a stumbling block to cooperation.

For your information, we attach a document which shows the allocation of AID population funds by countries and the population of those countries. It is interesting to note that no AID direct funds are allocated for programs in Brazil or Mexico, two countries which would be willing to cooperate in the university program. 

As I understand it, there is an informal arrangement that AID funds are given to the United Nations program for population activities. [STAFF NOTE.-Supplemental information retained in committee files.]

ALLOCATION OF AID POPULATION FUNDS 

Senator INOUYE..Many of us in the committee, Father, have been trying to wrestle with this problem. Obviously, none of us is an expert on population control. 

After reading much, we have reached some tentative conclusions that to solve this problem we cannot wholly rely on some of the programs that have been heretofore suggested. An example of these would be the issuance of contraceptives and other devices, and in the case of India, providing a transistor radio in return for a vasectomy. 

I think this is a shameful practice.

Our readings would lead us to conclude that in many of these less developed countries, since none of these people have old-age insurance, they are looking for some old-age insurance, and that would be some son or daughter to take care of them when they reach a certain stage in their lives.

If we can convince them that by certain means we can lower the mortality rate in children, increase the possibility of their children reaching adulthood, then we might be ready to provide education for family control.

But to do so at this stage before we can assure them of improving upon the infant mortality or improving upon providing longevity for the adults, we somehow feel that we are just wasting money. 

Is that a proper conclusion, sir?

Father COLLINS. Senator, I would distinguish it, if I may. I think that a judgment made by, I will speak specifically on behalf of the universities in this country, on the attitude toward population, that we would be remiss if we made a judgment on countries with which we have associations.

Our program asks the universities in those countries to address themselves to the precise point that you have made, that to use physical, clinical means as the instrument of our AID in a country that in many ways has been forced upon them by giving them money, I don't think is a good governmental or human way to approach the problem.

This statement is presented on behalf of the following voluntary agencies directly concerned with migration and refugee assistance in all areas of the world. Representative of major religious faiths, nationality groups, or nonsectarian, these agencies and their local community constituencies have as their primary concern, escapees, expellees, displaced persons and other refugees who seek asylum and resettlement in the United States. Through a broad network of cooperating organizations they provide resettlement and related services such as counseling, moral and spiritual guidance, vocational and linguistic training, and job placement. They also care for the aged, sick and handicapped and assist their adjustment in the resettlement process.

Mr. Chairman, it is our understanding that the Special Assistant to the 

Secretary of State for Refugee and Migration Affairs has as his mandate the following responsibilities: a. To formulate comprehensive policy and enunciate goals for all 

U.S. Government refugee efforts. b. C. d. e. f. 8.

To initiate and exercise supervision of fiscal policies, within the legal framework of budget practices and authority, for all refugee programs of the Executive Branch: to consult, advise and support budget requirements for all departments and agencies in the context of a total refugee program of the United States. 

To coordinate all refugee programs, efforts, and relationships within the U.S. Government and to conduct liaison with intergovernmental bodies and public groups: in this connection, he shall have the personal rank of Ambassador to facilitate the accomplishment of his duties.

To develop long-range contingency plans for anticipated refugee problems and problem areas. 

To continuously evaluate ongoing programs making modifications as appropriate and recommending policy changes as new conditions and needs arise.

To insure appropriate consideration of refugee affairs in major foreign policy decisions. 

To establish a focal point for information and action for all refugee affairs as they relate to the Congress, voluntary agencies, and the public.

It is our strong recommendation that this mandate be financed adequately so that the Office of the Special Assistant can in fact respond to worldwide refugee concerns in a meaningful, creative and responsible manner in keeping with the tradition of our government and the American people. This should include increasing attention to the special problems in Latin America, Africa, Asia and the Middle East, as well as to the new refugees in Europe. As recent experience has demonstrated, it cannot be predicted when new refugee crises will emerge nor from what areas.

In reviewing the proposed budget of $9,470,000 the agencies recognize that this is a minimal budget meant to apply to specified limited areas of the total refugee problem. However, we submit that the scope of the problem is far broader than would be provided for by the sums itemized in the ORM request, which in aggregate falls considerably short of what should constitute sufficient financing for the mandate. We earnestly suggest that in order to provide adequate assistance worldwide to refugees additional appropriations are essential.

This recommendation on the part of American voluntary agencies springs from a conviction of several years standing. In 1971 the American Council of Voluntary 

Agencies for Foreign Service, in its testimony on behalf of the Foreign Assistance Act, strongly endorsed the strengthening of the Office of the Special Assistant to the Secretary of State for Refugee and Migration Affairs: 

"United States Government concern for refugees and migration affairs is presently centered in the Office of the Special Assistant to the 

Secretary of State for Refugee and Migration Affairs. In order to fulfill its role in formulating policies and implementing programs in coordination with overall policy goals, this office should have

statutory authority to deal with the wide range of activities inherent in such responsibilities. Its mandate should not only be reaffirmed, but also enhanced so that the scope of the Office of Special Assistant includes refugee and migration activities now carried on by various other departments, bureaus and agencies in Government. "Special Recommendations "a. We support the proposal of the President to create an Office of Assistant Secretary of State for Humanitarian Affairs which should be sufficiently broad so as to make it the focal point of government-wide refugee and migration concerns. "b.

The traditional policy of the United States with regard to worldwide asylum for refugees and escapees should be reaffirmed and appropriately implemented. "c. Provision should be made for flexible authority in the basic immigration statute for admission of refugees in reasonable numbers and for authority to meet emergency arising from the rapidly changing world scene."

On several occasions the American Council has reiterated this position. 

In our testimony before your Committee last year we supported the proposal to create an Office of Assistant Secretary of State for Humanitarian Affairs sufficiently broad in responsibility to enable it to serve as the focal point of government-wide refugee and migration concerns. 

Today we again urge that careful consideration be given to this recommendation. We continue to be of the conviction that the United States concern for 15 million refugees around the world should be consolidated at the highest possible level so that the humanitarian concern of the American people can be consistently interpreted and administered through one office. 

It is apparent that needs of refugees outlined in the ORM material cannot be met by this minimum budget, and it is essential that there be an immediate increase in budget so that ORM would have available a minimum of $18 million to maintain the apparatus for assisting refugees. In taking this position we are not recommending that any other humanitarian programs be reduced, but rather that more adequate funding be available for refugees throughout the world. In particular we are concerned that at least token resettlement grants for all refugees coming to the United States be allocated on a non-discriminatory basis, and that the ORM budget should anticipate such needs for the year to come. 

Mr. Chairman, the Committee on Migration and Refugee Affairs appreciates this opportunity to present its earnest recommendation that in your consideration of appropriations for the Office of Migration and Refugee Affairs adequate funds be provided for assisting refugees wherever they may be.

MIGRATION AND REFUGEE AFFAIRS 

Mr. STERNBERG. It expresses the consensus of the organizations banded together in the committee, for which I speak here today. It is 

22 organizations religious, national, nonsectarian. 

They do, I believe, encompass a substantial segment of the population of the United States. 

With your permission, Mr. Chairman, I will not read our statement since it is part of the record. I would rather prefer to explain in some detail, briefly nevertheless, why we believe that the proposed budget for revenue assistance of the Office of Migration Affairs is a minimum budget, that it will be fully justified to double the figures from the roughly $9.5 million proposed now before your committee to up to $18 million to take care of needs which we consider pressing needs of the refugee population of the world today. 

This is a time of refugees. We know that refugee emergencies break out every year. We cannot predict which one will be the next one, but we do know that every year brings a new refugee situation. 

There are many ways of adding up figures on the number of refugees. There are many ways of compiling statistics. Some people have been talking of 50 million refugees; other figures are 8 million, 7 million; a recent study gives 6.9 million.

Whatever the figure, they are dealing with millions of people who are being excluded from totalitarian countries. It is always an excess of oppression, not an excess of liberty, which creates refugees. 

It would not be in our judgment proper however to leave the burden for caring for refugees to the countries of first asylum, the receiving countries, because they frequently are a matter of geographical accident.

When the Bengali refugees went into India it was not intrinsically a problem of India. It so happened it was a border they could cross from East Pakistan into India. India was hardly equipped to take care of 10 million more people. India, as you know, has quite a problem itself.

If then, as we believe, taking care of the basic needs of people who are chased across borders is the responsibility of the democratic countries of the world because they are the victims of totalitarian oppression, we take pride in the fact that the United States has been doing its full share in helping refugees. 

I have always thought it is a reason for satisfaction, it gives you a measure of satisfaction rather than a good reason for negative feelings about the role we have been playing in this refugee situation. which is part of the scene of our time which we have not been able to disregard, whatever we try to do in limiting the scope of our concern. 

We realize that the ORM budget, the ORM part in this U.S. total committee, ORM commitment to refugees' needs, is a small part, in the specific case, less than $10 million out of perhaps as much as $300 billion committed to refugee needs in different parts of the world. 

Nevertheless, it is an essential part because it is concentrating what we consider on a focal point. It is concentrating on something that is visible. It provides coordination and leadership for U.S. activities in the refugee field.

These moneys finance U.S. participation in international, intergovernmental activities. These moneys ought to be increased with a more thorough input into refugee needs in Africa. 

As an aside I might say that the $300,000 figure for the education needs of African refugees inside Africa becomes rather almost meaningless if we just look at the very recent changes. 

If Mozambique and Angola are moving to a degree of self-determination, self-rule, it may be that the development of the very near future, training a few hundred students in high schools hardly met even a fraction of the educational needs of Mozambique and Angola if these areas are not to get deeper into the economic situations against the present situation of colonial rule. 

I hope you understand me. I am not in favor of colonial rule but 

I fear a new nation emerging with a lack of educational structure is bound to worsen its economic situation and social condition. 

That was an aside. I did not intend to discuss Portuguese Angola here and Mozambique but I would like to explain to you why we believe that more moneys are needed for the refugee assistance program of the Office of Refugee and Migration Affairs. 

More money will be needed to establish a contingency fund with which we try to take the new emergencies as they arise. 

More funds will be needed to establish at least a total resettlement system of grants for refugees admitted into the United States and arriving here.

This is the case we would like to present to you today because it exceeds the budget proposal which your committee has before it. 

Since it has not been my intention to read the statement here today and since it certainly is not our intention to explain to you who we are, that can be ascertained in a much simpler way, I would like to briefly tell you why we are here, six of us.

We would hope that from here we can establish a dialog, a very frank expression of opinion.

We are definitely convinced, Mr. Chairman, that you approve our motivation. We do hope that you will permit us to bring our problems to you, not just in this setting of once a year appropriation hearings but whenever a refugee emergency arises which requires a compassionate and farsighted solution. 

Thank you very much. 

Senator INOUYE. Thank you very much, Mr. Sternberg.

I am pleased to assure you that my door is always open. This is substantiated by my very full office calendar. Some of my constituents have complained that I spend more time on non-Hawaiian matters. than on Hawaiian matters.

This committee has been trying for some time now to formulate a policy, a national policy, on refugees. I have been chairman for a yearand-a-half and during those months I have attempted on my own to formulate such a policy. 

I must say that I find it extremely difficult.

No. 1-you may be able to help us-we have tried to define the word "refugee." What is a refugee? Can you help us? 

Mr. STERNBERG. I cannot answer you in one sentence. We have to distinguish two groups of refugees, internal and external refugees. 

These are people displaced because of political, war, or religious op-

pression from their normal place of residence and forced into exile beyond the frontiers of their country or within their country because of a war like in Vietnam or to some extent in East Pakistan. 

Now, this is not a legal definition. This is an operational definition. 

That is what we have been working with. 

Senator INOUYE. I ask this question because oftentimes when Members of Congress and Members of this Government refer to refugees we do so when there is some political consideration involved. We concern ourselves when there is some political reason for the United States to be involved in certain matters. 

We have no formula or policy relating to all refugees. There is great confusion now. Is that person who has been requested to leave a certain area by his government to another area because of possible warlike activities a refugee? Is that man who wishes to leave the Soviet Union to go to Israel, is he a refugee? 

Mr. STERNBERG. To the first question my answer would be that it depends on the circumstances. The first is being forced to leave the theater of operation, because he is a victim of circumstances over which he has no control, I personally have no problem. 

Senator INOUYE. Even if the movement is temporary he becomes a temporary refugee.

As for the movement of largely Jewish refugees from the Soviet Union, I have no question whatsoever that they are full-fledged refugees in the same sense that the Cubans leaving Cuba with the permission of the government. Because that is the only way they can leave the Island. They are refugees.

But essentially the situations that force them out of their country and the motivations which led them from their country, whether they leave with consent, tacit or practical consent of their government, which may be the result of all sorts of international or national pressures, not directly related to the faith of the individual person, whether somebody leaves with the consent of the government, with a passport, if you will, those in the Soviet Union leave with documents, they have to pay a substantial amount of Soviet money in order to renounce Soviet citizenship prior to leaving, this I believe is not an essential factor in determining whether someone is a refugee. 

Is that young man who left the United States to go to Canada for reasons of his own, possibly of conscience, or that young man who decided that the United States was not his place of residence, and went to Australia, are these people refugees? 

Mr. ANDERSON. Since the 20 years now that I have been in this field we have discovered that the process of definition is also the process of determining degrees of responsibility. 

We have evolved a legal definition in the protocol of the Convention of Refugees. It is perhaps the most helpful definition for determining legal responsibility. I do not think any of us at this table in all of our experience in all of the years we have spent with refugees can fully accept that refugee as definitive in itself. 

In our case, for example, as men left their homes and our churches and departed from our shores because of what they claim to be reasons of conscience, part of our churches abroad and people in our churches at home considered that they had refugee status in the definition which we have accorded refugee status to those coming from other areas.

It is debatable but in the process of the debate and in the process of the discussion and definition of refugees we then evolved a possible solution.

Thus, those who seek a permanent definition of refugees that will last them in a fixed sense are going to be constantly confronted with situations which never fit those definitions. 

That is why we have strongly backed the Convention of Refugees but at the same time insisted on our part we have a broader responsibility internationally which has been encompassed and is not restricted to that definition. And the circumstances which caused their movement have to be analyzed in relation to the refugee status. When we respond in relation to refugee needs which interestingly enough for all groups regardless of under which definition have a similar set of needs and a similar set of responses which are required to make them self-supporting with new lives and new status in a new country. 

I don't know if that is helpful but that is the experience which has come out of our agencies here and abroad since World War II. 

Senator INOUYE. I would invite all of you, if you wish, to submit a memorandum on what you consider to be a refugee. It will be most helpful. 

Mr. STERNBERG. We will be glad to do that.

Soviet Union desiring to move to Israel we appropriated in excess of $50 million, the money to be used for various purposes, not just the cost of transporting men and women from the Soviet Union to, say, the shores of Israel but the maintenance of way-stations, the provision of receiving stations, the establishment of schools, the establishment of dormitories, the establishment of housing.

So, unlike this $9.5 million you are speaking of, this was way in excess of $50 million. In other countries refugee assistance has met an equivalent of one bowl of rice per day, no more, no less. How would you formulate a policy on the treatment of refugees by the United States. 

Mr. STERNBERG. Mr. Chairman, my personal bent is one of strong proletarianism. I believe in treating all refugees in the same way within the framework of the refugees' needs and expectations and within the framework of a purpose to be achieved in a certain refugee situation.

The movement out of Russia is not exclusively a movement to Israel. A certain percentage, perhaps right now, about 12, are coming 

West to the United States and Canada, Australia, and New Zealand. 

The movement of East European refugees, quite similar to this movement from Russia, is primarily to the West and close to 4,000 a year to the United States. The resettlement of the refugees, the Russians or East Europeans or Dutch during the Indonesian crisis, or Portuguese tomorrow will obviously not be solved by a bowl of rice. 

Any agency for settlement of refugees will have to be ready to spend a substantial amount. You cannot bring people to the United 

States to beg. You will have to provide the basic assistance which they need in order to become self-supporting, which is costly, which may run easily $2,000 or more per family.

As a matter of fact, the figure of U.S. assistance for the resettlement of Russians in Israel is roughly $1,000 which is not too different from the resettlement costs of the refugees, wherever they come from, if they come to the United States.

Now, to give you an example, when the Bengali situation erupted we went to India and tried to help. We thought the best way we could do that was to put Bengali refugees to work in the refugee camps for their own people, especially doctors and teachers. We offered to pay them a salary. The salary we offered them was equivalent to what the doctors and teachers made. It was roughly 300 rupees or less than $50 a month. 

Obviously we cannot resettle doctors in the United States as we are, whether from Russia, East Europe or China, it could not be at $50 a month. It could not be done at all at that level. 

So, my personal reaction, I understand your problem, I believe it is a serious problem, we should not dismiss it glibly and say one person just gets a better break and the other should do the best he can.
