INDOCHINA RESOURCE CENTER STATEMENT OF GUY GRAN, INDOCHINA RESOURCE CENTER ACCOMPANIED BY FRED BRANFMAN AMERICAN PRIORITIES OF AID REQUESTS FOR INDOCHINA 

Senator INOUYE. Our next witness is Mr.

Guy Gran of the Indo china Resource Center. 

Mr. GRAN. Thank you, Senator, for the opportunity to appear here this morning. 

I have with me my colleague, Mr. Fred Branfman.

We would like to split our time for oral testimony. 

Mr. Branfman will speak on the larger implications of American priorities and the magnitude of AID requests for Indochina. I will speak briefly on the economic contradiction of what we feel is an open ended burden for the United States and then discuss some alternatives to the AID proposals. 

Mr. BRANFMAN. I would like to state my testimony this morning is based not only on a daily monitoring of news from Indochina over the last 3 years but also on a trip I made there after the cease-fire last year in Cambodia and Thailand as well as 4 years spent in Indochina from 

1967 to 1971.

The main thrust of what I would like to say this morning is that we feel very strongly that the administration is intervening in Indochina this year precisely as they did in the early 1960's, that there is a massive covert attempt to support local government in Indochina of which the Congress and the American public are not yet fully aware and that unless it is stopped we will find ourselves as we did in the midsixties and late sixties faced with a situation where the executive has committed us to open involvement. 

There are a number of factors that make this clear. None make it clearer than the fact that this year the administration has proposed more aid to Indochina, $3.68 billion, than the rest of the world combined.

I would like to repeat that: More bilateral aid to Indochina than the rest of the world combined. Equally important, by its own definition, the administration proposals make it clear that at least 88 percent is war related.

Of the proposed Indochina funds only 12 percent are even defined as humanitarian reconstruction. In fact, we have found that only 2 percent is non war related. But we can talk about that later. 

The third thing I would like to stress on this point is that last year this committee showed the basic intent of Congress to disengage from Indochina by cutting the postwar reconstruction requests from $632 to $450 million. The administration, through a variety of subterfuges, a development loan here, a supplemental request there, but most importantly food for peace subsidies not only restored the cuts that the Congress made but wound up allocating over $1 billion in Indochina postwar construction last year, roughly 30 percent more than it had originally requested and almost 40 percent more than Congress had originally allocated for fiscal year 1974.

I think all of these dimensions show the tremendous emphasis that the administration puts on Indochina. If granted what would the administration's request this year achieve?

It is our belief that all that the administration can at best show, but slightly, is the deteriorating economic and military situation in Indochina. One element of this is that according to official statistics at least 

50,000 human beings were killed in Indochina last year, 70,000 were wounded and 1.3 million new refugees were created in South Vietnam and Cambodia.

More important, of course, the situation has deteriorated and we are probably now further from peace in Indochina than we were a year ago at this time. Why? We think that, once the record is quite clear, the problem in South Vietnam is that the Saigon government did not even want to sign the Paris peace agreement in the first place and since it was forced to sign it, it has gone out of its way not to allow the other side to enter the political arena. 

We think this is the key. One cannot expect either side to stop fighting unless they were allowed to enter the political arena. 

The Saigon government has outlawed the third force and refused to allow refugees to return to their villages. It has not released tens of thousands of political prisoners. Most important it continues to outlaw the PRG from any kind of political role in South Vietnam. 

We think that the only solution to this situation is an attempt on our part to see that our side does engage at least in a meaningful test of the other side's willingness to compete politically. 

I think it is very important that you remember that the governments in Cambodia and South Vietnam and Laos are the only governments in the world which have over 85 percent of their resources supplied by a foreign power.

We don't think it is quite accurate to say we are simply supporting the GVN in South Vietnam. The enormous degree of dependence gives us not only the right, but I would argue the responsibility, to see that whatever aid we do give Indochina this year is given in accordance with the Paris agreement. We are heading for more war in Indochina very likely a year or two from now unless this year we and the Vietnamese make basic political decisions. Unless this year sees a political settlement we will be headed for far more war than we have at the moment.

What is different now in 1974 as opposed to the late sixties is that there is a solution. In the late sixties the war was going on. We had no idea how it could end or what could be the solution. Now there is one. There is a Paris agreement. If adhered to by both sides, it does form the basis for some kind of settlement. 

We think that by the substantial cuts in aid which Congress makes and perhaps a suspension of aid until the Paris agreement is observed, some kind of solution can come into being in Indochina in this coming year.

If this does not happen we will be faced with a very ugly situation, at which point solutions will become much more complicated and difficult.

What is at stake in the Indochina situation this year goes far beyond Indochina. What we have seen in the last 2 years is a substantial shift in power. ངས་ངག་

Congress has begun to take us away from the presidential dictatorship towards global statesmanship around the world. 

Congress through its pressure and opposition to the Christmas bombing of Hanoi helped to pressure the President to sign the Paris agreement. Congress also stopped the bombing of Cambodia and has begun to regain a partnership in foreign policy. 

Foreign policy in this country must not be made by a small group of men in the executive branch. This is crucially important. Indochina, which has been a symbol of so many of the political problems in this country from Watergate to the notion of presidential dictatorship, once again has become a key. 

If we are going to restore rational priorities both worldwide and at home, it is absolutely essential for this committee to substantially reduce these requests. 

I think Mr. Gran now could give us a bit more detail on what this might mean.

Mr. GRAN. What the administration is arguing is that, given a larger amount of economic aid, $800 million to a billion dollars, over a period of 2 or 3 or perhaps 4 years South Vietnam could become an economically viable and reasonably self-sufficient state. 

In the testimony submitted for the record, I submit that this is an economic fantasy. IBRD economists and other economic realists in 

Vietnam would concur that to the contrary we are facing a situation of long term if not permanent dependence and only if present administration policies could continue and the war disappear. 

There are two basic reasons for this. As long as the political conflicts are fought out in a military rather than a political framework, it will require enormous security expenditures which the RVN alone can't afford. Simultaneously the present RVN policies to create more resources and to develop the economy generate the kind of opposition which create and perpetuate conflict. 

The thesis of my presentation is that economic costs and human costs of the present and the potential future are intolerable to the Vietnamese people and American people. The costs of the status and AID would perpetuate, are far greater than the costs of undergoing basic change.

I have tried in some considerable detail to paint those human costs, to describe the kind of economic conditions that AID would perpetuate, and to argue that AID cannot create stability with its programs.

One must talk of degeneration and not stability because of the institutionalized corruption and the institutionalized inflation. As an example I would like to raise the issue of refugee programs discussed a few minutes ago and go into one brief vignette from a serious new study of refugees that came from Saigon last week.

The essay describes in some detail how the refugee programs are carried out and why. Some of this material is in both of the formal statements we present for the record but I would like to go into what some French, Americans and Japanese are doing to support a generalization that the refugees are being used essentially as pawns. I quote:

In several cases the French, American and Japanese Governments and private firms are involved in the settlements in order to secure cheap labor forces for the existing or planned plantations and industrial enterprises.

2 In Lam-Dong Province the French tea and rubber plantations get new coolies in Tan-Rai. The "Gallia" rubber plantations of Phuoc-Tuy reduced the daily wage from 300 VN$ to 200 VN$ (620 VN$: 1 US$) for the plantation laborers when the refugees from Quang-Tri arrived at the settlement of Suoi-Nghe. The settlers of Quang-Thuan, Song-My etc. Quang-Thuan Province will provide a cheap coolies' force for the Japanese-Vietnamese sugar cane plantations in President Thieu's home province. Here the Japanese Government concentrated the 20 million US$ humanitarian aid in form of prefabricated housing units for the future workers on the Cam-Ranh Processing Port which is considered as an integrated economic unit of the Japanese imperium in sea. They found a competent and experienced collaborator in Pr. Do-Ba-Ai, former Caritas President of 

Quang-Tri Province who is clever enough to obtain sufficient funds for the understandings, such as social infrastructure and security measures, from church and humanitarian agencies abroad.

Most of this particular study deals with how the Buddhist groups and the Catholic Relief Agency groups treat the refugees that they manage to get control of. 

What we are dealing with essentially here is corruption, institutionalized so deeply that the Government is fundamentally incapable of operating on behalf of its citizens. 

We are dealing as well with inflation that is institutionalized so deeply by basic economic conditions that it cannot be alleviated, given present political policies. The vast majority of the people simply suffer ever greater burdens with no viable recourse.

The alternative to the status quo is an economic transformation away from this dependent state. We feel that the only way this is going to happen is through the political accommodations envisioned by the Paris agreement. We have two proposals on the way that Congress can create the conditions for such a solution. 

One way would be to suspend all money except truly humanitarian aid until the Thieu administration fulfills certain basic obligations that it has under the Paris agreement, most specifically the freedom of movement so that refugees can leave the cities and leave the refugee camps and go where they can find self-sufficient economic livelihood. 

A second alternative would be to substantially reduce the $910 million which in the total economic aid proposed by AID for the Thieu government to a figure of $200 million. 

Most of that would be for emergency needs, particularly for the starvation which is now going on in the central region, and such areas that might need it in the future. 

Obviously both of the alternatives incur costs to the Vietnamese people. What we are arguing is that those costs will be borne primarily by those Vietnamese who can afford it. Those costs will not be very great compared to the costs of the status quo which are appalling. 

Sometimes the cost of the status quo is greater than the cost of change. This I believe is one of those times. 

Senator INOUYE. I want to thank you very much, gentlemen.

On the matter of comparison it has been suggested by some that at the time of the signing by the signatories there was really very little intention on the part of the signatories to abide by the provisions set forth in the Paris agreement. 

What are your thoughts on that?

Mr. BRANFMAN. I think that the other side is quite interested in seeing the Paris agreement observed, not because they are nice guys or not nice guys, but because it is in their interest to carry on the competition in the political arena.

Senator INOUYE. Are they also abiding by the Paris agreement? 

Mr. BRANFMAN. I think they are substantially abiding in the sense that most of the attacks that they have carried out have been in marginal areas and after continual RVN provocation. Our own House Armed 

Services Committee reported last week that the change that has been taking place in the territorial control has seen the advantage going to the GVN. 

There are many complex issues involved in an analysis of ceasefire violation.

The refugees are now in the cities away from the PRG. If real freedom of movement, guaranteed under article XI of the Paris agreement, is implemented, the refugees would return to areas close to PRG control or under PRG control. This is not happening now in most instances.

If there is freedom of speech, freedom of meeting, freedom of political activity guaranteed by the Paris agreement, this will enable all elements to enter the political process. 

The PRG never said that it would not compete for power, but it has said it would be willing to compete for power politically. 

We believe it is in the PRG interest to do so because they don't need another war and because they can compete better politically. Even our own analysts agree that the DRV is interested in reconstructing the north, that it would like nothing better than to turn from war to rebuilding the northern part of Vietnam.

We think that they would prefer this kind of route. 

Even Air Force Gen. George Brown said that there would not be an offensive this year. We think this year is a year when this kind of thing could happen.

On the other hand if it does not happen, if we don't at least test, and no one is saying if the offer is tested and we were proven wrong that there should not be a policy review.

I would argue in the next 2 or 3 years you will see a gradually upsurge of the fighting which would culminate in another offensive. 

For that reason we believe that the other side is interested in entering political competition. It is in their interest. 

We believe that the reason that our side, the Thieu government, has shunned political competition is that it does not perceive it as being in its own narrowly defined self-interest of maintaining its war machine and its totalitarian control over the government that it controls. 

Senator MATHIAS. Do you think that the statement that is attributed to President Thieu that there is no third force in South Vietnam is true? 

Mr. BRANFMAN. I visited South Vietnam last year. They definitely exist. Even in a very controlled parliament which is by no conceivable means free in the lower assembly there is a fairly sizable block, about 

25 percent now, of third force.

Most strikingly, until this last August, there was a Catholic bloc in the Senate and Buddhist bloc in the Senate which together held about 60 seats and which voted against President Thieu's attempt to take over war powers during the offensive in 1972. They can be considered some kind of independent force. 

With the August elections they were wiped out. They hold very few seats in the Senate right now.

When the next election takes place this third force will not be represented in the House and Senate. 

Senator MATHIAS. You think that statement is not true today but it may become true?

Mr. BRANFMAN. There will always be a third force. They may not be sitting in the House and Senate. They have been forced out by 

Thieu. Tens of thousands of political prisoners are Buddhist monks and if they were not in the third force, and I am using the word force in a very real sense, a political bloc, there would be no reason for Thieu to imprison them.

The very fact we have and have had so many third force people such as Ngo Ba Thanh in prison is dramatic proof. 

Senator MATHIAS. I think that really goes to my question, do you think there are so many in prison, so many likely to go to prison, that the third force could be reduced to ineffectiveness? 

Mr. BRANFMAN. That is one potential result if we give Thieu the lavish kind of aid, a level which he does not even need. I should stress for the record the example of March 7, when Secretary of Defense Clements went before the House Armed Services Committee and said if the RVN did not get a $474 million supplemental, the RVN would be in dire straits.

A few weeks later the supplemental was defeated and DOD then said it turned out that they didn't need the money after all. The same thing happened on the economic side. Much of the money going there is being lost to corruption and the rest. If we reduce our aid substantially, as Mr. Gran suggests, to the level that we need to meet emergency needs during a period of transition to the formation of the National Council, then we would see a third force emerging. 

Senator MATHIAS. You think that even the limited aid necessary for the transition period should be conditional on the adherence to the terms of the cease-fire agreement, particularly the terms which deal with the evolution of a political settlement. 

Mr. BRANFMAN. My own position is to support what we call a pause for peace.

I might stress the only truly humanitarian aid we have been able to locate in the $3.7 billion is about $18.5 million, under 1 percent, for health care and child care in South Vietnam. We believe that all aid other than the humanitarian aid should be suspended until progress is made toward a political solution. 

If this is not politically feasible, we would support what Mr. Gran was outlining.

Senator MATHIAS. One final question. 

You mentioned Ngo Ba Thanh as a prisoner. 

Mr. BRANFMAN. She has been recently released.

Mr. GRAN. Could I add one point on suspending aid. 

The way the programs operate when we speak of suspending aid, we are talking about letting the pipeline of commodities work itself down so Thieu would have 3 or 4 or 5 or 6 months when he is still receiving commodities.

There will be several hundred million dollars worth of commodities in the pipeline at the end of this fiscal year. These commodities will be arriving to the end of 1974 and beyond. It is not a matter of a total cutoff at a point in time in July or August. 34-192 - 74-25

Even during the suspension there is a considerable period of transition where Thieu would have 2 or 3 months at least when he is still getting the money. He can contemplate the idea "I am going to have to make a political accommodation and conduct competition in the political arena rather than the military arena if I am going to continue to get aid."

If he made such choices he could do it in a short period of time. 

We are not asking a great deal in terms of time. 

Mr. BRANFMAN. Madam Ngo Ba Thanh was released last fall due to considerable international pressure but hundreds of thousands like her do remain behind, the most dramatic example being Huynh Tan Mam, president of the National Student Association, a very charismatic third force leader.

I want to close on the political prisoner question I was just mentioning.

We hope that the chairman and the members of this committee would consider the idea of pushing to get some really independent observers into those prisons. There is a gigantic dispute going up. The way to resolve it is not a lot more rhetoric going back and forth on both sides but to get some people into those prisons, some international organizations perhaps, to get at the truth and stop what we feel is the mockery of having the Thieu government claim that anyone in prison is a Vietcong sympathizer and constantly refuse to allow in the prisons those who are asking to go in.

Senator INOUYE. Am I to conclude from the statement that the government-involved corruption is worse today than it was a year ago?

Mr. GRAN. I think it would be pretty difficult to qualify but it appears so. I think there is an ever greater degree of economic desperation at a lot of levels which pushes people toward trying to create wealth while they still can. This contributes to a greater degree of corruption. The RVN officers now hoarding and selling scrap metal for private gain is one example. Corruption is most evident in the control of economic resources. 

Our very high level of economic aid and the import of commodities produces a wide variety of avenues. The major ongoing scandal involves imported fertilizer which is really fundamental to any kind of agricultural survival. RVN officials and others have been hoarding and speculating on most of the imports, a process which raises the price of rice production and thus of rice. This has been a major contributing factor why the poor, especially in the central regions cannot afford rice any longer and are slowly starving.. 

Mr. BRANFMAN. May I add one word from my own experience when

I was in South Vietnam. I asked this question of a large number of people including people in the American Embassy. The basic answer 

I got I can't prove because it is a very hard thing to prove, but I will share with you what I was told by everyone. Corruption has gotten worse for two reasons.

One because of the economic squeeze. The people at the lower level are feeling the pinch more and more. The essence of our argument is that you have a gigantic civil service and army in South Vietnam, 1½ million people who have no productive way of living. As their fixed incomes decline, they squeeze the people.

Second, the political initiative has shifted to the PRG since the cease fire because they represent peace while Thieu represents war. 

As a result some of the richer people and the Chinese in particular are growing increasingly more nervous, and there is a greater capital flight from the country.

MILITARY AND ECONOMIC AID TO INDOCHINA Analysis of the FY 1975 Request to the Congress Indochina Resource Center/NARMIC 

This year,

FOREWORD 

Congress has an excellent opportunity to help bring peace to Indochina. For the first time in a decade, American ground and air forces are not fighting there. For the first time in a generation, all sides in both Laos and Vietnam have agreed on blueprints for peace, the Paris and Vientiane Agreements of 1973.

Congress has played a crucial part in these developments. 

Its opposition to the Christmas bombing in 1972 was a factor in the Administration's decision to sign the Paris Agreement a month later. In the spirit of the Agreement, Congress halted the bombing of Cambodia in August, 1973 and passed legislation aimed at ending support of Vietnamese police and prisons in December, 1973. And in March of this year, Congress rejected the Administration's request for $474 million in supplemental military aid for the Saigon government.

These actions have saved countless lives in Indochina. 

In addition, they have made available millions of dollars for human needs at home. . 

Now the Nixon Administration's FY 1975 request for military and economic aid to Indochina presents Congress with a choice of whether or not to continue this progress. To state the matter frankly, we believe that Congress must choose between subsidizing narrow-based, military governments in Saigon and Phnom Penh and helping to restore peace in Southeast Asia. The actions of these governments during the last year have made it clear that political settlements are unlikely as long as American arms and resources offer them the option to fight. 

The analysis and findings presented here are a joint effort of the Indochina Resource Center and NARMIC, a project of the American Friends Service Committee.

U.S. EXPENDITURES FOR INDOCHINA IN FY 1975 SUMMARY 

War is still the overwhelming fact of life in Indochina today. In Cambodia, the last year's fighting has driven 

500,000 people from their homes." In Vietnam, despite the hopeful prospects of the Paris Agreement, nearly one million people have been killed, wounded or made refugees since the beginning of 1973. And the threat of an even larger conflict looms in the future unless the Saigon government alters its policy and accepts the political resolution provided by the Paris Agreement. 

Along with the threat of renewed, all-out fighting goes the danger of direct U.S. military reintervention. 

Despite the consensus at home for withdrawal from Southeast Asia, resumption of American involvement is not at all inconceivable. Even now, the U.S. remains deeply committed to the Saigon and Phnom Penh governments, providing over 85 percent of their operating costs. By supplying these governments with all their armaments, with military technicians and operational support, the U.S. is indirectly involved in the fighting. In addition, the U.S. maintains a substantial presence in Thailand to fly reconnaissance missions, supply spare parts, and remain ready to resume combat operations at a moment's notice. 

War in Indochina has brought the economies of Saigon and Phnom Penh to near collapse. They are unable to meet the basic needs of their people as rampant inflation and massive unemployment have brought thousands of people to the brink of starvation. Prolonged fighting in these countries will only continue the misery of Indochina's war-weary people.

The Administration's proposed $3.671 billion Indochina aid program for FY 1975--13 percent more than the amount programmed in FY 1974--will continue to underwrite war.

As shown in this table, the proposed expenditures have two main elements: 1) Direct support for the war efforts in 

Cambodia and South Vietnam, and 2) Support for the stabilization of the war economies of the two countries. These 20.0 16.2 2.5

TAL direct and indirect war-related categories account for 88 percent of the total Administration's request. Only 

10 percent of the total budget is available for reconstruccion and development and humanitarian aid. Even this aid has little chance of succeeding due to the continuing war and associated deterioration of economic conditions. 

So long as war continues in South Vietnam, funds for reconstruction and development will be used primarily for wartime economic stabilization. In Laos, however, the fighting has stopped and a coalition government formed, so it is assumed that non-partisan reconstruction and development can proceed. 

In South Vietnam and Cambodia, most "humanitarian" aid will be spent for refugee programs having strategic political and military purposes. Only the programs for health and child care can be considered humanitarian in South Vietnam. Programs in Laos may be genuinely humanitarian if approved and administered by the Provisional Government of National Unity.

Taking these considerations into account, it appears that only 2 percent of the Administration's proposal is for actual humanitarian or reconstructive purposes. 1 se 

SOUTH VIETNAM 

Heavy fighting continues in South Vietnam as President

Thieu refuses to order a ceasefire (Article 3 of Paris Agreement) and to demarcate zones of control (Ceasefire Protocol). The military situation remains highly unstable and may escalate to all-out war if Thieu continues to prevent a political settlement.

The economic crisis stems from the continuing state of war which has 1) dislocated rural populations, 2) taken 25 percent of the labor force out of gainful employment, and 

3) perpetuated a costly 1.2 million-man military and police apparatus.

Saigon's economic problems are not caused by inadequate levels of imports as AID claims. Even in constant dollar

values, present import levels are at $25 per capita today as compared with $21 in 1964.4 Rather, the crisis is due to the severe structural distortions in the economy which is being kept from complete collapse by U.S. aid. The U.S. taxpayer underwrites 86 percent of the costs of keeping 

Thieu's administration in power.

We propose that any future appropriations for aid to Salgon, other than humanitarian aid, be conditional on compliance by the RVN with the provisions of the Paris Agreement.

CAMBODIA 

President Lon Nol's government now controls little more than Phnom Penh and a few provincial capitals and has lost the support of even the small urban elite in Phnom Penh. 

The economy in the area controlled by the Phnom Penh government is disintegrating and is totally dependent on the U.S. for its everyday requirements. 

A ceasefire appears unlikely because the Khmer Rouge, which controls most of the country, considers the collapse of the Phnom Penh government inevitable. The unpopular government survives because of massive U.S. military support. 

As a result of the continuing war, a vast number of refugees are now concentrated in urban centers. These refugees need humanitarian aid, but the structure and corruption of the Phnom Penh government prevents U.S. aid from reaching those in need. The most humanitarian measure would be to stop funding the continuing war in Cambodia. 

LAOS 

Recent events in Laos demonstrate that even after years of bitter war, peace and reconciliation are possible if the local parties are allowed to make their own settlement. 

The two Laotian parties, the Vientiane government and the Patriotic Lao Forces (Pathet Lao) have agreed on the formation of three new governmental structures in accordance with the February 21, 1973 Agreement on Restoring Peace and

Achieving National Concord in Laos and the September 14,

1973 Protocol. 

To contribute to a durable peace in Laos, Congress should authorize and approve only that assistance which is in strict conformity with the Laotian agreements. Thus U.S. aid should be provided only at the request of all the parties within the Provisional Government of National Union, the body mandated to determine the form of foreign aid under Article 7 of the February Agreement. 

EXCERPTS FROM VIETNAM: THE HUMAN COSTS OF THE AMERICAN AID PROGRAMS An Alternate FY 75 Foreign Aid Proposal 

For Indochina

GUY GRAN INDOCHINA RESOURCE CENTER 

May 1974

PREFACE 

For Fiscal Year 1975 the Administration has requested the appropriation of at least $7.46 billion in direct bilateral foreign aid. By the AID presentation figures Indochina would receive $3.09 billion or 41% of the total aid for the whole world. A more precise accounting of total planned 

FY75 expenditures reveals that the real figure for Indochina would be at least $3.67 billion or about half of the world total. 

Most of these funds are intended to support the Republic of Vietnam (RVN) on the supposition that it can someday become an economically viable state. 

It would appear, however, that no amount of economic or military aid can ever overcome the essentially artificial nature of this state. The United 

States supplied 86% of the resources that permitted the RVN to exist in 1973. It is, however far morethan the degree of dependence which merits such a conclusion. The RVN state feels obliged to spend enormous to maintain a military and police bureaucracy. It is a very expensive way to maintain political control, and it keeps 19% of the work force out of commodity producing jobs. Various refugee and income maintenance programs also permit political control but drain the treasury. These fundamental distortions make the RVN economy structurally unviable. sums

The same drives for political control and the profits that accrue also destroy the RVN ability to generate substantial new revenue. While indirect taxes did rise last year, the RVN still fears to tax significantly the major pockets of wealth, land and personal income, because it is the rich who support it. With AID's urging the RVN pursues capital intensive agriculture in a labor rich country. Even if such processes show some success, agribusiness and trickle down development will add primarily to the wealth of those Thieu chooses not to tax. It is little wonder that such policies continue to create active opposition among the Vietnamese. 

The RVN answer to opposition is repression. Totalitarian control over economic transactions and individuals provides enormous possibilities for corruption. The present degree of corruption alone is enough to warrant the conclusion that the RVN government is incapable of acting in the best interests of its citizens. Meanwhile inflation, fueled by corruption, domestic "security" expenses, and world market conditions, is slowly but inevitably destroying the ability of a majority of Vietnamese to survive, let alone prosper. The appalling human costs of such processes are the most persuasive arguments for change. 

The Administration argues that it could perpetuate a status quo and a stability that in reality do not exist. AID's presentations ignore both the political fabric and the enormous human suffering it is largely responsible for. It is bad enough that the Administration's proposals are fundamentally irresponsible and inappropriate in economic terms. But it is totally unacceptable to continue and enlarge the psychological dehumanization, social degradation, poverty, and corruption on the present scale when other choices exist. 

These are sad conclusions to draw from 25 years of American aid programs in Indochina. To reach them requires intellectual energy, curiosity, and empathy. It takes political courage as well to recognize that the costs of the status quo can be greater than the costs of change. In

13e lieu of the proposed $911 million program of subsidies for the RVN, I propose a transitional aid program of $200 million. For it is substantial pressure on Thieu that offers the best chance that he and the RVN will begin to live up to the obligations of the Paris Agreement. Without the substantive political accomodation the Agreement outlines, there will be no peace, no viable government, and no viable economy in South Vietnam.

Without peace Congress will be facing another year with 100,000 Vietnamese casualties and 800,000 refugees followed by an FY76 request for $3 billion more in aid. The Vietnamese and the American people both deserve better. strate 11

These are considerable contradictions. They suggest more than political duplicity and fiscal irresponsibility. They point to a policy of permanently substituting material means for political appeal. And they reveal a basically artificial state, dependant upon another to a degree and durability which conjures few historical analogies, except perhaps Laos. In the analysis to follow I shall argue that such dependance has profoundly unhealthy results for the Vietnamese economy, the RVN state, and the people under its aegis. 

The RVN economy, in the manner of a heroin user, is addicted to American aid. This means, in the first place, that the Vietname se economy we subsidize is extremely ill in ways not apparent to traditional economic analysis and ways not considered in the surface picture of vibrant and healthy potential USAID will present. Most addicts don't appear very ill on the outside. They can carry out most normal functions over a long period of time. But the drug is slowly debilitating them. 

In like manner U. S. aid to Vietnam is sustaining a certain stability and economic health for some but the economy, the society, and the polity as a whole are being slowly destroyed. I shall try to describe the figurative and literal dimensions of this process and then assess the Administration's FY 75 economic aid package (the yearly fix) against the costs and potential rewards for the Vietnamese people of withdrawal from their habit.

PART VII. Toward Peace in Indochina 

By the AID fiscal summary the FY 75 foreign aid requests to Congress contain $7.46 billion in new obligational authority for bilateral military and economic assistance. Of that total the 60 countries of Africa and Latin 

America are to receive $886 million. On an average that is $10.4 million. a country in economic aid and $4.4 million in military, a total of $14.8 million. The three countries of Indochina alone are to receive $3.09 billion which is 41% of the total for the world, 29% of world economic aid and 55% of world military aid. Such an indication of Administration priorities requires serious contemplation from anyone interested in the me rit and continuation of foreign aid in general, never mind the wisdom of the Administration position. in Indochina.

The Administration wishes $550.7 million for Cambodia to prolong briefly this tragic and bloɔdy civil war. State Department officials admit candidly that the ONLY Administration purpose is to save face before its domestic critics as long as possible. Killing Cambodians is preferable to taking any responsibility and accepting the inevitable. By such moral and political cowardice, Congress is given two unpleasant choices. The most responsible position is a $50 million interim program of medical aid, sufficient until a new government can assess the situation. The Administration wishes to intrude another $143.5 million into the fragile new peace in Laos. In view of the existence of a new coalition government, it would appear wise to seek the advice of all of its leaders before deciding what should be done. The long and unhappy heritage of AID and the CIA in disrupting Laotian political settlements suggests that Congress make enormous extra efforts on behalf of the Laotian people. 

Last, but not least, the Administration is requesting $2.4 billion in new money (and $2.5 in spending authority) to support for another year one of the parties in a 40 year old revolutionary war in Vietnam. This is 32% of the TOTAL military and economic aid for the entire world, 23% of the economic aid and 42% of the military aid. Without such aid over the past two decades the RVN would not have come into existence and would not have survived. It is an anomalous historical situation. There are powerful emotional and psychological interests, involving personal image and political credibility, which argue for a continuation of such aid. 

Portions of the Pentagon, State Department, and international business community favor this policy. So naturally do the RVN leaders. 

The optimal scenario envisaged by Thieu and his supporters seems to be the following. First they would have Kissinger's secret diplomatic dialogues with Le Duc Tho be successful. To wit Kissinger should venture to Paris and conjure up yet another public relations triumph with a veneer of progress toward peace. Whatever actually transpires, a Kissinger diplomatic "breakthrough", peace perhaps "in hand" this time instead of "at hand", is likely to be staged to assist the passage of this aid bill. 

The long range dream for Thieu to retain power takes the following form. 

Because the economic problems are irresolvable with an army of 1.1 million men, Thieu will have to adapt the Paris Agreement to his own uses and make apparent compromises. The first step will be a sign of reconciliation, eliminating Article 4 from the constitution so "communists" can operate as a legal political party. At this point Thieu can hope to begin a negotiated partial de mobilization and the PRG will also de mobilize. Then Thieu will select secret supporters as members of the 

Third Force in the National Council of Reconciliation and Concord, so that his forces dominate that body. National election will then be scheduled and held. With Thieu's officials in control of the machinery, the communists can easily be held to 20% of the announced vote. 

Thieu's forces will remain in power. The present political economy, with adjustments for peace, will remain essentially intact. Foreign investors and tourists will flock in, and the need for American aid will diminish to far more politically tolerable levels. If this sounds possible to the reader, basic political reality should be remembered. The PRG position rests on a political heritage that is 2,000 years old. The present struggle to end foreign domination has been going on for four decades. Dreams of social justice and political independence remain healthy.

1 For 24 years in a row the American Executive branch, supported in varying degrees by the legislative branch, has struggled with diplomatic financial, and military means to mold the realities of Indochina to American perceptions and purposes. This Administration would continue such a pursuit. It would ignore the moral and human costs and insist that the American taxpayer support the financial burden to assure the status quo and the Administration's perceptions of Vietnamese reality. 

Last year Congress, hoping to presure Thieu toward political compromise and peace, cut the FY 74 aid requests slightly. The Administration ignored the Congressional intent and subsidized Thieu in every way possible.

In this essay I have tried to document what these choices have cost and will continue to cost the Vietnames people. It is not enough to add up the billions it has cost the American taxpayer and uncover the many 122 domestic programs that have been starved as a result. It is not enough to count the 120, 000 to 150, 000 Vietnamese who have been killed or wounded in the last year and the 800, 000 to 1, 000, 000 new refugees which have been created. One must consider whether the political and economic system as a whole functions in the best interests of the people. 

It is not an impossible question, for the empirical evidence from every sector of political and economic activity documents an inescapable answer. The present policies and practices of the RVN and its officials are fundamentally and irremediably contradictory to the basic needs of the Vietnamese people. For the poor it is now not even a question of tole rating this misery, it is a question of sheer physical survival. On 

March 22 Dien Tin reported that a pro-government Senator Tran Tan Tuan had announced that the RVN Ministry of Agriculture was considering the export of 50, 000 metric tons of rice. Last year 50, 000 tons was "loaned" to Lon Nol. Holding up decision was not the reality of PL 480 import shipments, 124, 000 tons in the first quarter of 1974, but the possible conflicts with American dealers on the world market! The

Ministry of Agriculture said there was plenty of rice, but people we re just too poor to buy it. Thieu does not permit them to cross into the PRG areas where rice land is freely available and where much of the Delta rice is now sold in preference to RVN government markets. The production, purchase, and consumption of rice is the heart of economic reality in Vietnam. The RVN government has ravaged the heart as it has every other part of the body politic in its quest for political power and economic wealth. Whatever the costs of political change, they are insignificant compared to the magnitude of human misery this Administration would perpetuate for the Vietnamese. 

Congress has another choice. That choice is to force this Administration and the Thieu government to live up to the political obligations they undertook with the Paris Agreement. The PRG has consistently urged this path to a peaceful political settlement. There is every indication that it would abide by its provisions. Thieu knows that the Paris Agreement means compromise and a sharing of the political power his officials find 

122 See the testimony of Fred Branfman before the Asia and Pacific 

Subcommittee of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, May 1, 1974 for a wealth of such material.

so profitable. He has thus ignored nearly every major element of the 

Paris Agreement. He will continue this pattern until or unless he is forced to do otherwise. Meanwhile at terrible cost to the Vietnamese the basic structural contradictions of the RVN economy are slowly destroying the RVN state. To change this situation Congress must considerably diminish the resources available to Thieu. 

Such a path will not be without costs and risks, but the se costs are far less than accepting the perpetuation of the present kinds of human tragedy, degradation, and corruption, a tiny portion of which I have chronicled herein. Such a path will also involve complex political and economic change in Vietnam which cannot be precisely mapped out. 

But the continuation of the known is fundamentally irresponsible in every sense of the word. Any decision made in June can be reviewed in 

December if it needs to be, but money once appropriated becomes inevitably fuel for further tragedy.

If Congress proceeds with a modest cut, $910 million down to $400-650 million, the RVN and AID will try to perpetuate the status quo with the same kinds of techniques I have chronicled. At great cost to the average Vietnamese Thieu may succeed a little longer. I propose an initial level of $200 million in economic aid and $400 million in military aid to be broken down in this fashion.

However, such speculation perpetuates precisely the same basic ethnocentric assumption Americans have made for two decades or more. It carries on the basic presumptions that the United States has the ability and the right to program the future. of any other country or people. That such a view cannot be defended and that such policies have failed for two decades in Vietnam do not seem to deter this Administration. But Vietnam is the business of the 

Vietnamese, not the Americans, as the Paris Agreement clearly and repeatedly states. 34-192 Q-74-26

The military evolution depends on the assumption that the PRG will not launch at attack in the middle of the transition. The PRG and DRV leadership have always been eminently pragmatic. Faced with major economic priorities at home, the DRV does not want to pursue with expensive bloodshed and uncertain outcome a political problem that can be solved with political means. If there is substantive political movement, the PRG and DRV will avoid bloodshed. An in-place military ceasefire could be negotiated fairly quickly. De mobilization,ne gotiated stage by stage, would mean DR V tanks and troops going north as well as fairly rapid RVN de mobilization of 4 to 600,000 troops. With little gas and no technicians, Thieu would be discouraged from offensive air operations.

Local commanders could afford peace in part because they could not afford war.

But the economy will collapse say the defenders of the status quo. 

I have documented that for most poor Vietnamese, which is most Vietnamese, the economy has already collapsed. The price of food is beyond the means of many poor, and the price and allocation system is controlled by corrupt officials and private speculators. It is hard to imagine how things could get worse. What is most likely to take place would be a slow cutback in certain commodities over six months as the CIP and PL 480 pipe line s were drawn down. This is NOT an immediate cutoff. It leaves 4 to 6 months at least for adjustments. In 1942 the Japanese conque red Indochina and there really was an abrupt cutoff of imports. The Vietnamese economy thrived as never before. It is a most instructive historical parallel. 

When a country is cut off a demand exists but no foreign supply is possible. Domestic entrepreneurs grab the opportunity. A wide variety of small enterprises would seize upon the scrap iron, for example, for agricultural needs like plows. Certainly the living standards of the wealthy would drop, but the Vietname se in RVN areas rather badly need a more egalitarian society if they ever hope to live in peace in one political community. Three basic imports provide most of the total yearly bill.

Petroleum for all RVN uses should be drawn from the military aid monies to insure that both the civilian and the military populations in RVN areas become acutely aware of how much petroleum costs and how little they can afford frivolous military exercises. Rice imports should be limited to the central regions. Given its corruption, the RVN will soon be unable to feed urban slum dwellers and refugees. They will vote with their feet. They will insist on returning to abandoned rice lands to begin farming. Hungry poorly paid soldiers on either side will have no incentive to stop them. Such movement is, in fact, already under way. In Finally, there is the problem of fertilizer. For the long term 1 propose funding of the urea plant which, by AID's description, would be operational in a year. In the short term there would be considerable movement back to labor intensive traditional agriculture. This provide s needed jobs and enormous incentive to rural migration and settlement. 

1974 1.9 million hectares by traditional methods will produce half the needed 

6.5 million metric tons. A majority of 900 million hectares now under cultivation in high yield varieties would have to be turned to traditional varieties to cut down on fertilizer needs. If another 800, 000 to 

1,000,000 hectares could be planted by traditional methods this fall, the RVN would need no imported rice and could survive on the fertilizer now in the pipeline. If RVN and PRG soldiers were turned to a giant WPA project of unexploded ordnance disposal and canal dredging such a

transformation would be quite possible. And if real efforts were made in both the political and economic transformation toward independence, Congress could consider filling any real gaps late this year. war.

The Administration proposes $910 million in economic aid to the RVN. 

It cannot demonstrate that such a funding level will avoid another year of It speaks not of another 100,000 Vietnamese casualties and another 1,000,000 refugees. It has no answer for the endless suffering of those millions of Vietnamese being ground to death by the institutionalized corruption and inflation of this artificial economy. For the irresolvable economic contradictions it offers fundamentally erroneous approaches to both agricultural and industrial modernization. For the social parasites it offers even greater resources to corrupt. For the Vietnamese people it offers the rhetoric of salvation but the reality of further degradation and dehumanization. Such a proposal rests manifestly contrary to any reading of our constitutional and ethical ideals. 

I propose instead a transitional economic aid program of $200 million. Certainly some Vietnamese will remain hungry in this interim. Urban living standards will decline. But if people are hungry with a tangible goal ahead, rather than starving for nothing as many are now, it will be far more bearable. What such a transformation means is the beginning of hope, of dignity, of self-sufficiency for millions of Vietnamese. It appeals to the positive instincts of mankind, not the instincts of fear, hatred, jealousy and aggression. It asks much of the 

Vietnamese people and much of the American people. But it promises even more. It promises the answer to the immortal question, "Papa, Qu'est ce que c'est la paix?"

Mr.

Chairman and members of the Committee 

I sincerely appreciate the opportunity granted to me to present testimony on behalf of the National Association of the Partners of the Alliance (more familarly known as the Partners of the 

Americas) before this Committee.

I have been an active participant in the Partners program since its inception and am currently Chairman of the Board of the Partners. In my Non-Partner life, I am Executive 

Assistant to the Governor of the State of Louisiana and Commissioner of Administration of the State of Louisiana, I have had extensive interests in various business enterprises and organizations.

As you have already mentioned, I am accompanied by Mrs. Francis 

W. Sargent, wife of the distinguished Governor of Massachusetts, who will utilize part of the time allotted to us. Mrs. Sargent is a director and is on the Executive Committee of our organization. I am also accompanied by Frederick Heldring who is President of the Philadelphia National Bank and who is also Treasurer of the Partners and a member of our Executive Committee. 

Last year the Congress included in the Foreign 

Assistance Appropriation Act (P.L. 93-240) a line item of 

$750,000 for The National Association of the Partners of the 

Alliance, Inc. (NAPA), otherwise known as "Partners of the

Americas". This appropriation was made pursuant to the "line item" authorization of $934,000 for each of the fiscal years 1974 and 1975, added to Section 25 (b) of the Foreign Assistance 

Act by Section 7 of last year's Foreign Assistance Act (P.L. 

93-189). This rather unique method of earmarking funds specifically for the Partners of the Americas was apparently made in recognition by the Congress of the contributions being made to international cooperation and understanding by the Partners through the Partners' people-to-people exchange and mutual assistance development programs.

For FY 1975 the Partners are seeking a similar line item appropriation of $825,000 to assist in carrying out its programs. The appropriation, as noted above, has already been authorized in the amount of $9,34,000. 

The programs for the coming year are even more important than they were last year. Secretary Kissinger in his major speech before the Organization of American States enunciated a "Good Partner" policy for Latin America and emphatically recognized the importance of programs of the type of those being carried out by the Partners of the Americas. He specifically called for increased emphasis on professional exchanges designed to link comparable institutions in the two areas and for the promotion of cultural exchanges intended to expand the mutual awareness of each others' cultures. The programs carried out by the Partners on a mutual cooperative basis are directly in line with the goals enunciated by Mr. Kissinger. 

The $750,000 appropriated by Congress last year has unfortunately not been utilized to the extent anticipated since AID had not as of May 15, 1974 made its FY 1974 grant of the funds appropriated last December. Instead, AID during the months of January and February provided funds at a much lower level and during the months of March, April and May provided funds on a month-to-month basis. The failure to make a timely grant as contemplated by the appropriation stems from AID's insistance on the inclusion in any grant of conditions which the Partners have found to be unacceptable and which they did. not believe to have been contemplated by the line item. 1 Among the numerous AID demands which have held up the grant are (1) that no part of the line item funds be utilized for cultural and sports people-to-people activities and (2) that NAPA adhere to the maximum extent possible to AID development criteria and priorities in carrying out its programs. Numerous

other significant items were also endeavored to be imposed on NAPA but these items have now been resolved. Unfortunately, these demands have resulted in the failure to fund the Partners in the amounts appropriated on a timely basis. Such lack of timely funding has tended to curtail the achievement of the intended results and has caused a delay in the implementation of some of the scheduled programs. 

The funds requested for FY 1975 will be used by the Partners to assist in the carrying out of their various programs which result in direct personal contacts between citizens of the U.S. and citizens of Latin America in the areas of agriculture, cultural programs, health projects, rehabilitation and special education projects, including physical education and sports, and cooperative self-improvement projects. Over and above the benefits flowing from such person-to-person contacts, the program also has a material benefit in that for every dollar of U.S. Government support or assistance provided through this program, some $15 or $20 are spent by American citizens acting as individuals. The program is supported, sponsored and carried out by private enterprise. 

Although U.S. Government investmant and involvement is minimal, the dividends in terms of international understanding and in development achievements are great. Background

The Partners of the Americas was established by administrative determination of the Agency for International Development on March 19, 1964, as the private sector component of the Alliance for Progress. The Partners have since that time been fulfilling the purpose of serving as a mechanism through which private citizens of the United States and Latin America work directly together not as donor-receivers, but on

a people-to-people basis, as "Partners" to improve understanding and cooperation in the Americas, while carrying out specific continuing self-help programs of economic, social and cultural development. Since June 30, 1970, the administrative and servicing functions of the Partners have been carried out by the National Association of the Partners of the Alliance, Inc. ("NAPA"), a private organization. As of March, 1974, 41

U.S. State partnerships were paired with 43 counterpart areas in 18 nations of Latin America and the Caribbean.

Activities Partnership projects emphasize the volunteer exchange of technicians and the implementation of programs in such areas as education, sports, medicine, mental health, rehabilitation, agriculture, culture, business investment, creative and performing arts, tourism, environmental protection, and emergency relief. A number of these programs also involve cooperative self-help development programs such as the construction of schools, the improvement of hospitals, the training of technicians, the improvement of communications, and the like. Except for 

NAPA service staff, the thousands of program participants are all volunteers and include educators, businessmen, physicians, students, housewives, agronomists, civic club leaders, and legislators.

The Partners do not work alone. They are affiliated with numerous other volunteer organizations in carrying out joint programs, including the Jaycees, the Lions, the Rotary, 4-H, the American Dental Association, and dozens of others which are listed on APPENDIX A. 

Although these programs cost the U.S. taxpayers only minimal amounts the program has far-reaching results. It is therefore even more important now that this country has become

more sensitive than ever before to large foreign aid expenditures.

This country is also questioning whether money alone Indeed can ever improve our relations with Latin America. 

Secretary Kissinger highlighted this fact in his "Good Partner" speech. In these circumstances, people-to-people contacts and the development of understanding and cooperative undertakings assume a supreme importance. Here the Partners stand as a shining example of what can be accomplished with a relatively tiny amount of government money, coupled with efficient, enthusiastic private volunteers. This success is due to the 

Partners working in consultation and cooperation with their Latin American counterparts in cultural, sport, educational, and health areas and on projects that the Latins want and need and are willing to do for themselves.

Indicative of the success of the program and of the high esteem in which it is held by other agencies of the United States Government and by some segments of AID are the following programs which are either currently underway or have been requested: 

1) Requests for short-term technical assistance from Latin American missions of the U.S. Agency for International 

Development, such as: a) training in highway safety procedures for officials of the Brazilian Ministry of Transport, provided by the State Partnership in Louisiana, Illinois, Michigan and Maryland; b) training in the care and breeding of rabbits as a high-protein low-cost food for rural Panamanian families, provided by Delaware Partners; c) technical services of a geographer to assist in national land-resource conservation and planning in Costa Rica, to be provided by Oregon; d) training in solution to problems of mass transit in Sao Paolo, currently being studied by Illinois. e) suggestion from the USAID Mission in Brasilia to the Partners that discussion be held concerning the possibility of having the 18-state Partner 

TAVAST

such as: framework with Brazi serve as the primary vehicle for technical assistance to Brazil after the planned phase-out of AID activities in 1978. 

2) Requests from U.S. Ambassadors in Latin America, a) a recent request from Ambassador William 

Stedman in Bolivia to provide hospital equipment for the Viedma Hospital in La Paz; b) a direct request from Ambassador Turner 

Shelton in Nicaragua to provide emergency aid to victims of the Nicaragua earthquake in 1972; 

3) The regular use of the Partners framework by the 

Bureau of Educational and Cultural Affairs of the State Depart ment for its international visitor program. Over the past two years more han 200 Latin American leaders from 16 countries have visited their U.S. Partner states through this liaison. 

4) The frequent presentation of community-level projects to the Partners by volunteers of the U.S. Peace Corps, seeking technical and material support from the U.S. Partner state. 

Approximately 50 projects per year originate with Peace Corps volunteers.

There are innumerable benefits for U.S. citizens participating in the program, such as unique opportunities for research and study in tropical agriculture and medicine, archaeology, architecture, Spanish and Portuguese, Latin American history, malnutrition, and mental retardation, to name a few. 

Innovative techniques used in Latin America health and welfare systems have been applied with great success in several U.S. 

Partner states. Cultural exchanges, sports exchanges, and the statewide publication of several high school and elementary school texts by Partner educators about the Latin Partner countries have broadened knowledge about Latin America among tens of thousands of U.S. citizens.

Examples of Projects 

There follow examples of the types of projects carried out by NAPA: 

1) Wisconsin 

Nicaragua Rural Health Project. 

For over 8 years the Wisconsin 

Nicaragua Partners have maintained a continuing program of medical assistance and training on the Northeast coast of Nicaragua. This project which is under the direction of the University of Wisconsin Medical School and the Nicaragua Ministry of Health has not only trained hundreds of physicians, nurses, dentists, and para-medical personnel, but has also served as a meaningful training base for University of Wisconsin senior year medical students. At the request of the Nicaragua Government, the University of Wisconsin has also participated in a complete restructuring of the Nicaraguan rural health delivery system. Nicaragua has gained the benefit of valuable medical training and U.S. medical students have gained valuable experience from being exposed to a totally different medical environment. Both have learned valuable lessons in rural medical systems. This long standing relationship was one of the reasons that the state of Wisconsin went to the immediate assistance of Nicaragua following the disastrous earthquake in Managua in 1972. Utah

the Campesino" approximately 100 miles from La Paz to train several hundred young farmers in basic soil management, livestock production and management, and in general agricultural extension work and, hopefully, thereby to improve the lot of this distressed area. It is expected that the graduates of this institution will participate in the training of the inhabitants of the altiplano in improving agricultural production methods; thereby, improving the standard of living.

Last 

Pernambuco Mass Citizen Exchange. fall, at a total cost to NAPA of only two airplane tickets, nearly 200 citizens selected from all areas of the state of Georgia engaged in a mass exchange via chartered jet with 200 similarly selected citizens of Pernambuco, Brazil. For 10 days all the participants lived in homes in their partner areas and met with their professional colleagues in an exchange that involved not only the 400 participants in the back-to-back chartered flights but also the 400 Georgians and Pernambucans who provided home stays. It will inevitably lead to more extensive assistance being provided by private enterprise and individuals, to increased trade, and most importantly to heightened awareness of basic human needs and to methods whereby assistance can be provided.

Antioquia, Colombia. For many years the Harvard Medical School has maintained a health training and nutrition outpost in rural Apartado, Colombia. 

This effort is directed toward improving the nutrition and health care requirements in Colombia. More recently, the

Massachusetts Partners are acquiring a river craft to trans-

Last year NAPA presented its request for an authorization for a specific line item on two bases; that is, the inability of NAPA to raise funds for administrative purposes and the decreasing funding levels contemplated by AID. 

The Inability to Raise Funds for

Administrative Purposes 

It was pointed out to the Congress that NAPA and the individual partnership committees had been relatively successful in raising funds for particular projects and for particular undertakings but that the corporations and foundations which provide funding to the Partners have been reluctant to provide funds for general administrative purposes and to provide travel funds other than for particular impact projects. This reluctance stems from the desire by corporations to fund projects which have a definite public relations impact in the countries where they operate. In the case of foundations there is a reluctance to provide money for office workers and for non-glamorous overhead undertakings.

This year the situation has improved somewhat in that NAPA has been able to secure some support for its overhead operations.

Even so, this support has been limited in that it has either been ear-marked for an administrative purpose in a particular project area, e.g. agriculture and nutrition, or it has been tied to a specific project, as for example, the sports and basketball programs.

The funds requested for fiscal year 1975 in this bill include $420,000 for administrative support. This compares with $423,000 provided for administrative support for the calendar year 1974, during which year the funds provided last year will be expended.

The argument is made that the Partners have not done enough to help themselves. The prior table of non-AID receipts shows that during FY 1973 and FY 1974 the Partners acheived substantial improvements in fund raising, i.e., $71,573 in FY 1973 and $548,079 in FY 1974 to date.

The 1974 figures include the gift of an aircraft to NAPA which NAPA sold for $265,000 and the grant in the amount of 34-192 O 74-27

$62,000 from the Lilly Foundation which was described above. The funds from the aircraft sale have been set aside, hopefully, as the basis for continuing endowment to be available when AID support is no longer granted. 

The grants which have been received are far from making NAPA into a self sustaining organization but they do indicate a helpful and hopeful trend in that direction. NAPA is making every effort to step up even further its fund raising efforts. 

These efforts include a direct mail campaign and the assignment of a staff member to full time fund raising activities. 

Although it is apparent that progress has been made both in the raising of funds generally and in the provision of private funding for administrative purposes, the results still demonstrate that it is exceedingly difficult to raise funds for unrestricted administrative purposes. This becomes particularly important in view of the fact that the administrative demands of the program are increasing. The demand for volunteer technicians has doubled over the last year and at the same time new states and countries wish to be admitted to the program, which admission obviously increases the administrative burden.

Cultural and Sports Funding 

It was noted previously that one of the principal elements delaying the execution of an agreement with AID this year has been AID's insistence that none of the line item funds be used for sports or cultural activities. This position was taken by AID despite the fact that the Partners' presentation on the line item last year specifically encompassed both sports and cultural programs.

The Partners are convinced that there is neither legal nor policy reason prohibiting them from utilizing AID provided funds for such programs. It is the 

Partners' position that the Congress has given specific endorse-

5 ! ment to those programs in the line item and that those programs are integral to the Partners' operations and, most importantly, are lead-ins to development assistance. 

The Partners were established as, and have traditionally operated as, a people-to-people program based on a Partnership principle, that is, the projects to be undertaken are to be mutually shared and are to be cooperative not imposed. Some 

This of the Partners' most successful projects have been in the cultural and sports areas, as for example, the sponsorship of the travel of prominent U.S. college basketball coaches to 

Latin America to conduct basketball coaching clinics. basketball program has been popular and has developed widespread interest in the Partners and in the United States in the countries in which the clinics were held. Similarly, interest in the Latin 

American countries involved has developed in the home states of the basketball coaches. Indeed there are projects underway to send soccer coaches from Latin America to the United States to conduct soccer clinics here.

A highly successful cultural program is the "Artist in Residence" program whereby the U.S. Partner state, the state university or some other organization in the Partner state accepts a prominent artisan, or performing artist from the Latin American Partner country and sponsors that person as an "artist in residence" for a long period of time. This program results in increased interest in the Partner country and in developing international understanding. 

Even more importantly, however, such programs are a definite lead-in to the development process itself. A tour of a musical group from the State of Oregon sponsored by the Partners to Costa Rica resulted in the establishment of broad scale formal cooperation between the University of Oregon and the 

University of Costa Rica. Such relationship leads directly

into the provision of technical assistance and the provision of development assistance. These results are precisely those called for by Secretary Kissinger in his speech before the OAS, where he specifically enumerated as desirable goals the establishment of cooperative ventures between educational institutions and a broadened cultural interchange. 

The Partners are perfectly willing, and indeed offered to AID, to enter into an agreement that no AID provided funds would be used for cultural or sport programs unless such funds were not available from other current sources. That offer was refused and AID continues to insist on the prohibition against the use of the line item funds for this purpose. 

We in the Partners hope that the Congress will make it clear that it is the intent of Congress that any funds appropriated pursuant to the line item may be utilized for the purpose of carrying out sports and cultural programs. 

Effect of Funding Reduction 

A reduction in the funding of the Partners would have a serious impact on several levels. It is important to remember that NAPA leverages every dollar of the Government's investment.

Dramatic examples can be shown of cases where the cost-benefit ratio exceeds 1 to 140 or 150. On the average over the past several years, for every dollar of U.S. funding there is a U.S. private investment of 10 to 15 dollars. There is also a further increase in benefits from private Latin American contributions, averaging 5 to 6 times the total U.S. benefits not even counting the value of the professional time of the expert volunteer technicians. Thus, on the average, every dollar of U.S. Government investment results in "matching" benefits of $50 to $90.

And, of course, conversely for every dollar of reduction, the benefits are reduced by 50 to 90 dollars. This multiplier effect is critical. It means, for example, that a reduction

of $100,000 could reduce the benefits of the program by $5 million to $9 million! 

Use of the Funds Requested

Of the $825,000 requested it is contemplated that $405,000 will be used for technician travel support purposes and that $420,000 will be used for administrative purposes.

The need for the administrative funds has been demonstrated above. The travel item represents the seed money for the initiation of projects and for the maintenance of the necessary liaison on developmental and people-to-people projects. A pro forma budget of the proposed utilization of the $825,000 is available. 

The Imperative Need for a 

Line Item

A description of AID's funding for fiscal year 1975 has already been given. The $500,000 programmed for the Partprogramming does not mean that the funds will ners by AID 

actually be made available to NAPA 

are totally inadequate for the continuation and expansion of the program. The history of last year's grant does not create any confidence that, if a line item is not provided this year, the program can be sustained at its present levels.
