THE AMOUNT REQUESTED 

Mr. ROEMER. We will not read all our statement but will direct ourselves to a discussion of what the Partners are, where they have been, where they are going, and why we need earmarked funds in the amount of $825,000 for our next year's budget.

As you and the committee members are aware, the Partners are a voluntary organization consisting of 43 partnership committees of some 41 States of the United States and corresponding committees in 

Latin America and the Caribbean.

These committees carry out general projects in numerous fields, including health, education, agriculture, rehabilitation, and other areas.

You will recall that last year a so-called line item was included in the authorizing legislation in the amount of $934,000 for each of the fiscal years 1974 and 1975, and a specific line item appropriation was included in the final appropriation bill for fiscal year 1974 in the amount of $750,000.

For the fiscal year 1975, we are requesting a single line item, sometimes called earmarking, of $825,000 for the Partners. These funds represent a 10-percent increase over the amounts appropriated last year. They do nothing more than cover the inflation which will have taken place over the year and the funding of certain programs which were earlier contemplated but have not yet been carried out. 

THE VALUE OF THE PARTNERS PROGRAM 

Mr. Chairman, although I have a very personal nonpecuniary interest in this program, I am convinced that the Partners is an effective and vital vehicle for promotion of international cooperation and understanding; and through this vehicle, which operates on a basis of mutual cooperation and joint effort, the United States has become better understood in the countries south of the border. 

In like manner, I think in many areas of the United States we have developed an increased consciousness and awareness of the heritage and of the problems experienced by 300 million neighbors south of us. 

Most important of all, the program has engaged in numerous development and technical assistance projects which have a benefit ratio far in excess of that experienced by any other program. 

Our leverage in many such projects runs in the order of 80 to 90 to 1. 

That is, for every dollar of U.S. funds invested, private contributions in dollars in local currencies and in contributed goods and service, amount to approximately $90.

I wish to note in this calculation we do exclude the assigned values of people input. We simply could not estimate that in hard figures. 

This is simply volunteer time.

EXAMPLES OF PROJECTS 

We carry out a vast variety of projects. I think the committee might be interested in a few examples of the type of things we do. This is, in fact, the best testimony of the value of this program.

WISCONSIN-NICARAGUA RURAL HEALTH PROGRAM 

In the State of Wisconsin, we have a program with Nicaragua on a rural health project. For over 8 years, the Wisconsin-Nicaragua 

Partners have maintained a continuing program of medical assistance and training on the northeast coast of Nicaragua. 

This project, which is under the direction of the University of Wisconsin Medical School and the Nicaragua Ministry of Health, has not only trained hundreds of physicians, nurses, dentists, and paramedical personnel, but has also served as a meaningful training base for University of Wisconsin senior-year medical students. 

At the request of the Nicaragua Government, the University of Wisconsin has also participated in a complete restructuring of the Nicaraguan rural health delivery system.

Nicaragua has gained the benefit of valuable medical training, and U.S. medical students have gained valuable experience from being exposed to a totally different medical environment. Both have learned valuable lessons in rural medical systems. 

This longstanding relationship was one of the reasons that the State of Wisconsin went to the immediate assistance of Nicaragua following the disastrous earthquake in Managua in 1972.

UTAH-BOLIVIA VOCATIONAL AGRICULTURAL SCHOOL 

The Utah-Bolivia Partnership has traditionally focused upon the education, medical, and dental needs of the rural impoverished altiplano region of Bolivia.

In an effort to relieve the crushing poverty of the area, the Partnership last year undertook a new program in agricultural training. 

Working in close cooperation with the Bolivian Department of Co operative Extension, the U.S. Agency for International Development, and several local agricultural experiment stations in the altiplano, the Utah-Bolivia Partners have helped establish and build a "College of the Campesino," approximately 100 miles from La Paz, to train several hundred young farmers in basic soil management, livestock production and management, and in general agricultural extension work; and hopefully, thereby to improve the lot of this distressed area. 

It is expected that the graduates of this institution will participate in the training of the inhabitants of the altiplano in improving agricultural production methods; thereby, improving the standard of living.

GEORGIA-PERNAMBUCO MASS CITIZEN EXCHANGE 

Last fall, at a total cost to NAPA of only two airplane tickets, nearly 200 citizens selected from all areas of the State of Georgia engaged in a mass exchange via chartered jet with 200 similarly selected citizens of 

Pernambuco, Brazil.

For 10 days, all the participants lived in homes in their Partner areas and met with their professional colleagues in an exchange that involved not only the 400 participants in the back-to-back chartered flights, but also the 400 Georgians and Pernambucans who provided home stays. The net cost to each traveler was only $250. 

I again point out the net cost to our program was the net price of two airplane tickets.

This exchange has resulted in new projects between Georgia and Pernambuco, in the establishment of new Partner cities, the exchange of medical expertise, and the design of course materials for retarded children.

It will inevitably lead to more extensive assistance being provided by private enterprise and individuals, to increased trade, and most importantly to heightened awareness of basic human needs and to methods whereby assistance can be provided. 

LOUISIANA-EL SALVADOR REHABILITATION PROJECT 

team

In Louisiana, we have many programs, but the technical program that I think is particularly impressive is one that deals with of orthopedic surgeons and prosthetic device specialists who have conducted a 1-week seminar in El Salvador, Colombia, and Costa Rica.

After a 2-week concentrated course on evaluation, diagnoses, and innovative techniques for the physically handicapped, five Louisiana rehabilitation specialists, working with 96,000 physicians and their counterparts and association workers, have completed this course. 

This program now is being implemented, and at the present time we expect in the month of June to send three more teams into the country of El Salvador where they will work with hospitals so as to give a "master's degree" in training to the people who are trying to implement the result of the first program. 

We have now brought to the State of Louisiana and to the LSU Medical School specialists who will receive specialized training as well as two students who are doing their basic research there. 

For the final example, I will ask Mrs. Sargent to give a statement relating to the State of Massachusetts. These are just a few of the many, many programs which the Partners carry out. 

PURPOSES OF THE PARTNERS 

The Partners have a broad base and operate in no less than 41 of the States of the Union and currently have requests for the establishment of new Partnerships in several other States.

The Partners are a voluntary organization embracing people from all walks of life working in cooperation with many voluntary agencies including the Rotary, Lions, Jaycees, and numerous clubs and organizations. Partners is an organization which is endeavoring to achieve two primary purposes.

The first is to develop the friendship and understanding between the Partner Country and Partner State involved and the second is to provide development assistance on a mutually cooperative basis where both the recipient country and the United States are in agreement on the goals to be achieved.

I want to point out that these two purposes go together to create the driving force for continuing success of this program. The Partners should be measured not only by the material parameters but by human values, pride, hope, health and better quality of life for the people involved.

FUNDING FOR THE PARTNERS 

Partners have traditionally received their funding through AID. 

In fact, we were a product effort of AID some 10 years ago. Last year, however, the Congress specifically earmarked funds for our use. Unfortunately, however, the AID grant to us contained in the fiscal year 1974 line item has not yet been executed although we hope to sign it at almost any moment.

This failure while difficult to us is not as disastrous as it could be since although our funds are provided on a fiscal year basis the grants to us from AID have traditionally been on a calendar year basis. 

Nevertheless, we have not been able to move effectively into the new directions and new programs that we contemplated last year and presented to the Congress last year.

We are confident however that the lost ground will be made up as we proceed. We are aware that there is a considerable reluctance within AID and within the executive branch to the use of the line item or earmarking technique.

I might add it is a fiscal difficulty also for the State of Louisiana. 

I am extraordinarily familiar with the difficulty of this type of funding, but where justified, it is a means which I think does serve a specific need.

We believe, however, that we are entitled to some special consideration in that we are an organization which is directly responsible for obtaining the goals which Secretary Kissinger set forth in his major speech before the OAS where he enunciated the "Good Partner" policy. 

Mr. Chairman, you will recall that in that speech he called for increased emphasis on cultural exchange and on the development of operating arrangements between institutions located in the United States and institutions located in Latin America. 

Our organization places specific emphasis on these programs. As set forth last year we have encountered continuing difficulty in raising purely administrative funds from private foundations and corporations. There has been no such reluctance on the part of certain institutions to provide funding to us and to the constituent State partnership for specific projects.

These institutions are reluctant, however, to provide our overhead costs. On the other hand, the amounts proposed to us by AID last year were not sufficient for us to maintain, or increase, our level of operations.

The same holds true for this year. Without the necessary assistance contemplated by our request for a line item we will be faced with decreased activity and possibly an end to our programs. 

CULTURAL AND SPORTS PROGRAMS 

One final word and that is concerning the value of cultural and sport programs.

In our presentation last year we pointed out that a part of our program consisted of programs in the sports and cultural fields. Thus we conducted basketball clinics in Latin America, utilizing some of the most successful basketball coaches in this country who are sent by the 

Partner State to the Partner Country in South America.

Similar programs are being run here and our Partner countries are sending soccer coaches here to conduct such clinics with our people. 

In like manner we have conducted and continue to conduct a highly successful artist in residence program. 

Although these programs are usually funded from non-AID sources such programs have traditionally been included within the ambit of those contemplated by the AID grant. This year, however, AID has taken the position that none of the earmarked funds may be used for this purpose.

This position completely ignores the fact that sports and cultural programs have historically led to developmental and technical assistance programs in voluntary organizations such as ours. 

I would like to point out, just like we do work on an individual partnership basis, we simply do not go to Latin America and direct our fellow partners as to what we think they should do but we join mutually in approving programs and developing areas where we have expertise, which they seek. In reciprocation they have programs to offer to us, including cultural or educational programs which might be meaningful to our people.

We develop programs with mutual cooperation and then proceed to find the resources available within our respective organizations to supply and accommodate that desire. 

It is our hope that Congress will make it clear that the funds provided to the partners through AID can be used for the purposes of our organization including the purpose of promoting sports and culture as seed operations to develop better the uses of our concept. 

I earnestly urge your support of our request for a line item in the amount of $825,000.

At this time I would like to ask Mrs. Sargent to make a statement. 

STATEMENT OF MRS. FRANCIS W. SARGENT PREPARED STATEMENT 

Mrs. SARGENT. I have a prepared statement, Mr. Chairman, which 

I hope may be reproduced in the record.

With your permission, I would like to summarize that statement. 

Senator INOUYE. Without objection, your statement will be made a part of the record. 

[The statement follows:] 

Mr. Chairman, I am delighted to have the opportunity to speak before this distinguished committee. I speak not only as a member of the Executive Committee of the National Association of the Partners of the Americas, but as a citizen of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts who has seen the excitement and commitment generated by the Partners programs.

Four years ago, I personally did not even know where Antioquia was or even that it was in Colombia-and I am sure most people in Massachusetts were no different. Our entire heritage is from the East to the West... we are European oriented, European educated; our Latin American friends just the same. 

But in 1970 all that was changed for me, when I began to work with the Partners of the Americas. Since that time, the Massachusetts committee has received hundreds of students, doctors, technicians, businessmen, sports coaches, musicians, artists, and educators from the State of Antioquia in Colombia. And in return, hundreds, and I would say almost thousands of Massachusetts citizens have traveled to Antioquia, and become our finest ambassadors.

I have met with junior high school kids from one of our inner-city areas, working with our neighborhood youth corps, whose entire lives were changed by a work-study visit to Medellin. 

Before they went, their lives were confined by the poverty and provincialism of their neighborhood. When they returned, their lives had expanded . . . not only with a new vision of family life, but by cultural differences, language, and a comparative vision of society. Now they are all in college, all motivated, all firm devotees of closer relations with Latin America. One day, their views will make a difference. And already their views are making a difference on our local perceptions of the increasing number of Spanish-speaking citizens who are settling in Massachusetts.

This summer, over 105 members of the Greater Boston Youth Symphony Orchestra are going to Medellin, at no cost to NAPA, to live with other musical families, conduct work sessions, and perform concerts. And this visit is at the express request of some of the citizens of Medellin who are eager to develop musical opportunities for school children in their city. And I want to emphasize that point... they requested our help.

This process of independence between two states-one in North America, one in South America-is, I think, a crucial point to realize about the Partners program. We do not tell our sister state what we think they should have; we ask them what they would like. This is a Partnership; a sharing. And we believe that by this cooperation, the image of the "big brother" is dispelled. Let me quote just one of the hundreds of letters that we received from our Partners in Latin America; "The United States," wrote one Latin friend from Brazil, “is perfectly able to sell its products but needs the Partners to 'sell' its image, which is far better than that which the world knows". 

Another friend, from Antioquia, the Partner state of Massachusetts, wrote after we had sent some medical equipment that "for years we have tried to get these supplies, and you were the first people to respond. The people of Santa 

Lucia now know that the people of Massachusetts care about them. Nothing could be more effective in achieving peace and solidarity between our two hemispheres".

We have, in the Partners, been criticized for participating in sports and cultural programs. But I must re-emphasize, Mr. Chairman, we do not make the priorities for our neighbors in the South-we do not tell them that soccer, basketball, music and art are not priorities for us-and that therefore we won't help them. We do not presume so much... we do know how effective sports and culture or any other jointly agreed project can be in creating mutual understanding, respect and an atmosphere where more fundamental problems can be attacked.

This September an exhibition of pre-Colombian gold requested by the Massachusetts Partners will be visiting Massachusetts and numerous other states in the Union, showing to our citizens the artistry and beauty of craftsmen in Colombia. If previous exhibitions of gold are any guide, this show should draw thousands of people-who are then exposed to a view of another culture that they might otherwise never have known. This nation can have all the aid programs in the world, but let me assure you, that the citizen I meet in Massachusetts doesn't know where his tax dollar is going. He has neither knowledge nor interest. But after such an exhibition as this, he will be both interested and possibly willing to become knowledgeable.

And finally, in terms of dollars well spent, there are surely few programs so prudent as the Partners. Most dollars are donated. Most expertise is voluntary. Most equipment is donated. Rarely is a program bigger than those who are sufficiently interested and it is their interest which makes sure that the program is well run and works. Nothing is institutionalized . . . there is no bureaucracy. The criteria for both sides is: can you help . . . do we have it . . . will it work? Obsolescence is never built in . . . programs are always relative and needed. now....

Never have citizens felt the pressure of inflation and taxation more than Partners of the Americas gets $90 in private contributions for every single public dollar spent. . . and untold donations of time and expertise that are without price.

Never have citizens felt so disenchanted about foreign aid. . . Partners of the Americas brings our two hemispheres together so that there are no foreign aid or "foreigners", only Partnerships and "friends".

As the Committee reviews the appropriations for fiscal 1975, I think that you will find that the Partners of the Americas, though a small item, is one of the most effective spokesmen for this nation. 

PARTNERS IS A TWO-WAY PROGRAM 

Mrs. SARGENT. Thank you.

I am honored to have the opportunity to speak before this distinguished committee.

I speak not only as a member of the executive committee of the National Association of the Partners of the Americas, but as a citizen of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts who has seen the excitement generated by the Partners programs. 

Four years ago, I personally did not even know where Antioquia was or even that it was in Colombia, and I am sure that most people in 

Massachusetts were no different.

Our entire heritage is from the East to the West-we are European oriented-European educated. Our Latin American friends are just the same.

But in 1970, all that was changed for me, when I began to work with the Partners of the Americas. Since that time, the Massachusetts committee has received hundreds of students, doctors, technicians, businessmen, sports coaches, musicians, artists, and educators from the State of Antioquia in Colombia. 

And in return, hundreds, and I would say almost thousands, of Massachusetts citizens have traveled to Antioquia, and become our finest ambassadors, a great many at their own expense. 

This summer, over 105 members of the Greater Boston Youth Symphony Orchestra are going to Medellin, at no cost to NAPA, to live with other musical families, conduct work sessions, and perform concerts.

And this visit is at the express request of some of the citizens of Medellin who are eager to develop musical opportunities for schoolchildren in their city. And I want to emphasize that point-they requested our help.

This process of inter dependence between two states-one in North America, one in South America-is, I think, a crucial point to realize about the Partners program. 

We do not tell our sister state what we think they should have, we ask them what they would like. This is a partnership, a sharing. And we believe that by this cooperation, the image of the "Big Brother" is dispelled.

SPORTS AND CULTURAL PROGRAMS 

We have, in the Partners, been criticized for participating in sports and cultural programs.

But I must reemphasize, Mr. Chairman, we do not make the priorities for our neighbors in the south-we do not tell them that soccer, basketball, music, and art are not priorities for us, and that therefore we won't help them.

We do not presume so much-we do know how effective sports and culture, or any other jointly agreed project, can be in creating mutual understanding, respect, and an atmosphere where more fundamental problems can be attacked. 34-192 O 74-28

This September, an exhibition of pre-Colombian gold, requested by the Massachusetts Partners, will be visiting Massachusetts and numerous other States in the Union, showing to our citizens the artistry and beauty of craftsmen in Colombia.

If previous exhibitions of gold are any guide, this show should draw thousands of people who are then exposed to a view of another culture that they might otherwise never have known. 

This Nation can have all the AID programs in the world, but let me assure you that the citizen I meet in Massachusetts doesn't know where his tax dollar is going.

He has neither knowledge or interest. But after such an exhibition as this, he will be both interested and possibly willing to become knowledgeable.

DOLLARS FOR PARTNERS ARE WELL SPENT 

In terms of dollars well spent, there are few programs so prudent as the Partners. Any program initiated is as big as the people interested.

There is no institutionalization, no bureaucracy. 

Never in the history of our Nation have citizens felt more alienated from Government. Partners of the Americas is a one-to-one program, never impersonal.

Never have citizens felt the pressure of inflation and taxation more than now. Partners of the Americas gets as much as $90 in private contributions for every single public dollar spent and untold donations of time and expertise that are without price.

Never have citizens felt so disenchanted about foreign aid. Partners of the Americas brings our two hemispheres together so that there is no foreign aid or foreigners, only partnerships and friends.

As the committee reviews the appropriations for fiscal 1975, I think that you will find that the Partners of the Americas, although a small item, is one of the most effective spokesmen of this Nation.

CORRECTED STATEMENT 

Mr. ROEMER. Senator Inouye, I have a corrected page I would like to submit for the record to the written testimony we gave. It is a page with some figures. The zeros were left out of some figures. That might be misleading. 

[STAFF NOTE: The following comments on Mr. Roemer's testimony were furnished to the subcommittee by the Agency for International Development and will be inserted in the record at this point:] 

1. Mr. Roemer's statement identified Secretary Kissinger's speech before the

Atlanta meeting of the OAS General Assembly as having "emphatically recognized the importance of programs of the type of those being carried out by the 

Partners of the Americas."

Mr. Kissinger's remarks were related to different kinds of programs, involving close contacts between planning and other officials, scientists, technologists, etc. 

Mr. Kissinger did not mention the Partners. 

2. Mr. Roemer criticized A.I.D. for "failure to make a timely grant as contemplated by the appropriation. ." He attributed this failure to "A.I.D.'s insistence" on the inclusion of conditions unacceptable to the Partners. 

The delay was due to a failure on NAPA's part to produce basic budgetary information which A.I.D. had repeatedly requested. A.I.D. was willing to move ahead on the grant, even with certain issues unresolved, and did so. Only during 

January and March were funds transmitted at a lower level than was contemplated. The Congress would surely not wish A.I.D. to forego sound bsuiness and management practices, and agree to a grant arrangement in the face of inadequate information, just to assure that NAPA received an equal amount of money each month. 

3. Mr. Roemer refers to A.I.D. "demands" and endeavors by A.I.D. to "impose" 

items on NAPA. 

A.I.D. has indicated to NAPA what it understands to be the Congressional consensus concerning the priorities on which A.I.D. funds should be used. It has also suggested development goals and criteria which it believes NAPA should seek to achieve and meet. It has set forth what it considers to be reasonable and responsible reporting requirements. These matters have been presented to, and discussed with NAPA, in a constructive, give-and-take series of negotiations, during which A.I.D. made several accommodations to NAPA. It is erroneous and misleading to refer to these matters as "demands" or "imposition." 

4. Mr. Roemer, in arguing for A.I.D. funding of NAPA's administrative expenses, states that "Congress, in providing a line item, had specifically taken into consideration NAPA's prior inability to raise funds for administrative purposes."

It is neither clear that Congress considered this issue, nor that it was reflecting any judgement on it by providing a line item. The legislative record shows that other points were stressed by supporters of a line-item appropriation, revolving around the attractions of the program, rather than NAPA's "prior inability to raise private funds for administrative purposes." "The 5. Mr. Roemer stated that "despite the Congress' authorization of $934,000 for fiscal year 1975, A.I.D. now, unilaterally, without consulting the Partners, proposes that the funding be reduced to an initial level of $500,000 amount to the Partners shown in A.I.D.'s FY 1976 program is $250,000." 

In view of the legislative history that calls for an end to A.I.D. funding for 

NAPA after 1976, A.I.D. has frequently requested NAPA to propose a schedule of phase-down in A.I.D. funding. NAPA has never responded to this request. 

Accordingly, in preparing A.I.D.'s presentation to the Congress, a schedule of $500,000 for FY 1975 and $250,000 for FY 1976 was proposed, as an orderly approach to the termination of A.I.D. funding. These figures were discussed with 

NAPA along with efforts to stimulate NAPA to develop a responsible financial program, including the establishment of annual fund-raising targets. Thus, A.I.D. has consulted with NAPA on this question, and has sought its collaboration on developing financial plans consistent with the legislative record. NAPA's cooperation in this area has not been forthcoming.

6. Mr. Roemer suggested that a reduction in A.I.D. funding could reduce the benefits of the program by 50 to 90 times the reduction-e.g., a reduction of $100,000 could reduce the program's benefits by $5 million to $9 million. 

This "arithmetic" assumes that a reduction in A.I.D. funding automatically means a reduction in program outlays. It neglects the hopefully-more-than offsetting funds to be raised from the private sector. Further, its "logic" would suggest that when A.I.D. no longer funds NAPA, the program would have zero benefits. Again, what seems to be involved here is a refusal by NAPA to accept the Congressional intention for NAPA to become self-sufficient and for A.I.D., in the next few years, to terminate its funding. 

7. Mr. Roemer states that the $500,000 programmed for fiscal year 1975 "are totally inadequate for the continuation and expansion of the program." 

In calendar 1973, NAPA raised $136,000 from non-AID sources (not counting the proceeds from the sale of an airplane which it has decided not to spend for the present). Together with the $450,000 of available A.I.D. funds (including a $50,000 carry-over from the previous year), this meant a resource level for 1973 of $586,000.

For 1974, Congress appropriated $750,000 which even with a modest estimate for private fund raising, would put resource availabilities at around $1 million. 

One of the reasons NAPA said it sought the Congressional line item last year was to make it possible to put itself in a position to become self-financing. Thus, if 

NAPA implements what it described were its reasons for seeking a large expansion in A.I.D. funding, a considerable sum will be spent in 1974 on private fund-raising efforts.

In 1975, if the Congress appropriates A.I.D.'s proposed figure of $500,000, these resources, together with private and other non-A.I.D. funds could result in resource availabilities of $800,000 or more, which would represent approximately a 40% increase above the 1973 program. (How it would relate to a 1974 program remains to be seen, depending upon how much is spent on fund raising.) 

Thus A.I.D.'s proposal for FY 1975 clearly allows for at least a continuation of program trends and, if NAPA does effective fund raising, would make possible an expansion of the program. 

1. Mr. Roemer requested an $825,000 line item for FY 75, to "represent a 10% increase over the amounts appropriated last year" to cover the inflation and "the funding of certain programs which were earlier contemplated but have not been carried out."

The request for an increase is in direct contradiction to the Congressional mandate from last year's legislative history that A.I.D. funds should cease after 

1976. Given this mandate and the increasing level of funds NAPA is receiving from private sources, it would be poor management for NAPA to allow itself to become increasingly dependent upon A.I.D. as the end of A.I.D. funding approaches. 

2. Senator Inouye asks "how long will the Congress be called upon to provide appropriations for administrative purposes" in light of the fact that when NAPA was established, it was understood that the original appropriation was seed money and that NAPA would finance itself in Senator Inouye's words, “in a short while."

Mr. Roemer's response was not entirely clear but he ventured the opinion that the time will come when this program will be self-sufficient. However, he did not foresee this result "by 1976, 1977." The point should be made that financial self-sufficiency is not obtained by seeking more and more funds from A.I.D. The incentive to raise funds from the private sector and the need to do it would be sharply diminished if NAPA were to receive the same or a higher level of funding as last year. (In fact, NAPA's approach to the Congres raises questions as to its intentions to become self-sufficient and as to the vigor with which it is pursuing its outside fund-raising.) 

3. Senator Inouye requested a list of NAPA employees and the payrolls for '73, 74, and '75 fiscal years. because "last year we know that your director received a salary which exceeded that of any of the A.I.D. employees with the exception of the Administrator and the Deputy Administrator "When one considers that your director receives a greater sum than the Saigon administrator who has to administer millions of dollars. I was outraged, to be very honest with you."

Mr. Roemer said that he understood the Senator's concern. It should be noted that NAPA's director's salary was increased without any consultation

with A.I.D. NAPA took this action internally, apparently seeking only the advice of its legal counsel as to the legality of the proposed increase salary level. When A.I.D. learned of what occurred, only during the process of acquiring long-delayed budget data from NAPA, steps were taken to assure that A.I.D. funds would not be used to fund the director's salary at a level above the ceiling for most U.S. Government employees. 

It should also be noted that NAPA has been reluctant to give A.I.D. specific salary data and, as of June 3, 1974, A.I.D. still does not have a complete salary schedule for all NAPA employees.

SEAN-135 he

Mr. Chairman and Members of the Subcommittee:

I am Benedict J. Kerkvliet, a professor of political science at the 

University of Hawaii and currently, for 1973-74, a Fellow at the Woodrow 

Wilson International Center for Scholars here in Washington. I am speaking today on behalf of myself and an organization of concerned Filipinos and Ameri cans called Friends of the Filipino People (FFP). 

We have been following closely events in the Philippines since President Ferdinand Marcos imposed martial law and curtailed all civil liberties in that country. I, for example, lived in the Philippines from March 1969 through 

November 1970 while doing research on peasant movements there, especially the Huk rebellion (1946-1954). And since then I have studied political developments in the Philippines and other countries in Southeast Asia, partly in connection with my teaching and my own research. My studies and those of others in the Friends of the Filipino People and organizations with similar interests have caused us to be alarmed at trends in the Philippines. We fear increased repression and violence under the present martial law regime. And we fear that the United States will continue to contribute directly to this repression. 

We want the United States government to show to the world this year that it will no longer continue to support military dictatorships. 

We want the United States to end all military and military-related assistance to the Marcos regime, the newest dictatorship in Southeast Asia. If the Administration of President

Richard Nixon fails to stop this aid, then we want at least the 93rd Congress of the United States to refuse to appropriate any more money to the martial law regime in the Philippines.

The basis for this position is the following argument. First, the martial law regime in the Philippines is a repressive one. Repression and abusive government practices have been major themes in the country's politics during the last one and one-half years. They far exceed whatever shortcomings the country had prior to martial law. Second, repression and abuses have provoked Filipinos from many different backgrounds and political orientations

to resist, often rebel. Rebellion is more extensive than before martial law. 

Third, the response of the Philippine government, in turn, has been more repression and further militarization of the government and the entire society. 

Fourth, this military apparatus, including the country's enlarged armed forces and modernized national police, is heavily dependent upon the United States. 

Whether or not Congress has approved, the United States government is perpetuating this dictatorship and its repressive policies. This not only makes a farce of our democratic principles and heritage, but it could easily drag the United States into another. "Vietnam" type of war in Southeast Asia. prospect scares me to death, and I should think that it would millions of other Americans and Filipinos, too. That

Political Repression in the Philippines Since September 1972, the Republic of the Philippines has been under martial law. This country, which once was widely known as America's "showcase of democracy" and one of the few countries in the Third World to have any semblance of democracy, has become a dictatorship. The dictator is Ferdinand 

E. Marcos, who is both President and Prime Minister of the Republic. so far.

The laws of the land under martial law are the Presidential Decrees, Letters of Instructions, and General Orders that only President Marcos or his own ministers can issue. He has proclaimed over 440 Presidential Decrees 

He has destroyed the legislative and judicial branches of government, silenced the press, ordered the arrests of thousands, and mobilized the military. 

One of President Marcos's first acts after declaring martial law was to dismiss the Philippine Senate and House of Representatives. political parties and cancelled all elections, including his own. and final, term as President should have ended December 1973. 

He banned all 

His second, He arrested prominent Senators and several delegates to the Constitutional Convention, which was then in session. These persons had been Marcos's political enemies and outspoken critics of the militaristic tendencies of the Marcos administration prior to martial law.

He also destroyed the previously independent judicial branch. General 

Order No. 3, which Marcos issued the first day of martial law, disrobes the court by excluding all acts, decrees, and other orders of Marcos or his representatives from judicial scrutiny. Also excluded are criminal cases involving such issues as "national security, ""the fundamental laws of the State," and 1 "public order."! He added four members to the Supreme Court, appointing persons known to be loyal to him. Then, as a journalist recently wrote, "to seal the collapse of the old independent judiciary, President Marcos not only squeezed resignation letters from all judges down to the Court of First Instance level (presided over by district judges); he also made sure the nine carry-over 2 Supreme Court justices took new oaths of office under his Constitution." 

President has also formed "military tribunals," one or more for each military region of the country, to try both civilian and military cases involving "crimes" against the government. The

The Marcos government was not content with simply cancelling all elections. It has wanted to give the appearance of free choice, especially for the benefit of the outside world. It has called, therefore, two referendums; one to approve a new Constitution, which allowed Marcos to stay in power indefinitely, and the other to approve the programs of the "New Society." For these referendums, the Marcos regime created "Citizen Assemblies" throughout the country. People had to vote in public, frequently in the presence of armed police, and with government officials coaching them on the "correct" ballots. 

As the highly respected Bishop Francisco F. Claver wrote recently, Probably the single most resented aspect of martial law (and this is true among the privileged as well as the underprivileged classes) is the loss of freedom of choice at the polls. 

The past two referendums have been unparalleled farces, a fact that is not lost on even the regime's staunchest supporters. For a people used to turning out of office unpopular administrations in the past through the instrumentality of the free ballot, having to vote according to 'suggested answers' is the ultimate indignity. The people feel the insult deeply, but they also realize they are not going to achieve anything in open demand for their rights. 3 1

The New Society prohibits the civil liberties of the "old society." As one recent study concluded, "... there is no freedom of the press, no freedom of speech, no freedom of assembly, no freedom from arbitrary arrest, and no 4 guarantee of a fair trial. " Where there were 15 or 20 daily newspapers before martial law, there are only three now -- all of them strictly controlled by the government, and one of them with close ties to President Marcos. The number of radio and television stations has similarly declined. All media must abide by the government's rules of censorship. These rules prohibit any criticism, let alone any dissent, of government policies and the President himself. "The media report virtually nothing but praise for the Marcos administration," wrote 5 one scholar. A correspondent remarked, as others have, "Manila's press after martial law counts among the dullest and most obedient in the world. " 6

Media people must adhere to government censorship lest they lose their licenses, be imprisoned, or both. Since martial law, the government has imprisoned numerous journalists, publishers, and broadcasters. At least one of them has been tried on charges of "subversion," and sentenced to several years of hard labor. Under martial law, "subversive literature" is, as Maryknoll priests told a Washington Post correspondent last November, "any article even mildly critical of the regime even articles from magazines such as 

Time or Newsweek "1 .... 

The government has banned from the country at least nine issues of Time, for example, because they had stories containing criticism of Marcos's policies. The government has outlawed strikes, political organizations, and unauthorized political meetings. "Strikes are a luxury we cannot afford in the 'New Society'," said Alejandro Melchor, the Executive Secretary to Marcos.

The regime has also dissolved labor courts and imposed compulsory arbitration in order to suppress labor and peasant unrest that had been common prior to martial law. Peasants, who comprise nearly 75% of the population, can only form associations that have the government's approval. In most localities the government has outlawed chapters of the two largest peasant organizations

prior to martial law, the MASAKA (Malayang Samahang Magsasaka, or Free 

Farmers Union) and the FFF (Federation of Free Farmers).

Fear and force are principal means the government uses to get compliance and obedience. Both the censored Manila newspapers and the foreign press report numerous police raids and mass arrests. During the first three months of martial law, the Philippine Constabulary (PC) stated that 8,261 persons had been arrested. After one year of martial law, the government admitted that it had arrested or, in the government's language, "detained" 10 11,697 persons. The figure must be far above that now because arrests and police raids have continued unabated in the eight months since last September. 

A common practice of the specially trained "Metrocom" (Metropolitan Command) police attached to the Philippine Constabulary is to surround an entire neighborhood, usually at night, force everybody out of their homes, and arrest people who look suspicious. These are called "zona" raids, named after the similar methods of the military during the Japanese occupation in World War II. In recent months, the police have focused especially on intellectuals and clergy. In December, for example, the PC raided the Baguio City branch of the University of the Philippines and arrested 150 professors and students. The PC released some of them a short time later, but they took the others to a PC prison or "detention center" for interrogation and imprisonment. Among the prominent persons recently arrested are Dr. Nemesio Prudente, former president of the Philippine College of 

Commerce in Manila; Attorney Charito Planas, a critic of martial law and a former delegate to the Constitutional Convention; and Lorenzo Tañada, Jr., a media executive and son of former Senator Tañada who has been a lawyer for several of those people arrested during martial law. 11 As for the clergy, the government has raided convents, church schools, church universities, and private homes in order to arrest ministers, priests, and nuns. At least 22 priests and nuns had been "detained" as of November 1973, according to a

New York Times report. By now the number is larger because the government, angry with those in the Catholic Church who continue to criticize the military for its abuses and martial law in general, has quickened its drive 12

against the clergy despite military assurances earlier that arbitrary arrest of Catholic clergy would stop. 13 Frequently, people arrested are never charged with a crime. People suffer, as priests in one Philippine province recently protested, "arbitrary arrests and acts of harassment on [grounds of] mere suspicion of so-called subversive activities. 1114 

Others, such as Baldomero T. Olivera, a former press secretary to a late Philippine President, are arrested for "rumor mongering, a punishable crime according to Presidential Decree No. 90.15 "Anyone who utters any criticism automatically becomes an enemy of the State, "' reported Professor John M. Swomley, Jr., after returning from a visit to 16 political prisoners in Manila. Still others are accused of specific crimes, including "subversion," but languish in prison for months without trial. From time to time, the government releases "detainees," after they agree to endorse the New Society and to report regularly to assigned police and military officers. 

Others, however, have been in prison for months. 

Senators Jose Diokno and

Benigno Aquino, Jr., for instance, have been in prison since the first day of [1 martial law. They still have not yet been formally charged. Their only offense seems to be that they were strong critics and threatening political opponents of 

Marcos prior to martial law.

Inside the prisons, government authorities often abuse the prisoners. 

A peasant whom the PC arrested, for example, fought the guards at the "detention camp. " The guards, in turn, electrocuted his penis. He had fought the guards in the first place because the reason he had been arrested was because he had tried to get the landlord to follow the rules of Marcos's land reform 17 program. A former prisoner wrote that many of those people arrested for subversive activity never make it to prison; "often as not, they are killed at the time of their capture by ambitious military men anxious to report 'battle' victories."

Those who escape murder "are taken to secret apartments and at times to military camps where they are squeezed for information through the use of a wide range of crude to sophisticated torture techniques. 18 In mid 1973, 27 priests reported .in a joint letter that they had documentary proof of men who had been "killed in

19 jail even before their guilt could be investigated and established. A pastoral letter of Sulu and Mindanao priests read to hundreds of congregations on Easter Sunday 1974 protested, "That some detainees, according to a growing number of reports, have been subjected to torture in violation of the United Nations Declaration of Human Rights, yet there are no signs that steps are being taken to correct ,,20 this.

A study in November 1973, based on a survey of key informants throughout the Philippines, found that, "There are frequent reports of physical torture from all regions of the country. The families and relatives of prisoners are [also] kept under surveillance. 21

Outside the prison, too, military officers and other government authorities abuse civilians and continue practices of corruption and favoritism. In the provinces, people report that military authorities get away with everything from murder to stealing funds from relief projects to siphoning gas from civilian 22 trucks into their own vehicles. A study of all regions in the country found, for example,

In the cities of Central Luzon, the 1st PC Zone Command protects gambling and houses of prostitution. In Cebu and Eastern Visayas, the 3rd PC Zone Command protects smuggling and vice, which are reported to be much worse now than before martial law. From 

Zamboanga del Norte, there are many reports of crimes committed by the military against defenseless Muslim civilians. In Mindoro, the PC are accused of land grabbing from the Mangyans (a tribal group).

The study concluded that instead of controlling the abuses of local politicians, who are by and large the same people as before martial law, the military in most of the eleven regions of the country are party to the abuses. There is a marriage of convenience from which both military and politicians profit. The ordinary people are the ones who suffer. There is no one to defend their rights. 

No one to whom they can appeal their grievances. They are intimidated, fearful. They have no recourse from either the abuses of 23 the military or the politicians, and abuses are common. 

A lawyer for recent refugees from heavy fighting in Sulu province said, "The efforts of the President to establish his New Society by martial law have failed because despite the various decrees, • • • the people are still suffering from want, fear, corruption, and iniquitious treatment from the people who have been 1124 charged with carrying out his presidential orders.

Since martial law began, the Marcos regime has increased its budget for propaganda from 3 million pesos to 68 million pesos ($10 million) in order to sell 25 the New Society both at home and abroad. But appearance of reform is not enough, not when repression is so harsh and the "reforms" themselves so empty. 

As a Wall Street Journal reporter wrotė a year ago, "Despite a few promising indications, his [Marcos's] 'New Society' remains more a matter of public relations than of profound reforms. Its momentum, moreover, 1126 sagging. seems to be

Land reform, for example, which Marcos has said repeatedly should be the only guage of success or failure for the New Society, has so far been a failure. And it shows every likelihood of continuing to be so because it excludes most tenant farmers, while those who are affected will probably end up as poor as they were before martial law. Corruption continues, even at the highest levels of government. The major difference is that corrupt 27 28 military officers have replaced some of the corrupt politicians. 

The widely advertised claim that "crime in the streets" is wiped out appears to have been only a temporary reality. Even the government censored press reports more stories of crime now than it did a year ago. Last October, the Department of 

Defense admitted to a delegation of Catholic bishops that the crime rate was on the rise and was fast approaching pre-martial law proportions. 29 30 Other

Those who have benefited from martial law include the foreign investors, particularly large American, Japanese, and multinational corporations. beneficiaries include Filipino political and economic elites. Talk about redistribution of wealth and undermining the wealthy families notwithstanding, the martial law regime has not posed a threat to the elite as a whole. Only a few of the oligarical families have lost some wealth and political clout. They did because they were political enemies of Marcos, who took his revenge once he had acquired so much power by virtue of martial law. Marcos and his family have benefited, too. 

Reputed to have been the wealthiest man in Southeast Asia before martial law, Marcos must be one of the wealthiest men in Asia now. He is also, in effect, President for life--or for as long as he can hang on to the position.

Growing Resistance and Rebellion 

Social, economic, and political conditions in the Philippines were bad before martial law. Since then, they have become in several respects even worse. But now Filipinos have far fewer legal options in order to express their discontent. The result, almost inevitably, has been increased illegal actions, resistance, and even armed rebellion. The authorities characterize the people who do these things as "subversives," " "communists, and "Maoists." If there is any truth at all to this, it accounts for only a small number of people. 

It is the government--its repressive policies and bad economics--that is provoking people to resist and to rebel. 

Take wage laborers, for example. 

Inflation exceeded 30 percent last year and it is still climbing; unemployment is increasing; employers lay off workers in violation of their contracts; and corporation executives connive with government officials to ignore minimum wage and other labor laws. 

The result is that workers want the right to strike. But the government continues to refuse. 

Some workers have publically protested and gone on strike, anyway, risking imprisonment or even death. The PC and local police have arrested many of the workers' leaders. 31

Squatter families, who compose one-fourth to one-third of Manila's population, have been organizing for years in order to protect themselves against forced eviction and government abuses. Now, under martial law, the evictions have been stepped up on order to make way for the regime's "beautification 11 projects, yet the squatters can no longer demonstrate or hold rallies. But because the situation had become so serious late last year, several hundred people dared to march toward the President's palace to protest "the government's violation of an agreement that no squatters would be ejected beyong the sixmeter distance from the Manila Bay shoreline." The PC's Metrocom police confronted the squatters, forced them to disperse, and arrested several leaders. 

The next week, the Metrocom raided the homes of those in the squatters' "ZOTO" organization and arrested more leaders. 32

5 

Presidential Decree No. 33 prohibits the "printing, possession, distribution, and circulation" of leaflets, handbills, papers, graffiti, or any other materials 33 that might "incite" people or criticize the government. Despite this decree and the prison sentence it carries, "underground" papers and leaflets continue to appear in increasing numbers. Many university people who were active in numerous nationalist organizations prior to martial law have now resorted to secret meetings and surreptitious methods in order to collect information and publish news that never gets into the government censored press. They do this despite the fact that police and the PC arrest and imprison people for these "subversive" and "communistic activities.

Meanwhile, there is considerable evidence that the number of groups prepared to fight in armed rebellion is increasing. One group, called the Filipino 

Freedom Fighters, pleaded with Marcos in a publically circulated letter last

September to lift martial law. When his term of office under the pre-martial law 

Constitution expired at the end of 1973, the Freedom Fighters stated that Marcos, in their view, was no longer the legitimate president and warned that force may be necessary in order to oust him. The Freedom Fighters reportedly include lawyers, professors, students, some libertarian-minded wealthy families, and even some disgruntled officers in the Philippine military.

In the countryside prior to martial law, organized rebellion was confined mainly to the small New People's Army in parts of the Cagayan Valley and Muslim rebels in parts of Mindanao. But since martial law, organized resistance and rebellion have appeared in most regions of the country. Reports from the Manila the and foreign press show armed groups have clashed with/Philippine military in several provinces in the following regions: Ilocos, Cagayan Valley, Central Luzon, Southern Luzon, Bicol, Western Visayas, Eastern Visayas, Mindanao, and Sulu-virtually every part of the country. The province of Pampanga in Central Luzon, for example, had a clash last October for the first time in over four years between d "insurgents" and the PC, 34 Armed rebels are also appearing again in other areas, such as Bulacan and Nueva Ecija, where the peasant-based Huk rebellion had been strong in the 1940s and 1950s. 35 The island of Panay in Western Visayas, 34-192 - 74-29

has become, according to another report, "a vertiable powder keg, " with 200 or more well armed rebels scattered across the three provinces there. The rebels reportedly 36 have considerable village support. Many students from universities in Manila and other cities have gone underground to join peasants in armed rebellion in different parts of the country. Prior to martial law, these students and peasants had been active in student political organizations and peasant associations. 

Martial law has banned these groups. A study last Fall noted, for example, that many of the approximately 100 armed rebels in Davao Oriental and Davao del Norte (in Mindanao) were young people who had been active in the "Khi Rho" before. 

The Khi Rho was a Catholic youth group that worked especially with peasant associations. Another report tells of four rebels whom the PC recently killed. 37 One had been the secretary-general of the SDK, which was a legitimate student political organization prior to martial law. Another had been the editor of the 

University of the Philippines student newspaper. Two more had been "campus 38 activists." Several priests and nuns, too, have joined armed peasant groups to prepare for armed rebellion. 39 Although the number of rebels may still be small and the degree of cooperation among these various groups may be weak, the rebels seem to be growing in strength 

and even in cooperation. Reports recently have said that the various underground groups within the "Christians for National Liberation" are making a "united front" with other underground groups and the so-called "Maoist" New People's Army. 40 

The New People's Army, too, seems to be larger now than it was when Marcos declared martial law in September 1972. A news report on a province in the Bicol région said, for example, "No more than a communist toehold before the imposition of martial law, this southern tip of Luzon has developed in the 16 months since September 1972 into what appears to be a solid spreading base of the . . . New People's Army. The NPA has taken hold of 

Sorsogon because it is rooted in the community. Its leaders here are former student activists, born here, and former Marcos political opponents led by a former local mayor. 41 The Philippine army has said that the number of "Communist regulars" has increased during martial law from 1, 710 to 2, 266. 42

Although the government characterizes most of these rebels and other "subversives" as "communists" and "Maoists," this is not a fair description, as I have tried to indicate here. A few may be communists, such as some of those in the New People's Army. But most people are doing things that the government considers illegal, including armed rebellion, first, in order to protect themselves against repression, and second, to work for improved conditions in their country. Most of these Filipinos would prefer legitimate channels of criticism, dissent, and protest, but martial law has closed those off. 

The situation reminds me very much of the conditions in which the large peasant movement in Central Luzon in the 1940s became a strong peasant rebellion that lasted until the mid 1950s. This was the Huk rebellion. Peasants had not wanted to take up guns to fight for economic justice and against the police and landlords' violent practices. But because of officially sanctioned repression beginning in 1945 and 1946, peasants had to fight back. They were forced to rebel. The government and US authorities at that time, too, called the Huks a "communist" rebellion. But it was not. 43 One would think that government officials would have learned better over the years since then. 

The largest and strongest rebellion during martial law thus far has been the Muslim movement in Mindanao and Sulu, the southern extreme of the Philippines. 

The Marcos regime has been terribly anxious to portray the Muslim rebels as "Maoists."

It is in the Marcos regime's interests to do this, first, in order to keep Muslim countries, upon whom the Philippines depends for most of its oil, from accusing the Philippine government of waging a genocidal war on Muslim brothers. 

Second, the Marcos government knows that the United States government is more likely to help in the counter-insurgency if the insurgents are "communists" and "Maoists."

But the Muslim rebellion is far more complicated than communist subversion. "The . . charge--that the rebels are 'Muslim Maoists'--remains the best illustration, among many, of the Manila [government] failure to see itself, or the problem, as Muslims see it, " wrote Harvey Stockwin, a close observer of the situation. "The rebels are no nearer reconciling Maoism to

Islam than are, for example, Sabah's Tun Mustapha or Libya's Colonel Moammer Kadaffi!44

The first complication is that there are several Muslim rebel groups, not just one. They do not want exactly the same thing and they are not under one unified leadership. Second, the current rebellion among Filipino Muslims is part of a long history of trouble between this minority group and the central government in Manila --whether under the Spanish, Americans, or Philippine Republic --and the Christian Filipino majority. The issues go way back: Muslim identity, landownership, and independence or at least an autonomous Muslim state. 45 Although fighting between Muslim rebels and the Philippine military occurred off and on during the 1960s, it was martial law that pushed an even larger number of Muslims into full-scale rebellion. One important reason was the increased presence of the Philippine military itself. The military's reputation is extermely bad among Muslims, and as the military started to exercise its new power under martial law, it easily angered these people. A second important reason was the government's demand that all citizens turn over their weapons to the military. Because Muslims have so frequently had to resort to weapons to protect themselves from the encroachements of Christian Filipinos and the central government, this demand was tantamount to surrendering their only means of selfdefense. This was all the more so in a martial law situation since other legitimate grievance channels were blocked.

From the earliest months of martial law until now, the rebellion has been gaining momentum among people in several provinces in Mindanao and in the province of Sulu. According to numerous reports, the rebels controlled much of Sulu. In January and February, the government decided it could no longer tolerate this and launched a series of heavy attacks. 

Military Force and Militarization

On several occasions last year, the Philippine military used airpower, naval bombardment, and heavy assaults against Muslim rebel positions in Mindanao and Sulu. A few months ago, in February 1974, the government put

their full might behind a sustained attack on Muslim rebels, numbering between 400 and 2,000, who had moved from the countryside to take control of the Muslim city of Jolo in Sulu province. It had been a city of 150, 000 people. After- 46 wards, according to a Manila newspaper, it had only 20,000 people. 

The city was in ruins, said a New York Times reporter; "it was acres of charred rubble and blasted concrete, from which bodies were still being recovered ... more than a week after the Philippine armed forces finally took Jolo back from the 47 

Muslim insurgents." 

Another reporter said that Jolo was 90 percent destroyed. 49

Between 1, 000 and 2,000 people were killed. The government's air force had bombed and napalmed the city, its navy had bombarded it with heavy artillary, and its army had fielded 5,000 heavily armed soldiers. This was, in Philippine military language, "a mailed fist approach" to end the rebellion. After the battle, the Marcos regime's Secretary of Defense, Juan Ponce Enrile, reflected on the method: "We should have taught these people a lesson a long time ago. 

We have been too easy on them. They must be forced to give up this foolish idea 50 11 of dismembering a portion of our country." One Muslim rebel told a foreign correspondent, "The [Philippine] army's aim is genocide, to wipe out all Moros [Muslims] and take our homeland. Why? Because Sulu is rich. Oil in the sea, crops, prestige for President Marcos's Manila Government. 

But Sulu [and] the greater islands of Mindanao and Palawan are Muslim lands, and we will 51 die to keep them." 52

Since the large battle in February, the Philippine military has continued what it calls "sanitizing operations" against Muslims beyond the ruins of Jolo. 

Several thousand Filipino refugees, both Muslim and Christian, try to find shelter and food in Zamboanga, Cotabato, Basilan, and other places. The Prime 

Minister of Malaysia recently reported that in his country alone, on the island 53 of Sabah, there were 22,000 Filipino Muslim refugees. But reputable observers say that rather than bringing the war to a halt, the government's military methods have strengthened the Muslim rebellion. As one foreign correspondent wrote recently about Jolo's destruction, "First, and last, it has increased the polarization between Christian and Muslim in the Southern Philippines .... 

Some of 48

the younger [Muslims] inevitably feel that joining up with the rebels is the only way out.

There are numerous swirling cross-currents, eddying all the more because of Jolo. They add up to vicious, gathering, circles of fear and suspicion, hatred and violence." 54 Other government military attacks similar to the one on Jolo have occurred during martial law. In October 1972, for example, a military commander in 

Northern Luzon forced 50, 000 Filipinos to move just as they were preparing to harvest their rice crops.

The commander said he wanted to "sanitize" the area with a "big military operation. " It was an area where the New People's Army was strong. "Everyone who remains in the area is NPA," General Tranquilino 

Paranis is reported to have said as he prepared the attack. Martial law, he added, had helped to persuade local government officials to cooperate with this military method. 55 I fear that government attacks like this, the one in Jolo, and other repressive methods will continue in many parts of the Philippines as the government continues to militarize and resort to large scale violence in order to rule. 

A major theme in Philippine politics under martial law has been militarization. Previously, the military played only minor roles. Now it has the center of the stage. In terms of size, for example, the military numbered between 60,000 and 65, 000 when Marcos declared martial law in September 1972. 

By late 1973, government news reports said that the Philippine military was 

The Marcos regime 

56 about 80,000. By May 1974, the number was 100,000. 

Some of the new plans that by mid 1975 the military will number 256,000. recruits will be volunteers, but the majority will be draftees. For the first time in the Republic's history, it will have a national draft. 

Military expenditures, too, are way above previous amounts, and they continue to rise. Although the regime's budget has been secret, one report said that, "a number of economists believe that military expenditures are far 57 ... more substantial than the level authorized in the pre-martial law budget." 

These military expenditures were a major cause for last year's record deficit 58 of 1.2 billion pesos ($150 million).

T Under martial law President Marcos has given this growing military organization increased powers in nearly every aspect of government. Several provinces have had Philippine Constabulary and Philippine Army colonels and generals for governors. In most regions, military officers are in charge of the important Regional Offices for Development, which supervise, among other things, public works and parts of the land reform program. 

Marcos has also made military officers responsible for the management of the Manila Electric company, a steel mill, and other companies that the regime took from rival political families after martial law. And there are the new military tribunals mentioned earlier that try civilians accused of certain crimes against the state. 

In addition to the military itself, there is the national police system. 

The National Police Commission, which was established a few years ago, is now making steady progress in bringing all of the country's 1,500 police departments under one integrated police system. The chief of the National Police 

Commission is the Secretary of Defense, Juan Ponce Enrile. As the police departments are integrated, the Philippine Constabulary will take control and supervise all police functions. In this way the integrated national police forces will 59 come under the Philippine armed forces. Accomplishments of this integration program thus far include, for example, unification of all police forces in metropolitan Manila, centralized data banks and communication systems for police work throughout the country, and training schools for all policemen and police chiefs. The Marcos regime has also released special funds to raise the salaries 60 and add fringe benefits for policemen throughout the country. This comes at a time when wages for most Filipino workers have been declining. 

Another important part of militarization is the government's efforts to watch or, as government reports say, "monitor" people. One part of this is the expanding role of several security, investigation, and spy agencies. In addition to enhancing the role of the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) and the National Intelligence Coordinating Agency (NICA), the regime has created related organizations, such as the Civil Intelligence and Security Agency (CISA).

The job assigned to CISA is to gather intelligence information on students, teachers, professors, and non-academic personnel at schools and campuses across the 61 country. Another method to keep track of people is the compulsory registration system that the regime has begun. This system requires, according to 

Presidential Decree 278 issued in August 1973, that, "... all citizens of the republic... shall be assigned a reference number and issued a national reference 

Citizens or nationals of foreign countries resident in the Philippines card .... shall likewise be assigned" a card to serve as "the official identification of the 62 person to whom it is issued. " These numbers and the registration information, together with the centralized computer system that will store the data, will help the government to track down criminals, subversives, critics, and complement its other surveillance methods. 

American Support

When President Marcos declared martial law, the US Embassy in Manila and the State Department in Washington had "no comment." Since then 

US diplomatic officials have avoided a categorical endorsement of martial law But by its actions, the United States does support President in the Philippines.

Marcos's regime and apparently it plans to continue to do so. arrested

For example, when the Philippine Constabulary and other police forces thousands of civil libertarians, prominent Senators, and other critics of Marcos's government during those first weeks of martial law, the United States Navy's Naval Command helped. It provided information to the Philippine police that led to the arrest of Filipinos and Americans who had been providing 63 legal services to American GIs there. More significantly, US military and economic assistance has continued even increased. Aid under the Military 

President Nixon's

Assistance Program (MAP), which had been going down since the mid 1960s, is now going up again. MAP aid increased from $14 million in FY 1972 to $15.7 million in FY 1973, and to $18.9 million in FY 1974.

Administration this year is asking for $17.9 million for FY 1975. On several occasions, US Ambassador to the Philippines William H. Sullivan has assured the Philippines that US assistance will continue, To the Marcos government

and its supporters, this assistance, which exceeds $100 million per year, constitutes both support and approval of martial law. For instance, a report in a government censored newspaper said when the US Senate voted last year for more assistance that, "In effect, the Senate action in committee constituted an unmistakable approval of the New Society being established in the Philippines 64 by President Marcos. " Another government censored newspaper said in its editorial, "In the case of the Philippines the US Senate action constitutes ... an unmistakable approval of the new order. It was held in US circles that affairs here are our own concern and that there are no indications that martial 65 law has endangered democracy in the Philippines." 

What is so disturbing is that aid from the United States has been the main source of money, materiel, and technical assistance for the buildup of the military apparatus in the Philippines over the years. Now, US economic and military aid have born fruit a dictatorship that relies increasingly on 

its military, which in turn relies heavily on more aid from the United States. 

It is hardly the kind of legacy that one would expect the oldest democracy in the world would like to leave.

The modernized police forces, including the Philippine Constabulary's infamous Metrocom, has raided hundreds of homes, arrested thousands of Filipinos, interrogated them, and collected dossiers on suspected "subversives" during martial law. This police system is, in large measure, the result of US AID's "Internal Security Program. So far the program has spent nearly $3.5 million of US taxpayers money.

According to the Executive Branch last 66 year, AID is reviewing the program "for possible increase in funding.!!

The program, according to AID, has achieved most of its original objectives. The 

Philippines now has facilities to train 4, 000 policemen per year; it can give advanced training to some of these police 

including training at such US counter-insurgency centers as Fort Bragg and the John F. Kennedy School for Special Warfare;

35 of the planned 55 police communications networks have been

installed;

and Philippine municipalities have developed a coordinated records 67 system.

Put into other terms, the program can take credit for such achievements as the ID card system now under way; the arrest of over 12,000 persons held in new "detention centers," and 1, 500 modernized police departments in which many policemen have the latest American riot guns, walkie-talkies, and patrol car computer consoles. 68 US AID continues to help the Marcos regime train and equip its police forces and integrate them under the command of Philippine Constabulary. Last year, Secretary of Defense Enrile thanked "our friends from the United States

Agency for International Development" for their assistance for police training when he spoke to a graduating class of the new Police Commission Academy. 

Just recently US AID gave the police department in Angeles City, Pampanga, 10 new motorcycles with radios (previously the department only had 2) and 15 69 jeeps with two-way radios. US assistance for "narcotics control, 11 too, seems to be helping the Marcos regime build a police state.

According to Liliosa Hilao's relatives, the PC officers who arrested her molested her at her home, then tortured her to death at Camp 70 Crame.

The principal justifications over the years for US assistance to the Philippine military have been to protect American bases and business interests and to help the Philippine government fight "communism" and "insurgency." 

Just last year, for example, Admiral Thomas H. Moorer, chairman of the

Joint Chiefs of Staff, told Congress during hearings on US military assistance,

Economic growth of the Philippines... has been slow and is still insufficient to permit the country to meet its full military requirements. This is particularly true in the face of the current insurgency. The people of the Philippines require assistance to modernize their armed forces and their constabulary. The security assistance material program amounting to $19. 3 million and $3 million FMS credit are designed to provide mobility, firepower, and communications---the three basic elements required to combat insurgency forces. 76

It was because of the "insurgency problem" in the Philippines last year that the Nixon Administration asked for more US military and military-related assistance to the Philippines for FY 1974.

During martial law, the Philippine military and police have continued to rely almost exclusively on weapons, materiel, and other US assistance in order to suppress growing dissent and rebellion. In order to combat insurgency, Admiral Moorer said, the United States supplied the Philippines in 1973-74 with "helicopters and transport aircraft, machine guns, recoilless rifles, and other weapons, together with long-range communication equipment. 

The Pentagon said last year that in order to help Marcos regime "cope with the current situation," the US military has been "moving up the delivery dates of some of the equipment most urgently needed by the Philippine Armed Forces--such as, M-16 rifles and UH-1H helicopters.... In addition we are ... providing the Philippines C-123K aircraft to help provide greater inter-island mobility."

Since the rebellion in Mindanao and Sulu has been the strongest one ,78 77 this past year, the importance of American weapons systems has been particularly noticeable in fighting there. When the Philippine armed forces bombed and attacked the city of Jolo in February for example, they used howitzers, .50-cal. machine guns, F-86 Sabre jets, C-47 gunships, armed helicopters, and naval 79 batteries---all supplied by the United States. The Philippine Air Force not only dropped US supplied bombs and fired US supplied machine guns, but they also dropped US supplied napalm. In other battles, too, according to a Filipino 80 consul in Honolulu, the Philippine armed forces has used napalm.

Surplus supplies from Vietnam, which were supposed to be used for peaceful purposes, and at least some US economic aid also went last year to the Marcos regime's counter-insurgency efforts. A New York Times correspon-

dent reported that during heavy fighting against Muslim rebels in 1973, the Philippine military used "crates of supplies, some adorned with the red, white, and blue handshaking label of the United States Agency for International Develop- ,81 ment."

Last October, an American official in Manila admitted that the Philippine air force had misused some planes that the United States had given to it from Vietnam surplus. Rather than using the planes for development projects, the air force mounted machine guns on them to battle Muslim rebels and to ferry 82 troops between the islands.
