In addition to US money and supplies, there are indications that American military personnel are also involved in helping the Marcos regime to suppress rebellions. If so, it would not be the first time that Ame rican troops have assisted the Philippine armed forces in counter-insurgency. example, the Philippine Constabulary asked the US Air Force at Clark Air Force Base to give helicopter support for a PC raid on "Huk insurgents," to do aerial photography in connection with counter-insurgency, and to provide transportation and communication services to Filipino officers directing counter-insurgency 83 operations.

One example of US military personnel directly involved with the Philippine military's operations is the assistance General Louis H. Wilson, commander of the United States Fleet Marine Force Pacific, has given. According to a 

Manila newspaper, Marcos awarded General Wilson the Philippine Legion of Honor "for his work in developing the Philippine Marine brigade.... Among other things, General Wilson led US Marines on joint exercises "with the Filipino marines without cost to the Philippine government to keep the marines abreast of developments in amphibian warfare. 84 In this context, it is important to remember that Filipino marines and "amphibian warfare" have been important during the campaigns against Muslim rebels, whose strongholds exist on several southern islands.

Another example of US military personnel helping the Marcos government with military and counter-insurgency is the work of US Army Green Berets. 

Over the last two years, the Green Berets have done "civic action" in many provinces. Some provinces are known to have rebel groups, such as the provinces of Iloilo and Capiz in the Visayas region, Zambales, Bataan, and Pampanga in Central Luzon, and Nueva Vizcaya and Isabela in Northern Luzon. 

The Philippine government and US military admit that the Green Berets are there; they say their purpose is to help build schools, distribute medicines, dig wells, and other "civic action" projects. American officials have added that the Green Berets are also in the Philippines for "training exercises. " 

Both American and Filipino officials deny that the Green Berets give military support to the Philippine government. But the underlying purpose of these 1185 Green Beret exercises appears to be counter-insurgency. Major J. Brunner, a Green Beret spokesman, told one reporter, "The Special Forces achieved a tainted image through Vietnam, as spies, killers, bayonet baddies. We're trying to change that image. " By conducting civic action with Filipino soldiers, he said, "you can build up the image of respectability of the host country's forces, and another Vietnam can be avoided. " But a Filipino priest and other 

Filipinos interpreted the Green Beret's presence slightly differently. The priest told the correspondent, the Americans are "getting smart. They're getting to know the terrain where the resistance is operating, trying to poison the water before the guerrillas get to swim in it. 1186

The Green Berets were on Panay. confirmed by very reliable sources.

There are several other disturbing reports. One is a newspaper's story from Manila last November that a United States Air Force helicopter crashed in a village of Nueva Vizcaya, a province in Northern Luzon. 88 The immediate question, of course, is why was the helicopter flying over that area?

2 That province reportedly has had some rebellion. Another report comes from a person who works in the Marcos government. He claims that he saw a film, taken by Filipinos working with a government agency, that shows uniformed 

American soldiers with Filipino soldiers fighting in Mindanao and Sulu a few months ago.

A related report comes from an American Air Force officer who, until recently, was stationed at Clark Air Force Base in the Philippines. He claims that it is widely known at Clark that American pilots flew American planes in bombing missions over Mindanao last year. 

Conclusion and Recommendation

Democracy and civil liberties are dead in the Philippines. The Marcos regime is a dictatorship. Resistance and rebellion, as a consequence of worsening conditions and political repression, are growing. And the Philippines is developing into a military state. These things are clear from what has happened since martial law.

It is also clear that the United States, through its military and militaryrelated assistance, has contributed immensely to sustaining the Philippine military before martial law. Today it continues to help the Marcos regime build an even larger military apparatus. If Congress appropriates more of the American taxpayers' money to give military or military-related assistance to the Philippines for FY 1975, that money, too, will further support the dictatorship. For this reason, the Friends of the Filipino People (FFP) and I recommend that Congress appropriate no military or military-related assistance for the Philippines. This year is an excellent opportunity for the United States 

Congress to draw the line. It can say now, before the situation in the Philippines becomes worse, that it will no longer be party to the growth of another antidemocratic regime.

V We further recommend that Congress conduct a thorough investigation to find out exactly what American military or para-military personnel have done or are doing in the Philippines. I have presented evidence that American

military personnel seem to be helping the Marcos government's counterinsurgency efforts. I have also reported what I have been told, but have not been able to verify positively, that American personnel in fact are directly involved in counter-insurgency there. This situation is reminiscent of the 

1950s and 1960s when there were many hints and unconfirmed reports that the US government was directly involved in counter-insurgency in Vietnam. Today we have similar hints and reports about the Philippines. And there are other similarities that seem ominous: Civic action missions, which the US government tried earlier in Vietnam, have reappeared now in the Philippines. The Philippines' national police system is an outgrowth of AID's internal security program in Vietnam. And William H. Sullivan, an architect of the US government's

Vietnam policy in the 1960s and the ambassador to Laos who coordinated the bombing of that country, is now the US ambassador to the Philippines. 

This time, hopefully, Congress and all other Americans will learn the truth of the matter before it is too late---before an American President presents a fait accompli and says Congress must appropriate much larger amounts to support "our boys" or "our commitments" in the Philippines. 

Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman and members of the Subcommittee.

EFFECT OF MARTIAL LAW RULING 

Mr. KERKVLIET. I will simply summarize the major emphasis that 

I would like to draw to the attention of the committee at this time. 

Following me Mr. Russell Johnson, representing another organization, is similarly concerned. 

We have been following closely events in the Philippines since President Ferdinand Marcos imposed martial law and curtailed all civil liberties. 

I, for example, lived in the Philippines from March 1969 through November 1970 while doing research on peasant movements there, especially the Huk rebellion-1946-54. 

And since then I have studied political developments in the Philippines and other countries in Southeast Asia, partly in connection with my teaching and my own research. My studies and those of others in the Friends of the Filipino People and organizations with similar interests have caused us to be alarmed at trends in the Philippines. 

We fear increased repression and violence under the present martial law regime. And we fear that the United States will continue to contribute directly to this repression. 

We want the U.S. Government to show to the world this year that it will no longer continue to support military dictatorships. We want the U.S. Government to end all military and military-related assistance to the Marcos regime, the newest dictatorship in Southeast Asia.

The basis for this position is the following argument. First, the martial law regime in the Philippines is a repressive one. Repression and abusive government practices have been major themes in the country's politics during the last 11½ years. They far exceed whatever shortcomings the country had prior to martial law. 

Second, repression and abuses have provoked Filipinos from many different backgrounds and political orientations to resist, often rebel rebellion is more extensive now than before martial law. 

Third, the response of the Philippine Government, in turn, has been more repression and further militarization of the government. 

Fourth, this military apparatus, including the country's enlarged armed forces and modernized national police, is heavily dependent upon the United States. Whether or not Congress has approved, the 

U.S. Government is helping to perpetuate this dictatorship and its repressive policies.

Since September 1972, the Republic of the Philippines, once known as America's "showcase of democracy," has become a dictatorship. 

Since he declared martial law, President Marcos has ruled by presidential decree. He dismissed the Philippine Senate and House of Representatives, banned all political parties, and canceled all elections. He destroyed the previously independent judicial branch and has instituted military tribunals to try civilians accused of crimes. against the government.

Because of martial law, there is no freedom of press, no freedom of speech, no freedom of assembly, no freedom from arbitrary arrest, no guarantee of a fair trial. Nor are workers allowed to strike or demonstrate.

The police and the armed forces have arrested over 12,000 peasants, workers, students, journalists, civil libertarians, nuns, priests, ministers, political opponents of Marcos, and other who criticize. 

One Presidential decree makes "rumor mongering" a punishable crime. Anyone who utters any criticism automatically becomes an enemy of the state. Inside the prisons, the police and soldiers have tortured and killed prisoners.

Outside the prisons, military officers and other government officials abuse civilians and continue practices of corruption and favortism. 

The Filipino people are still suffering from want, fear, corruption, and unequal treatment from the people who have been charged with carrying out Marcos' Presidential orders.

Economic and political conditions, which were bad before martial law, have since become worse. But now Filipinos have far fewer options in order to express their discontent. The result has been increased illegal actions, resistance, and even armed rebellion. 

The reaction, in turn, of the Marcos regime, is more repression. A recent example was the Philippine military's attack in February against Filipino Muslim rebels in the province of Sulu. It resulted in the destruction of Jolo, a city of 150,000 people. Between 1,000 and 

2,000 people died.

The government's air force bombed and napalmed the city and countryside, its navy bombarded the area with heavy artillary, and its army fielded 5,000 heavily armed soldiers. This was, in the Philippine military's language, "a mailed fist approach" to end the rebellion. 

Since that battle the military has continued what it calls "sanitizing operations" against the rebels.

A central theme in Philippine politics under martial law has been militarization. Whereas previously the Philippine military played only minor roles, it now has the center of the stage. Military officers are active in nearly every aspect of government. The military's numbers have also grown, from 65,000 men in 1972 to 100,000 men now. 

By mid-1975, the Marcos regime plans that the military will number 256,000.

What is so disturbing is that aid from the United States has been the main source of money, material, and technical assistance for the buildup of the military apparatus, over the years. 

Now, that U.S. assistance has born fruit-a dictatorship that relies increasingly on its military, which in turn relies heavily on more aid from the United States.

The Philippine national police system, for example, is in large measure in result of U.S. AID's internal security program. This 

AID police program can take major credit for such things as the citizen registration and ID card system now underway in the Philippines, the arrest of thousands of Filipinos held in new detention centers, and 1,500 modernized police departments in which many policeman have the latest American riot guns, walkie-talkies, and patrol car computer consoles.

Today AID continues to help the Marcos regime to train and equip its police forces and integrate them under the command of the Philippine constabulary.

U.S. assistance for "narcotics control," too, seems to be helping the 

Marcos regime build a police state. The Philippine constabulary's

anti-narcotics unit, which receives U.S. aid, is known to arrest suspected critics and "subversives" in Manila. 

In at least one instance, the arrested person, a young Filipino named Liliosa Hilao, died while detained at the anti-narcotics unit's building at Camp Crame-the PC headquarters in Quezon City. 

According to Liliosa Hilao's relatives, the PC officers who arrested her molested her at her home, then tortured her to death at Camp Crame.

Both the police and Philippine Armed Forces rely almost exclusively on weapons, materiel, and other U.S. assistance in order to suppress growing dissent and rebellion. 

Last year, for example, the United States supplied the Philippines with such things as helicopters, transport aircraft, machineguns, recoilless rifles, and longrange communication equipment in order that the Marcos regime could, in the words of one Pentagon spokesman, "cope with the current situation." 

During the battle at Jolo in February, the Philippine military used howitzers, .50-caliber machineguns, F-86 Sabre jets, C-47 gunships, armed helicopters, naval batteries, bombs, and napalm-all supplied by the United States.

Surplus U.S. supplies from Vietnam, which were intended for peaceful purposes, have also gone into the Marcos regime's counterinsurgency efforts. So have some supplies from U.S. AID. 

U.S. Army Green Beret units engaged in "civication" and training exercises in the Philippine countryside also appear to be involved in the counterinsurgency. There are reports of still other American military personnel who are directly involved with the Marcos regime's counterinsurgency.

The conclusions and recommendations we reach, therefore, are these: It is clear that the United States, through its military and military-related assistance, has contributed immensely to sustaining the Philippine military before martial law. 

Today it continues to help the Marcos regime build an even larger military apparatus. If Congress appropriates more of the American taxpayers' money to give military or military-related assistance to the Philippines for fiscal 1975, that money, too, will further support the dictatorship.

For this reason, the Friends of the Filipino People and I recommend that Congress appropriate no military or military-related assistance for the Philippines. This vear is an excellent opportunity for the 

U.S. Congress to draw the line. It can say now, before the situation in the Philippines becomes worse, that it will no longer be party to the growth of another antidemocratic regime. 

We further recommend that Congress conduct a thorough investigation to find out exactly what American military or paramilitary personnel have done or are doing in the Philippines. There is evidence that American personnel seem to be helping the Marcos government's counterinsurgency efforts.

In my full testimony, I present reports that American personnel, in fact, are directly involved in counterinsurgency there. This situation is reminiscent of the 1950's and 1960's when there were many hints and unconfirmed reports that the U.S. Government was directly involved in counterinsurgency in Vietnam.

Today we have similar hints and reports about the Philippines. And there are other similarities that seem ominous: Civic action missions, which the U.S. Government tried earlier in Vietnam, have reappeared now in the Philippines. The Philippines' national police system is an outgrowth of AID's internal security program from Vietnam. 

William H. Sullivan, an architect of the U.S. Government's Vietnam policy in the 1960's and the Ambassador to Laos who coordinated the bombing of that country, is now the U.S. Ambassador to the Philippines.

This time, hopefully, Congress and other Americans will learn the truth of the matter before it is too late before an American President presents a fait accompli and says Congress must appropriate a much larger sum to support "our boys" or "our commitments" in the Philippines. 

Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman and members of the subcommittee. 

Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman, and perhaps Mr. Russell 

Johnson should follow me.

Senator INOUYE. I would like to ask a few questions before proceeding to the next witness.

You have indicated that AID is at this moment providing assistance to the police system?

Mr. KERKVLIET. According to reports in the press which has recently as I believe, I think I footnoted in my testimony, I think it was last month, it showed a picture of equipment, particularly motorcycles and jeeps. It said that this latest equipment has come with the assistance of USAID.

This is to build up a police force in the town of Hongosa area by the way which has been in rebellion now. 

Senator INOUYE. Last year at the initiative of this subcommittee we closed down the activities of the public safety program. It is true that in the past AID through the public safety program provided assistance in equipment, training, motorcycles, and small arms. 

But your suggestion is that it is still going on? 

Mr. KERKVLIET. Yes. 

Senator INOUYE. If it is, it is in violation of the law. 

Mr. KERKVLIET. Yes; Mr. Chairman, I would assume so. According to these reports and not only this particular newspaper report but information I have been told by friends in the Philippines this kind of assistance is continuing. 

Senator INOUYE. We will check on this.

As to the communication system which the U.S. Government assisted in setting up in the Philippines, this is not provided for military purposes per se but to bring together the major island in a communication chain. We have done this in many countries where communication systems are faulty and as a result the Government was not able to keep in touch with activities in outlying areas. 

I suppose any system such as our telephone could be used for military purposes, although one would assume that our telephone system is primarily for domestic and private purposes. 

On the matter of military involvement I am certainly aware that last year, of the full appropriations for the military assistance program, approximately $18 million was for credit sales. It is still $18 million, but one should compare this with what has been granted in

the areas; this is one of the small appropriations made by the U.S. 

Government to any foreign government. 

Mr. KERKVLIET. I realize it is small in comparison to other countries, Senator, but we also have to think in terms of its meaning for the 

Philippine military, think in terms of their budget? I don't know whether we have recent information but as recently as 1971, as you are probably aware, the General Accounting Office in a report for the Congress showed that in the neighborhood of 80 percent of all Philippine military expenditures for administrative purposes, not saying anything about the arms and weapons that it needs, 80 percent was supplied from U.S. military assistance.

That means that roughly 20 percent as of 1971 was coming from the Philippine sources to pay their salaries and other administrative expenses and the other from the United States. 

We have ample evidence even from the Pentagon, as recently as last year's testimony before this committee, that ammunition and other supplies for strictly military purposes rely almost exclusively on the United States. The point is that even though it may be small in relationship to other countries it is very crucial assistance to the continuation of the military in the Philippines in terms of the Philippine Government. That is our concern. 

Senator INOUYE. Your concern is the concern of all of us here. I can assure you that your statement will be forwarded to the appropriate officials of the executive branch for their comments.

I would like to receive their views on your findings and suggestions. 

Thank you very much. 

Mr. KERKVLIET. You are welcome, thank you.

STATEMENT OF RUSSELL JOHNSON PREPARED STATEMENT 

Mr. JOHNSON. Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the opportunity of speaking at the same time as Professor Kerkvliet because my testimony perhaps will augment what he has delivered to you based upon my own personal experience 2 weeks in the Philippines in February 1974.

I have submitted a brief statement to the committee. I hope that will be published.

In the interest of saving time I would like to touch lightly on the major points. Senator

INOUYE. Without objection your full statement will be made a part of the record, sir. 

[The statement follows:] 

119

My name is Russell Johnson. I am a staff member of the American Friends Service 

Committee, by whom I have been employed for the past twenty-five years. From 1961 to 

1965 I served as director of the Committee's international conference and seminar program in South and Southeast Asia. I became at that time acquainted with nationals of the region with whom I have kept in touch through repeated return visits, the most recent of which occurred in January and February, 1974, including visits in South 

Vietnam, Cambodia and the Philippines.

I am especially concerned about developments today in the Philippines. Since 

September, 1972, there has been a martial law regime under Pres, Ferdinand Marcos in power, with repression of democratic process. The inequities between the elite minority and the majority of the people, urban workers and rural masses, continues to grow, aggrevated by spiraling inflation. Three kinds of insurgency threaten the regime: a full-scale Muslim rebellion in the southern islands, a Maoist New Peoples 

Army in the northern islands, and increasing resistance from militant Catholic and 

Protestant Christians. It

Foreign investment has been encouraged by the martial law regime and American business and banking corporations are taking advantage of the incentives offered. is now estimated that US investment is approaching the three billion dollars mark. 

Clark Air Force base and the Subic Naval base are the largest of the American military installations there. I cite these factors to indicate the size of the US stake in the islands, as compared with what it was in South Vietnam when I first visited that country in 1961: 1500 advisors, no bases, no investment. 

From the moment when we arrived in Manila, February 11, 1974, until our departure? two weeks later, we heard rumors of American military involvement in the counterinsurgency activity of the Philippine armed forces. It was not possible for us to pin down these reports in direct experience. In an hour and one half interview, the 

American ambassador William Sullivan denied to me that there is any such US direct involvement. The Civic Action teams are in the Philippines only for training purposes, he explained.

On the day before we left, a friend of ours, an American clergyman now working in the city of Manila, came to our hotel with his wife to share with great urgency the gist of a conversation he had had the night before with a corporal in the Philippine navy. I welcome the opportunity of sharing that testimony with you, even though it is not my own eyewitness account. It is essential that American citizens learn what is really going on before we find our nation more deeply involved militarily. 

From my experience elsewhere in Southeast Asia, I am convinced that the present insurgencies in the Philippines will grow and that military and police power will not suppress them.

The corruption in the upper levels of the martial law regime is widely known within the islands. Because of the great American economic and military stake in the country, the danger of direct American military complicity grows day by day. US military assistance to the Marcos regime shields it from its own people and makes the likelihood of armed revolution all the more certain. 

Report of a conversation held February 24, 1974, in Manila, Philippines, between a Corporal in the Philippines Navy and (name deleted), regarding U.S. involvement in the war in Mindanao.

Biographical background of the Corporal: about twenty years of age, native of (name deleted), son of a retired (deleted) of the Philippine Army. He is assigned to a supply (ammunition) boat operating between Manila, Mindanao and the Freedom Islands (Sprattly) which are located halfway between the Philippines and Vietnam. He confirmed the increased fighting in the Sulu area, particularly Jolo Island where several thousand RP army. Muslim "rebels" and civilians have been killed during the past few weeks. He stated that women and children are being shot as rebels they are bearing arms and shooting at government troops. All Muslims in the Mindanao area are labeled by government leaders as "traitors" and are to be shot. In one case a brigade of 28 army men were attacked and all beheaded by "rebels". He spent time in the Jolo area about three months ago. He has been involved in transporting by RP Navy ship ammunition and weapons from Freedom Islands to Mindanao a trip taking about 3 weeks by ship. Such supplies are 

USA supplies from Vietnam directly. He stated that the RP army needed these supplies in order to continue the war: "Filipinos killing Filipinos," he said. He also stated that 

US troop ships are being used for transporting RP army and marine troops to the Jolo area but since they are too big to land the troops, Philippine Navy boats are used to transport troops from US ships to land. These same big US ships are shelling "rebel held" positions in the Jolo area. This confirms reports from other areas that US ships. have shelled NPA (New Peoples Army) positions on Luzon.

The US Air Force from Clark Air Base is also being used in the Muslim War in Mindanao. US planes are bombing Muslim held positions. Not just conventional bombs are being used but also napalm, in an effort to deforest the jungle positions of the Muslims a job that is being finished by USA flame-throwers. US planes based at 

Clark Air Force Base, Angeles, Luzon, are also assisting the war by transporting weapons and ammunition from Luzon (Clark AFB) to Cebu City airport and even to Zamboanga City Airport (Mindanao). He stated, however, that most of the US supply planes are unloaded in Cebu for the final leg of their journey in Philippine Air Force planes (gifts of USA).

He was asked about the wounded men and their treatment. Philippine army, navy and air force personnel wounded are taken to Luzon (Manila mainly) for treatment. 

USA army, airforce and navy personnel wounded are taken to Freedom Islands where a US hospital had been set up to treat Vietnam casulaties. 

When asked about bombing of civilian centers in the Sulu area, he confirmed that such orders had been carried out. He stated that the usual practise was to warn civilians to vacate a town, barrio or area by a given time and to go to a designated place, on board a ship sometimes. If the civilians did not go, were held as hostages by the Muslims or refused to evacuate their homes, the orders to bomb and shell were carried out. Recent reports and pictures in the Manila papers confirm the almost complete destruction of Jolo. It is the policy of the RP government army that if threatened with being overrun by the rebels they are to attack and destroy the town. 

This was specifically in relationship to the army installation in Jolo. Those orders and the complete destruction of Jolo with the loss of civilian lives has been completed by the Philippine army and marines. 

The naval corporal, when asked about his training, states that all "reservists" called up are given training in Bataan, Luzon. He said his instructors were all 

Filipinos who had been trained by the USA military, some in the US and others in Luzon. He said that all of the books and materials used in the training were in 

English property of the US Army. Conclusion (of the American clergyman). US involvement in the war in Mindanao and the conflicts throughout the Philippines today is direct as well as indirect. It is channeled through Clark AFB and Subic Naval Base. It is being directed probably by the Joint Philippine/US Military Strategic Planning Council, Quezon City, Manila. 

It could not be happening without State Department knowledge, Pentagon and White House approval and knowledge and Ambassador Sullivan's knowledge. 

The war in Sulu and Mindanao is accelerating, as are the activities of NPA and other "rebels" in the Visayas and Luzon areas of the Philippines. Such areas are now described as "red hot". The Philippine army, navy and air force are on "red alert" status. The Corporal justified the war as a conflict being supported by Germany, Mainland China and Muslims. He stated that no "foreign" troops have ever been found in raids on rebel positions but that German-manufactured "double barrelled armour-piercing rifles" have been found in rebel caches. The public report on such weapons is that they come to the Muslims from Libya. The China "Maoist" support is not confirmed but Muslims are being described in Manila papers as "Muslim-Maoist rebels". Such terms are calculated to keep US involvement which protects the Philippines "for democracy" as the naval corporal put it. I have seen US military jets in Cebu and Catobato as well as amphibious carriers, weapons, etc. all U.S. manufactured. I have watched US military in battle dress board elevators in nice hotels in Cebu City. A second hand report came to me that a priest in central Mindanao watched Philippine army personnel unload automatic reifles from cartons clearly marked "CARE" package. US direct support and indirect assistance to the present Philippine Government is at the same level it was in South Vietnam before the US publically committed troops and bombs to support South Vietnam (the Saigon regime). I feel a strong responsibility to help the American people become aware of this situation. It cannot be allowed to continue.

PHILIPPINES A.LD. PUBLIC SAFETY AND NARCOTICS CONTROL ASSISTANCE TESTIMONY BY BENEDICT J. KERKVLIET OF MAY 24, 1974 

In his testimony before the Senate Subcommittee on Foreign Operations, Mr. Benedict J. Kerkvliet stated that the A.I.D. Public Safety program has aided the martial law administration in the Philippines and that the A.I.D. Narcotics 

Control project assistance is being misused for political and military purposes. 

The A.I.D. Internal Security Project in the Philippines was started in FY 

1968 to help the civilian police force in the priority areas of training, communications, records systems and administration. This project has resulted in the establishment of several police training academies, a uniform crime statistics reporting system, improved police management and administration procedures, and communications networks in fifty-five of the nation's provinces. The communications system, while set up for civilian police use, has been utilized primarily by other government agencies and provincial offices and has been essential in linking the distant parts of this island nation, especially during times of floods, typhoons and other natural disasters. This project had been extended one year until FY 1974 in order to complete the communications system. All but one police adviser will be phased out by June 30, 1974. The remaining communications technician will leave in August 1974.

The A.I.D. Narcotics and Dangerous Drugs Control Project, which began in 

FY 1972, is designed to assist the Philippine Government in the control of narcotics production and trafficking in the Philippines. A.I.D., working in coordination with the U.S. Drug Enforcement Agency, is providing technical advice, commodities and training to Philippine Government agencies concerned with the nationwide program of narcotics and dangerous drugs control. A.I.D. assist ance to the Philippine Constabulary Anti-Narcotics Unit (CANU) is restricted to the narcotics enforcement team and is in addition to the aid given to civilian narcotics agencies under the same project. According to the terms of the project agreement, this assistance is not related to military activities and careful checks have been made and are continuing to be made to insure that this assistance is not diverted to military purposes.

We have no information regarding the unfortunate death of Miss Liliosa Hilao referred to in Mr. Kerkvliet's statement. We requested any information available on this matter from the A.I.D. Mission in Manila. However, given the restricted nature of the A.I.D. narcotics control assistance, it is very difficult to see any relationship between this tragic occurrence and the U.S. economic assistance program in the Philippines. 

[STAFF NOTE.-The following information was subsequently sup plied by the Agency for International Development on July 10, 1974.]

DEATH OF MISS LILIOSA HILAO 

Pertinent Philippine Government documents relating to the death of Miss Liliosa Hilao have been examined by U.S. Mission officers in Manila. Based on these records it appears that on April 4, 1973, the Philippine Constabulary, acting under an arrest, search and seizure order signed by the Secretary of National 

Defense, and related to subversive activity, arrested Miss Liliosa Hilao along with two other women and four men. Liliosa Hilao was detained at Camp Crame as an alleged member of the New Peoples' Army, a communist military group. 

On April 7, 1973, while still being detained Miss Hilao drank muriatic acid in the lavatory and died about three hours later. The acid was stored in the lavatory and was used to clean the lavatory tiles and bowls. An official autopsy described the death as due to shock with pulmonary edema as a result of widespread corrosion of the intestinal tract, epiglottis and trachea with perforations of the greater curvature of the stomach. The Philippine Government autopsy revealed no evidence of sexual abuse or maltreatment. 

We recognize both the controversial nature of the measures taken by the Philippine Government since President Marcos proclaimed martial law in September 1972, and the problems experienced in the Philippines prior to that action. 

Imposition of controls and the suspension of some civil liberties has disturbed or disappointed many Americans, but at the same time many have been encouraged

by improvements in law and order, efforts at economic development, and the Philippine Government's avowed intention to promote social, economic, and administrative reforms, including a land distribution program. President Marcos has on several occasions stressed that he regards martial law as a temporary measure.

In any event, the A.I.D. program in the Philippines is not intended to indicate support for the martial law government and A.I.D. project activities there are carefully monitored to insure that they do not assist military or political programs. 

[STAFF NOTE.-The following information was also supplied by the Agency for International Development on July 10, 1974:] USE OF PUBLIC LAW 480 FUNDS GENERATED FOR MILITARY PURPOSES; 

TESTIMONY BY BENEDICT J. KERKVLIET, OF MAY 24, 1974 

In his testimony before the Senate Subcommittee on Foreign Operations, Mr. 

Benedict J. Kerkvliet indicated that the Philippine military has used $9 million from PL 480 (104) funds to buy essential military equipment and construct its bases.

In accordance with the legislative authority under Section 104 (c) of PL 480, as amended, the United States provided to the Government of the Philippines a total of $9.4 million in local currency for common defense purposes. These funds were granted during the periods of 1953-1961 ($2.8 million), 1962 ($4.8 million) and 1965 ($1.7 million) and were used for general military purposes of the type mentioned in Mr. Kerkvliet's testimony. 

There has been no use of PL 480 resources for military purposes in the Philippines since 1965. Beginning in 1967 all PL 480, Title I credit sales to the Philippines were made on a dollar repayable basis and the agricultural commodities imported have been used to meet food and fiber shortages in that country. The local currency generated from the importation of these commodities has been used by the Philippine Government, in consultation with A.I.D., for economic development purposes in support of projects in agriculture, rural development, nutrition and family planning.

BACKGROUND STATEMENT ON UNITED STATES-PHILIPPINE RELATIONS Recent Developments in the Philippines 

Since September 23, 1972, the Philippines has been under martial law, which was proclaimed by President 

Marcos under Section 11 (2) of the 1935 Philippine 

Constitution. (Tab A) President Marcos said that he had declared martial law because of increasing insurgency, declining law and order and a need for national reform. The Constitutional Convention, originally convened in mid-1971, completed its work and proposed a new Constitution on November 30, 1972, providing for a parliamentary form of government. Following deliberations by nationwide "Citizens' Assemblies" created early in 1973, President Marcos on January 17, 1973, declared the new Constitution to have been approved and to be in effect. At the same time he also redeclared martial law under the terms of the new Constitution. 

President Marcos' intentions for the future are not clear. He has said that martial law would last until normalcy has been restored. He has announced plans to pursue various reforms. Current projects include land reform, law and order, reform of the civil service and the armed forces, and the attraction of foreign capital investment. Some progress is evident in all these fields.

The Philippine economy seems to be performing well. 

The economic performance in 1973 was good, making a remarkable recovery from the disastrous floods of July- August, 1972, and aided by large inflows of private and official funds from abroad. The Government plans to devote more resources to economic development, and has been following a policy of encouraging the inflow of private investment from abroad. U.S. investors and traders are taking an active part in the expansion of mining, manufacturing and construction and in oil exploration activity.

The danger of severe internal disorder seems currently to be limited to the southwestern section of the southern island of Mindanao and the Sulu Archipelago.

This is the area where the Muslim population of the Philippines, totalling about three-and-a-half million, mainly resides.

In Luzon, dissident communist underground armed forces of some 1000 to 1200 men have been operating for several years. This threat seems at the present time to be contained successfully.

United States-Republic of the Philippines Security Relationship 

The United States and the Philippines have been associated in matters of mutual defense and security since 1898. In 1944, a joint resolution of the U.S. 

Congress called for granting independence to the Philippines, but with the U.S. retaining bases in the Philippines for the "mutual protection" of both countries. 

This was implemented by the Philippine Independence Act and the Treaty of General Relations of 1946. We subsequently entered into three basic bilateral security related agreements with the Philippines: 

(a) The Military Bases Agreement of 1947; 

(b) (c) 

The Military Assistance Agreement of 1947 

(which was superseded in 1953 by a new agreement); and

The Mutual Defense Treaty of 1951. 

The commitments undertaken by the United States in the Mutual Defense Treaty of 1951 are as follows: 

"Each party recognizes that an armed attack in the Pacific area on either of the parties would be dangerous to its own peace and safety and declares that it would act to meet the common dangers in accordance with its constitutional processes." 

An armed attack under the treaty includes: "An armed attack on the metropolitan territory of either of the parties, or on the island territories under its jurisdiction in the Pacific or on its armed forces, public vessels or aircraft in the Pacific."

We are not obligated under treaties or any other sort of understanding to become involved in an internal situation.

U.S. Military Presence in the Philippines 

We have over 17,000 U.S. military personnel stationed in the Philippines, nearly all located at our two major bases:

The extremely important Subic Naval Base complex provides a full range of naval, air, ship repair, logistics, and command and control functions. It is vital to support sustained use of mobile sea and air power in the area.

Clark Air Base is the largest U.S. air Force base outside of the United States. 

The American military presence in the Philippines from 1969 through the present is as follows:

January 1969 

28,300 

February 1973 16,000

March 1974 17,000

United States Military Assistance to the Philippines 

Since World War II, we have maintained that it is in the U.S. national interest that the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) be adequately equipped, maintained, and trained because of the historic and continuing importance of the Philippines as a U.S. ally in the western 

Pacific and because of the important role played by the AFP in preserving internal security and stability in the Philippines.

When U.S. Military Assistance was initiated in 

1947 the Philippine Armed Forces consisted of a small air corps, military police, and naval patrol force, all of which were poorly organized, trained and equipped. 

This austere base has been expanded by the GOP into an Army, Navy, Air Force and Constabulary, which has a modest capability for maintaining internal security and to a lesser degree to contribute to SEATO requirements. 

The U.S. Military Assistance program has provided much of the training, materiel, and services necessary to develop AFP capabilities to the current level and has enabled the AFP to deal more successfully with internal security matters and provide a relatively stable ground environment for the operation of U.S. bases in the Philippines.

Our emphasis is now placed on the development of greater self-sufficiency by the AFP, to reduce AFP dependence on MAP support for operating and maintenance (O&M) costs, and to increase the percentage of investment in the total MAP program. In addition to the change in the program's emphasis noted above, major goals of the MAP program for the FY 74-78 period are to assist the AFP in updating its equipment, and toward improving ground and air mobility, communications, and coastal patrol capability. In addition we plan to provide in FY 1974-75 15.6 million dollars in FMS credits to partially fund a M-16 rifle co-production facility in the Philippines.

U.S. grant military assistance has hovered around a magnitude of about $20 million, plus or minus, for some time now. Grant assistance was requested at $19 million for FY 1974 and as mentioned above for the first time we plan to extend FMS credits ($8.6 million) to the Philippines.

We have in the past supplied a broad range of military equipment to the Philippines, including F-5 aircraft, armored personnel carriers, mortars, ammunition, rifles, cargo transport aircraft, miscellaneous common use military equipment and training. We are not supplying napalm under the Military Assistance Program. 

Muslim Conflict in the Southern Philippines

Communal conflict and rivalry between Muslims and Christians in the Philippines have a long history and the predominantly Muslim population of the Sulu Islands and parts of Mindanao has from time to time in the past displayed resistance to the authority of the central government. These long-standing conflicts were inflamed to a relatively high level of violence during the latter months of 1972 and early 1973 as a result of Muslim resistance to a Philippine Government program to collect unregistered firearms. (The program was not resisted in the non-Muslim areas and was surprisingly successful, resulting in the collection of nearly a half million firearms.)

Intermittent fighting has continued in the Muslim areas up to the present time, with the most serious recent clash between the Philippine Armed Forces and 

Muslim insurgents occurring in February 1974. At that time, Jolo City in the Sulus was largely destroyed, several hundred people were killed and some 30,000 refugees fled the area.

The United States has not been involved in this conflict.

Security Assistance Force, Asia 

For the past two or three years small units of civic action specialists from the "Security Assistance 

Force, ASIA" (SAFASIA) have been coming to the Philippines to work with Filipino military and civilian officials in performing various civic action activities in needy areas and communities throughout the Philippines. 

These activities in themselves have little military content. They include providing medical/dental services to civilians in the towns and villages visited, performance of veterinary services, repair of bridges and roads and schools.

These civic action teams have had no overt or covert intelligence gathering or unconventional warfare training missions assigned to them, nor have they engaged in such. They have for the most part sought to avoid, rather than concentrate on high insurgency areas. 

One officer is stationed in Manila in a liaison capacity between the U.S. MAAG and SAFASIA. Courses at the Jungle Survival School at Clark Air Base are conducted routinely for U.S.

personnel, and while we

do not believe personnel are undergoing such training at this time, the courses could be resumed. A civic action team engaged in medical, dental, veterinary and engineering projects concluded its activities in northern Samar in May. The only men in the field, to the best of our knowledge, are a 13-man engineering detachment surveying central Luzon, the scene of severe flooding in 1972. They are scheduled to depart soon.

A detailed analysis of the activities of these forces may be found at Tab B.

Response to the issues raised by Professor Benedict J.

Kerkvliet and Mr. Russell Johnson in prepared statements for the Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on Foreign 

Operations dated May 24, 1974 While this report is annotated to reply to the statement submitted by Professor Kerkvliet on May 24th, the answers provided also cover the issues raised by

Recent Developments in the Philippines

Under the titles Political Repression in the Philippines, pp. 2-10; Growing Resistence and Rebellion, pp.

493 

11; and Military Force and Militarization, pp. 17-21,

Professor Kerkvliet provides his views regarding the internal situation in the Republic of the Philippines. 

United States policy toward the Philippines operates within the framework of the Nixon Doctrine, which was initially enunciated on July 29, 1969, in Guam on the eve of the President's visit to the Philippines. You will recall that the President again defined the basic character of America's role in the world in his second inaugural address, when he said, among other things: "The time has passed when America will make every other nation's future our responsibility, or presume to tell other people of other nations how to manage their own affairs. We recognize both the controversial nature of the measures taken by the Philippine Government since President Marcos proclaimed martial law in September 1972 and the problems experienced in the Philippines prior to that action. Some American citizens have been disturbed by the imposition of controls and the suspension of some civil liberties in a country whose history has been so involved with that of the United States. Others are encouraged by improvements in law and order, efforts at economic development and the Philippine Government's avowed intention to promote social, economic and administrative reforms, including a land distribution program. 

President Marcos has on several occasions stressed that he regards martial law as a temporary measure. 

It has been our view that the events leading up to the declaration of martial law, and the policies followed by the Philippine Government since that time, are fundamentally of an internal nature, and that any problems in the last analysis can only be dealt with by the Philippine people in the context of their own governmental processes and procedures. We have therefore felt that the interests of the United States would best be served if we did not attempt to comment on or characterize internal developments in the Philippines.

Under the section entitled American Support pp. 2730, there are a number of allegations which the Department has addressed below.

On page 22, it is alleged that the United States Navy's Naval Command "provided information to the Philippine police that led to the arrest of Filipinos and Americans who had been providing legal assistance to 

GI's there."

Shortly after the implementation of martial law, three United States citizens, Mr. Eugene Parker, Mr. 

Bert Lubow, and Mr. David Sorenson were arrested by 

Philippine authorities.

With respect to Mr. Eugene Parker and Mr. Bert Lubow, it is my understanding that their apprehension was accomplished solely by authorities of the Philippine government. 

With respect to Mr. David Sorenson, Philippine agents came to the U.S. Naval Base at Subic Bay and presented a warrant for his arrest. Mr. Sorenson was not subject to the jurisdiction of the U.S. armed forces. 

Accordingly, paragraph 2 of the Agreed Implementing Arrangements relating to Article XIII of the Military Bases Agreement, as revised, between the United States and the Philippines was applicable. This portion of the Agreement relates to criminal jurisdiction, and the relevant portions are quoted below: "2.a. The U.S. military authorities will normally make all arrests, or otherwise take persons into custody, within U.S. bases. This shall not preclude the Philippine authorities from doing so within the bases where the base commander or his authorized representative has given consent, or in the case of pursuit of a flagrant offender who has committed a serious crime. "If the Philippine authorities desire that persons not subject to the jurisdiction of the U.S. armed forces who are within U.S. bases be arrested or taken into custody, the U.S. military authorities will undertake, upon request, and within the limits of their authority, to make the arrest or take them into custody. All persons arrested or taken into custody by the U.S. military authorities who are not subject to the jurisdiction of the U.S. armed forces shall immediately be turned over to the Philippine authorities for compliance with formalities required by Philippine law and for custody except as provided by Agreed Minute Number 5."

Agreed Minute Number 5 is not pertinent to this situation. 

When Philippine agents presented the warrant for Mr. Sorenson's arrest at the Subic Naval Base, he was located and delivered to them by U.S. representatives at the gate of the Naval Base pursuant to the requirements of the Military Bases Agreement quoted above. 

Representatives of the Philippine government were nearby during this interval but took no action against Mr. 

Sorenson while he was on the Base. 

We are not in a position to evaluate the merits of the arrest of these three individuals by Philippine authorities. All three individuals were subsequently permitted to leave the Philippines.

That the United States has contributed in large part in the development of the Philippine military establishment and is continuing its military assistance to the Philippines is not contested and is documented in the background statement on that item. If Professor 

Kerkvliet is contending that the provision of such military assistance per se leads to military control over a society, it is a view with which the Department cannot concur.

Underlying Professor Kerkvliet's statement regarding the provision of military assistance to the Philippines by the United States is the view that we are becoming involved in another Vietnam-type situation by providing military equipment which can and is being used to contain the Muslim dissidence in the south. 

We sincerely hope and believe that we are not. 

First, the Philippine Government recognizes that the solutions to the Muslim dissidence require political, social and economic remedies and not only military action. 

Second, the particular frustrations and aspirations which fuel Muslim dissidence in the Philippines are not commonly felt by the nine-tenths of the Filipino population which is non-Muslim. Third, while MAP equipment has undoubtedly been used by the Philippine Armed Forces in this fighting-which, after all, presents the government with a serious challenge to public peace and security--U.S. policy and practice is to stay out of this internal problem. 

Professor Kerkvliet also appears to be contending that curtailment of U.S. military assistance to the 

Philippines will result in changing that government's internal policies in a manner which he believes is desirable. 

It is not clear to us that the curtailment of our military assistance would appreciably alter the present internal policies of the Philippine Government. We consider it much more likely that a curtailment would be resented as an effort to intervene, with results which would adversely affect our interests and our relations with the Philippine Government. 

As we said above, it is our analysis that Philippine problems in the last analysis can only be dealt with by the Filipinos.

Issues related to USAID's Internal Security Program 

(pp. 23-24), U.S. assistance to the Philippine Constabulary's Anti-Narcotics Unit (p. 24) and the Food for 

Peace program (p. 26) will be addressed in a separate letter drafted by USAID.

It should be noted that the assertion that the U.S. is supplying NAPALM to the Philippines is not correct (p. 27). 34-192 O 74-32

Professor Kerkvliet asserts (pp. 27-28) that there are indications that U.S. military personnel are also involved in helping to surpress rebellion in the Philippines. He observes that "it would not be the first time that American troops have assisted the Philippine armed forces in counter-insurgency" and cites two examples of such activity previously the subject of Congressional hearings. This is apparently a reference to the material appearing on pages 161 and 162 of the published transcript of hearings on the Philippines held by the Subcommittee on United States Security Agreements and Commitments 

Abroad on September 30, October 1, 2 and 3, 1969. This material was provided to the Subcommittee by the Department of Defense in response to a written request that it "describe in detail, circumstances and contributions made by U.S. agencies to the anti-Huk effort." Several specific instances of such contributions were listed. 

The transcript of the hearings on pages 233 and 235 covers a discussion of these instances of support by several of the witnesses responding to questions from Senator Symington. The incidents discussed there involved the furnishing on January 10, 1969, by Clark Air Force Base of one H-19 helicopter and crew at 0600 hours to furnich transportation and air to ground communications for General Rafael and General Zerrudo of the Philippine Constabulary in order to permit these two Constabulary commanders to observe a Constabulary action against a fairly large group of Huks. The discussion also centered around two other incidents in which U.S. 

Air Force reconnaissance aircraft performed aerial photography coverage of some areas adjacent to the Clark Air Force Base reservation in response to a Philippine Constabulary request for such coverage so that they could conduct raids in those areas. The transcript indicates that the witnesses made the point that these were exceptions to the United States Government's policy of not supporting counter-insurgency programs in the Philippines.

Units of the Armed Forces of the Philippines and 

U.S. military units have routinely conducted joint training exercises for over two decades. This in no fashion implies that U.S. forces are involved in counter insurgency operations in the Philippines, and to imply that General Wilson's activities have been of such a nature (p. 28) can only be accomplished by completely obscuring the very real difference between military operations and military training exercises. In this context, it would be useful I believe to make some observations regarding the role of U.S. Military Assistance Advisory Group personnel in the Philippines.

U.S. Army Advisors do not accompany Philippine Army or 

Philippine Constabulary units on field operations. There is a specific Country Team policy against entry of any JUSMAAG personnel whomsoever in areas where there are

anti-dissident operations. JUSMAAG Philippines is assigned a Military Assistance role only at the national level. U.S. Army personnel do not perform direct advisory functions below the level of the Department of Defense, the Armed Forces of the Philippines General Headquarters, or Service Department Headquarters level. 

These offices are all located in the Manila area.

Security Assistance Forces, ASIA. On pages 28-30 

of Professor Kerkvliet's testimony a number of allegations are to be found regarding the activities of Security 

Assistance Forces teams in the Philippines. General remarks regarding the activities of these forces may be found in the background material in section one of the Department's response and at Tab B. Certain additional observations, however, are warranted. 

As a general policy the presence of current insurgent/dissident activities or a recent history of such activities in the proposed exercise area eliminates the area from consideration. In so stating, it must also be observed that we are discussing activities of sufficient magnitude to be readily identified. The intent of the policy is clearly to avoid areas of significant insurgency which includes areas of Mindanao, all of the Sulus and parts of Northern Luzon. 

No U.S. Government personnel have been involved in the recent fighting at Jolo or Mindanao. 

The U.S. Navy has not been engaged in the shelling of coastal areas in the Southern Philippines, or 

Northern Luzon.

The U.S. has not supplied any logistical support to the Philippine Armed Forces fighting the Muslims. 

The U.S. Air Force did not, and is not flying bombing missions over Mindanao from Clark or any other base. 

While no U.S. military personnel actually have been stationed on or in the vicinity of Cebu Island during the past year, from October 73 to January 74 a

U.S. Air Force Mobile Technical Training Team was on temporary duty at Clark Air Base on Luzon and Mactan Air Base near Cebu City to train the Philippine Air Force in ground and flight skills necessary for operation of their recently acquired C-123K aircraft. The team's strength varied; the maximum number at any one time was 31, which occurred in December 1973. Flight training was conducted at Mactan, and was most active in December. The last technicians departed Mactan in mid-January to participate in similar training of the

Korean Air Force. Over the past year, up to 16 U.S. 

Army communications command technicians have been in

and out of Cebu City to assist the armed forces of the Philippines in constructing a troposcatter radio installation on Mount Luay which is located near Cebu City. 

Installation at this site should be completed by Octo ber 1975. Joint U.S. Military Advisory Group personnel make periodic visits to Mactan Air Base and Headquarters of the Philippine ground forces at Cebu City to observe and report on the utilization of materiel furnished and personal trained at the expense of the United States. 

There have been no U.S. calualties resulting from the Muslim insurgency in the South. Statistics relating to non-hostile death or injury of U.S. military personnel stationed in the Philippines may be found at Tab C in the Department's background statement.

[The statement follows:]

iir. Chairman and lembers of the Committee: 

We thank you for the opportunity to appear before your Committee to submit our views on the Administration's program for aid in the Middle East. 

I am speaking for the American Israel Public Affairs Committee and I am authorized by the Conference of Presidents of Major American Jewish Organizations, which includes 32 organizations, to state that the Conference supports our testimony, I am also informed by the American Jewish Committee that it associates itself with our proposals. (See appendix.)

At the outset, may we express our appreciation for your favorable vote on the Administration's emergency aid program for Israel last fall, when Congress recognized Israel's peril and helped to assure her survival. 

It is our hope that the 1975 aid bill will serve to promote a genuine peace in the Middle East. The aid program includes requests for $1.37 billion in military grants and economic supporting assistance for 51 countries. 

It recommends $430 million in military and economic grants to seven Arab countries including $100 million in military assistance and $77.5 million in supporting assistance for Jordan, $250 million in supporting assistance to Egypt. 

There may be an additional $100 million for Syria. Other Arab states to receive grant military aid: Tunisia, $2 million; Morocco, $860,000; Saudi Arabia, $220,000; 

Lebanon, $150,000; Sudan, $50,000. The program also includes $23.2 million for 

UNRIA. 

The amount proposed for Israel is $350 million, but of that amount $300 million is for credits and only $50 million is for a grant. These contrasting programs appear anomalous because the Arab states were the attackers last fall and 

Israel suffered heavy losses in her defense.

I call your attention to an editorial which appeared in The liew York 

Times on April 28, 1974: "The economic aid to Israel is considerably less than had been requested, and both Congress and the executive branch would do well to stay flexible in meeting this country's long-standing interest in preserving Israel's economic and military strength. 

Unlike the Arabs, Israel has no other major source of investment and economic aid."

We ask you to approve an appropriation for Israel which would be more responsive to her need to strengthen her defenses and to stabilize her economy. 

Earlier this year, Israel requested the Administration to recommend a supporting

1 assistance grant for $250 million, which, coincidentally, is the amount which the Administration has now proposed for Egypt. 

In supporting this request, we are fully aware of, and grateful for, the generous assistance approved by Congress last December. But subsequent developments do justify a request for additional aid. 

In voting the $2.2 billion last year, Congress provided that the Administration could grant Israel up to $1.5 billion and that the $700 million balance could be in the form of loans. The Administration recently announced an initial allocation under this legislation of $1 billion in grants, the balance in long-term loans at concessionary rates. It is our understanding that the $2.2 billion is to be spread over a three-year period: $300 million for the arms which 

Israel received during the war; $300 million in the current year; $600 million in 1975.

But Israel's arms procurement requests already exceed $3 billion. The agreements signed as of the end of March approximated $1.2 billion, and agreements approximating $1 billion were awaiting signature. The remainder were in various stages of negotiation. This means that Israel must continue to go more deeply into debt to pay for her survival, unless Congress approves additional grant assistance.

We submit the following reasons why legislation for additional assistance to Israel is justified at this time: 

1. The war did not end on Oct. 22. It has continued for more than seven months. Despite the U. . cease-fire, incessant shooting has violated 

Israel's cease-fire lines in a costly war of attrition. 

2. Israel suffered heavy losses in manpower and materiel. was shaken by the war and its prolongation and by worldwide inflation. 

Her economy 3. Israel's citizens have paid heavy taxes and loans to maintain their security and to amortize the heaviest per capita external debt burden of any people on earth. 

4. The military balance is beginning to tilt dangerously against Israel, partly because of Soviet shipments, partly because of the ominous proliferation of arms in the Persian Gulf.

5. A drastic contraction of American aid for Israel, coinciding with a substantial expansion of U. S. aid for the Arab states, may have a psychological impact on public opinion in the region, impeding progress toward a settlement. 

THE AR GOES ON 

The Administration's recommendation last year was made on October 19, just three days before the cease-fire. There has never been a real cease-fire since that time. The Egyptians kept shooting until the disengagement agreement was finally signed on January 17. Cyria's war of attrition on the northern front persisted even while Secretary of State Henry Kissinger was in the region attempting to negotiate a disengagement agreement. The Syrians punctuated their demands with shells.

The inability of the United Nations to enforce the UN-sponsored ceasefire and to curb the shooting beles ill for the effectiveness or durability of the disengagement agreements. Cease-fires are easily violated and disengagement is not synonymous with non-belligerence. 

We should note that between October 22 and May 1, the Israelis lost 90 men on both the northern and southern fronts. Thus, the Israel.. death toll in this war exceeds 2,600. Drew Middleton, veteran New York Times military analyst, has pointed out on ilay 12 that more than 600 of them were officers, who fight in the front lines in the Israel army. He drew the conclusion that the military balance was shifting against Israel. 

Nor has the UN been able to censure and halt shocking and brutal terrorist outrages against Israel civilians like the massacres at Kiryat Shemona and Ma'alot.

These unhappy developments inform Israel that she must continue to maintain adequate defensive strength to guard her frontiers and to take new precautions to protect civilians. She cannot rely on documents or third-party guarantees.

Throughout the war and for months thereafter, the Soviet Union poured sophisticated military equipment into the arsenals of Israel's neighbors, encouraging them to maintain a belligerent and negative posture toward: disengagement and a negotiated settlement.

At the same time, the wealthy oil states have financed the Egyptian and Syrian arms purchases from the Soviet Union, and, in addition, have enabled these countries to procure essential commodities to strengthen their home fronts. 

In the past, the Israelis were always assured that they did not need to maintain a quantitative balance because of the qualitative capacity of their soldiers. To some extent, the Arabs have now mastered sophisticated weapons. 

But the Arab military advantage during the October war was not due so much to sophistication as it was to the vast profusion of weapons, financed by oil dollars gleaned from the West and transmitted to the East.

The disastrous experience of last October, the overwhelming firepower of tanks and missiles, the rapid Soviet arms resupply, the alchemization of Arab oil into weapons, the prolongation of the war of attrition, the new wave of brutal terror 

all these compel Israel to maintain a larger and a much better equipped military force.

Before the war, Israel had some six to seven thousand in its mobilized reserves. In 1974, the Israelis estimate that they will need an annual average of 80,000 mobilized reserves, more than eight percent of Israel's labor force. 

THE COST OF THE WAR 

The war struck a hard blow at Israel's economy an estimated $7 billion dollars which means that every Israeli has to contribute almost a full year's labor to make up for it.

The replacement cost of materiel and damaged property is approximately $4 billion. 

The loss in production was about $400 million; it may be double that this year. 

When war came, the government moved swiftly to absorb purchasing power. It imposed a compulsory war loan of seven to twelve percent and a similar voluntary loan on top of that. Later there were five percent increases in custom rates, five percent increases in sales taxes, increases in cement excise. In addition to the reduction of subsidies on essential goods and salaries, there were increases in the price of fuel and electricity.

The total annual absorption of purchasing power came to 6.495 billion Israel pounds, the equivalent of more than $1.5 billion. 

If 1973 had been a normal year, the Israelis would have paid their government some $3.8 billion. As a result of the October war, the Israelis contributed almost $2 billion more to finance their own security.

ISRAELIS PAY A HIGH PRICE 

The Israelis are the highest taxed people in the world and they have the highest per capita external debt. 

The average Israeli had a per capita income of $2,100 in 1973. On this income, he paid $900 in taxes and $300 in loans, leaving $900 for living expenses. But this was further reduced by additional emergency taxes and by the abolition of subsidies.

In Israel, an Israeli with an income of $5,000 pays 52 percent in taxes and loans; on an income of $10,000 he pays 66 percent; on an income of $20,000 he pays at the rate of 75 percent.

The new taxes and compulsory loans mean that Israelis will be funneling 54 percent of the gross national product back to the treasury, according to 

Israel's Finance Minister Pinhas Sapir. The New York Times reported, on March 15: 

If one includes city tax rates and social security payments, the Israelis are actually contributing 62 percent of the gross national product to government treasuries, it was estimated by Moshe Neudorfer, Director of State Revenue. 

Israel's defense expenditures rose sharply in 1973. For that fiscal year, the total was $1.5 billion. In the per year, it was $4 billion. In the next twelve months, it is hoped, the figure will drop to $3.6 billion. 

In the last two years, 45 percent of Israel's defense expenditures were in foreign countries, about 95 percent of that amount in the United States. 

In 1972, Israel's imports for defense totaled $662 million. The figure rose to $1.57 billion in 1973 and it will rise to $1.8 billion in 1974. Along with this tremendous rise in imports for defense, there has been a sharp increase in imports for basic commodities. Inflation, world-wide and domestic, bit deeply into Israel's income. The cost of living rose some 26.4 percent this last year about three times the rate in the United States and an additional 19 percent in the first four months of 1974. Israel must import much of her foodstuff. The tonnage of soybeans, wheat and food grains which Israel required in 1972 cost $130 million. This year's estimated cost is $290 million. 

A few years ago, Israel paid about $25 million for wheat at PL480 prices. This year a similar quantity will cost $80 million.

While the cost of imports rose sharply, Israel's exportable goods have not commanded a comparable increase. Israel's largest exports are citrus and polished diamonds and these have not yet risen in price as rapidly as foods and other staples. Tourism, a dollar earner, declined because of the war. Exports have also been hit by dislocations in Israel's economy. Many of Israel's factories have lost production because key manpower and vehicles have been on battle lines instead of production lines. Heavily taxed consumers cannot afford to buy many domestically manufactured products. Manpower must shift to defense oriented industries. Israelis cannot compete as effectively as in the past for world markets. The domestic difficulties have been compounded by a worldwide monetary uncertainty. Currency devaluations have hit exports.

ISRAEL'S DEBT AND DEFICIT 

The high cost of defense, inflation, and lowered production have all combined to boost Israel's current accounts deficit which rose from $1.075 billion in 1972 to $2.475 billion in 1973, and which is expected to soar to $3.28 billion in 1974, bet to i ep back to $2.92 billion in 1975, assuming that there is peace and substantial increases in exports. 

Aside from her mounting current account deficit, Israel has carried a heavy debt burden because over the years she has borrowed large sums to finance her development as well as to pay for her arms. 

Always concerned lest U.S. aid to Israel should provoke a counterproductive reaction in the Arab world, the Department of State was always reluctant to meet Israel's requests for arms. AID's records show that between fiscal 1946 and fiscal 1973, more than 90 percent of all military assistance was in the form of grants. The United States provided $58.4 billion in grant military aid to more than 70 countries but not a grant military dollar was allocated to Israel. The fact is that Israel never asked for military grants. She wanted to pay her way and she went in to debt for her security. Even so, although the United States vas providing arms to Saudi Arabia and Iraq in the 1950s, it never sold Israel any military equipment until 1962, and it was not until last October that our Government provided her with grant military assistance of any kind. 

Those who complain that America favored Israel over the Arab states should reflect on this history, particularly in the light of the fact that Israel's neighbors have been at war with her all through this period and have been equipped by all the great powers: England, France, the United States, the Soviet bloc and even, to some extent, by the Peoples Republic of China. 

For many years,

The result has been a steadily mounting external debt. 

Israel's per capita external debt has been the highest in the world.
