billion at the end of 1973 are expected to drop sharply this year and next because of the mounting balance of payment deficit, resulting from inflation and Israel's inability to cover her heavy defense bill. 

Israel economists predict that after utilizing all foreseeable sources of foreign exchange, Israel will still be short $587 million this year and $840 million in 1975. Accordingly, foreign exchange reserves will drop to $1.1 billion by the end of 1974 or only 17 percent of imports and to a perilously low $270 million by the end of 1975 or a tiny four percent of imports, less than two weeks' requirements. 

This is the somber prospect confronting Israel unless there is an increase in grant military or economic assistance as well as a substantial restoration of PL480 surplus commodities.

Like all Americans, we are keenly aware of opposition to foreign aid in this country which has been fed by our own inflation and our heavy tax burdens. 

Our own citizens pay a heavy price for civic responsibilities, both in the areas of domestic and international concern, and we would hesitate to ask fellow Americans to contribute additional sums to assist Israel if the Israelis were not carrying such a tremendous burden to defend their survival. 

THE SHIFTING ARMS BALANCE 

The arms balance is shifting against Israel, partly because of the readiness of the Soviet Union to arm Egypt and Syria, partly because of mounting Arab oil wealth, partly because of the alarming arms race in the Persian Gulf. 

Soviet Aid to the Arabs There are conflicting estimates on the military strength of the Arab states when they launched their offensive, but all authorities agree that they had overwhelming superiority over Israel. They suffered heavy losses but the 

Soviets have more than replenished them. 

Syria is believed to have lost at least 600 tanks during the October fighting but it has since received 1,000 from the Soviet Union. The New York Times reported on May 5 that Syria now has 1,590 tanks, many of them T-62s, the heaviest and most advanced Soviet battle tank. Cuban, North Korean and possibly East 

European crews and technicians are reported to be manning the tanks while new Syrian crews are being trained. Syria also has received MiG-21J improved fighters and Sukhoi-20 fighter bombers. 

President Assad asked Moscow for MiG-25 Foxbat high altitude fighters when he was there in April, and Syrian pilots are now training in the USSR to fly the

SA MiG-23 Flogger fighter-bomber, a first line aircraft which the Syrian government has also requested.

Egypt, which began the war with about 1,950 tanks, now has 2,445 according to the ilay 5 New York Times. These include about 700 T-62s. Iraq has also received a number of these weapons, including Tu-22 supersonic medium range bombers.

Egypt has a Soviet-flown squadron of Foxbats flying reconnaissance missions far out of range over Israel.

Egypt and Syria have received a wide variety of support equipment which even Warsaw Pact countries have not obtained. These include radars, electronics countermeasures equipment (ECM), automatic quad-mounted anti-aircraft guns, bridging equipment and night fighting gear. 

presently under Soviet control 

Scud lb missiles are now in both Syria and Egypt. This missile has a 185 mile range, is capable of carrying a nuclear warhead and is a fearsome long-range bombardment system. Even with conventional warheads, the Scuds represent a quantum leap in the Arab offensive capacity. 

It should be stressed that all the above military estimates are regarded as conservative. 

Arab Aid 2 -3 The rich Arab states bankrolled the war. 

It is reported that Saudi Arabia and Kuwait donated $675 million to Egypt during the last year for arms and committed a smaller sum for economic aid to enable Egypt to buy food and subsidize officers' salaries. 

Debt-ridden Egypt was suddenly able to pay cash for imports to avoid high interest rates and she stockpiled a two-month's supply of wheat. She normally imports 21½ million tons a year.

Qatar gave Egypt $50 million; Algeria sent Egypt two million tons of oil after the war, and Sadat told a German newspaper that Algeria paid $100 million for arms which Egypt received from the Russians. (Algeria did the same for Syria.) 

Abu Dhabi borrowed $100 million, reportedly for Egypt, in November. And in April the Lebanese press carried news of an arms transfer from Saudi Arabia. 

Most Syrian defense financing came from Saudi Arabia. Estimates range between one-half billion and a billion dollars. After the war, Syria received $400 million in economic aid from Kuwait and $100 million from Saudi Arabia. Iraq recently announced that it would give Syria $50 million. After Assad's last visit to Moscow in April, Syrian analysts claimed that the Soviet Union would reconstruct all damage to the Syrian economy, estimated at $1.8 billion.

There is no doubt that Egypt and Syria could not have fought without substantial subsidies.

Production was slowed by the war in Egypt but not at the same rate as in Israel, where a much larger proportion of manpower and vehicles had to be diverted from production to defense; Egypt maintains a large standing army. .2

U. S. AID TO EGYPT 

Naturally, our Committee has some reservations about our aid to 

Egypt and Jordan.

We hope that the Administration is correct in the assumption

that Sadat wants peace, that he is ready to reactivate civilian life in the Suez Canal area and that he wants to liberate himself from the Soviet mortgage. 

But, having witnessed the futile and expensive efforts of former administrations to win President Nasser for the West, we are not convinced that our Government can prematurely enter into a partnership with the Soviet Union to revive the Egyptian economy and to raise Egyptian living standards, however desirable those objectives may be. There should be strong assurances, some genuine evidence, that Sadat is really ready to make peace.

Thus, if the United States and other powers are to join forces to help Egypt open the Suez Canal, the very least Sadat could do to signal his sincerity is to announce his intention. to respect the international character of that waterway, as well as the Straits of Tiran and Bab el liandeb, and the obligation to keep then open to the shipping of all nations.

But Sadat may now attempt to secure American, French and British weapons from his wealthy Arab allies, which they are now buying in great quantity. whether the American people approve or disapprove, there is really nothing to prevent Egypt from securing American weapons from other Arab states. Since they helped provide Egypt with the means to purchase Soviet weapons, they probably would not hesitate to transfer ownership of American weapons. 

The huge increase in the price of oil has made the Arab states in the 

Persian Gulf area a superb market for arms. Last year, the United States disclosed that it had offered Phantom jets to Saudi Arabia and other supersonic planes to Kuwait. State Department officials defended the proposed sales contending that the arms were intended to ensure a balance in the Persian Gulf area and that this region was not really involved in the Arab-Israel conflict. It was argued that 

Saudi Arabia had, over the years, "stuck to the notion that the question of security in the Persian Gulf, the question of oil, ought not be related to the political question of the Arab-Israeli dispute." 

But just a month earlic, King Faisal of Saudi Arabia had already made it very clear to Aramco officials that, he was prepared to use the oil weapon against the West on behalf of Egypt and Syria. There is no doubt that his alliance with Egypt was decisive in precipitating the October attack. 

At that time, Rep. Lee Hamilton, Chairman of the House Near East and 

South Asia Subcommittee, said that the United States Navy had a $600 million equipment and training program in Saudi Arabia and that we would sell her an additional $1 billion in arms, in addition to $600 million worth to Kuwait. 

Congressmen were quick to question whether the Persian Gulf states might transfer their planes to Egypt. On June 6, 1973, the Department of State told 

Congress that "none of the equipment can be transferred to any third party without prior approval of the United States." But later, in his testimony, Under Secretary of State Joseph J. Sisco said frankly, "I don't think anybody can give a guarantee.“

However, he felt that Saudi Arabia "would view the obligation seriously." 

As the October war neared, there were reports that Libya had sent its Mirage planes to Egypt and other French planes were used against the Israelis, who found it difficult to distinguish their own Mirage planes from those flying for Egypt.

As western nations competed for Arab markets, Arab leaders proclaimed their freedom from restrictions. Last July, Kuwait's Defense and Interior Minister 

Sheikh Sa'ad Abdulla Al-Salem pledged to refuse any arms contract which included restrictions on their use. "We are free to use our arms when and where we want, he said. 

When Sadat proclaimed that he no longer wished to be dependent on Soviet weapons and it is reported that the Russians are slowing down their supplies there were reports that other Arab states would come to Sadat's aid. 

The New York Times, on April 28, quoted "qualified Arab sources to the effect that, in the interim, Egypt might borrow non-3oviet equipment from other Arab states." 

On April 18, Ilenry Tanner reported from Cairo that: "officials of Saudi Arabia and Kuwait have reportedly said that they are free to put their new weapons at the disposal

of other Arab countries. 

They have been quoted in the Arab press as having said that the manufacturing countries had placed no restrictions on the use of these weapons. 

And Stanley Karnow wrote in The ileu Republic on March 23: 

... "Pentagon spokesmen are vague when asked whether the

Persian Gulf recipients of U. S. arms may be illegally transferring them elsewhere. 'We consider it unlikely, but we can offer no guarantee' is their routine reply.

The Saudis have for economic cooperation and the sale of American weapons. ordered 200 F-5Es this year. They may purchase A-7 Corsairs and F-14 Tomcats.

Saudi Arabia's national guard, which is established to preserve domestic peace and to guard petroleum installations, is scheduled to receive ii-60 battle tanks. The 

Saudis already have the lauk missile. Americans are training the Saudi national guard, helping to build a navy of 19 ships as well as ports. Ironically, the aid program includes a gift of U. S. training to Saudi Arabia. 

Saudi Arabia's oil revenues are expected to rise to $17.3 billion this year, as compared with $4.9 billion in 1973 The Economist estimated on May 4. 

There are reports that it will spend more than a billion on American arms, but this is unconfirmed because the information is classified. 

Saudi Arabia is also negotiating to buy French and British tanks. It is buying weapons from France: 38 Mirage-3 jets, -30 tanks, machine guns and missiles. Last year, Britain negotiated a five-year $600 million contract with Saudi 

Arabia for aeronautical equipment and has some deals with the United Arab Emirates. 

Tiny Kuwait, which has always lived in fear of Iraq, has also been in the market for arms. France has reached a deal to sell her 17 tirage F-1 fighter planes, and Kuwait Defense Minister Cheikh Sa'ad Abdulla Al-Salem claims that France has placed no restrictions on Kuwait's use of the equipment. And Kuwait may buy F-4 

Phantoms from the United States and Jaguar fighter bombers from the British. France has also sold 14 Mirage jets to tiny Abu Dhabi, which has no pilots; it will borrow some from Pakistan.

The Economist of April 27 noted that France is arranging to sell more than $150 million of advanced equipment to Arab states. 

The United States is also enlarging its arms sales to two of Israel's neighbors, Jordan and Lebanon. 

Jordan, which has received American tanks and planes in the past, is getting the TC anti-tank missile, which is better although much more expensive. than the Soviet Sagger missile. (It arrived in Israel after the war ended.) 

Jordan wants the Hawk anti-aircraft missile, but this would be an immediate threat to Israel aircraft flying in Israel's confined air space and Israel has objected. 

And the United States has offered two squadrons of A-4 Skyhawk jet fighters to Lebanon to replace 10 Mirage fighters. The United States has provided the 

Lebanese army with ii-16 automatic rifles. 

In the Persian Gulf, the Russians have been concentrating their attention on Iraq, which has nationalized oil and which is in a never-ending battle with Iran over access to the Persian Gulf. It is estimated the Russians have sold Iraq arms worth a billion dollars. The Russians also have a military interest in South Yemen and they compete with the Chinese in supporting the rebellion in Dhofar. It has just been reported that Libya will enter into a new arms deal with the Soviet Union. 

All this must surely be of some concern to Israel. Her danger grows because it is obvious that the great powers, anxious to share in Persian Gulf riches, no longer seem to care about slowing the arms race or restricting the proliferation

of weapons. Supersonic planes in the Persian Gulf area, like the F-4 Phantoms, are within range of Israel or could be transferred to Israel's hostile neighbors. 

Arab countries which have hitherto held aloof from the war against Israel may be tempted and will have little excuse to refuse to enter it if they have the power. 

There are tremendous dangers. Lethal weapons are now being amassed by oil-producing nations which demonstrated their propensity for blackmail and their massive irresponsibility when they vielded the oil weapon in their attempt to hijack the world, economically and diplomatically, just a few months ago. 

In an editorial on Feb. 16, The Washington Post declared that: "never in history have arms been amassed at such a rate in such a volatile region. 

It observed that: "new weapons create their om pressures to use them .... ... 1 The $2.2 billion for arms which the United States pledged to Israel after the war is a large sum, but it will be overwhelmed by the arms now coming to Egypt and Syria and their 

Arab allies.' 

And the editorial concluded: "It becomes all the more necessary for the United States to leave no doubt that its commitment to Israel's security is firm."

AID FOR UNRWA 

In addition to the funds proposed in the AID program for Jordan and Egypt, the Administration requests a $23.2 million contribution to the United 

Nations Relief and lorks Agency (UNRUA). We have never opposed this gift. But it is appropriate to point out that the United States is once again carrying a major portion of the burden. 

In 1959, Secretary General Dag Hammarskjold optimistically told the U. N. that the Arab refugees could be integrated in the Middle East and that they should be regarded not as a liability but as an asset for the future. His study showed that if $1.5 billion to $2 billion in capital could be invested in the area, this sum, together with the capital likely to become available from future oil revenues, could create a demand sufficient to absorb the refugees. 

But, regrettably, the Arab leaders, who were primarily responsible for the displacement of the refugees in the war against partition in 1948, rejected the Hammarskjold view because it implied resettlement in Arab countries. They ignored the humanitarian needs of the refugees. They preferred to turn the UNR!/A camps into military training camps and bases for terrorist warfare. 

Despite their rapidly expanding oil wealth, the Arab states have been miserly in their contributions to UNRIJA. The record shows that in the 23 years down to June 30, 1973, all Arab states donated just $26 million to UNRWA, a minuscule sum when compared with the $549 million donated by the United States and the $849 million contributed by all sources. 34-192 O-74-33

Arab rulers are ready to squander billions to subsidize a war against a hated Israel. But they have never been willing to help the Arab refugees to gain a new life in lands where there is room and opportunity for them. This refusal of the Arab states to recognize their responsibility for a tragedy which they created and which they have needlessly prolonged has brought misery, deprivation and violence to many thousands of men, women and children, Arabs and Jews, who might have shared life rather than death. 

This indifference to the fate of others is not limited to disregard for the Palestinian Arabs. The record shows that the wealthy Arab states have been similarly callous toward the appeals of UNICEF and the calls for food for the starving millions in drought-stricken African Sahel whose plight has been further aggravated by the inflated costs of oil-based fertilizers and fuels. 

In an article in The New York Times on April 4, Chester L. Cooper pointed out that approximately $350 million in aid had been contributed to help the stricken countries of Senegal, Mali, liauritania, Chad, Niger and Upper Volta. The United 

States gave more than a third, the EEC contributed slightly less than a third. As compared with these generous contributions, Libya a rich neighbor of the Africans contributed a nominal $760,000, Kuwait $300,000 and Saudi Arabia not a dollar in 1973 and only $2 million this year. 

1An article by Jim Hoagland in The lashington Post of March 15 points out that UNICEF spends about $5.4 million a year in 16 Middle East countries. Arab countries and Iran contributed only $871,000 to UNICEF; Saudi Arabia, where UNICEF spends $500,000, contributed a paltry $30,000. 

Then will the civilized world begin to call the rolls of those who vote for food and medicine for people and those who are for weapons to destroy them, of those who vote for peace and those who vote for var? 

IMPACT OF THE PROGRAM 

le offer some comment on the psychological impact of this aid program. 

In 1971, 1972 and 1973, Congress voted $300 million in military credits and $50 million in supporting assistance for Israel. Now the Administration proposes to revert to that pre-war figure, even as it greatly expands assistance to those who attacked Israel.

To many people in the ìfiddle East, and perhaps to people in Israel itself, this may suggest a retreat in American policy. I cannot believe that the Administration is diminishing its support for Israel, but Arab leaders have made extravagant claims to the effect that the United States now supports their views on the future of the Middle East.

J Many of you who have been to Israel since the war have been startled by the mood in that country. Israel's people won a military victory after initial reverses but they were abandoned by many of the governments of the free world and the third world.

As long as they were on the defensive, no one moved to stop the war. 

When victory was within Israel's grasp, the great powers interceded to save Egypt and Syria from a crushing defeat.

We have not criticized the United States for this action and for the policy it pursued during that period. On the one hand, our country maintained the balance of strength but it also sought to maintain the balance of influence. 

As a result, the United States has accumulated a substantial reservoir of goodwill in the Arab world.

If the effect of this new aid bill is to encourage the Arabs into believing that the United States is abandoning Israel in a campaign to win the Arabs avay from the Soviet Union, then there is scant hope for the attainment of an Arab-Israel peace. If Israel is to win the peace, she must be strong and the 

United States must continue to be clear and steadfast in her support. E -M

ASSISTANCE GRANT FOR ISRAEL 

Mr. KENEN. The administration has proposed a $50 million supporting assistance grant for Israel. We ask you to approve an appropriation which would be more responsive to Israel's need to strengthen her defenses and to stabilize her economy.

Earlier this year Israel requested a supporting assistance grant of $250 million which coincidentally is the amount which the administration later proposed for Egypt. We believe that the figure suggested by Israel merits your consideration.

In addition we would like to suggest that $100 million of the $300 million requested by the administration for military credits to Israel be appropriated in the form of grants, the remaining $200 million in the form of credits. This, incidentally, happens to be the amount of grant military assistance scheduled for Jordan.

Now, we are fully aware of and grateful for the generous assistance approved by Congress last December. Subsequent developments do in our judgment justify a request for additional aid.

In voting the $2.2 billion last year, Congress provided that the adminisration could grant Israel up to $1.5 billion in grants and that the $700 million balance could be in the form of loans. The administration recently announced an allocation of $1 billion in grants the balance in long-term low-interest loans.

ISRAEL'S ARMS PROCUREMENT 

But Israel's arms procurement requests already exceed $3 billion. 

This means that Israel must continue to go more deeply into debt to pay for her survival unless Congress approves additional grant assistance.

Now, we submit the following reasons why legislation for additional assistance to Israel is justified at this time: 

One, the war did not end on October 22. It has continued for 7 months. Incessant shooting has violated the cease-fire lines in a war of attrition costing many lives. 

The inability of the United Nations to enforce the U.N.-sponsored cease-fire and to curb the shooting bodes ill for the effectiveness or durability of the disengagement agreements. Disengagement is not synonymous with nonbelligerence. It is ironic, as Dr. Kissinger shuttles back and forth, that the shooting goes on.

Nor has the United Nations been able to censure and halt shocking and brutal terrorist outrages against Israeli civilians like the massacres at Kiryat Shemona and Ma'alot. If you read this morning's newspapers, you may have noticed Israel yesterday prevented another Ma'alot when they apprehended terrorists coming into the country from Syria. One of those terrorists confessed that if their mission had been accomplished the way they intended it to be accomplished, there would have been another massacre.

Now, this terrorist was trained in Lebanon and emanated from Damascus. This is all in this morning's paper. I am making the point because those who suggest that Lebanon has no responsibility for the continued warfare over her frontiers overlook the basic fact that there was a U.N. armistice agreement between Lebanon and Israel consummated in 1949. It is not a peace treaty. Lebanon and Israel are still in

a state of war, but Lebanon was obligated, as was Syria, to provide that there must be no paramilitary forces emanating from their side into Israel under that armistice agreement. 

What has been going on has been a violation of the agreement that was negotiated before. These unhappy developments inform Israel that she must maintain adequate strength to guard the frontiers and take new precautions to protect civilians.

Israel suffered heavy casualties in the surprise Arab attack last October. The war struck a hard blow at Israel's economy, an estimated $7 billion, which means that every Israeli has to contribute almost a full year's labor to make up for it.

ISRAEL'S HEAVY DEBT 

Israel's defense expenditures rose sharply in 1973. For that fiscal year, the total was $1.5 billion. In the war year it was $4 billion. In 

1972 Israel's imports for defense totaled $662 million. The figure rose to $1.57 billion in 1973 and it will rise to $1.8 billion in 1974.

The high cost of defense, inflation, and lowered production have all combined to boost Israel's current accounts deficit which rose from $1.075 billion in 1972 to $2.475 billion in 1973 and which is expected to soar to $3.28 billion in 1974.

Israeli economists predict that, after utilizing all foreseeable sources for foreign exchange, Israel will be short $587 million this year and $840 million in 1975.

The Israelis are the highest taxed people in the world. The average 

Israeli had a per capita income of $2,100 in 1973. Out of this income he paid $900 in taxes and $300 in loans, leaving $900 for living expenses, but this was further reduced by additional emergency taxes and by the abolition of subsidies. 

If one includes city tax rates and social security payments, the

Israelis are actually contributing 62 percent of the gross national product to government treasuries. The reason for this is that Israel never asked for military grants. She wanted to pay her way and she went deeply into debt for her security.

It was not until last October that our Government provided her with grant military assistance. As a result, Israel's per capita external debt has been the highest in the world for many years. The per capita foreign debt rose from $1,275 in 1972 to $1,510 in 1973 to $1,680 in 

1974 and it will be an estimated $1,940 in 1975.

The debt service has risen from $633 million in 1972 to $790 million in 1974 and it will be $1,080 million in 1974.

THE MILITARY BALANCE TILTS AGAINST ISRAEL 

Now, in addition to this, the military balance is beginning to tilt dangerously against Israel, partly because of Soviet shipments, partly because of the ominous proliferation of Western arms in the Persian Gulf.

Throughout the war and for months thereafter, the Soviet Union poured sophisticated equipment into the arsenals of Israel's neighbors. 

The wealthy oil states bankrolled the war, the Arab military advantage during the October war was due not so much to sophistication as

it was to the vast profusion of weapons financed by oil dollars, gleaned from the West and transmitted to the East. 

The disastrous attack of last October, the overwhelming firepower of tanks and missiles, the rapid Soviet arms resupply, the alchemization of Arab oil into weapons, the prolongation of the war of attrition, the new wave of brutal terror-all these compel Israel to maintain a larger and much better equipped military force. 

Before the war, Israel had some 6,000 to 10,000 people in its mobilized reserves. In 1974 the Israelis estimate they will need an annual average of 80,000 mobilized reserves, more than 8 percent of Israel's labor force.

U.S. AID TO EGYPT 

Now, on U.S. aid to Egypt. I speak for many organizations and therefore, I cannot say we are for it or against it because I have not polled them. If I were speaking for myself, I would probably vote for aid to 

Egypt at this time. But our committee does have some reservations about aid to Egypt and Syria. We hope the administration is correct in the assumption that Sadat wants peace, that he is ready to reactivate civilian life in the Suez canal area and he wants to liberate himself from the Soviet mortgage. 

But having witnessed over the years the futile and expensive efforts of former administrations, Eisenhower and Kennedy, to win President Nasser for the West, we are not convinced that our Government can prematurely enter into a partnership with the Soviet Union to revive the Egyptian economy, however desirable that objective might be.

There should be strong assurances, some genuine tangible evidence, that Sadat is ready to make peace. If the United States and other powers are to join forces to help Egypt open the Suez Canal, the least Sadat can do is to announce his intention to respect the international character of that waterway as well as the Straits of Tiran and Bab el Mandeb and the obligation to keep them open to the shipping of all nations as the United Nations Security Council ordered 

September 1, 1951. on

If the purpose of America's aid to Egypt and Jordan is to procure their assent to disengagement agreements, it should be borne in mind that authoritarian machines often have a short life expectancy. Experience has also taught that they are short on gratitude and long on appetite.

Sadat has announced his readiness to turn to the West for arms and to cease to be solely dependent on the Soviet Union. We do not believe that the American people favor U.S. military supplies to Egypt or 

Syria just 7 months after they opened up a vicious war against Israel and before consumation of a genuine peace. We hope that the administration does not intend to use any aid funds to strengthen Egyptian military capacity. There are third party conduits to consider. Whether the American people approve or disapprove, there is really nothing to prevent Egypt from securing American weapons from other

Arab states. Since they provided Egypt with the money to purchase 

Soviet weapons, they probably would not hesitate to transfer ownership of American weapons.

There are repeated statements from Arab leaders that there are no restrictions on the transfer of the weapons which they propose to acquire. These are very great dangers, Mr. Chairman. Lethal weapons are now being amassed by oil-producing nations which have demonstrated the propensity for blackmail and their massive irresponsibility when they wield the oil weapon in their attempt to hijack the world, economically and diplomatically, just a few months ago. 

I believe firmly that public opinion in this country does support Israel's cause and I will quote from two newspapers.

DISENGAGEMENT IS NOT PEACE 

Mr. KENEN. I would think so, Mr. Chairman, because disengagement, as I said, is a long, long way from peace. Even as this negotiation has been going on, terrorists crossed from Syria into Israel yesterday. 

Twenty-five years ago, I was on a TV program in New York hailing the first armistice agreement between Israel and Egypt. We were overjoyed by what happened. We thought peace was around the corner. 

We are a long, long way from peace, I fear, but like you, I hope that we achieve it. But I fear that if the Arab States begin to believe that 

America is turning away from Israel and is now joining them-I don't believe that it may be very difficult in the months ahead to negotiate a settlement.

A disengagement agreement really is tantamount to a cease-fire. 

That is what we had back last October when the U.N. approved Resolution 338, but the shooting went on in spite of the ceasefire.

Senator INOUYE. My final observation or question may require some lengthy response on your part. If you wish, you may return this afternoon. I must stop the hearing in a few minutes because I have another hearing to conduct.

This relates to the Palestinians. Very little has been said about the 

Palestinian, but I gather that he belongs to that part of the world. He was born there. Yet in this day no one wants him. He would be uncomfortable living in Israel. I don't suppose he is too welcome in Syria or in Egypt or in Jordan. I suppose that a Palestinian would like to have his own country, at least for identification purposes. 

How would you resolve this Palestinian problem? I can only conclude from my reading of the Middle East situation that even if you achieve cease-fire on all fronts, that as long as this Palestinian problem is unresolved, violence will continue.

I would hope that my observation is wrong, but this is my present observation. What is the solution to the Palestinian problem? 

Mr. KENEN. Do you want that in just one afternoon? I will be glad to come back and offer you my views. I don't pretend to be the architect of a utopian solution.

Senator INOUYE. If we are to resolve the Middle East problem, we should address ourselves to the Palenstinian problem. 

Mr. KENEN. I will come back.

SUBCOMMITTEE RECESS 

Senator INOUYE. The subcommittee will recess until 2:30 this afternoon, and our first witness will be Mr. Kenen. [Whereupon, at 1:20 p.m., the subcommittee was recessed, to reconvene at 2:30 p.m., the same day.]

T: 

(AFTERNOON SESSION, 2:30 O'CLOCK, Friday, May 24, 1974.) NONDEPARTMENTAL WITNESSES AMERICAN ISRAEL PUBLIC AFFAIRS COMMITTEE STATEMENT OF I. L. KENEN, CHAIRMAN, AMERICAN ISRAEL PUB- LIC AFFAIRS COMMITTEE Resumed PALESTINIAN PROBLEM 

Senator INOUYE. The subcommittee will resume its hearings. We will once again hear from Mr. I. L. Kenen. 

Mr. KENEN. Mr. Chairman, I have your question. I don't want to anticipate what may go on in Geneva. That is a long way off.

You indicated that it would take somewhat of a comprehensive statement. It will not be a long statement. I will be as brief as I can. 

I was at the U.N. back in 1947 and 1948. I am familiar with what went on. There would never have been an Arab refugee in Palestine in 1947 and 1948 if the Arab States had accepted the U.N. partition resolution at that time. There is not the slightest doubt about that. 

Even during the fighting in 1948, there were appeals directed to the 

Palestinians not to leave Israel.

I was at the Security Council when Sir Alexander Cadogan, the United Kingdom delegate, read the report from Haifa in which he told how the Jewish community in Haifa, which was half Arab and half Jewish, was appealing to the Arabs not to leave but to live with their people.

There were still about 120,000 to 150,000 Arabs in what is now Israel in 1948. They did not all have to leave, and some of them came back. 

Actually, I have interviewed an Arab labor leader from Haifa who recalled to me, and I have a tape of that, how the Histadrut issued appeals to the Arabs in Haifa not to leave at that time. But almost all of them left.

At the same time, Jews began to leave Arab countries. What we had actually was an exchange of populations. This concept of exchange of populations was first advanced by the British Labor Party in their preelection platform in 1945.

RESETTLEMENT IS THE SOLUTION 

I am sure you are more familiar with refugee problems than I am. 

I think it is a fact that no refugee problem has ever been solved by repatriation. All refugee problems have been solved by resettlement in many parts of the world.

We have always felt that the resolution of this problem was in a population exchange, bearing in mind that almost 700,000 Jews came out of Arab countries to settle in Israel during the same period.

As for our own American history, I would remind you that the United Empire Loyalists were refused permission to return to the United States after the Revolution. The British made that an issue in the peace negotiations. But, the American people refused to permit repatriation.

In view of the fact that there is now such a large Jewish population in what is now Israel, I think that it is totally unrealistic to expect Israel to repatriate any substantial number of Palestinian Arabs. Back in 1959, Secretary General Dag Hammarskjold of the United Nations brought in a report to the effect that the Palestinian refugees could be resettled in the Arab countries with the investment of $1 billion or $12 billion at that time, taking into account that there would be large oil revenues in the future.

This was prophetic. We have witnessed the tremendous increase in oil revenues. If the U.N. at that time had adopted the position that the time had come to resettle and not hold these people in camps, this would have been an ideal solution. But the Arab States all rejected that Hammarskjold proposal.

Where would they have been settled? There are now 20 Arab States. 

They are spread over 5 million square miles. They have rivers and rivers of oil. They have tremendous wealth. 

What we hear today is a great deal of talk about a Palestinian entity. 

Before 1918, Palestine was part of the Ottoman Empire, and it included what is now Jordan and what is now Israel and the West Bank. 

It was the British who, in 1922, having taken a mandate over the entire area, separated Jordan out, but Jordan, as we know it today, was originally part of Palestine. It is perfectly logical and sensible to suggest that the future of the Palestinians may well be found inside Jordan if and when the West Bank goes back to Jordan. 

When they talk about a secular Palestinian state in which Jews and Arabs will live side by side, you must look further into the documents because what they say in the documents is that all of the Jews who came after the "Zionist invasion" will have to leave. I am referring to the 

Palestine National Covenant of the Palestine National Council, adopted July 10-12, 1968.

What they are talking about is a secular state to include the Arabs and Jews who were there before 1948, or 1917, depending what they mean by the "Zionist invasion." What they are really talking about is eviction of a large number of Jews who certainly are never going back to the Arab States, in light of what has happened. It is completely unrealistic. 

What is ironic about this is that the people who have been talking most about a secular state in which Arabs and Jews will live in peace are the very same people who perpetrated the massacre in Ma'alot. 

Some of them say, "Let us have a separate Palestine on the West Bank." This is the other point of view among Palestinians. This is not very realistic because such a state would be a base from which there would be new attacks by terrorist groups. It would greatly endanger 

Israel. If you look at the West Bank, you will find that at some point it is only 7 miles from the Mediterranean. Israel had a very narrow corridor at that time. While I am not speaking for Israel, I know that many Israelis would not want to live next door to another new Arab

State, bearing in mind that many Palestinians could be settled in Jordan which was originally a large part of Palestine. 

I think that is pretty much a quick summary of the position. 

One further point. When people talk about Israel's counter raids, they misinterpret the meaning of the concept of an eye for an eye or a tooth for a tooth. The meaning of that was not revenge. The real meaning is "let the punishment fit the crime, be moderate in your response." 

Most people misunderstand that. That is the basis for what is happening.

As I pointed out earlier, Lebanon had an obligation under the armistice agreement not to permit its territory to be used as a headquarters for paramilitary forces invading Israel. Apart from that I think a great deal of blame must be placed on UNRWA because the United Nations Relief and Works Administration for years has permitted the camps to be taken over by the terrorist groups. They keep the civilians close by, as a result of which they are innocent victims of attempts by Israel to reply to the terrorists. What would you do if you were in 

Israel's place, if your people were attacking the government for its failure to protect people at Kiryath Shemome and Ma'alot. 

You would be compelled to take military action against those who were launching attacks against your people. This is an attempt by 

Israel to do something which the United Nations failed to do, which the United Nations has failed to discourage because the resolutions which have been adopted in recent years never condemn terrorism, they always condemn the reply. So the terrorists themselves feel they are immune from censure.

Years ago the Congress adopted an amendment to the Foreign Aid Act in which it provided that none of the funds that were voted for UNRWA should be used to pay for the training of military forces in camps. This was Mr. Freling Luysen's amendment.

Obviously, that resolution has never been respected because the UNRWA camps throughout this period have been bases for irredentism and regrettably for the preparation of raids against Israel's civilians. 

Thank you very much. I didn't mean to speak at this length. My newsletter recently published-I am not offering it for the record because I don't want to increase the expenses of your committee, but we recently published a document called "Myths and Facts, 1974" in which all these issues are discussed at length. 

I would like to offer you personally a copy of this publication. I will make it a point to send it to other members of the committee. I am sure all of you are very much concerned with this problem. 

Senator INOUYE. I thank you very much. The committee is aware of the United Nation's resolution of the forties and the solution that was suggested, but unfortunately the fact remains that today is 1974. It will not serve any good purpose to be going back into history and discussing that because it is, as you say, unrealistic. 

Now, you have indicated that some of the solutions suggested, for example, the settlement of the West Bank, are unrealistic. I gather that depending on one's perspective, all of the proposals that have been presented to date are unrealistic from one viewpoint or another. 

Mr. KENEN. I think that resettlement is not an unrealistic proposal. I don't know how many hundreds of thousands of Palestinians have

been resettled in other parts of the Arab world. The area of the Arab world today is larger than of the United States. 

Senator INOUYE. I just hope sometimes soon this matter will be resolved. I am afraid that if it is not, we will forever be holding hearings considering such appropriations. 

Mr. KENEN. I am going to retire in a few months and I wish you could settle it by then. 

Senator INOUYE. We will do our best, sir. Thank you very much.

NATIONAL ASSOCIATION OF ARAB AMERICANS STATEMENT OF PETER S. TANOUS, PAST PRESIDENT, NATIONAL ASSOCIATION OF ARAB AMERICANS CONCERN OVER MILITARY AID TO ISRAEL 

Senator INOUYE. Our next witness is Dr. Peter Tanous, past president of the National Association of Arab Americans. 

Dr. Tanous, do you wish to have Dr. Taylor with you or are you giving separate testimony?

Dr. TANOUS. That is right. I would like to introduce the vice president of the National Association of Arab Americans, Mr. Edmond 

Howar. 

The National Association of Arab Americans in appearance last year before this same committee, underscored our deep concern over large-scale military assistance to Israel; military aid which has been, and continues to feed the machines of war at a time when the seeds of peace are at hand.

In our previous statement before the Appropriations Committee, we asked that out of the $2.2 billion of military assistance being sought for Israel, that $1 billion be allocated, immediately, to the U.S. Armed 

Forces to replenish the stocks of military equipment-aircraft, tanks, guns, ammunitions, et cetera taken from our own combat units to supply Israel.

We further suggested that the remaining $1.2 billion requested for military aid be held in abeyance until such time as Israel indicated that it was willing to abide by the numerous U.N. resolutions regarding territorial integrity and military aggressions. 

If our suggestions had been acted upon, Israel would not be in an excessively superior military posture whereby it is able to attack the south of Lebanon, and other Arab countries at will, under the guise of "retaliation" against Palestinian commandos.

The continuous Israeli bombings of Lebanon with American supplied weapons in which reportedly 36 planes, in one raid alone, were engaged, has resulted in the deaths of almost 100 civilians; Lebanese civilians as well as Palestinian refugees.

Several hundred more civilians were wounded and hundreds of homes and shelters were destroyed. The toll is mounting daily, for these are not isolated retaliatory raids, but an attempt to destroy the political balance in Lebanon and to create a confrontation with Lebanon in order to justify Israel's intention to occupy the southern part of Lebanon.

Sixty percent of one refugee camp, Nabatiyeh which has been evacuated, was destroyed and the inhabitants have fled to nearby orange groves for shelter.

This tragic loss of innocent lives, unarmed children, babies and mothers, and the devastation of the UNRWA refugee camps are, and must be considered an outrage, at any time.

NAAA cannot understand how the U.S. Senate permits these acts of 

State terrorisms by Israel, which is a member of the U.N., to be committed without a pronouncement of condemnation. The sophisticated weapons used on civilians in Vietnam raised havoc in the House and Senate as inhuman acts against civilians and yet, not one word of condemnation has eminated from this body during these last acts of atrocity, where Israel is using the same horrible instruments of war. 

Don't you realize that Lebanon is not at war with Israel? That they have been living under a so-called armistice with Israel since 1947, and only Lebanon has not broken the armistice?

Mr. Chairman, the NAAA at its second annual convention held in 

Washington, D.C. delivered the following statement to a senior officer at the Department of State on May 17, 1974: "The National Association of Arab Americans in convention in our nation's capital, expresses our deep shock and dismay over the needless loss of innocent lives in the Middle East. "We are outraged by the Israeli bombing of Lebanon and the killing and wounding of civilians be they Lebanese or Palestinian refugees. We are also outraged by the recent series of events which occurred at Maalot. "We deplore all acts of extremism and violence and mourn the loss of innocent lives on both sides. We believe it essential for the American people and the 

American government to recognize the significant difference between the acts of desperate Palestinian individuals and the premeditated official acts of terror committed by the government of Israel. "The cycle of violence which has for so long characterized the Arab-Israeli problem is the result of the failure of the world community and the United States in particular, to resolve the fundamental issues at stake in the Middle 

East-which, among others, are: “1. A just and lasting peace for all nations of the Middle East. "2. Secure territorial boundaries of all nations of the Middle East. "3. Resolutions and return of occupied Arab lands, including Jerusalem. "4. And, of course, the most overriding issue to all of the above issues-and 

I was pleased that you brought this point up this morning-"recognition and resolution of the political and human rights of the Palestinian people." "We therefore call upon the United States government to use its good offices to work for the attainment of the above goals and strongly request reconsideration of our military assistance program to Israel in the light of recent and past events. Israeli technological capacity to inflict massive casualties, at will, without regard to other nations or people must be restrained. "We implore our government to expedite its peacemaking initiative in the Middle East so that this senseless slaughter will end once and for all and Israeli and Arab children can live in peace and security."

MILITARY DISENGAGEMENT 

At this time, may we state that economic assistance cannot replace a political settlement to the outstanding issues which have awaited a solution for the past 25 years.

Mr. Chairman, the present efforts at military disengagement are but a beginning in the long hard process toward a just and lasting peace. A peace which must involve not only withdrawal from Arab lands, but must also include Jerusalem, attainment of the national rights of the Palestinian people so long recognized by the international

community and, security for all nations in the area. May we emphasize that real security is not dependent upon military strength, nor upon indiscriminate bombing of civilians, but upon the resolutions of fundamental issues which have plagued the area for 25 years. 

It is therefore our hope, Mr. Chairman, that this committee will consider the following: 

1. Qualifying assistance to the countries in the area to their respective commitment to a just and lasting peace, and we further recommend that the issue of arms control for the Middle East be discussed in the 

Geneva talks. 

An emergency appropriation for UNRWA be immediately put forth in view of its current deficit of $12 million which is compounded by the recent damages which occurred in the continuing attacks upon the refugees residing in its camps. Such an appropriation would be but a holding operation until the basic issues of the just political and human rights of the Palestinians are resolved in the diplomatic process. 

In connection with this, we support Palestinian representation at Geneva.

Mr. Chairman, it is the consensus of opinion of the members of 

NAAA that any funds allocated to Israel, no matter whether it be for development, education, housing, or whatever, these same funds must be allocated for the Palestinian people who have suffered from grave injustices at the hands of Israel. 

Arms for Israel can only mean death to more hundreds of innocent civilians in Lebanon and in the camps. Again we state that economic assistance cannot be substituted for a just political solution; however, as we move into a hopeful era of peace, let us hope that future appropriations for assistance will be for constructive nationbuilding, rather than for the destructive military purposes which has unfortunately characterized our large-scale assistance in the past. 

Thank you, sir. 

Senator INOUYE. Thank you very much, Dr. Tanous. I am certain I speak for the subcommittee when I say that all of us are shocked and dismayed over the loss of innocent lives in the Middle East, be they Arab or Jewish. We are also outraged by the killings. Likewise, as you have called upon the United States, I think it would be equally appropriate to call upon Arab nations to urge their Palestinian brothers to stop their acts of violence. 

I am certain, just as much as Israel would find the most difficulty to maintain a strong military without American aid, the Palestinians, the guerrillas, would find it extremely difficult to carry out their acts without support of their Arab brothers. 

This, once again, just demonstrates the wisdom of the fundamental observation that violence begets violence. We cannot ever go on just pointing the finger of accusation. We will not solve problems that way.

I am just hoping we will have disengagement from Golan Heights and proceed from there.

Historically I gather that people lived in peace there at one time. 

I am certain we will return to that situation again. Beyond that, I don't suppose we can give much comfort from this standpoint because of certain commitments that we have made that the United States will continue to provide assistance to Israel.

We hope that the time will come when such assistance will not be necessary but it is a two-way street. 

What is your solution to the Palestinian problem, sir?

Dr. TANOUS. My solution basically is this. As Mr. Kenen, who preceded me here, stated, hundreds and hundreds of books have been written on this one subject. It appears to me that you cannot write off a nation of people as Golda Meir stated. When someone asked her about the Palestinians, she said, "Who are they?"

The Palestinians are a people. They are a people who were driven from their lands. They are people who are now proliberating the whole 

Middle East. I believe one impression in the United States is that all 

Palestinians are in refugee camps. This is not a fact. There are Palestinians working in Kuwait. Saudi Arabia. The Palestinian question cannot be written off until the aspirations of the Palestinian people are realized.

I am in no position to speak for anyone except America. I have no ties with any Arabic country. I have a deep affection for the United 

States, as all members of our association do. I think there will be no peace in the Middle East until the Palestinian problem is resolved. 

I think the problem can only be resolved with the establishment of a homeland for the Palestinians, whether it be in Israel, whether it be on the west bank-this of course is up to the negotiators. But I don't think, and I am sure you will agree, Mr. Chairman, that the Palestinian question cannot be swept underneath the carpet. It is here. It is crucial. 

It is the reason for the Middle East conflict today. 

There would be no conflict between Israel and Syria, Israel and Lebanon, Israel and Jordan, or Israel and Egypt if it was not for the Palestinian question. As long as that question remains, I believe there will never be peace in the Middle East. 

Senator INOUYE. In your statement, sir, your solution involves just two places-Israel and the west bank. Is that correct? 

Dr. TANOUS. I did not understand your question, sir.

Senator INOUYE. You suggested that two areas be considered for the resettlement of the Palestinians-the west bank of the Jordan 

River and Israel.

Dr. TANOUS. These are two geographic potentials; yes, sir. In other words, Israel to grant the rights to the people to return to their homeland. Jordan, of course, this would be for the negotiators, the Dr. Kissingers and the President Sadats, to decide.

But I would like to state this, Mr. Chairman, if I might. The continual bombing of southern Lebanon-I have heard on the radio today, much to my chagrin, that the home village of one of our descendants here in the Senate is Kaffir in southern Lebanon-was again bombed by the Israelis and the report that was announced on the radio was that a clinic in the cultural center in this very small village was eliminated. I repeat, it is the home town of the ancestors of Senator 

Abourezk. This is what concerns me, how we as Americans can tolerate a government, a member of the United Nations, performing acts of retaliation against innocent people. 

If we in America followed that approach, we would condemn every black in the United States because of what happened in California when Judge Boyle was murdered by some of the followers of Angela Davis. This is the wrong approach. We have a situation where you 34-192 O 74-34

have a handful of desperate radicals who are doing anything they can to either disrupt the Middle East talks or to focus attention on the plight of the Palestinians.

We, with all our wisdom here in the United States, from what I gather, continually sit back and provide the weapons of war for Israel to arbitrarily attack southern Lebanon. As an American citizen, I shake with horror when I see this.

AMERICAN NEAR EAST REFUGEE AID, INC. 

STATEMENT OF LAURENCE MICHELMORE, FORMER COMMISSIONER- GENERAL OF THE UNITED NATIONS RELIEF AND WORKS AGENCY (UNRWA) Senator INOUYE. Our next witiness is Dr. Laurence Michelmore, UNRWA Commissioner-General from 1967-1971, representing American Near East Refugee Aid, Inc. Welcome, sir. 

Dr. MICHELMORE.  

Mr. Chairman and members of the subcommittee. I am grateful for this opportunity to speak about the activities of the United Nations 

Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East 

(UNRWA). As you so kindly mentioned, I served as Commissioner 

General of UNRWA from 1964 until 1971. On the basis of that experience, I am firmly convinced that the services which UNRWA provides to the Palestine refugees are of vital importance and must be continued until there is some solution to the Arab-Israeli conflict, including a "just settlement of the refugee problem," to use the words of the Security Council's resolution of 1967. 

The three main parts of the UNRWA program are education and training, health services, and relief services.

Almost half of UNRWA's budget is spent on education and training. Over a quarter of a million boys and girls attend schools operated by UNRWA with the cooperation of UNESCO. This number increases by about 12,000 a year. Vocational training and teacher training is now given to about 4,500 young men and women. 

Palestinian children and their parents attach great importance to education, which they regard as their best hope for the future. 

UNRWA has done everything it could to meet the increasing demands for this service, believing that it is through education and training that the most constructive and lasting help can be given to the refugees. 

UNRWA provides a low cost but effective health program with special emphasis on preventive measures, including health education, school health service, maternal and child health care, and immunization. Curative services are also provided through a network of clinics. 

In the refugee "camp" areas, UNRWA provides for the water supply and for refuse and sewage disposal.

Health and sanitation expenses represent about 12 or 13 percent of the UNRWA budget.

Relief services include the distribution of basic food rations, supplementary feeding, and shelter. Together these activities account for about two-fifths of UNRWA's budget.

Food rations, consisting of flour, cooking oil, rice, and sugar are distributed to about 20.000 persons. This number has been limited by a ceiling, and is actually slightly below the figure of earlier years. The dollar cost of the rations has jumped tremendously because of the increased price of foodstuffs. In fact, the cost in 1974 will probably be more than twice the cost of the same number of rations 4 years earlier. 

Supplementary feeding is provided to small children and other vulnerable groups. The cost of food for this program has also risen sharply. 

About 644,000 persons live in areas known as UNRWA "camps".

UNRWA constructed most of the simple huts in these areas, as well

as the public facilities health centers, schools, latrines, food distribution centers, water points, drainage ditches, et cetera. After the initial construction, the continuing operating costs in relation to shelter are small.

The total expenditure on all relief services is equivalent to about $2 a month for each eligible person. This is far from complete support, but is very helpful to refugees on the edge of destitution. 

I am not including the $2 a month for the education and health services but the other relief activities as such. 

UNRWA costs have steadly increased over the years because of the growth of the refugee population with increased demands for education and health services, and because of the increase in the cost of goods and services needed in the UNRWA program. 

In the last 2 years the increase has been especially sharp because of the effect of inflation and rising prices, coupled with the revaluation of currencies and particularly the reduced value of the dollar in relation to currencies needed in the UNRWA program. 

Fortunately, over recent years, a number of governments have increased their contributions to UNRWA. Indeed, in the last 10 years, countries other than the United States and the United Kingdom have increased their contributions nearly tenfold. 

The U.S. contribution is still at about the level of 10 years ago, and the purchasing power of the contribution is considerably less. 

Until 10 years ago the U.S. contributed 70 percent of all governmental contribution to UNRWA. The regular U.S. contribution is now about half that figure, and if it is not increased will represent less than 23 percent of the amount needed from governments in 1973. 

The nine countries which belong to the European Economic Community contribute individually and through EEC. Together, their contributions are now at about the same level as the U.S. contribution. 

Several other countries contribute at a rate which might be regarded as more generous than that of the United States, in relation to their financial capacity. Among them are Greece, Japan, Norway, Spain, Sweden, and Switzerland, as well as several Arab countries. 

Encouraging as these developments are, they are not sufficient to meet the increased costs facing UNRWA. In 1973, UNRWA had a deficit of about $4 million, and reserves were virtually exhausted. I understand that income now expected by UNRWA in 1974 will be about $10 or $11 million short of present estimates of the amount needed, and the shortfall in calendar 1975 may be much greater. Unless this gap can be closed, the UNRWA program will be endangered, and education in particular may have to be severely cut. This would be catastrophic for the refugees, and could lead to serious difficulties for the governments of the area.

The United States has demonstrated a special concern for the problems of the Middle East, and has undertaken special responsibilities in relation to that area ever since the problem of Palestine was taken to the United Nations 27 years ago. This applies in particular to the Palestine refugees.

The United States has taken a leading role in establishing international relief programs for their assistance, and in financing those programs. The United States has had a major voice in United Nations debates concerning the refugees, and has often taken the lead in draft-

ing resolutions relating to the problems of the refugees and their assistance.

The refugees themselves, and the governments and the other inhabitants of the area, consider that the United States has a special position and a special responsibility in the search for peace in the Middle East. This is being demonstrated in the disengagement discussions now taking place. 

All these considerations underscore the importance of having the United States continue to provide major financial support to UNRWA and, in the present circumstances, of increasing U.S. support very significantly.

A breakdown in UNRWA services to the refugees would be a tragedy for them, a threat to stability in the countries in the Middle East, and a major handicap to efforts to secure peace in that area. A truly generous contribution by the United States to assure the continuation of essential services to the refugees, and to reestablish UNRWA finance on a sound basis would be in accordance with U.S. interests. 

Senator INOUYE. Thank you very much, sir. I can personally see the justification for American involvement, American assistance. As you are well aware, at the present time the United States contributes approximately 40-percent toward the various costs of the United Nations, in some cases as high as 80 percent, some as low as 20, but I believe the average is about 40 percent.

There is much debate in the Congress as to whether we should continue providing such high-level assistance, considering some of our problems at home. You have indicated that today our contribution represents less than 23 percent whereas at one time we contributed 70 percent. Are you suggesting that we contribute 70 percent of UNRWA costs?

Dr. MICHELMORE. No, Mr. Chairman. I understand the reasons that led the United States to want to reduce its share. Having borne 70 percent of the total for a good many years and with the United Kingdom bearing an additional 15 percent so that the two countries were really bearing the great bulk of the load, that they felt justifiably that other countries should bear some of that cost. 

However, other countries have increased their contributions. As I mentioned, countries other than those two which 10 years ago contributed less than $4 million to the program this year will be contributing $40. This is a substantial change. The situation in the area has also changed due to the events of 1967 which produced additional problems and additional costs for UNRWA due to the fact that the growing population of school age brings additional children to the schools in each year, at very heavy additional costs; also that the additional numbers of people requiring health services has been increased. 

The relief program as such, the assistance program as such, has not been increased. It costs more but it is not giving as much help as it did 10 years ago. The number of people receiving food rations are less. Some of the services formerly given have been eliminated but costs are higher. They are higher because inflation has taken place everywhere in the world because of increased goods and services. This is particularly notable in the UNRWA activities which are now conducted in the occupied areas administered by Israel where the rate. of inflation is about 30 percent a year.

This adds very materially to the cost there. The change in evaluation of the U.S. dollar has increased the cost substantially because of the fact that the dollar no longer has the purchasing power that it formerly did in terms of the Jordanian dinar and Syrian and 

Lebanese currencies.

It is for these reasons and because of the special responsibility which the United States has assumed and has demonstrated, because others have made real effort in this regard, that I think the time has come when it is perfectly justified and almost essential, if the program is to be maintained, for the United States to increase its support. 

Senator INOUYE. In the last 10 years much has changed in the economic profile of many countries; for example, the Japan of today is quite unlike the Japan of 10 years ago economically, just as much as the Kuwait of 1964 was a bit different than the Kuwait of 1974, and Saudi Arabia and Abu Dhabi and Libya. 

I am just wondering if it is not proper for countries that have done well in the last 10 years to pick up a heavier load than they did 10 years ago.

Dr. MICHELMORE. Mr. Chairman, I agree completely. You men tioned Japan. Japan this year I believe is contributing over $5 million to the program whereas 10 years ago it was in the-I don't remembercouple hundred thousand range, something in that order. Libya is contributing something like $600,000 compared to nothing virtually 10 years ago. 

Countries like Sweden, Denmark, Norway, Switzerland, Spain,

Greece, have increased their contributions very very significantly. 

Saudi Arabia has increased its contribution, nearly doubled its contribution, for this year. Now with the still greater oil revenues that some of the Arab oil producing countries are receiving, perhaps it should be possible for them to contribute still more. 

I understand that efforts are being made to try to persuade them to do that. I still would say that in my opinion the United States has taken from the beginning a special responsibility and it would be, I think, very important to keep this effort to which the United States has given so much support from breaking down while peace negotiations are hopefully a thing of the near future.

Senator INOUYE. I don't think the United States will do this. Finally, my question is, is there any national interest involved in our participation in UNRWA? Is it in the best interest of the United States to contribute to UNRWA?

States representation as a humanitarian state, an understanding state, as a friend of all peoples, I think is very much at stake. The United

States wants, particularly in the conduct of the health and education and training programs to prepare the Palestinian refugees, as much as the dollars that go to UNRWA will permit, for the greater re-

sponsibilities that they will have and the opportunities that they will have when peace some day comes.

MIDDLE EAST AFFAIRS COUNCIL STATEMENT OF DR. ALAN R. TAYLOR, CHAIRMAN, MIDDLE EAST AFFAIRS COUNCIL ACCOMPANIED BY CHRISTOPHER TAYLOR 

Senator INOUYE. Our final witness is Dr. Alan R. Taylor, the Chairman of the Middle East Affairs Council. 

Welcome to the committee, sir. 

Dr. TAYLOR. Mr. Chairman, I would like to introduce by son, Christopher Taylor. 

Senator INOUYE. Welcome, sir. 

CHRISTOPHER TAYLOR. Thank you very much. It is a great honor to be here. 

Senator INOUYE. Is he going to testify? 

Dr. TAYLOR. I think he would like to speak to the question you posed earlier about the Palestinian question. 

Senator INOUYE. Fine. You are welcome to speak.

Dr. TAYLOR. Mr. Chairman, the Middle East Affairs Council appre ciates the privilege of appearing once again before this subcommittee. 

We would like to reiterate our conviction that the United States can best serve its own interests and the cause of peace by working for a political solution which takes into account the legitimate rights and claims of all parties to the conflict. We therefore welcome not only the initiatives of Secretary Kissinger during the past few months, but also the general thrust of the Foreign Assistance Appropriations 

Bill now under consideration.

The initial position of the United States in the Arab-Israeli dispute was based on the principle of non-partisanship and recognized the right of both Arabs and Jews to establish a national existence in Palestine. This position was reflected in our support for the Partition 

Resolution of November 29, 1947, which called for the creation of an Arab state, a Jewish state, and an international administration in the 

Jerusalem area. Unfortunately, however, the Partition Resolution was never implemented, and the status quo has been determined by military "solutions" ever since. In this context, the United States gradually became identified as the patron of Israel, a role which undermined our potential as an effective mediator in the conflict. 

Mr. Chairman, recent events have opened new possibilities for 

America to exert its influence in behalf of a just and lasting peace in the Middle East. The determined efforts of Secretary Kissinger to resolve particular issues by tempering the demands of each party without preference to the broader interests of either marks an important step forward. But these diplomatic endeavors must be supported by an equally nonpartisan aid program, which is reflected in the proposed bill. The appropriation of assistance for Israel, Egypt, and Jordan,

and the establishment of a Middle East Special Requirements Fund would underline the intention of the United States to assume a neutral and positive role. The special requirements fund in particular could become an important instrument in demonstrating our good faith. 

As suggested in the working of the appropriations request, the fund could be used to support constructive projects in the West Bank, Gaza, and perhaps Syria as well.

With regard to the question of conditions, Mr. Chairman, we urge that no political riders be attached to this bill. Its purpose is to show our own impartiality and to foster positive endeavors within the recipient states. To attach political conditions would undermine not only the broader aims of the bill, but also the negotiating process which 

Secretary Kissinger has so admirably initiated.

For example, to insist that our assistance to Egypt be conditional upon an Egyptian agreement to permit the passage of Israeli flagships through the Suez Canal would force an issue that can only be resolved through negotiations. Furthermore, the assistance we have given to Israel in the past-far in excess of the amount now being considered for Egypt has never been conditional, though in that case an argument could have been made for general conditions involving principle.

Mr. Chairman, the Middle East Affairs Council is in full support of the proposed foreign assistance bill, and we urge its enactment into law. We commend the Congress for the initiative it has taken in helping to reconstruct an affirmative American role in the Middle East. 

The passage of this bill will become an important landmark in our relations with a troubled area which needs to be reassured of our commitment to the values upon which our own Republic was founded. 

 Now, Mr. Christopher Taylor. 

CHRISTOPHER TAYLOR. Senator, this morning I heard you ask Mr.

Dear Senator Inouye: 

I wish to convey my gratitude to you for allowing me to voice my opinion on the question of a final settlement for the Palestinian people. This question has for too long been obscured by other very complex dimensions of the Arab-Israeli conflict. My original purpose in attending the hearing was to observe rather than to testify. For that reason I was unprepared to make any formal statement; thus what I said came from my heart and I only trust my remarks made sense. In order to clarify my statements, I am submitting the following summary of my ideas. 

First I wish to state my opposition to all terrorism, whether it is carried out in the name of the Palestinian people of in the name of the State of Israel.

As a result of my acquaintance with Dr. Israel Shahak and others concerned with this issue, I have come to the conclusion that the only just and permanent settlement would be the creation of a state which incorporates both peoples, a singular and unified state which would be based on the principle of equality of all citizens and which would also recognize the right of both peoples to realize their national goals. 

After twenty-six years of hate and violence, this goal can hardly be accomplished overnight. Therefore, I urge the creation of a West Bank-Gaza Palestinian state as a beginning not an end. This temporary state would help to ease the anxieties of the Palestinians and, at the same time, would allow the people of Israel the opportunity to view the Palestinians with a new perspective. This measure can, I believe, work only. if it is understood by all parties concerned that this is only a first step. The eventual goal would be a union of both the states and peoples, achieved through a gradual social and economic integration. 

Mr. I.L. Kenen has dismissed both proposals as "utopian" and "impractical". He has stated his belief that the West Bank-Gaza state only offers terrorists a base to attack Israel. 

His concern is understandable; however, the problem of terrorism and counter terrorism can only be solved through tough negotiations between Palestinians and Israelis speaking to each other as equals. On the other hand, the "solution" of the current "terrorist problem" employed by Israel of indiscriminate bombing and shelling of refugee camps and villages serves to intensify not only the bitterness of the Palestinians but also the number and nature of the guerilla attacks.

Mr. Kenen has proposed a "solution" of "re-settlement" which seems to me to fall far short of true justice and is understandably unacceptable to the Palestinians. For hundreds of years the 

Palestinian people struggled for the right to determine their own national destiny and for freedom from the Ottoman Turks, and later they were forced to fight the English for the same reasons. Since 1948 most of the Palestinians have also been refugees from their own land, and not, I might add, refugees by their own choice. Mr. Kenen's proposal of "re-settlement" in the "Arab World" maintains their position as refugees from the land which has been their home for thirteen centuries and also fails to take into account their national aspirations. 

As a concerned human being who is anguished by the terrible wastes of the Maalots and the resulting raids of revenge, I continue to look to the Israel Shahaks, men who look around them and don't see Jew or Arab but rather human beings. I feel that a just settlement, however difficult to achieve, is the only way to stop the mutual hate which I see growing in the minds of both Palestinians and Jews of my own age whom I encounter in my everyday world.

The solution that I have presented may seem "impractical" to Mr. Kenen and many others on both sides; however, I submit, if they will only look at the Palestinian and Jewish nations of tomorrow, they will see the first seeds of hate and blind prejudice which are growing undisturbed in the minds of their youth. They must open their eyes and plant the seeds of justice and compassion, or otherwise they sentence my generation to stand helplessly by and watch a war of mutual genocide in which the question of a "solution" becomes merely academic. 

Senator Inouye, I feel that your question of what is to be done with the Palestinian people is the most relevant issue at hand. 

Therefore, it should be clearly established that the aim of the Special Requirements Fund is to promote a just and lasting settlement for both peoples and not to re-settle the Palestinian people outside their homeland. Thank you again for allowing me to testify before your subcomittee. 

Most sincerely, Christopher S. Taylor 

Christopher S. Taylor

Zembers of this committee for your consistent approval of UNICEF over the years.

The children of today are the potential leaders of the world tomorrow.

UNICEF stresses qualitative aid and operates on the principle of self-help. It is truly a miracle that it continues to help millions of mothers and children each year on less than the governments of the world spend on armaments and destruction in two hours of a day. 

We need to ask ourselves what are our priorities? Isn't one of our important priorities to support the catalytic effect of UNICEF'8 work in the developing countries? 

We are grateful for the Senate's approval of the $15,000,000 for fiscal year 1974 and we sincerely hope that you will continue to support the catalytic effect of UNICEF funds in the development of people and countries and continue to demonstrate our belief in, and leadership of, this emphasis on human worth and development.
