Much has happened during recent years both in national and international affairs that has undoubtedly affected the attitude of the American people on certain foreign policy issues. Whatever they may have decided on other questions, however, it is abundantly clear that public opinion in the United States is even more favorably inclined towards supporting UNICEF now than ever before, especially as people have become better acquainted with the accomplishments. 

Request for a U.S. Contribution of $18 million 

This group of national organizations supports UMI CEF's request for a U.S. contribution of 18 million for Fiscal 1975. This amount was authorized for Fiscal 

1975 by Public Law 93-189 on December 17, 1973; under international organizations and programs, Chapter 3 of Part I, Sec. 9, Item L, which reads: 

"(d) of the funds made available to carry out this Chapter for each of the Fiscal years 1974 and 1975, 18,000,000 shall be available in each such fiscal year only for contributions to the United Nations Children's Fund." 

A contribution of $18 million by the United States in Fiscal 1975 would represent about 28, or considerably less than one-third, of regular government contributions to UNICEF, according to present estimates. The percentage might be oven loser as other governments increase their gifts. So far in calendar year 1974 a number of goverments have indicated their intentions to increase their regular contributions. These include Canada, India, Japan, Norway, Sweden and the United Kingdom. If, however, in Fiscal 1975, the United States 

Government were to fail to contribute $18 million and leave the U.S. figure at $15 million, the percentage of the U.S. contribution would be reduced to 24.6% of total government contributions, or less than the accepted assessment rate of 25%. The U.S. contribution, in 1974, represents only 25.9% of regular government contributions.

Magnitude of the Unmet Needs of Children Children in 111 countries (with a child population of 780 million) are currently being aided by UNICEF. Of these 111 assisted countries, 99 contribute also to UNICEF's general resources. In other words, such contributions are in addition to their participation in UNICEF-assisted programs for children within their own borders. In all, 124 governments contributed to UNICEF in 1973. 

While UNICEF's total revenue from all sources amounted to $95.8 million in 1973, the sum is small in relation to the vast unmet needs of children and youth in the developing countries. UNICEF has a backlog of urgently needed programs which have been approved by the Executive Board but have been deferred until funds become available. At the conclusion of the present (1974) Executive

Board session it is expected that there will be urgently needed programs requiring $12,073,000 which have been approved but for which implementation must be postponed until funds become available. In addition a balance of $4,619,900 for projects noted prior to 1974 is needed, bringing the total to $16,692,900, apart from amounts required for relief and rehabilitation programs such as those mentioned on the following page. UNICEF maintains no reserves in the pipeline but strives instead to put the funds to work for children as quickly as possible, keeping working capital at a very low level. 

A major value of UNICEF's work lies in its catalytic effect in stimulating the developing countries to increase their own input. Two-thirds of UNICEF'S aid goes primarily to equip health, mutrition, educational and community centers directly benefitting millions of infants and children. With the remaining onethird, UNICEF provides transport, some training stipends, and other aid to assist the staff: doctors, murses, midwives, health and mutrition field workers, familychild welfare workers, etc. needed to run the services for children. Yet, despite the enormous strides made in the past quarter century to improve the daily lives of millions of children, three out of four still live in the shadow of hunger, disease and ignorance. Malnutrition, for example, is the biggest single factor contributing to infant and young child mortality in developing countries where 25-30% of these children die before reaching the age of five. Between 400 and 500 million suffer some form of malmutrition while approximately 11 million suffer severe Vitamin A deficiency which unless treated could lead to permanent blindness. 

It is only recently that scientists have begun to assess the full impact on young children of serious diet deficiencies. Disturbing findings relating malmutrition to childhood death rates, to physical growth, to mental development and to later productivity are causing increasing concern not only in the developing world, but wherever children may suffer its effects.

Emergency Needs 

In addition to its basic ongoing programs to benefit children, claims for assistance continue to reach UNICEF from emergency situations resulting from natural disasters and from wars. In addition to the emergency aid provided by 

UNICEF in 1972, Bangladesh, for example, no longer considered simply an emergency situation, contimos to require long-term rehabilitation assistance. 

Funds for other emergency aid for relief and rehabilitation still being sought from special contributions this year are: Indochina... 

Sudano/Sahelian drought.. Ethiopia..... 

Pakistan flood..

In millions of U.S. dollars 20.2 10.6 2.1 7.0

In addition, small amounts have had to be drawn from UNICEF's emergency reserve to assist Israel, Syria and Egypt following the Yom Kippur war.

Disasters make headline news. They attract great public concern and interest for a time. But old crises quickly fade from public memory as new ones monopolize the headlines. The effects of the disasters, however, remain long after the rest of the world has forgotten. After the initial emergency actions to supply food. and temporary necessities, UNICEF prefors to concentrate on the slow, undramatic long-term problems of reconstruction and rehabilitation that require funds, together with patience and persistence to overcome ultimately the damage caused by the original catastrophe. 

Currency Realignment and Price Increases

UNICEF receives payments in some 60 currencies and uses a similar number of currencies to buy supplies and maintain its field offices. The full impact on 

UNICEF's financial resources of the recent instability in international money markets cannot be measured with precision. The world-wide currency realignment of 1971 affected income and expenditures in 1972, and the further realignment of early last year included a second devaluation of the dollar by 10 percent. Based on the new rates of exchange, expenditures for program support and administrative services in 1973 and estimates for 1974 will result in an increase in total dollar costs of over $1 million for the two year period. 

Expenditures are affected by price movements as well as by currency realignments. Since 1971 prices for supplies purchased by UNICEF have increased

more rapidly than in earlier years. Based on average costs of purchases made in 

Europe, Japan and North America, prices for supplies purchased for 1972 seem to be approximately 7 percent higher than in 1971. UNICEF's financial experts expect a similar increase for 1973 over 1972. Thus, taking into account both the changes in the value of the dollar and other price increases, UNICEF's present income will provide a reduced amount of supplies and equipment for direct benefit to children. 

The full extent of such loss becomes almost impossible to measure because thore are thousands of items now being supplied to complex projects in the fields of child health, mutrition and education. As any householder knows, higher prices for the same goods will buy smaller quantities, given a fixed amount of money. 

As has been pointed out in previous years, however, a U.S. contribution to 

UNICEF does not adversely affect the U.S. balance of payments because UNICEF customarily spends all of its contribution from the U.S. in this country. UNICEF spent $27 million in the United States in 1973 while it received $25.5 million in funds from within the U.S. 

Ratio of U.S. Contribution to UNICEF 

The members of our organizations oppose an immediate reduction in the percentage of the U.S. contribution to UNICEF as too drastic and too abrupt. 

Goverments other than the U.S. have increased their regular contributions to 

UNICEF from $14,056,000 in 1965 to $30,624,000 in 1972, an increase of 118 percent. 

In the same period the U.S. increased its contribution from $12 million to $15 million, an increase of 25%. As the trend of contributions from governments other than the United States continues to increase, however, the ratio of the U.S. proportion to the total may decline without the application of a harsh and rigid formula.

A contribution by the U.S. in Fiscal 1975 of $18 million would represent approximately 28% of regular government contributions according to present estimates. 

Surely a sum equal to less than che-third of regular government contributions is a modest enough gift from the United States to the cause of building a better future for the world's children.

We are proud of U.S. leadership in UNICEF in the past and are confident that it will continue. We call attention to the President's words in his report to the Congress on U.S. Participation in Work of the United Nations, September 8, 1972, (H.Doc. 92-297) when he said: "This proposed reduction in our rate of assessment does not affect our voluntary contributions to various UN Programs. 

Indeed, the Lodge Commission recommended increases of at least corresponding size in voluntary contributions whose size depends on each nation's judgment of its own interests and capabilities."

This view seems a realistic and sensible approach to the issue of the appropriate ratio of U.S. support to international organizations. We hope that this Committee will give practical application to this interpretation of the Administration's recommendations by approving $18 million for the Children's Fund in Fiscal 1975.

STATEMENT OF JOHN M. KANE 

Mr. Chairman, Members of the Subcommittee:

I thank you for the opportunity to submit to you today the views of The American Legion on the Fiscal Year 1975 Foreign Assistance Act. This coming fiscal year is a crucial one for many of our allies and our friends around the world. A sound foreign assistance program is urgently needed to help protect those nations and to assist them further in strengthening their economic development and progress. 

The philosophy of The American Legion on foreign aid is contained in our Resolution No. 402-73, which was unanimously adopted by our National Convention held in Honolulu, Hawaii, on August 22, 1973. A copy of that resolution is appended to this testimony for your information. In essence we support 

United States foreign aid to those nations needing our help, who demonstrate a desire to help themselves, cooperate with us in promoting peace and international cooperation, and utilize our aid to enhance the security interests of the free world and to improve the economic and social well-being of their own people.

For many years The American Legion has supported United States foreign aid to deserving countries. We have supported aid as part and parcel of United States foreign policy, as well as a major humanitarian program of assistance to developing countries around the world. We have also supported foreign aid because it has contributed greatly to the capacity of our friends and allies around the world to defend themselves against aggression. 3

I believe we all realize that foreign aid has proven to be an indispensable tool of foreign policy since the end of WWII. Many of the nations we aided in the earlier years of our country's foreign aid programs now are able to go without aid they have developed strong economies and regained the confidence needed to provide political stability, economic progress, and an adequate defense. This, I believe, is the aim of the United States in providing economic and military aid to nations in Africa, Asia, and Latin America today.

Nations which we are continuing to aid today can look with hope to the examples of other countries which profited by our aid Western Europe, South Korea, the Republic of 

China and others and look forward to the day when they too will be self-reliant and no longer need large infusions of captial and technolocial knowhow from us. I hope our government will continue to make it clear that we are not going to substitute our aid for other nations' self-reliance forever and that we will not do for them what they can be expected to do for themselves.

Nevertheless, we realize that millions of people around the globe still lack housing, food and jobs - and that social unrest and economic chaos will threaten their future and ours and give openings for aggressive governments and aggressive ideologies seeking to change borders and institutions of other countries by force and civil strife. So long as these genuine threats exist and it looks as though they will exist for many years, despite talk of detente and cooperation among nations of differing ideologies and different political and economic systems 

we must continue to provide that level of economic

and military aid that will prevent aggression from succeeding and defeat subversion. 

For these reasons The American Legion supports Senate 

Bill S.3394, The Foreign Assistance Act of 1974, of April 29, 1974. 

We note that S.3394 provides for special assistance to two major problem areas today the Middle East and Indochina. 

We wholeheartedly endorse the Administration's programs in these two vital areas of the world. The United States has vital interests in seeing that peace and stability return to both critical areas. In the past we have devoted much money and in the case of Indochina much American blood to insure that democratic self-determination shall continue to exist in the Middle East and in Indochina. We cannot rest yet. Forces are unleashed in both areas that would swamp our friends and lead to further armed conflict, perhaps to an imminent threat of a major conflict between ourselves and the Soviet Union and its Communist allies. We must help our friends there; we also must strive to establish new friendships, especially in the Middle East, and to assist Arab and Jew to find a path to peace and cooperation. 

The most dangerous threat to world peace today lies in the conflict between Arab and Jew in the Middle East. Four times in the past 25 years, major warfare has broken out there. 

Both Israel and the Arab nations have suffered much bloodshed. 

They have suffered setbacks to their economies and have been forced to spend inordinate amounts of money on modern, sophisticated weapons instead of devoting these funds to the wellbeing and progress of their peoples. They seem caught in a

H 13 -5 never ending circle of fighting and sullen truce they cannot break out of without help.

The American Legion is proud of the part the United States is playing, through the offices of Secretary of State Kissinger, to mediate between Israel and its two major adversaries, Egypt and Syria. It appears that we are in a critical period, a period that may mean at least a limited peace in the Middle East. Egypt has shown a praiseworthy example for the entire Arab world. If Syria now agrees to a ceasefire and a troop withdrawal plan with Israel, we would hope that further steps can be initiated at once to insure a general ceasefire and to start negotiations leading to genuine peace throughout that troubled region. 1 We are therefore pleased to see that the President is seeking to implement a truly even-handed policy toward Jew and Arab alike and is asking the Congress for economic assistance for Arab countries as well as military security aid for Israel. For the first time in many years relations between Cairo and Washington have improved to the point where we can with confidence cooperate with Egypt in repairing the damages of war in the Suez Canal area and help restore and develop Egyptian trade. We are also pleased to note that an additional $100 million may be made available on a contingency basis, as the outlines of a political settlement take shape, for contingency forces, refugee aid and resettlement, and economic development projects in the region. 

We sincerely trust that, as the Administration states, this aid will contribute to the security of all the nations in the Middle East and give them the necessary confidence in the peacemaking process to lead to a lasting settlement. The

forces of moderation in the Middle East must take hold and go forward, with our mediation if it is desired by all sides, to establish the basis for a peaceful settlement. 

Second only to the Middle East in importance to the United States today is Indochina. Our nation fought for more than a decade to defeat Communist aggression in South Vietnam and to help give the Republic of Vietnam the opportunity to maintain its independence and its right of self-determination. 

We ourselves lost more than 54,000 Americans killed and over 

300,000 wounded. We cannot let them be considered to have died in vain.

We have a moral and a political commitment to South Vietnam.

S.3394 provides for the expenditure of $1.925.5 billion for security assistance around the world. The American Legion does not profess to have the knowledge necessary to determine

whether these are proper and effective levels of expenditure for grant military aid, for military sales credits, and for security supporting assistance. No nation can pursue economic development without military security, Through the security assistance portion of FY 1975 foreign aid program, the United States is striving to provide the security necessary for economic progress.

We support its emphasis upon the Middle East and Indochina and upon basic developmental aid to developing countries in the areas of food, health and education. We particularly approve the emphasis upon bilateral aid or multilateral aid when and where the United States has a voice in apportioning and supervising such aid.

The long-range interests of the United States depend upon helping our friends and allies economically and militarily and in assisting the developing nations in the interests of world peace and stability. We of The American 

Legion will continue to fight for, and to support, these objectives in all appropriate programs. 

STATEMENT OF DAVID L. HENDRY 

Our group, having a deep humanitarian concern over peace in the Middle East and a national concern over American interests in that region, submit for your perusal and that of other Senate members the following views pertaining to the Foreign Assistance Appropriations for Fiscal 

Year 1975.

Since World War II and the emergence of the United States as a major aid-extender, assistance to the Middle East has been of two types-economic and military--advanced for various raison d'etre. Perhaps it would be well to reassess the motives and objectives underlying our massive aid to the Mideast after almost three decades and relatively little success. 

First, for more than 25 years and until after the October 1973 War, the U.S. has progressively expanded assistance to Israel via military grants and loans, surplus food shipments under Public Law 480, credits through the Export-Import Bank with the lowest interest rate charged Israel of any recipient, economic aid through the regular channel of Foreign Assistance Acts as well as tremendous special arrangements which has led to American financial support for Israeli schools, hospitals, old-age and retirement housing, and resettlement of immigrants. This assistance has been given because Israel has been viewed, until recently, as a means to secure U.S. goals and objectives, or so we have been told. A militarily and economically strong Israel would, we were informed, keep the Mideast free from form war and secure for the West the continuous flow of oil. A strong Israel would curtail the influx of Soviet influence in the region. 

A strong

Israel would help to shore up the so-called "moderate" Arab governments and keeps the "radical" Arab states in line. The die was cast when the 

U.S. precipitatly withdrew its financial backing from the World Bank loan for Egypt's Aswan High Dam in 1955. Since then, continuing our policy in

assistance, including the refusal to sell wheat to Egypt under PL 480 let alone any military or major budgetary assistance, we have seen three major wars in the Middle East, rising governmental and group terrorism, increased Soviet penetration, decreased American influence, and more importantly, a complete boycott by all Arab oil producers ("moderate" and "radical" alike) on shipments to the United States.

The October 1973 War and the consequent petroleum cutoff to the West and the U.S. should have finally made it clear to all those Americans in leadership positions that our policy has been bankrupted: we did not have our oil, we did not have peace or even a hostile if silent status quo as during the six years after June 1967, we had become isolated internationally by our seeming support of Israeli territorial expansion, and Israel did not have security, even at the cost of American interests in the Middle East. 

Our Committee suggests that our aid should be premised upon our own national interests, not to secure the goals of another state (Israel), and that a position of neutrality on the part of the United States will serve to (1) increase American influence and ability to apply pressure on all parties in the area, (2) halt the bipolarization between the U.S. and USSR which has become an obstacle to a just and lasting peace, (3) secure sources of energy for the United States and strengthen economic ties, including outlets for our products. We do not advocate that the U.S. suddenly halt support of Israel through assistance or otherwise but that we halt our tacit support of Israeli conquests. 2 All Senators have been receiving from our organization over the years position papers which show what the cost to our nation has been of our open-ended commitment to Israel. Peace and stability in the Middle East can best be advanced by American support for the economic and social developmen of all countries in that area. We have, as well, a very special interest in the economic development of the pivot Mideast state of Egypt. With a reopened a 

Suez Canal and the Suez-Mediterranean pipeline as well as its oil and natural gas fields in Sinai, the Red Sea, off Alexandria, and in the Western Desert, Egypt is destined to become the most important single transitor of petroleum and very possibly a major exporter of energy itself. It has been largely 

American made and financed weapons which have rained down destruction on Egypt and the Arab states in 1967 and 1973, the deep penetration bombing of Egypt in 1970, the bombing and Israeli incursions into Lebanon and Jordan since and even before 1967, and Israeli air strikes against Syria in the late summer of 1973. With the scars of such destruction and the memory of the long U.S. alliance with Israel--an occupier in Arab and world eyes as witnessed by repeated United Nations votes--the United States has to overcome the hostility of the sweeping majority of Middle Eastern people. We believe a constructive, non-political presence through economic support of important development projects in the region would go a long way to refurbishing the tarnished American image. That tarnish is not an imagined one; 

Americans have simply been unaware and lulled because there was seeming quiescence in the Middle East from 1967 to 1973. And unlike the question of reconstruction aid to North Vietnam, the U.S. has neven been at war with nor have our troops been militarily engaged against those of any Arab state. 

Our Committee would support substantial long-term, low-interest loans or special grants to Egypt, Jordan, Lebanon, and any other Mideastern state which requires capital or technical cooperation to spur on its development. 

We would also support greater financial assistance for the health, education, and resettlement of Palestinian refugees. Along with a settlement for these 

Palestinians, in accordance with UN Resolution 242 and hopefully as formalized in the upcoming Geneva Conference, the United States should be prepared to extend sizeable economic support to enable a productive evolution of whatever solution is finally adopted by the Palestinian majority itself, whether a single or combination of solutions--a separate state, partial repatriation to Israel, and/or resettlement in other Middle Eastern countries

or the West. An economic success for the Palestinians would do much to defuse the more radical and desperate element permeating the Palestinian people.

Finally, our Committee requests a substantial cutback on military assistance to Israel since this policy has not achieved the hoped for results, including the security of Israel. Even the expanded borders of 

Israel did not protect it from war in October 1973 nor a blockade of Elath this time further south from Egypt's Sharm el Sheikh in Sinai. In fact, only a lasting peace can give Israel security and to be lasting, a peace must be just and meet a modicum for all those parties involved. 

In May 1972, almost a year and a half before the oil boycott, our position paper 

13, "Economic Realities and the Middle East," concluded: "There is nothing wrong or immoral in the United States pursuing its own national interests in the Middle East when those interests are enlightened and premised upon neutrality and the search for a just and lasting peace as well as improving American relations with all the countries in the region. 

Returning to our national energy crisis, we should recall that traditionally and historically there has been an excess producing capacity in oil on a world-wide basis. As a result we have been able to cope with both the threat of and actual disruption in petroleum flow. Now this is no longer true and because of the vast reserves of petroleum in Arab countries, stability in the Middle East is of ever increasing importance for the United States. It is no longer a question of "if" or "whether" our country will become dependent upon imported petroleum from the Middle East. The reality is when, to what extent, and under what conditions will the U.S. come to rely heavily on Arab oi. It is in our self-interest to work toward a high level of economic reciprocity in Arab-American relations, particularly as the energy crisis is a global one which bodes for greater interdependence between and among all consuming countries. "1 The past few months have proven our statement only too true; we hope that you will give credence and weight to the views we have expressed today on forthcoming U.S. economic assistance to the Middle East. 

Sincerely yours

STATEMENT OF DR. CARL E. TAYLOR Population Planning and Health Provisions of Public Law 93-189 (Foreign Assistance Act of 1973) 

The National Council for International Health endorses the new functional emphasis on population planning and health in the Foreign Assistance Act of 1973. Having reviewed the provisions of the Act, the Council believes that the provisions of the Act can be strengthened and clarified in order to improve the continuing population program emphasis within a social and political context which is flexibly adjusted to the varying needs of the less developed countries. I. 

Present Legislation

A. Relevant Provisions of the Authorizing Legislation 

(Public Law 93-189)

Section 102: 

Statement of Policy 

"(2) Future United States bilateral support for development should focus on critical problems in those functional sectors which affect the lives of the majority of the people in developing countries: food production, rural development and nutrition; population planning and health; and education, public administration and human resources development." "(5) United States bilateral development assistance should give the highest priority to undertakings submitted by host governments which directly improve the lives of the poorest of the people and their capacity to participate in the development of their country." "Section 104

Population Planning and Health. In order to increase the opportunities and motivation for family planning, to reduce the rate of population growth, to prevent and combat disease, and to help provide services for the great majority, the President is authorized to furnish assistance on such terms and conditions as he may determine, for population planning and health. They are authorized to be appropriated to the 

President for the purposes of this section, in addition to the funds otherwise available for such purposes, $145 million for each of the fiscal years 1974 and 1975 which amounts are authorized to remain available until expended." 

"Programs Relating to Population Growth Section 8. Section 292 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 is amended by striking out "For each of the fiscal years 1972 and 1973, $125 million" and inserting in lieu thereof "For the Fiscal year 1974, $125 million, and for the fiscal year 1975, $130 million." 

B. In Public Law 93-240, the Appropriations Act of January 2, 1974, the following provision is stated: For 

"Population planning and health, Development Assistance: 

necessary expenses to carry out the provisions of Section 104, $135 million: provided, that in addition to the amount provided for loans to carry out the purposes of this paragraph, such amounts as are provided for under Section 203 shall be available for loans, together all such amounts to remain available until expended: provided further,

ご ​R that no more than $112,500,000 appropriated or made available under this act shall be used for the purposes of Section 291 during the current fiscal year. "

II. The Difference Between Population and Health Funding Unlike the food or education sections of the Authorization Act which do not specify more detailed earmarking of funds, the population and health section (Section 104) specifies that $125 million will be authorized for population programs in FY 1974 out of the total $145 million authorization, thereby leaving $20 million for health other than population. 

As the population earmarking is increased to $130 million in 1975, only $15 million would be authorized for health during the second year. In the 

Appropriation Act, a ceiling of $112,500,000 for population is to be made available out of a total appropriation of $135 million for population and health, thereby leaving a balance of approximately $22.5 million for health. 

The Council endorses the continued need for a vigorous population program with the financial priority as indicated in the above legislation. 

However, since the funding authorization for population exceeds that of health by a factor of 10 in FY 1975 and by a factor of 5 in the current Appropriations Act, there is concern as to whether this balance reflects the most effective long-range approach to sustain a population program in less developed countries. Congressional intent is stated in the following way in the Senate Authorization Committee Report: "The Committee recognizes that slowing population growth requires more than access to birth control devices. Motivation to reduce family size can be increased if social and economic conditions in the developing countries improve." The House 

Authorization Committee Report reads: "New approaches going beyond traditional family planning programs are needed. The United States should be prepared to aid the developing countries in establishing low-cost systems of extending services to the urban and rural poor. For both humanitarian and logistic reasons, such delivery systems should be devised in an integrated strategy to combat the related problems of inadequate health care, insufficient nutritious food, poor sanitation, and excessive population growth."

Given the urgency of the population problem, and the limited resource availabilities in the Foreign Assistance Act, the Council recognizes that priority choices must be made. There is no illusion that the United States Government should undertake to sponsor major comprehensive health systems which would seriously dilute the effect of technical assistance in the population field. On the other hand, there is much experience which suggests that isolated population programs in developing countries have created public and political resistance to international assistance for population programs. 

III. 

Current Progress Towards Acceptance of Population Services in Developing Countries 

United States bilateral efforts have now been underway for eight years. Almost $500 million have been obligated for population programs. 

During this period of time, the major input of the United States, representing the largest donor in the population field, has contributed significantly towards to acceptance of official population policies by many developing governments. Recognition of the problem, policy formulation, and the beginning introduction of population services in many countries is a direct concrete response to Congressional support. In spite of this effort, the practice of family planning among couples of reproductive age in developing countries remains at about the 10%-15% level. Levels of practice parallel, to a considerable degree, the magnitude of the existing health infrastructure. The very high degree of participation in cities such as Hong Kong and Singapore and countries

such as Japan directly reflect the large public and private health infrastructure through which family planning services are made widely available. Countries with 25%-40% acceptance such as Korea and Taiwan also reflect a comparatively large availability of health manpower and facilities. For the largest developing countries, however, continuing contraceptive practice remains relatively low. In India and Pakistan where family planning programs have been official for over 15 years, modern contraceptive practice remains less than 15%. Indonesia is reported to have 8% participation on the Island of Java. In Latin 

America, outside of small countries with excellent services such as Costa Rica, family planning practice still remains relatively low. 

IV. 

Relationship Between Population and Health in Developing Countries 

Experience to date confirms that the development of national population programs in developing countries are dependent upon a distribution mechanism, commercial or non-commercial, public or private, through which services become widely available. For most developing countries, current marketing or delivery systems are poorly developed. In the absence of a network, neither population services nor any other health services can be made available to the majority of the population. 

Governments seek to cope with the problem in several principal ways. 

The first is to use the existing public and private health delivery system. 

Such systems are limited in the scope of coverage, and therefore, after . population services are introduced, levels of acceptance tend not to exceed the capacity of the system. For extension beyond the system, some governments such as Thailand seek to use auxiliary health personnel who perform the combined functions of providing health, population and nutrition services. Other governments such as Pakistan have sought to establish a special category of personnel who principally do family planning, but who also carry out minor services in the area of maternal and child health. In practice, population services are not readily accepted by users in complete isolation from other perceived basic health needs. Population programs draw heavily, although not exclusively, upon health trained personnel, health clinic facilities, health information systems, medical research and pharmaceutical supply systems. However,

It is often suggested that population planning is not entirely a matter of health because it involves such considerations as literacy, education of women, agricultural policy, legal sanctions, information, etc.. 

Certainly, the effects of population are all-pervasive. 

Influence upon human fertility behavior extends far beyond the control of a Minister of Health. Because of its importance it is desirable to have population policy determined at governmental levels above the Ministry of Health. the improvement of human well-being, whether in the area of nutrition, maternal and child health, occupational health, or in other specific health problems such as malaria and tuberculosis, are all influenced by the same non-medical considerations. None of these programs are effectively carried out without considerations of law, employment, availability of food, financial policies, public information and other factors which are considered to be outside of the area of health. Population measures are similar to health activities in that they share the common denominator that human biological and social behavior is changed by biological and social means.

In effect, population planning requires a thorough understanding of national health planning in the public and private sectors. It requires a thorough appreciation of resource management. It is estimated that A.I.D.assisted developing countries now have on the order of $10-$15 billion available for health expenditures in the public and private sectors. While this total investment is small in comparison to the very large investments in individual western countries, the total availability of resources is

not inconsiderable. Indeed, it would be wasteful to allocate funds for population or any other health field in an international assistance program if there were not a thorough understanding of what countries can do for themselves. If, for reasons of economy, less affluent governments elect to use health personnel for carrying out multiple related health tasks rather than establishing costly separate personnel systems for each separate health activity, United States policies should support the locally determined policy. V.

Number of Countries with A.I.D.-Assisted Population and Health 

Programs The special force of the current legislation permits active bilateral population programs in 39 A.I.D.-assisted countries and, in combination with voluntary and multilateral organizations, programs in approximately 69 countries. Under the category of health or "nonpopulation" programs, the United States is assisting only 21 countries. 

There are 28 A.I.D.-assisted countries which do not have bilateral health programs or personnel available to make the most effective use of existing national health plans.

Not more than eight A.I.D.-assisted countries have A.I.D. field personnel with the training and experience to help develop low cost delivery systems to reach the large majority of the population who now have limited or no access to population, nutrition or other minimal health programs on a convenient basis. The absence of this network now constitutes a major barrier to the accomplishment of population goals. 

Unless direct efforts are made to develop such programs which are socially acceptable, convenient to reach, and within the ability of a country to afford on its own, progress towards fertility reduction will remain slow. 

Given the limited state of population coverage at this point, the issue is not to determine the cheapest possible program, but the cheapest program which governments will accept and support. 

VI. 

Current Legislation 

The current budgetary allocations in present legislation continue to be open to the interpretation that the overwhelming thrust of U. s. population and health assistance is in "programs related to population growth". If these funds are indeed to be spent effectively on the more targeted population emphasis, an emphasis with which we entirely agree, it is essential that additional funds be made available for the provision of the minimal prerequisite health infrastructure. With few exceptions, LDC governments have clearly stated national policies which specify that population programs are to be an integral part of their national health system. If rapid progress towards population goals on a national scale is dependent upon input by the government or private sector to develop systems to achieve effective access to the majority of the population, the lack of such systems become an obstacle in progress in family planning. For the purpose of extending population programs rapidly, legislation should permit greater parity between population funds and those special MCH related funds which provide the long-range institutional network for population services. 

In contrast with the need for coordinated programs and administration, the force of the current legislation is to encourage implementation along separated lines in order to administer the separate provisions of the Act. 

Accordingly, the population program is administered separately from the health and nutrition structure in the Foreign Assistance Program.

Quite aside from considerations of efficiency and economy, the United States health interest is perceived by many developing countries as an effort primarily focussed on population control. Given the degree of human suffering around the world, a continued high prevalence of disease, the absence of trained manpower, and the particularly high toll of life among young children, over-emphasis on population is easily misunderstood. From a professional health point of view, there are probably no more effective elements in a program for maternal and child health than the practice of family planning. For this reason, the United 

States population goals could be vigorously pursued while clearly presenting an unmistakable concern for the well-being of the family. 

Since the goal of demographic transition is to achieve low birth rates and low death rates and since both conditions are essential for an improved quality of life, there is no need to contribute to the apprehension that reduction of disease and malnutrition are counterproductive when combined with effective population programs. 

VII. 

Recommendation In

The Council wishes to re-affirm support for continuing the high priority for population planning within the Foreign Assistance Act. order to present U. S. population assistance in the most favorable light, to effectively support the extension of delivery systems for population and health to the majority, to establish long-range institutions which can sponsor and support a high level of participation by couples of reproductive age, to reduce preventable disease, and to achieve the most effective use of limited health resources, it is recommended that legislation be revised to encourage joint health and population capability without decreasing the continued emphasis on population. 

In order to present a unified image of U. S. concern for the wellbeing of all people and without decreasing the emphasis on population programs, we would urge parity in funding between population and health programs.

If Congress feels that it is essential to retain the special earmarking for population funds in the Authorization and Appropriation Bills, (Programs Relating to Population Growth), the Council recommends that comparable earmarking be provided for the provision of the basic health infrastructure to support the rapid extension of population programs and for effective planning within the health sector.

STATEMENT OF DR. RANASAMY NATESAN 

Mr. Chairman and Members of the Committee, I would like to express my deepest appreciation for giving me an opportunity to submit my statements for your proposal on foreign aid for the international, social and economic development. 

At the time when the richest nations in the world are having economical crises, the world leadership like our nation has a moral responsibility to access the impact the economical crises around the world might have on the developing and the underdeveloped nations. Every citizen in our nation might appreciate the system of our government and our constitution. Although our branches of government are co-equal branches, at a time when there is a crisis in the executive branch obviously responsibility falls on the shoulder of the legislative branch in accessing the priority ofour programs domestic level as well as international level. Over the years by the cooperation of the foreign relations committee and foreign assistance appropriations committee as well as the Executive branch have made a very remarkable change in the developing nations and the underdeveloped nations by our contributions namely, money, material and men for the welfare of mankind. 

American contributions in pioneering this spirit throughout the world are indeed significant. Freedom to colonial people gave new spirit and aspirations. 

Growing strength of independence and responsibility gave clear national perspectives, development plans and above all a display of uncompromising determination to preserve freedom and national sovereignty. For example, a country like India took since World War II, the determined steps through planned development to transfer her economy from one of scarcity to self sufficiency maybe in the near future. In this planned development, India underwent difficulties and deficiencies caused by natural and other causes. In spite of these difficulties and deficiencies it pulled out its stagnant economy of British era to moderately rising levels, established basic industries and constructed impressive infrastructures of transportation, communication and power, and developed social overheads of education, health services and public administration. This unique process of economic and social development of the worlds largest free democracy has been accomplished largely by India's own resources. About 80 to 85% of the development investment has been made by India. The remainder has been furnished in grants and loans by international organizations and friendly nations throughout the world, chiefly the United States which has extended economic assistance totalling over $10 billion since 1947. When we help people around the world in good faith, we get it back from those people in return with gratitude, more than what we gave. For example, the recent report made by the United Nations Conference of Trade and Development:

When a medical doctor leaves India to settle in the United States it amounts to a loss of $44,336 for India and a gain of $710,000 in the U.S. Every scientist leaving India makes the country poorer by $23,698 while adding $260,000 to the wealth of America reports PTL. In 1970 a total of 3,141 Indian doctors and scientists emigrated to U.S. thus contributing a staggering 901.63 million dollars to that country in a single year by way of brain drain. These and other monetary effects of the brain drain have come out of the latest study by the United Nations 

Conference of Trade and Development of what is called "the reverse transfer of technology". Using a mathematical formula, UNCTAD for the first time analyzed the effects of brain drain in terms of an easily understandable quantity - money. 

Some 11,236 scientists and doctors from all developing countries emigrated to U.S. in 1970, the study says. In that year alone net income to U.S. from this brain drain was $3812.34 million which is more than 6.3 percent of its gross national product and 39 percent of what it spends on higher education. The income gained by U.S. as a result of immigration in a single year (1970) is in fact 1/8 of what was spent in 12 years for post-war recovery of Europe under Marshall Plan. The overall picture that has emerged from UNCTAD study "is one of a massive net income transfer from the developing countries to the United States in the form of brain drain. According to the study the "reverse transfer of technology" has reached massive proportions and biggest contributions are made by "countries that are among the poorest in the developing world itself." 

UNCTAD's brain drain study for 1970 has shown that in that year 69% of immigrants to U.S. came from developing countries. While taking foreign assistance for

its development, India was jealously guarding its political and economic freedom. 

This fear of foreign interference, a hangover of the past, perhaps had been carried too far to the disadvantage of securing rapid economic and social programs at national levels through free play of market economic forces and international cooperation. It is equally true to extend this negative factor at the world stage and have reflections on immediately recognizing how the differences born out of opposing ideologies, philosophies, national traditions, culture and economic interest shaped by varying geographies and histories keep people of the world divided and less united and cooperative. In pursuit of narrow national interest, at the cost of others, some powerful and rich nations pursue the part of outmoded mutual alliances, defense pact, balance of power gains and shrouded political diplomacy. This caused poor nations to spend unproportionately large amounts on defense and military hardwares, suppressing the popular aspirations of people and tending to become finally backward and repressive regimes. Step by step this process keeps the real development denied, large masses of people illiterate and poor and true exercise of democracy remote and receding. Unknowingly and definitely in the absence of real development, some poor nations have been driven to embrace political extremism. In an era of increasing interdependence, India in spite of its declared and demonstrated policy of nonalinement with any power blocs in international relationships is effected by foreign policies of other nations and this naturally effects the free flow of foreign assistance and national development. This condition is also applicable in the case of many other developing countries in varying degrees. It is here that the people of America, richly inherited with the constitution embodying high ideals of immortal values and truth have to seriously consider attitudes and approaches to human welfate, rights and dignity of life, freedom and democracy of governing institutions on a continuing basis of development of mankind. It so often happens that emphasis on outward differences and narrow national interest gets prior attention against the hidden fundamental unity of purpose and life amongst diversity. This promotes the nations of the world to devote over $250 billion per year on military expenditures. 

It continues to expand at a rate faster than general growth rates whereas development expenditures both in absolute and comparative growth interest is of a lower order. 

Foreign governmental aid forming significant shares of government aid flowing through developing countries is only on the order of about $7 to $10 billion per year. These figures speak for themselves. The magnitude of international cooperation and international non-cooperation is born out of selfish interest, distrust and fear. If this drag on military expenditures is reduced or even controlled at the present level, the world would enjoy higher levels of welfare and speed up development growth. The new order of growth alone will unfold vital scientific knowledge and secrets of nature on constructive development paths so far unknown to mankind.

The United States has produced outstanding leaders of world status and statesmanship. As the richest and stablest democracy of the world, our nation has a vision, vigor and vitality to deliver the rights and redeem two-thirds of the world population from the persistent poverty, ignorance and disease. This requires only rearrangement of priorities with emphasis on constructive development programs and relatively reduced roles of military strategy. For example, the executive branch has supported for the Vietnam war over $100 billion, killing men as well as wasting our resources and achieving a result which cannot be compared; by giving the same $100 billion through United Nations our money, men and material could have achieved a lasting peace in the world with a commanding world leadership for the United States.

Now before us a proposal to give over $2 billion for three million people in Israel in the name of foreign aid for the year 1974, whereas a country like Egypt with 35 million people our economical aid may be, if the legislative branch approves, $250 million. To the disappointment of the people of India and many members of the Contress as well as the people of our great nation, the economical aid for the nation that has over 580 million people is about $75 million. This type of disparity proposed by the executive branch may have to be corrected by the legislative branch.

In my judgment, I would urge you to persuade your colleagues to recognize the need for the priorities in giving social and economical aid for India. It should be increased to ten times the present seventy-five million proposed. This should be given in the form of food grains and economical assistance. 

As you know, for the year 1972 the earmarked aid to India was about four hundred million dollars but it was not passed by the Senate. During this period the administration took a harder line against India and cut our aid to India which crippled the slow growth towards progress. This particular crisis has been exposed to concerned American citizens by Mr. Jack Anderson (See Appendix I) in which you find the foreign aid given to the world. India has the least amount receivedduring this period although it has 580 million people living with the crisis. Although there is a controversy that poor nations like India should not have entered the nuclear club at a time when the resources for the economical growth is not sufficient; our nation may have to give any aid to countries like 

India in the form of material not in the form of money by which our justification in giving our resources may not be wasted. Resources, technical and managerial know-how available in rich countries are enough to wipe out the disparity existing between rich and poor countries. Again the straight requirement is the national will and determination to mount international cooperation in organized development efforts and programs. Experts have determined the development requirement of resources to the so called Third World of developing nations would be in the order of $25 to $35 billion per year for the next twenty years. This order of foreign assistance will soon set a self sustaining economy among the developing and underdeveloped countries. We also witness a phenomenon of hot money flow from one or two countries. West Germany has faced in a short period of time, a great deluge proportions of about $15 to $20 billion seeking refuge in the central banks of West Germany to benefit short term interest differentials and speculation being of marc re-evaluation during 1972.

On one side we face negative expenditures on armaments for which no nation is sure of any limit consistent with the requirements of national interest. On the other hand the international capitals flow from banking sectors creating excessive liquidity in a few countries, making inflationary economics and at the same time starving large numbers of developing countries for the lack of the same. 

Here again the unjustified foreign policy of our executive branch in reference to the Middle East which we persistently supported the three million people in Israel who disregarded the United Nations resolutions and the sovereign rights of Palestinian people due to the arrogance of power shown by Israel which is supported by our executive branch should be corrected by the legislative branch. 

The economical crisis created by the increased price of crude oil by the Arab Nations which boycotted the American goods as well as the rejection of American business has created a definite economical crisis for our nation today. It is a painful, big price that. the American people have to pay at the time that the executive branch is in a crisis. The moral leadership in the legislative branch given by men like Honorable Fulbright may not show much impact unless other membersof his committee exercise the authority and power to correct the mistakes made by the executive branch. At a time like this, when the Arab nations are expected to have a surplus of over $70 billion to $90 billion, our foreign policy is the greatest obstacle for our economical growth. The U.N. and U.S. should persuade oil producing countries to deposit their surplus money into the world bank to help close the gap between the poor and rich. 

The late Lester Pearson's commission officially known as the Commission of International Development, was appointed by World Bank to examine and advise the strategy for development in the second development decade. The Pearson 

Commission report addressed to world leaders in general and people at large end primarily at the policy makers of international aid have set definite targets, performance program measures connected with second development decade. 

This acceptance and implementation by all countries will have far reaching international development and this will insure enduring peace and progress on this shrinking planet, earth of man.

International development agencies have organized massive transfers of resources and know-how from wealthy nations to developing countries largely through governmental aids. This traditional method is influenced by commercial and national interest of aid giving nations, and to some extent, used as an instrument

to influence the receiver into power blocs. 

Self-interest with individual and national interest with countries are the real motivating forces in all development activities, but after certain limits it takes up defensive mechanisms to protect its status quo and this fact we witness in limited wars, exclusive alliance and balance of power through spheres of influence, and others. 

There are two areas which could be effectively put into operation for worldwide development programs.

Improved relationship in world trade and an increase in the present growth. 

Multinational corporations undertaking different functional activities like production, business, banking and other services should be channeled through the international development and servicing organizations. 

This will meet the needs of developing countries effectively and quickly, eliminate fears of outside interference and unilateral action of powerful countries in any manner affecting the interests of both. The rich countries should allow and help international agencies like UNDP, UNIDO, World Bank, regional development banks and international financial and development corporations with adequate revenue earning powers to establish sufficient executive agencies for international development. Then only the dependence on conventional armaments for national security and national interest can gradually be reduced and in its place international agencies for cooperation and development can come up through orderly evolution.

As with national development, international cooperation and development cannot be totally relied upon public finance and governmental support. Private industrial, business and banking corporations operating at national and international levels should be encouraged through incentives to increase their network of operations throughout the world. Such multinational corporations accredited and recognized by world agencies will find ready acceptance amongst developing counties for participation in their national reconstruction and development without fear or political interference. Simultaneously, a fraction of public finance of the rich countries finding its way as foreign governmental aid to the developing countries can now be diverted with greater advantage to the private corporations as incentives providing safeguards against compensation for nationalization, providing insurance against any local conflicts and other contingencies. These services can be extended through international agencies like UNDP, UNIDO, World Bank, regional development corporations and they may be allowed to collect some service charges. 

This will help these agencies to replenish any claims guaranteed to these private corporations. In this connection I would like your consideration to double the 

African Development Bank, Asian Development Bank, UNIDO and IBRD loan, credit or assistance. By your persuasion in taking the military aid from foreign aid to the defense budget; which would give sufficient funds to support these agencies without much hardship to find the resources for these above mentioned organizations to function more effectively. Through such programs, the flow of foreign aid can be considerably increased with smaller public finance and at the same time give confidence and assurance among the developing countries that their political freedom will not be affected. Multinational corporations operating industries, business and banking are adequately equipped to undertake development programs in underdeveloped countries. Priorities like development of power, roads, rails, shipping, processing of primary agricultural commodities as well as minerals like steel and nonferrous metals, refining of petroleum, establishing fertilizer projects, petro-chemical complex are the different areas which will help developing countries to close quickly the widening gap of economic disparity between the rich and the poor countries. The world is tending to grow smaller and moves toward a homogeneity with fast developing economies of the world, faster space commanication and other related developments. Each nation, large or small, is rapid-. ly coming to a state of economic interdependence. Increasingly, national economy, commerce, technology, banking and currency are internationalized giving scope for vider and greater international cooperation. World trade has great potential if allowed to develop in orderly manner and will bring much needed world peace and progress.

In the current world of modern era, epoch making scientific discoveries and application of new technologies open up expanding frontiers of dynamic

growth and calls for new values and dimensions of social structure, Toward the same, individuals and institutions at the national and international level have to prepare themselves for the new challenges and responses. 

Mr. Chairman and members of this committee, I want to remind you that our late 

President Kennedy said at his inaugural address that "If the free society cannot help many who are poor, it cannot save the few who are rich." I believe America has historic greatness in ability, vision, and faith. Americans can move the world closer to a durable peace and progress. Americans working with each other and with other nations can make this vision real. America is the pioneer in organizing the international aid program. 

We have difficulties domestically, so ве realize that we cannot extend more. This country stands for freedom and democracy and so we realize that we must assist other nations too. Our country spends a lot of money through the governmental aids. Why not direct the public revenue to the international agency directly instead of government to government. 

Multinational corporations should also be drawn in this effort. The international agencies do not have resources and staff as much as a multinational corporation. 

It is the commercial corporations throughout the world that are fully equipped for worldwide development. Now as with nations, internationally also we can build up economic development through the fiscal incentives and through certain other incentives. 

I plead for the developing countries that America alone can do that effectively because it is a leader and it is the strongest nation in every respect. 

I strongly suggest that you could negotiate with your own colleagues in your committee and the members of the House to drop the idea of any military assistance going through the foreign aid. By saving the amount earmarked for military assistance in foreign aid, you could capture the amount needed by giving priority to countries like india which need social and economic aid specifically earmarked for food, health, education and then for any development programs for social and economic growth. By the above mentioned methods, I assure you that you and your committee can help mankind, The method of innovation in foreign aid will help close the gap between poor and rich nations. It is very important matter that we can give serious consideration without further delay. By saving this amount going into military aid we could use it for assistance to refugees, international financial institutions, Peace Corps, Asian Development Bank, World Bank, UN, UNDP and Export-Import Bank activities which are doing the services for the welfare of mankind.

In concluding my remarks, I wish to emphasize America has a unique capacity of world leadership and unrivaled ability in organization and management of all human endeavor. This can be put to great advantage to us and the rest of the nations by suitably adopting our priorities and goals to changing requirements of the world.

Mr. Chairman, before closing my statement I want to state that the President's goal of bequeathing a generation of peace to America is a great ideal and a positive approach to world peace and progress. This goal has to be matched with constructive policies and programs at national and international levels. Western democracies and America in particular, have a great role to play in matching the instinctive urge to create, control and live a better life for all mankind rather than wasting our resources. I hope and wish that you, the members of this committee, Members of the Senate and House could give serious consoderation to my proposal as you the legislative branch of my government with a democratic power of our people with wisdom and judgment to shape the right kind of life for people of our nation and through us to serve the people of the world. 

I appreciate your and your committee giving me an opportunity to express my views on foreign assistance. I hope and wish that you recognize your authority and responsibility as the chairman of this committee; who could do a great deal to help mankind.

STATEMENT OF WINNIFRED E. MORGAN 

I strongly protest the appropriation of so much money for Israel, especially the fifty million dollars to house Soviet Jews who are to immigrate to Israel and the 1.5 billion dollars guaranteed to Israel for five years which is to be requested for Israel's defense. I believe that charity begins at home and we have urgent domestic priorities, including housing, on which that money could be spent. I am also opposed to making a commitment to a foreign nation which we do not make to our own institutions.

However, my strongest reason for opposing such ample funding for Israel's defense is my belief that the money is to be used for aggression. I simply do not want my tax dollars used to buy the means to devaste South Lebanon, a province of a Republic which not only has not harmed the United States but also has not harmed Israel, or to obliterate the Palestinian refugee camps. Israel deprived a whole society of its land and property and must take her part in solving the problem she created and, not by wiping out the Palestinians. I do not want a final solution to either the Jewish or the Palestinian problem. 

Israel has been an outlaw state since her inception. She bolstered her numbers in Palestine by illegal immigration, brought down the British mandate in a crescendo of terrorism, and, at the time of the partition of Palestine, although she owned only 5.66% of the land and represented only % of the population, was not satisfied with 56% of the area but had to seize another 22% and evict the inhabitants in so doing. She was admitted to the United Nations on condition that she take back the refugees but has always refused to do so. That was the first UN resolution Israel ignored. She has ignored sixty-two more. 

Israel began her policy of expansion in 1947 but has continued it ever since. 

When she occupies a territory she expels the inhabitants in order to make room for immigrant Jews. UNRWA estimated that on March 31, 1968, the number of refugees or newly displaced persons was as follows: U.A.R.
