The numbers have risen since. In the last war Israel bombed the cities of Ismailia, Port Said, and Suez so intensely that the estimate of civilian casualties is in the vicinity of 6,000 and up to 75,000 are homeless. Israel expelled most of the population of the Golan Heights after the 1967 war and planted paramilitary settlements and in this one she destroyed the villages as she advanced and forced the inhabitants over the cease fire line so we can add another 23,000 homeless from her advance into Syria. Lebanon estimates the number of her 

Palestinians as 300,000 or, ten percent of her total population. In addition, since 

Israel has been systematically destroying South Lebanon: houses, crops, olive groves, orchards, irrigation, automobiles, telephone and telegraph installations, schools, dispensaries, and has threatened on numerous occasions to make life there "unlivable" and to destroy all civil life in Lebanon, that country now has thousands of refugees from her own south, although she has never violated the 1949 cease fire line.

Unique among the nations of the world Israel claims the right to bomb, rocket, or invade her neighbour's territory in retaliation, an excuse unknown in international law and prohibited by the UN charter. The best answer to her persistent charge of "terrorism" was made by the President of the UN Security Council on April 18, 1974, when Israel was condemned, for the thirteenth time, for aggression against Lebanon. I would like to quote from it: "The main Israeli argument has centered on the claim that the three persons involved in the Qyriat Shmona attack had crossed from Lebanon. Members of the Council are well aware that the only evidence presented in support of that claim is the statement of the representative of Israel: hardly a conclusive piece of evidence.

Israel has never requested a United Nations inquiry to establish the facts; did not seek the aid of the United Nations Truce Supervision Organization personnel to corroborate its presumed findings; nor did it seek the judgment of the Council. On the contrary, Israel followed its established policy of aggressive-

1 ness, took the law into its own hands and arrogated to itself the dubious role of policeman, judge, and executioner.

Even if we accept, for the sake of argument, that those three unfortunate men had crossed from Lebanon, would it be fair or rational to hold Lebanon responsible? Would it be fair to ask any country, especially small Lebanon, with its limited security forces, to undertake the protection of Israel, when Israel itself, with its barbed wire fences, electronic devices, large security forces and para-military settlements all along the territories it holds has, as has been shown in this particular case, demonstrably failed to achieve that end? Is it reasonable to ask Lebanon, which shoulders the burden of caring in whatever way it can for the 300,000 Palestinians exiled from their homeland, to devote its resources to protecting the usurper and oppressor from the wrath of its victims? 

Only yesterday General Ariel Sharon, one of the leaders of the Opposition in the Israel Knesset, criticizing the Government security arrangements at the borders, charged Israel had been negligent in protecting Qiryat Shmona and demanded that the Government should not shirk its responsibility and should not try to put the blame on Lebanon. Yet General Moshe Dayan, according to today's issue of the Jerusalem Post, which reported the debate, insisted in his reply that his Government will hold Lebanon responsible for all acts of terror. 

Members of the Council are well aware of the fact that this cycle of violence and violent reprisals has marked Israel's policy toward Lebanon for a number of years. On each and every occasion that Israel has been brought before this 

Council to defend its aggression against Lebanon, it has emphatically stated that that is the only way to put an end to bloodshed. The months and years have passed and the hundreds of lives that have been lost should surely have convinced the Council of the fallacy of such a claim and the futility of such a policy, even in revenge. Unfortunately, as the present event has shown, Israel is not yet convinced.

The loss of a single human life is sad and tragic. To be fair, however, and to be able to put an end to this cycle of violence, the Council has a duty to consider events within their proper context. The desperate acts of some Palestinians which have brought such murderous punishment upon Lebanon and which the Israeli representative is so fond of labelling as Arab terrorism must be considered in the light of the unprecedented tragedy of the people of Palestine and the profound repercussions throughout the Arab world. For that tragedy Zionists must bear the primary guilt and responsibility. But none of us is completely blameless. The words of the eminent British historian, Arnold Toynbee are worthy of recall on this occasion. He said: "The Palestinian Arabs have an understandable vendetta against the Israelis, but they also have a grievance against all the rest of us. Half a century of massive indifference to their wrongs has had the same exasperating effect on them as a century of similar treatment has had on the black citizens of the United States. The Palestinians are now in a mood for sacrificing their lives if by wrecking the pillar they can bring the roof down on their Israeli enemies' heads; and if the crashing masonry were incidentally to stove in the skulls of the rest of the human race, why should the Palestinian Arabs care? What have the rest of us done to deserve consideration from them?" Professor Tonbee concludes his article by saying: "Today the Palestinian faces the human stone wall, and it is no wonder if, after beating his head against it in vain, he seizes a stick of gelignite and blows up himself, the wall, and his unresponsive fellow human beings on the far side. 

What else is he, or any one of us, to do? We have to face this fateful question frankly if we are to have any chance of finding the urgently needed answer to it."

It has become evident to the whole world, from which Israel has chosen to stand apart, that the end of violence and bloodshed, wars and destruction in the Middle East can be achieved only through the restitution of Palestinian rights. 

Nothing more is needed and nothing less will be sufficient to achieve that noble and just end, which is the primary concern of this Council. 

The representative of Israel has treated us to a tirade on Arab terrorism. 

Time and time again he dwelt on that theme, which is but a consequence of the Zionists' doing, in order to make the Council loose sight of the forest for the trees. Let us ask him about the horrendous atrocities committed by the Zionist terrorist gangs up to 1948 and the establishment of Israel. With your permission, let us seek his comment on the following examples. 

On 25 November 1940, ss Patria was blown up by Jewish terrorists in Haifa harbour, killing 268 illegal Jewish immigrants.

On 24 February 1942, ss Struma exploded in the Black Sea killing 769 Jewish immigrants. That incident was described by the Jewish Agency as an act of mass protest and mas suicide.

On 6 November 1944, Lord Moyne, British Minister of State in the Middle East, was assassinated in Cairo by Stern Gang terrorists.

In 1946, the King David Hotel was blown up by Irgun terrorists, killing 91 persons, mainly Arab and Jewish civil servants. 

From October 1946 to December 1947, letter bombs were sent by Irgun terrorists to British cabinet ministers and others. One person, Rex Farran, was murdered. The British Embassy in Rome was badly damaged. 

In 1948 occurred the Deir Yassin Massacre of 254 unarmed Arab villagers by Irgun and Stern Gang terrorists. Menachem Begin, the leader of the Opposition Party in Israel was the leader of that raid. 

After 1948, the terror gangs became an army. The Haganah, the Stern Gang. the Irgun Zvei Leumi became the Israeli defence forces, the regular army of Israel. The gang leaders-Menachem Begin, Yegil Allon, Yesrael Galili and others became Israeli statesmen, parliamentarians and generals. The terror policymethods unchanged, mentality unchanged and leaders unchanged. Just a few examples of the continuation of the methods and the mentality will suffice. 

In 1948, Bernadotte, United Nations mediator in Palestine, was assassinated by 

Stern Gang terrorists in Jerusalem.

From 1948 to 1967 Arab villages were obliterated. During that period, 385 

Arab villages were systematically obliterated within the territory of Israel. 

In 1953, Qibiya. A Jordanian village was attacked by half a battalion of Israeli troops, killing 42 villagers. Leader of the attack: no less than the present General Ariel Sharon.

In 1955, Kafr Kassem. Forty-seven inhabitants, including seven children and nine women, of an Arab village in Israel were massacred by border guards. 

The Canadian general in charge of UNTSO said that it was "sad proof that the spirit that inspired the notorious Deir Yassin Massacre is not dead among some of the Israeli armed forces."

In 1962 and 1963 parcel bombs were sent to West German scientists working in Egypt. Six persons were killed. Another German scientist was kidnapped and a private plane carrying people connected with an Egyptian military project exploded in mid air. 

On December, 1968, Beirut Airport. Israeli commando units transported by helicopter attacked the Beirut civil airport and destroyed 13 civil aircraft, causing damage estimated at $22 million.

In 1970 the Bahr El Baqr village school in the Nile delta was bombed by Israeli aircraft, killing 46 children. General Dayan's comment was that that school should not have been there.

From 1967 to 1972 there were attacks on Arab villages and refugee camps. 

Since the June war, Israel has launched repeated invasions with troops and tanks and repeated bombings and napalm attacks with aircraft against villages and refugee camps in Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, and Jordan. Over 1,500 civilians have lost their lives.

In 1972-1973, letter bombs were sent by Israeli terrorists to Palestinian spokesmen in Europe and the Middle East, killing four. 

In 1973 a civilian airliner was shot down by Israeli fighter aircraft over Sinai, killing 106 passengers and the crew.

Perhaps Mr. Tekoah may be so kind as to tell us in which Cabinet office, which 

Parliamentary room, and in which command posts, the perpetrators of those crimes are now languishing?

One of the great friends and supporters of the Zionist movement, Sir Winston 

Churchill, said on 17 November, 1946, following the destruction of the King

David Hotel in Jerusalem where 91 government officials lost their lives, and the assassination of Lord Moyne in Cairo, "If our dreams for Zionism are to end in the smoke of assassins' pistols and our labours for its future are to produce a new set of gangsters worthy of Nazi Germany"-these are the words of Sir 

Winston Churchill, not of the representative of Byelorussian SSR-"many like myself will have to reconsider the position we have maintained so consistently and so long in the past. If there is to be any hope of a peaceful and successful future for Zionism, these wicked activities must cease and those responsible for them must be destroyed root and branch"..

Members of the Council, they have not been destroyed either by root or by branch. Menechem Begin, the leader of the most murderous Zionist gang, is making a bid to become Prime Minister of Israel and will have a chance to instruct Mr. Tekoah so that he can heap more insults on the members of the Council. 4

Now, Mr. Tekoah, your actions-not people's bias or people's unfairnesshave brought you isolation from the world...

If anyone shames the United Nations by its presence it is Israel, which is the only country in the world with a membership which is conditional. I should like to quote from the record the very conditions on which Israel's membership to this Organization was accepted and which Israel has violated for twenty-five years. It states the following: "Noting furthermore the declaration by the State of Israel that it unreservedly accepts the obligations of the United Nations Charter and undertakes to honour them from the day when it becomes a Member of the United Nations, recalling its resolutions of 29 November 1947 and 11 December 1948"-and Mr. Tekoah knows very well what they refer to, they refer to the obligation of Israel to repatriate or compensate the Palestinian people whom they have evicted from their homes- "and taking note of the declarations and explanations made by the representatives of the Government of Israel before the Ad Hoc Political Committee in respect to the implementation of the said resolutions . . (General Assembly 

Resolution 273 (III) Your membership, Mr. Tekoah, is conditional and you have not honoured or fulfilled your conditions. You are highly qualified, if anyone is, for dismissal from this Organization." 

I am concerned, as a tax payer and a citizen, with two aspects of our relationship to Israel: the fact that Israel's existence as a state is due to our pressure on 

UN delegates for the Partition of Palestine and her continuing existence, to the support of the American Jewish community and that of the US Government, and yet, not only do we not control our client state but there is considerable evidence that it controls our foreign policy towards the Middle East and our news media.

In 1963 the Senate Foreign Relations Committee revealed a "conduit" operation run by an organization called the American Zionist Council. Over an eight year period this council received more than $5,000,000 from the Jewish Agency to create a favourable public opinion in this country for the Israeli Government. 

The Senate investigation closed that conduit, but, what do you think about even more money in another manner? From our bitter experience with the Committee to Elect the President and the Milk cooperatives we know that that much money can produce corruption in even the highest places. I would strongly suggest that since we hold the purse strings that we attach conditions, e.g., that 

Israel is to keep within her own borders and refrain from bombing peaceful villagers and UNRWA refugee camps. I would also suggest that we trim down a "defense" appropriation so that it is an amount really needed for defense and not aggression. Israel's frankly expressed expansionist views have kept the whole 

Middle East in a state of tension, and, although she seems to have calmed down a little since the October War, she is, apparently, still coveting Lebanon and the Litani River. One way to prevent her from casually bombing her neighbours would be to make her pay for the damage done to UNRWA camps and the province of South Lebanon out of her appropriation. Israel is not economically viable. 

She would soon decide that she could not afford the luxury of killing hundreds of Palestinians and Lebanese for every Israeli killed by the fedayeen. 

I am enclosing pictures furnished by UNRWA on the damage done to UNRWA camps in Lebanon. The news media would have us believe that Israel is striking at "terrorist bases" but wiping out the Nabatiyeh refugee camp would be analogous to destroying the city of Los Angeles because Patricia Hurst and some members of the SLA may be there. After looking at the pictures I am sure anyone will wonder whether Israel is not trying to find a "final solution" to the problem of a Palestinian nation which has risen up to confront her before the Geneva Conference.

I am also enclosing a list of the violations of Lebanese sovereinty committed by Israel since the raid on the Beirut airport, for the file.

DEPARTMENT OF THE TREASURY INTERNATIONAL FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS STATEMENT OF HON. JOHN M. HENNESSY, ASSISTANT SECRETARY OF THE TREASURY FOR INTERNATIONAL AFFAIRS ACCOMPANIED BY:

Senator INOUYE. The subcommittee will please come to order. 

This morning we turn to what we sometimes term the international financial institutions. More specifically, these are the International 

Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD) or more commonly referred to as the World Bank; its soft loan window, the 

International Development Association; plus the regional development banks-the Asian Development Bank (ADB), the Inter- 

American Development Bank (IDB), and the proposed African Development Bank.

It is through these institutions plus the United Nations development program that the United States shares with others a common concern to improve the lot of the less developed nations of the world. Few doubt that the United States should be involved in this international effort but there is considerable difference as to what constitutes a "fair share" for the United States. Over the past few years the committee has rejected a rigid percentile ceiling but has come to talk in terms of a 25 percent U.S. share as its target for these institutions. 

In the past contributions to these institutions we find the U.S. share ranges from 12.1 percent in the soft loan funds of the Asian 

Development Bank, to a high of 57.9 percent for the soft loan funds (569)

of the Inter-American Development Bank-a disparity which is exceedingly difficult to justify.

The specific request before us is for $500 million as an additional amount for the Inter-American Development Bank soft loans and $50 million as an additional contribution to the soft loan fund of the Asian Development Bank. In addition, $15 million is pending as an initial contribution to the African Development Bank, and $120,600,000 in paid-in and callable capital to the Asian Development Bank, once these amounts have been authorized. 

Without objection there will be inserted in the appendix of the hearing record a table reflecting past and projected U.S. contributions by dollar totals and as a percentage of the total funds contributed to each of the banks. In addition, accompanying this table will be a bar graph reflecting U.S. contributions to bilateral and multilateral development lending over the past 10 years. Also, there will be inserted in the Appendix a table reflecting subscriptions to ordinary capital and contributions to the fund for special operations of the Inter-American Development Bank.

PREPARED STATEMENT 

Senator INOUYE. Without objection, Mr. Hennessy, your full statement will be placed in the record at this point. 

[The statement follows:]

I am pleased to be here today to present the Administration's FY 1975 appropriations request totaling $1,006 million for the international development lending institutions. I strongly urge that this Committee and the Congress act favorably and appropriate the amounts requested. 

Before turning to the specifics of our appropriation requests for FY 1975, I would like to respond to the view that recent rapid changes in the world economy energy crisis in particular argue against our continued 

and the support of the international lending institutions. I believe the opposite is true, and that the arguments for continued U.S. leadership in this area are strengthened by recent events.

Doubts have been raised about the level of U.S. participation in the international development lending institutions in view of: 1) the overwhelming problem the developing countries face in paying for oil; 2) the possibility that money would go through borrowers' hands into oilproducers' pockets; and, 3) the possibility that the oil exporters will not assume responsibility for a fair share in the aid burden. These concerns are serious, but I hope to demonstrate that they are not well-founded. 

First, it is true that the problems confronting many developing countries are of serious magnitude 

the World

Bank estimates that the external capital requirements of the LDCs will increase by $10-12 billion per year from now until 1980, as a result of recent price increases of oil, food, and fertilizer. This added need for capital in the developing countries increases the urgency of assistance flows from industrialized countries. A reduction of our aid flows would only aggravate the precarious position now

facing many poor nations. It would also undermine our case that newly rich nations now have to join in the international effort by contributing their fair share of international assistance.

Second, the international development lending institutions cannot be used for paying the increased oil bill of the hard-hit developing countries. The institutions finance specific development projects, and do not support imports of basic commodities such as oil. 

Third, there is already concrete evidence that the oilproducing countries will recognize that their new affluence carries with it important responsibilities to poor countries. 

Iran has already made resources available for lending to developing countries. Venezuela is in the early stages of negotiating a trust fund under the Inter-American Development Bank of reportedly up to $500 million for financing development in poor Latin American countries, and has also pledged $30 million of new resources to the Caribbean Development Bank. Abu Dhabi, Oman, Kuwait, Libya, Saudi Arabia, and Bahrain are participating in the World Bank bond purchase programs. Several of the OPEC countries have pledged $3.3 billion toward the special new IMF facility aimed at providing assistance to countries with oil-induced balance of payments problems. An Arab Fund for African Development is under discussion, and additional resources are to be made available to Islamic countries.

There are positive overall economic and foreign policy reasons as well for us to move promptly on those appropriations which are related to the recently changed world economic situation. First and foremost, the United States cannot legitimately call for an international solution to such prob-

lems as energy, food supply, population, trade and monetary reform, if we shun our own responsibilities in the areas of international economic development. These problems are all intimately linked. To eliminate, or reduce, our contributions to the international development lending institutions would represent an inward turning on our part which could be used as a justification of similar measures by other countries, undermining the very cooperative system we are trying to strengthen. Of course, the work and effectiveness of these institutions in helping poor nations help themselves is important in its own right.

With this backdrop in mind, I would now like to discuss briefly the proposed appropriations. The total request of $1,006 million consists of a $500 million contribution to the Fund for Special Operations (FSO) of the Inter-American 

Development Bank (IDB); $320 million for the International 

Development Association (IDA); $50 million for the Consolidated Special Funds of the Asian Development Bank (ADB); and also two requests for which authorizing legislation is pending. The first of these is $120,635,000 for an increase in our Ordinary Capital contribution to the ADB; and the second is $15 million for the African Development Fund (AFDF).

While the amounts are large, the economic cost to the United States of supporting these institutions is much smaller than the aggregate figures indicate. Eighty percent, or $97 million of the $121 million requested for ADB Ordinary Capital, is in the form of a guarantee; thus only $24 million would require a budget outlay. In addition, the budgetary impact that would result from all of these appropriations would be spread over several years and much of our contribution to these institutions returns to us in the form of payment for the sale of goods and services.

According to a recent study prepared by the Congressional Research Service of the Library of Congress for the House Committee on Foreign Affairs, the aggregate balance of payments effect of U.S. participation in these institutions has been overwhelmingly favorable to the U.S. 

I would like to submit for the record in Annex I two very instruc tive tables developed for this report by the Congressional 

Research Service and highlight their conclusion: the cumula- tive balance of payments result of U.S.

involvement in the 

 (including IDA), the Asian Development Bank and the Inter-American Development Bank (including FSO) to date has been a net surplus of $2.1 billion for the United 

States. Of course, as disbursements on loans are drawn down over time there could be some decline in this figure the point is that in balance of payments terms we can well afford the program. 

but

In terms of our Gross National Product and our budget, these contributions represent less than one-tenth of one percent and only one-third of one percent respectively. 

The cost of maintaining an appropriate level of international responsibility in this area is a most reasonable one and the burden of development assistance falling on the U.S. has been shifting to other countries in keeping with this Committee's concern. This shift is already apparent in the present ADB and AFDB appropriations requests and will be incorporated in future IDA and IDB replenishment requests. 

INTER-AMERICAN DEVELOPMENT BANK 

For the Inter-American Bank the Administration is requesting $500 million for the Fund for Special Operations (FSO). This amount would represent the final installment of the U.S. contribution, totaling $1 billion, authorized

by the Congress in March, 1972, originally negotiated by the Executive Branch in April 1970. 

The Fund for Special Operations, as you know, constitutes an important part of the Inter-American Bank's structure. Its resources, which come entirely from member country contributions, are used to support projects in the poorest Latin American countries. 

Only about $100 million in convertible currencies will remain uncommitted in the FSO at the end of the present calendar year. The proposed $500 million U.S. contribution now requested would allow only for maintaining FSO lending in dollars for 1975 at this year's projected level of $400 million, with some provision for 1976. This would be a bare minimum given the loan demand from the relatively poor Latin American countries which borrow the bulk of FSO funds. 

Let me also address the question of the quality of the operations of the IDB, a matter that has been of major concern to this Committee. 

Specific steps have been taken since last year to improve its work and to strengthen its organization. Committee members already know about the 

Group of Controllers and the good work being done on external evaluation and review of projects. The U.S. member of the group is now Mr. Edward Tennant, who was formerly Auditor General for Foreign Assistance of the Agency for International Development. Thus far, the Group has completed 11 reports the most recent ones on Planning 

and Programming, Global Loans to Financial Institutions, and on a regional integration organization. Recommendations contained in these reports are in the process of being implemented. 34-192 O-74-37

In connection with the concern of the Committee and Congress about the follow-up on IDB loan projects, we can report the initiation by the Executive Branch of an active program of inspection trips to the field covering all the These have yielded concrete evidence that institutions.

IDB loans are contributing successfully to economic and social development in Latin America. For example, following the last IDB annual meeting in Santiago, Chile, Members of

Congress and other members of the U.S. delegation had the opportunity to see how IDB-financed projects contribute to economic and social development in Latin America. 

In concluding my statement on the IDB, I want to emphasize that our request for appropriation of $500 million takes on special meaning in the light of the closer ties we are attempting to forge with the countries of Latin America, based on a concept of a community of interest. One of the subjects of greatest concern to the Latin American Foreign Ministers at two recent conferences one in February in 

was the 

Mexico City, the other last month in Washington general decline in U.S. contributions to Inter-American institutions and to the IDB in particular. Secretary 

Kissinger pledged on those occasions that the Executive

Branch would do its utmost to maintain our aid flows to Latin America. In turn, the newly oil rich nations of the region were asked to join in helping to finance development. 

INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT ASSOCIATION 

The $320 million we are seeking today for the 

International Development Association (IDA) represents the third and final installment of our $960 million contribution to the IDA Third Replenishment.

As the members of the Committee are aware, IDA is an integral part of the World Bank, employing the same expert staff, and following the same rigorous standards of project appraisal and supervision. IDA funds go to the poorest of the developing countries, those with per capita incomes of less than $375 per year. These are countries which, because of their poverty, have extremely limited capacities for financing investment from their own savings. Similarly, their opportunities for obtaining external capital from sources other than IDA are limited, if not non-existent. 

IDA is thus crucial to the hopes of their citizens for better and more fruitful lives. Major sectors in IDA lending have been agriculture (28 percent), transportation (25 percent), and electric power (8 percent). Recently, new fields such as education and family planning have received increased emphasis, with the growing realization that improvement in human skills and the curbing of excessive population growth can be as important to economic development, if not more important, than the accumulation of physical capital. 

I would also like to call your attention to the fact that in its Report of May 11, 1972, on supplemental appropriations, the Conference Committee agreed that there was no intention of denying each of the three annual installments of $320 million in the three fiscal years beginning July 1, 1972.

I again urge the Committee to act, as you did last year, in the spirit of that joint explanatory statement, particularly in view of the fact that our payments are one year behind those of other IDA donors.

ASIAN DEVELOPMENT BANK For the Special Funds of the Asian Development Bank 

(ADB) the Administration is now requesting $50 million. 

This $50 million is part of a $100 million authorized contribution to the Special Funds of the ADB, of which the first $50 million was appropriated last year. 

Since authorization of the U.S. contribution of $100 million in 1972, a multilateral effort has been made to establish an Asian Development Fund (ADF). The $100 million already authorized would be counted towards the U.S. contribution to the Fund and would, by agreement with other donors, be tied to procurement of U.S. goods and services, ensuring direct benefits to U.S. suppliers and facilitating 

U.S. entry into key markets in Asia.

Last year when the Congress decided to reduce the Administration's request for the first $100 million to $50 million, it recognized the beneficial burden-sharing aspects of the new ADF proposal; and the Joint House Senate 

Conferees Report stated that the conference managers had no intention of denying a fiscal year 1975 request for the balance of $50 million when presented by the Administration. 

The conference managers supported the favorable burdensharing arrangements embodied in the proposal of which the $100 million was a part.

Our contribution of $50 million appropriated last year, combined with the request now before you will mobilize $250 million from other donors in their first stage contributions to the ADF. While there will be no commitment to the ADB concerning future U.S. contributions, we plan next year to request a third $50 million contribution. 

This would make a total U.S. contribution of $150 million, and taken with the $375 million contribution by other

donors, would complete the ADF's initial resource mobilization plan, providing a total of $525 million in concessional resources to the ADF. This is in addition to the $330 million in ADB Special Funds already contributed by other donors -- excluding the U.S. To the extent that such contributions were made since January 1, 1973, contributors are entitled to credit them against their ADF pledges.

The FY 1975 budget also includes an appropriation request for an increase in the U.S. share of capital stock in the ADB. This was also included in our request last year to this Committee, but the Congress did not take action on the authorizing legislation. It is now anticipated that action on the ADB Ordinary Capital authorization will take place shortly in the Senate and subsequently in the House. 

The total new U.S. Ordinary Capital participation would be $362 milion, of which 80 percent (about $290 million) would be callable guarantee capital and 20 percent, or about $72 million, would be paid-in. Budgetary expenditures result only from the paid-in capital portion as the guarantee capital serves to back ADB borrowings in private capital markets, and would only be called in the most unlikely event that the Bank experienced sizeable loan defaults. 

We strongly support this proposed U.S. participation in the Ordinary Capital increase, which became effective in 

November 1972 and has been subscribed to uniformly by other donor nations. As a result of our not subscribing, our present voting power has dropped from 18 percent to 

8 percent, putting us below that of Japan, India, and 

Australia. Participation in this capital increase will enable the U.S. to regain a level of voting strength which will reflect U.S. interests in the Bank and the Asian area.

Finally, Mr. Chairman, I would like to comment on the issue of procurement and the U.S. share in the Asian Bank. 

Both you and we have been greatly concerned about increasing the percentage of contracts resulting from ADB-financed projects awarded to U.S. business firms. In this respect, Mr. Chairman, our expectations were largely realized in 

1973. U.S. procurement from the Bank's Ordinary Capital lending operations more than doubled last year from 8 percent to 17 percent a marked improvement, which is largely attributable to the exchange rate realignments effected since 1971. Nevertheless, in order to improve the U.S. position further, we will intensify our contacts with U.S. firms, and improve the flow and distribution of information to private U.S. firms on upcoming ADB procurement opportunities.

ANNEX II PROSPECTIVE UNITED STATES PARTICIPATION IN THE AFRICAN DEVELOPMENT FUND 

The African Development Bank was established in 1964, when many of its member countries had just gained independence, and now has a membership of 39 African countries. The capital structure of the Bank is composed of both paid-in and callable capital just as in the other international financial institutions. amounted to $385 million, of which $130 million is paid in and the remainder callable. As of the same date, the Bank had authorized $130 million in loans for 60 individual projects in 31 member countries. All projects have been financed at near market terms, i.e., 6 and maturities of 10 to 20 years. 

As of the end of 1973, this capital - 8-1/2 percent interest

It has been recognized for some time that many African nations are in acute need of concessional lending resources from the industrialized nations. It was to meet this need and to encourage the commitment of resources from outside the African region that the African Development Fund was established. In 1966 the Bank started discussions with the United 

States and other developed countries on the possibility of establishing a concessional loan fund in association with the Bank. The donor nations, including the United States, agreed upon principles for the establishment of the Fund at a 

Development Assistance Committee meeting of the OECD in March, 1971. After approval by the Board of Governors of the Bank, the African Development Fund was established on June 30, 1973.

= .:

The United States participated actively in the drafting of the Articles of the Fund. We wanted to be assured that the Fund would be put on a sound basis and would be effectively managed. We believe we succeeded fully in this objective and that major efforts were made to meet well-known Congressional concerns. For example, the Articles of the Fund, alone among the development institutions, contain a provision requiring a comprehensive and continuing review of completed projects by an audit committee reporting to the Board of Directors. 

The Fund is legally separate from the Bank and managed by its own Board of Directors, consisting of six representatives of the donor countries and six Bank Directors, with each group holding 50 percent of the total voting power, and a 75% weighted vote for all operational decisions. As in the case of the concessional funds of the other international development lending institutions, the Fund uses the Bank's staff and draws upon its experience and expertise, By the end of last year, thirteen other industrial nations had ratified the Fund statutes and pledged a total of more than $90 million. In addition, the Bank has committed to the Fund approximately $6 million from its own earnings. Although only in existence a little over eight months, the Fund has already made three loans totalling about $5 million for irrigation and assistance programs in the countries of the Sahel, as a result of an initial decision to give priority in its lending to this drought stricken disaster area.

A soft loan window for Africa has been urgently needed. 

Africa is the least developed continent. Its peoples are the poorest in the world. In per capita GNP terms, 43 of its` countries have incomes of less than $360 and ten of these

have incomes of less than $100. Yet, the loans from the Bank's ordinary capital resources have had to be on near-commercial terms. This is a serious limitation since many of the pressing development projects in Africa cannot be financed on conventional terms. Many of these projects are not directly profitable in the short run but they are indispensable for economic and social progress. Their financing must be on more lenient terms and conditions than those offered by the Bank's ordinary capital resources. The Fund can provide the resources on the terms required. It can also promote the sort of regional economic integration and joint development projects which the U.S. has always supported as necessary in countries with small markets. 

The Fund can also serve as a magnet to attract capital from the oil-rich countries of the region. We already have indications of the willingness of oil-exporting nations of Africa to increase their contributions for the economic development of the continent. Libya, Nigeria, and Algeria will increase their participation in the African Development Bank's Ordinary Capital. Libya has also indicated its willingness to give the 

Bank access to a special pool of $100 million in development funds it has created. 

The U.S. stands to benefit substantially from a modest role in the Fund. Our relations with Africa have assumed greater significance as the developed world's need for industrial minerals and fuels has drawn U.S. investors and traders to Africa. A growing consciousness of the limits on world resources has highlighted the economic potential of the area. To illustrate, the continent possesses 42% of the cobalt, 34% of the bauxite, 17% of the copper, and about 23% of the world's known reserves of uranium ore. Africa will neces-

sarily be an increasingly important source of vital U.S. imports. Thus, our enlightened self-interest dictates that we build sound economic relations with the nations of Africa.

Participation in and support of the Fund is one means of furthering this goal. Participation in the Fund would also be perceived by the African nations as an indication of our interest in their growth and prosperity. 

Furthermore, under the Articles of the Fund, procurement of goods and services for projects financed by the Fund may only be from member nations. Thus, until the United States joins the Fund we will be precluded from this potentially substantial source of export earnings, particularly if the Fund should be expanded by the contributions of the other countries.

Senator INOUYE. Without objection, so ordered.

CONTRIBUTIONS AS PERCENTAGE OF GNP 

Mr. HENNESSY. In terms of our gross national product and our budget, these contributions represent less than one-tenth of 1 percent and only one-third of 1 percent respectively. The cost of maintaining an appropriate level of international responsibility in this area is a most reasonable one and the burden of development assistance falling on the United States has been shifting to other countries in keeping with this committee's concern. This shift is already apparent in the present Asian Development Bank and African Development Bank appropriations requests and will be incorporated in future IDA and 

IDB replenishment requests.

For the soft window of the Inter-American Bank, our request is for $500 million. In terms of levels, this would allow the bank to continue lending at the current rate through 1975 and what we have found is that in our normal internal U.S. Government processes by the time the appropriation action is through in recent years it has at least been at the end of the calendar year, so for orderly planning it would seem necessary that we should be able to count on a continuation of the current program through this year and through next year and this is what this amount would be designed to do. 

Now let me also refer very briefly to the fact that specific steps have been taken, internal steps, by the Inter-American Bank consistent with the concerns of this committee to improve their management and operations. I would like to also submit for this committee for the record a recent publication which came out last week by the bank which goes through this in much greater detail than I do in my remarks here. [The publication is retained in the committee files.] 

INSTITUTION INITIATIVES 

Mr. HENNESSY. I should also mention that one of the elements of strength we believe is that the independent audit group in the Inter- American Bank is now fully operational. The U.S. member of the group is Mr. Edward Tennant, the former Auditor General of AID, whose great experience and scope in this field we think brings special expertise.

We also initiated as a direct result of the concerns of this committee and other committees in the House a rather ambitious and active program of inspection trips to the field and these to date have covered some 39 countries and some 85 projects. 

Finally, in respect to the Inter-American Bank I would like to emphasize that Secretary Kissinger has underway a broad initiative to

try and build closer links with Latin America. This began in the form of the Foreign Ministers Conference in February in Mexico City and it was followed up last month in Washington with another Foreign Ministers Conference and then a meeting in Atlanta. At these meetings a new community of interest was sought with Latin America, the general concept being that there are many reciprocal areas in trade and we should be working together in trade negotiations and in similar fields.

In addition, the United States and the Latins voiced their concern that we had not been able to meet our aid promises. Secretary Kissinger went out of his way to say that the executive branch would do its utmost to maintain a close relationship with Latin America in the future.

INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT ASSOCIATION Turning to IDA, the International Development Association, I 

would like to point out that IDA goes exclusively to the poorest countries in the world. I think we are all aware today of the plight which is facing these countries today due to some $10 billion worth of increased energy bills the LDC's are going to have to pay and perhaps some $5 billion that they are going to have to pay in increased food costs. IDA goes to only those countries that have a per capita income of less than $375 per year.

This $320 million which is before you today is the last installment of the so-called IDA 3. I urge the committee to act as you did last year in the spirit of the joint explanatory statement of the conference committee of May 11, 1972, which stated that it was not your intention to deny these requests.

ASIAN DEVELOPMENT BANK 

In moving to the Asian Development Bank, there are two parts to our request before the committee this year. One is a second contribution of $50 million to the special funds of the Asian Development Bank. As you will recall, last year this committee appropriated a first $50 million. These two figures, last year's $50 million and this year's $50 million, if appropriated, would take with it an additional $250 million of other donors bringing a total of $350 million. 

We believe this has very favorable burden sharing elements to it. 

The committee again in its conference report recognized these as favorable and stated that they had no intention of denying a fiscal year 1975 request for the balance. I should point out that it would also be our intention to come up again next year for a third $50 million which would bring an additional $125 million from other nations but we have taken no commitment whatsoever on either the second $50 million or the third $50 million and it will depend entirely on the discretion of the Congress and its final decision in this request. 

The second part of our request this year, Mr. Chairman, has to do with the U.S. share of capital stock in the Bank. This was also on our appropriations calendar last year but it was knocked out due to the fact that neither House moved on the authorizing legislation. We now have been led to believe by both the Senate and the House that they will move on this authorizing legislation very shortly, in the Senate in particular, after the vote on the IDA. We expect that there will 34-192 O-74-38

shortly be a vote on our request to increase the U.S. share of capital stock by a total of $322 million and we have in the appropriations budget this year $120.6 million which will be the first out of 3 years' appropriation. Other nations have already gone forward on this increase in capital and as a result our share in the voting has dropped from 18 percent to 8 percent.

Let me also briefly mention in respect to this Bank, Mr. Chairman, that you had very just concerns resulting from your oversight of this Bank in your trip to the Asian Bank that our procurement share was unjustifiably low in the past. In 1973, we have seen a marked improvement. Our procurement percentage more than doubled last year. We were getting 8 percent of all the contracts let which is now up to 17. percent which we think is a very important improvement in 1 year. 

We are hopeful of seeing further improvements. We believe that the major reason for the improvement has been the new exchange rate realignments, but, also we ourselves have improved our internal processing of information and the dissemination of information to U.S. businesses.

AFRICAN DEVELOPMENT FUND 

Finally, I come to a new request for the committee. This is a request for an appropriation of $15 million to the African Development Fund of the African Development Bank. At the present time the United 

States is not a member of this institution and so I have attached to my statement a brief outline of both the Bank and the Fund for the committee's purposes.

AFRICAN REGIONAL BANK 

Briefly, the African countries have worked very hard to create their own regional bank and have contributed their own resources in an admirable demonstration of self-help.

The AFDF will contribute significantly to African development by specializing in small, high priority projects directed at the very poor of the region and by promoting the regional integration so essential to Africa's development. While the amount requested is small and is not contemplated to increase significantly in the next few years-for example, we are not planning any requests in addition to this $15 million for next year-it is important that the United States show its concern for, and interest in, the development of the countries of Africa through the concrete step of participation in the African Development Fund. All other major industrial nations except 

France have joined the Fund, and both Canada and Japan have already pledged contributions of $16.5 million each-more than our request before you.

The cost to the United States of participating in the Fund is small and entirely reasonable. We would be only 1 of 16 nations to contribute. 

The total contribution from these 16 donors and from the African Development Bank itself would be about $115 million, over $85 million of which is already subscribed. Our proposed contribution of $15 million is only 13 percent of this total. Contributions by the donor countries are being made over a 3-year period. The expected U.S. budget outlay would be only $1 million in fiscal year 1975. 

At the same time I wish to confirm to this committee that the United States has undertaken no commitment to participate in the Fund,

although the United States participated actively in drafting the arti cles of agreement of the African Development Fund in order to be assured that it would be put on an effective and soundly managed basis.

Legislation to authorize U.S. participation in the African Development Fund with a contribution of $15 million has been introduced by Senator Humphrey in the Senate. It is our hope that once Congress has completed its consideration of the pending authorizing legislation for the International Development Association it will then turn its attention to the request for the African Development Fund. 

In sum, Mr. Chairman, we feel that these appropriation requests deserve your approval and support. They are of great importance to our overall international economic objectives. The institutions involved are run on a sound basis and provide development assistance competently. This assistance is of direct and lasting benefit to the developing countries, and because of our worldwide interests to the United States itself. The current international economic situation lends added importance to this request. To withdraw our support from these institutions now would be shortsighted and particularly damaging to our broader interests.

It is, of course, the responsibility of the Congress to weigh this request against competing priorities. The thrust and weight of my testimony has been directed toward convincing you that this request deserves a very high priority. Its benefits are manifest, important, and affordable. I firmly believe it should receive your support. 

Mr. Chairman, that finishes my prepared testimony. Thank you. 

Senator INOUYE. Thank you very much, Mr. Secretary.

STATUS OF PORTFOLIO OF SUBLENDING BANKS 

Several years ago this subcommittee dealt rather extensively in the subject of subborrowers, and we noted that bank funds, funds that we have participated in, have been loaned out at rates in excess of 20 percent per annum, and that delinquencies and defaults were running as high as 50 percent. We earlier asked for an update on this information. Can you supply us with any information?

Mr. HENNESSY. We have now received information requested by the committee which we will supply for the hearing record. 

 DELINQUENCY RATES FOR INTERMEDIATE CREDIT INSTITUTIONS 

Listed below are the delinquency rates for the intermediate credit institutions utilizing loan funds from the international financial institutions. The data is of 

December 31, 1973 and includes loans made by the international financial institutions between January 1, 1964 and December 31, 1973. This limited time period was adopted to reduce the magnitude of the reporting effort; nevertheless, it is believed to be a representative sample. In the case of the IDA, the delinquencies are reported as a percentage of the intermediate credit institution's total portfolio, not just that portion stemming from the use of IDA's resources, whereas the reports for the IDB and ADB are limited to the portfolio stemming from their loans.

LENDING THROUGH INTERMEDIATE INSTITUTIONS 

Mr. HENNESSY. I don't have a full summary of it right here but what I could say, in a general sense, is that in terms of the percentage of the operations of all the institutions-World Bank, IDA, the Inter- American Bank and the Asian Bank-some 3 or 4 years ago 20 percent of their lending was going through these intermediate institutions. 

This has now been reduced to around 12 percent, but we feel it does fit a very broad and a very necessary area of lending. 

It is true that the disparity between the rate at which, for example, IDA or the World Bank lends and the rate at which it is relent is still high. We think there is very ample economic and financial justification for that but we do have the complete information on defaults which we will submit today to you and to the committee for your perusal.

The GAO has looked at this in some depth and to the best of our knowledge they do not quarrel with the practice of relending at a higher rate. Principally, I think the justification lies in the fact that the relending is done in local currency. 

Let's say if the World Bank lends to an institution in Brazil at 74 percent, that institution may turn around and lend it at 30 percent, you are right, but that institution is lending to its borrowers in cruzeiros, and at the end of 10 or 20 years those cruzeiros are paid in and then they have to buy dollars and pay back in dollars to the 

World Bank.

If you have a 2 or 3 percent devaluation per year, the interest differential does not even cover that amount. So the basic reason why there is such a differential is due to the inflation rates which in turn then leads to a higher rate of devaluation in those currencies than the dollar or the deutsche mark.

If there was not such a differential, the intermediate institutions would either have to take the exchange risks, which they are in no position to take, or they would be decapitalized over time. They also have to cover their administrative costs and also the costs of taking risks.

As regards the risks, in our perusal of full information which has now been provided us, we have not had a chance to study it in great depth. Our first analysis seems to say, the most recent figures, that there are certain problem countries where there are delinquencies which run higher than the average. Of course, one of the advantages of these institutions is that they are working in market segments that would not ordinarily get credit, so one would expect a somewhat higher risk or delinquency rate than you would on a normal commercial bank.

What we have pinpointed is that in special problem countries such as in Chile, for example, where they have gone through an abnormal economic period the intermediate institutions have a higher rate of delinquency and the Inter-American Bank is working on that and hopes to get them to make these loans current over a period of time. 

I think that our conclusion is-and Mr. Porges and Mr. Reynolds may be able to give more details-that the Bank should provide information on a more regular basis-and as a result of your hearings they will-to us in the executive branch and to the executive directors so

that we don't have to wait once a year, and even then with a considerable lag time, to see how the default or the delinquency rate is running on the secondary loans on these relending programs. 

ULTIMATE BENEFICIARY OF SUBLOANS 

Senator INOUYE. It would appear to me that the major beneficiary of our funds used for this purpose would not be the ultimate user of the funds, the peasant, but the intermediary local banks charging 30percent interest and with defaults in places such as South America extending beyond 35 percent. Is that the purpose of our contribution, to shore up these local banks?

Mr. HENNESSY. As I mentioned, the total percentage is now down to around 12 percent of all these institutions. For example, a good percentage of this goes into the agriculture sector and you just can't get at small farmers unless you work through cooperative and intermediate types of institutions such as that. 

The banks that are Washington based cannot make these loans. 

There is a dual purpose. The first purpose is trying to build local institutions; that is a very important part of it, institution building. 

The second part is providing credit to segments which would not normally in other cases be able to obtain credit. 

On the other hand, it is quite clear you have to strike a balance in providing capital to high risk areas and not getting your money back. It is obvious that the guy who got the money got the benefit. 

To give you some specific facts about the end user, the farmer-for example, I have a table here which the World Bank has done and which I would be glad to submit for the record, which shows for the Ivory Coast that the rate at which the institution relends there with 

World Bank funds is 10 percent. Commercial lenders are getting 150 percent. So for the farmer, if he can get a 10-percent loan that is great, as opposed to 150 percent.

In Vietnam the farmers are getting 30-percent money, through the intermediate institution but if they had to go outside they would be paying more. In Sri Lanka it is 12 versus 50. So the point is that it is lower than the prevailing commercial rate to people who would have to pay these other rates otherwise. It is true that they do have a higher default rate and delinquency rate but here again you are insulated because it is the intermediate institution who is taking the default risk, they are taking the credit risk.

So if an intermediate institution in Costa Rica lends and the farmer does not pay it back, the institution has to pay back on the order of 

100 percent on the loan.

FINANCIAL CONDITION OF SUBLENDING BANKS 

Senator INOUYE. Do we have any instance of any intermediary bank going bankrupt? 

Mr. HENNESSY. I don't know the answer to that question. I don't believe so, though.

Mr. PORGES. In the Inter-American Development Bank, I have no knowledge of any intermediate credit bank going bankrupt. Of course these loans would be guaranteed by the Government of the 34-192 - 74-39

country and there is no credit risk to the Inter-American Bank even if such a local bank did go bankrupt. 

Senator INOUYE. So the only person who is going down under would be the ultimate user of the funds?

Mr. PORGES. Well, sir, as Mr. Hennessy has mentioned, he has had the use of these funds. Of course we all know that the poor farmer, the small farmer, the small cattle rancher-these are areas depending on weather, supply, markets, road conditions. The risks are enormous for the small farmer. 

We feel that if these intermediate credit institutions were not able to finance them they would get no financing at all; the commerical bank certainly would not take care of them. So I think we feel this is a transfer of resources to that sector in Latin America. 

The overwhelming majority of the population works in agriculture and so this is a transfer of resources to that sector which is most needed, they are most needful of it, and where the risks are very, very high.

Mr. HENNESSY. On the other hand, I think as a general rule if over time the World Bank and the IDB find that an intermediary, institution is making a lot of bad loans and they would have to call in its loan because it looks like the bank is going to go bankrupt, they would modify their lending program. 

They are trying to build institutions on the ground and they are trying to get credit to end users who cannot otherwise get money. So if the institution building is not working, then the bank would reassess and reevaluate whether they wanted to make any additional relending loans even though repayment was guaranteed to the IDB or to the ADB. 

FUTURE CONTRIBUTIONS TO AFRICAN DEVELOPMENT FUND 

Senator INOUYE. I would like to now touch upon the last item, the 

African Development Bank. You have indicated that the contribution would be a small one. I just recalled that the original request made by our Government to the Inter-American Development Bank was not too big. I think the total was $450 million and today our total contribution is approximately $5 billion. 

For example, on our first subscription our contribution ran 45 percent of the total, it was $1 billion total of which we contributed $450 million. Today our participation exceeds 55 percent. These are from your reports.

What I am trying to find out is what do you consider would be a reasonable projection of our involvement in the African Development Bank?

Mr. HENNESSY. I recognize your point, Mr. Chairman. Great oaks from little acorns do grow, and in this field there is no doubt about it. 

We have requested $15 million which would cover both this year and next year. There has been some discussion internationally about further lending to this institution, about a replenishment at the end of next year, for example. No figures have been discussed. We have not participated in those discussions because we are not a member of the Bank or the Fund at this point in time. 

We would be very willing to put that into the record here and have it read back to us in future years. It is not our intention to build up

an enormous fund in a very short period. It would depend pretty much on how the Bank evolved. It is working almost exclusively on regional integration projects and the smaller projects that IDA cannot handle and the World Bank cannot handle. IDA and the World Bank both work in Africa so there would be very little justification if there is just a duplication of what they are now doing. 

But what does happen is that the World Bank and IDA operate on such a relatively large scale that they cannot look at $100,000, $200,000, nor do they give a focus to some of the regional integration aspects that the Africans are particularly interested in, road projects which help the markets. So our best estimate at this time would be for a flat line or small increase.

If we are talking about $15 million over a 2-year period we would not see this grow at any great length in the future or at any great order of magnitude. Of course in the other institutions we began with enormous amounts, $450 million has grown to $5 billion and beyond, but that has been over a 14or 15-year period.

NON REGIONAL PARTICIPATIONS IN AFRICAN BANK 

Senator INOUYE. These questions are asked in anticipation of questions I am certain will be asked by my colleagues. 

I note that in the African Development Bank the sponsors do not wish to have any participation by nonregional donors such as the 

United States. Is that correct?

Mr. HENNESSY. In the Bank itself. The Bank was set up in 1964 strictly by African nations and they contributed their own funds which were both Northern Africa and Africa contributing in some $300 million. At the same time, they felt for reasons, very understandable for newly independent states, that they wanted to do their own thing and they didn't want to be dependent on their old ex-colonial masters, so to speak. They set up their own bank and it has been operated on a very sound basis since then.

Three years ago they found that while they were able to obtain from their other members in the Bank the limited hard resourcessome $300 million-$350 million for relending-they could not come by enough soft funds so they joined together and with outside donors with the thought that they would set up a soft loan African Development Fund which would be similar to IDA and both African countries and non-African donors would participate.

The Bank has put some $6 million into it and the balance would be put in by some 15 or 16 developed countries. 

Now the question has come up in the past now that they have a fund, a soft loan window, and that has developed countries in partnership with the African countries, does it not make sense to open up the Bank and now have developed countries also in the Bank? 

A number of African countries still feel very strongly they would like to maintain the African character. They are in effect depriving themselves of our guarantee and the German guarantee or the United Kingdom. We think over time this may well change and we think it would make good sense for it to change because the institution's growth will be limited unless it can count also on some outside donors. 

I think we also want to recognize that this is a regional institution

and they have a lot of pride in it. We certainly would not want to force our way in.

On the other hand, we believe this a totally fair and appropriate manner to participate in the African Funds so that is what we are proposing today.

AUDIT OF AFRICAN DEVELOPMENT FUND 

Senator INOUYE. Without management participation, how do we audit the use of funds?

Mr. HENNESSY. We don't share in management of the Bank itself because we are not in their but the current donors do share in the management of the fund and if we made the decision to join we would be voting just like the other donors, with the ability to veto, as a group, any use of loans. We have, also, complete post audit capabilities for the fund.

Now, the fund will operate just the way the World Bank does. The 

World Bank has a soft loan window but the employees, the professionals, the economists, the engineers, et cetera, who develop the loans for IDA and the World Bank are one and the same people; the nature of the terms to the borrower changes. The same is true in the African Bank. The professional staff will service both the bank and the fund but in terms of use of audit capabilities of the funds in the African Development Fund, our directors and the governors of that institution will have the full authority to do it. In fact, because of the concerns of this committe and of the House in participating in the drafting of the charter of this institution, we had written into the charter of a provision that the Bank would have also a post valuation audit mechanism such as is now in the Inter-American Bank as a statutory provision. There was some concern by the Africans about this because at that time other banks had not yet moved to this but that was written in and does exist. So I think we have the type of guarantees we need if the Congress, in its wisdom, decides the United States can join this institution. 

I don't think there is any question but that we would have full purview over the use of our funds and a say in the management of the development funds in the fund although not in the Bank itself. 

ASSISTANCE TO SOUTH VIETNAM 

Senator INOUYE. Mr. Jordan, our Chief Counsel, was sent to the

Asian Development Bank's April meeting at the instruction of this subcommittee and he made several inquiries on the participation of the Asian Development Bank and other development banks in providing assistance to South Vietnam and other Southeast Asian countries.

I was most unhappy to learn that the responses were at best very vague and it is my understanding that at the present time ADB's assistance to South Vietnam approximates 1.8 percent of its resources. 

What sort of assistance is South Vietnam receiving from other development banks or the World Bank, or IDA? 

Mr. HENNESSY. The World Bank and IDA have not made any loans. to Vietnam. The Asian Bank is the only bank that has lent, and as you say, it is a very small absolute amount, a very small percentage. 

Of course Vietnam has 18 million people, so it is not one of the larger

countries. That 1.8 percent is not totally out of keeping with Vietnam's economic size.

As you well know, there are economic considerations on how well projects can be implemented during the period since January 1973. 

One of the banks has sent out numerous missions. The World Bank in particular sent out a mission last fall in October because of our concern, and other countries' concern, to see the banks take an active role in reconstruction. This is one of the things that, for example, the World Bank is very good at.

After the Second World War of course the first 40 years of activities were almost exclusively helping develop Europe and Japan. They have undertaken similar actions in Nigeria in Africa in their civil war, and in Bangladesh after the conflict there with Pakistan. So they do have an expertise and they have chaired together with the Asian Bank one informal meeting of potential bilateral and multilateral donors and that took place in November of last year. A subsequent meeting was scheduled to take place this year in February but it was cancelled after the House vote which rejected IDA. 

Now, a key point to see here is that Vietnam is only a soft loan borrower. Their financial situation is such that they can not hope to pay 7 or 8 percent or more than a fraction of their requirements, so they have to depend on concessionary funds. Right now they are depending exclusively on us. At the present time IDA 3, which is running out of money now on June 30, does not have any available funds left for Vietnam.

As you may recall from our letter to you last fall before we went to Nairobi we did make it quite clear to other donors that one of the concerns that we had in going forward with IDA 4 would beassuming that hostilities would reach a level that would permit projects to go forward-that IDA 4 would loan a significant amount of money to help in the reconstruction of all of Southeast Asia, Cambodia, Laos, as well as South Vietnam.

So there is right now a meeting being tentatively discussed for July again of potential donors. The hopes are that other countries will make advance contributions to IDA 4, and that these contributions will enable IDA to continue to operate after July 1, and that a portion of Vietnam's reaiurements will come from IDA and also from the Asian Bank. But there is a resource constraint these institutions don't have enough funds to go around.

There are also some security questions. I think at the time the 

World Bank mission went out-they first sent a mission out in May they sent another mission out in October-November. Their conclusion was at that time the level of hostilities would allow within certain areas carrying out let's say at the beginning of the program but the situation has not yet arrived where they can undertake a full-scale reconstruction program, for example, as they did in Korea, because there is still a security question there. 

U.S. SHARE OF INTER-AMERICAN DEVELOPMENT BANK CAPITAL 

Senator INOUYE. Many in the Congress feel that the American contribution to the Inter-American Development Bank would be difficult to justify at its present level of 68 percent which will jump over

70 percent if the pending request is granted. I also note that a 5-year straight line projection of the current level would not only maintain this high U.S. percentage but it would increase it slightly. 

Most of those with whom I have discussed this matter believe that the United States should put up seed capital for the emerging nations but three American tax dollars to one South American tax dollar is difficult to justify. How would you justify that, sir?

Mr. HENNESSY. I think that, on the average, per capita in South 

America is still around $400 to $700 so I don't think we can reasonably ask them to contribute more than $1 out of every $4 of the soft loan window at this time. What we have been trying to do is lend them the amount, to shift the burden from the United States to other countries to join with the Latins in inviting other nations-the Europeans, Japan, and Canada.

Now Canada has joined and made a contribution of some $300 million. The negotiations with the Europeans, quite frankly, has stalled for, I would say, 6 months or so because the Latins, and we agree with the Latins, have set a minimum target for them buying into an established institution. We thought, when this exercise began, of some half a billion dollars worth of new resources in paid-in form over a 3-year period, plus guarantee capital, they would agree. 

The Europeans have not yet been able to get together and meet that target and are almost $100 million below that. These were in 1971 dollars, not in 1974 dollars. So while we believe we would like to see our share diminished by having other nations join, we don't want to do it at cutrate or bargain rate or fire sale prices, so we are in the midst of a negotiation to do it. We want to do it on terms that we think are fair to us and to the Latins. 

We do have a special interest due to geography proximity and trade with Latin American, and therefore, a large U.S. share is not without some basis.

I note in your opening remarks there was this wide disparity between the amounts we contributed in one institution versus another. 

It is quite clear that at least traditionally the United States has thought we have had a special interest in Latin America. Secretary 

Kissinger, as I mentioned in my prepared text, has gone out of his way to try and rebuild some of the weakened ties that have emerged in Latin America. We think that in the world of the future in which more and more countries are building in blocs it is well for us to look to our own backyard to make sure we have extra good relations with the Latins and we may have to do slightly more than the hard-nosed numbers, which make good financial economic sense. 

RELATIVE TAX LEVELS IN THE UNITED STATES AND LATIN AMERICA 

Senator INOUYE. We are well aware that the per capita income of the South Americans is far below that of the United States. However, we are also aware of the statistics which indicate that an American citizen residing here and earning $50,000, say, would pay much, much more than a Brazilian citizen living in Brazil making $50,000. I think the American tax would be 4 times that of the Brazilian. 

The same situation would exist in places like Mexico, Chile, Venezuela. This is my concern.

Now, if we are going to be taxing our people very heavily to support our neighbors to the South, and we are committed to this, why can't our neighbors to the South tax themselves accordingly?

I am not suggesting that we tax the overtaxed peasant but those who are making $50,000 or $100,000. 

Mr. HENNESSY. The institutions have, themselves, I think, carried out a number of tax reform programs. I can recall in one country where the Inter-American Bank refused to grant any more credits until they passed an income tax because they didn't have one, and that has become the cause of some conflict with that country, but I think it has pushed them toward a system they needed. I think you have to recognize this. 

I would say first of all we do agree with the overall objective. We think that part of it means sharing the burden within the country and taking more of the burden on their own shoulders. By and large, on all the costs of the projects the banks contribute a small share, I think overall it is 35 percent of the total cost, and 65 percent is done by the countries themselves under their own general revenues. 

I think you do have a problem in making accurate comparisons. In 

Brazil, they depend more on indirect taxes. Brazil, because of the difficulty in collecting income tax, they found a more effective way to collect taxes is through value-added taxes, direct tax rather than income tax. I think this is a continuing problem and we need a continuing effort to improve the tax situation in all the countries of Latin America, and make sure that the upper end pays relatively more. 

I think the institutions when they sit down with the countries and look at their tax policy they will do this. 

We also provide tax assistance from the Treasury Department. The 

IRS has a number of tax technical assistance agreements with Latin American countries and it is one of the issues we did have on the Foreign Ministers' meeting in Mexico City which we hope to followup on. There is, I would say, a growing interest because we have had greater technification in the Latin American government but not sufficient taxation, so I hope there would be continued progress there, but it is an area where more can be done. 

Senator INOUYE. Do you really believe there is a sincere effort on the part of these countries to bring about tax reform? 

Mr. HENNESSY. I thing a great deal of them have done that. I think the Brazilians in particular. John Porges has some comments. He is closer to the actual steps that have been taken. 

I think we can provide data on the increase in tax take, for example, in a country like that, total tax taken from indirect and direct taxes in a country like Brazil.

TAX PRACTICES IN BRAZIL AND MEXICO 

Mr. PORGES. Mr. Chairman, I would like to add that Mexico has a retention-type tax the way the United States does, and the rates are fairly consistent for those who are on regular payroll, except agriculture, and those who run their own business. Those who are on a corporate payroll have a retention tax and they pay rates comparable to what we do.

Brazil's rates also have been climbing and are now on a level- I think it is after $10,000 you get up to 40 percent rate. The problem

in Latin America is that they are in a fairly early stage of industrialization and you have a proliferation of small family businesses. 

I think that it is in this area that the Internal Revenue Service has sent inspectors and people down to help the Governments in closing loopholes. In the corporate area the tax rates are high in Brazil and 

Mexico. I know one banker who went back from New York and found that he was paying more tax in Mexico than he was when he was on duty in the United States. I think there are areas which need to be improved but I think they are making a consistent effort in Brazil. 

They are now beginning to jail income tax evaders, which would have been absolutely impossible 10 years ago. 

Mr. HENNESSY. Let me add just one final note to this, as an example.

I would agree that more can be done and more should be done, perhaps in the consultative groups. A group of donor countries meets under the World Bank's chairmanship. They sit down and say to a developing country, "We are willing to lend you this amount of money provided you make this type of response and you have this amount of fiscal effort." In the case of Colombia, for example, there was a memorandum of understanding which contained an agreement that steady reform and certain increases would take place in the tax system. In other words, that was written right into what was expected of Colombia and so it is not unusual. 

Again, there is a long way to go and I think the tax ethic in many of the countries is very different from the ethic in our own country and needs to be worked on continuously. That is something, I think, again, perhaps we will be able to afford some report or some progress on.
