LATIN INFLUENCE ON BANK 

Senator INOUYE. I have been asking these questions because I noted in the recent meeting in Santiago, Chile, there is a very serious move to Latinize the Inter-American Development Bank; in fact, they are suggesting that the headquarters move to Caracas. 

What is the position of the Treasury Department on this? 

Mr. HENNESSY. I think at the Santiago meeting there were many speeches made for domestic political consumption. I would not say there was a strong move on to Latinize the Bank, I would say just the opposite. Most Latin Americans feel very strongly that the United 

States has a very important role to play in the Bank. Of course at that time there were some countries, with a somewhat different view. 

The Venezuelans, particularly in their speech, raised the question whether it didn't make more sense for the Latins to take a larger role and perhaps even put the head office of the Bank in Latin America, and I think they are hoping it would be Caracas. 

On the second point, where they relocate the head office, we would not have any strong feelings. Maybe it makes more sense to have the headquarters in the region like the Asia Bank does. 

I think what was clear to us as a result of this was this idea which emerged at Santiago which was that the vast majority of Latin Americans very much welcome, appreciate, and count on a continued U.S. support.

Now, I think the Venezuelan case will be a very interesting one to watch. We welcomed, very warmly, their suggestion that they would put in-I think the figure now is around $500 million in new capital to the Bank. If they want to use that to lower our share, I don't think it is up to us to say no and I think that would be in keeping with your committees' views.

If they are willing to buy shares at the same rate that we buy shares, then that is fine. Over time, maybe, that is the way these institutions go. They buy them back as they become more developed. So it all depends on the spirit in which it is done and the financial basis on which it is done. If it is on a fair financial basis and if it is what the members want, we would not oppose it. But at this time it seems unlikely, given the amount of money we have put in the Bank, that one nation-even with the oil wealth of Venezuela-would be able to purchase a major portion back so that is an open question. 

I think that the overwhelming support at that meeting in the public speeches and the private speeches was quite clearly that they wanted us to continue and they were very grateful for what had been done. 

ASSISTANCE TO COOPERATIVES AND CREDIT UNIONS 

Senator INOUYE. Some time ago a book was written entitled "You 

Can't Build a Chimney from the Top." With this theory in mind, that the building of capital begins with the thrift of individuals, this committee has sought to channel resources and financial backing to credit unions and savings and loan associations. I am certain you will recall we discussed this with you in the last 4 years and I would have to say that we have had very little success in this discussion particularly as it

pertains to South America and the Inter-American Development Bank.

Of the $3,741,311,000 total funds contributed to the Fund for Special Operations of which the United States contributed $2,540,350,000, or roughly 70 percent, how much has the Bank lent in direct support of credit unions or savings and loan associations?

Mr. PORGES. I don't have that figure, sir. 

Mr. HENNESSY. We don't have that figure but we will get it. 

Let me say this on this particular point. We agree on the trickle up theory as a theory, but, as a practice, it is very difficult and we would not like to mislead the committee into saying that it is just a question of turning the hose in a different direction. 

What has been found by institutions like the Inter-American Foundation, of which I am also a director, is that it takes an awful lot of time and effort and money and years to be able to develop a sound lending program for a cooperative or a credit union. Of course in the intermediate lending institutions some of these are going to go through cooperatives and credit unions, and here again we have some facts and figures which show that there may be higher credit risks involved. 

Now, I think part of the problem with the credit unions and the cooperatives which we have not totally bridged, is the fact, that, in the past the governments themselves, the nations involved, have not generally been willing to back them up financially.

In other words, if the Bank is going to lend directly to a cooperative in Ecuador, the Ecuadoran Government-this is a specific example, I am using it as an illustration-might not be willing to guarantee the credit to a small cooperative. So that would mean that the Bank would have to take that risk indirectly.

As we have seen from some of the intermediate lending institutions this can be high risk. We are not going faster than the Government wants to.

Senator INOUYE. We are talking about credit cooperatives here. If my memory is correct, I think we have provided less than $2 million out of this total $3.741 billion to credit unions and savings and loans. 

Mr. HENNESSY. I don't have the figure. I don't doubt that. One of the things that we are trying to do is work with institutions. For example, the Inter-American Bank is going to provide the Inter- American Foundation with up to $5 million and there will be a first grant proposed to provide for the Latin American country cooperatives. A $1 million grant to start off with so that 

Senator INOUYE. I am also impressed by the fact that of this nearly $2 million to credit unions and savings and loans in South America there have been no defaults. I think it might be well if the 

Treasury Department looked into this.

Mr. HENNESSY. We will be glad to do this. I am told by Mr. Reynolds that the IFC invested in an institution in Colombia. Again the record does not show that there has been a great deal of change but I think if you look at it very closely-the institution I know is the Inter-American Foundation and they have been in operation I believe 3 years now. It takes quite a period of time to mount a program that is really meaningful in this area and we would hope to see more and find better ways of doing it.

IDB ASSISTANCE TO INTER-AMERICAN FOUNDATION AND COLAC 

Mr. PORGES. Mr. Chairman, we feel that this agreement with the

So we are confident that the first million dollar loan by the Inter-American Foundation will be made. 

In the past I understand that this type of loan was a very small loan. Generally it is not in multiples of millions of dollars. These are small credit unions throughout South America and require the type of administration where you normally have to go through an intermediate institution in order to finance them.

So the Inter-American Foundation, in its short life, has opened up this network of foundations in the Dominican Republic, in Colombia, in Central America and in other places, and is therefore in a position both to monitor and to see that the small loans that are made on the basis of their loans to these foundations are wisely used. So we feel that in the future there will be a greater flow of resources to these instituitons.

That is not saying the bank could not directly do things themselves. 

I think we have become somewhat hesitant without a Government guarantee.

We were on the horns of a dilemma and the way that was resolved was not to make loans without Government guarantees. 

Senator INOUYE. Why can't these South American countries guarantee credit cooperatives? What is so bad about that?

Mr. HENNESSY. As a general rule that means picking out one group and there may be political implications. They have not been willing to do it and prefer to make the funds available through the local agricultural bank or development bank which again tends to make larger loans.

I think this is an area in which we ourselves could not set aside a contingency fund. Realizing that we come up before the Congress we say, well, they may have had a slightly higher default rate but we think that this is a segment that was not getting enough credit so that therefore we are supporting it, even though at the outset of the program, until we get some more expertise, there may be a high default rate. 

Senator INOUYE. The cooperatives have the lowest default rate in 

South America.

Second, we have been impressed at least by testimony presented to us that this is where the credit and money goes to the poor folks, the people we are trying to assist, not the governments. 

Somehow I feel that in these programs the main purpose would be to shore up these governments.

CONSTRAINTS ON LENDING TO COOPERATIVES 

Mr. HENNESSY. On all of them, the idea is to get them through to the end user. Again, you have to have institutions to do it and you are pointing out, I think, some very useful institutions that the banks have not used very much in the past.

It may well be we are agreeing with your objective and we will try and do something more concrete about it. These are institutions which can be used.

Now, in the past there have been restraints and constraints and concerns. I don't have the same figures. I don't have any figures before me right now on the credit risk but I worked for a commercial bank for a number of years in Latin America and we generally did not lend to cooperatives not because they don't have balance sheets, their legal status sometimes is in question. There are a whole set of associated problems in dealing with these very small types of energies. 

That does not argue that we should not do it and more can't be done, but if we look at the Inter-American Foundation, it has taken a very long period of time to do very little, on cooperatives. 

So, in order of magnitude next year if you have another $500 million out it would be an enormous amount in the entire region as far as cooperatives are concerned. I think maybe if you went up by $100,000 or $200,000 increments it would be a lot. Just sitting on the 

Board we do $5,000, $10,000 grants to these savings institutions-and they need technical assistance.

They sometimes have to find someone who knows how to make collateral loans, these types of things. 

I am not trying to belittle the importance of this, but it is a very difficult area and so the general thrust has been to work through already existing institutions.

In terms of development impact, our main interest is to provide credit to increase production, not to finance consumption, goods like appliances and cars-which is of course, what many of these cooperatives and credit unions do. But they also encourage saving and that is of value.

U.S. CONTRIBUTIONS ON "SUBJECT TO APPROPRIATION" BASIS 

Senator INOUYE. We shall appreciate that.

In establishing a target for the Inter-American Development Bank I recall that at the urging of the subcommittee the administration wrote into the letter of transmittal that these funds would not be available except upon an affirmative appropriation action. 

Do we have the language of that transmittal here?

Mr. HENNESSY. I don't have it before me but I believe it was "subject to appropriation" which was the catch word in there. 

Senator INOUYE. Why can't we place the same provision in establishing our target contribution to the World Bank also to the Asian 

Development Bank?

Mr. HENNESSY. Those are different institutions. We are not the only donor in those. That is the short answer. What that means is that if it is subject to U.S. appropriations with the United States being the only donor in the Inter-American Bank-with the exception now of Canada-that means as soon as we go ahead the whole thing goes ahead-if we don't, then the rest of it doesn't go forward.

In IDA where we have 24 other nations contributing, it is not a practical way of proceeding to have anyone saying that their contributions are subject to their internal situation of procedure each year. The bank needs a provision of funds over a period of time and it needs to be able to count on a set amount from each country. 

We sit around the table and each country agrees in the light of the agreement of other countries. What has changed, Senator Inouye, is that we have not taken any prior commitments without a full hearing and full authorization and an appropriation so we don't come to Congress and say "you have to appropriate these funds because we have committed you internationally."

We believe we have the most, let us say the only, practical way of dealing with both the Asian Bank and the World Bank IDA because of their broader membership. 

NATIONAL INTEREST RATIONALE FOR U.S. PARTICIPATION 

Senator INOUYE. Before calling upon Senator Chiles, I have just one observation and my last question.

Mr. Secretary, I am certainly aware that this area will receive the most intensive questioning and debate in Congress in the forthcoming weeks. It is not exaggeration to observe that foreign aid is the most unpopular program we have at the present time. 

For the past 2 or 3 years we have been able to pass upon these programs by small majorities. I anticipate once again that there will be intensive questioning and that is why I have been asking questions that may not seem relevant to you but these are the questions that have been asked of me by my colleagues.

My final question is one that is asked most often. What is the national interest which is involved in our participation with these banks? 

Is it in our best interest to participate in these banks?

Mr. HENNESSY. I think there are many answers and I think that one of the basic ones is humanitarian. I don't think I can get away from that, that we are trying to help people help themselves. That is part of the American tradition and that is obviously one of the fundamental motivations to get into this activity to begin with. 

I understand these programs are unpopular but in a recent survey taken by an independent organization it was found that something like 68 percent of the American people were in favor of foreign assistance but I think some of the problems that arise- Senator INOUYE. We checked on that, Mr. Hennessy, and if I recall when we questioned people most of those questions had assumed that this meant feeding the poor and the hungry. 

If that was the thrust of the question, I would have thought that 99 percent of the people of the United States would have approved and yet only 68 approved. 

I think that is an indication.

Mr. HENNESSY. It is our assessment, Senator Inouye, that the majority of the people do support it provided (A) that the money gets through to the people and this is obviously the thrust of your concerns asking about cooperatives and asking questions in general. 

We accept your questions and recognize they are absolutely essential to be able to defend these programs. 

So, the people are interested (A) if it gets through to the people, and (B) if the institutions themselves are effective and the money is being well spent. So we try to demonstrate that. 

Our assessment is based on at least some exposure to the public. All of us have been out-myself, Mr. Porges and others-talking about these programs at universities and before business groups. 

I think what we have found in the case of IDA's defeat in the House was that there has been quite a resurgence of concern and interest in development. We have had everyone from the National Foreign 

Trade Council including it in their platform as an important part of the proceedings, to other organizations doing likewise. Church groups and unions such as the AFL-CIO are in favor of the Inter- American Development Bank, and that is also true of the IDA legislation.

So, we think there are broad bases of support. 

Now, it is quite clear that there has also been some disillusionment because of our own internal situation and unmet needs at home. 

Besides the humanitarian aspects, there are some more narrow interests. For example, we sold $17 billion worth of exports last year to

less developed countries. One of the ways they pay for that is by borrowing for productive uses from these institutions. 

The increased production generates the exchange whereby they can turn around and pay us for that $17 billion worth of exports. 

Less developed countries are the only part of the world where we actually have had a surplus trade balance in our favor over the last 3 or 4 years when the trade balance deteriorated with other countries. 

So they are important markets for us for goods and also sources of supplies.

A very high percentage of our imports of critical raw materials comes from developing countries. The way you develop raw materials, of course, is to provide the infrastructure that these countries needthe dams, the powerplants, the roads, the ports, the factories so that they can produce basic commodities at lower prices. 

This allows us to keep our costs down here and also keep our factories going. The more production that is in different places in the world, of course, also allows us to have certain guarantees against one country or a small group of countries. monopolizing a particular raw material.

There is a great interest in seeing, for example, development go forward in Asia and all of Latin America to protect our bases of supply of raw materials.

We also have important export markets. They buy our goods. They are important sources of supply to us. We also have a lot of foreign investment in these countries and I think we are interested in their being a part of the market economy and free flow of capital as well. 

We have seen that they not only generate employment there, they also generate employment back here in the United States. 

I think, as I tried to touch very briefly on in my statement, that there is something which Secretary Kissinger as well as Secretary Shultz had touched on in their testimony in IDA and Secretary Kissinger's talks before the U.N., that the world today seems to be faced with a fundamental decision whether we are really going to go forward in a cooperative effort and build a world in which we will live in peace or that we are going to tear ourselves apart really in economic competition and this is perhaps even more serious that the problems of security and direct military warfare.

We think these programs are important because they build a fabric in which countries cooperate with one another. We find, for example, that Kuwait, although a small contributor to IDA, has continued to be a part of that program. There has been some demonstration effect. 

I think from Kuwait's putting in 0.6 percent of IDA which is a doubling of what they put in before.

They just recently set up a $3 billion development fund, compared with some $300 million which they have lent over the last 2 or 3 years. 

A small fund of about $500 million, it is now up to $3 billion, and they will be going forward.

So, it is part of a broad effort to hold the world together at a very critical time.

These institutions have proven themselves to be a useful means of helping countries help themselves and also to increase the ties between us.

So for all these several reasons it seems to us that it is in the U.S. national interest to support them and support them strongly; not at

t an amount that is more than the taxpayer can pay, not at a balanceof-payment cost that we cannot justly defend, but at a fair and reasonable level.

I tried to point out in my prepared text that in terms of our budget and balance of payments these are justifiable requests and we think they deserve a high priority consideration by this committee. 

INCREASING THE SHARE OF OTHER DONOR COUNTRIES 

Senator INOUYE. I agree with your rationale and your reasoning, but can't we call upon our neighbors on the other side of the world to also use this rationale in providing greater support for these banks? 

For example, we are providing 70 percent of the Inter-American Development Bank and you and I know that the Japanese are now doing big business with the South Americans, the Germans also, and yet for some reason they have not seen the humanitarian light or the national interest.

Don't you think we should somehow expose them to this? 

Mr. HENNESSY. I think that the record shows pretty good progress. 

For example, in IDA the U.S. share has gone from 40 percent down to 333 percent. We have had a good discussion on what is the appropriate amount and I think there are some basic differences between us, but in terms of our GNP and other figures which they think are reasonable, 3313 percent is hard to defend. We should have a larger percentage. I think the Inter-American Development Bank, we have to recognize, is a special case. 

In the Asian Bank, we have 8 percent now. We think our original 

18 percent is more reasonable. But in the case of the Inter-American 

Bank since the days of the Monroe Doctrine-for more than a century-the United States actually tried to keep European influence out.

So, I think one of the concerns both of the Latins and of ourselves was until recent years that we didn't really want to have a large European influence there. But the Europeans are doing business, they are making loans, they are there. 

So, that exercise began 2 years ago and has not yet come to fruition primarily because they were not willing to put up what we think is their fair share. We still need some light of reason to shine through to them about this.

On the other hand, we are asking them to take, for example, 8 percent of the votes in IDB and put up $500 million. That is a large amount of money. In terms of historic shares $500 million is not much but in terms of what we are putting in on a current basis it looks like a lot of money to them.

They think they are getting too little for their shares and that is the meat of the negotiation. 

I think that we can say that if you look back 10, 15 years when the United States was doing about everything, these institutions have been a mechanism for shifting the burden to other countries. 

For example, in IDA for every dollar we put in other countries will be putting in $2 and that is the grand-daddy, the largest one of course and a worldwide one. 34-192 O 74-40

So, I think there is ample evidence that the trend is in the right way; you and I might wish it were a little faster but I think there is a floor beyond which we should not go.

Eight percent in the Asian Bank seems to be below what we should have. We believe that in the Inter-American Bank we are somewhat above where we should be, and that is why we are in favor of the Europeans coming in.

Of course, if the Venezuelans are able and willing to put up a larger share, that lowers the European share and we don't have to call on the U.S. taxpayer to bear such a large burden. 

Senator INOUYE. Fifteen years ago this world had one remaining superpower, the United States of America. Now we have several superpowers and these superpowers, I don't think, are picking up their share.

These include the Japanese for one, the Germans for another, the British and French and other NATO countries to a lesser degree, the Soviet Union and recently the Arab nations. Yet, for some reason, we find ourselves being called upon to make the major share each year. 

I would hope that our administration and our representatives at these meetings would call upon our more affluent friends to also settle part of the humanitarian burden. 

Mr. HENNESSY. We will do that, sir. 

Senator INOUYE. We appreciate that, sir. 

Senator Chiles.

CONTRIBUTIONS BY VENEZUELA AND ECUADOR Senator CHILES. What about the Venezuelan contribution? How does that stand now, Mr. Secretary?

Mr. HENNESSY. They have set up the framework for a fund and they have been talking in general terms of putting in half a billion over 5 years, but the only concrete thing they have done is buy $25 million of IDB bonds and $23 million of IBRD bonds. 

They have set up the arrangements for their funds. They now have to go through a political process themselves to see how much actual money they can get through their own parliament. It is a democracy and a vigorous one as you well know. We are hopeful that they will meet that target and we hope that a large component will be concession, because that is what Latin America needs and Venezuela is in a position to give it.

So, we welcome, very warmly, their initiative and we hope to see it come to fruition in a very short period of time. 

The Bank has had one mission down there discussing it with them and they have not brought it to concrete terms. I think it is going to be very useful for some of these countries that were borrowers to become lenders. Their point of view will change, they will see how difficult it is to justify the duty and responsibility of any Congress to justify these expenditures and there may be a little more sympathy for what the United States has done.

So, we think it is a very helpful development and we are hopeful, both with regard to hard and soft funds. 

Senator CHILES. Ecuador now has some large foreign exchange reserves. Is there any prospect of their making a contribution?

Mr. HENNESSY. They have discussed with the Bank the prospect of buying World Bank bonds. I think their per capita income is such that while they will have excess liquidity for a short period of time they will absorb most of their new income on their own development. 

I foresee a very diminished amount of lending from the Bank that would go to Ecuador. For what lending does take place, they in turn would be willing to offset it or at least to partially offset it by buying IDB bonds, in other words, they would help provide funds for the banks to lend to other countries. 

That again is not at a concrete stage. 

One of the things that has happened, if I might remark, Senator Chiles, is that these countries, which have been poor and have been seeing themselves as poor for so long are suddenly seeing themselves on the other side and it has not yet totally penetrated their consciousness, so to speak.

I think there has not been as much progress as you and I might like ideally, but on the other hand, there has been progress and much more so than one might think. Looking at this historically, consider how long it took our European neighbors before they were willing to come forward with some contributions, once they became developed. 

ADMINISTRATIVE EXPENSES OF IDB 

Senator CHILES. In the conference last year the Senate went in with a considerably higher figure for IDB and the House was concerned with the administrative expenses of the Bank. What is the situation regarding the expenses and the concern for that? 

Mr. HENNESSY. I think the budget in the IDB has been a source of strength. John Porges has been working on this and I will let him. talk about the specific figures and what has been done. 

Mr. PORGES. Actual spending for 1973 came to within 1 percent of the budget. All the figures are not in but the estimates on the basis of those figures that are in came within one percent of the budget estimates.

Since last year, since my joining the Bank, I requested the President to set up a budgetary review committee of the Board and he did so. 

We now have quarterly budget reviews where we go into each item of the budget and continually impress upon the staff the need for greater control of expenditures and reduction of expenditures. 

We just had our first quarterly meeting and there are quite a few elements that need to be improved, but the Bank has indicated a willingness to do this.

I am hopeful that within a comparatively short time we will consistently be able to keep expenditures down. Of course, inflation has its result on salaries-for example there was a salary increase the end of last year which was reflected in this year's budget, and in these times. there is little we can do except try to keep these expenses down as much as we can and this is our effort on the board of the Bank. 

I think that more and more of a professional interest and push on the part of the committee of directors will accomplish this result.

LENDING COSTS OF IDR 

Senator CHILES. Can you give me some percentages and figures now of what it is costing IDB to put out money, and what percentage it is to administer your loans, and how does that rate with financial institutions? These are the kinds of things that you just tell me we are doing a better job.

This does not help very much if the House says, for example, again, that your expenses are way out of sight. 

Mr. PORGES. I agree with you, Senator Chiles. This is just a humble beginning. We feel we are starting in the right direction. As far as the Bank's financial expenses are concerned, we have stopped borrowing because of rates in the financial markets of the world. 

The Inter-American Bank has raised a total of $1.2 billion in the markets of the world. Of that $1.2 billion raised over the 14year life of the bank, $440 million was raised in the United States. 

With the cost of funds these days the Bank is not able to do So, since it does lend at 8 percent on its ordinary capital. It has been very difficult.

The control of expenditures is one which has been impressed on everyone in the Bank. The overseas offices are being utilized more and more to prepare the background for loans and the basic information on loans so that the costs of administration are lowered. In time, the establishment of the Comptroller's Office, with its emphasis on initiation and preparation of loan requests abroad, in time will bring down our expenditures.

On the actual cost for administration of loans I don't have the figures. I will submit them. I will obtain them and be happy to submit them for the record. The actual administrative budget for 1973 was $39 million.

Senator CHILES. $39 million. What I would like to have is some kind of breakdown showing what your costs are, how many employees that you have, what their total payment is, you know, how that breaks down for the number of employees that you have and get some idea of what it is costing you to administer a dollar or a thousand dollars of loan funds and how is that ranking with other lending institutions, both private and public. 

Then I can try to make some sort of a judgment for myself whether the charges of the House are correct or not. 

Mr. PORGES. I will be happy to submit the information. 

Mr. HENNESSY. I think we will have to put in some disclaimers. 

When you compare these institutions, for example, with the private institutions they do different types of activity.

CATALYTIC ROLE OF FOREIGN ASSISTANCE 

Senator CHILES. I have reached the opinion that the most valuable thing that can be done with our foreign aid is attempting to provide a catalyst rather than finance or build projects ourselves or even through international institutions. 

What efforts are being made in the Inter-American Development Bank especially to provide technical assistance so that the Latin Americans can prepare projects themselves and carry out their development process on their own initiative?

Mr. PORGES. Senator, technical assistance in the poorer countries is almost a sine qua non as part of the development loan. We do institution building. We have to furnish the type of economic and technical assistance to the country in drawing up the project, so in a typical development loan a certain percentage-it is not a large percentage but if it is a large $30 million or $40 million project, $1 million or $2 million might typically be a technical assistance part of the loan. 

The goals or objectives have to be realized before the rest of the loan can be drawn down and this I say is more difficult in countries which have less of a technically trained population, the Bolivians, for example, than it is in the case of a more developed country. 

On the question of acting as a catalyst in mobilizing resources the Bank has committed some $6.3 billion over its 14-year life and the Latin 

American counterpart for these project loans has been $13.3 billion and so this has resulted in $19.6 billion, the total cost of the projects, but they are over two to one in local contribution for these projects. 

IMPACT OF POSSIBLE APPROPRIATION CUTS 

Senator CHILES. Your lending authority at the beginning of this year or at the end of the year 1974 was $98 million carryover. 

Now, assuming that the United States made its full contribution I think you would have $181 million if we made the $500 million capital contribution.

What is going to be the status if the Congress comes out with, say, $200 million as our capital contribution this year? 

Mr. HENNESSY. Instead of $500 million? Well, it would mean that the Bank would have to reduce its programs or run right out of money. They have been lending at an annual rate from the soft loan window of $400-plus million. If they have a carryover of $100 million and you add $500 million to that that gives you $600 million which gives you a small carryover into the next year. 

Because of the delays that have occurred in the timing on approvals of appropriations in the past, as I tried to point out in my testimony, the Bank would be faced with a crisis not this year but sometime next year before this committee would have acted. 

So, it is our great concern that there not be cuts. You do have a small margin obviously in there but we think this full amount is the minimum needed to carry through on a sound management basis. 

These organizations obviously have longer leadtimes in making loans and they cannot start and stop, start and stop, depending on the flow of funds, so we believe a small margin has to be there for carryover from year to year.

Senator CHILES. The Congress gave you $255 million last year.

Mr. HENNESSY. Yes. 

Senator CHILES. Assuming that the Congress gives you $250 million this year, and I don't know that it would not, being an awful optimist, I don't think you are going to come out with a lot more than that by the time you get through the conference committee between the House and the Senate? Where is that going to put you in 1975?

Mr. HENNESSY. Well, that means they would have to reduce their lending program and, of course, they have already reduced it. They would cut back somewhere below, which depends on how much margin you want to leave from one year to the next, but a $100 million or $200 million carryover would seem to be a minimum, on an ongoing program of this size.

So, what you are talking about is reducing, as a matter of financial prudence, to, say, somewhere between $300 million and $350 million, on the order of magnitude of that. 

They could, of course, go ahead with $400 million depending on what was said in the conference report about future years, but the problem is in the planning and in the carrying forward of these programs there has to be some degree of certainty so that the institutions can continue to lend.

That has been very useful in the case of the Asian Bank and the IDA in that the institutions had a rough rule of thumb to go by from the conference reports and that allowed them to run a little bit closer to the bottom of the barrel. 

Let me just say that a cut of the order of magnitude which you mention would not only make them reduce their program well below the $400-plus million level, but it would also, I think, have a very disastrous impact on the effort which Secretary Kissinger is now engaged in trying to build closer ties with Latin America. 

So we would hope, very strongly, that that would not occur. 

Senator CHILES. You don't anticipate that there could be any help during the year of 1975 from the Europeans or from Venezuela that would help make the difference?on

Mr. HENNESSY. In our projections we don't have those in there, because those are in the middle of negotiation. To the extent that they are realized, then that would alleviate the burden. 

In other words, they could gain, run a little bit closer to the line, but both of those negotiations are in the negotiation stage. The 

Venezuelan one is in the initial stage and the European one is in the latter stage, but we have no certainty, we don't think for financial planning purposes that we can count upon them. 

Therefore, my statement would stand that a major cut would have the effect of cutting back the program way below its current level and would run the Bank dry toward the middle of next year before the Congress will have had time to act again. 

Senator CHILES. How soon do you think you ought to give the Bank a signal that that may happen?

Mr. HENNESSY. Well, we give signals and they watch themselves and what is clear is that they have already had to taper their programs. 

That was one of the-I won't say one of the bitterest, but it was certainly one of the bitter parts of our debate in Mexico City. 

Subsequently we made the impression of solidarity but we had not delivered when the time came to deliver.

What I would like to point out, of course, is that the FSO is

closely watched by the poorer countries in Latin America and these are the ones who are going to need it because of the increase in food prices, fertilizer prices, and in oil prices.

I think this would be probably the most inappropriate moment to make a major cutback. As I say, you do have some cause of carryovers and some tapering. You can ad hoc it, so to speak, and get through, but an enormous cut, I think, would have a very negative impact both in an economic and in a foreign policy sense. 

Senator INOUYE. Mr. Secretary, I would like to call upon the minority counsel, Mr. Rossiter, who has a few questions. 

IDA LENDING TO INDIA 

Mr. ROSSITER. Mr. Secretary, what percentage of IDA's loans go to India? 

Mr. HENNESSY. I believe last year it was 36 percent. 

Mr. ROSSITER. Do you have any projections on the percentage of the $320 million request for this year that will be allocated to that country?

Mr. HENNESSY. We are a year behind everyone else in a sense. That is, I think, another point which goes to Senator Inouye's point. Other countries have been much swifter in putting up their shares and paying it in. Those funds will have been committed based on the assumption that the United States will come in with its final installment, so that 36 percent you can apply to that $320 million.

Mr. ROSSITER. Future projections on the $1.5 billion that is requested for the replenishment. 

Mr. HENNESSY. One would assume it would be in that ball park.

REACTION TO INDIAN NUCLEAR TEST 

Mr. ROSSITER. Have you received any indication of how the other

IDA donors have reacted to the Indian explosion of the nuclear device and in terms of the continued contributions in vast amounts to that country?

Mr. HENNESSY. Of what? 

Mr. ROSSITER. The contribution of fairly vast amounts in comparative terms to that country out of IDA. 

Mr. HENNESSY. I don't have any direct knowledge of the implications of reports or reactions of other countries as it relates to their provision of development assistance to India. I think, from our own point of view, we do know that the great bulk of India's expenditures on nuclear development has been in the peaceful field, particularly in the field of power and energy, which we think is particularly important.

On the other hand, it is quite clear that this nuclear explosion does raise questions of India's own economic priorities and we think that probably all AID donors will want to carefully examine the implications for the future resources and their own economic priorities. I assume that will take place as a natural course of events. 

IDB LENDING TO CHILE 

Mr. ROSSITER. I have asked these questions along the same line as the chairman, because this is going to be a question that is going to

come up quite readily in the congressional debate and the Senate debate on the item. 

One other question relating to Chile. As you know, many individuals were surprised about two loans to Chile in a relatively short time after the Junta overthrew the Allende government. 

As I understand it, during Allende's years in power no IDB loans were granted to that country. Can you inform us why the loans were granted after the Junta took control, whereas there had been no loans previously in the Allende government? 

Mr. HENNESSY. To be factually correct, there were two loans made to the Allende regime. Something like $12 million was made available in January 1971 in those two loans after he took office. It is a fact, that after those initial loans were made in January 1971 to the Allende government, there were no new loans by any of the international institutions to Chile and that was due to two factors. 

One factor was that they had expropriated or were in the process of expropriating, without compensation, without due process, large American and other private interests, private enterprise. 

Under congressional mandate and under law, both the Gonzales amendment and the Hickenlooper amendment, the United States made its concerns known to these institutions in a specific way in the World Bank and in a general way in the IDA. Obviously, they cannot make loans when there are serious economic uncertainties ahead. 

That same policy issue occurred on several other occasions in Nigeria and the Belgian Congo, when there have been large scale expropriations not affecting the United States but others. That was problem 

No. 2.

Problem No. 1 was the economic situation in the country itself. We never got to problem No. 2, in a sense, because the lending institutions never got past problem No. 1, which was the economic situation in the country which went rapidly downhill. 

From all the economic reports made by the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank it was clear that there was economic mismanagement and, therefore, they could not meet their charter requirements that there was a reasonable certainty that they were going to be able to repay the loan.

Now, that situation changed very drastically after the new government came into Chile in September of last year. They agreed to pay up their defaults to the World Bank and the World Bank made a $10 million loan to them earlier this year after they had put their defaults in order.

They also called down missions of the international institutions everywhere from the Inter-American Committee of the Alliance for Progress, there was an IMF mission, there was a World Bank mission, there was an IDB mission who went down there and worked out an economic reconstruction program which they are carrying out. A part of this was what you might call a standby agreement, and, which was a normal economic antidote to inflation and a necessary condition for further economic growth, a stabilization. They drew on the International Monetary Fund earlier in February. I think there are some $80 million.

So the third step in the process was the Inter-American Development Bank making two loans, one for power of $75 million and another for

agriculture reconstruction and rehabilitation of some $22 million in March.

Here again the Government had an economic program which was one way. All the international institutions had studied and had given their staff approval to have a legitimate program which was going to entail certain sacrifices on the part of the Chilean population. 

At the same time the Government had begun to negotiate very seriously with the affected companies, not just the United States, but in other nations as well, in terms of returning seized assets. As a matter of fact there has been an agreement reached, I think it was some $40 million claimed by the Cerro Copper Co. That was taken out of the way and resolved, amicably and justly and fairly, and progress on the other three major outstanding copper claims seems to be proceeding in an orderly fashion and meeting the congressional, the legislative and legal requirement of good faith negotiations. 

Certainly the companies think so and as far as we can tell that is where that situation stands. 

So, the difference circumstances were (a) the better economic situation and (b) progress on the compensation issue.

So, it was not as many people would like to claim that it was: all political content. Those same criteria apply to any country that happens to be in that situation. 

Senator CHILES. Granted there are these different circumstances it does appear that there was a pretty strong gain. It may be a signal that we made in granting the $200 million agricultural loan in the abbreviated process.

If they are changing their economic policies, if they are granting compensation, if it appears that now some help could be done for the country to grant loans, all those I think are certainly circumstances towards resuming or granting some loans. 

But on the other hand when you abbreviate the process and you take less than 24 hours, and as I understand your technical review or something then that is a pretty strong signal the other way that you are not only granting the loans but that you are speeding up the process and that makes it look very strong as if it is a very favorable climate that we are setting rather than a business issue sort of thing. 

Mr. HENNESSY. On the agriculture loan that was an emergency loan. 

It was similar to the loan that was made in Nicaragua after their earthquake.

EMERGENCY AGRICULTURAL LOAN TO CHILE 

Senator CHILES. What is the emergency that you were getting ready to have a meeting in Chile?

Mr. HENNESSY. No, if they don't plant, a lot of people will starve to death this fall in Chile. That was the planting period and they needed fertilizer and they needed seed and that is why the Bank went to them.

Mr. PORGES. Senator, this is not the first emergency loan that the 

Bank has made reacting to extreme need of Chile. During the Allende regime after the earthquake the President of the Bank surveyed the damage done and the homeless condition of many of the people in the earthquake zone in 1971 and 1972. Since Chile in its condition was not able to make use and draw down several loans that had been approved but whose conditions for disbursement would not be met. The Presi-

dent of the Bank got the Board of Directors to reassign $16 million for rapid disbursement for earthquake relief and amelioration of the condition of the people. 

So, I think that we want to lay to rest the circulated rumor that we had no concern for the people of Chile during Allende's regime and are only concerned about it since the change of government. 

I think the Bank's record shows it has had a humanitarian concern throughout the Allende regimes.

Senator CHILES. How well did the Bank inform Canada of this emergency? Canada became quite concerned with the abbreviated process.

Mr. PORGES. We were all informed that it was absolutely necessary for the question of planting. The Chilean director brought figures up to show what had to be done, the amount of fertilizer that had to be imported or the people would be in a precarious situation in the fall. 

I don't know. Perhaps, again, the Canadian Government was reacting to certain local pressures or feelings there. I am not in a position to say.

If I may add, however, during the Allende regime Chile received the largest disbursement of foreign exchange in the Bank's history. 

All the loans that were on the books and whose preconditions for disbursement could be satisfied were disbursed in a rigorously objective fashion. The Bank didn't try in any way to slow down disbursement of loans, even though reports circulate that nothing went to Chile. 

Chile received $33,800,000 in 1971, $21,700,000 in 1972 and $14 million between January and September of 1973. This is the largest foreign exchange loan contributions the bank had ever made up to that time.

Mr. HENNESSY. I think that is an important point, as long as we are getting into the facts of this particular case, where you had the other banks' operations in there.

During the three years of the Allende regime they received a transfer of resources of $130 million versus the preceding years of $100 million, so there was a larger one. The fact that there were no new loans had no impact on the economic development of the country, in that there was a long leadtime, since you appropriate a loan and the machinery and equipment doesn't get down there until later. 

So, looking at the implications of the Banks' activities there, all the banks have given a greater transfer of real resources to that particular country in that particular time than they had in the previous 

3 years.

I might say that Chile started off that 3-year period with the highest historical level of reserves that they had in their nation's history and those were rapidly run through a negative figure. 

Mr. ROSSITER. I have no further questions.

Senator INOUYE. The committee is aware that the United States contributions to development banks are often reinvested in U.S. Government securities.

OPENING REMARKS 

Senator INOUYE. Many of us, particularly those of us who served in 

World War II, sometimes think of U.S. worldwide assistance as a relatively new program. 

When we stop to reflect, however, we realize that AID and its predecessor agencies have been in business for 28 years, over a quarter of a century.

During this period it has become an old line agency with many successes and fine traditions, but also with some rather fixed and perhaps too rigid and arbitrary ways of doing business.

In my opinion, AID is at a very critical juncture in its history. What it does and how it goes about doing it is of critical importance. It may even be the determining factor as to whether or not the foreign assistance program is to be continued. 

From our brief association I do not know of any man better qualified or more able to correct AID's administrative weaknesses and excesses and redirect its program in accordance with the intent of last year's Foreign Assistance Act than Dan Parker. 

It is with great expectation and great personal pleasure that, on behalf of the committee, I welcome you to present AID's 1975 budget request, sir. 

Mr. PARKER. Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman.

With your permission, I would like to submit a more complete statement for the record and speak briefly. 

Senator INOUYE. Without objection, your full statement will be made part of the record, sir. 

[The statement follows.]

Mr. Chairman and Members of the Committee: 

Today I have the honor of appearing before this Committee to support and explain the President's request for appropriations in FY 1975 under the Foreign Assistance Act. I regret that because of conflicting schedules the Secretary of State has not yet been able to speak with you of the foreign policy arguments which underlie our request for funding in the next fiscal year but assume that he will indeed have this opportunity as soon as schedules permit. Of the total appropriations of $4.182 billion requested under the F.A.A., the Agency for International Development would be responsible for a total of $2.568 billion. In my review today I would like to do three things:

17 review briefly the more general philosophy of our program; summarize the request by major components of the program; examine several aspects of our administration with which your Committee has been concerned during the last year. 

The President, in his message to you of April 24, underlined the basic fact of foreign assistance, that, "Foreign aid has become an indispensable element of our foreign policy." And this truth is seen no more clearly than in our request for funding in the next year. More than half of our funding request for the year would go to the Middle East and Indochina. In the former area the sharp increase in the funding of our programs is an essential ingredient in our efforts to bring peace to that part of the world through establishing a framework for cooperation. 

Indochina cur economic assistance makes possible not only the economic stability so essential to the region's well-being, it also provides a part of the resources needed for economic development by the nations of the area. With our aid--both economic and military--we achieve a degree of relative stability for that area and help to avoid, as Secretary Kissinger has said, "both the dangers of rivalry for domination by outside powers and to preclude domination itself." In

During the past year we have experienced major problems on the international economic scene which simply confirm the facts that the world is far more of a unity than many Americans have perceived and that we are far more dependent upon others and they upon us than many Americans have been wont to concede? In this newly perceived world foreign assistance has even a greater function than in the past. 34-192 O 74-41

It not only serves as the American signal of a willingness to cooperate with other nations of the world in seeking a new economic order for our mutual benefit. It provides us with a part of the resources essential to those tasks. 

The Middle East 

Let me turn now to the proposed allocation of the funds we seek. First to the Middle East. 

The program we present is designed to sustain the momentum toward peace by giving Israel that assistance necessary to maintain both its security and economic strength; cementing our new relations with various Arab countries; and 

encouraging the peaceful development of the area. 

For the region as a whole, we are requesting $477.5 million, $377.5 in Supporting Assistance, $100 million in special funds.

For Israel we propose $50.0 million in Supporting 

Assistance to be used for financing their imports from the U.S. This aid is designed to cushion the impact of the war upon Israel's economy. 

For Jordan we are asking $77.5 million in grants. 

The nation has been a force for moderation in recent years-its budget, too, is distended by the expenses of defense. 

For Egypt we seek a total of $250 million all in economic assistance to be made as follows: $20 million to finance work on the Suez Canal; $80 million in loans to finance general commodity imports mainly from the U. S. to provide raw materials,

semi-finished goods and equipment and machinery for industry and agriculture; 

$150 million to support the reconstruction of the areas bordering the Canal. 

We hope these funds will be part of a larger multilateral effort coordinated by the World Bank. 

And we request $100 million "Middle East Special

Requirements Fund" for use in meeting needs as we proceed We would consult closely with Congress with negotiations. prior to the use of this money. 

Indochina Postwar Reconstruction

Mr. Chairman, we are requesting appropriations of $940 million for Indochina of which $750 million will be for South Vietnam. For Vietnam this represents a significant increase compared with fiscal year 1974, and I would like to take a moment to explain why we consider this increase to be necessary. The basic justification for our continuing economic aid to Vietnam lies in our determination, as the Secretary has put it, to "enable the states of Indochina to move freely toward a future of self-determined political and economic stability.' 11 

Serious deterioration of South Vietnam's economy would jeopardize both the process of political accommodation and the military situation. And a failure of the economy to grow can only lead to political stagnation.

The justification for the high level of our aid lies in part in the effects of problems over which Vietnam has little control--declining dollar earnings as a consequence of the departure of U.S. troops, and the sharp increases in world price levels.

While South Vietnam has done well in meeting its economic problems--by adopting a domestic austerity program, by increased tax collections and by expanding exports, major resources from abroad are required to maintain economic stability and permit the economic growth essential to ultimate viability. Without these resources, the economy would near collapse with all that implies for political and social insecurity. Our request for $750 million in economic and humanitarian assistance is essential to ward off that danger. Humanitarian assistance is targeted at providing resettlement assistance to refugees.

Aid to Vietnam's development flows both to the rural and urban sectors. In agriculture for example we will support work on the repair and restoration of canals and salt-water intrusion barriers and in expanding agricultural credit. And in industry, we plan a large investment credit program with supporting technical assistance. 

Our request for $110 million for Cambodia will permit us to continue a commodity import program of $71 million, humanitarian assistance for refugees and others displaced by the continuing fighting and our contribution to the internationallysupported stabilization program. The $20 million for humanitarian assistance will support the activities of voluntary agencies such as CARE, Catholic Relief Services and the International Committee of the Red Cross in their activities on behalf of refugees and will also be used for refugee resettlement. And the balance of funds would go to the

Exchange Support Fund and technical assistance. 

In Laos, the United States supports the political solution now evolving.

We seek with our economic assistance of $57

3 million to help Laos make a successful transition from the disruption of war to the fruits of peace. 

Development Assistance 

I would like to expand, if I may, on the Development Assistance programs which together total $1.4 billion. Through our development assistance programs, the U.S. makes its contribution to those efforts to stimulate the economic and social growth of the poorest people and the poorest countries around the world. The developing countries must find ways to grow enough food to feed their people, to create enough jobs to employ their labor forces, to reduce population growth to manageable proportions, and to train their people in useful pursuits. Of course, we cannot do the job for these countries nor can we be the only donors. Fortunately the numbers of countries aiding the poorest countries of the world for development and the level of their aid have steadily grown. International financial institutions and multilateral bodies are also contributing significantly to the effort. 

Here I underline the remarkable economic events of the past year which have illuminated the fact of interdependence in the world economy. Our national interests are served by an open, global economy based on negotiation not confrontation, a means the LDC's may try if they feel thwarted in attaining an acceptable and adequate system for meeting their justified needs.

For our food and nutrition programs we have requested $546.3 million, an amount $262.3 million above the current year's program. We are confident that the Congress will understand the dimensions of the crisis which have led us to request additional funds. This increase is also in part

a response to the decision of the Congress last year to reduce our use of loan reflows by 50%. 

For Population Planning and Health, we are requesting $145 million, the full amount authorized. The Congress in its restructuring of our program last year identified these activities as keys to success in providing access of the poorest people to the basic prerequisite of a productive life.

For Education and Human Resources Development, we are requesting $90 million. We believe that our planned programs in non-formal education are responsive to the direction the 

Congress wishes us to follow. request

The Selected Development Problems category--for which we $53 million--permits us to undertake a limited number of basic infrastructure projects and other high benefit activities not directly limited to the three principal functional categories.

For Selected Countries and Organizations, we are requesting $39 million, the largest part of which, $20 million, is to support American private and voluntary organizations in their activities overseas. Here I would like to note the fact of our effort to improve our relations with private organizations. 

In the latter part of April, I met with representatives of more than 150 private and voluntary organizations to discuss ways and means in which we could work together to expand development assistance to the poorest majority of the people in the less developed countries. of the private agencies was very encouraging and the dialogue will be continued. We are examining problems of food 

The response distribution and methods of strengthening their

E capability to manage expanded programs and to support specific programs in the field of our major, functional areas.

For the five functional categories created by last year's legislation, we are then requesting appropriations of $873.3 million, which will make possible a program of $1,130 million. An analysis of our programs in these areas leads us to request that of these funds no less than $333.3 million in new authority be available for grants. 

Another category of our request concerns international organizations and programs for which we ask $153.9 million. 

I would like, here, to emphasize the close relationship between bilateral and multilateral assistance programs, and the responsibility which A.I.D. feels for ensuring that there is active collaboration between them. While Ambassador 

Buffum will be speaking in more detail at a later date, I want to convey my strongest support for these programs, and in particular for the U.S. voluntary contributions to the 

U.N. development system with primary emphasis on the UNDP. 

In CY 1970, we contributed $86 million to UNDP or 35.7% of total contributions. The CY 1975 tentative pledge of $100 million is expected to represent no more than 24.2% of all contributions--approximately equal to the 1974 level but below our 1972 and 1973 levels of 30.3% and 28% respectively.

I would also note our requests of $10 million for U.N. Environment Fund and $14.7 million for continuing the funding of work on the Indus Basin.

To complete our request, there is $10 million for American Schools and Hospitals Abroad, $30 million for the Contingency Fund, $45 million for our own administrative expenses and $5.9 million for certain administrative expenses of the Department of State.

Let me turn now to a number of issues with which your Committee has been concerned over the past year. These relate primarily to how we do our job and how we control the resources you make available to us each year. I fully recognize the appropriateness of your concern and wish to be as forthcoming as possible for only in this way can we arrive at useful understandings and appropriate solutions. 

I would like to deal first with three aspects of the way we do our job. Let me take up the question of the use of the fixed-cost reimbursement financing system. As a result of your interest, I have studied this and find many advantages to its use in a number of possible situations. 

Thus we shall consider new projects and proposals also in terms of the suitability of this approach. We share with you the belief that in certain circumstances this system can be highly efficient. In that our aid is in many situations directed at resolving problems of foreign exchange, there are limitations upon the effectiveness of the technique. Nonetheless, the system has been introduced for projects in Bangladesh and we contemplate using it for reconstruction work in Pakistan. 

Second, I would like to note that pursuant to the amended Act, all public safety activities are being terminated overseas. The last public safety advisers will have been withdrawn by August 15th. Furthermore, no additional A.I.D.-funded police training for South

Vietnam has been undertaken since this activity was prohibited and the last trainees will return to South Vietnam this month. We are continuing the activity of the International Police Academy, at approximately the level of last year, albeit at substantially lower levels

than in recent years. A small number of public safety advisers will continue or begin to work on narcotics control activities.

And there are a number of advisers requested by Saudi Arabia which reimburses full cost of these. 

Third, I am happy to report that we are completing a thorough overhaul of our policies for management of our loan portfolio. We are establishing tight and firm guidelines which will permit us to identify loans which are not going forward as rapidly as they should and thus to force prompt deobligation wherever called for. In fact, any 

3 deviation from the norms we are establishing must be reviewed personally by my Deputy to assure that the pipeline is constantly controlled and is reduced to its absolute minimum. I trust that you share with me the realization that authority to reobligate deobligated funds is a necessary concomitant of this process. The next item in this series of issues concerns A.I.D. management and operations. This Committee has in recent years expressed special interest and concern with the operational management of A.I.D. I certainly share your interest, and also your concern. I am instituting a new management approach, designed first to effectively meet our program objectives and second, to get the job done efficiently and economically. I have charged my new Deputy, John Murphy, with the responsibility. for infusing these objectives in the operations of the Agency. He is chairing a Senior Operations Group which has the responsibility for ensuring that our systems are not only designed but are working effectively and economically, both in terms of manpower and money.

As you well know, the A.I.D. staff has been reduced drastically in recent years. But numbers by themselves are inadequate in measuring operational efficiency. Today 

I am more concerned with the full utilization of skills we now have in A.I.D., getting the optimum mix of skills needed for our programs, and maintaining a top-quality staff. 

To support these most important human resources, we are now developing back-up systems, exploiting the techniques and facilities available to modern management. We have designed and propose to implement in FY 1975 an improved accounting system for operating expenses. A major system overhaul has been initiated, primarily to assist Agency managers to measure program performance. We intend to use modern computer technology in each of these management systems, again to achieve optimum utilization of our manpower resources. 

On the question of A.I.D. personnel, I know that your 

Committee has been concerned with the question of whether our missions overseas are overstaffed, whether their personnel is overgraded, and whether their allowances are too large. You have expressed concern about staffing and grade levels for A.I.D. in Washington. 

I would join you in your concern if I believed that A.I.D. was in fact overstaffed and over-compensated, and I have initiated a number of studies designed to determine whether this is in fact so. 

When these are complete, we shall report to you on the conclusions and the actions I propose to take.

I would note here that as the A.I.D. program has shifted over the years from activities in which A.I.D. technicians participated directly to those where A.I.D. exercises only managerial responsibilities with contractors performing the services, missions have become increasingly staffed with employees sufficiently experienced to fill this managerial role. Managers overseas are more costly 

1 than technicians. As for allowances, A.I.D. personnel are treated essentially the same as all U.S. Government civilian personnel overseas. 

I am glad to have had this opportunity to present our budget request and to explain to you some of the actions I have undertaken to assure sound management of the Agency and its programs.

I look forward to continuing to work closely with your Committee and hope that you will continue to give your support to our activities.

Our development assistance programs will be the U.S. contributions to working out resolution of these problems.

 INCREASED COST OF GRAINS

GRANTS AND LOANS 

In establishing the metes and bounds of these accounts a separate definition is requested for grants and loans. Your office has been advised of this question and you have responded with a memorandum which I wish to at this time have made a part of the record. 

It provides your definition and your metes and bounds as to what is scheduled in nutrition, population planning, health education, human resources, selected problems, and selected countries and organizations.

Let me first comment in general and then proceed to a more detailed description of the activities included within each functional appropriation. 

While the functional authorizations are quite broadly defined, they are substantially more precise in terms of program purpose than the previous grant and loan structure. In addition, when the new functional account structure is read in the context of the various committee reports, Congressional hearings and together with the policy directives set forth in the FAA of 1973, Congressional intent becomes quite clear. For example, the Agency is clearly directed by Congress to place greater emphasis on reaching the poorest majority and less emphasis on large scale resource transfers. These directives cut across the functional authorizations and help to give them more precision. 

While the functional account structure is considerably more precise in terms of program purpose, there are obviously some definitional problems that could arise in assigning an activity to a particular account. For this reason, we have taken special steps to assure that activities are carefully defined and assigned in a consistent and understandable manner. 

The following guidelines are used within the Agency to categorize activities by functional appropriation. 

1. Food and Nutrition includes projects conceived to achieve objectives such as: 

Increased food production 

Improved food distribution 

Improved nutritional content of food (those nutrition activities which are part of broad integrated health programs are funded from Section 104 funds Population Planning and Health) 

Provision of information regarding improved nutrition practices. 

Increased income for the rural poor Provision of necessary supplies and equipment: e.g., pesticides, fertilizer, machinery - Construction of new fertilizer production capacity 

- Development and improvement of rural cooperatives 

Improved rural electrification, farm-to-market roads and irrigation systems - Conduct of basic and applied agricultural research necessary to the achievement of a number of these objectives 

2. Population Planning and Health 

Involve family planning 

includes projects that: 

Improve health care, including maternal and child health - Extend health systems to rural areas 

Support training of health care personnel

Improve environmental living conditions, e.g., potable water better sewage systems, spraying of malarial mosquitoes, and so forth 

3. Education and Human Resources 

includes projects that relate to: 

General education (education projects which relete to specific sector activities are in other categories, e.g., agricultural education in Food and Nutrition, health education in Population 

Planning and Health) 

General manpower improvement, e.g., labor projects 

Public administration, e.g., tax administration, statistics research, general participant training, etc. 

Scholarship funds 4. Selected Development Problems includes projects that relate to: 

- Urban development 

-Industrial development or private enterprise 

Science and technology

Capital infrastructure development, e.g., dams for hydroelectric power, power transmission and distribution, transportation facilities, telecommunications, etc. 

Funding for feasibility studies which are non-specific, i.e., that do not relate specifically or singly to one of the three primary categories 

4. Selected Countries and Organizations 

All program loans includes: 

General, non-specific grants to international or private voluntary organizations In regard to the second portion of your question dealing with the difference between loans and grants, the definitional distinction is, of course, quite straightforward and I believe the Committee is familiar with it. Within each functional account we distinguish between grants, loans and operating expenses. As indicated in the Congressional Presentation, we propose a total grant program of $351 million for 1975. 

While in a general way the grant program in these functional categories conforms with the previous technical assistance and population appropriation accounts, the line between loans and grants on this basis is not firm. 

While constrained by the grant ceiling, we do attempt to take into account the recipient's stage of development as well as the nature of the project when deciding if loan or grant funds should be used. We are, for example, trying to grant fund certain projects in the least developed countries while similar projects in more advanced A.I.D. recipient countries are loan funded. Moreover, in almost all cases loan projects encompass a significant degree of technical assistance.

GRANTS AND LOANS 

Mr. PARKER. I appreciate having that go on the record and we will provide any further discussion you want.

Senator İNOUYE. I wish to now touch upon the matter of grants and loans.

In your opinion, what is the distinction between a grant and a conventional loan repaid over 40 years with an interest rate of less than 3 percent? This question has been asked many times by my colleagues. 

Mr. PARKER. Well, Mr. Chairman, the basic descriptive distinction between the two as we utilize it is that a grant is just that. There is no repayment expected for the grant.

The loan, and I think the crux of your question is, a loan on these terms is in part a grant, and I would say, yes, there is a grant element to these loans.

I think that the standard computation for a loan made as our development loans are, is 2 percent during the 10-year grace period and then a 3-percent interest rate on a declining outstanding balance over the succeeding 30 years. I think the grant element of that is calculated to be 65 percent.

Senator INOUYE. Would it be better if we stopped using the word "loan" and used something else such as "special grants"?
