As a businessman in the past myself, I would certainly agree with you that this would be a very desirable source of capital, but I think we have to recognize, Mr. Chairman, our purpose is to assist in the development of people and society so that we as a country can in fact avail ourselves of what they can produce and what their natural resources are.

Senator INOUYE. I understand this and I concur with you, but my purpose is not to change your objective, but to provide a more honest view to the people of the United States. 

Now, I would believe that most of the people of the United States reading your statement might get the impression that most of the countries are borrowing money from us, so therefore we are not giving anything.

I would prefer to have the people of the United States realize that our tax moneys are being used for grants, that these are not really loans in the sense that most Americans would understand them to be. 

Mr. PARKER. Well, I think in fact that these are loans. I think there is a grant element. I confess that possibly a better terminology might be used. The International Development Association does use the term "credits." We do in fact get back substantial interest payments and principal payments.

1 Senator INOUYE. I realize that, but we pay 8 percent to lend them money at 2 percent. I am just wondering where the loan comes in. 

Mr. PARKER. Well, I have to say that I do not think the term "grant" is descriptive of the loan. I would not debate with you that there is a substantial grant element on the loan. 

Senator INOUYE. Could you think up some other word or phrase that would be a bit more descriptive so that the people of the United States could get a clearer picture of what is happening? I have had several letters from people throughout the United States expressing horror that we have cited items as loans when in fact they claim rather correctly that this is a grant and they feel cheated. 

I think it would be very helpful if you could come up with some phrase that would, as I said, better describe what has actually happened.

Mr. PARKER. Indeed, Mr. Chairman, we will certainly pursue this. 

AID CRITERIA FOR TERMINATING ASSISTANCE 

Senator INOUYE. Several years ago AID prided itself on graduating countries from its assistance program and hailed Korea and Taiwan as showcase examples of what could be done in other countries. 

The subcommittee wishes to know what is AID's criteria for terminating assistance and redirecting resources to those countries with greatest needs. More specifically, when will this termination be applied to Brazil, Turkey, Korea, Guatemala, and Panama?

Mr. PARKER. This is a vast subject, Mr. Chairman, and it is one that in the brief time I have been here I have already begun to approach. I think that the traditional perspective-I think you used the term "graduate countries"-may have been a somewhat simplistic view and we are studying new criteria. 

It is not as it was assumed to be in the past that all of a sudden it is like a graduation; you flip the tassel from one side of the mortarboard to the other and are then a graduate. We can see very clearly that each developing country is unique unto itself and it has a development pace that has to be considered individually. 

I hope that we can go into this in some detail at some point after I have had a chance to give more study to it and I hope that we can reflect more accurately in loan terms and utilization of grants—I should use the term Senator INOUYE. I wish you would do this because it is rather basic. 

If I read my letters correctly, many Americans wish to know whether this program is a permanent program. That is, once you get on the recipient list do you stay on forever, or is there a point when our objective is reached? While we cite certain objectives, such as to make a country self-sustaining or to finish a certain project, it appears from the study of the record that once you get in on the program you are in forever. 

We would like to know if there is a point when one does get out or is it always destined to be United States give, and the rest of the countries receive. 

Mr. PARKER. Mr. Chairman, I can assure you that we are not going to let people just stay on. As a matter of fact, in this upcoming year 

Brazil will be completely phased out of receiving any development credits.

There are certain countries which have become due to the recent surges in prices-affluent but are still very much less developed. 

Senator INOUYE. Are you satisfied that we are meeting the needs of the so-called poorest majority of the world?

MR. PARKER. We are not meeting the needs but we are addressing what resources we can to serve those needs [and I think] in an overwhelming proportion of all of our activities.

I wouldn't want to begin to imply that doing so does not benefit the whole society, but this is the inverse, Mr. Chairman, of the assumption that prevailed some years ago that if you assisted the entire economy you would assist the entire population, the so-called trickle-down theory which I don't think is viable. 

I think the premise that we are now operating on is, in fact, more viable: that by assisting the poorest people, the less productive, those most needy, in fact you will help them and the entire economy. 

Senator INOUYE. I have just been advised in reaction to your statement that the program will be completely phased out in Brazil, that at the end of December there were $200 million in undisbursed loans and at the end of fiscal year 1975 you will have $100 million undisbursed loans. 

Mr. PARKER. Yes, I am talking, Mr. Chairman- 

Senator INOUYE. What will happen to that $100 million?

Mr. PARKER. Well, that is for projects which are already underway to the completion of implementation. 

Senator INOUYE. So, it will continue for a few more years?

Mr. PARKER. Yes, but we plan no additional congressional credits. 

LEVELS OF AID 

Senator INOUYE. In looking over the budget request I note that a large portion of AID's program has been utilized in South America which, compared with Africa, would be either a developed continent or a richer continent.

Do you feel that Africa is being provided the assistance necessary to keep some of their inhabitants out of the area of human misery? 

Mr. PARKER. Mr. Chairman, I think we have to approach from the perspective of total donor assistance. There is a unique relationship between North America and Latin America, and there is a unique relationship that exists between Europe, Western Europe in particular, and Africa.

I think thus we have to look at the totality of development assistance as it flows to the areas in need. 

In our own programs regarding Africa, we have had some constraints upon the ability of some of the countries that we are assisting in Africa to absorb the development assistance that we see as needed. 

Senator INOUYE. Did I hear that Nigeria was being phased out?

Mr. PARKER. Phased out of the loan credit, sir. I think we are now down to a transition to technical assistance only, and I don't think we have had we have $700.000 of the development loan credits in fiscal 

1974 to complete a school and none projected in 1975. and there was none in fiscal 1973. There is a continuing level of development grants and technical assistance down from fiscal 1973 of $8 million to $3.7 million projected for fiscal 1975. 

---

1 Senator INOUYE. I find this very interesting because according to 

1973 World Bank statistics Nigeria has 59 million people with a per capita gross national product of $150 and reserves of $600 million and I believe presently AID funds amount to $3.6 million. 

On the other hand we find, say, Panama with 1.6 million people with a per capita gross national product of $867 compared to $150 in Nigeria and reserves of $1.2 billion as compared to $600 million receiving $21 million.

This is the sort of mathematics that interests me, 59 million people, per capita $150. You are phasing them out but other countries such as 

Panama, Korea, with a per capita gross national product of $446, and $1 billion in reserves, Guatemala with a per capita national product of $406, and a reserve of $212. 

Mr. PARKER. Well, Mr. Chairman, let me take Nigeria first, if I may. The reason for the significant phasedown there-and the new 

1974 population figure that I have is somewhat more than you cited, it is closer to 80 million people, according to current census reports—is because of Nigeria's actual and projected oil revenue. I think that they have suddenly and very rapidly built up to having something like almost $2 billion by the end of 1973 in oil revenues, although foreign exchange holdings were considerably less at $60 million. I think that by the end of 1974 the projection I have seen is that they will have something like $3.9 billion and nearly $8 billion by the end of 1975 in oil earnings, so we are in fact phasing them out of credits. I hope that we could even phase down more quickly the grant portion of our assistance.

Senator INOUYE. Has your agency ever drafted a schedule setting forth gross national product, reserves, et cetera, to determine mathematically where the breaking point would be?

Mr. PARKER. This is an exercise, Mr. Chairman, that we are going through at the present time. I think a great deal of light can be shed by these economic and statistical analyses, but I think we also have to recognize and be able to factor into our decisionmaking the nonquantifiable aspects of the program. 

Senator INOUYE. I think it would be well for the people of the 

United States to know what sort of aid we give to what sort of country. 

I recall a few years ago when it was made known that we were providing heavy assistance to Brazil and Brazil was purchasing and maintaining an aircraft carrier; it didn't quite set right with the people of the United States.

If a country is that poor where did it get the money to buy an aircraft carrier? So if you could advise this committee what sort of schedule you look forward to, it would be most helpful in our determination also.

I realize it cannot be rigid and inflexible because each country has its special unique problems.

Mr. PARKER. Yes; and also I think that we have to bear in mind their ways of making sovereign decisions in their own interest. 

Senator INOUYE. But I think it would be helpful if we had some guidelines.

Mr. PARKER. I agree, Mr. Chairman, and we shall in fact work toward this and work with you on it.

AID TO SOUTH VIETNAM 

Senator INOUYE. The conferees on the fiscal year 1974 second supplemental agreed upon $49 million in funds for Indochina postwar reconstruction as provided by the House rather than $15 million provided by the Senate. The higher figure was agreed upon with the understanding that "no new development loan funds should be made available to South Vietnam without the express approval of the appropriations subcommittees of both Houses of the Congress." 

Is it your expectation that such a request will be forthcoming or is the matter now closed?

Mr. PARKER. Mr. Chairman, it is not yet closed. I have been doing my utmost, I have been having my associates do their utmost, and we have asked the Government of South Vietnam to do its utmost to obviate the need to do this. 

A great deal of the ultimate decision on this which will be rapidly approaching is related to the as yet unknown decision of the Congress as to the level of assistance that we can provide in fiscal 1975 to South Vietnam as well as the timeliness of the enactment of legislation. 

And I would say candidly it is my hope that we would not have to carry out any of this development loan. 

At this stage I must honestly say I don't yet know. We are running an awfully close margin in South Vietnam. The Government there has imposed even more strict austerity policies on importation of commodities than we had believed possible. 

They are doing one thing that I must confess a certain amount of ambivalence toward-the fact that a certain amount of fertilizer it was hoped could be purchased was unavailable for purchase, thus reducing the estimated commodity import requirements. But the other side of that coin is that to the extent that fertilizer is not available, the probability is that food production will be impaired. 

One other matter of good fortune has occurred there that again was not able to be factored in. This is a payment that is expected to be received, I believe, in July, from the oil companies who are paying for their right to explore for oil offshore. It is a close thing, Mr. Chairman, at the present point, but certainly you have a right to consult about it.

Senator INOUYE. As you are well aware, the House insisted upon the higher figure of $49 million because the House was impressed that if this were not done South Vietnam would go down the drain, you would have bankruptcy, et cetera. It was meeting a very critical point. 

So when the Senate approved and went along with the House, we anticipated that as soon as this matter was signed into law South Vietnam would be coming in requesting these loans. But, apparently, the urgency has ended.

Mr. PARKER. No; the urgency is still there. It is very, very close and I feel that this is a significant point in the relationship between the administration and the Congress. 

I feel the responsibility personally to avoid the diversion of development loan funds into Vietnam unless it is absolutely necessary. I am going to make every effort to avoid having to do so, but it is not that there is a lack of urgency. It is extremely urgent. 

I think it is due to very strenuous efforts on the part of the Vietnamese Government and people that they have been able to do what they

have. A level like this, Mr. Chairman, of assistance precludes them from growing. It means that they will be dependent upon external resources for a longer time, but we are requesting very substantial sums as I have stated through fiscal 1975. 

We see a substantial portion of that as going well beyond the mere level of economic survival-of getting into genuine development so that they can begin to grow, accelerate what growth they do have, and thus to enable us to reduce U.S. economic assistance to them. 

I would like to mention that we in fact are going to report to the Congress by the first of August with a 5-year phase-down projection. 

This was included with our concurrence by Senator Humphrey in his amendment to the State Department authorization bill and I welcome the chance to do this because I do not see it as hopeless. 

The Vietnamese people are industrious and capable and they have a country of resources. I believe that they can become self-sufficient. over a period of time with some reasonable external assistance. 

FIXED-COST REIMBURSEMENT 

Senator INOUYE. In testifying before the subcommittee on March 

25, 1974, Mr. Kenneth Fasick, Director of the General Accounting

Office, International Division, stated that his office found that AID has taken only limited action to utilize the cost reimbursement concept which the committee has supported so strongly over the past 2 years. 

Why is AID so timid in using this concept which I believe can do much to not only strengthen the AID program but promote more responsible planning by the recipient governments? 

Mr. PARKER. Mr. Chairman, as far as I am concerned, we are not timid. I have sent word to mission directors and I have talked to them personally of this concept, asking them to utilize it in principle and specifically wherever possible. In this current fiscal year there are a number of places where it is being used. 

There are a number of places projected for fiscal year 1975 where it would in fact be used. I hope to increase the number of applications. 

I think it makes every bit of sense, the virtues that you pointed out in the report of this committee before. 

Senator INOUYE. We have a small project in Tanzania. I know the cost overrun is $6 million and I am confident that if the cost reimburseable concept had been applied you would not have this extra cost. 

Mr. PARKER. I don't know the specifics of that case, but I agree in principle that this approach has a number of basic safeguards.

OBLIGATED UNEXPENDED BALANCE OF PIPELINE FUNDS 

Senator INOUYE. According to your schedule the obligated unexpended balance of pipeline money amounts to $2,811,420,000. 

Mr. PARKER. That is correct, sir.

Would you like this put into historical perspective, Mr. Chairman, because it is a reducing level of pipeline?

Senator INOUYE. Last year we pointed out a loan to Argentina which was at that time 10 years old. It is over 10 years old now. At that time there was $712 million which the agency insisted on disbursing at the original interest rate of three-quarters of 1 percent. What is the current status of that loan? The agreement date was October 10, 1963. 

Mr. PARKER. Well, frankly, from my point of view, this loan has not had a logical history. It is going to be disbursed by the end of this month. If it is not, it is going to be deobligated. 

Senator INOUYE. Well, what I can't understand is why we don't recover this loan and use it instead in a country that really needs it. 

Mr. PARKER. I have to be honest and say, Mr. Chairman, I don't know how to explain. I can give you all sorts of reasons, but the logic behind failing to change this loan somehow escapes me. 

It was confused by a number of changes in government in Argentina, by the change in project plan and scale, a number of things that were intended to improve it. I would have to honestly say that we probably should have renegotiated the terms of it on a number of occasions, and I would like to emphasize that we are trying to build policies now in the agency which will preclude this sort of thing. 

Senator INOUYE. Do you really expect that over 50 percent of this

Argentine loan will be disbursed within 2 months? That is what you have indicated.

Mr. PARKER. We are not going to extend the terminal date beyond the end of this month and we will deobligate the balance, but I would like to emphasize, Mr. Chairman, that the policies that we are putting into effect now simply will preclude this sort of thing. 

In brief, the policies which Mr. Murphy and I have worked out are going into effect the first of July. The beginning of the next fiscal year will basically limit the disbursement period to 3 years. Each stage of the loan will be considered as a module of the total loan. Each module has a set time period within which that element of the total loan must be accomplished. 

The assistant administrators have the authority to extend each of these modules for a limited amount of time, but not beyond the total period. 

Senator INOUYE. What will be the total of the period?

Mr. PARKER. This is 3 years, 36 months. Now, each time that they utilize this authority they must report to the deputy administrator because even though it is within their authority we consider it to be a possible aberration or deviation and it needs to be highlighted. We are frankly going to measure the performance of our regional bureaus. 

Senator INOUYE. Will you send this information to the committee also?

Mr. PARKER. Yes, we will be glad to, but we are going to measure the actual performance on the basis of how effectively they perform

within these periods the number of concessions they have to make and their actual performance. 

Mr. Murphy and I have discussed this and he has taken action to put this entire program into computers so that we can get this information quickly and maintain our knowledge of it for management purposes.

We are going to manage this basically, Mr. Chairman, on the principle of exceptions. I think we can set up very tight control to insure that we know what exceptions are made and to get early warning of when they might arrive.

I am not saying we will be totally without exceptions but we will know our exceptions and will minimize them.

AID PERSONNEL POLICIES 

Senator INOUYE. Recently there appeared in one of our national dailies an article which indicated that two State Department employees have been found guilty of embezzling large sums of money. 

I think the amounts exceeded $100,000, and they were forced into retirement, reprimanded and put on pension.

Usually in Washington, D.C. or in other areas within the United 

States if somebody stole a loaf of bread he ends up being convicted for something, possibly sent to prison.

I am just wondering what is the policy for AID if an employee is found in some corrupt activity, embezzlement, or receiving bribes? Do you prosecute them?

Mr. PARKER. Well, this is an area, Mr. Chairman, with which I don't have a great personal familiarity. I would say that we are quite alert to audit procedures of all to uncover any problems such as this. 

I believe that the procedure is to leave to the Department of Justice the actual prosecution of any criminal indictments. Now, as to what happens in terms of pension, again I am not really competent in terms of knowledge of this subject to answer fully. I would like to get the information to submit it or offer you a chance to submit it with others who may be more familiar with it.

The pension is, I believe, a contributory pension by the employees and I would presume that they would be entitled to that as part of their pension. I don't know, though, Mr. Chairman.

Senator INOUYE. Has any of AID's personnel been found guilty of criminal conduct and if so, what has been the disposition of this case? 

Can you think of one case in the past fiscal year?

Mr. PARKER. Well, I don't know of any directly. I have been told recently of indictments of one individual whose name I don't remember, who was connected with our Housing Guaranty Program. But the indictments did not relate to his work with AID. 

Senator INOUYE. I should have brought the article here because it has generated several letters from throughout the Nation. 

Mr. PARKER. I am informed, Mr. Chairman, that when we come up with information which indicates a problem of this nature we provide it to the Department of Justice which then takes the action. 

As to what specific actions have taken place, I do not personally know.

AID TO THE MIDDLE EAST 

On page 5 you write that "We hope that these funds will be part of a larger multilateral effort coordinated by the World Bank." 

Would you expand on that? 

Mr. PARKER. Under the Middle East is this?

Senator BROOKE. Yes. 

Mr. PARKER. Yes.

Senator BROOKE. Has there been any evidence that you will be sucsuccessful in achieving a large multilateral effort? 

Mr. PARKER. Yes, Senator Brooke, there has been considerable activity recently. I can't report that there are any concluded negotiations by any other possible donors to Egypt's reconstruction and development.

I have learned that Iran is proposing very significant assistance. 

More specifically, what I have heard is that they are discussing $250 million for assistance in the Suez area in reconstruction; another $400 million in reconstruction and development in other parts of the country.

Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, are other Arab countries which have had specific discussions.

In addition to that, West Germany is discussing assistance in the rebuilding of the Suez Canal. Japan has. There are quite a number of countries.

In addition to that, Senator Brooke, the World Bank is specifically engaged in discussions. It is our hope that the World Bank will in fact take the lead in orgaizing a coordinating mechanism so that the benefits to Egypt, first, can be enhanced by the external assistance and, secondly, so that there can be a means of stimulating other donors. Thus, no one has to bear more than what you would call a fair share.

Senator BROOKE. I don't want to minimize or even question the 

U.S. interest in the Middle East, but I can't help but wonder how much "peace" in the Middle East will cost the United States in terms of dollars over time.

We are very grateful, of course, that American lives are not being lost in the Middle East as was the case in Southeast Asia. Nevertheless, the American people may be asked to spend billions of dollars in the Middle East to promote "peace" on top of the billions of dollars we have already spent in that area. 

How long are we going to be committed in the Middle East in terms of large outlays of U.S. dollars? Do you have any idea at all?

The American people are going to be more and more concerned as to just what commitments we have made in the Middle East, and how much they will ultimately cost us. For example, what commitments have been made in order to bring about this disengagement? 

In this regard, is the $100 million special requirements fund committed informally to Syria to bring about disengagement and is this just the forerunner of millions and millions more that we have either committed or intend to commit in the years ahead? 

Mr. PARKER. Well, Senator Brooke, may I first address one technicality. There are no commitments made. 

Senator BROOKE. No commitments have been made? 

Mr. PARKER. That is correct, sir. 

Senator BROOKE. Is the $250 million for Egypt a commitment?

Mr. PARKER. No, sir, it is not. I say in all candor that obviously it is a strong implication that has been carried in the press and the very fact that we are requesting it of the Congress I think carried quite a message, but it is certainly conditioned clearly upon congressional approval and there is no specific commitment to that. 

Senator BROOKE. Of course it is conditioned on approval. Congress has to authorize and appropriate the funds. However, don't you, figuratively speaking, have a "gun at our heads or backs" in that our failure to provide these funds could be argued to jeopardize the whole structure of peace?

Mr. PARKER. Well, I certainly would choose not to use the phrase that we seem to have a gun at our head. 

Senator BROOKE. No, I don't suggest that you seek to have it at our head but isn't it assumed that an "obligation" exists to approve these funds?

Mr. PARKER. I would rather look at this as an investment in peace in contrast to what probably would be considered and was considered by the Congress an irrefutable investment of war. 34-192 O - 74-43

In 2 weeks of war it cost the U.S. taxpayers $2.2 billion for military assistance, a major component of which was on grant terms. 

Now, I don't know how to quantify where our break-even point is in terms of money. But I would say that the cost of investing in peace would be a great deal more than we are requesting if it were to be compared with the cost of war. 

Now, as to whether this is an open-ended thing, Senator Brookemaking a point that I think you want to get to and addressing it directly-I don't know. I would say that it is in the U.S. interests to keep investing in peace.

Now, this is not buying peace but it is investing in circumstances which will inherently tend to bring peace. For so long the people of this one area of the world, the Middle East, have been focusing upon what I would call the bad face of nationalism and the bad face of nationalism is to look at self, not just first but only, and as against external forces.

I think now the opportunity is to try and get these people to begin to look at how they might be able to develop, and thus how they might be able to utilize their own resources, their own energy, to develop positive and constructive things within their country. 

Senator BROOKE. I am not critical of the strategy of trying to help 

Israel and the Arab States to live together in peace and harmony. 

However you have indicated that our aid commitment might be openended.

Mr. PARKER. I would hope it wouldn't be open-ended. I addressed the question because I think that this is of interest to all of us and I think that you are touching upon something that is very useful. 

Senator BROOKE. I don't perceive thinking about the end of our aid commitment either in the Middle East or in Indochina in AID's congressional presentation. 

AID TO INDOCHINA 

We are constantly pouring money into Southeast Asia and I don't see any end to it. No projected phase-out program has been submitted to the Congress which would indicate this is a 2-year plan, 3-, 4-, 5or 10-year plan. The American people are entitled to projections as to further costs of our aid commitments, how long such commitments will continue, and what kind of results may be achieved. 

We don't expect many instantaneous results. The Middle East may be an exception. We are not even sure that the situation there will continue to improve, although we hope and pray that it will. But we have the Middle East on one side, Southeast Asia on the other, and we are literally spending and may spend billions of dollars in each of these parts of the world with no end in sight. The American people have been given little information about how much it has cost and how much it will cost us in these areas. 

Mr. PARKER. Well, Senator Brooke, I would like to point out that first of all that we intend to respond to the amendment that the Senate passed offered by Senator Humphrey, requesting a specific estimate of the phase-down of U.S. assistance to Vietnam by August 1. 

We welcome the chance to provide that estimate.

It obviously has to be based upon certain assumptions and, in brief, there are two key assumptions. One is beyond the control of the United 

States, and the other is beyond the control of the administration. The first assumption is as to the level of military activity. This is determined really by the Hanoi government and its sponsors because the fighting is going on in South Vietnam. South Vietnam is not fighting in the North.

So the level of assistance and the degree of military activity in South Vietnam obviously has to be one of the premises upon which we will project U.S. assistance levels. 

The other premise concerns the nature of development assistance as it relates to the ability of South Vietnam to develop itself and become productive. The premise that I would like to put forth is that if adequate funds are provided now, not only for economic survival, but also for investments for productive development, we can, in fact, reduce economic and over not too long a period of time to much more modest levels- Senator BROOKE. Mr. PARKER. As I say, we will make this report to the Congress by the 1st of August.

DEVELOPMENT ASSISTANCE

Hopefully, this will give us a much more enlightened position to look ahead to what development progress can be made. That could put

us in a position to make more useful estimates of progress to make sounder judgments about needed resources from external sources including the UN.

DOMESTIC AUSTERITY PROGRAM 

Senator BROOKE. Would you supply for the record a detailed description of this domestic austerity program? Also I would like to have some idea of how they have expanded their exports in the last 10 years. 

Mr. PARKER. Yes, Senator Brooke, I would be pleased to submit

that. The increase in exports has been really quite dramatic, but from a very small base. In 1971 the exports were something like $12 million. 

They have gone to $23 million in 1972, to $61 million last year, and our projected assumption is $90 million this year.

VIETNAM AUSTERITY PROGRAM 

The major objective of the austerity policy and program of the Government of South Vietnam is to take all feasible steps to insure that available resources are used to promote the security and the economic growth of the country and that uses of resources that do not support the achievement of those objectives are reduced or eliminated. In support of that policy, the GVN has worked hard and successfully to improve tax collections so that after-tax incomes conform to the requirements for austerity. In addition to the rise in per capita taxes noted in the table presented above, from 1972 to 1973 overall tax collections so far in 1974 are ahead of 1973 by 88%. (Much of the gain is attributable to inflation, but a solid gain of 13% is left after the effects of inflation are removed from the revenue figures.)

Most recently, the Government of South Vietnam has suspended the importation of so-called "C" and "D" goods, that is, goods that are in the "less essential" class as well as in the luxury class. The banned goods include many items of food, wood, cloth, paper and optical goods, cutlery, and some machinery, as well as spirits, perfumes, fur, clothing, musical instruments, etc.

The Government of South Vietnam has also boosted interest rates which will tend to maintain and augment incentives to save. If successful, this will somewhat diminish overall household expenditures, particularly on non-essential items. The improvement in tax collections will, of course, work in the same direction, further diminishing spending on non-essentials. 

Government policy has permitted upward rises in the prices of domestically produced essential goods. This action also tends to discourage the consumption of non-essential goods, as do the actions with respect to taxes and the interest rate, since the proportion of total income that will have to be devoted to essential purchases will rise (assuming, of course, that the government can arrange matters so that monetary incomes, in the meantime, do not rise to the point where they will offset the rise in the prices of expenditures out of income). Finally, the rise in the price of domestically produced essential goods should encourage the production of those essential goods.

DISASTER RELIEF 

Senator BROOKE. Mr. Parker, we are facing a major disaster in the 

Sahel region of Africa. Fortunately, only major disasters seem to be averted for the moment. It seems that AID has people and technical expertise and international contacts to deliver effective disaster relief and to deliver it quickly, although some confusion has been voiced lately as to AID's response in the Sahel. 

Is AID still the coordinator for disaster relief, and in your opinion, should it be?

Mr. PARKER. Senator, I believe that the policy within the U.S. 

Government has been to have the question determined when there is a major foreign disaster which requires U.S. assistance, and then on such occasions for the President to designate both the Agency and its special representative for disaster relief coordination. 

Notwithstanding that, I believe it is a responsibility of AID, since it is the Agency that does have knowledge of how to operate in the field and disasters rarely take place in convenient areas and they are by nature somewhat chaotic and disorganized-we do maintain within 

AID a disaster relief coordination office. 

We have been expanding our attention to these programs, and because of my concern that we in fact become as well prepared in advance as possible to overcome the effects of disasters that occur, we have engaged in simulation exercises in the facility that we have established, recognizing that you have to draw upon people from other agencies and from other bureaus within the Agency. We are training these people in simulation.

We also conduct a training program for government officials in countries that would like to come and avail themselves of this training. 

We are attempting to identify those countries in which there is a natural proneness to the occurrence of disasters and encourage these people to come.

We have had one class just recently. I have asked our disaster relief people to supplement their own management capabilities with thorough debriefings of each disaster and a review of the handling of each one in which we have had a part. 

I have asked our systems people to see if they can't help in developing a response capability that can indicate the quantity and nature of specific requirements, and then in addition to that, we have taken people who have had experience in the field in connection with disaster relief to debrief them before they are reposted or before they retire. 

I hope reasonably soon to be able to draw some of these programs together and we would be delighted to give you a status report on where we were and where we think we can improve.

NEW CONCEPTS AND RELATIONSHIPS BETWEEN A.I.D. AND THE PRIVATE AND VOLUNTARY ORGANIZATIONS 

The new concepts and relationships emerging between A.I.D. and the private and voluntary organizations, based on past experience and recent initiatives, are particularly exciting to me. 

We are proposing for FY-1975 an increase of $5 million to be used as Development Program Grants (DPG's) to strengthen the professional competence of the headquarters staffs of private and voluntary organizations to undertake specific overseas program development and planning efforts. 

We have also earmarked an additional $6 million for use as Operational Grants in support of overseas development assistance activities administered by private and voluntary organizations. 

The Development Program Grants (DPG's) will be made to qualified, interested private and voluntary organizations or consortia to augment their staffs and other capacities to enable them to plan, design, manage and evaluate whole program segments, related pilot/demonstration projects, negotiate in the less developed countries for roles in implementing program activities, or serve as resource agencies for specific projects as requested by host governments or groups, USAID's and/or international bodies. These grants are (a) to expand the ability of private and voluntary organizations to function as planning and/ or programming associates of A.I.D., rather than as resource agents only, and (b) to promote the involvement of private and voluntary organizations in vital development roles in the less developed countries, consistent with their purposes and host country and A.I.D. programs and priorities. 

The Operational Grants will be for private and voluntary organization activities and programs focussed on those critical functional problems which most affect the lives of the majority of people in developing countries. 

These new initiatives focus on combining A.I.D. resources with private experience and resources in expanding the area of our collaboration, with host country governments, in meeting basic human needs. Additionally, and of critical importance, a new form of relationship is emerging. 

This relationship will be a mutual one. A.I.D. is not simply contracting with private and voluntary organizations. We are more consciously recognizing the independence, experience, resources and competence voluntary organizations not only can bring, but have already brought, to the scene. We are saying: our objectives are synonomous, here are funds to use in mutually agreed upon ways, in pursuit of our common objectives. 

We will insist, naturally, that programs evolve with host participation; priorities, needs and objectives must be those of the host peoples. Further, we insist on sound fiscal management and substantive program accountability. 

But we seek a mutual association, a new equation (to cite the report of the Advisory Committee on Voluntary Foreign Aid, A Look to the Future) where private and voluntary organizations serve in tandem with A.I.D. in accordance with the individual organization's unique character and sense of mission. 

In this process it becomes essential to involve private and voluntary organizations at the earliest stages of development planning and facilitate their operations as associates in all phases of the program process. 

Already, 150 private and voluntary organizations have participated in a two-day conference here in Washington to discuss and comment upon the evolving new concepts. They participated actively, in small group working sessions, in contributing to the formulation of the guidelines which will govern the funding of private and voluntary organization programs. Our report of this conference will be published shortly; I will see that you receive a copy.

This initial conference was followed, in June, by a workshop held under the auspices of the Advisory Committee on Voluntary Foreign Aid. This workshop focussed on the administrative processes governing the Food for Peace programs. 

Voluntary agencies, A.I.D., OMB and USDA personnel spent a day reviewing the guidelines governing the system. A continuing joint working group, under the leadership of the Office of Food for Peace, is now studying the key aspects of the procedures with a view to increasing the participatory nature of the process.

Additional workshops will follow this Fall. The first three of these will deal with nutrition, food production and grant policies and procedures. 

Others will be planned throughout the year. They will be held here or abroad, as dictated by the topic and type of participants. Additionally, selected regional, country and functional conferences will be held annually. 

Further, we plan a program of continuing interchange and dialogue which will include several facets: regular and/or periodic exchanges of visits between A.I.D. and private and voluntary organization personnel; AID/W briefing in the field for USAID and private and voluntary organization personnel; home leave consultation visits among private and voluntary organization and A.I.D. personnel; opportunities to participate in training programs of mutual interest; and mutual participation in the orientation of new personnel. 

Additionally, we plan to counsel private and voluntary organizations on A.I.D. procedures including the availability of support, qualifying for support and the submission of proposals for grant assistance. We plan to assist private and voluntary organizations, where appropriate, to identify and obtain additional resources (beyond those available from A.I.D.) for the planning and implementation of development assistance activities. This will include resources such as those obtainable from the less developed countries themselves, from private donations, from the various multilateral banks, the United Nations Development Programme or other United Nations agencies, from foundations and other donors.

In concluding, I think it important to view these new concepts and relationships against the backdrop of A.I.D.'s existing and continuing relationships with private and voluntary organizations. Private and voluntary organizations receive funds from the Regional Bureaus, USAID's, and central AID/W offices the Bureau for Population and Humanitarian Assistance, for example. 

These relationships will continue. I expect they will expand. 

Equally important, however, the nature of our existing relationships with private and voluntary organizations will be influenced by the new directions. I expect we will see a greater degree of mutuality. Furthermore, the types of programs we undertake will increasingly reflect lessons drawn from private and voluntary organization experiences in meeting critical basic human needs in ways which involve people in the decision making process.

VOLAG ADMINISTRATION CAPABILITIES 

Senator BROOKE. Also supply for the record your assessment of the 

VOLAG's administration capabilities and their ability effectively to use foreign assistance funds.

Mr. PARKER. That is one of the main elements of the new program because we recognize that there are many organizations that have a great desire to function in development assistance, the large constituency, and some significant resources. 

They may not, however, have the resources or the capability to develop their own administrative mechanism, so within the selected organizations sector we are requesting a sum of $5 million that we could provide on a grant basis to these organizations to develop their capacity to function effectively. 

 ASSESSMENT OF PRIVATE and VOLUNTARY ORGANIZATION CAPABILITY FOR FOREIGN AID PROGRAMS 

The community of private and voluntary organizations is diverse; their capabilities are multifaceted. Some private and voluntary organizations will only wish to participate in project support or resource roles; others will have both the interest and scope to function more broadly as development planning and programming associates of A.I.D. With some additional professional staff and more assured public and private resources, such organizations could work with host country governments or private groups and with USAID's in planning whole development priorities recently determined by the Congress. 

Our assessment of their capability will be based on such factors as the following: potential for reaching large numbers of people at a reasonable cost; directness of impact on the people who constitute the poorest majority; clarity of definition of the target group; plans of the grantee, or tie-in with other programs which assure complementary efforts necessary to provide a higher standard of living to the target group; and potential interest and capacity of the grantee or other organizations to spread the program to large numbers of people over an extended period of time. 

The constituency of a voluntary organization is another important factor in any assessment of overall capability. Thus, the extent of private U.S. support available over time, whether financial or in kind, will be a consideration in determinations affecting A.I.D. funding of activities which have high substantive merit. It is recognized, however, that the circumstances surrounding each organization differ, requiring analysis of each situation individually, including an assessment of the merits of the ideas and programs advanced. Mobilization of private support is important both as a demonstration of unofficial American interest and as a complement to the severely limited appropriations available. 

Furthermore, substantial private support is conducive to the collaboration among equals that both A.I.D. and the private and voluntary organizations desire, and helps avoid compromising the independence of the organization. 

Another measure of capability is based on the ability of the private and voluntary organizations to demonstrate that their activities, whether directly or through indigenous agencies, are acceptable to host country governments and that they have formal or informal acceptance to function in agreed upon ways and for agreed upon purposes within host country jurisdictions. 

The acid test of capability, of course, is the evaluation to be based on actual performance as compared to planned program and project objectives, and results after reasonable periods of time. In this respect, progress and results must be seen in realistic contexts.

Those organizations which meet these criteria and thus are judged to have the capability/readines to work in areas of special emphasis will be considered for support by A.I.D. A.I.D. grants are intended to assist in the effort to expand the participation of private and voluntary organizations in the foreign aid program, while preserving the identity of the private and voluntary sector. To be eligible for a grant, an organization must satisfy A,I.D. that it possesses managerial competence in planning and carrying out development assistance programs 34-192 - 74-44

or projects and that it will practice mutually agreed upon methods of accountability for funds and other assets provided by the United States Government. Accordingly, the funding will apply both to (1) financing organizations for carrying out approved programs or projects in the less developed countries and (2) to grants to strengthen the capabilities of selected private and voluntary organizations to plan, design, manage and evaluate development programs and projects. 

Senator BROOKE. I have just two more questions, Mr. Chairman. 

Mr. Parker, is there a fundamental conflict between the need to maximize food production and the desire to promote the involvement of the small farmer in the development process? I ask this question because 

I believe that the fundamental priority for the world in the next quarter of a century will be to provide enough food to forestall tens of millions of deaths around the world. I am not convinced that food production can be maximized by giving the primary emphasis to the small farmer in our foreign aid program. I realize that this view runs counter to the general thrust of the new directions in foreign aid. However, the real world has a way of preempting "grand designs" and requires us to adjust our stated priorities to ones more in keeping with the needs of the moment.

Mr. PARKER. Well, this is a massive subject, Senator Brooke. 

Senator BROOKE. Yes; I know you can't treat it now.

Mr. PARKER. We could talk a great deal. 

Senator BROOKE. Well, I would appreciate your supplying for the record your views and comments and your defense of the emphasis on the small farmer if you do believe that is the way we should go; but I think it ought to be in the record. 

Mr. PARKER. I would like very much to do this and I would say that the two are not mutually preclusive, that the efforts that this agency is undertaking to try and stimulate production in developing countries is not preclusive of the high producing countries such as the United States and Canada increasing their food production as well. 

I would make note, though, that one of the principal inputs in determining agricultural productivity is that of labor. We in this country think of ourselves as the granary of the world, if you will. Yet I would like to point out that the yields per acre of wheat in this country are less than in a number of countries in Europe and even in Latin America-Mexico, for example, where they have a greater availability of labor.

FOOD PRODUCTION OF SMALL FARMERS 

So, it is not simply a factor of mechanization and large scale agricultural production. We view agricultural productivity in our economy here in terms of productivity in relation to labor. The AID programs are looking at increasing productivity per unit of land available.

INCREASING FOOD PRODUCTION BY SMALL FARMERS 

If we focus on the need to increase productivity per unit of land available it becomes clear that for most of the developing world there is no fundamental conflict between the need to maximize food production and the desire to involve the small farmer in the development process. Instead, there is a fundamental harmony between the two goals. I would go so far as to say that, except in the very short run, the two goals are so interdependent that the achievement of the one seems impossible without achievement of the other. The small farmer generally can produce considerably more per acre than the large farmer. Both experience and analytic projections can support this conclusion. (See chart below.) (Economists have developed the phrase "small-farm, labor-intensive agriculture system, which describes this productive utilization of the developing world's 200 million tiny (12 acres or less) farms to feed the rapidly growing population.)

The task of harmonizing the goals of increased food production and small farmer involvement requires not only high yielding technological inputs and cropping systems that are adaptable by small farmers but difficult and often painful changes of policies, plans and institutions on the part of many developing countries. 

Readiness on the part of governments to attempt these changes is increasing and we and other donors must do what we can to support the efforts, when they seem promising. AID is directing much of its program resources in this direction. "1 

Experience indicates that in the short run technological breakthroughs, such as those triggering the "green revolution, will be taken up quickly by the larger farmers and by the more progressive of the small farmers, if the rest of the system is ready to absorb the increased output and if price and other policies are right. However, the spurt in growth seems to level off quite soon if additional land is not devoted to the better technology. 

To keep the price of the increased food production as low as possible the basic factors of production (land, labor and capital) must be used as efficiently as possible in devoting more land to improved technology. 

For capital-scarce countries, especially those with a high population per unit of land, the concentration must be on maximizing output per unit of land and using labor intensive farming methods to do that rather than (as in most labor-scarce developed countries) investing in labor displacing capital equipment.

Employment creating capital equipment (such as small power tillers which speed the preparation of seedbeds

and thus permit multiple cropping) is to be encouraged. 

Experience shows that where labor intensive farming systems using improved technologies are adopted subsistence farmers begin producing surpluses for market and agricultural production increases rapidly.

It increases considerably faster than population and does so on a sustained basis. Production does not plateau, at least not for a long time.

For this encouraging result to happen, however, a country's policies, institutions and resources have to focus on providing the small farmer access to improved inputs and to markets as well as a degree of active participation in assessing what's needed and deciding what he should be expected to do.

Developing countries could promote increases in food production by relying initially on the few larger farmers and more progressive small farmers using improved technologies. At the same time governments could be concentrating their attention on adjusting their policies and on developing local-level input delivery systems and marketing and other institutions in which the local people participate. These latter could help change the mass of subsistence farmers into a powerful productive resource for the country. 

The risk in this is that during the initial year or two the larger farmers, with their financial head start, may displace the subsistence farmers, thus forfeiting for the country the best opportunity to employ high-yielding, labor intensive methods. 

AID will try hard to help developing countries to deal with these complex problems. However, because each developing country's situation will differ, because the tensions involved in essential internal changes are bound to be substantial and because we all have much to learn about what works, our approach must be pragmatic and characterized by a long, clear-eyed view.

Good morning Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to have the opportunity to appear before your committee today to review the operations of the Office of the Inspector 

General of Foreign Assistance (IGA). 

As you know, there is a new management team in place at IGA, so new in fact, that today marks our first formal appearance before any of our guiding committees on the Hill. 

Because of our newness, I will, in advance, ask your forebearance as to a detailed knowledge of what has gone before and concentrate primarily on what Mr. Constandy and I hope to accomplish in the future.

A brief review of the past years activities, the reports of which have been provided to the Committee, indicates that IGA was active and effective. Inspection activities have resulted in a number of program modifications which represent significant savings and increased efficiency and effectiveness in our foreign assistance programs.

I believe the managements of AID's assets have been improved based upon IGA reviews and recommendations. 

As examples, I cite the following: 

As a result of an inspection of Indonesia, a recommendation was made that AID financed procurement of oral contraceptives be centralized rather than be done by each AID mission individually; recommendation was accepted thereby saving approximately $2 million as a result of the first centralized procurement. 

In Brazil, IGA recommended the substitution of available and unused Brazilian-owned local currencies 

(generated thru U.S. AID) in lieu of U.S. appropriated dollars for support costs.

This action resulted in

annual budget and balance of payments savings to the U.S. of approximately $250,000. 

In reviewing U.S.-funded population control activities, IGA noted that the U.S. had obligated more funds than it was required to donate to the United Nations Fund for 

Population Activities (UNFPA) for calendar year 1972 

under the formula which governed the U.S. pledge. After this was brought to the attention of the Department of 

State's Bureau of International Organization Affairs, that office transferred the overfunding for 1972 to meet part of its pledge to UNFPA for calendar year 1973 and thus reduced the obligation of new funds for 1973 by $10,300,000. 

During inspections completed in calendar year 1973, IGA made a number of recommendations for deobligating funds which did not appear to be needed for their original purposes. 

Recommendations accepted resulted in deobligations totalling $10,125,458.

In considering the rather extensive responsibilities assigned IGA under our implementing legislation, Mr. Constandy and I have, through discussions with appropriate Washingtonbased people in the Departments of State and Defense, AID, OPIC and Peace Corps and members and staff of the concerned Congressional Committees, developed a better insight into our role and developed some ideas as to a new approach to our efforts which we hope will prove more effective. might add that we have also had the benefit of discussing our ideas with our Ambassadors and Mission Directors both in the field and when they have been here in Washington for consultation. I

Basically, our emphasis will focus on three broad areas:

1. 2. 3.

An improved internal management system within IGA to increase the quality and discipline of our own operation through better planning of inspections, more clearly defined objectives, and greater attention to follow-up. 

A reorientation of inspection efforts towards identifying endemic system and program weaknesses which have applicability far beyond individual instances, as well as increased ability to fulfill our other legislative responsibilities.

A reassessment of our available manpower allocation in light of the above-mentioned items which will, perhaps, result in a limitation of the total number of programs inspected within a given time period but should produce a greater bottom line impact on those reviews undertaken.

Within the context of these changes, it is our intention to retain maximum flexibility in our work so as to allow us to respond to suggested areas of inspection coverage from all appropriate sources including the agencies responsible for program management, the General Accounting Office, the Office of Management and Budget and the Congress. 

As regards the first change, we expect to implement a new organizational structure in the very near future. 

Currently it is undergoing final review within IGA and the Department of State. Essentially, it divides our office into three distinct though inter-related arms

a Planning Division, an Operations Division and a Reports/ 

Compliance Division. 

In this way, clear lines of authority and responsibility will be established so as to ensure that we achieve maximum effectiveness in whatever we do. 

With respect to systems evaluation, we have begun to tie together our past inspections and audits, reviews, and evaluations by others with future planning so as to concentrate our efforts and narrow the focus of our work. 

For example, we have undertaken a comprehensive review of P.L. 480 programs which will encompass detailed inspections of those operations in four to six selected countries. expect this type of effort to allow us to recommend both broad and specific modifications and improvements in this critical part of our AID effort. We have also continued our evaluation of the need for inspections which are of a more limited nature, such as OPIC and other specific instances brought to our attention which are much more narrow in scope and application.

These two objectives, if they are to be met, quite logically lead to the third impending change - that of striking a balance between single item inspections and the more comprehensive programmatic reviews which encompass more than one country or continent. I think of necessity, we will wind up with a lesser number of inspected items but with greater significance attached to those we do review.

We also feel that the reports of our inspections would be of more value to the users, that is the Secretary, the agencies involved and the Congressional Committees, if they were more concise, to the point, and complete in their coverage of the entire inspection to its conclusion.

Government of the Republic of Argentina. 

Purpose and nature of loan: to assist in financing (40%) of the construction of Argentine grain storage facilities--silos, elevators, and driers. This is an extensive modernization program providing the grain-producing areas with a network of storage facilities. (A complementary loan was made by the 

Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) to modernize and expand terminal facilities for exports at the major ports.) 

Loan signed October 10, 1963 for $21.7 million, requiring 60% 

U.S. procurement, repayment in 40 years, grace period on principal 10 years, interest rate 3/4%. --This AID loan is a two-step loan. AID loans dollars to Argentine Government who in turn loans the funds to sub-borrowers. The sub-borrowers repay their loans in local currency to the National Bank, Government of 

Argentina (GOA); the GOA repays AID in dollars. 

--The overall storage facility program is financed 40% by 

AID loan, 40% by the borrower, and 20% by individual sub-borrowers.

Loan amended in 1964 eliminating U.S. procurement aspect. 

Loan renegotiated on January 9, 1969, with principal amount reduced to $10.0 million. Interest remained at 3/4%.

Terminal Disbursing Dates (TDD) in December 1972 extended to June 30, 1974--not to be extended beyond this date. Undisbursed balance of loan to be deobligated. 

AID disbursements to June 30, 1974, $8.5 million, and AID will deobligate the residual $1.5 million.

$8,494,997 Background

This loan originally was for $21.7 million. The requirement for 60% U.S. procurement was a stumbling block to utilization inasmuch as most of the construction materials were available locally. This requirement was eliminated in 1964. However, further proceedings came to a temporary standstill pending the resolution of political problems. As a result no action was taken until early in 1966.

A further lengthy delay ensued after a change in the Argentine Government in June 1966 which occurred as the amendment to the loan was to be formalized. The U.S. Government's decision to go forward with the project was delayed until June 1967. Nonetheless, it was felt that the project should be revised on the basis of an additional study which was completed in March 1968. Because of changed circumstances resulting from Argentina's own efforts to increase on-farm storage, and the granting by the Inter-American Development Bank of a loan for port grain elevators, the AID project was reworked to limit it to intermediate grain storage facilities. 

The loan agreement was amended to reduce the loan to $10 million in January 1969. The interest rate remained at 3/4%. 

The Deputy Chief of Mission in Argentina informed IGA that at the time of the Argentine Government changeover in 1973 the U.S. Embassy recognized that the changes in the Government created problems in familiarization with the project. As a result the loan took on almost a new life. In December 1972, the Terminal Disbursement Date (TDD), i.e., as specified in the loan agreement, the last date on which Borrower may submit documentation in support of disbursement requests, was amended to June 30, 1974. In January 1973, a plan was defined in agreement with appropriate Government officials to effectively utilize the residual loan funds by the June 30, 1974 TDD, following which unexpended balances would be deobligated. 

These actions were in accord with the expressed concern of the U.S. Senate Appropriations Committee in its hearings in 

May 1973.

In these same Senate Appropriations Committee Hearings for 

FY 1974 (pg. 815), the Assistant Administrator for the

Bureau of Latin America included in his comments on the loan disbursements that, "On June 4, 1973, the U.S. Embassy in

Argentina reported that the currently agreed terminal disbursement date of June 30, 1974, continues valid and that it continues to expect full disbursement by that date. 

USAID/Buenos Aires in March 1974 reported of 481 installations in the private sector 345 were completed, and that implementation on the remainder and six in the public sector were progressing satisfactorily. 

On June 12, 1974, the AID Administrator made a policy determination that all future project loans will be executed for successful implementation and disbursement within three years. Comments 

1. The Regional Engineer, stationed in Asuncion, Paraguay, since last Spring, has been monitoring the construction activities under the AID Grain Storage Loan to Argentina and will continue to do so until completion of projects receiving AID financing. 2. 3.

This loan operation has been discussed with AID's Latin 

America Bureau and AID management. Their new policy statement, approved June 12, 1974, should preclude similar loan implementation and disbursement. difficulties in the future.

AID will prepare a completion report on the loan upon termination of these construction activities and will relay this information to the IGA.

ROCAP 

Central American Stabilization Fund AID Loan No. 596-L-009 

$10,000,000 

Borrower Central Banks of Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras,

Nicaragua and Costa Rica on behalf of the Central American 

Stabilization Fund.

Purpose of loan: By the provision of additional reserves, to assure the viability of the Central American Monetary Stabilization Fund (CAMSF) which was created in 1969 for mutual balanceof-payments assistance with up to 5-year credits to members, and to harmonize monetary, fiscal and exchange policies. A significant and broader purpose of the loan is to demonstrate U.S. support of 

Central American initiatives toward regional economic integration, including a common currency and central bank system, in the context of the Central American Common Market. CAMSF has subscribed capital of $20 million ($12.5 million paid up plus $2.5 million of accrued earnings) the $10 million AID loan, and commercial lines of credit for $70 million.

Background Since the establishment of CAMSF only two member countries, Honduras and Costa Rica, have incurred BOP deficits of a nature that may have warranted the use of CAMSF stabilization credits. 

Both found other solutions.

For Honduras to have used the CAMSF facility in 1970 would have required, under the CAMSF rules, the concurrence of El Salvador with whom she had just been at war and whose Central Bank would have participated in extending the stabilization credit. Instead, Honduras restored payments equilibrium by means of severe trade restrictions after renouncing Common Market agreements on free trade between members.

In Costa Rica's case, CAMSF assistance would have required that expansionary fiscal/monetary policies be curtailed which the government was unwilling to do. Accordingly, in 1972 Costa Rica resorted to higher cost commercial borrowing, which had no strings attached, in her efforts to return to payments equilibrium. 

Also, in moves contrary to Common Market and CAMSF policies at the time Costa Rica imposed a dual exchange rate for the colon and contrived a complex system of rules for external trade. 

Under the conditions by which CAMSF funds are now available, it is not clear that the AID loan will need to be drawn down prior to the TDD of December 31, 1975. 

Honduras and Costa Rica provide two examples of how member countries in BOP difficulty will seek alternatives to the CAMSF stabilization facility in preference to submitting to Common Market and CAMSF rules on trade and fiscal/monetary discipline when these impinge on national policies. But there is also some evidence that the rather strict CAMSF regulations have discouraged member borrowing in any case. 

Consequently proposals are now under serious consideration that CAMSF be restructured to accommodate member country needs more in harmony with their particular economic policies and situations.

The proposals would enlarge the lending facility by increasing the capital subscription of each member to $10 million, of which $4 million each would be called up. The types of accommodation would be expanded: a 1-year ("first window")

credit for short-term deficits; a 5-year ("second window") credit for deficits arising from "acts of God", e.g., crop failures; and a 7-year ("third window") credit for deficits having structural, or monetary, causes. The "third window" would be an extension of the present CAMSF 5-year stabilization credit and would also require a stabilization plan, i.e., fiscal/ monetary discipline, from the borrower. Drawings from the first two windows, however, would require only "letters of intent" which would not be subject to the same scrutiny as are stabilization plans. The proposed CAMSF restructuring would reduce the number of affirmative votes needed for approval of a given amount of credit and the interest charged, rather than being determined by the cost of money to CAMSF, would be at the discretion of the Central American Monetary Council, i.e., concessional rates would be possible.

The proposed reforms contemplate a new CAMSF role in assisting with the large payments deficit foreseen in 1974-75 as a consequence of the high costs of oil and other essential commodity imports. For 1974 alone this deficit is projected to be nearly $200 million for the five countries, in contrast to the healthy increases experienced in the area's aggregate reserve position for the years 1972-73.

Thus, the arguments advanced for continuing to make the AID loan available to CAMSF are: a. The original justification is still valid: The loan was a catalyst and by this tangible evidence of U.S. support 

CAMSF was able to attract capital subscriptions from its members and to negotiate commercial lines of credit. In this sense the loan has achieved one of its intended purposes without being disbursed. b. Progress toward monetary integration of the five 

Central American Common Market countries may falter without the demonstration of U.S. support of CAMSF. 

C. The money will be needed when the expected restructuring of CAMSF makes it the preferred source of funds for members. d. All funds possibly available from any origin will be required to cope with the substantial payments deficits for the area anticipated in 1974-75.

The latest thinking from the AID Regional Office for Central 

American Programs on the restructuring proposal foresees that borrowers would turn principally to the first two windows where the only condition for a loan would be a letter of intent. 

There is some question of whether AID funds can be dispensed at the first window since the AID Loan Agreement stipulates that they "be used only for stabilization loans, and not for short-term or seasonal loans" (Section 4.01 (h)). Moreover, the initial support given by the IMF and AID to CAMSF assumed that the latter would "avoid any possibility that insufficiently rigorous standards for the use of resources and criteria for stabilization programs render the CAMSF a substitute for the IMF and thereby a device by which individual countries might avoid taking the policy actions which their economic problems require." (Page 22 of the AID Capital Assistance Paper for 

CAMSF.)

The projected regional BOP deficit of $200 million may be overstated since the higher costs of commodity imports should be somewhat offset by substantial increases in Central America's export prices. Also, CAMSF anticipates a 20-year $75 million

€ However, line of credit from Venezuela plus a $25 million swap arrangement to assist with whatever deficit there may be. Additional assistance will be available from the special IMF facility established to finance deficits caused by oil pricing. deficits of the magnitude envisaged by the cost of oil imports cannot long be financed by credit from any source; importing countries will have either to negotiate a substantial reduction in oil prices or drastically reduce their oil consumption to avoid sinking hopelessly into debt, assuming the unlikely prospect in most cases of achieving a trade balance through higher export earnings.

We have asked that AID comment on the foregoing and their response follows:

AID Comments 

We agree that the AID loan to CAMSF is achieving important objectives even though the loan has not been disbursed. It is in the nature of a stabilization fund that drawdown requirements are not predictable. Accordingly, at the time the loan was authorized the possibility of a lack of loan disbursements for a considerable period was foreseen. Building on two prior reviews of the loan, an evaluation of the loan was recently undertaken by a team of AID officials assisted by a consultant. 

Although a final report has not yet been issued, the tentative findings are: (1) that the AID loan is achieving important objectives; (2) there are prospects for loan drawdowns before the

December 1975 terminal disbursement date in view of the significant changes in the balance of payments situation of the Central American countries induced in large part by the increased cost of petroleum products; (3) a deobligation at this time would be most inopportune because the Fund's ability to operate effectively would be curtailed and since such an action could be construed as an indication of indifference on the part of the U.S. toward progress in Central American economic integration; and (4) consideration should be given to restructuring the fund to facilitate member country access to its resources in such a manner as to strengthen monetary stabilization throughout Central America.

It should be pointed out that the evaluation has not been completed, and AID has not yet taken a position on restructuring. When the evaluation has been completed, AID will consider the options that emerge consistent with the original objectives of the loan and sound management of AID's portfolio. 4

COORDINATION OF FUNCTIONS 

Question. Mr. Todd, I have noted your intended organizational change. In the past, where a separation between planning and operations has been attempted (notably, President Eisenhower's National Security Organization), it has resulted in a confusion of lines of authority and responsibility. How do you propose to coordinate these functions?

Can you be assured that the planners will not construct plans to elaborate that the operators can't possibly carry them out? 

How will you assure that operators will carry out plans as planned?

Answer. The coordination of functions within IGA will be achieved through a redefinition of the structure of the organization, clear delegations of authority of those charged with the responsibility for the functions to be performed within that structure, and the application of systems management of inspections. 

Basically, the reorganization plan being developed for IGA recognizes and provides for the three fundamental elements of the IGA inspection process: the selection of suitable, well defined subjects for inspection under policy guidelines established by the Inspector General; the proper accomplishment of the factfinding portion of the inspection; and the appropriate use of the inspection findings.

These will be accomplished organizationally by the formation within IGA of three new subcomponents or offices. They are the Offices of Planning, Inspection and Report Management. 

Each office will be headed by a director to whom appropriate authority will be delegated by the Inspector General to fulfill the responsibilities of that office as defined within the functional statement for that office. 

Finally coordination is made an integral part of the operation by the implementation of a work flow management system which is basically a Critical Path Method and which requires coordination of function when more than one office has an interest or responsibility for action. 

Control to assure the selection of only feasible inspections of those developed by the Office of Planning will be maintained through a procedure requiring the approval of proposed inspections by the Inspector General or the Deputy Inspec tor General. 

A clear statement of inspection objectives and goals by the Office of Planning upon assignment of an inspection to a team, together with inspection supervision of work in progress by the Office of Inspections and a review of that work before reporting by the Office of Report Management should assure the completion of inspections as planned and the attainment of the specific inspection objectives. 

DIVISION OF ATTENTION BETWEEN ECONOMIC AND SECURITY ASSISTANCE PROGRAMS 

Question. There is evidence of some Congressional feeling that traditionally the 

Inspector General's office has almost exclusively directed its attention to scrutinizing developmental and humanitarian assistance programs while going rather light on military and military related programs.

Do you have any concerns regarding these programs which you would like to share with the Subcommittee?

What would you estimate to be the division of your effort or workload as between economic and security assistance programs. 

Answer. A recent IGA planning review of inspections completed during the past two years confirms the Congressional observation that insufficient coverage was afforded the Military Aid Program (MAP) by IGA. Efforts to bring the 

MAP workload into better balance have already been undertaken through surveys commenced within the IGA planning activity and through a series of meetings with a number of State and Defense Department officials involved in these programs. These efforts have not only been concerned with achieving a better distribution of the IGA workload as it relates to MAP, but extend beyond that to address some of the more significant aspects of those programs than has been the case in the past.

711

With IGA management being so new, it probably would be premature to draw any conclusions or reflect any concern regarding these programs at this time. 

It is anticipated that MAP related inspections will account for approximately 15% of the IGA expenditures of assets and manpower initially, with an increase beyond that as the inspection capability to assume a greater workload develops. 

It is less possible at the present time to give a definitive estimate of the future division of IGA workload as between economic and security assistance programs. 

As the planning process matures, however, it will be possible to project an annual program which would provide appropriate coverage of all the foreign assistance programs within IGA's responsibility.

Until then we stand in recess.
