The $28 million also includes support for the international agricultural research institutes which have been the leading force in the agency's attack on the less developed countries' major food production problems. That is planned at $10.5 million for fiscal 1975. 

Senator INOUYE. What is this organization?

Mr. BERNSTEIN. There are a series of eight international agricultural institutes around the world. The two oldest and best known, are the wheat and maize center in Mexico called CIMMYT, and the International Rice Research Institute in the Philippines called IRRI. These are private, autonomous organizations. 

Senator INOUYE. May I have a list of those, too? 

Mr. BERNSTEIN. Yes, sir. 

 AGRICULTURAL INTERNATIONAL RESEARCH INSTITUTES 1. International Center for Maize and Wheat Improvement (Centro Inter nacional de Mejoramiento de Maiz y Trigo; CIMMYT), Mexico City. Plays a catalytic role in development and utilization of the improved technology required to enable developing countries to increase production of wheat and maize. Those are the most important foodgrains, other than rice, in the developing world. 

Progrss to date includes high-yielding varieties constituting 30 percent of spring wheat plantings in developing countries, and commercial production of high protein maize in Brazil and Colombia. Proposed FY 1975 A.I.D. contribution 

$1,450,000. 

2. International Rice Research Institute (IRRI), Los Banos, Philippines.

Develops basic breakthrough technology for rice production in the tropics and assists developing countries to strengthen their own research and production programs. Rice is the staple food of more than one-half of mankind. The principal IRRI accomplishment has been development of higher-yielding rice varieties now being planted in close to half of the irrigated rice field of South and Southeast Asia. Proposed FY 1975 A.I.D. contribution $1,150,000. 

3. International Center for Tropical Agriculture (Centro Internacional de 

Agricultura Tropical; CIAT), Cali, Colombia. Develops research networks particularly regarding beef cattle, cassava, beans, and farm systems. Outreach activities include training of developing-country scientists and holding workshops for interchange of technologies. Among achievements to date, heavier beef cattle have resulted from higher-protein pasture grass and from partial immunization against blood parasites. Proposed FY 1975 A.I.D. contribution $1,650,000. 

4. International Institute for Tropical Agriculture (IITA), Ibadan, Nigeria. 

Helps improve the quantity and quality of food crops in the lowland humid tropics. Research and outreach activities concentrate on farming systems, cereal improvement (rice and corn), grain legumes (cowpeas and soybeans), and root and tubers (cassava, sweet potatoes, and yams). Work on mulching the land with crop residues to improve infiltration rates of rainfall and to reduce soil temperature has markedly increased yields of maize. Proposed FY 1975 A.I.D. contribution $1,800,000. 

5. International Crop Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics (ICRISAT),

Hyderabad, India. Develops more productive and dependable technology for a wide semi-arid tropical belt across South Asia, Middle East, Africa, and Latin America where food production is limited by erratic rainfall. Important crops in the area are sorghum, millet, chickpeas, and pigeon peas. ICRISAT was instituted in mid-1972. Since then it has forged links with Puerto Rico, Purdue, and other institutions, undertaken work on expanding and evaluating germplasm

of crops for use in breeding programs, and initiated research on cropping systems. Proposed FY 1975 A.I.D. contribution $2,400,000. 

6. International Potato Center (CIP), La Molina, Peru. Develops multi discipline research program addressing problems most limiting to increased production of potatoes. The potato is one of the world's principal food crops, is unusual in growing well at high elevations, and is very high in per-unit-area production of calories and protein. CIP has collected about 5,000 germplasm entries, and identification of important lines for breeding programs. Regional projects have been started in Mexico and Lebanon. Proposed FY 1975 A.I.D. contribution $550,000. 

7. International Livestock Center-Africa (ILCA), Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. 

Approved by the Consultative Group for International Agricultural Research in 1973. Strategy is to improve cattle production systems by integrating biological, socio-anthropological, and economic research. Will have close liaison with International Laboratory for Research on Animal Diseases (ILRAD), and the two organizations may amalgamate. Proposed FY 1975 A.I.D. contribution $1,500,000. 

8. West Africa Rice Development Association (WARDA), Monrovia, Liberia. 

Aims to help make West Africa self-sufficient in rice. Member governments are 

Dahomey, Gambia, Ghana, Ivory Coast, Liberia, Mali, Mauritania, Niger, Nigeria, Senegal, Sierra Leone, Togo, and Upper Volta. The Consultative Group for 

International Agricultural Research approved support in 1973 and funds were made available to WARDA in mid-1974. A.I.D. does not at this time propose a FY 

1975 contribution.

RURAL INCOME PROGRAM 

Senator INOUYE. What is involved in increased income for the rural poor?

Mr. MURPHY. Generally speaking, Mr. Chairman, the increased income will be the result of increased production of farm products.

If we can bring to them new seeds, fertilizers, and agricultural credit and extension services, their production, in our judgment, could be so increased as to put them in a market economy where they are actually going to be producing not just enough to feed them and their families but also to sell. RURAL ELECTRIFICATION 

Senator INOUYE. What is involved in improved rural electrification?

Mr. MURPHY. This represents part of the major transition which the program is undergoing as a result of the new initiatives introduced by the Congress last year. We are shifting our efforts to the distributing facilities to bring these power supplies out into the country for operation of low-lift pumps for irrigation, for rural industries, for providing simple light and other electrical needs for farm purposes.

It is a major shift in emphasis, as I say, resulting from the new thrust.

Senator INOUYE. Is this project a complete project taken on by the 

United States? By that I am referring to projects we have had in the

past where we were involved with several other countries. We would make the generator, and some other country was to make the distribution system. Then we find later the other country decides not to go through with its share. Then we are stuck with the whole thing.

Senator INOUYE. So this rural electrification is just for the Philippines?

DEVELOPMENT OF COOPERATIVES 

Senator HATFIELD. Mr. Chairman, I would like to go back to this rural cooperative on page 3. Will you tell us what you have in mind as to the development and improvement of rural cooperatives? 

Mr. MURPHY. Well, Senator Hatfield, we have had tremendous success here in the United States as you well know with the cooperative movement. Similar programs seem to have a very good place in countries overseas. We have a cooperative program, for example, in the agricultural sector pretty much the same as in the United States. It would also provide extension of credit services so the farmers would get small loans to buy the seeds to plant their crops and market them through the cooperative at the best price they can bring at the time. 

Senator HATFIELD. How much money are you allocating for development of cooperatives?

Mr. MURPHY. I am not sure we have a figure broken down specifically for cooperatives. In 1975, in agriculture, I believe the total figure is in the neighborhood of $55 million in all the agencies to help improve the rural cooperatives.

Senator HATFIELD. Will you provide a more concise figure for the record, please? 

Mr. MURPHY. Yes, sir; I will. 

Senator HATFIELD. In what way do you utilize the infrastructure in a particular host country to promote this type of cooperative? What is the base you start with? Is it a host country infrastructure or an imported-type infrastructure?

How do you teach people the concept of cooperatives? 

Mr. MURPHY. The basic approach, Senator, is to either use or to build, if they are not there, the existing institutions to pull these farmers in a particular area together and form a cooperative. Now the 

Senator HATFIELD. Did you say the existing institutions?

Mr. MURPHY. Yes, and if they don't exist, try to establish them. 

Agricultural extension can be a very effective means for organizing a group of neighborhood farmers to form a cooperative. In some countries there are extension services. 

COOPERATIVES IN THE SAHEL 

Senator HATFIELD. Let's take the Sahel. How do you begin a program there?

Mr. ADAMS. In Africa, in the Sahel, there usually are ministries of cooperatives, which may be rudimentary but have generally had the responsibility of trying to manage whatever the country regarded as its basic credit program. Sometimes these programs have been very limited. There is a need to try to assist them in organizing a whole range of inputs such as pesticides, fertilizer, improved seeds, et cetera. 

In the Sahel, I think the situation would have been more severe had not there been some rudimentary progress of the type Mr. Murphy has mentioned. It just happened there had been certain improved seed varieties which the governments are now trying to make available to farmers. The governments use the credit programs to try to organize farmers into some type of cooperative arrangement. Take for instance the case of Niger. There has been considerable input into peanut production. There is a cooperative organization which involves all the major peanut producers in the country. 

Senator HATFIELD. Do you use any expertise from existing cooperatives elsewhere in the world to bring assistance for those programs into those areas? 

Mr. ADAMS. Yes, sir.

Mr. MURPHY. Probably our most advanced project has been in Latin 

America. I would like to turn to Mr. Kleine and ask him to speak to that point because our experience there is of greater duration. 

COOPERATIVES IN LATIN AMERICA 

Mr. KLEINE. It is true Latin America cooperatives have been in being for many years. Many of them, I am pleased to say, were started under the Alliance for Progress program and by U.S. organizations representing our own cooperative movement. 

In recent years, Latin American organizations themselves developed considerable expertise of their own, and it is no longer necessary to

maintain the relatively high presence of U.S. experts in cooperative. 

We still utilize U.S. cooperative organizations, however, and based on the technical assistance they have provided and the know-how now in place, the Latin Americans organizations are working effectively through agricultural and cooperative banks and government ministries. 

Our programs in the agricultural field provide much of the credit and technical assistance needed to boost cooperative activity. 

Senator HATFIELD. Would you supply for the record some indication as to how many farmers are involved in Latin America as well as Africa? 

Mr. KLEINE. I would be pleased to. 

Mr. ADAMS. Yes. 

 FARMERS BENEFITED THROUGH AID-ASSISTED PROGRAMS IN AGRICULTURAL COOPERATIVE DEVELOPMENT

FOOD CRISIS 

Mr. MURPHY. Since the fiscal year 1974 program was conceived, we have witnessed a sharp deterioration in the precarious balance between worldwide food supply and demand. The resulting food crisis hit the 

LDCs with particular force. The remarkable production gains in the 

LDCs, associated with the green revolution, had at least kept pace with population growth over the past decade in most countries. 

But production gains were not sufficiently large to provide food stocks adequate to assure food security in the face of sustained periods of poor weather and increasing consumption requirements. Imports made at double or triple the prices of a few years ago threaten to undermine even the best of development plans. 

To further compound the problem, our own ability to help countries as we have in the past under Public Law 480 was, of course, severely curtailed and a worldwide fertilizer shortage was developed in the past 2 years. The energy crisis only exacerbated an already tight supply situation. As we think about the food problems of the LDC's we need to remember that even in good times, one-fifth of the people in the developing world are undernourished and a majority have inadequate diets.

EFFORTS TO INCREASE FOOD PRODUCTION 

Mr. MURPHY. While food aid can help tide over short-term food shortages, attaining adequate levels of food supply for developing countries depends fundamentally on increasing their own production. 

The potential for growth is there; it must be exploited. Improving agricultural production and rural development is imperative. 

Sufficient food supplies at prices poor people can afford is one of the great contributions to equity that a more productive agriculture can make. A vital, strong, growing agriculture sector, which engages the small farmer, can provide the basis for expanding job opportunities and improved income distribution.

Therefore, Mr. Chairman, we have sought to concentrate much of our economic development assistance on attacking this most basic world problem of increasing food production. 

THE FISCAL YEAR 1975 PROGRAM 

Increasing food production in developing countries is a complex and difficult task requiring a broad range of approaches, depending upon the specific country problems. It must be accomplished, in contrast with most past increases, primarily by raising output per unit of land because most of the arable land is already in use. The following sections describe key elements in our overall program. 

A. RESEARCH 

Production increases of wheat and rice have shown the high payoff of agricultural research. AID is supporting an extensive search for new varieties of grains and other crops-more productive and more nutritious as well as better fertilizers and improved farm practices. 

AID-financed research takes place at universities and other institutions in the United States, in eight major international centers-AID finances 25 percent of their annual budgets and at institutions in the developing countries; the entire effort is linked together through mutually supportive networks which assure that the results are fed into national production programs. 

Packages of technical assistance are being developed which will speed the transfer of these new production technologies from the research centers to the fields of smaller farmers. In addition to these efforts we plan to initiate in fiscal year 1975 a new TVA-related fertilizer center intended to become part of a new international plant nutrition institute supported by a consortium of donors. This institute would place increased emphasis on discovering improved and less expensive ways of providing the plant nutrients required for increased production as an important step in coping with the world food program.

NUTRITION REQUIREMENTS 

Senator INOUYE. At this point I might interrupt. 

You seem to be differentiating between problems of less developed countries and developed countries, and we are setting up now a system to build up nutrients in food of less developed countries. Isn't it true the nutrient requirements for less developed and fully developed countries are the same? 

Mr. MURPHY. Yes.

Senator INOUYE. The nutrient needs of people living in Washington, D.C., should apply to the people living in Bangladesh, should it not?

Mr. MURPHY. The problem basically is we simply can't take U.S. technology in agriculture and transfer it to a tropical area and have it work equally well. The basic problems of nutrition vary substantially as you move from zone to zone in terms of technology. So where we may have technology which works beautifully in Oklahoma and Texas, when we take those advances and move them to Bangladesh, they don't work that well.

LOCATION OF RESEARCH INSTITUTES 

Senator INOUYE. Where will the Institute be located?

Mr. MURPHY. This has not been determined. The fertilizer part would be located at TVA, but this is a proposal we have made to the Consultative Group on International Agricultural Research. It is under consideration by that group and has not yet been accepted or approved, but we sincerely hope it will be. 

A portion of that, if it is approved, would be the portion located at TVA, devoted to work on chemical fertilizers.

Mr. BERNSTEIN. Our whole effort is to develop international networks in which the institutions all over the world working on a problem such as rice, corn, cattle, or whatever can each contribute what they are best able to do. The whole system thereby gets strengthened. There are important skills which can be provided in the United 

States to help get at the problems, such as the disciplinary skills needed to attack the problems, the research methodology, and some of the research laboratory work which does not depend on climate. Some of the work is done at these international centers and they do it in collaboration with the national centers in the cooperating countries. 

For example, we finance 25 percent of the rice program at IRRI (International Rice Research Institute, Philippines), the leading rice center in the world.

There is a division of labor with each of the institutions in a particular global network doing what they can do best. They all contribute to a pool of results and every country can draw from that pool. They are developing better technologies and getting them down to the individual farm.

PRODUCTION PROGRAMS 

Mr. MURPHY. The production potential of small farmers has generally been underestimated and underemphasized, but there is considerable evidence that small farmers are able to produce yields comparable to or greater than larger farmers if they can get a fair price for what they produce and if they have access to the necessary agricultural technology, inputs, markets, and important social services such as health and education. AID's programs are helping to provide these essential elements. (1) AID's 1975 program will provide nearly $185 million to finance fertilizer and pesticide imports as well as a share of the costs of new fertilizer production facilities in Pakistan and Bangladesh. (2) Along with fertilizers, cheap and easily available water is also an important factor in raising production per unit of land. It is particularly important with the existing new seed varieties. A proposed $21 million loan to Indonesia will fund an expansion of local irrigation facilities used by small farmers while in Morrocco AID is considering two capital projects of the same type. 

Incidentally, Mr. Chairman, in the Indonesia project our planning includes provision for the use of the fixed-cost reimbursement technique which your committee has encouraged us to use more extensively. (3) Technical assistance in the whole range of production problems is a prime form of AID assistance in all parts of the world. In 

Ethiopia, for example, the production of beans and other food crops is to be spurred with the help of AID-financed advisers. (4) Livestock production is especially important in parts of Africa. 

Major multidonor assistance is being provided to Kenya's national livestock development program aimed at increasing beef production through ranch development, meat processing, improving essential infrastructure, and conservation. In the Lake Chad areas of central

Africa, comprehensive pilot programs are directed at the traditional herdsmen.

BALANCED APPROACH 

Mr. MURPHY. We are trying to strike a balance. Many of these projects we have talked to you about today are projects aimed at the long-term increase in production on the farm in various countries. I agree with you thoroughly that any country that is exporting its nutrients while its people starve is really exercising what I consider poor judgment. They are sovereign nations. If they make a decision to do something like that, there is nothing we can do about it. 

You know, on a lighter vein, a Scotsman has a hard time getting a good bottle of Scotch for the same reasons. They are exporting all the good-quality Scotch. Same thing with commodities. It depends on what their priorities are.

We are trying to strike a balance. The irrigation program is extremely important in increasing the yield per acre in the area where possible and at the same time we have our relief programs, and I certainly wish we could have a lot more to try to feed the people who are hungry today. 

Senator INOUYE. What you are telling me is that the decision to strike this balance take into consideration that at least half a million will stop this? 

Mr. BIRNBAUM. I think the Sahel is a very good example of the problem we are trying to address. For the immediate disaster, steps have been taken to prevent people from starving. The problem the 

Sahel is facing now arises from the fact there was no systematic effort to address the problems of the traditional farmers. The production per capita was falling. Producing food each year just to keep them going was not getting at the root of the problem. Livestock was growing but it was not commercialized. Land was being overgrazed.

The whole thrust of the program must be to address these problems so these people wouldn't be dependent on handouts. 

We don't pretend that we have adequate resources to do the job ourselves. Others must help and the countries themselves must shoulder the burden. But the underlying basis is sound-to help these people help themselves get on a sound economic footing. To do that, you have to help the country increase their foreign exchange earnings to pay for essential imports and move from just the traditional hand-tomouth society to one where people are participating in a viable economic system.

That is the new direction, not just keeping the traditional societies in place, but trying to increase their production and standard of living. 

In the interim, one must do everything possible to prevent people from starving to death. We are hoping our program will not be building monuments but engaging the peasant farmer, the small farmer in productive efforts that is one of the biggest problems.

The new seed varieties do increase yields and also increase the protein content. These varieties require inputs of fertilizer and water. We have a program to help these countries step-up irrigation facilities. 

It is all interrelated and I think what we are trying to do and we would like to submit is an overview of how we are trying to improve nutrition. Just looking at what is listed under the nutrition category does not give you a complete picture of the situation.

 AGENCIES RECEIVING FUNDS UNDER FOOD AND NUTRITION PROJECTS IN PAKISTAN

It is abundantly clear if progress does not occur within these domains and with rather considerable haste, one can expect further tragedies. We are aware of that; other nations are aware of it. 

NUTRITION PROGRAM 

Mr. BERNSTEIN. Mr. Senator, the matter Mr. White referred to is something the Agency can take great pride in-that is the fact that we have pioneered in an approach to nutrition which relates the total nutrition process. The countries are beginning to pick this up. Historically, the concern for nutrition was with a few scientists in laboratories who looked at the physiological processes and nice people who told us to eat a better diet. What has been developed is a methodology of looking at everything which happens in a country's development that affects its nutrition problem-looking at the whole process hap-

pening in a country, then strengthening its nutritional impacts through various kinds of intervention tools. 

For example, the major intervention that AID has greatly advanced is the one Mr. Birnbaum mentioned, improving the nutrient content of major foods. This is done by plant breeding, by fortifying basic foods with protein and other nutrients, and in other ways. Other interventions are in the health and planning area. The process of intestinal infection does severe damage to the nutrition of the groups most affected by malnutrition-the infants. So you work on that. For each situation, you pick the best way to help others get at the actual problem. For example, how to wean children and how to feed them through this vulnerable period. There are innovations in new food products. A number of countries are making progress here. We have just, for example, developed a new mix of whey and soybean flour as a lower cost and better substitute for powdered milk. These kinds of products will be distributed through our food distribution programs and are also going commercial. Also, the family planning program which improve the spacing of children again get at the basic nutrition problem.

There are about 10 or 12 countries now coming in asking for this type of help to provide systems of looking at their malnutrition problem and deciding what is the best way to get at it through the use of all these tools. This is a basic new approach. 

Senator INOUYE. Speaking of tools, in recent years I have read several articles which said the most inexpensive source of protein is fish. I have been further informed it is plentiful. We have nutrients all over. Some countries have gone into aquaculture. I have read through this statement of yours and there is not one word mentioned of using this less expensive source of protein. You have mentioned others.

FISHERIES AS A SOURCE OF PROTEIN 

World production of fish reached a peak in 1969-70 of about 70 million metric tons, roughly 60 percent table-grade and 40 percent animal feed. 

This equals some 40 pounds of live-weight fish (including shellfish) per person worldwide, but contributes only a tenth of the animal protein in an average diet. Nearly half of the world's fish catch is by developing countries, but an important part (including Peruvian anchovy) is exported to industrial countries for animal feed. 

The potential catch of fish by existing "hunting" methods has been estimated at two to three times present hauls, but this confronts cost and other feasibility problems in the fish catching and marketing phases. It will take more than a doubling or tripling of fishing activity to reach that potential, as stocks are reduced and the limits to sustainable yields are approached. It is also contingent on regulatory agreements to prevent overfishing and to control ocean pollution. Low-cost alternatives for reaching the mass of poor peoples in developing countries are being expanded by such measures as research to increase the protein content of the staple grain crops and to increase yields of high-protein vegetable crops. 

Another promising possibility is aquaculture fish farming in pools, lakes, and streams and increasing human control over the fish-producing environment in estuaries and other parts of the ocean. At present the world aquaculture harvest is about 5 million tons annually, largely from inland and brackish waters. It is estimated that 3-4 million hectares are presently utilized for aquaculture and that there could be added to it a potential of 25 million hectares not now used for food production. Expansion of aquaculture would not only improve diets but also expand employment, income, and in some cases foreign exchange earnings.

A.I.D. has made 211(d) institutional development grants in aquaculture to the University of Rhode Island and to Auburn University. 

We are also working with Florida State University. We plan to use those institutional resources to help launch projects for hatching selected fish eggs, growing juvenile stock, delivering small fish to producers, and marketing mature fish. Countries interested in and suitable for accelerating aquaculture development include the Philippines, Vietnam, Cambodia, Thailand, Indonesia, Tanzania, Brazil, El Salvador, Costa

Rica, Guatemala, and Honduras. The potential in the Philippines is indicated by an average fish consumption of 30 kilograms per person annually compared with production of only 8 kilograms. The Philippine 

Inland Fisheries Committee has agreed to implement a project for continuing research and training extension workers in pond fish production. 

The economics of expansion of aquaculture compared to other food production is being explored by A.I.D. In its further work in this field, A.I.D. expects to collaborate with the Overseas Development Council,

Rockefeller Foundation, and agencies such as the Department of Agriculture, World Bank, FAO, and the International Development Research 

Center in Canada.

COOPERATIVES DEVELOPMENT 

Senator INOUYE. Please proceed.

Mr. MURPHY. Strengthening the key institutions which serve the small farmers. Involving the small farmer in all the aspects of the production and marketing process is a powerful method of enhancing productivity. The cooperative movement, still weak in many countries, has great potential in this regard. 

In fiscal year 1975 we will encourage further expansion of cooperative programs. In Chile, for example, one of AID's objectives will be to strengthen co-op capacity to attack production and marketing constraints. Another example is in Tanzania where we intend to support the Rural Development Bank's program to facilitate loans to co-ops and district development corporations for the costs of seeds, fertilizers, and equipment.

INTEREST RATES 

Senator INOUYE. What will be the interest rate of the loan to the co-ops?

Mr. MURPHY. The standard rates to which you referred yesterday, 2 percent for the grace period, and 3 percent thereafter. 

Senator INOUYE. What would be the cost to the farmer? 

Mr. MURPHY. That I don't know.

Mr. ADAMS. Seven to eight percent in Tanzania. 

Senator INOUYE. Are you sure it is not closer to 16?

Mr. ADAMS. The best information I have is 8 percent. 

Mr. KLEINE. In Latin America, 12 percent.

Senator INOUYE. We loan to the co-op and they reloan? 

Mr. KLEINE. You have the two-step approach which was mentioned in which the concessional terms are to the government that accepts the risk, for the repayment of the loan, and the interest. Then the cooperative itself often will pay a somewhat higher interest rate and the difference is that which is considered desirable to help capitalize the cooperative to help the cooperative provide the supervision in these loans.

Senator INOUYE. Isn't it true the experience with co-ops has been almost perfect, no defaults?

Mr. KLEINE. Well, yes; there have been relatively few defaults. 

Senator INOUYE. Why should we give a concessional loan to the government and the government in turn through their banks exact huge interest from the co-op?

Mr. KLEINE. I would not characterize the spread between the terms the government pays to the U.S. Government and the terms paid by the cooperative bank to the government exorbitant. It is usually two or three points. We are attempting to promote higher rates of interest in our Latin American agricultural credit projects in order to attract greater participation of private capital. According to our research, the concession is more effective in the form of service and technical advice than artificially low rates of interest. 

Mr. BIRNBAUM. We do sympathize with the chairman that one wants to have an interest rate structure which can reach the small farmers. 

In many countries the rate of default for small farmers is very high. you just give them credit and they don't have the supporting extension facilities; the supporting infrastructure and marketing experience there can be a high rate of default. If 3

We did a study which indicated that a very low-rate of interest did not expand the volume of loans to small farmers. This has worked against them because a cooperative or land bank provides overhead and technical services. If the interest rate structure is very low, they tend not to deal with the small farmers because the bank cannot cover its costs.

We found unless the rate is 5 or 6 percent, or some rate which would provide the necessary spread, they have a tendency to stay away from the small farmer because of the tremendous work load and because of the default rate.

There is always a problem of finding a rate which satisfies the needs of the farmer. In traditional societies, if that farmer had to go try to get a loan in the marketplace the interest rate would sometimes be 15 to 20 percent. So interest rates of 7 or 8 percent for a cooperative or land bank is not uneconomic. 

RURAL DEVELOPMENT 

Mr. MURPHY. If the small farmer and the landless rural poor are to enhance their quality of life, the rural environment must be improved. 

The following examples suggest the range of assistance in this category, closely complementing the farm-oriented approaches described above. (1) Local public works projects will be supported in Indonesia where nearly 500,000 jobs are provided during the agricultural offseason on labor intensive road and land improvement projects. In this and other projects of this type we are also intending to use the fixed cost reimbursement procedures developed in the Philippines flood rehabilitation program. 

(2) Rural electrification projects will be financed in the Philippines where AID and the U.S. National Rural Electric Cooperative Asso ciation are helping the Philippines build cooperative electrical systems which will reach 75 percent of the population in 10 years; employment and income will be enhanced as the power is linked to irrigation projects and small-scale industry. (3) Market towns and areas are being developed in Guatemala and several other countries to help strengthen the small farmer's ability to engage more effectively in trade. 

IMPROVED POLICYMAKING AND INVESTMENTS 

AID is continuing to work closely with LDC governments to assist them to prepare sector assessments which help to identify critical problems and form the basis for informed decisions on resource allocation, cropping patterns, technology, institutional development, and price incentives, to which farmers react with great rationality. Analyses in 

Panama, Jamaica and Guatemala, for example, will lead to a variety of future projects which will emphasize price incentives. A current project in Costa Rica is directed toward improving the agriculture ministry's capacity to prepare, manage, and evaluate programs to improve the small farm operation; institutional capacity in programing, budgeting, and commodity management is being developed. 

Second programs enable AID to combine all the approaches discussed above in an integrated attack on agriculture and rural devel-

opment problems in a systematic fashion. These projects are based on an extensive analysis of the dynamics of the agricultural sector as a whole and all emphasize the problems of small farmers. About a dozen sector loans are planned for fiscal year 1975. 

For example, Nicaragua is seeking AID's assistance-following comprehensive section analysis for a program package which will include support for credit, co-ops, rural employment generation, inservice training, technical assistance, planning, agricultural statistics, marketing, land transfer, and agrarian reform. 

In the Dominican Republic, where an agriculture sector loan is in an advanced stage of planning, a sector assessment has been completed and there has been a striking turnaround in the government's willingness to take major steps to increase resource flows to production programs, including projects to increase agricultural production and marketing, rural public works, farm-to-market roads, local government administration improvement, and other efforts geared to agricultural development generally and small farmer agriculture in particular.

NUTRITION 

Poor nutrition exacts a heavy toll in lost labor efficiency, disease and child mortality. AID has developed a range of methods to improve nutrition at low cost, especially for vulnerable groups such as nursing mothers and preschool children.

A major goal of AID's nutrition strategy is to assist the developing countries in the search for the most effective ways to strike at malnutrition-at the levels of food production, the nutritive value of food produced, distribution, processing, and family feeding practices. Aid in nutrition planning will be provided in fiscal year 1975 to a number of countries, including Pakistan, Bangladesh, Zaire, and Kenya. 

Two important methods of acting against malnutrition are production of low-cost nutritious foods and devising affective techniques for delivering nutritious foods to preschool children. 

AID is taking the lead in improving food quality—particularly protein quality by demonstrating that the usable protein in cereal grains can be incerased by adding essential amino acids and protein concentrates during processing. Studies are underway to determine the value and feasibility of adding lysine to wheat and rice, and soy flour to corn and cassava. 

AID nutrition research has produced some notable successes: soywheat flour blends distributed through food for peace programs; a whey-soy drink powder which FFP programs will use to replace nonfat dry milk; edible coconut protein that the Philippine Government will produce on a pilot scale; a way to fortify tea with vitamin A which can lead to a substantal decrease in vitamin A deficiency blindness in tea-drinking countries like India, Pakistan, and Afghanistan. 

To reach preschool children, AID is (1) developing guidelines for selecting child feeding programs appropriate to national and regional resources; (2) evaluating supplementary child feeding programs to determine their effectiveness and capacity for improvement; and (3) training local staff and voluntary agency counterparts to carry out nutrition programs.

AID proposes to provide about $24 million in funding for nutrition programs in fiscal year 1975, up from $4.7 million in fiscal year 1974. 

In addition, AID's agriculture and health programs and Public Law 480 title II programs have important nutrition components. 

I appreciate the committee's patience in permitting me to make this full statement of our program in food and nutrition.

 COMMERCIAL RICE CONTRACT 

On August 3, 1973, Connell Brothers contracted with the Government of Indonesia, a non-A.I.D. funded commercial transaction, to provide 100.000 MT of 

U.S. rice at $420.00 MT. to be shipped September through December 1973. As world market prices for rice skyrocketed, Connell had difficulty finding rice to deliver at the agreed price.

Connell has shinned only 28,000 MT to date. It requested (and the Government of Indonesia agreed to) an extension of the contract from January 15 to February 28, 1974. However, no rice was shipped during the period of extension.

There appeared to be a break in the impasse in March, when Connell and the Government of Indonesia agreed to change the source of procurement from U.S. to non-U.S. and agreed to an appropriate new price. However, the agreement did not include a shipping schedule. Connell proposed to ship most of the remaining rice toward the end of this calendar year. 

We understand that during the past week the two parties have agreed on shipping not later than December 1974. The old contract will be amended accordingly. Thus, this longstanding dispute appears to be heading toward an orderly resolution.

A.I.D. support, as a matter of principle, the resolution of commercial disputes through private mediation or, if necessary, through the courts. Once again, this case bears no relation to past or planned A.I.D. or PL 480 assistance to Indonesia.

INDIA DEBT REPAYMENT Question. The Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 requires that most of AID's loans be made only on a finding that there are reasonable prospects of repayment. 

Recently, the United States has renegotiated outstanding loans to India and, in the past year, has had to "write off" some $2 billion in U.S.-owned rupees. Do

AID's assessments of India's financial standing suggest that she will be able to repay the $75 million loan you are programing for Fiscal Year 1975?

Answer. Yes. While we believe India's current economic situation is critical, we believe that she will be able to repay all of her prior and proposed dollar debts to the U.S. Government. Export earnings have recently shown some encouraging trends. If these trends continue, India will be in a better position to meet its foreign exchange requirements and help repay some of its outstanding debt obligations. As of March 1973, India's total foreign public debt was approximately $9.9 billion, of which the U.S. share is approximately $3 billion. To date, the 

Indian Government has never defaulted on the payment of any of its outstanding debts due to the U.S. Government, International Institutions and other donor countries.

As you have pointed out in your remarks, India's creditor countries, including the U.S., under the IBRD-led Consortium on India, have rescheduled some of 

India's debts to help counter the declining trends in net aid and to lessen the debt burden. These reschedulings have helped to ease India's debt burden which has averaged approximately $730 million annually. 

Question. A May 5, 1974 news article reported that Indian farmers' efforts to grow wheat were being severely handicapped by a series of Indian Government actions. Some of these actions were unrealistic land acreage ceiling, prohibitive land evaluations, and taxes that serve as a disincentive to farming, inadequate distribution of petroleum supplies even though there was adequate foreknowledge of the shortage, inefficient distribution of seed by state run corporations, and restrictive fertilizer import policies.

Given these conditions and other impediments to agriculture, can you specify in what way, if any, the proposed $75 million assistance to India will overcome these impediments to agricultural production and provide the crops necessary to feed India's ever expanding population? 

Answer. Yes, Sir. I would begin, however, by expressing reservations that some of the Indian Government actions cited-i.e., particularly land acreage ceilings and taxes are actually impediments to agricultural production. There is no evidence that land reform measures such as acreage ceilings have had prohibitive effects on production. Nor have land evaluations or the relatively light land taxes been prohibitive.The shortages of fertilizer and petroleum are real and serve as constraints to increasing agricultural production but are related, in large part, to world shortages and sharp price increases. We believe the $75 million requested for India's agriculture sector will help to ameliorate some of the immediate and major agriculture supply constraints. The lack of fertilizer is generally known to be a key constraint but there are others such as pesticides and various types of farm machinery which a U.S. loan of this magnitude could help make available.

THE AID PROGRAM IN ETHIOPIA IN TERMS OF THE PRESENT POLITICAL SITUATION 

Question. Ethiopia faces an uncertain political future. Unrest forced a complete change of government earlier this year (February 1974). Yet, A.I.D. is requesting appropriations under functional categories (Food and Nutrition, etc.) in excess of $25 million. What assurances do you have that this assistance will be used in a manner which will improve living conditions for the majority of people in Ethiopia?

Answer. The political and social unrest to which you refer and which began to surface earlier this year have been the result of pressure brought to bear on the Ethiopian Government by various groups (such as the military, labor unions, students, police and landless peasants) in order to achieve a more equitable distribution of benefits throughout the society. Although it is true that the specific future direction his movement will take is not yet clear, there are indications (such as accelerated attention to land tenure reform and the establishment of a drought relief commission) that the developments of recent months can in fact be considered positive in many respects and that the interests of a wide segment of the population may receive far more attention than in the past. 

Most recently for example, we have approved an Agricultural Sector Loan which contains conditions requiring the Ethiopian Government to outline specific policy measures for land reform, rural roads and small farmer production, which must be agreed upon before any loan disbursements are made. Although the legislative body has not yet approved the loan, pre-negotiations have taken place involving high level Ethiopian leadership. We feel that if the loan agreement is finally approved. this would indicate substantial progress and would provide us with assurances which even under the more stable conditions of the past would have been quite significant.

FOOD AND NUTRITION 

Question. Many authorities say that there is no long range solution to the food problem unless population growth is brought under control. How does A.I.D. determine the relative priority between food production and population control? 

Answer. Food production and population control are closely related. We certainly agree that in the long run the food problem cannot be solved unless population growth is brought under control. Similarly, couples are likely to continue to have big families for "social security" reasons until they can be relatively confident that their children will not die of malnutrition-related diseases and that they do not risk death by famine if they do not have children to support them. Food production is also a major element of the growth and modernization process that is closely associated with reductions in desired family size. 

Agriculture and family planning are A.I.D.'s highest sectoral priorities. In 

FY 1975 we are proposing increased programs in both the food and nutrition and family planning categories. The amounts of the increase are much larger in food and nutrition because agricultural production has much larger capital requirements. We were disappointed at the $112.5 million ceiling placed on our family planning program in FY 1974. We are requesting $137.5 million for FY 

1975, and plan to request significant increases in future budget levels as sound new programs are developed.

AID EFFORT IN POPULATION 

Question. Of eleven nations in the bilateral assistance programs for Africa, nine have population which are increasing faster than increases in agricultural production. What is AID doing to turn the tide?

Answer. Well, Sir. In our FY 1975 program we are requesting for these nine countries $5.9 million which is higher than the amount programmed for population-family planning in FY 1974 by $1 million. Our assistance is provided only upon request, and in accordance with the type of program chosen by the host nation and institutions. We are not oblivious of the sensibilities of the nations we assist.

Many African countries have recognized that maternal/child health care, combined with basic information about child spacing and limitation of family size, may provide a means to address long-range populations growth problems. 

AID has responded to this growing awareness by assisting integrated maternal and child health and family planning projects in many countries. These projects include efforts to establish departments in health ministries to organize and administer those programs, and to identify the most effective means of implementing integrated health and family planning programs, and to assist various institutions, among them paramedical training centers, universities and medical schools. In Tunisia AID has provided $783,000 during FY 1974 to help meet the costs of maternal and child health facilities, family planning services, technical assistance, commodities, and training. The FY 1975 requirements are estimated at $925,000 for these same components. About 300 health centers throughout the country are currently dispensing family planning services, with more than 100,000 women participating in the program. 

In Ghana, AID has financed population training and consultants in such areas as information, education, communication, and evaluation, foreign exchange costs of the contraceptives used in nationwide program. AID is supporting operational research to determine the most cost-effective way to integrate voluntary family planning services into rural comprehensive health programs. In two countries, Kenya and Morocco, AID is assisting the governments to develop and test new measures for collection of population and demographic data. The information will provide a basic for planning national programs. 

AID is also working closely with other donors on family planning activities. 

The World Bank has appraised the Kenyan five year population program and estimates the total cost including capital requirements at $30 million. The 

World Bank plans to finance most of the capital requirement of the project, $13 million, and the United Nations Family Planning Association and Sweden are considering financing $3 million and $4 million respectively. Other large contributors are expected to be Norway and Denmark. AID intends to provide support to the program with U.S. training for family planning personnel and technical and commodity assistance for the Ministry of Health's public health education activities.

The impact of population planning programs-including those assisted by AID on birth rates of developing African countries cannot yet be ascertained. 

However, in some African countries, notably Tunisia and Mauritius, birth rates are already falling; in others, where programs were initiated in the late sixties, substantial reductions in birth rates are not likely to be significant for several more years. Of course the ultimate resolution of the population problem requires national accelerated momentum, and internationally concerted efforts. There is growing evidence that family planning efforts will be successful only if they are based on interrelated policies affecting all aspects of a country's political and eonomic fabric. 

FOOD AND NUTRITION 

Question. Mr. Murphy, much publicity has been given to the fertilizer shortage and the increases in fertilizer prices. There are also reports that the developing countries can't obtain fertilizer to meet their needs and that consequently agricultural production will suffer severely. 

Because of the fertilizer and energy shortages and price increases, have the gains under the "Green Revolution" been lost? Some reports say that the countries have reverted to traditional methods. 

Answer. We would not say that the gains under the "Green Revolution" have been lost, This term has generally been used to describe radical increases in grain production that occurred in some parts of the developing countries, primarily in Asia, due to discovery and introduction of new technology-primarily new rice 34-192 O - 74 - 48

and wheat seed types that flourish in combination with high applications of fertilizer and water. Since these high-yielding varieties were first introduced in 

1966, acreage planted with them has expanded every year to the last crop year for which we have data, 1973. About 80 million acres were planted or about twice the acreage affected three years earlier. The extra production compared to the displaced traditional varieties was enough to feed about 160 million more people at a typical consumption level in a poor developing country, where cereals are the principal food. 

Recently, some developing countries have not been able to obtain as much fertilizer as their farmers need and want to support the newer high-yielding crop systems, because of a combination of high prices, foreign exchange shortages, and fertilizer supply shortages. This will certainly reduce their food production below what would otherwise occur. India is perhaps the hardest hit. Fertilizer use in India in 1973/74 is forecast at 13 percent below that in 1972/73. This fertilizer shortage will cause crop losses estimated at 3 million tons of rice, 2 to 3 million tons of wheat, and 1.5 to 2.0 million tons of coarse grains. However, we have no indication of any general shift away from higher-yielding technologies because of fertilizer shortages or for other reasons. Unless there is unforeseen very bad weather during the rest of 1974, developing country food production overall should be above 1973 though still well below these countries' needs. 

The most important effect of the "Green Revolution" was to demonstrate the value and necessity of much higher levels of investment in developing new agricultural technologies that will produce much higher yields under developing country conditions, and in making these improved farming systems effectively available to the mass of farmers. This demonstration has been followed by rising investments for this purpose,and we expect the trend of new technology application to continue and to spread more widely. The vigor of this movement depends, in considerable measure, on the extent of development assistance in this field.

II. Estimated Availabilities and Price: 

:

Although in the past A.I.D. limited financing of fertilizer to U.S. source, this policy was changed last year after consultation with the Fertilizer Institute, which represents domestic suppliers. As the fertilizer shortage developed, A.I.D. broadened the eligible source to permit procurement from free world sources. 

It is hoped that this broadening of approved sources will make possible substantial deliveries from major fertilizer producing areas. For instance, Cambodia traditionally gets some of its fertilizer from North Africa; and Bangladesh and Pakistan from European and Asian sources, in addition to American sources. 

Vietnam has recently been guaranteed approximately 40,000 tons of urea nitrogen fertilizer from Japan through an agreement between the two governments. A.I.D. expects that about 30 percent of the fertilizer it finances will come from such foreign sources in Y 1975. The 70 percent expected to be procured in the United States represents approximately 1% of U.S. fertilizer availabilities.

A.I.D. has no way of knowing with certainty how much Fertilizer will be available in international markets for A.I.D. A.I.D.'s last tender requesting offers for 350,000 metric tons received responses totalling only 112,500 metric tons. Of this amount, 67,500 tons complied with A.I.D.'s statutory price tests. faowever, the foreign recipients for whom the tender was made rejected 20,000 tons because the price was too high for their economies, considering the current resale value of the agricultural commodities for which the fertilizer would be used. 

Therefore, of the 350,000 metric tons requested, A.I.D. was able to award 47,500 metric tons. We believe that this was an unusual experience--since the tender was made just at the end of the spring planting season. For the remainder of the summer and into the fall, A.I.D. will make continous and diligent efforts both here and abroad, and fully expects to complete procurement of the 700,900 metric tons of fertilizer. 

Prices of fertilizer have continued to rise. For instance, urea is now being offered in the world market at $365 to $375 per metric ton, DAP at $420 to $450 per metric ton and TSP at $360 to $370. There is some reason to believe that these prices may be leveling off, but there is no assurance that this is the case.

III. 

Program vs. Project Financing: 

Most of the fertilizer financed by A.I.D. has been under program loans or grants, with some small amounts authorized under project loans. While future A.I.D. procurement may become more directed to sector type financing such as special Agriculture Development Loans, we expect that the pattern of financing will not change significantly in FY 1975. matter of information, in the $61.1 million of fertilizer 

As a

financed by A.I.D. in the first half of FY 1974, 88 percent was under program and 12 percent under project financing. 

See attachment for detailed breakdown.

IV. Procurement Arrangements: 

To preclude recipient countries from bidding against each other in a tight worldwide fertilizer market, A.I.D. held one fertilizer procurement for a number of countries early in June 1974. In this unusual situation, A.I.D. issues the Invitation To Bid on behalf of the recipient countries; however, the awards are then made by the recipient countries for those responsive offers approved by A.I.D. as to price and eligibility. We plan to hold another centralized procurement for A.I.D.-recipient countries in mid-July. To the extent that these consolidated procurements are successful in obtaining needed quantities of fertilizer, independent procurement actions by countries having A.I.D. funds available can be reduced or eliminated. 

The only exception to this procedure is where an odd lot of fertilizer may be offered to a country after one of A.I.D.'s centralized procurements, and the situation, considering price and need for the material, is such that A.I.D. will consider approval of this negotiated purchase.

V. Special Comment on Vietnam's Procurement Procedures: 

In the more normal procurement situation, the Governments of most of A.I.D.'s recipient countries rather than private importers handle the issuance of IFB's and awards thereunder, subject to AIO/W approval. Vietnam's procedure for developing fertilizer requirements and processing procurements parallels closely that of normal private commercial transactions, with Government of Vietnam only monitoring the entire process. The procedure operates essentially as follows: Private importers submit their import require ments to the Director of Commercial AID (DCA), Government of Vietnem, where they are reviewed and adjusted as required to conform to the country's estimates of realistic needs. The importers' requests are then consolidated and forwarded to AID/Washington for approval of the types of fertilizer, quantities and delivery dates. If approved by A.I.D., the request is then passed on to the GVN Overseas Procurement Office (VINOPO) in Washington for translation into an Invitation-For-Bids. AID/W assists VINOPO in the preparation of the IFB. The subsequent response to the IFB is evaluated by 

VINOPO, DCA and the private importers and recommendations are made to AID/W on proposed contract awards. Upon approval by AID/W, often involving an exchange of dialogue with our Mission and the GVN in Saigon on the acceptability of certain offers, DCA issues the contract award in the names of the private importers. AID/W then, at the request of DCA, establishes Direct A.I.D. Letter of

Commitment with the suppliers and makes payment upon receipt of documentation evidencing satisfactory shipments of the fertilizer as contracted. Concurrent with shipment of the fertilizer, private importer make full local currency payment through their commercial banks to the Government of Vietnam, which funds are deposited to the A.I.D.-GVN counterpart account. Upon arrival of the material in 

Vietnam, the importer clears the goods from the port and sells it through normal commercial channels.

Under A.I.D.'s current centralized procurement arrangements, discussed in Paragraph IV, AID/W (and not VINOPO) makes the actual solitication for offers but coordinates the proposed purchases through the same channels as mentioned in the above procedure.

1 AID's population program is helping developing countries bring rapid population growth into better balance with development potential and aspirations.

Nearly half of the 2.5 billion people in the developing countries are under the age of 15 and have most of their fertile years ahead. 

The immensity of the problem is clear-the present population of nearly every developing country will double in the next 18 to 30 years. 

Thus, major efforts are needed now if the population assistance program's long-term objective of sharply reduced population growth rates is to have any chance of realization. 

The effects of rapid population growth are becoming widely understood. For poor families, high fertility means poorer maternal health, higher infant mortality, and malnutrition. For countries, it means slower growth in per capita income, rising numbers of dependent children, labor force growth outpacing job creation, and ever-increasing numbers of mouths to feed, making dietary improvement and food self-sufficiency more difficult to achieve. 

And in recent months, the energy and food crisis have dramatically focused worldwide attention on the implications of uncontrolled population growth for a world with limited resources. 

In the early years of the program, the challenge was to use population funds to encourage others to join in programs to help check population growth. U.S. funds were used as seed money to encourage developing country governments and organizations to recognize the problem and to adopt appropriate policies and programs. 

We have encouraged the United Nations membership to create a special population fund and an action program. We bolstered the support for International Planned Parenthood Federation and its worldwide family planning associations. And we assisted many other public and private organizations. 

In part, as a result of these early efforts, there has been a recent marked upturn in interest in the subject of limiting population growth. 

Requests for assistance are mounting from critically affected countries. 

Requests for supplies of contraceptives began to move up markedly in late fiscal 1973, and have continued to accelerate in fiscal year 1974. 

Funding constraints and production limitations of U.S. manufacturers have hampered our ability to meet these growing requirements. 

Our present geographic coverage is worldwide. AID provides population assistance directly or indirectly to 70 nations. We are working through bilateral, regional, and interregional channels and through multilateral and private institutions. 

Even so, the greatest challenges are yet to be met. Exclusive of 

China, less than 15 percent of the LDC population is now reached by any kind of effective health-related services, and even less are reached with family planning services. 

Senator INOUYE. At this point, will you submit to us the list of all other countries that are participating in population control projects and the amount that we are providing?

Mr. MURPHY. Yes, sir, we will be happy to do that, Mr. Chairman.

INTEGRATED DELIVERY SYSTEMS 

Mr. MURPHY. To help reach this largely rural majority, AID is increasingly supporting (through the use of both title X population funds and non-title X resources) the development of integrated delivery systems which provide family planning, health, and nutrition services. By using existing manpower, such as midwives, village volunteers, and indigenous practitioners, we are striving to keep costs within LDC capabilities. 

We know that many of those people who have access to family planning services do not necessarily practice family planning; they may be getting only partial information, or they may not be taking full advantage of the services available to them. 

For these reasons, it is important to develop better understanding of how various factors economic, social, legal, cultural, religious, and technical-affect decisions regarding family size. 

For example, there is evidence that a willingness to reduce fertility is related to such factors as a decrease in infant mortality, availability of education, and the role of women in the society-specifically the opportunities available to them in pursuits other than child-rearing, such as access to education and employment. 

In general, a sense of participation in the benefits of economic development—a development strategy that draws in the bulk of the poor can be seen in some countries as contributing powerfully to declining fertility levels.

There are obvious lessons here: First, that assistance in raising agricultural productivity, education and health levels, and overall development, is a vital part of the broad effort to help the LDC's improve their population-resource balance. 

Second, that LDC population strategies must be broadened to take account of economic and social factors directly affecting fertility. We are currently exploring the implications these considerations have for assistance in research and action programs. 

RESTRICTIONS ON POPULATION RESEARCH 

Senator INOUYE. At this juncture, if I may ask, as you are aware, Congress recently adopted an amendment which placed certain restrictions on the use of AID moneys for this program. 

Now, how is this amendment affecting AID's operation?

Now, if you would like some specifics Senator INOUYE. Yes. I would like with some specificity to be advised how this amendment has affected your operations.

Mr. KEIFFER. Specifically, Senator, the amendment has been interpreted and now is in the form of a policy statement by the Administrator which he has just approved. It is very short. I could read it to you. 

Senator INOUYE. Yes, read the policy statement, please.

AGENCY POLICY ON ABORTION PROGRAMS 

Mr. KEIFFER [reading]. 

No funds available to carry out the Foreign Assistance Act will be used to procure or distribute equipment provided for the purpose of inducing abortions as a method of family planning. AID funds will not be used for the direct support of abortion activities in LDC's. However, AID may provide general population assistance program support to LDC's and institutions so long as AID funds are wholly attributable to the permissible aspects of such program. 

AID does not and will not fund information, education, training, or communication programs, that seek to promote abortion as a method of family planning. 

AID will finance training of developing country doctors in the latest techniques used in OBGYN practice. AID will not disqualify such training programs if they include pregnancy terminaiton within the overall curriculum. 

However, AID funds will not be used to initiate or expand the pregnancy termination components of such program and AID will pay only the extra cost of financing the participation of developing country doctors in existing programs. 

Such training is provided only at the election of the participants. 

AID will continue to support research programs designed to identify safer, simpler, and more effective means of fertility control. This work includes research on both foresight and hindsight methods of fertility control. 

AID funds are not and will not be used to pay women in less developed countries to have abortions as a method of family planning. Likewise, AID funds are not and will not be used to pay persons to perform abortions or to solicite persons to undergo abortions. Pursuant to the Foreign Assistance Act and AID policy, AID activities in family planning and population assistance to developing countries cannot incorporate coercive features relative to the practice of family planning or any mode thereof. 

In specific answer to your question as to the impact of this, we don't know yet obviously. We do know that abortion in many cases, legal or voluntary with the person, or self-induced is a rising practice all over the world.

And we know that the consequences of that in terms of bad health, death, and other dangers are severe. 

I would say that the net effect of the amendment will be that U.S. funds will not be available to do anything about that one way or the other. 

Senator INOUYE. Is it your recommendation that this amendment be deleted? 

Mr. KEIFFER. Well, it isn't going to help with the overall problem.

I don't know beyond that what to say. Without the amendment, we were moving in a relatively small way. With it we will not move. 

PROGRAMS IN ASIA 

Mr. MURPHY. We have noted signs of success in Indonesia, where a major effort is now under way-the number of acceptors has climbed dramatically from 181,000 in March 1971 to almost 1.4 million by

March 1974; Costa Rica, where there is enthusiastic support for the use of auxiliary health personnel to provide family planning information and services in the rural areas; the Philippines, where the Government is supporting more than 50 percent of the local costs of the program, a system of 2,400 multipurpose clinics has been organized and acceptor totals are climbing with approximately 800,000 new acceptors expected in 1974 contrasted to 686,000 in 1973 and 530,000 in 1972.

Other countries which show clear signs of potential for dramatic movement are Korea, Thailand, and Pakistan.

Despite these success stories, major problems need to be faced and overcome in a number of countries: India's family planning effort the world's first and largest-is losing momentum, for a variety of reasons; Bangladesh is just beginning to tackle the task, and may well have lost ground since its independence. 

PROGRAMS IN LATIN AMERICA AND AFRICA 

A few Latin countries are still arguing about whether they will have a population problem in their future. In some Latin countries we find laws and social and political practices constrain family planning programs at the same time that individual acceptance of contraceptives exists.

In Mexico and other countries the leaders are now convinced they have a serious problem and are seeking ways of coping with it. Many 

African countries are still concerned with political, ethnic, and methodological issues, but some leaders are beginning to grasp what their countries face and are beginning careful examination of what to do. 

ACCEPTORS AS AN INDICATION OF PROGRESS 

Senator INOUYE. May I interrupt there? I am impressed by the increase in the number of acceptors but has that been translated into population growth?

I say this because I recall receiving the same type of information on India where we were advised that this was a great success story, when in fact nothing had been done. Is it not true that instead of losing momentum they never had momentum ?

Mr. KIEFFER. I share your skepticism, Senator. Acceptor rates are simply an indicator. They don't tell the story. The story finally will be told in demographic terms, what happens to average family sizes, and then finally the number of children born after that and what these changes do to total population size. 

PROGRAM IN INDIA 

Senator INOUYE. What is the Indian situation now?

Mr. KIEFFER. I think what you have there is a government that has invested a considerable amount in family planning and has tried a variety of things. I think they locked onto the interuterine device rather heavily without exploring early enough other methodologies. They have had funding cuts because of the general constraints on their resources, and their the numbers are growing by 12.5 million net increase a year. I believe they are being swamped with people. 

Senator INOUYE. Are the Indians concerned?

Mr. KIEFFER. While I think they are very concerned there is so much that needs to be done that one could get the impression that they have not done anything that the problem suggests or requires. 

Senator INOUYE. Have we made an effort to provide India some advice in this area?

Mr. KIEFFER. We have. We had a staff here. We were working with them, and then about 2 years ago, they simply indicated to us that

they didn't wish that to continue. We dismantled our programs and pulled our people out. That has been the way it has been ever since. 

All AID programs were terminated, including this particular one. I spoke to Ambassador Moynihan in November about it, and he felt then that the situation had not really changed in terms of Indian attitudes. 

I think they simply feel they want to do this one themselves however that gets done. 

Senator INOUYE. All AID programs have been terminated?

Mr. WHITE. We have made no new aid commitments to India except for the title II program since 1971. 

The technical assistance effort which included the family planning effort was completed in 1973. I think a measure of Indian effort in family planning is the budget for the fourth plan in which they spent some $330 million equivalent. In their next plan they are allocating $600 million. So they are, I think, taking their problem seriously. They are trying to put more money behind the program which they see certainly as undercutting some of the possibilities for income gain unless the population growth rate is cut back. 

Senator INOUYE. You may continue, Mr. Murphy.

SUMMARY OF FISCAL YEAR 1975 PROGRAM 

Mr. MURPHY. A major constraint on our program at this time will be our financial inability to respond to initiatives which we have helped set in motion. At a time when our seed money is showing significant returns, the resources made available to the program have been cut. 

I strongly recommend favorable action on the $137.5 million request for fiscal year 1975, and urge Congress not to impose a restrictive ceiling on funds that AID could commit to the attack on this increasingly critical human problem. 

The fiscal year 1975 population program includes $105 million to support country and interregional programs. The currently anticipated fiscal year 1975 allocations to each of the following programs are noted in parentheses. 

These programs concentrate on: Assistance in collecting and analyzing demographic and social data ($10 million) as an essential tool for determining appropriate population policies and programs, and evaluating program impact ($8 million); extending the delivery of family planning services ($62 million)-including about $33 million worth of contraceptive devices; the training of medical and paramedi cal personnel, administrator and others in scientific, technical, managerial, and informational aspects of family planning programs ($20 million); and essential research on fertility behavior and better control techniques adapted for LDC use ($5 million). HEALTH PROGRAMS 

Mr. MURPHY. Health. In addition to the important emphasis on integrated low-cost health delivery systems described above (over $30 million is directed toward work in this area), AID's health program emphasizes projects in health planning and environmental health. 

One of the basic problems in poor countries is the maldistribution of existing health resources, particularly to the rural poor. AID is helping over 20 governments to undertake careful analyses of existing public and private health resources in the effort to design national programs which will not depend on major external donor support and will focus on priority health needs.

Training in American universities will be provided to permit developing countries to build a new cadre of professional staff capable of planning in the context of national economic development. 

Efforts are underway in central West African countries to help governments develop broad programs of health services. In the Cameroon, for example, AID is assisting development of a university center for health services which will be a major health training institution for the region. 

In an effort to protect populations of rural poor who are involved in rural agricultural development and in capital construction such as roads, dams, and irrigation systems, AID is following the intent of the National Environmental Policy Act which seeks to "stimulate the health and welfare of man.' 

We are supporting programs which stress major determinants of health status by improving the quality of water supply, the disposal of human waste, and the prevention of insect-borne diseases. (About $50 million will be directed toward these kinds of health projects in fiscal year 1975.) 

AID will seek to reduce the risk of cholera, other gastrointestinal, water-borne diseases, and several insect-borne diseases which have a major impact on morbidity and mortality such as malaria in Pakistan, Indonesia, Haiti and Nepal, and yellow fever in Central America.

In Africa, AID will help attack the parasitic disease river blindness which affects an estimated 1 million people in the Volta River Basin. 

Not only will this project ease human suffering but it will open up fertile river valleys for resettlement and productive agriculture. In so doing, it will help ease the population pressures created by the human dislocation caused by the Sahel drought. 

That concludes my prepared statement. 

Senator INOUYE. Thank you, sir.
