PROJECTIONS OF POPULATION GROWTH 

There is no "official" projection of the world population, because the future course of population growth depends upon a number of factors affecting both births and deaths which are difficult to forecast. The future level of fertility, for example, is dependent upon (1) the speed at which additional countries adopt population policies and programs; (2) the adequacy of these programs (that is, are they well organized and managed? Are service facilities located throughout the country in places conveniently accessable to the population?); (3) the resources allocated to the programs by both LDCs and donor countries; (4) the rate at which people who are not now regulating their fertility begin doing so; (5) the effectiveness of fertility control; and (6) the decisions individual couples make regarding the number and spacing of children they want, son preference, etc. Similarly, death rates will vary because of the influence of factors such as the adequacy of food supply, the degree of success of present or future health and sanitation programs, etc. 

Demographers usually make several projections at the same time, each based on differing assumptions about future levels of fertility and mortality. One such approach is to see what would happen if fertility declined from present levels to replacement levels by some specified time. Replacement level means that on the average couples would have only enough children to replace themselves. If none of the children died before reaching adulthood, this average would be two. However, since some children do die, the average number of children per woman (i.e., replacement level) is actually about 2.5 in the 

LDCs and about 2.2 in the developed countries. The table below shows what would happen if fertility declined to replacement level at varying points in time. These series further assume that once replacement fertility is attained, fertility will remain at that level. 

Today, mortality in most LDCs is still quite high despite the substantial declines that have occurred since World War II. If mortality rates decline to levels currently found in Taiwan, Hong Kong, and Singapore, rates could drop to a third or less of present levels. The projections below assume that mortality will continue to decline at fairly´ rapid rates for another 10-20 years, with slower declines occurring thereafter.

One final, but important, demographic fact of life for most LDCs is that their populations are quite young; half the populations of most LDCs are below 17 or 18 years of age. The young populations of these LDCs will continue to have an upward pressure on the number of future births even if fertility declines, simply because the number of people of

reproductive age will rise.

In the series of projections provided below, one consequence of this phenomenon may be seen: that is, even after fertility reaches replacement levels, populations continue to grow for another 50 or 

60 years.

With regard to the likelihood of attaining the various series, only the most optimistic believe that replacement fertility can be reached by the early 1980's. Replacement fertility by the year 2000 is, on the other hand, viewed by many as not only attainable but a desirable and necessary goal. This goal would require a substantial effort. Prolonging attainment of replacement fertility until well into the 21st century would produce an unmanageable situation in most people's views.

INDIA 

Question. The Committee is not convinced that India is prepared to take the measures necessary to improvement of her financial standing. For example, from past hearings the Committee has learned that India has virtually dismantled its own population planning program.

Uncontrolled population growth has been described as the most pressing problem thwarting India's ability to shoulder its increasingly large development problems. Should I assume that, as you have not programmed any population planning for Fiscal Year 1975, the Indian Government's position concerning this matter is unchanged?

Answer. While recent progress in India's Family Planning has not been as great as in the mid-sixties, India has in no way dismantled its family planning program. The program experienced enormous expansion in infrastructure, personnel and budgetary resources since the program was started in 1952. Some of its achievements include: (1) some 15-19 million couples currently practicing family planning; (2) approximately 14 million sterilizations performed since 

1956 and over 4.8 million IUD's inserted since 1966; (3) some 39,000 facilities established throughout India where family planning information, education and contraceptive supplies are available; and (4) approximately 125,000 family planning workers, doctors, nurses and paramedical workers trained. 

While results have been short of the targets called for in successive Five Year Development Plans, we need to recognize that the target group in India is some 100 million couples-an enormous number, larger than most countries in this world. We also need to recognize that there is no certainty about how to induce the large scale practice of birth control among the masses of poor, largely illiterate peasants in India. The latest IBRD figures note that Indian Government expenditures on family planning compare very favorable with those of other Asian countries. The Government actually spent a total of 2.77 billion rupees ($330 million equivalent) in its Fourth Five Year Plan (1969-74) and plans to allocate a total of Rs 5.16 billion rupees ($600 million equivalent) for its Fifth Five Year 

Plan. If the Government achieves this level of investment, some 40-42 million fertile couples are expected to be covered by the Family Planning Program by the end of the plan period. 

The Government is planning an integrated program strategy involving the total health needs of its rural population in the belief that better health for children will further reduce the pressures inducing large families. Consideration is also being given to experimental approaches, such as offering graduated government payments aimed at delaying age of female marriages, savings certificates to increase the intervals between births, and other community incentives. 

While the Indians have not requested us to provide assistance in the area of population planning in FY 1975, we are prepared to assist them, if requested, in appropriate programs. In addition, it should be noted that the United Nations 

Family Planning Agency has announced a 5-Year $40 million program in support of the Government's Fifth Five Year Plan. Since the U.S. Government contributes a substantial portion of the funds to this UN Program, we are indirectly con tributing to India's Family Planning program. 

POPULATION PLANNING AND HEALTH 

Question. The Committee, as you know, has an abiding interest in reducing personnel costs. In this regard, I was pleased to note that, in Pakistan, AID proposes to support a program which could reach 74 percent of the people on a person-toperson basis. Personnel costs for this program are approximately 10 percent of the total cost.

How does this compare with other AID programs? I have been told that personnel costs for other population programs run as high as 50-60 percent. 

Answer. The ratio of personnel costs to total program cost is not always a good measure of effectiveness or economy. For instance, the cost to AID of a person-toperson technical assistance program could consist almost exclusively of personnel costs of our technical advisors. However, in total, personnel costs for full-time 

AID employees in fiscal year 1974 will amount to 7.2 percent of our total program cost. This is a reduction from ratios of 9.4 percent in 1969, 8.2 percent in 1971, and 

7.5 percent in 1973. These reductions are significant, particularly in face of the pay raises accruing to government employees over these years.

[Brief recess.] EDUCATION SERIES 

Senator INOUYE. May we resume our consideration of the education series.

Mr. MURPHY. Educational accomplishments in LDC's during the past two decades have been extraordinary-educational systems were established where none existed, the numbers of secondary and primary schools increase vastly as did the numbers of teachers trained to cope with growing numbers of pupils, literacy rates were raised, and technical institutes and universities strengthened to the point that many of the development skills needed are now available without going abroad.

AID and other donors made a substantial contribution to these accomplishments. It has become increasingly apparent, however, that there is still a vast amount to accomplish if relevant quality education is to become available to the majority of people in the LDC's. 

LDC populations have been growing at such a rate that despite the educational improvements of recent years there are more children out of school today than in 1960.

In many areas there are still no schools and often no textbooks or teaching materials. Teachers are frequently ill-trained and unable to contribute adequately to the needs of national development. 

And most sobering of all is the realization that the costs of formal educational systems are so great that they simply are unacceptable as a technique for giving the bulk of the population access to basic education. Simply expansion of existing systems will not work. 

Devising the most appropriate education strategy for each country is not a simple task. It is first necessary to define the human resource and development problems and then determine the educational requirements and programs which can address these problems at a cost the country can afford. 

Increasingly, AID is helping LDC's address these basic problems through sector assessments. Based upon these careful analyses every effort is being made to develop high payoff, low-cost alternatives to

existing systems while retaining and strengthening those parts of traditional approaches that form a valid and essential base for educational development. 

AID's 1975 program gives increased emphasis to four promising and interrelated approaches to helping LDC's develop sensible and relevant broad based education programs: (1) nonformal education; (2) educational planning and analysis; (3) educational technology; and (4) development oriented higher education. 

At the same time we are continuing to support sound existing projects directed toward improved manpower development such as our general participant training programs and our programs with the AFL-CIO to strengthen free trade unions in Africa, Asia, and Latin America.

The program for nonformal education includes projects valued at over $20 million, up from about $4.5 million in fiscal year 1974. The increase is largely due to new projects in Latin America, such as a $6 million rural education loan to Bolivia, a major portion of which will be used to develop nonformal education services for selected rural populations.

A $2 million loan will support a major pilot effort to bring to the 80 percent of Pakistan's population that is functionally illiterate the practical knowledge and skills needed to make progress in agriculture, health, nutrition, and community management. 

Strengthened educational planning and analysis is critical to improved LDC capacity to establish and evaluate relevant human resource development goals. In addition to advisory efforts in several countries-for example, Pakistan, Indonesia, El Salvador, Ecuador, and Bolivia-there are projects underway now that build on earlier studies; for example, a $9 million Panama education sector loan will, among other things, finance programs designed to improve the quality of education while reducing costs to the central government. 

In Southern Africa a new curriculum development project will be initiated to help reform Swaziland's primary education system with a focus on the needs of rural people. 

A hopeful technique to provide low-cost education to large numbers of people involves making effective use of available technology, for example, use of radio in nonformal and formal education and the development of better and more relevant textbooks and curricula. 

KOREAN PROJECT 

In Korea a project now underway is totally restructuring elementary education through use of television and other new educational techniques.

In Honduras the development and distribution of seven million new textbooks to all public primary schools is transforming the prevailing rote system and bringing up-to-date basic education to the rural poor.

In addition to centrally funded research activities, regional projects are planned in fiscal year 1975 which use new technologies; in Bangladesh and Nepal, for example, projects are being developed to provide relevant expanded radio programing to reach rural communities. 

A $10 million educational innovation loan in Colombia will finance, in part, expanded use of educational television and radio.

There continues to be need for support of higher educational institutions where professionally competent personnel can be educated to meet the demands of increasingly sophisticated developing nations. 

In Asia support continues for the Bosphorus University in Turkey and Kabul University in Afghanistan.

In Ethiopia, Botswana, Lesotho, and Swaziland, AID is assisting in the development of universities where no institution of higher learning has existed, while in the Caribbean AID plans a $5 million fiscal year 1975 to help finance the expansion of the University of West Indies.

It should be noted that about $30 million for AID development assistance funds in all functional categories is directed toward the training of over 7,500 LDC participants.

These individuals, representing many development-oriented disciplines, receive training at hundreds of American and third country institutions before returning to their own countries to play an important role in the developmental process. 

By now over 166,000 participants have been trained by AID and predecessor agencies; it is through this avenue that much of America's most significant impact on the developing world can be seen; any discussion of manpower development should not neglect reference to this program even if many participants happen to fall outside this funding category.

Among the larger training programs included in this category for fiscal year 1975 are: (a) support of the Latin American scholarship program of American universities ($2 million); (b) two regional programs for training several hundred Africans, both in Africa and in the United States in development-related fields ($3 million); (c) the funding of up to 500 students at the American University of Beirut ($3 million); and (d) law enforcement training for about 400 public safety participants ($1.5 million). 

That concludes my statement. 

Senator INOUYE. Thank you very much, Mr. Murphy.

EDUCATION ASSISTANCE FOR BRAZIL 

Senator INOUYE. Mr. Murphy, I would like to quote from a report to Congress by the Comptroller General of the United States dated July 30, 1973, and it is entitled, "United States Foreign Aid to Education. Does Brazil Need It?". 

I don't know if you have seen this. 

Mr. MURPHY. I have not, Mr. Chairman.

Senator INOUYE [reading]. 

The United States has given education development in Latin America priority attention since the mid-1960's. Brazil, which accounted for a substantial part of this assistance, received about $187 million in direct and indirect aid for fiscal years 1965-72.

This is what they found:

The program was not designed to improve inequities in the Brazilian education system. U.S. efforts have not been directed to solving the basic cause of the shortage in qualified primary school teachers. Brazil has not complied with the financial commitments in the U.S. loans requiring increases in its Federal resources for education. Finally.

Increases in secondary school enrollment are being adversely affected by school site locations. U.S. aid to Brazil, in effect, supports an education system allocating a substantial amount of public resources to private schools which, because of tuition fees charged, discriminate against the less affluent. 

Available statistics indicate that although population is almost equally distributed between urban and rural areas in the four Brazilian states participating in the first U.S. education program, 78.5 percent of the enrolled secondary students in 1970 were in the urban areas. Nevertheless 88 percent of the sites selected at the time of this review were in urban areas. 

While this is not conclusive, it does indicate that in these states the greatest relative need for additional secondary schools is in rural areas, but schools being constructed with U.S. funds overwhelmingly are being located in urban areas. 

AID does not agree with this, but did not provide data supporting the contrary.

The per capita income varies widely, with northeast Brazil averaging $180 per, and south southern Brazil $550 per. Yet we spent most of our money in the urban areas supporting a private school system and did very little in the rural areas where the need obviously was located. 

If this is true, then I would suggest that you read this report. It is a staff report. I am just wondering how successful we can be in other 

Latin American countries where I gather private schools play a very substantial role in education. 

Mr. MURPHY. Well, from the date of the report, Mr. Chairman, I am sure that Mr. Kleine has read it. I have not read it. I didn't even know it existed. But I will ask Mr. Kleine to comment on that. 

AID COMMENTS ON REPORT 

Mr. KLEINE. Yes, Mr. Chairman, I have indeed read the report as have many in the Bureau, and as have the Brazilians themselves, and we did respond to the report at some length when it was made available to us.

The programs that are referred to in the report were launched some years ago and reflect the decisions made at that time. 

One of the critical aspects of the report was the question of location of schools, and here the Government of Brazil and the people of our mission working with them at the time took into account the question of population density, school deficits, and resources available, and the Government of Brazil thought that it could make its greatest impact on improving the educational system in Brazil if it were to begin to attack the problems where the people are. The people were moving from the rural areas in great numbers to the more urban areas, and the Government developed an approach to deal with this problem with their resources, supported by us. 

The Government of Brazil has its own programs which attempt to deal with the problem of education in the rural areas. 

We are not involved, as you know, in planning further loan programs for education or any other sector. 

Regarding the question of the private schools, it is true that throughout Latin America the best education that was available to people that could afford education was through the private school system.

That is changing. It began to change during recent years when governments began to apply more of their resources to the educational sector. 

Mr. Murphy has mentioned in his statement, as have others, that some of the governments have been putting as much as 30 percent of their total budgetary resources into the school system to begin to apply more resources to the problem. 

But merely going through the budgetary route has not yielded the required results, although it has been productive of more graduates and more teachers, et cetera. The shift that is now occurring is toward funding different ways, new ways to provide education for the people. 

Concerning Brazil, the GAO report dealt with the question of Brazil's ability to finance its own programs. The question was raised as to whether additional assistance should be made available to Brazil given the remarkable improvement in their economy. In fact, it is called by some a "miracle" that occurred in Brazil over the past 

4 years.

Our position, as described in our comments on the GAO report, was that AID had recognized the improvement in the Brazilian situation and had begun to phase down the program before the GAO study was undertaken. We have deliberately avoided an abrupt termination of our presence because we had commitments made earlier, particularly in the loan area. We now have a portfolio of loans whose pipeline we estimate, will be roughly about $200 million by the end of this June. 

Statutory and policy requirements on AID to oversee, monitor and evaluate the projects in the portfolio during the next several years provide the principal reasons for our retaining a nucleus of AID personnel in Brazil.

We have recognized for sometime that Brazil no longer needs large amounts of professional assistance from AID and that is reflected in our program proposals. 

Brazil has recently suffered something of a setback, as have so many countries because of the oil problem. What had appeared to be such a rosy picture for the next years has been clouded by this fact. For instance in 1973 the cost of oil imports to Brazil ranged in the neighborhood of $700-$800 million. In 1974, due to increased oil prices, the import bill for Brazil will run between $2.5 and $3 billion. Brazil imports about four-fifths of its oil requirements. Thus, the Brazilian situation is not quite as positive as it was at the time the GAO report was written. We are still optimistic, however, as are the Brazilians themselves, that they will be able to weather the oil crisis.

Mr. KLEINE. The $10 million would be addressing a separate but related aspect and that is to work with the Colombians on innovative approaches- Senator INOUYE. When do you intend to sign this loan and disburse the money?

Mr. KLEINE. Sir, we have been reviewing very closely these matters with our mission and the mission with the Government of Colombia. You will recall, sir, that this has been (a) an election year in Colombia, and (b) a year of inflation that has reached levels that they had not experienced in the recent past. As a result we feel that it will be possible to deauthorize some of these moneys because the slowdown on the part of the Colombians in terms of contributing resources to the educational sector means that some of our resources will not be called into use. So, to the extent that these resources will not be necessary there will be deauthorization. 

Now, to help the Colombians get a focus on new ways in educational innovation and educational techniques, TV, radio communications, et cetera, as a further adjunct to their normal system we would develop, if we can, a program in this field over this next fiscal year. 

Senator INOUYE. If there is any uncertainty as to whether Colombia can absorb this external assistance-you have just indicated, for example, that part of the $25 million will be deauthorized-what makes you think that they can absorb this new additional $10 million? 

Mr. KLEINE. We do anticipate, sir, that with the installation of the new Government and with the discussions that have already been under way with the representatives in the Government as well as with the existing Government that there is great interest in pursuing programs in the social areas of agriculture and education. 

It is our best educated belief that there will be a desire and a capacity for the Colombians to utilize this kind of assistance. 

If it doesn't materialize the program will not go forward. If they cannot use the resources already made available to them we will deauthorize and deobligate. 

We are not pressing on them the use of resources that are not needed or wanted.

LOAN PROGRAM IN BOLIVIA 

Senator INOUYE. The same kind of question for Bolivia. In the past 

10 years we have provided $50 million in foreign assistance loans. Of that sum about $35 million have not been disbursed but now you are requesting for fiscal year 1975, $6 million additional. 

What assurance can you give this committee that this amount will be promptly and effectively utilized for rural education? 

Mr. KLEINE. We do have the pipeline that you mentioned in Bolivia.

I mentioned first that Bolivia is the least developed country in South America. It is one of the most in need of assistance. The situation during the last 3 years has become more promising than in the previous past in terms of the ability and desire of the Government to move in the development area.

We have authorized and obligated the existing portfolio and while there are the usual kinds of problems in the initial implementation, the implementation problems are not that unique in Bolivia.

It will take time to utilize and draw down the existing portfolio. We feel that the interest of the Government is there to work in the area of

rural education and that there is an awareness of the need to try to reach out to those who have not had the benefit of any kind of systematized educational opportunity. Our discussions with the Government and the analysis itself are not yet far enough along to provide the conclusions that we will need to make the decisions. If we feel there is a problem of implementation, the loan will not go forward. 

I should note, Mr. Chairman, that some of the problems of the past which impeded the drawdown of assistance was the inability of the Government to mobilize the resources to make its counterpart contributions not only to our programs but to the IDB and to the World Bank. 

Bolivia is one of the countries that is benefiting, of course, from the oil situation and that will enhance its ability to make its contributions to programs that already exist and will be made available from external sources.

So, with that point of view, one serious past constraint should be alleviated. 

"BRAIN-DRAIN" FROM LDC'S 

Senator INOUYE. Mr. Murphy, one final question.

This subcommittee is very much concerned with the so-called braindrain problem of less developed countries. 

We have received reports which suggest that many of those men and women we have trained with AID funds have not returned to their homelands to assist their people as intended by our program. 

Do you have any statistics available which would indicate whether this is true or false?

Mr. MURPHY. I don't have them with me, Mr. Chairman, but I am sure we have them in the agency and I think, of course, the answer is that it is partly true but I hope it is mostly false. 

But the way to answer your question is to rack up the statistics and give them to you and if you like I will put them in the record at this point. 

 PARTICIPANTS' RETURN TO HOMELAND 

The "brain drain" is not a significant problem for AID. The current figures show that over the years since training began in current AID countries, a total of 712 participants out of a total of 97,589 failed to return to their home countries upon completion of their training. This is a world-wide "brain drain" figure for AID of less than three-quarters of 1%. The actual percentage of "brain drain" over the years has differed from one geographic region to another: 

Number of posts reporting 1. 

Total number of participants. 

Total number of nonreturnees. 

Percent "brain drain". 

Most recent data as of June 30, 1973. Latin Africa Asia America Supporting assistance countries

Total 14 12, 5111€ 24,289 19 41,240 19,549 44 97,589 323 89 53 247 2.6 1.3 

The differences are undoubtedly due to conditions in the home country at the time of the participants' scheduled departure for home. The highest rates of non-returnees (over 6%) have been among Vietnamese, Nigerians, Bengalis and Pakistanis, during times of trouble in those countries. Our records indicate that many in this category subsequently return when conditions in their home coun-

tries have stabilized. On the other hand, the exceptionally high rates of return of AID-sponsored participants is due to several facts. Prior to their training, all participants must sign a pledge to return to their home country on completion of training; their government must agree beforehand to have a job for them in their field of training awaiting them on their return; the visa provided them expires on completion of their training; and, the Immigration and Naturalization Act of 1951 (as amended) prohibits their remaining in the United States, or their re-entry in immigrant status, without having resided a minimum period of two years in their countries of origin. 

RELEVANT STATISTICS Mr. KLEINE. May I cite some statistics in the Latin American area that might bear on this because I believe this brain drain is not related to AID programs? It may be more a result of exchange programs financed from a variety of other sources and especially involving younger students.

In Latin America, sir, we have had a total of about 41,240 participants that have completed training in the United States or third countries. Of these, we know that 41,187 have returned to their countries at the completion of their AID training programs. Only 53, or one-tenth of 1 percent did not return and I believe that the performance record is one of which we can be proud. We also know, according to our annual AID mission followup reporting system that 95 percent are using the training that was provided for them. 

Now, in terms—I am not an expert on this-but there is a certain kind of visa that is given to them and once their education, unless they disappear in that case violating the laws of the United States, they must go back.

Mr. MURPHY. Mr. Adams tells me that in the African experience, Mr. Chairman, it is over 90 percent, we are absolutely certain that they have gone back after their training is completed. So we will get these statistics. 

Senator INOUYE. It will be most helpful, sir. 

Mr. MURPHY. And I hope they will show that the large majority do go back.

QUESTIONS SUBMITTED BY SENATOR INOUYE 

Senator INOUYE. I thank you once again, gentlemen, for your assistance this afternoon. I have some questions that I would like you to answer for the record. 

[The questions and answers follow:] EDUCATION PROJECT IN GUATEMALA 

Question. For fiscal year 1974 the Agency for International Development proposed to fund, at a cost of $180,000, a program for Expanding Educational Opportunity in Guatemala. The Committee is informed that AID has not implemented this project and, apparently, will not account for the use of this funding in any other program. These facts notwithstanding, AID is proposing the same project at an increased cost of $217,000. Why did AID fail to implement this program in fiscal year 1974? What use did it make of the $180,000? What does AID expect to accomplish with this new project that could not have been accomplished under the preexisting Educational Development Project (198) under which AID had obligated $953,000 through fiscal year 1974?

Answer. The $180,000 originally programmed for this project for FY 1974 was not allocated to Guatamela because the project was not ready for implementation in that year largely because the Guatemala Government was not in a position to launch a program of this type during an election year. I also note that our

1 total program for the Agency, and for Latin America, was considerably smaller than what we had requested for FY 1974. For Guatemala it was nearly $500,000 lower than what we had proposed in the 1975 Congressional Presentation. The $180,000 was therefore not available to be applied to another program. 

The project to expand educational opportunity was designed as a pilot project. 

The $217,000 in funding planned for FY 1975 represents an increase of $37,000 over that planned in the previous year. This is due to the decision to extend the educational opportunities to more of the Indian speaking students by furnishing translating services not previously contemplated. The extension of the activity for a second year (i.e., through FY 1975) will help assure the development of a capable organization to administer an educational opportunity project and provide sufficient time to determine the feasibility of the development of a broader program.

The Educational Development project (198) which began in FY 1971 has been directed at the primary school level. It has involved the development, through pilot schools, of the methodology, materials and curriculum necessary to upgrade the level and effectiveness of primary education in rural areas. The new project will complement the Educational Development project and the ongoing primary education loan program in that it will help provide opportunities for primary school graduates to continue their education. Its major focus will be the establishment of a system of scholarships for secondary education and loans for higher education for deserving students from rural areas. 

MAINTENANCE ALLOWANCE FOR AID'S ACADEMIC PARTICIPANTS 

Question. About two years ago this Committee was concerned about excessive student maintenance allowances being paid by A.I.D. to its participants. 

Under threat of an amendment, A.I.D. agreed to bring its allowances into line with those paid by the State Department. Has this been done? 

Answer. Yes, our allowances were made to conform to the same amounts as those paid by the State Department, effective January 1, 1973, and are continuing on this basis. 

Question. What are the monthly allowances for State and A.I.D. participants in the following four cities: Washington, D.C.; Cambridge, Massachusetts; Austin, Texas; and Portland, Oregon? And do you have comparable figures for

American students at institutions in these cities? 

Answer. Maintenance allowances for students sponsored by the State Department and A.I.D. in the first three cities are $300 a month. In Portland, Oregon, the allowance is $255.

According to university officials, the minimum comparable figures for American students are as follows: 

George Washington University, Washington, D.C--- 

Harvard University, Cambridge, Mass--.

Portland State University, Portland, Oreg--. $257 330 222 215 It should be noted that A.I.D. participants, unlike American students, are not permitted to supplement their incomes because of the terms of their J-1 visas.

JUSTIFICATION 

Senator CHILES. Mr. Murphy, please justify this item for us. I am curious to know if there are any limitations to the type of assistance that can be provided under this category. 

Mr. MURPHY. Mr. Chairman, I have a short statement which I will start to read and I will welcome interruptions at any point. 

Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, the Congress has authorized $53 millon for AID's fiscal year 1975 program "to help solve economic and social development problems in fields such as transportation, power, industry, urban development, and export development." (Section 106 of the Foreign Assistance Act) and appropriation of the full authorization level is requested. 

The fiscal year 1975 program totals $62.6 million. It is apportioned as follows:

As the energy crisis reminds us, not all urgent problems of the developing countries, and not all critical measures to improve the life of the poor in these countries, fall precisely within our three main areas of program concentration. 

We have, however, made a careful and determined effort to reduce the request in this category to a minimal level and the statistics bear out the results of AID's programing shift: In fiscal year 1973 we obligated $220 million in this category, and we anticipate $143 million to be our fiscal year 1974 level as compared to our proposed fiscal year 1975 program of $63 million. 

The program includes projects in the following major areas: 

Urban development; industry; science and technology; transportation; feasibility studies. 

URBAN DEVELOPMENT 

A $20 million loan for earthquake-related reconstruction in Nicaragua is the largest single project proposed for this funding category. 

The funds will support the rebuilding of Managua on a more functional pattern better able to permit government services to reach the

city's inhabitants. Loan funds will be concentrated on community improvements and infrastructure that will insure low population densities and an orderly expansion of the reconstructed city. 

Another important project in this category is the $3.5 million loan to provide seed capital to establish a central savings and loan bank in Honduras. This new national housing bank is expected to have a substantial impact on alleviating the growing housing deficit faced by 

Honduran families.

INDUSTRY, SCIENCE, AND TECHNOLOGY 

Two $5 million loans are proposed (to Korea and Colombia) to establish scientific and technological standards for local industrial and agricultural production and to promote the application of scientific research.

AID is also supporting research and advisory assistance by a variety of American institutions and organizations designed to increase the pace at which technology is transferred and adapted to LDC's. This is becoming increasingly important in the energy field where AID will assist LDC's in evaluating alternatives for meeting projected energy requirements.

TRANSPORTATION 

In Africa a $6 million loan is proposed for Tanzania as the final contribution to the Tanzania-Zambia Highway, an essential link in the movement of copper and other commodities from Zambia to the Port of Dar es Salaam. The as yet uncompleted section is the primary means of access to the large areas of Tanzania's southern highlands where livestock and cereal production are being developed. 

FEASIBILITY STUDIES 

As part of our effort to redirect AID's activities to the three primary concentration sectors we are including in this category about $1 million to finance project development studies in Asia and Africa. 

I appreciate the opportunity to make this statement, Mr. Chairman. 

My colleagues and I would be happy to answer your questions. 

FISCAL YEAR 1974 PROJECTS 

Now, in response to your opening remark, Mr. Chairman, I think I should say that we have regarded fiscal year 1974 basically as a year of transition.

In previous fiscal years very substantial sums were included in AID's appropriations and used for capital projects in this category. 

In this year we have much less, but still a substantial sum as compared to what is being requested for fiscal year 1975. 

We have a number of instances, for example, where power generation was financed in the previous years, say, fiscal year 1975, but the transmission and distribution facilities necessary to make that generated power useful were not done, so we did those. 

We had an instance of a large bridge in Africa where a substantial amount of money had been spent in preplanning and doing the design and engineering, and in 1974 we put in the money to build the bridge.

In other words, it was an effort to try to complete projects that were well along from previous funds but unless something further was done there would be no useful output from the projects. 

Senator CHILES. But you are not initiating any new capital projects now?

Mr. MURPHY. No, we are not initiating any new capital projects in the selected development problems category, Mr. Chairman. We are also eliminating the program loan variety of activities. We have only one program loan in fiscal year 1975 and in previous years there used to be substantial amounts. 

PROGRAM LOANS 

Senator CHILDS. Where is your program loan now?

Mr. MURPHY. In Sudan. 

Senator CHILES. What do you anticipate the continuation of that to be?

Mr. MURPHY. The amount for that I believe is $10 million, and it will probably be the final loan of that type, Mr. Chairman. 

Senator CHILES. What field is it in, agriculture?

Mr. MURPHY. It is a program loan designed to finance essentially imports. 

Mr. ADAMS. It is a balance-of-payments loan. 

Senator CHILES. And your $6 million for Tanzania is a completion loan again? 

Mr. ADAMS. Yes, sir; that is correct.

TANZANIAN HIGHWAY PROJECT 

Senator CHILES. As I understand, in the highway project a need arises due to claims brought by construction contractors against the Government of Tanzania for some $12 million. Do you believe the 

United States has the liability on these particular claims? 

Mr. MURPHY. I will ask Dr. Adams also to answer that, Mr. 

Chairman. 

Mr. ADAMS. We feel, sir, that the claims relate to valid problems which arose during the achievement of the project. For that reason, we have reserved an amount of $6 million to assist the Government of Tanzania to resolve the claims between itself and the contractor. The settlement concerns problems which arose in constructing a road which was more difficult to build than was initially anticipated. 

Senator CHILES. You note that additional claims may be made. Do you have any idea of how much they might be?

Mr. ADAMS. No, sir, we do not. Our estimate, of $6 million is a reserve for the U.S. contribution to assist the Government in resolving these claims. 

Senator CHILES. What have your claims people or your auditors said as far as what they feel Tanzania's legal liability is on these claims? Many times contractors get into difficulty because of weather or some unforeseen thing, but generally speaking, when they have entered into a contract to bid on the job, many times they are the ones that have to suffer the loss. I am trying to figure out whether there is a legal basis here or is this something out of which we are just bailing the contractor?

Mr. ADAMS. No, sir, I don't think it is a circumstance where we are trying to favor the contractor. We have done everything we can to provide encouragement, both to the contractor and the Tanzanian Government to undertake arbitration and try to find the most appropriate means for resolving the additional charges which the contractor wants to extract.

The assessment that we have made has been that in actually building the road, there were technical problems, engineering-designing problems, also problems of supply which were not anticipated and arose out of quíte justifiably more complex undertakings than either the government or the contractor were fully aware of when the project was first begun. It is in this context and without attempting to prejudge the outcome of the arbitration, that the concerns do appear to be legitimate ones which can be settled by arbitration and hopefully with justice both to the contractor and to the Tanzanian Government. 

SIZE OF CLAIMS 

Senator CHILES. Well, when we set aside the sum of $6 million, isn't that going to be what it is going to come out to, the claim is going to be in that amount once we have identified that is what the pot is? 

I mean, aren't we anticipating this before the fact? Maybe we ought to wait and see what the arbitration comes out with before we start appropriating some money.

Mr. MURPHY. Well, this is in the nature of a contingency item, Mr. 

Chairman, and there has been no decision to spend $6 million on this item.

We do want to wait until we see how the claims are finally adjudicated before deciding whether, and if so, to what extent it would be necessary for the United States to help out in this matter. 

Senator CHILES. I used to litigate a lot of claims with insurance companies, and if I ever knew what they had set aside for their reserve on that claim, I would have a good idea of what I could shoot for.

The lawyer on the other side always tried to keep me in the dark as to what they had and I always tried to find out what they had. 

I think if you set aside $6 million you are telling that contractor and his lawyers exactly what the pot of gold is. 

Mr. MURPHY. Well, we are certainly telling him what the limitation on any U.S. contribution to it could be, but his claim is double that amount at this point and it is possible that it will be negotiated downward, so that I think probably it is unlikely, Mr. Chairman, that we will negotiate it down as low as $6 million. 

Senator CHILES. I just bet you anything it will never be negotiated less than $6 million. 

Mr. ADAMS. Mr. Chairman, I can appreciate very much the kind of concern that you raise and the risk that you properly call to our attention. The one thing that is fundamental to consider is the Tanzanian Government's interest in not incurring obligations which are not justifiable. They will have as keen or even a more keen interest than ourselves in trying to make sure that the settlements do not add to the cost of the road. Also, one would hope that in having the elements of contention open to arbitration, that the arbitrators would

set the framework within which the claims can be regarded as just or unjust.

Mr. MURPHY. And, of course, this is a loan, Mr. Chairman, and to the extent that any part of it is used, the Tanzanian Government will have the responsibility of servicing the debt and in those circumstances they should be trying very hard to keep it at a minimum. 

Mr. ADAMS. They have. 

Senator CHILES. What is the interest rate on the loan?

Mr. MURPHY. It would be a typical development loan as in the past. 

I believe it is 2 percent for the first 10 years and 3 percent thereafter. 

FIXED-COST REIMBURSEMENT 

Senator CHILES. I note that in our report last year the committee spoke of the fixed-cost reimbursement method, saying that "the Committee strongly believes that the Agency for International Development should make greater use of the fixed-cost reimbursement method for dispensing economic assistance. ***" "To distinguish this method from traditional cost reimbursement methods, it should be noted that actual costs are not reimbursed. Other methods usually involve the incurring of costs by the assisted government for some agreed purpose, the submission of vouchers by the assisted government to AID evidencing the costs and legitimacy thereof, the auditing of the vouchers by AID, and the reimbursement. 

This approach tends to emphasize costs rather than projects.' 

I guess this is again one of cost rather than- 

Mr. MURPHY. That is right. I should say that Administrator Parker has directed some remarks to this subject in a previous session, Mr. 

Chairman, in which he indicated that we are very conscious of this committee's preference as expressed in that report. We have continued to use that technique in the Philippines, where it was first applied, we are now extending to Bangladesh, and we hope that we will also be able to use it in Pakistan this coming year, and we are well along the road on an agreement with the Indonesians, so that we are conscious of this.

We see some very definite advantages to it in specific situations where large amounts of local currency are involved and the supplies and materials and services can be obtained locally, and we are now looking at each project from the standpoint of whether or not it will lend itself to this particular kind of technique. 

Senator CHILES. On this particular project, of course, you wouldn't be here asking for $6 million if it had been a fixed-cost reimbursement project.

In other words, this is after the fact. 

Mr. MURPHY. Well, I believe it was started long before the committee expressed its preference.

Senator CHILES. I don't say that it didn't start before, but it would seem to me that particularly a highway project could be a very good indicator fixed cost.

Mr. MURPHY. I must agree it sounds logical and we are, in fact, going to use that technique in Indonesia next year on a road project there, so what the difference between that road project and this one might be, I don't know. But I do understand that there is some substantial

foreign exchange costs in this particular Tanzania project, and a foreign contractor involved. 

Senator CHILES. We may want to submit some other questions to you in this regard if we can. 

PREFEASIBILITY STUDIES IN YEMEN 

Prefeasibility studies in Yemen originally funded in 1973 are to be continued this year under AID's budget request of $416,000. In the past, funding for this project has been utilized to study the feasibility of tobacco industry improvements, of extending water systems in the city of Taiz, of dairy production, of tropical horticulture, and the feasibility of conducting a feasibility study on the Taiz airport. In fiscal year 1975, funding proposed for this project is to be allocated to help the government in Yemen "identify high-priority projects in important areas." 

What does that mean?

Mr. MURPHY. I will have to ask Mr. White to respond to that, Mr. 

Chairman. 

Mr. WHITE. We have used this project to identify areas of potential investment for the Yemeni. The Yemeni are in the fortunate position of having offers, and considerable offers in some instances, of assistance from other donors which they are unable to make effective use of because of the lack of basic feasibility work. These offers come from some of their neighbors. What we have been trying to do with this modest project is to identify particular project possibilities which might be eventually translated into investments using these other funds. For example, it could include groundwater development, which is an area that the Saudi Arabians are interested in financing, and so on.

Senator CHILES. What is the cause of a $300,000 overrun of estimated total cost and how is that justified? 

Mr. WHITE. I would not term the $300,000 as an overrun. It is really that the number of studies and their cost exceeded our estimate of a year ago. 

Senator CHILES. What studies have you completed?

Mr. WHITE. We have completed the pre-feasibility study on the construction of the airport at Taiz and the study of the tobacco industry.

The major study which we will have underway soon is for the expansion of the Taiz water supply system. That will be a major study which will be done during this next year. 

SAVINGS AND LOAN ACTIVITY IN HONDURAS 

Senator CHILES. AID requests $3,500,000 as seed money for establishing a savings and loan system in Honduras. The request is based on the assertion that the loan will assist in alleviating the growing deficit of middle- or low-middle income housing. 

Is it true that this Honduras saving and loan system is to be linked to the Central American Bank for Economic Integration, and that institutions' low-cost housing program? 

Mr. MURPHY. Mr. Kleine, will you respond?

Mr. KLEINE. Mr. Chairman, the institution will be an independent institution of Honduran nationality similar to about 18 other national savings and loan systems that have been established throughout Latin America.

It will relate to CABEI, the Central American Bank for Economic Integration, to the extent that CABEI may have housing investment guarantees for the Central America area and as projects are worked out, it would provide a channel for the utilization of those resources. 

It may also sell some of its mortgages to CABEI. 

CABEI has become increasingly involved in the Central American housing scene in terms of developing a secondary mortgage market and, as that is developed, the Honduran savings and loan system, as well as other systems in the area, will be able to benefit. 

Senator CHILES. I refer you to the grant activity data for the Central American program, page 205, Latin America program volume. 

I note that the home finance system will be based upon commercial interest rate mortgages. 

Are the poor able to obtain commercial mortgages? What is that commercial mortgage rate? 

Mr. KLEINE. The commercial rate? The rates vary, of course, with the availability of capital, but normally the rate that has been used through the savings and loan systems and the secondary mortgage market has been around 12 percent. While that seems relatively high, the fact is that this has been the only way in which long-term mortgage money has been made available.

Other than that, without this kind of facility, funds for housing have been available for much shorter periods of time and at higher interest rates.

LOW-INCOME HOUSING 

Senator CHILES. Which income group in Central America faces the most critical housing shortage?

Mr. KLEINE. I would say, Mr. Chairman, that it is the lower and lowest income categories that face the greatest requirement, the largest numbers who need housing. The savings and loan system does not yet reach out to these lowest income areas. 

We are attempting through the savings and loan system and through the use of the housing investment guaranty program to reach deeper and deeper into those categories. These are efforts that are under way and have not yet demonstrated themselves. So far, in order to reach the lowest income levels, subsidized housing financing has generally been necessary. The amounts required have been so large that governments by and large have not been able to sufficiently expand the subsidy in housing to pick up this requirement. We are, however, attempting to develop methods to provide low-income housing at commercial rates. 

We did, as you know, address this question, Mr. Chairman, in the 

Nicaragua low-cost housing loan under the disaster program, but that is not the normal function of the savings and loan system with which we are working to try to dip more deeply into that lowest income category. 

Senator CHILES. What kind of requirements are we setting forth or are we trying to see in the charter of savings and loan institutions to see that there is some dip made into the area?

Mr. KLEINE. The institutions, sir, are increasingly under pressure from their governments to address this need. They know that insofar as additional resources through the housing investment guarantee are concerned they will be made available in connection with serious efforts in this regard. 

What has been done in the savings and loan system thus far has been, I think, quite commendable in providing housing for the middle and lower-middle income range through systems, as I mentioned earlier, that have been set up in many countries of Latin America. 

But the large area of low-income housing is one that has not yet been addressed in a way that can show concrete results. 

Where governments have become sufficiently financially well off, such as in Brazil, they have been allocating budgetary and other resources available to reach out, but usually government budgetary structures are not quite as strong, and they are not able to take on the burden of providing subsidized housing for the great numbers that require it. It just has been thus far beyond their means. 

Senator CHILES. I think the concern is that in many of these countries that I have visited it seems that there is pretty good middleincome housing and a lot of construction going on in most of the cities and towns that I go to in the middle-income housing range. 

Of course, there are the poor conditions in the lower housing range. 

Somehow it seems that this middle income group is getting the money for construction starts or certainly housing is going on in that range, and so these programs perhaps facilitate or further encourage that as opposed to trying to get help where the most pressing need is. 

Mr. KLEINE. I share your views on this, Mr. Chairman. I should mention another approach that is being utilized by governments as well as external donors, and that is what is called the sites and services approach to the housing needs of very low levels of income, where they already have some very rudimentary kind of facility. 

The government provides sewage systems and some kinds of community services, As the individuals acquire some additional capital, they can borrow from a central source to develop their housing structure. This has been done in Colombia to some degree and I know it has been done in Brazil. Given our focus we expect we will be operating in the future in this housing field to find innovative ways to reach out. 

This system in Honduras in a sense completes a phase of association with the savings and loan system and support for the middle-income range in Latin America. This is the last of the savings and loan systems that would be set up under our program but it will help meet a need that does exist for the middle and lower-middle income group in Honduras.

Senator CHILES. I agree. I am glad that it completes it because certainly you are dealing with something that can be beneficial but I think that we can be of greater benefit if you do things like working on sites and services. 

SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY LOAN 

The committee finds that it is exceedingly difficult to assess the appropriateness of a $5 million loan request for Colombia under the broad title of science and technology.

Will you provide information with regard to specific programs we finance? What are the financial incentives about which you speak and how will they strengthen relations between the United States and Columbia universities and technical institutes in the private sector? 

Mr. KLIENE. The area of science technology and transfer of technology and science to Latin America is one area which has attracted the most keen interest of Latin Americans these past years. 

This was very evident, for example, Mr. Chairman, in the meetings that were held between Secretary Kissinger and the foreign ministers of Latin America during this spring and the recent sessions of the 

OAS General Assembly. 

In Latin America they are reaching the point where they feel that they have got to set up within their own national economies ways in which they can adapt more readily the science and the research results that are available, particularly in the United States, as well as elsewhere. Some of the countries have reached the stage where selected institutions are at a level where they can reach out and adopt new practices more readily than was the case some years ago. 

We have had one approach in this connection in Brazil that was launched a couple of years ago. Colombia is at that level of development where it needs and can utilize the facilities for linking the universities and-research institutes-in Colombia with those of the United States. This project would provide linkages between Colombian institutions and U.S. institutions, and will provide means of financing the adoption of new technology to Colombian needs. 

The precise elements of this loan proposal have not yet been worked out. There has been evidence of keen interest, as I mentioned, by the 

Colombians. The new government will be taking power in August and we anticipate that in discussions at that time the outlines of the project will become more clear. 

But this does meet an identified need, one which the United States has been looked to and is being looked to by Latin Americans with a great deal of interest and attention. 

TRANSFER OF TECHNOLOGY 

Senator CHILES. Well, in the area of transferring technology I happen to feel that that is one of the areas that we should be involved in AID.

I also feel that we ought to be allowing the country to decide what kind of technology it wants to transfer. We really should not be trying to sell our wares abroad in a broad shopping catalog or something like that because I think we have kind of done that in the past, and I am concerned about this project, whether again it is selling our wares or whether we are going to sit back and wait until Colombia decides what kind of technology they need from us. 

Mr. KLEINE. I fully agree, Mr. Chairman. The program will aim at enhancing the ability of the Colombians, through their institutions, to make their own decisions and to make their own choices as to the kind of technology that Colombia needs.

It is not directed at facilitating the promotion of our technology or that of any other country for its own sake. This is a build-up of the institutional capacities of Colombia to do exactly what you have in mind, sir.

Senator CHILES. I hope so. I hope it is not just to give them the appetite to see all of the wares that we have, to invite them to open the whole area, wherein they ought to be thinking about certain things that they need.

Mr. KLEINE. Right now much of Latin America feels it is at the mercy of those who travel from various developed countries selling certain wares and certain technologies. They recognize they don't have the ability to sort these out. 

They have a feeling they are being sold these technologies at exorbitant costs or being sold second-class technology at first-class rates when there already exists a new technology. It is this sense of frustration which has motivated them to put the question of technology so high on their agenda.

Mr. BERNSTEIN. Mr. Chairman, I might add that to help prepare. the ground for the kind of approach that you are mentioning, some of the central activity in this area is designed to help the countries of Latin America and other countries that are in position to do this to develop the kind of institutional strengths that they need in order to do their own selecting and their own adaptation of technology. 

For example, some of the funds here are to continue an activity in which the Denver Research Institute, collaborating with an association of industrial research institutes around the world, is working with developing-county members to train industrial research managers helping them to pick up the skill of relating that research to the practical needs of the industry-to do contract research for industry. This is a skill in which the United States excels and which is absent in most of these countries. 

They have industrial research institutions, they have some people with some pretty good disciplinary training, but they aren't adept at this process of adaptating technology to needs of specific companies. 

We are also working through Georgia Tech which is very strong in the small-industry area, particularly small rural industries-to help developing-county industrial service institutions build the capability to do selection and adaptation of technology for rural industry, with the idea that this would be followed by country activity which would apply these skills. The whole approach is designed to help get around the problem Mr. Kleine was talking about, where they feel kind of helpless if people come in with technology and they have to take it as is. The effort is to develop their capability to select. 

AGRICULTURAL RESEARCH GRANT 

Senator CHILES. AID proposes to grant $100,000 to Ghana for science, research and development. 

As I understand the project narrative, U.S. assistance would be limited to research in the agricultural and agro-industrial sector. 

Why, then, is this project not incorporated into the food production and nutrition function category of the bill?

Mr. ADAMS. What we are principally aiming to do there, Mr. Chairman, is to build upon the very excellent kind of cooperation that has begun between the National Academy of Sciences and the Coordinating Council of Scientific Research Institutes within Ghana. As outlined in the project sheet, the main objective is to strengthen Ghana's capability to improve the functioning of its own scientific

network. Therefore, we put the project in the category of selected development problems rather than listing it as being under the category of food and nutrition. It has a spinoff benefit which touches an area of the interests that Ghana has in improving its overall scientific capacity and building an evolving relationship between the National Academy of Sciences and the council. 

LOAN TO KOREA 

Senator CHILES. Why is AID proposing to award a $5 million loan to Korea for development of uniform standards and quality control assistance? Korea has the second highest per capita gross national product of all the Asian countries receiving assistance. Isn't it possible for the Korean Government to underwrite this undertaking? 

Mr. WHITE. The Koreans are relatively advanced on the industrial side. They have done extremely well in terms of moving exports in international markets. But they continue to have problems of meeting international standards in terms of measurements and levels of quality. 

The Koreans continue to have difficulties moving products at quality levels that meet international standards. We look at this project as one which is appropriate at this stage of Korea's development as we look to complete our own program. We would be helping to build a capacity for them to continue their strong export performance in the future.

An ability to meet quality standards is something that is lacking at this time. We think that the project would leave them in a much stronger position to continue the good growth and good performance that you have noted.

Senator CHILES. When do you anticipate that we would be completing our AID programs in Korea?

Mr. WHITE. I think in the relatively near future as we look ahead. 

Senator CHILES. That wasn't too definitive. 

Mr. WHITE. Pardon?

Senator CHILES. I didn't get a year out of that. 

Mr. WHITE. Well, the Koreans have received a setback from the energy problem. That is something that we want to take another look at. But it is possible that 1975 might be the last year. 

Senator CHILES. In 1975.

Mr. WHITE. For the loan program. 

Senator CHILES. Are you not requesting a loan funding before completion of project feasibility studies? 

Mr. WHITE. In Korea?

Senator CHILES. In Korea. 

Mr. WHITE. No. We have a feasibility studies loan under which we do the basic work to identify the feasibility of a further loan, or we have done enough work ourselves to believe that a loan is possible in fiscal year 1975. 

Mr. MURPHY.  

Senator CHILES. Thank you very much.

QUESTIONS SUBMITTED BY SENATORS INOUYE AND BROOKE 

The following questions will be inserted in the record at this point. [The questions and answers follow:]

QUESTIONS SUBMITTED BY SENATOR INOUYE SELECTED DEVELOPMENT PROBLEMS 

Question. A.I.D. proposes to grant $100,000 to Ghana for Science Research and 

Development. As I understand the project narrative, U.S. assistance would be limited to research in the agricultural and agro-industrial sector. Why, then, is this project not incorporated into Food Production and Nutrition functional category funding?

Answer. The project aims at strengthening both Ghana's research capability and the functioning of its own scientific network through experience in research on specific development problems affecting food production and nutrition. It will also continue the evolving relationship between the U.S. National Academy of 

Sciences and the Ghanaian Council for Scientific and Industrial Research. The project was therefore included in the Selected Development Problems functional category.

GHANAIAN SCIENCE FOUNDATION 

Question. Three-quarters of this grant is given over to an initial institutional grant to a Ghanaian Science Foundation. What specific information can you provide? Is the foundation in being or is it yet to be formed?

Answer. As yet, no foundation exists. Presently research by various specialized government institutions in Ghana is coordinated under the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR). The project is now in the early design stages. Recent discussions with Government of Ghana agencies including the 

CSIR have resulted in agreement that the purpose of the project will be to develop an institutional mechanism for focusing the research capabilities of various specialized Ghanaian institutions on important development problems which cut across the specialties of these individual institutions. A foundation is one alternative mechanism. Another could be the strengthening of the role and capacity of the CSIR itself. The project will include technical services to assist the Government of Ghana to determine the best alternative for managing their research in order to increase its relevance for development. It will be designed to develop, in the process of research on particular problems, effective research management and coordination. The first specific problem which has been identified for research is the decertification of the northern regions of Ghana. 

Question. A.I.D.'s Grant Activity Data for a $650,000 Asia Regional Grant is vague and uninformative. Technical Assistance funds proposed for Program 

Development Activities include $400,000 for U.S. Technicians and $250,000 for 

Other Costs. How is this being "responsive to the mandate to improve incomes and living standards of the poorer majority?" What are these "Other Costs?"

Answer. This project will provide funding for the specialized consultant services, feasibility studies, pilot field tests and other related activities needed to effectively identify and design development projects particularly responsive to the needs of the poorer majority. In FY 1974, for example, this project provided the funding for sending two poultrymen to the Yemen Arab Republic to assist the Yemen Government in designing a project to establish small farmer flocks of poultry. It also paid for two agricultural economists to travel to Nepal to help design a project to assist small impoverished hill farmers to improve productivity by the use of improved production technology. Next year it could be used to finance consultant services or pilot studies leading to a project to effectively extend low cost health services to rural poor now having little or no access to health services. Another need this project will meet is to provide funding for travel and conference costs to permit key Asian development planners and U.S. and other foreign specialists to exchange experiences on, for example, ways of increasing small farmers' participation in agricultural development programs. 

The "Other Cost" element of this project would include such items as confer. ences and rural development seminars, the costs of pilot studies, and consultant and technician support costs. I would also like to note, Mr. Chairman, that as the Grant Activity Data sheet for this project reflects, the $650,000 requested for FY 1975 is expected to be utilized primarily in the new areas of emphasis that is $200,000 in Food and Nutrition and Rural Development; $120,000 in Population Planning and Health; $230,000 in Education and Human Resources Development; and $100,000 in 

Selected Development Problems. 

34-192 - 74 - 52

ENTENTE AFRICAN ENTERPRISES 

Question. The Agency for International Development is presently sponsoring a Central and West Africa regional project designed to provide the mechanisms necessary to successful implementation of the $7.5 million African Enterprises 

Promotion loan authorized in June 1972. The project, for which $395,000 in grant funding is requested in Fiscal Year 1975, was started in 1974 and is scheduled to be terminated in 1976.

Would not the wiser course of action for AID to have taken in structuring this development program (and future programs of a similar nature) have been to assure that the necessary mechanisms were in place before seeking the loan authorization? Is it true that full implementation has been delayed for four years?

Answer. In fact, the necessary mechanisms were in place prior to seeking authorization of the African Enterprises Promotion loan. All of the participating development banks, with the possible exception of the Dahomean Development Bank, are relatively strong organizations, have experienced personnel, are receiv-. ing direct technical assistance, and have good financial records for the past several years. Several banks have already had considerable experience in evaluating loans in the private enterprise sector. 

The principal task, therefore, is to assure that they are geared to undertake a more intensive program to promote African enterprises, that their staffs are adequate for the evaluation of the increased number of applications which the AID loan will generate, that a coordinated program of cooperation exists between the banks and the promotion centers, and that in Dahomey and Niger, where such centers do not presently exist, alternate ways are developed to assure project development and follow-through technical assistance to potential entrepreneurs. 

In short, the financial component as provided by the AID loan is the essential catalyst to permit development and strengthening of an existing program. AID's technical assistance input with a development grant will assure its success and complete utilization of the AID loan. It is not true that implementation of the program was delayed for four years.

Question. The estimated total cost is $1,090,000. Would it not have been possible for qualified nationals of the Entente countries to learn how to organize and operate the banking and coordination centers by attending established institutions in the United States-with lesser costs and greater effect? 

Answer. As alluded to in my answer to your previous question, qualified personnel have already organized and are operating the development banks and private enterprise promotion centers. Several of the promotion centers have already made an impressive start in organizing training programs and seminars for African entrepreneurs. The funds provided in the A.I.D. grant will provide a modest amount of audio-visual equipment and training materials for continuing training programs on this businessman level. 

The failure to associate Africans more and more with their own economies can lead to a weakening of the political climate and consequent economic stagnation and retrogression. As well, the training of francophone Africans in the 

United States is more costly than in-country training because of the necessity for long-term instruction in English. 

QUESTIONS SUBMITTED BY SENATOR BROOKE TANZAM HIGHWAY 

Question. In your Congressional Presentation there is a request for $6 million for the TanZam Highway Project. This request arises from a possible need to pay the construction contractor additional funds. The Loan Activity sheet states: "Engineering and construction of the southern section of the road proved to be much more difficult than anticipated, and as a result, disputes have arisen between the construction contractor and the Government of Tanzania regarding payment for additional construction costs. The contractor has presented claims amounting to some $12 million."

The Data Sheet goes on to state: "Since the claims are still under discussion. 

A.I.D. has no means of predicting the results of these claims; however, it would appear to be prudent to anticipate that some awards could be made to the contractor and to provide for this contingency." You then request $6 million for this purpose.

My question is: Exactly what type of commitment do we have in this project that would necessitate the granting of a further additional loan to cover these overrun costs?

Answer. We have no commitment to the Government of Tanzania that would necessitate providing additional loan funds to cover these overrun costs. However, there are several factors which bear on our decision to consider extending such assistance to the Government. The TanZam Highway is an important factor in development of the southern highland area of the country which contains large areas of rich agricultural land. Tanzania is making strenous efforts to develop its rural economy and thereby raise the incomes and the standard of living of its rural people, who constitute about 90 percent of the population. Also, more recently Tanzania has suffered heavy crop losses during the past two years because of severe drought conditions and is presently using most of its available foreign exchange to purchase large quantities of food on the world market. We expect that upon completion of the arbitration of claims by the construction contractor, now in progress, the Government will request additional assistance in meeting these claims should a substantial proportion of them be awarded to the contractor. For the reasons I've mentioned, although there is no written commitment to provide additional assistance, we are prepared to give such a request sympathetic consideration. 

CONTINGENT REQUESTS 

Question. Would you supply for the record a list of all such contingency requests A.I.D. is making this year in either grant or loan program? I would like this information for all the functional categories. 

Answer. The Tan Zam Highway Project is the only one for which we are requesting contingent funding. 

DISASTER RELIEF IN NICARAGUA 

Question. I have received several letters charging that our disaster-related assistance to Nicaragua is being siphoned off into the bank accounts of government officials. In order to lay these fears to rest, would you provide us with some details as to how the proposed $20 million earthquake-related construction loan will be handled?

Answer. The transaction under the proposed AID loan for reconstruction will be subject to careful screening to ensure that our procurement procedures are being followed. There will be two types of payments made from the loan: direct payments to U.S. firms that are suppliers of equipment or technical services, and reimbursements made to the government on the basis of documented expenditures. In the first instance there will be little opportunity for AID funds to be diverted. Under the reimbursement procedure the expenditure documents provide a basis for auditing the transactions to see if the AID funds did go for the purpose intended. In September 1973 a special office of AID's Auditor General was established in Managua to monitor closely our assistance activities. Our AID 

Mission is scheduling audits of all our assistance activities to ensure that timely and comprehensive reviews are undertaken. A recent audit of the emergency relief in the immediate post-quake period has concluded that there was no evidence of diversion of U.S. inputs.
