Mr. MURPHY. 

Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, for the program in selected countries and organizations Congress has already authorized $39 million for fiscal year 1975 intended to "*** furnish assistance *** in support of the general economy of recipient countries or for development programs conducted by private or international organiza tions." (Section 107 of the Foreign Assistance Act.) The appropriation of the full amount authorized is requested. 

The fiscal year 1975 program totals $57.1 million and includes three types of activities:

Support to U.S. private and voluntary organizations, Contributions to selected international organizations, and 

Program loans.

It is apportioned as follows: Africa Asia

Latin America___. 

Centrally funded and other_ Millions $12.2 0.5 17.7 21.6 5.1 57.1 

Operating expenses----- Total 

In the past, program loans have accounted for the bulk of this category, but with the shift in AID's program emphasis away from large-scale resource transfers this account will be concentrated on support of AID's efforts to increase the contribution of U.S. private and voluntary organizations (PVO's) to economic and social development in the LDC's and assistance to the development programs of multilateral organizations (other than the United Nations, which is funded through the International Organizations appropriation). This year's $57 million program compares with levels of about $170 million in each of the last 2 years.

While these activities now represent a relatively small share of the total functional program (6 percent) we believe these programs to remain extremely important to the solution of development problems. 

U.S. private and voluntary organizations (PVO's) have a long history of working cooperatively with AID in furthering our objectives on a people-to-people basis. AID makes possible the provision of resources (including Public Law 480, title II) valued at $300 million annually to private agencies for humanitarian and technical assistance activities including a planned level of about $20 million in AID funds during fiscal year 1975. These funds will be channeled in the following manner:

As part of a special effort to involve the PVO's in a wider spectrum of community activities, AID's program includes $5 million for development program grants to strengthen the professional competence of headquarters staffs of PVO's and train overseas personnel. 

These grants will support qualified organizations in planning and implementing development activities enabling such groups to serve as development associates of AID. [In addition to the funds provided

in this account, a total of $6 million will be set aside in the other development accounts for regular bilateral project grants and loans which will be implemented by PVO's.] 

About $5 million is proposed to reimburse voluntary agencies for certain ocean freight costs. Without this support voluntary agencies would not be able to finance transport of donations made by American citizens to assist needy communities overseas. 

Slightly more than $4 million is programed to support the International Executive Service Corps (IESC), the private nonprofit organization that responds to requests from companies in the LDC's for short-term, highly skilled management advisors. These volunteers serve without salary. In fiscal year 1974, with a grant of $4 million from AID, IESC reached 650 projects; the fiscal year 1975 target is for over 700 projects. $3.75 million is planned as general funding support for the Asia 

Foundation. This experienced, privately managed organization supports important programs in the education and manpower, population, and rural development areas which effectively complement AID's own work in the Asia region. 

About $2.5 million is projected to help the work of 12 other organizations that provide important help to AID and the LDC's. These are, among others, the International Eye Foundation, the YMCA, the 

Cooperative League of the USA (CLUSA), the National Rural Electric Cooperative Association (NRECA) and Volunteers in Technical Assistance (VITA). 

Grants to selected international organizations in fiscal year 1975 (about $21 million) will include $17.7 million to support, in concert with other Western Hemisphere nations, three voluntary funds of the Organization of American States (OAS). 

Inter-American cooperation for development is stimulated by technical assistance and training programs of eight centers financed by the Special Development Assistance Fund, the Export Promotion Center, and the largest, the Special Multilateral Fund for Education, Science, and Technology whose basic science programs will be imple. mented in fiscal year 1975 by new programs emphasizing application of educational and scientific technology to specific development problems.

About $2 million is proposed for feasibility studies and projects sponsored by the African Development Bank and the Economic Commission for Africa, while $1.5 million is allocated to support of the 

Southeast Asia Development Advisory Group and CENTO develop programs. ment

In fiscal year 1974 AID plans to make four program loans totaling $139 million and in 1973 nine such loans valued at $214 million were made. In fiscal year 1975 we propose to make one loan of this type- $10 million for Sudan to finance essential imports, especially in the agricultural sector. This loan will help Sudan-whose foreign reserves are very low-overcome a serious balance-of-payments problem and bolster the IMF-aided stabilization program.

TRANSFER FOR REFUGEES AND MIGRATION

Mr. BIRNBAUM. It is section 2(c) of the Migration and Refugees 

Assistance Act of 1962. It states, "Whenever the President determines it is important to the national interest, not exceeding $10 million in any fiscal year of the funds made available for use under the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, as amended, may be transferred to and consolidated with funds made available for this act in order to meet unexpected urgent refugee and migration needs."

We have included $5 million as a possible transfer under this authority in anticipation that there might be some requirement in fiscal year 1975. In the last 3 years we have had such a requirement. 

Senator CHILES. Well, is that good policy? Shouldn't they be asking for the authorization where it is set up for instead of every time we are transferring some money, taking it out of this and putting it over there?

FOREIGN AID PROGRAMS OF RECIPIENT COUNTRIES 

Senator CHILES. I am curious about an item I noticed in the Latin 

America volume in the section dealing with inter-American organizations. I note on page 236 that the Israeli Government is providing $100,000 to the joint inter-American program. 

How prevalent is this? How many countries receiving U.S. foreign assistance have foreign aid programs of their own? And how large is the foreign aid program of Israel? 

Mr. MURPHY. This is a question, Mr. Chairman, which will require us to do some research in order to give you a full response and if wẹ may we would like permission to insert the response in the record at this point. 

Senator CHILES. Thank you. 

 FOREIGN AID PROGRAMS OF RECIPIENT COUNTRIES 

Virtually all countries make at least small contributions to the UNDP and to various other international aid giving institutions. This is normally a requirement for membership. Many countries also provide official credit to promote their exports and it is sometimes difficult to distinguish between that credit intended exclusively to promote exports and that with broader aid objectives. 

Of the countries receiving U.S. economic assistance in FY 1974, at least nine including Brazil, India, Nigeria, Venezuela and Israel also have on-going foreign aid programs of their own, including technical assistance, capital assistance or in some cases both. Israel budgeted about $6 million in 1974 for its foreign aid program. From the inception of its program in 1958 Israel has provided about 4,000 advisors and 15,000 fellowships involving some 80 countries in Africa, Asia and Latin America at an average of up to $10 million per year. 

In addition to the foregoing, some other countries including Kenya, the Philippines and Korea provide limited technical assistance, primarily to neighboring countries, mostly in the form of fellowships and facilities for training in host country institutions.

U.S. CONTRIBUTION TO OAS 

Senator CHILES. Projected U.S. contributions to the Organization of American States sponsored development programs for fiscal year 1975 total some $17 million. This represents the U.S. share amounting to 66 percent of total payments by member states. 

In view of the committee's desire to lighten the disproportionate burden the United States has carried in international organizations, how do you justify the United States carrying two-thirds of the cost of these programs? 

Mr. MURPHY. Mr. Kleine will answer that, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. KLEINE. The two-third to one-third ratio has been in being for 

OAS voluntary funds since 1965. Its adoption represented an improvement from the situation in the early 1960's, when voluntary technical assistance funds were supported exclusively by AID grants. There have been examinations of the cost-sharing formula matter periodically. We do feel that no one multilateral organization should depend on any one member for a predominant share of its financing. 

However, until it becomes more clear to all that the relative financial situation of individual member states has changed significantly, or new members do join, it appears that the prospect of achieving agreement with the other members on a reduced share is not very great. 

In terms of the per capita wealth and overall resources of the United States compared with the resources of Latin America, this ratio is not out of line. For example-

AFRICAN DEVELOPMENT BANK 

It is my recollection that in fiscal year 1974, Congress refused to approve your request for an African development bank-I think the sum was $10 million-to the President's proposal for U.S. contributions to international financial institutions now pending before the Congress.

It is the committee's view that this is the proper medium for allocating U.S. funding to international banks. Do you agree or disagree with the committee's position?

Mr. MURPHY. I agree with the committee's position, Mr. Chairman. 

There is a device that is established for making contributions to international financial institutions that is different than this, and I will have to ask Mr. Adams if he can explain why this particular one is in this program for fiscal year 1975. 

Mr. ADAMS. Mr. Chairman, we are really talking about two institutions. There is one, the regular program of the African Development Bank. There is also a request by the African Development Bank in which they have a particular interest in hoping the United States will join other donors in participating in the Development Fund. 

The African Development Bank proper is totally owned by the African governments themselves. It is only within the organization that constitutes the Fund that non-African nations have a role and are members.

What we have been attempting to do with respect to the opinion which you have just expressed a need, a very urgent need, for U.S. participation in both aspects of what is a major effort by the African governments. That would anticipate the United States participating in the Development Fund and also in contributing to the regular capital of the Bank. We would propose a loan of $10 million as a contribution to the regular capital of the Bank, which would enable the Bank to maintain and accelerate what has been an increasing growth in its capacity to place loans for infrastructure and development programs in 31 African countries.

The need for the Fund or the soft loan aspect of the Bank's program is made particularly urgent by the very special problems of some of the poorer of the African countries, those which are suffering extreme drought as well as those who face extreme development problems arising out of the energy crisis. When one looks at both, the Fund as well as the lending program which is projected for the regular capital program of the Bank, we find that this is small in comparison to the total need. Hopefully, the Congress would consider and view favorably the intervention on the part of the United States in both aspects of what has been a major effort on the part of the Africans themselves to help themselves.

Senator INOUYE. We are well aware of the special problems of the 

African Continent and I can assure you that the subcommittee will do whatever it can to assist people in that continent. 

However, I still cannot understand why this was singled out for this treatment instead of going through the regular route. Other banks are also involved in developmental loans.

I see really from the standpoint of procedure and organization very little difference between this bank and, say, the Asian Development Bank.

Mr. ADAMS. In the sense of there being two institutions, sir? The 

Fund does include both the African governments as well as the various countries of the developed world, and the regular African Development Bank is a separate institution which is run by the African countries themselves.

Mr. BIRNBAUM. Sir, if I may make a contribution. In the case of the 

Asian Development Bank or Inter-American Development Bank, we do subscribe to the capital, both paid-in and callable as well as making grants for soft loans which enable the banks to expand their operations. In the case of the African Development Bank, the member countries said that they would not allow developed countries to participate in the capital subscription. 

However, in an effort to help the African Development Bank in meeting the needs other than soft loan needs, we are proposing a development loan directly to the Bank. 

We feel it will serve a number of purposes. 

One, given the new directions that the Congress has identified in the Foreign Assistance Act, we would no longer be making loans for infrastructure, such as railroads, roads, and ports. This loan would be one way that we could help the Bank finance some of these harder loans.

We would then be able to reduce our activities in these areas and also strengthen this institution. 

Rather than our dealing with a series of small loans to small African countries, we intend to put this money into the Bank and this, as Dr. 

Adams was saying, in lieu of a capital contribution. We have no intention of making a capital contribution to the African Development Bank as we have in the case of the Asian Development Bank and Inter-American Development Bank.

In the short time that I have been in office-which commenced after this book was printed-I have come across a number of such situations which I think are going to require very careful study and which are going to get very careful study. 

Now, the first step in this procedure is to straighten out future loans, and the Administrator has signed a policy directive which, you

may recall, he referred to in his statement earlier before your committee, which is designed to really tighten up on the administration of future loans and that is only part of the exercise, but that part, Mr. 

Chairman, will put us in the position where any unconscionable delays in any of the loans steps, whether it be in time required between the time the loan was authorized and the time it was signed, or the time from when it was signed, until the time the conditions precedent to disbursement had been met, and then the time for disbursement of the loan will be under constant control and review. 

Now, the second part of this exercise is to go back and look over the inventory as of June 30, 1974, and we fully intend to do this, loan by loan, and to determine whether or not there is justification for retaining these loans in the active category, rather than deobligating or de authorizing the funds that are reserved for them.

U.S. GRANTS INVOLVING EGYPTIAN POUNDS 

Mrs. Sadat, wife of the Egyptian President, is the head of the Loyalty and 

Hope Society (Wafaa wa'l Amal), a humanitarian organization which, we understand, is undertaking the construction of a large treatment and rehabilitation center. This center is a humanitarian effort, being built for the purpose of relief and rehabilitation of the sick and injured, including victims of the recent hostilities. We understand the local currency amounts, £ 5,556,000 (U.S. $10 million), are to be used for local procurement of supplies and equipment and other local costs associated with activities of the center. Details concerning the authority under which the grant was made are included in the attached Justification for Presidential Determination as published in the March 18 FEDERAL REGISTER. 

In addition to the grant described above, there are two other grants involving Egyptian pounds: One for £ 5,556,000 (U.S. $10 million) was made to the 

Egyptian Government for use in assisting persons displaced by war along the border areas; the other for £ 1,667,000 (U.S. $3,000,000) was made available to the U.S. Navy for use in clearing the Suez Canal. We expect that there will be other uses to which these excess local currencies can be put in the future. However, these uses have not, as yet, been identified. 

JUSTIFICATION FOR PRESIDENTIAL DETERMINATION TO PERMIT GRANT TO EGYPTIAN CHARITABLE ORGANIZATION 1/ Problem: 

Section 620 (t) of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, as amended, prohibits the furnishing of assistance in or to a country that has severed diplomatic relations with the United States until such time as diplomatic relations are resumed. While we, in Cairo, and the Egyptians, in Washington, have diplomatic personnel attached to Interests Sections of Embassies of third countries, formal diplomatic relations have not yet been resumed. Thus, Section 620 (t) remains applicable at this time. 

In addition, several other potentially applicable provisions contained in Section 620 of the Act prohibit assistance to countries in default on debts owed to United States citizens (620 (c)), countries that have expropriated assets of United States citizens (620 (e)), the United Arab Republic (620 (p)), and countries in default of debts owed to the United 

States Government (620 (q)).

Section 614 (a) of the Act permits the President to waive the foregoing prohibitions if he determines it is "important to the security of the 

United States" to do so.

Justification: 

The nature of the proposed gift of United States-owned Egyptian pounds is that of a humanitarian gift to the people of Egypt. Wafaa wa'l Amal is headed by Mrs. Sadat. The organization will use the proceeds of the grant to alleviate human suffering resulting from the recent hostilities. 

The President's intention to authorize the gift, notwithstanding the absence of formal diplomatic relations and other potentially applicable Section 620 prohibitions under the Act, is based upon the positive humanitarian and psychological impact such a contribution will have on the people and leaders of Egypt. These benefits can be expected to contribute to our current efforts to achieve peace in the Middle East. 34-192 O-74-53

Egypt is central to these efforts, and our ultimate success will inevitably depend upon Egyptian confidence in our intentions to play a constructive role in the area. This humanitarian gift, in the new, improved atmosphere of United States-Egyptian relations and in the wake of disengagement of forces in which President Sadat played a key role, will constitute a tangible demonstration of our intentions. 

Under the circumstances, it is important to the security of the United States that the grant be made without regard to the prohibitions contained in Section 620 of the FAA, and without regard to any law relating to the receipts or credits accruing to the United States. 

1/ This Justification is not a legal opinion; a legal opinion did not serve as the basis for this grant. Rather, the prohibitions of 

Section 620 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, as amended, were waived by the President, under the authority of Section 614(a) of the Act, by Presidential Determination No. 74-15 dated March 7, 1974. 

(Published in Federal Register Vol 39, No. 53, March 18, 1974, at page 10113.) In accordance with Section 652 of the Act, the 

Speaker of the House of Representatives and the Chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee were notified by letter on March 4, 1974, of this exercise of the authority of Section 614. The 

Justification was attached to each letter.

SATELLITE TECHNOLOGY IN DISASTER WARNING And AssessmENT SYSTEMS 

Question. You are requesting $70,000 for Satellite Technology in Disaster

Warning and Assessment Systems. I am very interested in this program, especially as it relates to the Sahelian Drought. Can you provide the Committee with some details as to the results of the use of the satellite imagery support in the 

Sahelian area?

Answer. Study of the application of satellite technology to existing or incipient disasters is still in an early stage. The approach being taken is to examine imagery collected over the past several years, to ascertain what actions might have been possible had the imagery been received in a timely fashion. An analysis of such data relating to a number of past disasters is shortly to be reported

upon by the U.S. Geological Survey. In addition imagery covering known disasterprone areas, characterized by repeated disasters is being assembled to provide a "before disaster" data base. From the imagery analysis we hope to obtain a clearer idea of its practical application to emergency relief operations and its potential as a part of an early warning system. We are hopeful that USGS findings will confirm that such imagery can be useful in the future in ascertaining the general magnitude of some types of disasters and also in identifying the scope of critical disaster which might otherwise require many days of aerial reconnaissance.

Through a continuous monitoring system and expert analysis the existence or expansion of dangerous drought areas might be spotted at an early stage. The value of existing satellite imagery to the Sahelian drought situation remains a question yet to be answered but intensive study is underway. 

Question. Could you make effective use of more than $70,000 in this area?

Answer. Since we are in the pilot phase of this study, it is not felt that additional funding would be useful at this time. 

Question. What other complementary programs are being carried out by other government agencies?

Answer. There are many government agencies that have related imagery programs. Some of these are: NASA-Earth Resources Satellite Technology 

(ERTS); NASA-USGS Volcano Watch covering 15 volcanos in the U.S. and in 4 foreign countries. Bureau of Land Management, Range studies in the western States; Forestry Service, Forest Management studies in Alaska; Department of Interior, Flood study of Mississippi River; National Oceanic and

Atmospheric Administration-Marine studies.

BUREAU OF INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATION AFFAIRS STATEMENT OF HON. WILLIAM B. BUFFUM, ASSISTANT SECRETARY ACCOMPANIED BY: 

JOHN MCDONALD, OFFICE DIRECTOR, COORDINATOR OF MUL- TILATERAL DEVELOPMENT PROGRAMS CHRISTIAN HERTER, SPECIAL ASSISTANT TO THE SECRETARY OF STATE ON ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS SIDNEY CUMMINS, OFFICE OF INTERNATIONAL ADMINIS- TRATION PREPARED STATEMENT 

Senator INOUYE. We have with us for the first time Hon. William 

B. Buffum, Assistant Secretary of State for International Organization Affairs. 

Mr. Secretary, welcome to the committee, sir. Your entire statement will be inserted in the record at this point.

Mr. Chairman: 

I have come before this Committee today to express my support for the President's appropriation request of $208,450,000 in Fiscal Year 1975 for voluntary contributions to sixteen international programs.

Of these, the programs for which my Bureau has responsibility total $193,750,000. 

Most of these programs are well known to the Committee. 

Among them are: 11 

UNICEF 

an the United Nations Children's Fund organization whose prompt and effective response in providing food, clothing and shelter in all types of emergency situations has earned it universal respect; the World Food Program, which provides vital food aid both to meet emergency situations and to aid long-term development; 

the United Nations Fund for Population Activities, a rapidly growing program engaged in combating rampant population growth around the globe; 88 the UN Fund for Drug Abuse Control, which is working in such fields as crop substitution, police controls and addict rehabilitation to eliminate both the supply of and the demand for illegal drugs; 10 the United Nations Environment Program, which has begun work on systems for international pollution monitoring and exchange of environmental information; 

the World Meteorological Organization's Voluntary 

Assistance Program, which enables developing countries to participate directly in programs for global monitoring of weather and atmospheric pollution; 

the International Atomic Energy Agency's Operation 

Program, which provides technical assistance to developing countries to advance the peaceful uses of atomic energy.

Along with these programs, which are playing an important role in such areas of immediate and global concern as food, population, environment and energy, are three others which for many years have played a vital role in furthering political stability in the Middle East and South Asia. They are: 

the United Nations Relief and Works Agency, which is providing essential food, housing, schooling and health services to some 1.5 million Palestinians displaced as a result of the 1948 and 1967 Arab-Israeli conflicts; 

the United Nations Force in Cyprus, which has been a necessary factor in avoiding war among both the residents of the island and the other parties directly concerned; and 

the Indus Basin Development Fund, through which eight governments are financing construction of facilities to control the waters of the Indus River system, and to provide irrigation and power to millions of residents of India and Pakistan. The Indus Basin loans and grants are the only program in this group for which my Bureau does not have direct responsibility.

Funds are also requested for such important programs as the UN Institute for Training and Research, the International Secretariat for Volunteer Service, and the UN Fund for Namibia. 

This year we are also requesting for the first time funds for a contribution to the World Heritage Trust Fund. Proposed by 

President Nixon in 1971 and ratified by the Senate on 

December 7, 1973, this fund aims at protecting, preserving and restoring cultural sites and natural areas of outstanding significance to all mankind.

Chief among the programs for which we are requesting funds is the United Nations Development Program--the UNDP-which, along with its predecessor organizations, the

Expanded Program of Technical Assistance and the UN Special 

Fund, has been engaged for nearly a quarter century in providing countries with the technical assistance essential to their development.

Providing technical assistance is the major ongoing activity of the United Nations in the economic development field and the primary channel for that assistance is the UNDP. With programs in over 150 countries and territories and annual expenditures approaching $400 million, the UNDP has become the world's largest and most widespread program of grant technical assistance.

The measure of the UNDP is not its size, however, but the contribution it is able to make to development. Providing aid which is more universal in character and scope than any bilateral donor could possibly provide on its own, the UNDP has facilitated a broad interchange of technology, expertise and equipment and has furthered follow-up investment of benefit to recipients and donors alike. 

In the 1973 foreign assistance legislation, Congress expressed the belief that primary emphasis should be placed on assistance in agriculture, population, education and human resources development and on assisting the neediest countries. 

These are also the goals of the UNDP. 

Of the funds expended by UNDP, more than one quarter are 

Of those funds, 25 percent are in the field of agriculture. utilized in the area of applied research. Within the framework of an international consortium known as the Consultative Group on International Agricultural Research, the UNDP is helping to finance major research centers such as the Maize and Wheat Improvement Center in Mexico and the International 

Crop Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics in Hyderabad.

Research undertaken at these global research institutes and

3 at others established in cooperation with single governments, such as the Institute for Cereals and Technical Crops at Fundlea, Romania, is benefitting not only the developing countries but the developed countries as well. Scores of 

UNDP projects concerned with soil fertility and fertilizer use, plant protection, animal health and fisheries development are also helping to combat the threat of worldwide food shortages.

The development of human resources is another major field of UNDP activity. Apart from the provision made in virtually every project for the training of counterpart personnel, a considerable share of UNDP assistance is directed toward the establishment of institutions for the training of youth--as well as teachers--for work in such fields as public service, agriculture, industry and health. There has also been emphasis on educational planning and increasing attention is being given to educational reform. 

In 1973, recognition of the vital link between population control and development, the United Nations Fund for Population Activities was brought under the administrative and policy direction of the UNDP and of its Governing Council. This is a move which was advanced by the United States and supported by the vast majority of UN members. Our efforts to stimulate the growth of the Fund have also met with broad support. 

Contributions have grown dramatically and UNFPA projects are now underway in 78 countries.

Over the past few years, in accordance with the aims of the Second Development Decade, the UNDP has been engaged in an effort to provide assistance to the least developed countries which would be greater in terms of both volume and effectiveness. 

New methods have been devised, UNDP

staffing in these countries has been strengthened, and additional resources are being allocated for their benefit. 

Moving toward a goal of 25 percent of country program resources by 1977, resources currently allocated for the least developed countries now represent 22.5 percent of such funding-approximately four times the ratio for our own bilateral program. 

I might add another field of UNDP activity which is of particular importance--that of natural resources and energy. 

The total value of mineral deposits located through UNDP assisted projects is now estimated to have surpassed $20 billion.

Follow-up investment in the natural resources field in 1973 alone totalled over $1.2 billion, primarily for new sources of power. To give some idea of what this will mean to the developing world, the UNDP has reported that these new sources of power will surpass the currently installed capacity of India. In an effort to increase UNDP capability in the natural resources field, the United States has also led a successful effort to link the newly created UN Revolving Fund for Natural Resource Exploration to the UNDP in basically the same manner as the UN Fund for Population Activities. 

By plowing a portion of the receipts derived from natural resource discoveries back into the Program, it is hoped that UN mineral resource surveys will have a multiplier effect. 

As the Committee is aware, the United States and other major donors have been engaged for a number of years in furthering the ability of the UNDP to handle a substantially increased volume of technical assistance. Evaluation reports on UN assistance programs prepared by 95 foreign service posts this year give clear evidence that the reforms initiated in 1971 as a result of the Jackson Capacity Study and other

1 -= measures initiated since 1972 by the new Administrator, Rudolph Peterson, are bearing fruit.

Country programs have now been approved for 100 countries and plans are being made in many countries for the second cycle.

Annual reviews of these country programs are resulting in continuing modification of ongoing and planned assistance, with greater concentration on priority areas. All external assistance--including that of the bilateral donors--is being more closely coordinated, and several UN agencies not directly involved in the UNDP are participating in UNDP country programming exercises.

We are also encouraged by the extent to which the various UN agencies are increasingly pooling their talents to work together on such problems as drought and river blindness in 

Africa, earthquakes in Latin America, and floods in Asia.

Indications of the specific amounts of assistance which will be available during each multi-year period and a ceiling on assistance to relatively well-off countries are encouraging recipient governments to eliminate projects of lesser priority, to give greater consideration to regional projects and to projects undertaken jointly by the UNDP and other donors, and to initiate arrangements for cost sharing. 

Under the latter arrangements governments share in the foreign currency costs of projects--a cost normally borne by the UNDP alone. Iran, for example, has agreed to provide $12 million during the period 1973-1976 to pay a portion of the cost of 51 new projects in that country, thus supplementing $16 million available during this four-year period from the UNDP.

Such hard currency inputs are, of course, in addition to the counterpart contributions which made in local currency by all recipient governments. Similar arrangements, multiplying

the impact of UNDP assistance, have been undertaken in Iraq, Kuwait, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates. Funds provided by the latter three states under cost sharing arrangements now exceed the amount provided by the UNDP and these three countries also contribute more to the UNDP through voluntary contributions than they receive from the Program. Similar cost sharing is contemplated for Venezuela and a number of other countries in the coming year.

I should restate here, Mr. Chairman, a position that we have enunciated in several meetings of intergovernmental bodies, namely that despite their continuing need for technical assistance, the oil rich countries should all be at least net contributors to these international programs. The Administrator of the UNDP has just reported to the UNDP Governing Council that the governments of Iran, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela have expressed readiness to become, in fact, net contributors. 

We consider net contributor status only the first step required of the wealthier recipients and will continue to press for major contributions from them. 

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to detract in any way from the important role which our bilateral assistance program has played during the past quarter century and which it is. continuing to play. As Secretary Kissinger stated in his confirmation hearings last year however, "It has been the experience of foreign aid, and I believe it is the sense of many Members of the Congress, that American aid can now be more fruitfully channeled through multilateral institutions in many categories rather than through bilateral programs.' In response to a statement by Senator Scott that the Foreign Relations Committee was "very much interested in pursuing an expansion

of the multilateral approach whenever possible, Secretary Kissinger responded that this was consistent with his views. 

While exerting great effort during the past several years to enable the United Nations Development Program to handle an increased volume of development aid, we have increased our contribution to that program by only 4 percent. 

Other governments, on the other hand, have shown their confidence in the program by increasing their contributions by 96 percent. 

Time and again in recent years Presidential commissions and task forces and Congressional committees have recommended expanded utilization of international institutions for the delivery of U.S. development assistance. To accomplish this objective would clearly require an increase in the U.S. contribution. 

Mr. Chairman, this concludes my presentation of the

President's request for voluntary contributions to international organizations and programs in Fiscal Year 1975. I believe, Sir, it is worthy of your support. 34-192 O - 74-54

This is the United Nation's primary institution for encouraging training, resource development, and preinvestment surveys within the U.N.system.

It has gone through a period of transition in recent years under the leadership of its new director, Rudolph Peterson, formerly president of the Bank of America.

We do make the point, Mr. Chairman. that over the years the percentage of the total contributions received by the UNDP from the United States has been reduced materially.  U.S. SHARE OF OECD EXPENSES 

Contributions by Member Countries to the OECD are determined by national income statistics employing the Gross National Product for the most recent threeyear period in which definitive figures are available. This calculation is limited by the provision that no country will be assessed more than 25%. 

The 25% ceiling was adopted at United States insistence at the time the OECD was transformed from the Organization for European Economic Cooperation in the early 1960s. We insisted on the ceiling because we believed that we would otherwise have to pay a disproportionately high percentage. The matter was finally resolved in 1963 in the context of negotiations for Japanese entry into the Organization when the 25% ceiling was formalized. This ceiling has proved very beneficial to us. Without it our contribution for CY 1974 (FY 1975) would have been 47.2%.

In short, the United States percentage contribution was not reduced when Australia, Finland, and New Zealand joined the OECD because our percentage contribution was already much lower than it would have been had we not had the ceiling.

Mr. BUFFUM. The figures shown in the record for the last 2 years are somewhat misleading, Mr. Chairman, because as you have indicated, our total contribution level was at $4.8 million but the amount taken from the allocation for that fiscal year was less since there were carryover funds from previous years that were utilized. 

Senator INOUYE. We have received information to indicate that this force has been reduced by a total of 822 men, which would translate itself to a savings of about $3 million and if you take our proportion you come close to a million. 

Mr. BUFFUM. As I have suggested, Mr. Chairman, the estimated cost of the force despite the decrease in size, remains approximately the same.

I believe this is due not only to the increased costs which I have cited, but also is due to the fact that there have been substantial accumulated deficits for the United Nations in reimbursing troop contributors which are being equalized over a period of time and it is thought that the U.N. can catch up in meeting that deficit over this coming year.

Senator INOUYE. We would like to receive some justification for that if we may. 

Mr. BUFFUM. Yes, sir. 

 PAYMENT TO UNFICYP 

UNFICYP's deficit had been increasing at a rate of some $3 million per year for the past several years. As a consequence of the 25 percent reduction in 

UNFICYP troop strength completed in May 1974, UNFICYP cost esitmates for

CY 1975 have been reduced approximately $2 million a year, but some annual deficit remains. Moreover, in his most recent report, dated 22 May 1974, the

Secretary General reported an accumulated deficit in the UNFICYP Special 

Account of $19.9 million.

The major financial contributors have made no move as yet to reduce their contributions to reflect reduced costs. At the new stage of UNFICYP force levels and costs, annual income will more nearly balance annual expenditures. 

Current contributors to UNFICYP are seeking to maintain the current level of their support in order to avoid adding further to the deficits and in the hope of attracting additional contributions from other UN members. However, the U.S. has urged all concerned parties to consider significant additional reductions in UNFICYP's size, which if implemented, would markedly reduce current costs to the UN and permit a reduction in the level of U.S. support.

 U.S. PERCENT OF IN-KIND CONTRIBUTIONS TO LAEA 

The IAEA estimates in-kind contributions from all members in 1973 as totalling $2,472,558. U.S. in-kind contributions are valued at $910,059, 36.8 percent of the total. Of this amount, $804,400 was financed from the Foreign Assistance Act. 

The remainder consists of gifts of special nuclear materials from the AEC and contributions by the Export-Import Bank, AID, and AEC toward completion of a market survey of nuclear power potential in developing countries. 

We have interpreted our in-kind contributions as a special case and not a question of apportionment on a "fair share" basis. In-kind contributions generally come from the more advanced states and are contributed without regard to the in-kind contributions made by others. This is because in-kind contributions are intended to support Agency projects of special interest to the contributing state.

NUCLEAR TECHNOLOGY AND TERRORISM 

I hope you will excuse this rather lengthy background to my question, but I think it is necessary to convey the magnitude of the problem which I wish to discuss at this time. 

One of the key issues before Congress is that of assurance that nuclear power technology is developed safely and that the explosive and highly toxic fuel used in this technology can be prevented at all costs from falling into the wrong hands. 

In the gathering worldwide concern over developing resources of energy, there may be a strong temptation to overlook problems so grim and exotic as a terrorist's basement bomb. 

On May 28 my colleague, Senator RIBICOFF, had an editorial printed in the Congressional Record and that editorial reads: "The age of the home-made 'basement' nuclear bomb is upon us. The necessary materials can be stolen from nuclear powerplants, the necessary skills are widely available in the civilian economy, and the necessary information can be gotten from the public library." 

Fast breeder powerplants by the year 2000 will be generating plutonium at the rate of 1,200 tons a year in Europe and the United States and a good deal more will be generated elsewhere. 

Estimates of plutonium required to make an atomic bomb begin with as little as 13 pounds. The Atomic Energy Commission itself has conceded that 44 pounds of plutonium in the hands of skilled terrorists could result in an atomic bomb. This poses an incredible threat.

In the narrative supporting U.S. contributions to the International 

Atomic Energy Agency two statements are made which directly relate to this background I have given. The first is, "This program promotes the development of future export for U.S. nuclear equipment and material," and the second, "Many of the developing countries have only limited interest in the program of safeguards over nuclear materials . . ." 

NUCLEAR SAFEGUARDS PROGRAM 

My question is what steps are we taking to assure that the proper safeguards are implemented, because this has become a very important phase, the implementation of proper safeguards, especially in light of the recent underground explosion in India?

Mr. BUFFUM. Mr. Chairman, the administration is indeed concerned about the problem of safeguards and we have long been active in seeking to assure that they are established in countries which initiate atomic programs.

The IAEA is one of our main executing agents, if you will, to see that safeguards are applied in countries receiving assistance in the nuclear field.

We, of course, also have bilateral programs with a number of countries. We have the figures of the respective programs carried out by the IAEA and the United States bilaterally if the committee would wish to have that.

I might note that in its budget for next year the IAEA expects to expend approximately $3.8 million to develop and apply safeguards against the diversion of nuclear materials in countries which are parties to the non-proliferation treaty as well as in other countries which accept IAEA safeguards over nuclear material in their possession. 

I cite this activity, Mr. Chairman, to indicate that this is one of the major activities of the institution and one to which we have attached considerable importance. This particular safeguard program was carried out through physical verification by agency inspectors of reports submitted by participating states on nuclear material in their possession.

Under existing agreements in 1974, this calendar year the IAEA is applying safeguards in 27 different States in connection with the nonproliferation treaty and in 17 other States which have safeguard agreements with the agency.

This involves a total of 395 nuclear facilities and equipment supplied by the United States in the nuclear field is being safeguarded in 27 of these States.

The objective of the safeguards program is to defer and to detect diversion of nuclear material away from peaceful uses. The application of safeguards by an impartial and widely respected international organization such as the IAEA assures that safeguards are applied uniformly and effectively no matter what the source of the safeguarded material, and I might point out that we were pleased to be one of the major participants in the initial training of the IAEA safeguard staff. 

Therefore, I think it is fair to say, Mr. Chairman, that the IAEA safeguards thus play an important part in protecting U.S. security and meeting the kind of concerns which you have indicated and the fears that have been mentioned in your statement.

The acceptability, the implementation of these safeguards in our view may also offer a period of time to determine whether disarmament agreements going beyond a nonproliferation treaty which involve a surrender of some element of national sovereignty will prove feasible. 

The aspects of the agency's program involving safeguards, in our judgment, will continue to grow with the proliferation of nuclear powerplants, and as adherence increases to the nonproliferation treaty.

the IAEA operational program to enhance its capability of building a nuclear explosive device.

It simply was not working in that field. Nor were the IAEA safeguards applicable in the areas where they presumably obtained the fissionable material required.

CANADIAN NUCLEAR SAFEGUARDS 

Canada provided India with a large research reactor (called CIRUS) in the 1950's and, in conformity with international practice at that time, obtained assurances from India that the reactor would not be used for military purposes but only for peaceful uses. It was not until the 1960's that a formal international safeguards system was established, with the International Atomic Energy Agency being given the responsibility for carrying out safeguards inspections. Canada in later years informed India that its definition of "peaceful uses" did not include the development of so-called "peaceful nuclear explosives," but India did not acknowledge its acceptance of the Canadian position. Since the inception of 

IAEA safeguards, Canada has relied upon these safeguards in its nuclear relationship with other countries, just as the U.S. has.

CENTRALIZATION OF U.N. ASSISTANCE 

The United Nations Development System has grown without any particular plan or design. From a very modest beginning, United Nations development and humanitarian assistance is being dispensed through a complex network of organizations and programs and these consist of the U.N. and its component parts, such as UNDP, UNICEF, and about a dozen specialized agencies. Also involved are the World 

Bank, the World Food Program, and others.

The System is under the control of about 40 separate governing bodies. There is no central coordinating organization to exercise control over and direct the work of this group of organizations and agencies.

It has been suggested that there is a need for improved direction and control over activities and programs carried out under the System. 

What is the U.S. policy with regard to seeking changes in the structure of the U.N. to bring about more centralized direction control for the U.N. Development Assistance System? 

And if we do have any policy, what are we doing to improve this System? I have been told by some who have served that the organizational structure has built-in waste. This is a phrase they used. There is no concern for the usual common practice of, say, centralized purchasing, and there is no real effort to coordinate activities. As a result, you oftentimes have duplication of effort. 

Mr. BUFFUM. Mr. Chairman, I would have to concede immediately that there is a great deal to be done in coordination of the administration of economic development assistance through the U.N. family. 

There are too many autonomous bodies which are not adequately coordinated.

It is, however, a huge problem, given the independent character of some of these institutions, and the extent of the authority which can be wielded by any one supervisory instrumentality. 

We think in the first instance that this is a proper responsibility of the Economic and Social Council. We do seek through that institution

to provide some overall coordination and guidance. There is in addition an Advisory Coordinating Committee serving the Secretary General of the United Nations where the executive directors of each of these organizations meet with him-I think it is twice a year-to review their programs.

However, even this is not enough and we do wholeheartedly agree with the requirement that coordination be tightened up. The Secretary- 

General himself, I am glad to report, is concerned about this need. We will be consulting with him about it and while I do not take up the specifics of the kind of approach which we think would be practicable politically as well as administratively, it is one that is a problem to which we are giving continuing attention. 

Senator INOUYE. I appreciate that statement, sir.

Once again I welcome you to this committee and we will look forward to meeting with you often. 

I thank you, Mr. Secretary, for your assistance this morning.

Mr. BUFFUM. Thank you Mr. Chairman.

UN FINANCIAL SITUATION 

 The UN debt is currently around $90 million. What initiative is the U.S. taking in promoting a collective effort for a settlement of the debt? If the U.S. is not pushing for settlement of the debt, why isn't it?

Ambassador Buffum: The United States has consistently sought at Erd resolution of the UN financial problem. 

We played a major role, for example, in the formation of the Special Committee on the Financial Situation of the United Nations and in its work during 1972. Because of the negative USSR approach, however, the Committee 1980 aid Susain effect was able only to publicize the details of the problem. Subsequently, in order 34-192 O-74-55

to keep a constructive effort alive, we supported a resolution in the 27th General 

Assembly requesting the Secretary General to continue exploration of all possibilities for an over-all solution. His efforts led to voluntary contributions last year by Japan and the United Arab Emirates. 

The U.S. has consulted with other UN members looking toward an acceptable solution to the problem, and we shall continue to do so whenever we see an opportunity for progress. The basic ingredient for a solution, however, remains the readiness of those responsible for the deficit to make an appropriate contribution. Once that willingness has become apparent, we will wish to consult with the Congress on a suitable U.S. response.

Senator McGee .: 

Mr. Buffum 

What is the Administration's assessment of Country Programming? 

We believe country programming has been a very good thing. It has forced governments to really look at their needs, sort out priorities and allocate available resources. 

It has also done a great deal to eliminate wasteful squabbling and competition among UN agencies in each country by clearly establishing the UNDP Resident Representative as the coordinator of all UN development efforts in each country. Further, it furnishes a framework of coordination between UN and bilateral aid efforts. This is not to say that country programming is a panacea. There are differences in results from country to country and some evidence of lack of flexibility to adapt to changing circumstances or requirements. 

But UNDP is aware of these problems and country programming is an evolving system which can be modified if necessary.

controlled by the Provisional Revolutionary Government (PRG) in South Viet-Nam. 

Government policy did not allow the U.S. to participate in the special appeal and therefore no U.S. Government funds were contributed.

Is it possible to place restrictions on the use of U.S. contributions to UNICEF in order to preclude use of such contributions to fund programs in North Vietnam and the Viet Cong areas? 

Yes sir. At the 1974 Executive Board session UNICEF requested additional funds for the Indochina program which raised the total budget to $44.2 million for the period 1973 through 1975. In a statement to the Executive territory.

QUESTIONS SUBMITTED BY SENATOR INOUYE DOLLARS VS RUPEES FOR INDIA IN FY 75 

The fiscal year 1975 program presentation for India specifies several proposed purchases of equípment for agricultural production, rural electrification, and improvement of distribution systems. 

Is this dollar assistance necessary since these areas are covered, directly or indirectly, by the provisions regarding economic development of the recently concluded Indian Rupee Settlement Agreement?

They cannot be used to purchase, for example, badly needed fertilizer from abroad. QUESTIONS SUBMITTED BY SENATOR MCGEE RESEARCH CEILING 

Senator McGee: 

Mr. Murphy:

Under Section 106 of the FY 74 Appropriations Act, a $12 million ceiling was set on research funds. Is this amount sufficient to meet the existing need? 

The $12 million ceiling is not sufficient. 

The authorization and appropriation committee reports last year and the FAA of 1973 stress the need for stronger focusing of Development Assistance on the key factors impeding better lives for the mass of LDC peoples. This requires better answers for some very complex and stubborn problems. There are no ready means to accelerate agricultural yields sharply in poor countries, under tropical or semitropical conditions and in widely varying traditional rural societies. Or to provide effective health and education services to the mass of people at costs the countries can afford. Or to solve any of the basic problems faced by the developing countries.

Very little of the technology used in the U.S. and other developed countries is suitable for the very different ecological, social, economic and cultural conditions of the developing countries. A strong research and development program is essential to adapt known technologies or develop new ones to fit well the actual developing country conditions. 

AID's interregional research program is a key element in broader problem solving systems that the Agency is building to help developing countries meet their needs for better ways of growing food, for provision of basic health and education services to the bulk of their peoples, and for fuller employment and also better use of their material resources. These

systems mobilize the best U.S. scientific and technological resources to work with developed and developing country organizations addressing the same problems, and employ a variety of means to get successful R&D results applied in the developing countries. Efficient pursuit of the newly emphasizej problem solving mandate of the Foreign Assistance Act requires continuing gradual expansion of the interregional research component of these problem solving systems beyond the $12 million level at which it is now held by an appropriation ceiling. 

Since AID supports projects by annual increments of funding, and activity levels and costs have risen, most of the $12 million available under the present ceiling is required merely to sustain what is already under way. and Nutrition.

Most of the research increase in FY 1975 would go for Food Major food production and nutrition gains for developing countries are already in sight from AID generated research findings on wheat, corn and sorghum and on some key agricultural inputs. I am making available for the record a half dozen examples of major successes scored recently by AID research projects. These and other experience suggest that investment is well managed research on the key problems yields a very high return. New efforts are also planned in health, education, earth science and energy. 

The Food and Nutrition increase would investigate (1) innovative ways for approaching the problems of rural development with emphasis on the small farmer, (2) methods to conserve moisture and improve productivity in dryland agriculture, (3) new methods for microbial fixation of nitrogen which would be sufficiently more effective to supplement appreciably scarce manufactured nitrogen fertilizers, and (4) the microorganic

treatment of agriculture waste for converting into livestock feeds. 

Additional resources are needed also for on-going research on (1) improving the nutritional quality of grain crops, (2) combatting disease of legumes, e.g. bean and compea, (3) improving soybean production for use as foods in the LDCs, (4) improving market-oriented food systems, (5) producing lowcost nutritious foods, and (6) improving national agriculture and nutrition planning. Additional funds are needed in other appropriation functions for such important research as finding vaccines protective against intestinal diseases, utilizing non-professionals in teaching, and setting up hydrologic data networks. 

AID believes that it can pursue these and other research needs and integrate them most efficiently with assistance for country programs if the research ceiling is removed. This seems particularly appropriate in the light of the new stress on our legislation on problem solving. This committee did remove the research ceiling at its 1972 markup, but there was no further action on this item that year because AID was funded for the full FY 1973 under a Continuing Resolution.

If removal of the ceiling is not acceptable at this time, we request an increase of the ceiling to $15 million for FY 1975 with the expectation that further increases will be needed in subsequent years.

The examples of recent AID research project successes submitted for the record follow.

SORGHUM IMPROVEMENT 

get About 300 million people in the less developed countries most of their calories from the group of grasses known as "sorghums" and "millets." Virtually all of these are in the less developed countries generally the poorest countries and the poorest people, because these crops will produce at least some food on very poor, infertile and dry land land too poor to grow other crops. 

AID has concentrated its attention first on sorghums, about which most is known; we are broadening and adapting the sorghum work now to include the millets because of their importance in the more arid areas, especially of Africa.

The effort is designed to get the best genetic traits from wherever they may be found in the world and bring them together into varieties most suited to meet needs of LDC people for human food. 

These traits include: (1) improved yields; (2) disease and pest resistance; (3) higher protein content; and (4) better protein quality (improved amino acid balance). The effort involves Purdue, Texas A&M, Nebraska and Puerto Rico Universities and ICRISAT, the International

Research Center in Hyderabad, India, and many collaborating LDC university and other research centers. 

Because protein quantity and quality were the most serious limiting factors, the Purdue University program, focussing on these problems, began first. Results have been spectacular. 

Sorghum is modest in protein content (about 10%) and poor in protein quality being especially deficient in lysine, the principal limiting amino acid. By screening over 12,000 different varieties and genetic lines of sorghumns, from all over the world, genetic strains with 25% protein (or 2-1/2 times the protein of varieties in common use) were found. Several lines running from 50 to 80% above normal are being developed for field test.

Even more importantly, radically improved protein quality varieties were discovered. A group of high lysine varieties were discovered in 

Ethiopia with about 80% more total protein combined with about double the lysine values of ordinary sorghuns. Ordinarily, high protein content is associated with low lysine values (i.e., with low protein quality); so these lines are of outstanding significance. Their biological value, as determined by animal feeding experiments, are about 400 to 500 percent those of sorghums normally in use as human food. Sorghum kernels from these lines are somewhat softer, and probably less pest resistant, than normal varieties. Therefore, although some wider use might be made of these varieties themselves (AID plans such an introduction effort), their real contribution will come from the genetic introduction of these outstanding nutritional values into the lines being developed to have the other desirable traits such as high yields, disease and pest resistance, consumer acceptability, etc. 

Another extremely important result of this research has been the identification of another cause of severe malnutrition common among sorghum eaters. One of the greatest limiting factors to sorghum production is the very severe damage it suffers from birds, for many species of which it is a favorite food. Dark colored sorghums have proved over the years to be substantially more bird resistant than the commonly used varieties with light colored seeds, and therefore have been widely intro-

duced. Purdue University discovered that the bird resistance came from a chemical, "tannin" -- which caused the dark color. Unfortunately,. however, this chemical also caused the protein in the sorghum to be so chemically bound that it was unavailable for human nutrition. Rats fed on such dark, bird resistant sorghums -- even those of relatively good protein quality -- died from protein starvation. 

Fortunately, it now appears that the Purdue scientists have been able to separate genetically the bird resistance from the protein-binding traits of these chemicals, so that new, highly nutritious varieties of sorghums can retain the bird resistant qualities necessary to their production.

All these factors together mean the difference between death or bodily mutilation from protein dificient diets, and relatively normal development, of the sorghum eating children of some of the world's poorest people.

In the process of this work, these scientists have developed a very simple technique (known as the NINHYDRIN process) of testing, in the field, grains of any cereal crop for lysine content. This will greatly facilitate the effort to develop more nutritious lines of all the major cereal crops.

WINTER WHEAT IMPROVEMENT 

Wheat is the largest single human food source of calories in the world and, because so much of it is eaten, it is the largest total source also of protein. Winter wheat is of approximately equal importance with spring wheat although the latter has received much more research attention as relates to LDC conditions. 

All wheat is seriously deficient in total protein content (about 12.5%) and in protein quality, caused by lysine deficiency. 

AID sponsored a project with the University of Nebraska, which involves collaboration with USDA, with CIMMYT (the International Agricultural Research Center in Mexico) and with agricultural research centers in some 33 countries, about half of which are less developed countries.

The pattern of the research is to obtain the most desirable genetic traits from all over the world and to combine them into varieties which combine high yields, disease resistance, high protein content and good protein quality.

Over 16,000 varieties and strains of wheat have been screened at Nebraska to determine the nutritional values, and the best of these combined with other breeding lines and tested in some 55 field nursery sites in the cooperating countries. 

High yield qualities have come from varieties from the USSR, high protein content and good protein quality have come from lines developed in Nebraska; disease resistance factors have been incorporated from breeding lines from the less developed countries where pests and diseases abound against which resistance has evolved. 

The better lines of wheats that have been developed by these means have raised average protein content by some 50%. This has been done in high yielding lines. This is especially important as high yields are usually associated with lowered protein content. Similarly lysine 34-192 O-74-57

levels have been maintained in these high yielding/high protein content lines, whereas these values are usually obtained at the cost of reduced lysine values.

In the years ahead, emphasis will be placed on raising lysine levels. as this is the primary limiting nutritional value in wheat. 

A major side effect of this project has been a discovery of great importance to American and foreign agriculture. The effort to understand more fully the process by which plants manufacture protein led to a finding of the biological mechanisms by which herbicides kill weeds. 

This finding is being examined by various berbicide-producing companies as it should lead to much more efficient, less costly, environmentally more desirable weed control chemicals.

It permits development of herbicide chemicals to direct specifications of individual species, eliminating costly, blind screening of thousands of chemicals.

The more direct fit of chemical to specific plant killing requirements should result in much reduced herbicide application rates.

Finally, environmental damage should be lessened by reduced application levels, and greater species-or plant typespecificity..

IMPROVING FARM EQUIPMENT POWER FOR PRODUCTION OF RICE AND ASSOCIATED FOOD CROPS IN THE FAR EAST AND SOUTH ASIA 

In most countries in South Asia, more than half the population is engaged in agriculture with rice easily the major crop. Both land and labor productivity in agriculture are low, resulting in a poor living for a majority of the rural population. However, the development of high-yielding, fast-maturing rice varieties during the past decade has provided an incentive for farmers in the tropics to grow multiple crops and improve not only their productivity but also their diets.

To develop and realize the full potential of the new seed-fertilizer technology, more intensive production practices are generally necessary. 

In many countries of Asia, labor shortages are beginning to occur in periods of peak labor demand. Many farmers are finding that they cannot effectively till, plant and harvest their crops with traditional methods and take advantage of the new technology. For such farmers mechanization is becoming a means of supplementing both available labor and resources. The rise in seasonal labor costs in many Asian countries has created a favorable climate for agricultural mechanization. 

The drudgery of manual wetland rice farming has driven many farmers to the cities of Asia, where their lot is no better. Now that seedfertilizer technology is available to produce greater yields from the land, highly specialized equipment is needed to realize the benefits. 

Japan already uses specialized machinery on small farms. But the equipment for farmers in LDCs, if it is to be economically practical, must be tailored to their needs, inexpensive, and manufacturel in their own country. The tillage equipment must be so designed as to work well in mud, and water where ordinary equipment mires down. Harvesting and threshing equipment must work with relatively moist grain, where ordinary

threshers fail. The equipment is needed for the intensified operations of land preparation, transplanting, weeding, harvesting, and threshing.

Fast and efficient equipment for drying and processing is also needed. 

In view of these considerations, AID contracted with the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) in 1965 to develop the necessary equipment for the production of rice and associated food crops on the small farms (5-25 acres) of the Far East and South Asia. At its headquarters in 

Los Banos in the Philippines, IRRI has been developing and testing agricultural machinery suitable for use and manufacture in the tropics. 

Thus far, the IRRI farm machinery project has completed design work on the following equipment:

Irrigation Equipment 

Low-lift bellows pump

Field Production Machines 

Direct seeder for pregerminated paddy

Multi-hopper seeder for pre-germinated paddy 

Anhydrous ammonia applicator 

5to 7-hp tiller

Differential slip tiller 300-cm wide rotary tiller 360-cm wide rotary tiller 

400-cm wide rotary tiller 

Adjustable-blade cage wheel 

Extendible blade lug wheel 

Power rotary weeder

Post-harvest Equipment 

Drum thresher 

Table thresher 

PTO thresher 

Axial flow thresher 

Power rotary grain cleaner 

Batch type dryer 

Rice hull furnace 

Test tube miller

Many of these units are in commercial production in the Philippines. 

At present the greatest demand is for the tiller with an estimated current production of 8,000 per year and growing demand for other equipment. 

A tean is now in the field in Asia planning an industrial extension effort that will bring advice and guidance to local manufacturers of farm equipment. It is expected that this will result in production for profit by manufacturers in other countries of Asia including Bangladesh, Vietnam, Thailand, Indonesia, Cambodia and Pakistan.

The cost of this project to date has been $1,871,866.

CONTROL OF VAMPIRE BATS 

Vampire bats are a very real menace to farmers in Latin America. 

They transmit rabies by biting cattle, causing a loss of an estimated $250 million a year. Though statistics are poor, it is known that they cause many rabies deaths among humans. 

A research break through has been made on control of vampire bats, without endangering the interesting but troublesome creatures as a species. The technique has no adverse effect on the more useful bats that eat destructive insects.

In 1967 AID-supported research was begun by the Fish and Wildlife Service of the U.S. Department of the Interior to control these rabiescarrying bats.

Even if the bat does not transmit rabies, he can wreak havoc. 

Cattle that survive a bat's bite may suffer loss of blood, malnutrition, myiasis (a disease caused by maggots); this results in less meat and milk and animals are more prone to other infections. Bats may also be a carrier of the Venezuelan equine encephalomyelitis virus that killed thousands of horses in Mexico, Central America and the United States in 1969-71. 

After studying the habits of the vampire bat and the way in which his body functions, researchers came up with two methods of control. 

Both methods employ a blood anti-coagulant, ordinarily used for human heart patients, that is ingeniously geared to the peculiar, specialized physical makeup and behavior of the 3-inch, 1-ounce flying mammal.

In one method, the anticoagulant is injected into the rumen of cattle, one of their four stomach compartments. It is then absorbed into the cow's blood stream. The bat bites, laps the blood, and the anticoagulant enters the bat's digestive system. Because he consumes such an enormous amount of blood, virtually his own weight every 24 hours, and since blood, the bat's sole source of food, contains no vitamin K necessary for blood clotting, he cannot tolerate the anticoagulant. It prevents clotting of the bat's blood, and he dies of internal hemorrhaging within a few days. The anticoagulant does not harm the cattle, however, disappearing within approximately four days with no residue.

The other method is based on the bat's predilection for preening and cleaning itself and other bats. Fine nets are set up near corraled or tethered cattle. When the bats have been caught in these nets, men wearing protective garments smear the bats' back with anticoagulant mixed with petroleum jelly. Then they are released to return to their domiciles usually caves, mineshafts or wells where they contaminate the entire vampire bat colony. One such treatment of a few bats usually serves to eliminate a bat colony within two weeks. Control by this method reduced vampire bat bites on nearby cattle by 95 to 100 percent.. 

These methods are far more effective, cheaper and safer, than vaccinating cattle or attempting to shelter them in bat-proof enclosures. 

Estimates are that the costs of the chemical runs some 8 cents per cow. 

The effectiveness of this research is leading several countries to undertake all out vampire bat control programs.

In a series of demonstration workshops in Nicaragua, Brazil, Bolivia, Colombia, Panama and Ecuador vampire bat population and bite reduction of 90 to 100 percent have been demonstrated. 

Nicaragua is now spending $450,000 on a nationwide program over the next five years.

Brazil has assigned $2,000,000 dollars to a control program. 

Bolivia under Inter-American Development Bank loan funds has started a control program. 

Colombia has requested assistance in developing a program. 

Mexico is carrying out a country-wide program. 

CONTROL OF HEMOPROTOZOAL DISEASES IN LIVESTOCK 

Livestock, particularly cattle, are prey to a group of diseases of the blood stream (hemoprotozoal diseases) transmitted by ticks and other biting insects. These diseases, which occur in all tropical areas of the world, are particularly severe in Latin America, where they have been responsible for 50 percent of animal losses in some areas. 

In June 1968, AID contracted with Texas A&M University for research to determine the causes of these diseases and to develop preventive and immunization methods. Preliminary surveys indicated that altitude and' climate play a decisive role in the incidence of the disease. No cases of chronic infection are found above 5,000 feet of elevation. Below about 1,000 feet in tropical areas, infection with two or more of these diseases is so rapid that preventive steps must be taken within the first few months of an animal's life to be effective. 

Texas A&M scientists developed a technique, called "prenunization", in which the animal is injected with live organisms along with a drug that prevents it from seriously affecting the animal. This activates the animal's immunology system so that it becomes resistant to the disease. 

Subsequent bites by disease infected ticks serve, in essence, as booster shots.

Several experiments in Texas, Colombia and Mexico, have shown growth rates by the "premumised" calves consistently running 2 to 3 times higher than among the control group of untreated calves. 

Because of the success of these experiments, major field tests of these techniques are planned for Colombia, starting at this present time. About 20-30 small and medium size ranches, and some 6,000 head of cattle, will be involved in these field tests. Brazil is considering a similar effort with its own funds. 

If, as assumed, these trials prove successful, it may be anticipated that most Latin American countries where these diseases are prevalent will soon be developing major livestock disease control programs along the lines now evolving for vampire bat/rabies control. 

The importance of premunization is widely recognized by U.S. cattlemen interested in exporting cattle. Death losses as high as 70-80 percent are common in adult animals shipped from the U.S. to some infected areas. Even though a keen demand is present for U.S. breeding stock, buyers and importers are reluctant to import U.S. cattle into

infected areas. Premunization and vaccination techniques perfected through this research project should overcome this problem and permit increases in U.S. exports. 

. IMPROVING NUTRIENT VALUE OF CEREAL BASED FOOD 

Wheat is the largest source of calories for humans in the world and becoming larger, absolutely and relative to other crops. 

Though modest in protein content (12.%), so much wheat is caten that it is the largest single source also of protein for humans. (Source "Wheat in Human Nutrition," (FAO)

But, wheat has too little protein in relation to starch, and its protein is too low in lysine content, and also in methianine and threonine, to mect human protein needs, especially of young children. Because of the high starch-to-protein ratio, increased wheat consumption, unless supplemented by other foods, may actually worsen protein deficiency among children, whose requirements are high. 

Several angles are being pursued, each having its own role: These include improvement of protein content of wheat through breeding (University of 

Nebraska, CIMMYT); lysine fortification of wheat flour (INCAP in Central

America; Harvard in Tunisia, Johns Hopkins in Peru); plus efforts to improve general diets in a number of ways, especially by increased production and consumption of food legumes and livestock products. 

A Research project with Kansas State University, is directed at a number of problems, one of which is production of bread using a mixture of wheat and soybean flour.

Bread flour has severe problems of satisfying necessary baking properties, general texture, taste and appearance requirements of the bread. Addition of soy flour or other protein enrichers often results in poorer baking qualities.

The starting point of getting this flour built into LDC diets is demonstration of its value and acceptability through PL 480 programs. 

It is available for purchase under Title I.
