PREPARED STATEMENT 

Senator INOUYE. Mr. Murphy, please tell us the meaning of AID's administrative expenses. 

Mr. MURPHY.  Mr. Chairman, members of the committee, this morning, as you have indicated, we will present our requirements for administration and management for fiscal year 1975. 

This is a particularly complex subject and, from my review of the committee's hearings for the past few years, as well as the correspondence between the chairman and Administrator Parker during this year, it is apparent that it is a subject of considerable concern to the committee. 

At the outset, therefore, I should like to assure the committee that the subject is at least of equal concern to both the AID Administrator and to me. 

Since entering on duty as Deputy Administrator on May 1, I have spent a considerable amount of my time trying to master the subject in order to define the problems and to develop proposed approaches to their resolution. I wish I could say that I have succeeded, but that would be an overstatement. However, I believe it is fair to say that I have identified major areas of concern and I shall shortly speak to them individually.

This is the second year in which AID has included, in its presentation to the Congress, information concerning the total costs required to manage and operate the program. A concept has been developed which, simply put, requires that only the costs of technical personnel actually assigned to specific projects in the field be charged to the projects on which they are working. The costs of all other personnel that is, those not actually assigned to projects in the field-are considered as operating expenses. This latter group has been classified into 11 functional classifications ranging from executive direction to management support as set forth in table 4 on page 67 of the summary volume, which you have just inserted in the record, Mr. Chairman. An explanation of the composition of each of the classifications is set forth in appendix A of this statement.

There appears to be no question that some clear concept was sorely needed in order for AID and the Congress to understand what costs are being financed and to control and manage the costs. Thus, the important requirement that there be some basic understanding between the 

Congress and AID is now possible.

REQUIREMENTS FOR FUNDS 

You have before you, in the summary volume, narrative and tabular information about the requirements for funds for fiscal year 1975 together with some comparative data for fiscal year 1973 and fiscal year 1974. In total, these data show that such requirements have increased from $199.5 million for fiscal year 1973 to $216.7 million for fiscal year 

1974, and are expected to increase further to $220.1 million for fiscal year 1975.

TOTAL OPERATING EXPENSES 

I am sure that this apparent trend caused the committee concern. 

It certainly caused me concern-so I decided to dig into the subject. 

I couldn't understand how, in view of the frequent indications to the

committee about dramatic staff reductions since 1968, even taking into consideration the various pay raises enacted by the Congress and the inflation which plagues us, the money trend was in the opposite direction. My suspicion was well founded. A more accurate portrayal of the trend is depicted by the table on the page which follows, and as you will see, Mr. Chairman, this table starts off with the numbers that were shown in total in table 4 of the summary volume, and then it identifies four different categories of items which are necessary to take into consideration in order to get all 3 fiscal years on a comparable basis. The resulting changes in the totals show that, instead of the expenses going up as indicated in the numbers in table 4, in fact, on a comparable basis, the expenses are trending downward slightly from $234 million in fiscal year 1973 to $232.5 million in fiscal year 1974, and $220.1 million in fiscal year 1975.

AIR SUPPORT COSTS IN VIETNAM

1973 and fiscal year 1974 were paid from Department of Defense appropriations.

AIR AMERICA CONTRACT 

Senator INOUYE. On this Air America contract for Vietnam of $6 million, as I look through the summary, there is no justification for this. Is this something that you can explain to us here?

Mr. MURPHY. Well, I can certainly try, Mr. Chairman, and if I fail, I will give you whatever additional information you would like to have put in the record.

There is a requirement in Vietnam for extensive travel around the country to remote places where either there are no roads or the roads are not considered secure.

In other words, the safety of the traveler may be in danger. So, for some years there has been a contract with Air America to transport personnel around South Vietnam and to get them to places where they either could not get to because of the absence of roads or because of the safety considerations.

Now, in previous years when the American military were there, this cost was borne by the Department of Defense appropriations for military support to Vietnam. Now, with the withdrawal of the military, the requirement for travel within Vietnam still continues to exist but there is no basis for charging the military appropriations. 

So it was necessary to switch this cost from the Department of Defense appropriations to the AID operating expense and the estimate that we have, Mr. Chairman, of $6 million, is the annual cost of the contract for the past couple of years.

Now, there is some possibility, I would say, that as time passes, especially if pacification works, that there will be a decreased reliance on this kind of air transport and the possibility of increased use of the more normal ground transport, at least where roads exist, but we will have to watch this and adjust it downward as circumstances permit. 

Senator INOUYE. Does the justification narrative include some sum mary here?

AID PERSONNEL SYSTEMS 

Mr. MURPHY. Well, Mr. Chairman, this indicates to me that we have more than one area of misunderstanding, and we certainly do want to clear it up.

Our personnel problem is not like personnel problems in the normal Federal agency in Washington. We have a very serious problem that derives from the fact that our personnel are under two different personnel systems. 

In the one system, which is the standard civil service system, the determination of the salary to be paid for the job depends on the Classification Act, and the person who is put in that job as a GS employee can legally only be paid that salary. 

In other words, the salary relates to the functions to be performed. 

In the Foreign Service system, it is entirely different. They have what is called a "rank in man." In other words, the salary is assigned according to the officer's rank and not in accordance with the functions that he is assigned to perform. 

Now as you know, Mr. Chairman, our program necessitates the constant rotation of people from the field to Washington and from Washington to the field, so we have people coming in from overseas who are classified as Foreign Service Reserve people whose grade rests in them and not in the duties that they perform. 

We make every effort when they are assigned to a job in Washington to assign them to a job in which the grade level is as nearly equivalent to the salary that they earn because of their Foreign Service rank as we possibly can.

PROMOTION POLICY 

Senator INOUYE. I can understand that, Mr. Murphy, but these are not assignment problems. These were promotions. 

Mr. MURPHY. Well, let me get to that, Mr. Chairman.

In the Foreign Service the promotion system, as I think you are probably aware, takes place on the basis of annual reviews by evaluation boards, and a man progresses upward in the Foreign Service in accordance with the judgment of his peers about his performance relates to the performance of others in his class, and every- Senator INOUYE. It has no relation to the work he is doing?

Mr. MURPHY. Well, it has a relation, sir, in this sense. 

Let me see if I can give you a simple example. Say we have 25 Foreign Service Reserve class 4 officers on the agency payroll, and they are all, we'll say, agricultural economists. Now, we'll have an evaluation review each year of the agricultural economists class 4, and of those 25 maybe 2 will be promoted because their performance has been considered by the jury of his peers so outstanding as compared to the performance of the remainder of the 25 as to merit a promotion, so 2 people will be promoted to FSR-3. 

Now, they will still be agricultural economists, but they will have been picked out as people who are capable of deeper and more responsible performance, and their performance will be judged next year in comparison to other FSR-3's because next year they be FSR-3's. So it is a grade concept, Mr. Chairman, totally different from the Civil Service Classification Act, and this I think also contributes to some difficulty in the matter of the comparison of our average grades.

Mr. MURPHY. Now, Mr. Chairman, I should like to proceed to a discussion of the components which make up the estimate of $220.1 million for fiscal year 1975. The amounts required for Washington expenses are set forth in table 5 on page 68 of the summary volume.

Now, I am well aware, Mr. Chairman, that in the report on fiscal year 1973 the committee indicated very strongly its beliefthat separate appropriation of Administrative Expenses has outlived its usefulness and recommends that consideration be given to its elimination as an individual appropriation. This would permit "administrative" costs to be borne by and assessed against the several operating programs of the Agency for International Development as has often come to be the case through administrative determination.

Then, in its report on fiscal year 1974 the committee expressed a strong preference to have all operating expenses authorized and budgeted through the "Administrative expense" account and served notice that it would not again fund AID's cost of doing business through two accounts.

I should like to say, simply, that I believe I understand and that I sympathize with the committee's frustration in this matter. However, having said that, I express the hope that, as I continue with this statement, the committee will be convinced that Administrator Parker, with my assistance, is determined to rationalize this situation to the committee's satisfaction. We do know the meaning of "good manage ment" and we are going to take appropriate steps to achieve it. So, I plead with the committee to allow us just fiscal year 1975 to demonstrate the sincerity of our intentions. Because of the dynamic nature of the foreign policy problems that confront the United States and because the U.S. initiative and responses must be equally dynamic, we wish to express a definite preference for the course of action indicated by the earlier committee report, and we promise full accounting to the Congress and the American people.

I should like to preface my remarks with a few comments. As you know, I have been on this job only about 45 days so I cannot pose as an expert. This leads, Mr. Chairman, very logically to the question: 

What do we do about it?

Well, in the first place, we do not want to move on the basis of impressions, either our own or those of others. We must get the facts. 

So, on May 24, I appointed a task force to survey every Washington office to take a first cut at identifying excess positions. I emphasize positions because it is essential that this be done impersonally. When the work of the task force is completed, we shall have a report which, I expect, will pin down the obvious the positions which the senior officials would simply be unwilling to try to justify. With these data in hand, we propose to abolish those positions. But this will only be a first cut and, necessarily, it must assume continuation of existing systems for doing our work-an assumption which over the long run will prove erroneous because we have every intention to modernize and simplify our systems.

TRAINING OF AID PERSONNEL 

Meanwhile, we have had another task force working on training, including the retraining necessary to transform a number of our personnel into the technical generalists which will be needed to continue and expand the new program initiatives mandated by the Congress. 

Senator INOUYE. What is a technical generalist? 

Mr. MURPHY. He is defined, Mr. Chairman, as a very highly skilled man in one of our functional areas. For example, population planning. 

He is a man who knows just about all there is to know or as close to as we can find, who knows how you go about developing population

planning programs, designing them, executing them, and evaluating them. Now, there has been a tremendous shift in this agency in the past 3 years arising largely, Mr. Chairman, from a shift in focus in our program. 

We are now very definitely focusing on food and nutrition, population planning and health, and educational and human resources, and we therefore need people who are much broader and better skilled in these areas than conceivably might have been in the past when the emphasis was on the building of a powerplant, building a road, or setting up a telecommunication system-the type of capital project that used to involve so much money of this program. 

Now we have done some analyses on these and we have an indication that we are short of these types of people and that we are going to have to take a number of our people who we believe could absorb and usefully utilize additional training in these particular functional areas to equip them to go out into the field and do a better job than we otherwise can do, and we have this task force working on the training requirements and, as I say here, the next step will be to select from the number of people on this reassignment subcomplement which we earlier referred to, those that we really believe will be able to absorb the training and who will be able to usefully apply it for a reasonable number of years before they retire. That will be a difficult job to do but we are going to do it, and we will do it within the next several months and, again, Mr. Chairman, if you would like I will be glad to keep you informed of the progress on this effort. 

Senator INOUYE. I would appreciate that, sir.

Mr. MURPHY. When the report from this task force is available we shall then tackle the difficult task of determining which of the large number of personnel in the reassignment subcomplement should be retrained for further service overseas and arranging for the necessary retraining.

MANAGEMENT IMPROVEMENT PROGRAM 

These are, of course, only preliminary steps. A logical and methodical approach to the definition of real personnel requirements is obviously needed, and this will take some time. In the final analysis, I am sure the committee recognizes that personnel requirements are a function of the AID program and of the organization, systems, and procedures by which the program is planned and executed. We propose to embark on a management improvement program along the following lines:

Examine, refine, and update the definition of the functions and responsibilities of each Washington organization element. 

In the process, determine organizational changes necessary to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of the Washington headquarters and implement such changes.

Review the major systems and procedures and the coordinating mechanisms in use to identify opportunities for improvement and especially opportunities for introducing modern management concepts and techniques such as management by exception and electronic data processing.

1 Conceive, design, and implement improved management systems and procedures. 

Continuously review personnel requirements and adjust personnel ceilings as indicated to assure compatibility with improvement management systems and procedures.

The broad objectives are to improve the processes by which we: 

Plan and design programs and projects intended to achieve U.S. foreign policy objectives and goals.

Forecast personnel requirements of such programs and projects. 

Review, approve, and evaluate the execution of the resulting program and projects. 

In short, Mr. Chairman, we will be seeking a lean, busy and efficient organization alertly responsive to U.S. objectives.

Now, as I previously indicated, such a program will take time and the results will not be visible all at once. Rather, we envisage a gradual process which will reveal to the Congress and the American people steady improvement in the way AID discharges its responsibilities. 

This program has been the subject of extensive and intimate discus-. sion between Administrator Parker and me. We are determined to carry it out expeditiously and, in the process, we expect to resort to many techniques, both orthodox and unorthodox, about which I cannot go into detail at this time. 

Senator INOUYE. Mr. Murphy, I have noticed you have stated I think on four occasions that it will take time. How long will this take?

Mr. MURPHY. I think it will take all of fiscal year 1975, Mr. Chairman. Now, I quickly want to say that the results will start to be visible long before the end of fiscal year 1975, but it is an enormous undertaking. I trust you realize if we really go into every Washington office and examine every one of its functions and make sure they are necessary, and then we also examine all the major systems and procedures, that it is a major undertaking. 

Senator INOUYE. Who will conduct this study?

Mr. MURPHY. Well, let me put it this way: They all will be conducted under my direction. These people, of course, also are engaged, as I am, in policy formulation, but our emphasis is to be on operations and management, whereas the emphasis of the Administrator's Advisory Council is on the policy formulation processes.

园 ​Σ at varying times, and as the results of these become available we will act on them. I promise you we are going to act. We are not just going to study and argue, which has been the case in the past. 

I found, for example, one study that was done 2 years ago which made a whole series of recommendations. Various offices which were interested in the results got together and argued for 2 years. Well, I found out this was going on and I asked for the recommendations and inside of 24 hours, Mr. Chairman, I made the decisions and we are going to do something about the report. We are not going to have any more of this business of committees getting together and spending 2 years discussing and arguing about whether a recommendation is sound or not. 

We are going to have a system whereby the recommendations are put on my desk where the differing views are set forth so that there is no opportunity to squelch honest differences of opinion, I will weigh the views and I will make decisions on them and we are simply not going to take 2 years to implement recommendations. 

Senator INOUYE. Thank you. "GRADE CREEP" 

Mr. MURPHY. Now "Grade Creep," Mr. Chairman, is another area which has been of concern to the committee, as evidenced by previous hearings. On the Foreign Service side, it appears to me that there may be some justification for what may appear to be an average grade which I have been told is somewhat higher than State Department or U.S.I.A. In the field all three organizations have to leave out of the calculation of an.average grade the large number of local personnel who perform clerical functions such as typing, filing, and so forth, since these personnel are paid local salaries which vary considerably from post to post. So, from that standpoint, all would appear to be the same. However, there are other factors which are different. 

State and USIA, I am told, perform virtually all their own services and seldom contract. The result is that a large number of the relatively simple, repetitive tasks are performed by lower graded American personnel, which is not the case with AID. 

This is also true of most large organizations which are involved in performance of .routine or well-established repetitive services that lend themselves to vertical divisions of labor, in which a few senior professionals can direct the work of larger numbers of subordinates arranged in a pyramidal structure. This is not the nature of much of 

AID's business particularly the parts directly concerned with development problem solving and transferring know-how, which we are called on to make a growing part of our work. This requires senior professional leaders who can break new ground. Moreover, for this work, we are called on to reduce reliance on AID staff for the field implementation tasks-in which some pyramidal structuring has been feasible in the past-which leaves the Agency with the functions of deciding what should be done and mobilizing and managing the use of the very scarce, high-level expertise needed from outside to carry out the project assignments. To do this well, we need talent that can deal effectively with the highest professional levels and with senior policy officials and administrators. Thus, need for more junior staff

support is much less than if we were implementing projects we must have high average grade and pay levels if we are to do the job that our legislation calls for.

On the Washington side we have a very unusual situation. Most non-Foreign Service personnel occupy positions classified in the GS schedule. I have learned that when the Civil Service Commission last conducted a review circa 1966 overgrading was revealed. 

Howeyer, while I understand a substantial effort was undertaken to correct this situation, that effort halted because of a proposed major reorganization of the AID organization-arising from the Peterson report.

The Classification Act is the law of the land. It should be adhered to meticulously. It seems to me that, in instances where downgrading is indicated, substantial protection is afforded the incumbents under Civil Service rules. So, I promise the committee that action will be taken in fiscal year 1975 to regularize the situation with maximum fairness to all concerned and in strict accordance with the rules. 

Meanwhile we shall continue to see to it that whenever vacancies occur the position classifications assigned will be subject to careful scrutiny and that the necessity for the positions is reestablished. If it is necessary we shall seek assistance from the Civil Service Commission. 

Again, in complete candor and not to magnify the difficulty of the problem, I want to point to another factor that further complicates our Washington grade problems. We do operate under two personnel systems Foreign Service and Civil Service-and the systems are entirely different when it comes to establishing salaries. In the Civil 

Service the Classification Act rules the duties of the position determine the grade (and hence the salary)-but in the Foreign Service the grade attaches to the man and not the position he occupies This leads us inevitably into situations where returning Foreign Service officials may be assigned in Washington to positions graded under the Classification Act either above or below the personal grade carried by the official. I am advised that every effort is made to make assignments where salaries are comparable, but that this is frequently difficult if not impossible. Thus AID in effect is paying the only legal salary payable to the official, but a salary which may be above that payable to a classified official. I hope you will agree that this places us in a dilemma for which we have yet to discover a solution. We shall keep on trying.

SUMMARY OF STATEMENT 

In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I should like to introduce some perspective that is sorely needed to arrive at a balanced judgment of AID operating expenses. Our budget contemplates a direct-hire 

American staff of less than 5,000. While this is a large number in one sense it is also fewer personnel than man a single large U.S. aircraft carrier. These Americans are responsible and accountable for the "management", with all that word implies, of complex economic assistance programs of a wide variety and of substantial dimensions. So, I thought it might be helpful and informative to present some selected statistics to illustrate the management dimensions of AID's current operation.

AID plans, manages and monitors:

Bilateral economic/technical assistance programs in 1974 obligations and loan authorizations will exceed $1.8 billion in over 50 countries. . A loan portfolio of over 1,500 active loans with balances outstanding of $15.7 billion as of April 30, 1974.

Grant programs and projects with undisbursed balances of over $600 million at June 30, 1974.

Commodity procurement in the hundreds of millions of dollars in fiscal year 1974 of which the vast bulk was purchased in the U.S. from over 5,000 suppliers. 

1,226 technical service contracts with a value of $751 million as of 

December 31, 1973.

Training programs for 11,000 participants during fiscal year 1974. 

Public Law 480, title II, government to government grants of $60 million in fiscal year 1974.

Public Law 480, title II, grants of $143 million to over 90 private voluntary agencies in fiscal year 1974.

AID oversees participation in aid programs of: 

Seven major U.S. departments (USDA, Labor, Interior, HEW, DOT, Treasury, and Commerce). 

132 U.S. universities and educational institutions. 

AID coordinates: 

U.S. Government overseas disaster relief programs. 

U.S. development assistance policies and programs with other U.S. 

Government agencies and with various international institutions (e.g., IBRD, IDB, ADB, AFRDB, IDA, UN, OAS, DAC, etc.). 

AID participated with U.S. Department of Agriculture in development of Public Law 480, title I, programs in over 20 countries totaling almost $800 million in fiscal year 1974, including freight. 

OPERATING EXPENSES 

In short, Mr. Chairman, AID has a full platter-its work is of vital importance to the achievement of U.S. foreign policy objectives throughout the world. We hope the committee will agree and be patient and understanding with us and help us to gain our balance when we stumble, as we have many times and will surely do again. We, in turn, shall try to learn from our mistakes as we chart our future course.

Appendix A OPERATING EXPENSES 

Definition of the Concept A.I.D. operating expenses cover the salaries and supporting costs for personnel engaged in the basic operating functions of policy, planning, programming, coordination, management, and support in Washington and overseas. This type of personnel comprises about 93 percent of A.I.D. direct-hire employment. The 7 percent of A.I.D. personnel who are directly responsible for program and project implementation, as technical advisors attached to specific projects, are excluded.

Operations personnel and costs are grouped by functional categories representing the major operational and management responsibilities of the Agency. These functions (and their approximate share of total operating expenses) are: 

Executive Direction (5%) includes the top policy formulation and direction of the Agency. 

Program Planning and Budgeting (8%) includes identifying development needs, setting priorities for resource use, and resource allocation. 

Technical Analysis, Management and Evaluation (19%) 

includes technical planning and review of programs and projects, project management, and program evaluation. 

Central Backstopping of Overseas Operations (3%) involves program and administrative contact between

overseas missions and the Washington Country Desks in each of the Regional Bureaus.

External Relations and Information (18) includes legislative liaison and public affairs activities.

Administration of Special Programs (2%) includes management of the American Schools and Hospitals Abroad program, Disaster Relief, Food for Peace, and Private and Voluntary Cooperation programs.

Legal Services (18) involves provision of legal advice and services to all elements of A.I.D in Washington and overseas. 

Audit and Inspection Services (4%) includes the

Agency comprehensive internal audit program and the investigation of alleged irregularities and deficiencies relating to compliance and integrity of operations. 

Program Support Services (8%) includes functions directly supporting individual A.I.D. programs and projects; commodity management, contract services, engineering services, and participant training services. 

Financial Management Services (6%) includes the functions of accounting, statistics, internal financial control, advice and assistance on financial practices and procedures, and financial reporting. 

Management Support Services (43%) encompasses the full range of administrative management services (personnel, data processing) and the cost of general logistics support (communications, 34-192 O -74 - 59

vehicles, buildings, supplies) provided for all functions. 

Appendix B

Proposed Method of Allocating Operating Expenses to the A.I.D. Appropriation Accounts in FY 1975 

First, the amounts for operating expenses that are available from host country trust funds and from the housing investment guaranty and excess property program funds will be deducted. The remainder will be the amount of operating expenses that will be drawn from appropriated dollar funds. 

The next step will be to deduct from the appropriated funds requirement the "Administrative Expenses" appropriation, all of which will be available for operating expenses. The remainder will be divided among those of our regular appropriation accounts that fund activities involving operating costs. For 

FY 1975, there will be nine such accounts: the five functional appropriations, Indochina Postwar Reconstruction, Supporting

Assistance, Middle East Special Requirements Fund, and American 

Schools and Hospitals Abroad.

Since it is impossible to trace individual operating expense requirements back to each source appropriation, particularly in the case of the five functional appropriations, we will use the following simple approach that makes for a reasonably equitable distribution. In the case of the Indochina 

Postwar Reconstruction, Supporting Assistance, and Middle East Special Requirements Fund, we will determine the operating expense requirements in the field Missions involved with these

programs and add a percentage share of Washington costs to determine the operating expense charges to these appropriations. 

In the case of the American Schools and Hospitals program, we will charge that appropriation with the costs of running that program in Washington. Thus,

After the above calculations have been made, we will be left with an operating expense requirement which will be charged to the five functional appropriations. This will be done by dividing the remaining operating expense requirements among them on the basis of the program size in each case. for example, since Food and Nutrition programs are about 60 percent of the total program for all five appropriations, the Food and Nutrition appropriation will be charged with about 60 percent of the total remaining operating expense requirement. A similar calculation will be made for each of the other four functional appropriations.

The above calculations will be made at the time of our budget presentation to the Congress and reworked when we formulate the Operational Year Budget, which of course reflects the action by Congress on our various appropriation requests.

Without my knowledge, as I just described, they undertook an audit on this personnel thing and, as I say, I have read some of those points which you read out to me earlier from their report. I consider this very healthy, Mr. Chairman--I don't mean the results, but I mean the activity.

AUDIT PHILOSOPHY 

If you don't mind, I would like to just take a moment to expand a little on my philosophy in this regard, which I hope I can convince the committee is the correct philosophy to approach the whole auditor general question.

I believe, Mr. Chairman, basically, that each agency of the Government should run its shop well and efficiently and with the least possible expense to the U.S. taxpayer, and I think that in order for the top management of agencies to be reasonably assured that that is the case they need a management tool called audit working for them and in their shop to check on the activities of all other elements of the organization and to see that, in fact, bad situations are identified and corrected quickly.

Now, we have three organizations that are looking at us. We have our own Auditor General, we have the Inspector General of Foreign Assistance in the State Department and, of course, we have the General Accounting Office, which has provided extremely valuable services to Congress and the American taxpayer over the years. 

It is my philosophy, Mr. Chairman, that we should so conduct our operations in AID with the benefit of our own auditors that we could demonstrate to the Inspector General and hopefully also to the General Accounting Office over a period of years, that the need for their continued scrutiny and attention with the same intensity is decreasing and that, therefore, the total of all of the audit efforts put on the AID program would decrease. And hopefully it would first decrease in the 

Inspector General and next in the General Accounting Office, because both of those organizations came to be confident that AID itself was prepared to manage its own affairs and manage them well. 

Now, this is my philosophy and I believe that we should look on audit as a very important management tool. This is not to say, Mr. Chairman, that we should spend more money than is necessary on it or have more auditors than are necessary, and we will be focusing on that subject, too, and if I might digress, Mr. Chairman, we have here with us this morning the new AID Auditor General who entered on duty yesterday, Mr. Harry Carlton Cromer, and he is sitting here in the room. 

Will you stand, Harry, please.

BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCH

NUMBER OF AUDITORS VERSUS SIZE OF PROGRAM 

Senator INOUYE. Do you think as a management analyst we have too many auditors in AID? 

Mr. MURPHY. I don't know yet, Mr. Chairman, but I am going to find out. I do believe that there are some changes indicated in the way our general operation has been carried out, and I do propose to consult with Mr. Cromer about this as soon as I can finish my duties on Capitol Hill. 

For example, I don't believe our Auditor General in the past has used what I call selective auditing, or sampling or spot checking, whatever you will, to the extent that he should. I believe the practice has been to audit virtually every project and to do this on-well, originally on an 18-month cycle, although more recently that has been extended to a 24-month cycle, which, of course, is a step in the right direction.

I believe that we should approach the job on a sampling basis and that we should find where there is paydirt and then exploit that to the fullest extent. 

Senator INOUYE. May I suggest a little paydirt here? 

Mr. MURPHY. Yes, sir; you may.

Senator INOUYE. In fiscal year 1973 and 1974 we have had no AID program in Argentina and I see that none is contemplated for fiscal year 1975. However, we have had three AID auditors assigned in 

Buenos Aires, one FSR-3, another FSR-4, another FSR-4. Why do we need such expensive, $30,000, $24,000, $24,000 auditors in a city where we have no AID program? 

Mr. MURPHY. Well, sir, the simple answer, of course, is that these auditors are not limited in their duties to the city or country in which they are located. They cover areas, and my assumption, without knowing the facts, Mr. Chairman, is that the personnel stationed in Buenos 

Aires are covering Uruguay, Paraguay, and Chile, which would be the logical geographic territory for people stationed in Buenos Aires. 

I can assure you they have nothing to do with an Argentine program which, as you pointed out, doesn't exist. Their duties are related to the programs in neighboring countries.

Senator INOUYE. Last Friday when we brought up the irregularities in Nicaragua you correctly pointed out that even with a force of 314 auditors you couldn't expect them to be covering everything at the same time, but I am certain you realize that AID maintains two resident auditors in Managua, Nicaragua. Yet we had to hire Practical 

Concepts, Inc., to turn up information on misuse of AID material and

the phantom employees concerned with the project we have discussed. 

I am just wondering what the auditors were doing.

Mr. MURPHY. That is a very good question, Mr. Chairman. I will try to find out, but they may have been in a neighboring country working, they may have been in Managua working on other projects. 

Senator INOUYE. This is just a smattering example of auditors and the amount in the program. As I noted, in Argentina you have three and the AID program is zero dollars. In Brazil we have three auditors. 

Our program is $4.2 million. In the Dominican Republic you have two auditors. The program there is $7.8 million. In Liberia we have three auditors. The program total is $3.1 million. In Nigeria, four auditors. 

The program is $4.1 million. And in Honduras, zero auditors and $13 million. There is no relationship between the amount of the program and the auditors, or should there be?

Mr. MURPHY. Well, there certainly is no relationship by country, Mr. 

Chairman, because none of these auditors is assigned to a single country. In other words, they all have more than one country to cover and the place where they are assigned is simply their headquarters from which they travel. They work on the country in which they are assigned if there is a program there, and they also work on programs of neighboring countries. Now in Brazil, where you cited-What was it?

Senator INOUYE. In Brazil you have three and the program there is $4.2 million.

Mr. MURPHY. Well, here, this is another factor, Mr. Chairman, that 

I think has got to be considered. Brazil has a tremendous pipeline and so you can't measure the auditors simply by the amount of new aid that is being extended to the country. The unexpended balance of prior-year programs in Brazil exceeds $200 million and these auditors. are concerned with those projects much more than they will be with the 1974 programs. So that is a factor we have to look at, not only what the new aid with be; but also the extent of the previous aid and what remains unexpended and give attention to the proper use of those funds.

Now in the matter of the location of these people, Mr. Chairman, I do know that very recently some moves have been made within the office to reduce the number of individual places at which auditors are stationed in the interest again of some further economy, and the outgoing Auditor General made several recommendations and, as I recall, there were at least three places he eliminated where auditors had been stationed and they were combined, consolidated in other places, so that there were some economies developed from that, and I am sure again that is just a start.

There are probably further economies that can be achieved in that line.

DEVELOPMENT ASSISTANCE COMMITTEE Senator INOUYE. What is the responsibility of your representative on the development assistance committee stationed in Paris? 

Mr. MURPHY. Well, the development assistance committee, Mr. 

Chairman, was originated at the suggestion and urging of the U.S. 

Government. It is composed of all the developed countries. They all have representatives, and their purpose is to try to coordinate the

bilateral aid efforts of the developed countries to the developing countries, the LDC's and the U.S. representative meets with the French and the German and the British and the Dutch and the Swedish and Italian representatives, and becomes familiar with the programs that each of these countries has in mind for LDC's, share with them information about what the United States is doing, and the intent of it is to look toward an effective worldwide aid program on the part of all the developed countries which is coordinated and not overlapping.

Now, this committee not only has a U.S. member on it, Mr. Chairman, but it is chaired by a U.S. official and, in fact, my predecessor, Maurice Williams, is now chairman of the DAC and the U.S. member is John R. Mossler who formerly was the U.S. Mission Director in 

Saigon, Vietnam.

RESIDENCE AND REPRESENTATIONAL ALLOWANCES

Mr. MURPHY. I believe it does, Mr. Chairman. I believe it is the allowance but I could be wrong.

Mr. MURPHY. Oh, no. I believe that is the cost of not just residence of the member, Mr. Mossler, but also of one of his staff personnel. I would like to verify that for the record, Mr. Chairman. If the information I have given is incorrect I will correct it.

Dear Mr. Chairman: 

You will recall that during my testimony before your Subcommittee on June 18, 1974 regarding A.I.D. administration and management, you asked me about official residence expenses for our Development Assistance Committee (DAC) Representative in 

Paris. I have checked further into the facts and find that certain corrections should be made in the hearing transcript. 

I am writing this letter to make sure that you are aware of the changes.

A.I.D. provides official residence expenses to two officers in Paris: the Chairman of the DAC, Mr. Maurice J. Williams, and the United States Representative to the DAC, Mr. John R. Mossler.

We estimate that the total reimbursement for official residence expenses to these two officers will be approximately $20,000 in each of the fiscal years 1974 and 1975. These estimates are higher than the $11,600 shown for each of these fiscal years in a table provided to Mr. Jordan in connection with the hearings. 

The amounts shown in the table were based on the actual amount paid in FY 1973, but upon looking into the matter further, we find that the level for FY 1973 was low because the position of U. s. 

Representative to the DAC was vacant for most of that year. The higher estimates we now project for FY 1974 and FY 1975 are closer to amounts actually provided in years prior to FY 1973, when both positions were filled for the entire year. 

Official residence expenses are made available to A.I.D. Mission 

Directors and principal officers, such as the two DAC officers, to help defray the unusual expenses of operating and maintaining official residences. This allowance is a partial reimbursement for the extra

housekeeping costs which are incurred because of the need for these officers to use their residences in an official capacity. The allowance covers the cost of servants as well as miscellaneous household expenses. The first $1,500 of such expenses per annum is borne personally by each of these officers. While normally we limit the amount of reimbursement to $2,000 per annum, we have made an exception in this case because the cost of providing an equivalent level of support is considerably greater in Paris than in less developed countries. 

The amount which we do reimburse is in line with that provided to U.S. 

Representatives to other organizations in Paris, such as OECD and UNESCO. 

As indicated above, official residence expenses include the cost of servants. They do not include the cost of quarters, which is covered by a separate quarters allowance. I mention this to correct certain oral responses I made to you during the course of the hearing on June 18. 

We are in the process of correcting the hearing transcript to reflect the above facts. If you wish any further information, we will be happy to provide it. Sincerely, The Musking 

John E. Murphy

ADMINISTRATIVE EXPENSES AS PART OF ODA 

Senator INOUYE. I am just wondering, where would you place administrative expenses? Would you say that this is part of the U.S. economic assistance program?

Mr. MURPHY. I certainly would, sir. I was very shocked at reading your 1973 report to find the funds spent by the United States to administer this program are not considered and included in what is called Official Development Assistance. I certainly believe they should be.

Senator INOUYE. It would give a bad picture, wouldn't it? 

Mr. MURPHY. In fairness, I believe all such costs should be included. 

SUPPORT FOR FOREIGN ASSISTANCE 

Senator INOUYE. I am not suggesting that we should insist that AID conduct itself like an impoverished agency but we are dealing with the poorest of the poor, the most destitute people in the world. We have insisted that the Peace Corps, for example, keep down its expenses and that is why I have difficulty responding to my colleagues when they come up with these inquiries. Many of the inquiries that I am making today and other days come from my colleagues. I suppose they don't wish to ask you the questions. They want me to ask them. But the answers will have to be provided. Some of them are getting a bit apprehensive. I think it shows up in the votes. If you have followed you have noticed that we have had an eroded support and it is coming very close to defeat. I would hate to see good, meaningful programs going down the drain, so that is why we are trying our best to provide for Members of Congress the best justification we can find for continuation of this program. 

Mr. MURPHY. And we certainly appreciate that, Mr. Chairman, and I share your views thoroughly. I think it is a crying shame, if you will, that a relatively small item in the budget should become a bone of contention between Congress and the executive branch, and I am going to do my best to try to remove that by the most forthright presentation of the facts that I can make from now on. 

Senator INOUYE. You are absolutely correct. Oftentimes it is not the big thing. It is the smaller thing that may serve as an irritant and I suppose all of us are human and we pick on the small things. Small things we can understand. Big things are beyond our understanding, so we don't discuss those things. So it might do you well to concern yourself with small things also. 

Mr. MURPHY. We will.

PHASEOUT OF PUBLIC SAFETY 

Senator INOUYE. As you know, in December of 1973 we did away with the public safety program. What is the present status of the personnel phaseout? 

Mr. MURPHY. I have something here. On December 1, 1973, Mr.

Chairman, there were 89 personnel in 17 field programs. As of July 1, 1974 there will be seven visitors remaining in these countries phasing out and by August 15 those seven will have departed. We estimate that there will remain 10 host-country-funded advisers in Saudi

Arabia, 3 host-country-funded advisers in Venezuela, and 15 advisers who will be concerned with the narcotics program abroad. 

Now, according to my calculation, we have brought back about 60 personnel from overseas since December 1, 1973. Now we have the problem, Mr. Chairman, of what do we do with them. Ten of those personnel occupied foreign service "limited" appointments. In other words, they had no tenure so they were discharged on return. Nineteen of them have retired, or accepted other employment, or resigned. We are about to seek the assistance of the Civil Service Commission in efforts to place a number of the remaining personnel elsewhere in the Government. How successful we will be on this, I don't know. 

We also are looking at the possibility of retaining a number of them-in view of their extensive experience overseas-to be project managers in areas other than public safety. Of course we are forbidden to retain this activity overseas. Some of them undoubtedly will measure up to that capability but we are going to have, in my judgment, a necessity for what we call a selective reduction in force because it is clear that we will not need all these people. 

Now, in the last week in May, I approved a ceiling for the organization in Washington, and of course you know we are continuing the Police Academy, and this ceiling includes the personnel for the Police Academy.

We are in the process now of making up registers to see-given the approved ceiling-which of the personnel would have to be discharged in a reduction in force. 

Senator INOUYE. Like all Members of Congress, I hate to see any person, whether GS-16 or GS-13, losing his or her position as a result of congressional or executive decisions. RIF are three letters that many of us dread. In fact, in the U.S. Senate, every 6 years one-third of us do our best to stay in and keep employed, and I would expect you to do whatever you can to see that those who have been terminated find employment elsewhere. But I only hope that if you are going to place these men and women within other parts of your organization that they are placed in positions where their talents can be justified. 

Because we have received information that that is not the case, that they are just placed there for the sake of placing them. 

EMPLOYEE MORALE 

Now this is where you have problems. Someone sitting next to him in that same office will call us up and say, "We have a Mr. John Doe who just came in from Vietnam serving as such and such here, and he doesn't know bones about it, and he is my superior." Something like that.

Mr. MURPHY. I can understand that concern, Mr. Chairman, but I believe it is important that we do not mix up two separate problems here: job opportunity and job qualifications. What we are trying to do in the short run is to give everybody some work to do and, as a result, we do place Foreign Service officers in Washington jobs. I can understand the problems this causes to our GS employees who, as a result, may not have the opportunity to fill the job occupied by the Foreign Service employee. But in our Foreign Service placements in Washington, we make every effort to assure not only that the Foreign Service

person is qualified for the position, but also that we protect the GS employee. I suspect that some of the statements you receive about lack of qualifications really have to do more with the fact that placement of a Foreign Service officer in a job prevents the GS employee from filling that job.

Senator INOUYE. I am certain you realize that much of what we have here is information coming in from employees. 

Mr. MURPHY. I am sure it is.

Senator INOUYE. From those who are disgruntled, unhappy because of what they consider unfair treatment. Someone sitting next to them is getting more by doing less. Some of these letters come in like this [indicating] with no significance but we follow them through and it makes some sense. We hope that, for the agency's sake, that these things will be clarified and cleaned up because otherwise you are going to have a whole bunch of disgruntled people there. 

Mr. MURPHY. And we don't want that, Mr. Chairman, nor do we want a continuation year after year of justified or unjustified criticism in this area. We really want to eliminate this bone of contention, if you will, by trying to demonstrate that we are going to administer it effectively.

We will make some mistakes but we will try to keep them to the minimum. 

Senator INOUYE. I thank you very much, and I don't suppose you will be appearing before the subcommittee for a while, but may I say that it was a great pleasure to have you with us. 

Mr. MURPHY. It was a pleasure being here, Mr. Chairman. Even though I may not be coming back soon before the subcommittee, I hope that you and I, in the course of the year, are going to have frequent exchanges because I want you to be informed of what is going on.

Senator INOUYE. Fine, sir. I look forward to working with you. This is, as you say, a bone of contention for many of your fellow employees in AID. I will do what I can to assist, but I think much, if not all, of the work may have to come from your side. 

Mr. MURPHY. I agree with you, sir. Thank you very much.

STATEMENTS OF: 

ARTURO G. COSTANTINO, DIRECTOR OF OFFICE OF AMERICAN SCHOOLS ABROAD EUGENE D. TUCCI, PROGRAM ANALYST, OFFICE OF AMERICAN SCHOOLS AND HOSPITALS ABROAD, AGENCY FOR INTERNA- TIONAL DEVELOPMENT PREPARED STATEMENT 

Senator INOUYE. We are pleased to have with us again, Mr. Arturo G. Costantino, to justify the $10 million requested for this item in fiscal year 1975. Without objection, your full statement will be made a part of the record. 

Mr. COSTANTINO. May I submit my statement for the record, Mr. 

Chairman? I think you have probably read it, and we can save some time. 

[The statement follows:] 

Mr. Chairman: I am pleased to appear before the committee again to discuss the Fiscal Year 1975 budget request for the American Schools and Hospitals Abroad program which is carried out pursuant to Section 214 of the Foreign 

Assistance Act. 

As Director of the Office of American Schools and Hospitals Abroad it is my responsibility to administer this program. 

For Fiscal Year 1975, A.I.D. requests $10,000,000 plus $6.5 million equivalent in U.S.-owned local currencies to conduct the Section 214 program. The U.S.owned foreign currencies are required for projects in Egypt and Poland. 

The Egyptian currency, equivalent to about $4,425,000, will be used to complete construction of the library building at the American University, Cairo, ($2,750,000 equivalent) for which initial funding was provided in FY 1974, and partly to replenish the University's endowment funds granted by Congress in FY 1969 ($1,675,000 equivalent).

The Polish zloty equivalent of $2,075,000 will be used for (1) the design and construction of an American library at the birthplace of General Pulaski ($E 200,000), and (2) to supplement funds approved by Congress in FY 1974 for construction of Phase III of the American Children's Hospital in Krakow, Poland ($E 1,875,000).

The Agency's request for $10,000,000 is a substantial reduction from the $25,500,000 level approved by Congress for , and the $19,000,- 000 level appropriated for Fiscal Year 1974. This lower level was developed in consultation with the Office of Management and Budget and is responsive to the President's call for economies in government expenditures.

As was the case when we presented the Fiscal Year 1974 program, the Agency cannot now specify precisely how the $10,000,000 requested for FY 1975 will be allocated. However, a reduction of program funding to this level will preclude assistance to a majority of the institutions which have filed applications with the Agency and will necessitate a serious reduction in support levels to such institutions as the American University of Beirut, Project HOPE, the American Children's Hospital in Krakow, the University of the Americas, the American Hospitals in Paris and Rome, the Bologna Center of Johns Hopkins 

University, Robert College, the American University in Cairo, the Weizmann

Institute, and other smaller institutions which have been the core of the program over the past years.

The reduced level also will necessarily postpone into future fiscal years the effort initiated in FY 1973 to disperse the program geographically, thus correcting the over-emphasis on projects in the Near East. For example, if the FY 1975 budget permitted, a grant could be made to Silliman University in the Philippines for construction of a much needed library. A $10 million budget cannot accommodate this request nor further assistance to such institutions as Damavand College in Iran, which is building a new campus.

In the course of this hearing, I hope we can satisfy you that we have made good use of the funds appropriated. I also want to thank this committee for its past support and understanding.

[The criteria follows:]

1. 2. 3. 4. 5.

American Schools and Hospitals Abroad Criteria All institutions for which assistance is requested must be located abroad, and must have been founded or be sponsored by United States citizens. The Agency construes founding and sponsorship as requiring a preponderance of United States citizens in the founding or sponsoring group and an identification of the institution with the United States. 

The institution must be a private non-profit organization, not under the direct control or management of any government, or governmental organization, The sponsors must participate in the management of the institution and contribute to its financial support. No applications for assistance will be considered for ventures entirely dependent upon a grant under Section 214 for their initiation.

The institution should be open to all regardless of race, creed or color. No portion of the grant may be used to promote religious activities. 6.

Schools must have a student body comprised of a majority of citizens from countries other than the United States. 

In the case of medical institutions, the majority of students, nurses, other medical personnel receiving training shall not be U. S. citizens. and 7. 8. 9.

The faculty or staff must include United States citizens or other nationals train and graduated from United States institutions and thus be able to reflect American theory and practices in education, medicine and/or medical researc Full time schools will be expected to provide instruction in an American studie program designed to include aspects of American history, geography, cultural political and economic subjects. English should be used in instruction or taug as a second language.

Vocational and sub-professional training institutions should be planned to meet the needs of the host country. 

10. The institution must demonstrate competence in instructional skills, managem and financial operations. 11. Each application must include the information required to permit a firm estima of the total costs of the project to the U. S. Government and to demonstrate the capacity to ensure effective use of the assistance requested. 

N. B. The above criteria establish cligibility for a Section 214 grant. However, eligibility does not ipso facto imply that a grant will be recommended or approved by A. I. D.

United States Senate COMMITTEE ON APPROPRIATIONS WASHINGTON, D.C. 20510 

June 10, 1974 

The Honorable Daniel K. Inouye Chairman 

Subcommittee on Appropriations for 

Foreign Operations Committee on Appropriations United States Senate 

Washington, D.C.

Dear Mr. Chairman: 

I should like to call your attention and that of your subcommittee to the application of the American Library in Paris for a grant in fiscal 1975 from the appropriation "American schools and hospitals abroad". 

My reason for calling this matter to your attention is that I am informed that the budget request for this particular appropriation is $10,000,000 and that if this were to be the amount finally approved, this application could not receive consideration. As you know, in fiscal 1974, the budget request was also $10,000,000, however, the Congress approved $19,000,000 for this appropriation. Therefore, I am requesting your favorable consideration of sufficient funding so that this application may be approved. 

The American Library in Paris is a private, non-profit, tax exempt lending library which has been in existance for over 55 years. Being private, the Library's income must come from personal dues, donations and bequests. 

Under date of February 20, 1974, the Library submitted an application to A.I.D. for a grant of $257,400. This sum would be used to purchase additional bookshelves and other needed equipment, renovate the library quarters and replace the roof of the library building. All of these are in the nature of capital improvements, the cost of which is beyond the annual income available to the library from personal dues and contributions. For

The American Library was founded during World War I for the primary purpose of serving American servicemen in France, particularly those confined to hospitals. It performed a similar outstanding service in World War II. these reasons, the Library's application has received the strong endorsement of veterans organizations. 

The Library serves present needs in three ways: 

(1) It is a General Library providing an outstanding collection of over 150,000 books and over 700 magazines, all in English, for the thousands of American residents and visitors in Paris. (2) Since 1945, it has met an even more pressing and increasing need of servicing students and scholars from many European countries seeking research and reference materials in the growing field of "American Studies", which contribute in the so many ways to better international understanding. (3) To an increasing degree, the Library seeks to strengthen the bonds between the United States and other lands. This is a need which grows more urgent in these times of ever increasing international crisis and strain.

I am informed by officials of the U.S. Information Agency that the 

American Library in Paris and USIA enjoy a most cordial relationship and that the operation of the Library, open to the general public, completely complements the USIA Benjamin Franklin Reference Library which is designed to be a reference library for advanced students and facility of universities and government and professional people with scholarly interest. 

I wish to emphasize again that the application for a grant of the American Library is for repairs and improvements to its physical plant and is not for operating expenses or purchase of books or periodicals. I emphasize this distinction as I believe that whenever possible, operating expenses and purchase of books should come out of current income. However, the cost of improvements and repairs to plant, because of the lack of any surplus, cannot be paid for out of current income. 

Your favorable consideration of this request will be very much appreciated. 

Warm personal regards. Cordially Dan. 

Alan Bible

AMERICAN UNIVERSITY IN CAIRO 

Senator INOUYE. Is the American University in Cairo receiving assistance this year? 

Mr. COSTANTINO. Yes, sir.

Senator INOUYE. I asked this because I was under the impression that a trust fund had been established to take care of expenses; is that correct?

Mr. COSTANTINO. That is only partially correct, sir. An endowment fund in Egyptian pounds, 25 million Egyptian pounds, which is an equivalent of approximately $46 million, was granted, I believe, in fiscal year 1969. That endowment fund, however, was not released to the university because it was sequestered by the Egyptian Government after the break in relations with the United States. Our lawyers decided it would be unwise to release these funds to the university on the assumption that the funds might be seized by the Egyptian Government.

Since that time, there has been an interim arrangement, which is now going to be under review because the university was desequestered just last week, when the President was in Cairo. The arrangement was that the university could draw on the principal of the endowment fund to meet its Egyptian pound operating deficit on a yearly basis. The university justified these annual drawndowns to us, and we, of course, tried to limit these expenses to the degree possible. 

The endowment fund is now reduced to 17 million pounds. A year ago we made an agreement with AUC to initiate investment of a portion of the endowment funds. An office has been established in 

Cairo under Egyptian law to handle these investments for the university. So far, however, no specific proposals have been presented to us for approval. We agreed that AUC could proceed with investment of up to 3 million Egyptian pounds. that is about $5 million equivalent, to see what kind of earnings AID could generate. Clearly, the university needs a substantial amount of income to continue to operate and I am very concerned that their budget is far in excess of what can realistically be generated through that endowment fund. 

In addition to the foregoing, the university has received assistance from us over the past few years to meet their dollar expenditures, for such things as books, payment of salaries for U.S. teachers, and to some minor degree their overhead expenses in New York, though I think they have tried to meet those themselves. These sums have ranged from $200,000 to $500,000. In this connection their requirements for this current fiscal year were met from fiscal 1973 moneys.

This fiscal year the grant to the university was earmarked for the construction of a library, which has been under discussion for 3 years and for which we have requested both dollar local currency authorization and appropriations.
