959

AMERICAN SCHOOLS AND HOSPITALS ABROAD EVALUATION OF THE FUNDED PROJECTS 

Mr. Brooke: 

Mr. Costantino: 

Mr. Brooke: 

Mr. Costantino:

Mr. Costantino, some have argued that if your program is funded at the $10 million level, ineffective projects will be eliminated and only the best ones will continue to be funded. 

Is this the case or will the effect tend to be the opposite? 

If the Section 214 program is funded at the $10 million level in FY 1975, funds will be inadequate to cover the legitimate needs of projects that would be generally considered to be the best in the program, e. g., the American University in 

Beirut, the American Children's Hospital in Poland, the American Hospital of Paris, the University of the Americas, the Feinberg Graduate School of the Weizmann Institute,

Project HOPE, the American Hospital in Rome, the Bologna Center of Johns Hopkins, the Hadassah hospital in Jerusalem, the American University in Cairo, and other secondary and vocational schools and hospitals throughout the world which have received help or hope to receive help for the first time. 

That the institutions above are cited does not imply that other institutions are less "good" projects. It is hard, in fact, to say that any school or hospital isn't performing a useful social service. If the budget were increased A. I. D. would have the option of considering applications from many fine institutions which would otherwise have to be ignored and/or more adequately fund the institutions cited. 

Along this same line, how do you evaluate the effectiveness of the various projects that you fund? What qualitative and quantitative criteria do you use?

A number of techniques are used to evaluate the effectiveness of ongoing projects. (1) Each grant agreement requires the submission of periodic reports which are reviewed on receipt 34-192 O 74-61

by the Office of American Schools and Hospitals Abroad (ASHA). 

(2) Each project is visited periodically by a member of the ASHA staff, or by A. I. D. engineering staff in the case of construction projects. The American Hospital Association 

Surveyor's Listing Report form is used as a general guide for inspecting hospital facilities. In addition, educational, library, medical or management consultants are occasionally sent to institutions in the field to analyze and report on special situations or special problems. (3) Oral and written reports are received from time to time from personnel of the American Mission or the American Consulate commenting on the effectiveness of the institution, or on problems which arise, and which they feel require attention from ASHA. (4) 

All ASHA projects are audited periodically by various audit organizations both inside and outside of A. I. D. Copies of these reports are received and reviewed by ASHA, and 

ASHA is required to follow up on audit report recommendations.

The most effective of these techniques, of course, is the field visit by ASHA personnel. Perhaps the key element in making qualitative judgments is our evaluation of the management of the institution. ASHA personnel responsible for making these evaluations are senior officers experienced in the development of projects overseas. 

Quantitative criteria are difficult to use because of the great differences in the nature of the projects and the environments in which they operate. For instance, the performance of the highly sophisticated Hadassah Hospital in Jerusalem cannot be judged by the same standards used for the small cottage hospitals being operated in the back country of Nigeria by the World Mercy Fund.

Mr. Brooke: 

Mr. Costantino:

Can you provide the Committee with a detailed evaluation of each of your projects in terms of their effectiveness in meeting the objectives of the American Schools and Hospitals Program?

The objective of the American Schools and Hospitals Program is stated in the Section 214 legislation-- to support schools and hospitals overseas which serve as study and demonstration centers for ideas and practices of the United States. The following is an evaluation of our FY 1974 projects in terms of this objective: 

Admiral Bristol Hospital, Turkey. This small, excellent hospital with American medical and management direction has been known for years as the American Hospital in The hospital has been a pioneer in the development Istanbul. of a first-class, American program for the training of nurses, which has led to significant change of attitude towards the nursing profession in Turkey. Some of the largest hospitals in Turkey have asked for help in developing their own nursing systems along the lines of the American hospital. 

This project is highly effective. 

American Children's Hospital in Poland. This hospital was conceived and developed as a joint effort between the Governments of Poland and the United States for patient care, teaching and research. This 300 bed hospital serves as a center for acute pediatric care, a teaching center and a research center. The teaching role of this American center encompasses not only undergraduate, graduate and post graduate medical education, but also provides clinical instruction and experience for students in many disciplines, including nursing, medical technology, pharmacy, biology, dietetics, and midwifery.

The hospital has been operating at peak capacity since it opened in 1966, and is very effective in terms of a Section 

214 project.

American Farm School, Greece. The purpose of this unique institution is to disseminate knowledge of American agricultural methods in the classroom as well as through rural demonstration and extension. The 200 boys are selected for their interest in farming, leadership potential and scholastic ability. In addition to the general high school curriculum, they are taught the application of American agricultural technology in the agricultural enterprises of the school, including the dairy and dairy processing facilities, poultry, hog production, farm products marketing and field crop production, using primarily American agricultural machinery and equipment. The school is much admired and a respected symbol of the United States and its friendship for Greece.

The American Hospital of Paris, France. The American 

Hospital of Paris was opened in 1910, chartered by an act of Congress in 1913, and has long stood as a symbol of 

Franco-American friendship. Principal members of the medical and management staff are Americans and employ U. S. methods in the operation of the institution. 

The hospital is fully accredited by the American Joint Commission on the Accreditation of Hospitals. All U. S. physicians at the hospital are required to visit the U. S. at least once each three years to take refresher courses at U.S. hospitals or universities.

The hospital is well known throughout Europe, Africa, and the Near East as a center of the American medical profession, and is probably one of the most effective projects in terms of Section 214 objectives.

American Hospital in Rome, Italy. This is a relatively new institution with all the potential for impact on the local environment of the American Hospital in Paris or the Admiral Bristol Hospital in Istanbul. The general level of hospital management in Italy is so low that a small, modern American hospital in Rome to serve as a demonstration center for U.S. medical practices is proving to be highly beneficial to the community, and a catalyst to medical reforms. 

This 400-bed teaching hospital provides a broad program of medical education, nursing and paramedical training. English is the language of instruction, and the staff is American or 

U.S. trained.

American University of Beirut. This prestigious institution is the major project receiving support from the American Schools and Hospitals Abroad Program. Over 13, 000 degrees, as well as an additional 10, 000 diplomas and certificates have been granted by AUB since the school was founded in 1866. 

AUB maintains a mailing list of over 9, 000 living alumni.

Its graduates have risen to the ranks of national presidents, prime ministers, parlimentary leaders, ministers of foreign affairs and defense, principally in the Moslem nations of the 

Near East and Africa. Graduates have reached similar influential positions in the professional and business communities of the Arab world. Despite the volatile nature of the student body, and the some-time anti- U. S. demonstrations, experience has shown that when the graduates mature in their various professions, they almost invariably become the most staunch defenders in their social environment of the American nature of the university and of the United States.

American University in Cairo, Egypt. This is the only private, degree granting institution of higher education in Egypt. The university provides a strong and vital cultural link between the U. S. and the people of the leading country of the Arab world. The university, with course work conducted in the English language, provides educational services to 1, 500 undergraduates and graduate students and 4, 000 extension students. Effectiveness of the project in terms of the 

Section 214 program is frequently measured in terms of how the Egyptian Government or press feel about AUC, citing the healthy survival of the school as an American institution after the 1967 war; the Egyptian Government's favorable attitude towards AUC even at the lowest points in U.S.- 

Egyptian political relations. On May 18, 1973, when Egypt reduced U. S. official personnel by 50%, for example, the 

Government excluded AUC from the order and said AUC, 11 '... will remind us of the America with which we hope to have better relations."

Anatolia College, Greece. Anatolia College is a nonsectarian, non-profit American secondary school devoted to the education of Greek boys and girls from many parts of Greece. It is a school of exceptionally high academic quality. The college has been located in Thessaloniki since 

1923, when its directors were invited by the Greek prime minister to reestablish the school in Grecce. 

(Anatolia College had been founded in Turkey in 1886 by a group of American missionaries as a four-year liberal arts college for young men.) Chartered under the laws of Massachusetts in 1894, the Board of Trustees has 27 members in New York together with a seven-member advisory board in Greece. The school continues to function as an excellent vehicle for carrying out

the objectives of the American Schools and Hospitals Abroad Program. 

Beth Yaacov Avat Girls School, Israel. This girls high school with approximately 200 students is sponsored by the Beth Joseph Foundation. The school ... is fortunate in having American sponsors who guide the course of study... and formulate its educational policy. The influence of these sponsors is evident in the emphasis placed by the school's curriculum on the language, literature, and history of America. But the school's success as a workshop of 

American educational methods and ideas could not have been achieved without the quality of its instructors, a number of whom grew up in America and gained their schooling in its universities... In the classroom, students gain a new dimension of American society, government and culture hearing the first-hand experience of these instructors who imbue them with the ambition to introduce the best features of American life into the society which they will help build in Israel." (1) 

Bologna Center, Johns Hopkins University, Italy. Established in 1944 with assistance from the U. S. Government, the Bologna Center is an extension of the area studies program of the School of Advanced International Studies of Johns Hopkins University. The school exposes non- U. S. students to a U.S. system of graduate education with small classes, low faculty-student ratio. Bologna offers courses in 

American politics, history, culture and a contemporary U.S. approach to social sciences. Enrollment is approximately 

100. This unique, U. S. graduate school abroad promotes 

U.S. political and economic ideas among an elite group of (1) Beth Joseph Foundation application dated April 18, 1972.

European intellectuals.

There is an American Director with ten U.S. faculty out of a total of twenty eight. The cost/benefit ratio of this institution in terms of Section 214 objectives is probably among the most favorable in the program.

Cairo American College, Egypt. The school was founded in 1945 by American businessmen and missionaries living in the Cairo area. It was established and is operated to provide an American type of elementary and secondary education through a curriculum comparable to that of American schools of high academic standing. There are approximately 300 students in the school. Out of a total of 

35 professional staff, 22 are U. S. citizens. The school moved into its new campus in January 1970. It is located on the outskirts of Cairo, and comprises a group of welldesigned and well constructed buildings as well as typical American sports and recreation facilities. 

This excellent school is frequently under observation as a model for other schools to emulate.

Chemke Mercy Hospitals, Nigeria. The small cottage hospitals built by this project, sponsored by the World Mercy Fund, are located in some of the poorest regions of the country. They are partially staffed by American religious physicians and nurses. They were built in close cooperation with the Nigerian Government's Ministry of 

Health, and although these cottage hospitals are now privately run, they will eventually be taken over by the Government, when the Ministry is in a position to staff them. In the meantime, they provide an extremely valuable service in a part of the world where there are no other hospitals or health services available, and acquaint the

population with American medical practices, provided by the American involved in their operation. 

Cheng Hsin Rehabilitation Center, Taipei, Taiwan. The

Center treats post-polio children. It was opened during 

May 1966, and since that time, through corrective surgery, prothesis, physio-therapy and occupational therapy, has rehabilitated over two thousand children. The Center's facilities have been filled to capacity since the beginning of its operations. Section 214 help to this institution came after the bi-lateral A. I.D. program had ended in Taiwan, and perhaps more significantly, when the U.S. was engaged in its new relationships with Mainland China. We believe the establishment of the American wing at the hospital for the demonstration of U.S. medical techniques in this field was a timely and effective use of Section 214 funds in terms of the program's objectives in an important nation in the Far East.

Damavand College, Tehran, Iran. Damavand is a four-year liberal arts college for women. Its American style curriculum, all taught in the English language, prepares its students for careers in teaching, social work, and to be executive secretaries, all vitally needed now in Iran's developing society. Four graduates of this school are presently members of Iran's parliament. Damavand is a high-quality school, and the only American institution of higher learning for girls in Iran. It attracts girls from the leading families in the country. Considering the accellerating rate of the emergence of women into the industrializing society in the Middle East, Damavand is an exceptionally potent vehicle for demonstrating American educational practices during this time.

Escuela Agricola Panamericana, Tegucigalpa, Honduras. 

A. I. D. has helped support the Pan American Agricultural Schoo in Honduras for many years. Our evaluation has been that the 

Escuela is a well-managed American institution satisfying the need for trained agriculturists throughout Central America and northern South America. The boys are taught English as well as their agricultural specialties. Numbers of them come to the United States for graduate training upon completion of their work at the Escuela. The high-quality demonstration value of this institution in terms of the Section 214 program is without question. 

Feinberg Graduate School of the Weizmann Institute of

Science, Israel. In testimony before the Senate 

Appropriations Committee, July 16, 1971, Dr. Albert B.

Sabin stated: "The teaching methods, ideas and curriculum of the Graduate School are those of advanced universities in the United States. The faculty of the Graduate School is drawn from the principal scientists of the Institute and invited professors from the United States. A vital and expanding relationship exists between the Institute scientists and scientific and academic circles in the U. S. and elsewhere. 

Institute scientists have served and continue to serve as invited visiting professors and lecturers in leading scientific and academic institutions in the U. S., including: the 

California Institute of Technology, Rochefeller University, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Harvard University, Stanford University, University of California Berkeley, Princeton University and Columbia University. The demonstration nature of this program described by Dr. 

Sabin and confirmed by this Agency accords with the objectives of the Section 214 program.

Hadassah Medical Center, Israel. The Hadassah medical complex located in Jerusalem is a full service teaching hospital with a heavy accent on research. The Hadassah- 

Hebrew University Medical Center has a total teaching load of 2, 700, comprising undergraduate, graduate, and post graduate students. The number of students in the various medical disciplines range from 683 in the Nursing School, 551 in the Medical School to 4 in Clinical Psychology. 

All of Hadassah's medical and teaching institutions in Israel were established by U. S. citizens. Its policies and programs are formulated and directed by the National Board of Hadassah in New York. The teaching staffs and medical personnel include many U. S. citizens. In addition, many of the Israelis working for Hadassah are U.S. trained and they bring to their positions American standards and expert knowledge. This is an American institution overseas demonstrating American medical techniques and practices on a large scale. Hadera Institute, Israel. The main staff is made up of instructors and professors educated in the United States and graduates of major U. S. universities.

People-to-People Health Foundation (HOPE). HOPE is the acronym for "Health Opportunity for People Everywhere."

Pierce College, Athens, Greece. Pierce College, with about 1,000 English-speaking students (mostly Greek), is a full-fledged American undergraduate college institution providing a liberal arts education in Greece. The school began offering a degree-granting program about ten years ago. 

Its educational philosophy has developed along American lines. 

There is an emphasis on the professor's ability to teach and inspire intellectual depth and curiosity in the student through classroom and personal contact. Pierce has been regarded as a high quality American school since it was founded in Asia Minor in 1875, and continues to be a highly effective

Presbyterian Medical Center, Chonju, Korea. This medical center begun by Americans in 1893, is recognized as one of the outstanding medical facilities in Korea. The center provides medical services within and outside the hospital, operates a resident training program, and supports a school of nursing and various training programs for paramedics. 

The hospital has pioneered in a number of fields--training medical leadership, establishing medical records, speech

and hearing center, American accounting system, American nursing care, blood transfusions, post graduate education, etc. The center with 212 beds and associated rural health clinics makes a profound impact on the level of health care in the Southwestern region of Korea where it is located. 

Robert College, Istanbul, Turkey. Robert College was the first American college to be established outside the United States (1864). Since its beginning, the school has consistently maintained a high percentage of U. S. faculty and has enjoyed the endorsement and cooperation of outstanding U.S. educational institutions. Its graduates have achieved prominence in every sector of professional life, both public and private, in Turkey and abroad, in fields that range from architecture to zoology. Associated with Robert, was the 

American College for Girls founded in 1871. It was the pioneer institution in women's education in Turkey. Its impact and influence on Turkish Women and on the quality of their education and life style has been enormous. In

Sogang University, Seoul, Korea. This Jesuit university was founded in 1960, and is sponsored by a group of businessmen mainly from the Minneapolis area. University of the Americas, Puebla, Mexico. Mr. Costantino, for several years there have been attempts to limit funding for your program to no more than four projects in any one country. So far, these have not been successful. 

I wonder if there would not be some merit in placing limitations on the % of your funds that can be spent in any one country. 

I do not think so, Sir, because of the differences in the size and requirements of various institutions. Rather than placing a limit on the percentage of funds than can be spent in any one country, I believe it would be more useful to limit the number of institutions in one country that can receive assistance in any one fiscal year to two or three at most. Further, to deal in percentages could seriously hamstring administration of the program in a way not intended by the Committee. A percentage limitation prescribed with an annual level of approximately $20 million in mind could become either meaningless or unworkable if the total appropriation were to be drastically increased or decreased.

Also, would you provide us with your views on what would be an appropriate percentage limitation on the funding for any one country?

I think a percentage limitation by country would be arbitrary in view of the size, requirements and value of various institutions. For example, the American University in Beirut is a regional institution with students from over 60 countries.

Senator INOUYE. This morning we turn to those areas of our assistance program administered by AID's Supporting Assistance Bureau, namely, first, Indochina postwar reconstruction for which $939,800,000 in new obligational authority is sought and a total program of $943,300,000 is contemplated.

Second, security supporting assistance for which $385,500,000 in new obligational authority is sought, and a total program of $397,- 500,000 is contemplated. Of the total program $377,500,000 is requested for the so-called Middle East peace program, and $20 million for all other purposes.

Third, Middle East special requirements fund for which $100 million in new obligational authority is sought and a program of like amount is contemplated.

[The statement follows:] 

Mr. Chairman and Members of the Committee, it is a privilege to appear before you today to testify on behalf of our request for Security Supporting Assistance and Indochina Postwar Reconstruction for fiscal year 1975. I should like to turn first to the Middle East. 

MIDDLE EAST PEACE PROGRAM 

Secretary Kissinger has set forth the broad policy framework which guides our request for economic assistance in the Middle East. I should like to stress nonethless that we have an important opportunity to use our economic assistance to help consolidate the progress made through long and difficult negotiations. 

We have a responsibility to our own interests in peace to meet that opportunity. 

Our Supporting Assistance programs for the Middle East amount to $377.5 million $250 million for Egypt, $77.5 million for Jordan, and $50 million for Israel. 

In addition, military assista ice to Israel will be provided under the $2.2 billion military aid bill enacted last year plus $300 million in FMS credits contained in another part of this bill. Jordan will receive a MAP grant of $100 million and 

FMS credits of $30 million under this bill. Also, Israel, Jordan, and Egypt will be offered PL-480 sales agreements for surplus agricultural commodities, but the amounts cannot be determined until the current crop situation has been clarified. 

This will give us a well balanced program intended to reflect the needs of each country and the appropriate U.S. response to them. 

Each of the specific programs are described in greater detail in a separate Supporting Assistance Presentation Book. However, I would like to summarize them for you. Egypt We are proposing a significant program of assistance for Egypt for the first time since 1967. Egypt has the largest population, 35 million, and the lowest per capita GNP, about $243. of the countries directly involved in the Middle 

East conflict. Thus, its size gives Egypt both a key role in the affairs of the area and an immense task in raising the quality of life of its people. As a result, the largest single element, $250 million, of the proposed economic program is requested for Egypt.

President Sadat has recognized the urgent need to refocus the country's attention on reconstruction and economic growth. To succeed along this path, Egypt must rely heavily on external support. No one donor can be expected to provide all of the support required. Thus, our aid has a dual role: the provision of a share of the resources needed and a demonstration of our conviction that Egypt's development is of major interest to all who have a stake in peace in the Middle East. 

There is already evidence that other donors will make substantial contributions to Egyptian reconstruction, with offers of $240 million from Japan, $190 million from Kuwait and Saudi Arabia, and $870 million from Iran under consideration.

We plan to use the $250 million in Egypt for three basic programs. We will need an estimated $20 million to complete the clearing of ordnance and sunken ships from the Suez Canal. We see the reopening of the Canal as a priority task, one which demonstrates Egypt's intent to play a constructive role in world affairs, add to the general stake in peace, and in time produce significant foreign exchange earnings for Egypt. The British are also assisting with the mine. sweeping and we expect others, including the World Bank and Japan, to help complete the job of reopening the Canal. 

We plan to use $80 million to finance essential imports from the United States. 

Foreign exchange limitations have led to shortages of raw materials, spare parts, fertilizers, pesticides, and other imported goods required for full industrial and agricultural production. Financing for such imports will permit immediate reactivation of idle production capacity and thus have an immediate economic impact. 

The balance of the Egypt program, $150 million, will be used for reconstruction of the canal area, providing resettlement of the displaced population and the restoration of the productive capacity of the area. In concert with others, we plan to review and identify within the vast range of requirements those activities which each donor can finance. Reconstruction of water, power, and sewage systems are priority tasks. Housing, transport facilities, and industrial plants to provide employment are urgent requirments. The first element of this portion of the program will be used to set up a Reconstruction Fund under which replacement parts and equipment damaged or destroyed in the fighting can be financed. 

This will include electric generators, power cables, water pipes and valves, and the pumps and motors necessary to restore essential services in the canal area. 

This equipment will be of U.S. origin. Jordan

The proposed program for Jordan is basically a continuation of our current activities. An increase in our request for budget support is made necessary by the impact of higher world prices on Jordan's budget expenditures. The Jordanian economy remains extremely narrow and fragile and is not able to produce the revenues needed to cover essential governmental spending. Continued budget support is necessary for economic and political stability. We plan to use $67.5 million for this purpose in fiscal year 1975. 

The Government of Jordan has a sincere desire to reduce its dependence on external budget support and has launched a development program which holds promise, primarily through the exploitation of mineral resources and increased agricultural production, for economic independence for Jordan over the next decade. The Jordan River Valley is an area of great potential and we have concentrated the developmental side of our program in that area. In fiscal year 1975, we propose to use Supporting Assistance for two projects of $5 million each in the valley: one would help finance village resettlement and the other would be a sector loan for an increase in agricultural production in the valley. 

For Israel

While the October war put a number of strains on the Israeli economy, it remains relatively strong and Israel's foreign exchange position is good. However, domestic inflation poses a real problem to the Israelis, the population carries a very heavy tax burden, and foreign indebtedness is high. Thus, we propose in fiscal year 1975 to continue our program of economic Supporting Assistance to finance essential imports from the United States. We are requesting $50 million for this purpose, the same amount that was provided in fiscal year 1974. 

Special requirements fund

In addition, we are requesting a special fund of $100 million to enable us to move rapidly to meet economic and humanitarian needs elsewhere in the Middle East. As we are unable to identify the precise uses of this fund at this time, we have proposed a separate authorization with the stipulation that we would provide Congress in advance with a complete and timely explanation of uses.

It will be very important that we be able to move quickly to provide economic assistance elsewhere in the area as requirements arise. Resolution of the refugee problem will be a critical element of any peace negotiations and the United States must be in a position to assist in possible resettlement programs or development projects which could serve as a source of productive livelihood. Constructive programs must be developed and both the Arabs and Israelis will look to the United States for leadership and assistance. In this rapidly evolving situation, we must be able to respond as the need arises, if we are to play an effective role in creating the necessary conditions for a more permanent peace. 

OTHER SUPPORTING ASSISTANCE PROGRAMS 

We are also proposing continuation of the smaller, but nevertheless essential, Supporting Assistance programs not directly bearing on the Middle East. These programs total $20 million as follows: $9.5 million for Malta, $3 million for 

Spain, $4.8 million to support UN Forces in Cyprus, and $2.7 million for A.I.D. support costs. Malta

The island's strategic location is important to the defense of Europe and the Mediterranean. Thus, the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) supported the negotiation in 1971 of a renewal of the U.K.-Malta Defense Agreement providing Maltese facilities to the British military for a period of seven years. A number of NATO countries agreed to help the United Kingdom meet the annual payments for the retention of those facilities. The annual U.S. share, of $9.5 million, is paid through NATO. Spain

In the negotiations for renewal of the U.S.-Spanish Defense Agreement, signed in 1970, the Spanish Government requested that the new agreement provide for nonmilitary cooperation in the fields of agriculture, education, science and technology. Pursuant to this agreement, the $3 million proposed for FY 1975 will continue a program of cultural, educational and scientific exchanges administered by the Bureau of Education and Cultural Affairs of the Department of State, together with the National Science Foundation. 

U.N. Forces in Cyprus

Peace in Cyprus is critical to the maintenance of peace between Greece and Turkey, both NATO allies, and the U.N. has maintained a peacekeeping force there since 1964. Seven other nations provide armed forces and help to meet the financial costs. The United States provides financial assistance only and we are requesting $4.8 million for this purpose in 1975. 

INDOCHINA 

While in the Middle East we have a new opportunity, in Indochina we have a continuing responsibility. An adequate level of economic assistance is essential in order to preserve the degree of stability and peace which has been achieved in Indochina, and to provide the humanitarian support desperately needed by the people of Indochina after many years of war. 

There has been continued progress toward peace in Indochina during the past year, even though that progress has been somewhat uneven and more gradual than we would have liked. Nevertheless, a political solution has now been achieved in Laos with the formation of a coalition government and the complete cessation of hostilities. In South Vietnam, a political solution has remained elusive, but the level of fighting has declined so that military casualties have been about one-third of the 1965-1972 period. The South Vietnamese Government has demonstrated that it can cope with both its military and civilian problems so long as a reasonable amount of U.S. assistance is available. In Cambodia, fighting remains at a high level, and any serious discussions leading to a political settlement must await a clarification of the military situation. 

Progress toward rehabilitation and reconstruction has been slower than we expected, first of all due to the level of military activity in South Vietnam and Cambodia. This in turn has slowed down the economic support which we had expected would be forthcoming from other donors, although some, such as Japan and France, have increased their contributions. Also, the level of U.S. economic assistance approved by the Congress for FY 1974 was not adequate to undertake the capital development projects which are an essential part of moving these

countries to a state of economic self-sufficiency, and the real value of this assistance was even further diminished by sharp increases in the cost of the goods which Indochina imports.

Nevertheless, much progress has been made. I would like to comment on the impressions I had on a trip to Vietnam in April of this year. I have been traveling to Vietnam since January 1970, and never have I seen the present government look stronger, more competent, and more able to deal with the problems it is facing than now. We are closer to achieving a self-sufficient Vietnam than most 

Americans realize. The South Vietnamese economy is beginning to adjust to the economic impact caused by the withdrawal of U.S. military forces. Tax collections during 1973 increased by some one-third over the previous year, and are 25 percent higher during the first four months of 1974 than the comparable 1973 period. Exports, which were $13 million in 1971 and $23 million in 1972, jumped to $60 million in 1973. Refugees in camps, who numbered 489,000 on July 1, 1973, have now been reduced to 85,000, the lowest number since 1971.

We are requesting $943.3 million for economic aid to Indochina in FY 1975, for the following purposes: Cambodia.-.

A detailed description of the proposed country programs has been submitted in a separate Indochina Presentation Book. However, I would like to review these programs with you briefly. 

South Vietnam

We are requesting $750 million for economic aid to South Vietnam for the following purposes: 

Humanitarian assistance_ 

Reconstruction and development--.

The cutbacks in aid levels over the last several years and the sharp increase in world commodity prices have put a continuing downward squeeze on Vietnam imports during the past five years. In real terms, imports in FY 1974 are only 

55 percent of imports during the peak year of 1969, and are about the same on a per capita basis as they were in 1964-65 (See Attached Charts). This sharp drop in imports has led to severe strains on the Vietnamese economy, producing growing unemployment and severe economic hardships on substantial portions of the population. The urban population and Government employees have been particularly hard hit, with growing cases of malnutrition and misery on the part of those unable to find jobs. Statistics are not precise, but unemployment appears to be in the range of 800,000 to 1 million persons. 

The Vietnamese are a resourceful and hearty people, and they are adjusting to these reductions with great fortitude. However, there is a limit to endurance, and the Vietnamese are approaching that point. Further reductions would impose intolerable burdens on a people who have already suffered enough. 

Our program proposes to do three principal things: (1) to supply the humanitarian needs of the population through a series of programs in child care, health care, and refugee aid: (2) to meet the ongoing needs of the economy by the importation of fertilizer, pesticides, industrial raw materials, and petroleum products to maintain current Vietnamese production at about present levels; and (3) to undertake a greatly expanded program of capital investment projects so that the Vietnamese economy can begin to grow at a more rapid rate and hence to achieve economic self-sufficiency in the shortest possible time. While the numbers seem large, this is nevertheless a relatively austere program. It will only

maintain general imports at the current level, which is already greatly reduced as mentioned previously. Nevertheless, it will provide the possibility for Vietnam to begin to expand production, to create jobs in order to relieve the growing unemployment, and to increase its capacit: Leed and supply its own people without having to rely forever on foreign assistance. 

We are in the process of making some long range projections of economic requirements in the coming years. While these projections have not been fully completed, the general outline is now clear. The $750 million request this year should, in constant prices, be the peak request which we will present to the Congress. If the Congress grants this request, U.S. economic aid to Vietnam will decline steadily over the next five years, beyond which any further economic aid would be at nominal levels. This process cannot begin, however, unless we can make a sizable infusion during FY 1975. The sooner we begin, the sooner the 

Vietnamese economy will be restored to normalcy. 

I would like to say a word about the humanitarian programs. The $135 million request is needed not only to resettle refugees located in refugee camps, as we have done in prior years, but also to begin a program to resettle those refugees who fled or migrated to the cities during the war years and who now find they cannot make a living there any longer. We have also greatly expanded and accelerated our assistance to children under a new program to improve the nutrition, living conditions in orphanages and to provide more day care centers. 

We have increased support for out-of-country adoptions of war orphans. In all of these new programs for children we are relying very heavily on the services of American voluntary agencies. I have attached a short paper on our child welfare program, which is shown as Attm't. No. 1. 

Members of Congress have frequently expressed their support for the humanitarian element in this program, which we appreciate. However, it does not make any sense to be generous in our support for refugees and war orphans while cutting back on general economic support which provides the livelihood and means of support for the general population. The reports of misery and hardships which are coming out of Vietnam recently are not related to refugees which are being fed under U.S. support programs. Rather, they are average Vietnamese who have lost their jobs because of the general economic hardship being imposed on the country. Thus, in the broadest sense virtually the entire economic program can be thought of as humanitarian in nature. 

We have eliminated the term "Commercial Import Program" this year due to the consistent misunderstanding that the term has engendered in the past. In spite of our frequent explanation to the contrary, the general public has tended to identify the CIP with the importation of hondas or consumer goods, which it never was. Therefore, this year we have identified the imports which we finance by the purposes for which they are being used. Thus, fertilizer, pesticides and other imports required for the production of food has been identified as "Food and Nutrition", as would be the case in other aid-recipient countries. 

Industrial raw materials such as yarns and fibers, chemical products, iron and steel, and wood pulp are being requested under the category called "Industrial Production", and those imports needed to provide the inputs to operate Vietnam's transportation system have been so labeled. The control system developed under the CIP in past years, including close U.S. review and auditing, will, however, be retained in order to assure that goods are ordered and used for their intended purposes.

Before I leave Vietnam, I would like to call attention to the success of the land reform program there, which has really been a major success. I have attached a short paper on this which may interest the Committee (See Attachment II).

Laos 

The formation of a Provisional Government of National Union (PGNU) this past April represents a bona fide political resolution of Lao internal differences. 

The U.S. supports this effort and we seek, with our economic assistance, to help 

Laos make a successful transition from the disruptions of war to the fruits of peace.

The refugee population has exploded during the past year, and while earlier refugee groups were able to provide for themselves, this is becoming increasingly difficult for refugees now. We plan to use $20 million for humanitarian assistance. About half of the funds will support the growing programs of voluntary agencies such as CARE, Catholic Relief Services, International Committee for the Red Cross, and World Vision Relief Organization. The balance will be used to help resettle refugees, mostly on a temporary basis around Phnom Penh, so that they can provide for at least some of their own needs. A short paper on our efforts to help refugees is attached (See Attachment III). $71 million is for the ongoing Commodity Import Program under which we finance such essential goods as machinery and equipment, trucks, sugar, fertilizer, and oil products. Due to worldwide price increases, this amount will finance only the bare necessities which Cambodia needs to import. 

We plan to provide $17.5 million to the multilateral Exchange Support Fund, which helps Cambodia finance other needed imports and stabilize the economy. 

The U.S. contribution to this Fund is expected to be about half of the total. 

Luxury imports, including passenger vehicles and air conditioners, are banned and will continue to be. This import assistance from the United States and others allows the Cambodian economy to continue at a marginal level in what is a most difficult situation. 

Regional development

We are requesting $9.4 million in Indochina Postwar Reconstruction Funds for a variety of regional projects particularly focused on the Indochina countries, in addition to $5.8 million in other A.I.D. funds for regional development projects broader than Indochina.

The Indochina funds will be provided as a mixture of loans and grants. The largest of the grants, $2.2 million, is for the Mekong Basin Development Planning Project for a variety of activities including delta water systems and soils management, fisheries, navigation aids and dredging. The proposed loan, $4.5 million, is to increase the existing power generation at the hydro-electric plant at 

Drayling on a Mekong tributary in Vietnam.

CONCLUSION 

Finally, I would like to call your attention to a special problem which arises this year in connection with these programs. The usual extension of the Foreign 

Assistance Act under a Continuing Resolution for a number of months into the new Fiscal Year will have an adverse effect if the same pattern is followed this year.

For example, a Continuing Resolution at the FY 1974 level will not provide enough Supporting Assistance funds to undertake urgent new programs in Egypt, leading to a serious delay in reconstruction activities and a very undesirable gap in the pace of our growing contacts, both diplomatic and economic, with that country. A Continuing Resolution at the FY 1974 level would not contain money for a Special Requirements Fund, which is a new funding category in 1975. While we have not yet received a request for economic assistance from Syria, the absence of the Special Requirements Fund would preclude our taking important steps to

meet this or other urgent requirements which may arise. In Indochina, the FY 

1974 level is woefully inadequate to meet the funding requirements for even the maintenance of the present level of economic activity in view of rapidly rising world prices, much less making a serious beginning toward economic selfsufficiency.

Therefore, we ask your most urgent consideration of this bill, preferably with final passage early enough to preclude the necessity of a Continuing Resolution.

FISCAL YEARS

CHILD WELFARE 

ATTACHMENT 1 SOUTH VIETNAM 

The years of war have been very hard for children in South Vietnam, not only for the obvious cases of orphans and refugees but also for the many whose lives have been disrupted in manifold ways. 

In FY 1974, A.I.Ó. began an expanded $7.5 million special child welfare program. 

This was done, in part, in response to Congressional action earmarking $5 million for this purpose. We are proposing $8.2 million for FY 1975, to continue and carry forward this program. The speical program as funded this year includes the following elements: 

Orphanage Support and Improvement: Food and clothing allowances, health care, equipment, improvement of facilities and staff training. ($1,736,000) 

International Adoption: American agencies expanding and improving intercountry adoption programs and related welfare activities. ($469,000) 

Pediatric Clinics: Medical care for disadvantaged children with priority to those pre-adoption cases requiring special medical attention. ($340,000) 

Day Care Centers: Equipment, food and staff training for existing day care centers and support in the development of new centers. ($1,428,000) 

Home Nursery Care: Day nursery services for infants. ($760,000)

Nutrition Centers: Expansion of existing nutrition centers and creation of additonal centers for seriously malnourished children. ($630,000) 

Handicapped Children: 

Improved custodial care and therapy. ($178,000) 

Foster Care: Foster home care services for children as an alternative to their abandonment, institutionalization or adoption. ($570,000) 

Prevention of Infant Abandonment: Counseling service to emotionally distraught expectant mothers who might abandon their children. ($44,000)

Civilian Widows Assistance: Support, vocational training and small-scale capital assistance to widowed mothers. ($476,000) 

Training: Pediatric and nutrition training to midwives; child welfare services training to Ministry of Social Welfare employees. ($552,000) 

It is important to note that this special program by no means is the sum of U.S. assistance to Vietnamese children. If one also includes assistance to refugee children, child health services, and Food for Peace food supplements for needy children, the total would be over $30 million in FY 1973, over $40 million this fiscal year, and up again in the year to come. Further, our general economic support programs are of major, if less obvious, consequence for the welfare of Vietnamese children. A farmer who prospers, in part because he can get imported fertilizer, can take good care of his children.

On the other hand, the children of an unemployed adult can suffer just as much as the children in an orphanage with unadequate resources.

.

ATTACHMENT II LAND REFORM IN SOUTH VIETNAM 

South Vietnam recently marked the 4th anniversary of the signing of its revolutionary Land-to-the-Tiller Law of March 26, 1970, which set off one of the major non-communist land reform programs of the 

20th century.

The land reform was begun under the most difficult conditions imaginable. Widespread fighting was continuing on a major scale, and the administrative structure was creaky, so far as it existed at all. 

Further, this was not the reform of relatively few, very large estates. The tenancy rate on Vietnam's rice-land was among the highest in the world, roughly 60 percent, but on many middle to small sized holdings.

If the catalog of problems was endless, the land reform was pressed and the goal of 2,200,000 acres (1,000,000 hectares), which had seemed visionary, was in fact reached three years later in March 1973. By comparison, the often and rightly lauded land reform on Formosa distributed one-quarter of the acreage under conditions of peace and a full three years were taken simply for planning. 

When the goal was reached last year, tenancy was virtually eliminated in South Vietnam and ownership of half of the country's rice land had changed hands. The program has continued over the past year and title to another 330,000 acres has changed hands. To date, some 

750,000 farm families, composed of almost 5,000,000 members, have become property owners. 

Apart from the political reasons for land reform and considerations of equity, it has brought economic benefits to Vietnam's countryside. 

Tenants who once paid 25 to 35 percent of the crop to their landlords now have this to invest in better farming, seeds, fertilizer, improved irrigation, and there is much evidence that they have been doing so. 

South Vietnam's most significant social reform has received scant public attention. In fact, recent News stories `referred to landlords reclaiming land previously granted. These stories were carefully checked and found to be largely erroneous. 

ATTACHMENT III EMERGENCY RELIEF AND RESETTLEMENT NEEDS IN CAMBODIA 

Cambodia's refugee problems accelerated rapidly in FY 1974 as the fighting moved closer to the populated areas around Phnom Penh and the

province capitals. Registered refugees now total 885,039 compared to 

662,000 at the begining of the fiscal year. 

A number of emergency relief programs begun in FY 1973 were expanded at a rapid rate as Cambodia's refugee needs escalated. A.I.D. does not directly conduct emergency relief programs in Cambodia, but utilizes the services of a number of U.S. and International Voluntary 

Agencies as well as supporting Cambodian efforts to provide relief assistance. 

We have: 1. 2. 3. 4. 5.

Increased A.I.D. funding of the refugee programs from $1,175,000 in FY 1973, to about $14 million this fiscal year. 

Provide ten Packaged Disaster Hospitals for use in the areas with the greatest numbers of refugees. 

Provided grants to the Catholic Relief Services (CRS), the 

World Vision Relief Organization (WVRO) and the Indochina 

Operations Group (IOG) for the establishment and operation of four of the ten hospitals.

Provided additional grants to CRS, WVRO, CARE, and the IOG to enable them to supply emergency food, shelter and in-camp medical care to refugees and to begin a refugee resettlement program.

In addition, A.I.D. has begun this year to support the operations of the new Resettlement and Development Foundation which the Cambodian Government has established to manage refugee resettlement. The largest part of our FY 1974 refuge/ humanitarian aid, about $8 million, is to assist the Cambodians to resettle refugees in situations where they can grow more of their own food and can be reasonably self-supporting. 

The voluntary agencies have done an outstanding job is responding to these needs on short notice in an extremely difficult and frequently dangerous situation.

For FY 1975, these refugee/humanitarian assistance programs will continue to expand. About half of our $20 million request is needed for the voluntary agency programs, to provide food, medical attention, housing and other emergency relief assistance. The other half is needed for the 

Cambodian's own resettlement programs primarily around Phnom Penh, to clear and prepare land, help refugees construct simple houses, and prepare land, help refugees construct simple houses, and provide the tools, seed and some animals these people will need to lead more productive and self-reliant lives.

MIDDLE EAST 

With your permission, I would like to submit my statement for the record to save time, but to read certain excerpts from it just to give some of the flavor of the statement. 

SUMMARY OF STATEMENT 

It is a privilege to appear before you today to testify on behalf of our request for Security Supporting Assistance and Indochina Postwar Reconstruction for fiscal year 1975. I should like to turn first to the Middle East.

We have an important opportunity to use our economic assistance to help consolidate the progress made through long and difficult negotiations. We have a responsibility to our own interests in peace to meet that opportunity.

Our supporting assistance programs for the Middle East amount to $377.5 million: $250 million for Egypt, $77.5 million for Jordan, and $50 million for Israel. 

We plan to use $250 million from Egypt for three basic programs. 

We will need an estimated $20 million to complete the clearing of ordinance and sunken ships from the Suez Canal. We see the reopening of the canal as a priority task, one which demonstrates Egypt's intent to play a constructive role in world affairs, add to the general stake in peace, and in time produce significant foreign exchange earnings for Egypt.

The British are also assisting with the mine-sweeping and we expect others, including the World Bank and Japan, to help complete the job of reopening the canal. 

We plan to use $80 million to finance essential imports from the United States. Foreign exchange limitations have led to shortages of raw materials, spare parts, fertilizers, pesticides, and other imported goods required for full industrial and agricultural production. Financing for such imports will permit immediate reactivation of idle production capacity and thus have an immediate economic impact. 

The balance of the Egypt program, $150 million, will be used for reconstruction of the canal area, providing resettlement of the displaced population and the restoration of the productive capacity of the area.

The proposed program for Jordan is basically a continuation of our current activities. An increase in our request for budget support is made necessary by the impact of higher world prices on Jordan's budget expenditures.

The Jordanian economy remains extremely narrow and fragile and is not able to produce the revenues needed to cover essential governmental spending. Continued budget support is necessary for economic

and political stability. We plan to use $67.5 million for this purpose in fiscal year 1975.

The Government of Jordan has a sincere desire to reduce its dependence on external budget support and has launched a development program which holds promise, primarily through the exploitation of mineral resources and increased agricultural production, for economic independence for Jordan over the next decade. 

The Jordan River Valley is an area of great potential and we have concentrated the developmental side of our program in that area. 

In fiscal year 1975, we propose to use supporting assistance for two projects of $5 million each in the valley: one would help finance village resettlement and the other would be a sector loan for an increase in agricultural production in the valley. 

For Israel, while the October war put a number of strains on the Israeli economy, it remains relatively strong and Israel's foreign exchange position is good. However, domestic inflation poses a real problem to the Israelis, the population carries a very heavy tax burden, and foreign indebtedness is high. 

Thus, we propose in fiscal year 1975 to continue our program of economic supporting assistance to finance essential imports from the United States. We are requesting $50 million for this purpose, the same amount that was provided in fiscal year 1974. 

SPECIAL REQUIREMENTS FUND 

In addition, we are requesting a special fund of $100 million to enable us to move rapidly to meet economic and humanitarian needs elsewhere in the Middle East. As we are unable to identify the precise uses of this fund at this time, we have proposed a separate authorization with the stipulation that we would provide Congress in advance with a complete and timely explanation of uses. 

We are also proposing continuation of the smaller, but nevertheless essential, supporting assistance programs not directly bearing on the Middle East. These programs total $20 million as follows: $9.5 million for Malta, $3 million for Spain, $4.8 million to support UN Forces in Cyprus, and $2.7 million for AID support costs.

While in the Middle East we have a new opportunity, in Indochina we have a continuing responsibility. An adequate level of economic assistance is essential in order to preserve the degree of stability and peace which has been achieved in Indochina, and to provide the humanitarian support desperately needed by the people of Indochina after many years of war.

I would like to comment on the impressions I had on a trip to Vietnam in April of this year. I have been traveling to Vietnam since 

January 1970, and never have I seen the present government look stronger, more competent, and more able to deal with the problems it is facing than now.

We are closer to achieving a self-sufficient Vietnam than most Americans realize. The South Vietnamese economy is beginning to adjust to the economic impact caused by the withdrawal of U.S. military forces. Tax collections during 1973 increased in real terms by one-third over the previous year, and are 25 percent higher during the first 4 months of 1974 than the comparable 1973 period. 34-192 O-74-63

Exports, which were $13 million in 1971 and $23 million in 1972, jumped to $60 million in 1973. Refugees in camps, who numbered 

489,000 on July 1, 1973, have now been reduced to 85,000, the lowest number since 1971.

We are requesting $750 million for economic aid to South Vietnam. 

Our program proposes to do three principal things: 

1. To supply the humanitarian needs of the population through a series of programs in child care, health care, and refugee aid; 

2. To meet the ongoing needs of the economy by the importation of fertilizer, presticides, industrial raw materials, and petroleum products to maintain current Vietnamese production at about present levels; and 

3. To undertake a greatly expanded program of capital investment projects so that the Vietnamese economy can begin to grow at a more rapid rate and hence to achieve economic self-sufficiency in the shortest possible time.

I would like to say a word about the humanitarian programs. The $135 million request is needed not only to resettle refugees located in refugee camps, as we have done in prior years, but also to begin a program to resettle those refugees who filed or migrated to the cities during the war years and who now find they cannot make a living there any longer.

We have also greatly expanded and accelerated our assistance to children under a new program to improve the nutrition, living conditions in orphanages and to provide more day-care centers. 

We have increased support for out-of-country adoptions of war orphans. In all of these new programs for children we are relying very heavily on the services of American voluntary agencies. I have attached a short paper on our child welfare program which is shown as attachment No. 1.

Members of Congress have frequently expressed their support for the humanitarian element in this program, which we appreciate. However, it does not make any sense to be generous in our support for refugees and war orphans while cutting back on general economic support which provides the livelihood and means of support for the general population.

The reports of misery and hardships which are coming out of Vietnam recently are not related to refugees which are being fed under U.S. support programs. Rather, they are average Vietnamese who have lost their jobs because of the general economic hardship being imposed on the country. Thus, in the broadest sense virtually the entire economic program can be thought of as humanitarian in nature. 

Incidentally, we do plan in fiscal year 1975 that none of the counterpart, much less any of the direct aid will be used for military purposes from the fiscal year 1975 funds that are being requested in this presentation.

We are requesting $55.2 million for Laos and $110 million for Cambodia for purposes which are set out in the statement, and I won't go into that in detail at this time. 

Also, $9.4 million for a variety of regional projects. 

Finally, I would like to call your attention to a special problem which arises this year in connection with these programs. The usual extension of the Foreign Assistance Act under a continuing resolution for a number of months into the new fiscal year will have an adverse effect if the same pattern is followed this year.

For example, a continuing resolution at the fiscal year 1974 level will not provide enough supporting assistance funds to undertake new programs in Egypt, leading to a serious delay in reconstruction activities and a very undesirable gap in the pace of our growing contacts, both diplomatic and economic, with that country. A continuing resolution at the fiscal year 1974 level would not contain money for a Special Requirements Fund, which is a new funding category in 1975. 

While we have not yet received a request for economic assistance from Syria, the absence of the Special Requirements Fund would preclude our taking important steps to meet this or other urgent requirements which may arise.

In Indochina, the fiscal year 1974 level is woefully inadequate to meet the funding requirements for even the maintenance of the present level of economic activity in view of rapidly rising world prices, much less making a serious beginning toward economic self-sufficiency. 

Therefore, we ask your most urgent consideration of this bill, preferably with final passage early enough to preclude the necessity of a continuing resolution. 

Thank you, Mr. Chairman, and we would, of course, be glad to answer any questions the committee might have. 

Senator INOUYE. I thank you very much, sir.

SUEZ CANAL RECONSTRUCTION 

First, on the question of reconstruction of the Canal area, your statement indicates that equipment of U.S. origin will be financed under this reconstruction fund and the equipment and spare parts will include generators, pumps, motors, and so forth.

Is it true that much of the damaged equipment and equipment systems in place were of Russian or East European origin, and if so, do we have any Russian spare parts?

Mr. NOOTER. Well, of course, Mr. Chairman, we would not be providing spare parts for machinery that was not compatible with U.S. equipment, and I would also add that our program there obviously is a very new one.

In fact, the only thing that is now going on is the clearing of mines and ordinance from the Suez Canal, and there is a great deal of detailed work that needs to be done to refine the requests there. We have sent a small team out for a few weeks and we have one there now reviewing the situation. We know in general terms that the amount of the requirement is far, far in excess of what we are requesting, but the details and the exact nature of the requirements are still being worked out.

ASSISTANCE FOR JORDAN 

Senator INOUYE. In 1970, Kuwait and Libya cut off assistance to 

Jordan. I believe at that time it was about $64 million. And we were called upon to provide assistance and our assistance was $50 million per year.

Now that Kuwait has resumed payments I would believe that that should therefore offset to some extent Jordan's need for U.S. assistance. 

How do you justify your statement that Jordan will require $67.5 million in supporting assistance cash payments from the United States in fiscal year 1975?

Mr. NOOTER. You are correct in saying that Kuwait has resumed its subsidy payment of about $45 million a year. The principal reason behind our request is the rapid increase in world prices which impacts on Jordan's internal prices and their budget costs. The underlying requirement there is that Jordan maintain a. strong military establishment which is quite sizable, considering the size of this small country and its ability to raise revenues on its own. The Kuwaiti subsidy was taken into account when this requirement was calculated. 

Senator INOUYE. Was this a negotiated amount or was it based on specific criteria?

Mr. NOOTER. Each year the Jordanians review with us their budget requirements. I don't know if the word "negotiate" is exactly correct, but we do go over the budget with them and review their needs and try to determine what we think is the minimum amount that will permit them to finance their essential requirements.

USE OF ASSISTANCE 

Senator INOUYE. We have been advised that because this program is in the form of direct budget support, we cannot impose any limitations upon the use of these funds; is that correct? 

Mr. NOOTER. We do consider with them and have in the past entered into agreements with them about what their budget spending will be. 

Given the pattern of Jordanian imports we have not been able to tie these funds into an import program the same way which we have been able to do, for example, in Israel and as we propose to do in Egypt. 

Senator INOUYE. What I am trying to get, since this is direct budget support, isn't it possible for the Jordanians to receive the assistance and use it for some other purpose than that which was agreed upon? 

Mr. NOOTER. As I said, Mr. Chairman, we do have an agreement which refers to the budget levels, or budget spending that the Jordanians will have during that particular year. But I don't want to mislead you by saying that this is a very tight or restricted agreement. It is a general agreement in terms of what their spending will be, and we have never had any reason to find that they were diverting funds in ways that were undesirable.

I am not sure I understand the import of the question beyond that. 

Senator INOUYE. Let's assume that the United States and Jordanians get together and the Jordanians say, "We need support in the following areas: education, food for the poor, and housing." 

And so we provide $67.5 million. And after receiving this budgetary assistance they decide that education is not important. They will continue housing and feeding, but the amounts set aside for education will be used for military purposes. Can that be done?

Mr. NOOTER. We have not tied our budget support to any particular part of their budget and in that sense the money is fungible. This is 

Supporting Assistance, this is funds provided for general political and security purposes, and in that sense the use of funds for their military establishment is not considered in any way out of line with this kind of arrangement. That military establishment is a very important part of maintaining the stability in the Middle East. 

Senator INOUYE. The negotiations do not include that?

Mr. NOOTER. That is right. We have not tried to direct our budget support solely to the

Senator INOUYE. What you are trying to tell us is that we have absolutely no control over the funds?

Mr. NOOTER. We know what their general budget spending is for, and find that satisfactory for the purposes that we are providing this money. I will repeat again that the maintenance of a strong army which permits them to maintain their position in the Middle East is the principal purpose for this support. Mr. Breecher reminds me that their budget is submitted and approved by their Parliament and they have a budgetary process which keeps spending in line with the numbers which they go over with us when they present their needs for funds. 

Senator INOUYE. Would you advise us as to whether the Jordanian population will directly benefit from this program other than military security?

Mr. NOOTER. They will in the sense that maintaining a stable economic situation is to the benefit of all the people. But again, I will repeat, Mr. Chairman, this is a Supporting Assistance request intended for political as well as economic purposes. Jordan has been able to maintain a reasonable degree of economic stability with the assistance we have supplied them and with the assistance they receive from Saudia Arabia and now Kuwait. To that extent it is useful and helpful to the Jordanian people. 

TYING OF IMPORTS 

Senator INOUYE. Imports, as you indicated, may be financed from this program.

Mr. NOOTER. Yes. It is made available in the first instance for budget support- Senator INOUYE. But we have no control over what sort of import program they will have. 

Mr. NOOTER. In this program we do not, The reason we do not is that their import system, which is an open one without licensing, a system incidentally favored by the International Monetary Fund and many authorities as the most efficient and preferable, does not lend itself to controlling those imports in a tight and restricted manner without considerable disruption to the economy. Their total imports are also sufficiently small that it would be very difficult to attempt to tie these funds to U.S. exports. 

Senator INOUYE. Can we be assured that this import program will be helping the poor as we intend it to do, and that it won't be like some of the other programs we have seen where just the wealthy would be accommodated?

Mr. NOOTER. The distribution of funds that become available is in effect the spending within the Jordanian budget and is distributed throughout the economy in line with their budget expenditures. 

This is not part of the development assistance category in that sense and isn't intended to be directed specifically to the poorest of the poor, but obviously, we have a concern that the benefits of it do flow to the general economy.

NUCLEAR ASSISTANCE FOR EGYPT AND ISRAEL 

Senator INOUYE. Since our President's journey to the Middle East and his successive announcements of promises, we have tried our best to determine the nature of these promises.

Can you tell us the terms of the President's offer of a nuclear reactor plant and nuclear fuel to Egypt and Israel? 

Mr. SOBER. Yes, Mr. Chairman. The President has announced that we are agreeable to enter into negotiations with both Egypt and Israel for the conclusion of an agreement for cooperation which is an umbrella-type of agreement to cover nuclear cooperation with foreign countries.

In addition, the President has said that conditional upon the conclusion of that agreement for cooperation we are prepared to enter into an agreement with each one of these countries before the end of this month for the supply of fuel that would be needed for the nuclear powerplant which we have agreed to consider supplying them. 

Senator INOUYE. What sort of plant is this?

Mr. SOBER. This would be a powerplant. It is intended that it would add a significant increment to the power generating capacity of both 

Egypt and Israel.

They are thinking in terms of a plant, each one of which would supply some 600 megawatts of electrical power. Because of the problems inherent in planning for and constructing such a plant, these plants in both cases would not become available for operation until the early 1980's.

Senator INOUYE. Is this the type of agreement Canada entered into with India?

Mr. SOBER. It is very much different, sir, in that the agreement between Canada and India, to which I assume you are referring, applies to a research reactor near Bombay which was agreed to in the mid-1950's. I would say that that agreement was concluded at a time when the present system of safeguards administered by the IAEA was not in effect and in effect the research reactor which the Canadians supplied to India is not covered by specific safeguards. 

NUCLEAR SAFEGUARDS 

On the other hand, we have in mind the very firm intention that any agreement that we enter into with Egypt or Israel will be covered by the international safeguards administered by the IAEA, and I would like to add for your information, sir, that we also have in mind asking for certain special bilateral provisions. 

Senator INOUYE. Are you satisfied that these safeguards will be sufficient?

Mr. SOBER. We have been satisfied, sir. We will do everything that we can, using the best of technology and the best of brains and the best of the international community's system, to insure that any assistance which we have agreed to provide will be used only for the purpose that we have in mind, sir.

Senator INOUYE. I suppose that is what the Canadians had in mind also.

Mr. SOBER. They may have desired that, but I say there is a fundamental difference, in that safeguards do not apply to that particular reactor from which the Canadians, at least, believe the Indians got the technology to help them produce their nuclear capability. We have

something very firm in mind, sir, which is very different from the situation applying to the Canadian-Indian relationship. 

Senator INOUYE. I recall reading one of the reports issued by the 

U.S. Atomic Energy Commission in which it indicated that with all of the stringent safeguards that we apply to our nuclear powerplants, arsenals, or whatever you call it, we have "lost" about 100 pounds of uranium and about 60 pounds of plutonium. 

We don't know where they went and I have been further advised that all it takes is about 13 pounds of plutonium to make an adequate bomb to kill about 200,000 people.

I am further advised that in this world we have at least 50 international terrorist organizations, well-financed and well-armed. 

And I am further advised that all it would take would be some brain matter and some equipment you can purchase on the retail market and a good library, a public library, and you can produce a bomb. 

Is this advice wrong, the ones that we have been receiving?

Mr. SOBER. I am not in a position to deny anything that you have said, sir. I would like to make the point with regard to the agreement that we are contemplating with Egypt and Israel announced last week that indeed the safeguards and the special provisions which we have in mind are intended very explicitly to prevent anything like this happening.

We have no reason in terms of our past history of cooperation with foreign governments to believe that this cannot be done. 

Senator INOUYE. I suppose Syria would want one also.

Mr. SOBER. They might. I am not aware it has been raised, sir. It is certainly not under consideration at this time. 

RUSSIAN NUCLEAR ASSISTANCE

IS AID INVOLVED?

I would not rule this out as a later development because I simply don't know what might develop in the future, but based on the information we have available to us now, that has not been discussed. 

RATIONALE FOR AGREEMENTS 

Senator INOUYE. What was the rationale or the justification for making the promise in light of the many statements made by this Administration and others pointing to the Middle East as one of the most dangerous areas in the world today with greatest potential for warfare?

Mr. SOBER. Sir, the rationale was fundamentally economic in terms of the projections of increasing demand for electricity. As I said, the plants which we are talking about will not be available to produce electricity until the 1980's and projections indicate that the output from each of these plants would be very much in demand at that time.

We have in mind in terms of a political-economic background that the countries of the Near East need to look ahead to a firm economic base as part of what we hope will be a continuing process of increasing harmony and cooperation.

As for the issue we raised about the explosive nature of the region or the concerns about security, it is with regard to these risks that we do have in mind very, very firm assurances and provisions to be written into our agreement, sir, that relate to the safeguards to make sure that there is not a diversion for, if you will, military purposes of any assistance which we would provide.

SAUDI ARABIAN AGREEMENTS

What we have done is to come to an agreement with the Saudi Arabian Government to establish two commissions joint commissions, in the context of a long-standing close relationship which has had a very wide variety of aspects for quite a few years.

One of those commissions deals with economic cooperation. It does not, sir, I would like to point out, call for any American aid for Saudi Arabia, for obvious reasons. They don't need it. But they would like American firms to help them industrialize, they would like some assistance in how to deal with manpower problems, they would like to have the benefit of some of our know-how and technology in science and research, they would like to benefit from some of the things we have developed with regard to how you grow crops in very dry land, and things like that.

These are all subjects that would be within the scope of our economic cooperation with them.

There is also a commission on security matters which would give us a forum to discuss with them common matters of concern regarding stability in the Arabian peninsula.

With regard to your question about military sales, we have had a military sales relationship with Saudi Arabia for some 20 years or more. We do have a very small training mission there which has been there for quite a few years, more than 20 years also.

Mr. SOBER. No specifics in that context-no, sir.
