JOINT STATEMENT ON SAUDI ARABIAN-UNITED STATES COOPERATION WASHINGTON, D.C. 

JUNE 8, 1974 

Following the joint announcement of April 5, 1974, in which Saudi

Arabia and the United States expressed their readiness to expand cooperation in the fields of economics, technology, and industry, and in the supply of the Kingdom's requirements for defensive purposes, His Royal Highness

Prince Fahd bin Abd al Aziz, Second Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Interior, accepted an invitation to visit the United States on June 5-8 to discuss these matters with President Nixon and Secretary of State Kissinger.

His Royal Highness was accompanied by a number of high Saudi officials. 

Prince Fahd met with President Nixon on June 6, and he and his colleagues also had meetings with Secretary of State Kissinger, Secretary of the 

Treasury Simon, Secretary of Defense Schlesinger, Secretary of Commerce 

Dent, and other high government officials. 

The visit provided an opportunity for the two sides to agree on specific steps to strengthen relations in a variety of areas. Major attention was focussed on Saudi Arabia's economic and social development plans and defense requirements as well as on the ways in which the United States could be helpful in the realization of Saudi aspirations. There was a broad review of global problems of peace and security, and in this context, the situation in the Arabian Peninsula was examined. It was recognized that responsibility for maintaining security and promoting orderly development in this area belonged to the states of the region and that close cooperation among them is needed for their security. 

United States expressed its continuing support for cooperative measures. 

The 

The visit also provided an opportunity to review the current status of U.S. efforts currently underway to work towards a just and lasting solution in the Middle East in accordance with UN principles and resolutions. Both sides expressed satisfaction with the progress made and expressed their hope for continuing early progress in this regard. 

U.S. side reaffirmed its intention to continue its efforts looking toward a just and durable peace in the Middle East and noted the constructive support it has received from the Kingdom in these efforts. The

At the conclusion of the visit, His Royal Highness and the Secretary of State agreed on the following:

A. To establish a Joint Commission on Economic Cooperation. This 

Commission will be headed by the Secretary of the Treasury for the United States and by the Minister of State for Finance and National Economy for Saudi Arabia. Its purpose will be to promote programs of cooperation between the two countries in the fields of industrialization, trade, manpower training, agriculture, and science and technology. The first formal meeting of this Commission will take place in Saudi Arabia in October of this year. The Commission members will include representatives from the Departments of State, Treasury, and Commerce, and the National Science Foundation and possibly other agencies for the U.S. side. For the Saudi Arabian side, it will include representatives from the Ministries of Foreign Affairs, Finance and National Economy, Commerce and Industry, the Central Planning Organization, and other government departments concerned. The Economic Commission will review at this first meeting the recommendations and plans prepared by Working Groups that will be meeting in the meantime. These include the following: 

(1) A Joint Working Group of Industrialization will meet in Saudi Arabia beginning on July 15, 1974 to consider plans for Saudi Arabia's economic development, paying special attention to the use of flared gas for expanding the production of fertilizer. (2) A Joint Working Group on manpower and education will meet in Saudi Arabia shortly thereafter to consider projects aimed at the further development of Saudi technical manpower skills, the expansion of educational and technical institu-

tions, the transfer of technological expertise, the establishment of a comprehensive Saudi Arabian science and technology program keyed to the national goals of the Kingdom, and an expansion of sister university relations. (3) This will be followed by another Joint Working Group on technology, research and development in scientific fields of interest to examine specific cooperative endeavors in such fields as solar energy and desalination. (4) In addition a Joint Working Group on Agriculture will meet to examine agricultural development proposals in general and desert agriculture in particular.

The 

The Commission will encourage and facilitate periodic visits to Saudi Arabia by scientists, engineers and research specialists drawn from the U.S. Government, universities, and private business in order to supplement the operations of the Working Groups and to examine specific proposals for cooperation. The two governments have agreed to study a proposed technical cooperation agreement between them. two governments will also consider sponsoring an Economic Council composed of prominent American and Saudi participants from the private sector to work together to further the aims of the cooperative arrangements between the two countries. 

Consideration will also be given to the formation of a U.S.- 

Saudi Industrial Development Council, which might include government as well as private enterprise representatives. 

The U.S. Treasury Department and the Saudi Arabian 

Ministry of Finance and National Economy will consider cooperation in the field of finance,

B. To establish a Joint Commission to review programs already underway for modernizing Saudi Arabia's armed forces in light of "the Kingdom's defense requirements especially as they relate to training. The Commission will be headed by the Assistant Secretary of Defense for International Security Affairs for the U.S. and by His Royal Highness the Vice Minister of Defense and Aviation for 

Saudi Arabia. The first meeting of this Commission will take place in Saudi Arabia in the fall of this year. 

To that

It was agreed that Saudi Arabia and the United States will continue to consult closely on all matters of mutual interest. end, the Secretary of State and His Royal Highness Prince Fahd will remain in close contact with each other to oversee and to ensure that the activities of the joint commissions to be formed as a result of these talks are fully coordinated and are responsive to the interests of both countries.

This 

It was agreed that the visit of Prince Fahd not only enhanced the spirit of friendship and understanding between the two countries but that it also heralded an era of increasingly close cooperation. friendship is not based exclusively on material considerations but is derived from mutual respect and intimate relations over many years. The 

United States for its part hopes that this cooperation will be the benchmark for its evolving relations with the Arab world. Saudi Arabia for its part hopes that the era now opening will witness successful progress for its citizens and for all people of the area as they seek peace and security and the transformation into reality of their goals for prosperity and well-being. 

Fahd bin Abd al Aziz,

Second Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of the Interior 

Henry A. Kissinger,

Secretary of State

NUCLEAR SAFEGUARDS 

Senator CHILES. When you speak of international safeguards, are we talking about agreements that the countries will enter into? 

Mr. SOBER. Yes, sir. 

Senator CHILES. I am talking about the nuclear energy.

Mr. SOBER. Yes, sir, I understand. We are talking about negotiating with both Egypt and Israel on an agreement for cooperation. This is the umbrella agreement which we use that covers the Administration's cooperation with foreign countries. 

Part of that agreement has, for example provisions regarding the applicability of safeguards under the system administered by the 

International Atomic Energy Agency. And those are the safeguards which have been worked out by the international community, which we took a very active part in helping to formulate. 

We are, of course, members of the IAEA, and we are quite satisfied with what has been done.

I did say, sir, before you came in that with regard to the proposed agreements with both Egypt and Israel, in addition to the system of international safeguards administered by the IAEA with our participation, we have in mind negotiating also certain additional special bilateral provisions to give adequate assurance that there will not be any unintended diversion of the technology or equipment which we might supply.

Senator CHILES. But it still is all based on any respective country honoring the agreement. It is not anything where- 

Mr. SOBER. Largely, but not entirely, sir. A matter of trust is there, that is right, but the system of safeguards provides for physical in-

spections at periodic times so that there is an actual physical element which goes far beyond taking somebody's word. 

Senator CHILES. Tell me some more about that. Do we get a chance to make this inspection?

Mr. SOBER. Under the IAEA the international agency itself administers the safeguards and arranges for the inspections. 

Now, there may very well be Americans as part of an inspection team, but not necessarily. We, of course, will have access to the results of any safeguard inspection which is carried out. 

Senator CHILES. What provisions are there in case they say, "We are not going to allow you to inspect"?

Mr. SOBER. I would like to take that question and give you a response for the record because I don't have that much expertise to answer it in the way you might like. I would say one thing, for example, that would come into play is that normally when we have agreed to supply, sell, the nuclear power plant we undertake as part of that also to supply the fuel. The fuel has to be supplied on a continuing basis, so obviously we will have certain recourse as to what we might do to follow up on things like that. But I would prefer to supply an answer for the record to your question. 

 NUCLEAR SAFEGUARDS FOR AGREEMENTS WITH EGYPT AND ISRAEL 

The reactor and fuel to be supplied to Egypt anl Israel will be under the safeguards of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA). In the hypothetical case you mention, should either Egypt or Israel refuse inspection by the IAEA, it would be in violation of the safeguards arrangements. In such event, the Agency would report such non-compliance to its Board of Governors, of which the U.S. is a permanent member, and the Board would call upon the 

State to remedy the non-compliance forthwith. If the situation were then not remedied, the Board would report the non-compliance to all IAEA members and to the UN Security Council and General Assembly, and would have the right to: (1) call for the return of material made available to the State, (2) curtail or suspend IAEA assistance to the State, and (3) suspend the State from exercising its rights as a member of the IAEA. Non-compliance with agency safeguards would also, in effect, violate the guarantee given to the U.S. under the Agreement for Cooperation. Accordingly, should such non-compliance actually occur, the U.S. Government would have to assess carefully what political, economic or other steps it might desire to take in the circumstances. Among other things, the U.S. would have the right to halt further shipment of reactor fuel and to require return of U.S. material and equipment. 

TYING ASSISTANCE TO JORDAN Senator CHILES. The AID summary budget proposes a support fund for Egypt and Israel tied to U.S. exports. For Jordan, $67.5 million is listed as budget support. 

Is this money to be directed toward Jordan's internal government spending needs?

Mr. NOOTER. In the first instance, it is money provided to support their internal budgetary needs and the foreign exchange becomes available to them and can be used for importation of goods. However, Jordanian import patterns are such that we have not been able to find a way to tie that to U.S. goods without greatly disrupting the Jordanian economy. It is a small and rather fragile economy, and that system would be very difficult to administer. We have not found a way to work that out.

Senator CHILES. You mean we are giving them $67.5 million, but even though we are giving them that, we can't find a way to require that they spend that on American goods? 

Mr. NOOTER. That is the situation. 

Senator CHILES. You know, I just have a little difficulty; if we are going to help their economy that much because they don't have that $67.5 million, if their economy is so fragile and we are going to pump it in, it looks like there ought to be some way that we could have some provision to see that our balance-of-payment situation would be helped. 

Mr. NOOTER. That is always our objective wherever we can. As I say, in the case of Israel we have been able to work that out. We think that in the case of Egypt we can do so. We tie many of our import and other programs around the world, but in Jordan their system and import patterns are such that we have not found, technically, a way to be able to work that out. I wish I had a different answer for you. 

Senator CHILES. I wish I could understand the answer you are giving me.

Mr. NOOTER. The total level of their imports is such and their trade patterns with the world around them are such, that instituting a licensing system to provide for the control of goods and for those goods to come only from the United States would greatly upset their situation. 

Senator CHILES. And giving them $67.5 million isn't going to greatly upset their system?

Mr. NOOTER. The imposition of that licensing system to direct that those goods come from a particular country supplier would upset the balance that they have there and the confidence that has been generated in the dinar in that part of the world by having a free and fully convertible currency.

 EGYPTIAN DEBT 

Accurate statistics are difficult to come by on Egyptian debt matters. Nevertheless, Egypt's economic debt is estimated to be about $2 billion. This figure includes a cumulative deficit balance on barter trade of about $300 million for which there is no repayment obligation. The annual debt service is estimated to be approximately $200 million for the next several years. These estimates do not include Egypt's military debts about which virtually no information is available. Our assistance to Egpyt was outlined in our presentation to Congress proposing a $250 million package for FY 1975; $20 million on Suez Canal clearances; $80 million for commodities, and $150 million for Suez Canal area reconstruction. All of these funds will be used to procure goods and services in the United States. They would not support Egyptian debt repayment to the USSR.

NUCLEAR PROLIFERATION Senator BROOKE. Yes, Mr. Chairman. 

Mr. Nooter, I am concerned, as we all are, with the proposals made about the nuclear material for Egypt and Israel. Recently there were nuclear tests by India, China, and by France, that increased concern about the nuclear question.

It seems to me that we might be sounding the death knell for the nonproliferation treaty by our seeming willingness to proliferate "peaceful" nuclear technologies. 

Can I have your comment on that? Nuclear agreements with Israel and Egypt may be peaceful proliferation. Nevertheless, do such agreements indicate the beginning of the end of NPT? Argentina, South Africa, and many other countries might now, because of what is happening in the Middle East, want to increase their nuclear capabilities, even to the point of seeking a nuclear deterrent capability. 

Mr. SOBER. Senator, we support the nonproliferation treaty and we said as much last week at the meeting in Vienna of the International 

Atomic Energy Agency in commenting on the Indian test.

I think we have to make a very clear distinction between uses of nuclear power, nuclear energy. Nuclear power is something that many countries are beginning to think of using as they look ahead to the energy requirements of their populations in the decades ahead, and perhaps indeed, we should look ahead and expect a considerable increase in reliance on nuclear energy, not only in the United States but elsewhere.

But that is a very different thing from nuclear proliferation in terms of a nuclear explosion capability. We are very determined that any assistance and cooperation that we provide to foreign countries for nuclear power does not extend to nuclear proliferation or the ability to develop a nuclear explosive device.

And it is with this in mind that we pay a great deal of attention to the safeguards which will be applied to any cooperation which we accord.

And this is the point exactly in the question that we were discussing earlier this morning, sir, with regard to our willingness to negotiate agreements for cooperation in the nuclear field with both Egypt and Israel.

We have no interest, no intention, and no desire-in fact, we are dead set against the developing of a nuclear explosive capability, certainly from anything that we might do, and this will be an important part of our negotiation.

Senator BROOKE. India has denied that it is seeking a military nuclear capability as such, but the impression is there that it might be seeking a deterrent capability vis-a-vis Pakistan or China. It is not always what is that is important, but rather what is perceived to be the situation that determines reactions by others. 

Mr. SOBER. Senator, on that we make no distinction in this country in our looking at the policy ramifications of this question between a socalled peaceful nuclear device and any other nuclear device. Indeed, under the nuclear proliferation treaty the ability to explode something out of fissionable material is in question and we don't say one type is fine and the other is not. 

And, indeed, our anticipated agreements with Egypt and with Israel would not authorize them in any way to develop a so-called peaceful nuclear explosive capability.

That would be ruled out just as much as the intention to develop nuclear weapons capability.

Senator BROOKE. France doesn't insist upon similar safeguards does it?

Mr. SOBER. France does not endorse the international system of safeguards and of course it is not a member of the nonproliferation club. 

Senator BROOKE. For the record, there are certain questions that I would like you to supply answers to which hopefully will stimulate responses that will help clarify this matter. 

One, would you supply for the record a statement outlining the peaceful nuclear capabilities that exist in the Middle East at the present time.

ISRAEL ATOMIC ENERGY PROGRAM 

ORGANIZATION 

The Israel Atomic Energy Commission (IAEC) was established in 1952 and reorganized in April 1966. It now consists of 16 members with the Prime Minister as Chairman. The Director-General is Mr. Shalieveth 

Freier. The other members of the LAEC are drawn from governmental organizations, including ministries, and universities. The former 

Director-General, Professor Israel Dostrovsky is now President of the 

Weizmann Institute of Science.

FACILITIES 

Soreq Research Establishment (SRE), Nahal Sorea The SRE, located about 9 miles south of Tel Aviv, is the principal research organization of the IAEC. Its program centers about the Israeli Research Reactor (IRR-1), a 5 Mt, AMF pool-type light-water moderated reactor fueled with 90% enriched uranium. The reactor is used for research in physics and chemistry and for the production of isotopes. It achieved criticality in 1960.

A "hot lab" has been established and a fast neutron chopper is in use. 

Other equipment employed at SRE includes a 3.6 kilocurie cobalt-60 source and a 280 KEV x-ray generator..

The SRE is organized into approximately 20 departments and groups. 

The Reactor Physics Division cooperates closely with the Nuclear Science Department of the Israel Institute of Technology (Technion) 

at Haifa and the Solid State Physics Department of the Weizmann Institute at Rehovcth. 

Attached to the SRE is the Radioisotopes Training Center, administered jointly by SRE and the Weizmann Institute. The Center offers courses in the safe and effective use of radioisotopes in research, medicine, and industry, and conducts research programs in the application of radioisotopes. 

Negev Nuclear Research Center Government nuclear research is also conducted at the Negev Nuclear Research Center which includes a 26 megawatt natural uranium reactor supplied by the French. 

The Weizmann Institute of Science Located at Rehovoth, the Weizmann

Institute is Israel's largest institution of research in the physical sciences. Its nine departments are primarily concerned with physics. 

Their programs include work in infra-red spectroscopy, nuclear physics, solid state physics, experimental nuclear structure, high energy physics, x-ray crystallography, isotope research, physical chemistry, instrumentation, and micro-magnetics. The Institute has a 3 MEV Van de Graaff accelerator purchased in the U.S. In early 1955, a 6 MEV 

Tandem Van de Graaff accelerator manufactured by the High Voltage 

Engineering Corporation was installed for joint use by scientists from both the Weizmann Institute and the Hebrew University. The total

cost of the accelerator and the accompanying laboratories is reported to be $2.3 million. Construction was begun in 1973 on a 14 MEV accelerator. It is scheduled for completion in 1975. 

The Israel Institute of Technology (Technion) Technion at Haifa also has an important role in Israei's nuclear program. Studies are carried out in the fields of solar physics, megnetism, field theory, particle physics, cosmic rays, electronics, and nuclear physics. In cooperation with the Israeli AEC, Technion is in the process of establishing a 

Nuclear Science and Engineering Center at the New Technion campus near

Haifa to broaden the program of instruction and research in nuclear engineering. Plans call for a small reactor, a pulsed neutron generator and associated nuclear instrumentation. A reactor physics laboratory houses a D20-U02 natural uranium, exponential experiment for lattice studies.

NUCLEAR POWER 

Israel is expected to issue tenders within six months for their first -nuclear power reactor, a 660 Me plant scheduled for completion in 1982. 

No announcement has been made of the site for the reactor. 

The Israeli Minister of Commerce and Industry, Hain Bar-Lev, announced on April 15, 1974, that all new power stations built in Israel after 1980 will be nuclear. Four-power reactors are expected to be needed during the 1980's, according to the Director of the Nahal Soreq Nuclear 

Research Center. The Israeli Electric Power Corporation has been given exclusive responsibility for the nuclear power program in Israel.

RAW MATERIALS 

In 1948, the extensive Negev Desert phosphate beds were found to contain from 0.005 to 0.015% uranium. The average is about 0.006%. 

These resources are not economic for uranium at prices less than $10 to $15 per pound U303. By 1967, production of beneficialed phosphate had risen to about 600,000 metric tons per year. This production represents a potentially available high-cost uranium resource of about 

45 short tons U308 per year.

IRAN 1... 

ATOMIC ENERGY PROGRAM ORGANIZATION 

The National Atomic Energy Commission of Iran was established in 1959. 

It reports to the Ministry of Science and Higher Education. The Prine 

Minister serves as Chairman and other members include the Minister of Economy, the Chancellor of Tehran University, the Chairman of the Tehran 

University Nuclear Center, one other university chancellor and a number of scientists in the nuclear field.

Dr. Akbar Etemad, Deputy Prime Minister, was appointed to head a study group to outline the functions and draw up a table of organization for an atomic energy authority for Iran. Dr. Etemad, a nuclear physicist trained in Switzerland and France, delivered this study in April 1974,

and it is now under consideration by the Cabinet prior to submission to Parliament. Given the priority placed on it by the Shah, this legislation should pass into law in about eight weeks. 

Tehran University Nuclear Center - With very minor exceptions, all existing capabilities for the generation and study of nuclear energy in Iran are concentrated in the Tehran University Nuclear Center (UNC).

The principal facility at TUNC is a five-megawatt, pool-type reactor, constructed at Iranian expense but with a great deal of American technical assistance and about 80 percent American components, mainly from American Machine and Foundry. The reactor reached criticality 

November 13, 1967, but was closed down for about two and one-half years (1968-1970) to repair a leak in the coolant tank. 

This is a research reactor used primarily to produce isotopes, and the associated research program consists of scientific studies (nuclear physics, radiobiology, radiochemistry and activation analysis, and soils, medical, and petroleum studies) and technical (applied) studies (electronics and reactor operation). A program for the commercial production of radioisotopes for use in Iran is just being started. 

In addition to the reactor, TUNC has a 3.5 megavolt l'an de Graaff proton accelerator, ‘a cobalt source, a mass spectrometer, a pulse height analyzer, counters, scalers, and other nuclear equipment. The reactor itself is operated only once or twice a week due to insufficient experimental demand, and the basic problem at TUNC is lack of trained and experienced scientific and engineering manpower. The Center's program includes: Nuclear Physics, Radioisotopes, Physical Archeology, Radio-Biology, Agricultural Research, Materials Sciences and Electronics. 

The Center also has three service units. Technical Service perfoms laboratory special services. Health Physics includes protection within the Center and has a nation-wide film badge service. Radioisotope 

Production supplies isotopes produced at the Center to users in Iran. 

RADIOISOTOPE USES IN IRAN 

Radioisotopes are being used in agricultural pest-control studies in Iran.. In the medical field, the Cancer Hospital in Tehran is using a small radio-cobalt unit, and the Memazi Hospital in Shiraz is operating a radio-cesium unit produced by Harwell. The Institute of Taj Pahlanvi has a program in cancer research and therapy. Shiraz Medical College has a program in isotope applications. 

A food irradiation center has been established under the jurisdiction of the Institute of Standards and Industrial Research of Iran, with technical assistance, as needed, from the Tehran University Nuclear Center. Iran has been especially interested in irradiation of potatoes, onions, and tomatoes.

RAW MATERIALS 

Uranium deposits have been found near Yazd and near Anarak on the southwest margin of the Dasht Kavir (Salt Desert) Basin in east central Iran. The Anarak deposits reportedly are the richest (but grades are not reported), and have been analyzed by several countries. Occurrences have also been reported at five other localities; in Azerbaijan Province near the Turkish border, in Khurasar in northeast Iran near the Turkmen

SSR border, and near Hamadan, Isfahan, and Kashan in the Zagros Mountains of western Iran.

NUCLEAR TRAINED PERSONNEL IN IRAN 

The exact number of persons with masters and doctors degrees in nuclear sciences and engineering who are now in Iran cannot be more than about 80. 

Some of these are scattered among departments in other Iranian universities, but most are concentrated at Tehran University and are working at TÚNC. In 1973 the Harza Engineering Company, consultants to the Ministry of Water and Power, arranged for two special short-term courses in the United States for Iranians concerned with power production. 

Ten persons in management had an intensive series of visits lasting four weeks and 16 engineers stayed almost twice as long. It is anticipated that 20 more engineers will be sent off this year. Also, a much expanded program of training at the M.Sc. level will be initiated at TUNC in 1974, but the great majority of higher degrees will have to be sought from foreign universities. Because of the tremendous demand for highly trained manpower which will be created by the new atomic power program, the first task of the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran is seen as locating and enticing home Iranian expatriates trained abroad who have almost of necessity remained there in order to work in nuclear sciences. 

NUCLEAR POWER 

Within the past year the Shah has become increasingly interested in nuclear energy as a supplement, and ultimately a replacement, for petroleum as a source of electric power. He views petroleum as a noble resource, too valuable to be burned for its energy content. In March of this year the Minister for Water and Power revealed plans for an · initial. investment of $2.5 million for the development of atomic power plant's. The pattern of anticipated development is illustrated by the

Some additional water power will be developed from 12 new dams during the 5th Plan, and until 1980 oil and gas-fired power plants may be constructed, but the Ministry of Water and Power expects the price of petroleum will be too high thereafter. Nuclear energy will become the only economic source for additional power.

The Shah reportedly now is thinking in terms of atomic power plants producing a total of 20,000 megawatts, presumably toward the end of the 1980's. As part of a February 1974 trade and cooperation protocol with France, that country is to build in Iran five atomic power plants with a total capacity of 5,000 megawatts. There is considerable skepticism that France can deliver on this commitment. At any rate, there remains plenty of room for American enterprise to bid on the rest of the program.

EGYPT ATOMIC ENERGY PROGRAM Organization of the Atomic Energy Establishment The Egyptian Atomic Energy Establishment (AEE) is a governmental organi zation constituted by Presidential Decree number 288 of 1957. It took over the functions of the preceding Atomic Energy Commission which was constituted on 19 February 1955 by the Prime Minister's order and received legal status by act number 509 of 19 October 1955. 

The functions of the AEE are, in summary: (a) Training of specialists and conducting research in the various scientific fields related to atomic energy; (b) Establishing the necessary laboratories and institutions for training and research as well as for peaceful uses and applications of atomic energy; (c) Exploration, extraction, import, export, exchange and utilization of raw materials of interest for nuclear energy; (d) Production of materials, apparatus and equipment necessary for atomic energy and its applications; (e) Taking measures for public security and protection against radiation hazards, and proposing necessary legislation; (f) Following international progress in the field of atomic energy and representing Egypt in international atomic energy organizations and conferences; (g) Suggesting plans and projects that the State should undertake in order to derive the maximum benefit from the applications of atomic energy. 

The AEE is governed by a Board with twelve members. The members are drawn from amongst scientists and engineers working in the nuclear energy field, from universities and research institutions and from Ministries directly interested in the applications of nuclear energy such as the 

Ministry of Electricity and the Ministry of Industry. The Chairman of the Board is the President or a Minister acting for him. Members of the 

Board are appointed by Presidential decree for a term of three years which is renewable.

Decisions of the Board are sent to the Presidency of the Republic and to the Prime Minister. If objections are not made by them within are week, the decisions are considered as agreed. The decisions of the 

Board are executed through the Director of EE.

The budget and program of the AEE is proposed by the Board. The part containing personnel and running costs is sent directly to the Ministry of Finance for approval. The investment program is submitted to the 

Ministry of Planning, which has to approve the yearly investments and also AEE's contributions to Egypt's Five and Ten-Year Plans. When the

Ministry of Planning has agreed to the investment program, it is submitted to the Ministry of Finance for approval and for the appropriation of the necessary funds. 

The AEE operates the Nuclear Research Centre at Inchas, near Cairo, which has twelve scientific divisions including the reactor division. 

The Director of AE is advised by a Board of Heads of Scientific Divisions. 

He is assisted in his work by a Deputy Director for International and 

External Relations and Nuclear Power Projects, a Deputy Director for Scientific Planning and Nuclear Materials, and a Secretary General for Administrative and Financial Services. 

Major Facilities 

Inchass Research Center The Egyptian nuclear energy activities are centered? at the Inchass Research Center about 20 miles outside of Cairo. The heart of the Center, which includes about 20 buildings, is the Soviet built 2 Mit research reactor of the closed tank type. The reactor achieved criticality in July 1961. Other laboratories at the Center include: The Physics Laboratory, which has a 2.5 Mev Van de Graaff accelerator, the isotopes production laboratory, built by the Egyptians under an IAEA agreement, and an Activation Analysis Laboratory using a "SUNVIC" 100 channel analyzer and a 1" x 1 1/2" crystal. At this laboratory research is being conducted on uranium contaminants and ultra pure metals.

NUCLEAR SAFEGUARDS FOR AGREEMENTS WITH EGYPT AND ISRAEL 

Respecting safeguards that will cover U.S. nuclear equipment and material supplied to Egypt or Israel, these will be applied by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA). Nuclear materials accountancy is the fundamental 

IAEA safeguards tool, with containment and surveillance as important complementary measures. Accountancy is essential to the knowledge of how much safeguarded material is supposed to be at a given facility. To permit good accountability, facilities have to be designed to permit adequate measurement and control of the nuclear material being processed or used in them. The IAEA reviews nuclear facility design from this point of view. Detailed and accurate records and periodic reports need to be kept and submitted to keep track of the inventories, input, process losses, wastes, and shipments of nuclear materials. The 

IAEA reviews the system of records and reports for adequacy and, during periodic inspections, audits the records. The 

Agency also processes the periodic reports to assist in planning inspections, follows the flow of materials and checks for quantity agreement between shippers and receivers. 

The data also can be evaluated to determine if significant uncertainties are developing in the measurement of nuclear material quantities flowing through a process. 

The Agency conducts periodic inspections to verify information in records and reports, to account for the material which is supposed to be present, to review the methods of measurement, to investigate process losses and sources of uncertainties in the inventory and throughput, and to read and

service containment and surveillance devices. Containment and surveillance techniques (such as tamper indicating seals on stored nuclear materials, or tamper resistant automatic cameras providing unmanned observation of nuclear material in storage) give evidence as to whether the quantities of nuclear materials in a given location may have changed since the last inspection.

In addition to safeguards, the proposed Agreements for Cooperation with Egypt and Israel will include special controls in view of the sensitivity in the Middle East area. 

These controls relate to the following key points in the fuel cycle: (a) the reprocessing of irradiated fuel elements, involving the separation of the plutonium generated by the reactors from other components of the fuel; (b) the fabrication of special nuclear material; (c) the disposition and storage of recovered plutonium; and (d) physical security aggangements to protect nuclear material and the reactors from theft, diversion or sabotage. An explicit confirmation by Egypt and Israel that U.S. material will not be used for "peaceful" nuclear explosives would also be obtained.

Should the U.S. refuse to permit export of power reactors and fuel to Egypt or Israel, there are several other sources for such sales. In the process of developing nuclear programs to meet their own energy needs, commercial firms in the following countries have the capability-independently or through licensing arrangements--to provide power reactors to Egypt or Israel: France, Japan, Canada, the Federal Republic of Germany, the U.K., the

USSR, Sweden, Switzerland and Italy. Further, France, the 

U.K. and the USSR presently have the capability to produce enriched uranium for fueling the reactors. Uranium enrichment projects are also being developed which could be sources of such material for Egypt or Israel, e.g., a project in South Africa.

Negotiations on the proposed Agreements for Cooperation with both Egypt and Israel are in the initial stage. 

Once agreement is reached on the content and language of the respective texts, the formal procedures prescribed in Section 123 of the U.S. Atomic Energy Act will be observed. Accordingly, consistent with those requirements, the proposed agreements will be submitted to the Congress prior to their entry into force.

SUEZ CANAL CLEARANCE 

Senator BROOKE. What are our interests in hastening the reopening of the canal?

Mr. NOOTER. We think that the opening of the canal has a number of points of interest for the United States. One, let's say the canal is located in an area sufficiently between and near the existing lines that it represents an interest on the part of Egypt in maintaining the peace

in order to keep the canal open. Two, Egypt will realize revenues from it which will help it get back on its feet economically. I think the 

Egyptian Government now has a sincere interest in turning its attention to meeting some of the economic needs of its people which have been set aside for a number of years while they maintained a somewhat more warlike posture. We think that these are the two principal purposes that serve our interest in helping Egypt open the canal.

INDOCHINA POSTWAR RECONSTRUCTION Senator BROOKE.  

Now, Mr. Nooter, if we may go to Indochina. 

I have several questions which I will be submitting to you for your response at a later time.

SIZE OF LAOS MISSION 

According to your budget presentation the AID mission in Laos is the second largest mission in the world; Vietnam is the first. 

Yet, this aid program is not that large. It is $56 million proposed for fiscal year 1975.

I would like to make certain comparisons for the whole of Latin America-20 countries and two regional programs. For fiscal year 

1973, you had 388 persons operating in Laos under AID-the program was $45 million; and in Latin America you have 331 persons operating a program which amounted to $291 million. In fiscal year 1974, an estimated 324 persons with a $40 million program; and in Latin America, 368 persons and $202 million. For this fiscal year (1975), AID is requesting funds for 228 persons for a program of $55 million and in Latin America, 368 persons in a program of $267 million. 

How do you provide any rationale and justification for this type of comparison, on one hand a $55 million program with 228, and on the other hand, the whole of a continent, $267 million and 368 people? 

Mr. NOOTER. First, just to clarify, the figures which you cited on 

Laos are the same as the figures available here to me which include the direct hire and the so-called participating agency personnel, that is U.S. Government employees from other agencies, and the contractor personnel. I am not familiar with the Latin American figures but just for the record, I would like to clarify that they do include the contractor personnel because sometimes they do not include it when we talk about the number of U.S. employees. 

In a general way, though, I would say the large numbers of people in Laos compared to other programs around the world are the result of two things: One, the fact that Laos is a country with a GNP per capital of $60, or $70 per person, meaning that the skill level in that country very low. Second, the fact that there has been a long and grinding war there which now has come to a halt, but nevertheless involved us very people-intensive programs in refugee care and in health care and so on. is in 

Senator INOUYE. I could use your argument but instead of using

Latin America I could use Africa where the GNP is less than Laos. 

They have been involved in conflict for many years. 

Mr. NOOTER. But I think you will find that over the years our programs in Africa have had to have more people for the size of the program than we had in Latin America, but of course, without the influence of war there. But the per capita argument is similar. However, as your figures point out, we are reducing the levels of personnel in Laos and we will continue to do so. Even the figure which we cite for the end of 1975 we are reviewing constantly, and will review constantly during the year.

The new coalition government there is just getting started. We are still sorting out what our AID relationship will be with them, but I expect to see the manpower requirements in Laos dropping down during the course of the next several years. While it won't go down to 

Latin American levels for one of the reasons I mentioned, there will be a reduction of manpower. 

GAO REPORT ON VECCO 

Senator INOUYE. We have in our possession a GAO report which indicates that over $11 million of excess U.S. construction equipment furnished by AID to the Vietnamese Engineering and Construction 

Co. has been used less than 10 percent of the time. 

Have we recovered the unutilized equipment from them? 

Mr. NOOTER. We have recovered some equipment under that agreement and there have been some additional recoveries since that time. 

In addition to that I would like to say that VECCO, the organization set up for the use of this equipment- Senator INOUYE. If we don't recover this by July of 1974 we will lose title, won't we?

Mr. NOOTER. No. We are making provision to have that date extended so we won't lose our ability to remedy the situation while the question of whether the equipment should be recovered or not is still under study.

Senator INOUYE. We have recovered less than half, haven't we? 

Mr. NOOTER. I think total recoveries now are in the neighborhood of $5 million. But, as I started to say, VECCO is a relatively new organization, the utilization rate is going up, and our people in Saigon assure me that a lot of the equipment which was not being utilized at an earlier point is in use now and therefore they have asked for an opportunity for a little more time to review that and see how much should be recovered and how much should be permitted to stay there. 

Incidentally, the GAO report touches only lightly on another substantial part of that equipment in use in rock quarries and so on which is fully in use and has been utilized very well.

 FERTILIZER PLANT-VIETNAM 

The technical review which recommended the establishment of the urea fertilizer plant was prepared for the Government of Vietnam by the United 

Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO) for the United Nations 

Development Program (UNDP), which financed the study. The authors of the study were Messrs. W. G. Geren and P. M. Malk, individual American private consultants under contract to UNIDO.

No contractor has been selected for additional work. A notice has been published in the Commerce Business Daily seeking expressions of interest from potential consultants for the detailed study which would be the next step in this development effort. Selection of a consultant would only be made after a formal request for proposals and under AID procurement regulations applicable to such contracting actions.

USE OF U.S.-PURCHASED PIASTERS 

Senator INOUYE. The subcommittee understands that over a 2-year period, October 1971 through September 1973, about 5.2 billion piasters which were purchased with U.S. dollars and 1 billion U.S. counterpart piasters were handled by the Office of the Directorate General of Land Development and Hamlet Building in favor of war victims in South Vietnam.

1030

Of the 4.7 billion piasters distributed to 23 provinces, only 0.9 billion had been accounted for in December of 1973. 

Based on the fluctuating value of piasters during the period 1971 to 1973, the 3.8 billion piasters unaccounted for represents a U.S. expenditure somewhere between $32 million, and that is at the 1971 rate, and $7 million at the 1973 rate. 

We understand that in the past AID was only provided data on how many piasters were allocated to provinces and received no data on piasters spent for the balance of piasters on hand. 

If this is the case, this lack of control over U.S.-provided piasters, how do you know the extent to which U.S.-provided piasters have been properly used in South Vietnam?

Mr. NOOTER. I am puzzled by the statement and I will have to do some inquiring because my understanding is that the U.S. piasters are supplied on a reimbursable basis, but I will review that statement carefully and check with our mission.

Mr. NOOTER. I would have to trace through the specific accounts and see if we can track that down. 

Senator INOUYE. We will appreciate that because these are the little things that add fuel to the fire to stories of corruption in that part of the world.

CONTROL OF PLASTERS 

An audit report in December 1973, which was based on August 1973 information, is the source of the statement that 3.8 billion piasters distributed to 23 provinces have not been accounted for by the Office of the Director General of Land Development and Hamlet Building (LDHB). 

It should be noted that in mid-1973 the highest priority was placed on the return to village and resettlement of large numbers of refugees generated during the 1972 invasion and the post ceasefire hostilities. 

This necessitated placing funds into the field as rapidly as possible with an expected lag in the receipt of detailed expenditure data. 

The data has since been made available. 

Anxious to improve the financial control system, Dr. Dan, the Deputy 

Prime Minister who now is in charge of the Ministry of Social Welfare (MSW) as well as LDHB, has ordered his provincial Social Welfare Chiefs to report LDHB expenditures as well as those of MSW. Doctor 

Dan sent a special team to each province and obtained in April 1974 a complete accounting of provincial expenditures from the start of the LDHB program in 1971 to December 31, 1973, including the funds for which no accounting was provided in August, 1973.

The expenditures documents received from the provinces. are under review by AID personnel. Survey trips have been scheduled to the three provinces that have received the largest amounts of LDHB funds. 

Although the GVN does provide some funds from its own budget, USAID does not provide piasters to the GVN for the refugee program on a reimbursable basis. However, Project Agreements with the MSW have called for replenishment of the initial advance of piasters from USAID to be based upon signed receipts for expenditures. Given the emergency nature of the resettlement program, additional tranches of piasters provided to the LDBH were not based upon signed receipts for expenditures. Now that the GVN has completed the crash programs of assisting hundreds of thousands of refugees to leave temporary camps, the LDHB is able to use a more timely expenditure reporting system. 

Therefore, we are encouraging the Mission to find means to institute a system of providing piasters for the refugee program on a reimbursable basis.

RURAL CREDIT PROGRAM 

Senator INOUYE. I would like to now touch upon the rural credit program for Vietnam.

You are proposing $500,000 for an accelerated institutional credit program to the agricultural bank of Vietnam and private banks. 

I further understand that $60 million will be infused into the banking system.

Am I correct in assuming that this money will be channeled through private rural banks?

Mr. NOOTER. Through a combination of the Government's Agricultural Development Bank, which operates branches throughout Vietnam, and also certain private rural banks which are supervised by and in part financed by the Agricultural Development Bank.

Senator INOUYE. By providing funds for the expansion of this banking system we will be underwriting the profitmaking, private banking system, won't we?

Mr. NOOTER. Yes. The private bankers are in the business to make money. They put up some of their own funds and receive certain advances from the Agricultural Development Bank.

Senator INOUYE. Did you ever consider allocating this fund directly to rural cooperatives instead of a third party bank? 

Mr. NOOTER. I don't know that the term "rural cooperative" would be exactly right, but they do have what are called village credit committees which approximate cooperatives in Vietnam, and I understand that some of these funds would be channeled through them. 

But there is not at this time a very extensive cooperative system in Vietnam.

SOUTH VIETNAMESE REFUGEES 

Senator BROOKE. I have several questions, Mr. Nooter, which have to do with South Vietnamese refugees. 

How many South Vietnamese refugees are still in camps? 

Mr. NOOTER. 85,000. 

Senator BROOKE. How many have been resettled in the past year?

Mr. NOOTER. My understanding is that there are about 500,000 receiving resettlement benefits at the present time, and something around that number or somewhat higher have been in resettlement status during the course of the year. 

Senator BROOKE. Can you say exactly how many refugees have been actually resettled in the last year?

Mr. NOOTER. The figure in camps at the beginning of the year, as 

I said in my statement, is 489.000 and during the course of the year there would have been some relatively small number of new refugees, so that the total resettled would have been in excess of the 400,000 or so. That would be the difference between the number at the beginning and the end of the year.

Senator BROOKE. How many have been resettled in their home areas as opposed to resettled in new areas? 

Mr. NOOTER. I don't have a breakdown on that, Senator. 

Senator BROOKE. Can you get it for the record?

Mr. NOOTER. I can get it for the record. It has been some to old villages and some to new areas. 

 REFUGEES RESETTLED 

In FY 1974, approximately 555,000 refugees were settled, with 160,000 returning to their own villages and 395,000 resettling in new areas. This total is 120,000 larger than the difference between the beginning of the year refugee camp figure of 489,000 and the end of the year refugee camp figure of 54,000. The reason for this variance is twofold: first, newly created refugees were cared for in the camps in the course of the year, and second, some refugees who settled in agriculturally poor sites voluntarily resettled in areas with better agricultural potential.

REFUGEE CONTROL Senator BROOKE. What is the present policy of the South Vietnamese 

Government regarding the return of refugees to areas controlled by 

North Vietnamese and Vietcong?

Mr. NOOTER. This has come up frequently. When I visited Vietnam in April, I particularly asked about this question when we visited the northern part of South Vietnam. First, I asked Dr. Dhan, who is the deputy prime minister in charge of social welfare and refugee programs, and he said two things. First, he said, on the whole the subject has not come up; that is, those people who want to go back to the 

PRG controlled areas simply slip over and go there. But I said, "What would your position be if they did come to you and say, 'We would like to go back," and he said, "I would let them." Other people have claimed otherwise, as you know, but what I did confirm beyond any doubt in my mind is that when the refugees do want to go back, they simply do so. There have not been many who have, but there have been some. 

I must say there 

Senator BROOKE. Are you saying the policy of the South Vietnamese 

Government is to let them return to North Vietnamese and Vietcongcontrolled areas if they so desire?

STATUS OF MONTAGNARD REFUGEES Senator BROOKE. What about the Montagnards? I was there last year and I am concerned about the Montagnard refugees. I was impressed with the desire of the Montagnard people to return to their own mountain areas. Have their desires been met?

COMMITTEE'S PROPOSED ALLOCATIONS OF INDOCHINA POSTWAR RECONSTRUCTION FUNDS Senator BROOKE. The committee's report on the 1974 foreign assist ance narration recommended funds for South Vietnam be apportioned as follows: Humanitarian, $85.0 million; commodity import program, $195.6 million; reconstruction and rehabilitation, $25.0 million; technical support, $6.0 million; development, $20.0 million. 

Then you came back for an additional $49 million which was granted in a supplemental appropriations bill.

Can you state for the record the degree in which this committee's recommendations were followed and would you also provide a justification for any substantial deviations from the committee's recommendations? 

Mr. NOOTER. You are referring to the use of the $49 million?

Senator BROOKE. No, the use of the total fiscal year 1974 amounts, we would have to know whether there were deviations from our recommendations and if there were, the justification for the deviations? 

Mr. NOOTER. I will do that, Senator Brooke. 

 USE OF IPR FUNDS. 

The Committee's recommendation on how FY 1974 Indochina Postwar Re construction funds should be allocated for Vietnam was based on an over-all level of $400 million for Indochina. After the Congress acted upon our supplemental request, the total which became available for Vietnam was $397 million. 

This was an increase of some $65 million over the Committee's earlier proposal of $332 million for Vietnam, but it was significantly below the $475 million requested by AID. Within the total funds available, we were able to follow the 

Committee's recommendation on the amount allocated to humanitarian assistance. The additional funds for the commodity import program were justified to the Committee during the hearings on our supplemental request. The $282 million we set aside for the commodity import program was considered the minimum amount required to assure that the program could continue through the remainder of the fiscal year in view of the unforeseen, dramatic increases in prices for essential commodities such as fertilizer and petroleum as well as ocean freight.

The price increases discussed above when combined with the shortfall in the total funds available for Vietnam compared to our request, forced us to forego virtually all the capital development and reconstruction projects which had been contemplated for FY 1974. Our request for these combined categories amounted to $98 million. The actual allocation for these categories amounted to $15 million. This compares to the Committee's proposal of $45 million. 

Finally, our technical support program which totalled $15 million for the year was $9 million over the Committee's recommendation. Since these funds were primarily used for the payment of salaries and other costs related to AID personnel already on board, it was not possible to make any substantial savings in this category.
