HIGHWAY PROGRAM IN SOUTH VIETNAM Senator INOUYE. AID and the Department of Defense have invested about a billion dollars in Vietnam's road and highway system over the past several years.

As a result of the failure of the Vietnamese Government to enforce its vehicle weight control laws, roads designed and constructed to last 

15 to 20 years are breaking up and disintegrating after only 2 or 3 years.

The committee is in possession of a GAO report detailing the failure of the Vietnam government. In fact, the report notes that the AID mission director in Saigon has questioned the wisdom of additional investment for reconstructing highways and roads without effective safeguards to prevent destructive truck loading. 

In light of these findings, can you justify the request for $2,990,000 in fiscal year 1975 for highway advisory assistance projects? 

Mr. NOOTER. We think we can, Mr. Chairman, but I would like to speak to a number of points you have raised there. 

First, to put this in perspective, during the war years when the U.S. military was there the Defense Department was engaged in a broad-scale operational program for both building and maintaining roads, and the Vietnamese Department of Public Works was a relatively unimportant and undermanned and underfunded operation. 

Over the last couple of years that has changed, and I must say that the Vietnamese department now has some quite good people at the top. But because of the fact that the United States was playing such a large operational role they simply weren't called on to do most of the job. That has now shifted and they have had to begin taking on these responsibilities. Our program is designed to help them. 

On the matter of weight control for roads, the GAO report refers to some five weight inspection teams available, only five at the time that report was written. There are now 16 such teams in operation and 

I understand they have 26 additional teams in training.

I don't mean to say that is going to solve all their problems, but it is some indication of what is going on in that department. I think assistance to them is extremely important to help them build up their capability to maintain the road network that was constructed in part and at major cost by our Defense Department people while they were out there.

Senator INOUYE. According to the GAO, military traffic is a factor but it is not the major factor. 

They claim that the lack of weight control for civilian vehicles has brought about the disintegration of the road system. 

Mr. NOOTER. I didn't mean to contest that point. I can neither verify nor deny it. But my point is that the additional weight control inspection teams which they do need, and we agree they do need, are in process of being trained up and provided. Some are actually now in position in addition to the ones mentioned in the GAO report. 

Senator INOUYE. It is one thing to establish these teams. Is the

Government prepared to enforce the laws or the regulations? 

Mr. NOOTER. I don't know how to answer that in a general way. 

Certainly one of the things we will be doing is making sure that the assistance we provide is sensibly used and that would include reminding them, for one thing, of the necessity to enforce reasonable regula tions of this kind.

TERMINATION OF PUBLIC SAFETY ASSISTANCE 

Senator INOUYE. According to the narrative you state the following: "In accordance with the provisions of the fiscal year 1974 legislation. 

AID is terminating all assistance to the police and corrections system in Vietnam.

Can you assure us that you have taken necessary steps to prevent any possible diversion of AID support of other programs to the police and correction systems? 

Mr. NOOTER. Yes, I can, Mr. Chairman.

We issued very comprehensive instructions to our people in Saigon regarding the phaseout of any remnants of that program and it is all well in line. In addition, I have asked our auditor general to conduct an audit of those terminal activities to be sure that they were carried out in accordance with those instructions. I believe, also, that the General Accounting Office is going to have a similar audit, so I can say with great certainty that this phaseout will be consummated in accordance with our instructions and in accordance with the intent of Congress.

ACCESS TO PRISON SYSTEM 

Senator INOUYE. How do we investigate the system when to date we have been denied access? 

Mr. NOOTER. I don't understand your question.

Senator INOUYE. The GAO has been requesting access to the prison system and has been turned down at all times. The State Department has turned them down at each turn. 

Mr. NOOTER. I think what you are referring to is not an audit of the aid assistance. There was a request by a number of Congressmen to the 

GAO to conduct certain inspections of the Vietnamese prison system and that was turned down by the State Department and the Vietnamese Government on the ground that it was inappropriate to proceed in that way, but that was not a turndown of the audit of the AID sup- plies to the prison system, and to my knowledge it had no relationship whatsoever to the termination of the assistance to the police which is what we are referring to. 

Senator INOUYE. Why did you keep the GAO out of there?

Mr. STEARNS. Mr. Chairman, it seemed to us difficult to encourage the GAO to conduct an investigation of a prison system with the avowed purpose of discovering whether there were so-called political prisoners or not.

The embassy through normal consular access can and does visit a number of prisons, and it is one thing I think for an embassy which is accredited to the country to officially have that kind of access, but it becomes a much more difficult and delicate question for an investigatory branch of the U.S. Government coming from the United 

States to investigate the prison system. 

Senator INOUYE. On these visits what have you found?

Mr. STEARNS. After the March supplemental hearings, Mr. Chairman, we did submit to you a rather detailed dispatch submitted by the Saigon Embassy in December of last year in which they used data

which had been accumulated during the period in which there was a public safety program in Vietnam and cross checked that both through the consular visits and through a variety of other sources of information, part of it developed by the intelligence community, and reached the conclusion that as against the charges of 200,000 political prisoners there was a total prison population in Vietnam of no more than 

32,000 including all kinds of offenders. 

Senator INOUYE. Do we have any political prisoners there?

Mr. STEARNS. It is an extremely difficult question to answer because there is so little agreement on a definition of what a political prisoner is even in this country. It is sometimes suggested that Sirhan 

Sirhan is a political prisoner. I noticed, in the Senate debate on October 1 last year when the discussion of applications of section 32 of the

Foreign Assistance Act was debated that the Senate itself had problems defining political prisoners.

This is really the obstacle that we bump into, the fact that almost no country in the world has not at one time or another been accused of having political prisoners.

Senator INOUYE. Is this position of nonaccessibility to prison systems the same? Have you changed your position? 

Mr. STEARNS. No, sir; we still believe that a GAO inspection of the 

Vietnamese prison system would be an infringement on the South 

Vietnamese sovereignty. 

Senator INOUYE. Is this still the position of the Vietnamese government?

Mr. NOOTER. I believe that the Vietnamese Government has offered to have a representative group of U.S. Congressmen visit the prisons there, so long as they felt this was done in a way that would be impartial and would cover the spectrum of views on our program in that country. Is that not correct? 

Mr. STEARNS. I think the invitations have been issued. 

Senator INOUYE. Yes; I am well aware of that. 

I received one of the invitations myself.

If we can be invited, why can't we permit the GAO, an official arm of the U.S. Congress, to go in our behalf?

Mr. NOOTER. I believe it was more the nature of the request, the way it was phrased and worded, than the purposes for which it appeared to be intended.

I understand that the GAO is now doing an audit, for example, of the prison assistance that had been provided and they have had or do have some people in Vietnam at the present time.

CONDITIONS IN PRISONS 

Senator INOUYE. Are you satisfied that the so-called conditions which appalled Member of Congress have been corrected? 

Mr. STEARNS. We think there has been an improvement, Senator. 

Mr. NOOTER. Incidentally, I have visited some of the prisons there myself at the time we had a program there. I did not find the kind of conditions reported in Life Magazine. Some other Congressmen, in addition to the initial group that made a visit out there, also have visited these prisons. Of course one gets different reports from different people, but at least some portions of those Congressmen who made those visits said the same as I am saying now. My impression was that

the prisons were run in a reasonably humane way. Obviously, nobody can completely defend almost any prison system anywhere in the world including our own, but I did not find the conditions that received so much publicity 3 or 4 years ago.

RICE PRODUCTION STATISTICS 

Senator INOUYE. On numerous occasions in reporting on the progress in Vietnam AID has done so by comparing 1973, 1974 with a base year and the base year is always a year during the war. 

For example, on page 15 of the narrative you recited the following: "The 1968-1969 crop season paddy rice production has risen from 4.4 million metric tons to an estimated 6.3 million metric tons in 1973-1974."

What is the validity of statistics in comparing a period of intense warfare and one of supposed peace? 

Mr. NOOTER. You have a good point.

My information is that in the peak prewar years, and since wars have been going on out there for 20 or 25 years, but the peak year before 1965 when hostilities picked up, the crop was some 5.4 million tons of paddy rice compared to this year's 6.3 million. Although that is a peak year, it does give some comparison showing that recent crop production was higher than it was in any of the years prior to the heavy fighting.

Senator INOUYE. Do you attribute this to the slow-down in hostilities or efforts on the part of the government? 

Mr. NOOTER. It is a combination. About 25 percent of their crop now is in the high yielding varieties which has added to increased output. Certainly hostilities in the period that you refer to in 1968 and 1969 did lead to abandonment of some of the fields and a reduction in crop output. So I would say it is a combination of a more peaceful situation, ability of people to return to the fields and farms, a larger area as well as the improved varieties.

QUESTIONS SUBMITTED BY SENATORS INOUYE, CHILES AND BROOKE 

Senator INOUYE. As indicated in the beginning, we will be submitting to you the bulk of our questions on Indochina, including those by other members of the subcommittee, for your response. 

These questions, I believe, will require some study and some research for statistical information. [The questions and answers follow:] 

QUESTIONS SUBMITTED BY SENATOR INOUYE CONTINUING RESOLUTION AUTHORITY 

Question. If the Fiscal Year 1975 Continuing Resolution is written as it has been in the past, would AID have authority to initiate a new program or activity such as the one proposed for Egypt in Fiscal Year 1975?

Answer. Only if it has been justified to Congress in A.I.D.'s Congressional 

Presentation, or after other advance notification to the Congress. 

Question. Are there no limitations or restrictions so long as you operate within the overall rate for operations based on the lesser of last year's annual rate or the budget estimate?

Answer. Other appropriation restrictions also apply, such as the requirement for five days' prior notification to the Appropriations Committees before funds 34-192 O 74-66

are obligated, for almost all categories of funds. This is contained in Sec.

114 

of the Foreign Assistance Appropriations, 1974. 

SUPPORTING ASSISTANCE JORDAN (VILLAGE DEVELOPMENT) 

Question. I have a question concerning the proposed $5 million Village Development Loan in Jordan. How much will be required to capitalize the Government of Jordan financial institution and where will these funds come from? 

Answer. The funds from the proposed $5 million Jordan Village Development 

Loan are to be used by the Jordan Valley Commission. It is expected that the funds will be used principally for street construction, utilities (water and electricity), and funds to support construction of houses. About $1.5 million will go for the housing portion of this activity. There are several options for the management of these funds: through the agricultural bank, through the housing bank, or by a special division of the JVC. This question is now under study and will be settled in the course of the intensive review to prepare a final loan proposal. 

Question. What credit terms will be available to home buyers?

Answer. We are planning for 20 to 25-year mortgages with interest rates within the financial capacity of new buyers, although the actual rate is still under consideration.

MULTI-PHASED PROJECTS 

Question. I have a simple request to make. Whenever you have a multi-phased project, would you indicate the total estimated cost for all phases. Though not intentional, AID might mislead the Committee by giving only estimated cost for the first of several phases in its grant activity data sheet. 

Answer. Yes, we will try to do that, Mr. Chairman, to the extent possible. 

When we present a project it is always a discrete element and if a second phase of the project were to develop it would have to also be a discrete element that Congress could accept or reject without doing damage to the initial undertaking. 

However, we will try to cover all phases of a multi-phased project when we present it.

SUSTAINABLE ECONOMIC GROWTH 

Question. The underlying assumption in AID's fiscal year 1975 proposal for 

Vietnam is that "A short phase with a relatively high aid level will permit investments large enough to generate a chain reaction of self-sustaining growth." 

That assumption reads like a paraphrase of Walt Rostow's famous article "The Take-Off into Self-Sustained Growth." It is true that one of the preconditions for sustained economic growth, in Rostow's theory, is a rise in the rate of productive investment. U.S. foreign assistance can provide that. But, I suggest, there is another, more basic precondition which the United States. cannot provide. That is, namely, the domestic precondition of a political, social, and institutional framework which is capable of giving growth an on-going character. I do not believe that that precondition can be met today. 

To put the question in basic terms, what good will it do to put a finger in the dike, if the whole dike is collapsing?

Answer. I would certainly agree that more than capital injections are needed for sustainable economic growth. A viable political, social, and economic framework is necessary and I believe that Viet-Nam has this. It is not identical to ours nor is it desirable for it to be identical. Viet-Nam has an educated, highly productive labor force, a potential for surplus agricultural production, a diverse and well-equipped light industrial sector, and unexploited natural resources to go along with the institutional framework developed and tested in the crucible of war. In addition, the Paris Agreement with all of its imperfections, does provide a framework for political accommodation and a reduction of the military activity which has been the main factor for economic destabilization in the last decade.

REFUGEES 

Question. The Committee, indeed the entire world, has been deeply moved by the plight of refugees in Vietnam and it commends AID's attempts to assist in their resettlement. I do, however, have a few questions. Much of the land from which the refugees fled remains in the hands of the Provisional Revolutionary

Government (PRG). Will any of the refugees be relocated in these areas? If not, is there the possibility that refugees from these areas will eventually wish to return to them? In short, even after their relocation will they not be refugees from their native villages?

Answer. Obviously there will be no formal GVN relocation sites established on land controlled by the PRG. A limited number of refugees have returned to 

PRG controlled areas and others can just pick up and go if they so desire. Our experience to date indicates that not many refugees desire to place themselves under PRG control. In fact, hundreds of thousands of these refugees have volunteered for resettlement programs in Government of Vietnam territory in preference to returning to their old lands where these are under North Vietnam or PRG control. In any event the decision is an individual one. Dr. Dan, who is in charge of the refugee program, has stated that he would permit refugees to return to PRG areas if that is what they wanted. 

There certainly is the possibility that some of these refugees will eventually wish to return to their native areas when circumstances permit. On the other hand, some are doing quite well in their new location and will probably elect to stay where they are even when their villages become secure. 

Question. How many refugees remain in camps?

Answer. As of the end of June 58,000 refugees remained in 31 temporary camps. 

Of these over 28,000 are Cambodian refugees. 

Question. Will they be the first to relocate?

Answer. The refugees in temporary camps have the first priority for return to their villages or resettlement. It is unlikely, however, that the Cambodian refugees will return to Cambodia for some time to come. 

CITY-TO-FARM PROGRAM AND LAND REFORM PROJECT 

Question.

Is there any linkage between the City-to-Farm program and the 

Land Reform Project? 

Answer. There is no direct relationship between the City-to-Farm Project and the Land Reform Project, although both projects as well as the resettlement carried out under the War Victims Relief and Rehabilitation Project will result in the expansion of the number of owner-operated farm units throughout South Vietnam. Farmers will receive concessionary titles under the City-to-Farm and 

War Victims Relief and Rehabilitation Projects as these resettlements are carried out on government land, whereas farmers receive Land to the Tiller titles to expropriated private land under the Land Reform Project. 

There is a more direct relationship, however, if I speak more broadly of the policy of the Government of Vietnam to encourage former rural people now living in cities to return to income producing agricultural pursuits, rather than speak specifically of the City-to-Farm Project. Those city people who choose to settle on privately owned fallow land that comes under the purview of the Land to the Tiller law of the Land Reform program may apply for title after tilling the land for one crop year.

SYSTEM OF LAND TENURE IN VIETNAM 

Question. What was the system of land tenure in Vietnam prior to the war? 

Did the villagers hold title?

Answer. In longer settled Central Vietnam, individual peasant proprietorship was predominant on the eve of World War II. This was still true in 1955, with peasant proprietorship accounting for approximately three-fourths of the cultivated land. Land holdings were on a small scale with only 50 out of an estimated 

650,000 landowners owning more than 50 hectares each. 

The pre-World War II colonial system of large land holdings in the South continued after independence. In a total cultivated rice area of 2.3 million hectares, the concentration of land ownership in 1955 was one of the highest in the Far East or Southeast Asia. Approximately 2.5 per cent of the owners, with more than 50 hectares each, possessed roughly one-half of the cultivated land. 

On the opposite side of the scale, more than 70 per cent of the proprietors owned less than 5 hectares each, possessing an estimated total of 12.5 per cent of the cultivated land. In the province of Bac Lieu 9 per cent of the landowners had 

70 per cent of the land and 72 per cent of the farmers had no land at all or a hectare or two. In the province of Can Tho 4 per cent of the landlords possessed more than 50 per cent of the land, and roughly the same pattern repeated itself in province after province of the agriculturally rich Delta.

Question. Who now holds title to the land?

Answer. Title for 75% to 80% of the cropland is now held by owner-operators. 

The balance is owned by villages, religious organizations and private individuals. 

REFUGEES 

Question. Can you assure the Committee that when the Government of Vietnam purchases land for refugee resettlement war-profiteers are not the beneficiaries?

Answer. Resettlement sites are located on government-owned land, some of which is abandoned land that has reverted to the public domain. Abandoned land is acquired without cost by simply having the land revert to government ownership after an unsuccessful search is conducted (including advertisements) for the missing owners. Incidentally, the Viet-Cong destroyed land records in many resettlement areas of South Vietnam, making it almost impossible to trace ownership of this land, most of which has been abandoned for over 10 years. If proof of private ownership can be established for abandoned land, compensation to the owners cannot exceed that established under a set formula similar to that used for land expropriation under the Land Reform program. 

Question. In Fiscal Year 1975 voluntary agencies will be granted nearly $10 million for relief and resettlement activities in Cambodia. 

What controls do you have over the grants to voluntary agencies to assure that Cambodian refugees receive maximum assistance? 

Answer. We have grant agreements with each of the voluntary agencies spelling out the responsibilities and rights of both parties insofar as the refugee relief program is concerned. We receive regularly scheduled reports and have the right to audit. In addition, we have a small resident staff in Phnom Penh that monitors program implementation and tells us what is going on. 

We are quite satisfied that these agencies are doing what they can and are doing it well.

Question. The number of Cambodian refugees is rapidly approaching one million. What percentage received A.I.D. assistance through the voluntary agencies? 

Answer. Actually, in May 1,179,104 persons are reported as registered refugees.

I can give you figures for the month of May for those aided by voluntary and international agencies. Catholic Relief Services aided 250,000 refugees; World 

Vision Relief, 55,000; CARE, 36,000; the Indochina Operations Group of the Red 

Cross, 100,000; UNICEF, 32,000; and Save the Children Fund, 6,000, for a total of 479,000.

Is U.S. AID SOLD COMMERCIALLY? 

Question. Is it true that U.S. provided food has been sold commercially Laos?

Answer. There have been instances of, for example, vegetable oil provided under P.L. 480 turning up in the market place, but these have been minor and isolated cases. When these things do occur the Mission, as is the standard monitoring practice, traces the source of the leakage and cuts off the supply. 

DO LAO SELL U.S.-PROVIDED RICE? 

Question. Is it the practice for many Laotian hill-tribesmen to sell the rice they produce and then come to AID for U.S. provided rice? 

Answer. No sir, it is not. In the first place the hill-tribesmen are traditionally subsistence farmers with little or no real surplus to sell and have not been in the commercial marketing business. Secondly, when in the fall of 1973 it became apparent that a bumper rice crop was in prospect in many parts of Laos, the Lao government issued instructions to the provincial governors that no refugee was to be allowed to sell any rice unless he had in storage one year's supply for his family plus sufficient seed for the next planting. So far as we can ascertain there were only minor violations of this instruction. Although some 20,000 persons have returned to food support rolls mostly in the northern mountainous areas, this is a deficit area where we expected to resume food support. 

FOOD AND NUTRITION FUNDS ALLOCATIONS FOR COMMODITIES 

Question. Some $65 million is being set aside under Food and Nutrition for basic commodities, including major imports of fuel and pesticides. Can you inform the Committee as to what amount will be allocated to pesticides? To fuel?

1 Answer. A total of $185 million will be used to finance basic commodities in support of the Food and Nutrition sector. Of that amount, $16 million is allocated for pesticides and $55 million for fuel to run agricultural pumps and machinery.

Question. Vietnam is not known for its mechanized agriculture. Can you assure the Committee that this fuel will go for food production and distribution and not for military supplies? If not, why is it proposed under Food and Nutrition?

Answer. The procurement and allocation of fuel for the civilian and military sectors are handled through two separate and independent supply systems. Also 

A.I.D. maintains an inspection and control system which is designed to insure that A.I.D.-financed goods are used as intended. The combination of higher world prices and increased usage of motorized equipment, particularly for pump irrigation, might place our estimates of fuel requirements for the agriculture sector somewhat on the conservative side. Similarly, there has been a 15 percent increase in the number of motorized fishing vessels this past year. The annual fuel requirements for the fishing fleet alone is estimated to be around $13 million. 

PETROLEUM IMPORTS 

Question. What is the total dollar value of A.I.D. supported petroleum imports? 

Answer. $100 million.

INDOCHINA POSTWAR RECONSTRUCTION PROGRAM 

Question. Mr. Nooter, although Indochina Reconstruction has a new name and perhaps a more salable face, I see little difference between it and the old Supporting Assistance Programs. Just how much of the fiscal year 1974 Indochina 

Reconstruction Assistance Program has gone for real "reconstruction" as opposed to just maintaining the Vietnamese economy?

Answer. As you will recall, our FY 1974 request amounted to $475 million in 

Indochina Postwar Reconstruction funds for Vietnam. Within that request, we had planned to begin a major reconstruction and development program with an estimated cost of $98 million. These funds would have financed such development projects as the National Economic Development Fund and the rebuilding of agricultural facilities and basic infrastructure damaged by the war. The actual amount of funds which became available for Vietnam, i.e., $397 million, was significantly below the $475 million request. This fact when combined with the unforeseen dramatic increases in world prices forced us to forego virtually all the capital development and reconstruction projects which had been contemplated in FY 1974. Our FY 1975 request again emphasizes the urgent need to undertake a greatly expanded program of investments to increase Vietnam's productive capacity. Specifically, we have requested $219 mililon for productionoriented projects in irrigation, agricultural credit, fertilizer production and salt water intrusion barriers. 

MILITARY STABILITY 

Question. When the U.S. had 525,000 men in Viet-Nam, the other side demonstrated it could strike at will. How, then, can you now say, "The relative military stability which now prevails is adequate to permit substantial reconstruction and development in the secure areas of the country?" 

Answer. First of all, Senator Inouye, "security" is very much a relative term. 

As we have all learned in recent years, there is no part of the world-not Los Angeles or London or Saigon-which is totally secure from terrorist actions, for example. Many parts of the world-Israel and South Korea, for example, as well as South Viet-Nam-have long lived and will probably for some time continue to live under the threat of conventional military attack from hostile neighbors. The possibility of renewed or heightened warfare in these areas does not and should not, we believe, prevent continued economic development. 

Capital investment in South Viet-Nam is not without some risk, nor is life in some parts of the country without substantial danger from Communist terrorist and military attacks. However, during the last years of the war, particularly after 

1968, the South Vietnamese Government and armed forces, with American assistance, were successful in pushing both the Communist military forces and political infrastructure further and further away from the cities, the lines of communication and the highly populated rural areas. Simultaneously, the South Vietnamese, greatly aided by the Vietnamization program, gradually built up their

military and political strength so that they could defend themselves and the bulk of their populated territory without American combat support. Their progress in this regard was demonstrated by their success in turning back the massive North Vietnamese invasion in 1972 and their continued successful defense against the lower level of Communist aggression since that time. 

Consequently, we are confident that the degree of security necessary to permit substantial reconstruction and development work does now exist in South Viet- Nam and has existed for some time. Moreover, we believe the South Vietnamese can continue to maintain this security, provided we furnish them with adequate military and economic aid. Finally, we are persuaded that increasing prosperity and self-sufficiency in South Viet-Nam will contribute to increasing security and military stability, just as continued economic deterioration could lead to growing security problems. 

"SECURE" AREAS 

Question. Would you care to name, specifically, one area of South Viet-Nam that you consider "secure"?

Answer. As I pointed out in answer to your previous question, Senator, "secure" is a relative term.

Relative to what is required to undertake substantial reconstruction and development projects, with good prospects of successful implementation, we would consider "secure" virtually all the towns and cities of South Viet-Nam, most of the principal lines of communication, and well over half of the populated rural territory.

AVAILABILITY AND PRICE OF FERTILIZER 

Question. The program narrative for Vietnam notes that fertilizer costs have increased nearly 300 percent in the past two years. In the descriptive paragraph for the Food and Nutrition proposal, I find the estimate that at least $120 million worth of fertilizer will be required for rice production in Vietnam. That is close to 320,000 tons of fertilizer. From where is this fertilizer going to come? I ask this question because I am concerned with what has become a world-wide shortage of fertilizer. Among others, Vietnam, Cambodia, Egypt, Bangladesh and Pakistan will be the recipients of A.I.D. support for fertilizer purchases. I wonder, do you know, within a reasonable range, how much fertilizer is going to be available for A.I.D.'s world-wide programs and at what price?

Answer. Although in the past A.I.D. limited financing of fertilizer to U.S. source, this policy was changed last year after consultation with the Fertilizer Institute, which represents domestic suppliers. As the fertilizer shortage developed, A.I.D. broadened the eligible source to permit procurement from free world sources. It is hoped that this broadening of approved source will make possible substantial deliveries from major fertilizer producing areas, for instance, Cambodia traditionally gets some of its fertilizer from North Africa, Bangladesh and Pakistan from European and Asian sources in addition to America. Vietnam has recently been guaranteed approximately 40.000 tons of urea nitrogen fertilizer from Japan through an agreement between the two governments. A.I.D. expects that about 30% of the fertilizer it finances will come from such foreign sources in FY 1975.

A.I.D. has no way of knowing with certainty how much fertilizer will be available in international markets for A.I.D.-recipient countries. We hope to be able to finance about 700,000 metric tons this fiscal year, which will reflect only part of the total fertilizer requirement for most A.I.D. countries. 

Prices of fertilizer have continued to rise. For instance, urea is now being offered in the world market at $365 to $375 per metric ton, DAP at $420 to $450 per metric ton and TSP at $360 to $370. There is some reason to believe that these prices may be leveling off, but there is no assurance that this is the case. 

CENTRALIZED FERTILIZER PROCUREMENT 

Question. Are there proposals for centralized procurement or will A.I.D. missions be bidding against each other?

Answer. A.I.D. held one fertilizer procurement for a number of countries early in June, 1974. It is planning to hold another centralized procurement for all 

A.I.D.-recipient countries in mid-July. To the extent that these consolidated procurements are successful in obtaining needed quantities of fertilizer, independent procurement actions by countries having A.I.D. funds available can be reduced or eliminated.

IMPACT OF FERTILIZER PROCUREMENT ON DOMESTIC PRICES 

Question. What impact will A.I.D. fertilizer purchases have on the domestic price and, by extension, the cost of U.S. consumer goods? 

Answer. A.I.D. financing of fertilizer exports has only a marginal effect on domestic supplies and represents a minor share of the export market. For fiscal year 1973, A.I.D.-financed exports were less than 2 percent of the gross domestic supply, and about 11 percent of total exports from the United States. Thus, A.I.D.financed exports of fertilizer are only one minor factor contributing to the level of export prices, and have even less effect, if any, upon domestic prices of fertilizer or related commodities. The domestic average price for urea, as an example, is about $100 lower than the world price. The domestic price is influenced by farmer-owned production facilities who market their products at or near cost to owner/members. As a result, other producers competing in the domestic market sell at prices well below world prices. The maintenance of this substantial spread between domestic and export prices also reflects long-term relationships between domestic supplies and their customers. These established market relationships make suppliers unable or unwilling to take full advantage of higher export prices, which, as suggested above, are set by world supply-demand conditions on which A.I.D. has very little effect. 

QUESTIONS SUBMITTED BY SENATOR CHILES INDOCHINA POSTWAR RECONSTRUCTION REQUEST 

Question. The $939.8 million has been requested to a) relieve refugees, b) shore up import funds, and c) rebuild the depressed economies. Are these funds above and beyond PL 480 (Food for Peace) funds? If so, then your request is more than 27% up from your FY '74 request of $619 million and more than double the $435 million you actually expended. How do you justify this increase? 

Answer. Yes, PL 480 is in addition to our request here. The increase is our request, as discussed earlier here and in my formal statement, arises from two main factors. One is the sharp rise in prices, which means the same amount of real goods costs more. The other is that we are trying to get development going in South Vietnam so that it can move toward economic self-sufficiency and declining dependence upon our assistance. PL 480 Question. I have seen reports that P.L. 480 funds have been utilized almost exclusively to finance the SVN war effort as these funds are shifted by the Saigon Government out of the Food program. Do you have any information on such allegations?

Answer. P.L. 480 funds have been used as authorized by and justified by the 

Congress. Under the P.L. 480 Title I sales program, the food is purchased from 

United States suppliers with dollar payment made directly to the suppliers by the Department of Agriculture. The host country importers pay for this food with local currency. Section 104 of P.L. 480 has authorized the United States to enter into agreements with a recipient country regarding the use of these local currencies, including the use of local currency for common defense purposes. Under this authority, P.L. 480-generated local currency has been used to meet a share of the military budget requirements of South Vietnam. 

However, in compliance with Section 40 of the Foreign Assistance Act, no 

P.L. 480 currencies will be released for defense purposes after July 1, 1974, unless such currencies were obligated on or before December 17, 1973, the date of the enactment of Section 40. 

DISTRIBUTION OF AID IN LAOS 

Question. As you know, the U.S. has gone on record in support of the coalition government in Laos. I would be interested in knowing how agreements are being worked out within the coalition in Laos as between the different factions in regard to U.S. aid being channeled there? 

Answer. For the time being we are carrying out our aid program as before, that is, in accordance with written agreements with the appropriate ministry of the Lao government. We anticipate that as the Pathet Lao ministers settle into their jobs-they head the Ministries of Foreign Affairs, Public Works, Plan and

Economy, Religion, and Information-they will have their own views on aid. 

However, we do not know how these ideas may emerge in the Provisional Government of National Union which is obliged to operate on the basis of unanimity. 

SOUTH VIETNAM'S DEPENDENCE ON U.S. ASSISTANCE 

Question. Our AID policy to IndoChina has been formulated with the intent to enhance the ability of our Southeast Asian Allies to stand on their own feet. 

In this light I would like to know what percentage of SVN's budget is comprised of U.S. foreign aid? 

Answer. South Vietnam's budget for CY 1974 is 561.2 billion piasters. Support from U.S. foreign aid sources is expected to be 214.0 billion piasters or roughly 

39 percent of this budget.

Question. Have you any information as to the approximate percentage of 

SVN's total imports made up by goods from the U.S.? 

Answer. The best figures we have on GVN imports by country of origin are listed in the National Bank of Vietnam's Economic Bulletin for 1973. This document indicates that Vietnamese imports in CY 1972 were valued at $674.3 million of which $309.9 million, or 46.0 percent, were from the U.S. In the first nine months of CY 1973 Vietnam imported $504.1 million of which $243.9 million or 

48.4 percent were from the U.S.

NON-U.S. DONORS 

Question. What is the current status of efforts to involve non-U.S. donors in the aid program in South Vietnam? Has there been any indication that the members of the consultative group of donor nations of the World Bank have changed their view that conditions in South Vietnam are still too unsettled to permit any effective aid program funded by the World Bank? 

Answer. We are continuing to seek participation of other donors in support of Vietnam's development efforts. In 1973, other countries, principally Japan and France, contributed about $80 million to Vietnam. We expect that these countries will continue or increase their aid levels in the coming year. Other countries are continuing to provide smaller contributions for humanitarian programs.

We believe the Japanese are contemplating a further increase in their official aid program and private investments in Vietnam. Recently Japan announced that it was prepared to provide limited guarantees for Vietnam. Similarly, a relatively stabilized political and military environment and removal of restraints on OPIC participation in Vietnam would encourage increased flows from other donors and from the private sector. 

We have not tested the attitudes of the donors' group recently, although I understand that the Federal Republic of Germany has taken a more positive position several months ago.

DISTRIBUTION OF AID IN LAOS 

Question. Given the fact that there is now a coalition government in Laos, exactly how is our aid being distributed? Is some of it being utilized in areas that have been under the control of the Pathet Lac forces? 

Answer. The new coalition government, termed the Provisional Government of National Union, or PGNU, was invested only on April 5, 1974. U.S. officials in Laos have discussed U.S. aid with "Ministers of the PGNU, including communist ministers, and they have indicated that for the time being they wish to have the U.S. continue its on-going activities. It probably will be some time before plans for the Pathet Lao controlled zone are developed and coordinated with the Vietnamese side and become the accepted policy of the PGNU. 

MECHANIZATION OF SOUTH VIETNAMESE AGRICULTURE 

Question. In the wake of the energy crisis it has become apparent that serious problems will be encountered by societies making the transition from a nonmechanized economy to one dependent on mechanization, and hence on energy sources such as gas and oil. It appears to me that South Vietnam is one such country. Would you provide for the record an evaluation of the degree to which 

South Vietnam has become dependent on gas and oil for the effective functioning of its agricultural sector?

Answer. Agricultural mechanical equipment using petroleum products consists primarily of tractors and tillage equipment, with some thrashers and rice mills also in use. Thus, a conservative estimate is that at least one million barrels of gasoline and diesel oil are required annually just to maintain the present agricultural production in South Vietnam.

In addition, petroleum products are required for both the water and land transportation of agricultural output. 

Substantial gas and oil shortages would have a serious adverse effect on agricultural production as sufficient acreage could not be tilled to maintain present production levels. Also, double cropping would be drastically reduced without the use of pumps to control water levels. 

Question. How much emphasis are we giving in our aid program to South Vietnam to the mechanization of its agricultural production? 

Answer. AID procurement of agricultural equipment has been minimal; we provided some demonstration tractors and tillage equipment to the Agricultural Machinery Directorate in 1957 and only an occasional item of equipment since that date. We are encouraging the use of modern low-lift pumps to replace inefficient ones now in use and to permit the growing of crops in the dry season. 

The machinery procured by the private sector has been primarily equipment that does the heavy land tillage operation. This has brought additional land into tillage, much more land, in fact, than could have been prepared through the use of hand labor, which in turn has created more employment. Human skills and labor are required for transplanting, weeding, harvesting and thrashing in Vietnam. In relation to the increased modern low-lift pump utilization we are recommending, there will be a savings in energy through the replacement of inefficient pumps with new ones, and furthermore, the resulting broadening of agriculture production and employment will greatly offset the cost of pump installation and operation.

Question. Given the existence of the energy crisis and the weakness of the 

Vietnamese economy, would it not be wise to forbear from increasing the Vietnamese reliance on energy-related mechanization?

Answer. We agree with you. The only items of machinery that we can recommend importing are a limited number of tractors and tillage equipment (to be imported commercially) and essential irrigation equipment. This machinery is necessary if we are to bring into production sufficient land to utilize the available labor and to allow South Vietnam to attain self-sufficiency in its basic food requirements. The returns from this modest increase in equipment are much greater than the costs of installation and operation. 

OPTIMISM REGARDING SITUATION IN SOUTH VIETNAM 

Question. Several times in the past few months A.I.D. officials have given optimistic appraisals of the situation in South Vietnam to this committee. Yet, at the same time we have been asked for and have granted a supplemental ap-

propriation to stave off economic collapse. Can you explain these seeming contradictions? Specifically, can you detail for the Committee the positive alterations in the situation in South Vietnam that give rise to optimism expressed by yourself and others?

Answer. Our optimism is based on an assessment that the Vietnamese have both the commitment and ability to move forward with a serious and successful development program given adequate levels of economic support. We have already seen what the Vietnamese can do even under adverse economic conditions. Rice production has increased by 20 percent over the peak year of 1964. 

Sorghum has been introduced as a new crop and is making considerable impact as animal feed. Domestic tax collections during 1973 increased by 94 percent over the previous year (in real terms this represents an increase of 34 percent). 

Additionally, exports have increased from $12.5 million in 1971 to $60.6 million in 1973.

Obviously if Vietnam is denied even the minimum resources essential to sustain the economy at its current level, not only will there be lack of progress toward self-sufficiency, but unemployment will grow and the welfare problem will become more severe. All the economic reforms and policies which the Government of Vietnam has undertaken would be difficult to sustain under such conditions.

In sum, the alternatives before us are clear. The level of resources provided can either permit Vietnam's economy at best to stagger along or it can provide a real opportunity for Vietnam to lessen its dependence on high levels of foreign aid in the shortest time possible.

CAMBODIA 

Question. What percentage of the territory in Cambodia is now controlled by forces loyal to the Lon Nol government? What percentage of the population is in this territory? How do these figures compare to a year ago?

Answer. All of the major urban centers, in the populated areas, are controlled by the government. That's 15 percent of the area and about 75 percent of the people. It is hard to put percentage figures on the changes over the past year. 

The Government controls more people than then-over 70,000 refugees have come in from outlying areas in the past six months-and only one important city, Oudong, was lost. It has no strategic importance; however, it is of religious importance.

I should add that as much as 25 percent of the countryside is either contested, deserted or uninhabitable. 

Question. What are our objectives in Cambodia? At what point does our desire for a negotiated settlement become secondary to the desire to lessen the suffering of the Cambodian peoples? Perhaps we have lost sight of the fact that it is the peasant who is suffering most from the continuation of the fighting. 

Answer. Our objectives remain that of assisting the Cambodians to defend themselves, pursuant to a settlement of the fighting. As to ending the suffering of the Cambodian peoples-that is a decision for the Cambodians to make. So long as the Government is able to conscript an army and so long as the people support that army, then they appear willing to make the sacrifices required for their own defense.

The Khmer communists could end most of the peasants' sufferings immediately by accepting the GKR ceasefire proposal which has been offered for more than 

16 months.

MR. CHAIRMAN AND MEMBERS OF THE COMMITTEE: 

THE SECRETARY OF STATE HAS ALREADY APPEARED BEFORE CONGRESS TO GIVE THE BROAD OUTLINES OF THE PROPOSED FY 1975 SECURITY ASSISTANCE PROGRAM AND THE ROLE IT IS EXPECTED TO PLAY IN SUPPORTING THE FOREIGN POLICY OBJECTIVES OF THE UNITED STATES. MY PURPOSE, THEREFORE, IS TO DISCUSS SOMEWHAT MORE SPECIFICALLY THE MANNER IN WHICH THE TWO FORMS OF SECURITY ASSISTANCE ADMINISTERED BY THE DEPARTMENT OF Defense FOREIGN MILITARY SALES (FMS) CREDIT AND THE MILITARY ASSISTANCE PROGRAM (MAP) -- ADVANCE OUR OBJECTIVES. 

WITH ME TODAY FROM THE DEPARTMENT OF DEFENSE ARE ADMIRAL MOORER, CHAIRMAN OF THE JOINT CHIEFS OF STAFF, AND VICE ADMIRAL RAY PEET, THE DIRECTOR OF THE DEFENSE SECURITY ASSIST- ANCE AGENCY. 

I WOULD LIKE TO BEGIN, MR. CHAIRMAN AND MEMBERS, BY BRIEFLY PLACING OUR SECURITY ASSISTANCE PROPOSALS INTO THE OVERALL CONTEXT OF OUR PRESENT STRATEGIC DOCTRINE. 

EARLIER THIS YEAR, BEFORE THE ARMED SERVICES AND APPRO- PRIATIONS COMMITTEES OF BOTH HOUSES OF CONGRESS, I REVIEWED THE FUNDAMENTAL STRATEGIC ISSUES THAT WE FACE AND THE POLICIES AND PROGRAMS WE BELIEVE ARE IMPORTANT FOR THE LONG-RUN SECU- RITY OF THE UNITED STATES. I POINTED OUT THAT IT WAS NO LONGER SUFFICIENT, NOW THAT THE SOVIET UNION HAD ACHIEVED NUCLEAR PARITY, TO RELY FOR DETERRENCE ON NUCLEAR WAR SOLELY ON THE RHETORIC OF "ASSURED DESTRUCTION," WITH ITS IMPLICATION OF A RELATIVELY MASSIVE NUCLEAR RESPONSE. ACCORDINGLY, I HAVE PROPOSED CHANGES IN OUR TARGETING DOCTRINE WHICH WILL GIVE US THE WIDER RESPONSE OPTIONS NECESSARY FOR CONTINUING DETERRENCE. 

IN ADDITION, HAVING IN MIND THE AGGRESSIVE DEVELOPMENT AND

TESTING OF NEW ICBMS NOW UNDERWAY IN THE SOVIET UNION, WE ARE PROPOSING TO THE CONGRESS R&D PROGRAMS THAT WOULD BE NECESSARY TO HELP ASSURE ESSENTIAL EQUIVALENCE BETWEEN U.S. AND USSR STRATEGIC FORCES IF THE USSR DOES NOT AGREE TO ESSENTIAL 

EQUIVALENCE IN THE SALT NEGOTIATIONS. 

A BALANCE OF U.S.-USSR STRATEGIC NUCLEAR FORCES IS PART, BUT ONLY PART, OF THE WIDER NEED TO MAINTAIN A WORLDWIDE MIL- ITARY EQUILIBRIUM. DETERRENCE IS GREATLY STRENGTHENED IF THERE ARE REGIONAL MILITARY BALANCES IN CRITICAL AREAS OF THE WORLD. IN EUROPE, FOR EXAMPLE, WE AND OUR NATO ALLIES ARE SEEKING TO MAINTAIN A SATISFACTORY LONG-TERM BALANCE OF FORCES. 

SIMILARLY, WE WISH TO MAINTAIN A BALANCE OF NAVAL FORCES, FOR UNLIKE THE USSR, WHICH IS PREDOMINANTLY A LAND POWER, THE U.S. 

AND ITS ALLIES HAVE LONG AND EXPOSED SEA LINES OF COMMUNICATION. 

ACCESS TO VITAL SUPPLIES, SUCH AS OIL AND OTHER OVERSEAS RESOURCES, IS ESSENTIAL TO THE WEST. 

THE U.S., HOWEVER, CANNOT BY ITSELF MAINTAIN ADEQUATE CONVENTIONAL FORCES TO PROTECT ITS LARGER INTERESTS AND TO ENSURE STABILITY IN ALL POTENTIALLY VOLATILE AREAS OF THE WORLD. 

THE CONFLICT IN SOUTHEAST ASIA HAS DEMONSTRATED THE PROBLEMS THAT CAN RESULT FROM THE DIRECT INVOLVEMENT OF AMERICAN FORCES. 

HERE IS WHERE SECURITY ASSISTANCE HAS AN INDISPENSABLE ROLE. 

ΤΟ 

IT IS THE PRINCIPAL PURPOSE OF SECURITY ASSISTANCE BOTH THE GRANT AID AND THE MILITARY SALES PROGRAMS STRENGTHEN DETERRENCE AND PROMOTE PEACEFUL NEGOTIATIONS BY HELPING OUR FRIENDS AND ALLIES TO MAINTAIN ADEQUATE DEFENSE FORCES OF THEIR OWN. WE BELIEVE THAT HOSTILITIES CAN OFTEN BE AVOIDED ALTOGETHER; AND WHEN THEY CANNOT, WE SEEK TO ENSURE THAT OUR FRIENDS AND ALLIES HAVE THE CAPACITY TO DEFEND THEM- SELVES AND TO RESTORE STABILITY AS SOON AS PRACTICABLE. 

IN

THIS WAY, WE SEEK TO ACHIEVE REGIONAL STABILITY IN CRUCIAL AREAS OF THE WORLD WITHOUT THE NEED FOR DIRECT INTERVENTION BY AMERICAN FORCES. 

THE MIDDLE EAST IS AN EXCELLENT EXAMPLE. WE HAVE HELPED ISRAEL MAINTAIN SUFFICIENT DEFENSE CAPABILITY, THUS AVOIDING THE NEED FOR GREAT POWER MILITARY INTERVENTION AND THE DANGERS OF CONFRONTATION. WE HAVE BEEN FREE TO PURSUE ARRANGEMENTS FOR STABILITY AND A MORE DURABLE PEACE THROUGH DIPLOMATIC MEANS. 

THE RECENT INITIAL SUCCESSES OF THE DIPLOMATIC PROCESS ARE APPARENT AND ENCOURAGING. AS YOU KNOW, THE SECRETARY OF STATE CONSIDERS THE SECURITY ASSISTANCE PROGRAM TO BE ESSENTIAL TO THE SUCCESS OF OUR HOPES FOR A GREATER MEASURE OF MIDDLE EAST PEACE. 

THE VAST BULK OF OUR MILITARY ASSISTANCE AND FOREIGN SALES PROGRAMS RECOMMENDED FOR FY 1975 ARE AIMED AT TWO OF THE MORE UNSTABLE PARTS OF THE WORLD MIDDLE EAST AND ASIA. MORE THAN 80 PERCENT OF OUR PROPOSED GRANT AND SALES PROGRAMS ARE DIRECTED TO THE COUNTRIES OF THESE TWO AREAS. OUR LARGEST CREDIT SALES PROGRAM 

$300 MILLION

IS FOR ISRAEL, A COUNTRY WHICH ONLY RECENTLY WAS REQUIRED TO MOUNT A SWIFT AND SIZEABLE DEFENSE. 

BY FAR THE LARGEST GRANT PROGRAM $362 MILLION IS FOR CAMBODIA, A COUNTRY STILL STRUGGLING TO DEFEND ITSELF AND SURVIVE AS A FREE NATION. 

THE SECRETARY OF STATE HAS REPORTED ON THE PROGRESS OF HIS RECENT NEGOTIATIONS IN THE MIDDLE EAST. NOWHERE DO THE EFFORTS OF THE U.S. TO REDUCE TENSION, ENCOURAGE RAPPROCHEMENT, AND PRESERVE AN INCOMPLETE AND FRAGILE PEACE HAVE GREATER IMPORT THAN IN THE MIDDLE EAST. TO LIMIT THE POSSIBILITY OF DIRECT SUPERPOWER CONFRONTATION, TO PROVIDE THE CONFIDENCE NEEDED FOR NEGOTIATION, AND TO PERMIT ISRAEL AND CERTAIN OF THE MODERATE ARAB STATES TO HAVE THE CAPACITY TO DEFEND THEMSELVES WITHOUT

THE NEED FOR DIRECT U.S. MILITARY INTERVENTION, WE ARE RECOM- MENDING MAJOR GRANT AND SALES PROGRAMS TO CERTAIN MIDDLE EAST COUNTRIES. 

WE ARE PROPOSING CREDIT SALES PROGRAMS OF $300 MILLION FOR ISRAEL, $30 MILLION FOR JORDAN, $10 MILLION FOR LEBANON, $71 MILLION FOR GREECE AND $90 MILLION FOR TURKEY. WE ARE RECOMMENDING GRANT ASSISTANCE PROGRAMS OF $94 MILLION FOR JORDAN, AND $80 MILLION FOR TURKEY. ISRAEL AND JORDAN ARE AT THE CENTER OF THE PRESENT INSTABILITIES IN THE AREA, AND THEIR DEFENSE NEEDS ARE PARAMOUNT. GREECE AND TURKEY ARE, OF COURSE, KEY MEMBERS OF THE NATO ALLIANCE, AND THE MAINTENANCE OF ADE- QUATE DEFENSE CAPABILITIES IN BOTH COUNTRIES IS CRUCIAL TO THE ALLIANCE. 

IN ADDITION TO THE PARAMOUNT IMPORTANCE OF ACHIEVING AND PRESERVING THE PEACE THROUGHOUT THE MIDDLE EAST, THE UNITED STATES RECOGNIZES AN EQUALLY VITAL NEED TO PURSUE POLICIES CONDUCIVE TO CONTINUING ACCESS TO THE AREA'S TREMENDOUS OIL RESERVES. 

DENIAL OR CURTAILMENT OF THIS ACCESS WOULD REPRESENT A THREAT TO THE SECURITY AND ECONOMIC WELL-BEING OF THE UNITED STATES AND OTHER FREE-WORLD NATIONS. JUDICIOUS USE OF FOREIGN MILITARY SALES, BOTH CASH AND CREDIT, AND GRANT MILITARY ASSIST- ANCE, AS INSTRUMENTS OF NATIONAL POLICY TOWARD DEFLECTING THAT THREAT IS THUS CLEARLY CONSISTENT WITH OUR NATIONAL INTEREST. 

WE HAVE IN RECENT HISTORY INVESTED HEAVILY IN LIVES AND FORTUNE IN ASIA, FIRST IN KOREA AND THEN IN INDOCHINA. OUR PROMPT ASSISTANCE AND CONTINUING SUPPORT TO KOREA PERMITTED THAT COUNTRY TO MAINTAIN ITS INDEPENDENCE AN INDEPENDENCE THAT ALMOST VANISHED IN 1950. THE PROPOSED MILITARY ASSISTANCE TO KOREA FOR FY 1975 

$161.5 MILLION IN GRANT AID AND $52 

IS MEANT TO HELP MILLION IN FOREIGN MILITARY SALES CREDIT

STRENGTHEN AND MAKE MORE CERTAIN A SATISFACTORY MILITARY BALANCE THERE. MILITARY EQUILIBRIUM IN THAT IMPORTANT MEETING PLACE OF GREAT POWER INFLUENCE IS ESSENTIAL FOR DETERRENCE AND DEFENSE. 

SUCH A BALANCE IS ALSO AN ESSENTIAL UNDERPINNING FOR NEGOTIATIONS BETWEEN NORTH AND SOUTH KOREA. 

THE LARGEST PORTION OF OUR ASSISTANCE TO ASIA IS TO SOUTH- EAST ASIA, $544.3 MILLION IN GRANT ASSISTANCE, $15 MILLION IN FOREIGN MILITARY SALES CREDITS. THE REASONS FOR IT ARE WELL 

KNOWN.

WHEN WE WITHDREW AMERICAN FORCES FROM INDOCHINA, IT WAS UNDERSTOOD THAT WE WOULD PROVIDE THE MILITARY TOOLS TO ENABLE THE PEOPLE THERE TO DEFEND THEMSELVES. THE NEED TO DO SO HAS NOT LESSENED IN THE LAST YEAR. THE FLOW OF MILITARY EQUIPMENT, SUPPLIES AND PERSONNEL FROM THE NORTH TO POSITIONS ENDANGERING CAMBODIA, LAOS, AND SOUTH VIETNAM CONTINUES. CAMBODIA IS PAR- TICULARLY HARD PRESSED. THE SECURITY REQUIREMENTS OF THAILAND, INDONESIA AND THE PHILIPPINES ARE CONTINUING ONES WHICH THEY NEED HELP IN MEETING. IT WOULD BE UNWORTHY OF US AND WRONG, IN MY JUDGMENT, TO DEFAULT ON OUR OBLIGATION BY DENYING THE HELP NEEDED BY THESE SMALL NATIONS IN THIS DIFFICULT HOUR. 

ANOTHER OF OUR OBJECTIVES IN PROVIDING MILITARY ASSISTANCE IS CONTINUING AN UNINTERRUPTED ACCESS TO BASES AND FACILITIES IMPORTANT TO THE WORLDWIDE U.S. MILITARY POSTURE. IN ALL CASES, HOWEVER, DOD SECURITY ASSISTANCE PROGRAMS ARE DESIGNED TO FACILITATE AND ENCOURAGE GREATER CONTRIBUTION BY COUNTRIES TO THEIR OWN AND THE COMMON DEFENSE. THE INCREASE IN ALLOCATION OF FMS CREDIT PROPOSED CLEARLY INDICATES BOTH THE THRUST AND THE PROGRESS OF THIS EFFORT. A STRIKING CASE IN POINT IS THE SHARP DROP IN MAP GRANT AID PROGRAMMED FOR THE REPUBLIC OF CHINA FROM ALMOST $30 MILLION IN FY 1973 TO THE $400,000 TRAINING- ONLY PROGRAM PROPOSED FOR FY 1975. DURING THE SAME TWO-YEAR

1 

RISING PERIOD, FMS CREDIT SALES TO THAT COUNTRY NEARLY DOUBLED FROM $45 MILLION IN FY 1973 TO AN EXPECTED $80 MILLION IN FY 1975. 

A SIMILAR TRANSITION FROM GRANT AID RECIPIENT TO PURCHASING NATION STATUS IS ALREADY WELL UNDER WAY IN LATIN AMERICA. IN LESS THAN TEN YEARS, MAP GRANT AID PROVIDED THROUGHOUT THIS REGION HAS DROPPED BY APPROXIMATELY 75 PERCENT FROM A TOTAL OF ALMOST $80 MILLION IN FY 1966 TO THE LESS THAN $20 MILLION PROPOSED FOR FY 1975. LESS THAN $10 MILLION IN GRANT MATERIEL IS PROGRAMMED FOR ALL OF LATIN AMERICA. ONLY NINE OF THE 18 COUNTRIES IN THE REGION RECEIVING ASSISTANCE WILL RECEIVE GRANT MATERIEL. 

THE OTHER NINE WILL BE PROVIDED TRAINING ONLY, EITHER IN THE UNITED STATES OR AT U.S. SCHOOLS IN THE CANAL ZONE TRAINING WHICH SERVES OUR OWN INTERESTS AS WELL AS THEIRS AND PROMOTES THE SPIRIT OF COOPERATION AND PARTNERSHIP WHICH IS A BASIC OBJECTIVE OF SECURITY ASSISTANCE TO LATIN AMERICA. FMS CREDIT PLANNED FOR 16 OF TH 18 LATIN AMERICAN COUNTRIES PARTICIPATING IN FY 1975 DOD SECURITY ASSISTANCE PRO- GRAMS AMOUNTS TO $200 MILLION MORE THAN FIVE TIMES AS MUCH AS IN FY 1966. 

IN THIS CONNECTION, I NOTE THE OBJECTION RAISED BY SOME IN THE CONGRESS AND THE PUBLIC AT LARGE WITH RESPECT TO THE SALE OF U.S. MILITARY EQUIPMENT TO LATIN AMERICAN COUNTRIES WHOSE LIMITED RESOURCES, THEY CONTEND, COULD BE BETTER SPENT ON ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT. ACTUALLY, THE DEFENSE BUDGETS OF LATIN AMERICAN NATIONS ARE GENERALLY MODEST AND, BY COMPARISON, LOWER THAN THOSE OF EQUALLY ADVANCED COUNTRIES IN OTHER PARTS OF THE WORLD. BY COMPARISON, THE AMOUNT OF NATIONAL RESOURCES DEVOTED TO DEFENSE IS QUITE LOW AN AVERAGE OF ABOUT 2 PER- CENT OF GNP. THE MODERNIZATION REQUIREMENTS OF THEIR ARMED FORCES ARE NOT EXCESSIVE. 

LATIN AMERICAN COUNTRIES ARE OBVIOUSLY

DETERMINED TO MODERNIZE AND REPLACE U.S. EQUIPMENT OF WORLD WAR II AND KOREAN WAR VINTAGE. IT IS AND HAS BEEN FRUITLESS FOR THE UNITED STATES TO DICTATE TO THE GOVERNMENTS OF SUCH SOV- EREIGN NATIONS THE EXTENT TO WHICH THEY SHOULD SATISFY WHAT THEY HAVE DETERMINED TO BE THEIR MILITARY REQUIREMENTS. By REFUSING TO HELP THEM ACHIEVE MODEST MODERNIZATION PROGRAMS, WE DO NOT SPUR ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT OR AN ALTERNATIVE DISTRI- BUTION OF RESOURCES; WE SIMPLY ENCOURAGE THEM TO MAKE THEIR MILITARY PURCHASES ELSEWHERE. THIS IS INCONSISTENT WITH A FOREIGN POLICY WHICH SEEKS STRONG REGIONAL ASSOCIATIONS WITH THE NATIONS OF THE WESTERN HEMISPHERE. 

I DO NOT RECOMMEND MAJOR GRANT ASSISTANCE PROGRAMS TO LATIN AMERICA. I DO NOT RECOMMEND SELLING ARMS THERE OR ELSEWHERE IN A HAPHAZARD WAY, SIMPLY BECAUSE THERE IS SOMEONE WILLING TO BUY THEM. I DO RECOMMEND, HOWEVER, THAT WE GO AHEAD WITH PRUDENT GRANT AND ARMS SALES PROGRAMS TO OUR LATIN AMERICAN NEIGHBORS WHERE THOSE PROGRAMS MAKE SENSE FROM OUR POINT OF VIEW, AND NOT LEAVE THE SUPPLY OF ARMS LARGELY TO THOSE OUTSIDE THIS HEMI- SPHERE. THIS RESPONSE TO THE REASONABLE REQUESTS OF LATIN AMERICAN GOVERNMENTS FOR COOPERATION IN THE MODERNIZATION OF THEIR ARMED FORCES IS THE BASIS FOR OUR FY 1975 PROGRAMS.

THE HORN OF AFRICA IS OF PARTICULAR STRATEGIC INTEREST DUE TO ITS GEOGRAPHICAL PROXIMITY TO THE TROUBLED MIDDLE EAST. No FMS CREDIT IS PROPOSED FOR THESE OR ANY OTHER EUROPEAN COUNTRIES. ALL FOREIGN MILITARY SALES TO EUROPEAN COUNTRIES ARE MADE ON A CASH BASIS.

WHILE SUCH SALES CONTINUE AT A HIGH LEVEL, THE IMPROVED TECHNOLOGICAL CAPABILITIES OF EUROPEAN COUNTRIES TO PRODUCE MILITARY EQUIPMENT HAVE ENABLED THEM TO INCREASE THE VOLUME OF THEIR SALES TO COUNTRIES IN OTHER PARTS OF THE WORLD. 

IN 

THIS CONNECTION, AND IN THE CONTEXT OF MY EARLIER COMMENT ON OUR OWN MILITARY SALES TO LATIN AMERICA, IT IS NOTEWORTHY THAT WITH THEIR IMPROVED TECHNOLOGY BASE EUROPEAN COUNTRIES ARE COM- BINING THEIR TOTAL DEFENSE REQUIREMENTS TO INCREASE THE PRODUC- TION BASE AND FORMING CONSORTIA FOR LOCAL INDUSTRY PARTICIPATION IN A STRONG EFFORT TO COMPETE EFFECTIVELY FOR FOREIGN MILITARY SALES AND INFLUENCE IN THE WORLD MARKETS. 

MR. CHAIRMAN AND MEMBERS OF THIS COMMITTEE, I HAVE NOT TRIED TO BE ALL-INCLUSIVE TODAY. WHAT I WANTED TO EXPLAIN IS THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN OUR SECURITY ASSISTANCE PROGRAM AND OUR BROADER STRATEGIC AND DEFENSE POLICIES. 

I HOPE I HAVE MADE CLEAR THAT THE MAP AND FMS PROGRAMS ARE PART-AND-PARCEL OF OUR OVERALL POLICY. WE ARE SUCCEEDING IN OUR EFFORTS TO ADJUST OUR STRATEGIC NUCLEAR POLICIES AND PRO- GRAMS TO THE CONDITIONS WE CAN EXPECT IN THE NEXT DECADE. 

SIMILARLY, WE ARE GIVING SUBSTANTIALLY GREATER EMPHASIS TO THE CONVENTIONAL FORCES OF THE UNITED STATES, PARTICULARLY OUR NATO AND NAVAL FORCES, FOR IN A TIME OF NUCLEAR PARITY, DETER- RENCE IS MADE MORE LIKELY IF THERE IS A BALANCE OF CONVENTIONAL FORCES IN KEY AREAS AS WELL AS A BALANCE OF NUCLEAR FORCES.

Secretary SCHLESINGER. Mr. Chairman, I will make a few observations, if that is your preference. 

Senator INOUYE. Fine, sir. 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. As you have already indicated, Mr. Chairman, the assistance program encompasses more than foreign military sales and the military assistance program. This year the request by the administration is something on the order of $5 billion. 

Those parts of the program which are administered by the Department of Defense are the foreign military sales credit program and the military assistance program to which you have adverted. 

You have mentioned, Mr. Chairman, that there is a substantial increase in the program request by the administration for this year. That is correct. The increase, I think, is somewhat smaller than the numbers you cited for one reason, one prominent reason, and that is that last year in order to deal with the situation in Cambodia, the Department utilized the full $250 million in drawdown authority the Congress authorized in the Foreign Assistance Act to meet emergency requirements.

If that amount were added to the military assistance program for last year, the total would have been $700 million. The growth then between fiscal year 1974 and fiscal year 1975 would amount to $285 million rather than the $535 million figure you cited. 

I would hope that the committee would consider the use of drawdown authority in this connection.

There are two other items that I might mention. First, there is a $69 million pay back from the MASF program to MAP in 1974 in connection with Project Enhance.

And in addition, the Laos program which was funded through MASF in 1974 was shifted to MAP this year. When these adjustments are made, as your opening statement indicated, Mr. Chairman, there is still a sizable increase, but the size of the increase is on the order of 10 percent rather than the percentage implied by the $535 million increase you cited.

PURPOSE OF U.S. MILITARY ASSISTANCE PROGRAMS 

Mr. Chairman, the purpose of the United States in its military programs by and large is to attempt to maintain a worldwide military equilibrium. In that connection we, of course, have our strategic program and our general purpose forces program, with major deployments on the European continent. But when we pass beyond the European continent, and our forces in Korea and Japan, there are parts of the world in which this military equilibrium depends to a large degree on the security assistance programs of the U.S., including both MAP grant aid and foreign military sales credit programs.

During the last year, there was an excellent example of this in the Middle East through the support that was given to the state of Israel at the time of and following the events of last October.

The Secretary of State has worked industriously in pursuit of a permanent settlement in the Middle East. The Secretary of State has testified previously-not before this committee but will testify before

this committee that he regards the security assistance programs for the Middle East as essential to the success of our hopes for a greater measure of peace in the Middle East. 

BULK OF U.S. MILITARY ASSISTANCE TO MID-EAST AND ASIA 

As you know, Mr. Chairman, the vast bulk of our program is devoted to the Middle East and to Asia, something more than 80 percent of the two programs to which you have referred. The largest Foreign Military Sales credit program is $300 million for Israel; and by far the largest grant program, $363 million, is for Cambodia, a country which is attempting to defend itself and to survive against an insurgency. 

Another large element in our program, Mr. Chairman, is the support that we are giving in Korea. This year we are requesting for Korea 

1 $161.5 million in grant assistance and $52 million in Foreign Military 

Sales credit. It is intended through this program to help maintain the political-military equilibrium that has developed in Northeast Asia. 

By far the largest part of our program is allocated to Southeast Asia, $544.3 million in grant assistance and $15 million in Foreign 

Military Sales credit. The reasons for these programs are well known. 

When we withdrew American forces from Indochina, it was understood that we would provide the military tools to enable the people there to defend themselves. The need to do so has not lessened in this last year. 

The flow of military equipment, supplies and personnel from the north to positions endangering Cambodia, Laos and South Vietnam continues. Cambodia is particularly hard pressed. The security requirements of Thailand, Indonesia and the Philippines are continuing ones which these nations need help in meeting. 

There are a number of programs for which there have been reductions in the past year such as the drop in the MAP grant aid program for the Republic of China, from about $30 million in 1973 to $400,000 in training programs only proposed for 1975.

This reflects a growth of credit sales as opposed to grant military aid. FMS credit sales to the Republic of China have doubled, rising from $45 million in fiscal year 1973 to an estimated $80 million in fiscal year 1975. This reflects, Mr. Chairman, progress toward a general objective that we have for most of our assistance programs, which is to move countries from grant aid to credit sales, then ultimately to the extent possible from credit to cash sales.

MILITARY ASSISTANCE TO LATIN AMERICA 

Mr. Chairman, let me close my observations, which are a summary of my statement, by referring to the situation in Latin America for which there is a relatively small program in terms of grant military assistance.

Nine of the 18 countries in the region receiving military assistance will receive grant materiel. The other nine will be provided with training only either, in the United States or at U.S. schools in the Canal Zone. Training, I believe, serves our interest as well as the interest of the countries involved and promotes a spirit of cooperation and partnership which is a basic objective of the security assistance program for Latin America.

1064

The fiscal year 1975 FMS credit program for 16 of the 18 Latin American countries amounts to $200 million, more than five times as much as in 1966, almost a decade ago. In this connection, and in closing, Mr. Chairman, I should like to note the objection that has been raised by some Members of Congress and the public with respect to the sale of U.S. military equipment to Latin American countries whose limited resources, it is contended, could be better spent on economic development-a point of view, incidentally, that I share. 

However, one must keep in mind that the defense budgets of these Latin American countries are, in relation to gross national product, quite modest, and by comparison lower than those of equally advanced countries in other parts of the world. 

The modernization requirements for their armed services as these Latin American nations see them are not excessive and they are obviously determined to modernize and replace U.S. equipment of World 

War II and Korean war vintage.

It is, and has been, fruitless for the United States to attempt to dictate to these governments, governments of sovereign states, the extent to which they should satisfy what they have determined to be their military requirements. By refusing to help them achieve modest modernization programs, we do not succeed in spurring economic development or bringing about an alternative distribution of resources which we might prefer. We simply encourage them to make their military purchases elsewhere.

This is inconsistent with the foreign policy which seeks strong regional association with the nations of the Western Hemisphere. I do not recommend major grant assistance programs to Latin America. 

I do not recommend selling arms there or elsewhere in a haphazard way, simply because there is someone willing to buy them. I do recommend, however, that we go ahead with prudent grant aid and foreign military sales programs to our Latin American neighbors where those programs make sense from our point of view and not leave the supply of arms largely to those outside this hemisphere. 

Such a response to the reasonable request of Latin American governments for cooperation in modernization of their armed forces is the basis for our 1975 program for that region, the major item in which is, as I have indicated, $200 million, in Foreign Military Sales credit.

Mr. Chairman, I think that the rest of the statement deals with issues of a lesser magnitude which you may wish to take up at a later point in the hearings, but I am prepared to go on or close. 

Admiral Moorer may wish to make some comments.

Senator INOUYE. Before proceeding, our questions will be on both statements, so, Admiral, if you will proceed, sir.
