Mr. Chairman and Members of the Committee: 

As I respond to your request to present a military assessment of the Security Assistance Program for FY 1975, I am not unmindful that this is my fourth such assessment. 

Under these circumstances, perhaps you will permit me to preface my remarks with a very brief review of the 

Security Assistance Program over these past few years.

From FY 1972 through FY 1974, the Executive Branch requested that the Congress provide $3.

73 billion in regular Military Assistance and Foreign Military Sales funds. Congress appropriated $2.63 billion. These reductions have not been accomplished without cost. The 

Armed Forces of many of our Allies remain far short of their defense needs as they perceive the threat to their nations. The reluctance of some of these nations to revert to complete peacetime civilian governmental arrangements may stem from reduced US assistance. 

Other nations whose military requirements have not been met find themselves still engaged in an armed effort to maintain internal security when, under other circumstances, the insurgency may have been eliminated, Some nations are turning elsewhere for security assistance. The lack of capital investment funds had precluded even others from achieving greater, if not complete, self-sufficiency. The United 

States' access to bases has, to some extent, been influenced by the Security Assistance Program. 

I am well aware of the agonizing and complex problem the Congress confronts in the apportionment of scarce resources among competing and compelling national needs. 

These remarks are not intended as criticism. They are made simply to provide a backdrop for the current discus-

sion of this year's program 

a program designed to protect the security of the United States, her friends, and Allies.

This program is being proposed during a period when the strategic balance is in dynamic equilibrium and where each unprecedented challenge to our global interests produces an equal and opposite unprecedented opportunity for peace.

I believe that a brief strategic appraisal of the areas of the world where we, by sustained effort, expect to demonstrate continued progress toward our ultimate goal of a peaceful, free, and secure world would be of assistance.

EAST ASIA AND PACIFIC 

This area has, for hundreds of years, been beset by turmoil and aggression.

The United States has substantial interests and deep historical involvement in the region. We have been and must remain a Pacific power. 

Yet, the President and the Congress have signaled clearly a need for a new form of American participation in Asian affairs. The first anniversary of the Agreement on Ending the War and Restoring the Peace in Vietnam has passed. 

Since 1968, one-half million US military personnel have been withdrawn from the Asian mainland. It has been almost nine months since the last combat mission was flown by an American airman; and yet, the war continues unabated in Cambodia, and South Vietnam remains under periodic attack. 

The military situation in South Vietnam defies definition in the traditional terms of war or peace. It is an amorphous melange of the worst elements of both and lacks the graces of either. Over 200,000 NVA personnel remain. The GVN has suffered in excess of 63,000 casualties since the 27

1 

January 1973 ceasefire.

The Khmer insurgency has grown to between 50,000 and 60,000 troops. 

NVA/VC combat forces in Cambodia are advising the insurgents and represent about one-tenth of this effort. In addition, North Vietnam continues to provide the major portion of the logistical support to the tactical units of the insurgents. The 

Government, in spite of many dire predictions, retains effective control of 55 percent of the population and 20 percent of the territory. The remainder is either under insurgent control or vacated. The insurgents have interdicted all of the major land lines of resupply to the capital and are striving to crumble Phnom Penh's defenses and force a capitulation of the Government. If the North Vietnamese and their Khmer Allies are successful in defeating the legal Cambodian Government, the entire fabric of peace in the area would be severely weakened. 

South Korea, where the interests of four major powers converge, also faces a formidable threat. The dialogue between the two Governments, which began in 1972, has broken down, and North Korea has laid claims to the waters surrounding five UN-controlled and South Korean-occupied islands. The potential for conflict remains high. 

The Security Assistance Program for this area amounts almost two-thirds to $854 million for eight countries 

of which is for Cambodia and Korea. In Cambodia, 80 percent of the program is for basic ammunition essential to the survival of the nation. In Korea, we are striving to assure that this staunch and loyal ally, which determinedly has resisted continued aggression both at home and side by side with US forces in Vietnam, is sufficiently strong to deter North Korean aggression and provide stability on the

peninsula. In 1971, the United States undertook, with express Congressional approval, a balanced five-year force modernization program. Funding shortfalls amounting to almost $340 million have drastically slowed the pace of this effort. The goals remain valid. The distinguished 

House Majority Leader recently has added his voice to those of the Administration in support of the program. 

This program also includes $85.2 million for Laos and reflects the Congressionally dictated termination of funding within the DOD budget for this small nation, where it appears that peace may be returning after many bitter years of continuous conflict. 

We seek peace and security in the area. engaged in a vain defense of the status quo. 

We are not 

It is, however, important to US interests that there be an environment which will permit the nonviolent process of change to unfold free of force. There are nations in the area which have demonstrated a propensity to assume added risks in the face of weakness. Even with this program, no warranty of peace can be given; but without it, history's starkest military lesson will again be taught 

when aggression is rewarded anywhere, it is encouraged everywhere. 

NEAR EAST 

Strategically, the Middle East is important because 

of two major factors one geographic and the other geologic. Geographically, the Middle East is the corridor connecting the Eastern Hemisphere's three major continents. 

It is the avenue through which another strategic line of Soviet communication to the Indian Ocean and the Far East may be established. The eastern Mediterranean is also

vital to the defense of NATO's southern flank. Geologically, the primary resource of the Middle East is oil. Middle 

East oil supplied 13 percent of pre-boycott US demand, 75 percent of Western Europe's, and 85 percent of Japan's. 

Within the next decade, there is not likely to be significant diminution in the dependence of the industrialized West and Japan on the Middle East's oil. One-third of the non-Communist world's supply of oil is projected to come from Saudi Arabia and Iran alone.

Superimposed on these strategic considerations is the longstanding political commitment made by both the Congress and every President since Truman to the survival of Israel, most recently manifested in the Emergency Security Assistance Act of 1973. The credibility of this commitment, like all other US international obligations, depends on the proven past record of performance by the United States, including the performance of our Armed Forces. Further complicating the flammability of the situation is the fact that the area is the birthplace of three of the world's great religions.

It is against this background that the varied, compound, and interdependent objectives of the United States must be viewed.

Peace and stability are our principal national objectives, and defusing the Middle East crisis is central to global security. This point, where the interests of major powers converge, has all the necessary ingredients for being the cockpit for great power confrontation; and yet, there are political and military forces at work well outside the scope of the usual "Communist" and "Free World" interface. The area threatens to be the "Balkans" of the

late 20th Century. We seek mutually beneficial and nonexploitative relations with all the nations of the area. 

Second only to peace is the crucial need to insure access for both the US and her allies to the energy resources of the area. Until substitute energy sources are established, we will remain dependent, in part, upon oil from the Middle East. Also present here is the potential for divisiveness, which could damage severely the cohesion of the Atlantic community and US-Japanese relations. 

Serious diplomatic efforts have reduced this potential divisiveness.

These efforts are continuing. 

A further US goal remains the denial of hegemony over this strategic area by the Soviet Union or any other power with interests inimical to the United States ambitions not unknown to Russian history. Encroachment into or domination of the area by such a power would endanger NATO's southern flank principally guarded by Greece and Turkey, reduce US mobility, and endanger our lines of communication. It also would sever the economic and military relationships we have nurtured so carefully in the interest of the region's stability, progress, and independence.

Turkey and Greece play an essential role in NATO's military force. Astride important straits and strategically situated on the Southeastern flank, these nations demonstrate growing self-reliance. Their continued strength is essential to the process of deterrence, which, in the long run, alone will determine the durability of detente. 

I have just returned from a visit to several of the countries of the Middle East. I spoke at length with Arab leaders and with the Shah of Iran, and I can report to you

today that there remains in these nations and their leaders a deep reservoir of respect and admiration for the people of the United States. They view our willingness to share with them our military technology as an important factor in the effort to remove the incentive for war and to deepen the stakes for peace in the area. From 1955 through 1973, the USSR has delivered thousands of tanks to Middle East and North African countries approximately equal to our total inventory. 

a number Thousands 

of pieces of artillery also have been delivered level almost twice the US inventory. To counter this and to further the cause of peace, we seek a program of $174.2 million in grant aid for Jordan and Turkey; $501 million credit sales for Greece, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, and Turkey; and a training program of about $1 million for six other countries in the area. These costs may well be dollar-for-dollar our best investments in peace.

The threat to our NATO and other allies in the Near East may well have receded, but it has not ended. require and deserve our assistance until such time as they have recovered fully their self-confidence and economic They strength.

EUROPE 

For the most part, our Western European allies have demonstrated the vitality of this program and long ago have outgrown the material grant aid program. For this reason, it has been curtailed drastically. Grant aid to Portugal of less than $1 million is all the material assistance that is requested.

This program will assist Portugal's 34-192 O 74-68

1072

NATO-committed forces primarily in meeting the highly sophisticated air and submarine threat. I might add parenthetically that without Portugal's cooperation, manifested by her consent to the use of the Lajes Airbase in the Azores, the resupply operation which made Israel's survival possible could not have been conducted without great hazard to the lives of the crews and almost prohibitive cost.

AFRICA 

Of all the major areas of the world, Africa appears to offer the greatest hope of consensus in terms of policy goals. These are political stability; freedom from great power intervention; peaceful economic and social development; and bilateral relations founded on self-reliance, independence, and forms of support sustainable over the long term. Many Americans feel deeply their ancestral relationship to this vast and rich continent. The richness of African resources is demonstrated by accelerating direct US private investment now in excess of $4 billion. The over 40 African nations constitute almost one-third of the membership of the UN and other international forums. 

These nations are playing a major role in such diverse issues as the law of the sea, peacekeeping, the laws of war, and environmental protection far beyond the scope of traditional African interests. They are intensely aware that in these arenas, political influence is not tied necessarily to military strength or economic might. 

They also know that without this strength and might, the political vitality and functional stability necessary to independence and survival, soon may be lost to outside

NP interference or internal subversion. 

If conflict is to be avoided, they must be able to protect their independence 

a fragile commodity in many countries without regard to whether it is recent or ancient. 

The nature of the economic and political situation of the continent has not escaped the attention of the USSR and the PRC. Military assistance to Africa from these countries has been widespread, if not massive. 

The equipment ranges from small arms to sophisticated surface-to-air missiles and fighter aircraft. It is estimated that more than 30,000 Communist technicians an appreciable portion of which were military in Africa during 1973. Over 2,000 African military personnel were trained in the USSR, East Europe, or the PRC during 1973. 

served Again, the US proposes a modest program designed to further the national goals noted above. A small training program involving a total of 344 students from six countries is requested, together with limited FMS credit in the amount of $24.5 million 

$14 million of which is for Morocco's small, but efficient, army 

and a grant aid program for Ethiopia and Tunisia amounting to $13.3 million. 

The Ethiopian program is designed to assist that nation to defend its historic status as a free and independent nation from externally supported attack. We seek to preclude the loss of the Horn of Africa to a nation or group of nations with interests hostile to those of the United States. Tunisia also occupies strategically important territory astride one of the Mediterranean's most important chokepoints. The Tunisian security assistance program, composed primarily of spare parts for existing US equipment and rifles, is designed to provide

an adequate self-defense from both external and internal attack.

The operation of hostile ships and aircraft from Tunisian bases could disrupt severely NATO's defense of Europe.

This program will assist Tunisia in insuring her own independence.

Any discussion of security assistance in Africa, in general, and in Ethiopia, Morocco, and Tunisia, in particular, without some reference to the considerable influence these three nations exercise in the political councils of the continent would be far from complete. Their moderation and friendship for the United States transcend the military relationship carefully nurtured by all of us and include support for mutually beneficial programs in the UN and elsewhere.

LATIN AMERICA 

The vital interface between the security interests of the United States and the countries to our south are much too well known to require explanation here. Our relations with the Latin American nations and their military establishments, however, have been in a state of transition and, at times, crises since 1968. 

Kissinger, in a recent address to the OAS, termed this the law 

Secretary a transition from the "good neighbor" to the "good partner."

In October 1968, prohibitions on the sale of sophisticated weapons to "underdeveloped countries" were established by a move that many Latin American leaders, military and civilian alike, perceived as not only preemptory, but also arrogant. At the same time, our military presence in

Latin America long a symbol of our concern and commitment was caught up in the twin scoops of Administration concerns 

---

for the balance of payments and Congressionally directed reductions in such military presence abroad. Other events roiled the troubled waters: military leaders took on the surprising role of radical reformers; tuna boat seizures 

3d the subsequent suspension of military sales led to the expulsion of the US military presence in Peru and Ecuador;

Salvadore Allende was elected President of Chile and deposed; Peru took delivery of Soviet tanks 

the first

Latin American nation other than Cuba to acquire significant military equipment from the Soviet Union; and Cuban potential for inciting insurgency remains, even if somewhat reduced. 

The inflow of European arms, including French Mirage aircraft and French and Soviet armor, has impacted upon traditional relationship with Latin American leaders. Our This has exacerbated further our already declining relationship, which flowed, in part, from the decrease in the Security Assistance Program and the restrictions on sophisticated weapons systems. We must act now if we are to avoid, or at least mitigate, serious degradation of our lines of communication with Latin American leaders in furtherance of our strategic interests and overall security policy objectives.

The Military Assistance Program of $18.2 million and 

FMS credit of $200 million will not solve, of course, these longstanding problems, but it should be sufficient if coupled with our best diplomatic efforts to keep the door open at least while solutions are studied and prepared. From a military standpoint, we must give up totally any idea that Latin America is a "bloc" of nations beholden

to the United States. 

They are not, and I doubt that they ever were. They are individual nations who perceive their defense needs from the perspective of their individual nations, not as seen from any part of the United States 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue, the Capitol, or the Pentagon. 

CONCLUSION 

In conclusion, I would state simply that in my view, this program is essential to US security needs. I believe the hard choices have been made to separate the incidental from the fundamental. It is much more than a tangible indication of continuing US concern. It is, in effect, a shield behind which the free nations of the world can build a stable military equilibrium. This will permit the development in the still undetermined future of a fabric of common concern, where the relations between states can be conceived cooperatively and not in conflict or competition. The relatively modest Security Assistance 

Program is designed so that our allies and friends can develop the capability of defending their own vital interests without directly involving the Armed Forces of the United States. It also should insure that we are not isolated in a hostile world 

an isolation which is as susceptible of creation by a neglect of responsibility and power as from the abuse of power and authority.

WHY ARMS TO THE MIDDLE EAST COUNTRIES? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. That is a question, or rather a series of questions, Mr. Chairman, that goes to the heart of the issue. Let me attempt to deal with them, and if I forget any particular part of that complex of questions, please remind me.

As you know, the responsibilities for these programs are divided between the Department of State and the Department of Defense.

RATIONALE FOR EXTENDED ASSISTANCE PROGRAM FOR ISRAEL 

Senator INOUYE. I believe I am correct to assume that the Department of Defense is called upon by the administration to provide military assistance in that area and to provide recommendations. Now if your assessment is that there is no significant imbalance in the Middle East between Israel and her neighbors, how do you rationalize or justify an extended military assistance program? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. Once again, for policy on these matters, I would urge that the Department of State be consulted; but let me

relate my observations with regard to the military balance that by and large exists in the Middle East at the present time between Israel and her neighbors.

I would say this balance is based upon certain remaining qualitative advantages that the Israelis have in terms of training and manpower as offset by certain equipment advantages possessed by her neighbors, notably Egypt and Syria.

Now the Israelis, I believe, are concerned as a result of the war that occurred last fall that their prior estimates of the degree to which they could rely upon superior training and superior cohesion of their forces, must be reconsidered, and that the differences in terms of equipment should therefore be reduced. 

This is notably the case, I believe, in the ground forces area in which the use by the Egyptians and the Syrians of large numbers of antitank missiles reduced the prior advantages that the Israclis had possessed, or felt they possessed, in the employment of armor. So consequently, they do not feel that in the area of ground forces they can rely upon the advantages in training as compensating for reduced levels of equipment.

In the past they have been outnumbered in terms of tanks, for example, on the order of 212 to 1, and they would prefer to avoid such a contingency in the future.

I think that when you get down into these details, one sees why there would be particular equipment purchases. I think that equipment purchases are part of a long-term program that is designed to provide a continued security for the State of Israel. 

Now I adverted earlier to the question of the relationship between diplomatic and political activities and equipment activities. As this committee is aware, the Israelis have agreed to disengagement along the Suez Canal and to a withdrawal from the Suez, and there are prospects of further disengagement in the Sinai. They have more recently agreed to a disengagement in the Golan Heights area, and this would reduce the territorial protection that has been relied on by the State of Israel. To the extent that this territorial protection is reduced, there has been more concern, I believe, in the State of Israel about any equipment shortfalls; and so the Israelis may regard the provision of additional equipment as compensatory for the loss of territorial protection associated with the disengagement. 

Now, therefore, as this disengagement takes place, looking toward the protection of the State of Israel, the security of the State of Israel, one must adjust, I think, the levels of equipment. The purpose, I believe, of entering into this long-term arrangement, which is not prescribed in terms of design until such times as particular equipments are under order, is to provide the Israelis with the confidence that somewhere in the world there will be a supplier of military equipment.

I believe that the events of last fall, when a number of traditional suppliers of military equipment to the State of Israel, other than the United States, ceased to supply that equipment under pressure of a political nature, caused a degree of concern in Israel. I think an understandable concern, that in the future if they did not have a high degree of confidence in the supply of arms, they would not be assured of those arms when a moment of confrontation came. I think it is these larger political objectives that form the basis of our policy. 

Mr. Chairman, I hope that that illuminates the issue for you.

REQUEST FOR $100 MILLION CONTINGENCY FUND

Secretary SCHLESINGER. The $100 million has been discussed with me in a general and vague way. It is a contingency fund. Syria has been mentioned as a possible outlet for those resources, but I am not familiar with the details because it does not fall under those portions of the total foreign assistance request which are the responsibilities of the Department of Defense.

These are all interrelated. I, however, cannot state what the $100 million would be used for other than in these general terms that Syria has been represented as a very likely possibility for the utilization of these funds.

It is stated that this would be a special requirements fund for use by the President for assistance authorized by this act in accordance with the provisions applicable to furnishing of such assistance. That, I think, bears the earmark of flexibility; and therefore, it would be inconsistent with the flexibility intended for that $100 million for me or for anybody to say in advance that that $100 million is intended to serve certain prescribed purposes.

NUCLEAR POWERPLANTS FOR EGYPT AND ISRAEL 

Senator INOUYE. I have a question which does not directly involve your Department. There is some evidence that as part of the commitment in the Middle East, the President promised the Prime Minister to make available to Egypt and Israel nuclear reactor power generat plants.

I believe you have indicated that these power generating plants can be changed into a conversion plant. 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. Any nuclear reactor, Mr. Chairman, is a producer of plutonium, a producer of plutonium of various degrees of

qualities of material. The longer the reactor runs the greater is the quantity of that material. In any reactor plutonium is produced which can be utilized for nuclear explosives.

CHEMICAL SEPARATION FACILITIES 

When the core is extracted from the reactor, it is put into a chemical separation plant, which, by the way, does not exist in Egypt. There may be, I believe, a small chemical separation plant in Israel at the present time. We will check on that for the record, but it is the chemical separation plant that provides one with the plutonium that can be employed in nuclear explosives. 

 CHEMICAL SEPARATION FACILITIES 

The technology for chemical separation of plutonium from reactor fuel material is generally available to the public and required component equipment can be purchased, or constructed if necessary. 

We do not know if Israel has a chemical separation plant at the present time. 

However, such a plant, especially a small scale one, is not beyond the technical capabilities of the country.

SAFEGUARDS FOR NUCLEAR POWERPLANTS 

So a reactor, in itself, depending on where the core is processed and how the core is safeguarded, does not provide the material directly usable in nuclear explosives. If there is a system of safeguards for a nuclear powerplant and if that system of safeguards is effective, I believe that the likelihood of diversion of material from the purposes of the production of power to the provision of nuclear explosives is low.

Senator INOUYE. But as you have indicated, we cannot guarantee that these plants will not be employed for nonpeaceful purposes. 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. We can guarantee only that so long as the safeguards are effective they would not be so utilized; but if the safeguards are deliberately flouted, then there is a risk of diversion of this material into the purposes to which you refer. 

Senator INOUYE. How safe are the safeguard provisions employed in the United States?

Secretary SCHLESINGER. The safeguard provisions of the sort that we are referring to have not been employed extensively in the United States. In the United States, nuclear powerplants operate under regulations provided by the Atomic Energy Commission. The safeguards which are applied primarily to foreign plants, those plants that are supplied by the United States, are of a different nature. 

They require repeated inspections; they require the installation of containment and surveillance devices to avoid the diversion of material. 

These safeguards which are applied universally outside of the United States in the case of an American-supplied plant, are intended to detect any diversion of material from the purposes for which the plant was sold, namely power production. As you know, this whole strategy goes back over a period of 20 years to the so-called atoms for peace program. It has been the hope of that program over a period of almost 

20 years that the availability of nuclear power for peaceful purposes would lead away from the utilization of nuclear power for purposes of war.

LOSS OR DIVERSION OF NUCLEAR MATERIALS 

Senator INOUYE. I believe a recent report of the Atomic Energy

Commission indicated that the United States lost 100 pounds of uranium and 60 pounds of plutonium? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. I am not familiar with that report. I have been away from the Commission for some time, but there was a loss of U-235, I believe, some years ago; and I am sure that there have been losses of plutonium, Mr. Chairman, but I am not familiar with the details.

Senator INOUYE. If we can lose plutonium and uranium in the 

United States, can we anticipate that we might lose a little in Egypt and Israel? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. I would not assume so, but I cannot guarantee that that would not occur. I think that the loss of the uranium which is referred to occurred many years ago a decade ago, if I recall, maybe 15 years ago, something in that time frame and that it was a period of time which was characterized, I think, by a less meticulous attitude toward these problems than exists at the present time. In addition, I would point out that vast amounts of nuclear materials were being shipped in the United States at that time as compared to relatively small amounts of nuclear materials which would be shipped in the programs to which you refer. 

I would also point out, Mr. Chairman, that most of the nuclear materials that would be shipped would be fuel, which could not be utilized for weapons programs. 

The matter of concern would be the relatively small amount of plutonium which would be produced in the nuclear reactors in question, but I cannot suggest to this committee that nuclear powerplants are without risk of diversion. There is a system of safeguards that has been established with the intention of reducing risks of diversion to a low level, but there is no guarantee that diversion cannot take place.

PURPOSE OF DIEGO GARCIA 

Senator INOUYE. Do we intend to do this? Secretary SCHLESINGER. I think the arrival of vessels in the Indian 

Ocean is not dependent upon the reopening of the canal. The point that has been made is that the reopening of the canal would shorten Soviet lines of communication from the Black Sea area by some 8,000 to 10,000 miles approximately. 

The Soviets maintain substantial naval forces at the present time coming out of Vladivostok. The purpose of Diego Garcia is not to provide a permanent U.S. naval presence in the Indian Ocean. The purpose of Diego Garcia would be to provide us with the base facilities which are equivalent to base facilities already possessed by the Soviet Union so that if they employ their base facilities for the maintenance of fleets in the Indian Ocean, we also would have the capacity to do so.

In the period after the start of the war in the Middle East last October, the United States dispatched several task forces into the Indian Ocean. Those task forces were supported out of Subic Bay, which was some 4,000 miles away. This is a highly ineffectual way of supporting those task forces.

 PROCEDURE FOR AEC-DOD COORDINATION OF NUCLEAR POWER AGREEMENTS OF COOPERATION WITH EGYPT AND ISRAEL 

Under the Atomic Energy Act of 1954, no cooperation with any nation may be undertaken with regard to furnishing nuclear reactors or nuclear fuel materials until the President has approved a proposed agreement of cooperation and has made a determination in writing that the performance of the proposed agreement will promote and will not constitute an unreasonable risk to the common defense and security.

The proposed agreement must then be submitted to the Joint Committee on Atomic Energy for a period of thirty days while Congress is in session before the agreement can be implemented. 

In the case of such agreements with Egypt and Israel, the Department of Defense will be consulted by the Atomic Energy Commission concerning the provisions of the proposed agreements of cooperation. Department of Defense comments in this regard will be furnished the President for his consideration.

Secretary SCHLESINGER. In the case of a number of nations, we have pursued that, and the record to date is not an astonishing success. I will look into that, Mr. Chairman, and provide some citation for the record of the nations involved and the particular efforts of the U.S. 

Government in this regard. 

 NEGOTIATIONS AMONG WORLD ARMS SUPPLIERS 

The United States has consistently advocated controls or restraints on arms through statements by the President and by statement and positions taken by U.S. delegates to the Conference of the Committee on Disarmament (CCD), which includes most of the world's major arms suppliers and which convenes in Geneva twice a year. There was a statement submitted by the Director of Arms 

Control and Disarmament Agency (ACDA) in April 1966 (attached), a U.S. working paper on regional arms control submitted to the CCD in 1970 (attached) and, earlier this year, a statement by the U.S. delegate to the CCD, Ambassador Martin, which declared that it was time for the conference to begin serious study on this question. 

In 1970, the President in his Foreign Policy Report to the Congress said that the great powers should show restraint in their sale of arms to regions in conflict and declared that the U.S. stands ready to discuss practical arrangements to this end. The President made similar statements in his 1972 and 1973 Foreign 

Policy Reports. In sum, the United States has regularly made its position clear that it supports measures to control the flow of arms, particularly into areas of present or potential conflict.

Some arms producing states such as the FRG, Sweden, Japan, and Switzerland have enacted domestic legislation prohibiting the sale or transfer of arms to conflict regions and most arms producing states have, on occasion, made public statements that they would not supply arms to crisis areas. The French, for example, embargoed weapons to the four major participants in the 1967 Arab-Israel War. Other foreign governments, principally Western States, have indicated their interest in negotiating controls on weapons supplies. One example of this is the United Kingdom whose representative to the spring 1974 CCD session spoke in favor of regional control on conventional arms. 

The Administration is currently considering what further measures it might take in this field and will maintain its objective of developing constraints on conventional arms whenever possible.

ANNEX A CCD STATEMENT APRIL 19, 1966; US WORKING PAPER ON REGIONAL ARMS AGREE- MENTS, AUGUST 12, 1970 STATEMENT BY ACDA DIRECTOR FOSTER TO THE EIGHTEEN NATION DISARMAMENT COM- MITTEE: REGIONAL ARMS LIMITATIONS, APRIL 19, 1966¹ 

It happens that our meeting today coincides with the reconvening in Mexico City of the Preparatory Commission which is drafting a treaty to maintain Latin America as a nuclear-free zone. The initiative of the Latin-American countries in seeking a Latin-American nuclear-free zone is an outstanding example of regional activity to limit and control armaments. My Government fully supports that effort. It illustrates the constructive possibilities open to groups of countries 

1 ENDC/PV.257, pp. 15-19. 

2 See post, pp. 255-275.

when they co-operate in making a joint assessment of their national and regional security needs.3

In our discussions of late we have concentrated mainly on halting and turning back the nuclear arms race. This is, of course, as it should be. The United 

Nations has asked us to give priority to negotiation of a non-proliferation treaty, and we are doing so. In President Johnson's message to this Committee on 27 

January, the first six of his seven proposals deal with nuclear measures. At our last meeting I elaborated new means of verification for a cut-off in production of fissionable material and the destruction of nuclear weapons.' 

However, our proper emphasis on nuclear measures should not deter us from coming to grips with the problems of controlling conventional armaments. The seventh point of the programme proposed by President Johnson suggests a line of action for making progress in this area. The President said: 66 ... as we focus on nuclear arms, let us not forget that resources are being devoted to non-nuclear arms races all around the world. These resources might better be spent on feeding the hungry, healing the sick and teaching the uneducated. The cost of acquiring and maintaining one squadron of supersonic aircraft diverts resources that would build and maintain a university. We suggest therefore that countries, on a regional basis, explore ways to limit competition among themselves for costly weapons often sought for reasons of illusory prestige. The initiative for arrangements of this kind should, of course, come from the regions concerned. The interested countries should undertake not to acquire from any source, including production of their own as well as importation from others, military equipment which they proscribe. If such arrangements can be worked out and assurance can be given that they will be observed, the 

United States stands ready to respect them." "

We often use the phrase "conventional armaments" as a means of distinguishing them from nuclear armaments. However, there is nothing conventional about the death and destruction which can be inflicted by modern combat aircraft. They are capable of delivering enormous loads of rockets and bombs. Nor is there anything conventional about the havoc that can be created by a modern tank designed for offense warfare, or by modern naval vessels. 

These and other so-called conventional weapons have resulted in the loss of millions of lives. Over 8 million were killed in the First World War, over 22 million in the Second World War, and hundreds of thousands since the end of the Second World War. No one can question the vital importance of making progress in controlling conventional arms. 

If progress can be made, the benefits of increased security will accrue to both the smaller countries and the larger countries. Both have suffered greatly as a result of the conflicts of this century. The universal responsibility for arms control was summed up on 11 May 1965 at New York by the Nigerian representative to the Disarmament Commission. His wise words should be repeated: "At this point, we wish to underline the fact that the elimination of the armaments race is not a duty of the major Powers alone. The major Powers possess the most dangerous armaments, both in type and in quantity, and it is they who should give the lead in effecting reductions. But the medium and small Powers have a similar duty. There are countries in these categories which are making things awkward for themselves, awkward for their neighbours and awkward for the world by an arms build-up out of proportion to their legitimate security requirements."

The aim of this Committee is, of course, to consider measures which will increase the security of States and enhance international stability. Accordingly we shall wish to keep in mind any special military situations in various parts of the world. Some smaller countries are confronted by serious threats. Indeed, some countries have been subjected to external aggression. These countries, unfortunately, have been forced to make sacrifices in order to strengthen their defence establishments. On the other hand, some countries which have recently achieved independence are only now determining the extent of the military establishments which will be needed for their security. We do not suggest-indeed it would not be proper to suggest-that countries should set low levels for their defence establishments without regard to security. Legitimate security needs 

3 Ante, pp. 5-8. 

4 Supra. 

Ante, pp. 7-8. 

6 Disarmament Commission Official Records: 78th Meeting, p. 22.

must be met. Responsible officials will and should strive to acquire the armaments needed, but only the armaments needed, to meet those legitimate security requirements.

Regional and international peace is endangered, however, when nations seek armaments or weapons systems beyond their defence needs. Regrettably, an arms race can be set off by acquisition of weapons of excessive range of power. Whether such arms are acquired because of an inaccurate national security assessment or because of prestige considerations, other nations in the region will, as a result, feel pressure to acquire the same or similar weapons. Obviously an arms race of this type would create a tragic and unnecessary drain on resources badly needed for development. For many countries the exciting and challenging tasks of social, industrial and agricultural growth are just beginning. These should not be impeded by the burdens of spending for unnecessary armaments. 

For its part, the United States has pursued as a fundamental objective the promotion of economic and social development throughout the world. It has contributed billions of dollars to the economic and social efforts of other States. I feel confident that our willingness and ability to assist other countries seeking our help will continue. Regarding future assistance, I should like to repeat the statement which I made on 17 May 1965 before the United Nations Disarmament Commission. I said: "* * * in providing future assistance, the United States will continue to regard favourably efforts by the countries concerned to avoid excessive armament undertakings which would interfere with social and economic development" " In the search for regional co-operation to limit armaments certain principles might serve as a guide. First, the arrangement should contain an undertaking by the affected countries not to acquire from any source, whether indigenous production or importation, those types of military equipment which they agree to regulate. These would include the types of equipment that the participants decided were not required to meet their security needs, after taking into account the effect of the arrangements on other nations in the region. Restrictions would have to be placed on production as well as importation. It would serve little purpose if a country agreed to forego importation of certain military equipment while at the same time it undertook to manufacture such equipment. Nor would a regional arms race be averted if a country within the region agreed to forego production of certain costly military equipment but then imported it from supplier nations. 

Second, the initiative for an arrangement should come from within the region concerned. We have already seen that constructive initiatives in regional arms control are possible. This Committee cannot itself work out measures for particular regions. It can, however, provide encouragement and support. Such support might be furnished by discussing principles such as the ones I am suggesting today.

A third guiding principle is that the arrangements should include all States in the region whose participation is deemed important by the other participants. 

An arrangement could apply, as agreed by the participants, to either an entire region, a sub-region, or any two or more countries in the region. 

Fourth, potential suppliers should undertake to respect the regional arrangement by not supplying the proscribed types of equipment to the affected countries. Suppliers would, of course, be free to continue to assist in the economic development of the affected countries. They could supply equipment of types not proscribed and render other types of support and assistance deemed necessary to meet the defence and internal security arrangements of the affected countries. 

Fifth, the arrangement should contribute to the security of the States concerned and to the maintenance of a stable military balance. This principle should assist in guarding against any possible attempts to use regional arrangements to undermine existing security arrangements, contrary to the wishes of the States concerned. In addition, the arrangement should contain enough flexibility to permit adjustment to major changes in the political-military environment. 

Sixth, adequate provision should be made for satisfying all interested parties that the arrangement is being respected. 

Although I have suggested several principles which might guide the development of regional arrangements for limiting conventional armaments, one in particular should be emphasized. This is the principle that initiatives for regional 

Documents on Disarmament, 1965, p. 178.

arrangements should come from within the region concerned. Acceptance of the principle will best ensure that special regional security problems of the sort I have already mentioned, will be taken fully into account. This principle also contributes to the realization of the aims and aspirations of the countries concerned.

Regional initiatives present an opportunity for those countries to play a leading role in the attainment of basic arms control objectives. And the realization of such initiatives could enhance the security of the region as well as of the rest of the world. It could reduce regional tensions, promote the constructive utilization of economic resources, and contribute to the ultimate achievement of general disarmament.

The United States stands ready to co-operate to the fullest in implementing regional arms control arrangements. It recognizes the difficulties involved, but the potential benefits of regional arms limitations call for renewed efforts to achieve this goal. 

President Johnson has summarized the benefits as follows: "It can be a world where nations raise armies, where famine and disease and ignorance are the common lot of men, where the poor nations look on to the rich with envy, bitterness and frustration; where the air is filled with tension and hatred.

Or it can be a world where each nation lives in independence, seeking new ways to provide a better life for its citizens; a world where the energies of its restless peoples are directed toward the works of peace; a world where people are free to build a civilization to liberate the spirit of man.8 " 

UNITED STATES WORKING PAPER SUBMITTED TO THE CONFERENCE OF THE COMMITTEE ON DISARMAMENT: REGIONAL ARMS AGREEMENT, AUGUST 12, 1970 

On 19th April, 1966, the US representative to the ENDS, Ambassador William

C. Foster, described in the ENDC certain principles for regional conventional arms limitation agreements. The U.S. continues to believe that these principles could provide the basis for regional conventional arms agreements that would prove universally beneficial by reducing the likelihood and the potential levels of regional conflict. Moreover, we believe that agreements based on these principles would promote rather than undermine the vital interests of all the nations with direct interest in the security of the region concerned. The principles, as set forth in 1966, were as follows: "First, the arrangement should contain an undertaking by the affected countries not to acquire from any source, whether indigenous production or importation, those types of military equipment which they agree to regulate. These would include the types of equipment that the participants decided were not required to meet their security needs, after taking into account the effect of the arrangements on other nations in the region. Restrictions would have to be placed on production as well as importation. It would serve little purpose if a country agreed to forego importation of certain military equipment while at the same time it undertook to manufacture such equipment. Nor would a regional arms race be averted if a country within the region agreed to forego production of certain costly military equipment but then imported it from supplier nations. "Second, the initiative for an arrangement should come from within the region concerned. We have already seen that constructive initiatives in regional arms control are possible. This Committee cannot itself work out measures for particular regions. It can, however, provide encouragement and support. Such support might be furnished by discussing principles such as the ones I am suggesting today. "A third guiding principle is that the arrangements should include all States in the region whose participation is deemed important by the other participants. 

An arrangement could apply, as agreed by the participants, to either an entire region, a sub-region, or any two or more countries in the region. "Fourth, potential suppliers should undertake to respect the regional arrangement by not supplying the proscribed types of equipment to the affected countries. 

Suppliers would, of course, be free to continue to assist in the economic development of the affected countries. They could supply equipment of types not proscribed and render other types of support and assistance deemed necessary to meet the defense and internal security arrangements of the affected countries. "Fifth, the arrangement should contribute to the security of the States concerned and to the maintenance of a stable military balance. This principle should 

8 CCD/307, Aug. 12, 1970. 

Documents on Disarmament, 1966, pp. 226-230.

assist in guarding against any possible attempts to use regional arrangements to undermine existing security arrangements, contrary to the wishes of the States concerned. In addition, the arrangement should contain enough flexibility to permit adjustment to major charges in the political-military environment. "Sixth, adequate provision should be made for satisfying all interested parties that the arrangement is being respected."

We again commend these principles to the Committee. We note, however, that they relate principally to the general nature of the undertaking rather than to its arms control content. We note also that they do not attempt to suggest means of approaching the goal of regional armament limitation in situations, perhaps more the rule than the exception, in which achievement of a formal multilateral arrangement in one step, and as a first step, is extremely difficult. We therefore propose three more guidelines which touch on these aspects: 

1. One or more countries in a region might unilaterally undertake not to acquire certain types of expensive, technologically advanced combat equipment. Countries need from time to time to replace obsolete and worn out equipment and to modernize their forces. It should be possible, however, to distinguish the kinds of equipment suitable for replacing outmoded items in existing inventories from the types of highly sophisticated equipment whose acquisition would alter the balance of military capabilities within a region. The types of equipment that countries might undertake not to acquire would vary depending on the region in question, and it should be recognized that requirements for weapons systems for a region and within a region will change over time. The cumulative effect of unilateral decisions by a number of countries not to acquire certain categories of arms might well lead to the de facto exclusion from the region of major items of military equipment. The resulting stabilization of the arms situation in the region could then serve as the basis for formal agreement constructed along the lines of the principles described by Ambassador Foster. 

2. Responding to the initiatives of countries in a region that had taken the unilateral steps described above, states outside the region capable of supplying the equipment in question might similarly undertake, after consultation with the countries having taken the initiative, not to turn over the specified types of equipment to the countries involved. If other major suppliers were to undertake similar unilateral commitments, the effect would be to create a dual guarantee against the acquisition of the specified types of equipment by countries in the region. This double guarantee could be incorporated in an appropriate agreement. 

3. Countries might unilaterally undertake to make available to others in the region information regarding national policies as to production, purchase or supply of arms. While they might not wish to divulge order of battle or tables of organization and equipment, they might find no prejudice to their security interests in making known to others major policy decisions affecting acquisitions of armaments. Where appropriate, this information could perhaps be disseminated through existing regional organizations. If the example set by one or more nations in a region were to stimulate others to adopt similar practices, the result might be greater mutual understanding. The countries within a region that were exchanging information on their arms procurement policies might agree, in such an atmosphere, to discuss among themselves policies regarding specified types of equipment that would be most likely to cause new tensions and imbalances in the area. In the end, some degree of uniformity of policy might thus be achieved within the region. 

ARMS SALES 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. I think that your question is well taken. Let me make some slight modification of what I said earlier. I did not mean to suggest that we should not attempt to discourage arms sales. I think that it is appropriate for the United States to point out to many countries that a higher level of their resources are going into military expenditures than really would be desirable. I think we can attempt to discourage or attempt to bring about a more effective allocation of resources; but if that sovereign state has made that determination, then we cannot through persuasion alter that judgment. I think that we must accept it at that point.

IMPACT OF MILITARY AND ECONOMIC ASSISTANCE TO LATIN AMERICA 

Senator INOUYE. In the last 4 years I note, for example, that we have either sold or provided Latin American countries with over $200 million worth of jet fighter planes. Do you think these countries can support these sophisticated flying machines? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. The answer to that question is yes. They have the logistical capabilities to support them; and, of course, as I mentioned earlier, the proportion of resources devoted to military expenditures in Latin America, which are not necessarily related to discernible threats, tend to be far lower than they are in countries of comparable development.

Senator INOUYE. During that same period, Mr. Secretary, we provided these countries that purchased these planes with about $3 billion worth of economic aid. 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. That, I think, is a very significant aspect, Mr. Chairman. 

Senator INOUYE. I would think so, sir. 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. If one provides economic aid, should that economic aid be used indirectly for military equipment? If one provides military assistance so that a nation may save, in that manner, what it otherwise would have invested in military equipment, is that military assistance in effect functioning as economic aid? We must recognize that these resources are to a large extent fungible; and consequently, the particular objective that one intends may not be the objective that is ultimately served. 

Senator INOUYE. I am glad to hear that statement. 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. I regret that I have to make that statement,

Mr. Chairman, but I think we must recognize it. 

POLICY OF PROVIDING MILITARY EQUIPMENT TO "BOTH SIDES" 

Senator INOUYE. I, and many of my colleagues, have nightmares every so often of viewing some war in some distant part of this world where the opposing nations are using only military equipment furnished by the United States. 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. I think that that has occurred in the past, Mr. Chairman. 

Senator INOUYE. That is right. And I wonder if you think that is a good idea. 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. I think the policies of the United States have consistently been to urge restraint on both sides, and I hope that the policies of the United States will continue to be to seek a peaceful settlement, a peaceful resolution, wherever there is a possibility of a clash.

In many cases the facts that we have provided equipment for both sides gives the United States additional leverage. The fact that an area is provided military equipment by competing suppliers does not necessarily mean the way to peace in that area. I think that there are regrettable aspects of the sort that you mentioned, Mr. Chairman, but that there are favorable aspects as well in the United States providing supplies for both sides, because in the past, that has been useful in attempting to obtain restraint.

In the Indo-Pakistan war, for example, Mr. Chairman, a number of years ago, the U.S. role was to attempt to bring the parties to peace.

I do not know whether the fact that we had previously supplied military equipment to both sides was particularly efficacious. 

COUNTRIES REFUSED MILITARY ARMS Senator HATFIELD. Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the Secretary would provide the committee with a list of countries who have requested military aid which we have refused due to the type of weapons that were requested. 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. Yes. We would be delighted to do so. But there are many cases, Senator Hatfield, that I would strongly urge that the United States not provide certain classes of sophisticated military equipment because it is unsettling in the area. 

 SUBJECT: DENIAL OF GRANTING ARMS TO COUNTRIES 

Materiel grant assistance has been denied many countries, primarily because of dollar restrictions or legislative restrictions. Basic planning for grant materiel programs is, in most cases, a cooperative effort between our military representatives, acting under guidance from the Departments of State and Defense and in concert with their Ambassador in country, and the recipient nation. It is during this time that desires of the recipients are denied or channeled to another direc tion for various reasons: amount of funds available; efficacy of systems; our estimate of the threat; sophistication; and demonstrated needs. Other examples of denials are past arms embargoes because of conflicts: the Nigerian civil war during 1967 to 1970; the Honduras-El Salvador 1969 "Soccer War"; the India- 

Pakistan conflict of 1965-1967, where from 1967 to 1971 only spare parts and nonlethal equipment were provided; and the arms embargo during the 1967 

Arab-Israeli conflict. Still other examples are the denial of granting certain jets, missiles and tanks to Latin America and some military weapons to Africa in an effort to discourage arms escalation between countries. 

COMMITMENT TO PROVIDE MILITARY TOOLS TO INDOCHINA 

Senator INOUYE. Mr. Secretary, in your statement, the following is noted: "When we withdrew American forces from Indochina, it was understood that we would provide the military tools to enable the people there to defend themselves." 

Is this an open-end commitment, sir?

Secretary SCHLESINGER. I would not wish to describe it as an openended commitment, Mr. Chairman. On the other hand, I cannot state that there is any clear termination date. So, one could-uncharitably, if one wishes-describe it as an open-ended commitment. 

Senator INOUYE. This may be an exercise in semantics, but is this a commitment to the people there, or to the government in existence? 

To be more specific, what if there were a change in government in 

Vietnam quite contrary to the one you have today? Would this commitment still stand, sir?

Secretary SCHLESINGER. I think it would be available to a followon government. I think that such a government, in this hypothetical 

3 situation, might wish to review its policies. But if that government continued to strive to maintain South Vietnam's independence against either direct aggression or indirect quasi-aggression, I think that it would be my judgment that the supplies would continue to be avail. able to that successor government that you hypothesized. 

Senator INOUYE. Taking a realistic view of what is happening in that part of the world, and if this assertion is correct, would it be cor-

rect to assure that the United States will be providing arms and military tools to Indochina for many, many decades?

Secretary SCHLESINGER. I think, that as a matter of reality, that would not continue over many decades, but I cannot point to any particular termination date, Mr. Chairman.

[The Washington Post, Thursday, May 9, 1974] 

"HIDDEN" ARMS AID IN BUDGET DISPUTED 

(By Michael Getler)

The Pentagon acknowledged yesterday that its last three budget requests included a total of more than $1 billion to build a reserve stockpile of weapons for possible use by allies in Asia-rather than by American forces. 

The Defense Department denied, however, that it had sought to hide the money in its budget.

But, after lengthy questioning by newsmen at the daily Pentagon briefing and a subsequent Pentagon-ordered search of congressional testimony, Defense Department officials as of late yesterday were unable to produce any record showing that this request for funds had been clearly labeled or explained to 

Congress or the public.

The questioning arose after Sen. J. W. Fulbright (D-Ark.) charged that the administration was "hiding" $490 million in the new fiscal 1975 budget now before Congress. "This hidden item is typical of the way the executive branch tries to get around congressional cuts in foreign aid," Fulbright said. "Congress turns off or cuts down the flow from one foreign aid spigot and they open up another one somewhere."

The chairman of the Foreign Relations Committee leveled his charges after his aides attempted to get an explanation from the Pentagon about what specifically was included in that category of the defense budget which will cost $2.2 billion and is labeled as "Support of Other Nations."

This section includes $1.45 billion for military assistance to Vietnam. But it also includes, Fulbright was told, $490 million to buy and stockpile "war reserve" equipment and ammunition "earmarked specifically for use by" South 

Vietnamese, South Korean or Thai forces, if necessary.

Neither the official U.S. budget for the fiscal year 1975 beginning July 1 nor any other publicly released document at this time makes any mention of the $490 million for war reserves stocks for allies. 

In describing the $2.2 billion "Support for Other Nations" category, the official budget book describes only the separate military aid for South Vietnam and virtually all the other relatively small items in the category, but not the war reserve stocks.

In attempting to explain the situation, Pentagon spokesman Jerry W. Friedheim revealed that about $500 million had been similarly earmarked in fiscal 1974 and another $25 million in fiscal 1973, the first year in which funds were included for additional stockpiles that could be used by Asian allies. 

It has been known for many years that the United States stockpiled equipment for its own forces. But it was not known generally that weapons were being stockpiled for other nations, even though those weapons would be under U.S. control. 

Friedheim yesterday pointed out references in March by Defense Secretary

James R. Schlesigner and the chairman of the joint chiefs of staff, Adm. Thomas 

H. Moorer, about the prospects for stockpiling arms for allies. But these statements indicated that was a future plan, as a result of the Middle East war when the United States was forced to ship large quantities of arms out of its own inventories to Israel. There was no hint that almost $1 billion had already been requested for Asian forces in current and previous budgets.

One senior defense official said privately that Fulbright's statement marked the first time that Friedheim himself found out about the earlier stockpile requests.

The senator's challenge took on added interest since it came on the heels of a Senate vote denying the Pentagon a $266 million increase in aid for Saigon this year. Some Senate aides believe the stockpile funds may be a way to get around congressional denial of additional funds. 

Yesterday, however, the Defense Department said that the war reserve stocks for allies cannot be released from U.S. control "until a conscious presidential decision, with the appropriate congressional consultation, is made . . ." 

This means the President could act without full congressional approval. But, in discussing the situation with newsmen yesterday, the general tone of Friedheim's explanation was that the Defense Department understood that it was the intent of the Congress to limit military aid to Vietnam to the congressionally imposed $1.126 billion ceiling for fiscal 1974 and there would be no more legislative or bookkeeping attempts to get around it. 

Friedheim also appeared to take a less dire view of the effects of the congressional refusal of the extra $266 million than have some other defense and 

White House officials.

Friedheim noted that while the Pentagon has only somewhat less than $100 million left of the $1.126 billion ceiling on obligations for military aid to Saigon, only two months remain in the current fiscal year. 

He also noted that the ceiling does not affect equipment already in the supply pipeline to Saigon, that Saigon has some reserves of its own, that fighting has generally been at a reduced level recently, and that the rainy season that normally restricts combat comes to South Vietnam in June. 

Friedheim, under questioning, said, "There would not necessarily be a dramatic immediate effect in South Vietnam. At some point, however, there will be sort of a bubble in the pipeline and some reduction in the rate of deliveries." 

He said Pentagon supply specialists were now trying to figure out where the shortages will be, and will try to use the remaining money to plug specific shortages.

The basic rationale behind the stockpiling of weapons for allies is to have a ready supply of arms-other than those earmarked for U.S. units-which could be used in an emergency by such countries as Vietnam, Korea or Israel, for example, if they were attacked heavily and perhaps simultaneously. 

WAR RESERVE REQUIREMENTS 

Senator INOUYE. There are several paragraphs in this article that suggest that the last three Department of Defense budget requests, "included a total of more than $1 billion to build a reserve stockpile of weapons for possible use by allies in Asia-rather than by American forces."

Moreover, the article charges that the Defense Department officials "were unable to produce any record showing that this request for funds had been clearly labeled or explained to Congress or the public." 

Would you care to comment, sir? 

 And I think that that particular issue is based upon a misconception. Every shipment of munitions or equipment by the Department of Defense anywhere in the world must be authorized by the Congress. It must be authorized directly either in this appropriation account or in the MASF appropriation account which, of course, is down to the one country at the present time. 

The article in question and the charge in question was based, I think, on the view that somehow the Department of Defense could, because of these internal planning devices, deliver munitions or equipment out of this country to particular recipient nations. It cannot deliver anything that is not authorized by law and for which appropriations have not been made.

Now, in the planning process-and my understanding of this is not precise what had been anticipated, was that of the amounts that the Congress might approve for a particular year there was to be an internal earmarking of some materiel but that had nothing whatsoever to do with the ability of the Congress to control disposition of such material through its authorizations. 

Finally, Mr. Chairman, and this is perhaps the most significant point, this internal earmarking all occurred with regard to war reserves of particular munitions or equipment which were well below the specified war reserve requirements. Consequently, any funds which were requested for this purpose from the Congress were directly related to the war reserve requirements of the United States. 

Now, I might add one point, Mr. Chairman- 

Senator INOUYE. Excuse me. War reserves of the United States or of the recipient country?

Secretary SCHLESINGER. It was directly related to the war reserve requirements of the United States until such time as the total request approved by the Congress exceeded the specified war reserve requirements. The reason we have requested a readiness supplemental in fiscal year 1974 is that we discovered during the recent war in the Middle East that our war reserves were far below, dramatically below, specified war reserve requirements in many categories. 

There is one other aspect that I wanted to mention, Mr. Chairman, and that is when a contingency arises which was unanticipated, such as the recent contingency in the Middle East, at the present time we are forced to draw down from U.S. inventories and particularly from major equipment stocks such as tanks and aircraft. We have had to take items away from active duty or from reserve forces and this results in constraint on the effectiveness of those forces. 

This is a matter of considerable concern to us. I believe that the 

United States should do a better job in planning for these kinds of contingencies so that it does not have to strip its active duty forces, or reserve forces.

ESTIMATED CASH SALES 

Senator INOUYE. In reports to this subcommittee last year, DOD estimated that cash sales in fiscal year 1974 would amount to $3.678 million. The projected sales for fiscal year 1974 have now risen to $7,220 million. For fiscal year 1975 the estimate for DOD cash sales is $3,541 million.

In 1974 you were about $3.5 billion off the mark. Is there any reason for the committee to believe that you will be closer this year? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. I believe so, Mr. Chairman. I think that there were unique developments last year, and that the unique developments last year reflected the explosion that occurred in the Middle East, resulting in swollen sales for that particular year. 

The Iranian figure, which I cited earlier, of $3.5 billion was vastly in excess of anything that we anticipated at the beginning of the year.

Those sales, for example, of the F-14 aircraft to Iran represent orders that were placed in fiscal year 1974, but for which deliveries will occur in later years-until the end of this decade, in fact. So concentrated orders are placed in a particular year in which there are political developments of that sort, but the deliveries will be spread out over many years.

I would expect that the level of sales would fall back this year to a much lower level than that which applied in 1974. But I cannot guarantee that, Mr. Chairman.

BALANCE OF PAYMENTS AS A CONSIDERATION IN MILITARY SALES 

Senator INOUYE. Is it true that one of the major considerations in our military sales is the improvement of our balance of payments? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. Not in my judgment, Mr. Chairman, except for the one area of Western Europe. In the area of Western Europe, which I regard as a fundamental one for the United States, the Congress has required that the United States offset any foreign exchange costs of our deployment in Western Europe. We have, therefore, strongly urged our allies, as a result of this congressional decision, to purchase American equipment in such manner that the balance-of-payments costs of the deployments of American forces are offset.

In other regards, Mr. Chairman, I have opposed the kind of policy that you mentioned. I think that the sale of arms should be based upon considerations of U.S. foreign policy and in addition to that, sales should be limited in such a way that it serves the interests-as we interpret those interests of the countries concerned. The United 

States should be an honest broker in giving advice to other countries with regard to their military purchases, and it should not be engaged in a game of hawking military equipment.

RESTRAINTS VERSUS SUCCESS IN MILITARY SALES

We have been speaking of restraints in the distribution and sale of conventional arms but yet the record seems to indicate that we have done otherwise. 

The official policy of the United States, as expressed by the U.S. representative to the United Nations, suggests that the effectiveness of our work in the arms control field should match the solemnity of our declarations and I am wondering if this has been brought about by declaring on one hand that we favor restraint and on the other hand coming out as the number one salesman in the world. 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. I think that the reason for the high level of sales reflects certain foreign policy objectives not primarily economic, and that it reflects the prestige and the effectiveness of U.S. equipment. Sometimes equipment is purchased simply because it is 

American. I think, and I would hope, that this is the case, Mr. Chairman, that in a large number of cases the sales of American equipment reflect the belief on the part of purchasing nations, that the United States is a dedicated, honest broker that will give them good advice with regard to their equipment and that views of Americans will have value.

In addition, Americans provide a logistic support capability for the equipment they sell which is surpassed, I believe, by no other country. I believe that that is the appropriate way to engage in arms sales. The dumping of armament on countries which subsequently lack logistic support capabilities falls under the ban to which your question refers.
