THE CHAIRMAN COMMENDS THE SECRETARY 

Senator INOUYE. This is not a question. I would like to commend you and your office for your effort to reduce excess military personnel, particularly headquarters personnel. We would like to commend to you the review of the MAAG missions and MilGroups manned by over 2,000 military personnel and more than 25 general and flag officers. As you know, this committee has been urging all along an overall reduction in the number of these personnel and reduction of the number of missions without notable success. 

Senator INOUYE. And we look forward to receiving the results of your efforts there. 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. Yes, sir. You can look for some more cuts in that area. 

"FREE WORLD NATION"-WHAT IS IT? 

Senator INOUYE. I believe you agree with this statement because this comes from the sales and perhaps program facts. It says: "The programs through which security assistance supports the defense efforts of other free world nations are essential elements of U.S. foreign policy."

It must be a statement you can accept. 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. Yes, sir; I believe I accepted that.

Senator INOUYE. For the record, could you define a free world nation? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. I thought you were referring to the foreign policy, but I will make that attempt, Mr. Chairman. 

Senator INOUYE. Could you do it now? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. Oh, I thought you said for the record. 

Senator INOUYE. Yes, for the record today. 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. I think that one would recognize that there are variants amongst the category known as free world nations. In one category, there are a set of democracies, principally amongst the Western nations; but increasingly democratic forms and values have been developing elsewhere that I would describe as representing the heart, as it were, of the free world, the nations with which we have common values.

Those include certain kinds of democratic institutions. Obviously, these are matters of degree; and to some extent, some nations will fall away from what we would regard as the preferable form of government organization. Some will reduce certain types of liberties-by restricting electoral rights, for example and yet retain other types of civil liberties. Such nations I would regard on balance as preferable to even worse alternatives. And amongst these nations I would also include those which retain valuable aspects of freedom as compared to the alternatives. 

I would prefer, however, not to comment specifically with regard to individual nations. And finally, Mr. Chairman, I think that the preservation of national independence is something that the United States values that even where their internal forms have become degenerate-nations which desire to preserve their independence from external aggression, represent an area with which the United States would concern itself.

I shall attempt, Mr. Chairman, to provide a sharper definition in the record.

Senator INOUYE. It would be very helpful because in the rhetoric of government-not speaking of just the administration, but all of us here we very often use the phrase "free world nation" and I doubt if too many of us understand all its many meanings. 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. I would agree with the comment, Mr. Chairman, and I think that what one must recognize is that there is a gradation. If one seriously employs the term "free world nation," one is not referring with equal enthusiasm to all nations outside of what was formerly the Communist bloc. 

Senator INOUYE. So in your discussion, am I correct to assume that the major factor or the major characteristic of a free world nation is this: that a free world country is one which does not embrace what you call the alternative or, to put it more specifically, any country that opposes Communism? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. NO. I was proposing to be far more discriminating than that. I think that that was what your original question was getting at, Mr. Chairman, and I think that was a prior tendency on the part of many of us in the United States to describe any country that was not a part of the Communist bloc as, more or less by definition, a free world nation. I do not believe that that is tenable. 

We must look at a country in terms of the way that government comports itself in order to say to what extent it is part of the free world. 

Senator INOUYE. I would appreciate and I am certain the committee will also appreciate, as you would say, a sharper definition of "free world nation." 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. Mr. Chairman, I will give the statutory definition.

The Congress recognizes that the peace of the world and the security of the United States are in danger so long as international Communism and the Communist controls continue by threat of military action, by the use of economic pressure, by internal subversion or other means, to attempt to bring under their domination peoples now free and independent and continue to deny the rights of freedom and self-government to peoples and countries once free, but now subject to domination.

I think that represents an official statement. I am not sure that it is unambiguous. 

Senator INOUYE. Thank you very much, sir.

DEFINITION OF "FREE WORLD NATION" 

Senator HATFIELD. Mr. Secretary, in your refining the definition, I would like to have you perhaps go beyond the statutory definition and indicate to us what you think the major divisions of the world are. So frequently we have worked within the context of major divisions between East and West, when actually it is becoming increasingly a division geographically understood between north and south, as between the rich and the poor. As I see the major issues evolving today, as contrasted to the period of the cold war, these are issues involving resources, food, energy, development. 

I would like to know in that context if you accept that as a valid interpretation-

DEFINITION OF "FREE WORLD NATION" 

I would agree with the apparent thrust of the remarks of you both that the utility of the term "free world" may very well be on the wane. First, to the extent that its use may connote a "cold war" view of the world, the phrase was indeed more applicable 20 years ago than it is today. Second, to the extent that it could be understood as describing domestic political systems, it is misleading and imprecise. Finally, when antagonistic bi-polarity dominated the international political structure, "free world" generally referred to nations allied or closely connected behind U.S. leadership in containing potential communist direct or indirect aggression-from that perspective as well, it no longer gives us much help in dealing with the complexities of international relations. At the same time, while "free world," like "cold war," may approximately decline in fashion, it should not be assumed that important aspects of the international milieu which they characterized for many years no longer exist. Most significantly, the fundamental differences between ourselves and the Soviet Union have not disappeared. 

Indeed, those differences remain intrinsically irreconcilable on points such as personal liberty and basic economic organization. 

We can today as a nation gain-our political, security and economic goals can be served through relationships of many types with all kinds of countries. 

Furthermore, because we have maintained our strategic deterrent and sought to take advantage of negotiation opportunities which-for many reasons with which you are familiar-are expanding, the U.S. and U.S.S.R. seem now extremely unlikely deliberately to wage war over the incompatibilities of their respective systems. Thus it is in our interest fully to explore the potentials for harmony in our international relationships rather than to have our behavior characterized almost exclusively by the communist-non-communist competition. 

With respect to characterizing major divisions of the world, I find several perspectives useful-depending primarily on the context. The "north-south" or "rich-poor" division dramatizes world resource scarcity and resource distribution issues. Coincident with our continued effort to avoid war and to provide ourselves an adequate, across the board level of military security, the United States increasingly must concern itself with such issues. To the extent that we do not do so, indeed, the scarcity problems can become security problems. "East-west" shorthands the subdued but enduring communist versus non-communist competition.

Other divisions might consider gradations among nations based on our own sense of affinity with and ties to them. I do believe, for instance, as I indicated earlier, that there are nations with which we share common political idealsthough frequently a different cultural heritage and with which we accordingly have close ties. The most important of those ideals are, in my opinion, the high valuation of individual freedom and of just laws impartially, consistently applied. 

On the other hand, many nations fall, for one reason or another, outside that general grouping. With respect to those, we may be extremely critical of their internal systems and even uncomfortable about the intimacy of our relationships with them. Nevertheless, it is not our business, nor are we prepared philosophically or militarily to seek significantly to alter their internal politics. 

Finally, as I have also suggested above, the United States does have an interest in the maintenance of the independence or, if you will, freedom-of nations from external aggression. Aggression of any kind is not phenomenon that can be safely tolerated in international relations. The means by which we pursue our interest in minimizing aggression vary, of course, according to the risks and costs involved and our own capabilities. But there are many nations, representing many political systems whose strength and independence one way or another can contribute to international or regional stability. It is rarely in the U.S. interest to provide other countries their main defense, but it is frequently in our interest to provide a degree of support to supplement self-defense capabilities and efforts. It is in this context-pragmatic but in no sense a moral assessment of U.S. international goals and interests-that U.S. security assistance programs should be undertaken.

 SELECTED COMPARISONS IN CAMBODIA-1973 AND 1974 

While some quantification of progress is possible, any statistical analysis would be provided with reservations as to its usefulness in portraying the current situation in Cambodia. A brief comparison of the 1973 and 1974 dry season campaigns including, where applicable, such statistics as we have is as follows: 

The number of combat incidents since January 1973 show a marked trend upward during the year despite periods of pronounced lulls in fighting. In January 

1973, reported combat incidents were approximately 1,100. In January 1974 combat incidents were approximately 1,300. [Deleted.]

During the same period however, the number of maneuver battalions were reduced from [deleted]. This reduction largely resulted from improvements in 

FANK personnel accounting and pay systems which purged nonexistent or phantom troops from the FANK force structure and led to the consolidation of understrength and undermanned units with other FANK units in need of replacements. 

Reported Khmer Communists (KC) strengths have also increased during the year, growing from 40,000-50,000 in April 1973 to the 50,000 to 60,000 personnel currently estimated. During the same period, however, strengths of VC/NVA personnel in Cambodia dropped from an approximate level of 28,000-43,000 in April ´1973 to 10,000-14,000 personnel, possibly indicating a growing maturity of the KC movement and a lessening dependence on the VC/NVA presence. 

During the 1973 dry season campaign, the KC seized considerable territory in southern and northeastern Cambodia. FANK overall response to these initiatives was grossly inadequate. Numerically, FANK held a decided edge over the KC but other factors, the most significant of which was FANK's defensive mentality, worked to negate their advantage in numbers. FANK combat performance was characterized by poor leadership, low morale, and the refusal of units to advance against enemy resistance. Despite heavy US air support, FANK abandoned their positions to KC units with increasing frequency between February and July withdrawing into urban enclaves and positions along primary lines of communication leaving the population in the countryside largely to the KC. FANKS organic artillery fire support was generally not capable of supporting troops in the field. 

Although the Air Force and the Navy were fairly competent, FANK grew to rely almost exclusively on U.S. air strikes for fire support. The Cambodian Air Force was flying an average of only 10-15 strike sorties a day, most of which were against day-old targets derived from intelligence sources, rather than in response to calls for close air support from ground combat units. The Navy largely remained idle except for its routine escort of Mekong River supply convoys. 

The KC, on the other hand, became increasingly adept at concentrating multibattalion forces for attacks against FANK and took full advantage of the almost unrestricted movement afforded them throughout the country by FANK's defensive posture and lack of aggressiveness. Following a major effort to stop Mekong 

River shipping in March and April and the roll-up outposts along Routes 2, 3, and

6, the character of combat shifted to more intense sustained engagements. During 

June-August the KC continued to press their offensive, bringing the war to the outskirts of Phnom Penh before running out of steam in the face of heavy US air strikes and the suffering of unacceptable casualties. Following that failure, the KC pressed their attack on Kompong Cham and occupied half of that major provincial capital before being beaten back by a heavily reinforced FANK garrison. FANK was able to save Kompong Cham without US air support which served to raise both morale and confidence. 

In spite of improvements to their command and control apparatus and the extension and control around Phnom Penh, and the absence of US air support, the KC failed to achieve the decisive victory they expected in the 1974 season. 

The KC's failure did not result from a lack of preparation. At the height of the KC dry season campaign in January and February, KC combat strength in the Phnom Penh area rose to [deleted] troops-many of which were deployed from outlying areas to support the KC's major effort to bring about the capitulation of the Phnom Penh government. KC forces not only exerted heavy pressure on the capital and is environs but also interdicted all land lines of communication to the city.

However, the KC apparently underestimated their own military deficiencies, especially those relating to command and control and execution of attacks, while also underestimating the resiliency of FANK. While FANK remained on the defensive, KC inadequacies in coordinating their military operations allowed FANK to deploy its forces and use its superior firepower and mobility to maximum advantage and inflict heavy casualties. Most importantly, the fact that 

FANK was able to conduct a successful defense of Phnom Penh increased government confidence in its ability to defeat the enemy. 

In the absence of U.S. air support, the Cambodian Air Force continued to improve its support role increasing its average daily attack sortie rate to 80-90. In addition, the Khmer Air Force made good progress in improving command and control between Air Force headquarters and tactical ground commanders as well as more efficient use of aircraft by increased maintenance support and tactical deployments to outlying bases. 

The improvement in air support has been paralleled by the increasing employment of the Cambodian Navy which has played a key role in the defense of government enclaves. Naval units have been increasingly utilized to provide needed fire support, resupply and troop transport. 

Comparisons in FANK ammunition consumption between 1973 through to the present reflects a growing rate of expenditure. The first five months in 1973 show an average daily consumption of [deleted] short tons a day, whereas the average for the first five months in 1974 shows a daily consumption of [deleted] short tons a day. This increase is attributable to several factors including an increased intensity of fighting coupled with the increased dependence of FANK personnel on the use of supporting fires and finally, the increased inventories of weapons and combat aircraft. For example, during 1973 the Cambodian Army's artillery resources were significantly increased by the addition of [deleted] 155-mm howitzers and [deleted] 105-mm howitzers. Concurrently the FANK ability to control its fire support assets and effectively use them has improved by the establishment of several fire support coordination centers around Phnom Penh and in other key areas. The use of these and increased employment of aerial observers and forward air controllers has permitted FANK to achieve greatly increased coordination of field artillery, naval gunfire and close air support. For the first time the Cambodian Air Force is flying a significant portion of its total missions in response to on call requests from the infantry and artillery fires are being massed to support coordinated attacks. 

FANK's successful defense of Phnom Penh and increasing KC concern with popular disaffections in the provinces forced the KC to shift their strategy in early March to stem FANK advances and regain their offensive momentum. 

Generally, FANK has defended its enclaves well, however, the shift in KC strategy initially led to the capture of the provincial capital of Oudong and considerable territory northwest of Phnom Penh and along Route 4 in the southwest.

While FANK has shown improvement in 1974, the economic situation has continued to deteriorate. For the past two years the Khmer Republic has been experiencing serious economic problems. Steadily increasingly military expenditures in the face of a reduced tax revenue potential, have led to a severely imbalanced budget. Import requirements have increased, especially for rice, resulting in enormous trade deficits. Phnom Penh, the major urban area in the 

Khmer Republic, has experienced rising prices which, according to the Working Class Consumer Price Index have increased over 433 percent since December 1972. During the same period the Riel was officially devalued seven times. 

NATURE OF ESTRANGEMENT BETWEEN KHMER ROUGE AND NORTH VIETNAMESE 

Senator HATFIELD. Now also we have growing reports that there is an estrangement between the Khmer Rouge and North Vietnamese.

I am wondering if the claims are correct that the North Vietnamese strategy is finding a standoff situation more to their liking than a victory for the Khmer Rouge, and if you would make an assessment of this possibility or of this situation. 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. Historically, there have been strains and there will continue to be strains. I think that these strains can lead to greater promise of settlement. There has been fighting between the two groups, Admiral Moorer informs me. What I would suggest is that we prepare for the record a classified or unclassified version that you could employ, giving you the gist of the situation as we see it at the present time.

Undoubtedly, however, the Khmers are fierce nationalists who historically have resented the intervention of outsiders, particularly Vietnamese; and this would not be altered if the Vietnamese who are intruding are North Vietnamese Communists as opposed to South Vietnamese. 

Senator HATFIELD. In this assessment, Mr. Secretary, would you give us what in your judgment is the nature of the present conflict vis-a-vis the involvement of North Vietnamese troops in any particular conflicts? 

KHMER COMMUNIST FRICTION WITH THE NORTH VIETNAMESE 

Fighting between KC and VC/NVA elements broke out in southwest Cambodia in mid-July 1973 and intensified in August [deleted].

The North Vietnamese goal in Cambodia is primarily ancillary to their effort in South Vietnam. In that light, at the present time, they appear to be most interested in protecting their present free access to and control of eastern Cambodia. The traditional ethnic animosity between the Vietnamese and Khmer transcends Communist ideology and any Khmer Government, Communist or otherwise, would probably oppose occupation or domination by the North Vietnamese.

OBJECTIVES OF AID TO KHMER REPUBLIC Senator HATFIELD. What specific political or military objectives did we have in supplying the Khmer Republic with this extensive military aid? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. I think that the objectives fall under the heading of helping to protect the South Vietnamese regime on its back door. If that country were totally under the domination of North 

Vietnam, that would be a serious question. 

As your earlier question indicated, it might be only partially under North Vietnamese influence; but that in itself, while less serious, would be a matter of some concern. The impact of the fall of Cambodia upon 

Thailand is a matter of concern. So it is a question of their relations with their neighbors.

But in addition, the continued independence of the country in itself as opposed to its impact on the neighbors, the attempt to help the Khmer Republic avoid the hypothetical domination to which I referred to earlier is a matter of U.S. foreign policy. 

Senator HATFIELD. Mr. Secretary, it comes through to me that possibly we really have a higher priority in Saigon than we have as far as the needs of the Khmer people are concerned. Our involvement there is primarily related to the sustaining of the regime in Saigon or in Thailand and the Khmer people are caught in sort of an unfortunate whipsaw situation here. 

Would that be a correct assessment? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. I would not like to make invidious comparisons, but I accept the point. I reinforce the point that the impact upon the security of South Vietnam is a very important consideration. I

would think it would be inappropriate for American foreign policy to whipsaw the Khmer population for that purpose were that the only purpose. I think that we wish the Khmer Republic to survive. The defense put up by the Khmer Republic, which is greater than had been anticipated previously, is a matter of some satisfaction to the U.S. Government.

Senator HATFIELD. It would be almost like the ends justified the means if we should engage in a whipsaw type of activity.

Secretary Schlesinger. That would be a correct assessment in those circumstances.

Senator HATFIELD. Would a Khmer government that did not include 

Lon Nol be acceptable to the United States, in your opinion? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. Oh, I think that if such a circumstance were to arise, the answer might be yes, Senator Hatfield, but I think a more informed opinion should come from Dr. Kissinger. 

Senator HATFIELD. You cannot comment upon what type of coalition government might be acceptable to the United States? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. I think that the United States has in the past indicated that an ultimate settlement in Cambodia could well come in the same way that it came in Laos, through the formation of such a government, but I do not believe that the two parties in Cambodia have yet embraced that as a reality. I think that your earlier comment, however, is most germane at this point. 

Senator HATFIELD. Let's end on the upbeat. 

BASIS FOR DETERMINATION OF MILITARY ASSISTANCE BUDGET 

Senator INOUYE. I have several questions which I wish to submit to your office for response. I would like to close the hearings with three questions to Admiral Moorer if I may.

Admiral, in your statement, you have implied that because of Congressional reductions in budget requests for military assistance in foreign military sales, "The Armed Forces of many of our allies remain far short of their defense needs as they perceive the threat to their nations."

Admiral, are you suggesting that the United States make determinations as to its foreign military assistance budgets on the basis of what other nations perceive to be their military needs and their external threats? My question is do we make the policy or do they make the policy? 

Admiral MOORER. We make the policy, Mr. Chairman. I simply was pointing up that we, in fact, had exercised restraint and that in the case of the various nations, not all their requests had been honored. The approved programs for arms and supplies are developed in light of the resources available and what we, rather than they, consider would be the most useful. I simply was pointing up that there is a difference between their perception and our perception. 

Senator INOUYE. Do you suggest that their assessment is always correct, sir? 

Admiral MOORER. No, sir; I do not, and that is why we sometimes have differences in perception. I believe most people would take the position that those countries adjacent to the threat want to have a national force in order to reduce the risk as they see it.

IMPACT OF REDUCED U.S. ASSISTANCE 

Senator INOUYE. There is another statement. It is a sentence on your first page where you suggest that many of our allies are reluctant to revert to complete peacetime civilian governmental arrangements because of reduced U.S. assistance. Which countries are you speaking of? 

Admiral MOORER. Well, I think, Korea perhaps, would fall in that category, sir. They feel that in light of the threat from the North, they must allocate a large percentage of their resources to defense in addition to that which we have seen fit to provide for assistance. 

Senator INOUYE. Do you think that if we provide more military assistance it will back a more democratic country? 

Admiral MOORER. Well, I think that if we provide more assistance, they would feel more secure and might be in a position to move more into the area of economics.

Senator INOUYE. Are there any other nations besides Korea in this category?

ADMIRAL MOORER. Korea is the one to which I had prime reference. 

DYNAMIC EQUILIBRIUM OFFERS OPPORTUNITY FOR PEACE 

Senator INOUYE. So you have one country here. My last question concerns the sentence which occurs on the second page, and here you are discussing the military assistance program, and your quote is as follows: "This program is being proposed during the period when the strategic balance is in dynamic equilibrium and where each unprecedented challenge to our global interests produces an equal and opposite unprecedented opportunity for peace." 

Could you explain this, sir? 

Admiral MOORER. Yes, sir. What I am referring to is in essence what the Secretary has been discussing about regional balance; the idea being that if we can maintain this balance with an assistance program, we remove the temptation for aggression and, therefore, enhance the possibility of peace.

Senator INOUYE. More specifically, what is an equal and opposite unprecedented opportunity for peace? 

Admiral MOORER. Well, sir, I think that I just come back to the same point. I believe we have made significant progress toward acquiring a peaceful situation. When you have a military situation that is not in equilibrium you can, by bringing the friendly nation up to necessary military strength, enhance its stability and, therefore, reduce the risk of war.

CONGRESSIONAL JURISDICTION OVER SECURITY ASSISTANCE PROGRAMS 

Senator INOUYE. My final question, sir. It has been suggested by many in the Congress that this whole program should be taken out of the jurisdiction of the Foreign Relations and Foreign Affairs Com mittees and the two subcommittees concerned with foreign operations, that these programs should go where they belong, in the military committes. Do you have any observation to make? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. I have never suggested that, Mr. Chairman.

Senator INOUYE. No. I said that Members of Congress had suggested that.

Secretary SCHLESINGER. Well, I think that that issue arose primarily in association with the war in Southeast Asia and the whole question of MASF funding which ran at a high level. I think that these are foreign policy issues, and we are quite satisfied with the jurisdictional arrangements on the Hill as they exist at the present time. 

As you know, the Laos aid program goes back to the jurisdiction of the Foreign Affairs Committee, and it is planned that South Vietnam will also go back into that jurisdiction. 

Senator INOUYE. Mr. Secretary and Admiral Moorer, on behalf of the committee, I thank you and your staff for your participation in the hearings this morning.

QUESTIONS SUBMITTED BY SENATOR INOUYE 

The following questions will be inserted in the record at this point: [The questions and answers follow:] 

Question. You make the assertion that "Greece and Turkey are, of course, key members of the NATO Alliance, and the maintenance of adequate defense capabilities in both countries is crucial to the Alliance." 

Do other members of NATO agree with this assessment?

You propose credit sales of $71 million for Greece and $90 million for Turkey. 

Eighty million in grant aid and $35 million in excess defense articles are also programmed for Turkey. What is the total contribution of NATO countries, apart from the United States, to Greece? To Turkey?

Answer. The Allies recognize the strategic importance of Greece and Turkey, with their geography dominating the Southern Flank of NATO and the Black Sea approach to the Mediterranean. There is no misunderstanding of the importance of their military, strategic and participatory contributions to Alliance defense.

At one time Germany provided grant military assistance to Greece. However since the April 1967 coup in Greece, the FRG has furnished no grant assistance to 

Greece. The FRG has sold Greece submarines. Noratlas aircraft and a quantity of recovery vehicles and spare parts for tanks. Canada has furnished quantities of aircraft spares to Greece in the past. France has had no grant program for 

Greece but has sold patrol craft and AMX tanks. France is also attempting to sell Mirage aircraft to Greece.

The FRG has provided substantial quantities and varieties of ground force equipment to Turkey since 1964. This aid has been on a grant basis. Canada, Italy and the United Kingdom have also provided military equipment to Turkey, but only on a limited scale.

[The statement follows:]

MR. CHAIRMAN AND MEMBERS OF THE COMMITTEE: 

AS DIRECTOR OF THE DEFENSE SECURITY ASSISTANCE AGENCY, IT IS MY PRIVILEGE AND RESPONSIBILITY TO PARTICIPATE IN THE PRESENTATION TO THIS COMMITTEE OF THE PROPOSED FY 1975 SECURITY ASSISTANCE PROGRAM. PRE- VIOUS WITNESSES HAVE ALREADY ADDRESSED THE RELATIONSHIP OF THAT PROGRAM TO THE NATIONAL INTEREST IN TERMS OF BOTH U.S. FOREIGN POLICY AND THE MILITARY REQUIREMENTS ASSOCIATED WITH OUR NATIONAL OBJECTIVES. MY PART IN THIS PRESENTATION IS, THEREFORE, TO SPEAK TO THE CONTENT AND MANAGEMENT OF THE SECURITY ASSISTANCE PORTION OF THE PROGRAM, WHICH IS ADMINISTERED BY THE DEPARTMENT OF DEFENSE, AND TO ANSWER ANY QUESTIONS YOU MAY HAVE AS TO PAST PERFORMANCE, PRESENT STATUS, OR FUTURE PLANS. 

WHEREAS THE SECRETARY OF STATE IS RESPONSIBLE FOR DETERMINING WHETHER THERE SHALL BE A MILITARY ASSISTANCE PROGRAM OF A CREDIT SALE FOR A PARTICULAR COUNTRY, THE ACTUAL EXECUTION OF THE DEFENSE-ADMINISTERED SECURITY ASSISTANCE PROGRAM IS A FUNCTION OF THE SECRETARY OF DEFENSE ON WHOSE BEHALF I SERVE AS MANAGER OF THE PROGRAMS. HIS RESPONSIBILITIES WITH RESPECT TO THE MILITARY ASSISTANCE PROGRAM ARE, AS YOU KNOW, SPE- CIFICALLY STATED IN THE FOREIGN ASSISTANCE ACT. THEY PROVIDE A CLEAR AND CONCISE DESCRIPTION OF THE MAJOR MILITARY ASSISTANCE FUNCTIONS ASSIGNED TO THE DEFENSE SECURITY ASSISTANCE AGENCY. THESE INCLUDE THE PRIMARY RESPONSIBILITY FOR: 

THE DETERMINATION OF MILITARY END-ITEM REQUIREMENTS; 

- THE PROCUREMENT OF MILITARY EQUIPMENT IN A MANNER WHICH PERMITS ITS INTEGRATION WITH SERVICE PROGRAMS; 

- THE SUPERVISION OF END-ITEM USE BY THE RECIPIENT COUNTRIES; 

- THE SUPERVISION OF THE TRAINING OF FOREIGN MILITARY PERSONNEL; 

THE MOVEMENT AND DELIVERY OF MILITARY END-ITEMS; 

- THE ESTABLISHMENT OF PRIORITIES IN THE PROCUREMENT, DELIVERY, AND ALLOCATION OF MILITARY EQUIPMENT.

IN OVERSEEING THE PERFORMANCE OF THESE AND SIMILAR, CLOSELY RELATED FUNCTIONS FOR WHICH THE SECRETARY OF DEFENSE IS ALSO RESPONSIBLE, MY PRIMARY ROLE AS MANAGER IS TO ENSURE THAT THE SECURITY ASSISTANCE PROGRAMS ADMINISTERED BY THE DEPARTMENT OF DEFENSE ARE EFFICIENTLY IMPLE- MENTED. I MUST BE CERTAIN THAT THE PROGRAM IS IN ACCORDANCE WITH APPLI- CABLE PROVISIONS OF THE FOREIGN ASSISTANCE AND FOREIGN MILITARY SALES ACTS AND OTHER GOVERNING LEGISLATION, AS WELL AS WITHIN THE ESTABLISHED POLICY GUIDELINES AND THE BEST INTERESTS OF THE UNITED STATES. 

WHAT IT ALL BOILS DOWN TO IN ACTUAL PRACTICE IS THAT OUR JOB IS TO MANAGE THE SECURITY ASSISTANCE PROGRAMS IN A WAY WHICH WILL PROVIDE EACH RECIPIENT COUNTRY WITH THE KIND AND AMOUNT OF MATERIELAND TRAINING NEEDED TO STRENGTHEN ITS ARMED FORCES AND THEREBY ENCOURAGE AND ENLARGE THEIR CONTRIBUTION TO COMMON DEFENSE. 

COURSE, THE MILITARY GOODS AND SERVICES WE FURNISH A PARTICULAR COUNTRY MAY BE DESIGNED TO PROMOTE OTHER DIFFERENT, BUT EQUALLY IMPORTANT, OBJECTIVES ASSOCIATED WITH BROAD U.S. FOREIGN POLICY GOALS. 

OCCASIONALLY, OF WE HAVE TWO FORMS OF DEFENSE-ADMINISTERED SECURITY ASSISTANCE TO WORK WITH IN DEVELOPING THOSE INDIVIDUAL COUNTRY PROGRAMS. THEY ARE, AS YOU KNOW: (1) FOREIGN MILITARY SALES (CREDIT AND CREDIT GUAR- ANTEES); AND (2) THE MILITARY ASSISTANCE PROGRAM (INCLUDING EXCESS DEFENSE ARTICLES AND MILITARY-RELATED TRAINING PROGRAMS). 

ONE OF THE KEY FACTORS TAKEN INTO CONSIDERATION IN THE DEVELOP- MENT OF INDIVIDUAL COUNTRY PROGRAMS IS THE OPTIMUM "BLEND" OF THESE THREE TYPES OF SECURITY ASSISTANCE. OTHER INFLUENTIAL FACTORS INCLUDE: 

THE RELATIONSHIP OF THE RECIPIENT NATION'S DEFENSE CAPABILITY TO U.S. SECURITY INTERESTS; 

A REALISTIC FORCE LEVEL BASED UPON WHAT IS NEEDED, WHAT THE COUNTRY CAN SUSTAIN AND WHAT CAN BE PROVIDED;

17 

ECONOMIC AND POLITICAL CONDITIONS WITHIN THE COUNTRY; AND THE SCOPE AND PHASING OF ACTIONS LEADING TO ITS SELF-RELIANCE. 

THE DETAILS AS TO HOW WE PROPOSE TO MAKE USE OF THE AUTHORITY AND APPROPRIATIONS WE ARE ASKING FOR IN FY 1975 ARE SET FORTH IN THE REGIONAL AND COUNTRY PAGES OF THE CONGRESSIONAL PRESENTATION DOCUMENT WHICH YOU HAVE BEFORE YOU. I WOULD LIKE TO HIGHLIGHT CERTAIN KEY ELEMENTS OF THE PROGRAM WHICH I BELIEVE ARE ESPECIALLY PERTINENT TO YOUR CONSIDERATION OF OUR PROPOSALS. 

THE PROPOSED FISCAL YEAR 1975 CREDIT PROGRAM IS REQUESTED AT THE LEVEL OF $872 MILLION TO FACILITATE ANTICIPATED SALES TO OUR FRIENDS AND ALLIES DURING THE COMING YEAR. OUR REQUEST INCLUDES $555 MILLION IN NEW OBLIGATIONAL AUTHORITY FOR BOTH DIRECT DOD CREDIT AND TO GUARANTEE PRIVATE FINANCING (ESTIMATED AT APPROXIMATELY $353 MILLION IN FISCAL YEAR 1975). WE ANTICIPATE A NEED OF $520 MILLION FOR DIRECT FUNDING. THIS MIX OF DIRECT AND PRIVATE FINANCING IS A KEY ELEMENT IN OUR PROGRAM REQUEST. MANY DEVELOPING COUNTRIES AMONG OUR FRIENDS AND ALLIES ARE SELDOM ABLE TO EXPEND SUBSTANTIAL SUMS OF CASH FOR THE PURCHASE OF MODERN WEAPONS SYSTEMS OR TO OBTAIN CREDITS FROM PRIVATE SOURCES ON REASONABLE TERMS. OF COURSE, ALL REQUESTED FUNDS FOR DIRECT CREDITS WILL BE REPAID IN FULL TO THE U.S. TREASURY WITH INTEREST BY THE GOVERNMENTS TO WHICH THEY ARE MADE AVAILABLE. BUT CREDITS PRO- VIDED BY DIRECT MEANS OR THROUGH PRIVATE GUARANTEED FUNDS IN ACCORDANCE WITH THE PROVISIONS OF THE FOREIGN MILITARY SALES ACT ARE ESSENTIAL IF SUCH COUNTRIES ARE TO PURCHASE THE MILITARY EQUIPMENT AND SERVICES THEY 

NEED. 

COMPARING THE FY 1975 REQUEST WITH THAT OF LAST YEAR, WE ARE ASKING ONLY A SLIGHT INCREASE IN GRANT ASSISTANCE AUTHORIZATION FROM WHAT HAS BEEN AVAILABLE THIS PAST YEAR, IN FY 1974 CONGRESS APPROPRIATED $450 MILLION IN NEW OBLIGATION AUTHORITY. ADDING TO THIS THE LAOS PROGRAM,

​J 

WHICH WILL BE TRANSFERRED FROM THE DEFENSE BUDGET TO THE MILITARY ASSIST- ANCE PROGRAM AS OF THE BEGINNING OF FY 1975, AND THE $250 MILLION FY 1974 DRAWDOWN AUTHORITY, TOGETHER WITH THE $69 MILLION PAYBACK FUNDS WHICH WERE MADE AVAILABLE IN FY 1974, THE TOTAL FY 1974 FUNDING IS WITHIN 10 OR 12% OF THE $985 MILLION REQUESTED FOR FY 1975. 

AS FOR OUR REQUEST FOR GRANT MILITARY ASSISTANCE, I AM SURE THAT YOU WILL NOTE WITH SATISFACTION THAT ONLY TWENTY COUNTRIES WILL RECEIVE GRANT MATERIEL ASSISTANCE WHEREAS TEN YEARS AGO FIFTY-TWO COUNTRIES RECEIVED MATERIEL GRANT ASSISTANCE. AS THE ECONOMIC CAPABILITIES OF MANY OF THE ORIGINAL MAJOR RECIPIENT COUNTRIES HAVE IMPROVED, THEIR PRO- GRAMS HAVE BEEN REDUCED AND FINALLY ELIMINATED. CHIEF AMONG THE COUN- TRIES WHICH HAVE ASSUMED RESPONSIBILITY FOR MEETING THEIR OWN DEFENSE REQUIREMENTS ARE THE WESTERN EUROPEAN NATO NATIONS AND JAPAN. 

APPROXIMATELY 85% OF THE MILITARY ELEMENTS OF THE SECURITY ASSISTANCE PROGRAM WILL BE ALLOCATED TO ONLY TEN COUNTRIES, SEVEN OF WHICH WILL RECEIVE A MAJOR PORTION OF THIS ASSISTANCE IN THE FORM OF CREDIT FUNDS UNDER THE PROVISIONS OF THE FOREIGN MILITARY SALES ACT. 

THE CHAIRMAN OF THE JOINT CHIEFS OF STAFF CAN PROVIDE YOU WITH A MIL- ITARY ASSESSMENT OF THE NEED FOR THESE PROGRAMS, BUT I WISH TO REVIEW FOR YOU THE REQUIREMENT, AS I SEE IT, FOR THESE PROGRAMS IN THE TEN SELECTED COUNTRIES DURING FISCAL YEAR 1975 AT THE LEVELS PROPOSED BY THE ADMINISTRATION. THE RECENT WAR IN THE MIDDLE EAST AND THE U.S. 

STRATEGY FOR PEACE IN THAT AREA OF THE WORLD ARE IN THE FOREFRONT OF THE NEWS AND INTEREST OF THE AMERICAN PEOPLE, BUT THE SITUATION IN THE MIDDLE FAST IN NO WAY DIMINISHES THE MILITARY PROBLEMS THAT CON- TINUE IN EAST ASIA. FIVE OF THE SELECTED COUNTRIES ARE LOCATED IN THE EAST ASIAN AND PACIFIC REGION, SO I WILL BEGIN THERE, AND COME BACK TO THE MIDDLE EAST LATER.

EAST ASIA AND PACIFIC REGION. 

U.S. INTERESTS IN THE EAST ASIA AND PACIFIC REGION DERIVE FROM THE VAST POPULATION, NATURAL RESOURCES, INDUSTRIAL CAPACITY, U.S. INVEST- MENTS AND MARKETS, AS WELL AS THE IMPORTANCE OF THE AREA'S SEA AND AIR LINES OF COMMUNICATION TO U.S. GLOBAL STRATEGY. THE FRAGILE TRUCE BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENTS OF NORTH AND SOUTH VIETNAM AND THE ACCORD BETWEEN THE BELLIGERENTS IN LAOS HAVE PERMITTED AN EXTENSIVE REDUCTION OF U.S. 

MILITARY FORCES IN THE REGION. THE SUBSTANTIAL SECURITY ASSISTANCE PRO- GRAMS PROPOSED FOR THE REGION WILL PROVIDE TANGIBLE EVIDENCE OF THE MUTUAL INTEREST WE HAVE WITH OUR FRIENDS AND ALLIES OF THE REGION IN SECURITY AND STABILITY IN THE FAR EAST. 

THE IMMEDIATE THREAT TO THE REALIZATION OF OUR SECURITY ASSIST- ANCE OBJECTIVES IN THE KHMER REPUBLIC IS THE CONTINUING STATE OF HOS- TILITIES AND HIGH LEVEL OF COMBAT BEING EXPERIENCED IN THAT COUNTRY. 

THE CONTINUED ABILITY OF THE GOVERNMENT OF THE KHMER REPUBLIC TO MAIN- TAIN ITS PRESENT ACTIVE OPPOSITION TO COMMUNIST AGGRESSION ESSENTIALLY DEPENDS UPON U.S. MILITARY AND ECONOMIC AID. BECAUSE OF ACTIVE HOS- TILITIES, THE CONTENT OF THE PROGRAM PLACES MORE EMPHASIS ON OPERATIONS AND MAINTENANCE COSTS, ESSENTIAL FOR DAILY COMBAT, THAN ON INVESTMENT ITEMS. PRIMARY EMPHASIS IS BEING PLACED ON MAINTAINING A BALANCED KHMER FORCE OF ARMY, NAVY, AND AIR FORCE ELEMENTS. THE KHMER REPUBLIC WILL BE THE LARGEST GRANT RECIPIENT OF THE TOTAL MILITARY SECURITY ASSISTANCE PROGRAM. 

U.S. SECURITY ASSISTANCE OBJECTIVES IN THE REPUBLIC OF KOREA ARE TO ASSURE THAT ROK ARMED FORCES ARE SUFFICIENTLY STRONG TO DETER NORTH KOREAN ADVENTURISM AND PROVIDE STABILITY ON THE KOREAN PENINSULA TO MEET THESE OBJECTIVES, THE U.S. IN FY 71 INSTITUTED A BALANCED KOREAN FORCE MODERNIZATION PROGRAM, TO BE ACCOMPLISHED WITHIN FIVE YEARS. PRI- MARILY BECAUSE OF REDUCED MILITARY ASSISTANCE PROGRAM APPROPRIATIONS, THE MODERNIZATION PROGRAM HAS LAGGED BEHIND, AND THE FY 1975 PROPOSED PRO-

کے 

GRAMM IS FOCUSED ON EFFECTIVE CONTINUATION OF THE MODERNIZATION PROGRAM AT AN AUSTERE LEVEL. THE LEVEL OF FMS CREDIT PROPOSED FOR KOREA IN FY 1975 REFLECTS GROWING ROK FINANCIAL CAPABILITIES, AND REPRESENTS, IN OUR JUDGMENT, AN AMOUNT WHICH THE REPUBLIC OF KOREA CAN UNDERTAKE GIVEN ITS OVERALL ECONOMIC CONDITION. THE REPUBLIC OF KOREA WILL RECEIVE THE NEXT LARGEST PERCENTAGE OF THE TOTAL MILITARY SECURITY ASSISTANCE PROGRAM IN THE EAST ASIA REGION. 

THE SECURITY OBJECTIVES OF U.S. SECURITY ASSISTANCE TO LAOS ARE TO SUPPORT A BALANCED FORCE WHICH IS OF SUFFICIENT SIZE AND STRENGTH TO MAINTAIN THE SURVIVAL OF THE POLITICALLY NEUTRAL ROYAL LAOTIAN GOVERNMENT AND THE INDEPENDENCE OF THE PEOPLE; AND ENCOURAGE PURSUIT BY LAOS OF OBJECTIVES COMPATIBLE WITH U.S. INTERESTS. LAOS WILL RECEIVE APPROXIMATELY 5% OF THE TOTAL MILITARY SECURITY ASSISTANCE PROGRAM. THE AMOUNT INDICATED IN THE FY 1975 PRESENTATION DOCUMENTS REPRESENTS A DECREASE IN THE AMOUNT PROVIDED LAST YEAR FROM THE DOD BUDGET UNDER THE MILITARY ASSISTANCE SERVICE FUNDED PROGRAM. AS YOU KNOW, THE FOREIGN ASSISTANCE ACT OF 1973 DIRECTED THAT SERVICE-FUNDED MILITARY ASSISTANCE FOR LAOS BE TERMINATED AS OF JUNE 30, 1974; AND THE $85.2 MILLION REQUIRED FOR MATERIEL AND TRAINING MUST BE MAP- FUNDED IN FY 1975. 

THE REPUBLIC OF CHINA ON TAIWAN REMAINS AN IMPORTANT LINK IN THE ALLIED DEFENSE STRUCTURE STRETCHING FROM KOREA TO SOUTHEAST ASIA. THE MILITARY SECURITY ASSISTANCE PROGRAM FOR THE REPUBLIC OF CHINA IS NOW ESSENTIALLY ON A SALES BASIS. A SMALL, CONTINUING GRANT TRAINING PROGRAM IS ALSO PROPOSED TO HELP MAINTAIN CLOSE PROFESSIONAL TIES BETWEEN U.S. 

AND REPUBLIC OF CHINA MILITARY PERSONNEL. WITHIN THE OVERALL PROGRAM, EMPHASIS REMAINS ON FORCE DEVELOPMENT AND ROC SELF-RELIANCE ASSOCIATED WITH RESOURCES MANAGEMENT AND DEFENSE PRODUCTION CAPABILITIES. FORMERLY ONE OF THE LARGEST GRANT RECIPIENTS, THE REPUBLIC OF CHINA WILL RECEIVE ONLY FMS CREDIT FUNDS IN FY 1975, WHICH WILL BE FULLY REPAID TO THE UNITED STATES.

U.S. SECURITY ASSISTANCE REMAINS AN ESSENTIAL ELEMENT IN THE STABILITY OF THAILAND. AS A LEADER OF THE ASSOCIATION OF SOUTHEAST ASIAN NATIONS, THAILAND OCCUPIES A KEY POSITION IN THE AFFAIRS OF THIS REGION. WE ANTICIPATE REDUCING OUR GRANT MILITARY ASSISTANCE TO THAI- LAND AS THE CAPABILITIES OF THE THAI ARMED FORCES IMPROVE AND THAI- FINANCIAL CAPABILITIES INCREASE. HOWEVER, FOR THE PRESENT OUR MILITARY ASSISTANCE CONTINUES TO BE IMPORTANT. FOR FY 1975, OUR SECURITY ASSISTANCE WILL CONTINUE TO PROVIDE GRANT MATERIEL AND TRAINING TO UPGRADE THE ARMED FORCES IN SUCH VITAL AREAS AS RESOURCES MANAGEMENT, LOGISTICAL SUPPORT, AND COMBAT TRAINING. FORCE MODERNIZATION WILL CONTINUE, WITH EMPHASIS ON AERONAUTICAL MODERNIZATION, COMMUNICATIONS, AND VEHICLES. THAILAND WILL RECEIVE LESS THAN 4% OF THE TOTAL MILITARY SECURITY ASSISTANCE PROGRAM. 

OUR PROPOSED PROGRAMS IN INDONESIA, THE PHILIPPINES, AND MALAYSIA MAKE UP THE BALANCE OF THE EAST ASIA AND PACIFIC REGIONAL PROGRAMS WHICH CONSTITUTE NEARLY HALF OF OUR WORLDWIDE FY 1975 PROGRAMS. THE INCREASED SECURITY ASSISTANCE FUNDING REQUIREMENTS FOR THE REGION IN FY 1975 ARE NECESSARY TO OFFSET THE TRANSFER OF SUPPORT FOR LAOS FROM DOD FUNDING TO THE MILITARY ASSISTANCE PROGRAM, AND TO SUPPLY MINIMUM SUPPORT FOR THE CONTINUING HIGH LEVEL OF COMBAT ACTIVITY IN THE KHMER REPUBLIC. 

NEAR EAST AND SOUTH ASIA RECENT EVENTS HAVE MADE OBVIOUS OUR CONTINUING, STRONG SECURITY INTERESTS IN THE NEAR EAST AND SOUTH ASIA REGION. THESE INCLUDE NOT ONLY OUR INTEREST IN THE INDEPENDENCE AND SECURITY OF ISRAEL, IRAN, LEBANON, SAUDI ARABIA, AND JORDAN, AND SUPPORT FOR THE TRUCE NEGOTIATIONS, BUT ALSO INCLUDE OUR INTEREST IN THE IMPORTANT U.S. FACILITIES IN GREECE AND TURKEY. 

THE MILITARY CAPABILITIES OF BOTH TURKEY AND GREECE ARE ESSENTIAL FOR THE PROTECTION OF NATO'S SOUTHEASTERN FLANK, AND TO HELP CONTRIBUTE

3 1 3 1 

TO STABILITY IN THE EASTERN MEDITERRANEAN AREA. WE ARE PRESSING THE NATO NATIONS TO PROVIDE MORE MILITARY FORCES SO THAT THE RELATIVE SCALE OF AMERICAN CONTRIBUTION SHRINKS. BUT WE SHOULD NOT UNDERESTIMATE WHAT THEY ARE PRESENTLY DOING (OR OVERESTIMATE WHAT THEY ARE CAPABLE OF DOING). 

ALTHOUGH IMPROVEMENT IN THE TURKISH ECONOMY HAS ENABLED TURKEY TO UNDERTAKE THE FINANCING OF A SIGNIFICANT PORTION OF THE COSTS OF IMPROVING HER ARMED FORCES, A MIX OF U.S. MILITARY ASSISTANCE AND TURKISH RESOURCES WILL BE REQUIRED TO PROVIDE FISCAL BALANCE WHILE MAINTAINING THE MAXIMUM POSSIBLE EFFECTIVENESS OF HER FORCES IN BEING. THE INCREASING ABILITY OF THE TURKS TO UTILIZE THEIR OWN RESOURCES IS REFLECTED IN A GRADUAL TRANSITION FROM GRANT AID TO FOREIGN MILITARY SALES CREDIT TO THE EXTENT THAT WE NOW PROPOSE TO LEND HER MORE THAN WE GIVE HER THROUGH GRANT AID. TURKEY WILL BE THE FOURTH LARGEST PARTICIPANT IN BOTH THE GRANT AND FMS CREDIT PROGRAMS. SHE TOO WILL REPAY THE PRINCIPAL AND INTEREST ON THE SALES LOAN WE PROPOSE. 

THE DECISION OF THE GOVERNMENT OF GREECE IN JANUARY 1973 TO FOREGO FURTHER GRANT MILITARY AID REFLECTS HER INCREASED SELF-SUFFICIENCY. FOR- EIGN MILITARY SALES CREDIT IS, HOWEVER, REQUIRED TO PERMIT GREECE TO PURCHASE ESSENTIAL ITEMS TO MEET VALID MILITARY REQUIREMENTS. 

GREECE, THE EIGHTH LARGEST PARTICIPANT AND FORMERLY ONE OF THE LARGEST GRANT RECIPIENTS WILL RECEIVE ONLY FOREIGN MILITARY SALES CREDIT FUNDS, WHICH ARE ARE FULLY REIMBURSABLE TO THE U.S. 

THE SUPPORT OF ISRAEL'S EXISTENCE HAS BEEN A CARDINAL TENET OF AMERICAN POLICY IN THE MIDDLE EAST. IN PRACTICAL TERMS, THIS MEANS THE EXTENSION OF LARGE FOREIGN MILITARY SALES CREDITS AND GRANTS TO ASSURE THAT THE MILITARY BALANCE DOES NOT GO AGAINST ISRAEL. THE FY 1974 EMER- GENCY REQUEST FOR $2.2 BILLION IN MIXED GRANT AID AND CREDIT SALES PREVENTED AN UPSET IN THE MILITARY BALANCE AS A RESULT OF THE MOST RECENT WAR. THE REGULAR PROGRAM LEVEL OF $300 MILLION IN FOREIGN MIL-

ITARY SALES CREDITS IS AGAIN NEEDED IN FY 1975 TO ALLOW ISRAEL TO CON- TINUE TO PURCHASE THE MILITARY EQUIPMENT NECESSARY TO MAINTAIN THE MIL- ITARY BALANCE IN THE MIDDLE EAST, AND TO ENSURE THAT ISRAEL HAS THE CAPABILITY OF DEFENDING HERSELF. ALTHOUGH ISRAEL WILL BE THE SECOND LARGEST PARTICIPANT IN THE TOTAL MILITARY SECURITY ASSISTANCE PROGRAM, SHE WILL REPAY THE PRINCIPAL AND INTEREST ON THE CREDIT SALES PROGRAM 

PROPOSED.

JORDAN IS A MODERATE ARAB STATE WHICH MAINTAINS CLOSE TIES TO THE WEST. JORDAN HAS GENERALLY SUPPORTED A PEACEFUL SETTLEMENT OF THE ARAB-ISRAELI DISPUTE. JORDAN HAS DEMONSTRATED A WILLINGNESS TO USE HER ARMED FORCES TO COUNTER PENETRATION OF THE AREA BY RADICAL AND DISRUP- TIVE ELEMENTS. THE MILITARY ASSISTANCE PROPOSED FOR JORDAN WILL ASSIST HER TO MEET CRITICAL MODERNIZATION NEEDS AND HELP MAINTAIN THE COUNTRY AS A BULWARK AGAINST DISRUPTIVE ELEMENTS SEEKING TO ERODE THE NEGOTIATED PEACE SETTLEMENT IN THE MIDDLE EAST. 

LATIN AMERICA THE LARGEST PARTICIPANT IN THE SECURITY ASSISTANCE PROGRAM IN THE LATIN AMERICAN REGION, WHICH ROUNDS OUT THE TEN COUNTRIES CON- STITUTING 85% OF THE PROGRAM, IS BRAZIL. 

BRAZIL HAS A TRADITION OF INTERNATIONAL COOPERATION WITH THE UNITED STATES AND ITS ALLIES AND IS A POTENTIAL WORLD POWER. IT IS THEREFORE IN THE U.S. INTEREST TO REESTABLISH AND MAINTAIN THE TRADI- TIONAL U.S. ROLE AS BRAZIL'S PRIMARY SOURCE OF MILITARY EQUIPMENT; TO NURTURE THE FAVORABLE MILITARY-TO-MILITARY INFLUENCE COMPATIBLE WITH U.S. 

INTERESTS IN THE HEMISPHERE. BRAZIL WILL BE THE NINTH LARGEST PARTI- CIPANT, AND WILL RECEIVE FOREIGN MILITARY SALES CREDIT FUNDS AND GRANT MILITARY TRAINING, PRIMARILY IN THE UNITED STATES, UNDER GRANT AID. 

THE CREDIT FUNDS WILL, OF COURSE, BE REPAID TO THE UNITED STATES.

IN CONCLUSION, MR. CHAIRMAN, THE PROGRAMS THROUGH WHICH SECURITY ASSISTANCE SUPPORTS THE DEFENSE EFFORTS OF OTHER NATIONS ARE ESSENTIAL ELEMENTS OF U.S. FOREIGN POLICY AND MAKE A SIGNIFICANT AND SUB- STANTIAL CONTRIBUTION TO THE SUCCESSFUL IMPLEMENTATION OF THAT POLICY. 

THE SECURITY ASSISTANCE PROGRAMS HELP MAINTAIN A MILITARY BALANCE IN THE MIDDLE EAST CONDUCIVE TO RESTRAINT AND TO SUCCESS OF U.S. EFFORTS TO BRING ABOUT A LASTING PEACE IN THE AREA. THESE PROGRAMS ARE THE ESSEN- TIAL ELEMENT IN U.S. EFFORTS TO CREATE CONDITIONS REQUISITE FOR A TRUCE AND ULTIMATE SETTLEMENT IN THE KHMER REPUBLIC. AND, IN THE CASE OF LATIN AMERICA, SECURITY ASSISTANCE IS AN IMPORTANT FACTOR IN THE DEVELOP- MENT OF NEW RELATIONSHIPS AND AN IMPROVED SENSE OF COMMUNITY BETWEEN THE UNITED STATES AND OTHER NATIONS OF THE WESTERN HEMISPHERE. 

CONSIDERATIONS SUCH AS THESE EXPLAIN THE NEED FOR, AND WISDOM OF, CONTINUED USE OF SECURITY ASSISTANCE AS A CAREFULLY CONTROLLED AND SELECTIVELY APPLIED INSTRUMENT OF NATIONAL POLICY. 

IN THIS CONTEXT, I URGE THIS COMMITTEE'S SUPPORT FOR APPRO- PRIATIONS OF NEW OBLIGATIONAL AUTHORITY IN THE AMOUNT OF $985 MILLION AND TOTAL OBLIGATIONAL AUTHORITY FOR $1.024 BILLION, UPON WHICH THE FY 1975 MILITARY ASSISTANCE PROGRAM IS BASED. THESE FUNDS, WHICH REPRESENT APPROXIMATELY 1/20TH OF 1 PER CENT OF OUR ANNUAL GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT, AND APPROXIMATELY 1% OF OUR OWN DEFENSE BUDGET, ARE A REASONABLE PRICE TO PAY TO HELP STRENGTHEN THE SECURITY OF THE UNITED STATES AND HELP PROMOTE WORLD PEACE. 

I ALSO URGE THIS COMMITTEE'S SUPPORT FOR $555 MILLION IN NEW OBLIGATIONAL AUTHORITY TO BE USED FOR DIRECT CREDIT AND/OR GUARANTY OF COMMERCIAL CREDIT, AND A $872.5 MILLION TOTAL CREDIT PROGRAM DURING 

FY 1975.

INCREASE IN GRANT ASSISTANCE AUTHORIZATION 

Admiral PEET. I am happy to have the statement made a part of the record, Mr. Chairman. I might point out, if I may, however, that comparing the 1975 request with that of last year, we are really only asking for a slight increase in the grant assistance authorization over what was available last year. I arrive at that conclusion as follows:

The Congress appropriated $450 million in new obligational_authority for fiscal year 1974, and, adding to this amount the Laos program which will be transferred from the Defense budget to the military assistance program as of the beginning of fiscal year 1975, the $250 million drawdown authority used during fiscal year 1974, and the $69 million payback we received in 1974, the total 1974 funding is within 10 to 12 percent of the $985 million we are requesting for 1975.

It is not as big a difference as it would initially appear. 

Senator INOUYE. If I may, sir, I would like to proceed with the questioning. 

Admiral PEET. Yes, sir.

Senator INOUYE. My first question relates to section 506 of the Foreign Assistance Act. As you are well aware, under this section the 

President is authorized under certain conditions to drawndown DOD stocks up to a total of $250 million and transfer them through the grant military assistance program.

In acting on the fiscal year 1974 foreign assistance appropriation bill, the Senate knocked out this authority. However, the Senate position was dropped in conference on December 19, 1973, after the conference on the authorization bill reported that, "It is the intent of the committee of conference that up to $200 million of the emergency assistance requirements for Cambodia be furnished pursuant to the authority contained in this section." 

Just for the record, to what extent have you used the drawndown authority during fiscal 1974?

Admiral PEET. In 1974, we used the full $250 million. 

Senator INOUYE. What made you decide not to follow what most of us considered to be the clear intent of the conference report? 

Admiral PEET. I would like to ask advice of counsel. Our interpretation seems to be a little different. May I ask Mr. Forman? 

Senator INOUYE. Yes.

Mr. FORMAN. Mr. Chairman, we do not and did not regard the statement in the conference report as expressing an intention by the conferees that there be a limitation on the use of the drawndown authority for Cambodia during that fiscal year. That language was put in there in the context of a then-pending request by the administration for $200 million of emergency security assistance for Cambodia and as a separate authorization and appropriation. 

We had not asked for more. And rather than authorize that separate appropriation, the conferees simply indicated, in our judgment, that they would use $200 million of the $250 million available under the drawdown authority for that purpose, there being no indication that we are aware of that the Congress said no more than that could possibly be used.

The report merely reflected the factual situation that the President had asked for $200 million to meet MAP requirements foreseen in 

October of 1973.

Senator INOUYE. Well, our interpretation is different. First of all, I agree with your inference that this declaration of intention has no effect of law. We are clear about that. But it was hoped that the Defense Department would read this document and make the best effort to follow up. The language says, "It is the intent of the committee of conference that up to $200 million of emergency military assistance requirements for Cambodia be furnished pursuant to the authority contained in the section," which is 506. 

Mr. FORMAN. Senator, I did not state that we do not regard the conference committee report as not having the effect of law. We do try our best to carry out the intent of Congress, whether it be expressed in law or in a committee report.

What I said was we did not regard that expression of intent as being one which intended to impose a limitation on the use of a drawdown authority. 

Senator INOUYE. What did you think the intent was?

Mr. FORMAN. The intent was to tell us that in the judgment of the conferees it was better to use the drawdown authority to satisfy the then-existing request of the President for a special authorization and a special appropriation in the amount of $200 million. That was all we had asked for, and all the conferees were saying there was in lieu of having special authorization and appropriation, use the drawdown authority for the $200 million you have requested. 

The conferees certainly did not state in the report that you cannot exceed that $200 million, and there is nothing on the floor of the Congress or anywhere else which indicates that there was such intent. 

Senator INOUYE. Next time we will make it much more abundantly clear, sir.

DOD REIMBURSEMENT ANTICIPATED 

Has the Department anticipated reimbursement of these costs in the 

1975 request of $985 million?

Admiral PEET. We know we need to make reimbursement, but the administration has not decided as to how and when we are going to request funds for that reimbursement. 

Senator INOUYE. I suppose it comes in on a supplemental? 

Admiral PEET. That is certainly possible, Mr. Chairman.

Senator INOUYE. If it doesn't come through on the supplemental, how would you fund that?

Admiral PEET. There is also the possibility that it could go into next year's budget, or it may be that we would have to absorb it. 

Senator INOUYE. What was that last expression?

Admiral PEET. That we would have to absorb it and not ask funds for reimbursement. There are many different possibilities, Mr. Chairman. I don't know which one will be chosen by the administration. 

Senator INOUYE. Would I be correct to assume that you will be requesting an additional $250 million? 

Admiral PEET. I am not sure that is a good assumption.

Senator INOUYE. The foreign military sales credit program for fiscal 1975 proposes an obligation of $353 million guaranteed, $352.8

million in privately financed credit sales. Legislative requirements have established 25 percent as the desired reserve level for DOD guaranteed private financing.

Why are fiscal 1975 obligations for guaranteed private financing set at 10 percent?

Mr. FORMAN. The reason for that, sir, is that we have proposed in the authorizing bill which is now pending before the Foreign Affairs and Foreign Relations Committees that the statutory requirement of the 25-percent reserve be lowered to a 10-percent reserve, and therefore the budgetary figures reflect that request for change in the authorization language.

Senator INOUYE. Has that authorization bill cleared either one of the Houses?

Mr. FORMAN. No, sir; the bill is still pending in both committees. 

Senator INOUYE. Have you had hearings on it?

Mr. FORMAN. We have had hearings on the bills, but I don't- 

Admiral PEET. No, not specifically on that point.

Senator INOUYE. And you just assume that it is going to become law. 

Admiral PEET. Yes, sir; we did make that assumption in formulating the program. 

Senator INOUYE. What is the reason for lowering this? Is it to increase the volume of commercial credit sales underwritten by DOD?

Mr. FORMAN. No, sir; the reason for the decrease in the estimate is a decision by the Office of Management and Budget that, in view of our excellent history of never having a default under the guarantee program, the 25-percent reserve was unnecessarily high and that it could safely be reduced to 10 percent.

It is my recollection that the General Accounting Office some time ago also expressed the same conclusion. 

Senator INOUYE. If the authorization bill doesn't pass, what do you propose that the Appropriations Committee do about this arrangement here?

Mr. FORMAN. Well, if it doesn't pass, assuming the Congress however does approve the program ceiling that we have presented to the Congress, then we would need a budget increase of $52.9 million to accomplish the same program. 

Admiral PEET. The whole credit program, Mr. Chairman, has amounted to $5.1 billion. The arrearages as of March 31 of this year were only around $1 million and they are being negotiated right now. 

U.S. ECONOMIC INTERESTS CONSIDERED 

Senator INOUYE. In negotiating these sales, has our Government taken into consideration the economic interests of our country? 

Admiral PEET. I believe we have, sir. 

Senator INOUYE. What part does this consideration play in the full negotiation?

Admiral PEET. It plays a very important part in policy decisions by State, and I am sure Mr. Vest could amplify that. 

Senator INOUYE. What sort of guidance do you receive from DOD in this regard? Is there any policy, any policy document?

Admiral PEET. You have to consider many factors in connection with each sale. State determines the policies and decides whether or

not there will be a program for a particular country and the amount of each program. Sales are approved by State in one form or another by granting the export license or the proposed sale of particular equipment to a given country.

Senator INOUYE. I believe I can then safely assume that considering the immensity of the dollar amount involved and the significance in foreign policy, that this matter has been set down in writing in some sort of directive? 

Admiral PEET. Yes; as far as the Defense Deparmtent is concerned.

I have published a manual that does set forth the policies. I would like to emphasize that we are not promoting sales. At least the organization for which I am responsible is not promoting sales. 

We are available to answer questions and give out information to help our manufacturers make sales around the world, but we don't have a promotion policy as France and some of the other countries do.

Senator INOUYE. May we have a copy of this DOD directive? We would like to make that part of the record. 

Admiral PEET. Yes, sir.

December 20, 1972# NUMBER 5132. 3 

SUBJECT 

ASD (ISA) 

Department of Defense Directive Department of Defense Policy and Responsibilities Relating to Security Assistance 

Refs.: (a) DoD Directive 5132.3 "DoD Policy and Responsibilities Relating to Military Assistance," July 8, 1963 (hereby cancelled) I.

II. 

(b) through (p) (See enclosure 1)

PURPOSE AND APPLICABILITY A. This Directive establishes Department of Defense policy for carrying out the responsibilities of the Secretary of Defense under the Foreign Assist ance Act of 1961, as amended (hereinafter referred to as "the FAA") (reference (b)), the Foreign Military Sales Act, as amended (hereinafter referred to as "the FMSA") (reference (c)), related statutory authorities, and Executive Orders and Directives relating to the administration of security assistance.

B. The provisions of this Directive apply to the Office of the Secretary of Defense, Military Departments,

Joint Chiefs of Staff, Defense Agencies, Unified and 

Specified Commands, etc., (hereinafter referred to collectively as "DoD Components").

DEFINITIONS 

As used herein, the following definitions apply: A.

Defense Articles and Defense Services. (See Section 

644, reference (b)). 

B. Foreign Military Sales (FMS) refers to sales of defense articles and services to foreign governments and international organizations under authority of the FMSA or successor legislation. 

First amendment (Ch 1, May 24, 1974)

III. 

C.

D. E. F.

Military Assistance Advisory Group (MAAG) 

encompasses Joint U.S.

Military Advisory Groups, Military Missions, Military Advisory Groups, U.S. 

Military Groups and U.S. Military Representatives or other military organizations exercising responsibility at-the-government-level for securi- * ty assistance and other related DOD matters with the host government-to-which-they-are-accredited country's military establishment. Defense Attache 

System personnel will be included when assigned to Defense Attache Offices specifically designated by the Secretary of Defense to carry out security assistance responsibilities.

Military Assistance Program (MAP) refers to transfers of defense articles and services to foreign governments and international organizations as grant aid and loans under authority of the FAA or successor legislation.

Security Assistance includes all DOD activities carried out under the FAA, the FMSA, and related statutory authorities.

Security Supporting Assistance includes funds used to finance imports of commodities, capital, or technical assistance, provided either as a grant or loan in accordance with terms of a bilateral or multilateral agreement, to enable a recipient to devote more of its own resources to security purposes than it otherwise could do without serious economic or political consequences.

POLICY 

A. Security assistance shall be administered in accordance with the (1) provisions of the FAA (reference (b)), and the FMSA (reference (c)), and (2) subject to the limitations of the foreign policy and national security objectives of the U.S. lt shall support and be in consonance with 

U.S. military strategic plans and objectives and be guided by the policy and planning guidance issued by the Secretary of Defense, and by guidance issued by the Secretary of State.

B. The development of regional defense arrangements and self-support capabilities suitable for multinational participation shall be encouraged. 

C. There will be close coordination between U.S. military force planning and security assistance planning under the "Total Force" concept at all levels in the Department of 

Defense. 

D. The fundamental responsibility of foreign governments to determine the nature of their own security interests and the path of their own progress shall be recognized. U.S. advisory assistance and training provided to less developed countries will emphasize the development of a capability

to manage military resources with particular emphasis on planning, programming and budgeting activities at the national level. 

E. Security assistance plans and programs shall take into consideration the economic capabilities of the specific foreign country concerned and the support provided by third countries. If economic considerations are expected to restrict the attainment of needed military strength, security supporting assistance will be sought from other U.S. Government agencies as may be appropriate. 

F. The cost to the U.S. and allied/friendly countries of equipping, operating and maintaining recipient countries' military forces will be held to a minimum. Except for overriding military considerations, the buildup of military forces which the recipient country cannot ultimately support will be discouraged. G.

Consistent with other relevant considerations, grant aid (MAP) material assistance shall be reduced and terminated to any country having sufficient economic capability to enable it to equip and maintain its military forces at adequate strength without undue economic burden. Country plans and programs which facilitate the orderly phase-out of grant aid (MAP) material assistance will be encouraged and supported. 

H. To the extent practicable and consistent with overall security assistance objectives, allied/friendly countries will be encouraged to acquire U.S. defense articles (including excess defense articles) and services through purchase rather than grant aid. 

I. Direct procurement of U.S. defense articles and services from U.S. firms and manufacturers is preferred to procurement from the U.S. Government. DoD elements associated with security assistance will cooperate with and assist representatives of U.S. firms in the sale of U.S. defense articles and services to meet valid country requirements, consistent with over-all U.S. foreign policy and national security objectives. J.

In accordance with those same policy objectives, the development of the capability to counter insurgency and to provide for internal stability and security will be encouraged in less developed friendly countries. 

K. To the extent feasible, the use of indigenous military forces on activities helpful to the economic development of less developed friendly countries shall be encouraged, provided that such participation does not significantly detract from the capability of the forces to perform essential military missions. 

L. Security assistance shall be implemented in such a manner as to mitigate adverse effects on the U.S. international balance of payments.

IV. 

M. No commitment involving future U.S. programs, performance, or the availability of U.S. resources shall be made without specific prior approval of the Secretary of Defense in accordance with DoD Directive 2100.3, reference (d).

N. The selection and training of U.S. personnel engaged in security assistance activities will receive special attention. The standards, procedures, and responsibilities within DoD for the selection and training of security assistance personnel will be in accordance with the provisions of DoD Directive 2000.10, reference (e), and DoD 

Directive C-5105.32, reference (f). 

0. Material being procured or stocked specifically for MAP and FMS may be diverted to meet higher priority foreign requirements or urgent needs of U.S. forces with the prior concurrence of the Director, Defense Security Assistance Agency (DSAA). 

P. The security classification of security assistance information and the disclosure and safeguarding thereof shall be consistent with DoD Information Security Program Regulation 

5200.1-R, reference (g), and DoD Directive 5230.11, reference (h).

FUNCTIONS 

Subject to the direction, authority and control of the Secretary of Defense, functions with respect to security assistance are assigned as set forth herein. 

A. The Assistant Secretary of Defense (International Security Affairs) shall act for the Secretary of Defense in security assistance matters. In carrying out this responsibility the ASD(ISA) will: 1. 2. 

Serve as the principal DoD point of contact, representative, and policy spokesman relative to security assistance.

Coordinate and develop security assistance policy and over-all planning guidance for preparation of security assistance plans and programs. 

3. Coordinate the activities of DoD components related to security assistance matters. 

4. Develop comprehensive DoD security assistance plans and programs, including priorities, for approval by the Secretary of Defense. 

5. Provide the Director, DSAA, policy direction and primary staff supervision. 

6. Insure, through coordination with the ASD (Comptroller) that the security assistance program is integrated within the DoD Planning, Programming and Budgeting 

System (PPBS) (DoD Instruction 7045.7, reference (i)).

7. Obtain Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) comment and recommendation on security assistance matters including (but not limited to) the monetary value, development, preparation, refinement, and control of policy, plans, and programs to insure that the security assistance program supports and is in consonance with U.S. military strategic plans and objectives. 

8. Prepare and support before the Congress the annual request for security assistance legislation and funds in conjunction with other DoD components, as appropriate. 9. 

Review and approve recommendations of the Joint Chiefs of Staff pertaining to Terms of Reference for Chiefs of MAAGS, and to security assistance organizational and manpower requirements for MAAGS under Unified Commands. 

10. Approve on behalf of the Secretary of Defense the appointment of Chiefs of MAAGS, tour extensions or curtailments as recommended by the JCS. 

11. Review and approve recommendations of the JCS pertaining to the Military Service designation of the 

Chiefs of MAAGS. 

12. Provide security assistance policy guidance, as appropriate, to components of the DoD and to DoD representatives on U.S. missions and to international organizations and conferences. 13. 14. 15.

In conjunction with other agencies, maintain liaison with other governments which are planning security assistance to third countries in order to avoid duplication of effort and achieve maximum mutual effectiveness of programs.

Insure that the DoD security assistance effort is accomplished in the most effective and efficient manner possible.

Exercise those responsibilities and authorities assigned the ASD(ISA) in DoD Directive 5105.38, reference (j), and Secretary of Defense Memorandum, reference (k). 

16. Serve as the Chairman of the Defense Security Assist ance Council (DSAC) in accordance with DoD Directive 

5105.38, reference (j). 

17. Collaborate with the Director, Defense Intelligence

Agency, to develop arrangements to perform security assistance functions where such are assigned to attaches. 

18. Provide policy guidance, as appropriate, to the Director,

DSAA when material being produced or stocked specifically for MAP and FMS is being considered for diversion to meet higher priority foreign requirements.

B. The Director, Defense Security Assistance Agency (DSAA) 

is responsible for directing, administering, and supervising, within the policies established by the ASD(ISA), approved security assistance plans and programs. The 

Director, DSAA will perform functions in accordance with provisions of DoD Directive 5105.38, reference (j).

The Assistant Secretary of Defense (Comptroller) will establish policies and procedures involving financial management, fiscal matters, accounting, pricing, auditing, budgeting, statistical reporting, the Five-Year 

Defense Program and International Balance of Payments. 

Security assistance activities involving these functions will be in accordance with the policies and procedures established by the Assistant Secretary of Defense (Comptroller).

D. The Assistant Secretary of Defense (Installations and 

Logistics) will assure that DoD logistical policy and procedures provide for the most effective interface and integration with security assistance policy and planning. 

He will provide such technical assistance to the ASD(ISA) and Director, DSAA as necessary to accomplish the objectives of the security assistance program. He will provide recommended courses of action to the Secretary of Defense in cases where withdrawals and diversions from U.S. forces for MAP and FMS would significantly impair their operational readiness. .

E. The Defense Security Assistance Council (DSAC) will perform security assistance functions in accordance with provisions of DoD Directive 5105.38, reference (j).

F. Other Officials of the Office of the Secretary of Defense. 

The Director of Defense Research and Engineering; other Assistant Secretaries of Defense; the General Counsel of the DoD; Assistants to the Secretary of Defense; the

Director, Defense Supply Agency; the Director, Defense 

Advanced Research Projects Agency;

and the Director, Defense Intelligence Agency shall provide within the scope of their assigned functions, appropriate assistance as requested by the ASD(ISA) and the Director, DSAA with respect to security assistance.

G. The Secretaries of the Military Departments will serve as advisors to the Secretary of Defense on all matters of security assistance impacting on, or related to, their Department and will act for the Secretary of Defense where responsibility for actions is delegated. In carrying out this responsibility, the Secretaries will: 

1. Provide to the Secretary of Defense security assist ance policy, planning and programming recommendations considered appropriate and necessary to insure the successful conduct of security assistance, including its interface with and support of Military Department plans, programs and objectives. 34-192 O - 74 - 72

2. Provide data pertaining to price, source, availability and lead time for use in developing and reviewing security assistance programs, including FMS cases. 

3. Provide to elements of the Office of the Secretary of 

Defense, JCS, Unified Commands, and MAAGS, as appropriate, technical military advice as to weapons systems, tactics and doctrine, training, and pertinent logistic support. 

4. Conduct training and procure and deliver defense articles and services included in approved programs. 5.

Coordinate and establish delivery schedules and necessary internal procedures for follow-up, expediting, and related actions during implementation of approved programs. 

6. Provide such other technical assistance and facilities to elements of the Office of the Secretary of Defense as necessary to promote efficiency and economy in security assistance matters.

Within policies and criteria established by ASD(ISA), and under direction of Director, DSAA for approved programs, make sales of defense articles and services to eligible countries and international organizations. 

8. Integrate procurement for security assistance with military service procurement programs in accordance with policy guidance provided by ASD(I&L). 

9. Maintain appropriate records and furnish prescribed reports within the scope of their responsibilities. 

10. Assure that information with respect to purchases proposed to be made for the military assistance programs is made available, as far in advance as possible, to suppliers in the U.S. and, particularly, to small independent enterprises in accordance with Section 602 of the FAA, reference (b). 

11. Obtain from Unified Commands and MAAGs, as appropriate, such data as may be needed to carry out assigned responsibilities. 

12. With respect to the area or areas assigned, be responsible for providing administrative support needed to carry out security assistance functions, subject to the direction and policy guidance of the ASD(ISA). 13.

In accordance with approved tables of distribution and other authorizations, directives, and requests, recommend and provide qualified military personnel to carry out security assistance assignments. 

14. Provide estimates of MAP and FMS funding requirements, technical advice, and recommend changes when appropriate.

H. 

15. Assist the ASD(ISA) and the Director, DSAA, as requested, in government-to-government or inter-departmental discussions involving security assistance policies, plans and programs. 

16. Assist the ASD(ISA) and the Director, DSAA, as requested, in government-to-government negotiations for the sale of military equipment or services. 

17. Advise U.S. firms regarding the sale of U.S. defense articles and services to meet potential foreign country valid requirements, keeping MAAGS, Unified Commands, JCS, and DSAA informed. 

18. Assist the ASD(ISA), ASD(I&L) and Director, DSAA in developing and negotiating new or revised bilateral or multilateral agreements that commit the resources of the Military Department.

The Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) will provide the Secretary of Defense with military advice on security assistance matters, and will: 

1. Coordinate U.S. military force planning and security assistance planning under the "Total Force" concept. 

Identify tradeoffs as appropriate. 

2. Recommend military force objectives for allies or potential allies, general strategic priorities, tasks, and requirements for force development on a country and regional basis. 

3. Participate in planning, programming, and execution of security assistance to insure that it is in consonance with approved U.S. strategic concepts and plans by country, region and worldwide. 

4. Analyze and make recommendations concerning security assistance plans and programs submitted to the ASD(ISA) by the Commanders of Unified Commands. 5. 6. 

Recommend to the Secretary of Defense for approval

Terms of Reference for Chiefs of MAAGs and security assistance organizational and manpower requirements for MAAGS under Unified Commands. 

Recommend to the Secretary of Defense for approval the designation of Military Services responsible to furnish Chiefs of MAAGS. 

7. Recommend to the Secretary of Defense for approval individuals nominated as Chiefs of MAAGS or recommended for tour extension or curtailment. 

8. Conduct evaluations of the effectiveness of security assistance from the viewpoint of the security inter-

I. ests of the U.S. and conformance with security assistance planning/programming objectives as approved by ASD(ISA). 

9. Assign Force/Activity Designator to determine priorities in the allocation of materiel and equipment among recipient nations and between recipient nations and the U.S. Armed Forces within guidelines estab lished by the Office of the Secretary of Defense (DoD 

Directive. 4410.6, reference (1)). Recommend priorities of allocation of materiel and equipment when competing requirements cannot be resolved. 10. 

Recommend the selection, introduction, redistribution, and/or standardization of weapons systems for security assistance recipients.

Command and supervise the activities of the MAAGS in their respective areas, and provide necessary technical assistance and administrative support.

7. Coordinate offshore security assistance procurement activities carried out by their respective subordinate procuring agencies, including coordination, as appropriate, with the Chiefs of the U.S. Diplomatic Missions in the country concerned. 8.

In the development of security assistance plans and programs, obtain and consider recommendations of other affected Unified and Specified Commands.
