RELATIONSHIPS 

A. Pursuant to DoD Directive 5132.2, reference (n), the ASD(ISA) serves as the principal staff assistant to the Secretary of Defense in the functional field of international security; as one part of this larger responsibility, he coordinates and provides policy direction for the security assistance activities of DoD components. B. C. D. E. 

Pursuant to DoD Directive 5105.38, reference (j), the Director,

DSAA, serves under the direction, authority, and control of the Secretary of Defense, with policy direction and primary staff supervision by the ASD(ISA). The Director, DSAA, is also designated Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for

Security Assistance to the ASD (ISA), as an additional duty. 

In addition to the relationship of the MAAG to the Unified Command and the responsibilities contained in IV J, above, the Chief of the MAAG is under the generat overall supervision of the Chief of the U.S. Diplomatic 

Mission to the extent provided by law and in accordance with Executive-Orders the President's letter, reference (p), on the responsibilities of the Chiefs of Diplomatic Missions and such other instructions as the President may from time to time promulgate. As Chief of a separate element of the U.S. Diplomatic Mission he will: 

(1). Coordinate MAAG activities with other U.S. Govern ment agencies represented in the U.S. Diplomatic 

Mission which are concerned with the planning and execution of Foreign Assistance; (2) Refer unresolved differences between the Chief of the U.S. Diplomatic 

Mission and the Chief of the MAAG through the Commander of the Unified Command to the Secretary of Defense/JCS. 

The channel of communication with Unified and Specified Commands on matters relating to the implementation of the approved security assistance program shall be directly between those commands and the DSAA. The DSAA is authorized, in such matters, to communicate directly with Commanders of Unified and Specified Commands and with the Chiefs of MAAGS. All DSAA directives and communications to such commands, the Military Departments, and the MAAGS which pertain to security assistance affairs that have military operational, or policy implications shall be coordinated with the JCS, or ASD (ISA), respectively. Conversely, all JCS directives and communications to Unified and Specified

Commands, the Military Departments, or the MAAGS, which pertain to security assistance affairs, shall be coordinated with ASD (ISA).

Direct communication between the MAAGS and ASD (ISA), or 

DSAA for implementation of approved programs, is authorized for security assistance matters provided that: (1) The coordination requirements set forth in

Section V, C and D above are met; and (2) The policy, planning and programming responsibilities of the Commander of the Unified Command are not involved and

Direct communication is authorized between the MAAGS/ 

Service Sections of the MAAGS, Military Departments and

Use of the term "MAAG" in this Directive does not alter current command relationships between the Director, Defense Intelligence Agency and the Defense Attaches who report to Commanders of Unified Commands on security assistance matters only.

For the purpose of security assistance activities and coordination of MAAG activities only, the area of 

USCINCSO includes all of Central America, South America,

Mexico, and the islands of the Caribbean; the area of 

USCINCEUR includes the Mediterranean Sea and littoral, Middle East and eastern border of Iran, Red Sea and 

Persian Gulf and Africa South of the Sahara; and, the area of CINCPAC includes Japan, Republic of Korea, countries in Southeast Asia and South Asia and islands in assigned water areas. 

I. Existing responsibilities of Commanders of Unified 

Commands published by the JCS and in DoD Directive 

5100.1, reference (o), not related to security assistance shall not be affected by this Directive. 

TERMS OF REFERENCE 

Terms of Reference will be developed for each MAAG. They will be tailored to reflect only the minimum essential guidance to each MAAG; e.g., Mission, Command Relationships, Organization, Administration (to include release of classified information), Logistical Support, and, Responsibilities and Functions. As roles and requirements change for a given MAAG, additions or deletions, as required, will be made to the Terms of Reference.

CANCELLATION 

Reference (a) is superseded and hereby cancelled.

VIII. EFFECTIVE DATE 

This Directive is effective immediately. 

Kenneth Rush

Deputy Secretary of Defense

U.S. "HAWKING" OF MILITARY EQUIPMENT 

Senator INOUYE. Now you have just said you don't go out and sell; you just answer questions.

Admiral PEET. Let me make that clear. I don't say that our manufacturers and others don't sell. They have salesmen all over the world. 

We work with them. We will assist them. We will answer queries that come to the Embassy about the military equipment available in this country; but as a Government, we are not out hawking this equipment. 

Senator INOUYE. I would like to bring to your attention the testimony of Secretary Schlesinger of June 25. It appears on pages 1102 and 1103 of the hearings. 

My question: "And the Saudi Arabians will now purchase F-4 

Phantoms, I gather? "Secretary SCHLESINGER: We have indicated a willingness to sell 

F-4's to the Saudis. They have not requested them."

Admiral PEET. That is true, Mr. Chairman. That happened about the middle of last year. 

Senator INOUYE. This is not hawking it?

Admiral PEET. I don't think it is. The Saudi Arabians asked us if we would be willing to sell them F-4 aircraft. This government decided on an affirmative answer. Since then, they have not come to us with any request for purchase; and we are not pushing it one way or the other.

Senator INOUYE. You are just telling them that it is available. 

Admiral PEET. Yes, sir, in response to their request.

Senator INOUYE. The committee has been informed that several countries receiving FMS credit sales are considerably in arrears in their debt payments contrary to what you have just indicated, and some of them for more than 1 year.

What is DOD's policy on contract and credit sales of countries which are delinquent on prior credit agreements?

Admiral PEET. We make every effort to correct that situation; and, when we can't, I am very fortunate in being able to turn the matter over to State. The Embassies are actively engaged in collecting those bills.

As I indicated earlier, Mr. Chairman, we are talking about arrearages that represent less than one-tenth of 1 percent, BILLING NEGOTIATIONS WITH IRAN, ITALY AND JORDAN 

Senator INOUYE. I notice that Iran is about $1 million, Italy is over $160.000 and Jordan is $94,000. 

Admiral PEET. There is a long story associated with each of those. 

Either they claim they don't owe it or there is uncertainty as to what the interest was, that type of thing. We are negotiating, and and I would be glad to provide details on any particular case. 

Mr. FORMAN. Mr. Chairman, the figures that you just referred to are not arrearages on credit transactions, they are on regular cash. billings which arise from a variety of reasons, as Admiral Peet has said, including arguments about discrepancies in billing, questions as to whether goods that were purchased actually arrived, as to whether they are damaged and so forth.

Senator INOUYE. May we have the reasons for these three countries, Iran, Italy, and Jordan?

Admiral PEET. Yes, sir, we will provide it for the record. 

 DEBT ARREARAGES-FMS CASH SALES 

Jordan.-The arrearage of $94 thousand has been reduced to $22 thousand as of 30 June 1974. This arrearage has been largely due to administrative problems. 

Most recently, a discrepancy claim of $25 thousand has been submitted by Jordan which the Department of the Army will honor. This action will not only liquidate the debt, but will also result in a $3 thousand credit to the Jordan 

Trust Fund. 

Italy. The arrearage of $166 thousand has been reduced to $158 thousand as of 30 June 1974. This arrearage involves several FMS cases. The Department of the Army has recommended to the Italian Government that $68 thousand available in their trust fund which is not specifically earmarked for other contracts be applied to this debt. Approval of such action will reduce the arrearage to $90 thousand. The Army will continue their efforts to collect the remaining balance on a case-by-case basis via the MAAG. 

Iran. The arrearage of $940 thousand has been reduced to $491 thousand as of 30 June 1974. The remaining debt appears to be due to administrative problems within the Iranian Government. Most recently, the Department of the Army solicited assistance from the MAAG in obtaining settlement of this debt. MAAG response of 10 July 1974 indicated they had directly approached several elements of the Iranian Government concerning this arrearage and that an early response should be forthcoming. In addition, and by separate action, the Army billing agency has recommended to the Iranian Government that $387 thousand available in their trust fund not specifically earmarked for other contracts be applied to this debt. Approval of that action would further reduce the arrearage to $104 thousand.

STATUS OF IRAN 

Senator INOUYE. Is it true that Iran is no longer a recipient of foreign military sales credit?

Admiral PEET. Yes, sir, that is true. She also used to be a grant recipient.

Senator INOUYE. In fiscal year 1973 the U.S. Export-Import Bank authorized two credits each for 1 million for exports of U.S. military goods and services in conjunction with the Department of Defense. 

Both of these were for Iran.

During the first half of fiscal year 1974 one direct credit for $200 million was also authorized in exports of defense articles and services to Iran.

In short, Iran borrows money from one U.S. Government institution, then proceeds to use that money for the purchase of military items from another U.S. Government agency. If there is a significant difference between this and foreign military credit sales, the committee would like to know more about it. Can you enlighten us?

Admiral PEET. Yes, sir. The Export-Import Bank has been authorizing loans to Iran for a number of years. This was before the oil crisis of last year. In the particular case you mention, my office did put the Iranians in touch with the Export-Import Bank. The 

Export-Import Bank is authorized to make loans to developed countries for that purpose. I believe Iran is, currently negotiating with the Bank to close out those loans. 

Senator INOUYE. What is the purpose of giving such a wealthy country as Iran-and Iran did not become wealthy just 12 months ago-such favorable lending terms?

Admiral PEET. That is a question for the Export-Import Bank to answer, but I am sure they are doing it in accordance with their authority.

Senator INOUYE. But I gather that the Department of Defense is consulted on these loans.

Admiral PEET. Not as far as the terms of the loan or anything of that sort is concerned. We knew at the time-that is before the oil crisis that Iran was interested in borrowing some money. The Export-Import Bank was a legitimate source. 

Senator INOUYE. Are you aware if other oil rich nations are receiving similar credits?

Admiral PEET. No, I am not. In fact, I don't believe my office has been working with the Export-Import Bank on any others. Certainly not to my knowledge.

REDUCTION IN MAAG'S AND MIL GROUPS 

Senator INOUYE. The United States presently provides military assistance in the form of MAAG or MIL groups to a number of developed or oil-rich countries. The cost of operating these detachments places a drain on military assistance to more needy countries. Why are these military detachments not totally financed by the host countries? 

Admiral PEET. We are conducting extensive review of that very matter now, Mr. Chairman, and we are transferring more of them to funding by the host countries. However, each country is a little bit different; and there is a long history involved. I think I am making progress in cutting these numbers back, but what I find for the most part is that the Ambassador wants to retain these groups. He thinks they are in the best interests of the United States. 

Our commanders in chief in the area find them very useful. The host countries themselves resist any reduction in this type of American presence. The consensus is almost overwhelmingly in favor of maintaining these groups, Mr. Chairman; and I have a devil of a time cutting them back.

Senator INOUYE. It has been increased by 14 percent according to your fiscal 1975 presentation.

Admiral PEET. The numbers? I believe I have different figures for totals of MAAG personnel.

Senator INOUYE. Worldwide? 

Admiral PEET. On page 11 of the congressional presentation document, there is a summary. The totals, which are on page 12, show a total of 2,351 military in 1973 and an estimate for 1975 of around 2,100. 

Senator INOUYE. Why wasn't Argentina cut out?

Admiral PEET. A significant reduction is under active consideration right now. Might I provide the information on that for the record, Mr. Chairman? 

 REDUCTIONS IN MAAG PERSONNEL 

We cannot cut out the USMILGP in Argentina because of our continuing responsibilities for planning, administering and managing the sizable FMS Credit Sales Program we have there. However, we have just recently made significant reductions in the number of U.S. personnel assigned to carry out

these functions. Currently, there are only 23 U.S. personnel assigned to the 

MILGP in Argentina with further reductions to 20 projected by 31 July. This represents a 30% cut in the size of the MILGP this year. [Deleted.] We will reexamine the manning of the MILGP to assure that the number of personnel is in consonance with the Security Assistance Program we have with the Government of Argentina. [Information deleted was classified and retained in the Committee files.] 

MAAG'S IN IRAN AND SAUDI ARABIA 

Senator INOUYE. We have an active program in Iran and Saudi 

Arabia and the most conservative estimates seem to indicate that by the end of this calendar year the Persian Gulf oil-producing countries will make $105 billion more than they did last year. Assuming that they have the most expensive and most ambitious programs for the industrial development and military expansion, they will still have about $60 billion in surplus to spend. 

When it comes to foreign reserve, that far exceeds that of the United States. 

Admiral PEET. Yes, sir.

Senator INOUYE. And we are still insisting that we should pay their load?

Admiral PEET. No; we are not. I think we need to understand the whole story here. 

Senator INOUYE. I would like to know it.

Admiral PEET. The history and so on. For example, Iran this current year bought something in the neighborhood of $4 billion worth of equipment from the United States. Included in that $4 billion charge there was some 2-percent administrative cost, as is the case in practically all of the contracts. I would say that Iran is being charged for the services we are providing. 

Senator INOUYE. You have a $7.3 million MAAG in Iran. 

Admiral PEET. I am sorry 7?

Senator INOUYE. This is for your military. It will cost you $7,369,000.

Admiral PEET. Yes, sir. There is a history of MAAG presence in 

Iran. Some of the costs are provided by assistance in kind and that sort of thing, but it is quite true we do finance a portion of the MAAG cost in that country.

Senator INOUYE. We are constantly called upon, cajoled, and otherwise asked to cut down the cost of government. Sometimes it is rather difficult to explain to our constituents why we must pick up a tab for a small amount admittedly, $7 million, to a country that will have billions in surplus not knowing what to do with it. 

Admiral PEET. Mr. Chairman, I understand your point, but I would like to look at the other side as well. 

The 2-percent administrative charges which are in our sales contracts are not to cover the costs of operating the MAAG's. However, the operating costs of the MAAG in Iran are partially offset by the aid in kind which is provided by Iran. The 2-percent charge has proved to be satisfactory to defray the expense of administering our sales contracts. 

Senator INOUYE. Frankly, I think that 2 percent is not enough from the management standpoint. I think you should check with Mr. Roy

Ash who is the management expert. He will tell you if you want some-

thing out of that which is fair to the United States, it should be at least double that.

Admiral PEET. Mr. Chairman, it is not only the administrative charges. We also recoup nonrecurring R. & D. costs and things of that sort in these sales.

STANDARDS EMPLOYED FOR FMS 

Senator INOUYE. Part of your primary role as manager is to assure that the security assistance program is "in accordance with applicable provisions of the Foreign Assistance and Foreign Military Sales Act." 

Section 1 of the Foreign Military Sales Act restricts military sales to those consistent with the "extent and character of the military requirement of the recipient country." 

What objective standards are employed to determine that purchasing country's requirement? For example, it has been announced that Iran is buying a substantial number of F-14 aircraft. How does the Department of Defense determine that this type of aircraft is needed and in what quantity?

Admiral PEET. I am not sure it is the role of the Department of 

Defense to determine that that specific type of aircraft is needed and the exact quantity. That is up to the Iranians themselves. 

Senator INOUYE. Well, section 1 says that your sales are restricted to those which are consistent with the extent and character of the military requirements of the recipient countries. 

Admiral PEET. Yes, sir. When they make a request, we do evaluate it to make sure that it is consistent with the best interests of the United States and in conformance with our policies. It was decided that it was appropriate to sell the F-14 to Iran.

There are other cases, however, in which we may decide it is not appropriate; and we don't make the requested sale. 

Senator INOUYE. What sort of sales, for example?

CONDITIONS OF SALES OF MILITARY WEAPONS 

Admiral PEET. I would like to provide the answer for the record rather than go any further into detail here. 

Senator INOUYE. Is it classified? 

Admiral PEET. Yes, sir. [The information furnished was classified and retained in the committee files.]

MID-EAST ARMS RACE

MAP PROGRAM FOR ETHIOPIA 

Senator INOUYE. To what extent is the $11.3 million MAP program proposed for Ethiopia related to U.S. use of certain facilities in that country? 

Admiral PEET. There is a partial relationship, sir.

Senator INOUYE. Is it not true that the need for this facility has been greatly diminished and in fact has been largely phased out as of last month?

Admiral PEET. That is true. The importance of that facility has diminished.

Senator INOUYE. Then why can't you reduce the MAP program accordingly when you have almost nothing there? If the rationale is for the use of certain facilities and if the facilities are almost wiped out, what is the reason for maintaining this MAP program? 

Admiral PEET. That is not the only reason, Mr. Chairman. There are many other reasons for continuing our relationship with Ethiopia which are determined and best addressed by the Department of State. 

Mr. VEST. Sir, Ethiopia has been the major center of moderation in a geographically vital area sitting astride oil lines, the Soviet supported base in Somalia and the center for the various organs of African unity which have their headquarters there. 

The Ethiopians see themselves with an undecided border with Somalia, with a buildup from the Soviets, and they have asked us to support them, help them in this particular critical period. We have been doing so.

Senator INOUYE. There are many of us who are convinced that 

Ethiopia is in grave need of economic and humanitarian assistance. 

People are starving to death there. Why military?

Mr. VEST. Sir, this is a continuing program, not only with Ethiopia, but with many other governments with whom we do business. Their perception and their political views of their internal needs and their internal security programs as refers to their economic needs is often quite different from ours. We have discussions on these matters. This is why we end up with a mixed economic assistance with military aid, but a country which feels menaced and insecure is going to make its policy decisions in some part on its own perceptions and not on ours. 

Senator INOUYE. Some of us find it very difficult to understand how countries like India can support a carrier in light of what is happening to the economy. Do we advise them as to how we view their economic picture?

Mr. VEST. Sir, in discussions with countries not only are there diplomatic discussions, but there are discussions between various political leaders and at every level of society wherever democratic exchange goes on.

Senator INOUYE. So this is the price we are paying for the recall of our troops?

Chairman, but let me make sure I understand your point. Are you in effect saying that the Russians are doing much less than we are in that area of the world? 

Senator INOUYE. What I am saying is that for every dollar that the

Communist bloc nations put into North Vietnam, we put in eight. And it would seem from that standpoint that our friends in Indochina should be in good shape militarily. 

Admiral PEET. Mr. Chairman, I would like to provide the DOD comment on that for the record. Whenever I get involved in this sort of thing, I find that it is an apples and oranges proposition. It is hard to standardize on the value how we evaluate Russian currencies in terms of U.S. dollars. There are so many factors involved that it is very, very difficult to compare; but the general conclusion that I arrive at worldwide is that the amount of assistance provided by the Communist world and by our world is essentially equal. 

NATURE OF MILITARY SITUATION IN COMMUNIST NATIONS 

Senator INOUYE. Will you provide for the subcommittee under ´proper classification the critical nature of the military situation there? 

Admiral PEET. Yes, sir. [The information furnished was classified and retained in committee files.]

EXCESS ARTICLES 

Senator INOUYE. Briefly can you tell us how the Department determines which articles are excess? What is the process or procedure that is followed to determine whether something is excess? 

Admiral PEET. We have very strict rules and regulations as to what is excess and what is not and how it is determined, Furthermore, the Congress has imposed restrictions about whether it is located incountry or out-of-country. I would be glad to provide those regulations. In fact, counsel is going to give you some right now. 

Senator INOUYE. I would appreciate that.

Mr. FORMAN. Well, the definition of excess defense articles is contained in section 644 (G) of the Foreign Assistance Act, 1961, as amended last year. It enacts into law what was provided for in our existing DOD directives and it provides that it is the quantity of articles owned by the Government, not procured in anticipation of military assistance or sales requirements or pursuant to a military assistance sales order, which is excess to the approved force acquisition objective and the approved force retention stock of all Department of

Defense components at the time the article was dropped from inventory for delivery to countries or international organizations under the act.

When you get into in-stock stratification, you have in excess of the approved force acquisition objective the following stock levels stratifications: The contingency retention stock, economic retention stock, potential excess and excess. 

Senator INOUYE. How do you determine actual value? As you know, before the amendment to the foreign aid bill you determined the valuation of the excess articles as one-third of your acquisition cost, but now it is in actual value plus repair and rehabilitation costs. 

How do you determine this actual value?

Admiral PEET. Mr. Chairman, it is a difficult question; and we do have flexibility in determining the value. It sometimes relates in part to what the acquisition cost was. It also relates to the condition of the equipment at a given time. There are several factors involved here. 

Senator INOUYE. There is no standard?

Admiral PEET. No. We try to manage it in a way that we are consistent, but we do have some flexibility and we can also make the most of that flexibility for political reasons.

Mr. FORMAN. Mr. Chairman, there are to some extent some standards in that the regulations of the Department of Defense and the military departments do have what we call condition codes. Each type of condition in there-I have forgotten how many, let's say 10 conditions in which the item might be, that is, is it brand-new, is it used but in new condition, is it used but rehabilitated and so on down the line. Each will have a percentage sign for deduction from the original cost based on that condition, so to that extent there are standards, but however, as the admiral has indicated, of course, there is a question of judgment when the individual inventory manager looks at what he has got in inventory and what condition he says the item is in. 

This is not something done by Admiral Peet's office. It is done by the military departments of the inventory managers who are responsible for controlling their equipment. 

Admiral PEET. Mr. Chairman, along that line, what I try to do as much as possible to ascertain the actual replacement cost of items that we transfer. As the counsel is pointing out, that doesn't necessarily apply to excess but

Senator INOUYE. Oftentimes unused items, brand-new items are declared excess. How do you determine the value of that? Good working condition? 

Admiral PEET. Except for ammunition. I don't know of any brandnew items that were declared excess, Mr. Chairman. 

Senator INOUYE. You had better ask your counsel.

Admiral PEET. We do transfer some equipment from our stocks, but not as excess. When we sell used equipment, we have to determine what price to charge. What I was alluding to when I said it is not in the excess category is taking it out of DOD stock equipment and transferring it into the MAP or FMS program.

FORMER U.S. MILITARY PERSONNEL EMPLOYED AS CIVILIANS IN SOUTH VIETNAM 

Senator INOUYE. Do you have any information on the number of former U.S. military men now working as civilians in South Vietnam? 

Admiral PEET. I don't have it here with me, but I can look into the question and provide the answer for the record. 

Senator INOUYE. Do these technicians sometimes slip into the role of adviser?

Mr. FORMAN. Not in the sense of the word advisers as used in the cease-fire accords in Vietnam. If you mean by adviser, for example, do they give advice in the logistics area to the Vietnamese in how to set up a depot system or how to repair a piece of equipment, yes, but not in the sense of advising the Vietnamese of combat operations or any other actual military operation.

Senator INOUYE. I will be submitting to you several questions in this category because I believe your responses would require some thought. [The questions and answers follow:] 

Question. Do you have any information on the number of former U.S. military men now working as civilians in South Vietnam? 

Answer. Yes, I do. 

Question. How many are there?

Answer. Our records indicate that 2,722 of the employees of the Department of Defense and DOD contractors have served some time in the Armed Forces of the United States. This figure includes all employees with any service at all from the World War II period up to the present. I might add that when we first established the defense attaché office in Saigon we stipulated that no person who had retired from the military within the previous 3 years would be assigned to a civilian position in the defense attaché office and this has served to keep down the number of former military men in Saigon. Only last March did we revert to the more liberal civil service policy regarding employment of retired military personnel. 

Question. Do these technicians sometimes slip into the role of "adviser"?

Answer. No, every effort is made to separate the two functions. 

Qusetion. Is it true that many of these civilian technicians received their training in the U.S. military and, if so, does this violate the spirit of the Paris peace agreement?

Answer. Many of the tasks that the civilian technicians perform are related to military equipment maintenance, which is best learned in the military. Pro-

vision of maintenance services through military assistance on material and equipment permitted under the cease-fire agreement does not violate the spirit of the agreement. 

Question. Do American military men advise the Government of South Vietnam on what kind of military aid they should request from the United States? 

Answer. No. U.S. military personnel discuss with Vietnam armed forces representatives only the relative merits and availability of equipment and material which can legally be obtained. 

Senator INOUYE. Can you lay to rest charges that U.S. military personnel are acting as combat advisers in Cambodia in defiance of legislation which prohibits such activities? I think it is very important because there are constantly articles indicating otherwise. 

For example, in the Washington Post on March 13, 1974, there was an article indicating that we are providing illegal assistance to Cambodia. 

[The article follows:] [The Washington Post, Wednesday, March 13, 1974] ILLEGAL HELP TO CAMBODIANS-AMERICAN ADVISES IN COMBAT 

(By Elizabeth Becker)

KAMPOT, CAMBODIA.—During the dark hours of dawn the Cambodian insurgents were lobbing mortars around the government's command post at Kampot. 

Inside, U.S. Maj. Lawrence W. Ondecker was showing the Cambodian officers how to mount a counterattack. "I want you to respond very quickly," he said. "If even one mortar falls in your zone, you must answer back with fire immediately."

While the American major was poring over maps with the Cambodian staff officers, the Cambodian general officially in command of the post was writing in his diary, alone in an adjoining bunker.

The U.S. embassy in Phnom Penh has repeatedly denied reports that Americans are serving as military advisers in the field. Congress has passed a law that prohibits the U.S. mission here from direct involvement in the conduct of the war. 

But the situation in this coastal town about 80 miles south of Phnom Penh is critical, and Maj. Ondecker was flown down Sunday. "He was loaned to us from the 3d Infantry Brigade," Lt. Col. Choey Yeun said. “He is attached to the 3d and normally works in the field with them, but he is needed here. I am surprised that you did not know him."

In the past month rebel troops have moved within one to four miles of Kampot, capturing the city's main water supply and the country's only cement factory. 

They regularly shell the town with 75-mm. recoilless rifles and 81-mm. mortars. 

Although government intelligence officers warned of an impending offensive as early as January, the Kampot garrison made no defense preparations. Over the past week the Cambodian high command sent reinforcements—and they sent Maj. Ondecker. "Protect this area immediately," Maj. Ondecker said while the 81 rounds were falling in and around the city Monday morning. "Good, perfect," he said as a

Cambodian officer pointed on the map after accepting the American's proposal. 

The day before rebel gunners shot down one of the two helicopter gunships stationed here, and the second one was recalled to Phnom Penh. Maj. Ondecker arranged with the U.S. embassy on the morning of the attack that additional gunships would be sent to Kampot to support the infantry. 

A member of the U.S. military attaché's staff in Phnom Penh, Ondecker, is in 

Kampot officially to gather information. Chuck Bernard, known as Monsieur 

Jacques, is the other U.S. representative in town. He has approximately the same official duties as Ondecker except that his area is civilian matters. "Monsieur Jacques works with me," said Ker Sophay, director of political warfare. "He writes propaganda tracts with me. We have published and distributed 6,000 pamphlets in the three weeks he has been here." 

While junior Cambodian officers say Americans advise in the field around Phnom Penh, it has never been confirmed. In Kampot, however, it is difficult to hide. Ondecker was in and out of the command post, openly recommending mili-

四海 ​1 tary maneuvers. Sometimes he prefaced his proposals with "I suggest and the general also suggests that you immediately fire in this direction." 

The Cambodians were obviously pleased with the American's help. "Maj. Ondecker was very good with the 3d Brigade; he will be good with us," said Col. 

Choey Yeun. 

Changes were made quickly after Ondecker's arrival. Another infantry brigade was called in to bolster the 2,000-man government garrison, and the top command was replaced within 24 hours. The city's defense perimeter was stabilized for the first time throughout the siege.

Villagers are still leaving the town-the population has dropped from 50,000 to less than 20,000 in a month. Though all private shops are closed, and mortars still land within the city, the city's small open-air market reopened Sunday with some fruit and fish offered for sale. 

CAMBODIAN ROUTE PARTIALLY CLEARED 

Cambodian government forces yesterday cleared insurgent troops from a fivemile stretch of Highway 4, opening the road from Phnom Penh to the provincial capital of Kompong Speu 30 miles to the west, the Cambodian command said.

The highway, Phnom Penh's only land route to the sea, remain cut by rebel troops between Kompong Speu and the port of Kompong Som.

Meanwhile political sources in Phnom Penh reported that four prominent Cambodians, all of them former or present government officials, had defected to the government in exile of Prince Norodom Sihanouk, the deposed head of state. 

The most prominent figure among them was Ing Kiet, the minister of public works in Sihanouk's government before the latter was ousted in March 1970. 

The others were Khek Sisoda, onetime senior official in the Ministry of Commerce; Sieu Sophon, a magistrate in Takeo Province, and Siv Hak, an official in 

Tela Khmer, the government-owned petroleum complex. 

All four had been in Paris on either private or official business, when they defected and began working for Sihanouk's government there, the sources said. 

In Vientiane, the Laotian Foreign Ministry announced that North Vietnam's Ambassador Le Van Hien would return to his post today after an absence of nine years. Hien's return is seen by observers as an indication that a final agreement is imminent on a coalition government for Laos. Hien was last in Laos in 1965, departing in apparent protest over the collapse of an earlier attempt to form a coalition.

REIMBURESMENT OF COSTS FOR OVERHAULING AND OUTFITTING OF SHIPS 

Information available to the committee has suggested that contrary to legislative requirements the U.S. Navy has spent some $18 million overhauling and outfitting ships for loan to foreign countries. The governing legislation mandates that these costs should be paid by the recipient country or by military assistance funds.

1162

Nevertheless, the committee is informed that the Navy has not been reimbursed. What actions are being taken to insure that these costs will be reimbursed and that in the future the directives of Congress will be met with full compliance?

Admiral PEET. This is the subject of a detailed investigation by the 

GAO, and there is a report on it. We are doing everything we can to make sure we are complying with the law. I am attempting to get this whole ship loan, lease, and sale business resolved. 

For the most part, we are attempting to sell the ships outright to the foreign countries.

Senator INOUYE. I realize that the amount of $18 million is a small one, but the subcommittee feels that this may be just a tip of an iceberg because these were costs incurred during 1972 and 1973 during the transfer of 6 submarines and 10 destroyers. But since the inception of this program about 3,900 ships have been transferred. We have no idea whether these 3,900 have all been outfitted at American expense. 

Admiral PEET. I don't consider $18 million small. I agree with you, and it may well be that the matter warrants investigation. It has in fact, been investigated very thoroughly by the GAO, and we have cooperated fully. I don't know whether the report is on the street, but it should be before very long. 

Senator INOUYE. When can we get a report from your office?

Admiral PEET. We can provide a statement fairly shortly on this subject.

SHIP TRANSFERS TO FOREIGN COUNTRIES

COST OF TRANSFERS 

Senator INOUYE. Do you have any estimates as to what was spent by the Department of Defense in this area?

Admiral PEET. No; I do not, sir. Here again, the conditions are different in each transaction, depending on whether it is a grant country or a sales country. Some of the ships require overhaul, and some transactions include the cost of a 2-year supply of spare parts. They are not easy to compare. 

Ship transfers to foreign countries and authority for each transfer covering the past 5 years is attached. Costs associated with the transfers can be broken down into two categories, i.e., costs borne by the U.S. Government and costs borne by the recipient Navy. A lengthy case by case manual review will be required which will not define all costs since many pertinent transactions occur directly between recipient nation and commercial firms-without U.S. Navy participation. We will proceed with the audit of information which Navy is privy to, but we cannot forecast a time of completion.

ATOMIC EXPLOSION BY INDIA 

Senator INOUYE. This is in reference to the recent explosion of an atomic device by India. The committee has been assured that the 

United States has not provided India with nuclear materials which could be diverted to weapons systems. Can you confirm this, sir? 

Admiral PEET. I believe that is correct, but the matter is not in my purview, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. VEST. It is our understanding that that is the case sir. 

Senator INOUYE. Does India have any other so-called breeder reactors, those which generate plutonium?

Mr. VEST. Sir, I am not an expert in this field. I don't have an answer to that. I can get it.

Senator INOUYE. We would like to get the answer and we would like to know where she got this from. 

Mr. VEST. We will provide that for the record, sir. 

 INDIAN NUCLEAR DEVELOPMENTS 

The United States has not provided India with nuclear materials which could be diverted to weapons systems. The United States has provided slightly enriched uranium fuel for the Tarapur power station reactors and gram quantities of plutonium for research projects, all under IAEA safeguards. 

With the goal of producing electric power from fast breeder reactors by the 1990's, India has established a fast breeder development program. She has constructed a zero energy fast assembly and a pulsed fast reactor as part of this program. Neither of these systems is capable of producing significant quantities of plutonium. Currently India has a 35 megawatt (thermal) fast breeder reactor under construction at Kalpakkam which is scheduled for completion in late 1975. The project is being carried out with extensive French assistance. 

The reactor system will be designed to produce 15 megawatts of electric power and provide experimental facilities for engineering research. [Deleted.] 

This reactor is not part of the Indian thermal reactor program which undoubtedly produced the plutonium used in the Indian nuclear test. [Deleted.] [Additional information furnished committee files.] was classified and retained in the

Admiral PEET. My understanding of the policy I received from the Department of State is that it has not and does not.

 QUESTIONS SUBMITTED BY SENATOR INOUYE 

When nuclear materials are processed through elaborate chemical and physical procedures, small uncertainties in the measurement of the materials result in bookkeeping "losses". In some cases, minor quantities of nuclear materials are irretrievably lost in waste streams. These quantities are insignificant in comparison to the total quantities of materials processed. The sale of reactors to 

Egypt and Israel does not involve the processing of nuclear materials in those countries. Therefore, there is no relationship between processing "losses" in the 

U.S. and the sale of reactors.

Senator INOUYE. We will submit to you, if we may, several questions for your consideration. Most of them are of a technical nature. [The questions and answers follow:] 

MILITARY PRESENCE IN ECUADOR 

Question. How large is the present contingent of United States Military Attaches in Ecuador? How large is it to become? Are there any other United States military personnel in Ecuador? 

Answer. I assume by your question that you are referring to the number of

U.S. personnel assigned to manage the Security Assistance program in Ecuador. 

Currently, there are four U.S. military personnel temporarily assigned to the 

Defense Attaché's Office for that purpose. However, when USMLO is formally established on 15 July it will have an authorized manning of six U.S. military personnel and one U.S. civilian personnel. The only other U.S. military in Ecuador

are six personnel permanently assigned to the Defense Attaché Office who perform attaché functions, one officer assigned to Inter-American Geodetic Survey, and a small number who infrequently travel there for short periods of temporary duty.

OFFSET OF PERSONNEL COSTS IN ECUADOR 

Question. Are the increased personnel costs incurred by this and similar sales offset in the sales agreement?

Answer. There is a two percent surcharge added to most of the sales that we negotiate with foreign governments, and this is the case in Ecuador. This charge is made in lieu of separate computations of charges for the costs of general management and administrative expenses pertaining to supply and procurement and services and other DOD costs.

COMBINING MAAG AND ATTACHÉ FUNCTIONS 

Question. As you know this Subcommittee has been pressing for a substantial reduction in the number of U.S. MAAGS and MilGroups scattered throughout the world. The Pentagon has been slow to move. Yet, in Ecuador the Department apparently feels that the attachés are fully capable of performing MAAG and Mil- Group functions. Why is this not the case elsewhere? Do many of these MAAGS and MilGroups represent a "tail that could be cut"?

Answer. The arrangement in Ecuador wherein the Defense Attaché Office is currently managing the Security Assistance Program is temporary and in response to the Ambassador's request for immediate assistance in handling FMS cases and MAP training. To assist the Ambassador and meet personnel requirements to handle the increased workload, we augmented the DAO with four military personnel on a TDY basis beginning in April 1974. After coordination with Department of State, we have now approved the establishment of a U.S. 

Military Liaison Office (USMLO) in Ecuador effective 15 July 1974. Its author ized strength is six U.S. military and one U.S. civilian. Although officers assigned to USMLO will be accredited as attachés, by agreement with the Ecuadorian Government, there will be a notation in their credentials reflecting their security assistance duties in the U.S. Military Liaison Office (USMLO). The Chief of 

USMLO will be directly responsible to the Ambassador and not under the Defense Attaché.

Generally, we don't believe it advisable to combine the MAAG and Attaché Offices except in unusual circumstances, such as in Laos and South Vietnam, because of the dissimilarities in their duties and responsibilities. Most countries of the world utilize Defense Attachés, and they are traditionally recognized as overt intelligence collectors, whereas MAAG personnel are responsible for providing appropriate military advisory services and technological assistance to the host country, plus carrying out the Secretary of Defense's responsibilities under the Foreign Assistance Act. To carry out these necessary functions, our military advisors have to build and maintain a relationship of mutual trust and confidence with the host country's military establishment. A relationship of this nature is much more difficult for a combined MAAG/Attaché structure which has a recognized intelligence collection mission, and could well result in undesirable restrictions on our MAAG personnel and interfere with their access and free exchange of information with host government officials. We do not believe that 

MAAGS/MilGroups in any way represent a "tail" that could be cut, but rather are absolutely essential to carry out the SecDef's responsibilities under the 

Foreign Assistance and Foreign Military Sales Acts and review host countries' 

needs and requests from a U.S. national security standpoint.

REDUCTION IN THE NUMBER OF MAAGS 

Question. How many MAAGS and MilGroups are there presently in being? 

What steps are you taking to reduce this number? How many will there be in 

1976? 1977? What are your projections?

Answer. The Department of Defense has 44 MAAGs/Missions/MilGps world wide, including the Military Liaison Office which opens in Ecuador on 15 July. 

The major tasks of providing appropriate military advisory services and technological assistance to the host country plus residual responsibilities to monitor MAP end items to ensure their proper use and disposal after termination of a grant aid program preclude reducing the number of MAAGS at this time. However, we have made very substantial reductions in personnel assigned to these MAAGS over the past several years, and we are considering a continuation of these reductions through FY 75 and beyond. Although the number of personnel

assigned to MAAGS will decrease in the out years, we project that the number of MAAGS will remain approximately the same in the foreseeable future because of our residual responsibilities and other responsibilities delegated to the Secre tary of Defense under the Foreign Assistance and Foreign Military Sales Acts. 

SHIP LEASES 

Question. I have a series of questions which I would like to ask you in regard to this information:

If not as Foreign Assistance, how does DOD regard the leasing of non-excess defense articles to foreign countries? 

Answer. Like the Congress, DOD has never put a label on the exercise of the lease authority of 10 U.S.C. 2667.

Question. How do you construe the language of Section 2667 as giving DOD authority to make such leasing agreements? 

Answer. Section 2667 of Title 10 U.S.C. is a general statute which permits, except in the case of oil, mineral, or phosphate lands, the leasing of all manner of property in a broad sense. 

Question. Is there any limitation on the value or quantity which may be based under this interpretation?

Answer. There is no limitation on the value or quantity which may be leased under this interpretation. 

Question. Can you point to any reference in your Congressional Presentation which notifies the Congress that these leases are being made? 

Answer. There is no reference to these leases in our Congressional Presentation Document. However, we have over the past several years provided data to the Foreign Aid Committees about these leases during the course of our testimony. In addition, we have provided advance notice to the Armed Services Committees.

34-192 - 74-75 (1183)

ASSISTANCE TO HAITI 

The Committee has taken note of the discussion by Congress concerning our provision of assistance to countries whose governments appear clearly to be in violation of basic political and human rights of their citizens by blatantly imprisoning dissidents for political purposes. 

This Congressional sentiment resulted in Section 32 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1973, which reads as follows:

It is the sense of the Congress that the President should deny any economic or military assistance to the government of any foreign country which practices the internment or imprisonment of that country's citizens for political purposes. 

There is deep concern by the Committee that our foreign assistance, frequently justified in the name of protecting democracy and freedom, is furnished to certain regimes whose actions clearly violate these principles.

Also, the restructuring of the Foreign Assistance Act has stressed that our economic aid should be rendered according to its ability to directly meet the basic human needs of people rather than being used as a political tool for supporting the recipient government. The clear implication is that if a regime seems incapable of addressing itself forthrightly to the fundamental needs of its people, then our assistance to it, regardless of how well intended it may be, cannot be justified. 

Indeed, in such cases our economic and military aid can be perceived by the people of that particular country and by much of the world as undergirding a repressive and unresponsive government. 

The Committee intends, therefore, to evaluate proposed future foreign assistance at least in part on conditions within the prospective recipient countries, including the governments' commitment to basic human rights and its demonstrated dedication to serving the humanitarian needs of its poorest and most deserving people. 

As an illustrative case in point, the Committee has considered the $8.9 million in proposed economic assistance to Haiti that would be appropriated by this bill. 

Haiti is the poorest country in the Western Hemisphere, with a per capita income of about $70.00 per year. From 80% to 90% of her population is illiterate. About nine out of ten Haitians live in desperate poverty in rural areas, earning $25 to $35 each year and facing a life expectancy of about 33 years. Only a small urbanized elite enjoy any opportunities for education or employment. Yet an estimated 50% of the 200,000 to 300,000 work force living in urban areas are unemployed. 

Thus, the needs of the 4.8 million Haitian people are painfully obvious. 

The question remains, however, as to whether those needs are being adequately addressed by the present regime. 

With the death of Francois Duvalier in April of 1971, his 20 year old son, Jean Claude, succeeded him as "President for Life." While there is some evidence to indicate that the grim visible terror of Francois Duvalier's regime may have subsided, it seems that autocractic rule characterized by an unflinching willingness to suppress people has not.

The Human Rights Commission of the Organization of American States has issued statements and findings concerning the repression of human rights in Haiti.

In March of this year, Amnesty International, recognized as an international source on political prisoners, wrote to President Duvalier stating that:

Haiti's prisons are still filled with people who have spent many years in detention without ever being charged or brought to trial. Amnesty International remains seriously concerned at the continued repression of dissent in Haiti and the denial of human and legal rights.

When the Duvalier government announced last year that it had "amnestied" 130 prisoners, it was revealed that many of those named were not in prison at all, but were living abroad. Many hundreds of 

Haitians continue to suffer as political prisoners, to say nothing of those who have fled their homeland to escape persecution. 

The Inter-American Press Association, at the end of 1972, made the following observation in their report:

There is no freedom of the press (in Haiti). . . . The press continues to be unconditionally subjected to the whim of duvalierian dictatorship. 

In addition, there are serious questions as to whether the Haitian government has demonstrated capability and dedication in acting to meet the pressing social and humanitarian needs within their country. 

The current national budget of Haiti is $33.3 million. The government intends to spend a full $8 million on the Ministry of Internal 

Security and National Defense, 25% of her budget. That leaves only 

13% ($4.3 million) for the Ministry of Health, 12% ($3.9 million) for National Education, and 8% ($2.6 million) for agriculture, despite the fact that agriculture accounts for 80% of the nation's economic activity and is the only source of livelihood for the nearly 90% of Haitians who are rural peasants. 

Further, a memorial for Francois Duvalier is being built at the reported cost of $1 million, and the stadium at Port-au-Prince has recently been expanded at the approximate cost of $1.5 million, part of a $5 million governmental investment this year to host World Cup soccer elimination games. 

In recent years, the Haitian government has been aggressive in attempting to attract outside business investment. The principal types of investments, however, have been for luxurious tourist facilities and for assembly factories which take advantage of extremely low Haitian wages. Such factories, however, have created only about 1,000 new jobs per year on the average, which hardly makes a dent in the estimated 100,000 or more unemployed in the urban areas, or in the estimated 12,000 who leave the country each year in search of work. 

Moreover, while the parent American company having a product assembled in Haiti will pay the Haitian contractor approximately $1.70 per hour for each employee, the salary actually received by the workers averages about $.16 to $.20 per hour. It should be noted that the prospect of such investment ever "trickling down" to relieve the plight of the urban unemployed, or to have any effect on the abject suffering of Haiti's millions of destitute rural poor is remote if not impossible.

United States foreign assistance was suspended in 1963, and has been only gradually resumed since, until the past two years. The 

Committee notes that the proposed level of assistance to Haiti in AID's illustrative budget has almost tripled since FY 1972, to the current level of $8.9 million, not including an additional $2.1 million under P.L. 480. AID projects a continued increase in such assistance during the next two years. Further, the Committee notes with some concern that in August and October of this year weapons and ammunition worth about $275,000 were sold by our government to Haiti under the Foreign Military Sales program. (Also, last year and the year before licenses were granted for the private purchase of military equipment from United States sources.)

These amounts of assistance are relatively small. Yet, they represent a decision to begin a significant program of assistance to the Haitian government. Even now, the projected flow of U.S. resources to Haiti in FY 1974-$11.0 million-is equal to one third of Haiti's national budget.

For the reasons stated, the Committee questions the decision to resume and expand assistance to Haiti. It is Committee's opinion that despite the desperate need of the Haitian people, the conditions may not exist within the Haitian government which would enable our resources to be put to beneficial use. A primary effect of such aid, in the Committee's judgment, could be to make a regime whose violation of human rights seems to be flagrant and whose dedication to meeting the humanitarian needs of its people is dubious, dependent upon and undergirded by United States resources. 

For these reasons, the Committee intends to hold a special hearing immediately next year to examine our assistance program to Haiti. 

We will be investigating and closely watching developments within that country to determine whether our program of assistance is justifiable.

The Committee realizes that similar cases may be made against our giving of aid to other countries. The Committee intends to give critical examination to our assistance programs, particularly in those cases where governments are characterized by a denial of human rights and seem insufficiently committed to meeting the basic humanitarian needs of their citizens.

Regardless of how critical the need, the United States cannot do for the peoples of other countries what their own governments seem unwilling to do. Our foreign assistance must never subsidize the corruption, lack of commitment, unresponsiveness, or tyranny by other governments toward their own people. The Committee believes these perspectives are responsive to the intent of the Foreign Assistance.
