[New York Times, June 2, 1974] 

YOUNG DUVALIER RELAXES CURBS BUT THE HAITIAN PRESIDENT, LIKE HIS FATHER, PERMITS NO RIVALS TO HIS RULE (By Alan Riding) 

PORT-AU-PRINCE, HAITI-Three years after the death of President Francois Duvalier, the dictator's son and heir is firmly in power and assuming an ever larger role in the day-to-day Government of this impoverished Caribbean nation. 

Although still only 22 years old, the President for Life, Jean-Claude Duvalier, has already demonstrated his grasp of the politics of survival by purging the regime of over-ambitious or potentially threatening elements. 

He had also gained prestige among representatives of foreign governments and international development agencies by emphasizing the need to attack the country's critical economic and social problems. 

Foreign tourists, who were frightened away by the Duvalier regime in the sixties, are now flocking to Haiti in record numbers, while many Haitian exiles have either returned home or are at least investing their savings in the country. 

"A SERIOUS YOUNG MAN" 

Even some Haitians who were uncompromising opponents of the late President Duvalier, who was known as "Papa Doc," now concede that the young Duvalier has improved the political atmosphere since his father's death on April 21, 1971. "He's a serious young man who seems to be trying hard," a politically independent Haitian said.

Open criticism of the Government is still not heard and would be unwise. There is now little risk, however, in discussing its shortcomings in private or even debating the country's economic and social problems in public. 

But while political repression has eased and the economy is beginning to recover from a decade of stagnation, the Duvalier family has permitted no more challenges to its monopoly of power than did the late dictator during his violent 14-year rule of this tiny black republic. 

Opposition parties are still banned and "unnecessary" since Jean-Claude Duvalier is President for Life. But he and his influential mother, Mrs. Simone Ovide 

Duvalier, have nevertheless quickly smothered any emerging power groups within the regime itself.

MOTHER'S INFLUENCE WANES 

Adopting the tactics of his father, the young President has also made frequent Cabinet changes so that, today, no adviser or minister feels secure in his job or independently powerful. In just three years four men have headed the crucial 

Interior and National Defense Ministry. 

Even the 58-year-old Mrs. Duvalier, who made the principal decisions and preserved the continuity of the regime after Dr. Duvalier's death, is reported losing some of her power in face of the President's growing interest in government.

According to informed sources, the young ruler first challenged his mother by ousting one of her favorites, the much-feared Interior and National Defense Minister, Luckner Cambronne, in November, 1971. Since then, he has frequently ignored his mother's advice, the sources said. 

The family's obsession with security remains unchanged. The President has disbanded his father's brutal and unpopular private militia, the so-called Tonton Macoutes, but an elite army battalion known as the Leopards was created in 1971 and trained by United States war veterans to cope with possible invasions, uprisings or guerrilla activities. So far, the Leopards have seen no action. 

AID PROGRAMS RESUME 

Mr. Duvalier himself rarely leaves his shining white palace in downtown 

Port-au-Prince and, when he does, he is surrounded by bodyguards. But the 

President's treatment of his enemies and of aides who have fallen out of favor bears little resemblance to that of his father.

Although at least 150 political prisoners are still held in the Fort Dimanche Prison, most have been there since the previous regime. "Those who have gone to

jail under Jean-Claude were all involved in some concrete anti-Government activity." A foreign diplomat insisted, "No one has been arrested for his ideas."

The improvement in the political atmosphere here has enabled numerous United States and international assistance organizations to resume or step up their activities here. "We now think our help has a chance of getting to the right people," a foreign economist said.

One criticism still frequently heard, however, is that corruption is still rampant throughout the Government and the badly paid bureaucracy. 

When some foreign diplomats expressed encouragement at the dismissal in March of several Government officials with a wide reputation for dishonesty, others recalled that the President's private tax fund is still not included in the national budget and the revenue remains unaccounted for. [The Washington Post, May 21, 1974]

HAITI IS GRANTED BANK CREDIT FOR HIGHWAY WORK 

The first World Bank group credit to Haiti in 14 years was announced yesterday.

The International Development Association, the bank's soft-loan affiliate, has approved a $10 million credit for urgent rehabilitation works on the northern road from Port-au-Prince to Gonaives and Cap Haitien.

The credit is aimed at supporting the Haitian government's efforts to reconstruct the country's basic economic infrastructure.

The new IDA credit is for 50 years and is interest free, with a service charge of three-quarters of 1 per cent. 

[New Internationalist No. 12, February 1974] "TO HELL WITH PARADISE" 

To ordinary tourists the Caribbean offers an exotic refuge from the mists of Northern Europe. But how many pause to consider the effect of their care-free fortnight on the host country? In this radical analysis John Ash, who is currently engaged on a book about tourism with Louis Turner, shows how Haiti—an island which desperately needs to recover from a tragic history of corrupt government and retarded growth-is being hurt by the holiday trade. In the words of James Mitchell, the disillusioned Premier of St. Vincent. During 1973 Haiti's Habitation Leclerc opened its doors to international aristocracy, loudly proclaiming its intention to become "the most extraordinary, lascivious and decadent place on earth." The Habitation is an exclusive pleasure reserve, comprising a hotel and 38 chalets, situated on a hillside above Port-au- 

Prince. Each chalet is equipped with a private swimming pool, three Haitian servants, and gold-plated toilet fittings. The cost of a day in these surroundings is $150; the daily wage of the average Haitian worker is in the region of $1. A recent illustration in "Time" magazine of a Habitation interior displayed a beautiful creole girl reclining on a divan against a luxuriant backdrop of palm fronds.

Clearly the girl is to be regarded as another luxury fixture like the gold-plated taps. She has become an object for the amusement of wealthy foreigners. 

A report in The Guardian (15.10.73) gave the following list of the Habitation's financial backers: "Jean-Paul Belmondo, Mick Jagger, Alain Delon, the Duke of 

Bedford, Giovanni Agnelli, the Italian car magnate, Roger Vadin, Prince Egon von Furstenburg, Aristotle Onassis, Baron Edmund de Rothschild and other multinational business tycoons."

A TRAGIC PAST Haiti has an heroic and tragic past: in Aimé Cesairé's words it was the place "where negritude rose to its feet for the first time and said it believed in its own humanity".

In the 18th Century the island of Saint Domingue was considered the richest colony in the world. Its revenue surpassed that of all Britain's 13 American colonies combined. In this century it has been, consistently, one of the most wretched places of the earth. It now has a population of 3 to 5 million (exact statistics are unknown in Haiti)-90% illiterate, 50% unemployed, and many of them starving. It also boasts one of the world's highest infant mortality rates.

71 G 1 Much of the credit for this must go to the Duvalieriste regime that has been in power since 1957. Papa Doc resembles some monster of folklore with the difference that his many atrocities are well substantiated. Something between 3,000 and 12,000 "political opponents" were liquidated under his rule (the more modest estimate comes from sources close to the regime-the 12,000 from Haitian exiles). 

In particular the labour movement was ruthlessly suppressed; its leaders were variously tortured, maimed, driven mad and sent into exile. Decius Benoit, a prominent Trade Union leader was held down while petrol was poured over him and ignited; the unfortunate man somehow survived and was imprisoned without trial.

Papa Doc's rule was not only violently oppressive but criminally inefficient. Its economic policies were concerned only with finding ways of enriching the ruling elite. In consequence Haiti is still without proper roads or communications of any kind, and some of its richest agricultural areas have been reduced to famine conditions. In an article for The Sunday Times (23.8.70) Simon Regan described a trip to the peninsula as “a terrible experience". He was warned by his guide not to leave his horse unattended for long since it was likely to be eaten by starving villagers. One family offered to sell him "children between between 5 and 13 for a dollar each". In 1970 little or nothing was being done about this. International aid organisations were understandably reluctant to contribute funds when they knew they would serve only to increase the wealth of government officials in Port-au-Prince.

Foreign investors were discouraged by official corruption and incompetence, and tourists could even expect to find corpses in their hotel swimming pools (as 

4 in Graham Greene's "The Comedians'). Even the US Government was reluctant to lend support to a regime with such a sinister reputation, despite the obvious advantages of a strongly anti-communist state so close to Cuba. Papa Doc's death in 1971 did not bring about any real change in Haitian conditions, but all that was required by big business and the American Government was a semblance of change. "A SAP-FILLED TREE" Papa Doc was succeeded by his obese 19 year-old son, Jean-Claude Duvalier (or 'Baby Doc'). This most improbable of statesman inspired Luc Desyr, the 

Haitian Secret Police Chief, to lyrical effusions; he compared Baby Doc to "a young, leafy, sap-filled tree where birds caught in a violent storm can take refuge".

The US has resumed financial and military aid and American light industry has moved in to establish assembly plants for baseballs, belts, boots, brassieres, fishing lures, jeans, men's hair pieces, table cloth ensembles and tape cassettes. 

Baby Doc claims to be completing his father's "political revolution" with an "economic revolution". The Duvalieriste Revolution Mark II, as seen by most observers, consists of selling Haiti on the cheap to foreign investors. Wendell 

Phillips has been granted a 55 year oil concession covering Haiti's entire land and sea area; most of the coastline has been leased to foreign interests on the understanding that they will build hotels, as reported by Greg Chamberlain in The Guardian (14.9.71). The entire island of Tortue has been leased to a Texan group, Dupont Caribbean Inc., for 99 years. The island which is 24 miles long and 4 miles wide is at present inhabited by 5,000 desperately poor peasants; it is to be developed along the lines of Freeport, Grand Bahama, as a tax-free haven for the rich tourist.

The suppression of the trade unions made it possible for Dupont Caribbean to dismiss, summarily, 200 Haitian workers who had attempted to gain a pay increase by strike action. The firm's vice-president remarked: "One dollar a day is already too much for a Haitian worker". Dupont Caribbean is now, in all but name, the ruler of Tortue and its 5,000 inhabitants, and a clause in the firm's contract with the Haitian Government clearly shows that they have undertaken to maintain strict Duvalieriste standards: "No concession or agreement shall be granted or made with a Communist government or with a firm controlled by one and no subversive activity shall be permitted on the island". This is the true face of Haiti's new 'liberalism'. 

Haiti's new assembly industries have created only 15,000 new jobs which, in a country of something like 2 million unemployed, is hopelessly inadequate. 

Profits are not re-invested in Haiti, and any money that does stay in the country simply adds to the private fortunes of high government officials and established Haitian businessmen. This is dramatically demonstrated by the case of Luckner

Cambronne, the former Minister of the Interior and Defence. Until his recent fall from power Cambronne amassed an enormous fortune from the proceeds of tourism (he owned the country's chief travel agency and only airline) the 'quickie' divorce racket (which began when Mexico tightened her divorce laws), and, most scandalously, the blood export industry. Undernourished Haitians were paid $3 per litre of plasma which was then sold for a healthy profit in the States. A director of the US firm (by other accounts a German firm) running this operation merely commented that Haitians wouldn't know what to do with it; indeed they wouldn't as Haiti has one of the world's worst public health records. Since Cambronne's fall, blood export has been stopped, not, one imagines because of any sense of moral outrage, but because of bad publicity that was tarnishing the new, improved Duvalieriste image, and the fear that the blood might be substandard.

BEAUTIFUL AS LEMONADE 

For a variety of reasons Haiti is likely to become increasingly attractive to the tourist industry. Haiti has the requisite 'scenic beauty' and probably more 'historical interest' than any other Caribbean island. It has a thriving and much promoted school of primitive painting. Its culture is a fascinating hybrid of 

French and African, in which voodoo plays a leading role. And, amazingly, it seems to be true that Haitians are genuinely friendly toward visitors. There is little or no racial hatred of whites, indeed whiteness is frankly admired and envied. One astonished tourist was told by a black Haitian that he was "as beautiful as lemonade". Unlike the Jamaican or the Virgin Islander, the

Haitian is 'unspoilt'. He has not been contaminated by radical, black political theory, since his ignorance has been scrupulously preserved by the Duvalieriste regime, and all political opposition within Haiti has been effectively suppressed. 

It is ironic, in this context, that Haiti, the land of L'Ouverture and Dessalines, is becoming increasingly fashionable as a destination for colour-proud American blacks.

To the Caribbean tourist industry Haiti must seem an appealing refuge from a "violent storm". There is none of the violent and articulate political opposition to tourism which is becoming increasingly common in the long established Caribbean resorts. This opposition and resentment (summed up in the phrase "Tourism is Whorism') has gone beyond surly waiters and public abuse. Recently in St. Croix (US Virgin Islands) five young blacks walked onto the dining terrace of Rock-resort's lavish Fountain Valley golf club, and machinegunned eight people. For obvious reasons violent crime and political instability are inimical to the prosperity of the tourist industry. 

But in Haiti "Tourism is Whorism' in the most literal sense, and when Fanon described the resorts of the "Pleasure-Periphery" as 'brothels' he did not exaggerate.

Poor families often sell their daughters to the brothels of Port-au-Prince, not because they are unscrupulous but because this is the only way they can be sure their daughters will be fed. According to Jane Richardson of The Guardian (18.11.72) exquisitely dressed male prostitutes frequent the verandas of

Port-au-Prince hotels in the evenings "sweating with sincerity as they make conversational murmurs around their male or female targets". (One factor which may impede the advertised "lascivious decadence" of Haitian tourism is the appallingly high V.D. rate). In a more general sense, Haitian culture is in danger of being prostituted as tourism prospers; the famous 'primitive paintings' are already being mass-produced; voodoo ceremonies are staged purely for the benefit of tourists. (Habitation Leclerc, for example, was 'consecrated' by a voodoo ceremony).

The affluent tourist seems to represent a life-style of unimaginable ease and irresponsibility; the host community will strive to adopt the most obvious signs of affluence 'transistors, pop, sun-glasses, imported food and drink'. This has already occurred on other Caribbean islands. Things become desirable simply because they are foreign (i.e. Western). This is the negation of cultural identity; it is necessarily difficult for a nation of waiters, barmen, guides, hustlers and prostitutes to retain any sense of identity or dignity. 

Tourism is exporting a style of life the wisdom of which is being questioned, increasingly, in its countries of origin. Developing countries are not only selling their heritage to tourists but in doing so they are jumping on a bandwagon which is heading downhill. This kind of tourism is a display of consumption and wealth which has as its immediate audience some of the most desperate peoples of the world. It is a global agent of the process of 'absorp

12 7 1 P tion' and 'immobilisation'. To sum up, even if a tourism booms ould produce a general increase in Haitian prosperity (which is most unlikely), this economic gain will be vitiated by its destructive social and cultural consequences. 

EXOTIC PAGEANT 

The approch to the Habitation passes through some of Port-au-Prince's worst slums; of this George Bebe of The Miami Herald remarked: "The approach to the hotel may be distasteful to some guests, perhaps an exciting aspect to others". 

This element of social and cultural clash, in the tourist situation, must be controlled, of course, otherwise poverty, starvation and disease might interfere with 'the enjoyment of a pleasant holiday'. Against this tourism has a variety of defences, the most obvious of which is the isolation of the tourist in 'pleasure reserves.' The Habitation Leclerc is surrounded by a high wall; tourists are free to intrude on the host society when they wish, but the intrusion of the indigenous population into the tourist's fantasy world can be strictly controlled. 

More subtly, tourism has an in-built psychological defence mechanism, namely the conversion of social realities into the decorative elements of the picturesque and the exotic. Haitain life can be regarded as a pageant enacted for the diversion of the tourist. 

Far more puzzling than Mick Jagger's reported involvement in Habitation Leclerc is the Caribbean Travel Association's decision to hold its 1972 annual meeting in Haiti. The C.T.A. has a good reputation for its enlightened tourism policies. These policies center on the rather ill-defined concept of Caribbeanisation', and the complementary idea of "alternative tourism'. The chief instrument of 'Caribbeanisation' would be the small hotel. This would be locally owned, and its smallness and its siting within the community would lead to more genuine interaction between tourists and local people. These ideas represent a rejection of 'pleasure-reserve' tourism. It is argued that the small hotel run by local people, serving local food would attract a different kind of tourist, hence 'alternative tourism'. The new Caribbean tourist would be more aware of Caribbean problems, more inclined to experiment and less interested in buying a glossy 'package'.

There is some sincerity and a lot of enlightened self-interest in all this. The new discussion and the new initiatives are a direct response to the growing opposition to tourism within the Caribbean. Racial conflict and political activism have damaged the tourist industry and, along with external factors, have caused the Caribbean to lose a sizable percentage of its tourist trade to Europe. Tourism in Europe is cheaper than in the Caribbean and more varied. Thus a reform of the industry is necessary both to ease social tension and to attract the tourists being lost to Europe. The disillusionment with the present form of Caribbean tourism was summed up by James Mitchell, the Premier of St. Vincent when he declared: "To hell with Paradise!" He argued that as the Caribbean was no paradise for its inhabitants, it should not be sold as such to tourists. 

THE MYTHOLOGY OF ESCAPE 

In their response to this the C.T.A. have failed to face up to the full complexity of the situation. The C.T.A., and particularly its executive director and chief theoretician Herbert Hiller, wants to inject some reality into Caribbean tourism. 

This would require a complete revolutionisation of an industry that is based on illusion. Since the mythology of escape is indispensable to tourism it is not so easy to reject the image of "paradise." When tourists visit the Caribbean to forget the anxieties, frustrations and social responsibilities of the metropoles they can hardly be expected to take a serious interest in the problems of the society they are visiting. The tourist comes in search of a world of pleasure, an island of lotus-eaters. He expects the beach to be clean and the natives to be friendly; if they are not he is angry, he feels cheated, but he is unlikely to make much attempt to understand the root causes of polluted beaches or local hostility. A radical change in the nature of Caribbean tourism would have to be protected by a radical change in the attitudes of affluent North Americans and Western Europeans.

Tourism is, in every sense, the most inappropriate vehicle for the development of a Third World country. It exacerbates the most obvious symptoms of social injustice (illustrating on a local scale, a global situation). At the same time it tends to reduce the possibility of any radical solution to that injustice. 

It produces a "diversion of priorities"-the "demonstration effect" of the rich tourist leading to a pursuit of the material signs of affluence, while agriculture is

neglected. If large scale tourism development does come about in Haiti, it will be both too rapid, and inadequately controlled. This will cause maximum social disruption and environmental damage, and provide minimal benefit for the mass of Haitians. As we have seen, tourism cannot provide adequate employment, and while it will lead to an improvement in communications, the new roads and air-strips will give access to beach hotels, and not to Haiti's famine areas. It is, precisely, the last thing that Haiti needs. 

[To the Point, Jan. 12, 1974, a South African Journal] HAITI-THE RICH GET RICHER (By Alphonse Max, Port-au-Prince) 

Haiti is a country of apparent contradictions. Ninety per cent of the population are illiterates who live in huts that lack sanitation and other basic essentials of modern life. At least a third are jobless, and the average income of $80 a year is the lowest in the Western Hemisphere. The minimum daily wage of one dollar is enough to lure hundreds of Haitians to the capital of Port-au-Prince each month.

Despite the hardships, the mostly black, West African descendant population sings and laughs in the streets of the capital and in the jungle villages. Art is flourishing—both modern and traditional. It speaks of the talent and imagination carried across the ocean centuries ago, when the people were brought as slaves.

The country's 23-year-old "President for Life", Jean-Claude (Baby Doc) 

Duvalier, has loosened the rigid authoritarian rule exercised by his father. 

Francois (Papa Doc) Duvalier who died in 1971. The feared Tonton Macoutes, Papa Doc's personal elite force of gangsters, which numbered around 30,000 men, has been greatly reduced and lost most of its influence. 

Baby Doc is trying to bring better health and education as well as some comforts to his five million countrymen. One of his first moves was to encourage foreign investment, which is now pouring into Haiti at the rate of 80 million to 100 million dollars a year, attracted in part by recent tax exemptions, and the low cost of labour. Many factories import all raw materials and export the finished product.

As wages in Haiti gradually increase with improving economic conditions, part of these manufactured products may find an outlet in Haiti itself. But, it seems there is one product which will always remain an export: the baseballs hand sewn by Haitian workmen who boast that they are the only ones who still know this art. In one plant, 3.7 million baseballs are stitched together every year for export to the U.S.

Tourism is another basic pillar for projecting Haiti into the 20th century. Many of the newly established industries cater to this trade. U.S. companies are leading the way in hotel development. Humphreys Overseas Development, of Tennessee, early to recognise the potential, has built a modern 125-room hotel. They have been followed by Holiday Inns which has been granted permission to open a chain of motels. Dupont Caribbean is building a hotel complex on La Tortue 

Island, complete with recreation parks, swimming pools, indoor and outdoor sports facilities and a casino.

Baby Doc's authoritarian regime has survived nearly two years, which is no mean feat. Simply surviving the political storms within the Duvalier clan has been an accomplishment of note.

GNP INCREASES 

Few can deny the progress which has already taken place. The gross national product increased 5.7 per cent in 1971 and 6.5 per cent in 1972 against an average of 1.7 per cent during the Papa Doc era-further increases in the growth rate are expected. More than 150 U.S. manufacturing firms are now operating in Haiti. 

Further development is coming from international organisations such as the United Nations and the Inter-American Development Bank, who have offered long-term loans for roadbuilding and agriculture. 

The U.S. has granted military aid for about 10 million dollars, mostly for the defence of Haltian coastal water-Castro's Cuba is only a few miles away. 

National spending for health care and education has expanded five times since 

Papa Doc's rule.

These initial advances seem to have stemmed the immediate threat of a Marxist engineered revolt. The Parti Unifies des Communist, under the leadership of 

Jacques Dorsilien, had hoped for a quick takeover after the death of Papa Doc. 

But the expected chaos did not occur and Baby Doc has proven to be, unlike his father, a harsh foe of the communists. Under the old regime, several Marxists served in the cabinet and various agreements were negotiated with communist countries, including free passage for Cuban ships through Haitian waters and "flag of convenience" agreements for Bulgarian and other East European shippers. Notably, the cabinet of Jean-Claude had not included a single Marxist. 

Aided by his mother, Simone, young Duvalier is firmly in the saddle, and after the ouster of the powerful minister, Luckner Cambronne, there appears to be no one to question his authority. His older sister, Marie Denise, returned from exile with her husband, Colonel Max Dominique for a short stay. They originally left the country after participating in an aborted coup against her father. They left again when it was revealed they had been political rivals, but business associates of Cambronne. Their joint economic activities centered on the illegal exporting of large amounts of blood plasma to the U.S. 

The threat from other exiles, most of them in Canada, the U.S. the Dominican 

Republic, Cuba, and the Bahamas, seems small. The greatest number are in the 

United States and Canada and like the higher standard of living there. They are not anxious to return or to take part in any anti-Duvalier activities. The different rebel groups, some of them trained in Cuba, are considered hopelessly divided. 

After many years of oppression and economic stagnation there appears to be hope for Haiti, though not immediate spectacular success. Already the middle classes, while admittedly small, are better off than before. 

But with economic expansion comes rising expectation from the masses. It will take all the efforts of the rulers to keep the progress ahead of these rising hopes.

TWO-EDGED SWORD 

With the chill of winter in their bones it is understandable that the West Europeans have so far been complaining loudest about the blackmail by the Middle East oil sheiks. Yet now that Africa and the rest of the Third World have had a chance to take stock of the fuller implications of the oil crisis, the hard reality is beginning to sink in that it represents a terrible blow to them.

Although the sheiks have promised to keep their Third World friends (especially those in Africa who congratulated them so enthusiastically for shaking off the West's economic grip) fully supplied, they are also charging them the full price. And so rapidly has the price of oil escalated, that the World Bank now calculates that virtually the entire foreign aid of the West to the Third World will be offset by the higher oil prices. In other words, most of the foreign aid the 

Third World receives in cash will flow into the pockets of the Arab oil producers. 

INTO THE RED 

Another serious implication for the Third World is the boost the new oil prices will give to inflation in the industrialised countries. The rapidly rising prices the Third World must pay for essential industrial imports have long been a sore point among the poor countries. And with so many industrial products affected by the oil prices they will have to foot part of the West's higher bill. World Bank experts in New York predict that many Third World countries will go massively into the red this year in their balance of payments. As many of the industrialised countries will be landing in a similar situation as a result of the higher cost of oil imports, and a downturn in world trade, they will be unable to help. 

The extent to which the higher oil prices are going to hit the balance of payments of the industrialised states is reflected by the fact that in 1970 they had to spend more than 30 per cent of their total import bill on oil against a mere 18 per cent in 1960. And compared to the latest prices of oil was dirt cheap in 1970. 

The research division of the World Bank now estimates-after the recent doubling of Gulf prices-that most if not all of this year's projected $4500 million in foreign aid will have to be paid out for oil. The bank also points out that the poor countries will find it very difficult to cut oil consumption as it provides energy mostly for basic industries. To the officials of international aid organisations the oil crisis thus represents one of the biggest setbacks they have had to contend with.

To World Bank President Robert McNamara, who has been nicknamed Chair man Mac because of his many ideas on foreign aid, it provides confirmation of one of his key contentions: that too much of world aid lands in the pockets of too few. 

[From the Los Angeles Times, Monday, June 10, 1974.] FOREIGNERS TRY A POSITIVE LOOK AT HAITI REGIME RETURNING INVESTORS SEEK TO DISCOUNT THE EXCESSES LAID TO DUVALIER DYNASTY (By Stanley Meisler) 

PORT-AU-PRINCE, HAITI.—This is the year for foreigners to polish up the image of Papa Doc and his dynasty. 

It is an odd psychological phenomenon. Visitors to this Caribbean nation find many foreigners, especially Americans, both businessmen and diplomats, trying to persuade them and themselves that: -Despite his excesses, President Francois Duvalier, who died three years ago, achieved a social revolution in Haiti. -These excesses were probably exaggerated anyway by irresponsible foreign correspondents and Graham Greene in his novel, "The Comedians." -Papa Doc's successor, his 22-year-old son, Jean-Claude Duvalier, the new "president for life," is running a relatively stable, responsible and nonrepres sive government. Said one diplomat. "This is one of Haiti's peaceful and more promising periods."

The reasons for these beliefs are probably obvious. After a lapse of more than a decade, foreign aid technicians and foreign businessmen are coming back to Haiti. U.S. foreign aid is now almost up to the level that it was when President 

John F. Kennedy suspended it in protest against the excesses of Papa Doc. The foreigners, especially the Americans, would feel better if they could persuade themselves that the Duvalier dynasty was not as bad as its reputation. 

One belief can be dismissed out of hand-the argument that the terror of Francois Duvalier was exaggerated. It is not held as strongly as the others anyway. 

But it does come up. An American businessman who lived under Papa Doc said. "Things were not as bad as you reporters made out. Haiti is safer than New York.

Fewer people were killed here than in the Dominican Republic next door." 

But Papa Doc's reign, which lasted from 1957 until his death in 1971, was probably among the bloodiest in the Third World, rivaled only by that of Gen. Idi 

Amin in Uganda and by the Tutsi tribesmen in Burundi in Africa. 

In a recent study for the Twentieth Century Fund, Harvard University historian Robert I. Rotberg estimated that, between 1960 and 1964 alone, the Duvalier regime killed 2,000 Haitians in Port-au-Prince.

The other beliefs cannot be dismissed. There is some truth in the arguments that Duvalier achieved a social revolution and that his son is running a more humane government.

Throughout its chaotic history, Haiti has been a split society-a tiny elite, mostly of mulattoes, separated from the masses of black former slaves. In the past, the distinction was always easy to make. The elite spoke French, thought of themselves as European, practiced Catholicism, attended school and filled all the key posts of government and professional jobs. The black masses spoke Creole, followed African customs, practiced voodoo, kept out of school and tended their tiny plots of land for subsistence food and a few dollars a year. 

In the last decades, a new black class began to develop, a kind of middle class. Despite their impoverished background, this small group managed an education and aspired to some positions held by the elite. Francois Duvalier, a medical doctor, was a member of this class. He also belonged to a group of anti-mulatto writers who tried to turn Haitians toward their African roots.

In 1946, the black middle class made a breakthrough when Dumarais Estime was elected president. Estime began opening the elite-dominated bureaucracy to blacks. Duvalier was his minister of labor.

Duvalier, who came to power as president in 1957 with all the rhetoric about a black social revolution, finished the job that Estime had begun. The Haitian civil service is now heavily black. 

There are other signs that blacks have benefited from the Duvalier regime. 

The top secondary school in Port au Prince, which had an enrollment of only 10% blacks when Duvalier came to power, is half black now. Many prominent blacks insist that they have an entree into elite social life that would have been unthinkable in the 1950s.

But the black entry into power under Duvalier was very selective. In a sense, a new black elite developed. Duvalier ruled like a potentate, favoring those who pleased him at one moment, turning against them at the next moment. His henchmen, the infamous Ton Ton Macoutes, killed many more blacks than mulattoes. 

Some mulattoes, in fact, had power under his rule because he trusted them. The mulatto elite control of the economy was never broken. Duvalier didn't even try. 

On top of this, the black masses of Haiti, the peasants who make up more than 80% of the 4.5 million population, did not benefit at all from Duvalier's so-called revolution.

A trip to the countryside quickly reveals the neglect of the peasant. As ever, the black farmers, without any government help, hack at the ground with hoes in an attempt to extract their subsistence out of their tiny farms on eroded hills. 

Where there is outside help-piped water, a dam, a nutrition center-it invariably comes from a foreign organization like Church World Services. Not only did the 

Duvalier regime fail to build new roads for the peasants, it allowed the old roads to deteriorate.

Two centuries ago, Haiti was the richest colony in the New World. Now it competes with countries like Chad and Upper Volta for the desperate distinction of being the poorest place in all the world. It is among the 10 most hungry countries. The average Haitian eats 400 to 500 fewer calories a day than the minimum of 2,000 calories considered necessary for good health. Haiti has the highest death rate in Latin America.

From 1960 to 1971, the gross domestic product increased an average of 0.1% a year. In 1972, the gross domestic product averaged $87 a person, the lowest in Latin America. The average annual income of a peasant was under $10. 

Papa Doc did not take over a rich country and make it poor. He took over a poor country and left it poor, at least as poor as he found it. 

In his study, historian Rotberg had this to say about Duvalier's social resolution: The progressive social revolution never occurred. Instead, Haitians experienced tyranny, rapacity, and an all-encompassing, disfiguring dictatorship... More blacks from the lower-but not the lowest-stratum of society had been given a stake in the perpetuation of Duvalierism, but there has been no transformation of society."

In short, the so-called social revolution only brought a few loyal Duvalier followers to the top and left the black masses on the bottom. 

As for Jean-Claude Duvalier's government, there is no doubt that the son has been far less repressive and tyrannical than his father. Armed Ton Ton Macoutes no longer walk the streets of Port au Prince. It has been more than a year since the government rounded up political prisoners. Many exiles have returned to resume their life in Haiti.

But, as one diplomat put it in a recent interview, "Although there is no longer the great fear of terror, this is not a democratic society. Anyone talking against the government faces the threat of being picked up." 

Ever since Papa Doc died, many outsiders here have taken part in a guessing game about political power in Haiti. The son, named president for life, is a chubby, baby-faced young man with little experience. His detractors call him "tete du lard" (fathead) or "ti ton ton" (little uncle). At first, few people believed he could really run Haiti.

In the guessing game, foreigners concluded that Mrs. Simone Duvalier, the widow of Papa Doc, really ran Haiti, or Mrs. Marie Denise Dominique, the sister of Jean-Claude, or army officers or Luckner Cambronne, the minister of interior, who was finally ousted by the young president in November, 1972. More recently many outsiders have decided that Jean-Claude himself runs Haiti.

This game itself reveals a good deal about the irrationality of the political system bequeathed to Haiti by Papa Doc, who, before his death, annointed his son as the successor.

A cynical American who deals quite a bit with the government said recently, "If this government was one person, it would be committed. It's a classic case of paranoid schizophrenia."

A Haitian businessman, a longtime critic of Papa Doc, has this to say about young Jean-Claude: "He is president for life. You know what that means? He is our monarch. A monarch. Monarch of what?" The Haitian burst out laughing and then suddenly stopped his laughter. He rested his forehead in the palm of his hand. "You know," he said, "it is very humiliating here."

Posters around town show a photograph of Jean-Claude with the following quotation: "My father made the political revolution. I will make the economic revolution." There is no indication as yet, however, that Jean-Claude's regime 34-192 O - 74-76

has been any less neglectful of the black masses in the countryside than the regime of Papa Doc. 

On top of all this, the Jean-Claude regime may not be as stable as claimed by most foreigners here. In May, for example, Port au Prince was struck by two mysterious explosions, one at the cargo shed of Pan American World Airways at the airport, the other at the National Insurance Offices not far from the presidential palace. The second explosion destroyed all the social security and pension records of Haiti.

It is obvious that a good many foreigners here are guilty of self-delusion in their analysis of Haiti and the Duvalier dynasty. That does not mean that they are wrong to come to Haiti with foreign aid and investment. But it does mean that many of them, including American policymakers, may be ill-equipped to make the hard decisions about where to put the finances that the people sorely need.

Senator INOUYE. Our first witness is Mr. Herman Kleine, Assistant administrator for Latin America, who will be followed by nongovernmental witnesses who have advised the committee they want to submit their information on this subject. 

Once again, welcome, sir, and if you will introduce those accompanying you, you may proceed, sir.

GENERAL STATEMENT 

If I may, sir, I will proceed with my statement. 

Senator INOUYE. Please do, sir. 

Mr. KLEINE. Mr. Chairman, I welcome this opportunity to appear before your committee today to review with you the U.S. assistance programs to Haiti which are underway or which are proposed for this fiscal year.

First, I would like to discuss the background related to the resumption of our programs in fiscal year 1973. I say "resumption," although actually the term "intensification" more accurately describes the changes in our program in that year. From 1963, when our AID mission was withdrawn from Haiti, until 1972 humanitarian assistance was continued in the form of a malaria eradication program and through Public Law 480 title II supplementary feeding programs administered by U.S. voluntary agencies.

In the late 1960's, after a period of relative isolation for Haiti, the inter-American community became more concerned with the development needs in this most desperately poor country, the poorest of the hemisphere. The Organization of American States sent a team of consultants to Haiti to review the country's development plans and needs, its institutional capabilities and limitations, and the fiscal and budgetary performance of the Government. Specific supplementary studies

1 were also undertaken by the Inter-American Committee of the Alliance for Progress (CIAP) in several of the key sectors of the economy. The general conclusion of such studies was that the performance of the Government in addressing the economic and social needs of the country was increasingly satisfactory and warranted the resumption of external assistance to Haiti.

In 1972 the CIAP endorsed the conclusions of its secretariat and recommended to the donor community the resumption and intensification of economic assistance to Haiti. Subsequently in 1973, new assistance commitments to Haiti were made by France, Canada, and Venezuela and projects resulting from these commitments are now being implemented.

In January 1973 AID appointed a representative in Port-au-Prince and made an initial loan during the same year to improve Haiti's capacity to maintain its deteriorating road system. 

The international financial institutions also have resumed sizable programs, with the World Bank authorizing its first loan to Haiti in many years in 1974, with other proposals under consideration. Likewise, the Inter-American Development Bank, the IDB, through the initiation of two recent loans more than doubled its total lending to the country over the previous 12 years. 

The U.N. and OAS have intensified their technical assistance programs, and the U.N.'s world food program is expanding. The International Monetary Fund, which maintains a resident staff member in Port-au-Prince to advise the Central Bank on monetary and fiscal management, is providing technical assistance in selected other areas, such as customs administration. In addition, the Governments of West 

Germany, the Republic of China, and Israel are now providing bilateral assistance.

To complete the picture, Mr. Chairman, I should mention the several dozens of voluntary agencies both religious and secular-of both United States and other nationalities which are attacking the problems of health, nutrition, and education in the Haitian towns and countryside, with generally increasing budgets and staff resources. 

Thus the judgment that the climate in Haiti is conducive to a meaningful economic and social development effort is one which is shared by the entire international development community, the international institutions as well as an increasing number of donor countries. Furthermore, this substantial effort is one in which the United States is very much a partner. It is a reflection, too, that the development community cannot ignore the poorest country in the Western Hemisphere, but must respond in a way that directly improves the economic and social welfare of the common man in Haiti. 

Mr. Chairman, we feel this is an effort in which the United States should participate, but also in which we remain a significant but minor partner to other international institutions and donor countries. 

I would like to turn now to some of the economic developments and policies of the present Government of Haiti which have led the international development community to intensify its effort. First, the context. The economy of Haiti is small with a total GNP of only about $500 million; total Government receipts are about one-tenth of this amount.

For at least a decade the economy had been virtually stagnant. Its infrastructure was in an advanced state of disrepair, and, as mentioned earlier, the population of the country was and is by far the poorest in the hemisphere with less than 15 percent literacy, with infant mortality at a rate in excess of 150 per 1,000 live births and with a level of per capita income of less than $130 per year. Nevertheless, in spite of these great constraints, the Government is making serious attempts at development. Its achievements, while modest, are significant in the 

Haitian context. These include the following:

Installation of three electric generators completed with Haitian resources at the Peligre Dam, thus tripling domestic power generation. 

Modernization of the international airport at Port-au-Prince, again using its own resources. 

Increased operational and development budget allocations, especially for agriculture, health, education and physical infrastructure. At the same time no budgetary increases were included this year-the fiscal year runs from the 1st of October to the 30th of September-for the

Ministry of Defense and Interior. 

I should also note that the budget of the Ministry of Interior and National Defense includes not only that of the armed forces, but also the funds of the police and fire departments, the Presidency, cabinet officers, and certain other costs. Taking into account the development budget, which contains no funds for the Ministry of Interior and 

National Defense, defense expenditures approximate 13 percent of domestic government receipts, an amount less than 2 percent of Haiti's GNP. 

The Government also raised the price paid to producers of sugar cane by 50 percent. Most such producers are small farmers.

It revised its coffee export tax to assure more adequate returns to the farmer in times of declining prices. It regularized its external debt, payments. It eliminated the arrears in the payment of public salaries, which had been running at 3 to 4 months. It endeavored to raise public sector morality and, in fact, dismissed several notoriously corrupt high-ranking officials. It liberalized credit and savings policies. It increased the minimum wage, from 80 cents to $1 per day in 

1971 and to $1.30 per day in January 1974; and it has attempted to improve services to farmers, such as assistance in repairing irrigation canals, the provision of seeds and fertilizers, et cetera. 

Clearly, Mr. Chairman, much remains to be done, but we believe the Government of Haiti has demonstrated its intention to help meet the needs of the Haitian people. In the short run a government like 

Haiti's, with such limited means in financial and trained human resource terms, must concentrate on providing basic infrastructure and basic services, and the Government has moved to do so. 

During this period of gradual buildup of activities our AID experience with Haiti has been good. For example, one of the large activities we now support is a rural community development program in northwest Haiti, a particularly depressed area of some 400,000 people. To address the many needs of these people, a semiautonomous agency has been created, under the policy guidance of representatives of the national planning agency and the Ministries of Health, Agriculture and Public Works. Many of the professional staff of this organization have been seconded from other Government agencies which

have also made in-kind contributions such as facilities, bulldozers, and motor graders.

The Haitian-American Community Help Organization, better known as HAHO, promotes the establishment of community councils-of which there are now some 220 in the area-to identify community needs and to organize solutions to these needs. The organization provides certain basic services to the communities through the councils, such as health services, and provides technical and material assistance to the councils to carry out community projects. Some of the activities undertaken to date include road rehabilitation, reforestation and erosion control, potable water systems, irrigation, environmental sanitation, construction of health clinics, and agricultural production assistance to farmers.

This is not an isolated example. The Government of Haiti regularly makes available facilities and personnel to private voluntary organizations or in conjunction with official aid to facilitate the provision of services and assistance in rural areas, as it recognizes that, in the short run at least, it does not have the means or capacity to provide such services directly. Clearly the Government cooperates to facilitate efforts to improve the quality of life of the common Haitian. We believe it is sincere in encouraging such assistance and in its efforts to plan and organize so that it may begin to meet some of these needs directly.

U.S. assistance to Haiti is targeted on the rural sector where about 

80 percent of the people live. Our assistance is being designed to: (a) increase the quantity and quality of small farmer agricultural production so as to improve their economic well-being and (b) to increase the access of rural families to low-cost health services so as to improve their social well-being. In both sectors our assistance complements activities underway or planned by other donors. •· Agricultural production represents about 50 percent of Haiti's GNP and is the primary source of income for nearly 80 percent of Haiti's population. The Government of Haiti has assigned agricultural development a high priority. The challenge in the short run is to identify feasible projects within the economic and institutional capability of the Government, which will substantially benefit the common man. Analysis carried out by AID and other donors, in cooperation with Haitian authorities, suggest that priority should be given initially to the rehabilitation of rural infrastructure, primarily roads and irrigation systems, and to the intensification of production of traditional crops.

AID is currently providing assistance to rehabilitate and maintain the road system so as to provide access to farmers to agricultural inputs, such as fertilizers, and to enable the farmers to more efficiently market their production. AID is also cooperating with an agricultural mission from the Republic of China in a rice seed multiplication program and with the Mennonite Central Committee to test the acceptability and productivity of high-lycine corn varieties. Additionally, AID recently, in fiscal year 1974, approved a small farmer improvement loan design to increase rural income through the rehabilitation of coffee production.

An agricultural sector loan is planned for the current fiscal year, fiscal year 1975. The loan will center around the rehabilitation of com-

munity irrigation systems and will include also the provision of better seeds, improved storage and marketing facilities, and credit. It is anticipated that much of the physical work involved in the rehabilitation of these small irrigation systems will be performed directly by the farmer-beneficiaries with technical and organizational assistance provided by private voluntary organizations. 

As in the case of agriculture, serious institutional and financial limitations exist with regard to the health sector, where serious malnutrition and debilitating disease affect a large share of the country's population. The longer term objective of programs in this area is the establishment of a low-cost health delivery system for the rural population, appropriate to Haiti's resources and needs. Planning assistance to achieve this objective is being provided to the Government by 

AID and by the Pan American Health Organization. 

As an initial step in that direction the capacity of the previous malaria control agency is being expanded with AID assistance to address other communicable diseases, such as tetanus and tuberculosis, in addition to its continuing malaria control responsibilities. Additionally, the Government is working with AID, the United Nations Fund for Population Activities, and other donors to design a feasible family planning program for Haiti. It is anticipated that this program will be underway around the end of this calendar year. 

The requirement that Haiti finance 25 percent of the costs of our projects is a serious limit on our ability to be responsive to its development needs. With the increasing activity of several international donors which I have referred to and for which Haitian counterpart funding is also required the burden on the very small Haitian budget is increasing rapidly. Some flexibility in applying the 25 percent requirement in the 25 least developed countries would increase our ability to respond to their acute development needs. 

In sum, we believe the Government of Haiti is making an earnest attempt to follow constructive policies at home and in its international relations. Moreover, we consider it has done so with some measure of success. As the Government develops experience and confidence we would anticipate its record will progressively improve. We believe this trend is encouraging and should be recognized for the effort and direction it reflects, and for the promising-if modest-beginning it represents. This trend warrants encouragement because it offers some hope of alleviating the tragic poverty of the Haitian people.

HAITI'S BUDGETARY APPROACH 

Senator INOUYE. On page 16 of the report, the last paragraph intrigues me and I wonder, Mr. Administrator, if you have seen that.

I quote as follows: 

"One of the most serious deficiencies in Haiti's budgetary approach is the existence of nonfiscalized revenues. Estimates of funds flowing into the government that are not accounted for in the budget range as high as $10 million. This is a significant amount in a country whose official operating and development budgets total approximately $48 million." 

Are you aware of this, sir? 

Mr. KLEINE. Yes, sir. That is the funding account called the Regie du Tabac, which in essence is an agency for the collection of excise taxes from a number of commodities, and the estimates of the receiptsand they are just estimates-run to the neighborhood of about $10 million.

The need to fiscalize, to treat these receipts as general revenues, has been emphasized to the Government of Haiti by all the agencies working with the Government of Haiti. 

The IMF, the World Bank, the Inter-American Committee of the Alliance of Progress, when it has reviewed the Haitian situation, have been urging this further fiscalization. We think that the situation is improving and will improve as the Government finds greater confidence in its ability to deal with the problems and as it needs to support the development projects that are made available from other agencies.

As there is a pickup in the interest of the agencies and I do mention that the international agencies, the IDB and the World Bank, are the primary movers of resources, we anticipate in Haiti—as their activities increase, there will be an increased demand on the Government of Haiti to contribute resources to these projects, the counterpart, and this will be a pressure on them to release their resources for these purposes.

They use these resources in many ways. We don't know all the uses, but we do know that in times of need when prices go up on the commodities and the inflationary situation seems particularly bad, they increase imports into the market so that the population will have

greater access to supplies. But this is a problem and it has been mentioned to them. They understand it and we think that progress will come as this dialog increases with the Government over the future. 

Senator INOUYE. Is there any sort of accounting as to how these funds are being used? Without objection there will be inserted in the record at this point a table reflecting total U.S. assistance to Haiti from 1946 to 1973. The amount shown will be $139 million broken down as $134.9 million in economic assistance, $4.1 million in military assistance.
