SUSPENSION OF MILITARY ASSISTANCE 

Senator INOUYE. What were the circumstances under which U.S. military assistance to Haiti was suspended?

Mr. SHLAUDEMAN. I can say, Mr. Chairman, that at the time we suspended our other assistance activities we also suspended military assistance and withdrew our military group, and I might say in reference to your question to Mr. Corrigan we have no intention of reestablishing a military group in Haiti.

Senator INOUYE. Just for the record could you tell us why U.S. foreign assistance, military and economic, was suspended?

Mr. SHLAUDEMAN. I believe, Mr. Chairman-and I would have to go back to check the official records at this time--I believe in essence that we suspended assistance to Haiti because it was in our judgment not being effectively used. This was the basic rationale. 

Senator INOU YE. Did it have anything to do with the alleged activities of the predecessor regime?

Mr. SHLAUDEMAN. I think it probably did, Mr. Chairman. 

PROPOSED FISCAL YEAR 1975 MILITARY ASSISTANCE 

Senator INOUYE. Will you detail and justify the $200,000 in military assistance proposed for Haiti in fiscal year 1975?

Mr. CORRIGAN. Mr. Chairman, I understand that this consists mainly it is divided into two sections. A small training program on the one hand and then assistance to the Haitian Air Force on the other.

Senator INOUYE. This is part of the air-sea rescue program? 

Mr. CORRIGAN. Yes, sir, part of that, and the coastal patrol capability. A recent message from there indicates that at the present time there are three small 65-foot patrol boats in the Haitian inventory, of which no more than two are operable at any given time. Both crews lack training and overall expertise to conduct search and rescue operations.

Large tourist ships, small boats are arriving in Haiti in everincreasing numbers. The majority are from the United States. In the event of emergency the U.S. Coast Guard must be called upon at great expense to the U.S. Government to conduct these mercy missions. 

These operations are not only embarrassing to the Government of Haiti, but often place costly demands on the U.S. Coast Guard which could well use its resources elsewhere. 

In 1973 alone the U.S. Coast Guard participated in over 63 operations involving vessels, aircraft and personnel missing or in distress in Haitian territory waters and skies. The proposed grant training program would substantially assist the Haitian Government to assume a much greater share of search and rescue operations, thereby reducing to a significant degree the requirements placed on our own Coast Guard.

Essential proposed training for the Navy consists of the following: 

Basic English courses to prepare the French-speaking candidates to attend the appropriate service school, land, sea and surface communications, radio maintenance and repair, leadership, basic seamanship, boat-handling and small boat navigation, maintenance and repair of diesel engines, maintenance and repair of inner and outer harbor

navigational aids, basic supply and administration, maritime damage control, basic marine ordnance. So much for the Navy per se. 

The Haitian Air Corps represents an important element in the conduct of search and rescue operations. It has the potential of rapidly locating victims and providing timely evacuation. The aircraft currently in the Haitian inventory working closely with the Navy could adequately participate in such operations. 

Mention is made of the flexibility of helicopters. The Air Corps training, training for Air Force people, will consist again of English language training, air-sea-land communications, aircraft radio maintenance and repair, life support systems, search and rescue operations, air navigation, helicopter maintenance and repair, instrumentation repair, and finally supply management. 

In broad outline this is what the training hopes would consist of. 

Senator INOUYE. Although I realize that the training could be used for unintended purposes, are you, directly or indirectly training or equipping Haitians with guns or other offensive material? 

Mr. CORRIGAN. Certainly not. The Haitians- 

Senator INOUYE. I mean in the training program. Are you giving any training for the use of weapons? 

Mr. CORRIGAN. I am not entirely certain of that, Mr. Chairman. 

There might be some small weapons capability because these patrol boats have guns, of course, mounted on board. 

Senator INOUYE. Nothing beyond that, such as rockets, heavy weapons?

Mr. CORRIGAN. I think not, Mr. Chairman. 

Senator INOUYE. Mr. Administrator, may I request you and your colleagues to remain with us during the morning while we receive the testimony from other witnesses. I gather that some of the statements made will speak of certain activities which are alleged to be happening in Haiti at the present time on which I would like to have your thoughts also. 

Senator Brooke.

PROJECTION OF AID LEVELS Senator BROOKE. What are the projected U.S. aid levels for Haiti for the next several years?

Mr. KLEINE. Well, we are now, sir, preparing our internal budget reviews for the next fiscal year, fiscal 1976. This is an examination that is proceeding across the board for Haiti, for other countries in Latin America, and for other regions of the world. It will be sometime before decisions are made on the fiscal year 1976 program. Beyond that, our projections are in general terms only. In general, we visualize, sir, a continuation of the modest but significantly important program bilaterally supplied.

That is why the question of replenishment for the IDA is particularly important for a country such as Haiti. Haiti is one of the few countries in Latin America that benefits from the IDA replenishment. We would see those benefits providing for the largest capital inputs. We would be emphasizing the technical assistance component. 

And without being, of course, definitive in any way, it seems to me that the general magnitude that we have in mind for 1975 at some increase reflecting as it necessarily must the inflationary situation, would continue, but so much depends on things about which we cannot

forecast, the price of coffee, the availability of resources from other sides, and most important the ability of the Government of Haiti to come up with some counterpart to be able to draw down and draw upon the resources of other agencies. 

We fully agree that for every project or program there must be an earnest effort by a recipient government, and there is no better carnest effort than its willingness to put up some of is own resources. But the Haitian situation is one that is so tight that we have asked for greater flexibility, but its own ability to help finance the activities of the outside and its own institutional capacities are weak, as many of them still are, and these will take some time to develop, so its ability to utilize much larger volumes of technical assistance will be constrained over the next few years.

I am sorry I can't give you a precise indication in terms of levels, but I am trying to sketch as far as the U.S. bilateral program a modest but significant participatory role with the other agencies in helping Haiti move gradually but hopefully steadily forward in addressing the needs of its people. 

Senator BROOKE. This committee is concerned about long-range projections as well as annual programs. We need to have some indication as to how much we might be requested to appropriate for Haiti over a period of years.

I am well aware of the difficulties involved in formulating a multiyear plan given alterations in the environment such as worldwide inflation. Nevertheless, do you see a steady, modest but significant expenditure of U.S. funds for assistance to Haiti?

Mr. KLEINE. Yes, we do. The needs just cry out. Their ability to use our experience in their use of our assistance, these things will be factors that will have to be taken into account as we make these decisions.

COORDINATION WITH OTHER DONORS Senator BROOKE. What is the degree of coordination of U.S. aid with that of other donor countries?

Mr. KLEINE. There is a very active program of coordination, sir, that goes on both at the field level in Haiti and here in Washington amongst the agencies involved. The CLAP, the Inter-American Community of the Alliance for Progress, has taken perhaps a more active role in helping to coordinate in Haiti the assistance effort of donors than in other countries.

The annual session which is held to review progress and problems provides an opportunity each year to review with the Government of Haiti officials that it sends to these meetings and in combination. with representatives of all the other agencies to see what progress is and see where further efforts may be called for, further policy changes may be desirable.

In the field there is constant contact amongst representatives of the agencies. It is recognized particularly in a situation such as Haiti where there is such a thin small margin, if any margin exists, for waste in terms of duplication that we must avoid overlap and duplication, so the process goes on at both levels. It is a continuing process and it is one that is supported by all parties because of the very great need for such coordination.

CONTROLS ON AID 

Senator BROOKE. What controls exist to insure that U.S. aid is used for its intended purposes?

Mr. KLEINE. We have on-scene managers. In fact, even during the period when our program was totally humanitarian, with the provision of supplies for our feeding programs under Public Law 480, we had managers in our embassy in Haiti. We have a regular system of audits through our Auditor General's office and of course, we apply our regular evaluation system to our activities in Haiti as everywhere. 

We in Haiti are covered by the program of audits of the Inspector General of Foreign Assistance and, of course, it is subject to examinations by the General Accounting Office. We give very close attention to this element of our work. As one of the reasons we have deliberately decided to proceed cautiously in 1971 and to examine step by step the question of use of our resources and I am pleased to say, Mr. 

Senator, that the results thus far have been very encouraging. 

We have no indications of desire on the part of anyone to misuse or abuse our assistance.

POTENTIAL MISUSE OF FUNDS 

Senator BROOKE. Mr. Kleine, is there any point in the aid administration process at which the Haitian Government could misuse our funds?

Mr. KLEINE. Well, all our funds are provided on the basis of a project agreement. The agreement outlines the purposes. We have the right of audit, the right of inspection, and if there should be such abuse, we would catch up with it at some point and then ask them for a refund or other appropriate steps. Conceivably, as in any place, it is theoretically possible at least for some period of time that there be the use of certain equipment intended for a project used for another purpose. 

That would be observed at a later point and corrections made. 

But, as I said earlier, Senator, we have not seen any problems of this kind since the intensification of our activities in Haiti. 

Senator BROOKE. You know of no evidence of any misuse of U.S. aid to Haiti? 

Mr. KLEINE. That is correct.

Senator BROOKE. No further questions, Mr. Chairman. 

ISRAELI AID TO HAITI 

Senator INOUYE. I have two questions before proceeding, sir. First, I note that Israel is involved in some bilateral aid agreement with Haiti. 

Mr. KLEINE. Yes, sir 

Senator INOUYE. What sort of program is this?

Mr. KLEINE. It is technical assistance, the provision of advisers as they do in many countries in Latin America. They are very well regarded in the area of water and cooperatives, and so it is in these areas that they have been providing assistance in the past and we anticipate in the future, too.

THE DUVALIER GOVERNMENT 

Senator INOUYE. My final question. I realize this is a very broad one, very general one, but I believe it is a question in the minds of

many. The present government in Haiti has been described as being inhuman, repressive, dictatorial, not concerned with human rights. 

Many articles have been written to this effect, and I would like to get the official views of AID as to the charges made against the present 

Duvalier Government. 

Mr. KLEINE. I would make some initial comments, sir, and then ask

Mr. Schlaudeman to amplify, if I may. 

Senator INOUYE. We are not speaking of the old Papa Doc Duvalier, but the present regime.

Mr. KLEINE. Exactly. We, of course, took very seriously the comments made by your committee in its report of last year and proceeded to look at the situation again, both from our perspective in Washington and in the field. The concern of the committee in this regard, and indeed the general concern of the U.S. Government for these kinds of problems where they may exist it has been communicated to the Government of Haiti on a number of occasions and there is understanding on their part as to this interest. 

Now, with regard to the specific allegations as to the situation of Haiti now-and I think it is important to consider the present in the context of what it was-I would ask Mr. Schlaudeman to provide those comments.

Mr. SCHLAUDEMAN. Well, I think, Mr. Chairman, that the description in Senator Brooke's report of this aspect of the question is an extremely good one, one that we would generally endorse. In the long perspective of Haitian history I would think this government stands out in many respects for a somewhat more humane approach, a more civilized approach, I think a real desire to improve the lot of the 

Haitian people.

It is an authoritarian government, but it is a government which I think falls far short of any totalitarian practices. We believe there has been improvement. We believe this improvement continues. 

Senator INOUYE. Senator Chiles. 

REFUGEES 

Senator CHILES. Can you give us any idea how many refugees presently are outside of Haiti in the Bahamas or Haitians are presently in the Bahamas?

Mr. SCHLAUDEMAN. We don't have very accurate figures. We think somewhere around 50,000 probably in the Caribbean and elsewhere. 

That does not include Cuba where there is a large Haitian colony. 

Senator CHILES. How would you classify these 50,000? Are they political or economic refugees?

Mr. SCHLAUDEMAN. As far as we can tell, Senator, the great majority of them are what we would call economic refugees, people seeking employment elsewhere. 

Senator CHILES. Is that a growing figure today? Is there continuing to be Mr. SCHLAUDEMAN. It is a continuing problem. I don't believe it is growing rapidly, but it is growing, no question about that. 

Senator İNOUYE. I would like to follow up the refugee question. 

It has been suggested by some who are critical of the Duvalier Government that the American Government will only assist those refugees who flee Communist regimes and who may be nonblack regimes. They are suggesting that if the regime is black and non-

Communistic, the United States will not provide assistance. Is that a fair assessment?

This was brought about because recently I believe refugees were apprehended and deported when they insisted that they were political refugees, and I believe one of the refugees committed suicide. 

Mr. SCHLAUDEMAN. Mr. Chairman, we do not accept this allegation in any sense. Each refugee who arrives in the United States, each 

Haitian refugee is carefully interviewed and a study is made of each case. We try to determine on the basis of those interviews and of other information known to us whether the person has genuine cause for political fear, has left Haiti for political motives. 

There have been, I believe, around 20 who have in the course of this process been identified as perhaps having some cause for leaving Haiti because of political considerations and in all those cases they have been allowed to remain in the United States. 

Senator INOUYE. Senator Hatfield. 

Senator HATFIELD.  

THE HOUSING PROBLEM 

As I understand, there have been a number of American firms located, because of cheap labor, near Port-au-Prince and they established assembly-type operations and various other types as well, and this has caused some migration to the urban center from the dominant rural population pattern Haiti represents. 

What is the situation in the housing area there as far as aid or any other data that you may have concerning the housing problem in the urban center? 

Mr. KLEINE. Any problem one looks at in Haiti, one comes away with the feeling that the needs are overwhelming. So you have in 

Haiti the real test of what are the priorities, limited funds both on the part of the Government of Haiti and the part of donors. I do know that representatives of the Government of Haiti have talked about their need for assistance in this area. 

We have in the past considered tentatively the use of a housing investment guarantee program, but that is a high-cost program. The interest rates that flow with that program, it would address the needs of the middle and upper middle class in Haiti. It is a need that could be dealt with in part that way. But because of the great number of areas which require attention, because of our desire not to have the Government's efforts be dispersed so that nothing is effectively done in addressing any one problem, and because it has been identified that the agricultural rural areas where most of the people live and where the most abject poverty exists, we, with the approval of the Government of Haiti, have selected the rural area, the health area, the agricultural area, and have not yet moved in any way to be responsive in the housing area.

MOVE TO URBAN AREAS 

It is a fact that as in other countries there is a trend of a move from the rural areas to the urban areas. The fact is that Port-au- 

Prince has received perhaps a relative imbalance of the resources available to the Government to the neglect of in the past the allocation of resources to the field, the rural area.

Perhaps not by explicit design, but the difficulties involved in getting services and people out to stay in the rural areas, so our hope is that by working on improvement in the rural area we will tendthis is a hope tend to slow down the movement of people into the cities.

We will never eliminate it. That will go on. 

Senator HATFIELD. I don't quite follow how you expect to slow it down, because I understand much of the capital that is flowing into Haiti today is flowing primarily in two major economic directions, one is to provide better tourist facilities to attract the tourist industry, and No. 2 is for these companies-here is a rather extensive list of them—which have taken advantage of cheap labor by developing component parts of their general company or corporation in New York, Chicago, et cetera. This development is, of course, related closely to the transportation center of Port-au-Prince. 

Now, if the natives who are so poor and if they are suffering from such economic stress, they see these job opportunities in those two areas. They are going to tend to move in that direction, aren't they? 

Mr. KLEINE. You are absolutely right. The resources coming into these areas, tourism and industry, are in the private sector. It is in the public sector that I was addressing the resources from the World Bank, the IDB, the United States working in the rural area to give these people greater opportunities to improve their lot may tend to slow down the move.

I haven't seen the move slow down anyplace around the world. It goes on, and I should comment, sir, if I may, that these transformation industries do take advantage of the fact that labor costs are very low in Haiti, but they do provide jobs.

I was looking at figures in recent reports. Just from 1970 to 1973 an increase of 15,000 jobs in these industries. These industries contribute very significantly to the overall balance of payments to Haiti, so they are providing an assist to the economy, but as you suggest, also providing a magnet for people to come in. 

Senator HATFIELD. We are basically then depending on the trickledown theory in the application of some of this aid. 

Mr. KLEINE. I believe not, sir, with regard to the direct assistance that we are providing. For example, in the small farmer improvement loan our assistance will go-the loan was just recently approved to the beneficiaries directly in the form of credit, in the form of technical assistance, in the form of training. 

Senator HATFIELD. That is under the more updated policy as compared to the past?

Mr. KLEINE. The development program since 1973. We were out of Haiti in the development field for about 10 years. 

HAITIAN BUDGET 

Senator HATFIELD. Do we have a breakdown of the national budget as to what the Haitian Government is utilizing, how it is utilizing its own resources? 

Mr. KLEINE. Yes, sir, we do. 

Senator HATFIELD. Could you give us in general what percentage of this national budget goes for helping people in these same areas of rural, urban and job development, health education, as compared to 34-192 O-74-77

the other expenditures of police, security, overhead of government, and so forth? 

Mr. KLEINE. Yes, sir. Most of their budget goes to salaries.

Senator HATFIELD. To what? 

Mr. KLEINE. Salaries of personnel. They have two budgets. They have the operating budget for the normal operating expenses for their established agencies, and a development budget. The total is about $50 million a year. The Department of Interior and national defense receives approximately $8 million, which is the same level that it got the preceding year, but that figure includes activities that normally do not fall into a department of defense. As indicated in my statement, sir, there are allocations within this figure to the police and fire departments, the Office of the Presidency, Cabinet offices, and the total of the expenditures for this are all broad categories. The ministry represents about 13 percent of the total available under the operating and development budgets. 

The total funds going to agriculture, education, health, public health and general development represent about 58 percent of the budget and this is a percentage that has been going up. I believe the report of Senator Brooke also provides this breakdown. 

ROLE OF PRIVATE VOLUNTARY AGENCIES 

Senator HATFIELD. Have you observed the programs of the voluntary agencies as to whether or not they have formed a better record of getting aid and support directly to the people as in contrast to, say, governmental aid that flows from government to government? 

Mr. KLEINE. The role of private voluntary agencies in Haiti is a very active one and we believe, sir, one that will be even more active. 

The Government of Haiti recognizes that it just doesn't have a capacity and is not likely to have in some years to reach out. 

Senator HATFIELD. As far as infrastructure is concerned?

Mr. KLEINE. That's right. They encourage and facilitate the programs of voluntary agencies. They want to know what they are doing, of course, and that is not a problem. And so much of the activities that we had during the period of this humanitarian approach was carried out through the voluntary agencies and we are now proceeding with the voluntary agencies to examine what it is we have in prospect down the line, to see what they can do to participate in this, we hope, slightly expanding effort. 

Senator HATFIELD. You mean channel more resources of the AID 

program through the volunteer agencies? 

Mr. KLEINE. That is correct, sir.

Senator HATFIELD. We have a very fine record of that, you know, in Cambodia.

Mr. KLEINE. I understand, and I hope you will have the opportunity to visit in Haiti and see that the record in Haiti is a very good one, too.

NEEDS OF THE PEOPLE 

Senator HATFIELD. The thing that bothers me about foreign aid generally, and focusing down to Haiti particularly, is that, first, we oftentimes find that the aid, well-motivated and well-programed, is en-

meshed in a trickle-down structure to the actual people in need. Secondly, the aid is often a supplement to a national budget that has priorities in sustaining its political regime or in support of its own political ambitions with lesser priority to the needs of their own people. Thirdly, we find ourselves in a situation where our aid is really a form of American business enterprise subsidy in which we are merely indirectly subsidizing American economic enterprises because of cheap labor or because of such authoritarian regimes that they have stability. 

Those things bother me because they are, to me, a form of economic imperialism which the natives, even though they may not be educated, are very quick to sense and understand. Perhaps they understand this far more easily than some of our own American people, who see this only in terms of the theory and the procedures that are involved. 

I raise questions about this Habitation LeClerc or something that was advertised as seductive environment for people to come and enjoy the pleasures of a tropical climate. Well, to me the white American tourist enjoying that in the very presence of poverty, being waited on by poor people, certainly doesn't build a good strong American image abroad in the long run.

Even though we can use all sorts of economic justification for providing employment, etc., I think we have to examine this trend both in the long run as well as in the short. 

Mr. KLEINE. May I comment, sir? It is a very broad question.

The Habitation LeClerc was not an AID project, but it was an OPIC loan to help boost tourism, and while tourism itself does not help large numbers of individual Haitians, tourism as a sector has been one of the prime movers of the economy in these past few years. 

Tourism has grown from 1968 of 56,000 per year to 171,000 in 1973, and brought with it foreign exchange, quadrupled the availabilities in 1968, but that is not an area that AID is working in. But I would like to comment briefly on your general comments.

AID's programs these past several years have been almost exclusively in agriculture help to the small farmer, education to bring education to those who have not had the experience or to help governments reduce the costs which have become very great. Some governments are spending 30 percent of their budget for education, but reaching just a small percentage of their people. 

Likewise, we are trying to help them become more effective in health by bringing low-cost health services to those who have not yet benefitted from such programs. I don't see, sir, how assistance of this kind, which represents 80 percent of our program proposal of fiscal 1975the other balance is for the additional support to Nicaragua to help it recoup from the disastrous earthquake of December 1972-how that kind of assistance I have sketched fits into the mold that you have sketched. It may very well be that that is the image of past activities, but we are trying deliberately, and again under the thrust of the legislation that was enacted a year ago, to reach small people, and we are trying to find our way.

We are not subsidizing American business that way. We are only responding to these needs when the governments themselves have identified these as being priority needs and only then when they themselves are contributing significantly to these programs.

THE UNITED STATES-HAITI ECONOMIC RELATIONSHIP 

Senator HATFIELD. Well, that is fine. Let's take the full picture of 

American economic relationships here. Let's take both the insurance application in Haiti, and to further support my thesis, a chart that Mr. Mays provided for our committee. These loans and both insurance applications were compiled by both percentage and in amount of dollars. We find on the chart that manufacturing firms are 22 in number. This represents 51 percent of the total amount. Tourism is listed at 23 percent or $48 million. Finally, agribusiness drops to only 

14 percent.

So, the heavy emphasis here has been, at least in this one phase of our economic relationship, on manufacturing and tourism. Now these provide jobs, true, but the jobs exist at an almost exploitive level. In the meantime, small farmers and agriculture, under this particular relationship, are emphasized less and only fall into the 14percent category.

All I am saying is that beyond even your projects, taking the total relationship, these statistics tend to bear out the negative image of American investment in Haiti, an image that bothers me greatly. 

Thank you very much.

Mr. SCHLAUDEMAN. I would like to ask, Mr. Chairman, if you would excuse me. I have to appear before another Senate committee. Mr. 

Burke will be here to handle any further questions. 

Senator INOUYE. All right. 

Mr. SCHLAUDEMAN. Thank you. 

Senator INOUYE. Mr. Kleine, may I request that you and your colleagues remain here and be ready to respond to questions if such should arise.

NONDEPARTMENTAL WITNESSES STATEMENT OF HERMANN L. DESIR, CHAIRMAN, AMERICAN- HAITIAN COMMITTEE OF REFUGEES AND MEMBER OF THE BOARD, INTERNATIONAL LEAGUE FOR THE RIGHTS OF MAN VIEWS ON DUVALIER 

Senator INOUYE. Our first public witness is Mr. Hermann Desir, chairman of the American-Haitian Committee of Refugees and member of the Board of the International League for the Rights of Man. 

Welcome to the committee, sir. Please proceed.

Mr. DESIR. Dr. Francois Duvalier after his seizure of power in 1957 talked a lot about his revolution and his doctrine of "Duvalierism" which was to bring to Haiti an era of peace, prosperity, and happiness. The late president wrote voluminously on the subject, a veritable panegyric of the new regime under which Haiti was to witness extraordinary changes, an example to be followed if not by the whole world, at least by the black world. In a word, Haiti was to become a true paradise.

But the reality has been quite different. Far from bringing peace, prosperity, happiness and the promised equality, Dr. Duvalier behaved like a cruel tyrant. Far from assuring to Haiti the social, economic, and material welfare of all Haitians, whatever their color, religious beliefs or political opinions, Duvalier, his family and his myrmidons, have pillaged the country. They have embezzled public funds and exacted exorbitant taxes collected by force and terrorism, applied by the Macoustes and Leopards, killers of thousands of innocent and harmless citizens.

The Duvalier regime has plundered the people's exchequer, sending abroad for deposit in numbered accounts in Swiss banks important sums which could have served to educate the Haitian masses and institute an equitable system of distributing the national wealth. 

Dr. Duvalier holds the Haitian elite responsible for all the country's misery. No country can exist without an elite, and an honest Haitian elite, aware of its responsibilities to the people, could render great service to the Nation. Unfortunately this has not been the case up to the present. The so-called elite of the Duvalier era has been the worst of all, since it is made up not only of millionaires who have lied their way to great wealth, but of ruthless assassins who have not hesitated to cut down innocent and harmless citizens.

Let not the Duvaliers and their acolytes try to tell us that they are the champions and benefactors of the Haitian people. Lies, all lies. 

The Duvalierist clique has always been dominated by a policy of every man for himself, which of course includes larceny and pillage (public and private) as well as assorted frauds and swindles. All this is being done by the Duvaliers and their chief confederates under the guise of "revolution." (1219)

Under this pretext they have given arms to poor illiterate wretches who have known nothing but hunger and disease and told them that all their troubles have been due to the actions of a minority-the enemies of Duvalier-on whom they must wreck vengeance. Robbing, trampling and killing those men who have been designated enemies of the people, these blind militiamen have gone as far as murdering children, women and elderly men.

Instead of guaranteeing all Haitians a minimum basic education and teaching them the sacred principles of the declaration of the rights of man and the duties of citizenship in a democratic society. 

Duvalier has spent millions to maintain an armed militia. Under the orders of Duvalier and his accomplices this militia has kept an entire people in a state of terror.

After 16 years of barbarity and atrocious crimes, after wrecking the economy of the country, after 16 years of rule by the force of bayonets, Duvalier handed on his office of President for Life to a stripling, his son Jean-Claude, who was barely 19 years old. With this final act he violated the rights of 5 million free citizens and transformed Haiti into a monarchy of monkeys.

This rape of a once-free nation, without precedent in the history of the Americas, discredits not only the people of Haiti but also the great powers who in the name of democracy support this regime of assassins. To resume in a few words the dictatorship which for 16 consecutive years has abused and which continues to abuse the people of Haiti, is impossible.

The first words that come to mind, brutality, superstition, ruthlessness, mutilation, murder-are feeble and empty of meaning as applied to the magnitude of the crimes against Haiti. In fact, the policy of the government of Duvalier Junior today is based on total terrorism like his father. As this is written, 60 prisoners have just been murdered at Fort Dimanche, the concentration camp and torture chamber where a great number of political personalities still languish.

But we need not go as far as Fort Dimanche. In the cellars of the 

Palais National itself there are today haggard prisoners-bearded, long-haired, half-blind wretches whose only crime was to be denounced without proof by personal enemies hungry for vengeance, innocent men who wait impatiently for the liberation that death will bring.

Woe to him who opens his mouth to utter the slightest criticism, however benign, of any action by the government or a militiaman. 

Let us analyze the four points which represent the political philosophy of the Duvalier government: 

1. Democratic liberties reestablished. Sheer trompe l'oeil to create an illusion that would calm the fears of the United States aroused by the horrible crimes perpetrated by the regime and reported daily by the world press. Some American newspapers, rewarded by funds distributed by Jean-Claude Duvalier's secret police, have picked up the fiddle to play the government's golden tune while whole families in Haiti are dying of starvation. 

2. The country has attained political maturity. Another big lie. To justify this formula the government guarantees the safety of all political exiles who want to return to their country. What a cruel deception. More than one exile let himself be caught in this booby trap.

Once back home, no one ever heard of him again-except for those reported killed in auto accidents, shot in a family quarrel, or who committed suicide because of money troubles. Just 2 years ago anthropology professor Clovis Charlot was mysteriously killed in Port-au- Prince. No explanation has been furnished. 

To give faith to those doubting the attainment of political maturity, the government has just announced legislative elections. Is this not a mockery of that fine democratic institution, the legislature, which is a guarantee against the abuse of executive power? Avowedly there is only one power in Haiti, that of the President of the Republic. Note we have not said "the Executive," for the executive power is an organized extension of the function through a ministerial cabinet wherein each minister is responsible for his own department. 

But with this new and factitious apparatus the fledgling Jean- Claude Duvalier and his coterie of murders think they are presenting a new image of themselves to the civilized world. False hope, for this wolf in sheep's clothing will fool no one. 

3. National economy reconstituted on a solid basis. Again a false note in the siren song! Poverty has never been so widespread and deepseated in Haiti. The seductive serenade is simply to attract foreign capital on the pretext that the Haitian economy is entering the 

Golden Age.

The evident aim of this mendacious propaganda of the corrupt government of the junior Duvalier is to dangle before the eyes of American capitalists the glittering possibility of using cheap Haitian labor to the detriment of the already-depressed Haitian labor market. The 

Haitian worker earns in a day what the worker in neighboring Puerto Rico, for instance, earns in an hour. And the Haitian gets no social security benefits of any kind.

The American Government seems only too happy to see its industrialists profit by this type of exploitation which makes slaves of the Haitian people in a so-called democracy where human rights are being violated constantly. And yet this is the immoral government which receives American Government support on the pretext that the United States can tolerate no disorder in the Caribbean and that only a strong government can maintain peace and quiet. 

We call this sort of peace factitious because the idea that only force can control a people is a short-sighted concept. As oppression grows, so grows the hate of the people for the despotic regime until revolt must break out. And there is nothing more terrible or destructive than the revolution of a people driven by hate. Haiti today is a dormant volcano already rumbling with the precursory signs of an eruption. 

4. A strong government is necessary to prevent a Communist seizure of power. This last argument has already been used by dictators who, to reinforce their dictatorship, have raised the bogeyman of communism as a threat to democracy. What they call democracy is their power to oppress their people. 

Jean-Claude Duvalier pins a spurious badge of communism on every decent citizen who in the name of liberty demands respect for the law and the Constitution. But the decent citizen tends to forget that in 

Haiti there is neither law nor constitution. Only the Hougan, the witch doctor, can influence the decisions of the government. And these Voodo priests, evil and ignorant, make use of their power over officialdom

to gratify their personal vengeance on enemies and to grow rich at the expense of the impoverished populace. Under the Duvaliers Haiti has become the Kingdom of the Zombies and the Empire of Black Magic, all this in the very heart of the Americas and under the eyes of the Organization of American States. 

In the year three of Jean-Claude the country has reached the lowest depths of poverty and squalor. Whole families are dying of malnutrition and preventable disease. World statistics place Haiti among the lowest ranked three or four nations of Asia and Africa, the undisputed and unenvied titleholders as the most wretched have-nots on 

Earth. 

The 16 years of the fierce and criminal dictatorship established in 

Haiti by the Duvaliers, father and son, may be summed up as follows:

According to statistics furnished by the Haitian press in New York 72,000 innocent victims have lost their lives. At the time of the decease of Duvalier pére 450 political prisoners were impatiently awaiting death at Fort Dimanche, that temple of inhumanity from which only 

1 captive in 10 ever comes out alive.

It is in the name of the principles of justice, liberty, and international morality, therefore, that I denounce the intolerable conditions heretofore enumerated, and against which I believe it is imperative to appeal to the Organization of American States and to the International League for the Rights of Man to take the necessary steps leading to a halt in this bloodbath. 

Thank you. 

Senator INOUYE. Thank you very much, sir.

Before proceeding, I would like to refer all of the witnesses to the telegram that we sent to all of you, inviting you to testify. Because of restriction in time we hope that all of you can stay within the 10minute time limit requested by this committee.

Mr. Desir, I note that you have served as consul in the United States and in France and also a U.N. delegate and a director of tourism of 

Haiti. When did you begin your service for Dr. Duvalier?

Mr. DESIR. I never served Dr. Duvalier. I never. I served Mr. Magloire until 1957. When Mr. Duvalier came to power, he put an end to my services at the consulate and also in the tourism. 

Senator INOUYE. You were in service before 1957? 

Mr. DESIR. That's right.

Senator INOUYE. In all of the statements that we have looked over, we see many numbers being mentioned: 72,000 killed, 450 imprisoned, et cetera. Is there any way we can receive documented evidence?

Mr. DESIR. Well, it is not possible, Monsieur le Senator, because the work to establish the quantity of Haitians killed was made in Haiti and published by the Haiti-Observateur in New York and in the name of the party who signed it because it is not possible to have openly said anything about. You had to do it confidentially and we are very careful because the Government is watching everything they are doing when they try to denounce those crimes, but it is a fact. Unfortunately we cannot prove it.

Senator Inouye. Senator Brooke. 

Senator BROOKE. What alternative government do you believe would be possible for Haiti? 

Mr. DESIR. What is possible in Haiti is to save what you call the morality and dignity of 5 million human beings, to try by all means to

clean Haiti of the regime of Duvalier, to try to have a decent government by election of the people who is a participant of the Organization of American States, the Commission Internationale des Juristes de Geneve, and the U.S. internal press to support this, so that the government does have free elections, at least giving to the Haitian people the opportunity to choose a clean man, a man who loves his country.

We try not to become rich, but to save the country which is dying. 

Senator BROOKE. How do you propose to achieve this?

Mr. DESIR. That could be achieved by, for instance, suspending the diplomatic relations with this regime, which is illegal, because Haiti is not a monarchy. Mr. Duvalier had no right to appoint himself. It was enough for him to take the power for 15 years. He should have the decency to say, "Well, at least let me give to the Haitian people a chance to do something for themselves."

Senator BROOKE. You have agreed that there is dire poverty in 

Haiti. You are a Haitian and you have great love for the Haitian people. Do you advocate that the United States terminate its humanitarian assistance to the Haitian people?

Mr. DESIR. I am not in favor of starvation of my country. It is true when you give money to Haiti, a majority of your money goes to the Army, to the militiamen, the Macoutes and Leopards, and to those in power, and the education gets very little, the public health almost nothing.

Port-au-Prince is the most fatal city in the world, but I can't say no, don't give money to them. You should give them money, but you should control until the last penny the ways they are expending that money. 

We should never let anyone in Haiti among those in power have the right to write a check to the bank to take money. 

They should be controlled by the United States by all means in everything. That is the only way to save until better days will come, because we hope better days will come. 

I am not too young. I am 76 years old, but I hope I will see Haiti in better shape than now, and I will. 

Senator BROOKE. Mr. Desir, I went to Haiti at the request of the chairman of this subcommittee to seek out facts, with all of the objectivity and impartiality that I could muster, with the one exception that I have always had great respect and admiration for the Haitian people, their art, and their culture. 

Mr. DESIR. Thank you. 

Senator BROOKE. I hope you will believe my findings at least on this point, that American aid is not under control of the Haitian Government-and you heard testimony from Mr. Kleine to that effectthat our aid is given, if not exclusively, primarily for food and for agricultural purposes aimed at terminating some of the starvation in Haiti. If you can accept that, will you agree that this country and other countries should continue to give humanitarian assistance to the country of Haiti even with the present government in control? 

Mr. DESIR. Certainly, that would be wonderful if it would be possible to control everything to the last penny, where it is going and what it is doing. I am trying to save the masses who are dying, working for $1 a day while in Puerto Rico they make $1.65 an hour.

It seems to me I have no facts-but American industry establishing in Haiti is paying more than $4 a day for each Haitian worker. Why does the Haitian have only $1? Who got the $4?

Senator BROOKE. Mr. Desir, I will conclude with this. No man is infallible. Certainly I don't profess to be. I have had some training as a lawyer and State attorney general to make investigations and to look for facts and for truth. I saw no evidence of widespread terrorism. 

I inquired not just of the Duvalier government, but of many others, both Haitians and foreigners. I found no evidence of extensive political oppression at this time. I did find poverty. You might argue that they knew I was coming and they prepared for my visit in Haiti, but I can assure you that with what I consider to be a somewhat trained eye I found no evidence of many of the things that you have indicated in your testimony before this committee.

The chairman asked you about your figures, the deaths, tortures. 

I would like to know in my concluding question to you what are your sources of information within Haiti? How do you get your information?

Mr. JOSEPH. Mr. Desir has asked me to answer it. Sir, I have had time to read your report. I am Raymond Joseph, publisher of the

Haiti-Observateur in New York, and I will be next, so he wants me to answer those questions. However, I want to be specific with that question.

Senator BROOKE. Your sources of information? 

Mr. JOSEPH. My sources of information, I cannot give them because 

Haiti is a dictatorship Senator BROOKE. I am not interested in individuals. 

Mr. JOSEPH. All right. They are Haitian sources of information. The fact that I have been publishing a newspaper for the last 3 years starting with 1,500 copies, and now I have gone to over 25,000 weekly, and that each week I am giving information about what is going on in Haiti, not only about what is going on in New York, is proof of the accuracy of most of my information.

I am giving names of people arrested. You don't see anything about oppression there, you say. Well, in the last 2 months they have had a wave of arrests. Even Don Bohning, the Latin American editor of the 

Miami Herald, who recently visited Haiti has published in the Herald of June 23 the following:

Make no mistake, the present Government remains the most authoritarian in the hemisphere, political persecution does still exist, graft and corruption by most accounts continue at high levels and a free press is unheard of. 

Nor has the Government shown any genuine dedication to upgrading the lot of the more than 4 million Haitians who struggle to eke out a subsistence living in the countryside.

While arbitrary arrests do not occur on the scale they once did, they reportedly do still happen, although are hard to confirm. 

Recent and reliable reports have it that from 25 to 29 Haitians were arrested in the southern peninsula city of Jacmel for alleged subversive or Communist activity.

Also recently a French seminarian who had been in Haiti for several years was expelled for alleged anti-Government or subversive activities. 

In an unrelated incident earlier this year, demonstrating the Government's sensitivity, the resident representative of the United Nations was given 72 hours to leave the country for reasons that are still not fully known. . 

Now if they can do that to foreigners, just think what they are doing to Haitians. I will add a few names of Haitians arrested and you can check with the Haitian Government. 

Senator BROOKE. Would you submit those for the record rather than read them out?

Mr. JOSEPH. Fine. I will submit them.

STATEMENT OF RAYMOND ALCIDE JOSEPH Publisher, Haiti-Observateur (weekly) 

It is apparent that with the prevailing ethics of the times, the United States Government has decided to be less stringent when it comes to spending the taxpayers' money. For there is no way to explain the about face of the American Administration toward the Haitian regime of the Duvaliers. 

Back in 1962, the Kennedy Administration cut direct U. S. aid to the Duvalier dictatorship because of corruption, mismanagement of funds and blatant violence. 

Since then Francois "Papa Doc" Duvalier has died and a so-called new regime headed by his then 19-year old son came into being. Interestingly the new regime calls itself "a continuation of the revolution" started by Papa Doc. 

Indeed it is so. Recently Don Bohning, The Miami Herald Latin America Editor, visited Haiti and reported his findings in a series of articles. In the Sunday, June 23 issue of the Herald, Mr. Bohning said: "Make no mistake, the present government remains one of the most authoritarian in the hemisphere, political persecution does still exist, graft and corruption by most accounts continue at high levels and a free press is unheard of. "Nor has the government shown any genuine dedication to upgrading the lot of the more than four million Haitians who struggle to eke out a subsistence living in the countryside. "While arbitrary arrests do not occur on the scale they once did, they reportedly do still happen, although are hard to confirm. "Recent and reliable reports have it that from 25 to 29 Haitians were arrested in the southern peninsula city of Jacmel for alleged subversive or Communist activity. "Also recently, a French seminarian who had been in Haiti for several years was expelled for alleged anti-government or subversive activities. "In an unrelated incident earlier this year, demonstrating the government's sensivity, the resident representative of the United Nations was given 72 hours to leave the country for reasons that are still not fully known. 

I can confirm that in the last two months the regime has arrested more than 100 citizens under the pretext that they are subversives. Among them, I will mention Marc Romulus, a teacher who was lured back to Haiti from Canada by the propaganda of liberalization of the "new" Duvalier regime. Others include two physician brothers: Dr. Claude and 

Jacques Innocent; Dr. Alix Adam, an associate of the Innocent brothers. Also arrested is Lionel Charles, a student leader. I could continue enumerating those that have been arrested but it would serve no purpose, for their names mean nothing to you, gentlemen. 

Suffice to say that the relatives of those who have recently disappeared in the dungeons of the Duvaliers are filled with grief. For they know not what has become of their loved ones. 11 If the past, under the "new" Duvalier regime, is any indication, those that have disappeared will be forever gone. In August 1972, a full year into the Jean-Claude Duvalier 'presidency-for-life, some 200 Haitians disappeared without leaving any trace. Among them 

I will cite Jean Bernadel, a vice president of the Bank of Canada, Leon Jean, a former 

Duvalier congressman and four former colonels.

Certainly corpses of rebels are no longer tied to chairs on main thoroughfares as in the days of Papa Doc. The "new" regime is far more interested in the dollars of American tourists to continue that practice. But corpses there must be, because those that disappear in Port-au-Prince are never produced. They have done away also with the special holidays, when commerce, industry and school children were summoned to watch executions that were broadcast and televised. But is there enough of a change to warrant an embrace of the 

Haitian regime by the United States?

It is noteworthy that the Human Rights Commission of the Organization of American States condemned the regime last year for not producing the prisoners that disappeared under Papa Doc. In other words, that unit of the OAS recognizes a continuity of policy under Jean-Claude Duvalier.

As for mismanagement of funds, it can be observed right here in a suburb of this capital. The unemployed sister of Haiti's president recently acquired a $335,000 villa in 

Great Falls, Va. Maxine Cheshire reported it all in The Washington Post. Recently, the 

Canadian paper Montreal-Matin reported the acquisition of a $200,000 house for a consul in Montreal. All these expenditures sparked an editorial in the Haiti-Observateur which is very a-propos. (May 17-24, 1974 issue)

Meanwhile, the Haitian government takes full page ads in American newspapers as it did in the Washington Star-Daily News last April to propagate lies about its accomplishments. I will, however, draw attention to a more accurate picture that appeared in * your Congressional Record last December when the Honorable Senator Hatfield presented the case of Haiti. ... ...

But we may be barking up the wrong tree. When the life-presidency was first proposed, it was established in Article 197 of the Duvalierist Constitution of 1964 that the late President Duvalier had solved all of Haiti's problems. Among other things, he had "brought about a reconciliation between the political factions, ...laid the foundations of the country's prosperity by promoting agriculture and the country's progressive industrialization, placed the State on a stable economic and financial footing despite the sinister maneuvers of a conspiracy of domestic and alien forces, ensured effective protection of the toiling masses by bringing into harmony the interests and aspirations of capital and labor, brought justice to the peasant and opened the way to his complete rehabilitation, achieved the eradication of mass illiteracy and thus fulfilled the aspirations of the humble and weak for enlightenment and well-being, ... imposed respect for the rights of the people and the prerogatives of national sovereignty, gathered all social strata under his benevolent protection,... directed his every action towards building a strong nation capable of fulfilling its destiny in full freedom and dignity, for the happiness of all its sons and for the peace of the world. "1 For all of these things, "Therefore

Dr. Francois Duvalier, elected President of the Republic (exercised) his high functions for life." ... ... ... ...

His son is continuing in this same tradition of lies. The whole system is based on lies. Unless it is changed from top to bottom, the millions of dollars of the United States will accomplish nothing.

But I am speaking in vain, for the Haitian regime of Jean-Claude boasts that it has powerful voices defending its cause in the United States. I doubt that even the Honorable 

Senator Brooke is aware of the exploitation that is being made of his picture in Haiti. 

For the initiated of the inner Duvalier circle, the picture of the Senator, together with Jean-Claude Duvalier and the American Ambassador Heyward Isham is passed from one hand to the other. And it is said: "He (Mr. Brooke) is our defender in the Senate. We have nothing to fear." 

Raymond Alcide Joseran 

July 22, 1974

STATEMENT OF RAYMOND ALCIDE JOSEPH, PUBLISHER, HAITI- OBSERVATEUR, NEW YORK, N.Y. 

TESTIMONY CONTINUED 

Senator INOUYE. Our next witness has already begun his testimony. 

He is Mr. Raymond Joseph, the publisher of the Haiti-Observateur. 

Mr. Joseph, would you care to continue in your testimony.

Mr. JOSEPH. It is apparent that with the prevailing ethics of the times, the U.S. Government has decided to be less stringent when it comes to spending the taxpayers money. For there is no way to explain the about face of the American administration toward the 

Haitian regime of the Duvaliers.

Back in 1962, the Kennedy administration cut direct U.S. aid to the Duvaliar dictatorship because of corruption, mismanagement of funds and blatant violence. Since then Francois "Papa Doc" Duvalier has died and a so-called new regime headed by his then 19-year-old son came into being. Interestingly the new regime calls itself “a continuation of the revolution" started by Papa Doc. 

I won't repeat some of the things that I have said already. I say that these things are still continuing. I will not go into the list that 

I have here, a few names, because they won't mean that much to you. 

However, if the past is any test of what is going to happen in the future, the increase of aid of the United States will not free our political prisoners because the aid has been increasing and the political prisoners have not been released.

Certainly corpses of rebels are no longer tied to chairs on main thoroughfares as in the days of Papa Doc. The "new" regime is far more interested in the dollars of American tourists to continue that practice. But corpses there must be, because those that disappear in 

Port-au-Prince are never produced.

And it is a known fact that the vice president of the Bank of 

Canada, Jean Bernadel and Léon Jean, a Duvalierist congressman were arrested 2 years ago and we do not know what has happened to them yet. If it can happen to a vice president of a bank, just think what happens to the little people.

It is noteworthy that the Human Rights Commission of the Organization of American States condemned the regime last year for not producing the prisoners that disappeared under Papa Doc. In other words, that unit of the OAS recognizes a continuity of policy under 

Jean-Claude Duvalier.

For mismanagement of funds, I am very glad, Senator Brooke, that you mentioned it. Your figures of $10 million are a little bit low according to the Haitians themselves. It is not $10 million. It is $20 million a year which is dissipated by the Duvalier family. But you know for Haiti, where people earn $70 a year per capita, I think it is very important that we know what is happening with the $10 million that is unaccounted for. 

That has been going on for 17 years. Multiply that, and it is $170 million even taking your low estimates. Perhaps this is the money used to buy the house of Jean-Claude's sister right in the neighborhood. You can check it right at Great Falls, Va. The unemployed sister of the President has bought a $335,000 home. With what money?

The President was criticized in the press of Montreal recently for

buying a $200,000 villa for a consul, and Canada is giving Haiti $1 million a year for certain development projects. The Government is now spending $1 million for a tomb for Papa Doc. Just think, $1 million in memory of the man who did all the things that we say were wrong. But I think things may not be that bad at all. I don't think

Haiti is poor to the point of needing aid. 

According to the Constitution of 1964, here are the reasons for which the Presidency-for-life was created. 

Among other things, Papa Doc said- He had brought about a reconciliation between the political factions... laid the foundations of the country's prosperity by promoting agriculture and the country's progressive industrialization. placed the State on a stable economic and financial footing despite the sinister maneuvers of a conspiracy of domestic and alien forces. ensured effective protection of the toiling masses by bringing into harmony the interests and aspirations of capital and labor .. brought justice to the peasant and opened the way to his complete rehabilitation .. achieved the eradication of mass illiteracy and thus fulfilled the aspirations of the humble and weak for enlightenment and well-being. . . imposed respect for the rights of the people and the prerogatives of national sovereignty gathered all social strata under his benevolent protection directed his every action toward building a strong nation capable of fulfilling its destiny in full freedom and dignity, for the happiness of all its sons and for the peace of the world. ...

For all of these things, "Therefore Dr. Francois Duvalier, elected 

President of the Republic . . . (exercised) his high functions for life."

His son is continuing in this same tradition of lies. The whole system is based on lies. Unless it is changed from the top to bottom, the millions of dollars of the United States will accomplish nothing. 

That is part of the Constitution, the Constitution under which the 

Presidency for life is handed down to Jean-Claude Duvalier. But these are lies. If they were not lies we would not be asking today for 

U.S. aid.

Therefore, if the Government can base a whole structure on lies, helping it to maintain itself is not bringing peace or rehabilitation to the people. Perhaps my presence here is futile.

I will tell you why sitting here may be in vain. The Haitian Government has been exploiting the visit of Senator Brooke to Haiti. I am quite sure the Senator doesn't know it. But they are passing this picture around to their faithful. It's a photograph of Senator Brooke, standing between Jean-Claude Duvalier and the American Ambassador. With this picture they are telling their friends-and they have sent the message to us in their own ways—you are wasting your time. We have our defender, even in the U.S. Senate, meaning Senator Brooke.

Perhaps this may not mean anything to you but the Haitian Government exploited another picture back in 1969, when the United States was changing its policy toward Haiti. That is when Rockefeller visited the country. His picture, arms interlocked with Papa Doc, also was passed around and that picture signaled the change, the embrace of the regime. So, the embrace of Papa Doc by the executive branch started some time ago, and now they are saying it's happening in the Senate too. That is the reason why I feel it is so futile sitting here. 

Thank you, sir.

Senator BROOKE. Mr. Chairman, If I may respond. 

Senator INOUYE. Please do. 

Senator BROOKE. I knew the picture you refer to was taken, of course, but it is customary whenever a U.S. Senator visits a foreign country to have a meeting with the head of state which I thought was certainly important, to discuss the economic development of Haiti and the use of our assistance. However, I had no idea that the picture would be used as you say it is being used nor did President Jean- Claude Duvalier have any indication of what I was going to say in my report.

That report has just been submitted to this committee. No report has been sent to Haiti to my knowledge as yet. I did not discuss with Mr. 

Duvalier or any member of his Government what my findings and recommendations would be. I never discussed it with any member of 

AID. 

The first time I met Mr. Kleine was today when he testified before this committee. I did not even discuss it with my chairman or members of this committee before the report was written and submitted, nor have I discussed the report with Mr. Heyward Isham, American Ambassador to Haiti. Therefore, I don't think anyone had any knowledge, except the staff assistant who went with me, as to what would be contained in my report.

It was based upon objective findings of fact and representations. It is not the purpose of this committee to get into political questions involved in Haiti.

This is a subcommittee on appropriations considering foreign aid for Haiti. Our primary concern is the level of economic assistance the 

United States may provide to your country. We are also concerned with the $200,000 suggested by Mr. Kleine as needed for some form of training that may involve a number of members of the Haitian Armed Forces. I believe the main emphasis in such training would be the development of a sea rescue capability.

I think the testimony by administration witnesses indicated that there was no intent to give U.S. military assistance to Haiti at this time or in the foreseeable future.

So, we are talking primarily, about U.S. aid designed to promote projects such as the nutrition centers I visited in northwest Haiti. 

I have been in Southeast Asia and other poverty stricken places including some here in the United States. I think that it is important not only that we give aid to starving people in Haiti and elsewhere. 

U.S. aid to Haiti is extremely meager in comparison to what we provide to Southeast Asia, the Middle East, and elsewhere around the world.

Even though the Duvalier government is authoritarian and does not mirror some of the principles of government I live under, I believe it would be wrong to deny assistance to the Haitian people so long as we can be confident that such assistance is used properly. 

We are doing everything humanly possible to see that our aid is properly controlled. I talked to representatives of voluntary agencies and to ambassadors of other countries about the problem of controlling the use of aid funds and I came away convinced that the moneys spent by the United States for humanitarian purposes are going to the Haitian people who need it. To determine whether or not this was the case was the primary purpose of my trip.

1 So, I don't think we are that inconsistent and I don't want you to feel that your presence before this committee has been futile because someone has passed a picture around. They do that all the time. I have had pictures taken with other individuals whose policies, either in toto or in part, I have been opposed to and those pictures were used for "political purposes." A public figure cannot avoid this happening on occasion. 

You are directing your testimony primarily to a political issue and

I perceive the basic question to be one of economic aid designed to relieve the plight of Haitians. 

In reference to the statement just made by my distinguished colleague, is it your testimony that we should stop all the assistance? 

Mr. JOSEPH. No, that is not the thrust of my testimony at all. The thrust of it is that for a government which is spending millions of dollars which it cannot account for millions of dollars that have been collected, there should not be any bilateral aid to that government. 

If you are going to help, through the organizations I have heard about here, let's do it. I would not say don't give the Haitians food. I would be inhuman to say so. But if there is a way of giving directly to the Haitian people without giving to the Haitian Government, fine. 

I have worked in Haiti in the past with Church World Service and distribution of food has occurred without the Haitian Government being involved in it. I am saying if you give bilateral aid to a regime which is siphoning millions of dollars of taxes on the side-Mr. Brooke said $10 million, $20 million according to others that frees them to buy a $335,000 home and to build a mausoleum for $1 million. That is all I am saying. 

Senator INOUYE. Are you against the involvement of the Peace Corps in Haiti?

Mr. JOSEPH. No, I am not against the involvement of the Peace Corps in Haiti. I think that would be a very good program myself but Papa 

Duvalier opposed it. If Jean Claude now wants it, I think it is a very good idea.

However, I think the regime is totally illegal for us to deal with it, but the idea of the Peace Corps, in itself, is a good one. 

Senator INOUYE. If it is illegal to deal with the regime then we must stop all aid because we cannot unilaterally extend ourselves into any country without some sort of concurrence from the ruling government. 

Mr. JOSEPH. All right. Let's talk about it this way. There is something in the Congress now about giving preferential treatment to the Soviet Union. We say if we are going to give preferential treatment to the Soviet Union, at the same time the Soviet Union should let some of the Jews leave the U.S.S.R.

If we are going to give some aid to Haiti, as I said, you are not dealing with a legitimate political regime. If it were up to me I would not deal with that regime at all, but if you must deal with it, there should be conditions. Preferential treatment should also include the release of political prisoners. I think we can pressure the Haitian 

Government to do certain things and it will do them. 

Senator INOUYE. In other words, you want us to condition our assistance. 

Mr. JOSEPH. That is exactly what I want. 34-192 O-74-78

Senator INOUYE. Even if it means food? 

Mr. JOSEPH. Well, there is where the problem comes, but as I say, they have had some agencies working in Haiti throughout the years working directly with the Haitians. But when government-to-government aid itself comes into play, then we should put some restrictions on it. 

Mr. Hatfield. 

Senator HATFIELD. Mr. Joseph, do I understand your position to be that we continue our aid that goes directly to the people under careful scrutiny and supervision, but simultaneously that we utilize diplomatic channels and other methods of communication, maybe a détente, maybe a conference, maybe a summit, but diplomatic channels that are open to us to pressure this Government to allocate its resources so that we do not find ourselves providing foreign aid to merely subsidize an existing autocratic regime that then can take its own domestic resources to utilize and almost completely sustain itself in power? Is that what you are saying?

Mr. JOSEPH. I could not put it better, Mr. Senator. That is exactly what I am saying and I would ask something else. It is not beyond your means to ask a government, which is not following the dictates of the late Papa Doc to change the edicts that Papa Doc put in the books. 

Some 50 to 75 of us are condemned to death in Haiti. Now, we should apply some pressure to change this. Not for me personally, because I don't suffer from it. 

Senator HATFIELD. Do you have any evidence, Mr. Joseph, that there are volunteer agencies that are in a position to get more of these aid resources directly to the people than under existing structures that we are utilizing?

Mr. JOSEPH. The church groups are doing a wonderful work in Haiti. 

I think that is a way it can be worked out and I have not done exhaustive study but I am quite sure if Senator Brooke, who was in Haiti, who met with some people from private agencies can testify to that, and I firmly believe that they always did a far better job than the Haitian Government in these areas. 

Senator HATFIELD. And you feel that there are multilateral organizations that could bring about closer and better supervision bilaterally. Is that what I understand from your testimony? 

Mr. JOSEPH. That is my position.

Senator HATFIELD.  

Senator BROOKE. The problem is not quite as simple as an "eitheror" choice between bilateral and multilateral donors. For example, the Israeli Government has provided aid for a successful agricultural project. I believe it is in the field of irrigation where Israel has great expertise.

It is impossible to divorce food needs from irrigation development or road construction. If you grow crops you need roads from the farm to the market. This is important. Isn't it important to see the total picture?

Mr. JOSEPH. Yes, but, Mr. Senator, at the same time you are telling me that, after talking awhile with Jean-Claude you see a willingness on the part of that regime to change, to put more into economic development.

Well, if you are convinced of that let's see the regime put in the $10 million that are not fiscalized into these kinds of things. If we don't see that, I don't believe what he says. 

Senator BROOKE. I can only tell you what Jean-Claude Duvalier said to me. He said he was committed to an economic revolution, committed to improving the plight of the Haitian people. 

Now, that is what he said. You can disagree.

You mentioned the fact that you and other exiles were under condemnation of death. As I mention in my report, the exile problem is a serious one. One witness was asked whether the recent exiles from 

Haiti were economic or political exiles. I believe the Senator asking that question said that to the best of his knowledge most of them were economic exiles. It is understandable for many of them to be economic exiles because of the poverty in Haiti. 

I am sure that many Haitians believe if they get out they can make a better living elsewhere.

Political exiles are a different question, especially if they are individuals who advocate the forceful overthrow of a government. I don't know of any government in the world that wouldn't exile or jail someone who wants to overthrow it by force and I am sure the Duvalier government views the problem from that perspective. 

If someone advocates the forceful overthrow of the U.S. Government, they would be jailed.

The same thing would be true in Western Europe. It would be true elsewhere. How governments treat such individuals might be different from country to country. 

Do you feel those who are political exiles, if they were allowed to return to Haiti, would advocate the overthrow of the Government by force?

Mr. JOSEPH. First of all, I want to address myself to this dichotomy between political and economic exiles. I am definitely a political exile. 

There is no question about that. There are others that fall within the threshold of economic and political exiles.

However, let's understand. If the economic situation is getting better in Haiti it is the wrong time for us to leave, and for the first time some Haitians are taking their sailboats, not jets coming from Spain. 

They are taking to small sailboats, risking their lives on the high seas reaching here. I don't think- 

Senator BROOKE. Will you yield for just one moment? I don't want to prolong our dialog too long. 

You have made an excellent witness. You have made a worthwhile contribution. The mere fact that economic conditions are worse in 

Haiti, as you say they are- and I have no basis to compare, so I take your word for it could be due to the fact that economic conditions are worse all over the world. They are worse here. You could have the same amount of money today in Haiti that you had in 1957 and be much worse off. 

Mr. JOSEPH. I am not saying the economic situation is worse. I am saying that according to what is being said the economic situation is getting better in Haiti but at the time the economic situation is getting better for the first time Haitians are taking their little sailboats and leaving. Is it economic or is it because there is political persecution also? I have no way of telling. We have to ask those people themselves.

When they arrive in Miami, in 20 minutes it is decided that they aren't political but economic exiles. These same exiles after extensive questioning by other investigators, were found to have been in jail in Haiti. But since it is the administration's position that the new government is getting better politically, it is not in the U.S. interest to show that these are political exiles from Haiti. 

After 3 years of battle a young man, his name is Jean Lascouflair, was given political asylum in Boston. But he had to fight 3 years to get it. He has lost two brothers. They are still in jail in Port-au-Prince and we don't know anything about them. His father and mother were arrested and beaten up and released, and they aren't allowed to leave the country today under the new government of Jean-Claude. And it took 3 years for the U.S. authorities to reach the decision that he is a political exile. This is outrageous.
