[AFTERNOON SESSION, 1:30 O'CLOCK, TUESDAY, JULY 23, 1974]  NONDEPARTMENTAL WITNESSES STATEMENT OF GERARD GAETJENS, LEGAL ADVISER OF THE JOE GAETJENS FOUNDATION, LITTLETON, N.H. 

ACCOMPANIED BY: 

FRANCTZ BAZELAIS FATHER ADRIEN BAZELAIS  

Senator BROOKE (presiding). The subcommittee will come to order. 

The chairman will be coming very shortly. 

Mr. Gaetjens, I think we will have you present your statement. 

Mr. Gerard Gaetjens, legal adviser of the Joe Gaetjens Foundation, Littleton, N.H.

Will you identify the persons at the table with you, for the record? 

Mr. GAETJENS. This is Franctz Bazelais, and Father Adrien Baze lais, a Haitian priest. 

Senator INOUYE. (presiding). You may proceed.

Mr. GAETJENS. Senators, I am not in favor of substantial aid to Haiti.

As a descendant of those slaves who defeated the armies of Napoleon Bonaparte, who fought gallantly in the battlefields of Savannah, who helped Bolivar to free the slaves of Latin America, who helped Abraham Lincoln to free the slaves of the United States, I feel humiliated to come here begging you not to give to my country $12 million because the tyrant you have chosen to be our master wants that money only to prove to our people that he has the strong support of the United 

States of America. 

I am confident that most of you will hear my plea for a small country which has always been considered a troublemaker and a poor example by most of the white nations of this hemisphere. 

We were the second nation of the new world to become independent. 

In 170 years of history, we have learned that a man, whatever his color, is generally a wolf for his fellowmen, whatever their color. When we were slaves, the white men used Negroes to beat us. We were sold to slave traders by black kings.

Today we have the feeling that among our worst enemies in the United States there is a handful of black businessmen who want to have a piece of the action in our country. But, fortunately, as always we have found a lot of black Americans, the ministers of the Baptist Churches of Miami, for instance, who have been raising their voice in favor of hundreds of Haitian refugees who are in the jails of Miami because they wanted to live like human beings. (1235)

When in the past a few black imperialists were among those who instigated the U.S. Government to take over our country, we have found a white man in the American Senate to present our defense, the Honorable Senator from Massachusetts, Charles Summer.

Several streets of Haiti are named after John Brown and Charles Summer.

We venerate and honor these two great white Americans, but the Haitian people on behalf of whom I am talking today, that is to say, 4,000,000 men, women and children, will hate forever the former 

American Ambassador in Haiti, Dr. Clinton Knox, who praises himself as one of the best friends of the Honorable Senator from Massachusetts, member of this committee. 

Francois Duvalier used Dr. Knox as a trump card in what I call "Duvalier's African political games."

Our history has taught us that the color of his skin does not make a man compassionate or just.

Mr. Knox certainly did not understand the grandeur of the Haitian history. The independence of Haiti was not made only by blacks, it was made also by mulattoes. It was also made by thousands of white men (French priests and Polish soldiers).

The independence of Haiti is the victory of the oppressed against the oppressors. In our first Constitution, the Founders of our country proclaim: Whatever their color, black, yellow, or white, the Haitian, from now on, will be known under the generic term "black." 

Honorable members of this Commission: When I turn the pages of 

U.S. history, I realize that this powerful Nation of yours is the most powerful in the world because its foreign policy has been mostly oriented toward business, however, inhuman the profit may be. 

The slogan of the pragmatic school of the State Department is "Business is our business." Today, a new world has risen from two bloody wars. Human rights have become a reality. There is still, I know, a long way to go, but I sincerely think, like many of the Senators of the United States of America, that the country mood is now "Fair business is our business."

You will probably be told by the Department of State that the policy of the United States is not to intervene in the internal affairs of another country provided that this country entertains good business relations with the United States, but asking another country to respect the treaties on human rights signed by its representatives is not intervention.

It is the duty of the U.S. Senators to demand that the treaties signed with the United States be fully abided by the parties. As to 

Haiti, I do not dare believe that Dr. Kissinger will tell you that your concern about this country means intervention. The whole world knows that the United States is responsible for the making of the Duvaliers. 

For those who know the history of Haiti, this country, thanks to a few Americans, is now a keg of powder. The longer you avoid taking a decision the more the United States will be forced to intervene publicly as they did in the Dominican Republic. 

I see two solutions: 

First: A peaceful abdication from Mr. Jean Claude Duvalier in favor of a man who may immediately reconcile the nation with itself.

Second: If Mr. Jean Claude Duvalier does not love his country enough to make such a sacrifice, the American Senate will demand that prior to the granting of any financial help, he accept the setting of an ad hoc international commission with the following objectivs: (a) Registration inside and outside Haiti of those who have been arrested since 1957 and not brought to trial; (b) to the heirs of those prisoners who will not be found in the jails of Haiti, the Haitian Government will deliver a death certificate to put an end to the agony of their beloved ones; and (c) those who are still in jail will be brought to a fair trial before the representatives of this commission are allowed to communicate immediately with their parents or relatives.

Senators, because of the hearing this morning, may I change the following paragraph?

In addition, it seems illogical to me that the United States wants to have a regime which practices slave labor in violation of International Treaty on Human Rights signed by Haiti and the United States.

According to the report published by this Commission, it is my understanding that a contract between American and Haitian firms stipulated a salary of $36.60 a day while a decree signed by Duvalier in January fixed a legal salary for Haitian workers at $1.30 a day which, in fact, he receives after 8 hours of work. 

We have reason to believe that this $1.30 per day for worker is mostly pocketed now by the officers of the government. 

I return to page 3.

To finish the general part of my exposé, I will draw the attention of the honorable members of this Commission on something which is of vital interest for the little black investors of Haiti. They believe that the Haitian gourde is still guaranteed by the United States of America because of a misleading information on the gourde, which is read as follows: 

Ce billet, emis par la Banque Nationale de la Republique d'Haiti, en vertu de son contract de concession et conformement a la convention de 1919, est payable au porteur en monnaie legale des Etats Unis d'Amerique au taux de cinq gourde pour un dollar a presentation au guichet de la Banque a Portau-Prince et sous delai de route a ses guichets de province. 

Which means:

This bank note issued by the Banque Nationale of the Republic of Haiti according to its contract of concession, according to the 1919 convention is payable to the bearer in legal money of the United States of America at the rate of five gourdes for one dollar upon presentation at the counters of the bank in Portau-Prince and under travel time at its encounters in the provinces. 

I do not intend to discuss the monetary system of Haiti. It is an independent country and I am glad and proud it is so, but I do not want the U.S. Senate to be the accomplices of a few dishonest Haitians and Americans who are leading Haiti to the most disastrous and fraudulent bankruptcy of her history. 

The American Senate whose mission is to control the foreign policy of the United States of America should urge immediately the Secretary of State of the United States to gain acceptance from the Haitian Government that the 1919 Convention between Haiti and the United States is not in force and therefore demand that the Haitian Government modify its guarantee to the bearers of the gourde.

I want to conclude this written statement with four personal brief notes.

These two gentlemen who are beside me, Franctz Bazelais and Adrien Bazelais, have served in the American Army. They were at that time Haitian residents in the United States. They are now American citizens. Their father, retired Col. Max Bazelais, was arrested in 

August 1972, and I underline, under the administration of Jean Claude Duvalier.

This day were arrested 12 retired officers who, like Colonel Bazelais, were never brought to trial. This is a fact well known by Mr. Semms of the State Department.

Father Antoine Adrien, a Haitian priest in exile, told me a few months ago, that he was outraged by the said Mr. Semms maintaining in front of him that the regime of Jean Claude Duvalier has been totally liberalized.

I am being accompanied also by a young Haitian Michel Zaiden who fought gallantly in the jungle of Vietnam. After his return home, he became almost crazy when he learned that the Nixon administration had secretly given $1.5 million of weapons to Francois Duvalier before his death. Four months ago, I persuaded him to return to school because I told him that the Senate Appropriations Committee will have a hearing about Haiti and will probably smpathize with the thousands of Haitian men, women, and children who have been thrown in Duvalier's dungeons for years without any trial. He has come with me to express his gratitude to you.

In an article published 2 years ago by the Long Island Press, under the signature of Irma Ganze, one can read: "Baseball Has Its Babe 

Ruth; Boxing Its Joe Louis; and Football Its Red Grange; American

Soccer Boasts of International Hero Joe Gaetjens." 

From the Daily Express, July 28, 1971, I quote: "Today, the man who caused England's biggest sporting humiliation in 1950 is again in the spotlight at the center of an international mystery." 

Joe Gaetjens, my brother, was arrested on July 8, 1964, by Dr. Francois Duvalier's undercover squad. They put a gun to his head and forced him into a car; we have not seen or heard of him since. 

By note dated July 9, 1971, thhe International Committee of Human

Rights requested from the government of Jean Claude Duvalier the appropriate information about Joe Gaetjens' case.

The administration of Jean Claude Duvalier did not supply the requested information and in view of the fact that the term of 180 days provided by article 51 of the Regulations had elapsed, the International Commission of Human Rights resolves (paragraph 4) to recommend to the Government of Haiti that it grant reparation or compensation to whom it is due by law. 

On November 15, 1972, Mrs. Patricia Roberts Harris of Fried, Frank, Harris, Shriver and Kampelman, wrote to Mrs. Joseph Gaetjens:

Ambassador Knox does not believe that Joseph Gaetjens is now in any prison in Haiti, and I believe from my conversation with the Ambassador that it can be presumed that your husband is no longer alive.

It appears that the Haitian Government is refusing to act on our request for a death certificate for Joseph Gaetjens because of the political activities of his brothers. I believe that such an attitude on the part of the Government is

reprehensible but it appears that nothing further can be gained in working through the United States Department of State. 

When somebody realizes that Joe Gaetjens' wife and their three minor sons are American citizens, this letter speaks for itself. 

MONEY MISUSED 

Senator INOUYE. Thank you very much, Mr. Gaetjens. 

Senator BROOKE. I have one question. 

You state in the first paragraph that:

I feel humiliated to come here begging you not to give to my country $12 million because the tyrant you have chosen to be our master wants that money only to prove to our people that he has the strong support of the United States of America.

Do you mean that the U.S. Government chose Jean Claude Duvalier to be head of the Haitian Government? 

Mr. GAETJENS. Just a minute, Senator.

This is a question that I would like to answer fully. 

Since Haiti has always been considered by history as the black back yard of the United States, I refer you to many textbooks and chiefly to the books that have been published by Mr. Woodward, director of the political science department in MIT. 

You know that in 1950 Mr. Woodward said that it is now proven that you did it because you wanted to protect your interest in behalf of a few American businessmen.

In 1922, we were forced to elect Mr. Bonapresse because he had to sign a convention with the First National City Bank of New York prior to his nomination.

In 1946, for example, Mr. Bonapresse was overthrown because he had some difficulty with the First National City Bank of New York. 

When Mr. Duvalier was elected, I was personally involved in the election of Mr. Duvalier.

It was in part that the Ambassador, Mr. Clinton Knox, took over the government when Duvalier died, even before the Haitian people were ready to accept Duvalier's son as the successor. 

I refer you to this book. 

Senator BROOKE. I have never been blindly "my country right or wrong." I have always believed that it is possible to correct the wrongs.

I believe it is a serious charge to say that the United States put in a "tyrant," to use your words, as the leader of Haiti.

I don't think that history or the facts will support the contention that the U.S. Government put Jean Claude Duvalier in as leader of that country.

Mr. GAETJENS. I refer you to the book of an American Commission and the committee, Mrs. Harrington Sherman, and presided over by Mr. Woodward, the head of political science at MIT.

Senator BROOKE. I will read the book. 

As I said, I can't believe that we can accept a general charge like that as a fact. 

Senator INOUYE. Thank you very much, sir.

Your statement will be given most serious consideration. 

Mr. GAETJENS.

STATEMENT OF BENJAMIN DUPUY, EXTERIOR REPRESENTATIVE OF THE HAITIAN LIBERATION MOVEMENT, WHITE PLAINS, N.Y.

HAITI LIBERATION MOVEMENT 

Senator INOUYE. Our next witness is Mr.

Benjamin Dupuy, the exterior representative of the Haitian Liberation Movement. 

We welcome you to the committee, sir.

Mr. DUPUY.  

Mr. Chairman, and gentlemen, I would like first to express my appreciation for the opportunity to speak on behalf of the Haitian Liberation Movement.

Mr. Chairman, the present U.S. administration has recently decided to come out openly in support of the dictatorial and corrupt dynasty of the Duvaliers in Haiti.

To do this, the Nixon administration has felt the need to fabricate a myth-the myth of liberalization under the Government of Jean 

Claude Duvalier.

The death of Francois Duvalier in 1971 has offered indeed a timely opportunity for the present U.S. administration to set itself as an image broker for an incompetent political and administrative clique promoted and empowered by the late dictator. This clique bears the responsibility for what a recent study of the OAS calls, in its introduction, "the progressive deterioration of the Haitian economy up to its total stagnation during this last decade and the slim possibility of its recuperation and expansion in the near future." 

This study from which I have just quoted is entitled, "Haiti, Mission d'Assistance Technique Integree", and was made by the OAS, funded by the U.S. Government through AID. 

The present U.S. administration is the first to know that in fact nothing has changed in Haiti. What is construed to be in the interest of the United States in this part of the world seems to force this administration to rationalize its unconditional support for the most repressive government in the Americas.

Although any economic assistance under the present political structure cannot be channeled to any vital sectors of the Haitian economy, this administration has chosen, long before the death of the late dictator, to actively promote close ties between our country's most corrupt political figures and certain economic interests in the United 

States. 

The latter are, in many instances, interested in the exceptionally low level of salaries existing in Haiti. Their ties with underworld figures have been occasionally disclosed by the media; under the guise of promoting the tourist industry a flock of racketeers continues to invade the island with the blessing of the U.S. Government. Is it, in fact, in the long-range interest of the United States to nourish such putrescence? 

American journalists Hank Messick and Andrew St. George have documented the involvement of "the syndicate" in Haiti. 

Mr. Chairman, we have entered into the record 20 sworn affidavits submitted last month to the Immigration and Naturalization Service in the State of Florida by Haitian refugees, establishing their wellfounded fears of political persecution in Haiti.

[STAFF NOTE: Affidavits are retained in committee files.] 

Since September 1972, hundreds of refugees have been arriving on the shores of Florida. Crossing the Gulf of Mexico on small sail boats, those persecuted people have so far been subjected to all forms of harassment from the Immigration and Naturalization Service. 

The fact is that the arrival of people fleeing the "Duvaliers' Paradise" represents the most blatant demystification facing the Nixon administration policies toward the Haitian dictatorship. The testimonies of these refugees and those of the prisoners released in exchange for the kidnapped U.S. Ambassador, Clinton Knox, in January of last year are clear evidences of the tyrannical nature of the government of Jean Claude Duvalier.

To quote again from the same recent U.S. Government-funded study, here is the OAS description of the present government in Haiti. 

It summarizes the actual political structure that the U.S. Government is proposing here to assist. 

Considering the characteristics of the Central Government from a juridical standpoint, it adjusts itself to the model of Presidential Government and responsible Cabinet; however, in practice, the President of the Republic centralizes in his hands the almost absolute authority and responsibility for all the political and administrative direction of the State.

This description of the Haitian Government would certainly be accepted by most Americans as complying with their stereotype concept of a "banana republic". Such concentration of executive power would seem at first glance alien to the American political system. 

But isn't it a known fact that the Congress of the United States has been unable to block the end runs of the executive branch, especially in matters of foreign policy?

The Vietnam War, the secret war in Laos, the invasion of Cambodia are but a few examples.

It is today a real challenge to the American political system as to whether the executive branch has reduced congressional hearings such as this to mere rituals. 

It was very late yesterday afternoon when we had the opportunity to see Senator Brooks' report. We are sure that if we had read it before we would have the opportunity to comment about the report. 

If Senator Brooke is interested, maybe I would expect him to find out my opinion about what he wrote. 

Senator BROOKE. Mr. Chairman, I ask that the witness and others who wish to comment on the report be given an opportunity to do so. 

Senator INOUYE. Without objection, all witnesses who wish to comment on Senator Brooke's report may do so and it will be received for our files, sir.

SHOCKING STATEMENTS 

Mr. DUPUY. Thank you very much. 

Senator INOUYE. Thank you, Mr. Dupuy. 

Senator Brooke, do you have any questions?

Senator BROOKE. I am a little bit shocked at some of the statements you make, Mr. Dupuy. For instance, you say that, "a flock of racketeers continues to invade the island with the blessing of the U.S. Government."

That is one of the statements which is rather shocking to me.

I again saw no evidence of what you have referred to as the Mafia operating in your country of Haiti. I saw no evidence of extensive gambling casinos in Haiti. I don't know what the Mafia interests would be. I know what those interests are generally in some other countries, some other islands. I didn't see any similar interests in your country. 

You may have some documentation which you can submit to this committee which will support some of the allegations that you have made.

The second thing is that several times today we have talked about American interests in the cheap Haitian labor market. Everything is relative to cost. But American economic interests in Haiti are negligible. In fact, I hope to encourage more American private economic activity in Haiti because the Haitian people certainly want to work; they are a very proud people. The Haitian peasant, barefooted and poverty-stricken, is nevertheless very proud. 

You need more outside capital in Haiti. The United States with all its power and its wealth is always interested in attracting capital to its shores. Haiti is no exception in this regard. 

Do you think that we should just discourage "foreign capitalists" as you call them, from coming into Haiti? Would it benefit the Haitians to deny this possible source of employment? 

These are questions which I think you should consider in making recommendations to this subcommittee or to any other committees to whom you want to make recommendations.

I will be interested when you file your views with this subcommittee because they are very serious subjects and they affect thousands and thousands of poor people in Haiti who are very near starvation. 

Mr. DUPUY. Mr. Senator, in your report you seem to indicate that you had spent 4 days in Haiti.

Senator BROOKE. That is all. 

Mr. DUPUY. I have spent 10 years working with the peasants. I have been working with especially two American companies under contract with the Export-Import Bank and with the Bank for International Reconstruction and Development. I spent 10 years working as a field engineer.

One thing seems not to be very clear: the assistance that we propose today seems to be presented as though we had found a solution. It shows a total disregard for what was done before. There is a total disregard for past experiences. 

There have been tremendous investments in Haiti and not too long ago. That was just prior to the AID decision to withdraw assistance to the Duvalier regime. Now we are saying that it should be fine if roads could be built, if hospitals and education could be improved, if irrigation and drainage could be improved, as if we have just discovered the way to solve the country's problems, when those questions have been raised time and time again. 

My country by 1962 had an external debt of $60 million. Haiti committed itself deeply, borrowing money from all kinds of institutions, for the very thing that we are proposing today to start to do; the Ex-Im Bank gave $24 million to Haiti from 1952 to 1958 for the Artibouite Valley Project. I participated in the project. Now, I think the initial cost of the project was supposed to be $14 million. The total cost of the project when it was stopped was $40 million.

Yet, the production of foodstuffs in the Valley of Artibonite, it was a drainage and irrigation project had decreased after $40 million had been spent.

So, the OAS study, and I queried it before, said that the country is in a situation of total economic stagnation. Now, after 10 years since the United States withdrew their assistance how does the country find itself in such economic chaos? Do we have to forget about the $60 million and then we are going to start again on the same assumption that what is needed is a little help and we disregard the political and administrative structure of the country?

Senator BROOKE. I would not insult your intelligence by suggesting that the little aid that we propose to give Haiti is going to solve the problems of Haiti. I don't know how much money and what else will be needed to do that. I don't believe that it is our goal to solve the problems of Haiti. I am not for the United States imposing on Haiti or any other country a foreign political or economic structure. 

You suggest that we should go back to 1952. If we did we might profit by avoiding past mistakes but the economic problems of Haiti would still exist.

I hope you are convinced from the hearing today, after Mr. Kleine and others have testified, that what we are doing in Haiti today is aiding in a humanitarian way the Haitian people. Others who have spoken have said they don't want us to terminate American aid. It seems to me that the crux of your argument is that you feel that the United States should change the Haitian Government. I do not believe we should change the Haitian Government any more than I thought we should change the Government in Vietnam or the Government in Cyprus or any other government. It is not our job. It is not our role. 

We don't change the governments of other countries. 

I quite agree with those of you who have said that because of certain treaties and internal considerations the United States should withhold its aid under certain circumstances. I don't find sufficient evidence to warrant at the present time our withholding humanitarian aid to the country of Haiti. 

I think the real question is: What do you think we ought to do? 

What is your solution? What do you suggest that the U.S. Government do that it is not doing? What do you suggest that the U.S. Government stop doing what it is doing?

Mr. DUPUY. The Congress of the United States, and I am quoting: 

It is the sense of the Congress that the President should deny economic or military assistance to the government of any foreign country which practices the internment or imprisonment of that country's citizens for political purposes. 

If this is the sense of Congress, then the emphasis should be put on the political nature of the Governmet, not on the fact that American experts are going to insure that the money is well spent. 

But, unfortunately, during your 4-day visit, you put more stress on making sure that AID had everything under control. Now, we would have rather seen you telling the Government to open up the prisons for you to see. Maybe you could have gone with a list of people who have disappeared.

To be in harmony with the spirit of Congress in putting the stress on the political nature of the Government, the political nature of the problem, I think that we would have complied with the spirit of the 

Congress of the United States.

Now, if we blur the question and put the emphasis on how the aid is going to be used, what is going to happen is that you are going to have a colony because only American experts can be trusted. The more funds you put, the more experts we are going to have. 

Before we know it, it is practically a colonial situation where it is foreign experts and personnel that are doing the administration of the economy of the country.

So, we think that the economic question should not be the main subject or the good will of the government of Jean Claude Duvalier to go along with American help.

Now, I remember at the inauguration of "Papa Doc" he made a very famous speech. In the speech, he stated: "I want Haiti to become a second Puerto Rico," and maybe the U.S. 

Government, thought well, maybe we could help such a man. He offered all kinds of facilities. 

I am sure if Senators had gone there, "Papa Doc" would have said: "We will not interfere." 

Now, what has experience taught us?

It is that the minute the funds were coming then the government started to show its true face.

How can a government which is based on corruption, in which people who have 2 or 3 years in office buy jets, how can such people not finally come down and misuse the funds, whatever funds that there can be that are meant for the very people who are suffering? 

Another example would be the nonfiscalized millions of dollars flowing from the Regie du Taboc to Duvalier's bank account. Very conservative figures put it at $10 million yearly. Now, the same way we cannot tell you for sure how many people have disappeared although you seem to want us to present evidence of repressing, you know that evidence is not always available because of the very nature of the government.

Now, who is there to say that it is only $10 million? Why should we take your figure for granted?

Let us pretend it is $10 million. If we have $10 million nonfiscalized revenues and we have a development budget that is also $10 million, because this development project depends on earmarked taxes, as you have mentioned in your report, this means special taxes and who carries the brunt of the taxes? The poor peasant who is left to himself with no help whatsoever.

Now, the new taxes permit the Government to come with a development budget of $10 million. Those new taxes should not have been put on the peasants who are already overtaxed if they only had fiscalized the $10 million.

Senator BROOKE. The poor peasants in Haiti outside of the market economy do not pay a significant amount in taxes. They have little to pay with.

You talked about Haiti being a colony. I have always been against colonialism. I do not think you can say with seriousness that the United 

States desires Haiti as a colony. 

You also talk about removing all of the experts, the foreign experts, from Haiti. What would happen if this happened?

I believe it was the Reverend Jesse Jackson who said that you don't kick the white man out of the pilot's seat on the plane until you learn

j 1 at least to fly the plane. You may not agree with what Rev. Jackson said. It is not a question of black or white for me. But Haiti needs all the expertise that it can find. Haitians need to go to the best schools they possibly can; to become engineers, as you have become; to come back to Haiti and to use their expertise in their own country of Haiti. 

If you really feel for the Haitian people, you can't seriously want to remove those few experts who have gone to Haiti to help the Haitian people and sometimes help themselves, to be sure, with profits. 

Can Haiti really go it alone today even if you had a change in government? Do you really think they could go it alone? 

Mr. DUPUY. Senator, I would like to answer your first question concerning the peasants.

I think I have a pretty good idea of the economic structure of my country. I would say that the Haitian peasant is the most heavily taxed; maybe not in a visible way. The peasant will not fill in a form for income tax returns or anything of this nature. 

But you have to understand that what keeps the economy of the country going is the production of certain commodities like coffee, sisal, cacao, and so forth. Every time the Government puts a tax on coffee, it means a reduction in the amount of money that is paid to the peasant.

When the Government extracts something like 25 percent of the foreign market value of any raw material and when the Government spends such money to form its own militia, to form its own guard and repressive forces, when the Government spends such money to buy speedboats, villas, and puts the money in Swiss banks, it is the peasant who is paying the price for it. 

So, we should not establish a parallel with what we know here in this respect.

Now to the other question as to how bad it would be if all experts were taken away from Haiti. 

Now, we can continue to argue that the country is so poor that there is no way from a humanitarian vantage point to ignore the plight of the Haitian people. But, isn't it perpetuating this problem when we refuse to see the basic structural defect? 

What we are doing is just applying symptomatic treatment. We are not treating the cause. Maybe for good conscience purposes, you can go forever and ever having to give humanitarian help. Now, I do not think it is good for any country, and especially a small black country, to be receiving humanitarian help forever. I think the basic problem should be solved.

Now, when we ignore the political structure we are ignoring the basic problem and we are creating more misery for the future generations. 

That is why I have referred to past experiences. 

We have had governments that were not as bad as the government of Duvalier. In spite of that, they were still dictatorships. They were still people concerned about their clique. 

I have just offered some figures. The country owes such a large amount that there is no way to pay the debt without creating real economic chaos.

That is why we agree completely with the sense of Congress when they addressed themselves to the political problem because the political problem reflects a deeper threat. We can come and say, we cannot let

those people die; we cannot let those people starve. But, by looking only at this aspect of the problem, we are not offering any real solution.

Senator BROOKE. Do you advocate the overthrow of the present 

Government by force?

Mr. DUPUY. I would like the same question to have been put before 

George Washington when he realized that this country could not become free and prosperous if he had to go on the assumption that there were limitations to what should be done. We do not advocate violence for the sake of violence. But we think in the same way that the 

American people are so proud of their American Revolution we also look forward to our revolution. I seen no reason why, when a situation becomes inextricable, when there are no avenues for people to express their dissatisfaction with the Government, when it is repressed in the most brutal way, I do not see why we should limit the options. 

Senator BROOKE. Thank you. 

Senator INOUYE. Thank you very much, Mr. Dupuy. 

You have been most helpful. 

Mr. DUPUY. 

STATEMENT OF F. HOWARD MCGUIGAN, LEGISLATIVE REPRE- SENTATIVE, AFL-CIO, WASHINGTON, D.C. 

ACCOMPANIED BY: 

ELIZABETH JAGER, ECONOMIST MICHAEL BOGGS, INTERNATIONAL AFFAIRS DEPARTMENT  

Senator INOUYE. Our next witness is Mr. F. Howard McGuigan, legislative representative of the AFL-CIO. 

Welcome to the committee, Doctor.

Mr. MCGUIGAN. Thank you, Mr. Chairman, and Senator Brooke. 

I am accompanied by Elizabeth Jager, economist for the AFL-CIO, who works with trade and export; and by Michael Boggs of the International Affairs Department of the AFL-CIO.

We have a statement, Senator, which is within the time limits that your committee has set. There are several exhibits attached to it which we hope you will include in the record or make use of as you see fit. 

The AFL-CIO welcomes the opportunity to appear before this subcommitee to oppose the unrestricted appropriation of $8.9 million of so-called foreign aid to Haiti. 

We oppose the use of taxpayer funds to subsidize the exploitation of poverty-striken Haitians and of American workers to benefit the corrupt Haitian regime and some of the richest firms in the world. No amount of money-large or small-can change the political and economic facts which support this view. 

Popular mythology in the press and elsewhere that Haiti's corrupt, oppressive dictatorship has changed since the death of "Papa Doc" 

Duvalier on April 22, 1971. is false.

Midnight arrests, secret police (now called "Panthers" instead of "Tonton Macoute"), absolute suppression of all freedoms-political, social and economic-still characterize the Duvalieriste dictatorship. 

As in the past, freedom of the press does not exist.

J For foreigners, there has been one change: Tourists are no longer followed-as in the past, a novel change of the "Baby Doc" regime to stimulate tourism.

For Haitians, however, all forms of oppression remain: The trade union movement, brutally destroyed by "Papa Doc" Duvalier early in his lengthy reign of terror, will not be allowed to revive. This lack of freedom for workers is one of many attractions for Haiti's so-called "transformation industries."

The AID budget for foreign assistance would appear from its description to be unrelated to these political facts. The programs seem to be designed to help the people of Haiti only through food distribution and production, population planning, and agricultural development programs.

However, information about current U.S. operations in Haiti and about the Government, itself, lead us to question whether or not such well-intended objections would, in fact, be served by the Governments of the two countries. 

We therefore support the statement in the committee report of 

December 13, 1973, on H.R. 11771 that:

It is the committee's opinion that despite the desperate need of the Haitian people, the conditions may not exist within the Haitian Government which would enable our resources to be put to beneficial use. A primary effect of such aid, in the committee's judgment could be to make a regime whose violation of human rights seems to be flagrant and whose dedication to meeting the humanitarian needs of its people is dubious dependent upon and undergirded by 

U.S. resources.

Like the political mythology. the economic mythology of helping 

Haitians through "transformation industries" has proved a fraud on desperate Haitians at the expense of the American taxpayer and an increasing threat to the American worker. 

Haiti, in fact, is the most disgraceful example of the effects of mismanaged U.S. laws and policies. The United States exports jobs and production facilities from the United States to subsidize multinational firms at the expense of U.S. taxpayers and workers and of some of the poorest people of the world. 

Haiti is the newest area to receive "offshore" production emphasisa worldwide means of exporting jobs through special provisions of the U.S. tariff code and the combined efforts of the United States and foreign governments.

Thus, Haiti has been "exporting" or selling its labor, as United States firms-large and small-send parts of products to be assembled by $1-a-day labor-I understand it is now $1.30-and returned to the 

United States. The United States has been exporting United States jobs and taxpayer money.

The so-called trade in this exchange creates basically, apparel, electronic equipment, and a great many other products. Between 1971 and 1973, the offshore assembly has zoomed upward. Imports of offshore production from Haiti amounted to a total of $9.2 million-of which $6 million was in parts and $3.2 million in assembly labor. But in 1973, the total value of "offshore" exports to the United States was $28.3 million, of which $20.1 million was in parts and $8.2 million in 

Haitian labor payments. These labor payments are almost as high as the proposed AID budget request. 34-192 O 74-79

The "offshore" trade in Haiti, of course, as in other parts of the world, requires a duty only on the part of the cost added in Haitiin this case, Haiti's desperate labor. But that cost is rapidly expanding, as the attachments to this statement illustrate. In apparel alone, the value has doubled in the past year, according to an article in the New York Times on July 19, 1974.

American electronic manufacturers have been invited to have their work done in Haiti at labor rates of $1.60 per day, so that American workers can be thrown out of jobs. The attached photocopy of an advertisement reproduced in the March 21, 1974 Milwaukee Labor

Press illustrates how the manufacturers are lured to Haiti. 

Haiti now supplies "almost all the baseballs used in the United States, including those of the major leagues," the attached photocopy of the July 8, 1974 Los Angeles Times story on this fact explains. "Baseballs are sewn in Haiti because of its desperation."

What the newspaper report does not include is the fact that the baseball industry in Haiti-Tomar Industries of Haiti-is an offshoot of Rawlings Sporting Goods of St. Louis, Mo. and Overseas Sports Co. 

of Mayaguez, P.R., according to embassy reports. The pay for workers is $1.33 to $1.52 a day. 66 'According to the news story, the quality of the baseballs is not always good. But jobs have been moved to Haiti from different parts of the United States and Puerto Rico as firms seek the low labor rate." 

Other baseballs are sewn in Haiti by a leased operation of Wilson Sporting Goods, which is owned by Pepsico, a large multinational firm. Pepsico's president is Donald Kendall. He also heads a lobbying group of some of the richest multinational banks and firms in the world, the Emergency Committee for American Trade, which tells Congress of the benefits multinationals bring to American and foreign workers.

The multinationals have every reason to support AID programs for Haiti. They receive the fruits of the labor and political repression there, while U.S. workers and taxpayers bear the costs. 

There are many U.S. laws which benefit these firms and help them avoid U.S. costs of labor or taxes. At least two of the Haitian baseball operations, for example, appear to be on the books of the Overseas Private Investment Corporation, a government agency which insures multinationals against risks of expropriation. 

The multinationals also get the benefit of tax subsidies which help them to "export" to Haiti. One of these, the Domestic International 

Sales Corporation (DISC) program forgives 50 percent of taxes for U.S. exporters at U.S. Treasury and taxpayer expense. Other tax and trade incentives also exist. The largest firms and banks in the world thus join the scramble of sweatshop operators to benefit from cheap labor to sell products in the U.S. market.

Thus, the offshore trade between the two countries is largely within the accounting and tax structures of giant global firms or fastbuck operators.

The total trade between the two countries, which includes the offshore, is also subsidized by AID and other incentives. In 1973, the 

United States imported $63 million worth of total imports from Haiti and exported $77 million worth of products to Haiti, according to the Department of Commerce. The exports include some AID-subsidized sales.

The Commerce Department's Market Profile of Haiti, published in September 1973, shows that so-called U.S. exports to Haiti would probably increase.

The profile stated, "United States very likely will gain in share of market as U.S. AID assistance increases." Thus, the AID money, paid for by taxpayers, pays for some U.S. sales in the national export figures. 

The size of the fraud on the U.S. taxpayer becomes magnified as one examines a report of a luxurious hotel, for the benefit of business managers. The hotel was built in 1972. Described in the 1972 annual report of the Overseas Private Investment Corporation, as an effort "to attract tourist trade and to introduce overseas visitors to the many investment opportunities available in the country." 

The report continues, "In March a second project for the manufacture of sporting goods was covered and at year end several other tourist service industry and light manufacturing projects were in various stages of negotiation." OPIC claims it has changed its procedures to stop this runaway help, but it has neither the information nor the proof to support this claim. 

The attached list of some of the hundreds of firms which were operating with the help of U.S. Government agencies at taxpayer and worker expense was published in 1972 by the commercial section of the U.S. Embassy at Port-au-Prince. The Embassy is actively involved in promoting Haiti as a site for American industrial interests. 

We urge this subcommittee to secure a similar list for the year 1974. It will include the world's richest firms and banks or their licensees or subsidiaries who use the most oppressed and most pitiful labor in the hemisphere.

For Haiti is not an innovation in the multinational scheme of things, but a continuation of a practice used in the Far East and now as close to the United States as Mexico, Haiti, Trinidad, and Tobago. The practice is expanding in Communist countries, the Soviet Union and others.

The attached articles from the January 1973 American Federationist describes the operations in Haiti of many U.S. multinationals and so-called small firms-which produce clothing, electronic parts, fishing lures, men's hairpieces, et cetera. The article includes ample proof of the fact that the nominal wage of $1 a day is actually undercut by several ingenious Haitian schemes that go under the guise of legitimate deductions from the $1 a day. 

Conditions have not really changed since January 1973, as the newspaper reports in 1974 make clear.

Both the richest firms in the world and the smallest operators scramble to use the export of sweated labor by Haiti's 4 million povertystricken people and the tax support of the U.S. Government to compound the worldwide problems that have cost millions of American jobs and job opportunities. 

We, therefore, respectfully urge this subcommittee to recommend a denial of AID money to Haiti that merely assumes the benefits will accrue to starving people.

The hard facts of modern life are that corrupt governments and a maze of well-intentioned laws readily combine to frustrate the decent purpose of feeding the hungry and helping the poor to progress through aid.

Earlier, we have made clear our position that the United States is certainly giving material and economic assistance to Haiti-as well as to the U.S. interests in Haiti at the expense of the slave labor conditions in this pathetic nation, and at a cost of American jobs. 

This subcommittee cannot attach strings to such unprincipled forms of foreign assistance.

But any Government program to provide food and agricultural development in Haiti must be made contingent on internal changes which will enable the purpose of aid to be used to benefit Haiti's people. 

COUNCIL STATEMENT Mr. MCGUIGAN.  

Also attached to the statement is the AFL-CIO executive council's statement on human rights.

Senator INOUYE. Without objection, this material will be made a part of the record. 

[The material follows:] APPENDIX I STATEMENT BY THE AFL-CIO EXECUTIVE COUNCIL ON HUMAN RIGHTS AND DEMOCRACY FOR HAITI 

The AFL-CIO has decried the outrageous excesses of the tyrannical late Duvalier regime in Haiti since its assumption of power through "election" and chaos in 1957. In the first year of "Papa Doc's" reign, all of his open or suspected political opposition was murdered, imprisoned, or forced to flee the country. 

Despite repeated AFL-CIO protests, our government supported the Haitian gangster regime with millions of dollars in grants and loans, and even honored it with an official state visit by the then Vice-President Nixon. 

The Duvalier dictatorship has consistently refused to permit any objective survey of the conditions in Haiti. It has denied the OAS Inter-American Commission on Human Rights and the International Commission of Jurists the right to make on-the-spot surveys for fear of light being shed on the plight of the Haitian people under the Duvalier terror regime. 

Upon the death of "Papa Doc" Duvalier in April 1971 and the assumption of power by his twenty-year old son, Jean Claude Duvalier, the Nixon Administration gave tacit approval to the continued sale of arms and equipment to Haiti, as well as to the training of Haitian troops and police by a private organization employing former U.S. Marines as instructors.

Two months ago, in March 1972, a three-man "goodwill commission" from Haiti came to Washington, D.C., to convince the U.S. Government, the Organization of American States and international banking institutions that the new dictator planned to rule with an "enlightened" hand. But it is rather revealing that the Mission was headed up by Luckner Cambronne, the notorious henchman of the late Duvalier and now Minister of National Defense and Interior. 

The new Haitian Government has called for "all interested parties" to witness the "transformation" first-hand. The young Duvalier and the infamous Cambronne would have the world believe that all Haitian exiles are free to return to their homeland. One democratic leader, Clovis Charlot, who took this promise seriously, returned last December to his native land after a twelve-year exile. 

Less than three months after his return, (March 4, 1972), he was found dead in the morgue at Port-au-Prince. Despite this tragic reality, the recent Goodwill 

Mission to the United States has claimed that "enlightened" changes have been instituted in Haiti since the death of the old dictator. If this assertion is founded in fact, then the regime should welcome the opportunity to have its claim confirmed through a first-hand survey by responsible observers concerned with the preservation and promotion of human decency and democracy in the Hemisphere. 

Haiti is the poorest country in the Western Hemisphere, with one of the lowest per capita incomes in the world. Hence, it is all the more deplorable that the U.S. Department of Commerce should, in its own words, consider as a bright spot "in this picture of seemingly unrelieved gloom" Haiti's "supply of low-cost but adept and willing labor". In fact, the Department of Commerce considers the intolerable plight of Haitian labor as something "remarkable",

because it facilitates "the processing or assembly of U.S. origin components for export back to the United States." The Department of Commerce actually hails this export of American workers' jobs and the perpetuation of intense exploitation of Haitian labor when it thus encourages the American owners of runaway shops: "U.S. businessmen interested in assembly operations have access to an inexpensive nearby labor force which is guided by an experienced cadre of local entrepreneurs. The Haitian government welcomes and facilitates such business activities". (Commerce Today, October 18, 1971)

The AFL-CIO insists that the Department of Commerce should stop acting as a promoter of joblessness for American workers and miserably low wages for Haitian workers. The prosperity of the Haitian and American people demands better wages for the workers of Haiti and more, not less, jobs for the 

American workers.

We, therefore, call upon the Administration to spare no effort to have the new Duvalier regime permit the OAS, the International Commission of Jurists, and the International Labor Organization (ILO) to send observers to Haiti in order to establish, on the basis of first-hand gathered facts, what is the true status of the Haitian people's basic human rights and social justice. In addition, representatives of the Inter-American organization of Workers (ORIT) and the AFL-CIO, which have demonstrated a long and abiding interest in and concern for Haiti and its people, should be allowed to visit this beleaguered country in order to get a true and full picture of the conditons under which the Haitian workers and peasants live and work. 

In line with its Charter and the Declaration of Human Rights, the United Nations, of which Haiti is a member state, should demand unconditional amnesty for all exiles and freedom for all political prisoners in Haiti. 

The AFL-CIO Executive Council warns that mere promises by the youthful tyrant are not sufficient to right the terrible wrongs inflicted upon the Haitian people by a government universally condemned for its savage rule. The old tyrant is dead, but the tyranny continues. We urge that the United States 

Government and all international agencies impose strict economic sanctions against Haiti until its new regime translates its promises into performances by ending its despotic denial of all human rights and freedoms. 

APPENDIX II 

The following item speaks for itself: [From the Milwaukee Labor Press, Mar. 21, 1974]

JOBS GOING OVERSEAS RAM ELECTRONICS OF HAITI, 

Port-Au-Prince, Haiti.

DEAR SIR: We are an American owned company employing 600 people, assembling various products in Haiti. 

The average labor rate of $1.60 per day, is considered one of the lowest in the world.

We have the facilities and the trained staff to assemble your products at very significant labor savings. We receive and return all components by air at the low rate of only 10 cts per pound, since we are only 90 minutes from Maimi.

We would like you to come to Haiti for a few days, to see our operation. For further information please phone us collect. 

Yours truly,

RICHARD MARKOWITZ, President.

This letter sent to the Labor Press by a reader shows graphically the dangers facing American workers. This letter was circulated by the company to American manufacturers inviting them to have their work done on the island of Haiti where workers are paid the magnificent sum of $1.60 per day. What happens is obvious. Products made this cheaply with practically slave labor can be sold in this country for far below a normal price meaning that American workers are thrown out of work. 

The AFL-CIO is actively seeking legislation to prevent this kind of runaway activity.

APPENDIX III [From the New York Times, July 19, 1974] APPAREL MAKERS MOVING OPERATIONS TO CARIBBEAN 

(By Isadore Barmash) The constant search for readily available, and inexpensive, sources of labor nas taken an increasing number of American makers of apparel, electronics and other consumer products to Latin America and the Caribbean, it was reported this week.

The trend toward offshore manufacturing is being spurred by constantly rising labor rates here and the recent narrowing of the rate differential in Far Eastern countries, speakers said.

Addressing 100 executives of apparel companies who had paid $100 each to attend a seminar at the McGraw-Hill Auditorium, Seth M. Bodner, Deputy Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Resources and Trade Assistance, said. "There is no question in my mind that the Caribbean area and Latin America, because of their cheap labor and proximity to the United States, will become important textile suppliers in the years ahead."

In the last five years, he said, the amount of textiles and apparel that United States concerns have brought in from Caribbean countries has grown from 20 million square yards to 47 million. Trade with Latin-American countries in the same period has increased from 153 million square yards to 403 million, he added, with a heavy concentration in apparel. 

Rising costs and changing labor conditions in the Far East, particularly in Japan and perhaps also in Hong Kong, have "somewhat weakened [their] competitive positions," Mr. Bodner said.

INTEREST INCREASING 

But in Latin America, "there is a great economic expansion in progress and a tremendous desire to sell more in the U.S. market," Mr. Bodner added. Many 

United States companies, he said have also established contacts in that part of the world to sell both in Latin American markets and in the United States. 

Last year, Mexico accounted for about half of the big growth of offshore production in Latin America, while some countries, such as Haiti, doubled their production according to William R. Rinell, vice president of Summerour & Associates, a management-consultant company. 

Approximately 600 United States companies are assembling products in Mexico, with the largest number in the electronics and apparel fields, according to Alejandro Arellano, special advisor to the Government of Yucatan. In 1970, there were 350.

The increase has come since 1972, when the Mexican Government lifted its rule that United States companies could only build plants on the border and the seacoast.

In smaller countries, such as Trinidad and Tobago, a Government spokesman said, there are only about 20 United States concerns, but interest in going there has "increased sharply."

Estimates at the meeting were that United States manufacturers could cut their costs one-third by shifting to offshore operations. Martin J. Herman, a consultant, said that labor rates in Latin America and the Caribbean ranged from 20 cents to 80 cents an hour, compared with the $2-an-hour Federal minimum in the United States.

However, he and other speakers said that many problems were faced in building offshore plants, including an absence of managers among nationals, transportation delays and costly fringe benefits legislated by Governments. 

Reaction from United States labor unions to offshore operations, though virulent, has little effect on the trend. An official of the Amalgamated Clothing 

Workers Union of America attended the seminar but declined to comment. 

Management in the United States is obviously not about to abandon the movement overseas. 

TURNOVER DOWN 

Reporting on a Mexican border plant his company opened three years ago, Joseph Lipshie, chairman of the Salant Corporation of New York, said: "We feel we have an excellent operation there, both in terms of quality and costs. Employee turnover and absenteeism are much smaller than in the States, and productivity is just as good."

J. William Summerour, president of Summerour & Associates, said at the meeting that taxes on corporations in Latin America and the Caribbean varied widely "but are often no more severe than in the U.S." 

The seminar was sponsored by Summerour, the Singer Company, Willcox & 

Gibbs, Inc., and the Union Special Machine Company. :1 

APPENDIX IV 

(From the Los Angeles Times, July 8, 1974)

SEWING BASEBALLS AT $1.52 a Day-HaiTI'S ECONOMY PROFITS FROM CHEAP LABOR (By Stanley Meisler) 

PORT-AU-PRINCE, HAITI.-Like beautiful, multi-colored herons, the 400 black girls in the factory, all in yellow blouses and green skirts, flap their arms out to the side in rhythm. They must extend their arms to pull the stitches tight. 

The girls are sewing American baseballs. "Haiti," says William Johns, general manager of Tomar Industries, "is the world center of baseball, and no one plays it here."

But, although no one plays it, many people sew it. Almost all the baseballs used in the United States, including those of the major leagues, now come from Haiti. (This spring, however, some major league players were complainig about the quality of the balls-including th fact that some flew apart when struck.) 

Haiti has its monopoly not because of any special skill or resources. The monopoly is there because of cheap labor. The minimum wage in Haiti is $1.30 a day. 

Tomar Industries, one of several American companies that put baseballs together in Haiti, pays its workers 38 cents for every dozen baseballs sewn. The average girl can sew 32 to 4 dozen baseballs a day. That's $1.33 to $1.52 a day. 

Baseballs are sewn in Haiti because of its desperation.

Haiti is the poorest country in the Western Hemisphere and one of the poorest in the world. It is a country of 4.5 million people, mostly peasants, on a third of the island of Hispaniola in the Caribbean Sea. The gross domestic product of the country averaged out to $87 a person in 1972. 

Before its independence from France in 1804, Haiti was the richest French colony in the world. The exports from its plantations in 1789, the year of the 

French revolution, were almost double the value of the country's exports now. 

Now it has a stagnant economy. According to the latest figures from the 

Inter-American Development Bank, its per capita gross domestic product declined at a rate of two-tenths of 1% a year from 1960 to 1971, during the reign of the late president Francois Duvalier, the infamous Papa Doc.

In a country where 80% of the population is rural, agricultural production has been stagnant and even in decline. According to the latest statistics, exports of coffee, Haiti's main source of foreign exchange, dropped in 1970. The farmer is hampered by ancient techniques, the lack of roads, soil erosion, the minuscule size of farms, and his own illiteracy. On top of this, the government has slapped an export tax on coffee that discourages producers.

In the last few years, the woeful economy has managed to produce a few optimistic statistics. With Papa Doc dead and his son, 22-year-old Jean Claude 

Duvalier, ruling as "president for life," tourism is growing. In 1972, Haiti had 

137,000 visitors who spent $13.4 million. Both statistics show an increase of about two-thirds from what they were in the early days of the Duvalier dynasty. 

Construction also has been picking up. 

The sewing of clothing from American textiles is the largest assembly industry in Haiti. Baseballs are next. In third place is the assembly of transformers and other electronic equipment.

In the past, the baseballs had been sewn in Puerto Rico. But the cost of labor went up there, and the manufacturers decided to look for a cheaper source of labor. Puerto Rico also is beginning to lose its role as manufacturer of the cores of the balls because of labor costs. The assembly of the cores from American yarn is being shifted to Haiti. 

Some Americans say Haitian labor is 70 to 80% as efficient as American labor. 

Johns, the manager of Tomar Industries, says "Haiti has a fantastic labor pool that is intelligent enough to be trained if you have the patience." 

There has been some sensitivity here about Haiti selling its poverty. A few years ago, the government closed down Hemo-Caribbean, an American plant that was buying blood plasma from Haitians for $4 a pint and processing the plasma for export. According to the Haitian government, the plant was closed

"because of bad propaganda from the American press accusing the Haitian government of selling the blood of an underdeveloped people." 

But Americans here, both in private business and in the U.S. Embassy, say there is no similar sensitivity about the Haitians selling their labor to Americans for $1.30 a day.

The Americans say Haiti benefits from the assembly plants because they employ 15,000 Haitians full-time and 5,000 part-time, create a pool of skilled labor, and inject money into the Haitian economy. "For a Haitian," says one American, "$1.30 a day is a princely sum. Should we say to him that because it is less than the U.S. minimum wage, he shouldn't have any? I don't get that kind of logic."
