Appendix VI 

Through a series of complex tariff provisions, tax credits and trade policies, thousands of U.S. plants from Rhode Island to Wisconsin and California have shut down major portions or all of their national production facilities in order to produce abroad for the American market as well as to supply their other foreign-based subsidiaries which also produce for the 

U.S. market.

The scope of this multinational operation is breathtaking. For instance, in 1969 some 40 percent of 

Brazil's industrial exports were made by multinational companies for ultimate consumption in the U.S. market. And many multinational firms are now making a concerted effort to turn to Brazil as a production base for all of Latin America.

A typical example of the newborn Brazilian industry is Ford do Brasil, part of the U.S.-owned Ford 

Motor Co. complex which now breaks its Pinto model down into blocks made in Brazil, transmissions in Germany and body in Canada-part of a multinational framework which translates into destruction of the broad production base that is essential to the health of the American economy. . Previously, the closest example of the multinational operation was Mexico and the so-called Mexican 

Border Industry Program. But now Brazil is a developing target of the multinational firms and an even newer and more sinister pattern is developing in Haitiwhere a sordid political history gives a clear picture of how the worker can be manipulated.

The Mexican Border Industry Program was launched ostensibly as a system whereby U.S. firms with plants along the Mexican-U.S. border could set up twin plants immediately on the other side of the frontier for assembly purposes. The products were to have been finished in the United States largely for consumption in the U.S. consumer market. 

That was 10 years ago. Today, the Mexican Border 

Industry Program begins at Laredo and goes all the way to Yucatan. It embraces 350 assembly operation plants in Mexico, employing more than 46,000 work. ers at wages of 20 to 58 cents hourly. An increase of 1,000 new jobs per month has been reported in the last six months in these industries. Total employment in the Border program is expected to reach 

50,000 by 1973. Today there are few "twin plants" left across the border in the United States. In many cases, no production facilities at all remain in the United States-they have long since been transferred in toto to Mexico.

The corresponding development in Haiti may come as a mild shock to many who heretofore considered 

Haiti principally as a scenario for Graham Greene novels and a model for Caribbean intrigue. But Haiti

is much more than that. Its history is rich but pathetic, shot through with heroism, corruption and external meddling that makes its new role in international economics at once absurd and historic. 

Haiti, with 5 million people, 90 percent of whom åre illiterate, has attracted inordinate attention in newspapers and government circles in the United 

States. 

It is a land where the same illiterate 90 percent speak a patois of Arawak, Dahomey and Norman French while the ruling 10 percent speak French, where the life expectancy from birth is 47 years; where infant mortality is 180-200 per 1,000 compared with 21 per 1,000 in Sweden; where the per capita income is around $60 a year; where the labor force nunibers approximately 3.5 million but 50 percent are unemployed; where there exists one telephone per 1,000 people and one physician for 15,000.

Yet this pitiful spot of Caribbean geography has merited the attention of the American press, the dollars of the American government and the lethal hardware cast off by the American military. Haiti-the land of 

Papa Doc, voodoo and murder-has a history which makes it ripe for exploitation. By the mid-18th century, Saint-Domingue was an extremely valuable

French possession in the West Indies. The French used 

Saint-Domingue as an important military supply base during the American War of Independence. Six hundred black Haitian troops fought under Admiral d'Estaing in 1779 when he attacked Savannah, Ga., for the Americans.

After the War of Independence, the Americans turned to the French West Indies for trade and Saint- 

Domingue, then known as the "Gibraltar of the Caribbean" was the center of the action. Slaves manned more than '8,000 plantations on the island to produce sugar, coffee, cotton and indigo. At this point in history, Haiti was considered the world's richest colony, surpassing the combined economic importance of the 13 British colonies in America with an annual remittance to the French treasury of some $140 million. 

In 1794, the French emancipated all slaves within the French empire and Toussaint Louverture led black uprisings throughout the island, to the point where General Leclerc, Napoleon's brother-in-law, sailed for 

Saint-Domingue with 22,000 troops to restore order and-significantly-to restore slavery. Toussaint was trapped by Leclerc and sent to France, where he died in prison a year later.

In 1802, Napoleon legalized slavery on other islands in the West Indies, causing black generals in the service of Leclerc's army to mutiny along with a large body of mulatto troops. Yellow fever aided the struggle of black leaders Petion, Cristophe, Dessalines and

Clevaus against Napoleon's forces, wiping out Leclerc's army. On Jan. 1, 1804, Dessalines and his men proclaimed the independence of Saint-Domingue and

renamed it Haiti, the name the island bore when the 

Spaniards first saw it.

From then until 1957, when Francois (Papa Doc) Duvalier was elected, Haiti suffered an uncertain succession of 40 self-proclaimed emperors, prime ministers and presidents. At the same time, the American government intervened in Haitian affairs on several occasions to help elect its own favorites to the presidency of Haiti, thwart German designs there in the 1910s and protect American lives and property on various occasions. Franklin D. Roosevelt, as assistant secretary of the Navy in 1918, drafted a new constitution for Haiti permitting foreigners to own land outright for the first time, ratifying the acts of occupation and reducing the presidential terms to four years from seven. The Marines maintained a cooperative mission in Haiti until 1963.

Throughout this history, the great mass of Haitians lived in the darkest ignorance. Fluctuation in world coffee, sugar and cotton markets affected them most indirectly, since theirs was a subsistence economy not governed by economic vicissitudes in the international market.

Duvalier, a relatively obscure medical doctor, was elected President of Haiti Sept. 22, 1957, culminating a lifetime of stealth and careful planning through which he moved from propagandist to dictator. 

Duvalier's biggest break was $150,000 from the

U.S. government to fund a health and sanitation program in Haiti that was principally designed to rid the small nation of yaws. Duvalier, assistant to the director of the clinics, very quietly made himself known. In 

1943, he became director of the Gressier Clinic, Haiti's largest, and in 1944, he was selected along with other Haitian doctors to attend a special course at the University of Michigan.

From then on, Duvalier cemented his position within Haitian politics through modest but important steps. 

In 1948, he was appointed Sub-Minister of Labor. 

He was remembered as being very quiet and unobtrusive, as if he were waiting for the next move. The following year, he became Minister of Public Health and Labor. 

In 1954, President Magloire asked the Inter-American Cooperative. Health Program to fire Duvalier for using his post within the agency as a front for political activities. He stayed secreted away in various places until well into 1956. Early in that year, however, small disorders around Port-au-Prince were directly attributed to Duvalier's forces.

As the end of Magloire's term approached, he went to the American Embassy for assistance in prolonging his tenure in office. But the Americans had seen the obvious and suggested to Magloire that he abdicate. 

Magloire did so and tried to regain his position through

a series of maneuvers that resulted only in his fleeing to Jamaica and exile. 

Through the ensuing months, a political musical chairs game took place in which the government was ruled briefly by provisional presidents appointed by the Army, a triumvirate composed of the three principal candidates for the presidency and finally by the Army. The elections finally took place on Sept. 22, 1957. Duvalier was the victor-even though the defeated candidates protested the highly informal vote and a general strike followed. For the first time, the real face of the Duvalier force was revealed. Through wholesale brutality and physical intimidation, the strike was broken, stores were opened and Duvalier was clearly the undisputed leader. 

Francois Duvalier set about immediately to remove any opposition to his government in such a fashion that most of the political figures in Haiti fled the country within a few years. His private police, called the "Tontons Macoutes," were his prime instrument of extermination, as well as his collectors of money for the private treasury.

Probably the best description of the Haitian labor movement is that written by Gaston Jumelle, president of the Parti National Haitien, now in exile: "Labor or trade unions first came into being in

Haiti as a result of the revolution of 1946. and have been one of the great social benefits of that revolution. "Since Duvalier has come to power in Haiti, his government has liquidated the lawful head of the labor organizations of Haiti and substituted in their places people from his own political following and, more notably, members of his secret police. "Lyderic Bonaventure, the former head of the union of Chaufeurs and Taxi Drivers, was arrested, beaten and placed in prison, without trial, for a period of eight months. • "Nathaniel Michel. representative of the Haitian 

Free Trade Unions to the international labor movement, received the same unjustified treatment as that. to which Bonaventure was subjected and later was similarly released from prison. "Both Bonaventure and Michel had, at first, to go into hiding, then to seek asylum in the Embassy of 

Venezuela and later through safe conduct, arranged from friendly democratic sources (including the 

American Federation of Labor), were able to leave 

Haiti and go to Caracas; at present Bonaventure remains in exile in the United States and Michel, with assistance from the same friendly democratic sources, has arrived in Connecticut, where he remains in a mental health facility as a result of being tortured in Haiti. "Dacius Benoit, another union leader, was seized by the agents of Duvalier and restrained by his arms while gasoline was poured on him and ignited. Benoit miraculously survived this excruciating torture. He was released from prison at the same time as the release of Bonaventure and Michel. However, Benoit was later re-arrested and again confined to prison. • "Kesler Ciermont, another very prominent Hai-

tian labor leader, with a close association with the 

AFL, ORIT and the ICFTU (International Confed eration of Free Trade Unions), is now in exile working with the ILO in Africa. "In summary, and in brief, under the Government of Haiti of President Francois Duvalier, democratic free trade unions have been ruthlessly suppressed."

President Kennedy cut off diplomatic relations and aid to Haiti but it was resumed in June 1964 with a total of $6.8 million in loans and guarantees from the 

Agency for liternational Development and the Inter- American Development Bank, for a total of $100 million from U.S. sources since World War II. In that same month, Duvalier was installed as "president for life" through a rigged election in which more than 99 percent of the voters "approved" the constitutional amendment.

By far the most lucurative and dependable source of income for Duvalier and his closest adviser, Luckner Cambronne, was the agreement between the gov ernments of Haiti and the Dominican Republic for the sugar harvest labor force. Dominicans hold stoop labor, particularly in the cane fields, in low repute. 

As a result. Trujillo's government approached Duvalier in the late 1950s to get Haitians into the Dominican cane fields. Cambronne was put in charge of the contract. Some 30,000 Haitians went to the Dominican

Republic each year for the harvest. An initial head charge of $15 was levied for the Haitian workers, which the Dominican government paid directly to Cambronne and Duvalier. Of the average daily earnings of $4 per worker, $2 was remitted directly to the Central Bank of Haiti, the remainder to be paid to the workers in Haitian currency (gourdes). In interviews made in the sugar fields in the Dominican Republic, it was ascertained that the Haitian contract workers never were able to collect the sum that was, in theory, on deposit for them in Port-au-Prince as a guarantee for their return home. The Duvalier colfers were enriched by yearly contributions for each of the 30,000 field laborers who went to the Dominican Republic year after year under the contract, amounting to at least $7.5 million per year. 

When 21-year-old Jean Claude Duvalier was sworn in as president for life on April 22, 1971, on the death of his father, he inherited a morally and economically bankrupt power structure that in 14 years saw Haiti's incipient labor movement crushed and replaced by a puppet front; caused Haiti's unemployment to grow to 50 percent; kept its population illiterate; turned foreign investment to a steady pattern of disinvestment, at least until the U.S. Embassy began to intervene in the remaking of Haiti's image in 1968. 

Luckner Cambronne, Papa Doc's chief agent and go-between for years, beat out Jean Claude's ambitious sister Marie Denise and her husband, Max

Dominique, in their quest for power after Papa Doc's demise. Col. Dominique's recent history has been rather hectic. Once he was picked by Marie Denise as

her husband, he dumped his previous wife and family and has subsequently enjoyed a breathtaking upsurge in his career, from Palace Guard to colonel in the Haitian Army and confidant of Papa Doc. He fell from grace through the alleged political design of some of his military cohorts and was summarily banished from Haiti, as Ambassador to Spain and then France. His comrades were executed and it is said that none other than Marie Denise intervened with Papa Doc to save her spouse's neck.

Dominique and his wife, eventually relieved of their ambassadorship by Cambronne, came to the United States to reside in Florida, New York and Washington, D.C. Col. Dominique also engaged in an internecine competition with his brother-in-law and Duvalier confidant, Luc Desir, chief of Duvalier's dreaded secret police. Dominique lost out in that struggle, too.

With Dominique sidelined, Cambronne continued to cash in on his labors in the service of Papa Doc, amassing a fortune over a relatively short period of time. His white marble residence in the hills overlooking Port-au-Prince has been described as palatial, displaying luxuries unimagined throughout the rest of Latin America. Marie Denise has been described as one of the world's wealthiest women, testimony to her sizable share of the Duvalier fortunes. Her wealth adds to her political prowess, explaining her potentially disruptive role in Haitian affairs.

A Haitian goodwill mission headed by Luckner Cambronne came to Washington in March 1972 to sell the new image of Haiti under Papa Doc's son. 

Calling on the highest levels of the U.S. government, the mission undoubtedly succeeded in upgrading the prestige of their country, as indicated by the level of the offices in which they were received. 

Suddenly, in November 1972, the Haitian government announced that Cambronne had been stripped of his title as Minister of Defense and Interior. Along with his quick demise, his latest and most lucurative rackets were also discontinued. No longer is blood plasma collected from poor Haitians and sold at high prices through a U.S. firm in Florida; no longer does the $500, 48-hour quickic divorce mill operate in Port-au-Prince.

Cambronne himself took refuge in the Colombian 

Embassy in Port-au-Prince and headed for Miami.

In the meantime, Marie Denise and her husband Dominique were making preparations for their return from exile in the United States to Haiti where they will seek to fill the power vacuum created by Cambronne's abrupt fall.

The key to this power struggle is young Jean Claude 

Duvalier's mother, Simone Duvalier, widow of the late Papa Doc. Madame Duvalier was the real power behind the throne. Without her, Jean Claude is rudderless. When "Mama Doc" recently went to Miami for medical reasons, Cambronne, who tithed part of his fantastically lucrative "business" ventures to the old lady's bank accounts, fell in her absence. 

Seven months before Papa Doc's death, the United

States lifted the ban on the sale of arms to Haiti, allowing the sale of six patrol boats, six helicopters and $200,000 in arms, including armored personnel carriers, to the regime. And in August 1972 a military mission was sent from the United States to Haiti to review requests for $5 to $10 million in American arms-based on the four "threats" cited by the Haitian regime: Castro, communism, the Dominican Republic and Haitian exiles.

The first efforts of the new regime were geared to reform the external image of Haiti, but not its brutal system. To that end, Duvalier has "opened his arms" to Haiti's thousands of. exiles, informing them they are free to come home without fear of retaliation for their political "misdeeds." Few have accepted the invitation. 

Surrounded by the faithful nucleus of his father's government by terror, Jean Claude Duvalier continues to seek out new sources of international monetary assistance.

The character of Haiti's government-business projects are evident in some of the recent high points of Haitian commerce. In addition to Cambronne's contracting out of sugar cane workers, Haiti has adopted flags of convenience. Haiti began the practice of registry of ships, particularly of ships belonging to Iron Curtain or bloc countries, under the flags-ofconvenience racket in the early 1960s. When Castro was still in the throes of defeating Batista, a scheme to give the Cuban forces free passage through Haiti to Cuba would have cost the Cubans $28 million-but Cuba never went through with it. 

Haitian employment taxes have long been an effective money raiser for Duvalier and his henchmen. Of the pitifully low monthly minimum wage of $21, or 105 gourdes, an employe is compelled to pay taxes of 21 gourdes, or over 20 percent of his income, according to a table circulated by the U.S. Embassy. 

Included are such items as identity cards and lottery tax along with old age and accident insurance--the benefits of which are dubious, to say the least. Most of these levies are meant to bring revenue to the coffers of Duvalier and associates and do not bencfit Haitian workers.

Despite the character and tradition of Haitian business-particularly the notorious activities of high Haitian 'government officials-the United States continues to help. An airgram from the U.S. Embassy in Port-au-Prince to the U.S. Department of State, dated Aug. 20, 1971, says "Haitian firms pay their workers over 50 percent more per day than the national minimum wage and the operation is able to produce items for the U.S. market at at least 30 percent to 40 percent less than the same item produced within the United States (there is a) large pool of inexpensive labor... the fact that Overseas Private

Investment Corporation extended risk insurance is now available for U.S. investments in Haiti should in the near future entice numbers of U.S. manufacturers

of labor-intensive products, who are finding it increasingly more expensive to produce in the United States." 99 This bragging on the cheap labor available to assemble component parts shipped into Haiti-the "transformation" industry-makes it obvious that U.S. policy is to encourage the process and the accompanying export of U.S. jobs, just as it has in the similar arrangements by multinational firms in Taiwan, Hong 

Kong or Mexico. 

One of the sorest points among Haitian exiles is the continuing presence of U.S. Ambassador Clinton 

Knox in Port-au-Prince. The exile groups consider him a middleman between the Haitian government and the U.S. government and commercial interests and consequently view him as a significant factor in the continuing tolerance of the Haitian regime in Washington.

The U.S. involvement, through the U.S. Department of Commerce, Bureau of International Commerce, is sizable in seconding a massive buildup of transformation industries in Haiti. In what has become a typical client-broker relationship with several developing nations, particularly through the Department of State and Commerce, Haiti's attractions to U.S. manufacturers are being widely trumpeted. In August 1972 the Bureau of International Commerce cited "Haiti's favorable official attitude toward foreign investment, its supply of low-cost but adept and willing labor," and said "The importance of the relatively 40 35 30 25 20 15

The only negligible benefit such transformation industries have is to provide a few jobs for the underemployed or unemployed in a specific locale. They do not provide massive employment where it is needed. And the wages paid are by no means exemplary-such firms pay the going oppressive rate, for obvious reasons.

An appraisal from a Haitian Embassy publication in July, 1972 gives this rundown on the scope of 

Haitian operations: • Over 150 U.S. firms manufacture in Haiti. 

100 new transformation firms have been set up in the last 18 months.

Exports in 1970 were up 34 percent over the previous year and were expected to triple that amount for 1971. • 1970 legislation fixed minimum wages between

In a letter sent out by the thousands to prospective investors and manufacturers in the United States, the 

Archiconfrerie de la Saint Famille d' Haiti, one of the 25 Haitian firms involved in the transformation business, advertises low labor cost and no strikes. 

And these guarantees can be backed up by the

Duvalier regime's habit of suppressing any and all dissent.

No labor movement exists in Haiti today. It was eradicated by Papa Doc. The continuing labor situation, in the language, of the U.S. Department of Commerce, is one of the factors that "augurs well for the future of Haitian transformation industries."

Part of the rationale employed by the embassies and the U.S. government in support of their brokering activities argues that new industries create employment and ease critical unemployment problems. 

They do not. Mexican unemployment has not been diminished by the presence of hundreds of American companies operating in that country for export abroad. 

Even though 50,000 jobs will have been created in Mexico by these transformation industrics, that figure, while impressive in terms of American jobs lost, does little to ease Mexico's immense unemployment problem. Conservative estimates of unemployment in Mexico hover around 28 to 30 percent of Mexico's 14 million workforce.

The damage is acutely felt in the United States, though, where entire small communities are deprived of their sole or most important sources of employment

and income by movement south of the border. In 

Mexico, nearly 50,000 jobs were created under the 

Border Program at wages of 20 to 58 cents per hour, while in Haiti, 15,000 jobs have been established in similar transformation industries, paying 70 cents to $1 per day.

American companies are charged an average of $1.70 per hour for each Haitian employe. This figure is alleged to cover the Haitian company's overhead and profit margin. But for an eight-hour day, the U.S. company would be charged $13.60 per employe by a local labor contractor. Even if take-home pay were $1.60, as claimed by the Haitian government, the 

Haitian firm would show a profit of $12 per day per employee. In traditional fashion, this money goes to line the pockets of high government officials who are attracting the business and into the accounts of established Haitian businessmen. The workers share little of the profit boom from their labor. This is contract labor that performs the tasks assigned them in the transformation industries.

There is a labor contractor, either individual or in a firm, that provides laborers for the business interests who want to set up shop, be it in Mexico or Haiti. 

The businessmen reap the profits at both ends of the spectrum-the American in New Jersey or California and the labor contractor in Haiti or Mexico, who takes his cut off the top of his labor contract with the foreign firm.

In Haiti, the basic minimum wage was increased to $1 a day in August 1972, the same time the monthly minimum was declared to be $21 per month. In 1948; the official minimum wage ceiling was 70 cents per day. Payment in kind is officially condoned and may be in the form of food, lodging or clothing-making it easy to establish a Haitian version of the "company store." There are no formalized plans for retirement in domestic industry. When a worker reaches retirement age, the proprietor decides whether or not to grant a pension and in what amount. Foreign companies have retirement systems for supervisory personnel only. 

To take advantage of these conditions, scores of American companies have closed down their operations in the United States and gone to Haiti. Haiti is not an innovation in the multinational scheme of things, but a continuation of a practice begun in the Far East and now as close to the United States as 

Mexico, Haiti, Trinidad and Tobago.

The list of products assembled in Haiti now and for sale exclusively in the United States is fairly diverse, with apparel items dominant. The list includes baseballs, beaded articles, belts, boots, brassieres, cotton gloves, electrical and electronic parts, fishing lures, handbags, jeans, leather goods, men's hairpieces, neckties, nurses uniforms, ornaments, pants, paper aprons, ashtrays, toys, ribbon bows, sandals, screwdrivers, shirts, shoe uppers, softballs, sportswear, tablecloth

ensembles, wallets, women's wigs and tape cassettes. 

At first glance, it appears that the firms that have gone to Haiti are relatively small firms. Moody's Industrial Manual, however, reveals such surprising details as: Comel International Corp., Littlefuse, Inc., and Mel-Rain Corp. are all subsidiaries of TRACOR, a multinational with net sales in 1971 of almost $71 million; Colonial Shoe Ornament Inc. is a division of 

Lehigh Valley Ind., Inc., a producer and marketer of machinery, textiles, footwear, automotive supplies and motivational studies, with net sales for 1971 of nearly $109 million; Dudley Sports, Inc., is a subsidiary of 

Athlone Ind., Inc., a producer of everything from lingerie to tools and eyeglass lenses, with 1971 sales of $131 million; A. G. Spalding & Bros., Inc. is a division of Questor Corp., a multinational also into automotive and building products, with sales in 1971 of $286 million; Brunswick Royal Corp. is a subsidiary of Brunswick Corp., a firm that operates plants in at least 11 countries, with 1971 sales of $514 million; Wilson Sporting Goods, with sales in 1971, of $125 million, was recently obtained from Ling-Temco- 

Vought by PepsiCo, Inc., with sales in 1971 of $1.2 billion; Bayliss Bros. is a division of U.S. Industries

Inc., a multinational firm that had acquired some 140 companies through 1971, producing such diverse items as health products, mobile homes, furniture, clothing and building materials, as well as interests in financing, real estate, oceanography, geophysics, agribusiness, construction and equipment distribution. The firm, with some 17 overseas plants, had sales in 1971 of $1.4 billion.

Haiti's incipient transformation industry has paid handsome dividends. According to the Organization of American States' CIAP Country Review of Feb ruary 1972, small industries' exports from Haiti are estimated to be worth $14 million in 1971, compared to $3 million in 1967. The gross export value of the output of these industries has increased from $3 million in 1967 to $11 million in 1970. But the real import of these statistics lies in the fact that light manufacturing products made with domestic materials in Haiti had a total value of $3.1 million in 1970 while the rest of that $11 million was from products made with imported materials-which jumped from $2.2 million in 1967 to $8 million in 1970. 

In September 1972, the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) announced a loan of $10 million to the government of Haiti to "increase the cargohandling capacity of the country's principal port from its present 235,000 tons per year to 510,000 tons per year, to improve facilities for passenger arrivals and to strengthen the administrative and operational capacity of the Port Authority of Port-au-Prince." Further, and most significantly, "The central part of the structure will be widened to facilitate the movement of containers and roll-on, roll-off cargos." Containerization will serve the U.S. capital interests there, who are the major product exporters from Haiti. Con-

་ད་ ་་་་་་་ tainerized facilities will further irritate the unemployment problem in Port-au-Prince, with fewer jobs for longshoremen and freight handlers. Export companies' profits, however, will rise.

It can be assumed that the U.S. government played an important part in the approval of this loan to Haiti. 

The administrative body of the IDB is the board of governors which comprises one representative from each member nation, usually the secretary or minister of commerce or finance, as in the case of the United

States. The ruling body, the board of directors, is made up of seven members, six elected by member nations and one appointed by the United States. The voting position of each director is proportional to the capital contributions of the member country he represents.

The United States contributed 42 percent of the 

IDB's $2.2 billion in ordinary capital resources, 79 percent of the $2.3 billion Fund for Special Operations and $525 million to the Social Progress Trust Fund. The last was depleted in 1965, four years after it was funded.

With an expanded port facility to accommodate containerized shipping, ever increasing numbers of U.S. and other multinational firms flocking to Haiti to take advantage of the oppressive wage and work conditions and continuing U.S. government broker arrangements for the Haitian government, the future export tables will show vast increases in Haitian exports of multinational products back to the United States, as well as to other extranational multinational operations.

As in the Mexican case, thousands of small communities are deprived of their major sources of income in the United States as companies close up shop and move to Haiti, leaving unemployed Americans with nowhere to turn. As the Commerce Department says: "These items have been proven to be of as high quality as their U.S. equivalent and are produced with about 80 percent of the overall efficiency of a U.S. operation." Some firms go abroad because they are forced to by the leading competitors in their industry-if a company as large as General Electric goes to Mexico, Haiti or Taiwan to produce motors or transistorized circuit boards, a small competitor in Long Island will almost have to follow in order to compete.

In the Haitian example, the workers are bypassed by these sophisticated economic exercises, while the 

Duvalieristes pad their pockets. The "new" Haiti's expansive commercial outlook is evident: "numbered bank accounts as in Switzerland, are now available to foreigners at the Banque Nationale de la Republique d'Haiti, paying 5 percent interest per annum," the 

Embassy announces, and Hilton, Hyatt House, Playboy and American Airlines' Flagship hotel chains are reportedly examining Haiti for tourism development.

An elaborate mythology, created by multinational business interests, insists that an exodus of production facilities is required by still competition in the United States from manufacturers both at home and abroad; that goods produced abroad bring great benefit to the American consumer in price savings; and that the products are for various world markets, not just the U.S. market. The fact is that one pays the same price for an American brand television made in Mexico or Japan as he paid for the same set manufactured in the United States. This holds true for other products as well-hi-fi equipment, cameras or automobiles. The international market is manipulated, subsidized and subsequently rationalized by governments and industries alike, all in order to internationalize productive bases with the irrefutable profit gain reverting to the multinational companies and their parent firms or banks. And the advertising on the convenience of Haiti emphasizes its advantages over the Far East by being much closer to the U.S. market. 

Multinationals exploit resource capabilities of any nation from whose soil they operate. The consumer does not benefit because savings are not passed on to him-they emerge in the form of vastly increased profits for the parent organizations, which are then submerged in a sea of technicalitics that serves to disguise the actual earnings of these firms for tax purposes, both at home and abroad.

Products are assembled on a low-cost basis and sold at high prices, with savings not being passed to the consumer. The result is distorted resource allocation and a distorted total world income through the practice of deferring profits, transfer of capital from one subsidiary and one currency to another or to others and tax advantages and discounts offered on a worldwide basis to such multinational operations. 

Another myth devised by the multinationals is displayed in the halls of government agencies in Washington in multicolor, non-union-made posters that read "Exports Create Jobs." The result from the flight of capital and production from the United States, it is said, will be "millions of jobs in service." 

Unfortunately, the service industry is often a lowwage industry; will never accommodate the millions of workers unemployed today or those who will be displaced tomorrow; and has already seen its highand low-wage service jobs exported in forms varying from airline service to stagehands in the film industry. 

There are hundreds upon hundreds of examples of multinationals producing components in Taiwan, Mexico, Korea and Haiti to be employed in assembly of products in plants in France, Spain, Belgium or 

Germany for ultimate consumption in the American market. At the roots of this contemporary economic phenomenon is a central element: U.S. government irresponsibility in serving the establishment while the 'American unemployed suffer and their numbers grow. 

Now poor Haiti, once the Gibraltar of the Caribbean under French colonial rule, is fast becoming another

field for multinational operations. The corrupt government officials and business community of Haiti, in collusion with the U.S. government, are generating big business in hard currency at the expense of both 

American and Haitian workers. Goodwill missions to the United States and cheerful press releases from the Haitian Embassy in Washington to the contrary, Haiti is still a cesspool of terror, enforced ignorance and abject poverty. 

As recently as October 1972 an undisclosed number of persons were arrested in Haiti on questionable charges of their having plotted to overthrow Duvalier the Younger's government-their number included businessmen and army personnel. This is the real 

Hiti: knocks on doors at night, disappearing relatives .ind decomposing bodies found weeks later. 

Yet the U.S. Embassy in Haiti will say: "The sector m the future may well include industrial parks housing U.S.-Haitian partnership concerns assembling relatively large quantities of U.S.-origin components for sale on the U.S. market. The spinoff of such a development would surely affect in a fundamental way broad ranges of Haitian society, at least in the Portau-Prince area." 99

APPENDIX VII [From the New York Times, July 21, 1974] CONTINUED JOB DECLINES THREATENS CITY ECONOMY 

(By Michael Stern)

New York City is losing at an accelerating rate the jobs that sustain its economy and its government, and the declines are causing growing concern among city officials, private economists, businessmen and labor leaders. 

Leading the declines, which averaged 24,000 a month in the first four months of this year, are jobs in manufacturing. These are just the jobs that are most needed here to provide entry opportunities for the city's increasing population of poor and unskilled Puerto Ricans, blacks and other minorities. 

Though other American cities also are losing jobs, and some of them at a faster rate than New York, the problem here is more serious because New York is bigger and therefore is losing more-251,000 jobs in the last four years. 

The decline, which manifests itself in empty lots and factory buildings, a high rate of unemployment (7 per cent locally compared with 5.2 per cent nationally) and a huge burden of welfare dependency, is confirmed by an array of statistical evidence that has been pointing downward since 1969. 

After a decade of employment growth in the nineteen-sixties, the city lost 53,000 jobs in 1970, 135,000 in 1971, 49,000 in 1972 and 14,000 in 1973. The losses wiped out all the gains achieved in the previous decade. 

By far the largest part of the decline-169,000 jobs was in manufacturing employment, which had been falling continually through the fifties and sixties as well. However, in those years, the manufacturing losses were made up and even exceeded by growth in office work, services and government employment. 

For the two decades the city had net employment gains that were substantial but significantly below the growth rate of the nation as a whole. 

Since 1969, however, employment in nonmanufacturing pursuits also has been declining, and these losses have persisted even after the national recession of 1969-70 ended and employment began growing again in the country as a whole. 

The city's experience so far in 1974 gives no sign that the job slide is over here. 

Earlier this year, the slowing up of the rate of decline in 1973, coupled with a tiny gain of 1,200 jobs in January, had led officials of the city's Economic De velopment Administration and some private economists to hope that the decline had at last bottomed out.

But in February, the statistics began pointing downward again. There were 

22,000 fewer jobs in that month than in February, 1973. The March-to-March loss was 37,000 jobs and the April-to-April loss was 38.000 jobs. The losses average 

24,000 a month. Again, the largest part of the losses was in manufacturing. 

Many other cities are experiencing the same problem. Figures compiled by the 

Bureau of Labor Statistics from the Census Bureau's Current Population Survey show that while the job loss here from 1969 to 1973 was 6.4 per cent, it was 19.4 per cent in Detroit, 11.8 per cent in Baltimore, 11.3 per cent in Dallas, 9.7 per cent in St. Louis, 8.9 per cent in Milwaukee, 6.8 per cent in San Francisco and 6 per cent in Chicago. (Among the few gainers in those years were Los Angeles, up 

4.4 per cent, and Houston, up 11.3 per cent.)

MANUFACTURING LEADS DROP 

For those cities, as for New York, manufacturing was leading the declines. Only preliminary figures for a few cities are available for the most recent Census of Manufacturers, done in 1972, but they show that from 1967, when the previous census was made, manufacturing employment declined 13.8 per cent in New York, compared to 18.8 per cent in Philadelphia, 21.7 per cent in St. Louis, 15.2 per cent in Washington, 15.7 per cent in Baltimore and 12.5 per cent in San Francisco.

It has long been recognized that as the American economy matured, and as new technologies increased productivity, the number of people needed for the produc tion of goods would shrink in comparison with the number engaged in services, management, administrative tasks and government. This has been true for the nation and for New York, but the process has gone faster here. By 1970, 33 per cent of all national employment was in manufacturing, compared with 24 per cent of New York employment.

This trend has been considered normal for what has been called a "post-industrial society." But it creates special problems for New York and other major cities because they must bring their large and growing populations of poor blacks, Puerto Ricans and other minorities into their economies. Factory work, which can be learned quickly on the job, traditionally has been the way new people get a foothold in American life. 

MINORITIES GROW RAPIDLY 

In New York, these groups are the fastest growing part of the community. 

Together they made 13 per cent of the population in 1950, 22 per cent in 1960 and 33 per cent in 1970. In those two decades, the white population of the city declined by 1.5 million while Puerto Ricans, blacks and others increased by 1.6 million.

Cut off from the growing office sectors of the city's economy by lack of skills and low educational attainments, they have been forced into low-paying service jobs or into idleness. The manufacturing jobs that were moving to the suburbs were not available to them because they could not afford suburban housing or the high cost of traveling to remote factories by automobile. 

It is the concurrence of these two trends-the growth of the number of people needing factory jobs and the decline in the number of such jobs-that is thought to be the principal cause of welfare dependency here. 

Commenting on these trends in a recent study of the city's economy, the New 

York Urban Coalition said:

URBAN DEVELOPMENT BACKED 

"We argue strongly for urban industrial development as a basis for building job opportunities for male adults not likely to be adaptable to training for clerical or office positions. Only through adequate jobs for these men can we hope to reduce the level of aid to dependent children-the major welfare burden in New 

York City."

This view is shared by Alfred Eisenpreis, the city's Economic Administrator, who said in a recent interview: "It is true that we are in the post-industrial era, but the city cannot go on indefinitely losing manufacturing jobs. We cannot become an entirely nonindustrial society."

What hope has the city for reversing the factory job decline, or even slowing it? A look at some of the causes behind the decline suggests that there are few cures available to Mayor Beame and his administration. For many industries, New York is a disadvantageous location. Rents are high. Energy is two to three times more costly here than elsewhere in the country. Modern, large-scale horizontal factory space is hard to find here and even harder to develop. Taxes are high. Wages are high. Traffic congestion makes transportation costs high.

FORMIDABLE OBSTACLES 

These factors and others weigh differently for different businesses, but taken together they present some formidable obstacles to the growth of factory employment here.

In a free economy, businessmen seek out those sites where their costs are lowest and where their opportunities to turn a profit are best. Increasingly, those who can serve their customers from remote sites have been moving to the suburbs. Indeed, if the political boundaries of New York are ignored, and if the economy of the city is considered as a whole with all the satellite enterprises in the metropolitan area, as economists insist the economy should be seen, then New York's economy looks quite healthy. Its employment trends have been moving in tandem with those of the nation as a whole, even though its growth has been slower.

The difficulty is that despite the growth of state and Federal aid to the city in recent years, New York still must***. And increasingly, the part of its economy that is within reach of its taxing powers. And increasingly, the part of the economy that is within the city's reach is a smaller part of the whole. 

CHANGES HAMPERED 

Few of the disadvantages New York has as a site for manufacturing can be changed by the city. For example, in the three industries that together account for more than half the manufacturing employment here, wage scales are significantly higher than they are in the nation.

2 In apparel, average hourly earnings in 1973 were $3.46 here, compared with $2.61 nationally. In printing and publishing, the city rate was $6.47 an hour, the national rate $4.48. In food processing, the rate was 4.46 here and $3.60 nationally.

There is evidence to suggest that labor may be more productive here, narrowing the differential. But for most New York industries, where the cost of labor represents a large part of total costs, the possibility of getting labor cheaper elsewhere is a tempting lure to move factories out of the city. 

Similarly, the city has no hope of reducing energy costs. And at a time when the city is adding new taxes to pay its bills, there is small chance that it will lift the 3 per cent sales tax it imposes on new machinery and equipment. 

Moreover, it is unlikely that New York can move ahead in industries that are slowing down nationally. The city's largest single manufacturing industry, apparel, is on the decline nationally. So, too, is the city's second largest industry, printing, and its third largest, food processing. 

Indeed, most of the nation's growth in manufacturing is in durable-goods industries, those that are least well represented here. In 1973, the nation had 

11 million jobs in durable-goods manufacturing and 8 mililon in nondurable goods. For the city, these positions are reversed. Of 658,000 people employed in manufacturing here last year, 509,000 were in nondurable goods and only 149,000 were in durable goods. 

Increasingly, as world trade has grown, the United States has been buying more of its soft goods abroad because the cheaper labor available overseas has made foreign goods cheaper than those made by America's industries. The dollar devaluations in 1971 and 1973, plus a faster rate of inflation overseas than in this country, is lessening the advantage of cheap foreign labor, but it still exists and probably will for the foreseeable future. 

SOME HOPE SEEN 

There is hope, however, that the city can help to narrow some of the other differentials. It can and is, through its Public Development Corporation, putting together industrial parks to create more efficient factory space. A new Industrial 

Development Agency, created for the city by the last session of the legislature, will enable the city to issue bonds to build or buy new factories and to offer tax abatements to private developers who build industrial facilities. 

In addition, Mr. Eisenpreis is developing other aids for manufacturers in his agency. He has been working with the major banks to increase loans to small businessmen. He has been encouraging the city to buy from local manufacturers. 

And he is hoping to develop a capability to offer skilled management help to many small businesses that need more sophisticated leadership. 

Warning that there are no magic formulas that will radically change the facts of economic life here, he said: "Our goal is to reduce the preventable decline in manufacturing employment and to make the city as attractive as possible in the area where we can have an effect, for new enterprise. There is no one big thing we can do, but every little thing we do strengthens the whole fabric of the city. It has to be done strand by strand, but we are going to do it."

FREEDOM STILL SUPPRESSED Senator INOUYE. Senator Brooke.

Popular mythology in the press and elsewhere that Haiti's corrupt, oppressive dictatorship has changed since the death of "Papa Doc" Duvalier on April 22, 1971 is false. CIO. We have published many things in the past on the tragic situation in Haiti which we feel very strongly in continuing to this very day. 

The basis for the information we have supplied in this very brief report has been furnished to us by exiled leaders of the labor movement in Haiti, by sources in the Dominican Republic and in Venezuela who are also considered exiled groups from Haiti, by personal observations of our own people who have gone to Haiti as tourists and otherwise, by other groups, not Haitians, but other national groups in the neighboring Republic in the Caribbean who have firsthand knowledge of the situation in Haiti.

 STATUS REPORT ON SELECTED INDIVIDUALS 

In response to the Chairman's request, the Embassy in Port-au-Prince has received the following information from the Government of Haiti: 

Jean Bernardel, Leon Jean, Col. Max Bazelais: All three were implicated in a plot against the security of the State. In 1972 they kidnapped the son of the then Minister of Commerce, Leber Jean Pierre, and threatened that if the Head of Government did not step down, they would kill the child. They were judged by a military court, sentenced to prison terms, and remain under detention. No measures have been taken against their families. 

Joseph Gaetjens: Not in Haiti.

Dr. Jacques Innocent: Arrested in May 1972 during investigation of a Communist-linked conspiracy against the State. Dr. Innocent's wife was first married to a well-known Communist, Jacques Alexis, and Dr. Innocent himself is said to have strong Communist sympathies. Having cooperated in the investigation, Innocent was released in early August and has resumed the practice of medicine. 

Charles Innocent, Dr. Alix Adam, Dr. Lionel Charles: Unknown, not under detention in Haiti.

STATEMENT OF JAMES O. BYERS, PRESIDENT OF AEROTRADE, INC., MIAMI, FLA. 

PURCHASING AGENTS 

Senator INOUYE. To continue, our next witness is Mr. James O. 

Byers, president of Aerotrade, Inc., of Miami, Fla. 

Mr. Byers, welcome, sir. 

Mr. BYERS. Thank you, sir.

Mr. Chairman and gentlemen, we wish to, of course, thank the subcommittee for permitting us to present this brief statement. 

Aerotrade is a Florida corporation owned by U.S. citizens, whose officers and employees are U.S. citizens. We have been the purchasing agents for the Government of Haiti for the last several years. We

received substantial payments over the years. However, about a year ago we suddenly found ourselves in the situation that we had delivered over a million dollars' worth of supplies over and above the payments received from Haiti, and it was at this point that the Government took the position there was no longer any authority to, or funds to, pay us. 

At the outset, I want to be clear, of course, that I am in favor of assistance to Haiti, especially for the food and for the completion of highways such as the main highway through the country. 

We also want to say as one who has been in close contact with the Government for several years that the new President Jean Claude and his ministers are working, trying hard, in a most difficult situation. 

But I have to say that I am strongly opposed to "involuntary assistance," appropriating the property of U.S. citizens against their wishes without notice or by unilaterally nullifying contracts. 

Aerotrade and its officers do pay substantial income taxes, some small part of which support the foreign assistance program. But to select us to make a very large contribution directly to the Government, approximately $1 million, is most unfair, and until the situation is rectified, should be taken into account in making further foreign assistance grants and loans to Haiti.

We understand that this is the purpose of the Hickenlooper and the Gonzalez amendments. But in the past these have easily been defeated by, A, inability to deal with Haiti's fictitious counterclaim and, B, the requirement that a suit be instituted against the dictator claiming that he is in error in cancelling the Aerotrade contracts and refusing to pay for goods received. 

These two requirements are so grossly unfair to American citizens that Haiti cannot be found to be a country treating U.S. citizens fairly. 

The fictitious counterclaims seem to be present in all expropriations. 

It is especially mischievous where requests were made to the dictator to change his decision and then repeated requests for payment were made with the only response from the Government that "payment was not authorized."

How can Haiti's assertion for the first time a year after the nullification of the contract of a counterclaim of a million dollars paralyze the State Department? Or the requirement that a lawsuit must be initiated in Haiti when the last time an ex-employee of our corporation attempted to visit Port-au-Prince he was met by strong-arm men, hustled into detention and placed on the next plane out of Port-au- Prince, which incidentally happened to be going to San Juan. He was told a worse fate would meet any other member of the company should we come to Haiti.

Actually the program in which we participated was a modest one even considering the size of this small country and its dire financial situation. The largest items we shipped were several unarmed 65-foot 

Coast Guard cutters, a DC-3 aircraft with modification, several F-51's for patrol purposes, Cessna 150's and a T-28 for training, several helicopters for the use of medical teams and others, and orders to replace obsolete small arms.

In no sense were we engaged in rearming the country. We recently have been told of air shipments of military arm supplies by the plane load made by the U.S. Defense Department to Port-au-Prince by spe cial Pan American charter flights since our contracts were nullified.

If Haiti is to receive aid from the United States, we think it ought to treat the U.S. citizens fairly, appropriating money and property from U.S. citizens with one hand and grasping all the free aid and loans it can get on the other hand should not be encouraged. 

Senator INOUYE. Mr. Byers, thank you very much. 

Can you wait a few minutes? There is a bell for a vote on the floor.

We will have a short recess of about 10 minutes. [Brief recess.] 

Senator INOUYE. The subcommittee will please come to order.

The subcommittee has received some suggestion that Aerotrade has been related to activities of former Minister Luckner Cambronne. 

What is this relationship?

Mr. BYERS. He was the Minister of Defense. We were instructed by 

Jean Claude to report to him and receive all of our instructions and our orders for equipment from the Minister of Defense and Minister of the Interior.

Senator INOUYE. Were you in any way associated with the training program of the militia or police system there? 

Mr. BYERS. With the police we supplied them with their motor vehicles, some parts of their uniform, their revolvers, fingerprint kits, chemistry sets to detect drugs, such items as that.

Senator INOUYE. What sort of armaments did you provide the 

Government of Haiti?

Mr. BYERS. The government usually either directly from President 

Jean Claude or through his Minister of Defense asked for a considerable number of items which we felt were not in good taste, were not needed.

Senator INOUYE. What items were these that were not in good taste? 

Mr. BYERS. Jet aircraft, jet fighter aircraft, for example, 105-, 106millimeter recoilless cannons, rather sophisticated equipment. We explained it was a little too expensive, and we suggested other items to the Minister and to the President, which they agreed to. They included handgrenades, some rifles, pistols. But the majority of stuff was not arms or equipment like that. It was trucks, boats, and aircraft, helicopters.

Senator INOUYE. All of these sales were made with the knowledge and concurrence of the Government of the United States? 

Mr. BYERS. Most certainly, sir.

Senator INOUYE. In your relationship with this former Minister of Interior of Defense, Mr. Luckner Cambronne, were you required to make extraordinary payments? I say this because there are many articles which have been brought to our attention suggesting that former Minister Cambronne amassed huge fortunes which were acquired through unusual means.

Mr. BYERS. I don't know where these huge fortunes are. I do happen to know him personally. He lives in Miami. I don't know of any huge fortunes he ever attained. He did own a considerable amount of property and farms and so forth in Haiti. I presume that there is where some of his funds came from. 

I am sorry, Mr. Chairman. We made no payments. Permit me to clarify that. There are a lot of times when almost every high-ranking military officer and practically every Minister asked us to get some 34-192 O 74-81

furniture for their homes or a pair of boots, it became a little more involved. We always bought these things, shipped them to Haiti and never charged anyone for them. They included patio sets, shotguns for hunting purposes, suits of clothing, all manner of items, refrig erators, air-conditioning units. If you want to call it gifts, OK. 

Senator INOUYE. The costs of these gifts I presume was added on to the cost of the goods and material being sold to the Haitian Government, was it not?

Mr. BYERS. Added on? 

Senator INOUYE. Did you absorb the cost of the gifts? 

Mr. BYERS. Yes, in a great many instances; yes, sir. 

Senator INOUYE. You did not pass it on?

Mr. BYERS. No, sir. 

Senator INOUYE. On the matter of U.S. assistance to Haiti, are you suggesting that the sums that we may have appropriated be held up until your problem has been resolved with the Government? 

Mr. BYERS. Mr. Chairman, I am not saying to further burden and starve the Haitian people. That is unjust to them. Frankly, unless you have lived there and dealt with them for years as we have, we feel that it is very unfair, it is most discouraging, disappointing to us and our firm and most difficult for us to keep from becoming bitter when Haiti buys U.S. goods, U.S. material from U.S. citizens and U.S. companies, and then they refuse to pay, and then we turn around and loan them money. 

Senator INOUYE. What is the outstanding amount so far as your books are concerned? 

Mr. BYERS. Approximately $1 million, sir.

Senator INOUYE. Have you discussed this matter with the U.S. Government?

Mr. BYERS. We have talked to the U.S. State Department and asked them for whatever help, whatever assistance they could give us in reaching some kind of agreement with the Government of Haiti.

Mr. BYERS. I don't think we have received a final answer, Mr. 

Chairman.

STAFF NOT. Mr. Harry A. Bowen, attorney for Aerotrade, requested that the following statement be inserted in the hearing record with reference to informtion supplied by the Agency for International Development and reprinted on the following pages: 

Upon being shown the response of Mr. Kleine, Aerotrade advised the Subcommittee that when it first learned of the Raymond letter on July 24, it prepared and filed five affidavits of officers and employees to which were attached over a hundred pages of detailed records attempting to show the charges to be erroneous and misleading. Another affidavit asserts that false charges were similarly made against another American company and not supported. Shortly after the letter was written, Dr. Raymond was reportedly dismissed from Government service and counsel for the Government of Haiti withdrew the request for intervention in the New York Federal Court. Aerotrade asserts that false charges are a part of the modus operandi of the Haitian Government to cover its victimizing of 

U.S. citizens.

STATUS REPORT ON COMPLAINT BY MR. BYERS 

At the request of Aerotrade counsel the American Embassy has approached the Haitian Government informally and by diplomatic note dated July 30, 1974 indicating the interest

Aerotrade has in meeting with Haitian officials in an attempt to narrow their differences. As yet there has been no formal reply to the written inquiry. The U.S. Embassy in Port-au-Prince is continuing its contacts with the Haitian Government in regard to the matter. 

Aerotrade has been informed by State Department representatives that it still appears premature to address the question of official espousal of its claim. This is generally a last resort and follows a greater showing that all local legal remedies have been exhausted and that there has been a denial of justice. The 'Department does not believe that local legal remedies have been exhausted. 

The position of the Haitian Government regarding Aerotrade claims was presented in a diplomatic note dated September 26, 1973. This note charges that most of the material delivered was in a "deplorable state" despite the fact that the contract called for "new and unused" articles, and pointed out that the Haitian Government had received certain items valued at $1,196,289 and had paid $1,724,000 to Aerotrade.

It states that Aerotrade also is in debt to the Government of Haiti for $400,000 paid on credit to the company for the purchase of additional aircraft on a contract which subsequently was revoked by common agreement. Thus, the 

Haitian Government states that Aerotrade is in debt to 

Haiti in the amount of $927,711.

The Haitian Government has authorized the release of the following note: 

Department of Foreign Affairs 

Republic of Haiti 

Port-au-Prince September 26, 1973

SCT/274 

Mr. Charge d'Affaires a.i.

I have the honor to inform Your Excellency that as a result of a lawsuit undertaken by Aerotrade International, Inc., a Florida company of which Mr. James Byers is 

President, against the Government of the Republic of Haiti, for an amount of $867,000 plus interest, the latter has been informed that on August 21, 1973 Judge Weinfeld of "United States District Court Southern District of New

York" ordered the seizure of funds belonging to the Haitian Government and currently in the First National City Bank of New York until the payment of $867,000 with interest. It was also ordered that the sum of costs and expenses of the action of the said complainant be and

remained fixed at the sum of $40,000 of which $35,000 would be paid to the defendant to cover the costs of the trial that the latter would have agreed to in the case that judgment were rendered in his favor or if it is finally decided that the complainants are not entitled to seizure of the property of the defendant. The balance of $5,000 would serve to cover the court officer's fees. 

Finally the sheriff of the city of New York or of any county of New York state or any United States marshal is to levy in his jurisdiction at any time before final judgment upon such property in which the defendant has an interest and upon such debts owing to the defendant as will satisfy the plaintiff's demand in the complaint, together with probable interest, costs and the said officer's fees and expenses required by law. 

The Haitian Government must now provide the following details: 

1. The essential part of the complaint brought by the complainants against the Government of the Republic of Haiti deals with the contract signed February 7, 1972 for the acquisition of six (6) patrol boats and six (6)

Sikorsky S-58 helicopters provided with the necessary equipment for their operation (radio, radar for the sum of $97,155.00) armament ($239,410) and spare parts ($652,445). The only clauses of this contract which have been respected are those relating to the obligations of the Haitian Government mentioned in paragraph II of the agreement as is attested by the Notice of Receipt of Funds submitted by Mr. Byers himself. The complainants were to deliver within six months from January 20, 1972 the six boats and the six S-58 helicopters. The first payment of $400,000 having been made February 7, 1972 the Haitian Government expected to receive the twelve units by August 7 of the same year at the latest in the absence of a valid explanation for any delay which might occur. 

Three months after this due delivery date, only 4 helicopters and 2 boats were delivered (see paragraph I (B) and II (B) of the contract a copy of which is attached.) 

At the beginning of January 1973, Mr. James Byers reiterated in the name of Aerotrade his promises of overall delivery on condition that the Haitian Government agree to pay three months' instalments at one time. An amount of $198,000 covering October, November and December was delivered to Mr. Byers January 10 and 21 days later, that is, January 31 another sum of $66,000 was paid him, for a total of $264,000 for the month of January 1973 alone. (See document Note of Receipt of Funds by Mr. Byers.)

Despite the fact that Aerotrade had not yet delivered the totality of the order, the Haitian Government paid it 

July 2, 1973 the amortization for the month of June 1973. 

July 30, 1973, the Haitian Foreign Office received a note

No. 172 from the American Embassy in Haiti informing it that an American company, Swiftships Inc., with which the 

Haitian Government had never had a contract, claimed the

E payment of a debt of $676,000 unpaid on the orders that Mr. Byers had placed with it. At that time the Haitian 

Government definitively decided to break off all contact with Mr. Byers whom it blamed notably for: a) The non-delivery after eighteen (18) months of the totality of the material which should have been delivered in July 1972. b) The fact that the five (5) H-34 helicopters delivered have a unit value of about $85,000 while the Sikorsky S-58 helicopters of superior quality provided for in the contract were paid for at $126,550 each. c) That the spare parts for each helicopter of a value of $43,387.80 were not delivered. a) That the support equipment of a value of $65,353 for each boat was also not delivered. e) That the Haitian Government had been obliged to spend $120,340 of its own funds for the payment of personnel to assure the training of Haitian personnel and the maintenance of the aircraft bought whereas in the contract there is provided an amount of $243,845 that Aerotrade was to spend for this purpose. £) It must also be recalled that the Haitian Government paid $400,000 to Aerotrade under cover of contract signed for the purchase of 10 F-86 airplanes, a contract which was later revoked by common agreement. 

In summary the Haitian Government received: 

3 boats at $225,333 

5 helicopters at $85,000 

Radio and Radar for 8 units

Delivery of 8 units at $3,815 675,999 425,000 64,770 30,520 $1,196,289 On its side the Haitian Government paid $1,724,000 (see documents submitted by Mr. Byers).

Thus the Government of the Republic of Haiti received material whose overall value is estimated at $1,196,289 and has already paid Aerotrade Inc., $1,724,000, which makes a difference in its favor of $527,711. In adding to that amount the check for $400,000 received on the contract which was annulled for the purchase of F-86 airplanes, Aerotrade Incorporated is in debt to the Haitian Government in the amount of $927,711. 

It should be noted that Aerotrade Corporation and Mr. James Byers have never been empowered by the 

Haitian Government to act in its name in the capacity 2.

of "purchasing agent." They have never received remuneration for their services. The pro-forma invoices which they have drawn up have been built in their imagination for articles which the Haitian Government has neither ordered nor received. Such is above all the case of this Douglas C-47 aircraft the pro-forma invoice for which (attached) amounts to $64,455.00 which the Haitian 

Government again neither ordered nor received. 

3. Furthermore the Haitian Government is obliged to emphasize the deplorable state of most of the material delivered by Aerotrade despite the fact that it was provided in the contract that these articles should be "new and unused." This is why no Certificate of Receipt has ever been delivered for this material. The Government still is waiting for explanations to be provided by the seller.

It should be emphasized that the Haitian Government was not notified in the usual legal time period of the complaint of Aerotrade Corporation and that the Order of 

Seizure was made by default.

It flows from all that has been said above that the complaint of Aerotrade is neither legitimate nor with foundation.

Consequently the Haitian Government requests that the American Department of State recognize its right to sovereign immunity in conformity with: the universally recognized principles of international law which desire that the property of a foreign government are exempt from any seizure; b) the constant practice of the Department of State in these matters when it is a case of acts of "jure imperii; " c) the reciprocity which the Haitian Government intends to accord to that of the United States in any similar situation.

Also, the Government of the Republic of Haiti would be grateful to that of the United States if it would kindly intervene as soon as possible to put an end to these abusive lawsuits of which the Haitian state is victim before the District Court of New York, that is to say, to obtain the annulment of the Order dated August 21, 1973 and also to prevent any other action of the same sort.

I take this occasion to renew Mr. Charge d'Affaires the assurances of my high consideration.

INFORMAL MEETING SOUGHT 

Mr. KLEINE. I could at this point say that we have asked very recently our U.S. Embassy to use its good offices to help arrange an informal meeting between the organization testifying now and the 

Government of Haiti.

There is no such thing as a lawsuit against the President or the country, Mr. Chairman. We have tried.
