STATEMENT OF REV. ALFRED JOHNSON, EPISCOPAL MISSION SOCIETY, DIOCESE OF NEW YORK, NEW YORK, N.Y. 

EPISCOPAL MISSION SOCIETY 

Senator INOUYE. Our next witness is the Reverend Alfred Johnson, of the Episcopal Mission Society in the Diocese of New York.

Welcome to the committee, sir. 

Reverend JOHNSON. Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman.

I am Reverend Alfred Johnson, Director of Chaplaincy of the Episcopal Mission Society in the Diocese of New York, 38 Bleecker 

Street, New York, N.Y. I again thank you and the members of the subcommittee for affording me this opportunity to present my views which also conform to those of a resolution of the Diocesan Convention of the Episcopal Diocese of New York and those of the Ad Hoc 

Committee for Haitian Refugees, care of All Angel's Church, 251 

West 80th Street, N.Y., 10024.

The subcommittee is considering today proposals by U.S. Government agencies for allocation of funds for their operations in Haiti. 

It seems to me that this is a matter of considerable importance. At a time of serious inflation and increasing needs here at home, Americans are greatly concerned as to priorities and certainly that their hardearned tax dollars are not squandered to line the pockets of idle manipulators and to prop up the shaky regimes of dictators. 

The Department of State concedes that the Government of Jean Claude Duvalier who at age 19 was proclaimed President for life is authoritarian but asserts that the systematic political repression prevailing during the reign of his father Francois Duvalier no longer continues.

Miami Herald and Wall Street Journal reporters as well as many others with exprtise on conditions in Haiti, including some European diplomatic personnel in Haiti, maintain there has been no such improvement. They point out the Duvalier regime continues to operate without conformity to norms of law to the point where its instrumentality, the over-30,000 paramilitary Tonton-Macoutes, has free rein to arbitrarily arrest, imprison without charges or trial, and torture and even murder those having the slightest disagreement with governmental policies, or those falling prey to the animus or avarice of Tonton- Macoutes members who declare their victims to be opponents of the government, sometimes posthumously. 

Since the latter part of 1972 more than 400 Haitians have risked their lives in flimsy overloaded sailboats and asked for asylum here. 

Many drowned on the way. The State Department claims they are economic refugees, but over 50 representative affidavits based on indepth interviews of these Haitians by a task force under the direction of the National Council of Churches attest to their well-founded fear of political persecution.

These affidavits are corroborated by the Organization of American 

States Resolution adopted April 24, 1973, the findings in 1973 of

Amnesty International, and the resolution of the Governing Board of the National Council of Churches adopted February 14, 1974. A copy of this resolution and of one by the Diocesan Convention of the Episcopal Church in New York regarding Haitian refugees are attached. It is requested that they be included in the record as part of my statement.

The use of U.S. Government funds to assist the Duvalier regime's repression of the Haitian people can hardly be squared with our consciences or the national interests of the American people. Shall we only preach democracy, or shall we also practice it? Shall we only exemplify it for ourselves, or do we practice it and witness it else-

where? That is the question before us today. That is the question before us!

I urge that the Foreign Operations Subcommittee carefully scrutinize the appropriation of any funds for the support of the Duvalier dictatorship, either directly or indirectly.

Since being here today I have had occasion to discover their request for a fleet of rescue vessels. I would particularly point to your attention its capacity to prevent people escaping by the most usual means that refugees choose, the small sailboat. 

With that, I conclude my statement, except to add that I also represent the Bishop of New York, Bishop Jaul Moore, Jr. 

[The resolutions follow:] 196TH CONVENTION OF THE DIOCESE OF NEW YORK OF THE EPISCOPAL CHURCH, MAY 11, 1974 

HAITIAN REFUGEES 

(From the Reverend Alfred Johnson)

Whereas, an estimated 400 Haitian citizens have fled from Haiti and are now detained in Florida, some in jail, some out on parole, and Whereas, these people are faced with imminent peril of deportation back to Haiti which for many means physical torture and others execution, and Whereas, the United States Government has been unwilling to grant the status of political refugees to these people, therefore be Resolved. that the Secretary of Convention of the Diocese of New York express to the Secretary of State and the Attorney General and Members of Congress from the New York area our urgent request that these persons presently detained be granted refugee status and permitted to remain in the United States with whatever rights and limitations are appropriate to that status. 

Resolution adopted without amendment.

National Council of the Churches of Christ in the U.S.A. 

RESOLUTION IN SUPPORT OF HAITIAN REFUGEES 

(Adopted by the Governing Board, February 28, 1974)

Background statement to accompany the resolution The word of our Lord, "I was a stranger and you took me in," becomes especially incarnate in the plight of refugees fleeing from oppression. In the past fourteen months, more than 400 Haitian refugees, men, women, and children, have come to the United States. Ill and hungry after weeks at sea in flimsy boats, fifty at least having drowned when their overloaded boats sank somewhere along the 800 mile odyssey from Haiti to Florida, they were making their escape from tyranny to what they supposed would be freedom.

But since December 13, 1972, when the first contingent of sixty-five arrived, they have been denied political asylum and have become subject to deportation, despite the fact that twelve of the original sixty-five were former political prisoners. Subsequently, all Haitian refugees arriving by boat in Florida including those rescued at sea by a U.S. Coast Guard cutter on January 14, 1974, were, with the exception of the women and children, jailed or paroled under $1,000 bonds. As of February 21, 1974, there were 120 males imprisoned, some for periods exceeding four months.

The detention of Haitian refugees is in violation of United Nations Protocol on the Status of Refugees, ratified by the U.S. Senate on November 1, 1968, and reflected in Operating Instruction 108.1 of the Immigration and Naturalization 

Service calling for (a) attorney representation, (b) a hearing, rather than a mere interview, enabling the refugee to present a witness and documentary material in support of his or her claim, and (c) providing him or her any contrary evidence and opportunity to rebut it.

On February 5, 1974, in interviews held in Washington, D.C., between high officials of the Immigration and Naturalization Service and the State Department with lawyers and members of the New York and Miami-based Haitian refugee support committees and the Director of the Washington Office of the National Council of Churches, officials of both federal agencies acknowledged that cursory interviews rather than due process hearings had so far been the general practice in the cases of Haitian refugees. 

Senator Mark O. Hatfield, speaking for the Senate Subcommittee on Foreign 

Operations on December 17, 1973, made the following claims against the Haitian government, which are yet to be convincingly denied or contradicted by that government, that: (a) *** (b) At the end of 1972, the Inter-American Press Association asserted "There is no freedom of the press in Haiti. . . . The press continued to be unconditionally subjected to the whim of the Duvalierian dictatorship." (c) Of Haiti's current national budget of $33.3 million, the government intends to spend 25% on the Ministry of Internal Security, with only 13% to education and 8% to agriculture. This in a country where agriculture is the means of livelihood for 90% of the population, nine out of ten in agriculture earning only $25-$35 per year and with a life expectancy of thirtythree years. (d) While there are some indications that since Jean Claude Duvalier was declared "President for Life," the former grim, visible terror may have subsided, autocratic rule characterized by unflinching willingness to suppress people has not. (e) United States foreign assistance must never subsidize corruption of tyranny.

Due to inadequate legal defense funds, persistent violations of U.N. Protocol 

32 and I.N.S. Operating Instruction 108.1 on due process for refugees, compounded by problems of language and lack of knowledge of United States laws by Haitian refugees, few or no affidavits have been secured to document threat of personal persecution or jeopardy to life in the event of deportation; this despite an aggregate grant of $7,000 by the Office of Immigration of NCC Church World Service for legal defense, and smaller grants for complementary purposes by NCC member communions, chiefly the United Methodists and the United Presbyterians.

Fifty detainees have been removed from Miami for further detention in Port Isabelle, Texas, and another thirty-six to Collier County, Florida, an act which in itself reflects the continuing insensitivity of federal agencies to the cruel and unusual punishment which such removal visits upon the detainees and their families. In addition, parole bonds continue to be set at $1,000 per detainee, despite the fact that both the Haitian Refugee Center in Miami (composed of seventy-five local black churches) and the Archdiocese of Miami have offered to assume legal responsibility should the detainees be released on their own recognizance or on lesser bonds.

Deportation continues to be the most ominous threat faced daily by the refugees as long as they are not recognized as bona fide refugees. 

The racial overtones of the treatment accorded black Haitian refugees stands in tragic contrast to the generous United States government provisions for Cuban refugees who are, except for a few, white and skilled; which, by implication, seems to be saying that our doors are open only to those who are white, skilled, and fleeing from socialist governments, thereby sowing seeds of racial strife in Florida and elsewhere, and appearing by design or default a champion of dictatorships of the right, no matter how repressive they might be. 

Be it resolved that:

The Governing Board of the National Council of Churches of Christ in the U.S.A.- 

1. Expresses to the highest authorities of the United States government, especially the Department of State, its profound disquiet for what appears to be a fundamental violation of United States due process of law, required by U.N. 

Protocol 32 and I.N.S. Operating Instruction 108.1, particularly in the case of 

Haitian refugees. 

2. Calls upon NCC member communions to make urgent and continuing financial and legal assistance available to DOM's Church World Service Office of Immigration, the Division of Church and Society, the Haitian Refugee Information Center in Miami, and the Committee for the Defense of Haitian 

Refugees in New York City.

3. Commends the Immigration Office of Church World Service, the NCC Wash ington Office, the Division of Church and Society, the Commission on Justice, Liberation and Human Fulfillment, the Haitian refugee support groups, and the cooperating denominations, without whose well-coordinated efforts these 

Haitian refugees might now be despairing instead of hopeful. 

4. Authorizes the President of the Council immediately to appoint a task force to research the issue of Haitian refugees in the United States, such a task force to be assisted financially and otherwise by the above-named NCC agencies or units, availing itself wherever possible of specialized assistance from the Roman Catholic Church, Jewish organizations, civil liberties groups, labor organizations, Haitian refugee support committees and others, and to report to the 

June 12, 1974, meeting of the Executive Committee with appropriate recommendations for action.

Based on Policy Statements: 

United States Immigration and Naturalization Policy-March 21, 1952 

The Churches and Immigration-February 27, 1962

Human Rights-December 6, 1963 

The Governing Board understands that the work of this task force might have implications for the issue of refugees in a similar situation to which the National Council of Churches might be asked to respond.

STATEMENT OF DON PIERSON, PRESIDENT, DUPONT CARIBBEAN, INC., EASTLAND, TEX. 

FREE PORT DEVELOPMENT 

Senator INOUYE. The next witness is Mr. Don Pierson, President of DuPont Caribbean, Inc., of Eastland, Tex. 

Welcome to the committee. 

Mr. PIERSON. Thank you, sir. This is my son and counsel for our company, Dr. Grey Pierson. 

Senator INOUYE. Welcome, sir. It is good to see a father-son combination. 1 

Mr. PIERSON. I appreciate the opportunity you have given me to testify today. It is my hope that my testimony will result in a better life for the people of Haiti.

My involvement with Haiti began in 1967 when the Haitian Ambassador to Washington, Mr. Arthur Bonhomme, asked me if I might be interested in putting together a privately financed free port development in Haiti. The Government of Haiti had received a recommendation for such a project from a research report they had obtained from the Aero-Jet General Corp. of California.

Initially, I was somewhat hesitant about doing business with Haiti, because Haiti did not enjoy a very good world reputation at that time. However, in my dealings with Ambassador Bonhomme I found him to be a totally honorable and honest person, and after visiting Haiti, I could appreciate the great need and the remarkable business opportunities.

Several months later, after detailed research in Freeport, Bahamas, the only other privately financed and developed free port in the world, I commenced negotiations with Haiti. 

Haiti chose the island of Tortuga as the site for this project, and the years 1968, 1969, and 1970 were spent in negotiating this nonextractive contract. To avoid problems with future generations of Haitians, my conception was to share equal ownership of the operating company with the Republic of Haiti, and I insisted on a leasehold arrangement as opposed to ownership of the land area. 

Finally, in December 1970 the contract was signed, although it was not ratified in the official publication, Le Moniteur, until April 1971. 

We were ready then to start the project after 4 years of sitting, waiting, and negotiating with Haiti. The main reason the negotiations took so long is because we never bribed nor made payoffs to anyone. We wanted a clean, fair contract and we were able to obtain it with honesty and patience rather than payoffs.

Unfortunately, only a few days after the contract was ratified the President of Haiti, Francois Duvalier, died, and I was asked by Haiti to defer the beginning of the project until after a period of mourning. 

In the late summer of 1971, we were at last able to construct a small airstrip on Tortuga and thus establish a direct transportation link with Port-au-Prince. Before proceeding further we needed to have a business meeting of the Free Port Authority and one was finally scheduled to be held in October. When we arrived for the meeting, we were confronted by a demand from the new strongman, Luckner Cambronne, now a resident of Miami, Fla., that our contract be amended to identify the new government of Jean Claude Duvalier with the Tortuga Free Port project. Having no choice, we agreed. 

In January 1972, the amended contract was ratified, and we were at last free to officially start the development work; at this point 5 years had elapsed since I had begun my initial negotiations with Haiti. 

For the next 13 months we attempted to carry out development activities on Tortugas. We were hindered in these efforts by the 

Haitian Government in several ways. First, the Haitian Government refused to cooperate on such matters as appointing the Haitian directors to the Free Port Authority, thus blocking meetings of the Free Port Authority. Consequently, no licenses could be issued to business applicants, thereby depriving our company, Dupont Caribbean, Inc., of its major source of income. Also, the open and eager susceptibility to bribery of a few Haitian officials encouraged the subversion of Dupont Caribbean's contract by certain third parties.

In spite of these obvious handicaps, Dupont Caribbean was able to fulfill and surpass all of its contractual obligations to Haiti up until and through the month of February 1973.

By February 1973 we had proven the feasibility and profitability of our project. We had succeeded in bringing employment and opportunity to starving people in an area which had been utterly and completely undeveloped. Throughout the entire period of our dealings with Haiti, we had not, and have not, taken anything-not a lump of coal or an ounce of bauxite or a single dime-out of Haiti. 

Instead we had brought to Haiti capital, employment, and opportunity. In fact, we were told by the American Embassy that our project had brought more potential investors and tourists to Haiti than any other one thing-at no cost to Haiti.

We entered the month of February 1973 with the highest hopes for the future, but surrounded by reports that Haiti was about to resell our now valuable contract to a higher cash bidder. One of the things that gave us great encouagement in February 1973 was that, after many months of negotiations, Gulf Oil Corp. and Dupont Caribbean had reached an agreement which would have resulted in approximately $300 million being cumulatively invested in the Tortuga project.

This agreement was contingent upon Gulf's assurance by Haiti that Haiti would honor its contract with Dupont Caribbean. In order to ascertain the attitude of the Haitian Government, Mr. Greg Hohub, a 

Gulf vice president, met with the then Finance Minister of Haiti, Dr.

Edouard Francisque. Even though Dr. Francisque had signed the contract amendment as the official representing the Haitian Government, he told Mr. Holub that he knew nothing of the contract and had never heard of Dupont Caribbean.

A few days later Dr. Francisque called me into this office and told me Dupont Caribbean's contract was being canceled because the development work was too slow to suit him and we "had not performed our obligations to Haiti." Pressed for specifics, Dr. Francisque said that Dupont Caribbean had not made its cash payments to Haiti as required by the contract. He ignored my protests that the payments had been made in full and that I had the canceled checks to prove it. 

Since March 1973 Haiti has blocked Dupont Caribbean from proceeding with development activities on Tortuga through a series of purported "legal" actions in the Haitian "Courts." Not once has Dupont Caribbean received proper notice of the impending proceedings in the Haitian "Courts." Not once has Dupont Caribbean been allowed to present documentary or testamentary evidence to contradict the absurd charges of the Haitian Minister of "Justice." 99 It is apparently the view of Haiti that expropriation carried out by a so-called Department of "Justice" becomes a "legal proceeding,' and therefore acceptable, ignoring the fact that expropriation by any other name is still expropriation. Such behavior by a sovereign state is seldom admirable, but in our case it is especially unjust and wrong. 

Dupont Caribbean remains absolutely innocent of the ridiculous allega- 1 tions of the Haitian "Courts." Dupont Caribbean has gone out of its way repeatedly to avoid hurting Haiti and to allow Haiti ample opportunity to do the honorable thing. We have scrupulously avoided any involvement in the internal affairs of the Haitian State. Further, by

the very terms of the contract signed in good faith with Haiti, Haiti renounces both expropriation and nationalization direct or indirect and waives jurisdiction over disputes involving the contract. 

I might add that an AP dispatch this week stated that the Haitian Courts had canceled the contract and that Dupont Caribbean had no further avenues of appeal in Haiti. 

We have always acted in good faith in our dealings with Haiti. 

Haiti invited me to Port-au-Prince for a meeting on March 26, 1974, with Ministers Fourcand and Bayard of the Commerce Ministry and Minister Jeanty of the Justice Ministry. At that meeting they told me that Haiti had allowed itself to be misled into making the false allegations and that Haiti now wanted to do the right thing. We simply suggested that Haiti honor its contract. 

They asked if we would agree to a new contract wherein they would delete the two articles in which Haiti waived jurisdiction. As Haiti had ignored these provisions anyway, we agreed. The ministers thanked me profusely for our continued cooperation with Haiti, and I left the meeting feeling that the Tortuga project would now finally have the interest and support of the Haitian Government and that development work on Tortuga would quickly re-commence. Since that meeting, these same ministers have been extremely evasive about their intentions and it has become increasingly apparent that they have changed their minds.

Based on the integrity of our master contract with Haiti, we in good faith made subcontracts with American firms for development work on Tortuga. As Haiti has illegally blocked our master contract, we obviously are powerless to perform on our subcontracts, thus we are suffering litigation here in the United States because of Haiti's actions. 

Dupont Caribbean is the only company holding a contract with Haiti for the development of Tortuga. 

Had Haiti simply honored its contract with Dupont Caribbean, by this time Gulf Oil Corp. estimated $300 million generated investment would have been felt by all of Haiti. The estimated investment of another firm, Crutcher Resources, of $100 million would also have had a tremendous impact on the Haitian economy. These two investments alone would have provided more jobs and opportunity than any amount of proposed free aid. Most of all, we would be providing, at no cost to Haiti or the American taxpayers, a base of commercial activity that would be a source of employment and hope for thousands of impoverished Haitians.

It is my understanding that the purpose of any foreign aid to Haiti would be to assist in the economic development of Haiti to the benefit of the Haitian people. It is with this premise in mind that I tell you today that no conceivable amount of aid will be of any significant benefit to the average Haitian until certain changes take place in the attitude of the Haitian Government. 

In my modest opinion, the main problem Haiti faces in building a firm commercial base on which to support the nation is the lack of common, everyday business knowledge by those who hold key positions in the Haitian Government. Conversations with government officials almost always get around to getting more aid or grants or loans from somewhere, and practically never toward improving the commercial climate to attract the business endeavors that Haiti must have if it is ever to leave the charity rolls of the world.

Until Haiti makes the fundamental decision to act responsibly and with integrity in its dealings with private enterprise, Haiti will not advance one step toward the goal of self-sufficiency and an improved standard of living.

To the Haitian Government a contract is not a sacred document to be respected, but a piece of paper to play games with. Without the sanctity of contracts, meaningful construction and development with the attendant long-range planning is just not possible. Thus Haiti has discouraged serious, major investors and instead has become a magnet for fast-buck artists and fly-by-nights. The results are obvious to the visitor to Haiti.

Every businessman who visits Haiti is overwhelmed with the outstanding commercial possibilities in such an underdeveloped land, and some return to get in on the ground floor of what appears to be an awakening business opportunity unknown anywhere else in the hemisphere. After being initially encouraged, but finding that nothing ever happens to their requests, most leave Haiti in frustration. 

A conversation I had with a past Minister of Commerce has proven to be indicative of the attitude of a majority of the Haitian Ministers I have known. This man told me that he routinely rejected business contracts from private investors because of the danger that he would lose his job if the contract turned out to be bad. Since he didn't understand business, he felt that he was playing it safe by turning away private businessmen. However, he told me that he would be willing to "take the risk" if a businessman would "make it worth his while.

In other words, he was more concerned with a few thousand dollars personally than potential millions for his country. 

The World Bank recently approved a loan to Haiti of $10 million for new roads. Shortly thereafter there was a mad scramble to secure top posts with the Ministry of Public Works and small pseudo-subcontracting companies were sprouting up all over the place, not to do the work, but to find a way to siphon off some of the funds for Swiss bank accounts.

Our investment in the Tortuga project today is nearly $5 million, including actual investment, second and third party potential liabilities, and estimated legal fees caused by Haiti dishonoring Dupont 

Caribbean's master contract.

We are asking our U.S. Government to intervene on our behalf to get Haiti to either honor its legal contract or to immediately reimburse us. After we have gone to the risk and effort to prove the value of our free port project, it is inexcusable for Haiti to expropriate it under the thin veil of a kangaroo court proceeding. 

We are but a small company-no relation to the famous DuPonts of Wilmington, Del.-that has finally exhausted its resources in trying to get Haiti to do the right and honorable thing, and our voice is too small for Haiti to want to hear. Only our Government will be heard by Haiti at this point.

Haiti needs all the foreign aid it can get, and we do want a better life with opportunity for the Haitian people. We have found the 

Haitian people to be sweet, and kind, and gentle, and we call literally hundreds of them our friends. We want to help them, and have worked to help them for nearly 7 years. 

But to help the Haitian people, all foreign aid, loans, gifts, and grants should be stopped now.

The result of foreign aid in the past has been to cause the Haitian Government to exhibit a profound disinterest in private investment. 

It has apparently proven easier for Haiti to secure direct financial aid than to learn to deal responsibly with serious business people. As a result, Haiti remains as dependent on foreign assistance as ever, and the Haitian populace continues to suffer the lowest standard of living in this hemisphere. In fact, I suggest that this committee send a task force to Haiti to study the effects of past aid; I would be most surprised if even $100-and I use the term $100 as a grossly exaggerated figure to make this point of tangible improvement could be accounted for. Thus I must reiterate that the only way to help Haiti and her impoverished masses is, ironically, to immediately suspend all foreign aid.

Aid to Haiti should not be resumed until Haiti recognizes the importance of acting responsibly in creating a solid commercial base so that sometime in the future Haiti can look forward to a better way of life that her people have for so long been denied. Anything else will keep Haiti as the beggar of the Americas_forever. 

Senator INOUYE. Thank you very much, Mr. Pierson.

I note that you have an attachment, a copy of a telegram addressed to the Secretary of State, dated October 4, 1973. 

Mr. PIERSON. That is right.

GOVERNMENTAL REACTION 

Senator INOUYE. Did you receive any response? 

Mr. PIERSON. Not to this cable at all, Senator. 

Senator INOUYE. Have you received any sort of reaction from the 

Government of the United States?

Mr. PIERSON. The State Department has been very kind and very helpful. They suggested, even though our contract specifically waived legal jurisdiction from Haiti, that we take exception and let Haiti see it through the Haitian courts, which is what we have done. What they have done in Haitian courts, I can't say, but I can say this. This past 

December 18, 1973, in Port-au-Prince at the appeals hearing, I was approached after the appeals hearing by this man who said that he was the judge of the lower court that had found us guilty-no, not guilty, but had found us not complying with our contract. He was in a very agitated frame of mind. My interpreter interpreted for him. 

He said:

I am the judge that is in the lower court. I have been criticized by both prominent Haitians and foreigners for doing such a thing. I want you to know, Mr. 

Pierson, that was not my judgment. It was handed to me to read. As far as I know you are innocent.

That was this past December 18. After that time, I was informed by the Associated Press and also a few weeks ago by the State Department that the Supreme Court of Haiti had said that the contract was nullified.

Senator INOUYE. Throughout the so-called legal proceedings were you permitted to have counsel represent you? 

Mr. PIERSON. No, sir. May I read this cable into the record? I think it might explain some things here. It will take about 2 minutes. This was sent on October 3, 1973, and starts this way. It was sent to the

Department of State, Washington, D.C., Mr. Kissinger, Secretary of

State: 

Mr. KISSINGER: The following is a copy of a cable sent to Minister of Justice 

Fortunae-Palace of Justice-Port au Prince, Haiti. Respectfully, and for the record. I narrate the following facts with a copy going to Secretary of State 

Henry Kissinger, Washington, D.C.

Negotiations were begun with Haiti for the Tortuga freeport nonextractive contract in 1967, with Haiti sharing equal stock ownership in Dupont Caribbean Inc. as the founders, each having ten million shares. 

The project officially began in January 1972 with the publication of the Le Monituer granting the first phase one land release on Tortuga, and after only thirteen months and over two million cumulative dollars invested in the project later, was stopped by the false accusations of the Minister of Finance Francisque in February 1973.

Next, a provisional Haitian court judgement called for me to above all else call a meeting of the Dupont Caribbean Freeport Authority, which I immediately did. But no Haitian had the time to attend. Cable notices were sent to all appropriate Haitian Ministers, President ▲ Vie Jean-Claude Duvalier, and the 

American Embassy.

Next, Chief of Police Frank Romaine collected our international Canadian attornies and took them to his office and intimidated them. They left Haiti the next day.

The Haitian Justice Department then intimidated our Haitian attorney, Girard Noel, into leaving our employ, and discouraged all other Haitian attornies including Rouzier. 

The American Embassy protested and we were finally allowed to employ Gerald Merceron.

We were not told the date of the so-called trial. Therefore, we were denied the opportunity of being personally present of testifying and presenting facts that utterly destroy the false accusations and absolutely prove our innocence. The secret judgement was read to an empty Haitian courtroom and we found out about it only by accident. We are well aware of the rampant rumors in Haiti as to the reason for all of the false activity against us. Rumors say there are higher bidders for our nonextractive contract now that we have made it very valuable, if something legal looking can be done to get us out of the picture. It will not succeed. Such an action violates all civilized standards of equitable dealing and fair play.

We are confident that the true facts are being kept from his Excellency President a Vie Jean-Claude Duvalier and that he will order truth and justice to prevail when he hears the true facts. In the meantime, the world is becoming aware of what is being labeled a farce and a charade, with the resultant lowering of Haiti reputation among the nations of the world. There is no way to calculate the millions and millions of dollars that Haiti has already lost as a result of these illegal activities, and the probable millions Haiti is losing each month that this affair is allowed to continue. 

We have appealed the decision of the lower Haitian civil court, even though we are not optimistic that we will receive any justice and truth there. 

We are absolutely innocent and if given the opportunity, we will present true facts that will utterly destroy the false accusations and that will allow us to quickly resume our orderly business development of Tortuga. May we show you the true facts? We will fight with all of our might, for as long a time as it may take with every honorable means at our disposal, both in Haiti and outside of Haiti, for both Dupont Caribbean Inc. and for the benefit of the Haitian people, for truth and justice to triumph. 

We are absolutely innocent and have honored our contract. May we hear from you? 

Most respectfully and sincerely, DON PIERSON, President, Dupont Caribbean Inc., Eastland, Tex.

STATEMENT OF BERNARD SANSARICQ, MIRAMAR, FLA. 

NATIONAL RESISTANCE HAITIANS Senator INOUYE. Our final witness represents the Conseil Na tional Resistance Haitiane of the United States and Haiti. 

We have with us Mr. Bernard Sansaricq. 

You are Mr. Bernard Sansaricq? 

Mr. SANSARICQ. Yes, sir.

Mr. Chairman, I will try to keep my testimony as brief as possible. 

I will start by saying that Haiti is hell under Baby Doc.

If the United States really wants to help the Haitian people, foreign aid to Haiti should be cut off right away. For despite $80 million in 

U.S. aid in the past 20 years Haiti still has the poorest, hungriest, sickest people of this hemisphere. 

Where has the money gone? The Duvalier family is worth $50 million. Forty of those millions are in Swiss banks. $3 million were just spent to install special cable for closed-circuit TV so government

53 people in Port-au-Prince would watch the World Cup soccer games; $1 million to build a resting place for the body of François Duvalier. 

The Duvalier family is considering buying Hasco, Haitian-American 

Sugar Co., a sugar factory in Port-au-Prince, for approximately $5 million.

Marie Denise Duvalier spent a half million dollars in a lavish villa not too far from Washington.

Luckner Cambronne, Duvalier's greediest son, is worth at least $10 million. He just bought the Estrella Coffee Co. In Miami, Fla., for $500,000.

The rest of Duvalier's henchmen are all millionnaires. 

Fantastic sums of money are spent in police work, to spy on militant exiled leaders. Large sums of money are also spent on the foreign press to try to change the country's image. 

Lobbying in Washington is never neglected. Expensive cars and yachts for the President, expensive trips abroad for his relatives and followers.

Let us not forget: Weapons for the militia, the presidential guard, and the Leopards, three distinct repressive groups of Gestapo-type men trained by U.S. former military men with the blessing of the State Department.

The President's private tax fund in Haiti is not included in the national budget and the revenue remains unaccounted for. As long as the 

Duvaliers continue to dilapidate the public treasury, as they are, supported by the U.S. State Department, the United States can pour billions of dollars in Haiti without helping the unfortunate people of my country.

The U.S. Department of State maintains there is no political oppression in Haiti.

However, 3 weeks ago two well-known medical doctors, Innocent and Adams, were arrested. 

Mr. Romulus, a career teacher, Lionel Charles, a young student, and 

50 others were also arrested in Port-au-Prince. Earlier, still under 

Jean Claude, Colonel Kessner Blain, Mr. Clemart, Joseph Charles,

Jean Claude Brisson, Jean Robert Lherisson, and an eminent lawyer, Mr. Hubert Legros, were also arrested. 

Amnesty International, a London-based organization that intercedes for prisoners of conscience, have requested information on Mr. Legros and others, but the Haitian regime of Duvalier has remained silent. 

Also, 3 weeks ago Friar Michel Corignan was arrested in Port-au- Prince. The Catholic teacher had been at that school for 20 years. The 

Haitian regime accused him of being a communist. 

Now, Mr. Chairman, an Englishman, Mr. Edmund Burke, said a long time ago, "The only thing that is necessary for the triumph of evil is that good men do nothing." 

I am asking you today to do something.

Five million Haitians are begging for mercy. Their own country is just hell for them.

Some 300,000 are in the Dominican Republic, 20,000 in the Bahamas. and Jamaica, and they are coming by boatloads to Florida telling stories about the horrible killing taking place on the inside, but with much more finesse than before.

The Haitian people deserve more than this inhuman treatment, for their ancestors in the past have contributed more than any other American nation to the development and maintenance of other Latin American nations. This has persistently and maliciously been ignored for no one wants to be indebted to unfortunate Haiti. 

However, most of the Latin American nations-namely, Venezuela, Colombia, Bolivia, and Peru-owe their freedom to Bolivar. The South

American liberator would have perished of frustration in exile without Haiti's efficient help in arms and soldiers. It was not George Washington, champion of democracy, who furnished Bolivar with the needed help, but Petion of the newborn Haiti. Also by achieving independence in 1803 the Haitians had at the same time destroyed the dream of Napoleon to create a great French empire in the Mississippi Valley. The result was the sale of Louisiana to the United States. 

Mr. Chairman, I am asking you today to do something to help the 

Haitian people.

I firmly believe in the American Senate. I believe in the American 

Government, but I distrust the State Department. 

We need your help and we need the help of the American Senate to end this hemispheric nonsense in Haiti. 

Thank you.

PROPOSED ASSISTANCE PROGRAM 

Senator INOUYE. Of this year's proposed assistance program, $5.1 billion is reflected in the pending budget request for new obligational authority before this subcommittee.

This subcommittee began hearings on February 25 and will conclude them this morning with our very distinguished Secretary of 

State, Hon. Henry A. Kissinger. 

Mr. Secretary, I bid you a most cordial welcome for your first appearance before this subcommittee. Please proceed as you desire, sir.

STATEMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE Secretary KISSINGER. Mr. Chairman and distinguished members of the committee:

I deeply regret that the pace of recent events prevented me from appearing before you earlier for the foreign assistance program is of such urgent and fundamental importance to the entire range of our foreign policy concerns.

Developments during the past month alone-in the Middle East, at the Moscow summit, and with our Atlantic allies-demonstrate both the challenges and opportunities before American diplomacy today, and the central role that the assistance program plays. 

It is my profound conviction that programs of foreign assistance are not handouts. They are done on behalf of an international order and on behalf of an approach to the solution of problems that is in all nations' interest, and very much in the American interest. 

The test we must apply is whether what we are proposing is adequate to meet the need, and whether anything less would fulfill our purposes as a nation.

We believe that the program before you will substantially contribute to achieving these six goals:

Creating a lasting peace in the Middle East, not just another cease-fire;

Building the capacity of the peoples of Indochina to determine their own destiny;

Establishing the basis for relationships of mutual restraint and respect with the Soviet Union and the People's Republic of China; 

Avoiding the division of the world into competing blocs of developed and developing nations;

Bringing into balance food production and population growth; and 

Lowering the burden on the United States by building other nations' capacity for self-development and self-defense. 

We in the United States cannot alone underwrite the success of the quest to resolve old issues or alone persevere in the face of continuing obstacles to peace. Nor can we assure that the imperative of cooperation will overcome nations' temptation to pursue short-term advantage. 

But it is equally clear that hopes for a peaceful, cooperative, and just international order can only be realized with the strong participation of this Nation.

Our assistance programs are crucial vehicles for that participation. 

Our economic assistance is designed to reinforce developing nations' efforts to bring a better life to their citizens, increasing their stake in a cooperative global economy at a time when events threaten to divide the world anew-between North and South, developed and developing, consumer and producer. 

Our security assistance is designed primarily to help others strengthen the peace in areas where it is threatened, and to provide a framework of cooperation that will prevent new threats from emerging. 

Let me comment briefly on each of the principal elements of the program we have proposed: 

MIDDLE EAST 

In the Middle East, a new era is opening in our relations with both Arabs and Israelis and in their relations with one another. The program before you is vital to give substance to these new relationships and to preserve the momentum toward peace that has developed over the last 6 months.

We are witnessing one of the most arduous but also one of the most hopeful developments of the past generation. Thanks to the farsighted views of key leaders in the region, and with the active role of the United States, we have seen important steps toward peace and the partial erosion of decades of hostility and mistrust among the parties.

Our proposals have three basic purposes: 

First, to provide Israel with the assistance needed to maintain its security, giving it resolve to persevere in the negotiations, assured of its own strength, and of our support; 

Second, to give tangible expression to our new and fruitful relations with various Arab countries and encourage those which are seriously prepared to work for peace; and 

Third, to encourage the peaceful development of the area, reducing the incentives to violence and conflict, and deepening the interest of all the peoples in cooperation. 

More specifically, with this program we would: 

Make available to Israel $350 million in grants and credits to enable it to continue purchasing vitally needed military equipment from the United States and to relieve it of some of the burden of its onerous defense costs.

Extend to Jordan roughly $207 million in grants and credits both to enhance its security and to assist its economic development. This would strengthen Jordan's ability to hold the course of moderation it has consistently followed.

Provide $250 milllion in economic assistance to Egypt. Egypt has made the bold decision to move from confrontation to negotiation as a means of resolving the Arab-Israeli dispute. Its leaders have shown a desire to substitute friendship and trust in the United States for the hostility and distrust which has so long divided us. 

Make $100 million available in the form of a special requirements fund to be used to reinforce the peace process as we get further into negotiations. We would consult closely with Congress on the use of this money.

INDOCHINA 

Now let me turn to Indochina.

Sustaining the achievements of recent years-an honorable termination of direct American military involvement, peace in Laos, and a substantial reduction of hostilities in Vietnam, a prevailing military balance of forces, and a substantial lessening of the risk of confrontation among outside powers-now hinges on sums that are small in proportion to the total effort that has been made. 

Including the separate legislation for military aid, our total Vietnamese assistance request is about what we spent in a single month in 1968 at the height of U.S. involvement. 

But, the basic question is not what we have achieved or failed to achieve in the past. It is the kind of world we want to create for the future.

To help shape a world of negotiation, stability, and peace rather than confrontation, intervention, and force, our policy in Indochina is quided by these two objectives: 

First, to enable the states of Indochina to move freely toward a future of self-determined political and economic stability; 

Second, by thus strengthening their independence, to avoid both the dangers of rivalry for domination by outside powers and to preclude domination itself. 

We have submitted to Congress a 6-year projection which reflects our expectation of a gradually declining role in Indochina. 

But our present request for $750 million in economic and humanitarian assistance for South Vietnam is essential to make this transition. 

A stable military situation and eventual accommodation cannot be achieved if South Vietnam's economic problems are allowed to get out of hand.

In the past year, that nation has experienced problems over which it had very little control-a sharp decline in dollar revenue following the withdrawal of our troops, and world inflation.

At the peak of our involvement in the war, Vietnam's dollar earnings from U.S. Government activities ranged between $350 million and $400 million a year. Last year, following the withdrawal of U.S. troops, this figure dropped to just over $100 million. 

At the same time, the costs of Vietnam's imports soared as global inflation boosted the prices of raw materials and semifinished products. 

South Vietnam has been attempting to adjust to these challenges with its own resources. But its foreign exchange reserves have fallen severely.

Substantial assistance is still necessary. Our programs, however, are designed to do more than shore up the Vietnamese economy. They are shaped to nurture Vietnam's capacity for self-support by stimulating reconstruction and development; returning refugees to productive lives; and helping the Vietnamese to defend themselves. 

In the past, Vietnam has made good use of our assistance. We are confident it will do so in the future. 

We are also seeking $362.5 million in military assistance and $110 million in reconstruction funds for the Khmer Republic. The Cambodians are fighting for their survival against forces aided and advised by the North Vietnamese. The country's economy has been

shattered and the level of combat is intense. The people have paid a heavy price.

The Government of the Khmer Republic has consistently affirmed its desire for a peaceful settlement through direct negotiations with its adversaries. Clearly, a negotiated settlement of this war is the only responsible outcome.

In Laos, a cease-fire has been achieved and the process of political accommodation begun. The country is shifting from war to rehabilitation and reconstruction. The $142 million assistance package we are seeking will help it to carry out that transition. 

DEVELOPMENT ASSISTANCE 

Over two decades ago, the United States played the principal role in establishing the concept of economic assistance from the richer to the poorer nations. We can take pride in the record we have established. 

It both reflects humanitarian concerns and serves our national interests. 

Today our values and our interests continue to require an active assistance program by this Nation. But the old formulas and old justifications will not suffice.

In recent months the energy crisis has driven home the fact that interdependence is a condition, not a theory. That reality transcends any particular crisis and its lesson is clear: We live in a world economy under severe stress that makes cooperation an imperative if the open global economy is to be preserved and expanded. 

While the United States is in a better position than most nations to compete in a world where autarchy prevails, it is not in our interest for events to carry the world in that direction. Down that road lies an inevitable increase in political tensions which would unravel the fabric of global stability.

The programs we are proposing will place us in a better position: 

To enlist the developing nations' cooperation in sustaining an open global economy;

To promote a long-term balance between demands for goods and their supply; and

To be responsive to the concerns of countries and areas of importance to us.

The United States must pursue a comprehensive approach to our relations with the developing nations. To do so, we- 

Are requesting $1.2 billion for development assistance, which with loan receipts, interest payments, and deobligations will make possible programs of $1.5 billion;

We are seeking $1.006 billion for international financial institutions; and

We have Public Law 480 programs totaling $996 million. 

As you know, the focus of our assistance program is largely a product of congressional initiative. The develpment of this program exemplified the constructive bipartisan cooperation between the legislature and the Executive that we seek in the foreign affairs field. 

The program is designed to provide a more effective approach to assisting the poorest of the poor-the 800 million people who subsist on 30 cents a day and have no means to pay the sharply higher prices for fuel, food and fertilizer on which their survival depends.

The most critical challenge is to achieve a balance between food production and population growth-a balance the program's focus on agriculture, family planning and education will help realize. Thus: $676 million, almost half of our development assistance under the Foreign Assistance Act, is destined to support rural development and to increase food production; $226 million will go to family planning and health; $109 million will go to education. 

Developing nations meet more of their foreign exchange needs through trade than aid. Thus congressional passage of the administration's trade bill would be a crucial contribution to the development process.

The bill contains our request for authority to grant generalized tariff preferences which are of major economic and political significance to the developing nations.

SECURITY ASSISTANCE 

I have outlined the essential role our security assistance will play in nurturing the prospects for a stable and lasting peace in the Middle East and building the capacity for self-determination in Indochina. 

For similar reasons there is a continuing need for this country to assist nations elsewhere in meeting their legitimate defense needs. As you are aware, our approach has been to encourage other nations to assume an increasing share of the burden for their own defense. 

Refinement of our program does not mean that its objectives everywhere have been reached. Not all nations have developed a self-sustaining capacity for their own defense. And a climate of security is required if political and economic development are to take place. 

Thus our proposed program reflects a continuing need to do the following:

First, we should continue our assistance program to selected countries around the world as they develop their indigenous defense capabilities. The largest proportion of this assistance is directed to a selected group of countries where our direct security interests are involved.

But the program also will provide modest amounts of materiel and training to a number of nations in Latin America, Africa, the Middle East and East Asia-where our help can make a small but crucial contribution to their defense, or where our willingness to participate in their efforts is an important manifestation of a mutually beneficial relationship.

Second, we need to be able to provide adequate credit assistance to our friends and partners to supplement and in some instances to take the place of grant assistance. The foreign military sales program promotes the self-sufficiency of our friends. To increase the usefuless of this valuable tool, we are requesting that the guarantee requirement for foreign military sales be reduced to 10 percent, that the $150 million ceiling on credit sales to Latin America be deleted, and that the President be given authority to waive the $40 million ceiling on sales to Africa when he determines that it is in our national interest to do so.

LATIN AMERICA 

Latin America constitutes an area of special concern to the United 

States. 

The countries of this hemisphere are embarked on an exciting new adventure. We have determined to make the global agenda of interdependence a program for cooperation in the Americas. 

The initiative for this effort came from Latin America. The dialog we have launched with our friends to the south has opened up the possibility of a new and productive relationship in the hemisphere. 

But just as we expect to benefit from strong ties in the Americas, we must contribute in concrete ways to their establishment. The program before Congress contains essential elements in this direction: 

The $267.5 million bilateral economic program, focusing on food, rural development, and human resources, is a concrete manifestation of our interest in helping Latin America bring a better life to its citizens. 

Our request of $500 million to complete our share of the last replenishment of the Inter-American Development Bank is destined for an effective development organization. It also would demonstrate that we can keep our commitments by fulfilling an agreement made over 

4 years ago.

Passage of the trade bill, with its authority to grant generalized tariff preferences, would also fulfill an outstanding commitment to Latin

America, one which my colleagues in the hemisphere have repeatedly made clear is of utmost importance to their nations. 

Let me conclude.

CONCLUSION 

It is my strong belief that the central issue of our time is whether economic and politicial problems are going to be solved through cooperation or fester and fuel continuing confrontations. 

The programs we are requesting and the levels we are requesting are not arbitrary. The requests are made on behalf of a structure of peace that we believe is overwhelmingly in the American interest. 

They are indispensable tools to help us mold that structure. 

We are aware of both the limits and the possibilities for this Nation. The absolute sums involved are large indeed. But the burden is small-less than 1 percent of our national product. They are the resources required to carry America's role in building a more secure and stable world.

Economics, technology and the sweep of human values impose a recognization of global interdependence and the necessity of American participation in its management. 

Let us, therefore, resolve to act with both realism and compassion to reach a new understanding of the human condition and to build on that understanding a new commitment to helping meet the universal longing for justice, human dignity, and peace. 

COMMITMENTS IN THE MIDDLE EAST 

Senator INOUYE. I thank you very much, Mr. Secretary.

We realize that it is customary for the leaders of government and heads of state, when traveling abroad, to present gifts to their hosts,

and naturally we don't expect our President to be an exception to this custom.

During this recent trip we were made aware of certain gifts which were presented not through committee hearings or through briefings or consultation, but unfortunately by headlines. Apparently at every stop in the Middle East some sort of significant gift was presented. 

To this day I must confess that we are not aware of the real nature of the gifts, the commitments involved, the reasons or the rationale back of the gift. So if you would tell us why Israel and Egypt were presented with the nuclear plants and why the $100 million in the special fund, which apparently will assist Syria and the special fund for Israel, I think it would be most helpful to this committee if we had a broad explanation from you, sir.

Secretary KISSINGER. Mr. Chairman, our policy in the Middle East must have several components. It is in the interest of the United 

States and in the interest of world peace that the evolution toward moderation and a peaceful solution of the disputes in the area be given encouragement.

The energy crisis through which the whole industrialized world went last year brought home the crucial fact quite apart from danger of war that arose of the necessity to devise a peaceful solution to the conflict in the Middle East. 

Our policy therefore has several steps:

One, to contribute to the extent of our abilities to the negotiating process in the area;

Second, to provide incentives to the moderate countries in the area to pursue a peaceful evolution;

Third, where certain developments seem probable, to attempt to shape them in the most constructive direction possible.

All of these objectives afford an opportunity, of course, to contribute to the security of military strength. All of these objectives seem to be fulfilled by the various schemes to which you have referred. 

First, the $100 million special fund was not a gift that the President brought on his trip. It was part of our legislative proposals that were planned prior to that trip, and I believe I testified to them prior to the trip.

These funds are not earmarked for Syria as such, but they would be available for Syria as well as for other countries. The reason it was put in the form of a contingency item is that it was not possible to predict the opportunities that might arise to encourage a moderate course in particular countries in a situation as fluid as the one that now exists in the Middle East. 

NUCLEAR PLANTS 

With respect to the nuclear plants, those are not gifts. The decision to go ahead with the nuclear plants, which had been under negotiation for many months, was made because it is our judgment that we cannot control the nuclear future of the countries concerned. 

For example, France has sold five nuclear reactors to Iran under conditions of inspection much less restrictive than those upon which we will insist. And therefore, it seemed to us that by agreeing to these requests we had an opportunity to insist on safeguards which would reduce more than any alternative course that might be available-

the possibilities of diversion for military uses; and at the same time it would involve a long-term commitment, over an 8-year period, to a kind of peaceful construction which in itself would provide an incentive for peace.

Those were the reasons, Mr. Chairman, that led us to the specific decisions to which you have referred. 

Senator INOUYE. Why nuclear plants at a time of high tension?

I believe that many Americans interpret this sharing of nuclear information as fueling the fire.

Secreetary KISSINGER. Mr. Chairman, the nuclear plants-we have similar agreements I believe with 23 other countries-could not be considered as sharing nuclear information. The technology is quite well known. What is lacking in many countries is the engineering skill to produce it and the means to operate. 

Second, the danger that nuclear plants may represent is in the diversion of nuclear material. No nuclear material has been diverted from any plant under IAEA safeguards. The diversions that occurred in 

India were in a reactor that was built before the IAEA safeguards went into effect.

In addition, the nuclear plants to which we have agreed in the Middle East will be under safeguards stricter than the IAEA safeguards, and insofar as human ingenuity can provide for it, will prevent diversion of material for non-peaceful purposes.

It seemed to us that this was a better course in countries that had energy shortages and were almost certain to acquire nuclear reactors from some source than to refuse to participate. 

USE OF NUCLEAR MATERIALS FOR WARLIKE PURPOSES 

Senator INOUYE. The subcommittee has been advised, first, that the 

Aswan Dam is being used only to about 30 percent of its capacity, and if that is the case there is still much more potential available from the activities of the Aswan Dam; second, the AEC has advised us that last year we lost about 100 pounds of uranium and about 60 pounds of plutonium-it takes only about 13 pounds to make a first-class bomb; and third, the AEC also advises us that it doesn't take much to develop a bomb. You can get nonclassified material in libraries and in hardware stores and build a bomb, and this has been demonstrated quite adequately.

Aren't you fearful that this might be converted for aggressive or warlike purposes? 

Secretary KISSINGER. First, with respect to the energy situation in

Egypt, over the period that we have projected we expect that there will be an energy shortage in Egypt even with a full utilization of the 

Aswan Dam.

Second, it is quite true that the technology of building a bomb is fairly well known and much of it can be read in unclassified literature. 

But this condition will exist whether or not there is an American nuclear reactor in the area.

The possibility of not being able to account for some of the nuclear materials reflects accounting difficulties.

However, we believe that the new safeguards that we have developed with respect to the nuclear reactors for the Middle East will reduce this danger from what we consider insignificant proportions to nonexisting proportions. bd pd

HELICOPTER FOR PRESIDENT SADAT 

Senator INOUYE. The other item that was presented is not a very expensive one. In fact, in terms of the amounts involved in the appropriations, it is a small amount. And that is the helicopter presented to 

President Sadat.

We have had some difficulty trying to place this in the proper appropriations slot, and we find that after some discussion you have decided to put this under foreign aid.

I would like to have your justification on how this will help bring about the stability you seek in this world. 

Secretary KISSINGER. Well, Mr. Chairman, there always have to be judgments made to the degree to which the personal attitudes of leaders affect decisions of governments, and to what extent the visibility of an American helicopter as the Presidential vehicle in Egypt contributes to the image that the population of that area has of the role of the donor nation; the judgment in this case was that it would be in the interest of the United States to proceed with the gift of the helicopter for the reasons which I have outlined. 

MILITARY CREDIT SALES 

Senator INOUYE. In your statement you have suggested that we lift the restrictions placed upon military credit sales to Latin America and to Africa.

What is the threat that is being posed to our potential purchasers of military supplies in Latin America? Are there enemies- 

Secretary KISSINGER. Will you repeat that? What is the threat to which these sales are directed? 

Senator INOUYE. Yes. 

Secretary KISSINGER. Mr. Chairman, there are two aspects of the problem of threats. The first, what is objective reality; the second is, what is the perception of the country?

Now many countries in Latin America are either governed by or heavily influenced by their military establishment. They perceive that it is a question of national prestige, a question of national tradition, to require certain levels of armaments. The conditions in the world have been such that if we refuse to sell arms to them, they have many alternative sources of military suppliers.

With these military suppliers go training missions, and thus the general political relationship that is established through a constant exchange of information, training, and common attitudes. So we deprive ourselves in Latin America of a historical and natural relationship by refusing to do what many other countries are only too eager to achieve, and it is for this reason that we have proposed waiving the ceiling. Similar reasons, perhaps somewhat less strong, apply to Africa as well.

CURBING MILITARY SALES 

Senator INOUYE. I am certain you are aware that the condition of life in Latin America has been described by some as being degraded by disease, illiteracy, malnutrition and squalor almost second to none, and yet in the last 4 years we have sold these extremely impoverished countries nearly $250 million of military material.

In your statement and statements of predecessor Secretaries, I note that the purpose of the humanitarian aspect of foreign aid, and for that matter for the whole package, is to assist the poorest of the poor, and I also realize, as stated by you, if we don't sell, somebody else might sell.

But can't we get together with all the munitions makers in the world and possibly extend the coverage of the nonproliferation treaty to include conventional weapons? 

Secretary KISSINGER. Mr. Chairman, the requests for arms are not, of course, generated by us. As you know, we have in the past 12 years begun a new dialog with Latin America designed to spur development and to foster U.S. relationships with Latin America in the areas of development, increasing trade, and the fulfillment of the aspirations of the people.

So the question of arms purchases arises from the recipient countries, not from the United States. 

With respect to the desirability of curbing the arms trade in general, I believe that that is an interesting suggestion and one which we should explore with the chief suppliers on a worldwide basis of military equipment in order to be able to relate sales to needs. 

But under present conditions, in the absense of such an agreement, I think it would be a unilateral restriction on the United States that would serve no national purpose. 

Senator INOUYE. Mr. Secretary, I note, for example, that in the last 4 years our military export sales jumped from $1.3 billion to $8 billion in fiscal 1974, and just in recent days we have had two of our allies using our equipment to fight each other. 

We just came to the brink of a major war between Greece and Turkey, and I think many of my colleagues on this committee have persistent nightmares that these things will happen because we are the most successful salesman when it comes to arms. Someday you may see our weapons being used against each other in the Middle East. 

I am wondering if this does not concern us or should concern us. 

Secretary KISSINGER. I think it should concern us, Mr. Chairman, but of course in the case of Greece and Turkey the purpose of our military assistance is to permit them to defend themselves against an outside threat, as part of the NATO Alliance, in one of the geographically most decisive areas of the world. 

We made clear as soon as the tension started-I said so publicly in San Clemente that NATO allies would not be able to fight each other with an open American supply line and American equipment. We believe that thi was one of the factors that helped reduce the intensity of the crisis.

The circumstance in which two NATO allies are likely to go to war with each other is not very probable, though it was unfortunately near this last weekend. and we acted in the sense that I have described. 

In the Middle East I do not foresee a situation where both sides will be fighting each other with American equipment.

AID PROJECTION FOR SOUTH VIETNAM 

Senator INOUYE. Mr. Secretary, in your press conference of April 26 you stated with reference to future levels of assistance to Vietnam- We have told the Congress and we will reiterate this in our testimony that we will respond to their suggestions of putting before the Congress our expectations of the assistance that will be required over a period of time. 

A few days ago we received these projections, but to our disappointment they were classified "Secret." This restriction on the information and even on the gross figures severely limits their value to this committee.

Why can't these projections be placed in the public domain and be subject to open debate by the Congress and by the press, and for that matter by the citizenry? 

Secretary KISSINGER. Mr. Chairman, I don't know the reason for it.

It is our policy. But I tell you quite honestly I didn't know they were classified. 

Senator INOUYE. Can they be declassified this morning?

Secretary KISSINGER. The problem is that certain political and military assumptions were made; but may I review this and be in touch with you by the end of the week on this problem? 

Senator INOUYE. We will appreciate that because if we are called upon to make necessary decisions in determining the appropriation levels for Indochina, we will have to have an open debate at least in the committee, and it would be strange having a debate in executive session and on the floor of the Senate. So it would be most helpful if you would help us in this area. 

Secretary KISSINGER. Let me consider this and be in touch with you,

Mr. Chairman, to discuss our rationale. It is in our interest to have as full a discussion of the subject as we can generate without necessarily revealing the military assumptions on which it is based, since this might be a temptation. I suspect that we can work out some arrangements that will enable you to refer to figures in a way that contributes to the public debate. 

Senator INOUYE. Thank you. 

Secretary KISSINGER. May I be in touch with you no later than early next week? 

Senator INOUYE. I would appreciate that very much. [STAFF NOTE.-Those portions of the referencd table not relating to military assistance were subsequently declassified and are reprinted as follows:]

MILITARY ACTIVITIES BY NORTH VIETNAM 

Senator INOUYE. Mr. Secretary, you have communicated with this committee your concern that Hanoi will again seek the military solution in Vietnam if we should decide to cut off aid to Saigon. Can you further inform the subcommittee as to your views on the possible resumption of military activities by the Hanoi Government? Do we have any indication that this is the possibility? 

Secretary KISSINGER. Hanoi has put itself in a position over the past year where its military forces in the South are very substantial. It therefore has the option to resume military operations with a relatively small reinforcement effort. We have no indication of any imminent attack. Since this is the rainy season, it is not likely in the next month or so.

But the long-term strategy of Hanoi has always been to combine military with political pressure.

It is also our judgment that the military strength of South Vietnam has reached a point where this will not be an easy assignment for Hanoi to take on and where, if we continue an effort that is modest compared to the sacrifices that have already been made, we should be in a position to make this effort increasingly unattractive. Indeed, we have already made it substantially unattractive. 

SOVIET AND CHINESE ASSISTANCE TO NORTH VIETNAM 

Senator INOUYE. What is the level of assistance provided by the 

Soviet Union and the People's Republic of China for the North? 

Secretary KISSINGER. Mr. Chairman, this is a question about which there are endless debates. The debate arises partly because of insufficient information, partly because of the difficulty of establishing comparable price mechanisms, partly because of the difficulty in accounting. I have seen figures that vary wildly-from those which suggest they are far in excess of what we are supplying to figures that suggest they are supplying quantities substantially below what we are supplying.

Among the variables is that of whether you include transportation costs in the Soviet and Chinese totals as we do in our accounting. If you do the comparison in terms of physical quantity rather than in terms of dollar value. I think the figures are substantially comparable. 

Senator INOUYE. A recent news report indicated that the Defense 

Intelligence Agency has reported that our aid to Vietnam was 29 times greater than the aid received by Hanoi from China and from the 

Soviet Union.

Secretary KISSINGER. Before I testified before another committee on this subject, I attempted to obtain data on that question. At that time the estimate was nothing like that. It was something like half of the amount that we had supplied, and then it did not include transportation costs or differentials for labor costs in the product, so I never presented the figures, since I considered them too inconclusive. 

But "29 times" is certainly wrong. 

Senator INOUYE. That is too far-fetched, sir? 

Secretary KISSINGER. In my judgment, yes.

TURKEY OPIUM PRODUCTION 

Senator INOUYE. The committee is informed that in violation of the agreement with the United States, Turkey has lifted its ban on cultivation of opium poppies. On the 7th of May of this year we received testimony from Mr. Vance of your office:

Our commitment to provide them with a little over $35 million in grant assistance was conditioned on that undertaking, on that decree by the Turkish Government to ban the production of poppies. 

Is it the intention of this administration to continue aid to Turkey, and if so, why? 

Secretary KISSINGER. Mr. Chairman, we give aid to Turkey not for altruistic reasons but because of the enormous political and strategic importance of Turkey. It is geopolitically strategic at one of the most crucial locations. The defense of the Mediterranean, the ability to operate in the Mediterranean depend importantly on the independence and security of Turkey.

Poppy cultivation is a major domestic issue in Turkey. The restriction on this cultivation was accepted by a military government. 

Turkey is now under a democratic government which has a narrow majority. The pressures on the Turkish Government to resume cultivation of poppies have proved to be overwhelming. 

We were on the verge of beginning a dialog with Turkey looking towards effective controls of the traffic from the poppy cultivation and making sure that the production would not exceed the medical needs. 

This dialog could not start because of the Cyprus issue.

The policy of the U.S. Government will be to bring the trade in the product under effective control, and if that is achieved we believe that aid to Turkey should continue because it is done in our own interest and not only in the Turkish interest.

Senator INOUYE. Then our attempt to convince Turkey to stop its production was doomed to failure from the very beginning, wasn't it, sir?

Secretary KISSINGER. It failed, and one can explain in retrospect why it was almost bound to fail, given the narrow margin in the Turkish Parliament and the fact that all parties had made promises to resume cultivation during the election. 

Senator INOUYE. How can we in the legislative branch assist you in convincing the Turkish people of our concern over the cultivation of poppies? 

Secretary KISSINGER. Well, I think that the legislative branch should make very clear, Mr. Chairman, that we cannot interfere with a sovereign decision of the Turkish Government, but we can ask that the

results of these decisions not affect the health and welfare of the American people. Therefore, at a minimum, effective control of the poppy traffic is an absolute requirement. 

And, as I pointed out, Ambassador Macomber was on the way back to Turkey with a Presidential letter designed to open this discussion when the Cyprus problem interrupted the possibility of a dialogue on this issue.

As soon as the Cyprus issue is not solved, because that will take some time has been quieted to a point where the Turkish Government can deal with other problems, we will begin this dialogue and we would welcome legislative expressions of concern with it. 

Senator INOUYE. Mr. Secretary, without objection there will be inserted in the record at this point a table detailing the administration's proposed $378,412,000 in U.S. assistance to Israel in fiscal year 1975.
