ASSISTANCE TO ISRAEL 

Senator INOUYE. Does the administration favor any further assistance to Israel in fiscal year 1975, for example, in areas such as the refugees from the Soviet Union, military grant assistance, the nuclear plants, et cetera, or is this the extent of it? 

Secretary KISSINGER. Well, Mr. Chairman, the Government of Israel has presented to us on an informal basis various projections as to its future military and economic needs. They are based on the one hand on the security requirements which might be even heightened by the withdrawals that have taken place or may be in prospect, and second, they reflect the increase in oil, food, and other prices. 

These discussions have not yet reached a point where final conclusions or even preliminary conclusions have been reached that could be submitted to the Congress.

In fairness, I must point out to you, Mr. Chairman, that the projections would indicate that some additional requests may have to be made, though I would expect for fiscal year 1975 it would be of a rather modest measure.

Senator INOUYE. What is the present status of the $2.2 billion emergency appropriation that was made for fiscal year 1974? 

Secretary KISSINGER. The present state is that it has all been converted into grant loan, but my understanding is that it has been or will be substantially exhausted fairly soon. 

GREECE AND CYPRUS 

Senator INOUYE. Finally, Mr. Secretary, I am certain all of us would like to know what is happening in Greece and in Cyprus, to put it very mildly. Most of us are rather confused to see changes come about almost overnight.

Would you advise us as to what is happening within bounds of secrecy and the requirements of your office, sir?

Secretary KISSINGER. Well, Mr. Chairman, the coup that took place in Cyprus last week brought in a regime that Turkey believed would lead Cyprus to eventual union with Greece, a situation which Turkey strongly opposed.

Second, there was a fear on the part of Turkey that it would lead to complete domination of the Turkish minority by the Greek-Cypriot majority.

Finally, the leader of the government-or the administration-that succeeded Makarios was highly unacceptable also to Great Britain, which is one of the guarantee powers. 

Now as a result of the sequence of events that was started with the Turkish intervention there was yesterday a change back to constitutional processes in Cyprus.

The head of the national assembly, Clerides, has taken over as acting president, as is foreseen by the Cyprus constitution under conditions when the president is absent or incapacitated. 

On the mainland in Greece at the same time the military government seems to have been replaced by a civilian government headed by for mer Prime Minister Karamanlis. 

We welcome both developments during this crisis last week. We supported the constitutional processes in Cyprus. We welcome the return of Greece to civilian government. We have already established contact with the leaders of this government yesterday afternoon, and we will be in further touch with them today. 

Senator INOUYE. According to the latest news report, although the former head of state Papadopoulos has fled the country, it is reported that the military junta is still in firm control. Is this your conclusion, sir? 

Secretary KISSINGER. Well, it is very difficult to judge at this moment. Our impression is that civilian government has been substantially restored in Greece. The army will, of course, play a role, but it is our impression that it has not as dominant a role as it has had in the last 7 years. We expect a return to democratic processes in Greece. 

Senator INOUYE. Without objection there will be inserted in the record at this point tables reflecting the overall totals of U.S. assistance to Greece and Turkey.

MILITARY ASSISTANCE Senator INOUYE. Since World War II, the United States has provided 

$4.3 billion to Greece, of which $2.3 billion was in military assistance; $5.1 billion to Turkey, of which $3.7 billion was for military. 

I thank you very much, Mr. Secretary, and I am pleased to call upon my Chairman, Senator McClellan, at this time.

FOREIGN AID JUSTIFICATION 

First, I would like, Mr. Secretary, to ask you, in view of one of your statements in your prepared statement-I call your attention to it at the top of page 9 and I quote: 

Today our values and our interests continue to mandate an active assistance program by this Nation. But the old formulas and old justifications will not suffice.

What was our old formula and justification for beginning this foreign assistance program, particularly for our continuing aid after the Marshall plan had been carried out? 

Secretary KISSINGER. Mr. Chairman, I do not wish the sentence to be construed as a criticism of the previous justifications but rather as a statement to point out that world conditions have changed. At the time that the United States became involved in foreign assistance, we were the only country capable of providing the support for the reconstruction of war-torn society. 

At that time we were in a situation of global confrontation with the Soviet Union and in a period of the cold war, and also we believed that the economic assistance, economic progress, and political stability were casually related.

Since then, many of the world conditions have changed. The relationship between the United States and the Communist world have become more complex, more differentiated, and less characterized by day-to-day confrontation.

Many of the early recipients of our assistance, especially Europe and Japan, have become economically self-sustaining and are themselves contributing today to the process of economic assistance. 

On the other hand, new problems have arisen. First, the economic interdependence of the world has become much more sharply apparent than was the case even 20 years ago. Second, the gap between the least developed and the advanced nations has grown, and this contains the seeds of potential conflict or potential political instability. 

Therefore, the previous concern to use foreign assistance first to help reconstruct the industrialized nations of Europe and Japan, then to contribute to sustaining our friends in the cold war confrontation, and finally to begin economic development, now changes its focus in the direction that I have outlined in this statement. Our aid

becomes extremely important if we are not going to have a world economic collapse or world political confrontations between those who would exploit the despair of the least developed nations. 

Chairman MCCLELLAN. Well, I understand and I fully supported the justification and motivations for the Marshall plan, which was primarily to rehabilitate countries devastated from war. But that was a 5-year plan and since about 1952, we have continued foreign assistance programs, both military and economic. 

Now, the justification for the Marshall plan we know, I think. 

Those justifications were fulfilled and the Marshall plan ended, but what about the justifications that inspired the continuation of foreign aid? What were the justifications for that time after the Marshall plan?

Secretary KISSINGER. Well, the foreign aid program, of course, has gone through various phases. It went from the period in which we were helping with the reconstruction of the industrialized countries of Western Europe and Japan, to a period where we began to contribute to the economic development of the newly emerging countries, with the hope of thereby contributing to their political stability and to a more moderate international conduct, to the present situation where we are attempting to deal with the long term- 

Chairman MCCLELLAN. With what? 

Secretary KISSINGER. With the long-term problems that are produced 

DIFFERENCE BETWEEN OLD AND NEW JUSTIFICATIONS 

Chairman MCCLELLAN. Well, not this other long-term effort to promote economic development, and so forth. 

You say there is a new justification now in effect, different from the justification we have had in the past. I am trying to find out what that new justification is.

Secretary KISSINGER. The new justification, Mr. Chairman, is that events of recent years should bring home to us the interdependence of all of these societies and that it cannot be in our interest to bring about groupings of countries that control strategic materials and are fueled by desperation.

Rather, we should attempt to bring about a more cooperative international structure. This is a realization that has developed acutely in the last 2 or 3 years in a way that we had not been conscious of before. 

Chairman MCCLELLAN. I don't think we are making that quite clear.

Maybe there is a difference, but I think we are continuing what we have been doing all these years. I see no difference in it. 

If there is a difference, a real differentiation between what we are proposing to continue doing and what we have been doing in the past 

8 or 10 years, I wish you would make it just as explicit as you can. 

Maybe I am not following you. 

Secretary KISSINGER. Well, it depends, Mr. Chairman, upon what category you are talking about. 

Chairman MCCLELLAN. Well, whatever you were talking about here. 

Secretary KISSINGER. In the field of security assistance, for example, obviously the requirements have to be determined by the security

1 judgments that are made. Those will vary from time to time, but those do have significant, permanent characteristics. 

In the field of development assistance, we have shifted the emphasis substantially from helping to build infrastructure to an emphasis on the three sectors that Congress recommended last year; namely, food, health, and education, and to an emphasis on perhaps the least developed countries. These would be the changes as I have outlined in this statement. 

Chairman MCCLELLAN. Mr. Secretary, you say, "Our values and our interests continue to mandate an active assistance program by this Nation. But the old formulas"-and you might explain what you mean by "the old formulas"-"and the old justifications will not suffice." 

I take it you mean that what motivated us and what made it necessary up until now to have this foreign aid program no longer justifies a continuation of that program but some new justifications have intervened that now make it necessary to our interests to continue such a program. 

Secretary KISSINGER. Well, Mr. Chairman, I should not, before congressional committees, use sweeping professorial statements. Rather I should rest my justification on the reasons I gave why a foreign assistance program is necessary under current conditions without attempting to draw all the distinctions with previous experience. 

Chairman MCCLELLAN. Well, at any rate, I want to examine what you have said here and try to find out what the new justifications are. 

As far as I can tell, we still want to help the underdeveloped countries so far as economic aid is concerned, and we want to use it for political leverage, too, in a number of cases. Is that correct?

Secretary KISSINGER. That is correct, Mr. Chairman. 

Chairman MCCLELLAN. And the economic aid. Now, the military aid we propose to give, is there any difference in the justification for that now as to what we have done heretofore? 

Secretary KISSINGER. Well, in the military aid field, Mr. Chairman, we have attempted since 1969 to pursue a policy-the Nixon doctrine of strengthening the capacity for self-defense of countries in whose security we believe we have a national interest. 

So, our security assistance program attempts to achieve that objective. There is, perhaps, a change in emphasis but not a change in objective.

It is important to note that the figures provided in Table III for deployed forces represent a somewhat arbitrary assignment of costs to Europe and the rest of the world. force planning is based on an assessment of potential requirements for U.S. forces for contingencies in several parts of the world.

Shifting forces from Europe or Asia to the United States would not alter the requirement to maintain these forces in being unless there were a major and radical change in the security situation on the European continent. 

While some balance of payments relief might be forthcoming from such redeployments, the units would have to be kept in the force structure and room found for them to live and train in the United States, a requirement that might in the end cost more than maintaining them in their present overseas locations. 

The fact is that host governments in most cases provide facilities for these forces rent-free. Moreover, the capital investment that we have made in barracks and other facilities could not be recovered except in very unusual circumstances.

AID TO KOREA AND THE PHILIPPINES 

Mr. Secretary, both the Congress and the American people have voiced increased concern in the past few years over the nature of U.S. relations with regimes that can only be classified as authoritarian. 

I am not referring necessarily to the Soviet Union or the People's Republic of China, but rather to our aid relationships with countries such as South Korea, Brazil, and others. I am not one of those who believe we should have no aid relationship with countries with authoritarian governments because as I survey the countries of the developing world I can identify at the most two or three countries whose governments I personally would not classify as authoritarian in nature. 

Nevertheless, I believe it is the responsibility of both the Congress and the Executive to carefully evaluate whether or not a particular aid relationship with a particular authoritarian government is justified. 

In this regard would you provide the committee with your views as to the national interest justification for our continued and extensive aid commitments to South Korea and the Philippines. If you can, please place your comments in the context of what is occurring internally in those countries at the present time. 

Secretary KISSINGER. Well, Senator, I substantially agree with the way you have phrased the question or with the implications of your question.

I interpreted the implication of your question to be that we determine our aid requirements basically by our national interest, but we pay special attention to the fact that fostering our national interest may have consequences in the country concerned of a nature that would be quite inconsistent with our basic political values, and might go beyond what the national interest would dictate. 

Now, this is a very hard judgment to make because there are many examples where regardless-or almost regardless of the government, the consequences of a country collapsing or being swallowed up by a neighbor would be very severe.

For example, the position of South Korea is quite crucial to the future evolution of Japan. Therefore, our historic relationship with 

South Korea, which in turn was dictated by the strategic and political necessities of the areas, has led us to continue economic aid and military assistance when we would not have recommended many of the actions that were taken by the Government of South Korea. 

And those factors still exist. We are, of course, constantly re-examining the application or the modification of the strategic necessities of one period in the light of evolving relationships with all other countries in the region.

But until now our judgment, which I believe has been shared by the Government of Japan, has been that the stability and security of South Korea were crucial to the security of the East Asian area. 

With respect to the Philippines, we have, of course, had a historic relationship. The security interest is less immediate, but the adapta-

tion of our relationship in the light of historical circumstance has also been a major American interest. 

The Philippine situation has been extremely fluid and not always easy to assess, and often there is a certain lag between developments and one's ability to adjust policy to it. So, perhaps the best I can say now, Senator, is that the implications that I draw from your question are very much in our thinking. 

We are constantly examining our policy in the light of these implications. Where we believe that our vital national interest is at stake we proceed even when we disapprove of certain actions by some of the recipient governments. I would grant you that we should take their actions into account in shaping our aid program. 

Senator BROOKE. And you are doing this at the present time?

AID TO THE MIDDLE EAST 

Secretary KISSINGER. We are, yes.

Senator BROOKE. Turning to the Middle East, Mr. Secretary, it is my understanding that the basic objective of the proposed aid program for the Middle East is to foster the creation of a "vested interest," in nonviolent resolution of disagreements among the various belligerents. 

If this is the objective, please comment in detail on the manner in which you believe such a vested interest can be fostered. 

Secretary KISSINGER. To the extent that the countries in the area commit themselves to long-term economic programs, that is, programs that can be accomplished only under conditions of peace and over an extended period of time, to that extent incentives to resort to military means to resolve current problems will be reduced. It has been interesting that as part of the negotiation some of the parties have expressed a very great interest in determining what the economic reconstruction objectives of the other parties are in order to be able to determine their peaceful intention. The United States has attempted to contribute to this by giving some of the countries an incentive to commit themselves to the long-term economic programs. 

Take, for example, the reconstruction of the Canal Zone. That has implications for the long-term economic and political expectations of Egypt. If Syria commits itself to a long-term program of reconstruction, that has certain implications for its expectations for the future. 

That is what we are trying to encourage through the assistance that we are proposing directly for Egypt and on a contingency basis for Syria and, of course, we have a longstanding relationship with Israel which is based on a subtle difference. 

NUCLEAR DEVELOPMENT ASSISTANCE 

Senator BROOKE. Great concern has been voiced as to the possibility that countries receiving assistance in developing nuclear capabilities for peaceful purposes will eventually seek to develop a nuclear military capability.

The example of India, of course, is the prime case in point. The chairman has touched upon it, but I would like to explore this aspect of the nuclear problem with you in some depth.

First, do you believe that the countries to which we have recently and tentatively agreed to provide nuclear assistance will not eventually

have sufficient incentives to seek some form of nuclear military capability? 

Secretary KISSINGER. Well, Senator, I would suspect that we are now at a rather crucial point with respect to the nonproliferation treaty. 

The Department of State and the U.S. Government on an interdepartmental basis have made this one of our highest priority objectives, because if this further spread of nuclear weapons is not arrested within the next, say, 2 years, then-to answer your question-one would have to say that somewhere down the road, any nation that is capable of producing a nuclear explosive will do so one way or the other. And in that case, frankly, it wouldn't even make so much difference whether they have reactors supplied by us or not, because there will be enough nuclear material produced from reactors that aren't under the American control to be able to acquire it. 

We, for example, are now concerned with what India will do with the nuclear materials that it does not use in its own program and that it might make available to other countries. 

Therefore, we believe that the most urgent problem now, or one of the most urgent problems, is to get a universal policy of nonproliferation because the problem cannot be dealt with effectively country by country, no matter what.

As I pointed out, our safeguards are the most stringent, the safeguards that we are insisting on in the case of Egypt and Israel, in that human foresight can devise and probably will prevent the diversion of nuclear material.

It will not, however, prevent the desire for nuclear material and weapons if we cannot get a general nonproliferation policy. 

We are completing our internal studies, and we will be engaging in very active diplomacy starting in the fall with respect to this problem, which would then also contribute to enhacing the safeguards that I have already described. 

IMPLICATIONS OF INDIA'S NUCLEAR EXPLOSION 

Senator BROOKE. Your reply raises the question as to whether the 

Indian explosion and the enduring interest of others in obtaining nuclear technology has sounded the death knell of effort to prevent the proliferation of nuclear energy.

Secretary KISSINGER. This is one of the serious problems. First of all, it is unrealistic to make a distinction at the early stages of nuclear development between peaceful uses and potential military application because any capacity to produce an explosion has obvious military applications, no matter what purpose the country concerned asserts it is attempting to serve.

Now in, say, our relations with the Soviet Union, as concerns the threshold test ban that we are now negotiating, in advanced nuclear technology one can make certain exceptions for peaceful nuclear explosions because one can monitor whether a less sophisticated device is being used for useful explosions. In the beginning of a nuclear development of another country it doesn't make any difference. Any explosive serves potential alternative purposes and I mention this only to indicate that the nonproliferation problem is very serious. 

The Indian explosion has not helped. On the other hand, it has 

4 focused the issue very sharply and we are going to make a major attempt over the next year to get this problem under control.

MILITARY ASSISTANCE AND NUCLEAR CAPABLE AIRCRAFT Senator BROOKE. Of course, the acquisition of a credible nuclear capability or military nuclear capability has two basic components. 

First, the acquisition of the weapon itself; second, development of a credible delivery capability.

Now, in regard to the latter part, the delivery vehicle, what is the policy of the United States in terms of transferring nuclear capable aircraft to countries in which we have some form of military assistance or military sales relationship? 

Secretary KISSINGER. Well, Senator, almost any modern aircraft is likely to be capable of carrying nuclear weapons. Therefore, I don't know whether this is a useful distinction to make. I grant you that there are two aspects to the problem: the delivery of the bomb and the development of nuclear capability.

We will certainly, as part of this nonproliferation study we are making, examine the greatest degree of discouragement which our policy can bring to the spread of nuclear weapons. We have not yet formed a conclusion as to what degree of sale of delivery systems can be controlled. 

Senator BROOKE. I understand the F-4 can carry a nuclear lance but the F-5 cannot. 

Secretary KISSINGER. That is correct. 

Senator BROOKE. I am sure that such different aircraft capabilities should enter your considerations. 

Secretary KISSINGER. It certainly does.

Senator BROOKE [continuing]. As to what type of aircraft you are transferring in military assistance or military sales programs. 

Secretary KISSINGER. That is right.

ALLEGED MISUSE OF PUBLIC LAW 480 

Senator BROOKE. As you know, some Members of the Congress have been concerned over what seems to be the misuse of Public Law 480, Title I, foodstuffs to support military concerns in South Vietnam and in Cambodia. Many feel that the administration has used the 

Public Law 480 program to circumvent the desires of Congress in reference to aid levels for Indochina. 

Would you comment as to the validity of such allegations?

ALLEGED MISUSE OF PUBLIC LAW 480-VIETNAM AND CAMBODIA 

Two primary allegations have been made: 

One. That additional Public Law 480 was provided to South Vietnam and 

Cambodia for military reasons.

Approximately the same quantity as had been programmed and presented to the Congress was provided to South Vietnam last fiscal year. The dollar value rose sharply due to dramatic price increases of U.S. agricultural commodities, such as rice. For Cambodia, quantities were increased after Communist military action cut off food supplies, particularly rice, from the countryside, and price increases drove the dollar value up. In both cases, Public Law 480 foodstuffs were supplied to help feed the civilian populace and sold as usual through the normal commercial channels. Had the U.S. held to the dollar sums proposed to the 

Congress for South Vietnam and Cambodia, the actual consequence would have been a sharp reduction in the quantity of Public Law 480 foodstuffs supplied to the civilian populace of these two countries. 

Two. That local currency generated from Public Law 480, Title I sales, was used for military budget support in some way against the will of the Congress. 

Such local currency was used in accord with Sec. 104 (c) of Public Law 480, a section in the law for many years and which specifically and clearly authorized military budget support. The Congress recently eliminated this authority by passing a new Sec. 40 of the Foreign Assistance Act and such support is not to continue. 

Secretary KISSINGER. I frankly cannot comment on the validity of these allegations but I would like to look into it and give you my judgment.

I can tell you my general views. I do not believe in circumventing congressional intent by usng budgetary categories by means of loopholes and, therefore, our policy, I would like to say is-and if it isn't, it should be to inform the Congress of any use of funds that might have any problematical aspects. 

Senator BROOKE. Mr. Secretary, I have many more questions. I am going to ask you only two because my colleagues have been very patient and would like to ask their questions. 

CAMBODIA 

First, relative to Cambodia-and I have followed the situation in Cambodia since 1967 when I first visited that country. In general, I fear that our continued supply of military hardware to the Lon Nol government may be serving little, if any, useful purpose, and may be only prolonging the agony of that country. 

It seems to me that the situation in Cambodia necessitates some alteration in our current policy. Specifically, it would appear that some political accommodation involving Prince Sihanouk would be the proper objective of U.S. policy. 

Would you please comment upon this suggestion and also would you give us the benefit of your thinking as to the justification for continuing the supply of arms to the Lon Nol government? 

Secretary KISSINGER. We have attempted to prevent the forcible imposition of a political solution in Cambodia, but we are prepared to encourage any political process including any of the existing political forces that will lead to a resolution of the conflict. 

Senator BROOKE. Including Prince Sihanouk? 

Secretary KISSINGER. Yes, and, therefore, we would be prepared to encourage negotiations of the Phnom Penh government with all of the forces, and in fact we would strongly urge all of the forces to recognize the validity of what you have said. That applies not only to the

Phnom Penh government, it applies to all of the forces. The further objectives to be gained by violence do not justify the suffering that has been imposed, and the United States would use its influence to contribute to a political solution in that country. 

SPECIAL RELATIONSHIP WITH LATIN AMERICA 

Senator BROOKE. Finally, Mr. Secretary, several months ago, you met with the representatives of all of the Latin American countries and during that meeting you expressed the desire of the United States to join in true partnership with those countries in improving conditions for all peoples in Latin America.

Now, this, of course, is a very laudible goal which I believe all Members of the Congress can support. However, as I am sure you are aware, this committee feels a special responsibility to assure that partnership means that involved countries provide their "fair share" of the aid needed to bring to fruition our objectives for Latin America. 

Senator McClellan talked about this "fair share" concept; Senator 

Inouye talked about it as well. In this regard, members of this committee have questioned whether the continued and inordinately high percentage the United States contributes to the soft loan window of the Inter-American Development Bank computed in terms of total contribution by all donors is truly our "fair share." Our contribution is still close to 70 percent of the total contributed. In fiscal 1975, the administration has requested an additional $500 million. 

Now, will you provide the committee with your views as to why this amount of money should be appropriated? 

Secretary KISSINGER. The United States has had, historically, a very special relationship with Latin America and as a newcomer really to inter-American relations I am struck by the nature of this relationship, even in this age of all the conventional criticisms that are always being made in Latin America of U.S. policy. 

Now, it is not surprising that this special relationship should be reflected in the aid programs the United States has provided to its neighbors in the South.

The fact that geographic and historic relationships produce special patterns is seen in Africa where the European aid contribution shows the same disproportion that you have found in Latin America for the 

United States.

But I have the strong sense that relations between developed and developing nations will be one of the major problems of the next decade. If the United States cannot deal with this problem effectively in the Western Hemisphere, it will be even more difficult in other parts of the world. Conversely, if we can establish a relationship of partnership with the countries of the Western Hemisphere, it will have great symbolic significance also in other parts of the world, especially as many of the countries in Latin America are now seeing themselves also as part of the Third World structure. 

So, for all these reasons, I believe the relatively disproportionate role that the United States plays in Western Hemisphere aid programs is not only justified but from some points of view not undesirable explains why we have made special arrangements for consultation with Latin America in the trade negotiations and indeed in all other negotiations that affect them.

口​商 ​This is not to say that we want to preclude others from participating and we would greatly welcome the role of others. But we should not use the fact that other countries are not doing all they might to justify our not doing what the special relationship really imposes.

Secretary KISSINGER. Senator, I have testified more on behalf of the foreign aid program than of all other programs together, and I will do whatever I can to put my resources behind this program, which I consider essential.

Senator MCGEE. Thank you Mr. Chairman.

AMERICAN FOREIGN AID ROLE 

Mr. Secretary, I guess everyone is coming down to the crunch point this year, after an historic role in which for the first time we, as a major Nation, committed ourselves to the economic development of less developed areas. 

That program with all of those noble qualities is in more trouble than ever before. Many Senators and Congressmen are raising questions about the validity of economic assistance to the rest of the world. 

Many of them are couching it in the context that our own people are suffering for want of many things. Therefore, we should not be bothering with the needs of others.

My question to you, Mr. Secretary, is, is history about to be kind enough to us to give us a choice? 

Secretary KISSINGER. No, Senator, I don't think history will be that kind to us. In fact, when we started economic assistance we had a more apparent choice, and it is to the great credit of the leadership of that period that they could see that these long-term, enlightened U.S. self-interests required us to relate ourselves to other countries of the world, including those much less fortunate than we. 

Under present circumstances we do not have as wide a choice. With all the fatigue that decades of effort have imposed on us, the interdependence of the world is a reality and the American role is a necessity. It will be seen as the years go by that if we do not do what is necessary now, the burden on the American people caused by this failure will increase enormously. I understand that after decades of

effort it is very difficult to envisage the need for a continuance, but we are at one of those periods where the whole structure of international relations is changing and where the United States that used to be essentially self-sufficient is now becoming an integral part of a world community. For the United States to fail under those conditions would have very great consequences in the decades ahead. 

Senator MCGEE. The role that we played right after the war involved a very preponderant participation on our part. 

U.S. ASSISTANCE COMPARED WITH OTHER DONOR ASSISTANCE 

As the opposition to our role began to emerge in the public mind, particularly in the Congress, the suggestion was made that others ought to help more than they are. To what extent has the picture changed since the immediate postwar period? Have others shouldered an increased responsibility for economic assistance in the world? 

Secretary KISSINGER. Very much so, Senator. In the immediate postwar period, of course, we carried the entire load, but I have some figures here of the changes even in the last 12 to 13 years. 

In 1961, for example, the U.S. share was 57 percent of the total aid burden. Today it is 32 percent. In 1961 the European share was 

38 percent. Today it is 45 percent. Japan was 2 percent. It is today 

11 percent.

The U.S. share of its gross national product used for development aid was 0.56 percent in 1961, and it is 0.24 percent today. So, the objective is being increasingly met. 

Though, we should not delude ourselves that we can ever go to a zero level, our percentage has declined and can probably continue to decline. 

Senator MCGEE. When you talk about 0.56 percent of the GNP and 

0.24 percent, you are saying that in 1961 it was approximately one-half of 1 percent?

Secretary KISSINGER. Of our gross- 

Senator MCGEE. [continuing] Of our gross national product, and now it has dropped to about one-fourth of 1 percent. 

Secretary KISSINGER. That is correct, Senator.

Senator MCGEE. I am told that that percentage of our gross national product for economic development assistance is exceeded substantially by perhaps a dozen nations in the world who are contributing a larger percentage of their gross national product than is the United 

States. 

Secretary KISSINGER. That is correct, Senator, yes.

U.S. SELF-INTEREST 

Senator MCGEE. The reason I stress that is because I agree with you that the degree of our economic commitment around the world is probably going to have a good deal more to do in the long run with contributing to the lessening of tensions around the world than almost anything else that we could do. But you have also linked it to our selfish interest; namely, our dependence on the rest of the world for other strategic materials. 

To what extent is that true?

Secretary KISSINGER. It is becoming increasingly true that our objective dependence on the rest of the world is increasing. The tendency of many parts of the world to group themselves together in postures of confrontation with the developed nations is also increasing. If this tendency continues, the political structure of the next two decades is going to be very tense and very dangerous. Our effort has been, in the field of energy and in other areas, to attempt to encourage a pattern of cooperation in which the mutual obligations of countries is defined, For this reason the United States has to set an example of its commitment to a cooperative world by its continued role in these programs. 

Senator MCGEE. I recall better I guess than most people in this room the late 1930's when our arguments, including my arguments on campus, were that we couldn't afford World War II because we had just been swept through the throes of a depression. But we discovered that 

Mr. Hitler, Mr. Mussolini, and Mr. Tojo didn't respect our budget projections of those years.

We discovered we had to afford it. What I would express as the hope for now is that we don't make the same mistake over again. The parody of economic commitment, even in these binding times as we have heard here this morning, doesn't give us the free choice of saying we will do that later, but later becomes rapidly too late and then catastrophic. 

Secretary KISSINGER. And the economic cost of not doing enough is incomparably larger than efforts that would be needed now to do what is necessary.

Senator MCGEE. And I make no apologies for the severity of our economic bind here at home. Believe me, it is taking a severe toll, but from all that we gather from our studies, the rest of the world has not been freed from those tolls either, and yet in spite of the economic crunch around the world-and we have been spared much better than most-they are still increasing participation in economic development. I hope that we can somehow command that kind of perspective as we seek to judge what we have to do at this particular moment. 

Secretary KISSINGER. Again, I agree with you completely, Senator.

NEED FOR SECRETARY'S STRONG SUPPORT OF AID LEGISLATION

And I think that ought to become our priority even now as we talk increasingly about military assistance almost to the exclusion of economic assistance.

AID TO INDOCHINA

U.S. aid both foreign and military, is going to a part of the world with .8 percent of the population of the world. 

Would you care to comment on that study? 

Secretary KISSINGER. Senator, I have not had anyone check these statistics, but I believe the point is clear, that relatively large amounts are going to Indochina. The reason for that is the history which, regardless of whether we should have been there or not, has led us to commit the United States in a way that cost us 50,000 lives and

hundreds of thousands of casualties in order to avoid having Communist regimes imposed on nations of that area. 

Having made this effort for a decade, we will be judged internationally by other nations in that area-to some extent at least-by our willingness to make the really modest efforts that are now needed to complete the process toward self-sustaining economic development. 

Therefore, I would say that Indochina commitment has to be looked at in terms of the whole context of events over the last decade and in terms of the projections we have made to you, looking toward a reduction, not just in terms of what one would do today in the absence of this history. 

As a basic objective, I agree with you that over a 10-year period we should strive for a different balance in our aid program. But given the conditions that now exist and the history that has brought us to this point, we do have a moral and political obligation, in my judgment, to proceed along the lines we have proposed to the Congress. 

If they are not met, it may bring about the situation where in any one year we may do less than has been proposed but we reduce therewith the possibility of substantial reduction later on. 

Senator HATFIELD. Do I understand, Mr. Secretary, as of the budget proposed for fiscal 1975, you do not feel there is an inordinate amount of our resources, particularly economic resources, going to this one part of the world in light of the great problems in Sahel in Africa, Pakistan, Bangladesh, India, many parts of the world where famine is on the brink of crisis, and now you still do not feel that there is an inordinate amount of American resources going to Indochina? 

Secretary KISSINGER. There is a very large amount of American resources going to Indochina. I believe, in the light of the conditions 

I have described, it is the correct thing. 

If it were not for the present mood in this country and congressional sentiment, I would have said in reply to Senator McGee's earlier question that my real preference would be to increase the foreign assistance program and therefore take care of some of the needs that you have enumerated.

Since we have to operate on a very constrained budget, this dislocation becomes more apparent. Under the conditions that now exist, I have to support it, and I do support it.

INDOCHINA'S DEPENDENCE ON UNITED STATES 

According to the best estimates that I can acquire, it appears today that 86 percent of the resources for the Government of South Vietnam required for that government to function were provided by the United States. cally, militarily, and economically, and I do not see the trends changing.

Secretary KISSINGER. Let me say first Senator, that we provide far less than 86 percent of the South Vietnamese Government's resources.

WORLD FOOD PROBLEM

APPROACH ON TRADE

U.S. STRATEGIC DOCTRINE 

Senator BROOKE. Mr. Secretary, as you know, I have advocated for some time a moratorium on the testing and development of MIRV. 

Unfortunately, that "genie is out of the bottle" and will not likely return to it in the foreseeable future.

Recently, I questioned the Secretary of Defense regarding his proposals to increase our missile accuracy, up the yield of our nuclear warheads, and develop the MARV. 

My concern is that the United States might be viewed as moving toward a first strike capability, against land-based ICBM's, a course of action the President had previously foresworn in a letter to me. The proposals of the Secretary of Defense are likely to be provocative and cause an escalation in the nuclear arms race with the Soviet Union. 

Secretary Schlesinger recently appeared before the Defense Subcommittee of the Senate Committee on Appropriations. At that time 

I read a statement you were reported to have made regarding the

"counterforce issue." In my exchange with him I said, "Now, yesterday Secretary Kissinger was asked the value of the threshold test ban and he reportedly stated-and I want to quote-'It would make more difficult the combination of improved accuracy and larger yield, which may again bring about a situation in which a premium will be put on a first strike.'" 

I then asked him: "Now, is this not the very danger your proposed initiative threatens to make?" 

Secretary Schlesinger replied:

I think the first half of Secretary Kissinger's statement is correct; that a threshold test ban precluding the optimization of nuclear weapons to throw weight would inhibit the development of the capability that you are talking about.

In my judgment, the term "premium" unless more precisely defined, does not accurately describe the military balance as we know it today or as we will prospectively know it.

The concern that there will be a substantial premium on a first strike just does not comport with the threat of nuclear war as I understand it. That hypothetical concept does not comport with reality. Nuclear war is not attractive to either side. It would be the most agonizing decision that any leader of the 

United States or the Soviet Union or any other power would have to make and to talk about the premium on a first strike as suggesting that this is a decision that could be lightly undertaken, strikes me as being a rhetorical flourish, which should not be taken as a literal description of the underpinnings of reality. 

It is certainly not my purpose to start any conflict between the Secretary of Defense and the Secretary of State. Historically there have always been differences of opinion between the State Department and the Defense Department. I recognize this. 

But this is a very important issue, Mr. Secretary, and I waited especially on this matter to find out just what is the administration's position. Are we changing our strategic doctrine? Do we now seek a first strike capability against land-based ICBM's? What are your views on this as briefly as you can in the limited time? 

Secretary KISSINGER. Senator Brooke, first of all, when I speak I always make very sure that I understand what the President's views are and therefore I do not think my role is to participate in interdepartmental quarrels.

I have tried to reflect the administration's policy, not only as Secretary of State but as assistant to the President, and I believe that I can say accurately that what I say I take to be the President's views. 

Second, I did not mean to suggest that our present policy is to acquire a first strike capability. Therefore if I understand Secretary

Schlesinger's comment in rejecting the implication that our policy is a first strike capability, I agree with that. My comment was not directed against the existing defense program. If we look ahead 10 years, if we look at the trends and not at any one budget, then the doubts that may arise between the numbers of warheads and the numbers of launchers can be a temptation that did not exist when there were only single warheads. The multiplication of warheads around the world will remove the conditions of scarcity with respect to strategic weapons. This condition was one of the inhibiting features to the outbreak of nuclear war throughout much of this period. 

So, it is my view that the problem of the strategic nuclear forces over the next decade under conditions of very large numbers of war-

heads with improved accuracies and improved yield is one that requires careful thought. It is one of the reasons why the administration has attempted to put a ceiling on the arms race in the SALT negotiations. 

But I do not quarrel with Secretary Schlesinger about his description of our current military program. 

Senator BROOKE. Well, I agree with your position, but when I pressed the Secretary of Defense on this matter the Secretary said it wasn't a matter of whether it was your position or his position, but the administration's position, which was reflected in the budget request.

Of course, the budget request for this particular matter was for funds for research and development on increased yield and increased accuracy for Minuteman and the development of MARV. 

Secretary KISSINGER. What concerns me, Senator, what I have expressed publicly before, is not the budget as it now stands. What concerns me is some of the talk that takes place about the nature of the strategic superiority, I have serious question whether it is possible in the nuclear age to achieve a strategic superiority that is politically or militarily decisive. 

It does not mean that we can accept an inferiority, but it does mean that the traditional notions of warfare as applied to strategic nuclear forces do not seem to me to be relevant. 

Senator BROOKE. Then is it your position that even though the administration has requested funds for increased yield and improved accuracy and the development of MARV, the United States has not changed its position relative to seeking first strike capability against land-based ICBM's?

Secretary KISSINGER. That is my view and it is also that we must be prepared to limit military forces as a result of negotiations in strategic arms limitations and I believe that the Secretary of Defense agrees with me on that.

Senator BROOKE. If we move in this direction do you fear that it may be provocative? 

Secretary KISSINGER. I don't believe it will be provocative, but I

I would be worried if there were no SALT agreement and both sides . continued to exploit all the technical options that they have. So the problem each country has is to continue what it must prior to an agreement but to be prepared to limit its deployment and its development as the result. 

Senator BROOKE. Thank you, Mr. Secretary. 

PALESTINIAN PROBLEM 

Senator INOUYE. Mr. Secretary, one of the major areas of your concern is in the Middle East. I believe there is general concern that if we are to achieve peace in that part of the world we must somehow resolve this so-called Palestinian problem. 

Yet, in your statement I do not notice any mention of the Palestinian problem. How do you propose to resolve this matter, sir? What is your position?

Secretary KISSINGER. The Palestinian problem is perhaps the most complex aspect of the settlement. Our position has been to proceed step by step and to deal with the immediate issues first. 

I said publicly in the press conference that I thought the best or most efficient approach would be a negotiation between Jordan and Israel, and then a settlement between Jordan and the Palestinians of the precise political arrangements of the west bank. 

Now, whether that is achievable remains to be seen. If it isn't what then will happen we will have to decide. 

Next week the Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister of Israel is to be here to be followed by the Prime Minister of Jordan and Foreign Minister of Egypt and a representative from Syria. So, during the month of August we will have more detailed discussions of these issues and we will be able to give perhaps more comprehensive answers after these deliberations. 

Senator INOUYE. On behalf of the committee I thank you very much for appearing today.

Your testimony has been most helpful and I believe I speak for all when I say I wish you well in your quest for peace and stability in the world. 

Thank you very much.

QUESTIONS SUBMITTED BY SENATOR BROOKE U.S. FAIR SHARE OF FOREIGN ASSISTANCE 

Senator Brooke. 

Mr. Secretary, the FY 74 Foreign Assistance report of this

Committee placed great emphasis on ensuring that the United States pay only its "fair share" in helping the developing world improve the conditions of the world's poor. I believe this is a proper objective. However, I also believe that the "fair share" principle must also entail a recognition in the United States that we presently consume an inordinate amount of the world's diminishing natural resources. For instance, rough estimates place U.S. consumption of world energy resources at 1/3 of total consumption. To put this in proper perspective, one must realize that the United States has approximately 1/6 of the world's population. 

I also believe that our emphasis on "fair share" must be conditioned on the realization that we are becoming increasingly dependent on raw material resources from developing nations in order to maintain our own standard of living. This is, of course, an example of the well known growing interdependence of nations. 

Would you provide us with your views on what constitutes a "fair share" contribution of the United States in terms of foreign aid in light of our consumption of world resources and our growing interdependence with developing nations?

Secretary Kissinger.

The program proposals wẹ have submitted to you for FY 1975 represent a sizeable increase over our aid levels of previous years. It is difficult to say if the proposed levels constitute a "fair share" for the U.S. 

Based on our increasing economic relationships with the developing countries, their needs, and our resources, the proposed aid program in my opinion represents a justifiable contribution to the stability and growth of the LDC's and our international economy. 

There are a number of statistics I might mention, Senator, which further illustrate the increasing internationalization of the U.S. economy. An important part of our needs for industrial metals is supplied by other countries; imports account for between 50% and 

100% of eight important metals; and over a quarter of our iron ore needs is supplied from foreign sources. 

A large portion of these imports is from developing countries. U.S. investments, now totaling over $25 billion, are growing at 8% per year in the developing countries. From an economic standpoint, we have demonstrated interest in the prosperity and growth of these countries. However, the development prospects for the LDC's have been severely challenged by the energy situation and food shortages. A worsening of their terms of trade has diminished their ability to meet the basic needs of their people, not to mention their changes for increased growth. While the U.S. and

other developed countries are struggling with inflation, the price of development for many of these countries has gone far beyond their resources. 

As you know Senator, the United Nations has recommended to the developed nations, that their official development assistance to the LDC's should equal .7% of their GNP. 

Most major donors have agreed to work toward this goal; however, the U.S. has never officially endorsed this target. In comparison to the other donors belonging to the Development Assistance Committee, the aid effort of the U.S. is among the lowest in terms of percentage of GNP. In 1973, we contributed less than a quarter of 1% of our GNP for official development assistance. 

The U.S. bore more of the aid effort in the early years of the international aid effort. Since about 1960, other donors have taken on an increasing share of the development assistance provided to the LDC's. In the early sixties, the U.S. share exceeded 60% of the total of such flows. Since then, the U.S. portion of ODA disbursements has fallen steadily to 43% in 1973, 39% in 1972, and 32% in 1973. As a percentage of our GNP, U.S. ODA has dropped from .56% of GNP in 1962 to .23% in 1973.

WORLD FOOD RESERVE 

Is the United States willing to participate with other nations in the creation of a world food reserve? If so, on what terms? 

Secretary Kissinger.

The United States has agreed in principle to the FAO Director General's proposal for a system of national food reserves linked together at the international level through guidelines, consultations, and a better information system. 

Briefly, this system would involve a number of nationally-held food reserves which would be available for worldwide emergency needs, but held nationally rather than internationally. 

As part of our preparations for the World Food Conference, we are now in the process of reviewing possible procedures for the establishment and operation of such a reserve system as well as the costs and benefits of such a system. 34-192 O-74-86

Senator Hatfield.

WORLD FOOD SITUATION 

What programs are envisioned or in effect to promote agricultural production in the poor nations? 

Secretary Kissinger. eda et We are increasing our research to develop the tropical and semi-arid lands in the poor nations. Several of our present research programs have an impact for utilizing such lands. These include: water management in arid and semi-arid lands, agronomic-economic research on tropical soils, soil fertility in the humid tropics, sorghum and wheat improvement, weed control for less developed countries, and improved fertilizer for developing countries. 

We envision a set of generalized program packages of new technological opportunities that may be offered to the poor nations to increase the quantity and improve the quality of their food supplies. These include: production of high lysine corn, rice and multiple cropping systems; on-farm water management, soil salinity and irrigation water quality. In addition, we are planning an International Fertilizer Development Center to focus on research toward more efficient uo fertilizer for the developing countries, on making fertilizer factories more efficient, and on better systems to move fertilizer from the factory to the

small farmer.

We envision this Center as becoming part of an International Plant Nutrition Institute under multinational sponsorship.

OTHER NATION PARTICIPATION IN FOOD AID 

Senator Hatfield.

What efforts are being made to have other nations participate in food aid and/or agricultural production programs? 

Secretary Kissinger.

One of our major efforts in this area was, of course, the suggestion to the United Nations that a world food conference be convened to discuss these vital subjects. Two of the most important issues that will face the food conference deal with improved agricultural production and food aid. As a result of our food aid through public law 480 over the past 20 years, we have endeavored to set an example for other nations that they might also participate in food aid programs. 

This has been particularly successful through the United Nations World Food Program which began more than 10 years ago, largely as a result of U.S. initiatives, and which now includes more than 60 countries in addition to the United States. Over the years, the

U.S. share of World Food program contributions has decreased while those of other countries has increased, and we believe that this is an excellent indication that other nations are interested in participating in food aid programs. 

Regarding agricultural programs, we are hopeful that the Supplemental Appropriations requested for these programs in FY 75 will be approved by the Congress and allow us to set an example to others by indicating the extent to which we are prepared to assist agricultural production in developing countries. 

U.S. POSITION FOR THE WORLD POPULATION CONFERENCE IN BUCHAREST 

Senator Hatfield. 

What initiatives does the United States plan to offer at the World Population Conference in 

Bucharest in August? 

Secretary Kissinger. 

At the World Population Conference in Bucharest, the U.S. Delegation will view the issue of world food needs as an integral element of the population growth problem but will endeavor to postpone substantive and extended discussion of food shortages to the World Food Conference. At Bucharest, our

delegation will (1) stress the multiple relationships between continued population growth and the achievement of improved nutrition; (2) the need for urgent action to slow population growth and the appropriateness of the U.N. draft World Plan of Action as a vehicle for stimulating and orienting needed international efforts and (3) the general intention of the U.S. Government to continue and expand, as domestic conditions permit, our traditional programs of food assistance to the developing world. 

WORLD FOOD CONFERENCE 

Senator Hatfield.

What initiatives does the United States plan to offer at the World Food Conference in Rome in November? 

Secretary Kissinger.

As I have noted earlier, we are particularly interested in the major issues relating to agricultural development and food security. 

Within each of these categories, we are in the process of looking at a number of options that might be available for the United States to offer as suggestions for action at the 

World Food Conference. 

Within the field of

agricultural production, we are especially concerned about the need for additional research, both in an applied sense and in basic research over the longer term. In addition, we are reviewing the possibility of the United States offering various suggestions for action in this area.

We are also conducting detailed reviews of the possibility of an increase in our food aid programs and we are looking into various options and procedures on how best to participate in an international system of national food reserves. We believe that by concentrating our efforts on food production and food security, we can take initiatives that are most useful and in the best interests of the success of the Conference.

We are assisting on this problem at several levels With the help of U.S. universities and other sources of expertise, we are helping selected developing governments to analyze policy issues relating to their food distribution problems.

ASSISTANCE TO DEVELOPING COUNTRY CENSUS PROGRAMS 

Senator Hatfield.

Are any efforts being made or contemplated to assist developing nations in taking a census of their populations, so their needs may be ascertained? 

Secretary Kissinger.

The United States has been assisting other countries with censuses and other statistical programs for many years. 

These efforts have included short term assistance to help countries carry out a specific census or survey and long term assistance to help countries develop the infrastructure to enable them to carry out their own statistics programs. 

Programs have included the training of LDC personnel, the provision of U.S. technicians on short or long term assignments, research and development on new methodology particularly suited to conditions in LDCs and/or designed to reduce cost or speed results.

Assistance has not been restricted to population censuses, however. Censuses of Agriculture have helped countries assess their food situation. Surveys have provided data on fertility, mortality, nutrition, unemployment, and other factors. Vital registration systems provide data on births and deaths.

tensive and reportedly very effective effort from the standpoint of its potential value for other developing countries, and we have already received a great deal of information on this from a variety of American and international organizations. Conference being held in Bucharest 

August 19-30. We welcome this indication of Chinese interest in international cooperation on the population problem.

QUESTIONS SUBMITTED BY SENATOR INOUYE MIDDLE EAST PEACE Senator Inouye: 

Secretary Kissinger: 

Senator Inouye: 

Secretary Kissinger: 

Will you share with the Committee your judgement as to the importance of President Sadat, insofar as progress toward peace in the Middle East is concerned. 

How deep is the support within his government for the policies he has initiated?

President Sadat has already had profound influence on the course of events in the Middle East since the end of the 

October Arab-Israeli war. The most important contributions he made were his decisions to seek to resolve this long standing conflict by negotiation rather than through a continuation of war and to maintain an independent posture in Egypt's foreign relations. These courageous decisions were of far-reaching significance in that they helped create a new climate of hope in the Middle East and enabled the people in the area to begin thinking the unthinkable-that peace was something which could be achieved.

Egypt's role in the peace negotiations which lie ahead will be a critical one. 

We anticipate that, under President Sadat's leadership, it will also be a constructive one.

All indications are that President Sadat's political initiatives, enjoy popular support in Egypt.

In the Middle East Peace Proposals we find no reference to programs for Palestinian refugees. Support of UNRWA is, of course, proposed, but we seek to understand and to obtain your views on the more militant refugees--the so called fedayeen. Will you share your views with us? In particular, have you had any negotiations with leaders in the Palestinian guerilla movement? Is it within the capacity of the Palestinian guerillas to upset our, and the world's, hopes for peace in the Middle East?

We have had no negotiations with leaders of the Palestinian fedayeen organizations. 

It is certainly within the capacity of these organizations to make the peacemaking process more difficult but I do not believe the governments involved in the process will permit the pursuit of their national interests to be disrupted by the extremist elements in the Palestinian community. You will recall that Israel

Senator Inouye: 

Secretary Kissinger: 

and Syria reached a disengagement agreement in spite of the efforts of Palestinian extremists to prevent it by their seizure of Israeli school children at Maalot and their demands that they and other Palestinians in prison in Israel be given safe conduct to Damascus. The broader issue of the future of the Palestinians must remain for the Palestinians themselves and the parties to the dispute to resolve. 

Our position remains that this issue must be resolved if a peace in the Middle East is to be achieved and prove durable. 

IRAN/SAUDI ARABIA RELATIONS 

How would you assess the prospects for continued friendly relations between 

Saudi Arabia and Iran? We are making available to each substantial numbers of modern weapons, are we not?

It has long been U.S. policy to support friendly countries in the Persian Gulf area in their efforts to promote regional security. In this context, we have tried to respond positively to the requests from both Saudi Arabia and Iran for arms to meet their perceived needs for security.

Also in this context, we have sought to nurture cooperation between Iran and Saudi Arabia in providing stability and fostering orderly development in this region. Although there are traditional cultural and religious differences between the two countries, they share an interest in maintaining regional stability. In recent years Iran and

Senator Inouye: 

Secretary Kissinger: 

Saudi Arabia have cooperated to resolve a number of potential sources of tension, such as the Gulf Median- 

Line and Bahrain issues. They have also held a series of exchanges on matters of mutual interest. As recently as June of this year, Saudi

Minister of State for Foreign Affairs

MIDDLE EAST PEACE 

The advantages which will accrue to the Soviet Union by the reopening of the 

Suez Canal appear obvious. What advantages, if any, will accrue to the United 

States? To Israel? To the Arab nations?

Will all nations which are expected to benefit from reopening of the Canal contribute to the costs?"

The most important fact about the reopening of the Suez Canal is that there could be no peace agreement between Egypt and Israel until Egypt had regained control of the Canal and the right to reopen it. 

Progress toward peace in the Middle East is of incalculable importance in reducing the threat of war in the world. That fact, in our view is of overriding significance for Israel, the Arabs and the U.S. 

There will, of course, also be a general benefit to world commerce from reopening and lowering shipping costs. 

Another especially important benefit is that reopening the Canal, and reconstruction in the Canal area will create a vested interest by all concerned in continued area stability.

A settlement in the Middle East should eventually open the way for Israeli use of the Canal thereby opening Israel's 

Mediterranean ports to the Indian Ocean for the first time in more than twenty years.

As for the Arab countries, Egypt will gain from having an important new source of revenue, and it will also be able more easily to export its Suez 

Gulf oil production to European consumers.

In general, many Arab countries would share in the obvious benefits to world trade from reopening the Canal. 

Regarding the payment of costs for the Canal's reopening, it is expected that primary expenditures will be made by Egypt, with supplementary assistance from abroad. Maritime users of the

Canal will, in turn, bear part of this burden by the future payment of Canal transit dues.

In deference to his position as the only living former president of South Ko rea and a famous patriot, he had been brought to court that day from his home rather than from a prison cell.

He was not forced to wear the white prison garb or to have his arms tied behind his back, and he was permitted to sit down while addressing the bench..

On the steps of the courtroom that day the former president refused to permit a secret policeman to get into his car for the drive to his anti: que-filled mansion. The agent insisted.
