UCH SCENES and ironies are part SUCE 

Such the current political reality of

South Korea, a nation which owes its existence to U.S. policy at the end of 

World War II and massive US. efforts, including 33,000 war dead in 1950-'53 and more than $10 billion in military and economic assistance since then. 

The Korean war ended in an armistice agreement July 27, 1953, but 21 years later South Korea is not the democracy for which Americans hoped when GIs fought "in defense of freedom." Particularly in the past two years, since Park Chung Hee seized 

Tunchecked and unlimited power under a new constitution imposed by the guns and tanks of martial law, the fragile remains of political liberty have been fading fast.

Some 38,000 American troops remain here at South Korea's urgent request to guard against renewal of combat 1 from the north, and Korea continues to request-and obtain approval formassive injections of military assistance, food aid and U.S. Export-Import 

Bank loans as well as political support in the United Nations and other international bodies. Despite all this, American officials here have told callers they have "no leverage” to prevent democracy and dissent from being 

E ground under heel.

Since the first of the year 89 persons, many of them prominent citizens and a large number American-edu- 

1 cated, have been sentenced to harsh punishments by military tribunals for - violating the "emergency presidential decrees." According to informed diplomatic sources, about 150 more Koreans now languishing in jails are likely to be brought to trial on similar charges. 

The prisons of Korea are peopled with some of the country's outstanding citizens to cite only a few examples, the winner of an Aisa-wide Magsaysay

Prize for the promotion of democracy (sentenced to 15 years in prison for leading a peaceful petition drive to change the constitution), the country's foremost Lincoln scholar and the dean of theology at a famous university (on trial together for encouraging student demonstrations), the son of a retired navy admiral and descendant of the first baptized Protestant in Korea (sentenced to 15 years in prison for helping plan student demonstrations), the Methodist, minister who leads a labor mission in Inchon (in solitary confinement for two months, with no known charges yet lodged against her). 

Seven young Christian ministers are in prison for staging a prayer meeting in January at the office of the National Council of Churches to ask for a return to the old constitution which 

Park jettisoned two years ago and for a restoration of democracy. 

Student editors and a faculty adviser of the Sogan Jesuit University literary magazine were jailed (they have since been released) for publishing photographs and an article about a peaceful student demonstration' on their campus last fall. A politician of the opposition 

New Democratic Party was sentenced to five years in prison for "spreading groundless rumors" about the special presidential decrees.

In one of the greatest ironies, opposition politician Kim Dae Jung, who was snatched out of a 32d floor Tokyo hotel room and forcibly brought back to Seoul by the Korean CIA, is on trial while his kidnapers have never been officially identified or punished. Kim is accused, among other things, of saying during his 1971 presidential campaign that incumbent Park, if reelected, would destroy Korean democracy and seek to make himself the president for life. Kim has admitted he said so and declared that his prediction had come true.

A number of independent-minded people still at large are under close surveillance. Former foreign minister 

Chung Il Hyung, a leading assemblyman of the major opposition party, has a permanent visitor from the police in his outer office, checking to see who comes and goes. Another prominent opposition party member, Kim Young

Sam, was recently taken away by se-

cret police for a day of questioning after he scheduled a press conference to announce his opposition to growing repression.

The National Assembly, which is a nearly impotent debating forum under Park's new constitution, has not even met so far this year. The government has been refusing to convene a session until the opposition agrees in advance not to bring up Park's emergency "decrees." Last week a deal was made, under which the opposition can discuss some of the presidential edicts but not others, in a session to begin Aug. 1.

Hahm Sok Hon, a white-haired patriot who was imprisoned by the Japanese colonial rulers of Korea, by the invading Russian Communists and by the Syngman Rhee regime, was pulled in for interrogations by the Park regime and has daily visits at his home from his KCIA supervisor. "This is worse than Japanese [colonial] times.

Even under the Japanese, we could appeal to human feelings," Hahm told a visitor.

The 73-year-old Hahm, sometimes called "the Gandhi of Korea," was recently forbidden by the KCIA to address the local chapter of Amnesty International, the worldwide forum for concern about political prisoners. As an "act of witness," he decided to inform his secret police supervisor that "it is almost clear the [convicted] student leaders are not Communists and that they never formed any conspiracy against the state." Such a gesture does not seem small in today's climate. 

THE 

23

HE MAN WHO rules supreme in 

South Korea today is a one-time provincial schoolmaster who served in the Japanese army in World War II 

(during the Japanese colonial occupation of Korea). In the newly independent, divided Korea he was arrested in 

1948 and reportedly tortured and beaten on charges of being a Communist. Sentenced to death, he was saved by his willingness to cooperate with the authorities and by the intervention of friends. With the outbreak of the

Korean war in 1950, he was rehabili tated due to the shortage of trained officers. 

Hardworking, clever and secretive, he rose steadily through the officer ranks. After Syngman Rhee fell as a result of student riots and a virtual national revolt in 1960, somé elements of the military were dissatisfied with the relatively democratic but wobbly government which followed. In May, 1961, Gen. Park engineered a coup over the ineffective objections of the U.S. embassy, which failed to win strong backing from the Kennedy White House.

After ruling the country with an iron hand as chief of the military junta, Park reluctantly agreed under

U.S. pressure to establish a civilian regime. Despite an earlier promise not to participate, he was elected president in 1963 and again in 1967 (both times over former president Yun Po Sun, who is now on trial). After changing the constitution to permit himself a third term, he narrowly defeated Kim Dae 

Jung in 1971 following an election eve pledge never to run again. 

In October, 1972, Park declared martial law, jettisoned the old constitution, placed his opponents under arrest and suspended political activity, freedom of speech.and of the press. It is doubtful that he had the legal authority to do all this, but he had the guns. 

The United States, preoccupied with settlement of the Vietnam war and the 1972 elections, said and did nothing as the vestiges of democracy vanished. A new constitution giving him unlimited power and an unlimited tenure in office was approved by a national referendum, with massive government tubthumping and all opposition or even criticism banned.

Park has created a highly organized and centralized regime which has made major strides in economic growth via foreign investments and trade. Aided by clever management, a hard-working, literate and yet lowwage labor force and assistance and support from both the United States and Japan, Korean gross national product has shot up almost as rapidly

1 as the glossy skyscrapers in oncequaint Seoul. Political growth has not accompanied the economic growth, however.

When more than 30,000 students of at least 38 colleges demonstrated for a restoration of democracy last fall, Park fired his much-feared KCIA director,

Lee Hu Rak, and temporarily relaxed some of the restrictions on political freedoms. His critics, including an impressive lineup of senior establishment figures, took this as a sign of weakness and demanded a return to the old constitution. Early this year Park cracked down hard with an "emergency" decree banning all such talk or petitions, or even news reporting of them, on pain of 15 years' imprisonment at the hands of a military tribunal. When that failed to halt campus activity, he followed in April with mass arrests and a new decree providing death sentences or long prison terms for anyone involved in the student demonstrations, which he retroactively branded as Communist-inspired. As half of a bitterly divided and strategic peninsula, South Korea has undeniably serious security problems 1 with its counterpart regime in the Communist North. The division has also been among Park's most important 11 assets, for the Communist bogey is always at hand when the domestic public or overseas allies become restive. 

Nearly all opposition is branded as "Communist," "Communist-inspired" or "helping the Communists." With a large secret police apparatus, a controlled press and courtrooms closed to all but a few selected observers on "national security" grounds, it is diffi cult to distinguish between justified charges and sheer propaganda. Many 

South Koreans are ready to fear the worst. HA

AVING SUBDUED political opponents, the once virile Korean press and many of the active leaders of student and intellectual dissent, Park has found the churches a last troublesome reservoir of dissidence. 

Christianity has a long and honorable tradition in Korea, including an important role in the anti-Japanese resistance during colonial times. Christianity came hand in hand with Western influences, and many of its leaders have been abroad. Most of the churches of South Korea with a combined membership of 3.4 million 

Protestants and 800,000 Catholics in a total population of 31 million have international organizational links which can be sources of outside support. Moreover, they cannot easily be accused of being Communist. 

Both Protestant and Catholic churches are divided between conservative and less conservative wings. But as the crackdown of recent months begins to affect ministers, laymen and Christian student leaders, the churches have begun to rally round their own. "As far as freedom of worship is concerned, I think there is no problem," said general secretary Kim Kwan Suk of the National Council of Churches. "But when you confess your faith from your conscience, for example, about human rights, freedom of expression and social justice, then you may face some difficulties." During most of this year the Council of Churches and the Protestant groups it represents have been a center of conflicts with the government, while the relatively more conservative Catholics have been on the sidelines. Within recent days, however, this has begun to chance. 

DANIEL CHI is a born rebel. At the school in Pyongyang for refusing to bow to the Rising Sun as required by colonial authorities. He was the first of his family to become a Christian, and marked for special opportunities by the Roman Catholic Church because of his bold, independent ways.

Since 1965 he has been bishop of Wonju, a provincial district of some

26,000 Catholics (out of a district population of 1.1 million).

At the start of martial law in 1972, the governor of Wonju was sent to ask the bishop to support the new system, which was being sold to Koreans under the name of "Revitalizing Reform."

Chi flatly refused, saying he opposed it. In response, troops were placed around his residence "for his own protection" and his contacts outside were strictly limited. The government asked him to say he was not under house arrest. Characteristically, he refused.

Kim Chi Ha, the` poet, was a kindred soul and a valuable man in the bishop's eyes. After Kim was jailed, beaten and harassed for his verses of protest, Chi took him under his wing, giving him a place as an aide in Wonju. Late last year, the bishop gave the poet 'money-reportedly $2,500 in allwhich was passed along to students who were planning anti-government demonstrations. ).

After the arrest and trial of the poet for encouraging and financing demonstrations, it was clear that Chi was in- Ivolved in the same case. At this point the bishop was in Europe on a speaking tour. In an effort to avoid a confrontation, the government sought to convince the church and the bishop that Chi should remain abroad. The prelate refused. On July 6 he returned home to be arrested.

As he alighted from the airliner at 

Kimpo International Airport, several hundred priests, nuns and laymen lined the observation platform to wave greetings. The bishop disappeared from sight into the immigration area, where three men approached and demanded his passport. He refused, whereupon he was hustled to a waiting car and spirited to a first-floor room in the big KCIA înterrogation center at 

Nam Sam (South Mountain) in Seoul.

He was grilled by teams of interrogators for 30 hours before being permitted to sleep. 

Catholic concern and pressure mounted sharply despite secret police arguments to other bishops that this was a purely political matter unrelated to church business. After four days of detention, the bishop was released from the interrogation center as a big mass was being celebrated to pray for him and subtly protest. He was placed under secret police guard at a Catholic hospital on the cathedral grounds, and told he would be tried by court-martial beginning July 23. As the moment approached, the government sought to negotiate a modified form of house arrest in lieu of trial. The morning of

July 23, the bishop ignored the protests of his secret police guard and appeared in full regalia before newsmen to declare that he would refuse to submit to military court-martial and to state his views about democracy in Korea. The bishop's written statement threw down the gauntlet in unmistakable fashion. "The so-called Revitalization Constitution (Park's 1972 martial law revision) is invalid and contrary to truth, for it was forged with violence, intimidation and 'fraud. [it] stifles the least inalienable fundamental rights and basic human dignity... The so-called emergency decrees of the president number 1 and number 4, which they have indicted me for having offended, are among the cruelest violations of national law in our long history. The so-called extraordinary court-martial which exerts its jurisdic tion upon me is only a puppet which cannot by law and conscience judge independently..." ...

As the bishop was speaking to newsmen and handing out copies of his written statement, his distraught cret police supervisor tried to lung● through the knot of reporters to stop the action. The agent was unsuccessful because the newsmen and priests stood firm. A few moments later a 

Catholic father did an uncharitable and perhaps un-Christian thing: As several hundred nuns sang hymns before a statue of the Virgin Mary a few feet away, the priest landed a vigorous elbow to the face of the still-protesting secret policeman.

1 Within a few hours, the bishop had been taken back to the first floor of the KCIA interrogation center, but his defiance and his statement were widely known here and in the world at large. As he no doubt hoped, the line between the government and the chureh had been drawn sharply. The following day, secret police officials sent a representative to ask Korea's 

Catholic cardinal, Stephen Kim, why some of the priests are so rough.

WITH 

THE DEATH sentence for poet, the trial of an ex-president, the arrest of a bishop, the world has awakened with something of a start to the political condition of South Korea. 

Diplomatic pressures are beginning to mount on the Korean government, which is dependent on outside political support for its annual United Nations battle with Communist states and on outside economic support for its continued prosperity. The United States has publicly stated its concern and pri vately its displeasure, saying the Park regime has gone so far it is alienating its friends in Congress and elsewhere.

In a few days two subcommittees of the House Foreign Affairs Committee will begin public hearings on human rights in the Republic of Korea, a rare if not unprecedented hearing of this sort concerning a major U.S. ally.

Australia has let it be known it may have to issue a public statement condemning recent events in Korea. The 

Italians have said they may have to receive a North Korean trade mission because public opinion at home can no longer tolerate exclusive dealing with the South. New Zealand has asked its 

Seoul embassy for a special report. 

The French and Belgian ambassadors, in an unusual gesture of concern, attended a mass at the Catholic cathedral which was widely, billed as a serv ice in honor of Bishop Chi. The Neth erlands, which sponsored the pro- 

South Korean resolution in the United 

Nations last year, is reassessing its position. In Japan, which is an essen tial economic partner, public opinion is running strong against the Park gov. ernment, particularly since the arrest of two Japanese in connection with the student demonstrations. 

In response to mounting pressures, Park commuted to life imprisonment the death sentence for poet Kim Chi Ha and four college students. More such gestures may be ahead. The deep feelings and frustrations of his opponents at home appear stronger than ever.

His foes have not been convinced, only temporarily subdued. Any sign which they interpret as weakness could bring a new eruption of protest against a regime which seems unable to tolerate dissent. 

The United States has a grave stake in the present and future of South

Korea. Secretary of State Henry A. 

Kissinger suggested in recent congres sional testimony that the stability of South Korea is crucial to the independence and stability of Japan and East Asia. In his view, this justifies continued American support despite the faults of the present regime.

The United States is in no position to dictate the internal policies of South 

Korea today-but neither can the

United States and its citizens be eblivious to the practical and moral consequences, of repression there. The 

Seoul regime is fast losing its respectability abroad, and at home the bitterness is deepening. Moreover, there may be a limit to what Americans are willing to support in the case of South 

Korea, particularly when churches, churchmen and Western-educated people are involved. 

This peninsula is still an armed camp on both sides of the 38th parallel.

A lurch toward irrationality on either side could immediately involve the 

United States in a shooting war, possibly involving nuclear weapons, which are based here in profusion. The situation is cause for serious concern, to say the least. At the moment, however, Washington is preoccupied with other matters.

[From Mainichi Daily News, July 14, 1974] POET KIM GETS DEATH SENTENCE 

SEOUL (UPI)-South Korean military court handed down death sentences

Saturday to seven persons including six former student leaders and a poet for allegedly seeking to topple the government. 

A military spokesman said the court at the same time sentenced seven persons to life imprisonment, 12 to 20 years and six others to 15 years on the same charge.

The defendants were part of 55 men indicted in connection with an under ground student organization-the National Democratic Youth-Student League which allegedly tried to overthrow the government through street riots and set up a Communist regime. The group included two Japanese. 

With the sentencing Saturday, 14 persons have been sentenced to death, 15 to life terms, 18 to 20 years in prison and six to 15-year imprisonment in connection with the case.

Sentencing for the remaining co-defendants, Masaki Tachikawa and Yoshiharu Hayakawa of Japan, is expected sometime this week. The military prosecution demanded 20 year terms for both Tachikawa, 28, and Hayakawa, 37, at a court session Friday.

The seven who drew death sentences Saturday included Lee Chul, 26, Yu In 

Tae, 26, Yuh Jung Nam, 29, Kim Byung Kon, 21, Nah Byung Shik, 25, Kim Yong 

Il, 33, and Lee Hyun Bae, 30.

Four of them excluding Yuh, Kim Young Il and Lee Hyun Bae were student leaders of Seoul National University. Kim Young Il is a poet who has written a number of antigovernment poems. He is better known by his pen name of 

Kim Chi Ha. Yuh and Lee Hyun Bae are former student radicals.

Yu Kun Il, 37, an editorial writer for the daily Joongang Ilbo published here, was among the seven men who were given life terms at the Saturday session.

The court, handing down its verdicts, said the group organized more than 40 colleges and universities in the country into the underground body and tried to stage a nationwide uprising last April 3 to bring down the government and set up a Communist regime.

The court said the group deserved severe punishment as they sought insurrection in alliance with and under the control of Communist elements.

[From the New York Times, July 17, 1974] SEOUL COURT BEGINS TRIAL OF EX-PRESIDENT YUN AND 3 OTHERS FACING POSSIBLE DEATH PENALTY ON SUBVERSION CHARGE 

(By Fox Butterfield) 

SEOUL, South Korea, July 16.-A former President of South Korea went on trial before a military court today on charges of subversion that carry a pos sible death sentence.

Yun Po Sun, a frail, 77-year-old, was accused of having advocated the overthrow of President Park Chung Hee and having provided the equivalent of $1,000 to anti-Government student demonstrators. 

Three other prominent Koreans also went before the special court martial today on the same charges: the Rev. Park Hyong Kyu, an outspoken Presbyterian minister; Kim Dong Gil, a professor of American studies at Yonsei University in 

Seoul, and the Rev. Kim Chan Kook, dean of the theological seminary at Yonsei. 

The two clergymen are both graduates of Union Theological Seminary in 

New York.

The Government appeared so sensitive to putting a man of Mr. Yun's stature on trial that as late as yesterday the Premier's office had assured the United States Embassy that Mr. Yun would only be a "witness" in the case of the three other men. American officials today were reportedly angry at what they regarded as deception.

Long Series of Trials 

The court action today was the latest in a lengthening series of trials that have already resulted in the conviction of South Korea's best-known poet, the former publisher of the country's most respected intellectual magazine and 89 other clergymen, students and opposition party members. 

The trials grew out of demonstrations and a petition campaign last winter and spring against President Park's increasingly autocratic rule. Mr. Park responded, first in January and then more sweepingly in April, with a series of emergency decrees that now make virtually any dissent punishable by death. 

According to well-informed Western diplomats, more than 100 other Koreans who have been arrested this spring for involvement in the anti-Government dissidence are likely to be brought to trial soon. 

In court proceedings already completed, there have been these decisions : 

Kim Chi Ha, the country's best-known young poet, was sentenced to death last Saturday. He was alleged to have been connected with an underground group, the National Democratic Youth-Student League, which the court said organized demonstrations against Mr. Park on April 3. 

Fifty-two other Koreans and two Japanese were also convicted in the last week in the same trial. Thirteen were sentenced to death, and 15 to life imprisonment. 

Relatives of some of the defendants, who were largely students, said they had been severely tortured during interrogation. 

Chang Jun Ha, the publisher of Sasanggye, once South Korea's leading intellectual journal, was sentenced to 15 years in jail last February for advocating reform of the Constitution. The Constitution was revised in 1972 by Mr. Park to give himself sweeping powers and the means to continue in office as long as he wishes.

In eight other known trials during February and March, 35 other Koreans, including members of the New Democratic party, the leading opposition group, medical school students and students at Ewha Women's University were given terms ranging from one to 17 years in prison. 

In addition, Kim Dae Jung, the opposition political leader kidnapped from his Tokyo hotel room last August by South Korean agents, is now before a civilian court on charges of election law violations in 1967 and 1971. Mr. Kim was the opposition candidate against Mr. Park in the 1971 presidential election. 

The disclosure in today's newspapers that former President Yun was on trial brought incredulous responses from many Koreans, though they have grown used to learning of further trials.

Mr. Yun, who walks with the aid of a cane, was accompanied to the trial in the Ministry to Defense today by his wife and two lawyers. Under the strict rules of the special court-martial, each defendant may be accompanied only by his lawyer and one close family member. 

Because the court-martial is secret, no account of the proceedings today against Mr. Yun and the three others was available. But yesterday in an interview the fragile-looking Mr. Yun freely acknowledged that he had given money to the students through the Rev. Park Hyong Kyu. "Work for Democracy" Cited

Sitting in an old carved wooden chair in one wing of his sprawling, traditional style villa, Mr. Yun said: "I gave the money because the students are trying to work for democracy. The young people needed the money." "Do you think $1,000 is enough to overturn the Government," he asked, speaking in the English he learned 50 years ago as a student at the University of Edinburgh.

Mr. Yun, a member of an aristocratic family and a Presbyterian, was elected 

President in 1960 after the overthrow of President Syngman Rhee. He continued in office for a year after Mr. Park came to power in the military coup of 

1961 but finally resigned in protest over the junta's rule. He later ran unsuccessfully against Mr. Park for President in 1963 and 1967. 

Kim Dong Gil, the Yonesi University professor who is on trial with him, is an expert on Lincoln and is one of South Korea's leading specialists on American history. 

[From the New York Times, July 22, 1974] SPREADING TRIALS IN KOREA DEVASTATE POLITICAL ACTIVITY STUDENTS, PRESS AND CLERGY ARE SILENT AS PRESIDENT PARK USES THE COURTS TO ERADICATE RISING OPPOSITION (By Fox Butterfield) 

SEOUL, South Korea, July 20.-The wife of a man sentenced to be executed in one of Korea's spreading political trials stared at her hands and said, almost imperceptibly, "If I tell you he was innocent, they will send me to jail too."

It is a measure of the devastating effect of the trials, ordered by President Park Chung Hee to exterminate growing opposition to his Government, that even the families of the accused dare not talk about them. 

Students have stopped discussing politics, the clergy are giving circumspect sermons, the press prints only the official version of the trials, and businessmen mutter that stability is good for the economy. 

The impact of the trials, which began last winter after a series of small demonstrations against Mr. Park's autocratic 13-year rule, was suddenly intensified in the last week with a new wave of arrests, indictments and convictions. 

Sentences Commuted In the last eight days, 55 persons have been convicted before secret courtsmartial. Fourteen were sentenced to death, including South Korea's best known young poet, Kim Chi Ha, and six students.

Today, however, the death sentences of the poet and four other men convicted of an anti-Government plot were commuted to life terms after Defense Minister 

Suh Jong Chul reviewed their sentences.

A respected 77-year-old former President of the country, Yun Po Sun, was taken before another military tribunal this week, and a prominent Catholic bishop, the Most Rev. Daniel Chi, was ordered to stand trial next week, under emergency decrees proclaimed by Mr. Park. Both face a death sentence. 

Moreover, it appears that the trials will continue to spread. An Americaneducated lawyer who had defended several students and the poet, Mr. Kim, was arrested this week by the Korean Central Intelligence Agency after he bitterly objected in court to the death sentences given his clients. 

Also, 150 Koreans, including clergymen, professors and students, are being held in jail awaiting trial, well-informed diplomats say.

Among the few Koreans still willing to talk, although in furtive whispers, there is a feeling that the austere, aloof Mr. Park has gone too far. "He is mad, mad, there is no other explanation," said one opposition politician. 

But some other officials with access to the President and there are very few these days-insist that he is still under control. "Cold, calculating and selfconfident," a diplomat said. 

Three Traditions

According to associates, Mr. Park, who first came to power in the military coup of 1961 as a general, is the product of three related and rigorous traditions. 

One is Korea's borrowed heritage of Confucianism, with its stress on paternal government by stern leaders. Another is the bleak, often violent world of the 

Korean peasant, and the third stems from Mr. Park's highly disciplined training in the imperial Japanese Army, where subordinates were expected to follow orders.

"Park is only doing what his instinct and training have taught him to do: use force and terror to enforce his leadership," said one Westerner with long experience here. “It would be easier if we just recognized this is a dictatorship." 

Among Korean officials Mr. Park's crackdown is explained as "an unfortunate necessity" caused by the constant threat of North Korea, as Chung Il Kwon, the 

Speaker of the National Assembly said.

Mr. Chung, who was commander of the Korean Army at the outbreak of the 

Korean war, a former Premier and close friend of President Park, said, “Our American friends must understand our special situation and traditions. North 

Korea may invade any day, so we cannot afford the luxury of democracy as you can. "Anyone who creates unrest is really helping the Communists," Mr. Chung added. The interview was conducted in Mr. Chung's new hilltop house, in a woodpaneled room decorated with a tiger's head, a carved elephant tusk and a lacquered table from Vietnam. The last two were gifts from President Nguyen Van 

Thieu and former President Nguyen Cao Ky of South Vietnam.

Since the current crackdown began last January with the first of Mr. Park's emergency decrees, the Seoul Government has repeatedly stressed the imminence of an invasion.

Officials here point to several signs: two small new airfields the Communists have built close to the demilitarized zone, a new naval base on the west coast not far north of Seoul, and several attacks this year by the north on southern fishing boats and patrol ships.

Yesterday the Government said North Korean antiaircraft gunners had fired on a Korean Airlines civilian jetliner as it approached Kimpo International Airport at Seoul, though no bullet holes were found.

However, the American intelligence community here takes issue with the Government's analysis of the Communists' hostile actions and intentions at almost every point. There is a prevalent belief that Mr. Park has been using the threat more for his own domestic purposes. 

Economy Growing

Mr. Park's control over the Government and the population has no doubt been helped by the continued growth of the Korean economy. Despite dislocations caused by the oil crisis last winter-South Korea must import all its oileconomists here forecast a 12 per cent growth rate this year, down from last year's phenomenal 17 per cent but still excellent.

Inflation has become a serious concern, with wholesale prices up 30 per cent from last year and consumer prices 16 per cent by official estimate. But to offset the effects of inflation, the Government recently approved a 30 per cent raise for civil servants.

Both the 600,000-man army and the large Korean intelligence agency, Mr. 

Park's main power bases, remain loyal to him, as far as can be determined, knowledgeable diplomats say. The President has made a practice of regularly transferring the top army commanders to prevent any officer from accumulating power.

Thus Mr. Park's opponents who have been arrested and tried in recent weeks remain largely an isolated minority, like the liberals in China who were squeezed between Chiang Kai-shek and the Communists and the elusive third force in Vietnam caught between President Thieu and the Vietcong.

The dissidents are almost all urban, middle class and well educated, and many are members of South Korea's 12 per cent Christian minority. They have no real ties to the peasantry that still forms the backbone of the population, and they have only strictly controlled links to the growing working class. 

But the 1960 coup that toppled President Syngman Rhee was begun by students in Seoul, and there is still a feeling that the students can do it again. 

And despite the current wave of repression, there are still some surprising acts of courage. Bishop Chi, the Catholic leader under indictment, came back from a European trip even though he knew what would happen to him. "We cannot allow ourselves to become just the same as North Korea," said Mr. Yun, the former President now on trial. "I admit I gave money to the students to demonstrate," Mr. Yun related in an interview. "I would do it again if it would help." 34-192 - 74-88

[From the New York Times, June 16, 1974] SEOUL CONVICTION OF 2 JAPANESE EXPECTED TO AGGRAVATE STRAINS (By Fox Butterfield) 

SEOUL, SOUTH KOREA, July 15-Two Japanese accused of having been important go-betweens linking North Korean and Japanese Communists with the anti- Government student movement here were sentenced to 20 years in prison today. 

The action by a military court followed by a day the recall to Tokyo of Japan's Ambassador in South Korea and the summoning home of Seoul's Ambassador to Japan. The sentencing of the Japanese is expected here to aggravate already strained relations between the neighboring countries. 

The two men, Yoshiharu Hayakawa, 37 years old, a Japanese-language instructor at Kyonggi College, and Masaki Tachikawa, 27, a free-lance writer, were vital to the Government's case in a month-long trial that also involved 53 Koreans. Most of the 53 were charged with being members of an underground organization known as the National Democratic Youth-Student League. 

Fourteen of the Koreans were sentenced to death last week, including Kim Chi Ha, a satiric poet who has become widely known for his attacks on the Government. Fifteen others were sentenced to life imprisonment, 18 were given 20-year terms and six received 15 years. 

Accounts by the few outsiders who were allowed to attend the trial indicate that the prosecution failed to produce evidence proving that the two Japanese defendants had been dispatched to South Korea by North Koreans or by the Japanese Communist party. The two were said to have admitted however, that they had been in contact with some of the accused students and had talked about anti-Government actions. 

In a separate but related trial, a former President of South Korea, Yun Po Sun, is scheduled to go before a court martial tomorrow. Mr. Yun, 77, is accused of having provided the equivalent of $1,000 to student activists and having ad- Vocated the overthrow of the Government. Under an emergency decree proclaimed by President Park Chung Hee in April, Mr. Yun could be sentenced to death though that is considered unlikely. 

The emergency decree, which makes almost any dissent punishable by death, and the trials of the Koreans and Japanese arise out of last winter's anti- Government demonstrations and efforts by President Park to suppress them. 

By Government count, 253 activists have been arrested, including students, clergymen and intellectuals.

There was some doubt today whether Mr. Yun would actually be put on trial, though he was indicted and given a copy of the charges against him last week. 

[From the New York Times, June 16, 1974] SOUTH KOREA TRIAL STRAINS JAPAN TIES (By Richard Halloran) 

TOKYO, June 15.-The senior Japanese official toyed with his lunch a moment, then said thoughtfully and without bitterness: "The Koreans broke a promise they made to us, at least in spirit." 

He went on to say that if Kim Dae Jung, the South Korean opposition leader who is on trial in Seoul on charges of election violations,was convicted, the Japanese Government would be forced to take diplomatic steps against South Korea. He declined to say what they might be. 

Mr. Kim, who ran against President Park Chung Hee in 1971, was kidnapped from Tokyo by South Korean agents last August, which caused a public uproar here. In November, the Japanese and South Korean Governments reached a diplomatic settlement under which, according to the Japanese version, Mr. Kim would be allowed to leave Korea if he wished. 

The South Korean Government, however, has made clear that Mr. Kim will not be permitted to leave. That refusal is but the first on a long list of irritations that jeopardize the relations between the two nations. Recent conversations here and in Seoul indicated that the tensions were serious. 

The aggravations between Tokyo and Seoul are particularly important to the United States, which has military alliances with both capitals.

American officials said that there was not much they could do about the South Koreans' anti-Japanese campaign that is the root of the ill feelings. They asserted that they did not have much leverage to apply on President Park of South Korea, who has nearly absolute say in all his country's domestic and foreign policies.

The American officials said that their colleagues had done a lot of talking to President Park and other South Koreans behind the scenes, but that it had not done much good. They also said the United States was not willing to apply real pressure to Mr. Park-such as pulling out military forces or cutting off economic aid-for that might unsettle the situation even further. 

While the issue over Kim Dae Jung may be a diplomatic irritant, the question of the arrest and trial of two Japanese that started today on charges of attempted subversion in South Korea is potentially more explosive in terms of domestic politics here.

The two men, Masaki Tachikawa, and Yoshiharu Hayakawa, are vital to the South Korean Government's contention that North Korean Communists instigated an anti-Government student movement in Seoul in April. They are allegedly the "Japanese connection" bringing instructions and money from North 

Korean Communists in Tokyo. 

[From the New York Times, July 1, 1974] SEOUL ASKS DEATH FOR POET, 6 OTHERS ON PLOTTING CHARGE 

SEOUL, South Korea, July 10 (AP).-The prosecution has demanded death penalties for the Korean poet Kim Chi Ha and six other persons on trial on charges of attempting to overthrow the Government of President Chung Hee Park.

The seven are among a group of 55 persons on trial before a military court on related charges.

The prosecution yesterday demanded sentences ranging from 15 years to life for all but two of the defendants standing trial with Mr. Kim. The two others are Japanese, and the prosecution did not explain why it did not demand sentences for them.

Most of the defendants are students from Seoul National University, the country's most prestigious university. They were arrested after President Park issued a special decree April 3 following an outburst of anti-Government demonontrations by students demanding more democratic policies. 

The prosecution charged that the defendants had plotted to establish a Communist regime in South Korea by organizing mass uprisings and the occupation and destruction of key government office buildings. 

Government authorities said the moves had been blocked by the police. 

[From the New York Times, July 19, 1974] LAWYER IN SEOUL HELD AFTER TRIAL SOUTH KOREAN SAID TO HAVE TERMED CASES A FARCE (By Fox Butterfield) 

SEOUL, South Korea, July 18-A prominent South Korean lawyer who defended the nation's leading poet and 10 students in political trials last week has been arrested, associates disclosed today.

The lawyer, Kang Shin Ok, was taken from his office by plainclothes agents last Monday, apparently because he had denounced in court the military judges who imposed death sentences on several of his clients, including the poet, Kim Chi Ha. Mr. Kang, a leading advocate of civil liberties, holds a graduate degree from George Washington University and also studied at Yale. 

Kim Young Sam, vice president of the New Democratic party, the major opposition group, was detained this morning, apparently only for a brief time, for interrogation. He had scheduled a news conference at which, according to aides, he planned to call for suspension of the sweeping emergency decrees proclaimed by President Chung Hee this year. 

The arrests are part of a steadily lengthening series of political detentions, trials and convictions designed to suppress all opposition to President Park. In

recent months 91 people have been convicted of subversion, with 14 sentenced to death. Over 100 others are awaiting trial, informed diplomats say. 

Two other major court actions continued. 

In one a former President, Yun Po Sun, two Protestant clergymen and a professor of American history appeared for the second day before a closed courtmartial in the Defense Ministry. They are accused of violating emergency decrees by giving money to dissident students and calling for Mr. Park's ouster. 

Foreign correspondents have not been allowed to attend, and the strictly controlled press has not reported the proceedings. 

In a civilian appellate court another well-known Korean, Kim Dae Jung, argued that the case charging him with election law violations in 1967 and 1971 be thrown out because the judge was prejudiced. Mr. Kim is the opposition leader who was kidnapped from his Tokyo hotel room last August by agents of the South Korean Central Intelligence Agency. His appeal is given little chance of success.

The series of trials has produced a palpable atmosphere of fear, reducing conversations to whispers or shrugs of the shoulders and often leading to outright refusals to receive visitors. 

Partners in the law office of Mr. Kang declined to comment on why he had been arrested or what he had said in court that led to his arrest. "Do you think we want to be arrested too?" one of them asked.

Broad Prohibition 

Under an emergency decree issued April 3, it is a crime punishable by death for anyone "to advocate, instigate, propagate, broadcast, report, publish or otherwise communicate to others such act or acts as are prohibited" by the other emergency measures.

Others familiar with Mr. Kang's case said that in his criticism of the three judges he termed the trial a farce and asserted that he was ashamed to be a lawyer in Korea and that if he was a student he would have done just what the students did.

Mr. Kang, who is 39 years old, was arrested outside the courtroom with another defense lawyer. They were held for two days, then released, but Mr. 

Kang was rearrested. 

The Korean Lawyers Association met to discuss Mr. Kang's arrest, believed to be the first instance in which a lawyer has been detained in South Korea for his words in the courtroom.

Mr. Kim Young Sam of the New Democratic party has been one of the more outspoken members of the opposition in the National Assembly. According to his aides, he had intended to call not only for suspension of the emergency decrees but for the end of the courts-martial and freedom for Mr. Kim Dae Jung, who has been under virtual house arrest since his abduction. 

[From the New York Times, June 30, 1974] KOREA'S NEED FOR CONTINUING STABILITY 

TO THE EDITOR: Your newspaper can, of course, make its own judgments about events in Korea. But an article in your June 16 Week in Review section shows too much bias and creates a wrong impression. 

My Government has never said that "freedom is a luxury South Korea cannot now afford." We are far from perfect; but I see no reason why you should single out my country for such incessant criticism. 

In terms of economic, social and scientific development, Korea, under the dynamic leadership of President Park Chung Hee, has done far better than many other developing countries. We have, for example, increased our exports more than 100 times in the thirteen years since 1961. Surely you will agree that this is something more than merely an economic phenomenon. A sense of purpose, dedication, discipline and willing sacrifice lies behind this remarkable success. 

I may add that in 1974 our exports, despite the oil crisis, will probably reach $4.5 billion.

Regarding the trial of Kim Dae-Jung on charges of violating the election law. this is nothing but a move to clear up a case long pending before the courts. Premature judgment by the press on such pending cases should be avoided in order to ensure a fair judicial process to all parties concerned. Nor should isolated

events such as this blur the many other achievements that South Korea has attained so far under the present administration. 

I reject one-sided comments on my country by self-appointed, ritualistic liberals and academicians who are often indifferent to the hard realities that face the developing countries, including South Korea. Excessive criticism-colored by the element of bias toward other countries with different historical experience and cultural traditions not only wounds the national pride of the people concerned but might also be interpreted as undue intereference with their internal affairs. 

The Republic of Korea needs continuing political stability if it is to remain effective in containing the threat of Communist North Korean provocations and successful in accelerating economic and social development. The Armistice Line, manned by huge military forces on both sides, is only thirty miles from Seoul. 

This fact alone makes clear that Korea is in a situation unparalleled in most other countries. Accordingly, the Government is called upon to assume the extraordinary responsibilities in the field of national security.-TONG JIN PARK, Ambassador, Republic of Korea, New York, June 17, 1974. 

[From the New York Times, July 12, 1974] SOUTH KOREANS DOOM SEVEN STUDENTS 

SEOUL, South Korea, July 11 (AP).—A military court today found 21 persons guilty of having plotted student uprisings to overthrow President Chung Hee Park and sentenced seven of them to death. 

The sentences against To Ye Jong, head of the now defunct People's Revolutionary party, and six of his followers were the first death sentences since January when President Park cracked down on intellectuals, politicians and student leaders.

The three-man military court sentenced eight to life imprisonment and six to 20 years in jail. The verdicts are subject to review by higher authorities, and the defendants can also appeal to an appellate court-martial. 

Those sentenced were among 55 persons, including two Japanese, who went on trial June 15 on charges of involvement with the National Democratic Youth- Student Federation. The Government charged that the underground student group had conspired to overthrow President Park and to set up a Communist government that would merge South Korea with North Korea. 

The defendants were charged with having violated a decree by President Park on April 3 outlawing antigovernment activity and with having broken other security and antirebellion laws. 

A total of 253 persons have been arrested on suspicion of violating the April 3 decree, which provides a maximum penalty of death. Military courts now have convicted a total of 57 persons for anti-government agitation since Jan. 8, when the President issued the first in a series of decrees provoked by demonstrations against his rule.

A Roman Catholic bishop known for his outspoken criticism of the government was released yesterday after five days of questioning by intelligence agents, a church spokesman said.

The Most Rev. Daniel Tji Hak Soun of the Wonju diocese east of Seoul was arrested last Saturday upon his return from a European trip. He was suspected of working with the National Democratic Youth-Student Federation, according to the Rev. Lee Cho Hung, secretary general of the Catholic Conference of 

Korea. He added that he did not know whether the bishop had been cleared.

Secretary Kissinger: 

Senator Mathias: 

The factual reporting in these articles appears to coincide with the reporting of these same events by our Embassy in Seoul. In general, the press has been reporting indications of internal dissension in Korea, as a result of a series of Emergency Measures the government promulgated beginning last January. The Korean government has stated it took these steps because of the threat it perceives from the North, and the need, as a result, to tighten discipline in the South. of course we are distressed over reports of repression in Korea, At the same time, we are deeply concerned about the security of the peninsula, and our policies toward Korea are predicated with that essential interest in mind.

QUESTIONS SUMITTED BY SENATOR MATHIAS MIA'S 

What efforts have been made by the United States government to encourage the parties in Indochina to assist the United States in efforts to account for those missing in action? What funds have been earmarked to facilitate this effort? How many personnel have been assigned to this task in Indochina? 

Secretary Kissinger: Accounting for Americans still missing in Southeast Asia has been a major aim of our policy and diplomatic efforts in Southeast Asia. In Vietnam we have negotiated in the Four Party Joint Military 

Team (FPJMT) for information on the missing and the return of the remains of the dead, as provided in Article 8(b) of the Vietnam Agreement. Although the government of the Republic of Vietnam has cooperated in these efforts, to our regret the communist side has failed almost totally to live up to its obligations. It has been made clear that there could be no economic assistance or other accommodation with North Vietnam until a satisfactory accounting is

provided for the missing in action. In Laos, American officials have maintained continuing contact with the Pathet Lao side on this subject, before and since formation of the coalition government in 

April, 1974. Senior American officials have made clear to the communist side in Laos the importance we attach to resolution of this problem.

These efforts have been carried out by our embassies in Vietnam and Laos, with the support of our consular posts and in close cooperation with the American delegation to the PJMT. In addition to officers working on this subject in our diplomatic missions, for which separate funding information is not available, the FPJMT has an authorized strength of 15 U.S. military personnel and 7 U.S. civilians, supported by 22 local personnel, for which $158,000 has been earmarked in FY 1975. 

In addition, the U.S. funds weekly liaison flights between 

Saigon and Hanoi, in support of the FPJMT, at an estimated annual cost $425,000.

The Joint Casualty Resolution Center (JCRC) located in Thailand, is responsible for on-the-ground searches for our personnel and maintains records and information on our men. Under current estimates, $1,098,000 has been earmarked for JCRC in FY 1975.

Approximately 150 authorized American personnel are currently assigned to JCRC, out of an authorized strength of 175. 

NUCLEAR SAFEGUARDS IN THE MIDDLE EAST Senator Mathias 

8 

Has the Administration considered a proposal for a nuclear free zone in the Middle East? Iran has already proposed a nuclear free zone and in view of the agreement to supply nuclear reactors to both Egypt and

Secretary Kissinger : 

Israel, it would appear that a nuclear free zone could be a feasible way of achieving the purposes of the 

NPT. 

The safeguards we are insisting on in the case of Egypt and Israel are far more stringent than any we have hitherto applied elsewhere in the world. As 

I have indicated, one of our most urgent tasks is to develop a policy designed to prevent proliferation. 

We are engaged in intensive study of this problem now.

The idea of a nuclear free zone in the Middle East will be examined in the course of our studies. 

I might note that the U.S. has in : the past expressed support for nuclear free zones provided they meet certain criteria. These criteria are: the initiative should be taken by the states in the region concerned; the zone should preferably include all states in the area whose participation is deemed important; the creation of a zone should not disturb necessary security arrangements; and provisions should be made for adequate verification, which would include procedures for followup of alleged violations to give reasonable assurance of compliance.

It is impossible to be precise in comparing 

Sino-Soviet aid to the North with our aid ⠀ to the South because: (1) the Communists do not publish their aid figures, and our intelligence estimates are necessarily based on incomplete, fragmentary information; (2) for aid to the North we can only estimate the value of military hardware and commodities actually delivered, not total program costs, and it is very difficult to factor out hardware and commodity costs alone; and (3) aid to the North is normally computed on a calendar year basis, while our aid to the South is on a fiscal year basis. 

With these caveats in mind, the following is the best estimate we can develop of the value! of military hardware and economic commodities we have provided to the South, and the comparable value of hardware and commodities the Russians, Chinese, and East European

LIMITING WEAPONS SUPPLIES 

Would you detail efforts made by the United

States Government prior to arms sales agreements made with other countries to enter into negotiations with other supplier nations to agree not to supply weapons or to limit the supply of weapons by joint agreement. case of Peru, were efforts made with the other potential suppliers not to sell or supply arms to Peru? 

In the

United States Government efforts to negotiate mutual export restraints with other nations supplying military weapons have continued over a long period of time. Detailed information concerning this extensive effort is contained in a recent report to the Congress by the Arms Control and Disarmament Agency

entitled "The International Transfer of 

Conventional Arms," dated April 12, 1974.

Especially detailed information is contained in pages 83-91, and in Annex C, page 3. 

As you know, European supplies have mounted a vigorous sales effort in regard to recent arms purchases by Peru. The United States has been unable to restrain competition from new potential suppliers; France and the USSR have made sales of aircraft and 

A contributing factor tanks, respectively. in these sales to Peru was the reluctance of the United States to supply the types and quantities of modern equipment demanded by the Peruvian armed forces. Recent arms acquisition by Peru typifies a growing situation in Latin America 

where most countries are able to buy desired arms from suppliers of their own choice. U.S. restraint fails to halt arms acquisitions but merely risks conceding long-established supplier relationships to European competitors. This problem is important not only from the standpoint of the U.S. balance-ofpayments, but also in terms of the potential loss of political leverage.

FOOTNOTES: 

1FTEPP: Full Time Employee, Permanent Position 

2/ F.N.: Foreign National 

3/ The program in Brazil is in the process of being phased-out. 

4 ROCAP: The "Regional Office for Central American Programs," located in Guatemala City, Guatemala, provides support and assistance to Central American common market institutions and economic analysis, engineering, legal and financial analysis services to Costa Rica, Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras and Nicaragua. 

5/ The program in Venezuela is being terminated as of June 30, 1974. 

6/ Includes 3 U.S., 5 F.N.. employees in Argentina and 3 U.S., 23 F.N. employees in Mexico who are attached to the Regional 

Technical Aids Center. 

Includes 1 F.N. in Iran; 1 U.S., 4 F.N. in Lebanon in participant training functions; 3 F.N. in Taiwan. Nine U.S. employees in Saudi Arabia are entirely funded by the Government of Saudi Arabia and are only shown in the ASIA region because of their geographic location. 

8/ RED-Thailand: "Regional Economic Development Office" located in Bangkok, Thailand with 1 U.S. employee located in Manila,

Philippines attached to the Office of the Director of the Asian Development Bank. 

2/ Includes Vietnam Support Groups located in Taiwan (3 U.S., 14 F.N.), Philippines (4 F.N.) and Thailand (1 U.S., 21 F.N.) and operating expenses thereof totaling 553 thousand dollars. 

10/ Includes Malta, Spain and the U.N. Force in Cyprus. 

11/ CWR-Regional: "Central and West Africa Regional Office" manages program activities in the region which includes three Regional 

Offices: Senegal (covering Gambia, Mali, Mauritania, Sierra Leone, Guinea and Senegal); Niger (covering Ivory Coast, Togo, Upper Volta, Dahomey and Niger); and Cameroon (which covers Chad, Central African Republic, Gabon and Cameroon). These offices also handle the Sahel relief and rehabilitation projects. 

12/ OSARAC: The "Office of Southern African Regional Affairs Coordination," located in Mbabane, Swaziland, manages program activities in the region which includes: Botswana, Lesotho, Malawi, Swaziland and Zambia. 

13/ RDO-East Africa: The "Regional Development Office, East Africa," located in Arusha, Tanzania, manages program activities in the region which includes programs in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda. 

14 REDSO-East Africa: The "Regional Economic Development Services Office-East Africa" is located in Nairobi, Kenya. It provides economic and sectoral analysis, legal, engineering, contracting and supply management services on a regional basis to USAID's in Ethiopia, Kenya, Tanzania and offices in Swaziland and Sudan.

FOOTNOTES: (Cont'd) 15 REDSO-West Africa: The "Regional Economic Development Services Office-West Africa" is located in Abidjan, Ivory Coast. 

It provides economic and sectoral analysis, legal, engineering, contracting and supply management services on a regional basis to Ghana, Liberia, Nigeria, Zaire, and the various countries under the Central and West Africa Regional Office. 

The Uganda office was closed as of June 30, 1973. The U.S. direct hire and contract personnel physically departed the post by July 15, 1973. NOTES: 

(1) Post Differential allowances are paid to employees assigned to posts where extraordinarily difficult health or physical hardships exist. Living costs are not considered in determining differential allowances. 

The range of differential rates are from 0% (Rio de Janeiro, Tunis) to 25% (Monrovia, Vientiane). The maximum amount payable at the 25% rate is $9,500. (2) Benefits are the U.S. Government contributions to retirement funds, medical insurance plans, and life insurance premiums. (3) The following additional allowances are payable to A.I.D. employees when they are entitled to the allowance in accordance with provisions of the 

Standardized Regulations (Government Civilians, Foreign Areas): 

(a) Cost of Living Allowances are intended to reimburse an employee for certain excess costs, excess costs, exclusive of quarters costs which result from his being officially stationed overseas. Amounts are based on the salary of the officer and the "rating" of the post. 

Assignment to many overseas posts does not result in an employee receiving a cost of living allowance. Allowances range from $285 per year in Santo Domingo for a single person to $4,280 in Nouakchott for an officer with dependents. (b) Quarters Allowances are paid to employees stationed overseas to reimburse them for the majority of the costs of rent and utilities. 

They are paid at posts where living quarters are not provided by the A.I.D. Mission, and differ depending on the post, whether the employee has dependents, and the salary of the employee. They range from $600 for a single employee in Mbabane to $8,400 for a senior employee with dependents in Paris.

(c) Education allowances are paid to employees to assist them with the extra expenses incurred in providing an adequate education for their dependents. They vary depending on the school grade involved, whether the dependent is attending school at or away from the post, and the location of the post. These allowances range, per student dependent, from $50 per year for high school at post allowance in Niamey to $5,350 per year in Gaborone for away from post allowance. (d) Representation funds are made available to overseas A¡I.D. missions to help defray costs incurred for functions which are heid for the purpose of furthering U.S. foreign policy objectives. 

Representation allowances do not accrue to an employee because of his rank, title, or position. They are available only for expenses incurred on behalf of the U.S. Government. Effective for FY 1974, Representation ceilings were established at $3,000 for Missions with 

Class III Directors, $2,500 for Missions with Class IV Directors, 

$1,500 for Missions with FSR-1 Directors, $1,000 for Area or Regional

Offices, and $500 for posts with A.I.D. Affairs Officers. The objective of establishing these ceilings is not to require that more social functions be personally funded, but to set the pace for a new style for Mission program related functions. An exception to the above limitations may be granted only by the Assistant Administrator for Program and Management Services. Expenses to be reimbursed under this allowance in FY 1975 will vary considerably, ranging from an estimated $400 for Argentina to $3,000 for Indonesia. (e) Official Residence expenses are made available to A.I.D. Mission 

Directors to help defray the unusual expenses of operating and maintaining official residences. This allowance is a partial reimbursement 'for the extra housekeeping costs which are incurred because the Mission 'Director's position requires a household more extensive than otherwise would be necessary.

Effective for FY 1974 a ceiling of $2,000 was established for Official Residence Allowance. An exception to the above limitation may be granted only by the Assistant Administrator for Program and Management Services. Expenses to be reimbursed in FY 1975 under this allowance will vary considerably, ranging from an estimated "O" for 

Nepal to the $2,000 ceiling for Thailand.

STATION HOUSING ALLOWANCES: 

Housing and Cost-of-Living (COLA) Allowances are authorized for the purpose of defraying the average excess cost experienced by members on permanent duty assignments outside the United States. The excess costs are derived by comparison of the average cost-of-living and housing of members in each area outside the United States with the average cost-of-living and housing for similar members in the United States.

Depending upon the specific overseas location a member may receive either a housing allowance or COLA or both. In some locations where excess costs are negligible, neither COLA or housing allowances is authorized.

Housing and cost-of-living allowances for military personnel are autho rized by Vol. I of the Joint Travel Regulations (JTR). Rates prescribed therein are not special allowances applicable to military personnel on MAAG assignments but are applicable to all U.S. military members on permanent assignment outside the United States. 

The following are examples of allowances authorized at specific locations selected from Appendices A, B, and C of the JTR, Vol. I:

ENTERTAINMENT ALLOWANCES: 

Allowances to cover the expenses of official entertainment or representation are not cost-of-living allowances authorized by 37 U.S. Code 405. 

MAP Representation Funds are made available through State Department channels for use in the foreign country by MAAG for ceremonial and commemorative events and for entertainment of foreign dignitaries.

Representation Funds for all military assistance activities are administered in strict accordance with State Department Instruction, "Stand ard Regulations (Government, Civilian, Foreign Areas)." 

The maximum amount of representation is determined by an agreed-upon State/DOD formula based upon the number of field grade and fiag/general officers assigned to particular MAAG. The U.S. Ambassador annually approves the amount of representation funds made available to the YAAG.

FMS CREDIT SALES - SALES ORDERS (AS DISTINGUISHED FROM DELIVERIES) MADE ON THE BASIS OF CREDIT (DIRECT AND GUARANTEED) EXTENDED PURSUANT TO THE PROVISIONS OF THE FOREIGN MILITARY SALES ACT, IN THE CURRENT AND/OR PRIOR YEARS. 

FMS CASH SALES - FOREIGN MILITARY SALES ORDERS (AS DISTINGUISHED FROM DELIVERIES) FOR WHICH PAYMENT IS MADE EITHER "CASH IN ADVANCE" OR, IF THE PRESIDENT SO DETERMINES, WITHIN A REASONABLE PERIOD OF TIME NOT TO EXCEED 120 DAYS AFTER DELIVERY OF THE ARTICLE(S) OR THE RENDERING OF THE SERVICE(S). 

FMS SALES PAYMENT WAIVED -ISRAELI FOREIGN MILITARY SALES ORDERS (AS DISTINGUISHED FROM DELIVERIES) BETWEEN OCTOBER 6, 1972 AND MARCH 31, 1974, PAYMENT FOR WHICH WAS WAIVED BY A PRESIDENTIAL DETERMINATION, MADE PURSUANT TO THE REQUIREMENTS OF PUBLIC LAWS 93-199 AND 93-240, THAT RELEASED ISRAEL FROM ITS CONTRACTUAL LIABILITY IN THE AMOUNT OF $1.5 BILLION. 

COMMERCIAL SALES DELIVERIES (AS DISTINGUISHED FROM SALES ORDERS) BY U.S. INDUSTRIES TO FOREIGN PURCHASERS WHICH ARE NOT ADMINISTERED BY THE DEPARTMENT OF DEFENSE. The  he Group consists of the World Bank (International 

Bank for Reconstruction and Development), IDA 

(International Development Association) and IFC (International Finance Corporation). 

It provides both financial and technical help to improve the living standards of developing member countries. Bank loans, IDA credits and IFC investments are now being made at an annual rate of more than $3,500 million. In the latest fiscal year, about 58% of these funds came from the Bank, which has to borrow most of its resources in the private capital markets and charge a commensurate rate of interest. 

IDA was able to provide nearly $1,360 million in longterm, interest-free credits to the poorest borrowers; most of its funds are contributions from the wealthier member countries and the Bank itself, out of its net earnings. The balance consisted of investments by

IFC, which specializes in stimulating the private sector in developing countries. 

The combined ability of the Bank and IDA to help the poorest countries depends upon the level of contributions to IDA. Within the limit of its resources, IDA can help many countries that are too poor to borrow from the Bank, while the two together can help many others that are not quite so poor by lending side-byside, thus reducing the average burden of interest and repayments.

All but 19 of the independent countries listed in this 

Atlas are members of the Bank¹. Of these 122, 112 are also members of IDA, and 98 of IFC. Principal governments that have so far not participated in the Bank or its affiliates are those of seven countries in Eastern Europe, including the U.S.S.R., and the People's 

Republic of China. Together, they account for about 

30% of the world's population and 18% of its income. 

¹As of June 30, 1973.

1973 

World Bank Atlas 

This is the eighth edition of the World Bank Atlas. 

It incorporates several changes first introduced in the seventh edition, notably the expression of gross national product (GNP) in market prices rather than factor cost, and the use of weighted, multi-year exchange rates for converting domestic currencies into 

U.S. dollars.

Additional revisions and a somewhat revised format have been incorporated in the 1973 edition. Improvements in information have resulted in better understanding of the accounts of countries with centrally planned economies, and significant revisions have been made in the data for a number of these countries. The lengthening time series of data available for both GNP and population make it possible in this edition to show growth rates not only for the decade of the 1960s, but also for the more recent period 1965-1971. 

Users of the Atlas are again cautioned to recognize the necessarily tentative nature of the data and to interpret them with circumspection (see "Note," inside back cover). Many of the figures are derived from incomplete or unreliable basic data, and their conversion into U.S. dollars introduces an additional element of error. Further, they provide in any case only an approximate measure of average economic and social conditions and trends. They reveal little about the absolute state of poverty in the developing world, and nothing about its distribution within each country.

Bearing in mind these limitations, the 1973 Atlas confirms impressions conveyed in earlier editions. 

Real growth has continued in the developing world, in many cases at a rate equal to or greater than in the more developed countries. However, rapid population growth still prevails in large areas, and disparities in per capita income between rich and poor countries continue to increase. It is hoped that data presented in the Atlas will contribute to a fuller appreciation of the effort required to improve the conditions of life in developing countries, and especially for the poorest of the poor.

Note or purposes of international comparison, gross national product (GNP) estimates in 

U.S. dollar equivalents or some other numeraire should be calculated, ideally, on the basis of purchasing power parities or through direct real product comparisons. For several years, the World Bank has been participating in a major research effort in this area: the United 

Nations International Comparisons Project, initiated jointly by the U.N. Statistical Office and the University of Pennsylvania. Significant progress has been made, and the Bank expects to publish an interim report in 1974 on behalf of the sponsors. The project is expected eventually to provide a thoroughly documented basis for future studies on comparative incomes and related methodological research. To date, however, only a limited number of countries have been covered, and research on others is not sufficiently advanced to permit the formal presentation of results in this edition of the World Bank Atlas. 

In the absence of a more satisfactory basis, the present figures of GNP in U.S. dollars have been converted from domestic currency estimates, essentially on the basis of official exchange rates. In several cases, however, the rates have been adjusted to correspond more closely to realistic market rates. In early editions, the Atlas used 1964 as the base for conversion of domestic currencies to dollars.

Starting with the 1972 edition, a multi-year base period (1965-71) has been used, in an attempt to reduce the temporary distortions resulting from under-valuation and over-valuation of particular currencies in particular years. Under this procedure, GNP in domestic currency is first expressed in weighted average prices of the base period, 1965-71, converted to U.S. dollars at a weighted average exchange rate for the base period, and then adjusted for US inflation between the base

period and the current year before dividing by mid-year population to derive per capita GNP. 

It should be remembered that exchange rates equate at best the prices of internationally traded goods and services. They may bear little relationship to the prices of goods and services not entering international trade, which form the bulk of the national product in most developing countries. Agricultural products and services, in particular, are generally priced lower in relation to industrial output in developing than in industrialized countries, and agriculture typically accounts for much the largest share of total product in the developing countries. The result is that the currency conversion method tends to exaggerate real income differences between less developed and more developed countries. 

As noted in the Preface, the current edition of the Atlas gives GNP figures at market prices; editions prior to 1972 used GNP figures at factor cost. The former includes indirect taxes (net of subsidies), and thus relates more closely to the value of goods and services as they are sold in the market place. Detailed comparisons undertaken by World Bank staff now indicate that in global terms the market price expression of GNP is about 11 percent higher than GNP at factor cost. Further, on average there appears to be remarkable consistency in this relationship for groups of countries at all income levels, including the poorest and most highly developed. There are, of course, variations around the averages in a few particular cases, sometimes reflecting sharply differing national tax and subsidy policies and accounting systems. Differences in per capita GNP growth rates in market prices and at factor cost are minimal, however. 

Special considerations arise in preparing estimates for centrally planned (socialist) economies. National accounts for these countries are compiled originally on the basis of the 

System of Material Product Balances (MPS), rather than the standard U.N. System of National Accounts (SNA). There are also prob-

lems in selecting appropriate exchange rates for conversion of domestic currency estimates into U.S. dollars. In estimating GNP per capita for these countries, three principal types of adjustment have been made. First, as a result of additional information now available and better contact among international agencies, it has been confirmed that data for a few centrally planned economies have been expressed in the past in terms of gross rather than net material product. Accordingly, adjustments have been made to take account of intermediate consumption in the MPS accounts of these countries. Second, adjustments have been made to include product originating in the public and private service sectors, to bring the MPS accounts more into line with the SNA concept. Third, adjustments have been made in the various exchange rates used by a number of countries with centrally planned economies before linking them to the U.S. dollar through an adjusted dollar-ruble rate. It should be emphasized, however, that in the absence of market conditions, internal cost and price relationships in the countries with centrally planned economies differ substantially from those in other countries having similar per capita GNP levels. More than usual caution must be exercised, therefore, in using and interpreting the data for these countries. 

Revisions have also been made in the current edition of the Atlas in the basic data series of both GNP and population for a number of countries. Most notable in this respect is a sharp downward revision of the population estimate for the Peoples Republic of China, to bring this figure more into line with estimates available in other agencies, including the United Nations.br

Scholars and statisticians interested in fuller and more technical explanations of the methodology used in compiling the figures for the World Bank Atlas are invited to address their queries to the Economic and Social Data Divi sion, Economic Analysis and Projections De partment, World Bank.
